source: PubMed (NCBI E-utilities). Summaries written from abstracts only.
disclaimer: General information from published research, not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or midwife about your situation.

items.title: Adenomyosis and association between ultrasonographic features and pregnancy outcomes in women with infertility or pregnancy loss: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 29 studies of about 19,500 women with infertility or pregnancy loss, comparing women whose ultrasound showed adenomyosis with those whose did not. Women with diffuse adenomyosis, or adenomyosis in the inner part of the uterine wall, had lower odds of a live birth. Features near the womb lining and a larger uterus also seemed linked to poorer outcomes. The evidence was mostly low or very low certainty, because studies used different ways of diagnosing adenomyosis, so the numbers should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Diffuse adenomyosis was linked to lower odds of live birth than no adenomyosis (OR 0.52).
Internal adenomyosis was also linked to lower odds of live birth (OR 0.49).
Features close to the womb lining and a larger uterine volume pointed to poorer reproductive outcomes in a narrative summary.
Certainty was low or very low for 20 of 21 outcomes, and the authors call for standardised ultrasound definitions.

items.title: Global prevalence of adenomyosis and endometriosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pooled results from 127 studies covering nearly 199 million women to estimate how common adenomyosis and endometriosis are. In the general population, about 1% of women were estimated to have adenomyosis and about 5% endometriosis. Both conditions were much more common among women with infertility or gynaecological symptoms such as pelvic pain or heavy periods.
keyPoints: Worldwide, adenomyosis was estimated in about 1% of women and endometriosis in about 5% of the general population.
Among women with infertility, about 31% had adenomyosis and about 38% had endometriosis.
Among women with gynaecological symptoms, adenomyosis was found in 41%-49% and endometriosis in 18%-42%.
Endometriosis was found more often than adenomyosis across the groups studied.

items.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of reproductive outcomes after high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) treatment of adenomyosis
items.source: Best Practice & Research. Clinical Obstetrics & Gynaecology
items.journal: Best Practice & Research. Clinical Obstetrics & Gynaecology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 10 studies of 557 women with adenomyosis who wanted to become pregnant after HIFU, a treatment that uses focused ultrasound waves and does not remove the uterus. About 53% became pregnant and about 35% had a live birth. The authors say the evidence is very weak, because the studies varied a lot and none compared HIFU with other options in a rigorous way.
keyPoints: Across 10 studies (557 women), the pooled pregnancy rate after HIFU was 53.4%.
The pooled live birth rate was 35.2%.
The studies differed a lot from one another, so these numbers are uncertain.
The authors say better-designed comparison studies, ideally randomized trials, are badly needed.

items.title: Untangling the independent effect of endometriosis, adenomyosis, and ART-related factors on maternal, placental, fetal, and neonatal adverse outcomes: results from a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pooled many studies to see how endometriosis, adenomyosis and fertility-treatment (ART) factors affect pregnancy and newborn outcomes. Women with endometriosis had a higher risk of placenta previa, preterm birth and cesarean section, especially with severe disease. Adenomyosis was linked to miscarriage and pre-eclampsia. Much of the evidence was rated low or very low quality, so results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Endometriosis was linked to a higher risk of placenta previa (moderate quality evidence), and the link was strongest in severe forms such as stage III-IV and deep endometriosis.
Endometriosis was also associated with preterm birth and cesarean section (low quality evidence), whether or not the pregnancy came from fertility treatment.
Adenomyosis was associated with miscarriage and pre-eclampsia (low quality evidence), including in ART pregnancies.
The authors recommend against artificial-cycle frozen embryo transfer in women with ovulatory severe endometriosis and suggest single blastocyst transfer in this high-risk group.

items.title: Functional determinants of uterine contractility in endometriosis and adenomyosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine small studies that measured how the uterus contracts across the menstrual cycle in women with endometriosis or adenomyosis, compared with women without these conditions. Women with endometriosis were about nine times more likely to have contractions that push blood backwards during their period. Contractions were also more frequent and stronger in women with endometriosis or adenomyosis. There was very little data on adenomyosis, and the evidence was graded low certainty for most comparisons.
keyPoints: Women with endometriosis had about 8.6 times the risk of a backward (retrograde) contraction pattern during menstruation.
Uterine contractions were more frequent in the menstrual and luteal phases in women with endometriosis, and contraction strength was higher across all cycle phases in endometriosis or adenomyosis.
The authors suggest abnormal contractions may contribute to endometriosis and symptoms such as period pain and infertility.
Evidence for adenomyosis is limited, and most comparisons were rated low certainty.

items.title: A systematic review and Bayesian analysis of the adverse effects of dienogest
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 39 studies to see what side effects happen when dienogest is used to treat endometriosis or adenomyosis. Most side effects were common and not serious, with irregular uterine bleeding being the most frequent. The authors concluded dienogest is generally safe for these conditions, while noting that rarer serious problems, such as lower bone density in the spine, have been reported.
keyPoints: The most common side effects were abnormal uterine bleeding (about 55% of people), amenorrhea (absent periods, about 17%) and swelling (about 13%).
Uncommon side effects included abdominal pain, hives (urticaria), indigestion and peritonitis.
Serious reactions such as decreased lumbar spine bone mineral density, depression and hemorrhagic shock have been reported.
The authors concluded dienogest is generally safe for treating endometriosis and adenomyosis, but people should be aware of the serious reactions.

items.title: Ultrasound Elastography for the Diagnosis of Endometriosis and Adenomyosis: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 10 studies (744 women) on ultrasound elastography, a scan that measures how stiff tissue is, to help diagnose endometriosis and adenomyosis without surgery. Stiffer tissue was linked to more scar-like (fibrotic) tissue, and the scan matched biopsy results well for deep pelvic endometriosis. For adenomyosis, combining the studies showed good sensitivity and specificity. The authors conclude that elastography may be a promising non-invasive test, though for endometriosis there were too few studies to combine the results.
keyPoints: Elastography looks at how stiff pelvic tissue is, and stiffer areas were linked to more fibrotic tissue.
In deep pelvic endometriosis, scan findings matched histopathology (lab tissue examination) results, with high sensitivity and specificity.
For adenomyosis, combining the studies confirmed good sensitivity and specificity.
The authors say elastography may be a promising non-invasive way to diagnose endometriosis and adenomyosis.

items.title: Pregnancy Outcomes after Uterus-sparing Operative Treatment for Adenomyosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 13 studies of women with adenomyosis who had uterus-sparing surgery and wanted to have a baby. It compared surgery that cuts out the adenomyosis with other methods that destroy the tissue or cut off its blood supply. Pregnancy, miscarriage and live-birth rates were similar for both approaches, and the differences were not statistically significant. The authors suggest either type of treatment could be considered for adenomyosis-related infertility.
keyPoints: After excision surgery, about 40% of women trying to conceive became pregnant, and about 70% of those pregnancies ended in a live birth.
After non-excision treatments (such as focused ultrasound, ablation or uterine artery embolization), about 51% became pregnant, and about 71% of those pregnancies ended in a live birth.
Miscarriage rates were around 21-22% in both groups, and no differences between the approaches were statistically significant.
Excision may be worth considering for symptomatic adenomyosis with several years of infertility or repeated assisted reproduction failure.

items.title: Management of women with abnormal uterine bleeding: Clinical practice guidelines of the French National College of Gynaecologists and Obstetricians (CNGOF)
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: French gynaecology experts updated their national guidelines on abnormal uterine bleeding, covering diagnosis, teenagers, bleeding with no clear cause, polyps, fibroids and adenomyosis. They reviewed the research using a recognised method for rating evidence quality and produced 36 recommendations. Where the research gave no answer, they chose not to make a recommendation rather than rely on opinion alone.
keyPoints: The guidelines give 36 recommendations, 19 strong and 17 weak, for diagnosing and treating abnormal uterine bleeding.
They cover seven areas, including adolescents, endometrial hyperplasia and polyps, fibroids and adenomyosis.
For 14 questions the research did not provide an answer, so no recommendation was made.
The work was done by 26 experts independently of industry funding.

items.title: Impact of adenomyosis on the prognosis of patients with endometrial cancer
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review combined three studies of 2,505 women with endometrial cancer to see whether also having adenomyosis (a condition where the womb lining grows into the womb muscle) changes outlook. Women with both conditions had about half the risk of death, and a lower risk of the cancer coming back, compared with women who had cancer only. However, once other factors were taken into account, the link for cancer coming back was no longer clear, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Women with endometrial cancer and adenomyosis had about half the risk of death compared with those without adenomyosis.
Disease-free survival also looked better in the simple analysis.
After adjusting for other factors, the disease-free survival link was not clear.
The authors say more studies are needed to confirm the association is independent.

items.title: Adenomyosis as a Risk Factor for Myometrial or Endometrial Neoplasms-Review
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review looked at whether adenomyosis, a common non-cancerous condition where womb lining tissue grows into the womb muscle, could be linked to cancers of the womb. It also looked at how women with both womb cancer and adenomyosis fare over the long term. The researchers found that the genetic and cell-level changes that might lead to cancer in adenomyosis are still poorly understood. Results on survival in womb cancer are mixed and need more study.
keyPoints: Adenomyosis is a common benign gynecological condition.
The genetic changes and other cell-level mechanisms that could cause cancer in adenomyosis are still poorly understood.
Findings on whether adenomyosis affects survival in endometrial cancer seem contradictory.
More clinical and molecular research is needed.

items.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of adverse pregnancy outcomes after uterine adenomyosis
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pooled six studies comparing pregnancies in women with adenomyosis (322 women) to those without (9,420 women). Women with adenomyosis were more likely to have a baby born early, a baby smaller than expected for its age, and pre-eclampsia (a blood pressure problem in pregnancy). The authors conclude adenomyosis seems to have a harmful effect on pregnancy outcomes. The studies were observational and only a few women had adenomyosis, so the numbers are estimates, and the pre-eclampsia figure in particular is very uncertain.
keyPoints: Women with adenomyosis had about three times the odds of preterm birth (OR 3.05).
Their babies were about three times as likely to be small for gestational age (OR 3.22).
Pre-eclampsia was more likely too (OR 4.35), but the range around this estimate was very wide (1.07 to 17.72).
The review combined six observational studies; earlier studies had given conflicting results.

items.title: Reproductive, obstetric, and perinatal outcomes of women with adenomyosis and endometriosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 104 studies to see how adenomyosis and endometriosis relate to fertility, pregnancy and newborn outcomes. Both conditions were linked to a higher chance of miscarriage, and endometriosis was also linked to preterm birth, caesarean delivery and newborn unit admission. Endometriosis was also linked to fewer eggs collected and lower fertilisation rates during assisted reproduction. The authors say more evidence is needed, especially for adenomyosis and for different types of endometriosis.
keyPoints: Miscarriage risk was higher with both adenomyosis (OR 3.40) and endometriosis (OR 1.30).
Endometriosis was linked to preterm delivery (OR 1.38), caesarean delivery (OR 1.98) and neonatal unit admission (OR 1.29).
Endometriosis was linked to fewer eggs retrieved and lower fertilisation rates; ovarian endometriosis on its own was also linked to fewer eggs.
The authors suggest pre-pregnancy counselling and treating pregnancies with these conditions as higher risk until more evidence is available.

items.title: No. 164-Consensus Guidelines for the Management of Chronic Pelvic Pain
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This is a Canadian consensus guideline on how to assess and treat chronic pelvic pain in women. It notes that the causes of this pain are poorly understood, so treatments have had mixed success. The guideline supports care that looks at the whole person, including muscle problems, pain levels, physical therapy and psychological support. The goal is often better day-to-day function even if some pain remains.
keyPoints: Chronic pelvic pain is common and can be very debilitating, and treatments have had variable success because the causes are poorly understood.
Care should include checking for muscle (myofascial) pain, measuring pain levels in a practical way, and careful use of medicines, including opioids.
Teams that combine physical therapy, psychology (such as cognitive-behavioural therapy), gynaecology and pain specialists are recommended.
The guideline suggests rehabilitation should aim for better function with some pain rather than a complete cure, and recommends wider use of MRI and clear records of disease seen at surgery.

items.title: A meta-analysis and systematic review of advanced maternal age patients in IVF
items.summary: This review pooled 151 studies on IVF treatment choices for women over 35 (advanced maternal age). For most options, such as the type of stimulation protocol or FSH medicine, no clear benefit was found. Adding LH, using ICSI routinely, and genetic testing of embryos (PGT-A) did not clearly improve live birth rates, and assisted hatching was linked to lower live birth rates. The authors say better-quality trials are still needed to confirm most of these conclusions.
keyPoints: No stimulation protocol or FSH medicine showed a clear advantage for women of advanced maternal age.
Adding LH to FSH gave similar pregnancy and live birth rates; PGT-A gave similar live birth rates to no testing.
No good evidence supported routine ICSI, and assisted hatching was linked to lower live birth rates.
Low-quality evidence suggested transferring multiple embryos raised live birth rates but also raised multiple pregnancies.

items.title: Risk Factors for Thyroid Dysfunction in Pregnancy: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled data from about 65,000 pregnant women in 25 studies to see whether common risk factors, like age, weight and number of previous births, can predict an underactive thyroid in pregnancy. These factors predicted thyroid problems poorly, so they may not be a reliable way to decide who should be tested. Having thyroid antibodies in the blood was linked to a much higher chance of an underactive thyroid. Twin pregnancy was linked to a higher chance of an overactive thyroid.
keyPoints: Age, body mass index, number of previous births, smoking and gestational age at blood sampling were poor predictors of thyroid test abnormalities in pregnancy.
The risk factors recommended in current guidelines (age over 30, two or more births, BMI of 40 or more) would test 58% of women but detect only 59% of cases of overt or subclinical hypothyroidism.
Subclinical hypothyroidism risk was about 2.2% with no thyroid antibodies, 14.2% with TPO antibodies and 20.0% with both antibody types.
Twin pregnancy was linked to a higher risk of an overactive thyroid (5.6% vs 0.7%).

items.title: Does maternal age affect assisted reproduction technology success rates after euploid embryo transfer? A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined 7 studies covering over 11,000 embryo transfers in which the embryos had been tested and found to have the right number of chromosomes (euploid). It asked whether a woman's age still affects IVF success even when the embryo is chromosomally normal. Women under 35 had higher ongoing pregnancy or live birth rates than women 35 and older. The authors conclude that age-related decline in success is not explained by embryo chromosomes alone.
keyPoints: After transfer of chromosomally normal embryos, women under 35 had higher ongoing pregnancy or live birth rates than women 35 and over (about 6 percentage points higher).
Embryos were also more likely to implant in the youngest group.
Women under 35 did better than each older group studied (35-37, 38-40 and 41-42), with success tending to fall step by step as age rose.
The authors say these findings can help patients understand what to expect before choosing embryo genetic testing (PGT-A).

items.title: Relationship between advanced maternal age and decline of endometrial receptivity: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from 18 studies to see whether older maternal age is linked to a less receptive womb lining, which affects whether an embryo can implant and grow. Women of advanced maternal age had a higher chance of miscarriage and a lower chance of a live birth than younger women. Differences in implantation and clinical pregnancy rates pointed the same way but were not strong enough to be sure of. The authors say more studies are needed to confirm the link and understand why it happens.
keyPoints: Women of advanced maternal age had significantly higher miscarriage rates than younger women.
Live birth rates were significantly lower in older infertile women.
Implantation and clinical pregnancy rates trended lower with age but the difference was not statistically significant.
The authors conclude that older age is related to a decline in womb lining receptivity, and call for further studies.

items.title: Guidelines informing counseling on female age-related fertility decline: a systematic review
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: Researchers reviewed medical guidelines that tell doctors how to talk with patients about fertility declining with age. They found only a small number of good-quality guidelines on this topic, and the advice in them is inconsistent and incomplete. Most guidelines say fertility starts to fall somewhere between age 30 and the late 30s, but few say when to start the conversation.
keyPoints: Of 19 guidelines found that addressed age-related fertility decline, 11 were rated high quality.
Ten of the 11 high-quality guidelines named an age when female fertility declines, ranging from 30 to the late 30s.
Only one guideline recommended a specific age at which patients should be counseled.
Five of the 11 high-quality guidelines did not discuss the pregnancy and birth risks of advanced maternal age.

items.title: Guidance on the limits to the number of embryos to transfer: a committee opinion
items.summary: This committee opinion from two US fertility societies updates their guidance on how many embryos should be transferred during an IVF cycle. The aim is to encourage single pregnancies and reduce the number of twin and other multiple pregnancies. The guidance was refined using national IVF data and replaces the 2017 version. The abstract does not list the specific limits.
keyPoints: The guidance sets limits on the number of embryos transferred in an IVF cycle.
Its main goal is to promote singleton (one-baby) pregnancies and reduce multiple pregnancies.
It was refined using data from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine and the Society for Assisted Reproductive Technology.
It replaces the 2017 committee opinion on the number of embryos to transfer.

items.title: Advanced paternal age is associated with an increased risk of spontaneous miscarriage: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together results from nine studies to see whether a father's age affects the chance of miscarriage. Older fathers were linked to a higher risk, especially from age 40 and above, compared with fathers aged 25-29. The effect was smaller than the well-known effect of the mother's age, and the authors say the mother's age may still be partly influencing the results.
keyPoints: Compared with fathers aged 25-29, the pooled miscarriage risk was about 1.23 times higher at ages 40-44 and about 1.43 times higher at 45 or older.
Risks at ages 30-34 and 35-39 were not clearly different from the reference group.
For first-trimester miscarriage, the increase at age 45 or older was a little higher (about 1.74 times).
The authors say the paternal age effect is smaller than the maternal age effect, and it may be relevant to preconception counselling for couples with an older male partner.

items.title: Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidies (abnormal number of chromosomes) in in vitro fertilisation
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 13 trials with 2794 women to see whether testing embryos for an abnormal number of chromosomes (PGT-A) during IVF improves the chance of a baby. For the newer testing methods, it is uncertain whether PGT-A helps, because few trials exist and the evidence is low quality. The older FISH-based method probably lowered live births after the first transfer. The authors conclude there is not enough good evidence to support routine use of PGT-A.
keyPoints: For newer genome-wide testing methods, it is uncertain whether PGT-A increases the chance of a live birth (low-quality evidence).
PGT-A done with the older FISH method probably reduces live births after the first embryo transfer and probably reduces clinical pregnancies (moderate-quality evidence).
There is probably little or no difference in miscarriage rate with the FISH method; results for newer methods are uncertain.
Women should know it is uncertain whether PGT-A is an effective add-on to IVF, given its invasiveness and costs.

items.title: Advanced Maternal Age: Adverse Outcomes of Pregnancy, A Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined ten studies of single-baby, naturally conceived pregnancies to compare women aged 35 and over with women aged 20 to 34. Older mothers were more likely to have gestational diabetes, high blood pressure in pregnancy, induced labour, planned caesarean births, preterm birth, low birthweight babies and baby intensive care admission. Rates of stillbirth and perinatal death were also higher, and the risks were greater again in women over 40 than in women aged 35 to 40. The authors note that these risks may partly reflect age-related health conditions, but age appears to be a risk factor on its own too.
keyPoints: Women aged 35 and over were more likely to be overweight and to have gestational diabetes and gestational hypertension.
They had more induced labours and planned caesarean births, and more preterm births and low birthweight babies.
Babies of older mothers were more often admitted to neonatal intensive care and had lower Apgar scores.
Stillbirth and perinatal death rates were higher, and worse outcomes were more common in the oldest group (over 40).

items.title: Sperm recovery and ICSI outcomes in men with non-obstructive azoospermia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 117 studies of men with non-obstructive azoospermia, a condition where no sperm are found in the semen because the testes make very few. Surgery to take sperm directly from the testes found sperm in about 47% of procedures, and the two main surgical methods performed about the same. When the retrieved sperm were used for ICSI, about 24% of cycles ended in a live birth. The authors say a well-designed randomised trial is still needed to know for sure whether one surgical method is better.
keyPoints: Sperm were found in about 47% of testicular sperm extraction procedures, with no difference between conventional and micro-surgical methods (46% each).
Sperm retrieval was more likely when the testes were larger, and less likely in men with Klinefelter's syndrome; it did not depend on age or hormone levels.
About 29% of ICSI cycles led to a pregnancy and about 24% to a live birth, regardless of male or female age.
Fresh sperm gave a higher pregnancy rate than frozen sperm, but live birth rates did not clearly differ.

items.title: No-271-Delayed Child-Bearing
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looks at what is known about having children later in life. It says that a woman's age is the most important factor in fertility, and that medical risks in pregnancy and birth rise with age. Many women are not aware of the real success rates and limits of fertility treatments (assisted reproductive technology). The guideline aims to help doctors counsel women about their reproductive choices.
keyPoints: Maternal age is the most important factor in fertility.
Risks in pregnancy and birth increase with maternal age, including multiple births, preterm delivery, stillbirth and Caesarean section.
Delayed child-bearing is linked to a higher chance of infertility and pregnancy complications.
Many women do not know the success rates or limits of assisted reproductive technology.

items.title: Donor oocyte conception and pregnancy complications: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 11 studies to compare pregnancies from donor eggs with pregnancies from IVF using a woman's own eggs. Donor egg pregnancies had higher rates of high blood pressure disorders, babies who were small for their gestational age, caesarean birth and preterm birth. The extra risk did not seem to depend on the mother's age. The authors say women should be counselled carefully before choosing donor egg conception.
keyPoints: High blood pressure disorders in pregnancy were about four times more likely with donor eggs (odds ratio 3.92) than with IVF using own eggs.
Small-for-gestational-age babies, caesarean section and preterm delivery were also more common with donor egg pregnancy.
The higher risk held for both single and twin pregnancies and was independent of maternal age.
The authors recommend careful counselling before donor egg conception.

items.title: Oocyte or embryo donation to women of advanced reproductive age: an Ethics Committee opinion
items.summary: This opinion from a US fertility society's ethics committee looks at using donated eggs or embryos for women of advanced reproductive age (over 45). Donor eggs can make pregnancy possible again, even after menopause, but older women still face high rates of pregnancy complications. The committee advises a thorough health check before any embryo transfer and says treatment for women over 55 should generally be discouraged.
keyPoints: Advanced reproductive age raises the risk of infertility, pregnancy loss, fetal anomalies, stillbirth and obstetric complications.
Oocyte donation reverses the age-related drop in implantation and birth rates and can restore pregnancy potential beyond menopause.
Complications stay high in older patients, especially operative delivery and high blood pressure and heart-related risks.
Women over 45 should have a full medical evaluation before embryo transfer, and treatment should be strongly discouraged or denied if conditions raise obstetric risk.

items.title: Canadian Contraception Consensus (Part 1 of 4)
items.source: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.organisation: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline for health care providers covers how to use contraception to prevent pregnancy, including emergency contraception, and how to talk about sexual health. It says long-acting methods like implants and intrauterine devices (IUDs) are the most effective reversible options, and that the copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception. It also says family planning counselling should include how fertility declines with a woman's age.
keyPoints: Implants and IUDs (copper or levonorgestrel) are the most effective reversible contraception and have the highest continuation rates.
Counselling should explain that fertility declines as a woman gets older.
The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception and can be used up to 7 days after unprotected sex if pregnancy has been ruled out.
Emergency contraception pills work best when taken as soon as possible; ulipristal is more effective than levonorgestrel, and neither works on or after the day of ovulation.

items.title: DEFINING ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR FUNDING POLICIES AROUND IN VITRO FERTILIZATION
items.source: International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care
items.journal: International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care
items.summary: This review looked at 17 papers on how age, smoking and body weight affect the safety and success of IVF (in vitro fertilization). Most found that a pregnancy was less likely in women over 40, women with a BMI of 25 or higher, and women who smoked. Older age and higher BMI were also linked to more preterm births and low birth weight babies. The evidence came mostly from retrospective observational studies, so it shows links rather than proof of cause.
keyPoints: Most papers found a lower chance of pregnancy with IVF in women over 40, with a BMI of 25 or more, and in women who smoked.
Older maternal age and higher BMI were linked to more preterm birth and low birth weight.
The authors suggest maternal age and morbid obesity may be reasonable factors for public IVF funding policies.
The effect of smoking was inconsistent across outcomes, so support for using it in funding rules was weak.

items.title: Age and fecundability in a North American preconception cohort study
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This study followed 2,962 couples in the US and Canada who had just started trying for a baby, for up to 12 cycles, to see how age affects the chance of getting pregnant naturally. After 6 cycles, 62% of women aged 28-30 were pregnant compared with 28% of women aged 40-45; after 12 cycles the figures ranged from 79% (age 25-27) to 56% (age 40-45). The chance of conceiving each cycle fell steadily with the woman's age, staying fairly stable between 28 and 33. The man's age made little difference once the woman's age was taken into account, though few men over 45 took part.
keyPoints: Pregnant within 6 cycles: from 62% at age 28-30 down to 28% at age 40-45.
Pregnant within 12 cycles: from 79% at age 25-27 down to 56% at age 40-45.
Compared with women aged 21-24, the chance per cycle was 0.60 times as high at 37-39 and 0.40 times as high at 40-45.
Male age was not clearly linked to the chance of pregnancy after accounting for female age.

items.title: Risk of congenital genitourinary abnormalities in offspring and parental alcohol consumption during the periconception period: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 27 studies to see whether a parent's drinking around the time of conception is linked to birth differences of the genital and urinary system in babies. Mothers who drank had slightly higher odds of having a baby with hypospadias, and heavier drinking was linked to higher odds of undescended testes in a non-linear pattern. Overall results were mixed, and one unexpected lower-odds finding for undescended testes should be read with caution. The authors still recommend avoiding alcohol completely around conception and during pregnancy.
keyPoints: Maternal alcohol use around conception was linked to higher odds of hypospadias (OR 1.16).
Moderate-to-heavy drinking was linked to higher odds of undescended testes (cryptorchidism), but low-dose drinking was not.
When all types of genitourinary differences were combined, no overall link was found.
The authors recommend complete abstinence from alcohol around conception and during pregnancy.

items.title: Sleep disturbance in children with prenatal alcohol exposure: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies of children aged 3 to 10 who were exposed to alcohol before birth. These children slept worse than other children: it took them longer to fall asleep, they slept for less time, and they woke up more often at night. Sleep problems were linked to heavier alcohol exposure and to exposure earlier in pregnancy. The results varied a lot between studies, so the exact size of the difference is uncertain.
keyPoints: Children exposed to alcohol before birth had consistently worse sleep than typically developing children.
Sleep problems included longer time to fall asleep, shorter sleep, more night waking and lower sleep efficiency.
Heavier alcohol exposure, and exposure in early pregnancy, was linked to earlier and more lasting sleep problems.
The authors recommend early screening and support for sleep problems in these children.

items.title: Prevention of alcohol exposed pregnancies in Europe: the FAR SEAS guidelines
items.summary: These European guidelines look at how to prevent babies being exposed to alcohol in the womb, which can cause lifelong problems called fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD). The authors built 23 recommendations from a review of existing programmes, advice from international experts and a pilot project in Poland. They stress that support should respect women's choices and avoid blame or stigma, and that help should fit each woman's level of need.
keyPoints: Drinking during pregnancy is described as the leading cause of birth defects and child developmental disorders in Europe.
Recommendations call for screening all women of childbearing age for alcohol use, along with other risks such as domestic violence.
Women who need more help, such as those with alcohol use disorders, should get individual, multidisciplinary support, and their partners should be included.
Public health messages should combine information about risks with encouraging messages that help people feel able to change.

items.title: Psychosocial and medication interventions to stop or reduce alcohol consumption during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at eight trials (1369 pregnant women) testing ways to help women stop or cut down on alcohol during pregnancy. All of the trials tested talking-based support, mostly brief sessions, and none tested medications. Brief support may help more women stay completely alcohol-free than usual care, but the evidence is low certainty. The effect on how many drinks women had per day is very uncertain, and none of the studies looked at side effects.
keyPoints: Brief talking-based (psychosocial) support may increase the number of women who stay completely alcohol-free during pregnancy compared with usual care (low certainty evidence).
The effect on the number of drinks per day is very uncertain (very low certainty evidence).
Brief support probably makes little to no difference to how many women complete the treatment (moderate certainty evidence).
No trials tested medications for alcohol problems in pregnancy, and none reported adverse events, so more research is needed.

items.title: Prenatal alcohol exposure and associations with physical size, dysmorphology and neurodevelopment: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pulled together 306 studies on drinking alcohol during pregnancy and how children's growth, facial features and brain development turned out. More alcohol exposure was linked to smaller head size and body size, especially at birth, and to certain typical facial features and some development and learning difficulties. For several other outcomes there was not enough evidence to draw conclusions, and the certainty of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate.
keyPoints: Higher alcohol exposure in pregnancy was linked to smaller head circumference and body size, especially at birth, in a dose-response pattern.
Higher exposure was also linked to characteristic facial features and to many of the development outcomes used to assess fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD).
Evidence was lacking for several other features, such as seizures, sensory processing and brain MRI abnormalities, to support using them in diagnosis.
Data were often missing across the full range of alcohol amounts, so more well-designed pregnancy studies are needed.

items.title: Italian Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders
items.summary: These Italian guidelines cover fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD), a group of lifelong conditions that can result when a baby is exposed to alcohol before birth. They note that drinking alcohol in pregnancy is linked to birth defects, and that to be safe it is advised to avoid alcohol completely during pregnancy. They also say FASD is still hard to diagnose in Italy, and that early diagnosis and treatment matter.
keyPoints: Drinking alcohol during pregnancy can cause congenital disabilities, including facial differences, poor growth and learning difficulties.
To ensure safety, it is advised to abstain from alcohol during pregnancy.
FASD is still hard to diagnose in Italy, and more authorised diagnosis centres are needed.
Early diagnosis and treatment are described as critical for affected children.

items.title: Italian Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders: structural abnormalities
items.summary: This Italian guideline reviews Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD), a group of conditions caused by drinking alcohol during pregnancy. These can affect a child's body, behaviour and learning, and FASD is described as a major preventable cause of mental disability. The authors say prevention is the most effective way to reduce FASD, and that early diagnosis and support can improve outcomes.
keyPoints: FASD is caused by alcohol exposure before birth and can lead to physical, behavioural and learning difficulties.
It is a significant preventable cause of mental disability, affecting about 7.7 in every 1,000 people in the Western world.
Prevention is the most effective strategy, but public understanding of the risks is currently not good enough.
Timely diagnosis and appropriate support and management can significantly improve outcomes.

items.title: Italian Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders: multimodal approaches of treatment and intervention
items.summary: These Italian guidelines look at how to support children and adults living with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD), which are caused by alcohol exposure before birth. FASD can affect self-esteem, family and friendship relationships, and school success, and it often occurs alongside other conditions, which can delay diagnosis. The guidelines say that early diagnosis and early support may prevent further difficulties later on and improve outcomes. No single treatment worked best for every symptom, so care needs to be tailored to each person using a mix of approaches.
keyPoints: FASD can affect self-esteem, family and peer relationships, and school success.
Other conditions often occur alongside FASD, which may delay diagnosis and treatment.
Early diagnosis and support aimed at the main symptoms may prevent secondary difficulties and improve outcomes.
No one intervention was most effective across all symptoms, so each person needs an individual assessment and a combination of approaches.

items.title: Italian Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders: detecting alcohol drinking during pregnancy
items.summary: These Italian guidelines look at how to spot alcohol drinking during pregnancy, because alcohol exposure before birth can cause Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD). FASD can affect the brain, growth and facial features, and there is no known treatment, so finding alcohol use early matters. The guidelines say questionnaires may miss drinking because women may not feel able to answer honestly. They recommend adding tests for alcohol markers in blood, urine, hair or the baby's first stool to pregnancy care.
keyPoints: FASD is caused by alcohol exposure during pregnancy and mainly affects the brain, growth and facial features.
There are no known treatments for FASD, so early screening in pregnancy is important.
Questionnaires such as AUDIT-C, T-ACE and TWEAK may under-report drinking because of social pressure to answer in an expected way.
Alcohol marker tests (for example PEth in blood and EtG in urine) are recommended as part of pregnancy monitoring; urine EtG is very sensitive and can pick up occasional drinking.

items.title: Italian Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders: prevention and health promotion
items.summary: Italian guidelines reviewed the evidence on preventing Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD), a group of conditions caused by alcohol exposure before birth. They describe drinking alcohol in pregnancy as risky for both mother and baby. The guidelines recommend wide public education, routine alcohol screening and brief support during prenatal care, and targeted help for women who drink. They also stress avoiding stigma so women feel able to ask for help.
keyPoints: Alcohol use in pregnancy poses significant risks to maternal and fetal health and can cause Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders.
Public health campaigns, education and policy aim to raise awareness and promote not drinking during pregnancy.
Alcohol screening and brief intervention in routine prenatal care can help identify and support women who may be at risk.
Women with alcohol problems or earlier alcohol-exposed pregnancies may need treatment and rehabilitation, and stigma should be avoided.

items.title: Italian Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders: cognitive and behavioral deficits
items.summary: This Italian guideline reviews what is known about how drinking alcohol during pregnancy can affect a child's thinking and behaviour. Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASDs) are a group of conditions seen in people who were exposed to alcohol before birth. Brain scans show differences in brain structure and connections, which change how a child's brain normally develops. The paper also looks at whether a typical pattern of strengths and difficulties could help with diagnosis.
keyPoints: FASDs are conditions that occur in a person who was exposed to alcohol before birth.
Brain imaging in people with FASD shows differences in brain structure, cortical development, white matter and connectivity.
These differences are linked to difficulties in areas such as intelligence, memory, language, attention, learning, motor skills and social functioning.
A specific neurobehavioral profile may help in diagnosing FASD.

items.title: Baseline heart rate in infants with prenatal alcohol exposure: A systematic review and independent analysis
items.summary: Researchers looked at whether babies exposed to alcohol before birth have a different resting heart rate. Combining six earlier studies suggested their heart rate was slightly higher, by about 4.6 beats per minute. But when the team re-checked individual baby data from two larger datasets, resting heart rates were similar to those of unexposed babies born full-term and of healthy growth. The authors note that the review findings are limited by the small number of studies and the few that included comparison babies.
keyPoints: Pooling six studies, resting heart rate was about 4.6 beats per minute higher in babies with prenatal alcohol exposure than in comparison babies.
The review findings are limited because there were few studies and few included control babies.
In individual data from age-matched, full-term babies without growth restriction, resting heart rates did not differ between exposed and unexposed babies.
The authors conclude that babies with prenatal alcohol exposure appear to have normal resting heart rates.

items.title: Maternal alcohol consumption and the risk of miscarriage in the first and second trimesters: A systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from five studies to see whether drinking alcohol is linked to miscarriage in the first and second trimesters. Each extra drink per week was linked to a small rise in miscarriage risk (7% in the first trimester, 3% in the second), but these rises were not statistically significant, so they could be due to chance. Only one study looked at binge drinking and it found no link. The authors say more focused research is needed, and note that the usual advice to avoid alcohol in pregnancy is a precaution.
keyPoints: No statistically significant link was found between the number of drinks per week and miscarriage risk in either trimester.
Odds rose by 7% (first trimester) and 3% (second trimester) per extra weekly drink, but the confidence intervals included no effect.
Only one study looked at binge drinking, and it found no association with miscarriage.
The authors call for more focused research, especially on binge drinking and miscarriage.

items.title: Association between pregnancy intention and smoking or alcohol consumption in the preconception and pregnancy periods: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 23 studies to see whether planning a pregnancy is linked to smoking and drinking alcohol before and during pregnancy. Women whose pregnancy was unplanned were more likely to smoke and drink alcohol than women whose pregnancy was planned, both before and during pregnancy. The authors suggest health professionals should take a woman's pregnancy intentions into account when supporting healthier habits.
keyPoints: During pregnancy, women with unplanned pregnancies were 44% more likely to drink alcohol than those with planned pregnancies.
During pregnancy, women with unplanned pregnancies were 68% more likely to smoke.
Before conception, women with unplanned pregnancies were 20% more likely to drink alcohol and 30% more likely to smoke.
The authors suggest offering effective contraception in primary care could help prevent unplanned pregnancy, and that minimal-alcohol messaging and smoke-free laws could improve outcomes.

items.title: Ear Abnormalities Among Children with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 31 studies of children who were exposed to alcohol before birth or who have fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD). It looked at how often ear problems, both in how the ear works and in how it is shaped, were found. Some ear problems were very common in these children, such as long-lasting fluid in the middle ear and trouble filtering sounds. The authors say ears should be checked when children are assessed for FASD, and that the public should be told about the harms of alcohol in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Common ear function problems in these children included chronic middle ear fluid (about 88%), abnormal auditory filtering (about 80%) and conductive hearing loss (about 68%).
Common ear shape differences included microtia (a very small ear, about 43%), railroad track ear (about 17%) and misplaced ear (about 12%).
The authors recommend examining the ears when assessing children for FASD.
The authors call for public health messaging about the harms of alcohol exposure before birth.

items.title: The Universal and Primary Prevention of Foetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD): A Systematic Review
items.summary: Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is a group of lifelong brain and development conditions caused by alcohol use during pregnancy, and there is no cure. This review looked at 10 studies of programmes meant to prevent FASD in the general population. All but one of the programmes helped raise knowledge and awareness of FASD and lowered the risk of a pregnancy being exposed to alcohol. The studies varied a lot in quality, and many were small, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: FASD is caused by alcohol use during pregnancy and has no cure, so prevention is key.
Nine of the ten prevention programmes reviewed raised awareness and knowledge of FASD and reduced the risk of an alcohol-exposed pregnancy.
The quality of the studies varied widely, with small sample sizes and little testing of actual behaviour change.
More research is needed to find the best way to prevent FASD.

items.title: Cognitive and Behavioural Attention in Children with Low-Moderate and Heavy Doses of Prenatal Alcohol Exposure: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 13 studies comparing children whose mothers drank alcohol during pregnancy with children whose mothers did not. Children exposed to alcohol had more trouble shifting their attention between tasks. There were also hints, not firm proof, of attention problems with heavy exposure and with low-to-moderate exposure. The authors say the research so far is limited and not of high quality, so more study is urgently needed.
keyPoints: Any alcohol exposure in pregnancy was linked to a significant difficulty with shifting attention in children.
Heavy exposure showed a trend towards problems with encoding (taking in) attention.
Low-to-moderate exposure showed a trend towards greater odds of attention-related behaviour problems.
Many analyses had too few studies or showed no significant result, and the authors call for better research on low-to-moderate drinking.

items.title: Systematic review showed that low and moderate prenatal alcohol and nicotine exposure affected early child development
items.summary: This review looked at 17 studies on how low and moderate amounts of alcohol or nicotine during pregnancy affect children's development in their first 2 years. Alcohol studies reported reduced sensory sensitivity, smaller body size and, oddly, some increased thinking skills. Nicotine studies mainly found problems with orienting, communication and motor skills. The authors concluded that any amount of either appeared to put healthy development at risk, but said good representative data were missing and some findings were mixed.
keyPoints: 13 of the 17 studies looked at prenatal alcohol and reported reduced sensory sensitivity, smaller body sizes and increased cognitive capacities.
4 studies looked at prenatal nicotine and mainly found impairments in orienting, communication and motor skills.
The authors concluded that any amount of prenatal alcohol or nicotine exposure appeared to risk healthy child development.
Representative data from interdisciplinary research were missing, and some findings were controversial.

items.title: Guideline No. 405: Screening and Counselling for Alcohol Consumption During Pregnancy
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline sets out how health care providers should ask women of child-bearing age and pregnant women about alcohol, and how to support them. It recommends using validated screening tools and short counselling conversations (brief interventions). The aim is for providers to notice alcohol use and problem drinking earlier and help women reach the healthiest pregnancy possible. The abstract does not list the individual recommendations or their evidence ratings.
keyPoints: Pregnant women and women who could become pregnant should be asked about alcohol use and possible alcohol use disorder.
Validated screening tools and brief intervention approaches are recommended for providers.
The goal is for providers to feel confident and skilled in supporting women with alcohol use so they can reach the best health and pregnancy outcomes.
The guideline drew on trials, observational studies, reviews and consensus statements published between 2010 and September 2018.

items.title: A Systematic Review of Interventions to Improve Mental Health and Substance Use Outcomes for Individuals with Prenatal Alcohol Exposure and Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder
items.summary: This review looked at 33 studies of ways to support mental health and reduce substance use in people who were exposed to alcohol before birth, including those with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD). Most studies focused on building skills for children and supporting their families. Very few directly targeted mental health or substance use problems, and few were aimed at teenagers or adults. The authors describe the evidence as preliminary and emerging.
keyPoints: People with FASD have very high rates of mental health and substance use challenges, starting early in life and continuing into adulthood.
Most of the 33 studies focused on building skills and strategies for children and their families.
There was a clear lack of interventions aimed directly at mental health and substance use, and a major gap for adolescents and adults.
The evidence so far is preliminary but suggests several approaches may support better outcomes across a person's life.

items.title: Low-moderate prenatal alcohol exposure and offspring attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies looking at whether light-to-moderate drinking during pregnancy is linked to ADHD symptoms (attention problems or hyperactivity) in children. Ten studies were reviewed and six were combined in a meta-analysis. No increased risk of ADHD symptoms was found in children whose mothers drank up to 70 g of alcohol a week.
keyPoints: Eight of ten studies found no link between low-to-moderate alcohol in pregnancy and ADHD symptoms in children.
Combining results showed no association at up to 20 g, 50 g or 70 g of alcohol per week.
No increased ADHD risk was seen in children of mothers who drank up to 70 g per week.
In boys, drinking up to 50 g per week showed slightly lower ADHD symptom risk than in girls, though the authors did not claim this proves a benefit.

items.title: A systematic review of prevention interventions to reduce prenatal alcohol exposure and fetal alcohol spectrum disorder in indigenous communities
items.summary: This review looked at programs designed to reduce alcohol use in pregnancy and prevent fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) in Indigenous communities. It found ten studies, nine from the US and one from Australia, and all were rated as poor quality. Because of this, there is little evidence that these programs have worked so far. The authors say future programs should be built around cultural factors and history, and tested with stronger methods.
keyPoints: FASD is a lifelong condition caused by alcohol exposure before birth, and it is preventable.
All ten studies reviewed were rated as poor quality, with problems like people dropping out, no comparison groups and reliance on self-reported drinking.
There is little evidence that earlier prevention programs in Indigenous communities have been effective.
Future programs should address cultural factors and historical context and be evaluated rigorously.

items.title: Estimation of national, regional, and global prevalence of alcohol use during pregnancy and fetal alcohol syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from hundreds of studies to estimate how common drinking alcohol in pregnancy is worldwide, and how often it leads to fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), a birth defect caused by alcohol exposure before birth. They estimated that about 1 in 10 pregnant women worldwide drank alcohol during pregnancy. They also estimated that about 1 in 67 women who drank alcohol during pregnancy had a child with FAS. The authors conclude that better prevention and tracking of FAS are needed.
keyPoints: The global rate of alcohol use during pregnancy was estimated at 9.8%.
FAS was estimated to affect about 14.6 in every 10,000 people in the general population.
About 1 in every 67 women who drank alcohol during pregnancy was estimated to have a child with FAS.
This adds up to about 119,000 children born with FAS around the world each year.

items.title: Global Prevalence of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder Among Children and Youth: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 24 studies to estimate how many children and young people have fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD), a set of lifelong developmental problems linked to alcohol exposure before birth. It estimated that about 7.7 in every 1000 people worldwide have FASD, with big differences between regions and countries. The authors describe FASD as largely preventable and call for clear public health messages about the possible harm of drinking alcohol in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Worldwide, an estimated 7.7 per 1000 children and youth have FASD.
The WHO European Region had the highest estimated rate (19.8 per 1000) and the Eastern Mediterranean Region the lowest (0.1 per 1000).
Among countries, South Africa had the highest estimated rate (111.1 per 1000), followed by Croatia and Ireland.
The authors call for a universal public health message about prenatal alcohol harm, routine screening and brief interventions where appropriate.

items.title: Comorbidity of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 127 studies to see which other health conditions occur in people with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD), which is caused by alcohol exposure before birth. They found 428 different conditions linked with FASD, most often birth defects and mental, behavioural and language problems. The authors conclude that alcohol use in pregnancy causes many cases of preventable disability.
keyPoints: 127 studies were included, covering 428 conditions that occur alongside FASD across 18 of 22 ICD-10 chapters.
The most common were congenital malformations and mental and behavioural disorders.
In people with fetal alcohol syndrome, the most common conditions (50% to 91%) were nerve and sensory function abnormalities, conduct disorder, language disorders and chronic middle-ear infection.
The authors say alcohol exposure in pregnancy is a major risk factor for these conditions and a global public health problem.

items.title: Prenatal alcohol exposure and offspring liver dysfunction: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 23 studies to look at how drinking alcohol during pregnancy affects the baby's liver. Alcohol exposure was linked to lower fetal body weight but not lower liver weight. It was also linked to changes in liver proteins and enzymes, which suggests alcohol may disrupt how the baby's liver works.
keyPoints: Alcohol exposure in pregnancy was linked to a significant drop in fetal body weight.
It was not linked to a drop in fetal liver weight.
Exposure was linked to lower levels of protective liver substances such as glutathione.
Exposure was also linked to higher levels of oxidants and collagen, pointing to possible liver dysfunction in the baby.

items.title: Impact of fetal alcohol exposure on body systems: A systematic review
items.source: Birth Defects Research. Part C, Embryo Today
items.journal: Birth Defects Research. Part C, Embryo Today
items.summary: This review looked at 13 published studies on how alcohol exposure before birth affects different body systems in the baby. It found the brain is the organ most severely affected. Alcohol exposure in pregnancy was also linked to problems in the heart, kidneys, liver, digestive system and hormone (endocrine) system. The authors conclude that mothers need to take preventive steps during pregnancy.
keyPoints: The brain was the organ most severely affected by alcohol exposure before birth.
Prenatal alcohol exposure was linked to abnormalities in the heart, kidneys, liver, digestive tract and hormone systems.
The review pulled together 13 articles: five original studies and eight reviews.
The authors say preventive measures are needed during pregnancy.

items.title: Maternal gestational smoking, diabetes, alcohol drinking, pre-pregnancy obesity and the risk of cryptorchidism: a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies
items.summary: This review pooled results from 32 studies to look at whether smoking, diabetes, alcohol or being overweight before pregnancy are linked to cryptorchidism, where a baby boy's testicle has not moved down into place. Smoking during pregnancy was linked to a small increase in risk, while alcohol overall showed no clear link. Moderate drinking seemed to be linked to a slightly lower risk, but the authors say the results for alcohol and diabetes were unstable and need more research.
keyPoints: Smoking during pregnancy was linked to a modestly higher risk of cryptorchidism in baby boys.
Overall, drinking alcohol during pregnancy was not clearly linked to cryptorchidism.
A separate analysis suggested moderate drinking might be linked to lower risk, but the authors say this needs to be verified by further studies.
Being overweight or obese before pregnancy was not linked to cryptorchidism, and diabetes during pregnancy may be a risk factor but the result was unstable.

items.title: High feedback versus low feedback of prenatal ultrasound for reducing maternal anxiety and improving maternal health behaviour in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review compared two ways of running a pregnancy ultrasound: 'high feedback' (the woman sees the screen and gets detailed explanations) and 'low feedback' (she cannot see the screen and only gets a short summary). Four small trials with 365 women were included. High feedback did not clearly change anxiety. One small study found women given high feedback were more likely to stop smoking and avoid alcohol, but the evidence was low quality, so overall the review could not say which approach is better.
keyPoints: Three trials (346 women) found no clear difference in anxiety scores between high and low feedback during ultrasound.
One small study (129 women) found women given high feedback were more likely to stop smoking and to avoid alcohol in pregnancy.
The evidence was rated low quality, because of unclear risk of bias and wide uncertainty in the results.
The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to support either high or low feedback to reduce anxiety or promote healthy behaviour.

items.title: Serum anti-Müllerian hormone levels in women following bariatric surgery: insights from a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies to see whether weight-loss (bariatric) surgery changes levels of anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), a blood marker often used to estimate egg reserve. Overall, AMH did not change significantly after surgery. Results varied a lot between studies, with drops in some groups (for example, those with higher starting AMH or longer follow-up) and a rise in women described as fertile. The authors say these shifts should not be read as proof that egg reserve or fertility has changed.
keyPoints: Across 591 women, bariatric surgery was not linked to a significant overall change in AMH levels.
Results differed widely between studies, so the average hides a lot of variation.
AMH fell in some subgroups, such as women with higher starting AMH, and rose in the fertile subgroup.
Changes in AMH should be seen as shifting hormone levels, not direct evidence of altered egg reserve or fertility, as few studies reported reproductive outcomes.

items.title: The improvement effect of androgen priming on fertility in patients with diminished ovarian reserve and its impact on in vitro fertilization outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies (2,132 women) on androgen priming, meaning DHEA supplements or testosterone gel, before IVF in women with diminished ovarian reserve (a low egg supply). In the randomized trials, priming was linked to slightly more eggs retrieved (under one extra egg on average). Non-randomized studies also showed more fertilized embryos and a higher clinical pregnancy rate. The authors say it is still unclear whether pregnancy rates truly improve, and that larger, better-quality randomized trials are needed.
keyPoints: Androgen priming (DHEA or testosterone gel) increased the number of eggs retrieved in randomized trials, by about 0.8 eggs on average.
Non-randomized studies showed more fertilized embryos, more top-quality day-3 embryos and a higher clinical pregnancy rate.
Two months of priming, and an average age over 40, were linked to a bigger gain in eggs retrieved.
Whether priming improves pregnancy rates is not settled and needs more high-quality randomized trials.

items.title: Therapeutic management in women with a diminished ovarian reserve: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 38 randomized trials of treatments used during IVF in women with diminished ovarian reserve (a lower number of eggs). Only testosterone supplementation was linked to a higher live birth rate. Testosterone, DHEA and a delayed-start protocol also gave more eggs collected, and most other treatments showed no clear benefit. The authors say these findings need to be explored in further trials.
keyPoints: Testosterone supplementation was linked to higher live birth rates than no supplementation (four studies, 368 patients).
Testosterone, DHEA and a delayed-start protocol each increased the number of eggs collected.
Low-dose gonadotropin gave fewer eggs retrieved than high-dose gonadotropin.
The other treatments reviewed did not show significant improvements.

items.title: Evidence-based guideline: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency
items.summary: This international guideline from ESHRE and partner societies sets out 145 recommendations on diagnosing and managing premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), when the ovaries stop working normally well before the usual age of menopause. New data suggest POI affects about 3.5% of women, more than once thought. The guideline covers diagnosis, causes, effects on bone, heart, brain and sexual health, fertility, and treatment including hormone therapy. The authors note that for most management options, the supporting evidence in POI is limited.
keyPoints: POI is more common than previously thought, at an estimated 3.5% of women.
A single raised FSH result above 25 IU is now enough to diagnose POI; repeat FSH and/or AMH testing may be used when the diagnosis is unclear.
The guideline now covers the role of AMH in diagnosis, fertility preservation, muscle health, and hormone therapy after treatment-caused (iatrogenic) POI.
Recommendations on genetic testing, estrogen doses, the combined oral contraceptive and testosterone therapy were updated, but evidence for most options is limited.

items.title: ACOG Committee Statement No. 22: Anticipatory Counseling Regarding Ovarian-Factor Fertility Decline
items.summary: This statement from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists explains that fertility naturally falls with age as the ovaries lose egg follicles. It says people tend to overestimate their chances of getting pregnant at every age. It recommends that health professionals talk with patients early about this natural decline and about other, non-age-related factors that can speed it up. It also notes that better evidence-based resources are still needed.
keyPoints: Fertility declines with age as the number and quality of egg follicles in the ovaries naturally falls.
Patients significantly overestimate their chance of pregnancy at all ages.
Health care professionals should educate patients about ovarian reserve decline across the reproductive lifespan.
Factors other than age can speed up ovarian decline, and more evidence-based patient resources are needed.

items.title: The auxiliary effect of oral nutritional supplements on fertility in women with diminished ovarian reserve: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 studies with 2,773 women who have diminished ovarian reserve (a lower number of eggs than expected). It looked at oral supplements including vitamins, coenzyme Q10 and DHEA. Women taking supplements had lower FSH levels, higher AMH levels, more antral follicles, more eggs retrieved and higher clinical pregnancy rates. The authors suggest supplements may be a simple, relatively low-risk way to help support fertility in these women.
keyPoints: Supplements were linked to lower FSH, higher AMH and more antral follicles.
More eggs were retrieved, and clinical pregnancy was more likely (odds ratio 1.70).
Taking supplements for more than 2 months worked better for FSH, AMH and egg numbers.
Coenzyme Q10 alone appeared more effective than DHEA alone.

items.title: Individualised gonadotropin dose selection using markers of ovarian reserve for women undergoing in vitro fertilisation plus intracytoplasmic sperm injection (IVF/ICSI)
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 26 trials (8,520 women) of IVF/ICSI to see whether choosing the daily FSH hormone dose using ovarian reserve tests, such as AMH, antral follicle count or basal FSH, leads to better results. It is unclear whether dose-tailoring raises the chance of a live birth or ongoing pregnancy. Tailoring may lower the chance of moderate or severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), but the evidence is low certainty and the size of the effect is uncertain.
keyPoints: Using an ovarian-reserve-based dosing plan compared with a standard dose may or may not increase live birth or ongoing pregnancy (low-certainty evidence).
Ovarian-reserve-based dosing may reduce moderate or severe OHSS; for example, a 5% chance with standard dosing might fall to between 2% and 5%.
The evidence does not clearly support changing the standard 150 IU dose in predicted poor or normal responders, and higher doses mean more medication and cost.
Studies used different dosing plans, and some plans may work better than others.

items.title: The effect of COVID-19 and COVID-19 vaccination on serum anti-Mullerian hormone: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from studies looking at whether COVID-19 infection or COVID-19 vaccination changes levels of anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH), a blood marker often used to estimate egg reserve. After COVID-19 infection, AMH levels were slightly lower on average. After vaccination, there was no statistically significant change in AMH. The authors concluded that infection may affect ovarian reserve, while vaccination does not appear to.
keyPoints: Pooled results from 8 studies showed a small but statistically significant drop in AMH after COVID-19 infection.
Pooled results from 10 studies showed no statistically significant change in AMH after COVID-19 vaccination.
The authors concluded that infection may reduce ovarian reserve as measured by AMH, but vaccination has no impact on AMH.

items.title: The value of intraovarian autologous platelet rich plasma in women with poor ovarian reserve or ovarian insufficiency: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies of women with low egg reserve or early ovarian failure who had platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injected into their ovaries. AMH levels did not change in a meaningful way. The number of antral follicles (small egg-containing follicles seen on ultrasound) and the number of eggs retrieved were higher after PRP, and the authors report fewer cancelled cycles and more embryos in women with low reserve.
keyPoints: AMH levels showed no clear change after ovarian PRP (average difference 0.09, not statistically significant).
Antral follicle count was higher after PRP (average difference 1.73).
About 1 more egg was retrieved on average after PRP (average difference 1.21).
The authors report improvements in cleavage-stage embryo numbers and cycle cancellation rates in women with poor ovarian reserve.

items.title: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatment of the ovaries significantly improves fertility parameters and reproductive outcomes in diminished ovarian reserve patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 38 studies (2,256 women with diminished ovarian reserve) that looked at platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatment of the ovaries. After treatment, AMH levels went up, FSH levels went down, and women had more antral follicles, retrieved eggs and embryos. Some women also became pregnant, including a small share who conceived naturally. Most studies were observational (not randomised trials), and the authors say larger, better trials are needed to confirm the results.
keyPoints: AMH rose and FSH fell after PRP ovarian treatment, with changes seen at 1, 2 and 3 months.
Antral follicle count, retrieved eggs and embryos created all increased on average.
Spontaneous pregnancy rate was about 7%, biochemical pregnancy about 18% and live birth about 11%.
The studies were mostly observational with no comparison group other than the women's own earlier results, so larger randomised trials are still needed.

items.title: Anti-müllerian hormone as a diagnostic biomarker for polycystic ovary syndrome and polycystic ovarian morphology: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 82 studies to see how well a blood test for anti-müllerian hormone (AMH) can help diagnose polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). In adult women, the test picked up about 79 in 100 women with PCOS and correctly ruled out about 87 in 100 women without it. It worked less well in teenagers. The authors conclude that AMH alone is not enough to diagnose PCOS, and that no single cut-off level could be recommended.
keyPoints: In adults, AMH identified PCOS with a pooled sensitivity of 0.79 and specificity of 0.87.
In adolescents, results were weaker: sensitivity 0.66 and specificity 0.78, and AMH was nonspecific for polycystic ovarian morphology.
The 2023 international PCOS guideline now recommends AMH levels for defining polycystic ovarian morphology in adults, as part of its diagnostic algorithm.
AMH levels alone are insufficient to diagnose PCOS, and many factors affect AMH levels, so no international cut-off could be recommended.

items.title: Antioxidants and Fertility in Women with Ovarian Aging: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 20 randomized trials with 2617 women who had ovarian aging (a lower number or quality of eggs) and were having fertility treatment. Women who took antioxidant supplements had more eggs retrieved, more high-quality embryos, needed less fertility medication, and had higher clinical pregnancy rates. Coenzyme Q10 appeared to work best, especially in women under 35 with a low egg reserve. The authors describe antioxidants as an effective and safe add-on treatment, with lower doses working better.
keyPoints: Antioxidants increased the number of eggs retrieved and the rate of high-quality embryos, and lowered the dose of fertility medication needed.
Clinical pregnancy rates were higher with antioxidant use.
Coenzyme Q10 tended to work better than melatonin, myo-inositol and vitamins.
The best CoQ10 regimen for pregnancy rate was 30 mg a day for 3 months before the ovarian stimulation cycle, with the clearest benefit in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.

items.title: Clinical evidence of coenzyme Q10 pretreatment for women with diminished ovarian reserve undergoing IVF/ICSI: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled six randomized trials (1,529 women) of coenzyme Q10 taken before IVF/ICSI by women with diminished ovarian reserve. Women who took CoQ10 had higher clinical pregnancy rates, more eggs retrieved, fewer cancelled cycles and fewer miscarriages. They also needed fewer days and a lower total dose of fertility medication. The authors note that the trials were fairly small and poorly described, so larger, well-run trials are still needed.
keyPoints: CoQ10 pretreatment was linked to a higher clinical pregnancy rate (odds ratio 1.84) in women with diminished ovarian reserve having IVF/ICSI.
More eggs were retrieved with CoQ10, and fewer IVF cycles were cancelled.
Miscarriage rates were lower, and less fertility medication (gonadotropin) was needed in days and dose.
The authors say sample sizes were limited and methods poorly described, so better trials are needed.

items.title: Anti-müllerian hormone as a predictor for live birth among women undergoing IVF/ICSI in different age groups: an update of systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 27 studies with about 27,000 women having IVF or ICSI to see whether blood AMH levels (a marker of egg reserve) predict a live birth.
