AMH was linked to live birth overall, and the link was stronger in older women. In younger women, and in women with low egg reserve, AMH did not predict live birth well. The authors say AMH may be useful when counselling older couples about assisted conception.
keyPoints: AMH was associated with live birth after IVF/ICSI across 27 studies (27,029 women).
AMH predicted live birth better in women of advanced age.
In younger women and those with diminished ovarian reserve, AMH showed no predictive ability for live birth.
The authors suggest AMH may help with counselling older couples about assisted conception.

items.title: Clinical evidence of growth hormone for infertile women with diminished ovarian reserve undergoing IVF: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 randomised trials (852 women) of adding growth hormone during ovarian stimulation for IVF in women with diminished ovarian reserve, meaning fewer eggs than expected. Women who received growth hormone had more clinical pregnancies, more eggs retrieved and better embryo results. They also needed fewer days and lower doses of fertility medication, and fewer cycles were cancelled. The trials were at high risk of bias because of blinding, and the authors say better-designed trials are needed to confirm the results.
keyPoints: Growth hormone was linked to a higher clinical pregnancy rate (RR 1.63) and more eggs retrieved.
It was also linked to higher fertilization and embryo implantation rates, more good-quality embryos, and fewer cancelled cycles.
Women using growth hormone needed fewer days and a lower total dose of stimulation medication.
The trials had a high risk of bias in blinding, so the authors call for well-designed trials to verify the findings.

items.title: Endometrioma surgery-a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect on antral follicle count and anti-Müllerian hormone
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies (650 women) that measured egg reserve before and after surgery to remove endometriomas (ovarian cysts caused by endometriosis). Blood levels of anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), a marker of egg reserve, dropped by about 35-54% after surgery, and stayed lower up to 9-18 months later. Antral follicle counts on ultrasound did not change significantly. The authors suggest AMH may show the effect of surgery on egg reserve more reliably than follicle counts, though results varied a lot between studies.
keyPoints: AMH levels fell after endometrioma surgery by an average of 44.4%, 35.1% and 54.2% at early, intermediate and late follow-up.
The lower AMH was still seen 9-18 months after surgery.
Antral follicle counts on ultrasound showed no significant change at any time point.
The studies differed a lot from each other, partly because of different AMH tests, so exact figures are uncertain.

items.title: The Effect of Laparoscopic Endometrioma Surgery on Anti-Müllerian Hormone: A Systematic Review of the Literature and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 36 studies to see how keyhole (laparoscopic) surgery for endometriomas, which are ovarian cysts linked to endometriosis, affects AMH, a blood marker of egg reserve. AMH levels were lower after surgery in the short, medium and long term, with no clear recovery after a year. The drop was bigger with cysts on both ovaries and with cysts larger than 7 cm. The authors say the results should be read with caution because the studies differed a lot from each other.
keyPoints: AMH was significantly lower after endometrioma surgery at all time points, with no clear recovery after one year.
Bilateral endometriomas and cysts larger than 7 cm were linked to bigger drops in AMH.
The fall in AMH was greater after cyst removal (cystectomy) than after vaporization with bipolar energy or laser.
Using bipolar energy to control bleeding lowered AMH more than stitches or hemostatic agents.

items.title: Anti-Müllerian hormone as a marker of ovarian reserve and premature ovarian insufficiency in children and women with cancer: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 92 studies (over 9,000 patients) on anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), a blood marker of egg reserve, in girls and women who had cancer treatment. AMH dropped after chemotherapy or radiotherapy in most studies, sometimes to undetectable levels, and many studies saw at least partial recovery later. How much it fell and recovered depended on the treatment used, age and starting AMH. AMH is useful for showing the effect of treatment on the ovaries, but there is little data linking it to actual fertility or how long periods will last.
keyPoints: AMH was reduced or undetectable after chemotherapy or radiotherapy in 92% of studies (69 of 75).
About 79% of studies that followed patients over time (33 of 42) saw at least partial AMH recovery, but results varied widely by treatment type, age and starting AMH.
Some women with low or undetectable AMH still had periods or pregnancies, so AMH alone does not settle fertility.
More research is needed to link post-treatment AMH to fertility, length of reproductive life and time to premature ovarian insufficiency.

items.title: Does Anti-Müllerian hormone vary during a menstrual cycle? A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 11 studies of 733 women with regular cycles to see whether AMH, a blood test used to estimate egg reserve, changes during a natural menstrual cycle. AMH was slightly higher in the first half of the cycle (follicular phase) than in the second half (luteal phase), by about 11.5%. Levels around ovulation were not clearly different from either phase. The authors suggest the timing of the test in the cycle may matter when reading an AMH result.
keyPoints: AMH was significantly higher in the follicular phase than in the luteal phase, differing by about 11.5%.
AMH around ovulation did not differ significantly from the follicular or luteal phases.
The small shift may reflect how the ovaries respond to hormones during the cycle.
The authors suggest the cycle phase of the test should be considered when interpreting an AMH result.

items.title: Decline in anti-Müllerian hormone concentrations following radioactive iodine treatment in women with differentiated thyroid cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled four small studies of premenopausal women with thyroid cancer who had radioactive iodine treatment. Levels of anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), a blood marker of egg reserve, dropped by three months and stayed lower at 6 and 12 months. Another hormone, FSH, did not change. The review included only a small number of women (104 in the AMH analysis), and no data on antral follicle count were available.
keyPoints: AMH fell about 1.6 ng/ml at 3, 6 and 12 months after a single radioactive iodine dose compared with before treatment.
FSH levels showed no clear difference at 6 and 12 months after treatment.
Only four prospective studies were included, with 104 women in the AMH analysis.
No data were available for antral follicle count.

items.title: Dietary Modification for Reproductive Health in Women With Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 20 randomized trials with 1,113 women who have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) to see whether changing diet helps reproductive health. Diet was linked to more pregnancies, more ovulation, more regular periods and fewer miscarriages. It was also linked to lower AMH and androgen (male-type hormone) levels and less excess hair growth. Low-carbohydrate diets seemed best for fertility outcomes, and longer diets gave bigger improvements.
keyPoints: Diet changes were linked to higher clinical pregnancy, ovulation and menstrual regularity rates, and lower miscarriage rates in women with PCOS.
Diet was linked to lower AMH, free androgen index and total testosterone, and higher SHBG, a protein that binds sex hormones.
Low-carbohydrate diets did best for reproductive outcomes, while calorie restriction was key for lowering high androgen effects such as excess hair growth.
The longer the diet was followed, the greater the improvement; the authors suggest dietary advice be personalised for every woman with PCOS.

items.title: The Association between Vitamin D and Anti-Müllerian Hormone: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 24 studies (18 observational, 6 interventional) on whether vitamin D is linked to anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), a blood marker often used to estimate egg reserve. Studies that simply measured vitamin D and AMH gave very mixed results. When the supplement trials were combined, AMH went down after vitamin D in women with PCOS and went up in women who ovulate regularly without PCOS. The authors say the relationship is complex and larger randomized trials are needed.
keyPoints: Observational studies found very different results on whether vitamin D levels are linked to AMH, likely because the study groups differed.
In women with PCOS, AMH was lower after vitamin D supplementation (standardized mean difference -0.53).
In ovulatory women without PCOS, AMH was higher after vitamin D supplementation (standardized mean difference 0.49).
The authors conclude that large randomized trials are needed to understand this relationship and any benefit for female reproduction.

items.title: The effect of unilateral and bilateral laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis on Anti-Mullerian Hormone (AMH) level after 3 and 6 months: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Health and Quality of Life Outcomes
items.journal: Health and Quality of Life Outcomes
items.summary: This review pooled 19 studies to see how keyhole (laparoscopic) surgery for endometriosis affects AMH, a hormone blood test often used to estimate egg reserve. AMH levels went down 3 and 6 months after surgery, whether the operation was on one ovary or both. The drop looked larger after surgery on both ovaries. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: AMH levels fell 3 months and 6 months after laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis.
The fall was seen after surgery on one ovary and after surgery on both ovaries.
The authors concluded that this type of surgery has an effect on AMH levels.

items.title: Hysterectomy with opportunistic salpingectomy versus hysterectomy alone
items.summary: This review looked at whether removing the fallopian tubes during a hysterectomy for a non-cancer reason (to help prevent ovarian cancer) affects safety or ovarian reserve. It found seven small trials with 350 women, and the evidence was low to very low quality. No trials reported ovarian cancer rates, there were too few surgical complications to compare, and AMH (a marker of egg reserve) showed no clear difference, though the results were uncertain.
keyPoints: No trials reported whether removing the tubes during hysterectomy changed ovarian cancer rates.
There were too few surgery-related complications to tell whether the two approaches differ in safety.
AMH results were compatible with no difference or a small drop that the authors judged not clinically relevant (low-quality evidence).
Follow-up lasted only up to six months, and AMH can recover over several months, so longer-term effects, especially in younger women, are still unknown.

items.title: Anti-Müllerian hormone and assessment of ovarian reserve after ovarian toxic treatment: a systematic narrative review
items.summary: This review looked at studies that measured anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), a blood marker of egg reserve, after treatments that can harm the ovaries, such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Most studies found that AMH levels dropped compared with levels before treatment or in comparison groups, and the size of the drop depended on the type of treatment. The authors suggest AMH gives a more measurable picture of ovarian damage than menstrual patterns or FSH levels.
keyPoints: Most studies found AMH levels fell after ovary-harming treatments such as chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
How much AMH fell depended on the type of treatment.
AMH blood tests can measure ovarian damage in numbers, unlike menstrual changes or basal FSH, which are less precise.
AMH is becoming an important way to check egg reserve in people who want to keep fertility and natural hormone production.

items.title: Testing and interpreting measures of ovarian reserve: a committee opinion
items.summary: This committee opinion from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine looks at how tests of ovarian reserve (such as AMH) are used and understood. It explains that there is no agreed definition of 'decreased ovarian reserve', because the term can mean egg quality, egg quantity, or the chance of having a baby. The evidence on how well these tests work is limited, so results can be hard to interpret.
keyPoints: There is no widely accepted definition of decreased ovarian reserve.
The term can refer to three different things: egg quality, egg quantity, or reproductive potential.
Evidence on ovarian reserve tests is limited by small studies, differing study designs and a lack of validated outcome measures.

items.title: No. 469 Iron Deficiency and Iron Deficiency Anemia in Obstetrics and Gynaecology
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline explains how doctors should spot, treat and prevent low iron (iron deficiency) and anaemia caused by low iron in women, from first periods through to menopause. It pays special attention to pregnancy, periods and the time around surgery. It covers iron by mouth, iron given through a drip (intravenous iron) and ways to reduce heavy period bleeding. The abstract does not give the specific recommendations or the certainty ratings for each one.
keyPoints: Finding and treating low iron early is judged to be a cost-effective way to improve women's health and wellbeing.
Treating iron deficiency and iron deficiency anaemia can reduce the need for blood transfusion and its harms and costs.
Iron deficiency has a big effect on quality of life and work performance, which is weighed against the cost of iron infusions.
Reducing menstrual blood loss is highlighted as an important part of managing iron deficiency alongside oral and intravenous iron.

items.title: Recombinant erythropoietin for the treatment of iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy: A systematic review
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review looked at whether adding erythropoietin, a hormone that helps the body make red blood cells, to iron treatment helps pregnant women with iron deficiency anaemia that has not responded to usual care. Five small studies (about 207 women in total) were included, and the results could not be pooled because the studies differed too much. Three studies found that repeated erythropoietin doses plus iron raised haemoglobin more than iron alone, while two found no difference by day 28. The authors conclude that repeated doses plus iron may work better than iron alone for stubborn cases.
keyPoints: Five studies were included; all women got iron (by mouth or by drip), and half also got erythropoietin.
Three studies found repeated erythropoietin plus iron raised haemoglobin or haematocrit more than iron alone.
Two studies found no difference by day 28; one gave only a single dose, and in the other the erythropoietin group rose faster, with a bigger rise by day 11.
The authors say serial erythropoietin plus iron may be more effective than iron alone for refractory anaemia in pregnancy.

items.title: Effect of Nutrition Education During Pregnancy on Iron-Folic Acid Supplementation Compliance and Anemia in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 53 studies of 13,475 pregnant women in low- and middle-income countries. It looked at whether nutrition education during pregnancy helps women take their iron-folic acid supplements and lowers anaemia. Women who received nutrition education were more likely to take the supplements, had higher haemoglobin (the iron-carrying protein in blood), and had a lower risk of anaemia. Results varied quite a lot between studies.
keyPoints: Women who had nutrition education were about 2.8 times more likely to take their iron-folic acid supplements as advised.
Haemoglobin rose by an average of 0.88 g/dL in women who received nutrition education.
The risk of anaemia was 34% lower in the nutrition education group than in the comparison group.
The authors conclude that nutrition education programmes in pregnancy should be strengthened to help prevent anaemia.

items.title: The association between iron supplementation during pregnancy and the risk of childhood leukemia: a meta-analysis of case-control studies
items.summary: Researchers combined the results of 9 studies (over 4,000 children) to see whether taking iron supplements during pregnancy changes a child's chance of developing leukemia. They found no link between iron supplements in pregnancy and childhood leukemia overall, or for the two main types (AML and ALL). The studies were case-control studies, and the results varied somewhat between them, so the authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: No significant link was found between iron supplements in pregnancy and the overall risk of childhood leukemia (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.84-1.21).
No link was found for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) or acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) specifically.
The analysis combined 9 case-control studies with 2,327 cases and 1,954 controls.
The authors suggest further research on genetic and environmental factors.

items.title: Effect of prenatal multiple micronutrient supplementation compared with iron and folic acid supplementation on size at birth and subsequent growth through 24 mo of age: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 19 trials that compared multiple micronutrient supplements in pregnancy with the standard iron and folic acid tablets. Babies born to mothers who took the multiple micronutrient supplements were slightly longer and heavier at birth and grew a little better up to 6 months of age. These gains were no longer seen after 6 months. The differences in length and weight were small.
keyPoints: Compared with iron and folic acid alone, multiple micronutrient supplements led to greater length and weight from birth to 6 months, and larger head size from birth to 12 months.
At 3 months, babies whose mothers took multiple micronutrients had a lower risk of stunting (RR 0.86) and of being underweight (RR 0.86).
Risk of wasting at birth was lower with multiple micronutrients (RR 0.90).
Effects on length were not seen after 6 months, and some effects were bigger when supplements continued after birth and in places where low birthweight is more common.

items.title: Intravenous Iron Therapy Versus Blood Transfusion for Iron Deficiency Anemia: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review compared intravenous (IV) iron with blood transfusion for iron deficiency anaemia. It looked at 5 studies, including surgical patients, hip fracture patients and pregnant women. Blood transfusion raised haemoglobin faster in the first weeks, but IV iron tended to give a steadier and longer-lasting rise. The authors say the evidence is limited, with few trials and a high risk of bias, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Blood transfusion raised haemoglobin more quickly shortly after treatment started (less than 3 weeks).
At 3 weeks or later, 3 of 5 studies found haemoglobin was 0.7 to 1.4 g/dL higher with IV iron; the other 2 found similar levels.
IV iron seems to raise haemoglobin more gradually but with a longer-lasting effect.
Results are limited by the small number of trials and questionable study quality, and the studies covered mixed groups, not only pregnant women.

items.title: FIGO good practice recommendations on anemia in pregnancy, to reduce the incidence and impact of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH)
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This is a 2025 guideline from the international obstetrics federation FIGO on anaemia (low haemoglobin) in pregnancy. It reviewed the best available evidence and made recommendations on screening, diagnosis, prevention and treatment. It also highlights the link between anaemia and heavy bleeding after birth. Anaemia is still very common in pregnancy worldwide, especially in lower-income countries.
keyPoints: All pregnant women should be screened for anaemia at their booking visit and again at 28 weeks, using a full blood count.
Anaemia is diagnosed when haemoglobin is below 11 g/dL, in every trimester and after birth.
Routine iron and folic acid supplements, alone or as part of multiple micronutrient supplements, are recommended during pregnancy.
Anaemia is linked with postpartum haemorrhage (heavy bleeding after birth), so preventing it matters.

items.title: Impact of TMPRSS6 Genetic Variants on Maternal Iron Status in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at seven studies (about 1,094 pregnant women) that checked whether common variations in a gene called TMPRSS6 affect iron levels in pregnancy. Two gene variants were linked to lower iron in the blood and to higher risks of iron-deficiency anaemia, gestational diabetes and preeclampsia. The authors suggest gene testing might one day help tailor iron advice, but this is a suggestion and testing is not part of routine care.
keyPoints: Two TMPRSS6 variants (rs855791 T-allele and rs4820268 G-allele) were consistently linked to lower serum iron and lower transferrin saturation.
These variants were associated with higher risks of iron-deficiency anaemia, gestational diabetes and preeclampsia.
The gene affects a hormone called hepcidin, which can reduce how well the body absorbs iron from food.
The authors suggest TMPRSS6 genotyping in prenatal care could help personalise risk assessment and iron supplementation.

items.title: Intravenous iron versus blood transfusion for postpartum anemia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 20 trials (4,196 women) on treating anaemia after birth with iron given through a drip (IV iron), iron tablets or blood transfusion. Compared with iron tablets, IV iron reduced tiredness, raised haemoglobin and iron stores more, and caused fewer side effects overall. There was very little evidence on blood transfusion, so it could not be fairly compared with IV iron. The overall quality of the evidence was low to moderate.
keyPoints: IV iron reduced fatigue more than iron tablets after birth (standardised mean difference -0.40).
IV iron raised haemoglobin by about 0.54 g/dL and ferritin by about 58 mcg/L more than oral iron.
Total side effects were lower with IV iron than with oral iron (risk ratio 0.63).
Evidence on blood transfusion versus IV iron is very limited, so the better option is still unclear.

items.title: Pregnancy outcomes and iron status in β-thalassemia major and intermedia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 15 studies covering 684 pregnancies in women with two inherited blood conditions, beta-thalassemia major and intermedia, to estimate pregnancy risks. Pregnancy brought risks such as blood clots, pre-eclampsia and a high caesarean rate, and iron levels in the body rose because of extra blood transfusions and a pause in iron-removing treatment. The authors say this raises the risk of iron-related heart problems during pregnancy and labour, so heart monitoring and restarting iron-removing treatment after birth matter.
keyPoints: Blood clots occurred in 3.7% of pregnancies in thalassemia intermedia and 0.92% in thalassemia major, similar to before pregnancy.
Pre-eclampsia occurred in 11.3% and gestational diabetes in 3.9% of thalassemia major pregnancies; caesarean section rates were 83.9% in major and 67% in intermedia.

Blood transfusion needs rose in pregnancy (70% of intermedia pregnancies needed transfusions) and iron-removing treatment was stopped, so ferritin and liver iron rose and a heart MRI iron measure worsened.
The authors stress heart monitoring during pregnancy and restarting iron-removing (chelation) therapy after birth.

items.title: Age and sex-based impacts of maternal iron deficiency on offspring's cognitive function and anemia: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 14 studies, in people and in animals, to see whether low iron in mothers during pregnancy affects their children's thinking skills and risk of anaemia. Twelve studies found thinking and learning difficulties in children of iron-deficient mothers, usually milder in girls than boys. Two studies found more anaemia in these children, especially in boys and younger children. The authors conclude that looking after iron levels in pregnancy matters for children's health.
keyPoints: Twelve of fourteen studies found cognitive (thinking and learning) difficulties in children of mothers with iron deficiency.
Girls generally showed milder impairment than boys.
Two studies found more anaemia in children of iron-deficient mothers, particularly boys and younger children.
The authors say boys seem to be at higher risk of anaemia and cognitive problems in youth, while girls face higher risks in adulthood.

items.title: Screening and Supplementation for Iron Deficiency and Iron Deficiency Anemia During Pregnancy: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force
items.summary: This review pulled together 17 trials (about 24,000 pregnant women) that tested iron supplements during pregnancy. Taking iron lowered the chance of having iron deficiency or iron deficiency anaemia by the end of pregnancy. It did not clearly change other outcomes such as preterm birth, birth weight or gestational diabetes. The review found no studies on whether screening for iron deficiency during pregnancy helps or harms.
keyPoints: Iron supplements cut iron deficiency anaemia at term from about 20% to about 9% compared with placebo or no iron.
Iron supplements cut iron deficiency at term from about 70% to about 46%.
No clear differences were found in quality of life, gestational diabetes, bleeding, high blood pressure disorders, caesarean birth, preterm birth or baby size.
The main harm reported was short-lived stomach and gut side effects; no studies looked at screening.

items.title: Effect and safety of intravenous iron compared to oral iron for treatment of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 13 trials (3939 pregnant women) comparing iron given through a drip into a vein with iron tablets for iron-deficiency anaemia. Iron through a vein likely raises haemoglobin a little more and leaves fewer women anaemic before birth, and may do the same after birth. It likely makes little to no difference to blood transfusion or breastfeeding, and may make little difference to heavy bleeding after birth. Serious side effects were rare and poorly reported, so safety evidence is still limited.
keyPoints: Compared with tablets, iron through a vein likely raises haemoglobin slightly (about 0.5 g/dL) and likely reduces anaemia during pregnancy (moderate-certainty evidence).
After birth, haemoglobin may be slightly higher and anaemia may be less common with iron through a vein (low-certainty evidence).
There was likely little to no difference in blood transfusion or breastfeeding, and possibly little difference in postpartum haemorrhage (low-certainty evidence).
Side effects likely did not increase, but serious problems were rare and unevenly reported, so the effects on maternal death and intensive care admission are very uncertain.

items.title: Treatment for women with postpartum iron deficiency anaemia
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 33 trials with 4558 women to compare treatments for iron-low anaemia after childbirth: iron through a drip (intravenous), iron tablets, and blood transfusion. Intravenous iron probably eases tiredness slightly in the first weeks and causes much less constipation than tablets. Most of the evidence was low or very low quality, so many questions, such as rare serious reactions, are still uncertain.
keyPoints: Intravenous iron probably reduces tiredness slightly at 8 to 28 days compared with iron tablets, but probably makes little difference after four weeks.
Iron tablets probably cause a large increase in constipation compared with intravenous iron.

Intravenous iron may raise haemoglobin a little more than tablets, but results varied too much to combine; haemoglobin is an indirect measure, so decisions should rest on outcomes that matter to patients.
Effects on death, rare severe allergic reactions and breastfeeding are very uncertain or were not reported.

items.title: Micronutrients in Multiple Pregnancies-The Knowns and Unknowns: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at what is known about vitamin and mineral needs in women pregnant with twins or more. After searching three databases, the authors found 12 articles and one series of publications that met their criteria. They concluded that women with multiple pregnancies might be at risk of low vitamin D and low iron. For other nutrients, the evidence was mixed, scarce or missing.
keyPoints: Carrying more than one baby may raise nutrient needs and use up the mother's stores faster than in a single pregnancy.
Women with multiple pregnancies might be at risk of vitamin D and iron deficiency.
For other vitamins and minerals, the evidence is inconsistent, scarce or absent.
More studies are needed to know whether nutrition advice should change for twin or multiple pregnancies.

items.title: Effect of mass deworming with antihelminthics for soil-transmitted helminths during pregnancy
items.summary: This review pooled six trials of 7,873 pregnant women in lower- and middle-income countries to see whether worm-killing medicines (antihelminthics) given in pregnancy help. A single dose in the second trimester may lower anaemia by about 15% and reduce some intestinal worm infections, though the evidence is low certainty. The medicines probably make little or no difference to birthweight or low birthweight. The effect on preterm birth and baby deaths around birth is uncertain.
keyPoints: A single dose of antihelminthics in the second trimester may reduce maternal anaemia by about 15% (low-certainty evidence).
Treatment may reduce trichuris and ascaris worm infections, with moderate certainty for ascaris.
Treatment probably makes little or no difference to low birthweight or birthweight (moderate-certainty evidence).
The effect on preterm birth, perinatal mortality and hookworm is uncertain, and the benefits apply to places where worm infection in pregnancy is common.

items.title: Serum or plasma ferritin concentration as an index of iron deficiency and overload
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at how well a blood ferritin test can show whether someone has low iron stores (iron deficiency) or too much iron (iron overload). For people seeking medical care, a ferritin level below 30 micrograms per litre was fairly good at picking up iron deficiency and very good at ruling it in, though the evidence was low certainty. For iron overload, and for screening people with no symptoms, the evidence was too weak to draw firm conclusions.
keyPoints: At a cutoff of 30 micrograms/L, ferritin was reasonably sensitive (about 79%) and very specific (about 98%) for iron deficiency in people presenting for medical care, based on low-certainty evidence.
For iron overload, the evidence was very low certainty, and no studies included pregnant women, infants or children.
There is not enough evidence to know if ferritin works equally well for screening people who have no symptoms.
Ferritin can be raised by inflammation and infection, which can affect how the result is read.

items.title: Iron preparations for women of reproductive age with iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy (FRIDA): a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomised trials of iron treatments for pregnant women with iron deficiency anaemia. After 4 weeks, iron given through a vein (intravenous iron sucrose) raised haemoglobin and iron stores (ferritin) more than iron tablets (ferrous sulfate). Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose also raised haemoglobin more than tablets, but this rested on one trial. Many of the trials had a medium or high risk of bias, and there was not enough evidence to judge the other iron types.
keyPoints: Intravenous iron sucrose raised haemoglobin by about 7 g/L more than oral ferrous sulfate after 4 weeks.
Intravenous iron sucrose also raised serum ferritin, a measure of iron stores, more than oral ferrous sulfate.
Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose raised haemoglobin more than ferrous sulfate, based on one trial.
Oral iron commonly caused nausea, vomiting and bowel changes, while intravenous iron caused less of these but could cause local pain, skin irritation and, rarely, allergic reactions.

items.title: Risk of Infection Associated With Administration of Intravenous Iron: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review combined 154 randomised trials (about 33,000 people) that compared iron given through a drip (intravenous iron) with iron tablets or no iron. Intravenous iron raised haemoglobin more and made blood transfusions less likely, but it was also linked to a higher risk of infection. The authors rate the evidence for the infection risk as moderate certainty and call for better studies to weigh up the benefits and risks. The trials covered many patient groups, not only pregnancy.
keyPoints: Intravenous iron was linked to a higher risk of infection than oral iron or no iron (risk ratio 1.17, moderate certainty evidence).
It raised haemoglobin by about 0.57 g/dL and reduced the need for red blood cell transfusion.
There was no evidence of an effect on death or length of hospital stay.
The authors say well-designed studies with standard definitions of infection are needed to balance the risk against the benefits.

items.title: Iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy in Nigeria-A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at six studies from Nigeria, published between 1968 and 2017, on iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy. All six found that many pregnant women had iron deficiency anaemia. The review also listed factors linked to higher risk and to not taking iron supplements as advised. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is, and it covers only a small number of studies.
keyPoints: All six studies reported a high rate of iron deficiency anaemia among pregnant women in Nigeria.
Risk factors for iron deficiency anaemia included having had several births, being in the third trimester, and low socioeconomic status.
Factors linked to not taking routine iron therapy included poor use of antenatal services, low education, living far from a health facility, single or teenage pregnancy, older age, and rural living.
The authors suggest more education on family planning and antenatal care, better access to health facilities, and economic support for women.

items.title: Education of family members to support weaning to solids and nutrition in later infancy in term-born infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 21 trials (over 14,000 babies) that taught families about starting solid foods and compared this with usual care. Babies whose families received nutrition education probably grew slightly more by 12 months, but the gains were small and may not matter much in practice. It is unclear whether these early gains affect growth or development later in childhood.
keyPoints: Nutrition education about weaning probably gave small increases in weight-for-age and height-for-age scores by 12 months (moderate-certainty evidence).
Results at 18 months were mixed, and the two studies on brain development at 12 to 24 months gave conflicting results.
The authors say education may reduce the risk of undernutrition, but the evidence is low to moderate certainty because of study limitations and differences between trials.
No trials looked at long-term brain development, so longer-term benefits remain unknown.

items.title: Nutritional contributors to maternal anemia in Indonesia: Chronic energy deficiency and micronutrients
items.source: Asia Pacific Journal of Clinical Nutrition
items.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Clinical Nutrition
items.summary: This review pooled results from 10 studies of about 4,000 pregnant women in Indonesia to see which factors are linked to anaemia. Women with chronic energy deficiency (not getting enough food energy over a long time) had the highest risk. Having had more pregnancies, lower education and limited health knowledge were also linked to anaemia. Older age and not taking enough iron supplements were not clearly linked in these studies.
keyPoints: Chronic energy deficiency was most strongly linked to anaemia in pregnancy (about 3.8 times the odds).
Having more previous births, lower education and limited health knowledge were also linked to higher odds of anaemia.
Older age and inadequate iron supplementation were not clearly associated with anaemia.
The authors suggest paying attention to long-term undernutrition, not only single-nutrient approaches, when trying to prevent anaemia in pregnancy.

items.title: Treatment of Iron Deficiency Anemia in Pregnancy with Intravenous versus Oral Iron: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 11 randomised trials comparing iron given through a drip (intravenous) with iron tablets for pregnant women with iron-deficiency anaemia. Women who had intravenous iron were more likely to reach their target haemoglobin level, and their haemoglobin was higher after 4 weeks. They also had fewer side effects than women taking iron by mouth.
keyPoints: Women given intravenous iron were more than twice as likely to reach their target haemoglobin level as those taking oral iron.
After 4 weeks, haemoglobin was on average 0.84 g/dL higher with intravenous iron.
Adverse reactions were less common with intravenous iron than with oral iron.
The results stayed the same when the authors tested how much differences between studies affected them.

items.title: Oral vs intravenous iron therapy for postpartum anemia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 15 randomized trials comparing iron tablets with iron given through a vein (IV) for anaemia after birth. Six weeks after delivery, women who had IV iron had haemoglobin levels about 1 g/dL higher than those who took tablets. IV iron caused more skin flushing but much less constipation and indigestion. The authors say IV iron can be considered a viable treatment for postpartum iron deficiency anaemia.
keyPoints: At 6 weeks postpartum, haemoglobin was about 0.9 g/dL higher with IV iron than with oral iron (based on 4 studies).
Ferritin (iron stores) and early haemoglobin levels at weeks 1 to 3 were also higher with IV iron.
IV iron was linked to more skin flushing but less constipation and indigestion than oral iron.
Anaphylaxis was reported in 0.6% of women receiving IV iron, and the authors describe its safety profile as reassuring.

items.title: A systematic literature review of the relation between iron status/anemia in pregnancy and offspring neurodevelopment
items.summary: This review pulled together 27 studies (19 observational, 8 trials) on whether low iron or anaemia in pregnancy affects a child's brain development. There is some evidence that low iron in pregnancy, possibly especially in the third trimester, may be linked to poorer child development. Most studies measured haemoglobin, so the results may not apply directly to iron deficiency. Taking iron supplements in pregnancy did not seem to change children's neurodevelopment.
keyPoints: Iron status in pregnancy was linked to children's behaviour, thinking skills and school achievement, but the direction of the link for behaviour was unclear.
Conclusions on cognition and school achievement rested on only a few studies, and little evidence was found for links with motor development.
Most studies used haemoglobin, so applying the results to iron deficiency should be done with caution.
Iron supplementation during pregnancy did not seem to influence offspring neurodevelopment, and no conclusions could be reached beyond early childhood.

items.title: Fortification of rice with vitamins and minerals for addressing micronutrient malnutrition
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether adding iron and other vitamins and minerals to rice helps people who are short of these nutrients. It pooled 17 studies, mostly in children, with only two studies in non-pregnant, non-lactating women. Fortified rice may lower the risk of iron deficiency and may raise haemoglobin, but it may make little or no difference to anaemia, and the authors say the evidence is low quality. Evidence on side effects is limited.
keyPoints: Iron-fortified rice may reduce the risk of iron deficiency (low-certainty evidence).
It may make little or no difference to the risk of anaemia, and the overall conclusion on haemoglobin is uncertain.
Rice fortified with vitamin A or folic acid may make little or no difference to vitamin A deficiency or folate levels.
There is limited evidence on harms; one study reported slightly more hookworm infection.

items.title: Effectiveness of programme approaches to improve the coverage of maternal nutrition interventions in South Asia
items.summary: This review looked at nine studies from Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Pakistan on how to get more pregnant women to receive and take nutrition supplements such as iron and folic acid and calcium. It found that barriers exist at the level of the woman, her household and the health service. Programmes worked best when they tackled several of these barriers at once.
keyPoints: Barriers to getting and taking iron, folic acid and calcium supplements in pregnancy occur at the individual, household and health service levels.
Effective programmes addressed barriers at several levels at the same time.
Common features of effective programmes included community-based delivery, involving family members as well as pregnant women, and free supplements.
Effective programmes also used local research to design their approach and improved the training, supervision and motivation of front-line health workers.

items.title: Lactoferrin or ferrous salts for iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy: A meta-analysis of randomized trials
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled four randomised trials (600 pregnant women) comparing daily oral lactoferrin with daily oral ferrous sulphate iron tablets for iron deficiency anaemia. After four weeks, haemoglobin rose slightly more with lactoferrin overall, but in mild anaemia the difference was not significant, and the moderate-anaemia benefit came from just one trial. Women taking lactoferrin had fewer stomach and gut side effects, and no differences were found in outcomes such as preterm birth or birthweight. The authors concluded lactoferrin works at least as well as iron tablets and could be the preferred choice.
keyPoints: Haemoglobin after 4 weeks was higher with lactoferrin than with ferrous sulphate overall (mean difference 0.77).
In mild anaemia there was no significant difference between the two treatments; a benefit for lactoferrin was seen in moderate anaemia, based on one trial of 228 women.
Lactoferrin caused significantly fewer gastrointestinal side effects.
No significant differences were found in preterm birth, low birthweight, neonatal death or mean birthweight.

items.title: Vitamin supplementation for preventing miscarriage
items.summary: This large Cochrane review pooled 40 trials, covering over 276,000 women, to see whether taking vitamins before or in early pregnancy prevents miscarriage. Vitamin C, vitamin A, folic acid and multivitamins did not reduce miscarriage or total pregnancy loss. Women who took multivitamins plus iron and folic acid had a slightly lower risk of stillbirth than women who took iron and folic acid alone. There was not enough evidence to judge different vitamin combinations.
keyPoints: Taking vitamin supplements before or in early pregnancy did not prevent miscarriage.
Vitamin C (with vitamin E), vitamin A and folic acid showed no clear difference in miscarriage or total pregnancy loss.
Multivitamins plus iron and folic acid were linked to a lower risk of stillbirth than iron and folic acid alone (high-quality evidence).
There is not enough evidence to compare different combinations of vitamins for miscarriage.

items.title: Effect of administration of antihelminthics for soil-transmitted helminths during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether giving deworming medicine (antihelminthics) to pregnant women after the first trimester helps with anaemia and pregnancy outcomes. It combined four trials with 4265 women. A single dose in the second trimester made no clear difference to anaemia later in pregnancy, or to low birthweight, preterm birth or deaths around the time of birth. The reviewers say there is not yet enough evidence to recommend it, and that larger, better-designed trials are needed.
keyPoints: A single dose of deworming medicine in the second trimester was not linked to less anaemia in the third trimester (low quality evidence).
No clear effect was found on low birthweight, preterm birth or perinatal death (moderate quality evidence).
Results were similar when both groups also received iron supplements.
The evidence is not enough to recommend deworming treatment for pregnant women after the first trimester.

items.title: Intermittent oral iron supplementation during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether taking iron two or three times a week works as well as taking it every day during pregnancy. It combined 21 trials with 5,490 women. Babies had similar outcomes either way, and women taking iron less often reported fewer side effects. The quality of the evidence was low or very low, so the findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: No clear differences between intermittent (two or three times a week) and daily iron for low birthweight, birthweight, premature birth or newborn death.
Women taking iron intermittently had fewer side effects and were less likely to have high haemoglobin levels in mid and late pregnancy.
Mild anaemia near term was more likely with intermittent iron in some of the analyses, though anaemia at term overall showed no clear difference.
The authors say intermittent iron may be a feasible alternative for pregnant women who are not anaemic and have adequate antenatal care.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation in primary allergy prevention: Systematic review of randomized and non-randomized studies
items.summary: This review looked at whether taking vitamin D during pregnancy or breastfeeding, or giving it to babies, helps prevent allergies such as eczema, hay fever, asthma and food allergy in children. Only five studies qualified, and the quality of the evidence was very low. The studies suggest vitamin D may not lower the risk of these allergies, but the overall picture is uncertain.
keyPoints: Only one randomised trial and four non-randomised studies were eligible for the review.
Very low certainty evidence suggests vitamin D supplements may not reduce the risk of eczema, allergic rhinitis (hay fever), asthma or wheezing, or food allergy.
No studies were found on preventing allergies by giving vitamin D to children.
The authors conclude that information is limited and the effect of vitamin D on allergy prevention remains uncertain.

items.title: The Risk of Adverse Pregnancy Outcome After First Trimester Exposure to H1 Antihistamines: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from 37 studies on women who took H1 antihistamines (the type used for allergies, hay fever, hives and sometimes pregnancy nausea) in the first trimester. Babies of women who used them did not have more major birth defects than babies of women who did not. There was also no link to miscarriage, premature birth, stillbirth or low birth weight.
keyPoints: Taking H1 antihistamines in the first trimester was not linked to more major birth defects in cohort studies or case-control studies.
No increased risk was found for miscarriage, premature birth, stillbirth or low birth weight.
The authors concluded these medicines are not associated with an increased risk of major malformation or other adverse fetal outcomes.
The review pooled a large number of studies, with no sign of publication bias.

items.title: Physical Activity: An Accessible Prescription for Perinatal Mental Health
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian practice guideline looks at physical activity as a way to support mental health during pregnancy and after birth. It reports that moderate-to-vigorous physical activity is safe and low-cost, and can lower both the risk and the severity of mood and anxiety problems, with benefits similar to talking therapy. Fewer than 15% of women meet activity recommendations, often because of safety worries, little guidance and social barriers. Care providers are encouraged to offer clear advice and use a screening questionnaire to help women take part safely.
keyPoints: Perinatal mood and anxiety disorders affect up to 20% of patients and can lead to poorer outcomes for mothers and infants.
Moderate-to-vigorous physical activity is safe and cost-effective, and reduces the risk and severity of these disorders.
The mental health benefits of this activity are comparable to psychotherapy.
Fewer than 15% of perinatal individuals meet activity recommendations because of safety concerns, limited guidance and social barriers.

items.title: Digital Health Interventions and Psychosocial Outcomes in Women With Breast Cancer: Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 15 studies of apps, websites, text messages and other digital tools used to support women with breast cancer during or soon after treatment. Some tools gave modest, short-term improvements in quality of life, but results for anxiety, depression and self-confidence were mixed. The reviewers rated the evidence as low or very low certainty, so no strong conclusions can be drawn yet.
keyPoints: Digital tools favored quality of life in 8 of 15 studies, with modest and short-term benefits.
Anxiety, depression or distress improved in only 5 of 13 studies that measured them.
Benefits appeared more often when tools had active therapeutic parts or professional support, but this came from indirect comparisons.
Certainty of evidence was low for quality of life and emotional outcomes, and very low for self-efficacy.

items.title: Vasomotor Symptoms and Their Association with Depressive and Anxiety Symptoms in Peri- and Postmenopausal Women: A Systematic Review of Observational Studies
items.summary: This review pooled 12 observational studies of about 9,900 women to see whether hot flushes and night sweats go together with low mood and anxiety around menopause. Women with more troublesome hot flushes and night sweats had roughly 1.7 to 3 times the odds of depressive symptoms. The link with anxiety pointed the same way but rested on far fewer, weaker studies. The evidence is low quality for depression and very low for anxiety, and it cannot show that one causes the other.
keyPoints: Greater hot flush and night sweat burden was linked to higher odds of depressive symptoms, with adjusted odds ratios from 1.67 to 2.99.
The link with anxiety looked similar in direction but was weaker; only 5 of 12 studies looked at anxiety separately and none gave an adjusted estimate.
Poor sleep and fatigue may partly explain the connection, though some studies suggested a direct or two-way link.

Most studies were cross-sectional, so the review could not say whether hot flushes cause mood symptoms or the reverse; the authors suggest women with bothersome hot flushes may benefit from being asked about mood and anxiety.

items.title: Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Perinatal Mood, Anxiety, and Related Disorders: Guide de pratique 2024 du Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments pour le traitement des troubles de l'humeur, des troubles anxieux et des troubles connexes périnatals
items.source: Canadian Journal of Psychiatry. Revue Canadienne de Psychiatrie
items.journal: Canadian Journal of Psychiatry. Revue Canadienne de Psychiatrie
items.summary: This is a 2024 Canadian guideline on how to care for mood, anxiety and related problems during pregnancy and after birth. It was written with people who have lived experience of these conditions, along with specialist clinicians, and is based on reviews of the best available research. It covers medicines and non-medicine options, and how safe each is in the perinatal period. The abstract describes the guideline's scope rather than listing specific treatment findings.
keyPoints: The guideline covers depression, bipolar, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive and post-traumatic stress disorders in pregnancy and postpartum.
It sets out both medication and non-medication options, including lifestyle, psychosocial and psychological approaches, brain stimulation (neuromodulation) and complementary treatments.
Recommendations are ranked by lines of treatment, balancing how well they work with safety, tolerability and practicality.
It also covers finding cases early, how care is organised, high-risk situations and the mental health of fathers or co-parents.

items.title: Prevalence of Depression and Anxiety Among Adults With Chronic Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This large review pooled results from 376 studies covering about 347,000 adults with long-term (chronic) pain, 70% of them women. Around 4 in 10 had clinically significant depression, and around 4 in 10 had clinically significant anxiety. Rates were highest in women, younger people and people with nociplastic pain (pain without tissue damage, such as fibromyalgia). The authors say routine screening and fair access to specialist care are needed.
keyPoints: About 39% of adults with chronic pain had clinically significant depression and about 40% had clinically significant anxiety.
Women, younger people and people with nociplastic pain were most likely to have depression and anxiety.
Rates were highest in people with fibromyalgia (about 54% for depression and 55% for anxiety) and lowest in arthritis conditions.
The authors call for routine screening in clinical settings and equitable access to specialty care.

items.title: Psychotherapies for Generalized Anxiety Disorder in Adults: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
items.summary: This review pooled 65 trials of talking therapies for adults with generalized anxiety disorder, with about 70% of participants being women. Cognitive behavior therapy (CBT), newer 'third-wave' versions of CBT, and relaxation therapy all reduced anxiety symptoms more than usual care in the short term. Only CBT was still clearly better when people were checked 3 to 12 months after treatment ended. People were no more likely to drop out of these therapies than out of usual care.
keyPoints: CBT and third-wave CBTs reduced anxiety symptoms compared with usual care, with moderate certainty of evidence.
Relaxation therapy also helped in the short term, but the evidence was low certainty and the benefit disappeared when high-risk-of-bias studies were left out.
Only CBT stayed significantly more effective than usual care 3 to 12 months after treatment finished.
The authors suggest CBT may be the first-line therapy for generalized anxiety disorder, with third-wave CBTs and relaxation therapy as other options.

items.title: French Society for Biological Psychiatry and Neuropsychopharmacology and French-speaking Marcé Society guidelines for the management of mood disorders in women before, during, and after pregnancy
items.source: French Society for Biological Psychiatry and Neuropsychopharmacology and French-speaking Marcé Society
items.organisation: French Society for Biological Psychiatry and Neuropsychopharmacology and French-speaking Marcé Society
items.summary: Two French psychiatry societies wrote expert guidelines on using psychiatric medicines for women with depression or bipolar disorder before, during and after pregnancy. They combined scientific evidence with a survey of 48 psychiatrists who have expertise in mood disorders or pregnancy-related mental health. The experts recommend treating mood symptoms during pregnancy and keeping up medication, even when someone feels well and stable.
keyPoints: Experts recommend treating mood symptoms during pregnancy rather than leaving them untreated.
They recommend keeping up a medication treatment during pregnancy, even in women who are stable.
First-choice medicines during pregnancy are only those with no known risk of causing birth defects.
While breastfeeding, first-choice medicines are only those with no evidence of harm to nursing babies.

items.title: Association Between Mental Health and Reproductive System Disorders in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 31 studies to look at how often mental health conditions and reproductive health conditions occur together in women. Women with a reproductive system disorder had about 2 to 3 times the odds of also having a psychiatric disorder. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and long-lasting pelvic pain were each linked to higher odds of depression and anxiety. The authors note that most other condition pairings have been studied very little, so many links are still unknown.
keyPoints: Women with a reproductive system disorder had roughly 2 to 3 times the odds of also having a psychiatric disorder.
PCOS was linked to higher odds of depression and of anxiety.
Chronic pelvic pain was linked to higher odds of both depression and anxiety.
Few studies looked at other reproductive conditions or at whether mental health conditions come first, so the evidence is limited.

items.title: Management of Anxiety and Depression in Adult Survivors of Cancer: ASCO Guideline Update
items.summary: The American Society of Clinical Oncology updated its guideline on managing anxiety and depression in adults who have survived cancer, based on a review of 17 systematic reviews and 44 randomized trials. Talking therapies, education and other psychosocial approaches helped with depression and anxiety, while the evidence for medicines was mixed. The guideline suggests matching the treatment to how severe symptoms are, starting with the least resource-intensive option that works.
keyPoints: All people treated for cancer should be offered education about depression and anxiety.

For moderate depression or anxiety, options include cognitive behavior therapy, behavioral activation, structured physical activity, and mindfulness-based stress reduction (for depression) or acceptance and commitment therapy (for anxiety).
For severe symptoms, therapies such as CBT, behavioral activation, cognitive therapy, mindfulness-based stress reduction or interpersonal therapy are recommended.
Medicines may be offered if first-line therapy is unavailable, has not helped, or the person prefers medication or has responded well to it before.

items.title: Listening Visits for maternal depression: a meta-analysis
items.summary: Listening Visits are a gentle, non-directive counselling approach delivered by nurses to mothers with depression after birth. This review pooled six trials with 703 mothers to see how well they work compared with usual care or other control conditions. Overall the visits showed a moderate benefit for depression symptoms. The authors say this supports offering them as an early step in care for mothers with mild to moderately severe symptoms.
keyPoints: Six trials with 703 mothers were combined; the overall effect on depression was moderate (0.66), though results varied a lot between studies.
After removing outlier studies, four similar studies with 651 mothers showed a smaller but still moderate effect (0.43).
The authors support Listening Visits as a first-line option in a stepped care approach for mild to moderately severe depression symptoms.
Nurses and other non-mental-health specialists can deliver the visits, which makes them easier to offer.

items.title: Implementation and Effectiveness of Nonspecialist-Delivered Interventions for Perinatal Mental Health in High-Income Countries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 46 trials (about 18,000 people) of counselling for depression and anxiety around pregnancy and after birth in high-income countries, delivered by people without formal counselling training, such as nurses and midwives. Compared with usual care or other comparison groups, the counselling was linked to lower depression and anxiety scores, with the biggest effects seen in trials that treated women who already had symptoms. Results differed a lot from trial to trial, and many trials left out important details about how the counselling was delivered. The authors conclude that non-specialist providers may be effective but more research is needed.
keyPoints: Counselling delivered by non-specialist providers was linked to lower depressive symptoms and lower anxiety scores than comparison groups.
Interventions that treated women with existing symptoms showed benefit for both depression and anxiety.
Most counselling was given by nurses and midwives, mainly face to face; only 2 trials used online delivery.
Results varied widely between trials, and many studies did not report details such as supervision and fidelity.

items.title: Screening for Anxiety in Adolescent and Adult Women: A Recommendation From the Women's Preventive Services Initiative
items.summary: The Women's Preventive Services Initiative, a group of women's health organisations and patient representatives, recommends that clinicians screen for anxiety in girls and women aged 13 and older who have not already been diagnosed with an anxiety disorder. This includes pregnant and postpartum women. No studies directly tested whether screening itself improves outcomes, but the screening questionnaires were moderately to highly accurate, and both talking therapies and certain medicines helped symptoms. A positive screen is a first step, and further assessment is needed to confirm a diagnosis.
keyPoints: Screening for anxiety is recommended for women and girls aged 13 or older without a current anxiety diagnosis, including during pregnancy and after birth.
No studies directly looked at the overall benefits or harms of screening itself.
Twenty-seven screening tools were moderately to highly accurate at spotting anxiety.
Psychological therapies and SSRI or SNRI medicines improved symptoms and reduced relapse; the best screening interval is unknown, and a positive screen needs further evaluation.

items.title: Recommendations of the Polish Psychiatric Association for treatment of affective disorders in women of childbearing age. Part III: Approach to pregnancy loss and unsuccessful in vitro treatment of infertility
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from the Polish Psychiatric Association on caring for women after pregnancy loss or unsuccessful IVF treatment. Pregnancy loss and the death of a baby around birth are described as among the most stressful life events, and they raise the risk of depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress. Repeated IVF failures can cause similar emotional effects. The guideline sets out how health staff should support women, and gives basic advice on talking therapy and medicines.
keyPoints: Pregnancy loss and perinatal death carry an increased risk of depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorders.
Care should be individual and based on respect, empathy and expertise.

Recommended support includes full information from the doctor about the woman's health, possible causes and next steps, access to a psychological consultation at any time, and clear information on legal rights such as health insurance and labour law.
Repeated IVF failures can bring emotional effects like those after miscarriage, and prolonged frustration may lead to depressive symptoms and more anxiety.

items.title: Best practice for community-based management of postnatal depression in developing countries: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 12 studies on community-based care for postnatal depression in developing countries. It found that talking therapies based on cognitive behavioral therapy, infant stimulation and problem solving can improve outcomes for mothers. Putting these programs into practice can be hard, because they rely on trained health workers who need support and close supervision.
keyPoints: Cognitive behavioral therapy, infant stimulation and problem-solving approaches can improve outcomes for postnatal depression.
Challenges include dependence on specific types of health workers and the motivation and capacity of those delivering the care.
Programs need a high level of supervision and systems to make sure they are delivered as intended.
The authors say more research is needed to fill remaining gaps.

items.title: First-Trimester Pregnancy Exposure to Venlafaxine or Duloxetine and Risk of Major Congenital Malformations: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pooled results from eight studies of babies whose mothers took the antidepressants venlafaxine or duloxetine in the first three months of pregnancy. For venlafaxine, there was no sign of a higher risk of major birth defects. There was much less data on duloxetine, but it also did not point to a meaningful increase in risk.
keyPoints: Venlafaxine in the first trimester was not linked to a higher risk of major birth defects (3,186 exposed babies, 107 with major malformations).
Duloxetine data were much smaller (668 exposed babies, 16 with major malformations) but did not suggest an important increase in risk.
These antidepressants (SNRIs) have far less research behind them than SSRIs, so the duloxetine findings are less certain.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the association between unintended pregnancy and perinatal depression
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to see whether unintended pregnancy is linked to depression around the time of pregnancy and birth. About 21% of women with an unintended pregnancy had depression. The link held across different types of unintended pregnancy, timing of measurement, study designs and settings, although the studies varied quite a lot from one to another.
keyPoints: About 21% of women with an unintended pregnancy had perinatal depression.
The chance of perinatal depression was about two times higher in women with unintended pregnancy.
The link appeared across different study types, settings and timing of measurement, though the studies differed considerably.
The authors suggest perinatal care could ask about pregnancy intention and depression, and link family planning with mental health services.

items.title: Psychological and Interpersonal Dimensions of Sexual Function and Dysfunction
items.summary: This systematic review looked at research from 2010 onwards on how mind, relationship and life factors affect sexual function in women and men. It found that things like depression, anxiety, stress, past trauma and relationship dynamics can all contribute to sexual difficulties. Psychological treatment was strongly supported for low desire and orgasm difficulties in women. The authors recommend checking for these factors as a routine part of care.
keyPoints: Depression, anxiety, stress, substance use and past trauma can contribute to sexual difficulties and should be assessed at the first evaluation.
Sexual function is linked between partners, so a problem for one person often affects the other's function or satisfaction.
There is strong support for psychological treatment for sexual desire and orgasm difficulties in women.
Menopausal status has its own effect on reported changes in sex life and difficulties with intercourse.

items.title: Fetal death: Expert consensus of the French College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
items.source: French College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.organisation: French College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
items.summary: The French College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists issued an expert consensus on fetal death, meaning loss of a baby's heartbeat after 14 weeks of pregnancy. For women in the general population, it does not recommend aspirin to prevent fetal death. Low-dose aspirin is recommended only after a previous fetal death caused by vascular (blood vessel or placenta) problems, to reduce risks to the baby around birth.
keyPoints: Aspirin is not recommended to prevent fetal death in the general population.
After a previous fetal death due to vascular problems, low-dose aspirin is recommended to reduce perinatal illness and complications.
For other previous fetal deaths, the evidence is not enough to recommend aspirin.
If the cause of a fetal death is identified, care should be adjusted case by case.

items.title: Risk Factors of Subchorionic Hematoma Under Assisted Reproductive Technology
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research
items.summary: This review pulled together 50 studies on subchorionic hematoma (a collection of blood between the pregnancy sac and the womb wall) in pregnancies conceived with assisted reproductive technology such as IVF. It found that several things were linked to a higher chance of this bleed, including high hormone levels, embryo transfer, polycystic ovary syndrome, fluid-filled tubes, and using low-dose aspirin during pregnancy. The authors say more high-quality studies are needed to understand why these links exist.
keyPoints: IVF and its steps, such as embryo transfer and hormone treatment, were described as a central risk factor for subchorionic hematoma.
High estrogen and progesterone levels, low blastocyst grading, PCOS and tubal hydrocele were linked to a higher risk.
Using low-dose aspirin during pregnancy was linked to a higher risk of subchorionic hematoma.
The authors call for better-quality studies to explain the mechanisms and improve outcomes for people having ART.

items.title: Low-molecular-weight heparin for the prevention of preeclampsia in high-risk pregnancies without thrombophilia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 randomised trials (1,758 women) to see whether low-molecular-weight heparin, a blood-thinning injection, helps prevent preeclampsia in high-risk pregnancies. It found that heparin lowered the chance of preeclampsia, but the benefit was only clear when it was used together with low-dose aspirin. The combination also reduced preterm birth and poor baby growth, and it worked better than aspirin alone. It made no difference to placental abruption. The women studied did not have a clotting disorder (thrombophilia).
keyPoints: Low-molecular-weight heparin reduced the risk of preeclampsia in high-risk women without thrombophilia (relative risk 0.67).
The benefit was only significant in studies where heparin was added to low-dose aspirin.
Heparin plus low-dose aspirin also lowered the risk of preterm birth and fetal growth restriction.
The combination was reported as better than low-dose aspirin alone, with no effect on placental abruption.

items.title: Impact of low-dose aspirin exposure on obstetrical outcomes: a meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Psychosomatic Obstetrics and Gynaecology
items.journal: Journal of Psychosomatic Obstetrics and Gynaecology
items.summary: This review pooled 47 placebo-controlled trials (59,124 pregnant women) to see how low-dose aspirin affects birth outcomes. Overall, aspirin slightly lowered the risks of small-for-gestational-age babies, preterm birth, low birth weight and NICU admission, but it raised the risk of placental abruption. The benefits were clearest in women at high risk of preeclampsia, where placental abruption was not increased. In healthy, low-risk women, aspirin did not clearly improve outcomes and was linked to a higher chance of placental abruption.
keyPoints: Across all trials, aspirin lowered the risk of small-for-gestational-age babies, preterm birth, low birth weight and NICU admission, but increased the risk of placental abruption.
In women at high risk of preeclampsia, aspirin reduced small-for-gestational-age babies, preterm birth and perinatal death, without raising placental abruption risk.
In healthy pregnant women, aspirin did not significantly improve outcomes and increased the risk of placental abruption.
In high-risk women, doses of 100 mg or more and starting at or before 20 weeks gave clearer benefits; the authors say more research is needed on the best dose and timing.

items.title: Low-molecular-weight heparin in the prevention of unexplained recurrent miscarriage: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled six randomized trials (1016 women) to see whether low-molecular-weight heparin, a blood-thinning injection, helps women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage have a live birth. It was used on its own or together with low-dose aspirin, starting early in pregnancy. The heparin did not increase the chance of a live birth, and this held across the different subgroups looked at. The authors rate the evidence as moderate quality.
keyPoints: Low-molecular-weight heparin did not raise live birth rates in women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage (pooled odds ratio 1.01).
No significant benefit was seen whether heparin was used alone or with low-dose aspirin, or in any other subgroup.
The review included 6 randomized trials with 1016 women in total.
The authors describe the evidence as moderate quality.

items.title: Effect of IVIG therapy on pregnant women with unexplained recurrent spontaneous abortion: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 trials with 751 women who had repeated miscarriages with no known cause, to see whether intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) helps more babies to be born alive. Overall, IVIG did not raise live birth rates compared with other treatments or placebo. For women who tested positive for antiphospholipid antibodies, a combination of low-molecular-weight heparin plus low-dose aspirin gave a higher live birth rate than IVIG.
keyPoints: IVIG did not significantly increase live birth rates compared with the non-IVIG groups overall (OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.75).
Compared with placebo (multivitamins, albumin or saline), IVIG showed a possible benefit that was not statistically significant (OR 1.43, 95% CI 0.99 to 2.07).
In women positive for antiphospholipid antibodies, heparin plus low-dose aspirin led to more live births than IVIG.
The review included 12 studies and 751 participants in total.

items.title: Guidelines-similarities and dissimilarities: a systematic review of international clinical practice guidelines for pregnancy hypertension
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review compared 17 international guidelines on high blood pressure in pregnancy and found that 15 were clinically useful. The guidelines agree on many things, including using aspirin to help prevent preeclampsia, treating severe high blood pressure, and using magnesium sulfate to prevent seizures in severe preeclampsia. They differ on how to spot who is at risk early in pregnancy, how aspirin should be given, and whether adding calcium helps.
keyPoints: Guidelines consistently recommend aspirin to help prevent preeclampsia.

Guidelines agree on treating severe high blood pressure in pregnancy with labetalol, nifedipine or hydralazine, and on using magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prevention and treatment in severe preeclampsia.

Guidelines disagree on how to identify preeclampsia risk early and how aspirin should be given; tools combining clinical risk, blood tests and ultrasound can substantially reduce preterm preeclampsia.
Guidelines differ on whether calcium should be added to aspirin, especially for women with low calcium intake and higher risk.

items.title: Management of primary headaches during pregnancy, postpartum, and breastfeeding: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at which medicines are used to prevent or treat migraine and other primary headaches during pregnancy, after birth and while breastfeeding. Most of the 16 studies had a high risk of bias, and the evidence for safety was low to moderate. Low-dose aspirin, triptans, calcium channel blockers and antihistamines may not be linked to harm for the baby, while acetaminophen (paracetamol) and several other medicines may be linked to possible effects on the baby. No evidence was found on how well preventive medicines work, and there was too little evidence on non-drug treatments.
keyPoints: Low-dose aspirin and triptans may not be associated with harm to the baby, based on low-to-moderate certainty evidence (the aspirin evidence was indirect).
Acetaminophen (paracetamol), prednisolone, indomethacin, ondansetron, antipsychotics and intravenous magnesium may be associated with adverse effects in the baby or child.
For prevention, calcium channel blockers and antihistamines may not be linked to harm, but the review found no evidence on how well any preventive medicine works.
For treating migraine or tension headache, metoclopramide plus diphenhydramine may work better than codeine (one trial, low certainty); there was too little evidence on non-drug treatments.

items.title: Aspirin Prophylaxis During Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 35 placebo-controlled trials, covering 46,568 pregnant women, to look at low-dose aspirin taken to prevent pre-eclampsia. Aspirin lowered the risk of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, perinatal death and poor growth of the baby in the womb, and it did not raise bleeding risk. The benefits were clearest when aspirin was started before 20 weeks of pregnancy. The effect of different aspirin doses was unclear and needs more study.
keyPoints: Low-dose aspirin lowered the risk of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, perinatal death and slow growth of the baby in the womb, without raising bleeding risk.
