Starting aspirin before 20 weeks of pregnancy gave a clearly lower pre-eclampsia risk (RR 0.76) and better birth weight and gestational age at delivery.
Aspirin did not reduce the risk of gestational hypertension (high blood pressure in pregnancy).
The effect of aspirin dose on outcomes was not significant and needs further study.

items.title: Impact of low-dose aspirin on adverse perinatal outcome: meta-analysis and meta-regression
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 40 randomized trials (nearly 35,000 pregnant women) to see how low-dose aspirin affects babies' health around birth, beyond its known effect on pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and low birth weight. Starting aspirin by 16 weeks was linked to fewer deaths around the time of birth, and no extra harms were seen. Starting after 16 weeks was linked to fewer low Apgar scores and less bleeding in the baby's brain, but also a possible small rise in placental abruption that did not reach statistical significance.
keyPoints: Starting low-dose aspirin at or before 16 weeks was linked to about half the risk of perinatal death (RR 0.47), with a number needed to treat of 92. This effect was seen only with doses of 100 mg or more a day.
Starting after 16 weeks was linked to fewer low 5-minute Apgar scores and less periventricular hemorrhage (bleeding in the baby's brain).

After 16 weeks there was also a trend toward more placental abruption (RR 1.20), which was not statistically significant. No significant increase in adverse events was seen when aspirin was started by 16 weeks.
Aspirin had no effect on the way women gave birth, whenever it was started.

items.title: Does low-dose aspirin initiated before 11 weeks' gestation reduce the rate of preeclampsia?
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 8 randomized trials with 1,426 women to see whether starting low-dose aspirin before 11 weeks of pregnancy lowers the risk of preeclampsia. The women studied were at higher risk of pregnancy problems. Early aspirin did not clearly reduce preeclampsia, high blood pressure in pregnancy, or poor baby growth. It might lower the chance of preterm birth, but the authors say larger trials are needed to confirm this.
keyPoints: Starting low-dose aspirin before 11 weeks did not significantly reduce preeclampsia, gestational hypertension, or any high blood pressure disorder of pregnancy.
It did not change the risk of fetal growth restriction (poor growth of the baby in the womb).
Early aspirin might reduce preterm birth (before 37 weeks), though this result was less steady in the checks the authors ran.
The authors conclude that larger randomized trials are needed to confirm the findings.

items.title: Aspirin for the prevention of preterm and term preeclampsia: systematic review and metaanalysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 16 trials with almost 19,000 pregnant women to see whether aspirin lowers the risk of preeclampsia, a pregnancy condition linked to high blood pressure. Aspirin reduced the risk of preterm preeclampsia (preeclampsia leading to early delivery), but not preeclampsia that develops at term. The benefit was seen only when aspirin was started at 16 weeks of pregnancy or earlier and taken at 100 mg or more a day. Half of the trials were of good quality and half were of poor or uncertain quality, but the benefit was also seen in the high-quality studies.
keyPoints: Aspirin was linked to a lower risk of preterm preeclampsia (relative risk 0.62), but had no significant effect on term preeclampsia.
The reduction in preterm preeclampsia was found only when aspirin was started at or before 16 weeks of pregnancy at a daily dose of 100 mg or more.
In that early, higher-dose group the risk of preterm preeclampsia was about two-thirds lower (relative risk 0.33).
Results were mixed across trials overall, and 8 of the 16 trials were of poor or uncertain quality.

items.title: Care prior to and during subsequent pregnancies following stillbirth for improving outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at treatments given before or during a pregnancy that follows a stillbirth, to see if any improve outcomes. It found ten small trials covering only 222 women who had a previous stillbirth, testing medicines such as low-dose aspirin and blood thinners (heparin). The evidence was low or very low quality, so it is not clear whether any of these treatments help prevent another stillbirth. The authors say there is not enough evidence to guide care and that larger, well-designed trials are urgently needed.
keyPoints: No clear evidence that low-dose aspirin or heparin reduces stillbirth, neonatal death or preterm birth in a pregnancy after stillbirth.
Some birthweight differences were seen with low-dose aspirin, but these were very unreliable because the trials were so small.
No trials tested emotional or psychological support for parents, which the authors call an urgent priority.
The authors conclude there is insufficient evidence to guide care and call for larger, well-designed trials.

items.title: The role of aspirin dose on the prevention of preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 45 randomized trials with about 20,900 pregnant women to see how the daily aspirin dose affects preeclampsia and poor baby growth. When aspirin was started at 16 weeks or earlier, it lowered the risk of preeclampsia, severe preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction, and higher doses (within the 50-150 mg range studied) worked better. When it was started after 16 weeks, the benefit was small or absent.
keyPoints: Aspirin started at 16 weeks or earlier cut the risk of preeclampsia by about 43% (relative risk 0.57), severe preeclampsia by about 53%, and fetal growth restriction by about 44%.
With early starts, higher aspirin doses were linked to a bigger reduction in all three outcomes.
Aspirin started after 16 weeks had a modest effect on preeclampsia and no clear effect on severe preeclampsia or fetal growth restriction, with no dose-response pattern.
The authors say women at high risk should be identified early in pregnancy.

items.title: Aspirin for in vitro fertilisation
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 13 randomised trials with 2,653 women having assisted reproduction treatment such as IVF. It looked at whether taking aspirin (80 to 100 mg a day) improves the chance of a live birth. Women who took aspirin had about the same rates of live birth and pregnancy as women who took a placebo or nothing. The evidence was moderate to very low quality, and it cannot rule out possible harms.
keyPoints: Live birth rates were similar with aspirin and with placebo or no treatment (moderate-quality evidence).
Clinical pregnancy rates were also similar between the two groups (moderate-quality evidence).
Miscarriage, multiple pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy and vaginal bleeding showed no clear difference, but the evidence was low to very low quality.
The authors found no evidence supporting routine aspirin use in a general IVF population, and the evidence does not exclude possible side effects.

items.title: Low-Dose Aspirin for Preventing Preeclampsia and Its Complications: A Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 29 randomized trials to see whether low-dose aspirin helps prevent preeclampsia (a pregnancy condition involving high blood pressure) in high-risk pregnancies. Aspirin lowered the chances of preeclampsia, severe preeclampsia, preterm birth and slow growth of the baby in the womb. Starting before 16 weeks of pregnancy worked better than starting later. Aspirin slightly raised the chance of placental abruption, but not other major complications.
keyPoints: Low-dose aspirin reduced preeclampsia (odds ratio 0.71) and severe preeclampsia (odds ratio 0.37) in high-risk pregnancies.
It also reduced preterm birth and intrauterine growth restriction (slow growth of the baby in the womb).
Starting aspirin before 16 weeks of pregnancy was more effective for preeclampsia and growth restriction than starting later.
Aspirin increased placental abruption (odds ratio 1.35) but not other major complications; the authors concluded there was no major safety risk to mothers or babies.

items.title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus in Pregnancy
items.summary: This review looked at 65 studies to see how lupus (SLE) and pregnancy affect each other. The authors concluded that a pregnancy with lupus cannot be thought of as risk-free, even though lupus treatment has improved. They say close, team-based monitoring before, during and after pregnancy is needed to keep both mother and baby as healthy as possible. They also note that more research is needed to understand why complications happen.
keyPoints: Pregnancy in women with lupus cannot be considered without risk.
Care from several specialists and regular monitoring before, during and after pregnancy is needed.
Better treatments and new biomarkers could lead to care tailored to each woman's lupus and pregnancy needs.
The reasons lupus raises the chance of complications are still not fully understood.

items.title: Autoimmune diseases and adverse pregnancy outcomes: an umbrella review
items.summary: This review pulled together 32 earlier reviews, covering 709 studies, to look at how autoimmune conditions relate to problems in pregnancy. Women with several autoimmune conditions, such as lupus, type 1 diabetes, Sjögren's syndrome, systemic sclerosis, inflammatory bowel disease and coeliac disease, had a higher risk of problems like miscarriage, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and stillbirth. The authors conclude that better care before, during and after pregnancy is needed for women with these conditions.
keyPoints: Miscarriage risk was higher in women with Sjögren's syndrome and lupus (SLE).
Pre-eclampsia and preterm birth were more common in women with type 1 diabetes and lupus.
Stillbirth risk was higher in women with type 1 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease and coeliac disease.
Growth problems in the baby were more likely with systemic sclerosis and coeliac disease, and low birth weight with lupus and systemic sclerosis.

items.title: Global epidemiology of systemic lupus erythematosus: a comprehensive systematic analysis and modelling study
items.summary: This review pooled results from 112 studies to estimate how common lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE) is around the world. It found that lupus is much more common in women than in men, with about 79 women per 100,000 living with it compared with about 9 men per 100,000. Rates differ by age and region, and data are missing for roughly 80% of countries, so the estimates carry a lot of uncertainty.
keyPoints: Worldwide, about 5 in 100,000 people are newly diagnosed with lupus each year, and about 3.4 million people are living with it.
Women are affected far more often than men: about 78.7 vs 9.3 per 100,000 people.
Lupus appears more frequently in high-income countries, and rates vary by region and age group.
No lupus data exist for 79.8% of countries, so the true picture is still unclear.

items.title: Belimumab for systemic lupus erythematosus
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled six trials (2,917 adults, mostly women) of belimumab, a biologic medicine for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). At the approved dose, more people on belimumab had improved disease activity at about 52 weeks than people on placebo, and more were able to cut their steroid dose by half or more. Evidence on harms was less clear, with no obvious difference in serious side effects or serious infections, but some of that evidence was low or moderate quality. The review did not look at pregnancy, and longer-term data are still needed.
keyPoints: At the approved 10 mg/kg dose, belimumab was probably linked to a meaningful improvement in lupus disease activity compared with placebo (high-certainty evidence).
More people on belimumab were able to reduce their glucocorticoid (steroid) dose by at least half (high-certainty evidence).
Quality of life probably changed little or not at all between belimumab and placebo (moderate-certainty evidence).
Serious side effects, serious infections and deaths may not differ from placebo, but evidence on harms is inconclusive and mostly low to moderate certainty.

items.title: Interventions for cutaneous disease in systemic lupus erythematosus
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 61 trials of treatments for skin problems in people with systemic lupus erythematosus (lupus). Hydroxychloroquine probably reduces skin flares compared with a dummy treatment, and chloroquine and methotrexate may help skin clear. Most of the evidence is low or moderate quality and based on small studies, so results should be read with caution. Methotrexate is known to carry a risk of harm to a baby during pregnancy.
keyPoints: Hydroxychloroquine probably reduces clinical flares at 6 months compared with placebo (moderate-quality evidence).
Chloroquine and methotrexate may improve skin clearance compared with placebo, but the evidence is low quality and from small studies.
Hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine and methotrexate all have known side effects, including stomach upset, liver problems and eye damage (retinopathy) with the two quinine-type drugs.
Methotrexate can harm a developing baby (teratogenicity) during pregnancy.

items.title: Tai Chi for rheumatoid arthritis
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether Tai Chi helps people with rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune condition that causes painful, stiff joints. It combined seven small trials with 345 people, mostly women, with programs lasting 8 to 12 weeks. It is uncertain whether Tai Chi improves joint pain, disease activity or everyday function, because the evidence was very low quality. People in Tai Chi groups were less likely to drop out of the studies, and few minor side effects like joint and muscle soreness or cramps were described.
keyPoints: It is uncertain whether Tai Chi improves pain, disease activity or physical function in rheumatoid arthritis; all of these results were very low-quality evidence.
People doing Tai Chi were less likely to withdraw from the studies than those in comparison groups (low-quality evidence).
Side effects were not clearly reported, but a few minor ones such as joint and muscle soreness and cramps were mentioned in two studies.
The review found no data on whether Tai Chi affects joint damage seen on X-ray, and the studies did not look at pregnancy.

items.title: Celecoxib for rheumatoid arthritis
items.summary: This review pooled eight trials (almost 4,000 adults, most of them women) of celecoxib, an anti-inflammatory painkiller, for rheumatoid arthritis. Compared with placebo, celecoxib probably improved symptoms and pain. Compared with older anti-inflammatory drugs, it gave only a small symptom benefit but caused fewer stomach and gut ulcers. The evidence was moderate to low quality, and results on serious side effects and heart risks were uncertain. The review did not study pregnancy.
keyPoints: Celecoxib improved symptoms and pain more than placebo in rheumatoid arthritis (moderate to low quality evidence).
Compared with older NSAIDs, celecoxib gave a small symptom improvement that may not matter much in practice.
Celecoxib caused fewer gastroduodenal ulcers than older NSAIDs (moderate quality evidence).
Results for serious side effects and cardiovascular events were uncertain, and regulators warn of a possible heart risk.

items.title: Sudden deaths in infancy and pesticide exposure: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 17 studies to see whether pesticide exposure is linked to sudden unexpected deaths in infancy, including SIDS. The results were mixed. Some studies linked parents' work-related pesticide exposure to SIDS, while studies of pesticides at home gave conflicting results. The authors concluded that no clear link can be established and that more research is needed.
keyPoints: Three studies found a link between SIDS and a parent's job-related pesticide exposure.
Studies of pesticide use at home gave conflicting results, and half found no link.
Pesticides were found in the brain tissue of some infants who died of SIDS, but many of these studies were old and may not reflect current exposure.
The authors say a clear link between pesticides and sudden infant death cannot be established and call for further studies.

items.title: Mother-Infant Bed-sharing Is Associated with Increased Breastfeeding: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This systematic review looked at 24 studies on whether mothers who share a bed with their baby breastfeed more. Most of the studies found that bed-sharing was linked to more breastfeeding. The link was not seen in African American women in the U.S., who had lower breastfeeding rates overall. The authors suggest that health care providers could teach women how to bed-share without hazards for those who plan to do it.
keyPoints: Most of the 24 studies found a positive link between bed-sharing and breastfeeding (73% of longitudinal and 69% of cross-sectional studies).
Many postpartum women share a bed with their infants.
No such link was seen in U.S. African American women, who had lower breastfeeding rates overall.
The authors suggest educating women about bed-sharing without hazards, which may be one way to support breastfeeding.

items.title: Can behavioural interventions delivered using digital technologies influence infant sleep? A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 4 randomised trials of sleep advice for babies delivered through digital tools such as apps or online programmes. Babies in the digital programmes had their longest unbroken sleep stretch lengthened by about three-quarters of an hour on average, but total night-time sleep did not clearly change. The studies were small in number and all had a high risk of bias, so the evidence is low certainty and larger, better trials are needed.
keyPoints: Digital sleep programmes were linked to a longer longest continuous sleep period (about 0.76 hours more on average).
There was no clear effect on total night-time sleep.
Digital programmes may also improve a child's morning mood and how well the child sleeps, based on exploratory outcomes.
Only 4 trials were found, all at high risk of bias, so the certainty of the findings is low.

items.title: Infant sleep interventions with sleep measurements using actigraphy: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 11 studies that tested ways to help babies sleep better and measured sleep with a wrist-worn movement sensor (actigraphy). Three studies used extinction-based behavioural methods and eight used parent education programs. The programs generally helped both babies' and parents' sleep, with fairly consistent effects on night wakings and time taken to fall asleep. Effects on parents' emotional wellbeing were mixed, and only two of the 11 studies had a low risk of bias.
keyPoints: Infant sleep programs had positive effects on sleep for both babies and parents.
Effects on how often babies woke at night and how long they took to fall asleep were fairly consistent.
Effects on parents' emotional and social wellbeing were inconsistent across studies.
Only two of the 11 studies had a low risk of bias, and better standardised methods are needed for measuring infant sleep.

items.title: Inconsistency Between Pictures on Baby Diaper Packaging in Europe and Safe Infant Sleep Recommendations
items.summary: Researchers looked at 631 types of baby diaper packaging sold in 11 European countries to see whether pictures of sleeping babies matched safe sleep advice. About half of the packages showed a sleeping baby, and around 8 in 10 of those pictures broke at least one safe sleep recommendation. The authors say manufacturers and lawmakers should act so parents are not shown misleading images that could lead to unsafe sleep habits.
keyPoints: 49% of the diaper packages showed a picture of a sleeping baby.
79% of those pictures were inconsistent with at least one safe sleep recommendation.
About 45% showed a baby not sleeping on their back, and about 51% showed pillows, blankets or other soft items.
About 10% showed a baby sharing a sleep surface with another person.

items.title: Group-based sleep trajectories in children and adolescents: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 36 good or fair quality studies that tracked how sleep changes from birth to age 18. Most found three or four common sleep patterns, and sleep length in young children became more similar to each other over the first six years. Lower family income, a mother's depression and night feeding were the most often reported links to different sleep patterns. Children with persistently short sleep were linked to higher chances of problems such as obesity and mood or behaviour difficulties, but the authors say cause and effect cannot be shown and study quality could be better.
keyPoints: Most studies found three or four distinct sleep patterns over childhood, and sleep duration patterns grew more alike in the first six years of life.
Lower socioeconomic status, maternal depression and night feeding were the most commonly reported links to sleep patterns.
Persistent adverse patterns, such as ongoing short sleep, were linked to higher risks of obesity, weaker immunity, neurological problems and emotional or behaviour symptoms.
The authors note that cause and effect cannot be concluded and that study quality could be improved.

items.title: Maternal depressive symptoms and mother-infant cosleeping (including room sharing and bedsharing): a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 14 studies to see whether a mother's low mood after birth is linked to where her baby sleeps, such as in the same room or the same bed. The results were mixed: some studies found no link, one found bed-sharing was linked to lower low mood, and others found co-sleeping linked to higher low mood. Because the studies were designed and measured things so differently, the review could not find a consistent relationship.
keyPoints: Five of 14 studies found no link between a baby's sleep location and mothers' depressive symptoms.
One study found bed-sharing was linked to fewer depressive symptoms, while five found co-sleeping linked to more.
Where the link was found, it was often unclear whether low mood led to co-sleeping or the other way round.
Differences in how studies were run and defined co-sleeping meant no consistent pattern could be found.

items.title: Prenatal and postnatal factors associated with sudden infant death syndrome: an umbrella review of meta-analyses
items.summary: Researchers pulled together eight earlier reviews (152 studies in total) to see which factors are linked to sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Smoking or drug exposure during pregnancy, smoking around the baby, bed sharing, and a baby's head being covered by bedclothes were linked to higher SIDS risk. Sleeping on the back and pacifier use were linked to lower risk. The strength of the evidence varied a lot, and the authors say more research is needed where it was weak.
keyPoints: Prenatal drug exposure, prenatal opioid exposure and prenatal maternal smoking were linked to higher SIDS risk, with evidence rated from suggestive to highly suggestive.
Bed sharing and postnatal maternal smoking were linked to higher risk, but the evidence for these was rated weak.
Babies found with their heads covered by bedclothes after sleep had a much higher risk, with evidence rated suggestive.
Sleeping on the back (supine) and pacifier use were linked to lower risk; the evidence was rated suggestive for back sleeping and weak for pacifiers.

items.title: Effect of biotic supplementation on infant sleep and settling behaviours: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 23 randomised trials to see whether probiotics, prebiotics or similar supplements change how well full-term babies (0-12 months) sleep. Probiotics did not make babies sleep longer in the first 4 weeks. By week 5, babies given a placebo slept about 35 minutes longer than those given probiotics, a borderline result. There were too few studies to say anything firm about prebiotics, synbiotics or other types.
keyPoints: Probiotics did not increase infant sleep duration in the first 4 weeks of supplementation.
In week 5, babies on placebo slept about 35 minutes longer than babies on probiotics (borderline significance).
Too few studies were available to judge prebiotics, synbiotics and post-biotics, or effects over the full first year.
The authors call for future research on the full range of sleep behaviours, feeding type and the gut microbiome.

items.title: Exploring paternal postpartum depression and contributing factors in Ethiopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled five Ethiopian studies with 2,055 fathers to see how common depression is after a baby is born and what raises the risk. About 1 in 5 fathers (20.86%) had postpartum depression. Risk was higher with low family income, substance use, poor social support, unplanned pregnancy and a baby with sleep problems. The studies differed a lot from one another, so the exact figures should be read with care.
keyPoints: About 21% of fathers in the Ethiopian studies had postpartum depression.
Infant sleep problems were linked to higher odds of depression in fathers (OR 4.78).
Poor social support, unplanned pregnancy, low income and substance use were also linked to paternal depression.
The authors call for routine depression screening for fathers, better social support and education on managing infant sleep.

items.title: The effects of Yakson touch and gentle human touch on preterm infants: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomised trials of two gentle touch methods, Yakson touch and gentle human touch, in babies born early. Babies who received these touch methods had lower pain scores during and after medical procedures than babies who did not. The review also reports that both methods improved infant sleep and behaviour, while heart rate and oxygen levels did not change. The authors describe the methods as easy, safe and drug-free.
keyPoints: Pain scores on the Neonatal Infant Pain Scale were lower in preterm babies given Yakson touch or gentle human touch, both during and after procedures.
Both touch methods improved infant sleep and behaviour.
Heart rate and oxygen saturation in preterm babies were not affected by either method.
The authors describe the touch methods as non-drug, easy and safe for use during painful procedures.

items.title: Periodic change of body position under phototherapy in term and preterm neonates with hyperbilirubinaemia
items.summary: This review looked at whether regularly turning a newborn to a different position (for example from back to tummy) during light treatment for jaundice helps the jaundice clear faster. It found five small studies of 343 babies, and turning them seemed to make little or no difference to how long treatment lasted or how fast bilirubin fell. The evidence is low quality, so firm conclusions cannot be drawn. None of the studies looked at sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
keyPoints: Periodic change of body position under phototherapy may make little or no difference to how long treatment lasts.
It may also make little or no difference to how fast bilirubin levels fall in the first 24 hours, though only one study measured this.
The evidence is low certainty because the studies were small and at high risk of bias.
None of the studies reported on SIDS, exchange transfusions or bilirubin-related brain damage.

items.title: The Effect of High and Low Ambient Temperature on Infant Health: A Systematic Review
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: Researchers reviewed 26 studies on how hot and cold weather affects babies under one year old. Hot weather was linked to a higher risk of infant death, hospital admissions and hand, foot and mouth disease. Cold weather was linked to infant deaths and breathing illnesses in several studies. Findings on temperature and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) were inconsistent, and evidence was limited for some groups and for lower-income countries.
keyPoints: Higher temperatures were linked to more infant deaths, hospital admissions and hand, foot and mouth disease.
Several studies found cold temperatures were linked to infant deaths and episodes of respiratory (breathing) illness.
Results on temperature and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) were inconsistent.
Only five studies were from low- or middle-income countries, and evidence on specific groups and infections was limited.

items.title: Cultural variation in factors associated with sudden infant death during sleep
items.summary: This review looked at 218 research articles from Asian and Western countries to see which factors are linked to sudden unexpected death in infancy (SUDI). In both regions, the most commonly discussed sleep-related factors were sleep position, bed-sharing and sharing a room with the baby. Some factors, such as overheating, swaddling or bedding, place of death and smoking, were discussed differently between the two regions. The authors suggest that health professionals should be aware of cultural differences in how babies sleep.
keyPoints: Sleep position (44%), bed-sharing (22%) and rooming-in (16.5%) were the three most discussed sleep-related factors for SUDI in both Asian and Western articles.
Sleep position, male sex, bed-sharing and genetics were among the top 10 factors named in both regions.
Overheating, swaddling or bedding standards, place of death and smoking were discussed differently between the two regions.
Asian countries had far fewer articles on SUDI, and smoking received little attention there, so the authors suggest adding smoking-cessation support to prevention plans.

items.title: Association between auditory system pathology and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS): a systematic review
items.summary: Researchers reviewed 12 earlier studies to see whether problems in the hearing system of the brain and ear are linked to sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Studies using hearing tests on infants gave inconsistent results. Four of five studies that looked at the brainstem after death found more hearing-related abnormalities in babies who died of SIDS. The quality of the evidence was very low, so no clear link can be confirmed yet.
keyPoints: No clear link was found between hearing system problems and SIDS.
Hearing tests on infants (otoacoustic emissions and auditory brainstem response) gave inconsistent results across studies.
Four of five brainstem studies found more auditory abnormalities in SIDS cases than in controls, which may point to an association.
The quality of evidence was very low, and larger, better studies are needed.

items.title: A systematic review of the burden and risk factors of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) in Africa
items.summary: This review looked at 32 studies to understand how common sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) is in Africa and which risk factors are involved. Many infants shared a bed with their parents and many were put to sleep on their tummies, both known SIDS risk factors. Reported SIDS rates were high in some countries, and Africa may have the highest SIDS rate in the world. Most studies came from South Africa, so the findings may not apply to the whole continent.
keyPoints: Bedsharing with parents was very common, ranging from 60% to 91.8% of infants across studies.
Putting babies to sleep on their tummies (prone sleeping) was frequent, ranging from 26.7% to 63.8%.
SIDS rates ranged from 0.2 per 1000 live births in Zimbabwe to 3.7 per 1000 in South Africa.
Most studies were from South Africa, so better research from other African countries is urgently needed.

items.title: Interventions to Improve Safer Sleep Practices in Families With Children Considered to Be at Increased Risk for Sudden Unexpected Death in Infancy: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at programs designed to help families with babies at higher risk of sudden unexpected death in infancy (SUDI) follow safer sleep practices. It found 23 intervention studies sorted into five types, such as providing a safe sleep space with education, home visiting, peer educators and digital health messages. Some programs are moving from simply giving information to a two-way, longer-term, personalized approach, which may be an improvement. The authors say stronger evidence is still needed to show which approaches actually work.
keyPoints: Safer sleep advice has cut infant deaths worldwide, but progress has slowed, and most deaths now occur in families facing social and economic hardship.
Five types of intervention were found: sleep space plus education, intensive home visiting, peer educators, general awareness campaigns and targeted digital messages.
Newer programs use personalized, relationship-based support rather than only giving out information.
More robust evidence is needed to know how well these interventions reduce risk.

items.title: Sleep during Infancy and Associations with Childhood Body Composition: A Systematic Review and Narrative Synthesis
items.summary: This review pulled together 19 studies that followed babies from their first two years of life into childhood, to see whether how long babies sleep is linked to body weight and body fat later on. The results were mixed. The evidence for longer infant sleep being linked to a healthier body composition in childhood was inconsistent, and the quality of the studies varied from strong to weak.
keyPoints: 19 studies were included; most measured sleep duration, and only 2 looked at sleep problems.
Study quality was rated strong for 5 studies, moderate for 5 and weak for 9.
Evidence that longer infant sleep leads to a healthier body composition in childhood was inconsistent.

items.title: The influence of bed-sharing on infant physiology, breastfeeding and behaviour: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 59 studies to understand how sharing a bed with a baby affects the baby's body, breastfeeding and behaviour. Babies who shared a bed had more waking moments, warmer bed temperatures and breastfed for longer than babies in their own cot. They also showed differences in sleep patterns, heart and breathing control, and stress hormone responses. The authors say many of these differences depend on the situation and on parents' views and culture, and that more research is needed to understand the risks and possible benefits.
keyPoints: Bed-sharing babies had more behavioural arousals, warmer in-bed temperatures and longer breastfeeding than cot-sleeping babies.
Differences were also found in infant sleep patterns, heart and breathing control, and cortisol (stress hormone) responses.
Many differences depend on context, parents' views and cultural values.
Risk arises if a baby cannot respond properly to their sleep environment; more studies are needed to clarify infant risk and any benefits of a safer setup.

items.title: Non-pharmacological interventions for improving postpartum maternal sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 15 studies of non-drug approaches, such as massage and exercise, to help mothers sleep better after birth. Overall these approaches improved how well mothers said they slept, with massage and exercise showing the biggest effects. They also slightly improved babies' night-time sleep, but did not clearly change mothers' depression symptoms. The authors say more research is needed on how long the benefits last, using objective sleep measures.
keyPoints: Non-drug sleep interventions improved mothers' self-reported sleep after birth.
Massage and exercise had the largest effects on maternal sleep quality.
Interventions overall showed a small positive effect on babies' night-time sleep.
No clear effect on maternal depression was found, and more research is needed on how long benefits last.

items.title: Dietary modifications for infantile colic
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether changing a baby's diet, or a breastfeeding mother's diet, can ease colic in babies under four months old. It found 15 small trials of 1121 babies in total, testing things like low-allergen maternal diets, special formulas and herbal extracts. The evidence was very low quality and the trials had serious flaws, so the reviewers could not recommend any particular dietary change.
keyPoints: 15 randomised trials (1121 babies aged 2 to 16 weeks) were included, but all were small and at high risk of bias.
Some single studies reported benefits, such as a low-allergen diet for the breastfeeding mother or a herbal extract, but results for hydrolysed formulas were inconsistent.
The reviewers rated the overall evidence as very low quality and could not recommend any dietary intervention for colic.
Where adverse effects were reported, none were found, but better-designed studies are still needed.

items.title: Infant pacifiers for reduction in risk of sudden infant death syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for randomised controlled trials testing whether giving babies a pacifier (dummy) during sleep lowers the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). It found no eligible trials. Earlier observational studies had linked pacifier use with fewer SIDS cases, but the review could not confirm or rule out that benefit from trial evidence.
keyPoints: No randomised controlled trials were found on pacifiers and SIDS risk.
The review authors could not support or refute pacifier use for preventing SIDS.
Studies since the early 1990s have linked pacifier use with fewer SIDS cases, but those were not randomised trials.

items.title: Duration of Breastfeeding and Risk of SIDS: An Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled data from 8 studies, covering 2,267 babies who died of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) and 6,837 comparison babies, to see how long breastfeeding needs to last to be linked with lower SIDS risk. Breastfeeding for less than 2 months was not linked with lower risk, but breastfeeding for 2 months or more was, and longer breastfeeding was linked with more protection. The protection was seen even when breastfeeding was not exclusive. The authors note the studies collected slightly different information, so not every other factor could be accounted for.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding for less than 2 months was not linked with a lower risk of SIDS.
Any breastfeeding for 2 months or more was linked with about half the risk of SIDS, and longer duration was linked with more protection (over 6 months: about a 64% lower chance of SIDS).
Breastfeeding did not need to be exclusive to be linked with this protection.
The studies varied slightly in what information they collected, which limited how fully other factors could be accounted for.

items.title: Brief Resolved Unexplained Events (Formerly Apparent Life-Threatening Events) and Evaluation of Lower-Risk Infants
items.summary: This American Academy of Pediatrics guideline is about babies under 1 year who have a sudden, brief scary episode that then fully passes, such as turning blue or pale, breathing oddly, going floppy or stiff, or not responding normally. The old name for this was ALTE; the guideline replaces it with 'brief resolved unexplained event' (BRUE). A BRUE is only diagnosed when a careful history and physical exam find no explanation. Babies are sorted into lower-risk and higher-risk groups, and the guideline gives evidence-based advice on evaluating and managing the lower-risk group, aiming to avoid unnecessary and costly tests and treatments.
keyPoints: The term ALTE is replaced by 'brief resolved unexplained event' (BRUE) for infants younger than 1 year.
A BRUE involves a sudden, brief episode that has resolved, with one or more of: blue or pale colour, absent or irregular breathing, a marked change in muscle tone, or altered responsiveness.
It is diagnosed only when no explanation is found after an appropriate history and physical exam.
Infants are grouped as lower-risk (with evidence-based recommendations) or higher-risk (needing further investigation, but no recommendations given).

items.title: Swaddling and the Risk of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome: A Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled data from 4 observational studies to look at whether swaddling a baby for sleep is linked to sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Across all four studies the link was not clear-cut, but removing one study gave a small increased risk. The risk was much higher when swaddled babies were placed on their front or side, and possibly higher in babies older than 6 months. The authors note the evidence is limited and hard to interpret.
keyPoints: Advice to avoid front or side sleeping applies especially to swaddled babies.
Swaddled babies placed on their front had the highest risk, followed by side sleeping, then back sleeping.
Limited evidence suggested the risk rises with age, with about twice the risk in swaddled babies over 6 months old.
The authors suggest considering an age after which swaddling should be discouraged.

items.title: Effects of Pilates on the quality of life of pregnant women during pregnancy: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at ten studies with 499 pregnant women to see how Pilates affects quality of life during pregnancy. Women who did Pilates reported better quality of life, sleep and movement in some studies, and less lower back and pelvic pain in most of them. A few studies also found lower anxiety and depression. The authors conclude Pilates appears helpful, with exercise supervised by nurses or midwives.
keyPoints: Lower back and pelvic pain was reduced in the Pilates groups in eight of the ten studies.
Two studies found better quality of life, sleep quality and physical mobility with Pilates.
Two studies found less anxiety and one found lower depression scores in women who practised Pilates.
The authors conclude Pilates benefits pregnant women, with physical activity supervised by nurses and midwives.

items.title: The effect of pelvic belts to manage low back and pelvic pain during pregnancy a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled seven studies on pelvic belts for low back and pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy. Belts gave a modest drop in pain and little change in disability. The quality of the evidence was low to very low, so no firm recommendations can be made yet.
keyPoints: Across 6 studies, pain scores fell by about 20 points on average with a pelvic belt, but the range of results was wide and included no change.
Across 5 studies, disability improved only slightly, and the range of results also included no change.
The evidence was rated low and very low quality using GRADE.
The authors say more research is needed before clinical recommendations about pelvic belts can be made.

items.title: Effects of the combination of exercise and education in the treatment of low back and/or pelvic pain in pregnant women: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pooled 13 randomised trials of pregnant women with low back and/or pelvic pain. It compared exercise plus education with exercise alone or education alone. Exercise combined with education reduced pain and disability more than education on its own. Only one study looked at fear of movement, and it found no clear change.
keyPoints: Exercise plus education lowered pain more than education alone (standardized mean difference -0.29).
Exercise plus education also lowered disability more than education alone (standardized mean difference -0.37).
Only one study measured fear of movement (kinesophobia), and it showed no significant change.
The authors conclude the combination seems more effective than education alone for low back and/or pelvic pain in pregnancy.

items.title: Efficacy of pelvic floor muscle training with physical therapy for low back pain: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 19 randomised trials to see whether pelvic floor muscle training helps people with low back pain. It found that training these muscles may reduce pain, and adding it to standard physical therapy may improve both pain and disability. The authors say the benefit may be especially relevant for pregnancy-related back pain. The evidence was low certainty, so the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training showed low certainty evidence of reducing low back pain, at a level the authors describe as clinically meaningful.
Adding pelvic floor training to standard physical therapy improved pain and disability, again with low certainty evidence.
Compared with other interventions, pelvic floor training improved pain but did not clearly improve disability.
The authors conclude it is potentially beneficial, particularly for pregnancy-related back pain, but note concerns about study quality and risk of bias.

items.title: Prevention of low back and pelvic girdle pain during pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials with GRADE recommendations
items.summary: This review pooled six trials with 2,231 pregnant women to see whether anything can prevent low back and pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy. Exercise on its own was the most promising option: moderate-quality evidence found it was acceptable to pregnant women and probably slightly lowered the chance of low back pain in the long term. Other approaches did not show clear benefit, but the evidence was mostly moderate to very low quality and only a small number of trials were included. The authors say larger, higher-quality trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Exercise on its own was acceptable to pregnant women and probably slightly reduced low back pain episodes in the long term (moderate-quality evidence).
Other prevention approaches did not show clear benefit, based on moderate to very low quality evidence.
No strategy had high-quality evidence for preventing back or pelvic girdle pain or reducing sick leave.
Only six trials were included, so more large, high-quality studies are needed.

items.title: Effect of the pilates method on pain and quality of life in pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies
items.journal: Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies
items.summary: This review looked at whether Pilates exercise helps with low back pain in pregnancy compared with usual prenatal care or no exercise. Only two small trials, with 65 women in total, were good enough to include. Women who did Pilates probably had less pain in the short term, and no side effects were reported. The review rates the evidence as moderate quality, and the trials were small and could not hide who was getting Pilates.
keyPoints: Pilates was linked to a significant drop in low back pain compared with a group that did no exercise.
Only two trials (65 women) met the review's criteria.
No adverse effects were reported.
The authors rate the evidence as moderate quality; the studies were small and lacked blinding.

items.title: The global prevalence of low back pain in pregnancy: a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 28 studies with almost 13,000 pregnant women to estimate how common back pain is in pregnancy. About 4 in 10 women (40.5%) had back pain during pregnancy. It became more common as pregnancy went on, and the studies differed a lot from one another, so the exact figures are uncertain.
keyPoints: Overall, about 40.5% of pregnant women had back pain (95% CI 33 to 48.4).
Back pain was reported by about 28% of women in the first trimester, 37% in the second and 48% in the third.
The studies varied a great deal (very high heterogeneity), so the numbers are rough estimates.
The authors say back pain in pregnancy is common and call for more awareness and timely diagnosis and treatment.

items.title: Predictive Factors for Pregnancy-Related Persistent Pelvic Girdle Pain (PPGP): A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 10 studies to find out which factors make pelvic girdle pain that starts in pregnancy more likely to still be there 3 to 6 months after birth. Several factors seen during pregnancy, such as high pain levels and a history of back or pelvic pain, were linked to pain lasting longer. The studies were too different from one another to combine their numbers, so the findings are descriptive and more careful research is needed.
keyPoints: Strong predictors of pelvic girdle pain lasting after birth were high pain levels in pregnancy, many positive pain provocation tests, and a past history of lower back or lumbo-pelvic pain.
High disability in pregnancy, neurotic behaviour and strong fear-avoidance beliefs (avoiding movement for fear of pain) were also strong predictors.
Evidence for emotional distress, catastrophizing and sleep problems as predictors was weak or contradictory.
The studies were too varied to pool results, so better-designed future research is needed.

items.title: Health Outcomes after Pregnancy in Elite Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.source: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
items.journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
items.summary: This review looked at what happens after pregnancy for elite athletes, meaning women who competed or trained at the highest level before or during pregnancy. It pooled 11 small studies. Elite athletes were much more likely than non-elite athletes to return to sport within 6 weeks of giving birth, and some had injuries such as stress fractures. The evidence was rated very low certainty, so the findings are uncertain and better research is needed.
keyPoints: Elite athletes were more likely than non-elite athletes to return to sport before 6 weeks postpartum.
Fourteen elite athletes across three studies had injuries after birth, including stress fractures and running injuries.
About 40% of elite athletes in five studies reported improved performance after giving birth.
The authors say higher-quality research is needed to guide a safe return to sport.

items.title: Effect of kinesio taping on low back pain during pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 7 randomised trials with 444 pregnant women to see whether kinesio taping (stretchy therapeutic tape applied to the lower back) helps low back pain. Taping was linked to lower pain scores and less difficulty with daily tasks than in comparison groups. The authors concluded taping has a positive effect, though results varied quite a bit between trials and the abstract does not rate the overall certainty of the evidence.
keyPoints: Kinesio taping lowered low back pain scores and improved back-related disability compared with control groups.
Pain improved in the second and third trimesters.
Taping for more than 1 week still improved pain, but the improvement in daily function was not statistically significant in that subgroup.
The authors suggest more research on preventing and treating low back pain in pregnancy.

items.title: Exercise for the prevention and treatment of low back, pelvic girdle and lumbopelvic pain during pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 32 studies of over 52,000 pregnant women to see whether exercising during pregnancy affects low back pain and pelvic girdle pain. Exercise did not lower the chances of having this kind of pain. However, women who exercised reported less severe pain during pregnancy and in the early weeks after birth. The quality of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate.
keyPoints: Exercising in pregnancy did not reduce the odds of having low back, pelvic girdle or combined lumbopelvic pain, during pregnancy or after birth.
Women who exercised during pregnancy reported lower pain severity during pregnancy and in the early postpartum period than women who did not exercise.
The evidence behind these findings was rated very low to moderate in quality, with other study types giving very low quality support.

items.title: Exercise for the prevention of low back and pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from 11 randomized trials with 2,347 pregnant women to see whether exercise can prevent back and pelvic pain. Exercise gave a small reduction in the risk of low back pain, and fewer women took sick leave because of lower back and pelvic pain. There was no clear sign that exercise prevented pelvic girdle pain.
keyPoints: Exercise lowered the risk of low back pain in pregnancy by about 9%.
Exercise did not clearly prevent pelvic girdle pain.
Women who exercised were less likely to start a new period of sick leave because of lower back and pelvic pain (about 21% lower risk).
The authors describe the protective effect on low back pain as small.

items.title: Women's experiences of pregnancy related pelvic girdle pain: A systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together eight studies in which women described what living with pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy was like. The pain affected daily life at home and at work, and many women felt they lost their independence. They described frustration, guilt, irritability and sadness at not being able to do their usual roles, and some worried about caring for their children safely. The authors say health professionals should take this pain seriously, be sensitive about it, and refer women for treatment early.
keyPoints: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy affected women's daily lives at home and at work.
Women reported frustration, guilt, irritability and upset, and said it affected their sense of identity and independence.
Women may become socially isolated, and there is a risk of overusing painkillers if they lack support.
Women with young children may face safety worries when carrying babies and managing toddlers.

items.title: Prognostic factors for pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain, a systematic review
items.summary: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy is common, and for some women it carries on after the baby is born. This review looked for factors linked to whether the pain lasts, but only three small studies met its criteria. Past low back pain, pain in several pelvic locations, being overweight or obese, other pain conditions and emotional distress in pregnancy were linked to slower recovery. The evidence was low to very low quality, so the findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: About a third of women still have pelvic girdle pain three months after birth, and 8.5% still have symptoms two years later.
Previous low back pain, pain in three to four pelvic locations, and being overweight or obese were linked to a lower chance of recovery by 12 weeks after birth.
At six months after birth, pain was more likely to continue with crutch use, other pain conditions, obesity, earlier first period, or emotional distress during pregnancy.
Only three studies were included and evidence quality was low to very low, so no firm conclusions can be drawn.

items.title: Osteopathic manipulative treatment for low back and pelvic girdle pain during and after pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies
items.journal: Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomised trials of osteopathic manipulative treatment (hands-on osteopathic care) for low back pain in pregnant and postpartum women. In pregnancy, moderate-quality evidence showed it reduced pain and improved everyday movement and function. For postpartum women the evidence was low quality but pointed the same way. The authors say larger, higher-quality trials could change these estimates.
keyPoints: Five trials looked at osteopathic treatment for low back pain in pregnancy and three looked at it after birth.
In pregnancy, moderate-quality evidence showed a medium-sized reduction in pain and improvement in function.
After birth, low-quality evidence showed a moderate-sized reduction in pain and improvement in function.
The authors call for larger, high-quality trials with robust comparison groups.

items.title: Treatments for pregnancy-related lumbopelvic pain: a systematic review of physiotherapy modalities
items.summary: This review looked at physiotherapy treatments for back and pelvic pain during pregnancy and after birth. It found strong evidence that acupuncture and pelvic belts help with pain in pregnancy. Evidence for exercise was low, and for many other treatments it was very limited. No specific side effects were reported for any treatment, but the studies were too different to combine their results.
keyPoints: Strong evidence supports acupuncture and pelvic belts for lumbopelvic pain during pregnancy.
Evidence was low for exercise in general and for specific stabilising exercises.
Evidence was very limited for water gymnastics, muscle relaxation, osteopathic manual therapy, craniosacral therapy, electrotherapy and yoga.
For pain after birth, evidence was very limited for clinic-based treatments and self-management programmes.

items.title: Interventions for preventing and treating low-back and pelvic pain during pregnancy
items.summary: This review pooled 34 trials with 5121 pregnant women to see what helps prevent or ease low-back and pelvic pain in pregnancy. Exercise may reduce low-back pain, disability and sick leave compared with usual prenatal care. Single studies also suggested benefits from acupuncture, craniosacral therapy, osteomanipulative therapy and combined treatment programmes. The quality of the evidence was low to moderate, so these results could change with more research.
keyPoints: Low-quality evidence suggests that exercise on land or in water may reduce pregnancy-related low-back pain and improve daily function.

Moderate-quality evidence suggests an 8 to 12 week exercise programme probably reduces the number of women reporting low-back and pelvic pain, and land-based exercise probably reduces related sick leave.
Single studies suggested acupuncture or craniosacral therapy improved pelvic pain, and osteomanipulative therapy may help low-back pain and disability.
When side effects were reported, they were minor and short-lived.

items.title: Barriers and facilitators of choosing a vaginal birth after cesarean: A mixed-methods systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 55 studies from 19 countries to look at what makes women more or less likely to choose a vaginal birth after a caesarean (VBAC). It found that the decision is shaped by the woman herself, her relationships, the healthcare system and wider social factors. The authors say hospitals should offer better support for VBAC and involve women in the decision. The quality of the studies was rated moderate to high.
keyPoints: Choosing VBAC is influenced by four areas: the woman's own factors, her relationships, the healthcare system and social factors like culture and law.
Personal factors include background, physical health, what a woman knows and believes, and how she feels about birth.
Emotional support, good communication, and how willing healthcare staff and facilities are to support VBAC also matter.
The authors conclude that hospitals should improve care, build capacity to support VBAC, and respect women's preferences by involving them in decisions.

items.title: FIGO good practice recommendations for vaginal birth after cesarean section
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: These international good practice recommendations look at vaginal birth after a caesarean (VBAC) as an option instead of a repeat caesarean for suitably selected women. VBAC succeeds in about 60% to 80% of attempts, and the risk of the womb scar opening (uterine rupture) is low, around 0.3% to 0.7% after one previous low transverse caesarean. VBAC generally gave similar or better results for mothers and babies than a planned repeat caesarean. The guidance stresses good counselling, a hospital able to do an emergency caesarean, and continuous monitoring of the baby in labour.
keyPoints: VBAC success rates range from 60% to 80%, and are highest with a previous vaginal birth, a non-recurring reason for the earlier caesarean, a gap of 18 months or more between births, BMI under 30, and labour starting on its own.
Uterine rupture is the main concern but is low risk, about 0.3% to 0.7% for women with one previous low transverse caesarean.
VBAC generally led to similar or better outcomes than planned repeat caesarean, including lower maternal mortality, fewer infections and shorter hospital stays.
Care should include proper counselling, a facility ready for emergency caesarean, and continuous fetal monitoring during labour.

items.title: The safety of trial of labor after cesarean section (TOLAC) versus elective repeat cesarean section (ERCS): a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 13 studies covering over 676,000 women who had a previous caesarean. It compared trying for a vaginal birth (TOLAC) with a planned repeat caesarean. Trying for a vaginal birth was linked to a higher chance of uterine rupture, newborn asphyxia (low oxygen at birth) and perinatal death. The authors note that the risk of every complication was small in both groups.
keyPoints: Uterine rupture was more likely with a trial of labour than with a planned repeat caesarean (odds ratio 3.35).
Neonatal asphyxia (odds ratio 2.32) and perinatal death (odds ratio 1.71) were also higher with a trial of labour.
No significant difference was found for hysterectomy around the birth, blood transfusion or infection after birth.
The risks of all complications were small in both groups, and the authors say this information can help women and providers choose the type of birth.

items.title: Increased risk of obstetric anal sphincter injury in women undergoing vaginal delivery after caesarean section: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 23 studies from 11 countries to see whether women who give birth vaginally after a previous caesarean (VBAC) have more severe tears involving the anal muscle (OASI) than women having a first baby. Tears were more common after VBAC: about 8.2% compared with 6.6% in women having a first baby. The studies differed a lot from one another, so the exact size of the difference is uncertain.
keyPoints: OASI occurred in 8.18% of VBAC births compared with 6.59% of births in women having their first baby.
The pooled odds ratio was 1.27 (95% CI 1.10-1.47), meaning somewhat higher odds of OASI after VBAC.
The studies varied a great deal in their results (I2 = 98%).
The review concluded that VBAC was linked to a higher prevalence of OASI than first vaginal births.

items.title: Prediction models of vaginal birth after cesarean delivery: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 33 studies describing 20 tools that estimate the chance of a successful vaginal birth after a previous caesarean. The tools often use factors such as body mass index and whether the woman has had a vaginal birth before. One widely used tool, Grobman's model, was checked in several different groups of women. Most of the studies had methodological weaknesses, so the authors say better-designed tools are still needed.
keyPoints: Twenty prediction models for vaginal birth after caesarean were identified across 33 studies.
Common factors in the models were body mass index, previous vaginal birth, maternal age and the reason for the earlier caesarean.
Grobman's model was tested in multiple outside populations and performed acceptably.
Most studies (27 of 33) had a high risk of bias, so more rigorous models are needed.

items.title: Classical Cesarean: What Are the Maternal and Infant Risks Compared With Low Transverse Cesarean in Preterm Birth, and Subsequent Uterine Rupture? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This review pooled results from 24 studies on classical caesarean (an up-and-down cut in the womb) compared with the usual low sideways cut when babies are born early. It found no clear difference in maternal death or intensive care admission, but the data are scarce. In women who had a classical cut and did not go into labour in a later pregnancy, about 1 in 100 had a uterine rupture (a tear in the womb).
keyPoints: No significant difference between classical and low transverse caesarean in maternal death or ICU admission after preterm birth, though the evidence is limited.
At 28 to 31 weeks, the classical cut was linked to higher rates of womb infection, blood transfusion and ICU admission.
The low vertical cut was linked to lower odds of injury to nearby organs than the low transverse cut.
Uterine rupture in a later pregnancy was about 1% after a classical cut when no labour was planned.

items.title: Trial of labor after cesarean delivery in twin gestations: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 11 studies of women pregnant with twins who had a previous caesarean, comparing planned vaginal birth with a planned repeat caesarean. Uterine rupture (the scar opening during labour) was more common with a trial of labour. But it was no more common than in women with one baby trying for a vaginal birth, and the chance of a successful vaginal birth was similar. The authors say planned vaginal birth may be a safe alternative to a repeat caesarean for some women with twins.
keyPoints: Uterine rupture was more common with a trial of labour than with a planned repeat caesarean in twin pregnancies.
The rate of uterine rupture did not differ significantly between twin and single-baby pregnancies trying for a vaginal birth.
Trial of labour with twins did not raise the risk of scar separation, heavy bleeding, blood transfusion, or baby illness or death compared with a repeat caesarean.
Women with twins had similar vaginal birth success rates to women with one baby.

items.title: Trial of labor versus elective repeat cesarean delivery in twin pregnancies after a previous cesarean delivery-A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 10 studies comparing a planned vaginal birth (trial of labour) with a planned repeat caesarean in women pregnant with twins who had a previous caesarean. About 7 in 10 women who tried labour gave birth vaginally, and uterine rupture was rare (under 1%). Trying labour was linked to a higher risk of newborn death, but the authors say this may be influenced by prematurity and needs more research. Women who tried labour had fewer infections, and the risks of blood transfusion and hysterectomy were similar between the two groups.
keyPoints: Around 72% of twin pregnancies that attempted labour after a previous caesarean ended in a successful vaginal birth.
Uterine rupture occurred in about 0.87% of women who tried labour.
Trying labour was linked to a higher risk of neonatal death (relative risk about 3), which may be influenced by prematurity and needs further investigation.
Maternal infection was lower with trial of labour, while risks of blood transfusion, hysterectomy and uterine dehiscence were similar to a repeat caesarean.

items.title: Methods of term labour induction for women with a previous caesarean section
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for trials comparing ways to start labour (induction) in women who have had a previous caesarean. It found eight small trials covering 707 women, each comparing different methods, so results could not be combined. The evidence was moderate to very low quality, and no method could be shown to be better or safer than another. The review says more research is needed, though large trials are unlikely, so careful observational studies may be the best way forward.
keyPoints: Eight trials (707 women) were included, but each compared different induction methods, so no pooling of results was possible.
For most comparisons there were no clear differences in caesarean rates between methods.
One trial of vaginal misoprostol versus oxytocin stopped early after one woman had a uterine rupture and another had a uterine dehiscence.
The authors conclude the evidence is inadequate to say which induction method is best after a previous caesarean.

items.title: Elective repeat caesarean section versus induction of labour for women with a previous caesarean birth
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for randomised trials comparing a planned repeat caesarean with a planned induction of labour for women who have had a caesarean before and need their labour started. It found no such trials. Both options have benefits and harms, but what we know comes only from non-randomised studies, which can be biased, so conclusions should be treated with caution.
keyPoints: No randomised controlled trials were found comparing planned repeat caesarean with planned induction of labour after a previous caesarean.
Both options carry benefits and harms.
Current information comes from non-randomised studies, which have a high potential for bias.
The authors say randomised trials are needed to give the most reliable answers.

items.title: Practice Bulletin No. 184 Summary: Vaginal Birth After Cesarean Delivery
items.summary: This guideline looks at trying to give birth vaginally after a previous caesarean, called a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC). A successful vaginal birth after caesarean (VBAC) is linked to fewer health problems for the mother and fewer complications in future pregnancies. A trial of labor that ends in a repeat caesarean is linked to more health problems for mother and baby than either a successful VBAC or a planned repeat caesarean. Because of this, the guideline stresses checking each woman's chance of success and her individual risks when deciding if a trial of labor is a good fit.
keyPoints: TOLAC is appropriate for many women who have had a previous caesarean.
A successful VBAC is linked to less maternal illness and fewer complications in future pregnancies.
A failed trial of labor is linked to more maternal and baby health problems than VBAC or a planned repeat caesarean.
Doctors should assess the likelihood of VBAC and each woman's individual risks when counselling about who is a good candidate.

items.title: Practice Bulletin No. 184: Vaginal Birth After Cesarean Delivery
items.summary: This guideline looks at planned attempts to give birth vaginally after a previous caesarean, called a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC). When it works, it is called a vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC). VBAC is linked to fewer complications for the mother and fewer problems in future pregnancies. However, a trial of labor that does not succeed carries more risk than a successful VBAC or a planned repeat caesarean, so it is important to check each woman's chances and risks.
keyPoints: TOLAC is appropriate for many women who have had a previous caesarean and want a vaginal birth.
A successful VBAC is linked to lower maternal complications and fewer complications in future pregnancies.
A failed trial of labor is linked to more maternal and newborn complications than a successful VBAC or an elective repeat caesarean.
Doctors should assess the likelihood of VBAC and the individual risks when counseling about who is a good candidate.

items.title: Screening for Osteoporosis to Prevent Fractures: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force looked at whether checking for osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) helps prevent broken bones in adults aged 40 and over who have not been diagnosed. It found that screening has a moderate benefit for women aged 65 and older, and for postmenopausal women under 65 who are at higher risk of fractures. For men, there is not enough evidence to say whether screening does more good than harm.
keyPoints: Screening for osteoporosis is recommended for women aged 65 or older (B recommendation, moderate certainty of moderate net benefit).
Screening is also recommended for postmenopausal women under 65 who are at increased fracture risk, as estimated by a clinical risk assessment.
For men, the evidence is insufficient to judge the balance of benefits and harms of screening.
Osteoporotic fractures can lead to distress, further fractures, loss of independence and death.

items.title: Optimal resistance training parameters for improving bone mineral density in postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research
items.journal: Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research
items.summary: This review pooled 17 randomised trials (690 postmenopausal women) to see how resistance training affects bone density. It found that resistance training improved bone density in the lower spine, the neck of the thigh bone and the total hip, but not clearly at one hip site (the trochanter). Heavier lifting (at least 70% of the most a person can lift once), done three times a week for longer periods, looked best. The studies differed a lot from one another, so the results may not apply to everyone and more high-quality trials are needed.
keyPoints: Resistance training improved bone density at the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip in postmenopausal women.
No clear benefit was seen at the trochanter (a part of the hip bone).
A programme of high-intensity training (at least 70% of one-repetition maximum) three times per week for a longer duration may be best.
Large differences between the studies limit how far the findings can be generalised, and more high-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Resistance training effects on healthy postmenopausal women: a systematic review with meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 randomized trials of resistance (strength) training in healthy postmenopausal women. Compared with no training, strength training improved fitness, including aerobic capacity and both leg and arm strength. The effects on bone density and body measurements were less clear. The authors suggest training 3 days a week for about 60 minutes per session.
keyPoints: Resistance training clearly improved maximal oxygen uptake (a measure of aerobic fitness) compared with control groups.
Lower body and upper body strength both improved significantly.
The effect on bone mineral density and body measurements such as size and shape is still debated.
The authors suggest sessions of 60 minutes, 3 days per week, to support quality of life, function and disease prevention.

items.title: Effects of mind-body exercise on perimenopausal and postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 11 randomized trials with 1,005 women who were perimenopausal or postmenopausal. It looked at mind-body exercises such as tai chi, yoga, Pilates, qigong, baduanjin and mindfulness-based stress reduction. Compared with control groups, women doing these exercises had better bone density, sleep quality, anxiety, depressed mood and fatigue. Results for sleep, anxiety and depression varied quite a bit between studies.
keyPoints: Mind-body exercise was linked to higher bone mineral density compared with control groups.
Sleep quality improved in women doing mind-body exercise.
Anxiety, depressed mood and fatigue were all reduced.
Results for sleep, anxiety and depression differed a lot between the included trials.

items.title: Bone-modifying agents for reducing bone loss in women with early and locally advanced breast cancer: a network meta-analysis
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 34 trials (about 33,800 women) of bone-strengthening medicines given to women with early or locally advanced breast cancer, whose bones can thin during treatment. Several of these medicines, such as zoledronic acid, ibandronate and clodronate, likely raised bone density and lowered fracture rates compared with no treatment or placebo. They made little to no difference to overall survival, and they may cause more side effects, including a rare jaw problem and kidney issues. The authors say choosing the best option is hard and more head-to-head trials are needed.
keyPoints: Most bisphosphonates (except alendronate and pamidronate) and denosumab likely increased bone density and reduced fractures versus no treatment or placebo.
Clodronate and ibandronate lowered fractures from about 70 to about 40-42 per 1000 women (high certainty).
Overall survival showed little to no difference with these medicines (low certainty).
Denosumab, ibandronate and zoledronic acid probably raise the chance of osteonecrosis of the jaw, and ibandronate probably raises the chance of kidney impairment (moderate certainty).

items.title: Oral vitamin D supplementation for adults with obesity undergoing bariatric surgery
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether vitamin D supplements help adults with obesity who are having weight-loss (bariatric) surgery, and which dose works best. It found five small trials with 314 people. A moderate dose (3200 IU a day) may raise vitamin D blood levels compared with placebo, and a high dose may raise them a bit more than a moderate dose. The evidence is low to very low quality, and no trial reported on fractures, so it is still unclear what dose is best for bone health.
keyPoints: Moderate-dose vitamin D (3200 IU/day) may improve vitamin D blood levels compared with placebo, based on low-certainty evidence.
High-dose vitamin D (over 3500 IU/day) may raise vitamin D levels more than a moderate dose, but the evidence is very uncertain.
Neither moderate nor high doses seemed to change parathyroid hormone levels much, though the evidence for the high dose is very uncertain.
No trials reported on fractures, and information on side effects was scarce, so more research is needed.

items.title: Prevention and treatment of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis in adults: recommendations from the European Calcified Tissue Society
items.summary: The European Calcified Tissue Society issued guidance on preventing and treating bone thinning (osteoporosis) caused by glucocorticoid medicines such as steroid tablets. It covers adults expected to take these medicines for 3 months or more. It sets out who should have a fracture-risk check, who should be offered bone-protecting treatment, and which medicines suit different levels of risk.
