keyPoints: For anyone taking glucocorticoids for 3 months or more, general measures are advised: enough calcium and protein, a vitamin D level of 50-125 nmol/L, and steps to lower the risk of falls.
A fracture-risk check is advised for people likely to take oral glucocorticoids for 3 months or more who are aged 50 or over or already at higher risk of fracture.

Bone-protecting treatment is advised for people aged 50 or over with a recent fracture, a glucocorticoid dose of 7.5 mg/day or more, age 70 or over, a low bone density score, or a high FRAX risk score.
Premenopausal women and men under 50 with low bone density or a past fragility fracture are advised to be referred to a bone specialist.

items.title: Efficacy of traditional Chinese exercise on postmenopausal osteoporosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research
items.journal: Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research
items.summary: This review pooled 16 trials with 1,288 women after menopause who had osteoporosis. It looked at traditional Chinese exercise, which includes practices like tai chi, alongside usual treatment. Adding these exercises improved bone density, pain, balance and quality of life compared with usual treatment alone. The authors say results should be read with caution because the trials differed a lot from one another on some measures.
keyPoints: Traditional Chinese exercise plus usual treatment improved bone mineral density compared with usual treatment alone.
It also reduced pain, improved balance and improved quality of life.
Blood levels of calcium, phosphorus, osteocalcin and alkaline phosphatase did not change significantly.
The authors suggest it can be used as a non-drug treatment, but note large differences between studies for some measures.

items.title: Effectiveness of whole-body vibration on bone mineral density in postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 23 studies (20 in the meta-analysis) on whole-body vibration, where you stand on a vibrating platform, in women after menopause. Vibration improved bone density at the lower spine and, in some analyses, the hip. The strongest evidence was for high-frequency, low-intensity vibration over a high total time of use. Other settings looked promising but need more research, especially stronger vibrations where safety needs care.
keyPoints: Whole-body vibration had significant effects on bone mineral density in postmenopausal women, mainly at the lumbar spine and trochanter (part of the hip).
High-quality evidence supported high frequency (about 30 Hz), low magnitude (about 0.3 g) and high total dose (about 7000 minutes) to improve lumbar spine bone density.
Other vibration settings were promising but had weaker evidence and need better study.
Safety should be considered, especially with stronger vibrations (1 g or more).

items.title: Dietary recommendations in the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis
items.summary: French rheumatology groups reviewed research on how diet affects bone density and fractures, mainly using meta-analyses and dietary intervention studies. They recommend a Mediterranean-style diet with 2 to 3 dairy products a day, which supplies calcium and good-quality protein and is linked to lower fracture risk. They advise against unbalanced Western diets, vegan diets, weight-loss diets in people who are not overweight, alcohol and daily sodas. For many other foods and supplements, the evidence was too limited or mixed to give advice either way.
keyPoints: A Mediterranean-type diet and 2 to 3 dairy products daily are recommended for bone health and are linked to lower fracture risk.
Unbalanced Western diets, vegan diets, weight-loss diets in non-overweight people, alcohol and daily sodas are advised against.

Evidence is too limited or divergent to recommend for or against tea, coffee, vitamins other than vitamin D, phytoestrogen-rich foods, calcium-enriched plant drinks, oral nutritional supplements, prebiotics or probiotics.
These are the first recommendations of their kind, and more research is needed.

items.title: Effectiveness and Safety of Treatments to Prevent Fractures in People With Low Bone Mass or Primary Osteoporosis: A Living Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis for the American College of Physicians
items.summary: This review pooled results from 34 randomized trials and 36 large observational studies to compare treatments that aim to prevent broken bones in adults with low bone mass or osteoporosis. Several medicines, including bisphosphonates and denosumab, lowered the chance of hip, spine and other fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. Some treatments carried risks: longer bisphosphonate use may raise the chance of two rare problems, and two bone-building medicines led more people to stop treatment because of side effects. Few studies looked at men, people with low bone mass, Black-identifying people, or treatment beyond 3 years.
keyPoints: Bisphosphonates and denosumab reduced hip, spine and other clinical fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis (moderate to high certainty).
Bisphosphonates used for 36 months or more may increase the risk of atypical thigh bone fractures and jaw bone damage, but these events were rare.
Abaloparatide and teriparatide reduced spine fractures but more people stopped them because of side effects.

In older postmenopausal women at very high fracture risk, abaloparatide, teriparatide, or romosozumab followed by alendronate may work better than bisphosphonates over 17 to 24 months (low to moderate certainty).

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D for increasing bone mineral density in premenopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled seven trials (941 healthy women, average ages roughly 18 to 42) comparing calcium, vitamin D, or both against placebo for at least three months. None of the combinations made a meaningful difference to bone density at the hip or lower spine. The authors say the evidence is of moderate to low certainty, and most studies had some risk of bias. No trial reported fractures.
keyPoints: Calcium alone, vitamin D alone, or both together did not improve bone mineral density at the hip or lumbar spine compared with placebo in healthy premenopausal women.
The authors conclude these supplements are unlikely to help prevent fractures in this group and do not support them as a public health measure to improve bone density.
Studies of women with low bone mass, osteoporosis, or a higher risk of bone disease may still be useful, according to the authors.
The certainty of the evidence was moderate to low, and no trials reported fractures.

items.title: Exercise training and bone mineral density in postmenopausal women: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of intervention studies with emphasis on potential moderators
items.summary: This review pooled 80 controlled trials (5,581 women) that tested exercise programmes lasting at least 6 months in postmenopausal women. Exercise led to small but real improvements in bone mineral density at the lower spine, the neck of the thigh bone and the hip. The benefit looked similar whether women had normal bone or osteopenia/osteoporosis, whether they were early or late after menopause, and whether the exercise was supervised or not.
keyPoints: Exercise programmes of 6 months or more improved bone density at the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip in postmenopausal women.
The bone benefit did not differ significantly between women with normal bone and those with osteopenia or osteoporosis.
Results were similar for early versus late postmenopausal women.
Supervised and non-supervised exercise programmes gave similar bone benefits.

items.title: The Clinical Effectiveness of Denosumab (Prolia®) for the Treatment of Osteoporosis in Postmenopausal Women, Compared to Bisphosphonates, Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators (SERM), and Placebo: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 trials (about 25,900 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis) to compare denosumab (Prolia) with bisphosphonates, SERMs and placebo. Denosumab raised bone density in the spine and hip compared with placebo, but some bisphosphonates raised bone density more at certain sites. The medicines did not differ clearly in vertebral fractures or safety. The authors say some results were imprecise and should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Compared with placebo, denosumab significantly increased bone mineral density in the lumbar spine and total hip.
Denosumab increased total hip bone density more than raloxifene and bazedoxifene (SERMs).
Alendronate, ibandronate and risedronate improved femoral neck and lumbar spine bone density more than denosumab.
No significant differences were found between denosumab and the comparison drugs for vertebral fractures or safety outcomes.

items.title: Fracture risk reduction and safety by osteoporosis treatment compared with placebo or active comparator in postmenopausal women: systematic review, network meta-analysis, and meta-regression analysis of randomised clinical trials
items.summary: This review pooled 69 trials with over 80,000 postmenopausal women to compare osteoporosis medicines for preventing broken bones. Bisphosphonates, parathyroid hormone receptor agonists and romosozumab all lowered the risk of clinical fractures compared with placebo, and all treatments reduced spine fractures. Bone-building (anabolic) medicines worked better than bisphosphonates for clinical and spine fractures, and no harms were seen in the trials. The certainty of the evidence was moderate to low, mainly because of limits in how the studies were reported.
keyPoints: Bisphosphonates, parathyroid hormone receptor agonists and romosozumab reduced clinical fractures compared with placebo.
Bone-building (anabolic) treatments were more effective than bisphosphonates at preventing clinical and spine fractures, whatever the person's baseline risk.
Denosumab, parathyroid hormone receptor agonists and romosozumab were more effective than oral bisphosphonates for preventing spine fractures.
Certainty in the results was moderate to low, and no harm outcomes were seen.

items.title: 2022 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Prevention and Treatment of Glucocorticoid-Induced Osteoporosis
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Rheumatology updates advice on preventing and treating bone thinning (osteoporosis) caused by glucocorticoid medicines, such as prednisone. It applies to people taking these medicines at 2.5 mg or more daily for over 3 months. It recommends checking bone fracture risk soon after starting treatment and offering bone-protecting medicines to those at medium or higher risk. It also covers special groups, including people who may become pregnant.
keyPoints: Adults starting or continuing glucocorticoids for over 3 months should have their fracture risk assessed as soon as possible, including a bone density scan and a fracture risk tool if aged 40 or older.
People at medium, high, or very high fracture risk are strongly recommended to take bone-protecting medicine, with the choice made together with their clinician.
Bone-building (anabolic) medicines are conditionally recommended as first treatment for people at high or very high risk.
The guideline gives advice for special groups, including children, people with organ transplants, and people who may become pregnant, and for stopping or switching osteoporosis treatment.

items.title: UK clinical guideline for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis
items.summary: The UK National Osteoporosis Guideline Group updated its guideline on assessing and managing osteoporosis and preventing fragility fractures (breaks from low-impact falls) in postmenopausal women and men aged 50 and over. It draws on systematic reviews, meta-analyses and randomised trials, with recommendations graded by the strength of the evidence. It covers diagnosis, fracture-risk assessment, drug and non-drug treatments, and how care services should be organised. The guideline is accredited by NICE.
keyPoints: The guideline covers postmenopausal women and men aged 50 and over.
It gives recommendations on diagnosing osteoporosis, assessing fracture risk and deciding when to treat.
It covers non-drug and drug treatments, including how long to take and how to monitor anti-resorptive medicines, and steroid-related osteoporosis.
It has been accredited by NICE and endorsed by international osteoporosis bodies.

items.title: Risedronate for the primary and secondary prevention of osteoporotic fractures in postmenopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled results from randomised trials of risedronate, a bone-strengthening medicine, in postmenopausal women. In women already at higher risk of fractures, daily risedronate 5 mg probably lowered the chance of non-hip, non-spine fractures and may have lowered hip fractures, without more serious side effects than placebo. For women at lower risk, the evidence was limited and very uncertain, so no clear benefit or harm could be shown.
keyPoints: In higher-risk women, risedronate 5 mg/day probably reduced non-vertebral fractures by about 20% (moderate certainty).
It may reduce hip fractures by about 27% in higher-risk women (low certainty).
Risedronate probably did not increase serious side effects compared with placebo, and stopping because of side effects was about the same in both groups.
For women at lower fracture risk, the evidence was limited and highly uncertain, and effects on spine and wrist fractures remain unclear.

items.title: Management of Postmenopausal Osteoporosis: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 2
items.summary: The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) updated its guidance on treating osteoporosis in women after menopause. The guideline looks at who should be offered osteoporosis medicines, the benefits and risks of the different medicine options, and how treatment should be monitored. It also covers what role calcium and vitamin D play. Each recommendation is rated by strength and quality of evidence, and where evidence was lacking, the authors gave general good practice points instead.
keyPoints: Gives updated recommendations on who should receive osteoporosis medicines after menopause.
Weighs the benefits and risks of the available medicine options.
Covers how treatment should be monitored and followed up.
Addresses the role of calcium and vitamin D in managing postmenopausal osteoporosis.

items.title: Pharmacological interventions versus placebo, no treatment or usual care for osteoporosis in people with chronic kidney disease stages 3-5D
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether osteoporosis drugs work and are safe for women who also have chronic kidney disease (CKD). It combined seven trials of postmenopausal women, but all of the trials had a high risk of bias. In people with milder CKD (stages 3-4), the drugs may lower the chance of spine fractures, though the evidence is low certainty. For people with severe CKD or on dialysis, it is still unclear whether the drugs help.
keyPoints: In CKD stages 3-4, osteoporosis drugs may reduce spine (vertebral) fractures (low certainty evidence).
In CKD stages 3-4, the drugs probably make little or no difference to overall clinical fractures or to adverse events (moderate certainty evidence).
In CKD stages 5 and 5D, it is uncertain whether the drugs reduce fractures or deaths (very low certainty evidence).
The drugs may slightly improve lumbar spine bone density in severe CKD (low certainty), but larger studies, including men and children, are needed.

items.title: AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF CLINICAL ENDOCRINOLOGISTS/AMERICAN COLLEGE OF ENDOCRINOLOGY CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINES FOR THE DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT OF POSTMENOPAUSAL OSTEOPOROSIS-2020 UPDATE
items.summary: This is a 2020 update of clinical practice guidelines from two American endocrinology organisations on diagnosing and treating osteoporosis after menopause. It contains 52 recommendations, most graded A or B, built on reviews of the evidence. New or updated topics include how osteoporosis is diagnosed, sorting patients into high-risk and very-high-risk groups, a new dual-action treatment option, and how to switch between treatments.
keyPoints: The update has 52 recommendations: 40% Grade A, 46% Grade B and 14% Grade C, with none at the weakest grade.
Of 368 citations, about 70% were the highest or intermediate levels of evidence.
The diagnosis of osteoporosis is clarified, and patients are grouped by high-risk and very-high-risk features.
It adds a new dual-action therapy option and guidance on moving between treatments.

items.title: Effects of combined calcium and vitamin D supplementation on osteoporosis in postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials to see whether calcium and vitamin D together help bone health in women after menopause. Taking them together improved bone density at several sites and lowered the rate of hip fractures. The benefit on bone density was clearest for dairy products fortified with calcium and vitamin D, and not clearly seen for supplements alone.
keyPoints: Combined calcium and vitamin D increased bone mineral density in the whole body, lumbar spine, arms and femoral neck.
It reduced the rate of hip fracture in postmenopausal women (relative risk 0.864).
Femoral neck density improved only when the vitamin D dose was 400 IU a day or less.
Only fortified dairy products showed a significant effect on total and lumbar spine bone density, not the supplements.

items.title: European guidance for the diagnosis and management of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women
items.summary: This European guidance reviews how osteoporosis is diagnosed and managed in women after menopause who may be at risk of fractures. It covers bone density scans, fracture risk assessment, general lifestyle and medicine-based management, and how treatment is monitored. The update adds new information on bone microstructure, the FRAX risk tool, Fracture Liaison Services, diet over the long term, and the higher fracture risk seen after stopping drug treatment.
keyPoints: Bone mineral density measurement is reviewed for diagnosing osteoporosis and assessing fracture risk.
The update covers general and medicine-based management, treatment monitoring and case-finding strategies.
New sections look at the FRAX risk tool, Fracture Liaison Services for preventing a second fracture, and long-term effects of diet on fracture risk.
Fracture risk can rise when drug treatment for osteoporosis is stopped.

items.title: Exercise and Sports Science Australia (ESSA) position statement on exercise prescription for the prevention and management of osteoporosis
items.journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
items.summary: This position statement from Exercise and Sports Science Australia reviews research on how exercise can help prevent and manage osteoporosis. It found that bone responds well to impact activities and to high-intensity resistance training that gets progressively harder. Building muscle strength, balance and mobility also lowers the chance of falls, and so of fractures. Exercise should be tailored to each person's bone health, other health conditions and fracture risk.
keyPoints: Bone responds positively to impact activities and high-intensity progressive resistance training.
Improving muscle strength, balance and mobility reduces the risk of falls and therefore fractures.
Exercise programs should come with enough calcium and vitamin D.
Loaded spine flexion is not recommended, and impact activities may need changing for people with osteoarthritis or frailty.

items.title: Physical exercise training interventions for children and young adults during and after treatment for childhood cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether exercise programmes help children and young people with cancer. It included six small trials with 171 participants, all children having treatment for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Some fitness measures, strength and bone density improved with exercise, but the evidence was low quality and the overall effects were not yet convincing. Only one study measured bone density, and it found a benefit.
keyPoints: Only one study measured whole-body bone mineral density, and it found a statistically significant benefit from exercise.
Some measures of fitness, flexibility and muscle strength were better in the exercise groups, but not all measures showed a difference.
No significant differences were found for fatigue, daily activity or adverse events, each assessed in one study.
The studies were small and all children had leukaemia, so more and larger studies including other cancers are needed.

items.title: Calcium intake and bone mineral density: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 59 randomised trials in people over 50 to see whether getting more calcium from food, or from supplements, changes bone density. Both approaches raised bone density by a small amount, roughly 0.6-1.8%, and the gains did not keep growing over time. The authors concluded the increases are unlikely to make a meaningful difference to fracture risk.
keyPoints: More calcium from food raised bone mineral density by about 0.6-1.0% at one year and 0.7-1.8% at two years at most sites measured, with no effect at the forearm.
Calcium supplements raised bone density by about 0.7-1.8% at all five sites, and the gain at later time points was similar to the gain at one year.
Results were similar for food versus supplements, calcium alone versus with vitamin D, higher versus lower doses, and low versus higher starting calcium intake.
The authors concluded these small, non-progressive increases are unlikely to lead to a clinically significant reduction in fracture risk.

items.title: Calcium plus vitamin D supplementation and the risk of fractures
items.summary: This large trial followed over 36,000 healthy postmenopausal women aged 50 to 79 for about 7 years. Half took calcium (1000 mg) with vitamin D3 (400 IU) each day and half took a placebo. The supplements gave a small boost to hip bone density but did not significantly lower the risk of hip fracture. They were linked to a higher chance of kidney stones.
keyPoints: Hip bone density was about 1 percent higher in women taking calcium plus vitamin D than in those taking placebo.
The supplements did not significantly reduce hip fractures, spine fractures or total fractures.
Kidney stones were more common in the calcium plus vitamin D group (hazard ratio 1.17).
When only women who kept taking the supplements as directed were counted, the hip fracture risk was lower (hazard ratio 0.71).

items.title: Contrast-Enhanced Mammography for Breast Cancer Screening: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies of contrast-enhanced mammography, a type of mammogram that uses an injected contrast dye, when used for breast screening or follow-up checks. Compared with standard low-energy mammography, it found about 9 more cancers per 1,000 women screened. It may find a similar number of cancers as breast MRI, but only a few studies compared the two, so firm conclusions cannot be drawn yet.
keyPoints: Contrast-enhanced mammography found 9.3 more cancers per 1,000 women screened than standard low-energy mammography.
This result came from seven screening and surveillance studies combined, with consistent findings across them.
Cancer detection with contrast-enhanced mammography may be broadly similar to MRI in some screening settings.
Few studies and differing designs mean no definite conclusion can be made about how it compares with MRI.

items.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Supplemental Breast Cancer Screening Based on Breast Density: 2024 Update
items.source: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Radiology looks at extra breast cancer screening tests for women with dense breasts or higher breast cancer risk. Standard mammograms lower breast cancer deaths by about 30%, but they pick up less cancer in dense breast tissue. The panel says which extra tests may be appropriate depending on a woman's breast density and risk level.
keyPoints: Mammography lowers breast cancer deaths by about 30%, but it is less sensitive in women with dense breast tissue and some higher-risk groups.
Digital breast tomosynthesis (3D mammography) improves screening sensitivity in all women.
Average-risk women with heterogeneously dense breasts may also benefit from breast MRI, abbreviated MRI or breast ultrasound.
Breast MRI or abbreviated MRI is usually appropriate for all high-risk women, whatever their breast density.

items.title: The impact of mammographic breast density on locoregional recurrence in breast cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together seven studies of about 3,000 people treated for breast cancer to see whether dense breasts on a mammogram are linked to the cancer coming back in the same breast, chest wall or nearby lymph nodes. The cancer came back locally in 17.0% of those with dense breasts, compared with 9.9% of those with less dense breasts. Overall, dense breasts were linked to a higher risk of local recurrence (pooled relative risk 1.41). The authors say density may be worth considering when planning follow-up care after treatment.
keyPoints: Locoregional recurrence was seen in 17.0% of patients with dense breasts (BI-RADS C-D) versus 9.9% with less dense breasts (BI-RADS A-B).
Dense breasts were linked to a higher risk of the cancer coming back locally (pooled relative risk 1.41; 95% CI 1.17 to 1.70).
Five of the seven studies found a link between higher density and local recurrence.
The authors suggest care teams may consider breast density when planning follow-up and local treatment after breast cancer.

items.title: American Society of Breast Surgeons and Society of Breast Imaging 2025 Guidelines for the Management of Benign Breast Fibroepithelial Lesions
items.source: American Society of Breast Surgeons and Society of Breast Imaging
items.organisation: American Society of Breast Surgeons and Society of Breast Imaging
items.summary: Two US breast specialist societies wrote guidelines on how to manage benign (non-cancer) breast lumps called fibroepithelial lesions, which include fibroadenomas and benign phyllodes tumors. The guidelines are based on expert consensus and available evidence. They say many fibroadenomas confirmed by biopsy do not need to be removed, and that people can usually return to routine breast screening afterwards.
keyPoints: A biopsy-proven fibroadenoma without atypia only needs removal if it causes symptoms, the patient prefers it, it reaches a certain size, or it clearly grows over time.
Patients with a biopsy-proven, matching fibroadenoma do not need follow-up imaging and can return to age-appropriate screening.

Lesions suspected to be phyllodes tumors, including benign ones, need surgical removal of the whole mass; a second surgery for a positive margin is not required but may be considered if the mass was cut through or disease may remain.
After a benign phyllodes tumor is removed, no follow-up imaging is needed and age-appropriate screening can resume.

items.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Female Breast Cancer Screening: 2025 Update
items.source: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.summary: This is an updated guideline from the American College of Radiology on how to screen for breast cancer. It says routine screening lowers the risk of dying from breast cancer because cancers are found early. Mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis (a 3D mammogram) are recommended for everyone with native breast tissue, whatever their risk level. People at high risk may start earlier and may also have breast MRI.
keyPoints: Routine screening substantially reduces breast cancer deaths and illness through early detection.
Screening advice depends on risk, which is grouped as average, intermediate or high.
Mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis are recommended in all risk categories for people with native breast tissue.
For high-risk people, breast MRI is recommended from as early as age 25 to 30, and mammography or tomosynthesis from between 25 and 40 depending on the type of risk.

items.title: European guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of breast lesions with uncertain malignant potential (B3 lesions) developed jointly by EUSOMA, EUSOBI, ESP (BWG) and ESSO
items.summary: This European guideline covers breast lesions that are not clearly cancer but are not clearly harmless either (called B3 lesions). They can sit alongside breast cancer or slightly raise the chance of developing it later. The guideline says next steps after a biopsy depend on the type of lesion, its size, and the woman's own preferences, and that doctors and patients should decide together. It also notes that less invasive options, such as vacuum-assisted excision, may reduce the need for surgery.
keyPoints: After a biopsy shows a B3 lesion, a team of specialists should review whether to remove it with a vacuum-assisted procedure or with surgery.
Decisions should be shared between the woman and her care team, taking into account atypia, lesion size and her preferences.
Using vacuum-assisted excision is expected to reduce how often surgery is needed.
Written information alongside talking with the care team is recommended, and lifestyle changes should be suggested to women at higher breast cancer risk after a B3 diagnosis.

items.title: Breast cancer screening and early diagnosis in China: a systematic review and meta-analysis on 10.72 million women
items.summary: This review pooled results from 35 studies covering about 10.7 million women in China to compare two ways of finding breast cancer: organised population screening and opportunistic screening (check-ups done outside an organised programme). Population screening found cancer in fewer women overall, but a higher share of the cancers it found were early-stage. Results varied with how screening was done, women's age, where they lived, and follow-up. The authors call for more high-quality, well-organised population screening programmes to widen coverage.
keyPoints: Population screening had lower cancer detection rates than opportunistic screening, but a higher proportion of the cancers found were early-stage (about 80%).
Detection rates were higher for women in urban areas, when ultrasound was used together with mammography, and at the second screening round.
The proportion of early-stage cancers was about 86-90% in those same subgroups.
Results differed by screening process, age, population and follow-up method, and the authors call for more high-quality population screening programmes in China.

items.title: ESR Essentials: screening for breast cancer - general recommendations by EUSOBI
items.summary: This is a European radiology society guideline on breast cancer screening. It says regular mammography is still the main way to screen, because it finds cancer early and lowers deaths from breast cancer. Women at high risk, and women with extremely dense breasts, are advised to have MRI as an extra screening test. Screening choices should be made together by each woman and her doctor.
keyPoints: Mammography screening has helped cut breast cancer deaths by at least 20% over the last 30 years, and is still the mainstay of screening.
Women at high risk should start screening earlier, with yearly breast MRI, and can add mammography from age 35-40.
Breast MRI should also be offered to women with extremely dense breasts; ultrasound can be used if MRI is not available, though its added benefit is limited.
Screening plans should be decided through shared decision-making between the woman and her doctor.

items.title: Screening for Breast Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence on breast cancer screening for women at average risk who are aged 40 or older. It recommends a mammogram every two years for women aged 40 to 74, and rates the overall benefit as moderate. For women 75 and older, and for extra scans such as ultrasound or MRI in women with dense breasts, it says there is not yet enough evidence to weigh the benefits against the harms.
keyPoints: Mammogram screening every two years is recommended for women aged 40 to 74 at average risk (B recommendation).
The Task Force has moderate certainty that this screening has a moderate net benefit.
Evidence is insufficient to judge the balance of benefits and harms of mammograms in women aged 75 and older.
Evidence is insufficient to judge extra screening with ultrasound or MRI for women with dense breasts and a normal mammogram.

items.title: Shared decision-making for supporting women's decisions about breast cancer screening
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 19 trials with over 64,000 women aged 40 to 75 to see whether shared decision-making (talking through the evidence and your own values with a health professional) helps women decide about breast cancer screening. Shorter forms of shared decision-making and clearer communication of risks seemed to improve knowledge and may reduce decision conflict, without raising anxiety. Overall, though, the evidence is uncertain, because few studies measured satisfaction or confidence in the decision, and much of the evidence is low or very low quality.
keyPoints: Clearer communication about risks increased women's knowledge about screening, based on high-certainty evidence.
Shortened shared decision-making that included personal values may have reduced decision conflict and improved knowledge, but the evidence was low to very low certainty.
These approaches made little to no difference to anxiety or depression, and clearer risk communication lowered cancer worry.
Full shared decision-making was tested in only two studies, and its effects remain uncertain; better trials are needed.

items.title: Prevalence of Breast Cancer Screening in Asia: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Prevention
items.journal: Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Prevention
items.summary: This review pooled results from 41 studies across 14 Asian countries to see how many women have breast cancer screening. In China, Iran, Japan and Korea, about 24% of women had a clinical breast examination and about 18% had a mammogram over the last ten years. The authors found that many Asian countries do not have enough good national data on screening, so the full picture is unclear.
keyPoints: Pooled across China, Iran, Japan and Korea, about 24% of women had a clinical breast examination in the last ten years.
About 18% of women in those four countries had mammographic screening in the last ten years.
Most Asian countries lack nationally representative surveys or cancer registries, so screening data are limited.
The authors say breast cancer control policies, including screening programmes, need strengthening.

items.title: Implants versus autologous tissue flaps for breast reconstruction following mastectomy
items.summary: This review looked at 35 non-randomised studies (over 57,000 women) comparing breast reconstruction after mastectomy using implants versus the woman's own tissue. Women who had their own tissue used reported somewhat better emotional and sexual well-being and more satisfaction with the reconstruction. Implant surgery may be shorter, but much of the evidence is low or very low quality, so firm conclusions are hard. The authors say no single technique is best for every woman.
keyPoints: Own-tissue reconstruction may give better psychosocial and sexual well-being than implants (low-certainty evidence).
Women with implants may be less satisfied with the reconstruction (low-certainty evidence).
Implants may lead to more long-term complications and a shorter operation, but the evidence is very uncertain.
No technique suits all women, and randomised trials are lacking to guide the choice.

items.title: Supplemental Breast Cancer Screening in Women with Dense Breasts and Negative Mammography: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 22 studies covering over 261,000 women to compare extra breast screening tests for women with dense breasts whose mammogram showed no cancer. These women were at average or intermediate risk of breast cancer. MRI found more cancers that the mammogram had missed than the other extra tests (3D mammography, handheld ultrasound and automated breast ultrasound), which did not differ much from one another. There were too few studies to compare cancers that appear between screening rounds.
keyPoints: Across studies, 541 cancers missed by mammography were found using extra screening tests in women with dense breasts.
MRI found about 1.5 more cancers per 1000 screenings than the other extra tests, including both invasive cancers and early (in situ) disease.
The other extra tests (3D mammography, handheld ultrasound, automated breast ultrasound) did not differ significantly from one another.
The chance that a recall or biopsy turned out to be cancer was similar across all the tests.

items.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Breast Cancer Early Detection Program in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 12 studies on whether breast cancer early detection programs offer good value for money in low- and middle-income countries. Mammograms were found to be cost-effective but cost more and need more skilled staff than clinical breast exams. Mammograms before age 40 were not cost-effective. The authors suggest that screening based on age and risk could work in countries with limited resources, though the studies used quite different methods.
keyPoints: Mammograms were cost-effective but cost more and need more skill to carry out than clinical breast exams.
Mammogram screening before age 40 was not cost-effective.
An age- and risk-based mammogram approach could be workable where resources are limited.
The studies varied in their methods, which limits how firmly the results can be compared.

items.title: Mammography in combination with breast ultrasonography versus mammography for breast cancer screening in women at average risk
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether adding a breast ultrasound scan to mammography helps find more breast cancer in women at average risk. It found that the combination detected more cancers and missed fewer, but it also caused more false alarms and more biopsies. No study checked whether adding ultrasound actually reduces deaths from breast cancer.
keyPoints: In the main trial (about 72,700 women), adding ultrasound found about 2 more breast cancers per 1000 women over two years (5 versus 3 per 1000), and cancers that appeared between screens were less common (high certainty).
Adding ultrasound led to about 37 more false-positive results and 27 more biopsies per 1000 women screened (high certainty).
In women with dense breasts, cohort studies also found more cancers detected with the combination; in women with non-dense breasts, cohort studies found no clear difference.
None of the studies looked at breast cancer deaths or overall deaths, so it is unknown whether finding more cancers saves lives.

items.title: Training health workers in clinical breast examination for early detection of breast cancer in low- and middle-income countries
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether training health workers to do clinical breast exams helps find breast cancer earlier in low- and middle-income countries. It combined four large trials from India, the Philippines and Rwanda. Training may help more women be diagnosed at an early stage and fewer at a late stage, but the evidence is low quality. The effect on deaths from breast cancer is uncertain.
keyPoints: Training health workers in clinical breast examination may increase early-stage diagnoses (45% versus 31%), based on low-certainty evidence.
Training may reduce late-stage diagnoses (13% versus 42%), also low-certainty evidence.
The effect on breast cancer deaths is uncertain (very low-certainty evidence).
Health worker exams picked up about half of cancers (sensitivity about 52-53%), and the accuracy and follow-up results are uncertain.

items.title: Lifestyle Quality Indices and Female Breast Cancer Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 29 observational studies that looked at healthy lifestyle scores (such as healthy weight, diet and physical activity) and breast cancer risk. Women with the most healthy lifestyle scores had about a 20% lower risk of breast cancer than women with the least healthy scores in studies that followed women over time. The link held for different breast cancer subtypes and, mostly, for both before and after menopause. Most studies were at low risk of bias, and the certainty of the evidence was moderate.
keyPoints: In studies following women over time, the healthiest lifestyle group had about a 20% lower breast cancer risk (HR 0.80).
Studies that looked back in time also found lower risk (OR 0.74).
Lower risk was seen across breast cancer subtypes, including ER+/PR+, ER+/PR- and ER-/PR-.
The link held by menopausal status, except for premenopausal breast cancer in the studies that followed women over time.

items.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Palpable Breast Masses: 2022 Update
items.source: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Radiology looks at which imaging tests are usually best when a woman finds a lump in her breast. The right first test depends on age. Ultrasound is usually the first choice under 30, while a mammogram or tomosynthesis (a 3D type of mammogram) is usually the first choice from age 40. If tests show the lump is benign or probably benign, no further imaging is usually needed, though a biopsy may still be considered depending on the situation.
keyPoints: For women under 30, ultrasound is usually the appropriate first imaging test for a lump.
For women aged 30 to 39, ultrasound, diagnostic mammography and tomosynthesis are all usually appropriate.
For women 40 and older, diagnostic mammography and tomosynthesis are the appropriate first imaging tests.

If imaging looks suspicious for cancer, the next step is usually image-guided biopsy; if results are benign or probably benign, no further imaging is usually needed unless the clinical picture calls for a biopsy.

items.title: Global guidelines for breast cancer screening: A systematic review
items.summary: Researchers reviewed 23 breast cancer screening guidelines from 11 countries or regions to see what they recommend. Most suggest mammograms every one or two years for women at average risk, usually between ages 40 and 74. Women at higher risk are generally advised to start earlier and have a mammogram or an MRI scan every year. The guidelines varied in quality, and the review calls for better-made guidance.
keyPoints: Most guidelines recommend mammograms every year or every two years for average-risk women aged 40-74, with 50-69 seen as the best age group for screening.
All the guidelines named mammography as the main screening test for average-risk women.
Higher-risk groups include women with a personal or family history of breast cancer, known genetic risk, past chest radiation, or dense breasts.
For higher-risk women, most guidelines advise yearly mammography or yearly MRI, starting at a younger age.

items.title: Mammographic breast density and the risk of breast cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine studies to see how breast density on a mammogram relates to breast cancer risk. Women with extremely dense breast tissue (called BI-RADS D) had about twice the risk of breast cancer compared with women with scattered dense tissue (BI-RADS B). The authors say this is lower than earlier estimates, which may be because newer digital mammograms and an updated density scale were used.
keyPoints: Extremely dense breasts (BI-RADS D) were linked to about a 2.11-fold higher breast cancer risk than scattered density (BI-RADS B).
After adjusting for age and BMI, the increased risk was about 1.83-fold.
This is a lower risk estimate than previously reported.
The difference may be explained by digital mammography and the 5th edition of the BI-RADS system.

items.title: Breast cancer screening using synthesized two-dimensional mammography: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 13 studies with more than 1.3 million women having breast cancer screening. It compared a newer 3D scan (tomosynthesis) paired with a computer-made 2D image against the same 3D scan paired with a standard 2D mammogram, and against standard 2D mammography alone. The computer-made image found about the same number of cancers as the standard image but led to fewer women being called back or needing a biopsy. Compared with standard mammography alone, the 3D approach found more cancers, but the rate of cancers appearing between screens was similar. The authors suggest it could replace the standard pairing and reduce radiation dose.
keyPoints: Computer-made 2D images plus 3D scanning found a similar number of cancers as standard 2D plus 3D scanning.
The computer-made approach led to fewer recalls and fewer biopsies than standard 2D plus 3D scanning.
Compared with standard mammography alone, it found about 2 more cancers per 1000 screens and reduced recalls.
Cancers appearing between screening rounds were similar to standard mammography, and the authors suggest it could replace standard 2D plus 3D scanning to lower radiation dose.

items.title: Performance of ultrasonography screening for breast cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 23 studies to see how well breast ultrasound works as a screening test. It looked at ultrasound used on its own and ultrasound added after a normal mammogram. Adding ultrasound after a normal mammogram found cancers the mammogram had missed. In women with dense breasts, ultrasound alone performed about as well as mammography, but more women were called back for extra checks.
keyPoints: Ultrasound added after a normal mammogram could pick up occult (hidden) breast cancers that mammography missed.
In women with dense breasts, ultrasound alone was comparable to mammography for sensitivity, specificity, cancer detection rate and biopsy rate.
Ultrasound alone led to significantly more women being recalled after a positive screen than mammography.
Ultrasound alone also detected significantly more invasive cancers than mammography.

items.title: Adjuvant Endocrine Therapy for Women With Hormone Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer: ASCO Clinical Practice Guideline Focused Update
items.summary: This update to a cancer guideline looked at how long women with hormone receptor-positive breast cancer should keep taking aromatase inhibitor medicines. Six trials of treatment beyond 5 years found fewer breast cancer recurrences and fewer cancers in the other breast, but no overall survival benefit. Bone-related side effects were more common with longer treatment. The panel noted the benefits were modest and that decisions should be shared between patient and clinician.
keyPoints: Extending aromatase inhibitor treatment beyond 5 years lowered the risk of breast cancer coming back and of cancer in the other breast, but did not improve overall survival.
Bone-related side effects were more common with extended treatment.
Women with node-positive breast cancer are recommended to receive extended therapy, including an AI, for up to 10 years in total.
Many women with node-negative cancer should consider extended therapy, with an individualised approach for lower-risk cancers based on benefit and tolerability.

items.title: American Cancer Society/American Society of Clinical Oncology Breast Cancer Survivorship Care Guideline
items.source: American Cancer Society/American Society of Clinical Oncology
items.organisation: American Cancer Society/American Society of Clinical Oncology
items.summary: This guideline from two major cancer organisations gives advice to doctors caring for women who have finished breast cancer treatment. It is based on a review of 237 studies plus expert opinion. It recommends regular check-ups and screening for new breast cancers, but says most of the evidence is not strong enough for firm recommendations.
keyPoints: Survivors should have regular check-ups for breast cancer coming back, including a cancer-related history and physical exam, and should be screened for new primary breast cancer.
Routine blood tests or scans are not supported for people with no symptoms, as a way to look for recurrence.
Primary care clinicians should counsel on healthy lifestyle, watch for after-treatment symptoms that affect quality of life, and check that women keep taking endocrine (hormone) therapy.
Most of the evidence is not strong enough for a firm evidence-based recommendation, so many recommendations rest on expert consensus.

items.title: Effectiveness of Breast Cancer Screening: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis to Update the 2009 U.S. Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to see whether mammogram screening for breast cancer helps average-risk women. Screening generally lowered the chance of dying from breast cancer, but the effect was small, and it was strongest for women in their 60s. Screening did not change the chance of dying from any cause. The authors note that most trials used older technology and treatments.
keyPoints: Breast cancer deaths prevented over 10 years per 10,000 women screened: about 3 (ages 39-49), 8 (ages 50-59), 21 (ages 60-69) and 13 (ages 70-74).
Results were not statistically certain at every age, including the 40s and the 70-74 group, and the size of benefit was small.
Screening did not reduce deaths from all causes.
Advanced breast cancer was less common with screening in women aged 50 and older, but not in women aged 39 to 49.

items.title: Follow-up strategies for women treated for early breast cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at five trials of more than 4,000 women who had been treated for early breast cancer, comparing different ways of doing follow-up checks. Regular check-up visits plus yearly mammograms worked as well as more intensive schemes with extra scans and blood tests, for survival, spotting a return of cancer and quality of life. Follow-up with a general practitioner worked as well as hospital specialist follow-up, and patients were more satisfied with GP care. The review notes that the trials were conducted almost 20 years ago.
keyPoints: Check-ups with physical examinations and yearly mammography were as effective as more intensive follow-up with extra laboratory and scan tests.
Overall survival did not differ between simple and intensive follow-up (high-quality evidence), and quality of life was similar.
Follow-up by general practitioners in an organised practice setting was as effective as hospital specialist follow-up for survival, recurrence detection and quality of life.
Patients reported greater satisfaction when followed up by general practitioners.

items.title: Guidelines for anaesthesia and sedation for patients who are breastfeeding: Guidelines from the Association of Anaesthetists
items.summary: A group of experts, including anaesthetists, pharmacists, midwives, infant feeding advisers and parents, wrote guidance on breastfeeding around anaesthesia or sedation. Anaesthetic, sedative and pain-relief medicines pass into breastmilk in only very small amounts. For almost all of these medicines there is no evidence of harm to a breastfed baby. The advice is now 'sleep and keep' rather than 'pumping and dumping'.
keyPoints: Anaesthetic, sedative and pain-relief medicines move into breastmilk in only very small amounts.
For almost all medicines used around surgery, there is no evidence of harm to the breastfed child.
Throwing away breastmilk after anaesthesia ('pumping and dumping') is not necessary; 'sleep and keep' is recommended.
Anyone with a child under 2 years should be asked before a procedure whether they are breastfeeding or expressing milk.

items.title: Effect of Cue-Based Feeding on the Feeding Outcomes of Preterm Infants: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies of 2,239 premature babies to compare cue-based feeding (feeding when the baby shows signs of readiness) with feeding on a set schedule. Babies fed by cue reached full oral feeding sooner and had fewer feeding problems like feeding intolerance. Parents also took part more and felt more satisfied, and health professionals agreed it helps. The abstract does not rate the certainty of the evidence.
keyPoints: Cue-based feeding shortened the time for preterm babies to reach full oral feeding.
It reduced the chance of feeding intolerance compared with scheduled feeding.
Parents were more involved and more satisfied with cue-based feeding.
The authors recommend cue-based feeding for preterm infants.

items.title: Breastfeeding interventions for preventing postpartum depression
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 10 trials (1573 women) testing whether support with breastfeeding could help prevent postpartum depression. Psychosocial breastfeeding support (such as counselling and emotional support around feeding) may lower the chance of postpartum depression in the first one to three months, and may help women breastfeed for longer. However, the evidence is low quality and based on very few small studies, so the results are uncertain. No harms from the interventions were reported, but it is unclear whether harms were actually measured.
keyPoints: Psychosocial breastfeeding support may reduce postpartum depression one to three months after the programme, but this came from one small study (82 women) and is low-certainty evidence.
Psychosocial support may increase how long women breastfeed in the long term (low-certainty evidence).
The effect on depression symptom scores, anxiety and exclusive breastfeeding is very uncertain, and 'alternative' relaxation-type interventions showed no clear benefit.
No adverse events were reported, but most studies may not have measured them; larger, better-run trials are needed.

items.title: Breastfeeding Support Provided by Lactation Consultants: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 40 randomised trials (8,582 mothers) in high-income countries to see whether support from a lactation consultant helps with breastfeeding compared with usual care. Mothers who got lactation consultant support were a little less likely to stop exclusive breastfeeding or stop breastfeeding altogether, and they breastfed for about 3.6 weeks longer overall. The effects on how long babies were exclusively breastfed, on mothers' confidence, and on infant weight were uncertain.
keyPoints: Lactation consultant support slightly reduced the risk of stopping exclusive breastfeeding (risk ratio 0.96) and of stopping any breastfeeding (risk ratio 0.92).
Any breastfeeding lasted about 3.63 weeks longer with lactation consultant support.
Evidence was weak that it changed exclusive breastfeeding duration, mothers' breastfeeding confidence, or the risk of infant overweight.
Support worked better when breastfeeding was measured earlier after birth, and more consultant visits worked better at reducing stopping any breastfeeding.

items.title: Breastfeeding and Health Outcomes for Infants and Children: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 29 earlier reviews and 145 newer studies on breastfeeding and children's health in developed countries. More breastfeeding was linked to a lower risk of several problems, including moderate-to-severe chest and tummy infections, ear infections, asthma, obesity, type 1 diabetes, childhood leukemia and infant death. The studies were observational, so they show links rather than proof of cause, and there were risks of bias.
keyPoints: More breastfeeding was linked to lower risk of moderate-to-severe respiratory and gut infections, ear infections, allergic rhinitis and asthma.
Links to lower risk were also seen for obesity, rapid weight gain, high systolic blood pressure, type 1 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, childhood leukemia and infant mortality.
No clear length of breastfeeding stood out as the most beneficial for any outcome.
There were few data on whether the type of breastfeeding or the source of breast milk changed the results.

items.title: Assessment of growth status and nutritional management of prematurely born infants after hospital discharge: A position paper of the ESPGHAN Nutrition Committee
items.journal: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.summary: This position paper from a European paediatric nutrition committee gives advice on feeding and growth checks for premature babies after they leave hospital. It is based on 101 published studies plus expert opinion where studies were lacking. It recommends regular growth checks, breastfeeding when possible, extra nutrition for babies who need to catch up, and starting solid foods based on the baby's development rather than a fixed age.
keyPoints: Weight, length and head size should be measured regularly after discharge to spot slow growth or undernutrition.
Breastfeeding is highly recommended for all preterm infants when feasible; babies needing to catch up may be given supplements such as human milk fortifier.
Solid foods should start when the baby reaches developmental milestones, rather than at a strict set age.
Vitamin D and iron supplements are recommended through at least 12 months corrected age, with regular ferritin (iron store) checks.

items.title: Predictors of exclusive breastfeeding: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from observational studies (38 articles, 19 in the meta-analysis, over 70,000 mothers) to find out what is linked to exclusive breastfeeding. Mothers who knew the benefits of breastfeeding, had support with child-rearing, and started breastfeeding within 24 hours of birth were more likely to breastfeed exclusively. Higher education, better family income and normal vaginal delivery were also linked to more exclusive breastfeeding. These studies show links, not proof of cause, and the abstract does not report an overall certainty rating.
keyPoints: Mothers who understood the benefits of breastfeeding had about 2.7 times the odds of exclusive breastfeeding.
Support with child-rearing was linked to about 2.57 times the odds, and starting breastfeeding within 24 hours to about 1.85 times.
Higher maternal education, better family income and normal vaginal delivery were also linked to more exclusive breastfeeding.
The authors conclude that better education, social support and economic conditions for mothers are linked to improved exclusive breastfeeding.

items.title: Text messaging interventions for breastfeeding outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 studies testing whether text messages can support breastfeeding. Mothers who got text messages were more likely to be exclusively breastfeeding, and they felt more confident about breastfeeding, than mothers who got no messages or general health information. Messages that started in pregnancy, continued after birth and were sent weekly worked best.
keyPoints: Text messaging raised exclusive breastfeeding rates at under 3 months, at 3-6 months, and at 6 months or more.
Mothers who received texts reported higher breastfeeding self-efficacy (confidence in their ability to breastfeed).
Weekly texts covering both pregnancy and the time after birth were the most effective approach.
Texts were compared with no messages or general health information.

items.title: Relaxation Therapy and Human Milk Feeding Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 randomised trials with 1871 breastfeeding parents to see whether relaxation (music, guided relaxation, mindfulness, breathing or muscle relaxation) helps with breastfeeding. Relaxation was linked to more breast milk, better weight gain in breastfed babies, and a slight drop in stress and anxiety. It did not change the amount of protein in breast milk. The authors say relaxation can be offered to parents who want to improve well-being or milk supply.
keyPoints: Relaxation was linked to an increase in the amount of breast milk produced.
Breastfed babies of parents who used relaxation gained more weight.
Parents reported a slight reduction in stress and anxiety.
Relaxation did not change the protein content of breast milk.

items.title: Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine Position Statement: Breastfeeding in Emergencies
items.summary: This position statement from the Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine explains why breastfeeding matters so much in disasters and conflict. Breastfeeding gives babies safe food and protection from infections without needing clean water, electricity or supplies. The statement says emergency plans should protect and support breastfeeding, keep mothers and babies together, and quickly help mothers who struggle or are separated from their babies.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding gives reliable nutrition and protection against infections without clean water, feeding equipment, electricity or outside supplies.
Dehydration and missed feedings can affect milk production, but stress alone does not.

Emergency support should keep mothers and babies together, give private or protected places to breastfeed or express milk, and quickly find mothers having difficulties or who are separated from their babies.

Babies who are not breastfed need priority support, and options like relactation, wet-nursing and donor milk should be considered; formula should only be given when babies cannot be breastfed, with a full package of support, and donations of formula, bottles and pumps should not be accepted.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of breastfeeding and neurodevelopmental outcomes in preterm infant
items.summary: This review combined 16 studies (one trial and 15 cohort studies) looking at breastfeeding and brain development in babies born early. Preterm babies who received any breast milk tended to have better thinking (cognitive) scores later on and a lower risk of neurodevelopmental impairment than babies who never received breast milk. The effect on movement (motor) skills was unclear, and there was no clear advantage for exclusive breastfeeding or donor breast milk over preterm formula. Most of the evidence came from cohort studies, and possible publication bias means the motor skills findings need caution.
keyPoints: Preterm babies who received any breast milk had better long-term cognitive scores than those who never did.
Any breastfeeding was linked to a lower risk of neurodevelopmental impairment in preterm infants.
Evidence on motor development was inconclusive, apart from a possible benefit in extremely low birth weight infants.
Neither exclusive breastfeeding nor predominant donor breast milk showed clear superiority over preterm formula for neurodevelopment.

items.title: Skin-to-skin contact after birth: Developing a research and practice guideline
items.summary: This guideline used the World Health Organization process, including a systematic review and expert panel, to clarify how skin-to-skin contact should be done after birth. The panel gave a strong recommendation for immediate, continuous, uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact for all mothers and babies, after every type of birth. It reported high confidence in the evidence and said the practice does not need many resources. Delaying non-essential routine care so this contact can continue was found to be safe.
keyPoints: Immediate, continuous, uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact should be standard care for all mothers and babies after all modes of birth.
Babies weighing from 1000 g can have skin-to-skin contact, with experienced staff if help is needed.
Delaying non-essential routine care in favour of uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact is safe.
Skin-to-skin contact lets newborns move through their instinctive behaviours, and the practice is not resource intensive.

items.title: Breastfeeding or breast milk for procedural pain in neonates
items.summary: This Cochrane review pulled together 66 trials on whether breastfeeding or giving a little expressed breast milk eases pain in newborns during procedures such as heel pricks, blood draws and vaccinations. Breastfeeding likely shortens crying time and lowers pain scores compared with no comfort measure, being held, or other non-drug approaches. Breast milk given by other means also seemed to help, though most of that evidence was low certainty. No side effects were reported in the studies that looked for them.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding during a painful procedure likely reduces how long a newborn cries and lowers pain scores (moderate-certainty evidence).
Breastfeeding may also reduce the rise in heart rate compared with being held or skin-to-skin contact (low-certainty evidence).
Supplemental breast milk likely reduces crying time compared with positioning, massage or placebo (moderate-certainty evidence).
Moderate-strength glucose or sucrose may work about as well as breastfeeding, but this is low-certainty, and more research is needed in preterm babies.

items.title: Oral dextrose gel for the treatment of hypoglycaemia in newborn infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether a sugar (dextrose) gel rubbed inside a newborn's cheek can treat low blood sugar in babies. It included two studies of 312 late preterm and at-risk full-term babies in high-income countries. The gel probably helps correct low blood sugar, probably means fewer babies are separated from their mothers for treatment, and probably makes exclusive breastfeeding after discharge more likely. The evidence on later brain-related disability and on the need for a drip is uncertain, and only a small number of studies were available.
keyPoints: Oral dextrose gel (40%) probably helps correct low blood sugar in at-risk newborns (moderate-certainty evidence).
It probably reduces the chance a baby is separated from their mother for treatment (moderate-certainty evidence).
It probably increases the chance of exclusive breastfeeding after going home (moderate-certainty evidence).
No adverse events such as choking or vomiting were reported, and the effect on later neurological disability and need for intravenous treatment is still uncertain.

items.title: Support for healthy breastfeeding mothers with healthy term babies
items.summary: This large Cochrane review looked at 116 trials (nearly 99,000 mother-baby pairs) testing extra breastfeeding support compared with usual maternity care. Support focused only on breastfeeding probably means fewer women stop breastfeeding, especially stop exclusive breastfeeding. Evidence for support bundled with wider health programmes was less certain. Support seemed to work whether it came from health professionals or peer supporters, and in person, by phone or online.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding-only support probably reduces the number of women who stop any breastfeeding or exclusive breastfeeding at six months (moderate-certainty evidence).
Support may be more helpful when delivered over a schedule of four to eight visits.
Support from professionals or lay/peer supporters, face-to-face, by phone or digitally, all appear useful.
Evidence for 'breastfeeding plus' support (combined with wider maternal and child health care) was less certain and less consistent.

items.title: Workplace programmes for supporting breast-feeding: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at programmes at workplaces that support breastfeeding among employed mothers, and some aimed at expectant fathers. Women who took part in these programmes were more likely to be exclusively breastfeeding at 3 or 6 months than women who did not. The authors say the programmes may work, but no randomised controlled trials were found, so better-quality research is still needed.
keyPoints: Fourteen studies were included, mostly from the USA, and none were randomised controlled trials.
In three studies comparing groups, exclusive breastfeeding at 3 or 6 months was about three times more likely among programme participants (odds ratio 3.21).
Across single-group studies, about 76% of women were still breastfeeding at 6 months and about 41% at 12 months.
Workplace programmes may help employed mothers and the partners of employed fathers, but stronger research is needed.

items.title: Breastfeeding Challenges: ACOG Committee Opinion, Number 820
items.summary: This guidance from ACOG looks at common problems that can stop women from breastfeeding as long as they hoped. Many women stop early because of ongoing pain or nipple injury, and only about 25% of women in the United States breastfeed exclusively at 6 months. Care professionals are advised to take a careful history and examine the woman to find the exact cause of pain and choose the right treatment. Worries about medicines, and issues like limited paid leave or workplace barriers, can also lead to early weaning.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding is linked to lower risk of breast cancer, ovarian cancer, diabetes and hypertensive heart disease for the mother.
Pain or nipple injury is a common reason for early, unwanted weaning, so a focused history and exam is needed to find the cause and the right treatment.
Pain with breastfeeding may be linked to postpartum depression, so screening for postpartum depression is an important part of care.
Advice about medicines during breastfeeding should rely on current resources such as the LactMed database.

items.title: EAACI guideline: Preventing the development of food allergy in infants and young children (2020 update)
items.summary: This European guideline looked at ways to lower the chance of babies and young children developing immediate-type food allergies. It suggests introducing well-cooked egg, and peanut in places where peanut allergy is common, as part of starting solids, with the best timing appearing to be around 4 to 6 months. It suggests against avoiding common allergy foods during pregnancy or breastfeeding. The authors say there is still a lot of uncertainty about how to prevent food allergy.
keyPoints: Introducing well-cooked egg (not raw or uncooked pasteurized egg) as part of complementary feeding is suggested, with moderate certainty of evidence.
Where peanut allergy is common, introducing peanut in an age-appropriate form as part of starting solids is suggested; egg and peanut seem most effective when introduced at 4 to 6 months.
Avoiding regular cow's milk formula as a top-up feed for breastfed babies in the first week of life is suggested, though the evidence is low certainty.
Avoiding allergy foods during pregnancy or breastfeeding, and using soy formula in the first 6 months, are both suggested against for preventing food allergy.

items.title: Diagnosis and management of Non-IgE gastrointestinal allergies in breastfed infants-An EAACI Position Paper
items.summary: This is a position paper from the European Academy for Allergy and Clinical Immunology (EAACI) on non-IgE-mediated food allergies in breastfed babies. Food proteins such as egg, soya, cow's milk and wheat can pass into breastmilk and are detectable for hours or days after a mother eats them. This exposure helps babies build tolerance, but sometimes it can trigger allergic symptoms. Because this type of allergy is not well understood, diagnosis and management vary, so an expert group used evidence review and consensus to set out practice points for healthcare professionals.
keyPoints: Food proteins like egg, soya, cow's milk and wheat can be found in breastmilk for many hours or days after being eaten.
Exposure to these proteins is part of how babies develop tolerance, but can sometimes cause allergic symptoms in breastfed infants.
Non-IgE-mediated allergy, apart from allergic proctocolitis and eosinophilic oesophagitis, is not well understood, so diagnosis and management vary.
The EAACI aims to support breastfeeding in all infants, including those with food allergies.

items.title: Oral galactagogues (natural therapies or drugs) for increasing breast milk production in mothers of non-hospitalised term infants
items.summary: This large review pooled 41 trials (about 3,000 mothers) of drugs and natural remedies, such as fenugreek, fennel and moringa, taken by mouth to boost breast milk. Drugs like domperidone and metoclopramide may increase milk volume a little, but the evidence is low quality. Natural remedies may help some babies' weight and milk volume, but the studies were so different and weak that the size of any benefit is very uncertain. Side effects, where reported, were minor.
keyPoints: Drugs such as domperidone, metoclopramide and sulpiride may increase milk volume (low-certainty evidence).
Natural remedies may help infant weight and milk volume in some studies, but the size of the effect is very uncertain.
Reported side effects were minor, such as tiredness, nausea, headache, dry mouth, and maple-syrup-smelling urine in mothers, but safety data were limited.
It is not known whether any remedy helps mothers keep breastfeeding longer, or whether one remedy works better than another.

items.title: Infant formulas containing hydrolysed protein for prevention of allergic disease
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 16 trials to see whether feeding babies a hydrolysed formula (where milk proteins are broken down) prevents allergies better than standard cow's milk formula or breast milk. For babies who could not be exclusively breastfed, long-term hydrolysed formula made no clear difference to allergic disease such as eczema, asthma or food allergy. A few days of extensively hydrolysed formula in hospital might lower cow's milk allergy slightly, but the evidence was very low quality and needs more trials.
keyPoints: No evidence that short-term or prolonged hydrolysed formula prevents allergic disease compared with exclusive breastfeeding.
Prolonged hydrolysed formula versus standard cow's milk formula showed no clear difference in allergic disease, eczema, asthma, rhinitis or food allergy.
Very low-quality evidence suggests a few days of extensively hydrolysed formula might reduce infant cow's milk allergy, but the result was borderline and from a single study.
The authors recommend further trials before this practice is adopted.

items.title: American Society of Hematology 2018 guidelines for management of venous thromboembolism: venous thromboembolism in the context of pregnancy
items.summary: The American Society of Hematology issued guidelines on preventing and treating blood clots (venous thromboembolism) linked to pregnancy. These clots affect about 1.2 in every 1000 deliveries, but they are a leading cause of serious illness and death in mothers. The panel made 31 recommendations on treatment, diagnosis and prevention, using a structured method to rate the evidence.
keyPoints: Low-molecular-weight heparin is strongly recommended over unfractionated heparin for treating an acute blood clot in pregnancy.
Blood-thinning prophylaxis during pregnancy is strongly recommended for women with a past clot that was unprovoked or linked to hormones, though the certainty of the evidence is low.
Prophylaxis during pregnancy is conditionally advised against when a past clot was tied to a resolved, non-hormonal trigger.
Most other recommendations were conditional, including either once- or twice-daily heparin dosing and starting treatment as an outpatient for low-risk clots.

items.title: Skin-to-skin care for procedural pain in neonates
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 25 trials (about 2,000 newborns) to see whether skin-to-skin contact, also called kangaroo care, eases pain during procedures such as heel pricks and injections. Babies held skin-to-skin had lower heart rates, cried for less time and scored lower on pain scales than babies given no treatment. No harms were reported in any study. The authors note that some measures gave mixed results and that more research with consistent methods is still needed.
keyPoints: Skin-to-skin care appeared to reduce pain in newborns during a single painful procedure, based on combined pain scores, heart rate and crying time.
Babies cried for a shorter time with skin-to-skin care after heel pricks and injections.
Skin-to-skin care alone worked better than glucose alone in two studies, and was about as effective as breastfeeding or expressed breast milk where compared.
No adverse events were reported, and the authors judged it safe for a single painful procedure.

items.title: Frenotomy for tongue-tie in newborn infants
items.summary: This review looked at five small trials (302 babies under three months old) of frenotomy, a quick procedure that releases a tight tongue-tie, to see if it helps with breastfeeding. Mothers reported less nipple pain in the short term after their baby had the procedure. The results for how well babies fed were mixed, with no consistent benefit, and no serious problems were reported. The trials were small and had weaknesses, so the findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: Frenotomy reduced breastfeeding mothers' nipple pain in the short term.
There was no consistent improvement in how well babies breastfed; two trials showed no change and one showed improvement.
No serious complications were reported, but the number of babies studied was small.
No trial could say whether frenotomy leads to successful breastfeeding in the long term.

items.title: Comparative safety of antiepileptic drugs for neurological development in children exposed during pregnancy and breast feeding: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 29 studies of about 5,100 children whose mothers took epilepsy medicines (antiepileptic drugs) during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Valproate, alone or combined with other medicines, was linked to the highest chance of delays in thinking and movement development. Oxcarbazepine and lamotrigine were linked to higher rates of autism, though the estimates were very imprecise. The authors advise counselling for women who are planning a pregnancy so the safest regimen can be chosen.
keyPoints: Valproate was the only medicine linked to more cognitive developmental delay compared with no medicine (OR 7.40).
Valproate was also linked to more psychomotor delay, as was a combination of carbamazepine, phenobarbital and valproate.
Oxcarbazepine, valproate, lamotrigine and lamotrigine plus valproate were linked to higher odds of autism, with wide uncertainty ranges.
Counselling is advised for women considering pregnancy to tailor the safest regimen.
