items.title: Breastfeeding in the 21st century: epidemiology, mechanisms, and lifelong effect
items.summary: This large review pulled together many studies on breastfeeding and health for babies and mothers, in both rich and poor countries. Breastfeeding was linked to fewer infections and bite problems in children, higher intelligence scores, and probably less overweight and diabetes. For mothers, it was linked to lower breast cancer risk and longer gaps between pregnancies. No link was found with asthma, allergies, blood pressure or cholesterol, and longer breastfeeding was linked to more tooth decay.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding protected children against infections and malocclusion (poorly aligned teeth) and was linked to higher intelligence, with probable reductions in overweight and diabetes.
No link was found with allergic conditions such as asthma, or with blood pressure or cholesterol; longer breastfeeding was linked to more tooth decay.
For mothers, breastfeeding protected against breast cancer, improved birth spacing, and might also protect against ovarian cancer and type 2 diabetes.
Near-universal breastfeeding could prevent an estimated 823,000 deaths in children under 5 and 20,000 breast cancer deaths each year.

items.title: Kangaroo mother care to reduce morbidity and mortality in low birthweight infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 21 trials (3042 babies) of kangaroo mother care, where a low birthweight baby is held skin-to-skin against the mother's chest with frequent breastfeeding. Compared with usual newborn care, babies who had kangaroo care were less likely to die, develop serious infection or become too cold, and gained weight a little faster. Mothers were also more likely to be breastfeeding at discharge and at one to three months. The authors say the evidence supports kangaroo care as an alternative to conventional care, mainly where resources are limited.
keyPoints: Kangaroo care was linked to a lower risk of death (about 33% lower at latest follow-up) and of severe infection or sepsis in low birthweight babies.
It reduced the risk of low body temperature (hypothermia) and increased weight, length and head growth.
More mothers were exclusively breastfeeding at discharge and at one to three months, and more were breastfeeding at least partly.
No clear difference was found in movement and learning development at 12 months; more research is needed on long-term outcomes and on very early or continuous kangaroo care in unstable babies.

items.title: Early skin-to-skin contact for mothers and their healthy newborn infants
items.summary: This review pooled 46 trials (3,850 mothers and babies) that compared skin-to-skin contact straight after birth with usual hospital care for healthy newborns. Mothers who held their baby skin-to-skin were more likely to be breastfeeding one to four months later, and to be breastfeeding exclusively. The evidence for benefits to babies' body functions, such as blood sugar, was weaker, and many of the trials were small and had quality problems.
keyPoints: Mothers who had skin-to-skin contact were more likely to be breastfeeding one to four months after birth (moderate-quality evidence).
They were also more likely to breastfeed exclusively, both from discharge to one month and from six weeks to six months (moderate-quality evidence).
Babies who had skin-to-skin contact were more likely to breastfeed successfully at their first feed, and had higher blood sugar levels (low-quality evidence).
No differences were found between starting contact within 10 minutes of birth or later, or between shorter and longer contact times.

items.title: Systematic review with meta-analysis: early infant feeding and coeliac disease--update 2015
items.summary: This 2015 review pulled together 21 studies, including two large randomised trials in babies at high risk, to see whether breastfeeding or the timing of first gluten foods changes the chance of coeliac disease. Breastfeeding, whether exclusive or any, and breastfeeding while gluten was first introduced did not lower the risk of coeliac disease in childhood. In high-risk babies, starting gluten at 4, 6 or 12 months gave similar rates of coeliac disease. Waiting longer delayed when the disease appeared but did not reduce the overall risk.
keyPoints: Exclusive or any breastfeeding, and breastfeeding at the time gluten was introduced, did not reduce the risk of coeliac disease in childhood.
In high-risk infants, introducing gluten at 4 months (in very small amounts), 6 months or 12 months led to similar rates of coeliac disease in early childhood.
Later gluten introduction was linked to later onset of coeliac autoimmunity and disease, but not to lower total risk.
Observational studies suggest that eating larger amounts of gluten at weaning may raise the risk.

items.title: Breast-feeding and postpartum weight retention: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from eleven studies to see whether breastfeeding affects how much weight women keep after pregnancy. Compared with formula feeding, breastfeeding for about 3 to 6 months seemed to be linked to less retained weight, while breastfeeding for more than 6 months had little or no effect. The authors say the evidence is not strong enough yet, and more robust studies are needed to know how the pattern and length of breastfeeding matter.
keyPoints: Eleven studies were included in the meta-analysis.
Breastfeeding for 3 to 6 months seemed to be linked to less postpartum weight retention than formula feeding.
Breastfeeding for more than 6 months had little or no influence on weight retention.
More robust studies are needed to judge how breastfeeding patterns and duration affect weight.

items.title: Giving women their own case notes to carry during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at four small trials (1,176 women) where pregnant women carried their own case notes instead of the hospital keeping them. Women who carried their own notes were more likely to feel in control and more of them wanted to do it again in a later pregnancy. There was no clear difference in satisfaction, smoking or breastfeeding. One or two trials found more operative deliveries and caesarean sections in the group carrying notes, but the trials were small and the evidence was low to moderate quality.
keyPoints: Women carrying their own notes were more likely to feel in control of their care (moderate quality evidence).
More women who carried their notes wanted to do so again in another pregnancy.
No clear difference was found in satisfaction, smoking, breastfeeding, labour pain relief, depression, miscarriage, stillbirth or newborn deaths.
More operative deliveries and caesarean sections were seen in the case notes group, but the trials were small and the review says there is not enough evidence to be sure.

items.title: Effectiveness of non-pharmacological traditional Chinese medicine therapies in promoting human milk feeding outcomes: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 33 randomized trials (5,710 mothers) of non-drug traditional Chinese medicine treatments, such as massage, acupressure and acupuncture, used alongside usual breastfeeding support. A massage plus acupressure combination ranked best for exclusive breastfeeding rates and for how soon milk 'came in'. Acupuncture combined with ear-point pressing ranked best for milk volume and prolactin, a hormone involved in making milk. Massage and acupressure on their own also helped across all outcomes measured. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Massage plus acupressure ranked most effective for exclusive breastfeeding rates and for shortening the time until milk comes in.
Acupuncture plus ear-point sticking-pressing ranked highest for breast milk volume and serum prolactin levels.
Massage and acupressure used alone showed a consistent benefit across all outcomes studied.
The authors see these therapies as complements to, not replacements for, conventional lactation support.

items.title: American Society of Breast Surgeons, Society of Breast Imaging, and College of American Pathology 2025 Guidelines for the Management of Infectious and Inflammatory Lesions of the Breast
items.source: American Society of Breast Surgeons, Society of Breast Imaging, and College of American Pathology
items.organisation: American Society of Breast Surgeons, Society of Breast Imaging, and College of American Pathology
items.summary: Three US medical societies wrote guidelines on how doctors should manage breast infections and inflammation, including mastitis in breastfeeding women. They say infectious mastitis (which may need treatment) should be told apart from non-infectious mastitis (which needs supportive care only). The guidelines are based on evidence plus expert consensus, because few strong studies exist for these conditions.
keyPoints: Doctors should tell infectious lactational mastitis apart from non-infectious mastitis, as the first often needs procedures and the second needs supportive care only.

Infectious lactational mastitis with thick fluid collections usually needs a small cut with a drain placed in the clinic; surgery in an operating room is only needed if the patient cannot manage an office procedure.
If a firm inflamed mass (phlegmon) is present, antibiotics should be given for at least 10 days.
Granulomatous mastitis needs a biopsy to confirm the diagnosis, often comes back, and can take up to 18 months to clear.

items.title: Postpartum and Lactation-Related Genitourinary Symptoms: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 65 studies on vaginal and urinary symptoms in women who are breastfeeding after birth. Vaginal dryness, thinning of the vaginal tissue, painful sex and sexual difficulties were all common. Painful sex was most frequent at 3 months after birth and became less common by 12 months, though it stayed higher than in women who had not recently given birth. The authors link these symptoms to the low-estrogen state that breastfeeding can cause.
keyPoints: About 64% of breastfeeding women had vaginal atrophy (thinning of vaginal tissue) and about 54% had vaginal dryness.
Painful sex affected about 60% at 3 months, 40% at 6 months and 28% at 12 months after birth.
Women who were postpartum had roughly 1.5 to 2.3 times the odds of painful sex compared with women who were not postpartum.
About 73% of breastfeeding women reported sexual dysfunction, and their average sexual function score fell below the cut-off for dysfunction.

items.title: Quantitative impact of frenotomy on breastfeeding: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 21 studies on frenotomy (a small procedure to release a tight tongue-tie) in babies with tongue-tie who were having trouble breastfeeding. After the procedure, mothers reported more confidence in breastfeeding and less nipple pain, and latch scores and baby reflux symptoms also improved. The authors concluded that providers should offer frenotomy when tongue-tie is linked to breastfeeding difficulties. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is, and the studies compared scores before and after the procedure.
keyPoints: Mothers' breastfeeding self-efficacy (confidence) improved after frenotomy, with a larger effect at 1 month than at 5-10 days.
Nipple pain dropped substantially after frenotomy, at 5-15 days and at 1 month.
Latch scores (a measure of breastfeeding quality) and infant reflux severity improved after the procedure.
The authors recommend offering frenotomy to mother-baby pairs with tongue-tie-related breastfeeding problems.

items.title: Nonpharmacological Interventions for Treating Breastfeeding Nipple Pain: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 19 trials of non-drug treatments applied to the skin for sore nipples while breastfeeding, such as lanolin, breast milk and light therapy. The evidence was uncertain and the trials were not high quality, so it is not clear which treatments work best. The authors say better trials are needed before firm recommendations can be made.
keyPoints: 19 randomised trials were included, and all had unclear to high risk of bias.
Light therapy (photobiomodulation) compared with placebo showed uncertain effects on pain.
Lanolin compared with breast milk showed uncertain effects on pain and wound healing, and no side effects were reported in either group.
Other treatments showed similar results, and the authors call for higher-quality trials to support recommendations.

items.title: The effect of Orem's Self-Care Deficit Theory-based care during pregnancy and postpartum period on health outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine studies (839 women) that tested nursing care built around Orem's Self-Care Deficit Theory, an approach that helps women look after themselves, during pregnancy and after birth. Women who received this kind of care had less nipple pain and greater confidence in breastfeeding, and they felt more ready to go home from hospital. The authors note there is still little research on this approach, so the findings are early.
keyPoints: Care based on Orem's theory reduced nipple pain after birth.
It improved breastfeeding self-efficacy, which means a mother's confidence in her ability to breastfeed.
It improved self-care, adaptation and readiness for hospital discharge after birth.
In pregnancy, it was linked to a longer pregnancy, fewer preterm labours and better hygiene behaviour.

items.title: The effect of frenotomy in infants with ankyloglossia on maternal nipple pain - a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether cutting a baby's tight tongue-tie (frenotomy) eases a breastfeeding mother's nipple pain. Pooling three trials, mothers whose babies had the procedure had a small short-term drop in pain, about 1.2 points on a 10-point scale. The authors question whether a change that small really matters, and the studies were of low to very low quality, so the true benefit is still unproven.
keyPoints: Frenotomy was linked to a short-term reduction in maternal nipple pain of about 1.2 points on a 10-point scale.
The authors question whether a 1.2-point drop is clinically meaningful, even though it was statistically significant.
Risk of bias in the studies ranged from some concerns to high, and evidence quality was low to very low.
The definitive benefit of frenotomy for nipple pain remains unproven and larger, better-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Effects of GLP-1 agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors during pregnancy and lactation on offspring outcomes: a systematic review of the evidence
items.summary: This review looked at what is known about GLP-1 agonist and SGLT2 inhibitor diabetes and weight-loss medicines during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Most of the evidence came from animal studies, with very little human data. The authors found signs of possible harm to offspring and broadly support stopping these medicines during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
keyPoints: In animal studies, GLP-1 agonists were linked to lower fetal weight and growth, and these medicines passed into breast milk.
In animal studies, SGLT2 inhibitors affected kidney development when given at a stage matching late pregnancy in humans, and they passed into breast milk and affected newborn growth.
A database of unplanned pregnancies on SGLT2 inhibitors found more miscarriages and birth defects.
The authors broadly support stopping both medicine types during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and note that human data are scarce.

items.title: The preventive and therapeutic effects of probiotics on mastitis: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled six randomized trials to see whether probiotics (helpful bacteria taken by mouth) can prevent or treat mastitis, a painful breast infection linked to stopping breastfeeding. Taking probiotics during pregnancy was linked to about half the rate of mastitis, and bacteria counts in breast milk went down. The authors say probiotics may help to a certain extent, but high-quality multicenter trials are still needed to confirm this.
keyPoints: Oral probiotics taken during pregnancy were linked to a lower rate of mastitis (RR 0.49).
Bacteria counts in breast milk fell after probiotics, both in healthy women and in women with mastitis.
Probiotics are being looked at as an option because antibiotic use in breastfeeding raises safety and drug-resistance concerns.
Only six trials were included, and larger high-quality trials are still needed.

items.title: Vegan or vegetarian diet and breast milk composition - a systematic review
items.source: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
items.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
items.summary: This review looked at 13 studies on how a vegetarian or vegan diet affects breast milk. It found that mothers who eat meat, vegetarians and vegans all make milk of similar nutritional value. The main differences were in fatty acids and a few micronutrients, mostly vitamin B12. The authors say this holds as long as the mother takes suitable supplements to meet her needs while breastfeeding.
keyPoints: Breast milk from non-vegetarian, vegetarian and vegan mothers was of comparable nutritional value.
Differences were mainly seen in fatty acids and some micronutrients, especially vitamin B12.
Vegetarian and vegan mothers can make nutritionally valuable milk if appropriate supplementation covers their nutritional needs.
The authors conclude that diet choice should not permanently exclude women from donating to human milk banks.

items.title: Oxytocin and postpartum depression: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 16 studies on whether oxytocin, a hormone involved in labour, breastfeeding and bonding, is linked to postnatal depression. In 8 of 12 studies on the body's own oxytocin, lower oxytocin levels went with more depressive symptoms. For oxytocin given by drip during labour or after birth, the 4 studies were too few and too different to say anything firm. The authors say the research so far has limits and better studies are needed.
keyPoints: In 8 of 12 studies, lower natural oxytocin levels in the blood were linked to more depressive symptoms after birth.
No conclusions could be drawn about synthetic oxytocin given in labour and later postnatal depression, because only 4 studies exist and they differ a lot.
Studies varied in lab methods and in how well they accounted for things like breastfeeding.
The authors strongly recommend more rigorous research on both natural and synthetic oxytocin and postnatal depression.

items.title: Interventions for preventing mastitis after childbirth
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 10 trials with over 3,000 breastfeeding women to see what helps prevent mastitis (a painful breast inflammation) after childbirth. Probiotics, acupoint massage, and breast massage with low frequency pulse treatment may lower the chance of mastitis compared with placebo or routine care. For antibiotics, ointments, breastfeeding education and special cereal, results were uncertain. Most of the evidence is low quality, and a large probiotics trial has not shared its results, so the picture is incomplete.
keyPoints: Probiotics may reduce the risk of mastitis compared with placebo (low-certainty evidence).
Acupoint massage probably reduces both mastitis and breast pain compared with routine care (moderate-certainty evidence).
Breast massage with low frequency pulse treatment may reduce mastitis (low-certainty evidence).
Antibiotics, antibiotic ointments, specialist breastfeeding education and special cereal showed no clear benefit, but the evidence is too uncertain to be sure.

items.title: Effectiveness of breast massage for the treatment of women with breastfeeding problems: a systematic review
items.source: JBI Database of Systematic Reviews and Implementation Reports
items.journal: JBI Database of Systematic Reviews and Implementation Reports
items.summary: This review looked at whether breast massage helps women with breastfeeding problems such as blocked ducts, engorgement and mastitis. It found six small studies, and all of them reported less pain after massage, whatever technique was used. The studies were very different from each other and used unvalidated measuring tools, so the results could not be combined and are hard to repeat.
keyPoints: All six included studies reported a reduction in pain after breast massage, whatever technique was used.
Different types of breast massage helped reduce immediate pain and resolve symptoms.
Small studies, differing methods and unclear descriptions of the massage techniques limit how far the results can be trusted or repeated.
The authors call for better-designed trials, including in mothers of preterm infants, and longer follow-up to see if massage affects how long women breastfeed.

items.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Breast Imaging of Pregnant and Lactating Women
items.source: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Radiology looks at breast imaging for women who are pregnant or breastfeeding. Breast changes in these times can make lumps and other symptoms harder to assess, but symptoms should still be checked promptly. Mammography is described as safe in pregnancy, and imaging while breastfeeding is much like imaging for women who are not breastfeeding.
keyPoints: Breast cancer linked to pregnancy is becoming more common as more women have children later, and imaging of symptoms should not be delayed.
Symptoms that may need imaging include a palpable lump, nipple discharge, diffuse breast enlargement, focal pain or milk rejection.
Mammography is safe during pregnancy, and screening should be tailored to a woman's age and breast cancer risk.
Breast imaging during lactation is very similar to imaging in women who are not breastfeeding, while imaging in pregnancy is adjusted to protect both mother and baby.

items.title: Potential protective effect of lactation against incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus in women with previous gestational diabetes mellitus: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 9 observational studies of women who had gestational diabetes in a past pregnancy. It looked at whether breastfeeding was linked to a lower chance of later developing type 2 diabetes. Women who breastfed for longer, and those who breastfed exclusively rather than using formula, had a lower risk. Because the studies only observed women rather than testing breastfeeding directly, they cannot prove breastfeeding is the cause.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding for more than 4 to 12 weeks was linked to a lower risk of type 2 diabetes than shorter breastfeeding.
The link looked stronger when women were followed for longer; at more than 5 years the odds ratio was 0.22.
Exclusive breastfeeding for more than 6 to 9 weeks was linked to lower risk than exclusive formula feeding (OR 0.42).
All the evidence came from observational studies, so more research is needed to show a true cause-and-effect.

items.title: Supplementation with multiple micronutrients for breastfeeding women for improving outcomes for the mother and baby
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for trials testing multivitamin-and-mineral supplements (three or more nutrients) taken by breastfeeding mothers, to see if they help mother or baby. Only two very small studies (52 women in total) were found, and they gave no usable numbers. So the review could not say whether these supplements help or whether they cause harm.
keyPoints: Only two small trials (52 women) were found, one in Brazil and one in the USA.
Neither trial reported the main outcomes, such as maternal illness, side effects or infant deaths.
One study said supplements helped mothers recover from anaemia, but it gave no data to confirm this.
There is no evidence on possible harms, including from taking too much; better, larger studies are needed.

items.title: Consensus clinical practice guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of restless legs syndrome/Willis-Ekbom disease during pregnancy and lactation
items.source: International Restless Legs Syndrome Study Group (IRLSSG)
items.organisation: International Restless Legs Syndrome Study Group (IRLSSG)
items.summary: Restless legs syndrome affects about one in five pregnant women in Western countries, and many have moderate or severe symptoms that disturb sleep. An expert group from the International RLS Study Group wrote consensus guidelines for diagnosing and managing it during pregnancy and breastfeeding. They suggest starting with gentler approaches such as reassurance, exercise and avoiding things that make symptoms worse, and they explain when iron supplements may help. Only a few medicines are rated as something that "may be considered", and only when symptoms do not improve with gentler measures.
keyPoints: About one in five pregnant women in Western countries has restless legs syndrome, and many report moderate or severe symptoms that affect sleep.
First-line management is non-drug: reassurance, exercise and avoiding factors that make symptoms worse.
The guidelines give a rationale for iron supplementation.
A few medicines are rated "may be considered" in pregnancy and breastfeeding, only when symptoms are refractory to more conservative approaches.

items.title: Combined hormonal versus nonhormonal versus progestin-only contraception in lactation
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 11 trials (1482 women) on whether hormonal birth control affects breastfeeding or infant growth. Most trials found no clear difference between groups in how long women breastfed, in milk composition, or in how babies grew. A few older studies suggested combined pills (with estrogen) may lower milk volume or breastfeeding duration, but results were often not well reported. Overall the evidence was limited and not consistent across methods.
keyPoints: Most trials found no significant difference in breastfeeding duration, breast milk composition or infant growth between contraceptive groups.
One combined pill trial showed lower milk volume than placebo, and an older pill trial reported shorter breastfeeding, though results were not always quantified.
Trials of the progestin-only pill, the hormonal IUD and the etonogestrel implant mostly showed no significant effect on breastfeeding.
The evidence was limited for any single method and results were not consistent across trials.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 637: Marijuana Use During Pregnancy and Lactation
items.summary: This is a 2015 opinion from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists about marijuana (cannabis) use before and during pregnancy and while breastfeeding. It advises that women who are pregnant or planning pregnancy be encouraged to stop using marijuana, including for medical reasons, because of concerns about the baby's brain development and the effects of smoking. There is not enough data to know how marijuana affects breastfed babies, so use during breastfeeding is discouraged.
keyPoints: Women who are pregnant or thinking about pregnancy should be encouraged to stop using marijuana.
Doctors should be discouraged from prescribing or suggesting medical marijuana before pregnancy, during pregnancy, or while breastfeeding.
Women using marijuana for medical reasons should be encouraged to switch to an alternative therapy that has better pregnancy safety data.
There are not enough data on how marijuana affects babies during breastfeeding, so use is discouraged.

items.title: Treatments for breast abscesses in breastfeeding women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at how best to treat breast abscesses (a painful pocket of infected fluid in the breast) in women who are breastfeeding. It compared needle aspiration with cutting and draining the abscess, and also asked whether adding antibiotics helps after draining. The reviewers found the evidence too limited to say which approach is better.
keyPoints: Four small trials with 325 women were included, and most had an unclear risk of bias because of poor reporting.
Needle aspiration failed more often than incision and drainage (low quality evidence), with women then needing drainage; all abscesses treated by drainage were treated successfully.
Results on faster healing and on continuing breastfeeding were inconsistent between studies and could not be combined.
Adding antibiotics to incision and drainage made no clear difference to treatment failure or wound infection in the one study that looked at this.

items.title: Guidelines for antenatal and preoperative care in cesarean delivery: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Society recommendations (part 1)-2025 update
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This updated guideline from the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Society gives six recommendations to help people prepare for a planned caesarean birth and recover well. Three apply during pregnancy (education, staff training, and managing health conditions) and three apply just before surgery (skin cleaning, fasting rules, and a carbohydrate drink). The strength of the evidence behind them ranges from very low to moderate.
keyPoints: Education for patients before a scheduled caesarean is strongly recommended, although the evidence is low to very low quality.

Health conditions such as anaemia, obesity, high blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, heart disease, epilepsy, autoimmune disease and asthma should be managed well during pregnancy (moderate evidence, strong recommendation).
Cleaning the abdominal skin with a chlorhexidine cloth the evening before a scheduled caesarean is weakly recommended (moderate evidence).
Fasting time before surgery should depend on what was eaten, and a clear carbohydrate drink before surgery is strongly recommended (low to moderate evidence).

items.title: Guidelines for postoperative care in cesarean delivery: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Society recommendations (part 3)-2025 update
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: The Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Society updated its 2019 guidance on care after a caesarean birth. Experts reviewed studies up to September 2024 and agreed on 13 steps to help mothers recover well. These include eating and drinking early, getting up and moving soon, and taking scheduled pain relief. The strength of the evidence behind the steps varies from very low to high, and the steps should be considered unless there is a medical reason not to.
keyPoints: Early eating and drinking, early removal of the urinary catheter and drip, and getting up and walking early are all recommended.
Pain relief should be scheduled: regular acetaminophen (paracetamol) and regular anti-inflammatory drugs, with oral opioids as rescue pain relief and a standard plan for managing side effects.
Other recommended steps are blood clot prevention, treating anaemia, breastfeeding support and education, rest periods, and a patient-centred plan for going home.
All 13 recommendations are strong, but the evidence behind many is low; anti-inflammatory drugs have high-quality evidence and acetaminophen and anaemia treatment moderate.

items.title: Guidelines for intraoperative care in cesarean delivery: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Society recommendations (part 2)-2025 update
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This is an updated set of recommendations from the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Society on what care to offer during a caesarean birth, to help recovery and improve outcomes for mothers and babies. The authors reviewed recent trials and large studies, then agreed on ten areas of care. All ten came with a strong recommendation, though the strength of the evidence behind them ranges from very low to high.
keyPoints: Having a support person present is recommended, although the evidence for this is very low quality.

Antibiotics given to prevent infection, keeping the mother warm, careful use of medicines that help the womb contract, and early skin-to-skin contact with the baby are recommended, backed by moderate to high quality evidence.
Preventing nausea and low blood pressure after a spinal, keeping fluid levels balanced, and using several types of pain relief together are also recommended, based on low quality evidence.
The guideline says these steps should be considered for people having a caesarean unless there is a reason they are not suitable.

items.title: Elective induction versus expectant management for suspected large-for-gestational-age fetuses: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled three randomised trials (almost 4,000 pregnancies) where the baby was suspected to be larger than expected. It compared planned induction of labour at 37-39 weeks with waiting for labour to start on its own. Induction probably led to fewer shoulder dystocia cases (when a baby's shoulder gets stuck) and fewer caesarean births, and more spontaneous vaginal births. Babies in the induction group needed phototherapy for jaundice more often. The certainty of the evidence was moderate for most main outcomes.
keyPoints: Induction probably reduced shoulder dystocia (RR 0.65) and caesarean birth (RR 0.87), and increased spontaneous vaginal birth (RR 1.12).
No differences were seen in instrumental delivery, severe perineal trauma or perinatal death.
Babies born after induction weighed about 177 g less on average but were more likely to need phototherapy (RR 1.63).
The authors suggest discussing these benefits with each patient, taking her preferences and circumstances into account.

items.title: Intrapartum Doula Support and Cesarean Delivery Rates: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 18 studies to see whether having a doula (a trained birth support person) during labour is linked to fewer caesarean births. In the randomised trials, about 17.5% of people with a doula had a caesarean compared with 23.6% with standard care. Operative vaginal birth (forceps or vacuum) was also lower with a doula. The studies differed quite a bit from each other, and there were signs that smaller studies may have reported more favourable results, so the findings should be read with some caution.
keyPoints: In randomised trials, doula support was linked to a lower caesarean rate (17.5% vs 23.6%; pooled relative risk 0.71).
Operative vaginal delivery was lower with doula support (7.9% vs 13.2%).
No clear difference was found in low 5-minute Apgar scores or use of regional anaesthesia (such as an epidural).
In US-only trials the caesarean difference was not clear-cut, and the authors note substantial variation between studies and possible publication bias.

items.title: Immediate or early skin-to-skin contact for mothers and their healthy newborn infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 69 trials (7290 mothers and babies) to see what happens when a healthy newborn is placed skin-to-skin on the mother's chest right after birth, compared with usual hospital care. Skin-to-skin contact probably helps more mothers breastfeed exclusively, both up to one month and from six weeks to six months. It also probably helps babies keep up their blood sugar and body temperature. Effects on the mother's blood loss and the time to deliver the placenta were unclear, and no trial met all the criteria for high quality.
keyPoints: Skin-to-skin contact probably increases exclusive breastfeeding from hospital discharge to one month (RR 1.36) and from six weeks to six months (RR 1.38), based on moderate-certainty evidence.
Babies probably have higher blood sugar levels, and slightly higher temperature (about 0.28 °C, not clinically meaningful), with skin-to-skin contact.
Babies may be more stable in heart and breathing function, but this evidence is low certainty from small studies.
Evidence on maternal blood loss and placenta delivery time was inconclusive, and no trials were done in low-income countries.

items.title: Impact of enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) guidelines implementation in cesarean delivery: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review combined 16 studies of about 19,000 women who had a caesarean birth, comparing hospital care that followed enhanced recovery (ERAS) guidelines with usual care. Women in the ERAS groups stayed in hospital about 14 hours less and used less opioid pain medicine. Rates of readmission, infection at the wound and sickness or vomiting were similar between the two groups. The authors note that few of the studies were randomised trials and the studies differed a lot, so the evidence has limits.
keyPoints: Enhanced recovery care after caesarean was linked to a shorter hospital stay, by about 14 hours on average.
Opioid use was lower with enhanced recovery care.
Readmission, overall complications, wound infection and vomiting were not different from usual care.
Evidence is limited because few trials were included and the studies used different protocols.

items.title: Midwife continuity of care models versus other models of care for childbearing women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 17 trials with about 18,500 women to compare care from the same midwife (or small midwife team) through pregnancy and birth with other models of care. Women in midwife continuity models were probably a little more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth and probably a little less likely to have a caesarean or an instrumental birth (forceps or vacuum); they may also have fewer episiotomies. Most trials did not include women at high risk of complications, and some findings are less certain than others.
keyPoints: Midwife continuity of care likely increases spontaneous vaginal birth (about 66% to 70%) and likely lowers caesarean sections (about 16% to 15%), based on moderate-certainty evidence.
It likely reduces forceps or vacuum births (14% to 13%) and may reduce episiotomy (23% to 19%).
There was little or no difference in preterm birth, postpartum haemorrhage or admission to neonatal care; results for fetal loss and neonatal death were very uncertain.
Women in these models generally reported more positive experiences, and some cost savings were noted before and during birth.

items.title: Treatments for cesarean scar pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 176 studies covering over 13,000 women treated for a cesarean scar pregnancy, where the pregnancy implants in the scar from a previous cesarean birth. Many different treatments have been used, and most worked in the large majority of women, with success rates ranging from about 72% to 98% depending on the approach. The authors concluded that the treatments seem about equally effective, but better-designed trials are needed to work out which is best for which situation.
keyPoints: Success after the first treatment was about 86% with ultrasound-guided suction curettage, 72% with systemic methotrexate and 82% with local methotrexate.
Laparoscopy (96%), hysteroscopy (90%) and high intensity focused ultrasound (93%) had high success rates when used on their own.
Combined treatments, such as curettage with a balloon or focused ultrasound followed by curettage, reached success rates of 96-98%.
Systemic and local methotrexate did not differ in success, and curettage was linked to a higher chance of successful treatment in comparison studies.

items.title: Tranexamic acid for preventing postpartum haemorrhage after caesarean section
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether giving tranexamic acid (a drug that helps blood clot) to everyone during a caesarean birth prevents heavy bleeding afterwards. It combined six trials with almost 16,000 women, most at low risk of heavy bleeding. The drug made little to no difference to heavy blood loss when estimated by eye, and probably a slight reduction when blood loss was measured more precisely. Need for blood transfusion or extra surgery was about the same in both groups, and the evidence on serious side effects such as blood clots is very uncertain because so few occurred.
keyPoints: Tranexamic acid given routinely at caesarean made little to no difference to estimated blood loss of 1000 mL or more (high certainty evidence).
It likely slightly reduced blood loss of 1000 mL or more when measured by calculation (moderate certainty evidence).
Blood transfusion and extra surgery to control bleeding were similar with or without the drug.
The evidence on blood clots, hysterectomy and maternal death is very uncertain because very few events occurred.

items.title: PROSPECT guideline for elective caesarean section: updated systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations
items.summary: This guideline reviewed 145 trials to find the best ways to manage pain after a planned caesarean birth done with a spinal or epidural block. It recommends a combination of pain relief given before, during and after the operation, with regular paracetamol and anti-inflammatory medicines after surgery and stronger opioids kept for pain that breaks through. Some options were left out because they carry risks or because the evidence was not strong enough. The advice may not apply to emergency caesareans or those done under general anaesthesia.
keyPoints: For planned caesareans under spinal or epidural anaesthesia, recommended pain relief includes intrathecal morphine or diamorphine before surgery, paracetamol, anti-inflammatory medicines and intravenous dexamethasone after delivery.
If no intrathecal opioid is given, wound numbing injections or infusions, or nerve blocks in the abdominal wall, are recommended instead.
After surgery, regular paracetamol and anti-inflammatory medicines are advised, with opioids used only as rescue.
Surgical choices recommended include a Joel-Cohen incision, leaving the peritoneum unclosed and using an abdominal binder; TENS can be used as an extra pain aid.

items.title: Sleep disturbances during pregnancy and adverse maternal and fetal outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 120 studies of more than 58 million pregnant women to see whether poor sleep in pregnancy is linked to health problems. Poor sleep, including insomnia symptoms, very short or long sleep, restless legs and sleep apnea, was linked to higher rates of pre-eclampsia, high blood pressure, gestational diabetes, caesarean birth, preterm birth and stillbirth. These are links seen in observational studies, so they do not prove poor sleep caused the problems. The authors say sleep problems are easy to overlook and deserve more attention in prenatal care.
keyPoints: Sleep disturbances in pregnancy were linked to pre-eclampsia (odds ratio 2.80), gestational hypertension (1.74) and gestational diabetes (1.59).
They were also linked to caesarean section (1.47), preterm birth (1.38), large-for-gestational-age babies (1.40) and stillbirth (1.25).
No clear link was found with small-for-gestational-age babies or low birth weight.
The links were stronger in women aged 30 or older and those who were overweight before pregnancy.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 205: Vaginal Birth After Cesarean Delivery
items.summary: This American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists guideline looks at trying to give birth vaginally after a previous cesarean (called TOLAC, with a successful result called VBAC). It says VBAC can meet a woman's wish for vaginal birth and is linked to fewer complications for the mother and in later pregnancies. A trial of labor that does not succeed carries more risk than a successful VBAC or a planned repeat cesarean. Because of this, it is important to look at each woman's chance of success and personal risks when deciding if TOLAC is a good fit.
keyPoints: TOLAC is a planned attempt at vaginal birth after a previous cesarean, and a successful attempt is called VBAC.
VBAC is linked to lower maternal complications and fewer problems in future pregnancies.
A failed trial of labor is linked to more maternal and newborn complications than VBAC or an elective repeat cesarean.
Counseling should weigh the likelihood of VBAC and each woman's individual risks.

items.title: Efficacy of vitamin D supplementation in gestational diabetes mellitus: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials
items.summary: This review pooled six small trials (456 women in total) to see whether vitamin D supplements help pregnant women who have gestational diabetes. The number of caesarean births did not differ between women who took vitamin D and those who did not. Some trials hinted at fewer newborn problems such as jaundice, but the evidence was low or very low quality. Overall, the authors found no moderate or high quality evidence that vitamin D improves blood sugar control or pregnancy outcomes in gestational diabetes.
keyPoints: Caesarean delivery rates were not significantly different between women given vitamin D and those given placebo or no treatment.
Vitamin D may reduce some newborn complications (such as hyperbilirubinemia) and hospital stays, but this evidence was low or very low quality.
No trials looked at preeclampsia, preterm birth, gestational hypertension or side effects of vitamin D.
No moderate or high quality evidence showed that vitamin D improves glucose metabolism or outcomes related to gestational diabetes.

items.title: The effect of exercise during pregnancy on gestational diabetes mellitus in normal-weight women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled eight randomised trials to see whether exercising during pregnancy affects gestational diabetes in women of normal weight. Women who exercised had a lower chance of developing gestational diabetes and gained less weight during pregnancy. Exercise did not change the length of pregnancy, the baby's birth weight, or the chance of a caesarean birth.
keyPoints: Exercise during pregnancy was linked to a lower risk of gestational diabetes in normal-weight women (about 40% lower in the pooled results).
Women who exercised gained less weight during pregnancy.
Exercise made no significant difference to gestational age at birth or birth weight.
Exercise did not significantly change the odds of a caesarean section.

items.title: Prenatal ultrasound diagnosis and outcome of placenta previa accreta after cesarean delivery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies of nearly 3,900 pregnancies where the placenta was low-lying or covering the cervix (placenta previa) and the woman had already had at least one caesarean birth. About 8 in 100 of these pregnancies had placenta accreta, where the placenta grows too deeply into the womb wall. Ultrasound found most of these cases before birth when skilled operators did the scan. Most women with accreta in the studies with detailed data ended up having a hysterectomy at the time of caesarean birth.
keyPoints: Placenta accreta occurred in 8.4% of pregnancies with placenta previa and a previous caesarean; the rate was 4.1% after one caesarean and 13.3% after two or more.
Ultrasound detected about 91% of accreta cases before birth, and performed well when done by skilled operators.
A caesarean hysterectomy was performed in about 90% of cases with detailed management data.
The authors say a prenatal screening protocol is needed so delivery can be planned individually; no data were found on screening at routine mid-pregnancy scans in non-expert units.

items.title: Position in the second stage of labour for women without epidural anaesthesia
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 30 trials with about 9,000 women to compare upright positions (such as sitting, squatting or kneeling) with lying down during the pushing stage of labour, in women without an epidural. Upright positions were linked to fewer assisted births (such as forceps or vacuum) and fewer episiotomies, and possibly a slightly shorter pushing stage. They were also linked to more blood loss over 500 mL and possibly more second degree tears. The trials varied in quality, so the authors say results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Upright positions were linked to fewer assisted deliveries and fewer episiotomies compared with lying down.
The pushing stage was about 6 minutes shorter on average, but the evidence was very low quality and the difference was no longer clear when higher-risk trials were left out.
Upright positions were linked to more blood loss over 500 mL and possibly more second degree tears; there was no clear difference in caesarean rates or in third or fourth degree tears.
The authors say better-designed trials are needed to confirm the true benefits and risks of different birth positions.

items.title: Continuous support for women during childbirth
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 26 trials with nearly 16,000 women to see what happens when someone stays with a woman throughout labour, compared with usual care. Women with continuous support may be more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth and less likely to have a caesarean birth. They may also have shorter labours and be less likely to report negative feelings about their birth. Much of the evidence was rated low quality, and no harms were found.
keyPoints: Continuous support in labour increased spontaneous vaginal birth (average RR 1.08) and reduced caesarean birth (average RR 0.75), though this evidence was low quality.
Labours were about 0.69 hours shorter, and women were less likely to use pain relief medicines, have an instrumental birth (forceps or vacuum), or report negative feelings about their birth.
Babies were less likely to have a low five-minute Apgar score, with no clear effect on special care nursery admission or breastfeeding.
The review found no evidence of harms. Some subgroup results (such as a bigger caesarean reduction with a doula) were exploratory and should be read with caution.

items.title: Amnioinfusion for chorioamnionitis
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether adding fluid into the womb during labour (amnioinfusion) helps when a woman has chorioamnionitis, an infection of the membranes around the baby. Only one very small trial of 34 women was found, and it was at high risk of bias. There was no clear effect on womb infection after birth, newborn infection or caesarean rate, so the evidence is too limited to say whether it helps or harms.
keyPoints: Only one small trial (34 women) was found, so no firm conclusions can be drawn.
No clear effect was seen on womb infection after birth, newborn infection or caesarean section rate; this evidence was low quality.
Women who had amnioinfusion had a slightly lower temperature at delivery, possibly a cooling effect of the room temperature fluid rather than less infection.
The review can neither support nor refute use of amnioinfusion for chorioamnionitis outside clinical trials; larger trials are needed.

items.title: Effect of postoperative coffee consumption on gastrointestinal function after cesarean section, a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review combined 6 small trials (555 women) from Iran and Turkey looking at drinking coffee after a planned cesarean section. Women who drank coffee may have passed wind, had a bowel movement and had bowel sounds return sooner than women who had water or routine care. The effect was clearest when coffee started 2 hours after surgery rather than 8 hours. The authors say few studies were included and the evidence quality was low, so the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Coffee after a planned cesarean may shorten the time to first passing wind by about 2.75 hours.
Time to first bowel movement was about 3.20 hours shorter, and bowel sounds returned about 0.68 hours sooner.
The benefit was seen mainly when coffee began 2 hours after surgery rather than 8 hours.
Only 6 small trials were included and the quality of evidence was low.

items.title: Coffee intake after cesarean section and postoperative gastrointestinal recovery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled eight trials with 1,269 women who had a cesarean birth, comparing coffee with caffeine after surgery to water, decaf coffee or usual care. Women who drank caffeinated coffee may have passed gas and had a bowel movement sooner, felt less nausea, and left hospital a little earlier. The quality of the evidence was low to very low, and results varied a lot between studies, so the findings should be read with caution. The authors say more well-designed trials are needed.
keyPoints: Caffeinated coffee after cesarean was linked to passing gas about 5 hours sooner and having a bowel movement (defecation) about 3 hours sooner.
Nausea was less common with caffeinated coffee, and hospital stay was about 9 hours shorter on average.
There was no clear difference in time to first bowel movement, eating solid food, or vomiting.
The authors describe coffee as a possible simple, low-cost aid to recovery, but note the evidence is weak and more trials are needed.

items.title: The effects of coffee versus gum chewing after cesarean on bowel functions: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 20 trials (2,876 women) to see whether drinking coffee or chewing gum after a cesarean helps the bowels start working again. Both coffee and gum chewing shortened the time to first bowel movement and first passing of gas compared with doing nothing. Gum chewing also shortened hospital stay, reduced complications and improved satisfaction, while coffee did not shorten hospital stay. Results varied a lot between the gum chewing studies, and the authors concluded gum chewing was more effective overall, although the direct comparison of the two found no clear difference in bowel recovery times.
keyPoints: Coffee after cesarean shortened the time to first bowel movement (about 4.4 hours) and first passing of gas (about 4.6 hours) compared with no intervention.
Gum chewing shortened the time to first bowel movement, gas and bowel sounds, with larger average reductions, but the gum studies differed a lot from one another.
Gum chewing was linked to a shorter hospital stay, fewer complications and better patient satisfaction; coffee was not linked to a shorter stay.
The network comparison found no significant difference between coffee and gum chewing for time to first bowel movement, gas or bowel sounds.

items.title: Maternal Coffee Consumption During Pregnancy and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Offspring: A Case-Control Study and Meta-Analysis
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: Researchers looked at whether drinking coffee during pregnancy is linked to ADHD in children. They ran a case-control study in Egypt (176 mothers of children with ADHD and 504 mothers of children without) and then combined it with earlier studies. Both found that frequent coffee drinking in pregnancy was linked to a higher chance of ADHD in the child. The authors say this is an association only, and better studies are needed to show whether coffee is the cause.
keyPoints: In the Egyptian study, frequent coffee drinking in pregnancy was linked to higher odds of ADHD in children (OR 1.85), and the link held after extra adjustments.
Combining seven studies also showed higher ADHD risk with maternal coffee intake (OR 1.33).
The authors note that cause and effect is not proven and that safe amounts of coffee are still unclear.
They call for prospective studies that measure caffeine objectively, for example with biomarkers.

items.title: Relationship between caffeine intake and small for gestational age and preterm birth: a dose-response meta-analysis
items.source: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
items.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 22 studies to look at caffeine intake during pregnancy and two outcomes: babies born small for their gestational age (SGA) and preterm birth. Higher caffeine intake was linked to a higher chance of SGA, with each extra 100 mg of caffeine a day linked to a 13% greater risk. No reliable link was found between caffeine and preterm birth. The abstract does not rate the certainty of the evidence, and these studies show an association rather than proof of cause.
keyPoints: Higher caffeine intake in pregnancy was linked to a higher risk of small for gestational age (pooled estimate 1.28).
Each extra 100 mg of caffeine per day was associated with a 13% greater risk of SGA.
No reliable link was found between caffeine intake and preterm birth.
The review pooled 22 studies (15 cohort and 7 case-control).

items.title: Prenatal caffeine consumption and neurobehavioral disorders - A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 14 observational studies on whether drinking caffeine during pregnancy is linked to behaviour, learning or attention problems (like ADHD) in children. Seven studies suggested a possible link, six found no clear effect, and one found fewer peer problems. The studies were mixed in quality and affected by other factors, so the evidence is very uncertain and cannot show that caffeine causes these problems.
keyPoints: Of 14 studies, 7 suggested a possible link between caffeine in pregnancy and neurobehavioral or development problems.
6 studies found no significant effect, and 1 found fewer peer problems with caffeine exposure.
The studies had a moderate risk of bias and the certainty of evidence was rated very low.
The evidence is not enough to confirm that caffeine in pregnancy leads to neurobehavioral disorders.

items.title: Maternal smoking, consumption of alcohol, and caffeinated beverages during pregnancy and the risk of childhood brain tumors: a meta-analysis of observational studies
items.summary: This review pooled results from many observational studies to see whether smoking, alcohol or caffeinated drinks during pregnancy are linked to brain tumors in children. Drinking caffeinated drinks in pregnancy, especially coffee, was linked to a somewhat higher chance of childhood brain tumors. Passive smoking was also linked to higher risk, while active smoking and alcohol showed no clear link. The authors say stronger studies that follow mothers and children over time are still needed.
keyPoints: Caffeinated drinks in pregnancy were linked to a higher risk of childhood brain tumors (OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.07-1.26), especially coffee (OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.00-1.38).
Passive smoking was linked to higher risk (OR 1.12), but active smoking was not (OR 1.00).
No significant link was found between alcohol in pregnancy and childhood brain tumors.
The authors call for more prospective cohort studies to give a higher level of evidence.

items.title: The association between antenatal coffee consumption and preeclampsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled seven studies to see whether drinking more coffee during pregnancy is linked to preeclampsia, a pregnancy condition involving high blood pressure. Women who drank the most coffee had somewhat higher odds of preeclampsia. But the link disappeared or weakened when the analysis was limited to better-quality studies or to women without chronic high blood pressure. The authors conclude that the link is still unclear.
keyPoints: Across seven studies, the highest coffee intake was linked to higher odds of preeclampsia (pooled OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.86).
The link was no longer statistically significant after removing one cross-sectional study, excluding women with chronic high blood pressure, or excluding low-quality studies.
All the studies looked back in time (six case-control and one cross-sectional), which limits how firm the findings are.
The authors say the association remains inconclusive and call for prospective cohort studies.

items.title: Maternal caffeine consumption during pregnancy and risk of low birth weight: a dose-response meta-analysis of cohort studies
items.source: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
items.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
items.summary: This review pooled results from seven cohort studies to look at whether caffeine intake during pregnancy is linked to low birth weight (a baby born under 2500 g). Women who had more caffeine had a higher chance of having a baby with low birth weight. Each extra 100 mg of caffeine a day was linked to a small rise in that chance. These studies show a link, not proof that caffeine is the cause.
keyPoints: Higher maternal caffeine intake was linked to a higher risk of low birth weight (RR 1.70, 95% CI 1.19-2.43).
Each extra 100 mg of caffeine per day was linked to a 12% higher risk of low birth weight (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.03-1.22).
The link between caffeine and low birth weight was not a straight line, according to the dose-response analysis.
The review combined seven cohort studies, and earlier studies on this question had given conflicting results.

items.title: Mendelian randomization study of maternal coffee consumption and its influence on birthweight, stillbirth, miscarriage, gestational age and pre-term birth
items.summary: Researchers used a genetic method (Mendelian randomization) to test whether drinking coffee itself causes pregnancy problems, since randomized trials on this are lacking. They used genetic and health data from very large groups of women and babies. They found no change in the risk of miscarriage, stillbirth or preterm birth linked to coffee, and no effect on length of pregnancy. Higher coffee intake was linked to slightly higher birthweight, but the size of this effect was not consistent between analyses.
keyPoints: No change in risk of sporadic miscarriage, stillbirth or preterm birth was linked to coffee consumption.
No effect on gestational age (length of pregnancy) was found.
Higher coffee consumption was associated with higher birthweight, but the size of the effect was inconsistent.
The authors conclude coffee during pregnancy might not itself cause these adverse outcomes.
keywords: can i drink coffee while pregnant

items.title: Maternal caffeine consumption during pregnancy and offspring cord blood DNA methylation: an epigenome-wide association study meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers looked at whether caffeine from coffee, tea and cola during pregnancy changes the way genes are switched on or off (DNA methylation) in babies at birth. They combined data from six European studies covering 3,725 mother-baby pairs. They found very few changes and little evidence that caffeine affects this process in the womb. The study may not have been large enough to spot very small effects, and the mothers drank only small amounts of caffeine.
keyPoints: Only one DNA methylation change was linked to total caffeine intake and one to cola intake, out of the whole genome.
This gives little evidence that caffeine in pregnancy changes babies' DNA methylation at birth.
Mothers in the study had low caffeine intake, so results might differ in people who drink a lot.
Current guidelines advise limiting caffeine to under 200 mg a day, though there is no clear proof of its effects on human development.

items.title: Prenatal smoking, alcohol and caffeine exposure and offspring externalizing disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 63 studies on whether smoking, alcohol or caffeine during pregnancy cause behaviour problems in children, such as ADHD, conduct disorder and oppositional defiant disorder. For caffeine, the studies were mostly about ADHD and did not support a causal effect. Smoking also showed no clear causal link to ADHD in the largest, most carefully designed analysis, and alcohol results were mixed. The authors say more research is needed, especially on caffeine and alcohol and on conduct and oppositional defiant disorders.
keyPoints: Studies of caffeine in pregnancy were mainly limited to ADHD and do not support a causal effect.
Findings on caffeine and conduct disorder or oppositional defiant disorder need more research.
The largest analysis found no clear causal link between prenatal smoking and ADHD in children.
Alcohol studies gave inconsistent results, so no strong conclusions about causality can be drawn.

items.title: The association between caffeine exposure during pregnancy and risk of gestational hypertension/preeclampsia: A meta-analysis and systematical review
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research
items.summary: This review pooled results from ten observational studies covering almost 115,000 pregnant women. It looked at whether caffeine during pregnancy is linked to gestational hypertension (high blood pressure in pregnancy) or preeclampsia. No significant link was found, including when low-to-moderate and high caffeine amounts were each compared with none or the lowest intake.
keyPoints: No significant link was found between caffeine during pregnancy and gestational hypertension.
No significant link was found between caffeine during pregnancy and preeclampsia.
Results were similar for low-to-moderate and for high caffeine amounts compared with none or the lowest intake.
The review combined ten observational studies with 114,984 pregnant women.

items.title: The association between caffeine and alcohol consumption and IVF/ICSI outcomes: A systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies of 26,922 women and/or their partners having IVF or ICSI fertility treatment. It looked at whether caffeine or alcohol intake was linked to getting pregnant or having a baby. Caffeine intake, in women or men, was not linked to pregnancy or live birth rates. Alcohol was linked to lower chances of pregnancy (women) or live birth (men) once weekly intake was above 84 g.
keyPoints: Neither women's nor men's caffeine intake was significantly linked to pregnancy rate or live birth rate after IVF/ICSI.
Women's alcohol intake above 84 g per week was linked to a lower chance of pregnancy after IVF/ICSI.
Men's alcohol intake above 84 g per week was linked to a lower chance of their partner having a live birth after IVF/ICSI.
Compared with not drinking, 84 g of alcohol a week was linked to a 7% lower pregnancy chance in women and a 9% lower live birth chance for partners of men.

items.title: Association of maternal caffeine intake during pregnancy with low birth weight, childhood overweight, and obesity: a meta-analysis of cohort studies
items.summary: This review pooled results from 15 studies that followed about 102,000 pregnant women. Women who had the most caffeine during pregnancy were more likely to have a baby with low birth weight, and their children were more likely to be overweight or obese. The authors say the studies show an association, not proof of cause, and that more research on how this might happen is needed before recommending complete avoidance of caffeine in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Highest versus lowest caffeine intake in pregnancy was linked to a higher risk of low birth weight (relative risk 1.33).
Each extra 100 mg of caffeine per day was linked to a small rise in low birth weight risk (relative risk 1.07).
Highest caffeine intake was also linked to higher risk of childhood overweight and obesity (relative risk 1.39).
The authors suggest more research on possible mechanisms before advising complete avoidance of caffeine in pregnancy.

items.title: Maternal diet and offspring telomere length: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at seven studies on what mothers eat or their nutrient levels during pregnancy and the length of telomeres (a marker of cell ageing) in their babies. Higher maternal folate and vitamin D levels, and higher dietary caffeine intake, were linked with longer telomeres in the babies. Other dietary intakes, such as carbohydrate, omega-3 fats, vitamin C or sodium, were not linked. The authors describe the evidence as limited but suggestive, and say more and larger studies are needed.
keyPoints: Higher maternal blood folate and vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D3) were linked with longer offspring telomere length.
Higher maternal dietary caffeine intake was also linked with longer offspring telomere length.
Dietary intake of carbohydrate, folate, omega-3 fats, vitamin C or sodium was not linked with telomere length.
The evidence is limited, and larger long-term studies of pregnant women are needed.

items.title: Smoking, alcohol and coffee consumption and pregnancy loss: a Mendelian randomization investigation
items.summary: This study used genetic data from two large groups of women to look at whether smoking, alcohol and coffee might cause pregnancy loss. Genes linked to starting smoking were tied to a higher chance of pregnancy loss. Genes linked to drinking more alcohol or coffee were not clearly tied to pregnancy loss. The authors say this points to smoking, but not moderate alcohol or coffee, as a possible cause.
keyPoints: Genetic predisposition to smoking was linked to a higher risk of pregnancy loss (combined odds ratio 1.31).
No significant link was found between genetically predicted coffee consumption and pregnancy loss (odds ratio 0.96).
No significant link was found between genetically predicted alcohol consumption and pregnancy loss (odds ratio 1.09).
The authors conclude that moderate alcohol and coffee intake were not shown to be linked to pregnancy loss.

items.title: Relationship between caffeine intake and infertility: a systematic review of controlled clinical studies
items.summary: This review pulled together four studies (one cohort and three case-control) with nearly 13,000 people to see whether caffeine intake is linked to infertility. Low, medium and high amounts of caffeine did not appear to raise the risk of infertility. The quality of the evidence was low, so the authors say the conclusion should be treated with caution.
keyPoints: Four studies with 12,912 participants were included in the review.
Low, medium and high caffeine intake did not appear to increase the risk of infertility.
The evidence for every comparison was rated low quality.
The authors advise that the conclusion be treated with caution.

items.title: Effects of maternal caffeine consumption on the breastfed child: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether caffeine that a breastfeeding mother consumes affects her breastfed baby. Only five small studies were found, and their quality was limited. A few showed no clear effect on a baby's heart rate or sleep, while others hinted at links with colic or eczema, but it is unclear whether caffeine was the cause. Overall, there is not enough good evidence yet to give firm advice on caffeine while breastfeeding.
keyPoints: Caffeine passes into breastmilk, but the evidence on its effects on breastfed babies is scant, limited in quality and inconclusive.
Small studies that looked directly at maternal caffeine found no significant effects on the baby's 24-hour heart rate, sleep time or frequent night waking.
One study found a lower rate of full breastfeeding at 6 months postpartum.
Chocolate and coffee intake was linked with more infant colic and worse eczema in two studies, but it is questionable whether caffeine was the cause.

items.title: Systematic review of the potential adverse effects of caffeine consumption in healthy adults, pregnant women, adolescents, and children
items.summary: This systematic review looked at research published from 2001 to mid-2015 on whether caffeine causes harm in healthy adults, pregnant women, teenagers and children. After weighing study quality and consistency, it found that up to 300 mg of caffeine a day in healthy pregnant women is generally not linked to harm to reproduction or development. Information on children and teenagers was limited. The authors say more research is needed on people who may be more sensitive to caffeine.
keyPoints: Up to 300 mg of caffeine a day in healthy pregnant women is generally not associated with adverse reproductive and developmental effects.
Up to 400 mg a day in healthy adults is not associated with overt harm to the heart, behavior, bones, or reproduction and development.
Little data exists for children and teenagers; 2.5 mg per kg of body weight per day still seems an appropriate limit.
Future research should look at groups who may be at higher risk, such as people with existing health conditions.

items.title: Coffee, Caffeine, and Health Outcomes: An Umbrella Review
items.summary: This review pulled together results from many earlier studies on coffee and caffeine and a wide range of health outcomes. Coffee was linked to a probably lower risk of several cancers (breast, colorectal, endometrial), heart disease, Parkinson's disease and type 2 diabetes. Caffeine was linked to a probably higher risk of pregnancy loss, and to a rise in blood pressure in short-term trials. The authors concluded that coffee can be part of a healthful diet.
keyPoints: Coffee was linked to a probably lower risk of breast, colorectal, colon, endometrial and prostate cancers, cardiovascular disease, Parkinson's disease and type 2 diabetes.
Caffeine intake was linked to a probably increased risk of pregnancy loss in the observational studies reviewed.
In short-term trials, caffeine raised blood pressure and coffee raised blood fats, though the blood fat result varied a lot between studies.
The authors concluded that coffee can be part of a healthful diet.

items.title: Coffee consumption and health: umbrella review of meta-analyses of multiple health outcomes
items.summary: This large review pulled together results from 201 earlier studies of coffee and health outcomes in adults. For most outcomes, coffee drinking was linked to benefit more often than harm, with the biggest gains at three to four cups a day. In pregnancy the picture was different: high coffee intake, compared with low or none, was linked to low birth weight, preterm birth and pregnancy loss. These are links seen in observational studies, so they do not prove coffee is the cause.
keyPoints: High versus low or no coffee in pregnancy was linked to low birth weight (odds ratio 1.31), preterm birth (1.22 first trimester, 1.12 second trimester) and pregnancy loss (1.46).
Outside pregnancy, most other harmful links were largely explained away once smoking was accounted for.
Coffee seems generally safe at usual intakes in the general adult population, with most benefit seen at three to four cups a day.
Coffee drinking was also linked to fracture risk in women but not in men, and robust randomised trials are needed to tell if the links are causal.

items.title: Maternal caffeine intake during pregnancy and risk of pregnancy loss: a categorical and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 14 studies, covering over 130,000 people, to see whether caffeine in pregnancy is linked to pregnancy loss. Higher caffeine intake was linked to a higher risk, while low and moderate intake showed no clear link. The authors say the results are inconclusive, partly because of possible publication bias and because smoking and pregnancy symptoms may not have been fully accounted for.
keyPoints: Low intake (50-149 mg a day) showed no clear increase in pregnancy loss, and moderate intake (150-349 mg a day) was not clearly different from none or very low intake.
High intake (350-699 mg a day) was linked to 40% higher risk and very high intake (700 mg or more a day) to 72% higher risk, compared with no or very low intake.
Each extra 100 mg of caffeine a day (about one cup of coffee) was linked to a 7% higher risk of pregnancy loss.
The authors call the findings inconclusive but say following guidelines to avoid high caffeine intake in pregnancy appears prudent.

items.title: Maternal Coffee Consumption During Pregnancy and Neural Tube Defects in Offspring: A Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This study combined results from seven earlier studies (six case-control studies and one cohort study) to see whether drinking coffee during pregnancy is linked to neural tube defects in babies, such as spina bifida. The researchers found no significant link between coffee drinking and neural tube defects overall, or spina bifida specifically.
keyPoints: Seven studies were pooled: six case-control studies and one cohort study.
Coffee drinking in pregnancy was not significantly linked to neural tube defects overall.
No significant link was found for the spina bifida subtype either.

items.title: A meta-analysis of risk of pregnancy loss and caffeine and coffee consumption during pregnancy
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pooled results from 26 studies (20 on caffeine and 8 on coffee) to see whether caffeine or coffee in pregnancy is linked to pregnancy loss. Both were linked to a higher risk of pregnancy loss, and the risk rose as intake went up. The authors concluded that caffeine and coffee during pregnancy seem to increase the risk of pregnancy loss. The abstract describes an association found in earlier studies, which had been inconsistent, and does not report a certainty rating.
keyPoints: Higher caffeine intake was linked to a higher risk of pregnancy loss (odds ratio 1.32, 95% CI 1.24-1.40).
Higher coffee intake was also linked to a higher risk (odds ratio 1.11, 95% CI 1.02-1.21).
Risk of pregnancy loss rose by 19% for every extra 150 mg of caffeine per day.
Risk rose by 8% for every extra two cups of coffee per day.

items.title: Effects of restricted caffeine intake by mother on fetal, neonatal and pregnancy outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for randomised trials testing whether cutting down caffeine in pregnancy changes outcomes for mothers and babies. Only two trials qualified, and only one gave usable results. In that trial, regular coffee drinkers (3+ cups a day) who switched to decaf in the second and third trimester had babies with similar birthweight, similar rates of preterm birth and similar rates of being small for gestational age. The evidence was low quality, so the review could not confirm or rule out a benefit of avoiding caffeine.
keyPoints: Only two trials met the review's criteria, and just one contributed data.
Cutting caffeine by about 182 mg a day (by switching to decaf) did not change birthweight, preterm birth or small-for-gestational-age rates in that trial.
Evidence for birthweight and preterm birth was low quality because of the small sample and wide confidence intervals.
