The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to confirm or refute that avoiding caffeine affects pregnancy outcomes, and call for better double-blinded trials.

items.title: Maternal Caffeine Consumption during Pregnancy and Risk of Low Birth Weight: A Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 12 studies (8 cohort and 4 case-control) to see whether caffeine during pregnancy is linked to low birth weight. They found that women with the highest caffeine intake had higher odds of having a baby with low birth weight than women with the lowest intake. The risk went up steadily as caffeine intake rose, by about 3% for every extra 100 mg a day (roughly 1 cup of coffee or 2 cups of tea). These were observational studies, so they show an association rather than proving caffeine is the cause.
keyPoints: Highest versus lowest caffeine intake in pregnancy was linked to higher odds of low birth weight (pooled odds ratio 1.38).
Each extra 100 mg of caffeine a day (about 1 cup of coffee or 2 cups of tea) was linked to a 3.0% rise in the odds of low birth weight.
The risk appeared to rise in a straight line as caffeine intake increased.
Results varied moderately between studies, and there was no sign of publication bias.

items.title: Maternal and childhood consumption of coffee, tea and cola beverages in association with childhood leukemia: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 case-control studies (3,649 children with leukemia and 5,705 comparison children) to look at whether a mother's coffee, tea or cola intake was linked to childhood leukemia. High maternal coffee intake was linked to higher rates of two types of childhood leukemia, and cola showed a similar link. Tea intake was linked to slightly lower leukemia rates. These studies show associations only and cannot prove that a drink caused the leukemia; the authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: High maternal coffee intake was linked to more acute lymphoblastic leukemia (OR 1.43) and acute myeloid leukemia (OR 2.52).
Any or low to moderate maternal cola intake was also linked to more leukemia overall and acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
Low to moderate tea intake was linked to slightly lower leukemia risk overall (OR 0.85), though the trend was not significant.
A child's own cola drinking showed no link to leukemia.

items.title: Effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists on kidney and cardiovascular disease outcomes: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 11 large trials (about 85,000 people, roughly 29,000 of them women) that compared GLP-1 medicines, such as those used for type 2 diabetes and weight loss, with placebo. In people with type 2 diabetes, the medicines lowered the risk of serious kidney problems, heart attack, stroke, and death. Serious side effects were no more common than with placebo, but more people stopped taking the medicine because of side effects. The abstract does not report results for women separately.
keyPoints: In people with type 2 diabetes, GLP-1 medicines reduced a combined measure of serious kidney outcomes by 18% compared with placebo.
They reduced major heart events (heart-related death, non-fatal heart attack or stroke) by 13% and death from any cause by 12%.
Results were similar when a trial in people with heart disease and excess weight but without diabetes was included.
Serious adverse events, including pancreatitis and severe low blood sugar, were not more common, but stopping treatment because of side effects was more frequent with GLP-1 medicines.

items.title: Collaboration on the optimal timing of anticoagulation after ischaemic stroke and atrial fibrillation: a systematic review and prospective individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (CATALYST)
items.summary: Researchers combined data from four trials of 5,441 people who had a stroke caused by a blood clot and also had an irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation. They compared starting a blood-thinning tablet (a direct oral anticoagulant) within 4 days of the stroke with starting it 5 or more days later. Starting early meant fewer repeat strokes in the first 30 days, and there was no sign of more bleeding in the brain. About 45% of participants were women, but the results were not reported separately for women.
keyPoints: Within 30 days, the main outcome (repeat clot stroke, brain bleed with symptoms, or unclassified stroke) happened in 2.1% of those who started early and 3.0% of those who started later.
Repeat clot-related stroke was lower with early treatment: 1.7% versus 2.6%.
Symptomatic bleeding in the brain was the same in both groups: 0.4% each.
The authors say the findings support starting these tablets within 4 days in clinical practice.

items.title: Clopidogrel versus aspirin for secondary prevention of coronary artery disease: a systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis
items.summary: This study pooled data from seven randomised trials covering about 29,000 people who already had coronary artery disease, most of whom had had a stent or an acute coronary syndrome. It compared two blood-thinning medicines taken on their own, clopidogrel and aspirin, to prevent heart attack, stroke or death from heart disease. People taking clopidogrel had fewer of these events than those taking aspirin, and there was no clear difference in major bleeding or in deaths. The authors conclude clopidogrel may be the better choice for long-term prevention in people with established coronary artery disease.
keyPoints: Clopidogrel was linked to fewer heart attacks, strokes or cardiovascular deaths than aspirin (hazard ratio 0.86).
Major bleeding was similar between the two medicines.
Overall death rates did not differ between the groups.
The authors support using clopidogrel in preference to aspirin for secondary prevention in established coronary artery disease.

items.title: Tranexamic acid for postpartum bleeding: a systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
items.summary: Researchers combined data from five large, well-run trials involving over 54,000 women giving birth to see if tranexamic acid, a medicine that helps blood clot, reduces dangerous bleeding after birth. Life-threatening bleeding was less common in women who got the medicine (0.65%) than in those who got a placebo (0.85%). Blood clot problems were equally rare in both groups (0.2%). The authors do not suggest giving it to every woman who gives birth, but say it could be considered earlier for women at high risk of death from bleeding.
keyPoints: Life-threatening bleeding after birth occurred in 0.65% of women given tranexamic acid versus 0.85% given placebo.
No difference was found in blood clots (thromboembolic events): 0.2% in both groups.
The benefit did not clearly differ by type of birth, anaemia, underlying bleeding risk, or timing of the dose.
The authors do not recommend routine use for all births but suggest considering it early for women at high risk of death.

items.title: Adherence to CPAP Treatment and the Risk of Recurrent Cardiovascular Events: A Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined data from three trials of CPAP (a breathing machine worn at night) in 4186 adults who had both heart disease and obstructive sleep apnea. Overall, people offered CPAP had about the same risk of another heart attack, stroke or similar event as those given usual care. But people who used CPAP well, for at least 4 hours a night, had a lower risk of these repeat events. Most participants (82%) were men, so results may apply less clearly to women.
keyPoints: Overall, offering CPAP did not change the risk of repeat heart or stroke events compared with usual care.
People who used CPAP for at least 4 hours a day had about a 31% lower risk of repeat events.
Average CPAP use in the trials was only about 3 hours a day, so many people did not use it enough.
The authors suggest sticking with treatment is a key factor in preventing further heart problems in people with sleep apnea.

items.title: Replacing salt with low-sodium salt substitutes (LSSS) for cardiovascular health in adults, children and pregnant women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 26 trials (about 35,000 adults) comparing low-sodium salt substitutes, which swap some of the sodium for potassium, with regular salt. In adults, the substitutes probably lower blood pressure slightly and probably cause slightly fewer non-fatal heart problems and heart-related deaths. They also probably raise blood potassium slightly, though the trials found little to no difference in high potassium (hyperkalaemia) overall. No studies in pregnant women were found, and the evidence in children is very uncertain.
keyPoints: In adults, low-sodium salt substitutes probably lower blood pressure slightly (about 4.8 mmHg for the top number and 2.4 mmHg for the bottom number), based on moderate-certainty evidence.
They probably slightly reduce non-fatal stroke, non-fatal acute coronary syndrome and cardiovascular deaths in adults.
They probably raise blood potassium slightly, but may make little to no difference to the risk of hyperkalaemia; all trials excluded people for whom extra potassium could be harmful.
No studies in pregnant women were found, and evidence for children is very uncertain, so no conclusions can be drawn for these groups.

items.title: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis for women at risk during pregnancy and the early postnatal period
items.summary: This review pulled together 29 trials (3839 women) testing treatments to prevent blood clots, such as heparin injections and compression stockings, in women at higher risk during pregnancy and just after birth. Blood clots are rare but can be serious. The evidence was very uncertain, so the review could not say clearly whether these treatments help or cause harm. One finding was that low molecular weight heparin led to fewer people stopping treatment because of side effects than unfractionated heparin, but this too rests on very low-certainty evidence.
keyPoints: Blood clots in pregnancy and after birth are rare but are a major cause of illness and death for mothers.
All the key findings were rated very low-certainty, mainly because of study limitations and too few events, so benefits and harms remain unclear.
Fewer women stopped treatment because of side effects with low molecular weight heparin than with unfractionated heparin (very low-certainty evidence).
The authors say larger, high-quality studies are needed, and that good registry data analyses may help because big trials are unlikely to be funded.

items.title: Exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation for coronary heart disease
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 85 trials with over 23,000 people who have coronary heart disease to see whether exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation helps. It found that rehab lowers the chance of a heart attack and of being admitted to hospital, and may slightly improve quality of life. Longer-term, it may also reduce deaths from heart causes. Fewer than 15% of participants were women, so the findings reflect mostly men.
keyPoints: Within 6 to 12 months, exercise-based rehab reduced the risk of heart attack (high certainty evidence) and of any hospital admission (moderate certainty evidence).
It likely makes a small reduction in deaths from any cause, and made little to no difference to bypass surgery or stent procedures.
Over longer follow-up, rehab may reduce deaths from heart disease and heart attacks.
Women were still a small share of trial participants (under 15%), so more trials representing women and everyday care are needed.

items.title: SGLT2 inhibitors for primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular and renal outcomes in type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cardiovascular outcome trials
items.summary: This review pooled three large trials of SGLT2 inhibitors, a type of diabetes medicine, in more than 34,000 people with type 2 diabetes. The medicines lowered the risk of major heart events by about 11%, but this benefit was seen only in people who already had heart or blood vessel disease. They also cut the risk of heart failure hospitalisation or cardiovascular death by 23%, and kidney disease progression by 45%, whether or not people had existing heart disease.
keyPoints: Major heart events (heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death) were reduced by 11%, with benefit only in people with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
The risk of cardiovascular death or hospital stays for heart failure fell by 23%, with similar benefit with or without existing heart disease or heart failure history.
Progression of kidney disease was reduced by 45%, regardless of existing heart disease.
Benefit varied by kidney function: bigger reductions in heart failure hospitalisations but smaller reductions in kidney disease progression in people with more severe kidney disease.

items.title: European Stroke Organization guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of cerebral venous thrombosis - endorsed by the European Academy of Neurology
items.summary: The European Stroke Organization updated its guideline on cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT), a type of blood clot in the veins that drain the brain. It covers how CVT is diagnosed and treated, and includes advice for women who have had CVT before. The guideline says women who have had CVT should avoid contraceptives containing oestrogen, and that later pregnancies are considered safe, with preventive blood-thinning injections (low-molecular-weight heparin) considered during pregnancy and after birth. The authors say more research is needed to strengthen many of these recommendations.
keyPoints: MRI or CT angiography is suggested to confirm a CVT diagnosis.
Women who have had a previous CVT are advised to avoid contraceptives containing oestrogen.
Later pregnancies are suggested to be safe, but preventive low-molecular-weight heparin should be considered throughout pregnancy and the weeks after birth.
Blood-thinning treatment by injection or drip is recommended in acute CVT, and low-molecular-weight heparin is suggested over newer oral blood thinners.

items.title: Amniotic fluid embolism: diagnosis and management
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine reviewed the research on amniotic fluid embolism, a rare and serious emergency in which a woman suddenly collapses during labor or soon after birth. The guideline says there is no lab test that can confirm it, so doctors diagnose it from the signs. It sets out how care teams should respond, including immediate resuscitation, support for breathing and blood pressure, and fast treatment of bleeding.
keyPoints: Amniotic fluid embolism should be considered when a woman in labor or just after delivery suddenly has heart and breathing collapse.
No specific lab test can confirm or rule it out, so it remains a clinical diagnosis.
If the heart stops and the baby is 23 weeks or more, immediate delivery is recommended along with high-quality CPR.
Care should involve a multidisciplinary team, support for oxygen and blood pressure, avoiding too much fluid, and early checks and treatment for blood clotting problems and bleeding.

items.title: Association Between Lowering LDL-C and Cardiovascular Risk Reduction Among Different Therapeutic Interventions: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 49 trials with over 312,000 people (24% women) to see how lowering LDL cholesterol, often called 'bad' cholesterol, relates to heart and blood vessel events. Statins and several other treatments that work the same way gave a similar drop in risk for each amount of LDL lowered. People who reached lower LDL levels had fewer heart attacks and coronary deaths. The results are not reported separately for women.
keyPoints: For every 1 mmol/L (38.7 mg/dL) drop in LDL cholesterol, the risk of major vascular events fell by about 23% with statins and about 25% with similar non-statin treatments.
Lower achieved LDL levels were linked to fewer heart attacks and coronary deaths, both in people without heart disease and in those who already had it.
Fibrates lowered risk more than expected, while CETP inhibitors lowered risk less than expected from their LDL effect.
Only 24% of participants were women, and results were not broken down by sex.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of LDL-lowering therapy among men and women: meta-analysis of individual data from 174,000 participants in 27 randomised trials
items.summary: This study pooled data from 27 trials with about 174,000 people, including nearly 47,000 women, to see whether cholesterol-lowering statin drugs work as well in women as in men. For the same drop in LDL ("bad") cholesterol, women and men had similar reductions in heart attacks, strokes and other major vascular events. Statins did not raise the risk of cancer or of deaths from non-heart causes in either sex. The authors conclude that at the same level of heart disease risk, statins work about equally well in women and men.
keyPoints: Statins lowered LDL cholesterol by similar amounts in women and men.
Major vascular events fell by about 16% per 1.0 mmol/L LDL reduction in women and about 22% in men, a difference that was not statistically significant.
Benefits were also similar for women and men at lower predicted heart risk (under 10% over 5 years).
No harmful effect on cancer rates or non-heart deaths was seen, and overall death rates fell in both women and men.

items.title: Self-collected vaginal specimens for human papillomavirus testing and guidance on screening exit: An update to the American Cancer Society cervical cancer screening guideline
items.summary: The American Cancer Society updated its cervical screening guideline for people at average risk. Self-collected vaginal samples for HPV testing are now an accepted option, though a sample taken by a clinician is still preferred. The update also changes when it is safe to stop screening, because cervical cancer remains common in people over 65.
keyPoints: For ages 25-65 at average risk, a clinician-collected cervical sample for HPV testing is preferred, and a self-collected vaginal sample is acceptable.
After a negative self-collected HPV test, repeat testing is recommended in 3 years; after a negative clinician-collected test, it is every 5 years.
To stop screening, a person at average risk should have negative HPV tests (preferred) or negative HPV and cytology co-tests at both age 60 and age 65.
Self-collection can help people who face barriers to screening, but most who test HPV-positive need extra follow-up, and long-term real-world data are limited.

items.title: Applying Results of Extended Genotyping to Management of Positive Cervicovaginal Human Papillomavirus Test Results: Enduring Guidelines
items.source: Enduring Consensus Cervical Cancer Screening and Management Guidelines Committee
items.journal: Journal of Lower Genital Tract Disease
items.organisation: Enduring Consensus Cervical Cancer Screening and Management Guidelines Committee
items.summary: A US consensus committee set out how doctors should act on a positive HPV test when the lab also reports which HPV type was found. HPV 16 and 18 carry the highest risk and lead to a colposcopy, a closer look at the cervix. Other higher-risk types usually lead to a follow-up cytology (cell) test or a special stain test, while a few lower-risk types can be rechecked in a year.
keyPoints: A positive test for HPV 16 or 18 is followed by colposcopy.
For HPV 45, 33/58, 31, 52, 35/39/68 or 51 (without 16 or 18), follow-up with a cytology or dual stain test is recommended.
For HPV 56/59/66 alone, repeat HPV testing in 1 year is recommended when screening with HPV testing alone, and when cotesting with a normal, ASC-US or low-grade cytology result.
If there is a history of high-grade cell changes or treatment for CIN2 or worse, the 2019 guidelines are used instead of these genotype-based steps.

items.title: Self-Collected Vaginal Specimens for HPV Testing: Recommendations From the Enduring Consensus Cervical Cancer Screening and Management Guidelines Committee
items.source: Enduring Consensus Cervical Cancer Screening and Management Guidelines Committee
items.journal: Journal of Lower Genital Tract Disease
items.organisation: Enduring Consensus Cervical Cancer Screening and Management Guidelines Committee
items.summary: A US expert committee wrote guidance on using a swab you collect yourself from the vagina for HPV testing as part of cervical cancer screening. For people without symptoms and at average risk, a sample taken by a clinician from the cervix is still preferred, but a self-collected vaginal sample is acceptable. The committee says self-collection widens screening options and could help people who are not currently getting screened.
keyPoints: For routine HPV screening in people without symptoms and at average risk, clinician-collected cervical samples are preferred and self-collected vaginal samples are acceptable.
After an HPV-negative result on a self-collected sample, repeat testing in 3 years is recommended.

A positive test for HPV 16 or 18 should be followed by colposcopy with cytology and biopsies; other high-risk types are followed by further clinician-collected testing or repeat testing in 1 year, depending on the type.
Little data exist on self-collection for follow-up after abnormal results, colposcopy or treatment, so clinician-collected cervical samples are preferred in those situations.

items.title: The Burden of HPV Infections and HPV-Related Diseases Among People With HIV: A Systematic Literature Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 221 studies published between 2018 and mid-2023 on HPV infection and HPV-related disease in people with HIV. People with HIV had more HPV infections and more HPV-related diseases than people without HIV. Women with HIV had up to six times the rate of new cervical cancer, and the review calls for better HPV vaccine delivery and uptake in this group, for example alongside routine HIV care.
keyPoints: People with HIV had higher rates of HPV infection and HPV-related disease than people without HIV.
New cervical cancer was up to six times more common in women with HIV than in women without HIV.
The most common high-risk HPV types linked to disease were HPV16, 18, 52 and 58, which are covered by HPV vaccines; HPV35 was also common in people of African descent.
The authors call for stronger HPV vaccine delivery and uptake in people with HIV, potentially by combining it with routine HIV care.

items.title: Factors that influence caregivers' and adolescents' views and practices regarding human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination for adolescents: a qualitative evidence synthesis
items.summary: This review pulled together 71 qualitative studies from around the world to understand why parents or carers and teenagers do or do not accept HPV vaccination. It found that many things shape these views, not just how much people know about the vaccine. The review authors lowered their confidence in some findings because of how studies were run or gaps in whose views were included.
keyPoints: Views on HPV vaccination are shaped by eight themes, including knowledge, perceived risks and benefits, family decision-making, trust in institutions, cultural beliefs and access to vaccination services.
Social, political, economic, structural and moral factors matter as well as individual knowledge.
Programmes that tried to raise uptake mostly focused on knowledge and risks and benefits, leaving other influences largely unaddressed.
The authors say tailoring efforts to the local setting could make vaccination programmes more acceptable and effective.

items.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination in women with conisation
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether getting the HPV vaccine around the time of cervical conisation (a procedure to remove precancerous cells from the cervix) helps prevent precancerous changes from coming back. Across 13 studies, vaccination may reduce the chance of high-grade cervical changes (CIN 2 or worse). However, most of the evidence comes from non-randomised studies with serious risk of bias, so confidence in the results is low. Only two randomised trials exist, and evidence on other outcomes, including cervical cancer, was very uncertain.
keyPoints: HPV vaccination around the time of conisation may lower the risk of CIN 2+ (high-grade precancerous changes) compared with no vaccination.
Results for CIN 3+ varied between studies, and evidence for cervical cancer and persistent HPV infection was very uncertain.
One trial reported minor local reactions such as redness and rash, headache, and severe allergies in about 1% of women.
The authors say more randomised trials with a placebo group are needed to get stronger evidence.

items.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination for the prevention of cervical cancer and other HPV-related diseases: a network meta-analysis
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 60 randomised trials with over 157,000 people to see whether HPV vaccines are safe and prevent HPV-related disease. Vaccination lowered the risk of cervical pre-cancer and genital warts in young women, and no safety concerns showed up. The trials were too short for cancers to develop, so cervical cancer itself could not be measured, and there was no pre-cancer data for people vaccinated under age 15.
keyPoints: In females aged 15 to 25, HPV vaccination reduced cervical pre-cancer (CIN2+): by about 30% overall and by about 60% for the HPV types the vaccine targets (moderate certainty).
Anogenital warts were much less common after vaccination, about 25 fewer cases per 1000 people (high certainty), and fewer people needed treatment for HPV-related pre-cancer (moderate certainty).
Serious side effects were no more common in vaccinated groups than in control groups (high certainty).
No data were available on cervical cancer or other cancers, and none on pre-cancer outcomes for vaccination under age 15.

items.title: Effects of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programmes on community rates of HPV-related disease and harms from vaccination
items.summary: This large Cochrane review looked at 225 studies covering over 132 million people to see how HPV vaccination programmes affect cervical disease and whether the vaccine causes harm. It found that vaccination lowers the rate of cervical cancer, pre-cancer changes and genital warts, and that the benefit is biggest when girls are vaccinated at or before age 16. Several health problems often discussed online were not linked to the vaccine. Most of the evidence was rated moderate certainty.
keyPoints: Moderate-certainty evidence shows HPV vaccination reduces cervical cancer; for those vaccinated at or before age 16, the risk was about 80% lower.
Vaccination also reduced high-grade cervical pre-cancer (CIN3+ was 74% lower in those vaccinated by age 16) and anogenital warts (about 47-53% lower).
Vaccination was not linked to chronic fatigue syndrome, complex regional pain syndrome, premature ovarian failure, infertility or increased sexual activity (moderate-certainty evidence).
Evidence on Guillain-Barré syndrome was low certainty but suggested no increased risk; no studies reported community rates of serious adverse events.

items.title: Causal attribution of human papillomavirus genotypes to invasive cervical cancer worldwide: a systematic analysis of the global literature
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 1174 studies worldwide to work out which types of human papillomavirus (HPV) actually cause invasive cervical cancer. They found 17 HPV types that are likely causes, with HPV16 and HPV18 together responsible for about three-quarters of cases. A group of seven types, covered by the 9-valent vaccine-style grouping (HPV16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58), accounted for roughly 92% to 96% of cases depending on the region. The authors say this can help shape vaccination and screening plans to reduce cervical cancer.
keyPoints: 17 HPV types were judged to be causes of invasive cervical cancer.
HPV16 caused the largest share of cases worldwide (61.7%), followed by HPV18 (15.3%).
Seven types (16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58) together accounted for 92.1% of cases in Africa and 95.9% in central, western and southern Asia.
HPV35 played a larger role in Africa (3.6%) than in other regions (0.6-1.6%).

items.title: Electronic Health Interventions and Cervical Cancer Screening: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 articles (15 randomized studies, 23,102 women) testing electronic health tools such as text messages, phone calls, web videos and online booking to encourage cervical cancer screening. Women who received these tools were more likely to get screened than women who had usual care. The results varied a lot between studies, and the authors say larger studies on cost-effectiveness are still needed.
keyPoints: Electronic health interventions raised cervical screening participation compared with usual care (relative risk about 1.46).
Phone calls, combined (multimode) approaches, text messages, and video or online booking each worked better than usual care.
The tools had a bigger effect in low- and middle-income areas.
No clear improvement was seen among women with HPV, and results differed a lot between studies.

items.title: Human papillomavirus vaccine effectiveness by age at vaccination: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 21 studies to see whether the age at which someone has the HPV vaccine changes how well it works. It checked protection against HPV infection, genital warts, cervical abnormalities and cervical cancer. Most studies found the vaccine worked best when given at the youngest ages. The authors conclude that getting vaccinated on time matters.
keyPoints: Seventeen of the 21 studies found the highest vaccine effectiveness in the youngest age group.
Effectiveness for ages 9-14 ranged from about 74% to 93%.
Effectiveness for ages 15-18 was more variable, ranging from 12% to 90%.
The HPV vaccine works by preventing infection before natural exposure, so earlier vaccination is likely more effective.

items.title: Global and regional estimates of genital human papillomavirus prevalence among men: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 65 studies covering about 44,800 men in 35 countries to estimate how common genital HPV infection is in men. Around 3 in 10 men had at least one genital HPV type, and about 2 in 10 had a high-risk type linked to cancer. Infection was most common in young adults, peaking at ages 25 to 29. The authors say men are an important source of HPV spread, so prevention plans should include them.
keyPoints: About 31% of men worldwide had any genital HPV, and 21% had a high-risk HPV type.
HPV-16 was the most common type (5%), followed by HPV-6 (4%).
Infection was highest between ages 25 and 29 and then levelled off or fell slightly.
Rates were similar across most world regions but about half as high in Eastern and South-Eastern Asia.

items.title: Worldwide use of HPV self-sampling for cervical cancer screening
items.summary: This review looked at how many countries use HPV self-sampling, where a woman collects her own sample for cervical cancer screening instead of having a clinician do it. Earlier evidence suggests self-sampling works well and reaches women who are not being screened. Worldwide use is still limited: only 17 of the countries with screening programmes (12%) recommend it. The authors expect use to grow, partly because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
keyPoints: Evidence supports self-sampling as a valid alternative to clinician collection for HPV screening.
Self-sampling can reach women who are underscreened, in both low- and high-resource settings and across target ages.
Only 17 countries (12%) with screening programmes recommend it: nine as the main method and eight to reach underscreened groups.
Ten pilot projects are testing a switch to self-sampling in established screening programmes, and use is likely to increase.

items.title: Role of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination on HPV infection and recurrence of HPV related disease after local surgical treatment: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies of people who had HPV-related cervical changes removed by local surgery. It looked at whether getting the HPV vaccine was linked to fewer repeat problems afterwards. Women who were vaccinated had fewer recurrences of serious cervical changes (CIN2+), especially changes caused by HPV types 16 and 18. However, the quality of the evidence was rated very low to moderate, so the findings are not yet conclusive.
keyPoints: Vaccinated women had about 57% lower risk of CIN2+ coming back after local surgery (risk ratio 0.43), across 11 studies and 19,909 participants.
The benefit looked stronger for disease linked to HPV16 or HPV18 (risk ratio 0.26).
There was no clear evidence of benefit for vulvar, vaginal or anal changes, genital warts, or HPV infections, but few studies looked at these.
The authors say the evidence is inconclusive and call for large, high-quality randomised trials.

items.title: Secondary Prevention of Cervical Cancer: ASCO Resource-Stratified Guideline Update
items.summary: The American Society of Clinical Oncology updated its worldwide guideline on screening to catch cervical cancer early. It recommends HPV DNA testing in all settings, with how often and at what age depending on the resources available in a country or health system. Women living with HIV are advised to be screened more often, and screening after pregnancy is also covered.
keyPoints: HPV DNA testing is recommended in all resource settings; visual inspection with acetic acid may be used in basic settings.
In the best-resourced settings, screening is advised from age 25 to 65 every 5 years; in settings with fewer resources it starts at 30 and may happen only 1 to 3 times in a lifetime.
Women who are HIV-positive should have HPV testing after diagnosis, twice as many times per lifetime as the general population.
Screening after pregnancy is recommended at 6 weeks postpartum in basic settings and at 6 months in other settings.

items.title: HPV self-sampling for cervical cancer screening: a systematic review of values and preferences
items.summary: This review pulled together 72 studies with over 52,000 people to see how women feel about collecting their own sample for HPV cervical screening. Women generally found self-sampling highly acceptable, whatever their age, income or country. The main reason some still preferred a clinician to take the sample was worry about not collecting it correctly.
keyPoints: Women generally found HPV self-sampling highly acceptable regardless of age, income or country of residence.
Lack of confidence in collecting a reliable sample was the most common reason for preferring a clinician-collected sample.
Most women preferred self-sampling at home over self-sampling at a clinic.
The cervical swab was the most common and most accepted sampling device.

items.title: Improving vaccination uptake among adolescents
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 16 studies of ways to get more teenagers vaccinated, including against HPV. Health education about the HPV vaccine improved uptake compared with usual practice, and this finding was backed by high-certainty evidence. Several other approaches, such as financial incentives and school-based delivery, may or probably help too, but most of the evidence was low to moderate certainty and many studies had a risk of bias.
keyPoints: Health education improved HPV vaccine uptake compared with usual practice (high-certainty evidence).
Financial incentives may improve HPV vaccine uptake (low-certainty evidence).
Giving vaccines by school class rather than by age group probably led to slightly higher HPV vaccine uptake (moderate-certainty evidence).
Reminder prompts for healthcare providers probably made little or no difference to vaccination completion (moderate-certainty evidence).

items.title: EBCOG position statement: Gender neutral HPV vaccination for young adults
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This position statement from a European gynaecology body looks at HPV vaccination. HPV is linked to several types of cancer in both women and men. The statement says national vaccination programmes should make sure both young women and young men get the full vaccine course in their teenage years, so that more of the population is protected. A review it cites found that vaccinating boys and girls is most cost-effective when the cost per person and the vaccination coverage are both low.
keyPoints: HPV has been linked to the start of several types of cancer in both females and males.
National programmes should ensure young women and young men both receive full HPV immunisation in their teenage years.
Vaccinating both sexes helps build herd immunity.
A recent review found vaccinating boys and girls is most cost-effective when individual costs and coverage are low, and it could greatly reduce HPV-related cancers in later life.

items.title: Cervical cancer screening for individuals at average risk: 2020 guideline update from the American Cancer Society
items.summary: The American Cancer Society updated its advice on cervical cancer screening for people at average risk. It now recommends starting at age 25 and preferring an HPV test every 5 years, up to age 65. Where HPV testing is not available, screening with an HPV test plus a Pap test every 5 years, or a Pap test alone every 3 years, is still acceptable.
keyPoints: Screening should start at age 25, rather than 21 as in the 2012 advice.
The preferred option is a primary HPV test every 5 years from age 25 to 65.
If primary HPV testing is not available, an HPV plus Pap test every 5 years or a Pap test alone every 3 years is acceptable.
People over 65 can stop screening if they have had no serious cervical pre-cancer (CIN2 or worse) in the past 25 years and have had adequate negative screening in the past 10 years.

items.title: Human Papillomavirus Vaccination: ACOG Committee Opinion, Number 809
items.summary: This is guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on HPV vaccination. HPV can cause cancers and genital warts in women and men, and the vaccine greatly lowers the chance of these. The vaccine works best when given in early adolescence, before any exposure to HPV. Older adults up to age 45 can also be vaccinated, with the decision made together with their health care professional.
keyPoints: HPV vaccines are among the most effective vaccines available, with over 99% efficacy in women not previously exposed to that HPV type.
The vaccine significantly reduces anogenital cancer and genital warts in women and men.
Ideally the vaccine is given in early adolescence, before exposure to HPV through sexual activity.
Unvaccinated women aged 26 or younger are advised to get the vaccine series regardless of sexual activity, prior HPV exposure or sexual orientation.

items.title: Cervical Cancer, Version 3.2019, NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology
items.journal: Journal of the National Comprehensive Cancer Network
items.summary: This is a guideline summary on cervical cancer from a US cancer expert group. It notes that most cervical cancers can be prevented through HPV vaccination, routine screening and treatment of precancerous changes. Even so, cervical cancer is still the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide, largely because screening is not good enough in many regions. The rest of the guideline covers how early and locally advanced cervical cancer is checked, staged and treated.
keyPoints: Most cervical cancers are preventable through HPV vaccination, routine screening and treatment of precancerous lesions.
Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women globally.
Inadequate screening in many parts of the world is why it remains so common.
The guideline covers workup, staging and treatment of early stage and locally advanced disease.

items.title: Population-level impact and herd effects following the introduction of human papillomavirus vaccination programmes: updated systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 65 studies in 14 high-income countries, covering about 60 million people, to see what happened after HPV vaccination programmes began. Within 5-9 years, HPV infections, genital warts and precancerous cervical changes (CIN2+) all dropped, especially in girls and young women. Genital warts also fell in boys and men, which points to a 'herd effect' (protection spreading beyond those vaccinated). Programmes that vaccinated several age groups and reached more people had bigger effects.
keyPoints: After 5-8 years of vaccination, HPV 16 and 18 infections fell by 83% in girls aged 13-19 and by 66% in women aged 20-24.
Genital wart diagnoses fell by 67% in girls aged 15-19, and also fell in boys aged 15-19 (48%) and men aged 20-24 (32%).
Precancerous cervical changes (CIN2+) fell by 51% in screened girls aged 15-19 and by 31% in women aged 20-24 after 5-9 years.
Programmes with multi-age vaccination and high coverage had greater direct and herd effects.

items.title: Human Papillomavirus Vaccination for Adults: Updated Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices
items.source: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.journal: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.summary: This report gives the updated US vaccine advisory committee (ACIP) recommendations on HPV vaccination for adults. HPV vaccination is meant to prevent new HPV infections and HPV-linked diseases, including some cancers. Catch-up vaccination is now recommended for everyone through age 26. For adults aged 27 to 45, the committee did not recommend vaccinating everyone, but said some people might benefit and suggested deciding together with a health care provider.
keyPoints: Routine HPV vaccination is recommended at age 11 or 12, and can start from age 9; this has not changed.
Catch-up HPV vaccination is recommended for all people through age 26.
Catch-up vaccination is not recommended for all adults aged 27 to 45.
Adults aged 27 to 45 who are not adequately vaccinated may benefit, so the decision is made together with a clinician (shared clinical decision-making).

items.title: Comparison of different human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine types and dose schedules for prevention of HPV-related disease in females and males
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 20 trials with about 32,000 people to compare different HPV vaccine types and dose schedules. Two doses gave similar antibody responses to three doses in girls aged 9 to 15, and the nonavalent and quadrivalent vaccines gave similar protection against cervical precancer and cancer. In males, the quadrivalent vaccine probably reduced genital lesions and genital warts. Evidence on serious side effects was low or very low certainty, because there were few events.
keyPoints: Two-dose and three-dose HPV vaccine schedules gave similar antibody responses in girls aged 9 to 15 for up to five years (moderate- to high-certainty evidence).
A longer gap (6 or 12 months) between the first two doses gave stronger antibody responses than a shorter gap in 9- to 14-year-olds.
The nonavalent and quadrivalent vaccines gave similar protection against cervical precancer or cancer in women aged 16 to 26 (high-certainty evidence).
In males aged 10 to 26, the quadrivalent vaccine probably reduced external genital lesions and anogenital warts, with more injection-site pain or redness than control.

items.title: Screening for Cervical Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence on cervical cancer screening and updated its recommendations. It found that screening women aged 21 to 65 greatly lowers cervical cancer cases and deaths. It recommends cytology (Pap test) every 3 years for ages 21 to 29, and for ages 30 to 65 a choice of Pap test every 3 years, HPV testing every 5 years, or both together every 5 years. It advises against screening in women under 21, in older women with adequate prior screening who are not at high risk, and after a hysterectomy that removed the cervix (unless there was a high-grade precancerous lesion or cervical cancer).
keyPoints: Screening women aged 21 to 65 substantially reduces cervical cancer cases and deaths.
Ages 21 to 29: Pap test (cytology) alone every 3 years.
Ages 30 to 65: Pap test every 3 years, HPV test alone every 5 years, or HPV plus Pap test together every 5 years.

Screening is not recommended under age 21, over 65 with adequate prior screening and no high risk, or after hysterectomy with cervix removal without a history of high-grade lesions or cervical cancer.

items.title: Detecting cervical precancer and reaching underscreened women by using HPV testing on self samples: updated meta-analyses
items.summary: This large review pooled results from 56 accuracy studies and 25 participation trials to look at HPV testing on samples women collect themselves. When a PCR-based HPV test was used, self samples found precancerous cervical changes about as well as samples taken by a clinician. Mailing self-sampling kits to women's homes got more underscreened women tested than invitation or reminder letters. Results varied a lot between studies, so the authors suggest local pilots before wide roll-out.
keyPoints: PCR-based HPV tests were as sensitive on self samples as on clinician samples for detecting CIN2+ or CIN3+ (pooled ratio 0.99).
Signal-amplification HPV tests were less sensitive on self samples (pooled ratio 0.85).
Mailing self-sample kits to women's homes led to higher participation than invitation or reminder letters (relative participation 2.33).
Opt-in strategies, where women must request a kit, were generally not more effective than invitation letters; direct offers in underscreened communities gave participation above 75%.

items.title: Cytology versus HPV testing for cervical cancer screening in the general population
items.summary: This review pooled 40 studies of more than 140,000 women to compare HPV testing with cervical cytology (the smear test) for finding serious cervical changes (CIN 2+). HPV tests were better at picking up these changes, but they also flagged more women who did not need follow-up. A negative HPV test was more reassuring than a negative smear, because smears are more likely to miss real disease.
keyPoints: HPV testing found more cases of CIN 2+ than cytology (pooled sensitivity about 90% for the HC2 HPV test versus about 63% for conventional cytology and 73% for liquid-based cytology).
HPV tests were slightly less specific, so they lead to more unnecessary referrals.
A negative HPV test is more reassuring than a negative cytology result, which has a greater chance of being falsely negative and delaying treatment.
Results did not differ between women under and over 30, but longer-term studies are still needed to confirm the clinical impact.

items.title: Assessment of cortisol as a neonatal pain biomarker in the application of non-pharmacological analgesia therapies: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 studies to see whether non-drug comfort methods ease pain in newborns, using the stress hormone cortisol as a pain marker. Skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding lowered cortisol, which suggests they reduce pain from procedures like heel pricks. Sucrose (sugar solution) did not clearly lower cortisol. This is about comforting babies, not about painkillers taken by breastfeeding mothers.
keyPoints: Skin-to-skin contact had a large effect on lowering newborn cortisol, and was described as the most effective method for pain from procedures like heel pricks in preterm babies under 28 weeks.
Breastfeeding had a moderate effect and was described as an effective and safe way to ease newborn pain and lower cortisol.
Sucrose had only a small effect and was not found effective at reducing newborn pain based on cortisol.
Non-drug therapies overall reduced pain as measured by cortisol, though the size of the effect varied by gestational age.

items.title: Labor neuraxial analgesia and breastfeeding: An updated systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether having an epidural or spinal (neuraxial) pain relief during labor affects how likely a mother is to breastfeed. It pooled 15 studies with over 16,000 women, and the results were very mixed: some found no difference, some found lower breastfeeding rates after neuraxial pain relief, and some were in between. The authors think other factors, such as skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding support, may explain much of the difference. The studies were mostly observational, so they cannot prove cause and effect.
keyPoints: Across 15 studies, 6 found no difference in breastfeeding, 6 found lower breastfeeding with neuraxial pain relief, and 3 had mixed results.
Results were very inconsistent, likely because of other factors that can muddy the picture, such as immediate skin-to-skin contact and maternity leave.
Education programs and breastfeeding support are likely more important for long-term breastfeeding success than the type of labor pain relief.

items.title: Supporting breastfeeding for women on opioid maintenance therapy: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at ways to help women on opioid maintenance therapy (such as methadone or buprenorphine treatment for opioid use disorder) breastfeed their babies. Only four studies were found, and in all four breastfeeding rates improved. Three of the four had moderate to serious risk of bias, so the results should be read with caution. Programs that worked well used a team approach, kept mother and newborn together, and put the woman's needs at the centre of care.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding rates are low in women on opioid maintenance therapy, even though breastfeeding has known benefits.
All four studies found a statistically significant improvement in breastfeeding rates after an intervention.
Three of the four studies had moderate to serious risk of bias because of confounding factors.
Successful programs shared an integrated approach, a well-prepared multidisciplinary team, keeping mother and newborn together, and patient-centred care.

items.title: The pharmacogenetics of opioid therapy in the management of postpartum pain: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 17 studies on how a mother's genes may affect how opioid painkillers work after childbirth. It looked at both pain relief and side effects for mothers and their breastfeeding babies. The review found that variations in a few genes (CYP2D6, OPRM1 A118G, UGT2B7 C802T and ABCB1 G2677AT) may affect how well these medicines work or how likely side effects are. The authors say this could help tailor pain care after birth, though the abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Opioids are commonly prescribed for pain after childbirth, but balancing pain relief with safety for mother and breastfeeding baby can be hard.
Seventeen studies were included, covering different opioids, gene variations and outcomes.
Variations in the CYP2D6, OPRM1 A118G, UGT2B7 C802T and ABCB1 G2677AT genes may influence pain relief or side effects.
The authors suggest these findings may help personalise pain care after birth.

items.title: Labor Epidural Analgesia and Breastfeeding: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 23 studies on whether having an epidural for pain relief in labor affects breastfeeding in the first days after birth. The results were mixed: 12 studies linked epidurals to poorer breastfeeding success, 10 found no effect, and 1 found a positive link. Most studies were observational and had weaknesses, so it is not clear whether epidurals themselves cause any breastfeeding difficulty.
keyPoints: Of 23 studies, 12 found a negative link between labor epidural and breastfeeding success, 10 found no effect, and 1 found a positive link.
Most studies were observational, and the few randomized trials had inadequate or unclear randomization.
Many studies were small or did not account for things like a mother's intention to breastfeed, social support, or the type and dose of pain relief.
It is unclear how much any effect might be due to factors like infant alertness, maternal fever, oxytocin release, labor length, or instrumental delivery.

items.title: The Analgesic Efficacy of Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Agents (NSAIDs) in Patients Undergoing Cesarean Deliveries: A Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 22 randomized trials of women having a cesarean delivery to see whether NSAID painkillers (like ibuprofen-type medicines) help with pain after surgery. Women who received NSAIDs reported lower pain scores at 12 and 24 hours, used less opioid medicine, and felt less drowsy. Nausea and vomiting were no different between the groups. The authors say more research is needed on the best NSAID regimen and on effects such as breastfeeding.
keyPoints: Women given NSAIDs after cesarean delivery reported lower pain at 12 and 24 hours than those who did not receive them.
They used significantly less opioid painkiller medicine after surgery.
They had less drowsiness or sedation, but no difference in nausea or vomiting.
The pain benefit at 24 hours was seen with NSAIDs given by injection or drip, but not by mouth or rectally.

items.title: Colorectal cancer screening: An update to the American Cancer Society guideline, 2026
items.summary: The American Cancer Society updated its bowel (colorectal) cancer screening guideline for people at average risk. It still recommends starting screening at age 45 and continuing to age 75 if life expectancy is over 10 years. Two newer stool tests are now recommended, while blood tests were found less effective at catching early cancers and precancerous growths and are advised only for people who decline or do not complete other tests.
keyPoints: Average-risk adults should start bowel cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75 if their life expectancy is more than 10 years.
A next-generation stool DNA test and a stool RNA test are recommended, along with yearly high-sensitivity stool blood tests (FIT or guaiac), as preferred stool-based options at 3-year intervals.
Blood-based tests were less sensitive for precancerous growths and stage I cancers, so they are suggested only for people who decline or do not complete preferred tests.
A positive result on any non-colonoscopy test needs a follow-up colonoscopy, preferably within 6 months.

items.title: Linked color imaging versus conventional white-light colonoscopy for the detection of colorectal polyps
items.summary: This review looked at whether a special colonoscopy imaging mode called linked color imaging (LCI), which boosts color contrast, finds more bowel polyps than standard white-light imaging. It combined 16 trials with about 12,800 adults having colonoscopy for screening, symptoms or follow-up checks. LCI found slightly more adenomas (a type of polyp that can turn into cancer) and more polyps overall, with no adverse events needing medical treatment reported. No trial measured whether this led to fewer bowel cancers appearing after colonoscopy.
keyPoints: LCI slightly increased the adenoma detection rate compared with standard white-light colonoscopy (high-certainty evidence).
LCI slightly increased the overall polyp detection rate and likely found more sessile serrated lesions and more adenomas per person (moderate-certainty evidence).
No adverse events needing medical treatment were reported with LCI (moderate-certainty evidence).
No study measured cancers appearing after colonoscopy, so the effect on cancer prevention is not yet known.

items.title: Disability and Participation in Colorectal Cancer Screening: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 20 studies, mostly from the USA, to see whether people with disabilities take part in bowel cancer screening as often as people without disabilities. People with disabilities were less likely to be screened overall. The gap was biggest for stool-based home tests (FOBT/FIT) and for people with intellectual disabilities, while colonoscopy rates did not differ significantly.
keyPoints: People with disabilities had lower odds of bowel cancer screening overall (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.73-0.87).
Stool-based tests (FOBT/FIT) were less likely to be done by people with disabilities (OR 0.72), with no significant difference for colonoscopy.
People with intellectual disabilities had the lowest participation (OR 0.65), especially for stool tests (OR 0.58).
The authors call for more research and coordinated efforts to improve early cancer diagnosis for this group.

items.title: Guaiac-based faecal occult blood tests versus faecal immunochemical tests for colorectal cancer screening in average-risk individuals
items.summary: This Cochrane review compared two stool-based bowel cancer screening tests, the older guaiac test (gFOBT) and the newer faecal immunochemical test (FIT), in people at average risk. It pooled results from dozens of studies. FIT was better than the guaiac test at picking up bowel cancer and advanced pre-cancerous growths, and the two tests gave a similar number of false alarms in most studies. Neither test is perfect, and both can miss some cancers.
keyPoints: FIT found more bowel cancers than the guaiac test: about 76% versus 39% in studies where everyone also had a colonoscopy.
In studies following people with negative tests, FIT detected about 89% of cancers versus 59% for the guaiac test.
For advanced growths (advanced adenomas and cancer combined), FIT picked up about 26% to 33% compared with 15% for the guaiac test, so both tests still miss many.
Specificity (correctly clearing people without disease) was similar in some studies, but in others the guaiac test had fewer false alarms leading to unnecessary colonoscopy.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of cytology and HPV-related biomarkers for anal cancer screening among different risk groups
items.summary: This review pooled results from 39 studies on tests used to find anal precancer, which is caused by HPV. About 20% of people in higher-risk groups had precancer or worse, ranging from 22% in men who have sex with men and live with HIV to 13% in women. Anal cytology (a swab-based cell check) and HPV testing both found most cases, but each also gave many false alarms, and using the two together did not clearly improve risk prediction. The authors say the findings can help shape screening guidelines.
keyPoints: About 1 in 5 people tested in higher-risk groups had anal precancer or worse; the rate was 13% in women.
Cytology picked up 81% of cases and HPV testing 92%, but specificity (correctly clearing people without disease) was only 62% and 42%.
Using both tests together found 93% of cases but correctly cleared only 33% of those without disease.
Newer tests (HPV E6/E7 mRNA and p16/Ki-67 stain) seemed better at avoiding false alarms but missed more cases, though data were limited.

items.title: Screening for Colorectal Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence on screening for bowel (colorectal) cancer in adults at average risk, meaning people with no prior bowel cancer, polyps, inflammatory bowel disease or known inherited risk. It found that screening clearly helps adults aged 50 to 75, and also helps those aged 45 to 49. For adults aged 76 to 85 the benefit is small, so the choice depends on the person's health, past screening and preferences.
keyPoints: Screening is recommended for all adults aged 50 to 75, with high certainty of substantial benefit.
Screening is also recommended for adults aged 45 to 49, with moderate certainty of moderate benefit.
For adults aged 76 to 85, screening is offered selectively because the benefit is small; people who have never been screened are more likely to benefit.
Bowel cancer is the third leading cause of cancer death in both men and women, and cases in adults aged 40 to 49 have been rising.

items.title: Global Prevalence of Colorectal Neoplasia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 70 studies covering more than 637,000 people to estimate how common bowel growths (adenomas) and bowel cancer are worldwide. About 1 in 4 people had an adenoma, about 1 in 20 had a more advanced adenoma, and fewer than 1 in 200 had bowel cancer. Rates were lower in women than in men and lower in younger adults than in older adults. The authors say this points to a need to expand bowel cancer screening for groups with high rates.
keyPoints: Overall, 23.9% of people had adenomas, 4.6% had advanced adenomas and 0.4% had bowel cancer.
Women had lower rates than men: adenomas 19.3% vs 29.7%, advanced adenomas 3.8% vs 6.5%, and cancer 0.4% vs 0.8%.
Rates were higher in older adults than younger adults, and higher in European countries than in other regions.
The authors conclude that screening programmes should be expanded for groups with high rates of bowel neoplasia.

items.title: Screening for Colorectal Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomised trials to see whether bowel cancer screening helps adults with no symptoms. Stool blood tests (guaiac fecal occult blood test) and a camera test of the lower bowel (flexible sigmoidoscopy) both lowered deaths from bowel cancer and cases of late-stage disease. The benefit was clearer for adults aged 60 and over. Neither test changed the overall chance of dying from any cause, and sigmoidoscopy carries some risks such as bleeding or bowel perforation.
keyPoints: Stool blood testing (gFOBT) cut bowel cancer deaths by 18%, and flexible sigmoidoscopy cut them by 26%, compared with no screening.
About 377 people needed screening with gFOBT, and about 864 with sigmoidoscopy, to prevent one bowel cancer death.
Neither test reduced deaths from all causes combined.
Benefit was much greater in adults aged 60 and over, so younger adults may face the harms of screening without much benefit.

items.title: Clinical effectiveness of progestogens compared to combined oral contraceptive pills in the treatment of endometriosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled seven studies with 948 women who have endometriosis. It compared progestogen-only treatment with the combined pill for pelvic pain, painful periods, pain during sex, and mood or psychological health. The two treatments worked about equally well, and side effects such as breast tenderness, weight gain, and bleeding changes were also similar.
keyPoints: No clear difference between progestogens and the combined pill for pelvic pain, painful periods, or pain during sex.
Psychological health outcomes were similar for both treatments.
Side effects such as breast tenderness, weight gain, absent periods, and bleeding were not significantly different.
The authors conclude both are equally effective options for managing endometriosis symptoms.

items.title: Dienogest vs. combined oral contraceptive: A systematic review and meta-analysis of efficacy and side effects to inform evidence-based guidelines
items.summary: This review pooled five studies (four randomised trials and one observational study) comparing dienogest, a progestin-only treatment, with the combined contraceptive pill in women with endometriosis. Both treatments eased pelvic pain to a similar degree. Side effects such as bleeding, nausea, headache, hot flushes and hair loss were also similar, and a similar number of women stopped each treatment. Pain during sex was lower in the combined pill group. The included studies had a moderate risk of bias.
keyPoints: Dienogest and the combined pill improved pelvic pain by a similar amount in women with endometriosis.
Pain during sex after treatment was lower with the combined pill.
Rates of bleeding, nausea and vomiting, headache, hot flushes and hair loss did not differ between the two treatments.
The authors conclude that the choice between them can rest on a woman's preference, medical history and experience.

items.title: Metformin and Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills in the Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This review pooled 36 randomised trials in women with PCOS to compare the combined pill, metformin, and both together. For excess hair growth (hirsutism), there was no difference between metformin and the pill, or between the pill and the combination. Metformin was better at lowering insulin and triglycerides, while the pill was better at improving male-type hormone measures. The authors conclude that the choice should be based on symptoms, and that combining both treatments gave some blood-test benefits.
keyPoints: Hirsutism did not differ between metformin and the combined pill, or between the pill alone and the pill plus metformin.
The combined pill was better than metformin for male-type hormone measures (free androgen index, SHBG and testosterone).
Metformin lowered insulin and triglycerides more than the pill did.
Pill plus metformin gave some better blood-test results than the pill alone, including insulin, insulin resistance, free androgen index and SHBG.

items.title: Guidelines of care for the management of acne vulgaris
items.source: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
items.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
items.summary: This 2024 guideline reviewed the evidence on treating acne and made 18 recommendations. Treatments with strong support include benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline. Combined oral contraceptive pills were given a conditional (weaker) recommendation as one acne option, alongside spironolactone and several other treatments.
keyPoints: Strong recommendations were made for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline.
Combined oral contraceptive pills received a conditional recommendation for acne, meaning the evidence supports them less strongly than the first-line options.
Oral isotretinoin is strongly recommended for severe acne, acne causing psychosocial burden or scarring, or acne that has not responded to standard treatment.
Good practice advice includes combining topical treatments that work in different ways and limiting the use of antibiotics taken by mouth.

items.title: Are natural estrogens used in contraception at lower risk of venous thromboembolism than synthetic ones? A systematic literature review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled five studies, covering over 560,000 women over time, to compare blood clot (venous thromboembolism, or VTE) risk in combined pills containing synthetic estrogen (ethinylestradiol) versus natural estrogen (estradiol). Pills with natural estrogen were linked to about a 33% lower risk of blood clots. The authors say this supports a re-look at contraceptive guidelines, though most of the included studies were observational.
keyPoints: Combined pills with natural estrogen (estradiol) were linked to a 33% lower risk of VTE than pills with synthetic estrogen (ethinylestradiol).
When both were paired with the progestogen levonorgestrel, estradiol-based pills showed a 49% lower VTE risk.
Most earlier research looked at the progestogen type, so estrogen type has had less attention.
The authors suggest contraceptive guidelines may need re-evaluating to put patient safety first.

items.title: The effects of exogenous estrogen in women with SAR-CoV-2 infection: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from five studies to see whether taking estrogen affects the chance of dying from COVID-19 in women. Women past menopause who used menopausal hormone therapy were less likely to die from COVID-19 than women who did not use it. Premenopausal women taking the combined pill showed no clear difference in COVID-19 deaths compared with women not taking it. Most of the evidence came from cohort studies, so certainty was limited for most outcomes.
keyPoints: Menopausal hormone therapy was linked to a lower chance of dying from COVID-19 in postmenopausal women (moderate certainty evidence).
The combined oral contraceptive pill made no significant difference to COVID-19 death rates in premenopausal women (2 studies, 5,099 women).
Menopausal hormone therapy users had a slightly higher rate of hospital and ICU admission, but no clear difference in needing breathing support.
Certainty was low for outcomes other than death, because the included studies were mostly cohort studies and hormone doses and durations varied.

items.title: Harms of third- and fourth-generation combined oral contraceptives in premenopausal women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 33 studies with over 629,000 women to look at side effects of newer combined pills (third- and fourth-generation) in women before menopause. Fourth-generation pills were linked to lower LDL ('bad') cholesterol and, compared with older levonorgestrel pills, a lower risk of arterial blood clots. There was no difference in clots in the leg veins (deep vein thrombosis), and for the other outcomes the data were mixed and showed no clear difference.
keyPoints: Fourth-generation pills were linked to lower LDL cholesterol than comparison pills.
Arterial thrombosis was less common with fourth-generation pills than with levonorgestrel pills.
No difference was found in deep vein thrombosis between fourth-generation pills and levonorgestrel pills.
For the remaining outcomes, results varied between studies and no clear difference was found.

items.title: Different kinds of oral contraceptive pills in polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 19 randomised trials comparing different combined contraceptive pills in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Pills containing an anti-androgen (ethinyl estradiol with cyproterone acetate) lowered male-type hormones and excess hair growth more than conventional pills. However, this pill carries a higher risk of blood clots, so the upcoming PCOS guideline will not recommend it as a first choice. The authors say better evidence on real-life outcomes is still needed for newer pills.
keyPoints: Ethinyl estradiol with cyproterone acetate reduced excess hair growth, testosterone and BMI more than conventional combined pills.
Fourth-generation pills gave slightly lower BMI and testosterone than third-generation pills, but no difference in excess hair growth.
There was no difference in excess hair growth between high and low estrogen doses.
The cyproterone pill will not be a first-line choice in the pending PCOS guideline because of a higher risk of venous blood clots; no evidence was found on natural estrogens in the pill.

items.title: Combined oral contraceptives: update recommendations of the Latin American contraceptive association
items.summary: This review looked at how combined birth control pills (pills with both an estrogen and a progestin) have changed over time. Newer pills use lower estrogen doses, natural estradiol options and different types of progestin, which has helped reduce side effects and risks. The authors conclude that these changes have improved the balance of benefits and risks, so a pill can be matched more closely to each woman's needs.
keyPoints: Lowering the ethinylestradiol dose over time helped reduce side effects and adverse events.
Natural estradiol and estradiol valerate are now available and are a valid alternative to ethinylestradiol.
Newer non-androgenic progestins have different hormone and metabolic effects, so the pill can be tailored to each woman.
Overall, newer pills have improved the balance of benefits and risks.

items.title: Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System in Women Using Combined Oral Contraceptive: A Systematic Review
items.source: Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia E Obstetricia
items.journal: Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia E Obstetricia
items.summary: This review looked at 10 small studies (501 women aged 18 to 49) to see how the combined pill affects a hormone system that helps control blood pressure, called the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. The studies found higher activity of this system in women using the combined pill. The authors say this supports the idea that using the pill is linked to a higher risk of heart and blood vessel problems, including high blood pressure. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Ten studies with 501 women in total were included in the review.
Women using the combined pill showed increased levels of renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone, which are part of the blood pressure control system.
The authors conclude the combined pill activates this system more strongly.
They say this supports a link between pill use and higher cardiovascular risk, including high blood pressure.

items.title: Recurrence after stopping anticoagulants in women with combined oral contraceptive-associated venous thromboembolism: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 19 studies to look at how often blood clots (venous thromboembolism, or VTE) come back after anticoagulant (blood-thinning) treatment stops. It compared women whose clot was linked to the combined contraceptive pill with women whose clot had no clear cause. Clots returned less often in the pill-linked group, at about 1.2 per 100 person-years versus about 3.9 per 100 person-years. The authors concluded that the chance of another clot after a pill-associated clot is low.
keyPoints: Women with a clot linked to the combined pill had a recurrence rate of about 1.22 per 100 person-years after stopping blood thinners.
Women with a clot that had no clear cause had a higher rate, about 3.89 per 100 person-years.
The risk of recurrence was roughly one third as high after a pill-associated clot as after an unprovoked clot (rate ratio 0.34).
The included studies were judged to be at low risk of bias.

items.title: Options for Prevention and Management of Menstrual Bleeding in Adolescent Patients Undergoing Cancer Treatment: ACOG Committee Opinion, Number 817
items.summary: This guidance from ACOG covers how to prevent or manage heavy periods in teenagers having cancer treatment. Most teens with sudden severe bleeding can be treated with medicines, and surgery is rarely needed. Taking combined hormonal contraceptives (the combined pill) continuously can stop periods, though it cannot be guaranteed. People with cancer already have a higher risk of blood clots, so any use of estrogen needs a careful, individual decision with the health care team.
keyPoints: Teens with severe sudden bleeding usually need only medical treatment; surgery is rarely needed.
Surgery may be considered if a patient is not stable or medicines have not worked.
Combined hormonal contraceptives used continuously are effective at stopping periods, but complete absence of bleeding cannot be guaranteed.
Cancer treatment raises the risk of venous thromboembolism (blood clots), so estrogen use should be tailored to each patient with close monitoring for clots and liver problems.

items.title: Association between polycystic ovary syndrome and venous thromboembolism: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled five large observational studies to see whether polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is linked to venous thromboembolism (VTE), which means blood clots in the veins. Women with PCOS had higher odds of VTE than women without PCOS. The link remained when the researchers accounted for excess weight and use of hormonal treatments such as the combined pill. The authors suggest this should be considered when choosing medicines for PCOS.
keyPoints: Women with PCOS had about 1.7 times the odds of a venous blood clot compared with women without PCOS.
After adjusting for obesity and hormonal treatments, the odds were about 1.9 times higher.
PCOS appears to be a risk factor for blood clots independently of excess weight and combined pill use.
The authors say this should be taken into account when choosing medicines for PCOS.

items.title: Metformin versus the combined oral contraceptive pill for hirsutism, acne, and menstrual pattern in polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 44 trials (2,253 women) comparing metformin with the combined pill, alone or together, for women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). For excess hair growth, results depended on body weight. Metformin may work less well than the pill for women with a BMI of 25 to 30, and the evidence is unclear for lighter or heavier women. Metformin may cause more severe stomach problems than the pill. The quality of the evidence was low or very low.
keyPoints: In adult women with a BMI of 25 to 30, metformin may be less effective than the pill for excess hair growth (hirsutism).
Metformin may cause more severe stomach and gut side effects than the pill, but fewer other severe side effects.
Metformin or the pill alone may work less well for hirsutism than metformin and the pill together, though the combination may cause more stomach side effects than the pill alone.
In teenagers with PCOS, it is unclear whether the treatments differ, because the evidence is missing or very low quality.

items.title: Combined hormonal contraceptives for heavy menstrual bleeding
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled eight trials (805 women) to see whether combined hormonal contraceptives (the pill, vaginal ring or patch) reduce heavy periods. Moderate-quality evidence found the combined pill reduced heavy bleeding compared with placebo over six months. A hormonal coil (LNG IUS) worked better than the pill, and the pill and vaginal ring looked similar. For other comparisons the evidence was too limited to draw firm conclusions.
keyPoints: The combined pill improved heavy bleeding compared with placebo: between about 12% and 77% of women had a successful response versus about 3% on placebo (moderate-quality evidence).
Minor side effects, especially breast pain, were more common with the combined pill.
The hormonal coil (LNG IUS) was more effective than the combined pill at reducing heavy bleeding (low-quality evidence).

There was not enough evidence to compare combined hormonal contraceptives with anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) or long-course progestogens; the pill and vaginal ring appeared to have similar effects.

items.title: Drug interactions between rifamycin antibiotics and hormonal contraception: a systematic review
