items.summary: This review looked at whether rifamycin antibiotics, which are mainly used to treat tuberculosis, make the combined contraceptive pill work less well. Eleven studies were included, and all of them looked at combined pills. Rifampin lowered hormone levels in the body and made ovulation more likely in some studies, and rifabutin had a smaller effect. No studies measured actual pregnancy rates, and there was little information on other rifamycins.
keyPoints: Rifampin reduced estrogen and/or progestin levels in five studies and increased ovulation in two of four studies.
Rifabutin caused smaller changes in hormone levels than rifampin.
Rifaximin and rifalazil did not change hormone levels in the one study of each.
No studies looked at pregnancy rates or at contraception that is not taken by mouth, so the real-world risk is unknown.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of venous thrombosis risk among users of combined oral contraception
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pooled results from 22 studies to compare the risk of blood clots in veins (venous thromboembolism) among users of low-dose combined pills with different progestogens. Pills containing cyproterone acetate, desogestrel, drospirenone or gestodene were linked to a higher clot risk than pills containing levonorgestrel, with risk ratios of about 1.5 to 2.0. The authors conclude this may mean a small increase in risk.
keyPoints: Pills with cyproterone acetate, desogestrel, drospirenone or gestodene had about 1.5 to 2.0 times the clot risk of levonorgestrel pills.
Results were similar when only 30 μg ethinyl estradiol monophasic pills were looked at.
After adjusting for differences between studies, the risk estimates were slightly lower.
The authors describe the extra risk as small.

items.title: Evaluation and Treatment of Hirsutism in Premenopausal Women: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This Endocrine Society guideline gives advice on checking for and treating unwanted excess hair growth (hirsutism) in women before menopause. For most women who want treatment, it suggests starting with the combined pill, and adding a medicine that blocks male-type hormones after 6 months if the response is not good enough. Hair removal methods such as laser can be added for extra cosmetic benefit.
keyPoints: Testing for high androgen (male-type hormone) levels is suggested for women with an abnormal hirsutism score, but not for women with regular periods and only local unwanted hair growth.
For most women, the combined estrogen-progestin pill is the suggested first medicine; an antiandrogen can be added after 6 months if the response is not good enough.
Antiandrogen medicines on their own are not recommended unless reliable contraception is also used.
Insulin-lowering drugs are suggested against, and laser or photoepilation is suggested for most women who choose hair removal.

items.title: Nonoral combined hormonal contraceptives and thromboembolism: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether the contraceptive patch, vaginal ring or combined injections carry a higher risk of blood clots than the combined pill. Eight studies were found, and their results were mixed: some showed a higher clot risk with the patch or ring, others showed no difference. The authors describe the evidence as limited, and say any extra risk probably means only a small number of clots across the whole population. No studies were found on combined injections.
keyPoints: Studies disagreed on whether the patch or the ring carries a higher risk of venous blood clots (VTE) than the combined pill.
Two studies found no increased risk of arterial clots (such as heart attack or stroke) with the patch compared with a combined pill.
Any extra risk likely means a small number of events across the population.
No studies on combined injectable contraceptives were found, and more research is needed.

items.title: Combined hormonal contraception and the risk of venous thromboembolism: a guideline
items.summary: This guideline from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine looked at whether combined hormonal birth control raises the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), which is a blood clot in a vein. VTE is rare in young women of reproductive age. Combined oral contraceptives do increase the risk. For women for whom combined hormonal contraception is appropriate, it is reasonable to use any currently available type.
keyPoints: VTE (blood clots in the veins) is rare in young women of reproductive age.
Combined oral contraceptives increase the risk of VTE.
If combined hormonal contraception is appropriate for a patient, it is reasonable to use any currently available preparation.

items.title: Oral Spironolactone for Acne Vulgaris in Adult Females: A Hybrid Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at whether spironolactone tablets help acne in adult women, as an option besides antibiotics and the combined pill. It found 10 trials and 21 case series, but the evidence was weak and the trials had a high risk of bias. One trial showed a 200 mg daily dose reduced inflamed spots compared with placebo, but results for lower doses were unclear. The reviewers concluded there is limited good-quality evidence behind how spironolactone is usually used.
keyPoints: All 10 trials were at high risk of bias, and the quality of evidence was low or very low for every outcome.
Only one crossover trial clearly showed benefit, for a 200 mg daily dose against placebo.
Menstrual side effects were more common at 200 mg, and taking a combined pill alongside it significantly reduced them.
Pooled results supported the recent advice that routine potassium blood tests are not needed in this group.

items.title: Drospirenone-containing oral contraceptive pills and the risk of venous thromboembolism: a systematic review of observational studies
items.summary: This review looked at 17 observational studies on whether combined pills containing drospirenone raise the risk of blood clots in the veins (VTE) compared with older pills containing levonorgestrel. The studies gave very different answers, and many had flaws in how they were done. Because of this, the true clot risk of drospirenone pills is still unknown. The best-quality studies suggest little or no extra risk, or a slightly higher risk, but they cannot rule out the risk being almost double.
keyPoints: Across 17 studies, the relative risk of blood clots with drospirenone pills versus levonorgestrel pills ranged from 1.0 to 3.3.
Only three studies were rated moderate risk of bias; ten were serious and four were critical.
The three highest-quality studies found relative risks between 1.0 and 1.57.
Because of study limitations, the clot risk of drospirenone pills remains unknown.

items.title: Superficial venous disease and combined hormonal contraceptives: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether women with superficial vein problems (such as varicose veins or clots in veins near the skin) have a higher chance of a deep blood clot (VTE) if they use combined hormonal contraceptives like the combined pill. Only two studies of fair quality were found. Both suggested a higher clot risk in pill users who had these vein conditions, but the authors say no firm conclusions can be drawn because there are so few studies and they have limitations.
keyPoints: Only two fair-quality studies were found, so the evidence is limited.

One study found women with a superficial vein clot who used the pill had a much higher odds of VTE than non-users without the condition (about 43 times), compared with about 4 times for pill users without it and about 5 times for non-users with it.

The other study found women with varicose veins who used the pill had a higher rate of VTE (1.85 per 1000 women-years) than pill users without varicose veins (0.84) or non-users with varicose veins (0.31).
The authors say no definitive conclusions can be made and more research is needed.

items.title: Combined hormonal contraceptive use among breastfeeding women: an updated systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 13 studies of breastfeeding women who used combined hormonal contraceptives (pills with estrogen) compared with women who did not. The studies were of poor to fair quality, and results were mixed: some found more formula supplementing and less breastfeeding in pill users, while others found no difference. Starting the pill before 6 weeks after birth sometimes went with lower infant weight gain, but starting after 6 weeks showed no effect on infant weight gain or other infant health outcomes.
keyPoints: Evidence on combined pills and breastfeeding success was limited, of poor to fair quality, and inconsistent.
Some studies linked starting the pill before 6 weeks postpartum with lower infant weight gain, while others found no effect.
No studies found an effect on infant weight gain when the pill was started after 6 weeks, or on other infant health outcomes at any start time.
Women in the first 6 weeks postpartum have the highest risk of blood clots, and estrogen may add to this, so they should be told about the full range of safe alternative methods.

items.title: Combined oral contraceptives, thrombophilia and the risk of venous thromboembolism: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 15 earlier studies to see how much extra blood clot (venous thromboembolism) risk the combined pill adds for women with inherited clotting conditions called thrombophilia. In pill users, mild thrombophilia (factor V Leiden or prothrombin mutation) raised clot risk about 6-fold and severe thrombophilia about 7-fold. The actual yearly risk was much higher with severe thrombophilia than with mild. The authors advise against the pill in severe thrombophilia, but say it can be offered with mild thrombophilia if other good contraceptives are not tolerated and there are no other risk factors.
keyPoints: Among pill users, mild thrombophilia raised clot risk almost 6-fold and severe thrombophilia about 7-fold.
Absolute clot risk was far higher with severe thrombophilia (4.3 to 4.6 per 100 pill-years) than with mild (0.49 to 2.0 per 100 pill-years).
The results support discouraging the combined pill in women with severe inherited thrombophilia.
With mild thrombophilia and no other risk factors such as family history, the pill can be offered if reliable alternatives are not tolerated.

items.title: Safety of hormonal contraceptives among women with migraine: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether women with migraine have a higher chance of stroke when they use hormonal birth control. It found seven studies, all of fair to poor quality, and all looked at combined pills. Taken together, the limited evidence suggests women with migraine who used the combined pill had about two to four times the risk of stroke compared with women who did not use it. There was no evidence on other hormonal methods, and more research is needed.
keyPoints: Four studies found the combined pill was linked to about two to four times the stroke risk in women with migraine, compared with not using it.
The only study that looked at migraine types found a higher stroke risk in migraine with aura, and this risk was similar whether or not the pill was used.
No evidence was found on methods other than pills, such as the patch, ring, implant or hormonal coil, or on heart attack risk.
The studies were all case-control studies of fair to poor quality, so the evidence is limited.

items.title: Co-administration of St. John's wort and hormonal contraceptives: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether taking the herbal remedy St. John's wort alongside the combined contraceptive pill changes how well the pill works. Only four small studies met the review's criteria. Some showed more breakthrough bleeding, lower hormone levels in the body, and possible signs of ovulation. The evidence is limited and mixed, but it raises concern that the pill may be less effective when taken with St. John's wort.
keyPoints: Three of four studies found more breakthrough bleeding when the combined pill was taken with St. John's wort.
One study found more follicle growth and probable ovulation, though two others found no change in ovulation markers.
Three studies found lower hormone exposure with St. John's wort; the one study that did not used a product low in hypericin.
The evidence is limited, but it raises concern about reduced contraceptive effectiveness.

items.title: Combined hormonal contraception and its effects on mood: a critical review
items.source: European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care
items.journal: European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care
items.summary: This review looked at studies from the past 30 years on how combined hormonal contraception (such as the combined pill) affects mood. Most women using it had no change in mood, or even a better mood, and bad mood effects were uncommon. The authors say the research is limited and inconsistent, so strong conclusions about who is at risk are hard to draw.
keyPoints: Most women using combined hormonal contraception showed no effect or a beneficial effect on mood, with few adverse effects.
Products containing less androgenic progestins may cause fewer mood side effects.
Continuous dosing and possibly non-oral forms seemed to have the fewest mood effects.
Women with existing mood disorders may be more prone to mood effects, but this may reflect which contraception they were given rather than the disorder itself.

items.title: Clomiphene and other antioestrogens for ovulation induction in polycystic ovarian syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review pulled together 28 trials (3377 women) of clomiphene and similar tablets used to trigger ovulation in women with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) who are struggling to conceive. Clomiphene seemed to raise the chance of becoming pregnant compared with a dummy tablet, but the size of the benefit is very uncertain. Most of the evidence was low or very low quality, and few trials reported live births, so the authors advise caution.
keyPoints: Clomiphene citrate was linked to a higher chance of clinical pregnancy than placebo, but how big the benefit is remains very uncertain (low-quality evidence).
No clear difference in live birth, miscarriage or pregnancy rates was found between clomiphene and tamoxifen (low-quality evidence).
Compared with gonadotropin injections, clomiphene may lead to fewer pregnancies and live births (limited evidence).

Adding dexamethasone or the combined oral contraceptive to clomiphene might help, and a 10-day course might work better than a 5-day course, but the evidence was very limited and more research is needed.

items.title: Combined oral contraceptives: the risk of myocardial infarction and ischemic stroke
items.summary: This review pooled results from 24 observational studies to see whether women taking the combined pill have more heart attacks or strokes caused by blood clots. Pill users had about a 1.6-times higher relative risk than non-users, and the increase was similar for heart attack and for stroke. Pills with higher estrogen doses seemed to carry more risk, and the type of progestagen did not clearly change the risk.
keyPoints: Combined pill users had about a 1.6-fold higher risk of heart attack or ischemic stroke than non-users.
The increase was similar for heart attack (1.6) and ischemic stroke (1.7).
Risk seemed to rise with higher estrogen doses and was highest for pills with more than 50 micrograms of estrogen.
The risk did not vary clearly by progestagen type or generation; with clot data from other studies, a levonorgestrel plus 30 microgram estrogen pill appears the safest oral option.

items.title: U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, 2024
items.summary: These are the 2024 US Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use from the CDC, which say which contraceptive methods are suitable for people with particular health conditions or circumstances. They replace the 2016 version. Updates include new advice for chronic kidney disease, revised advice for breastfeeding, after birth or abortion, obesity, blood clots, clotting disorders, lupus, sickle cell disease and other conditions, and newer pills, patches, rings and hormonal IUDs. The aim is to remove unnecessary barriers to contraception and support person-centred counselling.
keyPoints: Replaces the 2016 US Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use.
Adds recommendations for people with chronic kidney disease.
Revises recommendations for breastfeeding, postpartum and post-abortion use, obesity, deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, thrombophilia and several other conditions.
Includes newer methods such as new pill doses, patches, vaginal rings, progestin-only pills and levonorgestrel IUDs.
keywords: which contraception is safe for me

items.title: Hormonal contraception for women at risk of HIV infection
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled four randomised trials (9,726 women) in places where HIV is common, comparing hormonal contraceptives with the copper coil and with each other. The contraceptive injection (DMPA) and the hormonal implant (LNG) probably made little to no difference to HIV risk compared with the copper coil. The injection probably slightly raised HIV risk compared with the implant, though the range of possible effects was wide. All methods prevented pregnancy well, and many women reported condomless sex whichever method they used.
keyPoints: DMPA injection compared with the copper IUD likely made little to no difference to HIV acquisition (moderate-certainty evidence).
The LNG implant compared with the copper IUD likely made little to no difference to HIV acquisition (moderate-certainty evidence).
DMPA compared with the LNG implant probably slightly increased HIV acquisition (about 11 more women per 1000, moderate-certainty evidence).

DMPA slightly reduced pregnancy compared with the copper IUD (the LNG implant probably did too, moderate-certainty evidence), and DMPA users were less likely to stop their method than copper IUD or implant users (high-certainty evidence).

items.title: U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, 2024
items.summary: This is the 2024 update of the US guidance for health care providers on starting and using specific birth control methods. It was updated by the CDC after reviewing the scientific evidence and meeting with national experts. The goal is to remove unnecessary medical barriers to getting and using contraception and to support respectful, person-centred counselling without pressure.
keyPoints: Updated advice on which medications can be given for intrauterine device (IUD) placement.
Updated advice on managing bleeding changes while using a contraceptive implant.
New advice on testosterone use and the risk of pregnancy.
New advice on self-administering injectable contraception.

items.title: Progestin intrauterine devices versus copper intrauterine devices for emergency contraception
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether a hormonal coil (levonorgestrel IUD) can be used for emergency contraception as well as the copper coil, which is the most effective emergency option. Only one trial of 711 women met the review's criteria. The evidence was very uncertain about pregnancy rates, failed insertions, expulsions, removals and how acceptable women found each coil. The review cannot yet say whether the hormonal coil works as well as, better than, or worse than the copper coil for emergency use.
keyPoints: Only one trial (711 women) was found, with one month of follow-up.
Evidence on pregnancy rates, failed insertions, expulsion, removal and acceptability was very uncertain.
The copper coil may cause slightly more cramping, while the hormonal coil may cause slightly more bleeding and spotting days, but this evidence is also uncertain.
More studies are needed before the hormonal coil's effectiveness for emergency contraception can be confirmed.

items.title: Contraception values and preferences of people living with HIV: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 21 studies, mostly from sub-Saharan Africa, to understand what matters to people living with HIV when choosing contraception. Choices were shaped by many things, including how easy a method is to get, how well it works, side effects, protection from HIV, plans for having children, and advice from healthcare providers. Male condoms were often preferred because they are affordable, easy to find and protect against both HIV and pregnancy. The review concludes that these personal preferences should be respected so people can choose the method that suits them.
keyPoints: Preferences were shaped by availability, convenience, perceived effectiveness, safety, side effects, fertility wishes and relationship dynamics.
Male condoms were often a preferred method because they give affordable, accessible protection against both HIV and unwanted pregnancy.
Fears of infertility and side effects made some people less interested in hormonal methods.
Healthcare providers influenced how safe, tolerable and effective women thought different methods were.

items.title: Values and preferences for contraception: A global systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 423 studies from 93 countries on what people care about when choosing contraception. People's priorities differ, but the same main themes came up in many places. The most common were side effects, how well a method works, and how easy it is to use. The authors note that studies reported their findings in very different ways, which made it hard to combine and count the results.
keyPoints: The most common concerns were side effects, effectiveness, and ease, frequency or length of use.
Effects on sex and partner relationships, periods, reversibility, cost and availability, autonomy, and discreet use also mattered to many people.
People generally felt satisfied with, and knew more about, the method they were using.
Values and preferences vary from person to person, though core themes were similar across settings.

items.title: Systemic hormonal contraception initiation after abortion: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 16 studies on starting hormonal birth control (pills, injection, implant and similar) right after an abortion, or on the same day as the first abortion pill. For most methods, starting early did not make the abortion less likely to work, and no bleeding-related safety concerns were found. One study found a small rise in ongoing pregnancy when the DMPA injection was given right away rather than later. The studies were of poor or fair quality, so firm conclusions are limited.
keyPoints: Starting most hormonal contraception right away did not reduce how well a first-trimester medical abortion worked.
One fair-quality study found ongoing pregnancy in 3.6% with immediate DMPA injection versus 0.9% with delayed DMPA.
No bleeding-related safety concerns were found when hormonal contraception was started after medical or surgical abortion.
Starting a hormonal method as early as the day of the first abortion pill is an option for those who want contraception.

items.title: Health Care for Transgender and Gender Diverse Individuals: ACOG Committee Opinion, Number 823
items.summary: This guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) covers inclusive, affirming health care for transgender and gender diverse people, including hormone therapy and preventive care. It says gender-affirming hormone therapy is not effective contraception. People who are sexually active and still have their gonads, and who do not want a pregnancy (or do not want to cause one), should be counselled about the chance of pregnancy.
keyPoints: Gender-affirming hormone therapy is not effective contraception.
Sexually active people with retained gonads who want to avoid pregnancy should be counselled about pregnancy risk when sexual activity involves sperm and oocytes.
Not every transgender person has gender dysphoria or wants hormone treatment.
Inclusive, affirming care is essential to reduce the health inequities transgender people face.

items.title: The effect of different contraceptive methods on the vaginal microbiome
items.summary: This review looked at how different contraceptive methods affect the vaginal microbiome, the community of bacteria that normally lives in the vagina. A healthy vagina is usually dominated by Lactobacillus bacteria, which help protect against infections. The review reports that contraception can influence bacterial vaginosis, the most common imbalance of vaginal bacteria. It concludes that hormones taken by mouth or through the body tend to support a healthy, Lactobacillus-dominated vaginal microbiome.
keyPoints: The vaginal microbiome is normally dominated by Lactobacillus bacteria, which give some protection against infections.
Bacterial vaginosis is the most common imbalance of vaginal bacteria, and contraceptive use can influence how common it is.
Available evidence suggests oral or systemic female sex hormones help promote a healthy vaginal microbiome with Lactobacilli predominating.
The review covered combined pills and vaginal rings, progestin-only injections and implants, and copper or hormonal intrauterine devices.

items.title: Reasons for rejecting hormonal contraception in Western countries: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 42 studies from Western countries to understand why some women and their partners reject or complain about hormonal contraception (pills, patches, rings, injections, implants and hormonal IUDs). It found eight main reasons, ranging from physical and mood side effects to worries about future fertility and a wish for something more natural. The authors conclude that these reasons are complex and varied, not simply an irrational fear of hormones.
keyPoints: Eight main reasons for rejecting hormonal contraception emerged: physical side effects, altered mental health, negative impact on sexuality, concerns about future fertility, invocation of nature, concerns about menstruation, fears and anxiety, and side effects not being taken seriously.
The reasons given were complex and multifactorial, not only a general fear of hormones.
Some people felt their reported side effects were dismissed, and the authors call for more research on the provider-patient relationship.
The authors say birth control should better meet the needs and expectations of both women and men.

items.title: 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Reproductive Health in Rheumatic and Musculoskeletal Diseases
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Rheumatology gives advice on reproductive health for people with rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases, such as lupus. It covers contraception, fertility treatment, fertility preservation, menopausal hormone therapy, pregnancy and medicines. The experts say the overall evidence specific to these conditions is low, so many recommendations are conditional rather than strong.
keyPoints: Using safe and effective contraception to prevent unplanned pregnancy is a guiding principle.
Pre-pregnancy counseling is encouraged so that conception happens when the disease is quiet and while taking pregnancy-compatible medicines.
Reproductive health decisions should involve ongoing talks between the patient, their rheumatology doctor and obstetrics/gynecology.
Many recommendations are conditional because there is little or low-level data, so choices should reflect each person's values, preferences and other health conditions.

items.title: Evaluating different pain lowering medications during intrauterine device insertion: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 38 randomized trials (6,314 people) that tested different pain-relief medicines during IUD (coil) insertion against placebo. A numbing cream containing lidocaine and prilocaine, applied to the genital mucosa, reduced pain the most at tenaculum placement and during insertion. Numbing injections of lidocaine near the cervix ranked second. The authors concluded that the other medicines studied were not effective.
keyPoints: Lidocaine-prilocaine cream significantly reduced pain at tenaculum placement compared with placebo.
The cream ranked highest for reducing pain during IUD insertion, followed by paracervical lidocaine.
The authors conclude it is the most effective medication for IUD insertion pain and that the other medications were not effective.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 208: Benefits and Risks of Sterilization
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists looks at the benefits and risks of sterilization, a form of permanent birth control. It states that both female sterilization (tubal occlusion) and male sterilization (vasectomy) are safe and effective. The document reviews how female sterilization compares with male sterilization and with other types of contraception.
keyPoints: Female and male sterilization are both described as safe and effective permanent contraception.
More than 220 million couples worldwide use sterilization, including about 600,000 tubal occlusions and 200,000 vasectomies a year in the United States.
For women, sterilization removes the need for contraception that must be remembered or used correctly throughout the reproductive years.
It is described as an excellent option for women who have medical reasons they cannot use reversible methods.

items.title: Interventions for emergency contraception
items.summary: This Cochrane review pulled together 115 trials with over 60,000 women to compare ways of preventing pregnancy after unprotected sex, including emergency contraception pills and the copper IUD. Levonorgestrel and mifepristone worked better than the older Yuzpe combination pills, and ulipristal acetate and mifepristone may work better than levonorgestrel. Nausea and vomiting were the main side effects, and some methods changed the timing of the next period. The quality of the evidence for pregnancy outcomes was moderate to high.
keyPoints: Levonorgestrel caused fewer pregnancies than the Yuzpe combination pills, with fewer side effects such as nausea and vomiting.
Ulipristal acetate was linked to fewer pregnancies than levonorgestrel, and mid-dose mifepristone (25 to 50 mg) was probably more effective than levonorgestrel.
Ulipristal acetate made a later-than-expected period more likely, and mifepristone caused period delay that seemed to depend on the dose.
The copper IUD and mifepristone showed no clear difference in pregnancy risk (low-quality evidence), and the copper IUD may cause more abdominal pain.

items.title: Hormonal contraception in women with endometriosis: a systematic review
items.source: European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care
items.journal: European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care
items.summary: This review looked at studies of hormonal contraception in women with endometriosis, focusing on pain, quality of life and whether the condition came back after surgery. Combined pills and progestogen-only methods helped reduce period pain, and often pelvic pain and painful sex too, while improving quality of life. Some combined pills lowered the chance of endometriosis returning after surgery, but progestogen-only methods did not. The authors say there is not enough evidence to name one hormonal contraceptive as better than the others.
keyPoints: Combined hormonal contraceptives and progestogen-only contraceptives were linked to clear reductions in period pain, often with less non-period pelvic pain and painful sex, and better quality of life.
Only two combined pill types (EE/NETA and a flexible EE/drospirenone regimen) were shown to work significantly better than placebo.
Three studies found combined pills used after surgery reduced the risk of endometriosis coming back; there was no evidence that progestogen-only methods did this.
There is not enough evidence to say any one hormonal contraceptive is better overall.

items.title: Interventions using social networking sites to promote contraception in women of reproductive age
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether social networking sites, such as Facebook, can help women of reproductive age start or keep using contraception. Only two US studies were good enough to include, and both had a high risk of bias. One study saw a small rise in use of long-acting methods after 12 months, but there were no differences in consistency of use, knowledge of methods or condom use. Overall, there is little scientific evidence that social media programmes improve contraceptive use.
keyPoints: Only two studies met the review's criteria, and both were at high risk of bias.
In one trial of 2284 women, a web-based social networking intervention led to a small but significant increase in use of long-acting reversible methods at 12 months.
Neither study found differences in self-reported consistency of use, knowledge of method effectiveness, or condom use and intention.
The authors concluded there is little evidence that social networking sites improve contraceptive use or adherence.

items.title: Clinical practice guidelines for contraception by the French National College of Gynecologists and Obstetricians (CNGOF)
items.journal: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.summary: The French College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (CNGOF) published its first full set of guidelines on contraception. The guidelines are based on research published up to December 2017 and cover 12 themes, including intrauterine contraception, emergency contraception, natural methods, and contraception for teenagers and women over 40. They also cover women at higher risk of blood clots, heart problems or cancer. The authors conclude that the future of contraception depends mainly on making better use of the methods we already have, through clearer information and easier access for all women.
keyPoints: The guidelines give graded, evidence-based advice on 12 contraception topics, including intrauterine and emergency contraception.
They include specific advice on patient information, follow-up, and contraception for teenagers, women over 40, and women at higher clotting, heart or cancer risk.
Male and female sterilization and off-label hormonal treatments were left out of the review.
Better information for users and wider access to contraception for all women is seen as the main way to improve contraception.

items.title: Steroidal contraceptives: effect on carbohydrate metabolism in women without diabetes mellitus
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 31 trials of hormonal contraceptives (pills, injections, a vaginal ring and implants) to see whether they change how the body handles sugar (glucose and insulin) in women without diabetes. Most comparisons found no notable difference between methods, and the few differences seen were small and inconsistent. The authors say the evidence is limited, so they cannot make strong statements, and very little is known about women who are overweight.
keyPoints: Current evidence suggests no major differences in carbohydrate metabolism between different hormonal contraceptives in women without diabetes.
Of 34 comparisons, only eight showed any notable difference between groups, and results were often inconsistent.
Few studies compared the same types of contraceptives, many trials were small, and some lost many participants.
We still know very little about women at risk of metabolic problems because of being overweight.

items.title: Contraceptive Counseling in Clinical Settings: An Updated Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at whether talking with a clinician about contraception (contraceptive counseling) makes a difference. It updated an earlier review and found 10 new studies. Overall, the evidence supports counseling as useful, with many studies showing a positive effect on at least one outcome. The authors say better records of what counseling includes, and comparisons of different counseling styles, would make the evidence stronger.
keyPoints: Across the older and newer studies, 6 of 9 studies in adolescents and young adults found a statistically significant positive effect of counseling on at least one outcome.
16 of 23 studies in adults or mixed age groups also found a significant positive effect on at least one outcome.
Overall, the evidence supports contraceptive counseling in general, as well as some specific counseling approaches and features, such as personalization.
More research is needed to compare which counseling approaches work best.

items.title: Use of intrauterine devices in nulliparous women
items.summary: This clinical review looked at whether intrauterine devices (IUDs, or coils) are suitable for women who have never given birth. Five IUDs are available in the US: four hormonal ones and one copper one. All have very low failure rates and high satisfaction, yet fewer women who have not had children use them. The review concludes that IUDs are safe and effective for most women, including those who have not had children.
keyPoints: IUDs are safe and effective for most women, including those who have never given birth.
All five IUDs available in the US have very low typical-use failure rates and high acceptability ratings.
Women who have not had children use IUDs less often than women who have.
IUDs should be routinely included in the contraception options offered to women who have not had children.

items.title: Brief educational strategies for improving contraception use in young people
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at short educational programs (one to three sessions in a clinic) meant to help young people up to age 25 use contraception. It found 11 studies with about 8,300 people, and five showed some improvement in contraceptive use. Only one of those five gave moderate-quality evidence; the other four were older studies with low-quality evidence. Because the programs and measures varied so much, the results could not be combined.
keyPoints: Five of 11 brief education studies showed some effect on contraceptive use in young people.
Counseling followed by phone calls helped young women (16 to 24) use the pill more consistently at 3 and 6 months and use condoms more at last sex.
Comprehensive contraceptive services after an abortion led to more use of effective contraception and correct condom use at 6 months.
Few studies tested brief strategies, and most of the evidence was low quality; more intensive programs might work better but are harder for clinics to deliver.

items.title: Hormonal contraceptives for contraception in overweight or obese women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether hormonal birth control works less well in women who are overweight or obese. It pooled 17 studies with about 63,800 women. Most studies did not find a higher pregnancy risk in women with a higher weight or BMI, though a few methods showed some differences. The overall quality of the evidence was low, and there were few studies for most methods.
keyPoints: Most studies did not show a higher pregnancy risk in overweight or obese women using hormonal contraceptives.
No link between weight and pregnancy was found for the progestin injection (subcutaneous DMPA), the levonorgestrel hormonal IUD, the two-rod levonorgestrel implant or the etonogestrel implant.
Results were mixed for some pills, the patch and the older six-capsule levonorgestrel implant, with differences found in a few studies.
The review rated the overall quality of evidence as low, and the methods studied are among the most effective when used as directed.

items.title: School-based interventions for preventing HIV, sexually transmitted infections, and pregnancy in adolescents
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at eight large trials (over 55,000 students) of school programmes meant to prevent HIV, other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and teenage pregnancy. Classroom sex education programmes on their own did not show a clear effect on HIV, herpes, syphilis or pregnancy. Programmes that gave cash payments to keep girls in school may have lowered herpes infection and pregnancy, but the evidence is limited and more trials are needed.
keyPoints: Education-only school programmes showed no clear effect on HIV, herpes, syphilis or the number of young women who were pregnant.
Monthly cash incentives to stay in school were linked to lower herpes infection and fewer pregnancies in young women, based on low or very low certainty evidence.
Free school uniforms alone did not show a clear herpes benefit, but uniforms combined with sexual health education reduced herpes infection in one trial (low certainty).
The authors say adolescents still need services that include contraceptive choices and condoms, and that schools may be a good place to offer them.

items.title: Hormonal and intrauterine methods for contraception for women aged 25 years and younger
items.summary: This review looked at hormonal and intrauterine birth control in women aged 25 and younger, focusing on how often pregnancies happened and how many women kept using the method. Five small trials with 1,503 women were included, and the methods compared did not differ clearly in how well they worked or how long women stayed on them. Women using a hormonal coil (LNG-IUS) seemed to keep using it at least as often as those on the combined pill. The authors say the evidence is moderate to low quality and not strong enough to say which method is best for this age group.
keyPoints: Five trials (1,503 women aged 25 and under) compared pills, patch, vaginal ring, hormonal coils (LNG-IUS) and the copper coil.
When different types of methods were compared, pregnancy rates and continuation rates did not differ significantly.
Different doses of the hormonal coil (LNG-IUS) appeared equally effective over three years.
In three trials of hormonal coils, at least 75% of young women were still using them after 6 to 36 months.

items.title: Contraception for adolescent and young women. A consensus conference results
items.source: European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care
items.journal: European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care
items.summary: Italian experts reviewed the evidence on hormonal birth control for teenagers and young women, covering how well it works, bleeding patterns, acne, sex life, mood and bone health. They then voted on recommendations, and every statement reached the 75% agreement needed. The panel suggests long-acting methods such as implants or coils as first choices for teens because they work well and are easier to keep using. They also stress choosing a method that fits each person.
keyPoints: Long-acting reversible methods are recommended as first choices for adolescents because they are very effective and easier to stick with.
Talking through likely bleeding changes and other side effects before starting can help people keep using their method.
Combined hormonal methods are effective for managing acne.
Formulations can be chosen to support sexual health, steady mood and bone health, with the best choice depending on the individual.

items.title: Contraceptive use among women with inflammatory bowel disease: An updated systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 15 studies on women with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) who use hormonal contraception, looking at flare-ups, other health risks and whether the pill still works as expected. Results were mixed and mostly not statistically significant, and the evidence was rated very low certainty. Blood levels of pill hormones looked similar in women with and without IBD.
keyPoints: Studies gave inconsistent results on whether hormonal contraception raises or lowers the chance of IBD flare-ups or relapse (very low certainty).
Two studies found no significant link between the pill and blood clots (VTE) in women with IBD, and one found no link with abnormal cervical smears.
Two small studies suggested pill hormone levels in the blood were not different in women with and without IBD.
No evidence was found on bone thinning (osteoporosis) in women with IBD using contraception, and most studies had a high risk of bias.

items.title: Modifiable risk factors in women at high risk of breast cancer: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 93 studies on whether lifestyle factors such as alcohol, smoking, weight, physical activity and hormone use affect breast cancer risk in women with an inherited higher risk (family history or BRCA gene changes). Most studies found no link, but some suggested more activity may lower risk, and that hormonal contraception, menopausal hormone therapy, smoking and alcohol may raise it in women with a family history. Results were mixed and sometimes pointed in opposite directions for women with BRCA changes. The studies were small, measured things in different ways, and were limited in number, so no firm conclusions can be drawn yet.
keyPoints: For women with a family history, most studies found no link between these lifestyle factors and breast cancer.
Some studies suggested physical activity lowered risk, while hormonal contraception, menopausal hormone therapy, smoking and alcohol raised it in women with a family history.
For women with BRCA mutations, most studies found no link, and the few that did showed conflicting results.
Small studies and varied methods mean more research is needed.

items.title: Impact of estrogens on resting energy expenditure: A systematic review
items.summary: Many women worry that hormonal contraception or menopausal hormone therapy will cause weight gain. This review pulled together 10 studies on how estrogen medicines affect resting energy expenditure, the calories the body burns at rest, in healthy normal weight and overweight women. Estrogen use was linked to a higher resting calorie burn, by up to about 208 kcal a day with contraception and up to about 222 kcal a day with menopausal hormone therapy. The authors suggest estrogen may help protect against weight gain, though the abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: The review found 10 studies on estrogen medicines and resting energy expenditure in healthy women.
Estrogen in contraception raised resting energy expenditure by up to +208 kcal per day.
Estrogen in menopausal hormone therapy raised resting energy expenditure by up to +222 kcal per day.
The authors suggest estrogen may have a preventive effect on weight gain and obesity development.

items.title: Are Endogenous Androgens Linked to Female Sexual Function? A Systemic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from many studies to ask whether women's natural androgen hormone levels (such as testosterone) are linked to sexual desire and overall sexual function. It found a moderate link: women with higher testosterone tended to report better desire and sexual function. The link was weaker in the more precise lab-measured studies, there was evidence of publication bias, and the authors say more research is needed and that psychological and relationship factors still matter.
keyPoints: Higher natural total testosterone was moderately linked to better sexual desire and better overall sexual function in women.
The link did not differ by menopausal status, menstrual cycle phase, or use of hormonal contraception.
DHEAS was linked to overall sexual function but not to sexual desire.
Psychological, relationship and other hormonal factors should not be overlooked, and more research is needed.

items.title: Association of levonorgestrel intrauterine devices with stress reactivity, mental health, quality of life and sexual functioning: A systematic review
items.summary: This systematic review looked at what studies say about how hormonal coil (levonorgestrel IUD) use relates to stress, mental health, quality of life and sexual functioning. Results on mental health were mixed and unclear, and there was little data on stress. Quality of life and sexual functioning seemed to improve with the coil more consistently. The studies varied a lot in how they were done and how good they were, so firm conclusions are hard to draw.
keyPoints: Data on stress responses with the hormonal coil (LNG-IUD) is scarce.
Findings on mental health are ambiguous, with no clear pattern.
Quality of life and sexual functioning seem to improve more consistently with LNG-IUD use.
No studies were found on effects of the LNG-IUD on the brain, and more high-quality research is needed.

items.title: Migraine and Ischemic Stroke in Women. A Narrative Review
items.summary: This review looked at the research linking migraine, especially migraine with aura, to ischemic stroke (a stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel) in women. It found that migraine with aura goes along with several stroke risk factors, including hormonal contraceptive use, pregnancy and blood clots in the veins. Strokes linked to migraine with aura were more common in women under 45 who had frequent migraine attacks, used hormonal contraception, or had pregnancy complications such as preeclampsia. The authors say more research is needed, but suggest that migraine with aura may deserve a check-up similar to the one used for mini-strokes.
keyPoints: Migraine with aura is linked to stroke risk factors such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, smoking and some heart conditions.
In women, migraine with aura is also linked to hormonal contraceptive use, pregnancy and venous blood clots.
Stroke tied to migraine with aura is more common in women under 45 with frequent migraines, hormonal contraception use, or pregnancy and preeclampsia.
The authors suggest a diagnostic check for migraine with aura that mirrors the one for transient ischemic attack (mini-stroke), while noting more research is needed.

items.title: Dietary intake and eating behavior in depot medroxyprogesterone acetate users: a systematic review
items.source: Brazilian Journal of Medical and Biological Research = Revista Brasileira de Pesquisas Medicas E Biologicas
items.journal: Brazilian Journal of Medical and Biological Research = Revista Brasileira de Pesquisas Medicas E Biologicas
items.summary: Many women stop the contraceptive injection DMPA because of weight gain, so researchers reviewed studies on whether it changes what women eat or how they eat. They found only seven relevant studies. The one randomized trial found no link, and the others were inconsistent, with some showing no change and some showing more appetite in the first six months. There is not enough evidence to say whether DMPA changes eating habits in a way that causes weight gain.
keyPoints: Only seven studies looked at eating habits in DMPA users: one randomized trial, one non-randomized trial and five cohort studies.
The randomized trial found no link between DMPA and changes in diet or eating behavior.
Other studies were inconsistent, ranging from no change to increased appetite in the first six months of use.
The available data are not enough to conclude whether DMPA leads to weight gain through changes in eating.

items.title: Hormonal contraception among electronic cigarette users and cardiovascular risk: a systematic review
items.summary: Smoking while using combined hormonal contraception is known to raise the risk of heart and blood vessel problems. This review looked for evidence on whether using e-cigarettes alongside hormonal contraception does the same. It found no studies on women using both together. Limited, mostly short-term data in the general population suggested heart problems are rare with e-cigarettes and that they may affect heart rate and blood pressure less than regular cigarettes.
keyPoints: No studies were found on heart and blood vessel outcomes in women using both e-cigarettes and hormonal contraception.
In the general population, heart rate and blood pressure mostly stayed in the normal range after e-cigarette use.
Three studies found smaller changes with e-cigarettes than with regular cigarettes.
The authors say more research is needed on using hormonal contraception and e-cigarettes together.

items.title: Safety of hormonal contraception and intrauterine devices among women with depressive and bipolar disorders: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether hormonal birth control is safe for women who have depression or bipolar disorder. Only six studies met the criteria, so the evidence is limited. Across these studies, using birth control pills, the hormonal IUD or the DMPA injection was not linked to a worse course of illness than using no hormonal method.
keyPoints: Six studies were found; the review calls the evidence limited.
Pill, levonorgestrel IUD and DMPA use was not linked to worse depression or bipolar illness compared with no hormonal method.
In one study of adolescent girls with raised depression scores, combined pills were linked to improved scores after 3 months compared with placebo.
In bipolar disorder, one study found no more psychiatric hospital stays with DMPA, IUDs or sterilization.

items.title: Drug interactions between hormonal contraceptives and psychotropic drugs: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether hormonal birth control and common medicines for anxiety or depression affect each other when taken together. The 18 studies found suggest little cause for concern: pregnancy rates did not differ, and the mental health medicines worked the same with or without hormonal birth control. The evidence was limited in quality and amount, and a small amount of data raised a possible concern for two older antidepressants (amitriptyline and imipramine).
keyPoints: Studies found no difference in unintended pregnancy rates when hormonal contraceptives were taken with or without psychotropic drugs.
Treatment outcomes for the mental health medicines did not differ when taken with or without hormonal contraceptives.
Limited data suggest hormonal contraceptives may raise blood levels of amitriptyline and imipramine, which could theoretically be a safety concern.
No data were found for non-oral forms of hormonal contraception (such as patches or rings), and more research is needed.

items.title: The definition of unexplained infertility: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at how 375 studies defined 'unexplained infertility', which is the diagnosis given when standard tests find no clear cause. It found that studies used very different tests and cut-offs to decide who counted. Most checked semen, fallopian tube openness and ovulation, but often in different ways. The authors say agreed international criteria would improve research and future care.
keyPoints: There is no agreed set of tests for diagnosing unexplained infertility.
Of 375 studies, only 258 stated how they defined unexplained infertility.
Most studies checked semen (85%), fallopian tubes (90%) and ovulation (79.5%), but used different methods and cut-offs.
Other checks, such as the womb cavity and hormone levels, were used in fewer than half of the studies.

items.title: A critical systematic review and meta-analyses of risk factors for fertility problems in a globalized world
items.summary: This review pooled results from 62 studies (almost 112,000 people) to look at risk factors for fertility problems that are often overlooked, especially in lower-income regions. Genital tuberculosis, HIV and bacterial vaginosis were linked to a higher chance of being unable to become pregnant, and some forms of female genital cutting were linked to blocked-tube infertility. Parents who are blood relatives had a higher chance of stillbirth and newborn death. The authors suggest that health promotion and early detection could help prevent fertility problems.
keyPoints: Genital tuberculosis was linked to about a ninefold higher risk of being unable to become pregnant, though the estimate was imprecise.
HIV and bacterial vaginosis were each linked to an almost threefold higher risk of being unable to become pregnant.
Female genital mutilation/cutting (Type II/III) was linked to about twice the risk of tubal-factor infertility.
Consanguinity (parents related by blood) was linked to higher risks of stillbirth and neonatal death.

items.title: Innovative Approaches to Menstruation and Fertility Tracking Using Wearable Reproductive Health Technology: Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at wearable devices, such as wrist, finger, in-ear and intravaginal sensors, that track body signals like temperature, heart rate and breathing rate to follow the menstrual cycle. Most of the devices reviewed had high accuracy for detecting fertility and could tell apart the fertile window, the luteal phase and menstruation. The authors say these devices hold promise, but research is still scarce and more studies are needed to confirm the results.
keyPoints: Fertility-tracking wearables can be worn on the wrist, finger, inside the ear or intravaginally.
Most devices had high accuracy for detecting fertility and could separate the fertile window, luteal phase and menstruation.
They work by measuring changes in heart rate, heart rate variability, temperature and respiratory rate.
More validation studies are needed, especially for breathing rate as a way to stage the cycle, and data privacy concerns need to be addressed.

items.title: University students' fertility awareness and its influencing factors: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 21 studies on how much university students know about fertility, including risk factors for infertility and fertility treatments. Overall, students showed low to moderate fertility awareness. Female medical students knew the most, while links between awareness and age or years of education were unclear.
keyPoints: Across 21 studies, university students generally showed low to moderate fertility awareness.
Female medical students had higher fertility awareness than other groups.
Evidence linking age or years of education to fertility awareness was insufficient.
The authors suggest more fertility education is needed, especially for male and non-medical students.

items.title: Timed intercourse for couples trying to conceive
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at seven trials with 2,464 women or couples to see whether timing sex around ovulation helps people conceive. Using urine ovulation tests probably increases the chance of a live birth and of a positive pregnancy test compared with having sex without tracking ovulation. For fertility awareness methods such as temperature or cervical mucus tracking, the evidence was too limited to say whether they help. The evidence ranged from moderate to very low quality.
keyPoints: Urine ovulation tests probably increase live birth: if the chance is 16% without tests, it is about 16% to 28% with them (moderate-quality evidence, one trial).
Urine ovulation tests probably also increase the chance of a clinical pregnancy or positive pregnancy test (moderate-quality evidence, four trials).
It is uncertain whether fertility awareness-based methods change live birth, pregnancy, time to pregnancy, stress, anxiety or depression, because the evidence was limited and low to very low quality.
The benefits seen were in women under 40 who had been trying for less than 12 months; no trials tested timing sex using ultrasound.

items.title: Effectiveness of fertility awareness-based methods for pregnancy prevention during the postpartum period
items.summary: This review looked at how well fertility awareness-based methods (tracking signs of fertility to avoid pregnancy) work in the months after having a baby, whether or not someone is breastfeeding. Only four studies met the review's standards, and most were low quality. Typical-use pregnancy rates in the early months after birth ranged from about 8.5 to 26.8 per 100 women, depending on the method and group studied. The authors conclude that the evidence is very limited and more good-quality studies are needed.
keyPoints: Only four studies gave usable data on postpartum effectiveness: none were high quality, one was moderate and three were low quality.
Typical-use pregnancy probability in the first 6 cycles postpartum was 12.0 per 100 women years for the Marquette Method.
For the Billings Ovulation Method, typical-use pregnancy probability ranged from 9.1 (non-lactating women under 30) to 26.8 (lactating women under 30).
Evidence for each method in postpartum people is very limited, so more high-quality studies are needed to guide counselling and shared decisions.

items.title: What do people know about fertility? A systematic review on fertility awareness and its associated factors
items.summary: This review pulled together 71 studies on how much people know about fertility, risk factors for infertility, and the effects of delaying childbearing. Overall, people of reproductive age showed low-to-moderate fertility awareness. Women, people with more education, people who had struggled to conceive, and those who planned their pregnancies knew more. The authors say the studies measured awareness in very different ways, so the conclusions should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Across 71 studies, fertility awareness was generally low to moderate.
Higher awareness was seen in women, highly educated people, people who had difficulty conceiving, and those who planned their pregnancies.
Having or wanting children was not linked to awareness level, and the link with age was inconsistent.
The authors suggest awareness programmes, especially for men, people with low education, and family planning settings, but note the studies varied a lot.

items.title: Effectiveness of Fertility Awareness-Based Methods for Pregnancy Prevention: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 53 studies on how well fertility awareness-based methods prevent pregnancy. None of the studies were high quality, and the rest were moderate or low quality. Pregnancy rates varied a lot between methods and even within the same method, so the studies cannot be used to say that one method works better than another.
keyPoints: Of 53 studies, none were high quality, 21 were moderate quality and 32 were low quality.
In moderate-quality studies, typical-use pregnancy rates in the first year ranged from about 2 to 34 per 100 women, depending on the method and study.
Perfect-use rates were lower, from 0 to about 12 per 100 women in the first year.
Studies covered different groups of women, so the methods cannot be fairly compared with each other.

items.title: Knowledge of age-related fertility decline in women: A systematic review
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pulled together 41 studies that asked people how well they understand the way a woman's fertility falls with age. Across studies, knowledge was often poor, especially about when fertility drops sharply. Educational campaigns and programs did raise knowledge, but only a few have been tested. The authors say better public education is needed so people can make informed choices about when to try for a baby.
keyPoints: Awareness of age-related fertility decline varied widely between studies and was judged insufficient overall.
People were least sure about when female fertility drops markedly: only 5.6% to 60% correctly named the 35-39 age range.
Targeted education can improve knowledge, but only six intervention studies (four randomized trials) have been done.
The authors call for campaigns aimed at people of reproductive age and at healthcare providers.

items.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria® First Trimester Vaginal Bleeding: 2025 Update
items.source: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Radiology looks at which tests to use when someone has vaginal bleeding in the first three months of pregnancy. Bleeding is common and can be caused by a normal pregnancy, a pregnancy that is not developing, an ectopic pregnancy, or, rarely, a molar pregnancy. Most causes can be found using an ultrasound scan, blood tests for the pregnancy hormone hCG, and a physical exam. An MRI scan without contrast dye is only sometimes used for hard-to-solve cases.
keyPoints: Most causes of first trimester bleeding can be diagnosed with ultrasound, hCG blood tests and a physical examination.
When the diagnosis is unclear, repeat examinations and close follow-up are very important.
Care is taken to avoid early treatment that could harm a pregnancy that may be normal.
MRI of the pelvis without contrast may help in difficult cases, such as when ultrasound is limited or an ectopic pregnancy outside the fallopian tube is strongly suspected.

items.title: Effectiveness of treatment options for tubal ectopic pregnancy: A systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 31 trials (2,938 women) comparing ways to treat a tubal ectopic pregnancy: waiting and watching, medicines such as methotrexate, and surgery. Most medical and conservative options worked about as well as expectant management (waiting) for clearing the pregnancy. All options had a higher chance of failing than surgery to remove the tube (salpingectomy). The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to say that any medical treatment is better than expectant management.
keyPoints: Methotrexate was not clearly better than expectant management for resolving a tubal ectopic pregnancy.
Most conservative treatments had similar results to expectant management in the network analysis.
Every treatment option had a higher risk of failure than salpingectomy (surgical removal of the tube).
There is insufficient evidence to support any medical treatment over expectant management.

items.title: Methotrexate vs expectant management for treatment of tubal ectopic pregnancy: An individual participant data meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled the original data from two randomised trials (153 women) comparing methotrexate (a medicine) with careful watching and waiting for tubal ectopic pregnancy with low hCG levels. Treatment worked for about 79% of women given methotrexate and about 69% of those who waited, and this difference could have been due to chance. Rates of needing surgery and time to recovery were also not clearly different. Side effects from methotrexate were reported far more often than in the waiting group, so the authors suggest starting with watchful waiting may be a reasonable choice.
keyPoints: Treatment success was 79.3% with methotrexate and 68.6% with expectant management, not a statistically significant difference.
Surgery was needed for 9.8% after methotrexate and 18.6% after waiting, also not a clear difference.
Average time to success was about 20 days with methotrexate and 21 days with waiting.
Methotrexate side effects were reported in 33 women, compared with 4 in the waiting group.

items.title: Cesarean Scar Pregnancy: A systematic review on expectant management
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: A cesarean scar pregnancy is a type of ectopic pregnancy where the pregnancy implants in the scar from an earlier cesarean birth. This review looked at 194 women whose pregnancies were monitored rather than ended early. About 1 in 4 reached a term birth, but more than half needed a hysterectomy, and the condition carried a high rate of serious complications. Some ultrasound signs may help predict how a pregnancy will go, but they need more research before being used with confidence.
keyPoints: Of 194 women managed expectantly, about 26% had a term delivery and 42% had a preterm birth.
About 20% had a miscarriage, 8% had foetal death, and 53% had a hysterectomy.
Placenta accreta spectrum was common and linked to more complications, including bleeding and surgical problems.
Certain ultrasound signs, such as lower myometrial thickness and type II or III classification, were linked to worse outcomes but need further validation.

items.title: Methotrexate versus expectant management in ectopic pregnancy: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This study pooled results from four randomised trials comparing methotrexate (a medicine that stops the pregnancy tissue growing) with watchful waiting in women with an ectopic pregnancy. All the women were medically stable. The two approaches worked about equally well, and the need for surgery was not clearly different between them. The authors concluded that watchful waiting was not worse than methotrexate when pregnancy hormone (β-hCG) levels were already low or falling.
keyPoints: Ectopic pregnancy affects about 1-2% of pregnancies and can sometimes need emergency surgery.
Methotrexate and expectant management had no significant difference in treatment success (hormone levels falling without complications).
Need for surgery was also not significantly different between the two approaches.
Expectant management was not inferior to methotrexate in stable patients with low or declining β-hCG levels.

items.title: Interventions for non-tubal ectopic pregnancy
items.summary: This review looked at treatments for ectopic pregnancies that implant outside the womb cavity and the fallopian tubes. Only five small trials (303 women) were found, and all were about pregnancies in a caesarean scar. For most outcomes, such as how often treatment worked or caused complications, it is unclear whether the treatments differ, because the evidence is low or very low quality. Blood loss was lower when scar pregnancies were treated with uterine artery blocking treatment before suction curettage than with methotrexate alone.
keyPoints: Only five trials were found, all on caesarean scar pregnancy; none covered other non-tubal sites such as the cervix, ovary or abdomen.
It is uncertain whether uterine artery embolization (with or without chemotherapy) differs from methotrexate alone in success rates, complications or side effects (low-quality evidence).
Blood loss was lower when suction curettage followed uterine artery embolization than when it followed methotrexate alone (moderate-quality evidence).
It is uncertain whether suction curettage guided by hysteroscopy or by ultrasound gives different results (very low-quality evidence).

items.title: Endometrial injection of embryo culture supernatant for subfertile women in assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether injecting a fluid that embryos have been grown in (embryo culture supernatant) into the womb before embryo transfer helps women having fertility treatment. Five trials with 526 women were included. The review could not say whether the injection improves live birth, ongoing pregnancy or miscarriage rates, and the evidence was mostly of very low quality. Ectopic pregnancy was also unclear, with too few cases to draw any conclusion.
keyPoints: It is uncertain whether the injection improves live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates compared with no treatment (very low-quality evidence).
It is uncertain whether it changes miscarriage, clinical pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, multiple pregnancy or preterm birth rates.
There may be little or no difference in foetal abnormality rates, based on one small trial (low-quality evidence).
The authors say larger, well-designed trials reporting live births and harms are still needed.

items.title: Surgical treatment for tubal disease in women due to undergo in vitro fertilisation
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 11 trials (1,386 women) of surgery for blocked, fluid-filled fallopian tubes (hydrosalpinx) before IVF or ICSI. Removing the affected tube (salpingectomy) probably raises the chance of a clinical pregnancy compared with no surgery, and blocking the tube may also help, though the evidence for that is weaker. Most of the evidence was low or very low quality, and no trial reported long-term fertility results. Too little evidence was found to say whether the surgery changes the risk of complications.
keyPoints: Salpingectomy before IVF probably increases the clinical pregnancy rate compared with no surgery (moderate-quality evidence).
Tubal occlusion may increase the clinical pregnancy rate compared with no surgery, but the evidence is low quality.
There was not enough evidence to compare the different surgeries with each other or to judge surgical complications.
No trials reported live birth for most comparisons or any long-term fertility outcomes, so more high-quality trials are needed.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 191: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists explains tubal ectopic pregnancy, where a pregnancy grows outside the womb, most often in the fallopian tube. When it is found early, most cases can be treated successfully, either with minimally invasive surgery or with a medicine called methotrexate. If a person is unstable, it is a medical emergency that needs prompt surgery.
keyPoints: Ectopic pregnancy means a pregnancy outside the uterine cavity, and the fallopian tube is the most common site.
Most tubal ectopic pregnancies found early can be treated successfully with minimally invasive surgery or with methotrexate.
A tubal ectopic pregnancy in an unstable patient is a medical emergency that needs prompt surgery.
The guideline aims to support timely diagnosis and management based on the best available scientific evidence.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 193: Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists reviews tubal ectopic pregnancy, which is a pregnancy that grows outside the womb, most often in the fallopian tube. When it is found early, it can usually be treated successfully, either with minimally invasive surgery or with a medicine called methotrexate. If a patient is unstable, it is a medical emergency that needs prompt surgery.
keyPoints: An ectopic pregnancy is a pregnancy outside the uterine cavity, and the fallopian tube is the most common site.
Most tubal ectopic pregnancies found early can be treated successfully with minimally invasive surgery or with methotrexate.
A tubal ectopic pregnancy in an unstable patient is a medical emergency that needs prompt surgery.
The guideline aims to support timely diagnosis and management based on the best available scientific evidence.

items.title: Oocyte cryopreservation for patients with endometriosis: where are we now? A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 10 observational studies on freezing eggs in women with endometriosis. Fewer eggs were collected when women were older at the time of freezing and when they had already had surgery for endometriosis. There is very little follow-up data on what happens when the frozen eggs are later used, so it is not yet possible to say for certain how well egg freezing works for all women with endometriosis.
keyPoints: Fewer eggs were retrieved as age at freezing increased and after previous surgery for endometriosis.
The number of eggs retrieved did not seem to depend on the type of endometriosis, or on the side or size of ovarian endometriomas.
Egg maturation rate did not appear to be affected by a history of endometriosis surgery.
Not enough follow-up data exist on using the frozen eggs, so the benefit of preventive egg freezing cannot yet be confirmed for all women with endometriosis.

items.title: Fertility preservation for cancer: referral guidelines, treatment options, and specific considerations
items.summary: This review looked at how fertility preservation is offered to people having cancer treatment, which can harm future fertility. It found that egg and embryo freezing are the standard options, and that ovarian tissue freezing suits children before puberty or people who need to start treatment urgently. Guidelines recommend an early fertility consultation, but referrals are still low because of provider, hospital and cost barriers.
keyPoints: Chemotherapy, radiation and surgery can seriously reduce the ability to have children later.
Egg freezing and embryo freezing are the standard fertility preservation options.
Ovarian tissue freezing is suitable for prepubertal patients or those who need urgent cancer treatment.
Early referral, individual assessment and a team approach give the best chance of a good outcome, but cost and access barriers remain.

items.title: Planned oocyte cryopreservation: a systematic review and meta-regression analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 10 studies of women who froze their eggs to protect against age-related fertility decline. About 11% of women came back to use their frozen eggs, and 28% of the women who returned had a live birth. Success was much higher when eggs were frozen at 35 or younger than at 40 or older. The authors say success rates are limited overall and that better-quality data are needed.
keyPoints: Across 8,750 women, about 11% returned to use their frozen eggs.
Live birth rate per woman was 28% overall, 52% if eggs were frozen at 35 or younger, and 19% at 40 or older.
About 78.5% of frozen eggs survived thawing.
Egg freezing is a feasible option for later conception, but the chance of a live birth falls as age at freezing rises.

items.title: Live birth rate after female fertility preservation for cancer or haematopoietic stem cell transplantation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the three main techniques; embryo, oocyte and ovarian tissue cryopreservation
items.summary: This review pooled results from 34 studies of women who had fertility preserved before or around cancer treatment. It looked at how often these women went on to have a live birth after freezing embryos, eggs or ovarian tissue. The authors say the studies were too different to compare the three methods directly, so the figures give only limited guidance when counselling patients.
keyPoints: After frozen embryos were used in IVF, about 41% of women had a live birth.
After frozen (vitrified) eggs were used, about 32% had a live birth.
After ovarian tissue was frozen and transplanted back, about 21% had a live birth through IVF and about 33% through spontaneous pregnancy.
Long-term follow-up registries are needed to track how many women return to use their frozen material and how many go on to have babies.

items.title: The Impact of Oocyte Vitrification on Offspring: a Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 13 studies covering 4,159 babies born from eggs that were frozen using a fast-freezing method called vitrification. It checked things like birth weight, Apgar scores, birth defects and general baby health. The authors concluded that vitrification seems safe for babies, at least in the short term.
