All the studies were observational, and children were followed for six years at most, so longer-term data and better-designed trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Vitrification (fast freezing) of eggs appears safe for babies and child health in the short term.
The review included 13 observational studies and 4,159 babies, with follow-up of up to 6 years.
Outcomes checked included birth weight, gestational age, Apgar scores, congenital anomalies and baby health.
The authors call for more long-term data and randomized controlled trials to strengthen the evidence.

items.title: Oocyte and embryo cryopreservation before gonadotoxic treatments: Principles of safe ovarian stimulation, a systematic review
items.summary: This systematic review looked at whether freezing eggs or embryos before treatments that can harm fertility, such as cancer treatment, is safe. It drew on 2 randomized trials, 60 cohort studies and 20 expert reviews or opinions. The authors concluded that for most patients, fertility preservation can be done safely within about 2 weeks without affecting disease severity or long-term survival.
keyPoints: Modern fertility preservation gives a high number of eggs collected.
Protocols can be started at multiple points in the menstrual cycle and keep estrogen from reaching very high levels.
For most patients, the process can be completed within 2 weeks without affecting disease severity or long-term survival.
More than one quarter of patients who preserve fertility later return to use fertility services.

items.title: Women Electing Oocyte Cryopreservation: Characteristics, Information Sources, and Oocyte Disposition: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 29 studies on women who freeze their eggs for non-medical reasons, often called planned egg freezing. Most women who freeze or consider freezing were single, highly educated, in work, and around 37 years old. Most first heard about it from the media or friends rather than a health professional. Most had not tried to use their frozen eggs, and they did not regret freezing them.
keyPoints: Women who freeze or consider freezing eggs were mostly single, highly educated, employed, and about 37 years old on average.
Media and friends were the most common first sources of information; health professionals were less common.
Most women who froze eggs had not tried to get pregnant with them, yet did not regret the decision.
Women's plans for unused frozen eggs (discard, donate to others, or donate to research) were inconsistent across studies.

items.title: Planned oocyte cryopreservation (Planned OC): systematic review and meta-analysis of cost-efficiency and patients' perspective
items.summary: This review pulled together 43 studies on planned egg freezing, which is freezing eggs for future use when there is no current medical reason to do so. It looked at cost-efficiency, how often frozen eggs are actually used, and what patients think. The authors concluded that planned egg freezing is an adequate way to preserve fertility, but many people lack knowledge about the process and overestimate its success rates.
keyPoints: Planned egg freezing was found to be cost-efficient at age 35 if 60% of banked eggs end up being used.
Up to 15% of banked eggs were used within 22-58 months, and 9% of warmed banked eggs led to live births.
Most patients think egg freezing is ideal before age 35, but many are not fully aware of what the process involves and tend to overestimate success rates.
Worries about health effects or limited success were the main barriers to wider use; online resources and treating doctors were equally important sources of information.

items.title: PERSPECTIVE: Cryopreservation of Human Oocytes and the 'Carryover' Effect on Early Embryo Development
items.summary: This review pooled results from 27 studies of frozen human eggs to see how freezing affects early embryo development. Vitrification (fast freezing) did better than slow freezing for egg survival, fertilization, early cell division and implantation. Even so, freezing seems to have a small negative 'carryover' effect on how embryos develop after fertilization, and this effect was bigger with slow freezing. The reasons for this effect are not yet known.
keyPoints: Vitrification gave better egg survival than slow freezing (84.7% vs 58.0%).
Fertilization, early cell division and implantation rates were also higher with vitrification than slow freezing.
Egg freezing can negatively affect early embryo development, more so with slow freezing than with vitrification.
The cause of this 'carryover' effect is unknown; the authors suggest future research look at epigenetic changes.

items.title: Social Freezing: Pressing Pause on Fertility
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review looked at research from the past ten years on social egg freezing, where women freeze eggs for non-medical reasons to protect against age-related fertility decline. It covered how freezing is done, its safety, how often frozen eggs are used, ethical questions and cost-effectiveness. The authors report that egg vitrification (fast freezing) is the preferred method and that it may help women feel more secure and in control of their reproductive choices. The abstract does not give success rates or rate the quality of the evidence.
keyPoints: Fertility can be preserved for non-medical reasons by freezing eggs, embryos or ovarian tissue.
Egg vitrification is described as a new and optimal approach.
Planned egg freezing is seen as a chosen strategy against age-related infertility, despite some controversies.
It may help women feel more socially, psychologically and financially stable before motherhood.

items.title: Fertility preservation for transgender adolescents and young adults: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 40 studies on fertility preservation (such as freezing eggs or sperm) for transgender teenagers and young adults who may take gender-affirming hormones or have surgery. It found many barriers to preserving fertility, including not knowing the options exist, high costs, invasive procedures, and the emotional impact of the process. Hormone treatment is expected to harm fertility, but it is not known how far those effects can be reversed. The authors say high-quality medical data is lacking, so advice often relies on expert opinion and on studies in cisgender people.
keyPoints: Barriers to fertility preservation include low awareness of options, high costs, invasive procedures and possible psychological impact.
Gender-affirming hormones are expected to affect fertility, but how reversible this is remains unknown.
The authors recommend fertility preservation counselling as early as possible, as standard care before hormone treatment starts.
Because high-quality medical data is lacking, current advice relies on expert opinion and studies in cisgender people.

items.title: Practical recommendations for fertility preservation in women by the FertiPROTEKT network. Part I: Indications for fertility preservation
items.summary: This German-network guideline explains when fertility preservation, such as freezing eggs or ovarian tissue, may be worth considering for women facing illnesses like cancer. It looks at how serious the disease is, how much the treatment could harm fertility, and a woman's own plans for having children. The advice depends on the type and stage of the illness, so decisions are made individually.
keyPoints: In breast cancer, freezing ovarian tissue or eggs is especially recommended for low-stage cancer and for women under 35.
In Hodgkin's lymphoma, the need depends on the chemotherapy plan, since some regimens harm the ovaries very little and others a great deal.
In borderline ovarian tumours, fertility is usually protected through fertility-sparing surgery, and ovarian stimulation may also be considered.
The choice for or against preservation depends on prognosis, risks to fertility and personal family planning.

items.title: Fertility preservation for medical reasons in girls and women: British fertility society policy and practice guideline
items.summary: This is a guideline from the British Fertility Society on protecting fertility in girls and women who face medical treatments, such as cancer care, that could harm their ability to have children. It looks at four options: freezing embryos or eggs, freezing ovarian tissue, using hormone-suppressing medicine (GnRH agonists), and moving the ovaries out of the way of treatment. Freezing ovarian tissue is still thought of as experimental, though more babies have now been born after the tissue was put back. The guideline says these options carry risks and that research is still ongoing.
keyPoints: Options considered are embryo and egg freezing, ovarian tissue freezing, GnRH agonist suppression and ovarian transposition.
Ovarian tissue freezing is still considered experimental, but more live births have been reported after tissue was transplanted back.
Girls and women should be counselled by a multidisciplinary team about fertility risks and options, with psychological support to help them decide.
Women need to be medically fit for these invasive procedures, and they are appropriate when the main treatment aims to cure the illness.

items.title: Risks associated with fertility preservation for women with sickle cell anemia
items.summary: This small study looked at seven women with sickle cell anemia who froze eggs, embryos or ovarian tissue before a stem cell transplant. Three of the seven had serious sickle cell complications around the time of treatment, including life-threatening breathing failure and painful crises. The authors say women with sickle cell anemia face real risks during fertility preservation and that better, evidence-based ways to lower those risks are needed.
keyPoints: Seven women aged 15-32 with sickle cell anemia had fertility preservation before a stem cell transplant: 4 froze eggs, 1 froze embryos and 2 froze ovarian tissue.
Three of the seven had sickle cell complications around the procedure, including life-threatening respiratory failure and painful crises.
One painful crisis was serious enough that a stimulation cycle had to be stopped.
The authors conclude that evidence-based ways to reduce these risks and improve fertility preservation results are needed.

items.title: Update on fertility preservation from the Barcelona International Society for Fertility Preservation-ESHRE-ASRM 2015 expert meeting: indications, results and future perspectives
items.summary: Experts from three major fertility societies reviewed a decade of progress in fertility preservation, including egg and embryo freezing. They found that freezing eggs or embryos is the first-choice option for women past puberty, and that freezing mature eggs by a fast-freezing method called vitrification is preferred. Most of the evidence was of limited quality because there were few large or randomised studies, so more long-term research is needed.
keyPoints: Embryo and oocyte (egg) freezing are first-line fertility preservation methods in women after puberty, with vitrification of mature (metaphase II) eggs preferred.

Counselling about fertility preservation options is recommended for people whose fertility may be affected by illness, treatment, age or planned gender-affirming care, including women who want to delay having children.

Transplanting frozen ovarian tissue back has restored ovarian function and led to spontaneous pregnancies and pregnancies with assisted reproduction, supporting its future use as an open clinical option.
Most evidence reviewed was level three or below, and international registries tracking short- and long-term outcomes are strongly recommended.

items.title: Ovarian stimulation in the luteal phase: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies that started ovarian stimulation for egg collection in the second half of the menstrual cycle (the luteal phase) instead of the usual first half. Luteal-phase cycles took about one day longer and used more fertility medication. The number of eggs collected was similar, slightly more of them were mature, and more eggs fertilised. Only three studies reported pregnancy rates, and these did not differ between the two approaches.
keyPoints: Luteal-phase stimulation took about 1 day longer and used more total gonadotropin medication (about 817 IU more).
The total number of eggs retrieved was not significantly different between luteal and follicular starts.
Slightly more mature eggs were retrieved and fertilisation rates were higher with luteal-phase starts.
Pregnancy rates after frozen embryo transfer were similar, but only three studies reported this.

items.title: Emergency fertility preservation for female patients with cancer: clinical perspectives
items.summary: This review looked at the options available for preserving fertility in women who need cancer treatment quickly. It found that several options exist, including freezing eggs, freezing embryos and freezing ovarian tissue, though some are still experimental or debated. The authors say these options are under-used and propose a step-by-step approach for urgent cases.
keyPoints: Options for urgent fertility preservation include emergency ovarian stimulation, embryo freezing, egg freezing, ovarian tissue freezing and re-transplanting, in vitro maturation, and ovarian protection techniques.
Some options are established, while others are experimental or debated.
These options are under-used in women with cancer.
The authors suggest a new multi-step strategy for emergency fertility preservation.

items.title: Network meta-analysis of progestogen administration routes for luteal phase support in fresh embryo transfer IVF cycles
items.summary: This study pooled results from 24 randomized trials to compare how progesterone-type medicines, given in different ways, support the second half of the cycle after a fresh embryo transfer in IVF. Oral and injected-into-muscle forms showed a statistically significant boost in live birth rates compared with placebo, while vaginal and under-the-skin forms did not. The authors note that the confidence ranges overlap, so it is unclear whether any route is truly better, and more studies are needed.
keyPoints: Oral progestogen was the only route with a statistically significant increase in clinical pregnancy rate.
For live birth, only oral and intramuscular routes were significantly better than placebo; vaginal and subcutaneous were not.
Overlapping confidence intervals mean it is uncertain whether any route is clinically better than another.
Results held up when low-quality and older studies were left out, but the authors say further studies are needed.

items.title: Revisiting natural cycle frozen embryo transfer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 70 studies on how to prepare the womb for a frozen embryo transfer, looking mainly at natural cycle approaches. Adding vaginal progesterone after transfer raised live birth rates in true natural cycles but not in modified natural cycles. A newer approach called natural proliferative phase transfer had higher live birth rates than hormone replacement therapy, but the evidence for this was very low certainty. The authors say high-quality evidence is still limited.
keyPoints: Vaginal progesterone support after transfer improved live birth rates in true natural cycle transfers compared with no support (moderate-certainty evidence).
Progesterone support showed no benefit in modified natural cycle transfers (moderate-certainty evidence).
Natural proliferative phase transfer had higher live birth rates than hormone replacement therapy transfer, but this was very low-certainty evidence.
Cycles where ovulation occurred had higher live birth rates than cycles with a luteinized unruptured follicle (very low-certainty evidence).

items.title: Endometrial injury in women undergoing in vitro fertilisation (IVF)
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 24 trials with 7,234 women to see whether deliberately scratching the womb lining before embryo transfer helps IVF work better. When the most reliable trials were pooled, it was unclear whether the procedure increases the chance of a baby or a pregnancy, because the results fit with no effect or a small benefit. It probably causes mild to moderate pain. The conclusion is the same as the previous version of the review.
keyPoints: The effect of endometrial injury (scratching) on live birth and clinical pregnancy in IVF is unclear, based on moderate-certainty evidence.
In the example given, if the usual chance of live birth is 27%, with scratching it would be somewhere between 27% and 32%.
It may make little to no difference to miscarriage risk (low-certainty evidence).
The procedure probably causes mild to moderate pain.

items.title: Techniques for preparation prior to embryo transfer
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at simple steps taken just before an embryo is placed in the womb during IVF: having a full bladder, removing mucus from the cervix, and 'afterloading' (first placing the catheter, then loading the embryo). Across 11 trials, none of these steps clearly changed pregnancy rates or pregnancy loss, though the evidence was low or very low certainty. The review did not make any recommendations for practice and called for larger, better-designed studies.
keyPoints: A full bladder versus an empty bladder made no clear difference to pregnancy rate, pregnancy loss or difficulty of transfer, and the evidence was very low certainty.
Removing cervical mucus may make little to no difference to pregnancy rate, and the evidence was low certainty.
Afterloading the embryo may make little to no difference to pregnancy or pregnancy loss, and the effect on how difficult the transfer is remains very uncertain.
No specific recommendations for practice were made because the evidence is limited; larger and better-designed trials are needed.

items.title: Endometrial preparation with vs without ovulation for frozen-embryo transfer: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 17 randomized trials (10,611 people) comparing two ways of preparing the womb lining for a frozen embryo transfer: cycles where the body ovulates (natural, modified natural or stimulated) and artificial cycles using medication without ovulation. Cycles with ovulation lowered the risk of pregnancy loss, with high-certainty evidence. Overall live birth rates were similar, though they were higher with ovulation when the less reliable trials were left out.
keyPoints: Preparing with ovulation reduced pregnancy loss compared with artificial cycles (high-certainty evidence).
Clinical pregnancy rates were about the same with both methods.
Overall live birth rates were comparable (moderate certainty), but were higher with ovulation after excluding high-risk-of-bias studies and one outlier trial.
There was a possible trend towards fewer hypertensive disorders of pregnancy with ovulation, but this was not statistically significant.

items.title: Reproductive outcomes after letrozole stimulated versus artificial frozen-thawed embryo transfer cycles in women with PCOS and/or oligo-anovulation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 17 studies (mostly observational) comparing two ways of preparing the womb for a frozen embryo transfer in women with PCOS or irregular ovulation: using letrozole to stimulate the body's own cycle, or using artificial hormones. Letrozole cycles were linked to slightly more live births and fewer pregnancy losses, and to lower risks of high blood pressure in pregnancy and very large babies. The certainty of the evidence was low, and the one trial that reported live birth found no real difference, so more good trials are needed.
keyPoints: Letrozole cycles were linked to a modest rise in live birth (odds ratio 1.37, about an 8% risk difference) compared with artificial cycles, but the one trial reporting live birth found a similar rate.
Letrozole cycles were linked to fewer pregnancy losses, though the two trials reporting this varied a lot, so the result is uncertain.

Letrozole cycles were linked to lower risks of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and large-for-gestational-age babies, with no clear difference in gestational diabetes or small-for-gestational-age babies.
The authors suggest letrozole may be a viable alternative to artificial cycles for women with ovulatory disorders while better trials are awaited.

items.title: Pregnancy outcomes in freeze-all versus fresh embryo transfer cycles of women with adenomyosis and endometriosis: a systemic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled earlier studies to compare freeze-all embryo transfer with fresh embryo transfer in IVF/ICSI for women with endometriosis or adenomyosis. For women with endometriosis, freeze-all was linked to higher rates of implantation, clinical pregnancy and live birth. Miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy rates were similar between the two approaches. For women with adenomyosis, outcomes were similar whichever approach was used.
keyPoints: In endometriosis, freeze-all had higher clinical pregnancy (OR 1.25), live birth (OR 1.31) and implantation (OR 1.27) rates than fresh transfer.
Miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy rates were comparable between freeze-all and fresh transfer in endometriosis.
In adenomyosis, IVF/ICSI outcomes were comparable between freeze-all and fresh transfer.

items.title: Utility of GnRH Agonists before embryo transfer in women with adenomyosis: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled eight earlier studies of women with adenomyosis (a condition where womb lining tissue grows into the womb muscle) having IVF. It looked at whether GnRH agonist medicines, used before ovarian stimulation or before a frozen embryo transfer, improve pregnancy outcomes. No clear benefit was found from long or ultra-long GnRH agonist treatment, and using one before a frozen transfer did not improve results. The studies were all retrospective, and the authors say proper prospective trials are needed.
keyPoints: Pretreatment with a GnRH agonist before frozen embryo transfer did not improve reproductive outcomes in women with adenomyosis.
No evidence of benefit was found for long or ultra-long GnRH agonist protocols before ovarian stimulation or frozen transfer.
An antagonist protocol gave a higher live birth rate than a long GnRH agonist protocol (OR 2.59, 95% CI 1.03-6.52).
All eight included studies were retrospective, so prospective trials are needed.

items.title: Economic evaluation of embryo transfer strategies in in vitro fertilization (IVF): a systematic review
items.source: Journal of Health, Population, and Nutrition
items.journal: Journal of Health, Population, and Nutrition
items.summary: This review looked at 16 studies that compared the costs and benefits of different ways of transferring embryos during IVF, mostly single versus double embryo transfer. Single embryo transfer, including plans that mix fresh and frozen transfers, was often better value for money than double embryo transfer, especially for younger women. This is partly because it lowers the chance of complications for mothers and babies and cuts later healthcare costs. The results depend on a woman's age, the healthcare system, the type of model used and personal preferences, and most studies came from high-income countries.
keyPoints: Single embryo transfer and plans built around it were often more cost-effective than double embryo transfer.
The benefit was clearest for younger women, partly because fewer maternal and newborn complications means lower long-term healthcare costs.
Cost-effectiveness varied with maternal age, healthcare system, modelling approach, patient preferences and how much society is willing to pay.
Most of the evidence came from high-income countries, mainly in Europe.

items.title: Outcomes after assisted reproductive technology in women with cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 42 studies comparing fertility treatment (ART) results in women with a history of cancer and women without cancer. On average, women with cancer were less likely to return for an embryo transfer and less likely to have a clinical pregnancy or a live birth. The studies varied a lot, and some did not fully account for age differences, so the results are uncertain.
keyPoints: Women with a history of cancer were less likely to return for embryo transfer than women without cancer.
They also had a lower likelihood of clinical pregnancy and of live birth after ART.
Results differed a lot between studies, and 11 studies did not adequately account for age differences.
There was too little data to judge effects of cancer type, stage, treatment, or fresh versus frozen transfers.

items.title: Endometrial receptivity array before frozen embryo transfer cycles: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from eight studies of about 2,800 women having frozen embryo transfer during IVF. It compared women who had an endometrial receptivity array (ERA) test beforehand with women who did not. The test did not lead to a clear difference in live birth or ongoing pregnancy, and it is still unclear whether ERA can raise pregnancy rates.
keyPoints: Live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates were not significantly different between women who had ERA and those who did not.
No difference was seen whether women had fewer than 3 or more than 2 previous failed embryo transfers.
Implantation, biochemical pregnancy, clinical pregnancy and miscarriage rates were also similar between the two groups.
The authors conclude it is not clear whether ERA increases the pregnancy rate.

items.title: The effect of progesterone supplementation for luteal phase support in natural cycle frozen embryo transfer: a systematic review and meta-analysis based on randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled four randomised trials (1,116 women) of frozen embryo transfer done in a natural cycle, where the body makes its own hormones. It looked at whether adding progesterone after the transfer (called luteal phase support) improves results. Progesterone was linked to more live births and more clinical pregnancies, with moderate-quality evidence. The benefit was clear in true natural cycles but not shown in modified natural cycles, where more research is needed.
keyPoints: Progesterone support was linked to more live births (RR 1.42) and more clinical pregnancies (RR 1.30) in natural cycle frozen embryo transfer, based on moderate-quality evidence.
The benefit was seen in true natural cycles but was not found in modified natural cycles, so larger trials are needed.
Only one trial compared oral dydrogesterone with vaginal progesterone in modified natural cycles and found similar pregnancy and miscarriage rates, but the evidence was low to very low quality.

items.title: A comprehensive analysis of chromosomal polymorphic variants on reproductive outcomes after intracytoplasmic sperm injection treatment
items.summary: This study looked at 929 embryo transfer cycles (fresh and frozen) in 692 women having ICSI treatment at one fertility centre in Sri Lanka. Researchers checked whether common harmless-looking chromosome variations (called chromosomal polymorphic variants) changed the chances of pregnancy, miscarriage or live birth. They found no evidence of a difference between women with and without these variations, whatever the type or number. The authors say larger, better-powered studies in more diverse groups are still needed.
keyPoints: No difference was found in pregnancy, miscarriage or live birth rates between carriers and non-carriers of chromosomal polymorphic variants.
The results differ from some earlier studies that linked these variants to more miscarriages.
The authors suggest testing for these variants before assisted conception may turn out to be a futile diagnostic tool.
More prospective, adequately powered studies in multiethnic populations are needed.

items.title: Recurrent implantation failure: reality or a statistical mirage?: Consensus statement from the July 1, 2022 Lugano Workshop on recurrent implantation failure
items.summary: An international group of fertility experts reviewed studies from 2015 to 2022 on 'recurrent implantation failure' (RIF), when embryos repeatedly fail to implant during IVF. They concluded that RIF has often been over-diagnosed and over-treated. True RIF appears to be very rare, affecting fewer than 5% of couples with infertility, and in most cases of failed treatment, reassurance and continuing standard care are suitable.
keyPoints: True recurrent implantation failure is extremely uncommon, occurring in fewer than 5% of couples with infertility.

The experts suggest not giving this diagnosis until a woman has failed at least 3 transfers of chromosomally normal (euploid) embryos, or the equivalent number of untested embryos adjusted for her age.
Other factors that could reduce the chance of implantation should be ruled out first, since treatment failure often has several causes that are not repeated each time.
In most cases of failed IVF or other assisted reproduction, reassurance and continued conventional treatment are considered appropriate.

items.title: Obstetric and neonatal outcomes after natural versus artificial cycle frozen embryo transfer and the role of luteal phase support: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 30 observational studies (over 110,000 singleton pregnancies) comparing two ways of preparing the womb for a frozen embryo transfer: a natural cycle, which uses your own ovulation, and an artificial cycle, which uses medicines to prepare the womb lining. Pregnancies after natural cycle transfers had lower risks of several complications, including pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and heavy bleeding after birth. The evidence quality was rated very low to moderate, and the studies varied a lot. The authors say natural cycle transfer should be preferred for women who ovulate, but they could not make a recommendation about progesterone support (luteal phase support) in natural cycles.
keyPoints: Compared with artificial cycles, natural cycle frozen transfers had lower risks of pre-eclampsia (OR 0.50), hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (OR 0.60) and postpartum hemorrhage (OR 0.43).
Natural cycles also had lower risks of preterm birth, very preterm birth, early pregnancy loss, low birthweight, large-for-gestational-age babies and placenta previa.
The authors estimate natural cycle transfer may prevent 4 to 22 cases per 1000 women for each adverse outcome.
Preterm birth risk was lower when luteal phase support was used in natural cycles, but this rests on very low quality evidence, so no recommendation on luteal phase support could be made.

items.title: Endometrial thickness and live birth rates after IVF: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 20 studies covering about 20,500 women to see how the thickness of the womb lining, measured by ultrasound, relates to live birth after IVF or ICSI. Live birth rates varied widely, from about 5% to 49% with fresh embryo transfers and about 6% to 39% with frozen embryo transfers. The authors concluded that lining thickness and other risk factors do affect live birth rates, but results also depend on more than the lining alone. Most studies were looking back at past records, mainly from China, and used different thickness cut-offs, so the results are hard to compare.
keyPoints: Womb lining thickness and other risk factors significantly affect live birth rates in both fresh and frozen embryo transfer cycles.
Live birth rates ranged from 4.8% to 48.99% in fresh cycles and 6.06% to 39.19% in frozen cycles.
IVF results in women with a less receptive womb lining do not depend only on the state of the lining.
Studies used different thickness thresholds and mostly looked back at past records, limiting how firmly results can be compared.

items.title: Does endometrial compaction before embryo transfer affect pregnancy outcomes? a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 18 studies covering about 16,000 embryo transfer cycles to see whether the womb lining getting thinner ("compaction") in the days before an IVF embryo transfer affects the chance of pregnancy. Overall, there was no meaningful difference in pregnancy, live birth or miscarriage rates between women whose lining compacted and those whose lining did not. Some subgroup results looked better with compaction, but these depended on how the lining was measured.
keyPoints: Across 18 cohort studies, lining compaction made no significant difference to clinical pregnancy, ongoing pregnancy, live birth or miscarriage rates.
Compaction was not linked to any harm for pregnancy outcomes.
In subgroups using combined transvaginal and abdominal ultrasound, or compaction of 15% or more, ongoing pregnancy was higher with compaction.
Differences in how the lining is measured may explain why earlier studies disagreed.

items.title: Association of embryo transfer type with infertility in endometriosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review pulled together six studies of 3,010 women with endometriosis who had IVF-type treatment, comparing frozen embryo transfer with fresh embryo transfer. Women who had frozen transfers had more live births and fewer miscarriages. Clinical pregnancy rates were similar between the two groups. The evidence was rated moderate quality, and the authors say there is not yet a lot of it, so more carefully designed studies are needed.
keyPoints: Live births were more frequent with frozen embryo transfer than with fresh transfer (odds ratio 1.53).
Miscarriage was less frequent with frozen transfer (odds ratio 0.70).
Clinical pregnancy rates were similar for frozen and fresh transfers.
The authors note the evidence is not yet abundant and call for more strictly designed research.

items.title: Obstetric and perinatal outcomes following programmed compared to natural frozen-thawed embryo transfer cycles: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies comparing two ways of preparing the womb for a frozen embryo transfer: using hormone replacement medicines (programmed cycle) or following the body's own natural cycle. Pregnancies from programmed cycles had higher rates of high blood pressure disorders, pre-eclampsia, heavy bleeding after birth and caesarean birth. Most of the evidence was low or very low quality, so the authors say firm recommendations for clinical practice cannot yet be made.
keyPoints: Programmed (hormone replacement) frozen transfer cycles were linked to higher risks of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, postpartum haemorrhage and caesarean section than natural cycles.
After adjusting for other factors, only high blood pressure disorders, pre-eclampsia, postpartum haemorrhage and caesarean section stayed significantly linked to hormone preparation.
Most findings were rated low or very low quality evidence because studies differed in hormone timing and dose, embryo stage and genetic testing.
The authors call for well-designed prospective studies to find a safer way to prepare the womb for frozen transfer.

items.title: Endometrial preparation for frozen-thawed embryo transfer cycles: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review pooled results from 26 randomised trials and 113 cohort studies to compare ways of preparing the womb lining for a frozen embryo transfer. Natural cycle preparation (using the body's own hormones) was linked to higher live birth rates than artificial cycles (using medication to build the lining). After artificial cycles, pregnancies also had higher rates of high blood pressure in pregnancy, heavy bleeding after birth and very early birth. Most of the comparisons came from observational studies, which cannot prove cause and effect.
keyPoints: Artificial cycle ranked last for live birth rate among the preparation options compared.
In observational studies, artificial cycles had lower live birth odds than modified natural cycles (OR 0.85) and trigger natural cycles (OR 0.81).
Pregnancies after artificial cycles had higher odds of pregnancy-induced hypertension, postpartum haemorrhage and very preterm birth than after trigger natural cycles.
The authors conclude natural cycle treatment gives a higher chance of live birth and lower risks of these complications.

items.title: Assisted reproductive technology and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: systematic review and meta-analyses
items.summary: This review pooled results from 85 studies to compare high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy (including preeclampsia) after IVF/ICSI versus natural conception. Pregnancies from IVF/ICSI had higher odds of these conditions, whether it was one baby or more. The odds were higher still with frozen embryo transfer than fresh transfer, and highest with donated eggs.
keyPoints: IVF/ICSI pregnancies had higher odds of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy than natural conception, for both single pregnancies (OR 1.70) and multiple pregnancies (OR 1.34).
Frozen embryo transfer was linked to higher odds (OR 1.74) than fresh embryo transfer (OR 1.43).
Pregnancies using donated eggs had the highest odds (OR 4.42 for single pregnancies).
Results for preeclampsia were similar to those for hypertensive disorders overall.

items.title: Preparation of the Endometrium for Frozen Embryo Transfer: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at the different ways the womb lining can be prepared before a frozen embryo is transferred during IVF. Low-quality evidence suggests that natural cycle approaches may work better than hormone replacement treatment. The review also suggests that timing matters, and that progesterone levels can vary a lot between women even on the same dose. The authors say better-designed trials are urgently needed.
keyPoints: Low-quality evidence suggests natural cycle protocols (true or modified) may be better than hormone replacement treatment.
Suggested timing for a warmed blastocyst transfer is day 6 of progesterone start, day 6 after the LH surge, or day 7 after hCG, depending on the protocol.
Progesterone levels can differ markedly between women on the same dose and route, which may affect outcomes.
Well-designed trials comparing protocols on live birth and maternal and baby outcomes are urgently needed.

items.title: Serum luteal phase progesterone in women undergoing frozen embryo transfer in assisted conception: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies of women having a frozen embryo transfer (FET) as part of fertility treatment. It looked at whether blood progesterone levels during the luteal phase (the time after transfer) were linked to pregnancy outcomes. Among women with levels below 10 ng/mL, higher progesterone was linked to more ongoing pregnancies or live births, more clinical pregnancies and fewer miscarriages. It is not clear whether levels at or above 10 ng/mL make a difference, and trials are still needed to show whether raising the dose of progesterone support helps women with low levels.
keyPoints: Below 10 ng/mL, higher blood progesterone was linked to more ongoing pregnancies or live births (RR 1.47) and more clinical pregnancies (RR 1.31).
Higher progesterone below 10 ng/mL was also linked to a lower risk of miscarriage (RR 0.62) in cycles using only vaginal progesterone and blastocyst embryos.
For levels of 10 ng/mL or above, results were uncertain because the studies differed a lot and had wide margins of error.
The authors suggest there may be a minimum progesterone level needed for implantation, and call for trials testing higher-dose luteal support in women with low levels.

items.title: Number of embryos for transfer following in vitro fertilisation or intra-cytoplasmic sperm injection
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 17 trials (2505 women) comparing how many embryos are put back during IVF or ICSI. Transferring two embryos in one cycle gives a higher chance of a live birth than transferring one. But if a single embryo transfer is followed by a second single transfer (fresh or frozen), the overall live birth chance may be similar, with far fewer multiple pregnancies. The evidence is low to moderate quality, and the benefit was seen mainly in women with a good outlook.
keyPoints: One cycle of single embryo transfer may give a lower live birth rate than one cycle of double embryo transfer (low-quality evidence).
Two single transfers in a row (repeated single embryo transfer) may give a live birth rate little or no different from one double embryo transfer (low-quality evidence).
Single embryo transfer, repeated or not, probably lowers the chance of a multiple pregnancy compared with double embryo transfer (moderate-quality evidence).
Miscarriage rates may be little or no different between the approaches.

items.title: Endometrial preparation for women undergoing embryo transfer with frozen embryos or embryos derived from donor oocytes
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 31 trials (5,426 women) comparing ways to prepare the womb lining for frozen embryo transfer or transfer of embryos from donor eggs. The authors found not enough good evidence to say that any one method is best. Some small differences appeared, for example a stimulated cycle may give more clinical pregnancies than a fully medicated (programmed) cycle, and a natural cycle probably leads to fewer cancelled cycles. Most of the evidence was low or very low quality, so these results are uncertain.
keyPoints: Overall, there is insufficient evidence to recommend any one method of womb-lining preparation for frozen embryo or donor-egg transfers.
Stimulating the cycle (with FSH, letrozole or clomiphene) may improve clinical pregnancy rates compared with a programmed cycle (low-quality evidence).
A natural cycle probably reduces cycle cancellations compared with a programmed cycle, but the effect on live birth is uncertain.
Adding a GnRH agonist may improve live birth rates (low-quality evidence), while GnRH antagonists probably give better clinical pregnancy rates than agonists (moderate-quality evidence).

items.title: Association Between Endometrial/Subendometrial Vasculature and Embryo Transfer Outcome: A Meta-analysis and Subgroup Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 studies (895 women who became pregnant and 882 who did not) to see whether blood flow in the womb lining, measured by ultrasound, relates to IVF and frozen embryo transfer results. Women who became pregnant tended to have higher blood flow measures in the womb lining on the day of embryo transfer. The authors say how well these measures can predict pregnancy still needs to be tested in larger studies.
keyPoints: Blood flow in the womb lining on the day of embryo transfer was higher in women who became pregnant than in those who did not.
Blood flow just beneath the womb lining on the hCG trigger day was also higher in women who became pregnant.
The link was clear in frozen embryo transfer cycles, and these measures might help pick the best timing for a frozen transfer.
The authors say larger studies are needed before these ultrasound measures can be used to predict pregnancy.

items.title: Revisiting embryo assisted hatching approaches: a systematic review of the current protocols
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: Assisted hatching is an IVF add-on where the outer shell of an embryo (the zona pellucida) is thinned or opened to help it implant. This review looked at 69 studies comparing hatched and non-hatched embryos. Thinning the shell of fresh embryos gave very limited benefit. Opening the shell of thawed blastocysts was consistently reported as helpful, and lasers were reported to work better than mechanical or chemical methods.
keyPoints: Thinning the shell of fresh embryos, by chemical or laser methods, gave very limited benefit for clinical outcomes.
Studies were consistent that opening the shell of thawed blastocysts helps.
Laser-based methods were consistently reported to be better than mechanical or chemical ones.
The review notes assisted hatching was introduced with poor proof of safety and biological plausibility.

items.title: Application of seminal plasma to female genital tract prior to embryo transfer in assisted reproductive technology cycles (IVF, ICSI and frozen embryo transfer)
items.summary: This review looked at whether placing seminal plasma (the fluid part of semen) in the vagina before embryo transfer helps women having IVF, ICSI or frozen embryo transfer. It pooled 11 trials with 3215 women. There was not enough evidence to say whether it changes live birth or miscarriage rates. It may slightly raise clinical pregnancy rates, but this result is very uncertain and was not seen in the most reliable studies.
keyPoints: Not enough evidence to tell whether seminal plasma changes live birth rates or miscarriage rates (low quality evidence).
Little or no difference was found in the combined rate of live birth or ongoing pregnancy, or in multiple pregnancy rates.
Clinical pregnancy rates may be higher, but the evidence is very low quality and the difference disappeared when only the lowest-risk-of-bias studies were analysed.
No data were available on infections or other side effects, so the authors say more research is needed.

items.title: Cycle regimens for frozen-thawed embryo transfer
items.summary: This review pulled together 18 trials (3,815 women) comparing different ways of preparing the body for a frozen embryo transfer: a natural cycle, hormone therapy to build the womb lining, or drugs to trigger ovulation. Overall, there was not enough evidence to say that any one approach is better than another for women with regular ovulatory cycles. The quality of the evidence was low or very low, so the results are uncertain.
keyPoints: No clear difference in live birth rates was found between natural cycle and hormone therapy approaches for frozen embryo transfer.
Evidence was too limited to recommend one cycle regimen over another for women who ovulate regularly.
A few single trials suggested differences, such as hormone therapy with GnRHa suppression doing better than hormone therapy alone, but these were based on very small, low-quality evidence.
Many trials did not report important outcomes such as live birth or miscarriage.

items.title: Fresh embryos versus freeze-all embryos - transfer strategies: Nuances of a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled five randomised trials that compared transferring an embryo right away (fresh) with freezing all embryos and transferring later, in people having IVF or similar treatment. When many eggs were collected, freezing all embryos tended to give somewhat better pregnancy results, and possibly fewer miscarriages, though that result was borderline. When fewer than about 15 eggs were collected on average, freezing everything did not seem to help.
keyPoints: Freeze-all may be helpful when a high number of eggs is collected during stimulation.
Across trials averaging 12 to 21 eggs, freeze-all had a higher ongoing pregnancy rate than fresh transfer.
Miscarriage rates were lower with freeze-all in these trials, although the result was borderline.
When the average number of eggs collected was under 15, freeze-all did not appear to be advantageous.

items.title: Systematic review of interest-holder perceptions of pharmacist-prescribed ulipristal acetate emergency contraception
items.source: Journal of the American Pharmacists Association
items.journal: Journal of the American Pharmacists Association
items.summary: This review looked at what pharmacists, patients and others think about pharmacists prescribing ulipristal acetate (a type of emergency contraception) in the United States. Seven small studies were found, mostly from California. Patients saw benefits such as lower cost, less time and easier access, and other groups supported the idea. Pharmacists named barriers like lack of time, payment for the service and staff support. All seven studies had a high risk of bias because few people responded to the surveys, so the findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: The authors conclude that pharmacist prescribing of ulipristal acetate could improve access to emergency contraception.
Patients in one of two reports described lower cost, less time and better access.
Pharmacists most often cited barriers of time, payment for services, and staffing and workflow support; some wanted more training.
All seven studies had a high risk of bias due to low response rates.

items.title: Mifepristone versus other interventions for the prevention of pregnancy in reproductive-age women using emergency contraception
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 87 trials (about 36,000 women) comparing mifepristone with other emergency contraception methods taken within five days of unprotected sex. Mifepristone, at both mid and low doses, probably led to fewer pregnancies and fewer side effects than levonorgestrel, and was likely more effective than the older Yuzpe regimen. The main downside was a delayed next period. Most trials were done in China, and some evidence was of lower quality, so results may not apply everywhere.
keyPoints: Mid-dose (25 to 50 mg) and low-dose (under 25 mg) mifepristone probably cause fewer pregnancies than levonorgestrel.
Mifepristone is likely more effective than the Yuzpe regimen, and nausea and vomiting were less common with all mifepristone doses.
A delayed period is probably the main side effect of mifepristone, and higher doses seem to delay periods more often.
Evidence comparing mifepristone with the copper IUD was very low certainty, and most trials were in China.

items.title: Society of Family Planning Committee Statement: Contraception and body weight
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from the Society of Family Planning about how body weight and contraception fit together. It says body weight and size may affect how well some birth control methods work, but that people of all body sizes should still be offered the full range of methods, including emergency contraception. It calls for respectful, unbiased counseling that helps each person choose what suits them.
keyPoints: Clinicians should offer the full range of contraceptive methods to people of every body weight and size.
Counseling should cover any risks and benefits linked to body weight when choosing a method, including emergency contraception.
People should be told about possible weight change, especially weight gain, with some contraceptive methods so they can factor it into their decision.
Weight management approaches such as bariatric surgery and GLP-1 medicines may affect how well contraception works, and this should be discussed.

items.title: Risk factors for ectopic pregnancy occurrence: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pooled 11 observational studies (25,051 women) to find out which factors are linked to ectopic pregnancy, where a pregnancy grows outside the womb. The strongest links were a past ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, abdominal or pelvic surgery, and previous tubal ligation. Smoking, older age, more than one partner, past miscarriage or abortion, earlier use of emergency contraception, and an intrauterine device were linked to a slightly higher risk. The authors suggest screening women who have the strong risk factors.
keyPoints: Strongest links to ectopic pregnancy: a past ectopic pregnancy (OR 9.03), abdominal or pelvic surgery (OR 5.60), previous tubal ligation (OR 5.59), pelvic inflammatory disease (OR 4.00) and infertility (OR 3.70).
Previous use of emergency contraception, an intrauterine device, smoking, older age and more than one partner showed only a slightly increased risk.
Oral contraceptive use was linked to a slightly lower risk, and condom use appeared to have very limited effect.
The authors suggest screening for ectopic pregnancy in women with the strong risk factors.

items.title: Comparative effectiveness and safety of different progestins in combined oral contraceptives: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 18 randomised trials comparing four hormones (progestins) used in combined birth control pills: gestodene, desogestrel, drospirenone and levonorgestrel. All four worked about equally well at preventing pregnancy, but they differed in bleeding patterns and side effects. Gestodene had the least unexpected bleeding, drospirenone had the fewest reported side effects, and levonorgestrel was highlighted for emergency contraception.
keyPoints: The four progestins had comparable contraceptive efficacy overall.
Gestodene had the lowest rates of breakthrough bleeding and irregular bleeding.
Drospirenone had the lowest rate of adverse events, while gestodene had the highest.
The authors suggest desogestrel for routine use, gestodene for bleeding control, drospirenone to limit androgenic effects, and levonorgestrel for emergency contraception.

items.title: Emergency Contraception Update for Adolescents and Young Adults: Guidance for Health Care Professionals
items.source: Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine
items.organisation: Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine
items.summary: This guidance paper from the Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine looks at emergency contraception (EC) for teenagers and young adults. EC can prevent pregnancy after unprotected or underprotected sex, some methods are easy to use and get, and very few people cannot use it. Young people often face barriers such as age, relying on family for insurance and transport, cost, wrong information and worries about privacy. The paper suggests ways for health services to make EC easier to reach quickly for this age group.
keyPoints: EC can prevent pregnancy after unprotected or underprotected intercourse, and there are very few reasons someone cannot use it.
Teenagers and young adults are at considerable risk of unintended pregnancy.
Barriers to timely EC include age, dependence on family for insurance and transport, cost, misinformation and privacy concerns.
The paper offers strategies to improve timely, young-person-focused access to EC.

items.title: Drug-drug interactions between antiretrovirals and hormonal contraception: An updated systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 49 studies on how HIV medicines (antiretrovirals) interact with hormonal contraception, including emergency contraception. Most combinations appear safe and effective together. The main concern was the HIV medicine efavirenz, which in most studies lowered the levels of hormones from implants, emergency contraception and vaginal rings, with higher pregnancy rates or signs of ovulation. The overall quality of the evidence was moderate.
keyPoints: Most HIV medicines and hormonal contraceptives can be used safely and effectively together.
Efavirenz reduced progestin hormone levels or was linked to more pregnancies or ovulation in 15 of 18 studies of implants, emergency contraception and vaginal rings.
One study found about double the bone density loss when the injection DMPA was used with an HIV regimen containing TDF, compared with TDF alone.
Even with efavirenz, pregnancy rates with an implant were lower than with other hormonal methods, so counseling on the relative risks is advised.

items.title: Over-the-counter provision of emergency contraceptive pills: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at what happens when emergency contraceptive pills can be bought over the counter or from a pharmacy without a prescription. Across 19 studies on effectiveness, people used the pills no more or less overall, but they were more likely to take them in good time. Pregnancy rates and sexual behaviour did not change, and abortion rates were similar or lower where pharmacies stocked the pills. Most users and providers supported over-the-counter access, and nearly all the studies came from high- and middle-income countries.
keyPoints: Over-the-counter or pharmacy access led to more timely use of emergency contraceptive pills compared with prescription-only access.
No differences were found in overall pill use, pregnancy rates or sexual behaviour.
Abortion rates were similar or lower in areas where pharmacies offered the pills.
Privacy, convenience and cost shaped decisions to use them, and modelling studies suggested pharmacy access would lower health system costs.

items.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Adverse Effects of Levonorgestrel Emergency Oral Contraceptive
items.summary: This review pulled together 47 studies on the side effects of levonorgestrel emergency contraception (the 'morning-after pill'). Most side effects were common and not serious. Some uncommon and a few serious events were reported, but the abstract does not say how often or whether the pill caused them. There is very little data on what happens when the pill is used repeatedly.
keyPoints: Most side effects of levonorgestrel emergency contraception were common and not serious.
Uncommon reactions included loss of appetite, rash, skin darkening (chloasma), miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy and weight gain.
Serious events such as convulsion, stroke, anaphylaxis and ovarian cyst rupture were reported in the studies.
Side effect rates were not statistically different between the two-dose (0.75 mg) and single-dose (1.5 mg) regimens.

items.title: Drug interactions between non-rifamycin antibiotics and hormonal contraception: a systematic review
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review looked at whether common antibiotics (other than rifamycins) make hormonal birth control work less well. It pulled together 29 studies covering birth control pills, emergency contraception pills and the vaginal ring. The studies did not show that these antibiotics reduce how well hormonal contraception works. The authors note that for some types of antibiotic there is only a small amount of lower-quality evidence.
keyPoints: Two studies found no difference in pregnancy rates in women using birth control pills with or without these antibiotics.
No study found changes in ovulation suppression or breakthrough bleeding when hormonal contraceptives were taken with an antibiotic.
Progestin levels in the body did not drop significantly with any antibiotic; estrogen (ethinyl estradiol) levels dropped only with dirithromycin.
The authors conclude most women can expect no reduction in contraceptive effect, though data for some drug classes are limited.

items.title: Endometrial changes during ulipristal acetate use: A systematic review
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: Researchers reviewed ten studies (1,450 women) looking at what ulipristal acetate, a medicine used for emergency contraception and for shrinking uterine fibroids, does to the womb lining. In studies that took lining samples, the medicine caused changes to the lining in 41-78.8% of women, and these mostly went away after treatment stopped. Endometrial hyperplasia (thickening of the lining) was reported in 6 of 1,450 women (0.4%), and no lasting pre-cancerous or cancerous changes were found after up to four courses. Most studies were short and followed women for a limited time, so the authors say more information on long-term use is needed.
keyPoints: Specific, non-normal changes to the womb lining occurred in 41-78.8% of women who had biopsies during ulipristal acetate treatment, and these were reversible after stopping.
Womb lining thickness usually rose during treatment and returned to normal within a few weeks of stopping.
Endometrial hyperplasia was reported in 6 of 1,450 women (0.4%), and the one cancer case was already present before treatment.
Follow-up after up to four courses showed no lasting pre-cancerous or cancerous changes, but most studies were short-term and long-term safety is not yet known.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 710 Summary: Counseling Adolescents About Contraception
items.summary: This is a guideline summary from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on how doctors should talk with teenagers about birth control. It says modern contraceptives work very well when used correctly, and that talks should start with the most effective methods. Emergency contraception should always be part of the conversation, including how teens can get it. Teens should be able to choose their own method and keep their visits private where possible.
keyPoints: Modern contraceptives are very effective when used correctly, so good counseling and access matter in teen health care.
Contraception talks should begin with the most effective methods first.
Emergency contraception should routinely be included in contraception discussions, including how to access it.
A teenager should never be forced to use a method chosen by someone else, such as a parent, partner or health care provider.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 710: Counseling Adolescents About Contraception
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on how doctors should talk with teenagers about birth control. It says modern contraceptives work very well when used correctly, and that emergency contraception should be part of every conversation about contraception, including how to get it. It also says teens should never be forced to use a method chosen by someone else.
keyPoints: Modern contraceptives are very effective when used correctly, so good counseling and easy access matter in teen health care.
Conversations about contraception should start with the most effective methods first.
Emergency contraception should routinely be included in contraception discussions, including how to access it.
A teen has the right to refuse or stop a method, and should not be made to use one chosen by a parent, partner or health care provider.

items.title: Intervention Now to Eliminate Repeat Unintended Pregnancy in Teenagers (INTERUPT): a systematic review of intervention effectiveness and cost-effectiveness, and qualitative and realist synthesis of implementation factors and user engagement
items.summary: This review looked at programmes meant to stop teenagers and young women from having another unplanned pregnancy, including one emergency contraception programme. Overall, there was little or no good evidence that any of the programmes worked to reduce repeat pregnancy. Fewer of the young women in the programmes went on to have a baby, but the number of repeat pregnancies was not clearly different. Young women's circumstances, motivation and having a real say in how programmes are designed seemed to matter.
keyPoints: Repeat pregnancy rates were similar with or without the programmes (43% vs 48%), a difference that was not statistically significant.
Fewer young women in the programmes had a subsequent birth (12% vs 21%), based on four studies.
Many repeat pregnancies happened alongside poverty, low expectations and few opportunities.
The authors say more carefully designed and tested programmes are needed, with young women playing an active role.

items.title: Safety and effectiveness data for emergency contraceptive pills among women with obesity: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether emergency contraceptive pills work as well for women with obesity as for women without. The studies found were few and of poor to fair quality. They suggest levonorgestrel pills may be less effective at higher body weight, and ulipristal pills may be somewhat less effective too, though that result was less certain. The authors say all women should be told about the full range of emergency contraception options.
keyPoints: One analysis found about a 4-fold higher chance of pregnancy after levonorgestrel emergency pills in women with obesity (BMI 30 or more) than in women of normal or lower weight.
For ulipristal, women with obesity had roughly double the pregnancy risk, but the results were uncertain and did not reach statistical significance.
Another analysis of three trials of levonorgestrel found no increase in pregnancy risk with higher weight or BMI, so the evidence is mixed.
The authors advise counselling all women at risk of unintended pregnancy, including those with obesity, about all emergency contraception options, including an emergency copper IUD.

items.title: School-based interventions for improving contraceptive use in adolescents
items.summary: This review looked at 11 trials of school-based programs meant to help teenagers use contraception. Some multi-session programs that included interactive lessons led more students to report using effective contraception and condoms, and fewer to report sex without a condom. A lesson on emergency contraception helped students learn the time limits for using the emergency pill and the copper IUD. The overall quality of the evidence was low.
keyPoints: One multi-session school program led more students to report using effective contraception and condoms at last sex, and another led fewer students to report sex without a condom.
Students who had an emergency contraception session were more likely to know the time limits for the emergency pill and the IUD used as emergency contraception.
Most programs focused on preventing STIs/HIV and pregnancy, so they mainly stressed condoms, though some covered a range of methods.
The authors rated the overall evidence as low quality, partly because of limited information on how well programs were delivered and high dropout.

items.title: Physiotherapy for endometriosis-associated pelvic pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 7 studies of women with endometriosis-related pelvic pain. It compared physiotherapy with other (non-physiotherapy) approaches. Physiotherapy reduced pain more than the comparison treatments, and the biggest drops were seen with electrotherapy and laser devices. Treatments applied to the painful area worked better than general ones.
keyPoints: Physiotherapy lowered pelvic pain more than non-physiotherapy comparisons (average difference about 2 points on a pain scale).
Electrotherapy and laser devices gave the greatest pain reduction.
Techniques applied locally to the painful area reduced pain more than general techniques.
The review concluded physiotherapy is effective for pain in women with endometriosis.

items.title: Diagnosis of Endometriosis
items.summary: This is a clinical practice guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on how endometriosis should be evaluated and diagnosed. It covers the clinical, imaging and surgical steps of diagnosis for adults and adolescents who have symptoms that could point to endometriosis. The abstract does not list the specific recommendations. It notes that for adolescents the advice rests on limited evidence, data from adults and expert consensus.
keyPoints: The guideline gives recommendations on the clinical, imaging and surgical evaluation and diagnosis of endometriosis.
Recommendations are graded by strength and evidence quality, with ungraded Good Practice Points where evidence is lacking.
The advice also applies to adolescents unless stated otherwise.
For adolescents, recommendations draw on limited evidence, adult data and expert consensus.

items.title: Guideline No. 468: Clinical Management of Endometriosis
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This is a Canadian clinical guideline on how to manage endometriosis and its symptoms, written for health care providers. It says that finding and treating endometriosis early may reduce pain, improve fertility and quality of life, and support long-term health. Early care may also lower the costs that come from delayed diagnosis and treatment. The abstract does not list the specific recommendations, so the details are not given here.
keyPoints: Timely, effective management of endometriosis may reduce pain and improve quality of life.
Good management may also improve fertility and long-term health outcomes.
Early intervention may reduce the health and financial burden of delayed diagnosis and treatment.
The guideline covers women and gender-diverse people affected by endometriosis and used the GRADE method to rate evidence.

items.title: Salivary miRNAs in the diagnosis of endometriosis An invited narrative scientific literature review, commissioned by European Board and College of Obstetrics and Gynaecology (EBCOG)
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review looked at whether a simple saliva test could one day help diagnose endometriosis without surgery. Researchers have been studying tiny molecules called miRNAs in saliva, and one pattern has shown promise. But the studies so far are few and small, and the pattern has not been tested in other countries. Saliva testing is not yet ready for everyday use.
keyPoints: Endometriosis has long been diagnosed with invasive surgery such as laparoscopy, and blood-based miRNA tests have not become routine.
Saliva is easy to collect and causes the patient no inconvenience, so it is an appealing way to test.
All published saliva studies are small, which makes it hard to draw clear conclusions.
It is still unclear whether the saliva findings reflect endometriosis itself or the body's general inflammation or immune response.

items.title: Time to Diagnose Endometriosis: Current Status, Challenges and Regional Characteristics-A Systematic Literature Review
items.summary: This review looked at how long it takes for women to be diagnosed with endometriosis, using 17 studies published since 2018. Reported times ranged from about 4 months (0.3 years) to 12 years, depending on how the delay was measured, where women lived and who was studied. The authors conclude that diagnostic delay still happens and is mainly driven by doctors. The quality of the studies ranged from poor to good.
keyPoints: Time to diagnosis in the studies ranged from 0.3 to 12 years.
The length of delay varied with how it was defined, the country and the type of patients studied.
Diagnostic delay is still present and is mainly driven by physicians.
The authors call for standard definitions, more awareness and targeted diagnostic approaches.

items.title: Progestagens for pain symptoms associated with endometriosis
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 33 trials with 5059 people who have endometriosis to see whether progestagen hormone treatments ease pain. Compared with placebo, oral progestagens probably reduce overall pain and period pain and improve quality of life. Compared with other hormone treatments such as the contraceptive pill or GnRH agonists, pain relief looked similar, but there were few studies, so the evidence is less certain.
keyPoints: Oral progestagens versus placebo probably reduce overall pain and period pain, and improve quality of life (moderate to high certainty).
Oral progestagens may make little to no difference to pelvic pain compared with placebo (low certainty).
Compared with the contraceptive pill or GnRH agonists, oral progestagens showed little to no difference in pain, mostly based on low-certainty evidence.
Side effects varied: oral progestagens probably caused more side effects than GnRH agonists, while depot (injected) progestagens probably caused fewer.

items.title: Guideline No. 449: Diagnosis and Impact of Endometriosis - A Canadian Guideline
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looks at how endometriosis is diagnosed and how much it affects people's lives. It says diagnosis can be supported by a detailed history, a physical exam and imaging tests, ideally with providers who have experience in endometriosis care. Surgery with lab testing can confirm the diagnosis, but it is not needed if imaging has already confirmed it. The guideline calls for earlier recognition and better education to cut delays in getting care.
keyPoints: Diagnosis can be made using a detailed history, examination and imaging tests with providers experienced in endometriosis care.
Surgery with pathology confirms endometriosis but is not required if imaging has already confirmed the diagnosis.
Earlier recognition is needed so people can get timely care and support.
Education for the public, patients, families, health care providers and administrators can help reduce delays in diagnosis and treatment.

items.title: The role of fibrosis in endometriosis: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 142 studies (human, lab and animal) on scarring-like tissue, called fibrosis, in endometriosis. It found that fibrosis is a central feature of endometriosis lesions and is closely linked to nerves in the lesions, which is likely a cause of endometriosis pain. Most of the studies had a moderate to high risk of bias, and many of the treatment ideas have so far only been tested in animals. The findings point to possible future non-hormonal treatments rather than anything available now.
keyPoints: Fibrosis is an important feature of all types of endometriosis lesions, driven mainly by cells called myofibroblasts.
Nerves and nerve chemicals sit close to fibrotic tissue in lesions and are likely a cause of endometriosis-related pain.
Endometriosis fibrosis shares features with other fibrotic diseases, which may help researchers find new non-hormonal treatments.
Treatments aimed at fibrosis have mostly been tested only in animals, and most studies had a moderate to high risk of bias.

items.title: Understanding the impact of endometriosis on women's life: an integrative review of systematic reviews
items.summary: This review pulled together 15 earlier systematic reviews to see how endometriosis affects women's quality of life. It found that the condition touches many parts of life, including pain, fertility, sex life and mental health. Many women also felt let down by the care they received. The authors note the studies varied a lot and most were cross-sectional, so the picture has limits.
keyPoints: Pain is a hallmark of endometriosis, and infertility and sexual problems are also common.
Depression, anxiety and stress were major contributors to lower quality of life.
Long diagnosis, treatments that did not work well and symptoms that kept going left women frustrated with healthcare.
Negative thinking patterns such as catastrophizing and fear-avoidance can make pain feel worse.

items.title: Effect of Dietary Interventions on Endometriosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from 11 trials (716 women) testing diet changes and supplements for endometriosis. Most trials reported less pain, and antioxidant supplements were linked to a reduction in period pain compared with placebo. They did not clearly help chronic pelvic pain or pain during sex. The studies varied a lot and many had a moderate or high risk of bias, and the better-quality studies did not show a clear benefit over placebo.
keyPoints: Most of the 11 trials reported a positive effect on endometriosis pain scores, but many had moderate or high risk of bias.
Antioxidant supplements were linked to a reduction in period pain (dysmenorrhea) compared with placebo.
Supplements did not significantly reduce chronic pelvic pain or pain during sex.
Studies with low risk of bias did not show significant results versus placebo, so more and better trials are needed.

items.title: Excisional surgery versus ablative surgery for ovarian endometrioma
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled nine trials (578 women) comparing two keyhole surgeries for ovarian endometriomas, which are endometriosis cysts in the ovary. Cutting the cyst out (excision) may work better than draining and burning it (ablation) for reducing painful periods, pain during sex, and the cyst coming back. Chances of pregnancy in the first year looked similar with both methods. The evidence is low certainty, and very little was reported on safety.
keyPoints: Excision may lower the chance of painful periods returning within two years (about 10% to 34% after excision versus 49% after ablation).
Excision may lower the chance of painful sex returning within two years (about 4% to 23% versus 58%).
Excision may reduce the chance of the cyst coming back and of needing more surgery within a year.
There may be little or no difference in spontaneous pregnancy in the first year, and few safety data were reported.

items.title: Benefits of physical therapy in improving quality of life and pain associated with endometriosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pooled six trials of women with endometriosis who tried non-drug, conservative therapies such as physical therapy, compared with placebo. These therapies lowered pain intensity and improved physical function. They did not clearly change the other quality-of-life areas that were measured.
keyPoints: Non-drug conservative therapies reduced pain intensity in women with endometriosis compared with placebo.
Physical function, one part of quality of life, also improved.
No statistically significant differences were found for the other quality-of-life measures analyzed.
The authors conclude these therapies are a treatment option for improving pain and physical function.

items.title: The genetic basis of endometriosis and comorbidity with other pain and inflammatory conditions
items.summary: Researchers combined genetic data from over 60,000 women with endometriosis and about 700,000 women without it. They found 42 places in the genome linked to the condition, including genes involved in how pain is sensed. Endometriosis shared genetic links with other pain conditions such as migraine and back pain, and with inflammatory conditions such as asthma and osteoarthritis. The authors say more work is needed to turn this into new treatments.
