keyPoints: 42 genome regions were linked to endometriosis, with the strongest effects seen in more advanced (stage 3/4) disease driven by ovarian endometriosis.
Some of the linked genes are involved in sensing and maintaining pain.
Endometriosis showed genetic overlap with 11 pain conditions, including migraine, back pain and chronic pain in several body sites.
It also overlapped genetically with inflammatory conditions such as asthma and osteoarthritis.

items.title: Association of endometriosis and adenomyosis with pregnancy and infertility
items.summary: This review pulled together findings from recent meta-analyses on how endometriosis and adenomyosis relate to getting pregnant and to pregnancy outcomes. Both conditions were linked to lower pregnancy and live birth rates and more miscarriages, with a bigger effect for adenomyosis. Women with mild forms of endometriosis do not seem to face much higher risks of major pregnancy complications, but those with severe endometriosis or adenomyosis may. The studies varied a lot in quality and design, so the authors say conclusions should be drawn with caution.
keyPoints: Endometriosis and adenomyosis were linked to lower pregnancy and live birth rates and a higher miscarriage rate, with a larger effect in adenomyosis.
Women with superficial or ovarian endometriosis do not appear to have a considerably higher risk of major pregnancy or newborn complications.

Severe endometriosis is linked to a several-fold higher risk of placenta previa, and deep endometriosis to surgical complications at cesarean section and rarely bleeding inside the abdomen in pregnancy.

Adenomyosis is linked to higher risks of preeclampsia, preterm birth, baby not head-down, heavy bleeding after birth, low birth weight and small babies; women with deep endometriosis or severe adenomyosis may benefit from care at specialist centers.

items.title: Prolactin and pain of endometriosis
items.summary: This review looked at whether prolactin, a hormone that is higher in women, plays a role in the pain of endometriosis. A systematic search of clinical studies found that blood prolactin levels are higher in people with endometriosis. The authors suggest that high prolactin may make pain nerves more sensitive and could add to pelvic pain, though this is a possibility rather than a proven cause. They propose that treatments aimed at prolactin may one day help manage endometriosis pain.
keyPoints: A systematic review of clinical studies found higher blood prolactin levels in patients with endometriosis.
Lab studies show prolactin can make pain-sensing nerves more sensitive, especially in females.
High prolactin may contribute to pelvic pain and to other pain conditions that occur alongside endometriosis.
Targeting prolactin or its receptors might improve endometriosis pain management in future.

items.title: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues for endometriosis
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 72 trials (7,355 women) to see how well GnRH analogues, a type of hormone treatment, relieve endometriosis pain and what side effects they cause. Compared with placebo, they may reduce pain, including period pain and painful sex, after three months, but they may also cause more hot flushes. They may also lower bone density, though this evidence came from comparisons with other treatments, not placebo. The evidence was low to very low quality, so the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: GnRH analogues may reduce overall pain, period pain and painful sex compared with placebo after three months, based on low-certainty evidence.
They may cause more hot flushes and other side effects than placebo or gestrinone.
Bone mineral density may drop with GnRH analogues, and taking them alongside calcium-regulating agents may reduce this loss.
The effect compared with danazol or intrauterine progestogens is uncertain because the evidence was very low quality or missing.

items.title: Barriers to a Timely Diagnosis of Endometriosis: A Qualitative Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 13 qualitative studies on why endometriosis takes so long to diagnose, which can be up to 11 years. It looked at the views of both women with symptoms and health care professionals. The studies pointed to four kinds of barriers: personal factors, influences from other people, problems in the health system, and features of endometriosis itself. The authors say the findings show where the path to diagnosis could be improved.
keyPoints: Diagnosis of endometriosis can be delayed by up to 11 years, during which symptoms can affect quality of life, work and relationships.
Women often find it hard to tell abnormal pain from normal periods, and period stigma and the normalization of menstrual pain add to delays.
Health system problems included limited training and attitudes among health care professionals, late referrals to specialists, and poor explanation of how the pill is used in the diagnostic process.
Endometriosis itself adds challenges: symptoms vary, they overlap with other conditions, and there is no non-invasive test.

items.title: Prophylactic procedures associated with gynecological surgery for the management of superficial endometriosis and adhesions. Clinical practice guidelines from the French College of Gynecologists and Obstetricians (CNGOF)✰
items.journal: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.summary: These French guidelines look at whether extra procedures should be done during gynecological surgery when mild (superficial) endometriosis or scar-like tissue (adhesions) is found. Surgery is not recommended for mild endometriosis that causes no symptoms, but removing it may improve pain and quality of life in women who do have pelvic pain. Routine release of adhesions is generally not advised. All recommendations are based on low-quality evidence, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Surgery for symptom-free superficial endometriosis is not recommended to prevent pelvic pain, as there is no evidence it will become painful (low level of evidence).
In women with pelvic pain, removing superficial endometriosis lesions found during surgery may improve pain and quality of life (low level of evidence).

In infertile women, cutting out (excising) superficial endometriosis is recommended over burning it (monopolar coagulation), as it may give a higher spontaneous pregnancy rate (low level of evidence).
Routine adhesiolysis (releasing adhesions) is not recommended to prevent pelvic pain or to improve pregnancy chances, because benefit is unclear and surgery carries risks (low level of evidence).

items.title: Pentoxifylline for the treatment of endometriosis-associated pain and infertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether pentoxifylline, a medicine that affects the immune system, helps with endometriosis pain or fertility. It found five small trials with 415 women in total. The evidence was very low quality, so it is not clear whether the medicine helps with pregnancy rates, miscarriage, recurrence or pain. The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to support using it for endometriosis.
keyPoints: No trials reported on live birth rate, the main fertility outcome the review looked for.
It is uncertain whether pentoxifylline changes clinical pregnancy rate, miscarriage rate, recurrence or pain compared with placebo or no treatment.
All the evidence was rated very low quality, with problems such as unclear trial methods and many women lost to follow-up.
The authors found insufficient evidence to support using pentoxifylline for endometriosis-related pain or subfertility.

items.title: Effect of physical activity and exercise on endometriosis-associated symptoms: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether physical activity and exercise help with endometriosis symptoms such as pain. Only three small studies, with 109 women in total, were good enough to include. One study found less pain and one found lower stress, but the studies were too different and too limited to say whether exercise really helps.
keyPoints: Only three studies (two randomized trials and one without a control group) with 109 women were included.
Only one study found improved pain, and one showed lower stress levels.
The effect of exercise on endometriosis symptoms could not be determined because of major limitations in the studies.
Better-designed trials are needed that measure pain, quality of life and what patients think of the exercise.

items.title: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device (LNG-IUD) for symptomatic endometriosis following surgery
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether a hormone coil (LNG-IUD) placed after endometriosis surgery helps with symptoms. It found only four small trials with 157 women in total, and the evidence was low to very low quality. Some small studies suggested better period pain, quality of life and satisfaction with the coil than with no treatment, but the review could not say for sure that it works. More large, well-designed studies are needed.
keyPoints: Four small trials (157 women) were included, and the certainty of the evidence was very low to low.
The review is uncertain whether an LNG-IUD after surgery improves period pain, quality of life or chronic pelvic pain compared with no treatment or with GnRH-a drugs.
One study reported more melasma (skin darkening) and bloating with the LNG-IUD, while irregular bleeding was the most common side effect compared with hot flushes and night sweats with GnRH-a drugs.
The authors conclude there is no high-quality evidence to support the widespread use of an LNG-IUD after endometriosis surgery.

items.title: Extrapelvic Endometriosis: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at published reports of endometriosis found outside the pelvis, such as in the abdominal wall, abdominal organs, chest and nerves. It found that this form is reported more often than once thought, but most evidence comes from case reports and small case series. Symptoms often follow the menstrual cycle, and surgery was the most common treatment. There are no studies comparing treatments, so the best approach is not yet known.
keyPoints: Endometriosis outside the pelvis was traditionally thought to be rare, but a considerable number of cases have been reported.
Abdominal wall lesions usually caused a palpable mass, with cyclic pain and cyclic bleeding in some patients; wide local excision was the main treatment, with 5% recurrence.
Chest (thoracic) endometriosis typically showed catamenial pain, collapsed lung (pneumothorax) and coughing up blood, mostly on the right side, with 29% recurrence after surgery.
No comparative studies exist to show the best way to diagnose or treat extrapelvic endometriosis; heightened awareness and a team approach across specialties are recommended.

items.title: Laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 14 trials (1563 women) looking at keyhole (laparoscopic) surgery for endometriosis, a condition linked to pain and difficulty getting pregnant. Compared with a look-only keyhole operation, surgery probably increases the chance of an ultrasound-confirmed ongoing pregnancy. It is uncertain whether surgery reduces pain, and no trials reported live birth. Many of the studies were small or poorly reported, so the evidence for most outcomes is weak.
keyPoints: Laparoscopic surgery probably increases the rate of viable pregnancies confirmed by ultrasound compared with diagnostic laparoscopy only (moderate quality evidence).
It is uncertain whether surgery reduces overall pain, as the evidence was very low quality and based on very few women.
No studies looked at live birth, and there was not enough information on adverse events to draw conclusions about safety.
There was not enough evidence to say whether ablation or excision works better, or whether one heat tool is better than another.

items.title: Pre- and postsurgical medical therapy for endometriosis surgery
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 26 trials (3457 women) to see whether hormone-suppressing medicines work better when taken before surgery, after surgery, or both, for endometriosis. Taking medicine after surgery may lower the chance that the disease returns and probably increases pregnancy rates compared with surgery alone. For taking medicine before surgery, or comparing before with after, the evidence was too weak to draw conclusions. No trials looked at medicine both before and after surgery, and there was not enough data on serious side effects.
keyPoints: Hormone medicine after surgery may reduce disease recurrence within 12 months compared with surgery alone (low-quality evidence).
Hormone medicine after surgery probably increases pregnancy rates compared with surgery alone (moderate-quality evidence).
Evidence on medicine taken before surgery, or on before versus after, was uncertain (low to very low quality).
Not enough data to judge serious side effects, and no trials tested medicine both before and after surgery.

items.title: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 738 Summary: Aromatase Inhibitors in Gynecologic Practice
items.summary: This ACOG committee opinion looks at aromatase inhibitors, medicines that lower estrogen, and how they are used in gynecologic care. For women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and a body mass index above 30, letrozole (an aromatase inhibitor) should be considered the first choice to trigger ovulation, because it led to more live births than clomiphene citrate. The opinion also notes these medicines may help endometriosis pain when combined with progestins, and that women with breast cancer on long-term treatment should have bone density checked.
keyPoints: For women with PCOS and a BMI over 30, letrozole should be considered first-line treatment for ovulation induction because it gives a higher live birth rate than clomiphene citrate.
Lifestyle changes that lead to weight loss should be strongly encouraged for women with PCOS.
Aromatase inhibitors are a promising option for endometriosis-related pain when used together with progestins.
Compared with tamoxifen in breast cancer care, aromatase inhibitors are linked to fewer blood clots, endometrial cancers and vaginal bleeding, but long-term use needs bone density screening.

items.title: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 738: Aromatase Inhibitors in Gynecologic Practice
items.summary: This ACOG committee opinion reviews how aromatase inhibitors (medicines that lower estrogen) are used in gynecologic care. For women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and a body mass index over 30, letrozole is advised as the first medicine to consider for helping ovulation, because it led to more live births than clomiphene citrate. Aromatase inhibitors may also help with endometriosis pain when taken together with progestins.
keyPoints: For women with PCOS and a BMI over 30, letrozole should be considered first-line for ovulation induction because it gives a higher live birth rate than clomiphene citrate.
Lifestyle changes that lead to weight loss should be strongly encouraged for women with PCOS.
Aromatase inhibitors are a promising option for endometriosis-associated pain when combined with progestins.
With long-term use in women with breast cancer, bone density screening is recommended because low estrogen raises the risk of osteoporosis.

items.title: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain in women with endometriosis
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs, such as naproxen) help with pain from endometriosis. Only one very small trial of 24 women could be used, and it did not show clear evidence that naproxen eased pain compared with a placebo. The quality of the evidence was very low, so the review could not say whether NSAIDs work for endometriosis pain.
keyPoints: Only one trial with 24 women could be analysed, and the evidence was judged very low quality.
Naproxen showed no clear evidence of easing endometriosis pain compared with placebo.
It was unclear whether naproxen reduced the need for extra pain relief or caused more side effects.
There was no evidence that any one NSAID works better than another, and NSAIDs can have unintended effects.

items.title: Imaging modalities for the non-invasive diagnosis of endometriosis
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at how well scans such as transvaginal ultrasound and MRI can diagnose endometriosis without surgery, compared with surgical diagnosis. It included 49 studies with 4807 women, but most studies were of poor quality. No scan was accurate enough to replace surgery for finding endometriosis overall, though ultrasound and MRI did well for ovarian cysts caused by endometriosis (endometriomas). The authors say the findings should be interpreted with caution.
keyPoints: No imaging test was accurate enough to replace surgery for diagnosing endometriosis in the pelvis overall.
For endometriomas (ovarian endometriosis cysts), transvaginal ultrasound was good at confirming the diagnosis, and MRI looked accurate enough to possibly replace surgery, though data were scant.
Transvaginal ultrasound could help show which areas are affected by deep endometriosis, which can help plan surgery.
Most included studies were of poor quality, and newer scan techniques had too few studies to judge properly.

items.title: Blood biomarkers for the non-invasive diagnosis of endometriosis
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether a blood test could diagnose endometriosis without surgery. It pulled together 141 studies of 122 different blood markers, all compared against surgical diagnosis. None of the markers was accurate enough to replace surgery or to help decide who needs it, and all of the studies were of poor quality.
keyPoints: Endometriosis affects about 10% of women of reproductive age, and surgery (laparoscopy) is still the gold standard for diagnosis.
None of the blood markers that could be pooled (anti-endometrial antibodies, IL-6, CA-19.9 and CA-125) consistently met the accuracy needed for a replacement or triage test.
All 141 studies were of poor methodological quality, and results varied a lot between studies.
No blood biomarker was accurate enough to be used clinically outside a research setting.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 663 Summary: Aromatase Inhibitors in Gynecologic Practice
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from a US obstetrics and gynecology committee on aromatase inhibitors, medicines that lower estrogen. It says that for women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and a body mass index above 30, letrozole should be considered as the first medicine to help trigger ovulation, because it led to more live births than clomiphene citrate. It also describes aromatase inhibitors as a promising option, alongside progestins, for endometriosis pain. Lifestyle changes that lead to weight loss are strongly encouraged.
keyPoints: For women with PCOS and a BMI over 30, letrozole should be considered first-line for ovulation induction because it gave a higher live birth rate than clomiphene citrate.
Lifestyle changes that result in weight loss should be strongly encouraged.
Aromatase inhibitors combined with progestins are a promising option for endometriosis-associated pain.
With long-term use in breast cancer treatment, bone density screening is recommended because low estrogen can raise the risk of osteoporosis.

items.title: Combination of the non-invasive tests for the diagnosis of endometriosis
items.summary: This review looked at whether combining non-invasive tests (such as blood or urine markers, vaginal ultrasound and clinical examination) can diagnose endometriosis without surgery. It found 11 small studies with 1,339 women in total, and all were of poor quality. A few combinations looked promising, but each was tested in only one study with wide margins of error. The authors conclude that keyhole surgery (laparoscopy) is still the gold standard, and non-invasive tests should only be used in research for now.
keyPoints: About 10% of women of reproductive age have endometriosis, and surgery (laparoscopy) is still the gold standard for diagnosis.
Some test combinations, such as a vaginal examination plus transvaginal ultrasound for rectal endometriosis, looked accurate in single studies.
All 11 studies were of poor quality and each test combination was studied only once, so the real-world usefulness remains unclear.
The authors say non-invasive tests for endometriosis should only be used in a research setting for now.

items.title: Clinical practice guideline "preconception care"
items.summary: The Swiss Society of Gynecology and Obstetrics issued a guideline on preconception care, which means getting healthy before pregnancy. It describes counseling that helps women and couples spot health, lifestyle or environmental risks early and act on them. Healthy eating, physical activity and avoiding substance use are named as part of getting ready for pregnancy. The abstract does not rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Preconception care is an ongoing part of routine gynecological care, not a single visit, and is adapted to each person's needs.
It aims to manage chronic conditions, encourage healthy nutrition and physical activity, and avoid substance use before pregnancy.
Planned pregnancies are linked to lower illness for mother and baby than unplanned ones.
Counseling should ideally start well before stopping contraception, because many helpful changes take weeks or months to work.

items.title: Effects of strength training on quality of life in pregnant women: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at nine randomized trials (1,581 pregnant women in total) that tested strength training during pregnancy. The studies found that strength training may help limit excess weight gain, ease low back and sciatic pain, lift mood, and improve sleep and wellbeing. The authors say future studies need more standard methods and clearer reporting, but suggest strength training could be added to general exercise advice for pregnancy.
keyPoints: Strength training in pregnancy was linked to less excessive weight gain and less low back and sciatic pain.
It was also linked to better mood, sleep quality, muscle strength, flexibility and overall quality of life.
The review covered nine randomized controlled trials with 1,581 participants.
The authors call for standardized methods and more detailed reporting in future research.

items.title: Resistance training in pregnancy: systematic review and meta-analysis of pregnancy, delivery, fetal and pelvic floor outcomes and call to action
items.summary: This review pooled 50 studies (nearly 48,000 pregnant people) to look at resistance training, such as exercising with weights or resistance bands, during pregnancy. Resistance training, on its own or as part of a mixed exercise programme, was linked to lower odds of gestational high blood pressure, gestational diabetes, mood problems around birth and very large babies. Most programmes mixed several types of exercise, so it is hard to know how much of the benefit came from resistance training itself. The authors say better-designed studies are needed.
keyPoints: Resistance training was linked to lower odds of gestational hypertension (OR 0.42) and gestational diabetes (OR 0.62).
It was also linked to lower odds of perinatal mood disorders (OR 0.48) and macrosomia, or a very large baby (OR 0.67).
About 90% of the studies used mixed exercise programmes, and the amount of resistance training was generally low to moderate.
Because the programmes were mixed and poorly described, the effect of resistance training alone is hard to pin down.

items.title: Influence of pelvic floor muscle training alone or as part of a general physical activity program during pregnancy on urinary incontinence, episiotomy and third- or fourth-degree perineal tear: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
items.summary: This review pooled 30 randomized trials (6,691 women) to see whether pelvic floor muscle training during pregnancy helps prevent bladder leaks and serious tears during birth. Training lowered the risk of urinary incontinence and of third- or fourth-degree perineal tears. It did not change how often episiotomy was needed. The authors conclude that pelvic floor training should be part of antenatal care.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training in pregnancy lowered the risk of urinary incontinence (relative risk 0.72).
It also lowered the risk of third- or fourth-degree perineal tears (relative risk 0.50).
It made no clear difference to the chance of having an episiotomy.
The training worked whether done on its own or as part of a general exercise program.

items.title: Effects of Dietary Approaches and Exercise Interventions on Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Network Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 39 trials involving 2,712 women with gestational diabetes to compare different diets and types of exercise. The DASH diet (rich in fruit, vegetables and whole grains) and low glycemic index diets were linked to better blood sugar control and lower baby birth weight. Resistance exercise and the DASH diet were also linked to less need for insulin. The certainty of the evidence was low or very low, so the authors say better-quality research is still needed.
keyPoints: The DASH diet and low glycemic index diets improved blood sugar control, though the certainty of evidence was very low to low.
The DASH diet and resistance exercise each reduced the need for insulin therapy.
Both diets lowered newborn birth weight, and the DASH diet was also linked to fewer large babies (macrosomia) and fewer cesarean births.
Exercise did not change infant outcomes; effects on babies were seen mainly with diet changes.

items.title: Effectiveness of exercise interventions on urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in pregnant and postpartum women: umbrella review and clinical guideline development
items.summary: This review pulled together 9 earlier systematic reviews (covering 89 studies) to see whether exercise helps with bladder leaks and pelvic organ prolapse during pregnancy and after birth. Exercise and pelvic floor muscle training during pregnancy had the strongest evidence for preventing bladder leaks after birth. Evidence that training reduces leaks was moderate, while evidence that it eases prolapse symptoms was low.
keyPoints: The strongest evidence was that exercise and pelvic floor muscle training during pregnancy help prevent bladder leaks after birth.
Moderate-level evidence showed exercise and pelvic floor training are likely to reduce the symptoms and severity of urinary incontinence.
Evidence that pelvic floor training reduces pelvic organ prolapse symptoms was low.

The guideline group recommends encouraging pregnant and postpartum women to exercise and train their pelvic floor, and referring those with symptoms to a pelvic floor specialist such as a physiotherapist.

items.title: Physical exercise in pregnancy: benefits, risks and prescription
items.summary: This review pulled together the strongest published research (57 articles, including 32 meta-analyses and 16 randomized trials) on exercising during pregnancy. It found that regular exercise is linked to many benefits and was not linked to a higher risk of problems for the mother or baby. The authors say the type and amount of exercise should fit a woman's earlier fitness level, health history and the details of her pregnancy.
keyPoints: Exercise can help prevent gestational diabetes, excessive weight gain in pregnancy, hypertensive disorders, urinary incontinence and large babies (fetal macrosomia).
Exercise can also help prevent lower back and pelvic pain, anxiety and depression during pregnancy.
Exercise was not related to an increased risk of adverse outcomes for the mother or baby.
Following current exercise guidelines is enough to get the main benefits, and exercise type and intensity should be based on a woman's previous fitness level.

items.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines That Address Physical Activity and Exercise During Pregnancy: A Systematic Review
items.summary: Researchers compared 13 clinical guidelines on physical activity during pregnancy. The guidelines from the World Health Organization and NICE were rated as the best quality. Most guidelines agreed on how long, how often, how hard and what type of activity to do. They disagreed on a few details, such as how to screen before exercising, the best heart rate, and when in pregnancy to start.
keyPoints: Physical activity is recommended for healthy pregnant women.
Across 13 guidelines, advice on exercise duration, frequency, intensity and type was consistent.
Guidelines differed on pre-exercise screening tools, how to measure exertion, target heart rate, and when to start exercising.
Only 2 of the 13 guidelines were judged to have good methodological quality (WHO and NICE).

items.title: Executive summary of evidence and consensus-based clinical practice guideline for management of obesity and overweight in postpartum women: An AIIMS-DST initiative
items.summary: This is a new clinical guideline from India on managing overweight and obesity after birth. It gives healthcare providers advice on starting conversations about weight and on lifestyle-based first-line management, covering diet, physical activity and breastfeeding. The abstract does not report the specific recommendations or how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: The guideline covers screening and starting a discussion about weight with women who are overweight or obese after birth, and with women who had a normal pre-pregnancy weight but kept extra weight.
Recommendations cover assessing and managing diet, physical activity and breastfeeding behaviour as first-line lifestyle management.
It includes behaviour-change techniques to help women stick with weight management advice.
It also gives advice on how long and how often follow-up visits should be.

items.title: Aerobic or Resistance Exercise for Improved Glycaemic Control and Pregnancy Outcomes in Women with Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review looked at 14 studies with over 758 pregnant women who have gestational diabetes, to see whether aerobic exercise or strength training works better for blood sugar and pregnancy outcomes. None of the studies compared the two types of exercise directly. About half showed that adding exercise improved blood sugar control compared with usual activity, and exercise mostly did not change outcomes for the mother or baby. The studies were too different from each other to say which type of exercise is best.
keyPoints: No study directly compared aerobic exercise with strength training in gestational diabetes.
Half of the studies found better blood sugar control with extra exercise than with usual physical activity.
Exercise largely had no effect on pregnancy or newborn outcomes, and the studies support that exercise in pregnancy is safe.
Because the studies varied so much, no specific best type of exercise could be recommended.

items.title: Physical Activity and Exercise During Pregnancy and the Postpartum Period: ACOG Committee Opinion, Number 804
items.summary: This guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) looks at exercise during pregnancy and after birth. It says that for most women without pregnancy or medical complications, staying active or starting safe activity is safe and desirable. Women who were already active, even at vigorous levels, can generally keep going, though some routines may need small changes as the body changes.
keyPoints: Without pregnancy or medical complications, physical activity in pregnancy is safe and desirable, and women are encouraged to continue or start safe activities.
Women who were active before pregnancy, including vigorous aerobic activity, can continue during pregnancy and after birth.
Observational studies link exercise in pregnancy to less gestational diabetes, fewer cesarean births and assisted vaginal deliveries, and faster postpartum recovery.
Physical activity may help prevent postpartum depression, and some exercise routines may need adjusting for normal body changes in pregnancy.

items.title: Interventions to prevent women from developing gestational diabetes mellitus: an overview of Cochrane Reviews
items.summary: This overview pulled together 11 Cochrane reviews (71 trials, over 23,000 women) to see which approaches might prevent gestational diabetes, a form of diabetes that develops in pregnancy. No approach showed clear benefit or harm. Combining diet and exercise, myo-inositol, vitamin D and metformin were of possible benefit, but the authors say better evidence is needed. Omega-3 supplements did not change the risk of gestational diabetes, and the evidence for diet alone or exercise alone was too weak to draw conclusions.
keyPoints: No intervention in the 11 reviews showed clear benefit or harm for preventing gestational diabetes.
Diet and exercise together, myo-inositol, vitamin D and metformin were of possible benefit, but more high-quality evidence is needed.
Omega-3 supplements had no effect on gestational diabetes risk (high-quality evidence).
There was not enough good evidence to judge diet alone, exercise alone, probiotics or vitamin D with calcium.

items.title: Techniques for preventing hypotension during spinal anaesthesia for caesarean section
items.summary: This review looked at 125 trials with 9,469 women to see which methods help prevent low blood pressure after a spinal anaesthetic for caesarean birth. Fluids through a drip, certain medicines (ephedrine, phenylephrine, ondansetron) and compression of the legs all lowered the chance of low blood pressure. None of them removed the need to treat low blood pressure in some women. The evidence was low to very low quality, so the findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: Drip fluids, ephedrine, phenylephrine, ondansetron and leg compression can reduce the chance of low blood pressure after spinal anaesthesia for caesarean.
None of these methods removed the need to treat low blood pressure in some women.
Ondansetron also reduced slow heart rate and nausea or vomiting compared with a placebo, and ephedrine was linked to less slow heart rate than phenylephrine.
The evidence was low to very low quality, and rare side effects (for example with colloid fluids) could not be assessed.

items.title: Interventions to Prevent Perinatal Depression: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed ways to prevent depression during pregnancy and after birth, which affects as many as 1 in 7 women. It found convincing evidence that counseling, such as cognitive behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy, helps prevent it. The Task Force is moderately certain this approach has a moderate benefit and little risk of harm. Evidence for other approaches, such as exercise, education or supplements, was too limited to judge.
keyPoints: Counseling such as cognitive behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy is effective in preventing perinatal depression.
Women with past depression, current depressive symptoms, or risk factors like low income or young or single parenthood would benefit from counseling and could be considered at increased risk.
Harms of counseling were judged to be no greater than small.
There was not enough evidence to judge the benefits and harms of other non-counseling approaches.

items.title: Benefits of Physical Activity during Pregnancy and Postpartum: An Umbrella Review
items.source: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
items.journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
items.summary: This review pulled together 76 earlier reviews to see how physical activity affects a mother's health during pregnancy and after birth. Moderate-intensity activity was strongly linked to a lower risk of gaining too much weight in pregnancy, gestational diabetes and symptoms of postnatal depression. For other outcomes, such as pre-eclampsia, high blood pressure in pregnancy and anxiety, the evidence was limited or not strong enough to say.
keyPoints: Strong evidence: moderate-intensity physical activity lowered the risk of excessive weight gain in pregnancy, gestational diabetes and postnatal depression symptoms.
Limited evidence suggested activity may lower the risk of pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension and anxiety or low mood during pregnancy.
There was not enough evidence to say whether activity helps with weight loss after birth or postnatal anxiety.
There was not enough evidence to tell whether the benefits differ by age, ethnicity, income or weight before pregnancy.

items.title: Treatments for women with gestational diabetes mellitus: an overview of Cochrane systematic reviews
items.summary: This overview pulled together 14 Cochrane reviews (128 trials, about 18,000 women) on treatments for gestational diabetes. Lifestyle changes (healthy eating, physical activity and checking blood sugar) was the only approach that showed possible benefit: fewer babies were large for their age. It may also lead to more labour inductions. For many other treatments there was not enough good-quality evidence to draw conclusions.
keyPoints: Lifestyle changes (healthy eating, physical activity and blood sugar checks) probably reduce the number of babies born large for gestational age.
Lifestyle changes may increase the chance of labour being induced.
Exercise on its own did not help women return to their pre-pregnancy weight, and results for caesarean birth were inconclusive.
Insulin compared with tablets probably raises the risk of high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy; for many other treatments evidence was too limited to say.

items.title: No. 367-2019 Canadian Guideline for Physical Activity throughout Pregnancy
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looked at research on exercise during pregnancy. It found that staying physically active in pregnancy brings moderate benefits, including less excessive weight gain, and no harms were identified. Most pregnant women without medical reasons to avoid exercise can take part, and the guideline says to do what you can on days when tiredness or discomfort get in the way. The quality of evidence varied across the recommendations, from very low to higher.
keyPoints: Physical activity in pregnancy is linked to less excessive gestational weight gain and lower total weight gain.
It is also linked to lower risk of gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, gestational hypertension, Caesarean section and depression, and to fewer large-for-gestational-age babies.
Exercise was not linked to miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, low birth weight or birth defects.
Women not yet active are advised to build up gradually, and those with certain medical conditions should talk to their obstetric care provider first.

items.title: 2019 Canadian guideline for physical activity throughout pregnancy
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looked at research on being physically active during pregnancy and whether it affects health problems for the mother, baby or newborn. The guideline panel found that the benefits of prenatal physical activity are moderate and that no harms were identified. Women, health professionals and exercise professionals who gave feedback said following the recommendations would be feasible, acceptable and fair, and would need few resources.
keyPoints: The benefits of physical activity during pregnancy are moderate.
No harms of prenatal physical activity were identified.
Most stakeholders and end users said the recommendations would be feasible, acceptable and equitable.
Following the recommendations is likely to need minimal resources from individuals and health systems.

items.title: Prenatal exercise for the prevention of gestational diabetes mellitus and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 106 studies (over 270,000 pregnant women) to see whether exercising in pregnancy lowers the chance of gestational diabetes, high blood pressure in pregnancy and pre-eclampsia. Moderate to high quality trial evidence showed that exercise on its own was linked to roughly 40% lower odds of each condition compared with no exercise. Programmes that combined exercise with other changes, such as diet advice, did not show the same benefit.
keyPoints: Exercise-only programmes lowered the odds of gestational diabetes (OR 0.62), gestational hypertension (OR 0.61) and pre-eclampsia (OR 0.59) compared with no exercise.
Programmes that mixed exercise with other components did not show a reduction in these conditions.
At least 600 MET-min/week of moderate-intensity exercise was linked to a 25% or greater drop in the odds of these conditions.
600 MET-min/week is about 140 minutes of brisk walking, water aerobics, stationary cycling or resistance training.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 201: Pregestational Diabetes Mellitus
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on caring for women who already have diabetes before they become pregnant. It explains how to counsel and manage women before and during pregnancy, including frequent monitoring and medication changes. The update also covers insulin pumps, oral diabetes medicines in pregnancy, and the option of long-acting reversible contraception (such as an IUD or implant) after the baby is born. The abstract notes that few well-designed studies exist, so many recommendations rest on expert and consensus opinion.
keyPoints: Diabetes that starts before pregnancy needs frequent monitoring and medication adjustment, and it carries risks for both mother and baby.
Women with pregestational diabetes can be counselled and managed before and during pregnancy using the updated guidance.
The update adds more on insulin pumps (continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion) and on oral diabetes medicines in pregnancy.
Long-acting reversible contraception is an option in the postpartum period for women with pregestational diabetes.

items.title: Psychosocial interventions for supporting women to stop smoking in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 102 trials to see whether support programmes help women stop smoking in pregnancy. Counselling, feedback and incentives helped more women stop smoking in late pregnancy, while the effect of health education and social support was less clear. Women who got these programmes were less likely to have a low birthweight baby, and no harmful effects on mood or wellbeing were seen.
keyPoints: Counselling increased the number of women who had stopped smoking by late pregnancy, compared with usual care or less intensive support (high-quality evidence).
Women who received these support programmes had 17% fewer low birthweight babies and 22% fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.
Exercise on its own compared with usual care had an unclear effect on stopping smoking.
There did not appear to be adverse psychological effects from the interventions.

items.title: Lifestyle interventions for the treatment of women with gestational diabetes
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 15 randomised trials (4501 women) of lifestyle treatment for gestational diabetes, usually healthy eating, physical activity and blood sugar monitoring. Women who had lifestyle treatment were less likely to have babies born large for their age and were less likely to have postnatal depression, and more of them reached their weight goals a year after birth. Several of these findings came from only one trial and were low-quality evidence. Long-term effects for mothers and children were poorly reported.
keyPoints: Lifestyle treatment probably lowered the chance of a baby being born large for gestational age (moderate-quality evidence from six trials).
Postnatal depression was less likely with lifestyle treatment, and more women met postpartum weight goals at one year, but each came from a single trial with low-quality evidence.
There was no clear difference in pre-eclampsia, caesarean section, perineal tearing, induction of labour or neonatal low blood sugar.
Long-term outcomes for mothers and children were poorly reported, so lasting benefits or harms remain unclear.

items.title: Combined diet and exercise interventions for preventing gestational diabetes mellitus
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 23 trials with nearly 9,000 pregnant women to see whether combining healthy eating and exercise programmes helps prevent gestational diabetes. Women in the programmes had a possibly lower chance of gestational diabetes and caesarean birth, and gained a little less weight during pregnancy. There were no clear differences for pre-eclampsia, high blood pressure, large babies or baby deaths. The programmes in the trials varied a lot, so the review says its findings have limited ability to guide practice.
keyPoints: Diet and exercise programmes may reduce the risk of gestational diabetes slightly (moderate-quality evidence), though the result was borderline.
Women in the programmes gained about 0.9 kg less weight during pregnancy on average (moderate-quality evidence).
A possible small reduction in caesarean section was seen (moderate-quality evidence).
No clear differences were found for pre-eclampsia, high blood pressure, large-for-gestational-age babies or perinatal death (low to very low-quality evidence).

items.title: Bed rest in singleton pregnancies for preventing preterm birth
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether being prescribed bed rest, at home or in hospital, helps prevent early (preterm) birth in women at high risk. Only two studies qualified, and only one (1266 women) could be analysed. Early birth before 37 weeks was similar with bed rest (7.9%) and without it (8.5%). The authors found no evidence for or against bed rest, even though it is widely used.
keyPoints: Only two studies met the review's criteria, so the evidence is very limited.
In the one analysed study, preterm birth before 37 weeks was similar with bed rest (7.9%) and without (8.5%).
There is no evidence that bed rest at home or in hospital prevents preterm birth, and none showing it does not.
Because bed rest may have downsides for women, families and healthcare costs, the authors say pros and cons should be discussed with women at risk.

items.title: Diet and exercise interventions for preventing gestational diabetes mellitus
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 13 trials (about 5,000 women) that tested diet and exercise programmes during pregnancy against usual care. The programmes did not clearly lower the chance of gestational diabetes, caesarean birth or very large babies. Women in the programmes did have a lower chance of preterm birth. The review says the evidence has limits and is not strong enough to guide practice.
keyPoints: No clear difference in gestational diabetes risk between women given a diet and exercise programme and those given usual care.
No clear difference in caesarean section or large-for-gestational-age babies.
Preterm birth was less likely with the combined diet and exercise programmes (risk ratio 0.71).
Weight gain in pregnancy tended to be a little lower, but there was no clear difference in weight kept after birth.

items.title: Diet or exercise, or both, for preventing excessive weight gain in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 65 trials (49 with usable data, about 11,400 women) testing diet, exercise, or both to prevent too much weight gain in pregnancy. These approaches lowered the chance of gaining more weight than recommended by about 20%, and the reviewers rated this as high-quality evidence. There were possible extra benefits for some outcomes, especially for women at higher risk, but several results were uncertain or based on limited evidence.
keyPoints: Diet, exercise, or both reduced the risk of excessive weight gain in pregnancy by about 20% (high-quality evidence).
Low glycaemic load diets, exercise alone, and diet plus exercise all gave similar reductions.
Women in the programmes were slightly more likely to gain less weight than recommended (moderate-quality evidence).

There was no clear difference in pre-eclampsia, caesarean birth, preterm birth, or large babies overall. In higher-risk women, combined diet and exercise counselling was linked to a borderline lower chance of a large baby, and babies of higher-risk women in the programmes had fewer breathing problems.

items.title: Fetal neurobehavior and consciousness: a systematic review of 4D ultrasound evidence and ethical challenges
items.summary: This review looked at 74 studies that used 4D ultrasound to watch how babies behave in the womb. Behaviours such as yawning, hand-to-face movements and startle responses became more complex between 24 and 34 weeks of pregnancy, in step with known brain development. No study showed that these movements mean a baby is consciously aware, so the authors urge caution in how they are interpreted.
keyPoints: Yawning, hand-to-face movement and startle responses became more complex between 24 and 34 weeks of pregnancy.
These changes matched known stages of brain development, such as the growth of connections between brain areas.
No study gave clear evidence linking a baby's movements to conscious experience.
Artificial intelligence tools may help spot patterns on ultrasound, but they have not yet been checked by independent testing.

items.title: The association between increased fetal movements in the third trimester and perinatal outcomes; a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined seven studies to look at what happens when a woman feels more baby movements than usual in the third trimester. Women with increased movements had a lower chance of cesarean delivery than comparison groups, but were more likely to have labour induced. Increased movements were not linked to differences in birth weight, NICU admission, gestational diabetes or high blood pressure, so they do not appear to be a strong sign of problems.
keyPoints: Increased baby movements in the third trimester were linked to a lower risk of cesarean delivery.
They were also linked to a higher likelihood of labour induction, which the authors say needs further study.
No significant differences were found in birth weight, small or large babies, NICU admission, gestational diabetes or hypertension.
Increased movements may not be a major predictor of poor outcomes for mother or baby.

items.title: Pregnancy, birth and neonatal outcomes associated with reduced fetal movements: A systematic review and meta-analysis of non-randomised studies
items.summary: This review pulled together 39 studies of women at 24 weeks or later who went to be checked because they felt their baby moving less. Compared with women who did not report this, they had higher odds of stillbirth and of having a smaller-than-expected baby. They were also more likely to have an induced labour, an instrumental birth or a caesarean. No link was found with preterm birth or newborn death. The studies were not randomised trials, so they show associations rather than proving cause.
keyPoints: Reduced baby movements were linked to higher odds of stillbirth (OR 3.44) and a baby small for gestational age (OR 1.37).
Women who reported reduced movements were also more likely to have induction of labour, instrumental birth and caesarean section.
No association was found with preterm birth or neonatal death.
The review describes reduced movements as an important alarm signal for possible risk of problems in pregnancy.

items.title: Effect of encouraging awareness of reduced fetal movement and subsequent clinical management on pregnancy outcome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology MFM
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology MFM
items.summary: This review pooled 18 studies to see whether encouraging pregnant women to notice and report reduced baby movements, or to count movements, lowers the chance of stillbirth. The evidence is uncertain about any effect on stillbirth. Raising awareness of baby movements may be linked to fewer newborn intensive care admissions and fewer low Apgar scores, without more caesareans or inductions. Counting movements may help mothers feel more attached to their baby and less anxious.
keyPoints: The effect of movement awareness or movement counting on stillbirth is uncertain.
Encouraging awareness of baby movements may be linked to fewer newborn intensive care admissions and fewer low Apgar scores at 5 minutes.
Awareness interventions may not increase caesarean deliveries or induction of labour.
Counting movements may increase maternal-fetal attachment and reduce anxiety.

items.title: Does fetal size affect maternal perception of fetal movements? Evidence from an individual participant data meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined data from five studies of 851 women who had a late stillbirth and 2257 women whose pregnancies continued to a live birth. They looked at how women felt their baby's movements in late pregnancy, and whether this differed by baby size. Feeling stronger movements was the most common experience through to full term, whatever the baby's size. Feeling fewer movements was linked to a higher chance of stillbirth, and more so when the baby was small.
keyPoints: Stronger movements were the most commonly reported change from 28 weeks to full term, for babies of all sizes.
Feeling stronger movements was linked to lower odds of stillbirth in every baby-size group.
Reduced movements were linked to higher odds of stillbirth in all size groups, and especially in the two smallest quarters of babies.
Increased strength of movement in late pregnancy is a positive finding regardless of baby size.

items.title: A better understanding of the association between maternal perception of foetal movements and late stillbirth-findings from an individual participant data meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined data from five studies of 851 late stillbirths and 2,257 ongoing pregnancies to see how a mother's report of baby movements after 28 weeks relates to stillbirth. Feeling movements get stronger was linked to lower odds of stillbirth, while feeling fewer movements in the last 2 weeks was linked to higher odds. The link with fewer movements was strongest before 37 weeks. Baby hiccups and regular bouts of vigorous movement were linked to lower odds.
keyPoints: Most women (over 60%) reported movements getting stronger in late pregnancy, which was linked to lower odds of late stillbirth.
Feeling fewer movements in the last 2 weeks was linked to more than double the odds of late stillbirth, and this link was strongest at 28-36 weeks.
Baby hiccups and regular episodes of vigorous movement were linked to lower odds of late stillbirth after 28 weeks.
A single episode of unusually vigorous movement was linked to higher odds of stillbirth, especially at term.

items.title: Fetal Movement Counting and Perinatal Mortality: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled five randomized trials covering about 468,000 pregnancies. It compared women taught to count their baby's movements with women who were not given this instruction. Teaching movement counting was not linked to a clear drop in baby deaths around the time of birth. It was weakly linked to slightly more preterm births, labor inductions and cesarean births.
keyPoints: Perinatal death was 0.54% with movement counting and 0.59% without, a difference that was not clearly significant (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.85-1.00).
No clear differences were found in stillbirths, neonatal deaths, low birth weight, Apgar scores or NICU admissions.
Small increases were seen in preterm delivery (7.6% vs 7.1%), induction of labor (36.6% vs 31.6%) and cesarean delivery (28.2% vs 25.3%).
The authors concluded that instructing women to count movements is not associated with a clear improvement in pregnancy outcomes.

items.title: Mobile applications providing guidance about decreased fetal movement: Review and content analysis
items.summary: Researchers reviewed 24 pregnancy apps to see what they tell women about a baby moving less than usual. All of the apps mentioned decreased baby movement, but few linked it to stillbirth or other serious outcomes. The advice varied a lot between apps, and the review found a lack of evidence-based clinical guidance in them.
keyPoints: All 24 pregnancy apps reviewed mentioned decreased fetal movement, but few explained that it can be linked to stillbirth or other adverse outcomes.
Advice on monitoring baby movements varied widely: about two-thirds recommended kick counting and one-third offered a kick counter.
One in four apps suggested eating or drinking something to stimulate the baby to move.
The authors concluded that the apps lacked evidence-based clinical advice and that accurate content on fetal movement is essential.

items.title: Risk factors for reduced fetal movements in pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled 27 studies of pregnant women who came in worried about their baby moving less than usual. It looked for what these women had in common compared with women who did not report reduced movements. Smoking, an anterior placenta, and too little or too much amniotic fluid were linked to reduced movements. The authors say the results can help raise awareness and encourage women to contact their maternity care provider if they have concerns.
keyPoints: Women who reported reduced fetal movements were more likely to be Caucasian, smokers, and to have an anterior placenta, oligohydramnios (low amniotic fluid) or polyhydramnios (high amniotic fluid).
Age and number of previous births (parity) did not differ between women with and without reduced movements.
Previous caesarean section, pregnancy past 42 weeks, diabetes and high blood pressure disorders did not predict reduced movements.
Perceiving reduced movements is an important sign for identifying women at higher risk of poor outcomes, so the authors encourage women to contact their maternity provider if concerned.

items.title: Understanding the associations and significance of fetal movements in overweight or obese pregnant women: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether a larger body size in pregnancy changes how baby movements are felt or how often women seek help for fewer movements. Women with a higher body weight did not seem to feel movements any differently, but they were more likely to report reduced movements to their care team. Among women who did report reduced movements, those with a higher body size had a higher chance of stillbirth and slow baby growth. The evidence was limited and mostly low or very low quality.
keyPoints: Higher maternal body size was not linked to feeling baby movements differently (very low-quality evidence).
Women with higher body size were more likely to present with decreased fetal movement (low-quality evidence).
Among women with decreased movement, higher body size was linked to more stillbirth and fetal growth restriction (very low-quality evidence).
The authors conclude the evidence is limited.

items.title: Care of pregnant women with decreased fetal movements: Update of a clinical practice guideline for Australia and New Zealand
items.source: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology
items.journal: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology
items.summary: This is an updated clinical practice guideline from Australia and New Zealand on caring for pregnant women who notice their baby moving less than usual. It gives 12 recommendations and a suggested care pathway for health professionals. The aim is to spot higher-risk pregnancies earlier and improve outcomes for mothers and babies.
keyPoints: The guideline offers 12 evidence-based recommendations and a suggested care pathway for women who report decreased baby movements.
It was updated by the NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Stillbirth and the Perinatal Society of Australia and New Zealand.
Wider use of the guideline by clinicians and maternity hospitals could mean earlier identification of higher-risk pregnancies.
The authors say this could improve health outcomes for women and babies and reduce stillbirth rates.

items.title: Interventions to enhance maternal awareness of decreased fetal movement: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 16 studies of ways to help pregnant women notice when their baby moves less than usual. The studies were of fair to poor quality and too different to combine, and results were mixed: one large trial found no drop in stillbirth, while another trial and several non-randomised studies suggested a possible drop. The review found no clear evidence of benefit or harm, and no sign that these programmes made women more anxious.
keyPoints: Decreased baby movement is linked to poorer pregnancy and birth outcomes, and reporting it quickly may help prevent stillbirth.
Evidence on awareness programmes was mixed: one large trial found no reduction in stillbirth, while another trial and some non-randomised studies found reductions.
No evidence was found that these interventions increased maternal concern.
The best way to support women in monitoring their pregnancies is still unknown, but women should be told about the importance of baby movements.

items.title: Fetal movement counting for assessment of fetal wellbeing
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether counting your baby's movements helps keep babies safe in pregnancy. It combined five trials covering about 71,000 women. The authors found there is not enough good evidence to change current practice. Counting did not clearly lower stillbirth rates, but it did seem to reduce mothers' anxiety and led to more hospital check-ups after reduced movements were reported.
keyPoints: No trial compared movement counting with no counting at all, so it is still unclear whether counting saves babies' lives.
Routine counting did not change stillbirth or caesarean section rates in the trials, though the evidence was mostly low quality.
Maternal anxiety was lower with routine movement counting (moderate quality evidence), and there was no clear change in mother-baby attachment.
More women were admitted to hospital after reporting fewer movements, and women found counting to 10 once a day easier to keep up than counting several times a day.

items.title: Planned early delivery versus expectant management of the term suspected compromised baby for improving outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at what to do at term (37 weeks or later) when a baby is suspected to be compromised, such as when growth is slow or fluid around the baby is low. It compared planning an early delivery with waiting and monitoring. Across three trials of 546 women, there were no clear differences in deaths, serious illness for babies or mothers, or development at two years. The trials only covered slow growth and low fluid, so the findings cannot be applied to every suspected problem, such as reduced baby movements.
keyPoints: No clear difference in perinatal death, major newborn illness, or disability at two years between early delivery and waiting.
Early delivery meant birth about 10 days earlier on average, more inductions, and more babies admitted to intermediate care nursery.
Caesarean rates, vaginal birth, pre-eclampsia and breastfeeding did not differ between the two approaches.
Only three trials were included, covering slow growth and low amniotic fluid; reduced fetal movement and abnormal heart tracings still need their own trials.

items.title: Caesarean myomectomy in pregnant women with uterine fibroids
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether removing fibroids during a caesarean birth (caesarean myomectomy) is safe and helpful. It pooled 23 non-randomised studies with 7504 women. The evidence for every outcome was very low certainty, so the review could not draw firm conclusions about blood transfusion, bleeding, hospital stay, operation time, major surgery or postpartum fever. No studies reported on future fertility.
keyPoints: All 23 included studies were non-randomised, and the evidence for every key outcome was very low certainty.
Women who had caesarean myomectomy may have had slightly longer operations (about 11 minutes more) and hospital stays (about 0.3 days more), but the review says no firm conclusions can be drawn.
No clear conclusions could be made about transfusion, haemorrhage, major surgery or postpartum fever.
No studies reported whether the procedure affects later fertility.

items.title: Uterine Leiomyoma in women of reproductive age: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at published research on how uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) show up, are diagnosed and are treated in women of reproductive age. It concluded that women who become pregnant while having fibroids are at higher risk of pregnancy and newborn complications. The authors recommend against simply watching and waiting in women of childbearing age, and suggest surgery that removes the fibroids while keeping the uterus. The abstract does not describe how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Pregnancy with uterine fibroids is considered high risk for complications for the mother and baby.
Hospital care in a specialised obstetric unit is recommended during the riskiest periods of pregnancy.
The authors advise against passive watch-and-wait management in women of childbearing age with fibroids.
Fibroid removal surgery that keeps the uterus (leiomyomectomy) is recommended to protect the ability to have children.

items.title: Minimally invasive treatment options for uterine fibroids - state-of-the art 2021
items.summary: This review looked at treatments for uterine fibroids that avoid open surgery and can keep the uterus. It found that uterine artery embolization (blocking the blood supply to the fibroid) is a proven and widely accepted option for suitable patients. Newer methods such as high-intensity focused ultrasound, microwave ablation and radiofrequency ablation look promising but need more research before they can be seen as full alternatives to surgery.
keyPoints: Uterine artery embolization is a proven, widely accepted treatment that works well in appropriately selected cases.
High-intensity focused ultrasound is still experimental, but early studies look promising and need confirming in randomized trials.
Microwave and radiofrequency ablation may become recognized fibroid treatments in future.
More research is needed before these minimally invasive methods are accepted as full alternatives to surgery.

items.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Fibroids
items.source: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Radiology covers uterine fibroids, which are the most common growths of the uterus. It says pelvic ultrasound and MRI are the best imaging tests for first diagnosing fibroids, planning treatment and checking after treatment. Fibroids are very common, especially in Black women (over 80% by age 50, compared with close to 70% in White women), and heavy periods are the most frequent symptom.
keyPoints: Fibroids are the most common growth of the uterus, and their cause is multifactorial, involving genes, hormones, environment, race, age, parity and body mass index.
More than 80% of Black women and close to 70% of White women have fibroids by age 50.
Heavy periods (menorrhagia) are the most frequent symptom, though symptoms vary widely.
Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler and MRI (with and without contrast) are the best imaging tests for diagnosis, treatment planning and follow-up.

items.title: Association between obesity and the risk of uterine fibroids: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health
items.journal: Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health
items.summary: This study pooled results from 22 articles (24 studies) covering about 326,000 women to look at whether obesity is linked to uterine fibroids, which are common non-cancerous growths in the womb. Women with obesity had a somewhat higher chance of having fibroids than women with a normal weight. Gaining weight since age 18 was also linked to a higher chance of fibroids. The link between body mass index (BMI) and fibroids was not a straight line.
keyPoints: Obesity was linked to a higher risk or prevalence of fibroids (odds ratio 1.19).
Women with the highest BMI had about 19% higher odds of fibroids than women with a normal BMI.
Women with the biggest weight gain since age 18 had higher odds of fibroids (odds ratio 1.26) than women with no change.
The link between BMI and fibroids was non-linear, following an inverse J-shaped pattern.

items.title: Uterine Morcellation for Presumed Leiomyomas: ACOG Committee Opinion, Number 822
items.summary: This is a guidance document from ACOG about morcellation, a surgical technique that cuts the uterus or fibroids into smaller pieces so they can be removed through small cuts. The concern is that an unexpected cancer called leiomyosarcoma could be spread if the tissue is cut up in the open. This cancer cannot be reliably found before surgery, so a woman having surgery for presumed fibroids may have one without anyone knowing. ACOG advises that doctors and patients talk through the risks, benefits and alternatives together before choosing an approach.
keyPoints: Before morcellation is considered, a woman should be checked for signs of an increased risk of cancer of the uterus.
Leiomyosarcoma cannot be reliably diagnosed before surgery, so a presumed fibroid could turn out to be a cancer that morcellation might spread.
Open abdominal surgery may lower the chance of spreading cancer cells but carries more complications than minimally invasive approaches.
Doctor and patient should make the decision together, with informed consent covering the risks and benefits of each approach and alternatives to morcellation.

items.title: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 770: Uterine Morcellation for Presumed Leiomyomas
items.summary: This guidance from ACOG looks at morcellation, a technique that cuts fibroid or uterine tissue into smaller pieces so it can be removed through small cuts. Open morcellation has raised concern because a rare, hidden cancer called leiomyosarcoma could be spread during the procedure. This cancer cannot be reliably found before surgery, so a fibroid that looks harmless could occasionally be cancer. Open abdominal surgery may lower that risk but carries more complications than minimally invasive surgery, so the guidance says patients and doctors should talk through the options together.
keyPoints: Open (uncontained) morcellation may spread an unsuspected leiomyosarcoma in a woman thought to have only fibroids.
Women should be checked before surgery for signs of increased cancer risk, and morcellation is not appropriate if a cancer is present.
Leiomyosarcoma cannot be reliably diagnosed before surgery.
Open abdominal surgery may reduce the chance of spreading cancer cells but has more complications than minimally invasive approaches.

items.title: Hysteroscopy for treating subfertility associated with suspected major uterine cavity abnormalities
items.summary: This review looked at whether removing growths or scarring inside the womb with a thin camera (hysteroscopy) helps women with fertility problems get pregnant. Only two small studies were found. For women having IUI who had womb polyps, removing the polyps may have raised pregnancy rates, but the evidence was low quality. For fibroids, it is still unclear whether removal helps.
keyPoints: Removing polyps before IUI may raise clinical pregnancy rates: about 63% of women versus 28% with diagnostic hysteroscopy only (low-quality evidence).
For women with unexplained subfertility and submucous fibroids, it is uncertain whether removal improves pregnancy or miscarriage rates (very low-quality evidence).
No data were found on live birth or complications, and none for septum, adhesions, or women going on to IVF/ICSI.
The authors say more research is needed.

items.title: Three-dimensional saline infusion sonography compared to two-dimensional saline infusion sonography for the diagnosis of focal intracavitary lesions
items.summary: This review looked at two ultrasound tests, 2D and 3D saline infusion sonography, used to find growths inside the womb such as polyps and fibroids in women with abnormal bleeding or fertility problems. Both tests were very accurate when compared with hysteroscopy, a camera look inside the womb. 3D scans scored slightly higher, but the difference was not statistically significant. The authors rate the evidence as low quality.
keyPoints: 3D saline infusion sonography found womb-cavity abnormalities with about 94.5% sensitivity and 99.4% specificity across 11 studies.
When 2D and 3D were compared directly, 3D scored slightly higher, but the difference was not statistically significant.
Because 2D is already very accurate, the room for improvement with 3D is small.
Both 2D and 3D saline sonography can be considered alternatives to diagnostic hysteroscopy in women with abnormal uterine bleeding or subfertility.

items.title: ART and uterine pathology: how relevant is the maternal side for implantation?
items.summary: This review looked at how problems with the uterus, such as fibroids, may affect success with assisted reproduction (ART) like IVF. The authors found strong evidence only for surrogacy when a woman has no uterus. For other uterine problems, there is very little evidence that treatments improve results, or that the problems themselves lower ART success.
keyPoints: Surrogacy is strongly supported as effective for women born without a uterus (uterine agenesia).
For other uterine conditions, there is very little evidence that usual treatments improve ART outcomes.
The real effect of many uterine and womb-lining problems on ART is not known.
Tests to check whether the womb lining is ready for implantation are still being developed, and the authors call for better-designed studies.

items.title: Use of misoprostol in myomectomy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled five studies (283 women, average age 34) looking at misoprostol, a medicine that reduces blood flow to the uterus, given before myomectomy (surgery to remove fibroids). Women who received misoprostol lost less blood during surgery than those who received a placebo. Operation time, need for blood transfusion and fever after surgery were not meaningfully different between the groups. The authors conclude it is easy to use, with minor or no side effects.
keyPoints: Misoprostol reduced estimated blood loss by about 149 mL per operation compared with placebo.
Hemoglobin (a blood count marker) fell less after surgery in the misoprostol group, by about 0.68 g/dL.
No significant differences were seen in operation time, transfusions needed or fever after surgery.
The authors describe misoprostol as easy to use with minor or no side effects, whatever surgical technique is used.

items.title: Folic acid supplementation and malaria susceptibility and severity among people taking antifolate antimalarial drugs in endemic areas
items.summary: This review looked at whether taking folic acid affects malaria in people living in malaria areas who also take antifolate malaria medicines. For people being treated for malaria, folic acid (mostly at doses above 1 mg a day) meant the parasites cleared less often and treatment failed more often. One trial using the usual 400 microgram daily dose, the amount recommended to prevent neural tube defects, found little to no difference. No trials reported on whether folic acid changes the risk of getting malaria in the first place.
keyPoints: In malaria treatment trials, folic acid with antifolate medicines meant parasites were less likely to clear by day 3 and treatment failed more often (moderate-certainty evidence).
Most trials used folic acid doses above the 1.0 mg daily upper limit.
One trial using 400 micrograms a day, the dose recommended to prevent neural tube defects, showed little to no difference in parasite clearance or treatment failure.
No trial reported whether folic acid changes the risk of uncomplicated or severe malaria in people taking these medicines to prevent it.

items.title: Effects of excess folic acid and high blood folate during preconception and pregnancy: systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at what happens when women take a lot of folic acid, or have high folate levels in their blood, before and during pregnancy. Folic acid is recommended because it helps prevent neural tube defects, but too much was linked to some problems. The clearest link was with gestational diabetes. The authors say clear safe upper limits are urgently needed.
keyPoints: Folic acid is widely recommended before and in early pregnancy because adequate folate helps prevent neural tube defects.
Very high folic acid intake or high blood folate was linked to a higher risk of gestational diabetes, which was the most notable finding.
High supplement intake or high blood folate was also linked to neurodevelopmental issues in children, larger-than-expected babies and higher birth weight.
The authors say clear safe upper limits for folic acid intake and blood folate levels are needed urgently.

items.title: Preconception Folic Acid and Multivitamin Supplementation for the Prevention of Neural Tube Defect: An Umbrella Review of Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This study pulled together 10 earlier reviews, covering nearly 300,000 people, to see whether folic acid or multivitamins taken before and during pregnancy lower the chance of a baby having a neural tube defect (a problem with the early development of the brain and spine). Taking either type of supplement was linked to about a 57% lower chance of these defects. Results varied a lot between the reviews, and the authors say more large studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Folic acid or multivitamin use was linked to a 57% reduction in neural tube defects in children.
Folic acid on its own showed a bigger reduction (77%) than multivitamins (37%).
The reduction was similar in reviews of randomised trials (57%) and observational studies (55%).
The authors recommend considering these supplements in the preconception period, and say more research is needed on the best dose, duration and timing.

items.title: Folic acid supplementation in European women of reproductive age and during pregnancy with excessive weight: a systematic review
