items.summary: This review looked at whether women in Europe who have overweight or obesity take folic acid as recommended before and during pregnancy. Across 8 studies, only about 4% to 9.5% of pregnant women with obesity followed the recommendations, and most (61%) started folic acid only after they had conceived. The authors say recommendations differ between countries and that women with excess weight may need closer monitoring and tailored supplement plans.
keyPoints: Standard advice is 0.4 mg of folic acid daily, starting before conception and continuing through the first trimester, to help prevent neural tube defects.
Women with obesity often have lower folate levels, and the World Health Organization recommends a higher 5 mg dose for them.
Only 4% to 9.5% of pregnant women with obesity followed folic acid recommendations, and 61% started after conception, missing the key early window.
The authors call for consistent recommendations across European countries and for checking folate status in women of childbearing age with excess weight.

items.title: Folic Acid Supplementation and Risk of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review of the Literature
items.summary: This review looked at 12 studies on whether taking folic acid before or during early pregnancy is linked to gestational diabetes. Results were mixed. Some studies found that high daily doses (800 micrograms or more) or long use (over 3-6 months) may be linked to higher odds of gestational diabetes, while the standard dose of about 400 micrograms looked neutral or possibly protective. The authors say the evidence is not conclusive and more research is needed.
keyPoints: High daily folic acid (800 micrograms or more) or prolonged use (over 3-6 months) was linked to higher odds of gestational diabetes in several studies, especially when started before conception.
Standard-dose folic acid (about 400 micrograms) appeared neutral or possibly protective in some groups.
High folate levels combined with low vitamin B12 were linked to higher gestational diabetes risk.
The authors suggest cautious use of high-dose folic acid and individualised prenatal nutrition, including checking B12 status.

items.title: Influencing factors of neural tube malformation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined 49 case-control studies to look at what raises or lowers the chance of a baby having a neural tube defect, a problem with the development of the brain or spine. Folic acid use was linked to a much lower chance of these defects. Fever, obesity, passive smoking, antiepileptic drugs and mercury exposure were linked to a higher chance. The authors recommend that women who could become pregnant take folic acid and zinc supplements before and during pregnancy.
keyPoints: Folic acid was linked to lower odds of neural tube defects (odds ratio 0.31).
Fever, obesity, passive smoking and antiepileptic drugs were linked to higher odds of neural tube defects.
Mercury exposure was linked to higher odds of neural tube defects.
The authors recommend folic acid and zinc supplements for women of childbearing age before and during pregnancy.

items.title: The concept of folic acid supplementation and its role in prevention of neural tube defect among pregnant women: PRISMA
items.summary: This systematic review looked at how folic acid helps prevent neural tube defects, which are serious birth defects of the baby's brain and spine. Folic acid is needed for the rapid cell growth of the developing baby, and the neural tube closes in the first trimester. The review concludes that women are recommended to take 400 micrograms of folic acid a day from before conception until the end of the first trimester.
keyPoints: Folic acid is the synthetic form of vitamin B9, found in supplements and fortified foods, while folate occurs naturally in foods.
Low folic acid levels disrupt DNA and RNA production, which can lead to neural tube defects.
The first trimester is the key time for the baby's neural tube to close.
Women are recommended to take 400 micrograms of folic acid daily from preconception to the end of the first trimester.

items.title: Periconceptional folic acid supplementation for women with epilepsy: A systematic review of the literature
items.summary: This review pooled results from 23 observational studies of women with epilepsy to see whether folic acid taken around conception lowers the chance of major birth defects. It did not find a protective effect. Birth defects were slightly more common in those who took folic acid, and the authors called this result unexpected. Folic acid may help the child's brain development and behaviour, but the evidence for this was limited.
keyPoints: No evidence was found that folic acid lowered the risk of major birth defects in babies of women with epilepsy.
Birth defects were relatively higher with folic acid around conception (OR 1.34), a result the authors called unexpected.
Taking 4 mg or more was linked to a similar birth defect risk as not taking it.
Folic acid may benefit the child's neurodevelopment, but the evidence was limited.

items.title: Folic Acid Supplementation to Prevent Neural Tube Defects: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force
items.summary: This review looked at newer studies on whether taking folic acid around pregnancy helps prevent neural tube defects, which are serious birth defects of the brain and spine. The studies suggested folic acid lowered the chance of these defects, and found no signs of harm for twin pregnancy, autism or cancer in the mother. The new findings matched what earlier reviews had found. Most of the evidence came from observational studies rather than trials.
keyPoints: One large cohort study found a lower risk of neural tube defects with folic acid taken before pregnancy, during pregnancy, or both.
The lower risk was seen only in the later study period (2006-2013), not the earlier one (1999-2005), and no other significant benefits were reported.
No study found significant harms linked to folic acid in pregnancy, including multiple births, autism or maternal cancer.
The new evidence agreed with previously reviewed evidence on benefits and harms.

items.title: Structural congenital anomalies in resource limited setting, 2023: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from ten studies covering about 95,755 women who gave birth in places with limited resources. It looked for factors linked to structural birth defects (differences in how a baby's body forms). The pooled rate of birth defects was higher than in better-resourced countries. The authors advise preconception care and enough folic acid before and in early pregnancy.
keyPoints: The overall rate of structural birth defects in resource-limited settings was higher than in better-resourced countries.
Maternal illness, unidentified drug use, birth weight, chewing chat and chemical exposure were linked to birth defects.
Not taking folic acid during pregnancy was linked to birth defects, although the abstract words this result confusingly.
The authors advise preconception care and adequate folic acid before and during early pregnancy.

items.title: Maternal folic acid supplementation and the risk of ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) in infants; a systematic review
items.summary: Some public messages have suggested that folic acid supplements in pregnancy might cause tongue-tie in babies. This review searched four major databases and found only one study that looked at the question. That study had design problems that make its findings unreliable, so there is not enough evidence to link folic acid with tongue-tie. The authors conclude that the benefits of folic acid, which helps prevent neural tube defects, far outweigh the risks.
keyPoints: Folic acid supplements are known to protect against neural tube defects in babies.
Only one study of 93 articles found directly addressed folic acid and tongue-tie, and it had limitations in design, selection bias and confounding.
There is insufficient evidence for a link between folic acid supplementation and tongue-tie.
The authors say the benefits of folic acid currently far outweigh the risks.

items.title: Periconceptional folate and gestational diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies
items.summary: This review pooled results from ten cohort studies covering about 40,000 pregnancies to look at whether folate (folic acid) around the time of pregnancy is linked to gestational diabetes. Overall, higher folate exposure was linked to a somewhat higher chance of gestational diabetes. The link was seen for folate during pregnancy and in studies from China, but not for folate taken before pregnancy or in studies from western countries. These studies only show an association, not that folate causes gestational diabetes.
keyPoints: Across ten cohort studies, higher folate exposure was linked to a modestly higher risk of gestational diabetes (OR 1.24, 95% CI 1.01-1.52).
The link was seen for folate exposure during pregnancy, but not for exposure before pregnancy.
The link was seen in studies from China but not in western countries.
The authors conclude that periconceptional folate exposure is positively associated with gestational diabetes risk, especially during pregnancy.

items.title: Birth prevalence of neural tube defects in eastern Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 20 studies covering about 750,000 births in Eastern Africa to estimate how common neural tube defects (NTDs) are. NTDs are serious birth defects of the brain and spine. The rate was about 33 per 10,000 births, around 5 times higher than in Western countries where folic acid is added to foods. The authors suggest that adding folic acid to staple foods may lower NTD risk in the region.
keyPoints: About 33 in every 10,000 births in Eastern Africa were affected by an NTD, with the highest rate in Ethiopia (60 per 10,000).
Spina bifida was the most common type, followed by anencephaly and then encephalocele.
The rate is about 5 times higher than in Western countries with required folic acid fortification.
The authors conclude that mandatory folic acid fortification of staple foods may reduce NTD risk in Eastern Africa.

items.title: Guideline No. 427: Folic Acid and Multivitamin Supplementation for Prevention of Folic Acid-Sensitive Congenital Anomalies
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline gives updated advice on folic acid and multivitamin supplements for women who could become pregnant, to help prevent neural tube defects and other folate-sensitive birth defects. A low daily dose of folic acid is recommended for all women who could become pregnant, before conception and throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding. A higher dose is advised only for women who have had a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect or similar condition. The abstract does not give the specific doses or the certainty ratings.
keyPoints: All women who could become pregnant are advised to take a low daily dose of folic acid before conception and throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding.
High-dose folic acid is recommended only for women who have had a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect or other folate-sensitive birth defect.
Folic acid, or folate from food plus a multivitamin, is linked to lower rates of neural tube defects, other birth defects and some pregnancy complications.
Women with complex risks (genetic, medical or surgical) may benefit from a personalised approach, possibly including folate blood testing.

items.title: Directive clinique no427 : Suppléments d'acide folique et multivitamines en prévention des anomalies congénitales sensibles à l'acide folique
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian clinical guideline gives updated advice on folic acid and multivitamin supplements taken before and during pregnancy to help prevent neural tube defects and other birth defects that folic acid can reduce. Women aged 12 to 45 who could become pregnant are advised to take a low daily dose of folic acid before conception, during pregnancy and while breastfeeding. A high dose is advised only for women who have had a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect or another folic acid-sensitive birth defect. A more personalised approach may be considered for women with complex genetic, medical or surgical risks.
keyPoints: All women who could become pregnant are advised to take a low daily dose of folic acid before conception, during pregnancy and during breastfeeding.
High-dose folic acid is recommended only for women with a past pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect or another folic acid-sensitive birth defect.
Women with complex genetic, medical or surgical risks may be offered a personalised approach, which could involve blood folate testing.

Taking oral folic acid, or adding multivitamins or micronutrient supplements to dietary folate, is linked to fewer neural tube defects, fewer other folic acid-sensitive birth defects and fewer obstetric complications.

items.title: Women Taking a Folic Acid Supplement in Countries with Mandatory Food Fortification Programs May Be Exceeding the Upper Tolerable Limit of Folic Acid: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at how much folate and folic acid women of childbearing age and pregnant women get in high-income countries that add folic acid to foods by law. It found that women do not get enough folate from food alone, even with fortified foods. However, almost all women who take a folic acid supplement go over the upper tolerable limit of 1000 mcg a day. The authors say the supplement advice and this limit should be reviewed, because going over it may affect how folic acid is absorbed and used by the body.
keyPoints: Food sources alone, including fortified foods, did not give women of childbearing age enough folate.
Almost all women taking a folic acid supplement went over the upper tolerable limit of 1000 mcg per day.
The 1000 mcg limit was set to avoid hiding a vitamin B12 deficiency, not based on how folic acid is absorbed and processed.
The authors call for a careful review of supplement recommendations and the upper limit.

items.title: Preconception and periconception interventions to prevent low birth weight, small for gestational age and preterm birth: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled 58 studies of things women do before and around conception, such as taking supplements or improving general health, to see if they prevent low birth weight, small babies or preterm birth. The evidence was very uncertain for those outcomes, mostly because few studies tested any single approach. One clearer finding was that supplements containing folic acid taken before and around conception were linked to a lower risk of birth defects.
keyPoints: Evidence was generally very uncertain on whether preconception or periconception interventions prevent low birth weight, small for gestational age or preterm birth.
Supplements containing folic acid taken before and around conception were linked to a lower risk of birth defects (risk ratio 0.37, 10 studies, over 313,000 people).
Studies varied a lot in the interventions tested, so few studies were available for any single comparison.
The authors call for more research on a wider range of interventions.

items.title: Effectiveness of preconception interventions in primary care: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 22 randomised trials of preconception care given in primary care (such as GP surgeries) to people planning a pregnancy. Brief or longer education, supplements and diet changes helped improve health knowledge, increase folate intake and reduce risks like drinking alcohol or smoking before pregnancy. Few trials looked at actual pregnancy outcomes, and most trials were of low quality, so it is still unclear whether this care improves pregnancy outcomes. Almost all trials focused on women, so there is little evidence for men.
keyPoints: Brief education improved health knowledge, reduced alcohol and tobacco use, and increased folate intake.
Intensive education reduced alcohol-exposed pregnancies and increased physical activity; one trial found fewer spontaneous pregnancy losses.
Supplements increased folate intake, and dietary changes were linked to less pre-eclampsia and higher birth weight in one trial each.
Only eight articles reported pregnancy outcomes, and most trials (12 of 22) were of low quality.

items.title: Maternal biomarkers for early prediction of the neural tube defects pregnancies
items.summary: This study pooled results from earlier studies to see whether blood levels of certain nutrients in mothers are linked to pregnancies affected by neural tube defects (serious birth defects of the brain and spine). Higher homocysteine was linked to a higher risk, while higher folate and higher vitamin B12 (cobalamin) were linked to a lower risk. The authors suggest these blood markers might help predict neural tube defects early. The results varied a lot between the studies that were combined.
keyPoints: Higher homocysteine in the mother was linked to a greater risk of a neural tube defect pregnancy.
Higher folate levels in the mother's blood were linked to a lower risk.
Higher vitamin B12 (cobalamin) levels were also linked to a lower risk.
The authors suggest these maternal blood markers may help with early prediction of neural tube defects.

items.title: Association of the Maternal Folic Acid Supplementation with the Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review
items.source: Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia E Obstetricia
items.journal: Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia E Obstetricia
items.summary: This review looked at 17 studies on whether taking folic acid around pregnancy is linked to autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in children. The studies pointed to a protective effect when folic acid was taken before conception and in early pregnancy. The authors say more research is needed, because taking too much folic acid may not be harmless.
keyPoints: The review found 17 eligible studies out of 384 articles searched.
Folic acid taken before conception and in early pregnancy was linked to a protective effect against autism spectrum disorder.
The authors suggest folic acid be indicated in this period as prevention.
More studies are needed on its effects in pregnancy, since excessive folic acid may not be harmless.

items.title: Effects of Preconception Care and Periconception Interventions on Maternal Nutritional Status and Birth Outcomes in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 45 trials from low- and middle-income countries on care given before and around the time of conception. Taking folic acid around conception was linked to fewer babies born with neural tube defects, and iron plus folic acid was linked to less anemia. Education programmes also helped more women use contraception, which can help delay a first pregnancy or space pregnancies. The authors say more robust trials from these countries are still needed.
keyPoints: Folic acid taken around conception reduced neural tube defects (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.41-0.77; two studies, 248,056 women).
Iron-folic acid supplements lowered anemia rates (RR 0.66), especially when taken weekly and given in a school setting.
Education programmes raised contraception use among those aiming to delay a first pregnancy (RR 1.71) or space pregnancies (RR 2.25).
The authors call for more robust randomized trials from low- and middle-income countries.

items.title: Fortification of wheat and maize flour with folic acid for population health outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether adding folic acid to wheat or maize flour helps population health, including pregnancy outcomes. Only 10 small studies were found, and the evidence is low or very low quality. One non-randomised study found fewer neural tube defects (serious birth defects of the spine and brain) with fortified wheat flour, and several studies found higher folate levels in the blood. No studies reported side effects, so safety is not yet clear.
keyPoints: Folic acid-fortified wheat flour may reduce neural tube defects, but this was reported in only one non-randomised study (low-certainty evidence).
Fortified wheat or maize flour may raise folate levels in the blood, though most of this evidence is very low certainty.
Evidence on effects on haemoglobin or anaemia is limited; a trial in children found no clear effect.
No studies reported adverse effects, and the review's small number of studies limits what can be concluded.

items.title: Folic acid supplementation during the preconception period: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Guidelines advise women to take folic acid before pregnancy to help prevent neural tube defects in babies. This review pulled together 105 studies from 34 countries to see how many women actually do this. Use varied a lot between countries, and in many places a large share of women may not reach folate levels high enough to protect against these defects.
keyPoints: Guidelines recommend folic acid supplements in the preconception period to prevent neural tube defects (NTDs).
Reported use before pregnancy ranged widely, for example 32-51% in North America, 9-78% in Europe and 4-34% in the Middle East.
Use was higher in more highly educated groups and in fertility clinic settings.
Only about a third of studies reported when women took folic acid, and fewer reported whether they took it consistently.

items.title: Elevated homocysteine levels in mothers with neural tube defects: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 17 studies (3,237 people) to see whether mothers of babies with neural tube defects have different blood levels of homocysteine, an amino acid linked to folate. Mothers of affected babies had slightly higher levels, about 6% higher on average. This difference was not seen in countries that add folic acid to foods by law. The authors say other factors could not be fully ruled out and larger studies are needed to confirm the link.
keyPoints: Mothers of babies with neural tube defects had about 6% higher average homocysteine levels than mothers of unaffected babies.
The higher levels were seen in women tested during pregnancy or before taking folate supplements.
No link was found in countries with mandatory folate fortification of food.
Other factors may explain the finding, and larger or cohort studies are needed to confirm it.

items.title: Folic Acid Supplementation for the Prevention of Neural Tube Defects: An Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force
items.summary: This review looked at 24 studies on whether taking folic acid around the time of conception lowers the chance of a baby having a neural tube defect (a birth defect of the brain or spine). Studies done before food fortification began in the US in 1998 found that folic acid supplements gave protection. Newer studies done after fortification have not clearly shown this protection, but the authors note these studies may be affected by recall bias and misclassification, which can hide a real benefit. No clear increase in twin pregnancies, asthma, wheezing or allergy was found.
keyPoints: Before food fortification in 1998, folic acid supplementation was linked to protection against neural tube defects; one trial found 0% vs 0.25% incidence with folic acid vs trace elements.
Studies done after fortification did not consistently show a protective link, though the authors say bias and misclassification could weaken the measured effect.
No statistically significant increase in twinning was found with folic acid.
Three systematic reviews found no consistent evidence of increased asthma, wheezing or allergy in children.

items.title: Folic Acid Supplementation for the Prevention of Neural Tube Defects: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force looked again at folic acid supplements for women who could become pregnant. Neural tube defects are serious birth defects of the brain and spine, and most women do not get enough folate from food alone. The Task Force found the benefit is substantial and the harms at usual doses are no more than small. It recommends a daily supplement of 0.4 to 0.8 mg (400-800 micrograms) of folic acid for all women planning pregnancy or able to become pregnant.
keyPoints: All women planning pregnancy or capable of becoming pregnant are recommended to take a daily supplement with 0.4 to 0.8 mg (400-800 µg) of folic acid.
Daily folic acid taken around the time of conception can prevent neural tube defects.
Most women do not get the recommended daily amount of folate from diet alone.
Harms to mother or baby from folic acid at usual doses are no greater than small.

items.title: Practice Bulletin No. 187: Neural Tube Defects
items.summary: This guideline from a leading obstetrics group explains neural tube defects, which are birth defects of the brain, spine or spinal cord. It notes that, unlike many other birth defects, these can be prevented in the first place with folic acid. It also says screening and diagnosis in pregnancy are widely available and that fetal surgery has improved outcomes for some babies.
keyPoints: Neural tube defects are the second most common major birth defect after heart defects.
Primary prevention of neural tube defects is possible with folic acid, unlike many other birth defects.
Prenatal screening and diagnosis for neural tube defects are widely available.
Outcomes depend on the level and extent of the defect; most babies with spina bifida survive after surgical repair, while anencephaly is not compatible with life.

items.title: Pre-conception Folic Acid and Multivitamin Supplementation for the Primary and Secondary Prevention of Neural Tube Defects and Other Folic Acid-Sensitive Congenital Anomalies
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline explains how folic acid, usually taken in a multivitamin, helps prevent neural tube defects (serious birth defects of the brain and spine) and possibly some other birth defects. It advises eating a folate-rich diet, but says supplements are needed to reach the folate levels that give the best protection. The recommended dose depends on whether a woman's risk of a neural tube defect is low, moderate or high.
keyPoints: A healthy folate-rich diet is advised, but a folic acid/multivitamin supplement is needed to reach folate levels linked to maximum protection against neural tube defects.
For low-risk women, a daily multivitamin with 0.4 mg folic acid is advised for at least 2 to 3 months before conception, through pregnancy, and for 4 to 6 weeks after birth or while breastfeeding.

For moderate-risk women, 1.0 mg folic acid daily from at least 3 months before conception until 12 weeks of pregnancy; for high-risk women (such as a past neural tube defect pregnancy), 4.0 mg daily over the same period, then a multivitamin with 0.4 to 1.0 mg.

Because many pregnancies are unplanned, all women who could become pregnant should be told about folic acid; folic acid is unlikely to hide vitamin B12 deficiency, and no tests are needed before starting.

items.title: Effects and safety of periconceptional oral folate supplementation for preventing birth defects
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined five trials with 7,391 women to see whether taking folic acid around the time of conception prevents birth defects. Daily folic acid, taken alone or with other vitamins and minerals, clearly reduced neural tube defects (serious defects of the baby's brain and spine), including in women who had a previous affected pregnancy. There was no clear effect, good or bad, on cleft lip or palate, heart defects, other birth defects or miscarriage, though the evidence for most of these was low quality.
keyPoints: Folic acid reduced neural tube defects by about two-thirds compared with no folic acid (risk ratio 0.31), based on high quality evidence.
The protective effect held for first-time and repeat (recurrence) neural tube defects, and was the same at 400 micrograms (0.4 mg) a day or higher, alone or with other vitamins.
No clear effect was found on cleft lip, cleft palate, heart defects or other birth defects, but the evidence was low quality.
Folic acid did not appear to raise the risk of miscarriage (moderate quality evidence).

items.title: Prevention of neural tube defects: results of the Medical Research Council Vitamin Study. MRC Vitamin Study Research Group
items.summary: This large trial followed 1817 women who had previously had a pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect (such as spina bifida). Women took folic acid, a mix of other vitamins, both, or neither around the time of conception. Neural tube defects were far less common in the folic acid groups: 6 cases compared with 21 in the groups without folic acid, a 72% protective effect. The other vitamins did not show a clear benefit, and no harm from folic acid was seen, though the study could not rule out rare or slight side effects.
keyPoints: Folic acid cut the risk of neural tube defects by 72% in women who had a previous affected pregnancy.
The mix of other vitamins (A, D, B1, B2, B6, C and nicotinamide) showed no significant protective effect.
No demonstrable harm from folic acid was found, but the study had limited ability to detect rare or slight side effects.
The authors recommended folic acid starting before pregnancy for women who have had an affected pregnancy, and diets with enough folic acid for all women who may have children.

items.title: Dietary fat intake with risk of gestational diabetes mellitus and preeclampsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies
items.summary: This review pooled 21 studies that followed pregnant women over time to see whether the fat in their diet was linked to gestational diabetes (diabetes that starts in pregnancy) or preeclampsia (a pregnancy blood pressure problem). Women who ate more total fat, animal fat, vegetable fat, cholesterol or omega-3 fats had a small but statistically significant higher risk of gestational diabetes. No link was found between dietary fat and preeclampsia. These studies show links, not proof that the fats caused the diabetes.
keyPoints: Higher intake of total fat, animal fat, vegetable fat, dietary cholesterol and omega-3 fatty acids was linked to a small increase in gestational diabetes risk.
Animal fat (relative risk 1.56) and dietary cholesterol (relative risk 1.48) showed the largest increases in risk.
No significant link was found between dietary fat and preeclampsia.
Every 10% rise in energy from total fat was linked to about 15% higher gestational diabetes risk.

items.title: Global seroprevalence of Toxoplasma gondii in pregnant women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 138 studies covering about 135,000 pregnant women to see how many have antibodies showing past infection with Toxoplasma gondii, the parasite that causes toxoplasmosis. Around 37 in 100 pregnant women worldwide had these antibodies, with big differences between regions. The authors say toxoplasmosis in pregnancy can cause serious, lasting harm to mother and baby, so awareness and health programmes are important for prevention and early diagnosis.
keyPoints: Worldwide, about 36.6% of pregnant women had antibodies showing they had been exposed to Toxoplasma gondii.
Rates were highest in South America (52.8%) and Africa (46.8%), and lowest in North America (19.7%) and Europe (24.6%).
The authors say exposure levels mostly depend on age, lifestyle and how much people know about toxoplasmosis.
The authors say public awareness and health programmes are needed to help prevent or catch toxoplasmosis early in pregnancy.

items.title: Systematic Review of Nutritional Guidelines for the Management of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: A Global Comparison
items.summary: Researchers compared 12 nutrition guidelines for gestational diabetes (diabetes first found in pregnancy) from health organisations around the world. All agreed on moderating carbohydrates and eating enough fibre. They disagreed on the type of carbohydrate to focus on, the blood sugar targets after meals, and whether extra supplements such as chromium, selenium and omega-3 are useful. Guidance on adapting advice to different cultures and on counselling support was limited.
keyPoints: All 12 guidelines stressed moderating carbohydrates and eating enough fibre.
Guidelines differed on carbohydrate quality (low glycaemic index versus restricting total carbohydrate) and on after-meal blood sugar targets.
Supplements like chromium, selenium and omega-3 fatty acids were generally not recommended as routine.
Cultural fit and behavioural counselling were rarely covered, and the authors call for clearer, more consistent guidelines.

items.title: Fish Consumption and the Risk of Depression: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies
items.summary: This review pooled 35 observational studies to look at whether eating more fish is linked to a lower chance of depression, including depression during pregnancy. People who ate more fish had about a 21% lower risk of depression, and the result for pregnancy-related depression was similar (about 22% lower). The link was only clearly seen at around 68 g of fish a day or more. Because these studies only observe people's habits, they show a link, not proof that fish prevents depression.
keyPoints: Higher fish consumption was linked to lower depression risk overall (RR 0.79).
A similar link was found for depression related to pregnancy (RR 0.78).
A clear link appeared only in studies where fish intake was at least 68.4 g/day, hinting at a possible threshold.
Each extra 15 g/day of fish was linked to a 6% lower depression risk.

items.title: Nut Consumption and Fertility: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled four studies (875 adults) on eating nuts and fertility. In two trials of healthy men, eating about 60g of nuts a day (roughly two servings) improved sperm movement, vitality and shape, but not sperm count. Other studies found no link between nut intake and embryo implantation, pregnancy or live birth in people having fertility treatment. The evidence base is small, so the findings are still limited.
keyPoints: Eating at least 60g of nuts a day improved sperm motility, vitality and morphology in healthy men in two trials.
Nut intake had no effect on sperm concentration.
Non-randomised studies found no link between nut intake and implantation, clinical pregnancy or live birth in people having assisted reproduction.
Only four studies were included, so the evidence is limited.

items.title: A systematic review of maternal TORCH serology as a screen for suspected fetal infection
items.summary: This review looked at eight studies (2538 pregnancies) where mothers had a blood test panel called 'TORCH' after an ultrasound showed possible problems with the baby. The panel checks for toxoplasmosis, rubella, CMV and herpes. Only CMV infection was confirmed in the babies (26 cases), and none of the studies found toxoplasmosis, rubella or herpes. The authors conclude the panel is of little use when the ultrasound shows only one non-specific sign, such as slow growth or extra fluid on its own.
keyPoints: Across 2538 pregnancies, 26 cases of congenital CMV were confirmed, and 15 of them had more than one ultrasound abnormality.
No cases of congenital toxoplasmosis, rubella or herpes were confirmed in any of the eight studies.
The TORCH blood test has low usefulness for isolated findings such as fetal growth restriction or polyhydramnios alone.
The authors suggest retiring routine 'TORCH' panel ordering in favour of more targeted investigation.

items.title: Listeriosis in pregnancy: An umbrella review of maternal exposure, treatment and neonatal complications
items.summary: This review pulled together nine systematic reviews on listeriosis, an infection caused by Listeria bacteria that can be found in processed and prepared food. Listeriosis is rare but serious in pregnancy and can lead to miscarriage, preterm birth, stillbirth and infection in the newborn. Prevention relies on following strict food advice, such as reheating leftovers until steaming and avoiding unpasteurised dairy products. Most of the reviews included were of moderate to high quality.
keyPoints: Pregnancy raises the risk of being diagnosed with listeriosis compared with the general population.
Prevention is based on strict dietary advice, such as reheating leftovers until steaming and avoiding unpasteurised dairy products.
Infections were most likely in the third trimester (66%) and rarely in the first trimester (3%).
Symptoms are mostly fever and flu-like symptoms such as fatigue; first-line treatment is intravenous amoxicillin or ampicillin.

items.title: Hygiene measures as primary prevention of toxoplasmosis during pregnancy: A systematic review
items.source: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.journal: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.summary: This review looked at 67 studies on whether hygiene steps during pregnancy help prevent toxoplasmosis, an infection that can pass to the baby. It covered food advice, pet care, and other environmental measures. The authors concluded that hygiene measures are an effective and practical way to lower the chance of toxoplasmosis and congenital toxoplasmosis.
keyPoints: The authors conclude hygiene measures are an effective, practical first line of prevention against toxoplasmosis in pregnancy.
They can help reduce congenital toxoplasmosis, where the infection passes to the baby, and its consequences.
The reviewed measures included dietary recommendations, pet care and environmental steps.
The review also looked at how well pregnant women and health professionals know the risk factors.

items.title: Prevention and Management of Hypertriglyceridemia-Induced Acute Pancreatitis During Pregnancy: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This systematic review looked at how to prevent and manage acute pancreatitis caused by very high triglycerides (blood fats) in pregnancy. Severe high triglycerides can lead to pancreatitis, which carries a maternal death rate of about 20%. The authors suggest that women at high risk have their triglycerides checked once each trimester, with diet changes, omega-3 fatty acids and other treatments stepped up if levels climb higher.
keyPoints: Women at high risk are suggested to have triglycerides checked once every trimester.
Fasting triglycerides above 250 mg/dL should prompt monthly checks, gestational diabetes screening, a strict low-carbohydrate, low-fat diet and exercise.
If triglycerides stay above 500 mg/dL despite diet and lifestyle changes, omega-3 fatty acids and a fat-restricted diet with a registered dietitian are advised.

Fibrates are a second-line option because their risks and benefits in pregnancy are unclear and they may harm the baby; plasmapheresis should be considered early for very high levels or signs of pancreatitis.

items.title: Interventions to prevent spontaneous preterm birth in women with singleton pregnancy who are at high risk: systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pooled 61 trials (over 17,000 pregnant women) to compare treatments that aim to prevent early birth in women expecting one baby who had a past early birth or a short cervix. Vaginal progesterone worked best, with about half the odds of birth before 34 weeks compared with placebo or no treatment, and the evidence was rated high certainty. Fish oil or omega-3 might also lower the chance of birth before 34 weeks, but the result was uncertain and could not rule out no effect.
keyPoints: Vaginal progesterone was linked to fewer births before 34 weeks (odds ratio 0.50) and was the only treatment with clear evidence of fewer perinatal deaths.
Fish oil or omega-3 might reduce birth before 34 weeks (odds ratio 0.30), but the range of results was wide and included no effect (moderate certainty).
Only progesterone treatments were linked to fewer breathing problems, infections, bowel complications and intensive care admissions in newborns.
The authors conclude vaginal progesterone should be the preventative treatment of choice for women at high risk because of a past early birth or short cervix.

items.title: Maternal Mercury Exposure and Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy: A Systematic Review
items.source: Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia E Obstetricia
items.journal: Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia E Obstetricia
items.summary: This review looked at whether mercury exposure, for example from eating fish or from dental fillings, is linked to high blood pressure problems in pregnancy such as pre-eclampsia. Only six studies met the criteria, and the results were mixed: two found a link in the most exposed groups and four did not. Most studies did not properly account for fish eating, which can also be good for health, so the picture is unclear and more research is needed.
keyPoints: Only six studies were found, covering 4,848 pregnant women.
Two studies found a link between higher mercury and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in the most exposed group; four found no link.
Five of the six studies did not properly adjust for fish consumption, which may blur the results.
The authors say more studies are needed to understand mercury's effects on blood pressure in pregnancy.

items.title: Toxoplasmosis infection among pregnant women in Africa: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined 23 studies of 7,579 pregnant women attending antenatal clinics in ten African countries. It found that about half (51%) had antibodies showing they had been infected with Toxoplasma, a parasite that can harm a baby if the mother is first infected during pregnancy. Results varied a lot between studies. The authors conclude that the risk of catching toxoplasmosis in pregnancy is high and that preventive measures to avoid exposure should be strictly applied.
keyPoints: The pooled rate of positive toxoplasmosis blood tests among pregnant women in Africa was 51.01%.
Findings differed widely between studies, so the true rate may vary by place.
Congenital toxoplasmosis happens when the mother is infected during pregnancy.
The authors say preventive measures to avoid exposure during pregnancy should be strictly applied.

items.title: A fresh look at the role of spiramycin in preventing a neglected disease: meta-analyses of observational studies
items.summary: Toxoplasmosis is an infection that can pass from a pregnant woman to her baby; undercooked meat and some other foods are common sources. This review combined 33 observational studies covering over 15,000 mothers and babies. It found that mothers treated with the antibiotic spiramycin passed the infection to their babies much less often than untreated mothers. The studies were observational rather than trials, so the results show an association.
keyPoints: The rate of mother-to-baby transmission was about 19.5% in treated women versus about 50.7% in untreated women.
Spiramycin on its own was also linked to lower transmission, to about 17.6% compared with 50.7% untreated.
The authors conclude that treating suspected or confirmed toxoplasmosis in pregnancy significantly reduces transmission to the baby.

items.title: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine Consult Series #52: Diagnosis and management of fetal growth restriction: (Replaces Clinical Guideline Number 3, April 2012)
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This guideline from the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine explains how doctors should diagnose and manage fetal growth restriction, when a baby is measuring smaller than expected in the womb. It affects up to 10% of pregnancies. The guideline sets out how it is defined, which tests to offer, how closely to monitor the baby, and when to plan delivery. It does not cover food safety or fish in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Fetal growth restriction is defined as an ultrasound estimated weight or abdominal size below the 10th percentile for gestational age.
Once it is diagnosed, regular ultrasound Doppler checks of blood flow in the umbilical cord are recommended to watch for changes.
Timing of delivery depends on the Doppler results and how small the baby is, ranging from about 30-32 weeks up to 38-39 weeks.
Low-molecular-weight heparin, sildenafil and activity restriction are recommended against as treatments for fetal growth restriction.

items.title: The congenital toxoplasmosis burden in Brazil: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 21 studies from Brazil covering 469 children born with congenital toxoplasmosis, an infection passed from mother to baby during pregnancy. About half of the children had eye damage (retinochoroiditis) and nearly 1 in 5 had calcium spots in the brain. Children whose mothers received anti-toxoplasmosis medicine during pregnancy tended to have a better outlook, and were more likely to have no symptoms. Many mothers did not get prenatal care or treatment, and over half of the children were only diagnosed after birth.
keyPoints: Eye inflammation (retinochoroiditis) was the most common problem, seen in 48.2% of the children, followed by brain calcifications in 17.7%.
Mothers who were treated with anti-Toxoplasma medicine during pregnancy had children with a better prognosis, and treatment was linked to children having no symptoms.
Only 44.6% of the mothers had prenatal care, and 22.5% of those received no toxoplasmosis medicine.
57% of the children were diagnosed only after birth.

items.title: Omega-3 Fatty Acid Supplementation for Perinatal Depression: A Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 18 trials with 4,052 women to see whether omega-3 supplements (fish oil) help with depression around the time of pregnancy and birth. Overall there was a small benefit compared with placebo, but the results varied a lot between studies. Omega-3 showed almost no effect during pregnancy, while the effect looked larger after birth, though those individual results were uncertain.
keyPoints: Across all trials, omega-3 gave a small overall improvement in depressive symptoms compared with placebo.
During pregnancy, omega-3 had a negligible effect, and the authors advise against using it to treat or prevent depression in pregnancy.
After birth, the effect looked medium to large, and the authors say omega-3 may be a promising add-on treatment for postpartum depression.
Results differed a lot between studies, so the subgroup findings should be read with caution.

items.title: Antenatal interventions for preventing stillbirth, fetal loss and perinatal death: an overview of Cochrane systematic reviews
items.summary: This overview pulled together 43 Cochrane reviews to see which care during pregnancy might prevent stillbirth and newborn death in low-risk or general groups of women. Some approaches showed a clear benefit, including balanced energy and protein supplements, midwife-led care, training traditional birth attendants, and computerised heart-rate monitoring of the baby. Having fewer antenatal visits probably led to more baby deaths around birth. For many other interventions the effects were uncertain, and results varied between settings.
keyPoints: Balanced energy and protein supplements probably reduce stillbirth (moderate-certainty evidence).
Midwife-led models of care reduced fetal loss and newborn death, mainly for low-risk pregnancies (high-certainty evidence).
A reduced number of antenatal care visits probably increases the risk of death around the time of birth (moderate-certainty evidence).
Most other interventions, including most nutrition ones, had uncertain effects, and the authors call for more high-quality trials, especially in low- and middle-income countries.

items.title: No. 285-Toxoplasmosis in Pregnancy: Prevention, Screening, and Treatment
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looks at toxoplasmosis, an infection that can pass from a pregnant woman to her baby. It is rare, but when it happens in the womb it can cause serious eye, brain and heart problems. The guideline says prenatal care should include education on preventing infection. Routine screening of all pregnant women is not currently recommended in Canada, because the infection is uncommon and tests and treatments have limits.
keyPoints: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy can pass to the baby, which is called congenital toxoplasmosis.
Congenital toxoplasmosis is rare but can cause severe brain or eye disease, including blindness, and heart and brain anomalies.
Prenatal care should include education about preventing toxoplasmosis.
Routine screening is not currently recommended because the disease is uncommon in Canada and diagnosis and treatment have limitations.

items.title: Dietary patterns, foods and nutrients in male fertility parameters and fecundability: a systematic review of observational studies
items.summary: This review pulled together 35 observational studies on what men eat and how it relates to sperm quality and the chance of a couple conceiving. Healthy diets rich in fish, fruit, vegetables, whole grains and certain vitamins and omega-3 fats were linked with better sperm quality. Diets heavy in processed meat, full-fat dairy, sugary drinks and sweets were linked with poorer quality, and a man's high alcohol, caffeine and red or processed meat intake was linked with a lower chance of pregnancy. Because these studies can only show links and not cause and effect, the authors say larger and better-designed trials are needed.
keyPoints: Diets rich in omega-3 fats, antioxidants, vitamin D and folate, and low in saturated and trans fats, were linked with better semen quality.
Fish, shellfish, poultry, cereals, vegetables, fruit and low-fat dairy were linked with better sperm quality in several studies.
High male intake of alcohol, caffeine, and red and processed meat was linked with a lower chance of pregnancy in partners.
The studies are observational, so they show associations rather than proof of cause, and need confirming in larger trials.

items.title: Maternal prenatal and/or postnatal n-3 long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFA) supplementation for preventing allergies in early childhood
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 8 randomised trials (3366 women, 3175 children) to see whether omega-3 supplements taken in pregnancy or while breastfeeding reduce allergies in children. Some small benefits were seen at certain ages, for example fewer medically diagnosed IgE-mediated allergies at 12 to 36 months. Most allergy outcomes showed no clear difference, and the review concludes the evidence is limited. Supplementation in pregnancy did not appear to raise the risk of postpartum bleeding or early childhood infections.
keyPoints: Omega-3 supplements were linked to fewer medically diagnosed IgE-mediated allergies in children aged 12 to 36 months, but not beyond 36 months.
Food allergy was lower in the first 12 months, and eczema was lower at 12 to 36 months, but there were no clear differences for hay fever or asthma/wheeze.
Few differences in childhood allergic disease were seen overall, so the authors say the evidence is limited.
Omega-3 supplementation in pregnancy did not show a higher risk of postpartum haemorrhage or early childhood infections.

items.title: Prenatal education for congenital toxoplasmosis
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether teaching pregnant women about toxoplasmosis (an infection that can harm a baby, caught through things like undercooked meat, unwashed produce and cat litter) helps prevent it. Only two trials, covering 5455 women, were found, and both were low quality with many women lost to follow-up. One trial found better hygiene habits, while the other found better knowledge but no change in behaviour, and infection rates did not clearly differ between groups. The evidence is too limited to say whether prenatal education prevents congenital toxoplasmosis.
keyPoints: Only two cluster-randomised trials (5455 women) were found, and both were of low quality.
One trial reported improved pet, personal and food hygiene after education; the other found better knowledge but no change in behaviour.
Infection (seroconversion) rates did not differ clearly between education and comparison groups, but there were too few cases to draw conclusions.
The authors say more good-quality trials are needed, even though observational studies suggest education may help.

items.title: Vulvovaginal estrogen therapy for urinary symptoms in postmenopausal women: a review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 17 studies (2,111 women) on vaginal estrogen applied locally for urinary symptoms after menopause. Women had fewer urinary symptoms after treatment than before, including recurrent urinary tract infections, leaking urine, urgency, needing to pass urine often, and waking at night to pass urine. Vaginal acidity (pH) also improved. The authors say the findings support current guidelines recommending vaginal estrogen for these symptoms.
keyPoints: After vaginal estrogen, women were much less likely to have recurrent urinary tract infections, stress or urge incontinence, urgency, frequency and nocturia than before treatment.
Vaginal pH went down after treatment (average change of about 1.3 units).
The authors conclude that topical vaginal estrogen appears to improve all the urinary symptoms studied.
The results back up existing guidelines that recommend vaginal estrogen for these symptoms in menopausal women.

items.title: Platelet-rich plasma in the management of vulvovaginal disorders: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 18 small studies on platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections, made from a person's own blood, into the vulva and vagina. People treated had conditions such as vulvar lichen sclerosus, sexual dysfunction and vaginal atrophy (thinning and dryness). Studies generally reported better symptoms, sexual function and vaginal health, with few and mild side effects. The studies were small and used very different methods, so no firm conclusions can be drawn yet.
keyPoints: 18 studies with 480 patients were included, mostly small single-arm trials and only two randomized controlled trials.
PRP injections were linked to improved symptoms, sexual function and vaginal health.
Side effects were few and mild.
Differences in how PRP was prepared and given, small sample sizes and methodological limits mean better randomized trials are needed.

items.title: Vaginal estrogen use in breast cancer survivors: a systematic review and meta-analysis of recurrence and mortality risks
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 8 observational studies of women who had breast cancer and used vaginal estrogen for menopause-related vaginal and urinary symptoms. Vaginal estrogen use was not linked to a higher risk of breast cancer coming back, dying from breast cancer, or dying from any cause. The studies were observational, so they show an association rather than proof.
keyPoints: Vaginal estrogen was not associated with a higher risk of breast cancer recurrence (6 studies, 24,060 women).
It was not associated with higher breast cancer-specific death (4 studies, 61,695 women).
It was not associated with higher overall death (5 studies, 59,724 women).
The authors concluded that vaginal estrogen does not appear to raise these risks in breast cancer survivors.

items.title: The AUA/SUFU/AUGS Guideline on Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause
items.summary: This guideline from US urology and gynaecology bodies reviews the evidence on genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), the vaginal and urinary symptoms caused by falling estrogen around menopause. GSM is diagnosed from a person's symptoms, with or without physical findings, once other causes have been ruled out. Many hormonal and non-hormonal treatments have been studied, and low-dose vaginal estrogen has the strongest evidence. There was not enough information to say that one hormonal treatment is better than another.
keyPoints: GSM is diagnosed from symptoms, with or without physical changes, after other causes are ruled out.
Urinary symptoms of GSM can look like other common bladder conditions such as overactive bladder.
Local low-dose vaginal estrogen has the most robust evidence among the treatment options.
There is not enough evidence to favour one hormonal therapy over another, so treatment is chosen through shared decision-making based on patient goals and preferences.

items.title: Vaginal lasers for treating stress urinary incontinence in women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether vaginal laser treatment helps women with stress urinary incontinence (leaking urine when coughing, sneezing or exercising). It combined nine trials with 689 women, comparing lasers with sham (pretend) treatment or with topical treatments such as oestrogen. Lasers may make little or no difference in the first year, and any small improvement in symptom scores may not be noticeable to patients. The evidence is very uncertain, and no major side effects were seen.
keyPoints: In the short term (under one year), vaginal lasers may make little to no difference to stress urinary incontinence compared with sham or topical treatments.
The small improvement seen in symptom questionnaire scores may not be big enough for patients to notice.
One small study suggested more women were continent after one to five years with laser, but the evidence is very uncertain.
No major adverse events were reported with lasers, sham treatment or topical oestrogen.

items.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Managing Genitourinary Symptoms Associated With Menopause
items.summary: This guideline looks at genitourinary syndrome of menopause, a group of vaginal and urinary symptoms caused by low estrogen after menopause. These include dryness, burning, pain with sex, urinary urgency, painful urination and repeat urinary tract infections. It says the symptoms can strongly affect wellbeing and quality of life, and it describes several treatment options.
keyPoints: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause is caused by low estrogen and includes genital dryness, burning or irritation, sexual discomfort, and urinary symptoms such as urgency, painful urination and recurrent UTIs.
The symptoms can have a profound effect on wellbeing, daily functioning and quality of life in postmenopausal women.
Vaginal moisturizers and lubricants are used to give symptom relief.

Hormonal treatments help thicken the vaginal lining and increase vaginal secretions, and pelvic floor physical therapy and behavioral therapies address pelvic floor tightness and psychosocial factors.

items.title: Impact of vaginal estriol on serum hormone levels: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether vaginal estriol, a form of estrogen used for menopause-related vaginal and urinary symptoms, changes hormone levels in the blood. Across the studies, blood levels of estrone, estradiol, testosterone, progesterone and sex hormone binding globulin did not change after using it. A few studies saw small, short-lived changes in other hormones, which stayed within the usual postmenopausal range. The authors say this supports the safety of vaginal estriol products.
keyPoints: No changes were found in blood estrone, estradiol, testosterone, progesterone or sex hormone binding globulin after vaginal estriol.
Some studies showed a small, temporary drop in gonadotropin hormones, but levels stayed within the postmenopausal range.
Only a few studies reported a small, temporary rise in blood estriol; most found no change.
No clinically relevant long-term changes in blood hormone levels were found, supporting the safety of vaginal estriol.

items.title: European Board and College of Obstetrics and Gynaecology (EBCOG) position statement on the use of laser vaginal devices for treatment of genitourinary syndrome of menopause, vaginal laxity, pelvic organ prolapse and stress urinary incontinence
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: The European Board and College of Obstetrics and Gynaecology (EBCOG) looked at vaginal laser treatments for menopause-related vaginal symptoms, vaginal looseness, prolapse and bladder leaks when coughing or exercising. Lasers have become popular over the last decade, but the statement says there is not enough strong evidence to support their routine use. It calls for high-quality studies that measure outcomes that matter to patients before lasers become standard care.
keyPoints: Lasers for genitourinary symptoms of menopause, prolapse and stress urinary incontinence have become popular, but robust evidence for routine use is lacking.
Conservative management (non-surgical approaches) is recommended as first-line treatment for pelvic organ prolapse and stress urinary incontinence.
Vaginal estrogens are often prescribed for symptomatic vaginal atrophy.
EBCOG calls for high-quality evidence with patient-reported outcome measures before laser use becomes routine.

items.title: Nonestrogen Therapies for Treatment of Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 136 studies of treatments that are not estrogen for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which includes vaginal dryness, discomfort and sexual symptoms. Most of the non-estrogen options studied helped with symptoms, and they were similar to or better than estrogen or placebo, with only a small rise in side effects. There was not enough evidence to say which non-estrogen option works best compared with the others.
keyPoints: Vaginal DHEA, ospemifene, erbium and CO2 lasers, polycarbophil-based vaginal moisturizer, tibolone, hyaluronic acid and testosterone all improved signs of vaginal atrophy.
Vaginal DHEA, ospemifene, tibolone, fractional CO2 laser, polycarbophil-based moisturizer and testosterone also improved sexual function.
Non-estrogen options were similar or better than estrogen or placebo, with minimal increase in side effects.
There were not enough data to compare the non-estrogen options with each other.

items.title: Injection Treatments for Vulvovaginal Atrophy of Menopause: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at injection treatments (such as platelet-rich plasma and hyaluronic acid) for vaginal dryness and related symptoms after menopause. It found eight small studies with 236 women in total, mostly observational. Most of the treatments were linked to symptom improvement on questionnaires, but the authors say the data are still poor and more studies are needed.
keyPoints: Eight studies with 236 women were included; only one was a randomized trial and seven were observational.
All injection types tested except micro-fragmented adipose tissue (MFAT) seemed to improve symptoms on validated questionnaires.
Treatments that showed improvement included hyaluronic acid products, platelet-rich plasma (PRP) alone or with hyaluronic acid, and microfat/nanofat grafting with PRP.
The authors conclude that further studies are necessary.

items.title: Treatment of urge incontinence in postmenopausal women: A systematic review
items.summary: This review pooled 35 randomized trials on treatments for urge incontinence (sudden, strong urges to pass urine with leaks) in women after menopause. Systemic (whole-body) estrogen did not help bladder leaks and was linked to lower odds of improvement compared with placebo. Local (vaginal) estrogen helped vaginal symptoms but mostly did not improve urinary symptoms. The authors conclude that good evidence for effective treatment is still lacking.
keyPoints: Systemic estrogen was linked to lower odds of improving incontinence than placebo (OR 0.74).
Local estrogen mostly did not improve urinary symptoms, though it helped vaginal symptoms.
Oxybutynin (an anticholinergic) worked better than placebo in one trial; adding local estrogen did not add benefit over anticholinergics alone.
Vitamin D, phytoestrogens and estrogen modulators were not effective or gave contradictory results; physical therapy looked positive but needs better trials.

items.title: Safety and Serum Estradiol Levels in Hormonal Treatments for Vulvovaginal Atrophy in Breast Cancer Survivors: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 17 studies on hormone-based treatments for vaginal dryness and related menopause symptoms in women who have had breast cancer. Low-dose vaginal estrogen caused the smallest changes in blood estradiol levels and had the most research behind it. Even so, its safety is still unclear, especially for women taking aromatase inhibitors. Other options such as vaginal testosterone, DHEA (prasterone) and ospemifene had less data.
keyPoints: Women treated with vaginal estriol or estradiol had an average rise in blood estradiol of 7.67 pg/mL.
Vaginal testosterone caused temporary peaks in blood estradiol, and one study found levels stayed above the normal postmenopausal range.
One study of DHEA (prasterone) found no rise in blood estradiol, and one study of ospemifene found no increase in breast cancer recurrence risk, but both need more data.
Because of cancer recurrence concerns, the authors suggest aiming for the lowest possible hormone concentration.

items.title: Vaginal laser therapy for genitourinary syndrome of menopause - systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 64 studies on vaginal laser treatment for genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), which includes vaginal dryness and related urinary and sexual symptoms. Scores for symptoms, sexual function and vaginal health seemed to improve in the short term. However, most studies had no comparison group, safety was poorly reported, and the authors say better trials are needed.
keyPoints: Vaginal laser seems to improve symptom, sexual function and vaginal health scores in the short term.
Only 10 of the 64 studies were controlled trials; 47 were before-after studies with no control group.
Safety results were underreported and only covered the short term.
The authors call for well-designed trials with sham-laser control groups before the benefit can be confirmed.

items.title: CO2-Laser therapy and Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 25 studies (1,152 women) looking at CO2 laser treatment for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which includes vaginal dryness, painful sex, itching, burning and pain when passing urine. All the studies reported symptom improvement, and no major side effects were reported. However, the studies were quite different from each other, most were single-centre and not randomised, and the authors rate the overall quality of the evidence as low or very low.
keyPoints: All 25 studies reported a significant reduction in symptoms such as dryness, painful sex, itching, burning and pain when passing urine.
Sexual function scores improved in all 8 studies that measured them, but the improvement was large enough to be clinically meaningful in only 2 of them.
No major adverse events were reported, and the authors describe CO2 laser as a safe option for postmenopausal women.
The quality of the evidence is rated low or very low because the studies varied a lot and most were not randomised.

items.title: Efficacy of Hormonal and Nonhormonal Approaches to Vaginal Atrophy and Sexual Dysfunctions in Postmenopausal Women: A Systematic Review
items.source: Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia E Obstetricia
items.journal: Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia E Obstetricia
items.summary: This review looked at 55 randomized trials of treatments for vaginal dryness (atrophy) and sexual problems after menopause. The treatments included lubricants and moisturizers, plant estrogens, DHEA, ospemifene, vaginal testosterone, pelvic floor exercises and others. The studies used many different treatments and ways of measuring results, so the findings are hard to compare. Most of the trials were judged to have a low risk of bias.
keyPoints: 55 randomized trials were included, covering hormonal and non-hormonal approaches.
Lubricants and moisturizers (18 studies) and phytoestrogens (14 studies) were the most studied options.
Other options studied were DHEA, ospemifene, vaginal testosterone, pelvic floor exercises, oxytocin, vaginal CO2 laser, lidocaine and vitamin E suppositories.
The research was inconsistent in treatments and outcome measures, though most trials had a low risk of bias.

items.title: Vaginal Rejuvenation: A Retrospective Review of Lasers and Radiofrequency Devices
items.summary: This review looked at 59 studies covering 3,609 women who had laser or radiofrequency treatment for vaginal laxity or menopause-related vaginal dryness and thinning. The studies reported better symptoms and sexual function, high satisfaction, and only minor side effects such as pain, swelling or discharge. The authors say more research is still needed on which conditions these treatments suit, whether repeat treatments are required, and long-term safety.
keyPoints: Across 59 studies (3,609 women), laser and radiofrequency treatments were linked to improved symptoms of genitourinary syndrome of menopause and vulvovaginal atrophy.
Sexual function improved and patient satisfaction was high in the reported studies.
Side effects were minor, including pain, swelling or vaginal discharge linked to treatment.
More research is needed on which conditions can be treated, whether maintenance treatment is needed, and long-term safety.

items.title: Hyaluronic Acid in Postmenopause Vaginal Atrophy: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at whether hyaluronic acid, a non-hormonal vaginal gel, helps with vaginal atrophy (thinning and dryness of the vagina) after menopause. It pulled together 5 small studies with 335 women in total, comparing the gel with vaginal estrogen. The gel did not appear to work differently from estrogen for tissue thinning, vaginal pH, painful sex or cell maturation. The studies measured results in different ways, so the numbers could not be combined, and the findings should be read with that in mind.
keyPoints: Hyaluronic acid showed no significant difference from vaginal estrogen for epithelial atrophy, vaginal pH, painful sex and cell maturation.
The authors suggest it has comparable effectiveness, safety and tolerability to vaginal estrogen for vaginal atrophy symptoms.
It may be a possible alternative for women who cannot use hormonal treatment.
The studies were few and measured outcomes differently, so a meta-analysis was not possible.

items.title: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause: a systematic review on prevalence and treatment
items.summary: This review pulled together 27 studies on genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), which covers symptoms like vaginal dryness, irritation, itching and painful sex after menopause. These symptoms were very common, affecting between 13% and 87% of women across studies. Many women did not know the cause or the treatment options, and most who had tried treatments were not satisfied with them.
keyPoints: Symptoms such as vaginal dryness, irritation, itching and painful sex affected 13% to 87% of women in the studies.
Over-the-counter lubricants and moisturizers were the most used treatments, followed by low-dose vaginal estrogen.
Vaginal health is not often discussed at doctor visits, and many women are unaware of GSM or its treatments.
Many women worry about the long-term safety and side effects of hormonal treatment, and most were dissatisfied with the treatment they had used.

items.title: Joint recommendations for the diagnosis and treatment of vulvo-vaginal atrophy in women in the peri- and post-menopausal phases from the Società Italiana per la Menopausa (SIM) and the Società Italiana della Terza Età (SIGiTE)
items.summary: Two Italian menopause societies published joint guidance on vulvo-vaginal atrophy (VVA), the thinning and dryness of vaginal tissue that can happen around and after menopause. The guidance says VVA is very common after menopause, yet most women who have it are not treated well. Diagnosis is simple and mostly based on a clinical check-up. Many treatments exist, and the guidance encourages open conversation between women and their doctors.
keyPoints: VVA is very common in postmenopausal women, and most women with it are not adequately treated.
Diagnosis is simple and largely clinical.
Treatment options range from preventive education and local non-hormonal therapies to local hormone-receptor agents, systemic therapy, laser and radiofrequency.
Better communication between doctor and patient is encouraged, because VVA is hard to talk about and treatment can improve quality of life for the woman and her partner.

items.title: A systematic review of intravaginal testosterone for the treatment of vulvovaginal atrophy
items.summary: This review looked at six small clinical trials of testosterone placed inside the vagina to treat vaginal dryness and thinning (vulvovaginal atrophy), including in women taking aromatase inhibitor medicines. The studies hint that it may lower vaginal pH and improve the balance of healthy vaginal bacteria. But the trials were small and short, and most had no placebo group, so the effect on sexual function and the long-term safety remain unclear. The authors say larger, well-designed trials are needed.
keyPoints: Six small trials (10 to 80 participants, lasting up to 12 weeks) were found; only one was double-blind.
Intravaginal testosterone may lower vaginal pH and increase protective lactobacilli bacteria, and possibly improve vaginal cell health.
Effect on sexual function is uncertain because most studies had no placebo and did not account for baseline differences.
Safety is uncertain because few women were studied, studies were short, and hormone-level reporting was incomplete.

items.title: Local oestrogen for vaginal atrophy in postmenopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 30 trials (6,235 postmenopausal women) of oestrogen put directly into the vagina as a ring, cream or tablet to treat vaginal atrophy, which causes dryness, itching and painful sex. The different forms worked about equally well when compared with each other. Compared with placebo (a dummy treatment), the oestrogen treatments improved symptoms, though the evidence was mostly low quality.
keyPoints: No clear difference in symptom relief was found between oestrogen ring, cream and tablets.
Vaginal oestrogen improved symptoms of vaginal atrophy more than placebo, based on low-quality evidence.
Oestrogen cream may be linked to a thickening of the womb lining compared with the ring, possibly because higher doses of cream were used.
Overall side effects did not clearly differ between the oestrogen forms or compared with placebo.

items.title: Gestational diabetes mellitus and adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes in twin and singleton pregnancies: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to compare pregnancies with and without gestational diabetes, in both single-baby (singleton) and twin pregnancies. In both groups, gestational diabetes was linked to higher chances of problems such as high blood pressure in pregnancy, caesarean birth, preterm birth, very large babies and newborn intensive care admission. The effects looked milder in twin pregnancies for some outcomes, and neonatal death was lower in twin pregnancies with gestational diabetes. These are links seen in observational studies, not proof of cause.
keyPoints: In singleton pregnancies, gestational diabetes was linked to higher risks of hypertensive disorders (RR 1.85), caesarean delivery (RR 1.31), preterm birth (RR 1.36) and neonatal intensive care admission (RR 1.43).

In twin pregnancies, gestational diabetes was also linked to higher risks of hypertensive disorders (RR 1.69), caesarean delivery (RR 1.10), preterm birth (RR 1.19) and neonatal intensive care admission (RR 1.20).
Twin pregnancies with gestational diabetes had a lower risk of small-for-gestational-age babies and of neonatal death compared with twin pregnancies without it.

Twin pregnancies had a lower relative risk than singletons for caesarean delivery, neonatal intensive care admission, stillbirth and neonatal death, so gestational diabetes may have a milder effect in twins.

items.title: Prevalence of gestational diabetes mellitus in Pakistan: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from nine studies of about 27,000 pregnant women across Pakistan to estimate how common gestational diabetes is. About 1 in 6 women (16.7%) were found to have it, though rates differed a lot by region and by which test and criteria were used. The authors note that many studies reported poorly and disagreed with each other, so the exact figures are uncertain.
keyPoints: The overall pooled rate of gestational diabetes in Pakistan was 16.7% (95% CI 13.1 to 21.1).
Rates varied by region, from 35.8% in Balochistan to 11.4% in Punjab.
Different diagnostic criteria and cut-off values gave different rates, with some criteria showing rates above 25%.
The authors call for agreement on recommended screening methods and ongoing training for doctors to help detect and treat it in time.

items.title: Induction of labour at or near term for suspected fetal macrosomia
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at four trials (1190 women) comparing induction of labour at or near term with waiting for labour to start, when a baby was thought to be very large (over 4000 g). Induction did not clearly change the chance of caesarean birth or instrumental delivery. It did lower the chance of shoulder dystocia and of broken bones in the baby, and babies were born a little smaller on average. The authors suggest the pros and cons of induction be discussed with parents.
keyPoints: Induction did not clearly change the risk of caesarean section or instrumental (forceps or vacuum) delivery.
Shoulder dystocia and birth fractures were less common with induction; about 60 inductions would be needed to prevent one fracture.
Scan estimates of baby weight are often inaccurate, so many women may worry unnecessarily and many inductions may not be needed.
One large trial saw more use of phototherapy for newborns after induction, and the trials were too small to show an effect on the rare nerve injury called brachial plexus injury.
