items.title: Smoking during pregnancy and gestational diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from 35 studies covering almost 24 million pregnant women to see whether smoking during pregnancy raises the chance of gestational diabetes. Overall, smoking was not linked to a higher risk of gestational diabetes. The studies differed a lot in how they diagnosed gestational diabetes, which makes the picture less clear.
keyPoints: Across 35 studies, smoking during pregnancy was not clearly linked to gestational diabetes (pooled odds ratio 1.06, not statistically significant).
A smaller group of studies using the same two-step diagnostic method also showed no clear link.
The studies varied a great deal, partly because gestational diabetes is diagnosed in different ways.
The authors say agreed diagnostic criteria are needed to better understand any link between smoking and gestational diabetes.

items.title: The Effects of Exercise during Pregnancy on Gestational Diabetes Mellitus, Preeclampsia, and Spontaneous Abortion among Healthy Women-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of exercise during pregnancy in healthy women. Exercise lowered the risk of gestational diabetes, and the type, intensity and supervision of exercise did not seem to matter. Overall, exercise did not clearly lower the risk of pre-eclampsia, though mind-body exercise and low-intensity exercise looked helpful in smaller subgroup checks. Exercise did not increase adverse events, but the authors say more high-quality studies are needed on pre-eclampsia.
keyPoints: Across 18 trials, exercise compared with no exercise was linked to about a one-third lower risk of gestational diabetes (RR 0.66).
Any type or intensity of exercise seemed equally effective for gestational diabetes prevention.
Across nine trials, exercise did not clearly reduce pre-eclampsia (RR 0.65, range 0.42 to 1.03), but mind-body and low-intensity exercise looked beneficial in subgroup analyses.
No effect of exercise on withdrawal from studies or adverse events was found, and the authors conclude exercise in pregnancy is beneficial and safe; no studies reported on spontaneous abortion.

items.title: Different intensities of glycaemic control for women with gestational diabetes mellitus
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at four trials (1731 women) comparing tighter versus less-tight blood sugar targets for women with gestational diabetes. Tighter targets may slightly raise the chance of high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy, but the result was uncertain and could point either way. Tighter control probably made little to no difference to caesarean rates, induction of labour, or babies being born large. The evidence was low to moderate quality, and the review says more good-quality trials are needed.
keyPoints: Tighter blood sugar targets may increase hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (low certainty), but the range of possible effects includes both benefit and harm.
Caesarean section, induction of labour, large-for-gestational-age babies and newborn low blood sugar were likely similar between tighter and less-tight control (moderate certainty).
Women on tighter targets were more likely to need medication and less likely to stick with treatment.
Current international target recommendations vary widely and rely on expert consensus rather than strong trial evidence.

items.title: Prevalence and Risk Factors of Postpartum Depression in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 27 studies including more than 133,000 women to estimate how common postpartum depression is and what raises the risk. About 14 in 100 women were affected, with rates ranging from about 5% to 26% depending on the country. Having gestational diabetes, depression in pregnancy, or a past history of depression was linked to a higher chance of postpartum depression. The authors note that high-quality reviews on this topic are limited, and results varied a lot between studies.
keyPoints: Pooled prevalence of postpartum depression was 14.0% across all studies, and it varied by country from 5.0% to 26.32%.
Gestational diabetes, depression during pregnancy, and a history of depression were linked to higher risk.
Having a baby boy was also linked to higher risk, though the abstract does not explain why.
Knowing these risk factors may help healthcare staff screen for and support women with postpartum depression.

items.title: IDF Diabetes Atlas: Estimation of Global and Regional Gestational Diabetes Mellitus Prevalence for 2021 by International Association of Diabetes in Pregnancy Study Group's Criteria
items.summary: This large review pooled results from 57 studies to estimate how common gestational diabetes (diabetes first found during pregnancy) is around the world, using one standard set of diagnostic criteria so the numbers can be compared. About 14% of pregnancies worldwide were estimated to be affected. Rates differed a lot by region, from about 7% in North America and Europe to nearly 28% in the Middle East and North Africa.
keyPoints: The estimated global prevalence of gestational diabetes was 14.0% when studies were standardized to IADPSG criteria.
The highest rates were in the Middle East and North Africa (27.6%) and South-East Asia (20.8%).
The lowest rates were in North America and the Caribbean (7.1%) and Europe (7.8%).
Among country income groups, high-income countries had the highest standardized prevalence (14.2%).

items.title: Gestational diabetes mellitus and adverse pregnancy outcomes: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pulled together 156 studies covering more than 7.5 million pregnancies to see how gestational diabetes relates to problems in pregnancy and for babies. After accounting for other factors, gestational diabetes was linked to higher chances of caesarean birth, preterm birth, larger babies and some newborn complications. For several other outcomes, such as stillbirth and shoulder dystocia, no clear difference was found. Only about a third of the studies had a low or medium risk of bias, and results varied between studies.
keyPoints: In studies where no insulin was used, gestational diabetes was linked to higher odds of caesarean section, preterm delivery, macrosomia (a very large baby) and a baby born large for gestational age.

In studies where insulin was used, gestational diabetes was linked to higher odds of a large-for-gestational-age baby, neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, newborn jaundice and neonatal intensive care admission.
No clear difference was found for stillbirth, neonatal death, shoulder dystocia, postpartum haemorrhage or instrumental delivery.
Differences between countries, screening methods and whether body mass index was adjusted for explained some of the variation between studies.

items.title: Prevalence of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus in Nepal: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Nepal Health Research Council
items.journal: Journal of Nepal Health Research Council
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 9 studies in Nepal, covering about 20,865 pregnant women, to estimate how common gestational diabetes is. Overall, about 2.6 in every 100 women were found to have it, but the figure changed depending on which test criteria were used. The authors conclude that gestational diabetes is becoming more common in Nepal and that larger local studies are needed.
keyPoints: Pooled prevalence of gestational diabetes in Nepal was 2.61% across 9 studies.
The rate varied by diagnostic criteria, from about 1.1% (Carpenter and Coustan) to 6.6% (IADPSG).
Prevalence appeared higher in studies published in or after 2015 than before 2015.
The authors call for larger local studies to measure the true burden, risk factors and ways to prevent it.

items.title: Probiotics for preventing gestational diabetes
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled seven trials with 1647 pregnant women to see whether probiotic supplements prevent gestational diabetes. It is unclear whether probiotics change the risk of gestational diabetes, because the evidence was low quality. However, probiotics were linked to a higher risk of pre-eclampsia, and the review authors urge caution about using them in pregnancy.
keyPoints: It is uncertain whether probiotics lower the risk of gestational diabetes compared with placebo (low-certainty evidence).
Probiotics increased the risk of pre-eclampsia compared with placebo (high-certainty evidence).
Probiotics made little to no difference to the chance of caesarean birth (high-certainty evidence).
The authors urge caution in using probiotics during pregnancy given the possible harm and little observed benefit.

items.title: Screening for Gestational Diabetes: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence on screening for gestational diabetes, which is diabetes that develops during pregnancy. It recommends screening pregnant people without symptoms at 24 weeks of pregnancy or later, because this is moderately beneficial for the health of both mother and baby. There is not enough evidence to say whether screening before 24 weeks does more good than harm.
keyPoints: Screening for gestational diabetes is recommended at 24 weeks of pregnancy or later for people without symptoms (a B recommendation).
The Task Force has moderate certainty that screening at this stage gives a moderate net benefit for mothers and babies.
Gestational diabetes raises the risk of problems such as preeclampsia, a larger-than-average baby (macrosomia) and low blood sugar in newborns.
The evidence is not enough to judge the benefits and harms of screening before 24 weeks (an I statement).

items.title: The 2019 Flemish consensus on screening for overt diabetes in early pregnancy and screening for gestational diabetes mellitus
items.summary: This is a 2019 consensus statement from several Flemish (Belgian) medical groups on how to screen for diabetes in pregnancy. It recommends checking for existing diabetes at the start of pregnancy, ideally with a fasting blood glucose test. Gestational diabetes is then screened for at about 24 weeks, with a one-step or two-step approach depending on a woman's situation. Women who had gestational diabetes should also be checked for blood sugar problems after the birth.
keyPoints: All women should be screened for existing (overt) diabetes when planning pregnancy or at the first prenatal visit, preferably with a fasting blood glucose test.

Women with impaired fasting glucose, women with obesity and normal glucose, and women who had gestational diabetes before are advised lifestyle counselling and a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 weeks.
All other women are advised a two-step approach at 24 weeks: a 50 g glucose challenge test, followed by a 75 g glucose tolerance test if the 1-hour result is 130 mg/dl or higher.
Every woman who had gestational diabetes should be offered screening after pregnancy for later blood sugar problems.

items.title: Macrosomia: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 216
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists looks at babies who are expected to be born very large (macrosomia). It explains that as birth weight goes up, the chances of a difficult labor, shoulder dystocia (a baby's shoulder getting stuck), birth injury and lasting harm to the newborn also go up. It also covers how accurate the methods for estimating a baby's weight are, what their limits are, and how care can be managed when a large baby is suspected. It has been updated with newer research, including on preventing macrosomia.
keyPoints: The larger the baby's birth weight, the higher the chance of labor problems, shoulder dystocia, birth trauma and permanent injury to the newborn.
Methods for estimating a baby's weight before birth have limits in how accurate they are.
The guideline suggests how to manage a pregnancy when a very large baby is suspected.
It has been updated with recent research on preventing macrosomia.

items.title: Maternal Race/Ethnicity and Postpartum Diabetes Screening: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 27 U.S. studies covering about 96,000 women who had gestational diabetes. It looked at how many were screened for diabetes after giving birth, and whether this differed by race and ethnicity. Fewer than half were screened (about 42%). Screening was lowest among white and black women and higher among Hispanic and Asian women, though studies varied a lot in how they measured and reported this.
keyPoints: About half of women with gestational diabetes may go on to develop type 2 diabetes, with the highest risk among black women.
Only about 42% of women with gestational diabetes had diabetes screening after pregnancy.
Pooled screening rates were about 35% for white, 33% for black, 45% for Hispanic and 50% for Asian women.
Programs to improve screening were most common and most effective among Hispanic women.

items.title: Maternal Arsenic Exposure and Gestational Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from nine studies to see whether exposure to arsenic, a natural and industrial contaminant, is linked to gestational diabetes. Overall, women with higher arsenic exposure had about 1.56 times the risk of developing gestational diabetes. The studies differed quite a bit from one another, so the authors say the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Pooled results from nine studies (1,984 gestational diabetes cases) showed higher arsenic exposure linked to about 1.56 times the risk of gestational diabetes.
The link was confirmed in studies that measured arsenic in urine.
Risk estimates varied by region and by the criteria used to diagnose gestational diabetes.
The authors describe this as a possible association and say the data need careful interpretation because the studies differed.

items.title: Polyphenol-rich foods and risk of gestational diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 12 studies, covering nearly 125,000 women, to see whether eating foods rich in polyphenols (plant compounds found in things like fruit, vegetables, tea and coffee) is linked to gestational diabetes. Results for individual polyphenol-rich foods were mixed: some studies found lower risk, some found no link, and two found higher risk. Women who followed a Mediterranean-style diet most closely had about half the risk of gestational diabetes compared with those who followed it least. These were observational studies, so they show a link rather than proving cause.
keyPoints: Across 12 studies, results for individual polyphenol-rich foods were inconsistent: 5 found lower risk, 5 found no link, and 2 found higher risk.
Women with the highest Mediterranean diet scores had about half the risk of gestational diabetes compared with those with the lowest scores.
The authors suggest that overall dietary patterns rich in polyphenols may reduce gestational diabetes risk, though evidence for specific food groups is inconclusive.
Included studies were observational (mostly cohort studies), so they cannot prove that diet causes the difference.

items.title: Fetal biometry for guiding the medical management of women with gestational diabetes mellitus for improving maternal and perinatal health
items.summary: This review looked at whether using ultrasound scans of the baby's size, on top of mum's blood sugar readings, helps decide how closely to treat gestational diabetes. It found three trials with 524 women. For caesarean birth and newborn low blood sugar, the scans may make little or no difference, but the evidence was low or very low quality. The authors say there is not enough evidence to know whether this approach helps mothers or babies.
keyPoints: Three trials (524 women) compared ultrasound of baby's size plus blood sugar levels with blood sugar levels alone.
Adding ultrasound may make little or no difference to caesarean birth or newborn low blood sugar (low-certainty evidence).
Results for large-for-gestational-age babies, shoulder dystocia and perinatal death were unclear (very low-certainty evidence).
There is insufficient evidence to judge this approach, and larger trials are needed.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 190 Summary: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
items.summary: This is a summary of a practice guideline from ACOG, an organisation of obstetricians and gynaecologists, on gestational diabetes. It gives a brief overview of what is known about the condition and reviews management approaches backed by well-conducted research. It also points out areas where knowledge is still lacking and more research is needed. The abstract notes that debate continues about how best to diagnose and treat gestational diabetes.
keyPoints: Gestational diabetes is one of the most common medical complications of pregnancy.
There is still debate about how to diagnose and treat it, even after several large recent studies.
The guideline reviews management approaches that have been validated by appropriately conducted clinical research.
It identifies gaps in current knowledge for future research to address.

items.title: Perioperative management of adult diabetic patients. Specific situations
items.summary: This French guideline covers how to manage diabetes around surgery and childbirth. For women with gestational diabetes (high blood sugar first found in pregnancy), it says blood sugar should be kept in a set range during labour using an insulin drip together with a glucose drip. After delivery, insulin is stopped, and diabetes medicine is only needed again if blood sugar stays high.
keyPoints: Gestational diabetes is defined as glucose intolerance discovered during pregnancy, and is treated differently from diabetes that existed before pregnancy.
During labour, blood sugar should be kept between 0.8 and 1.4 g/L (4.4-8.25 mmol/L), using a continuous insulin infusion together with a glucose infusion.
After delivery, insulin therapy is stopped in gestational diabetes.
Diabetes treatment is needed again if blood sugar stays above 1.26 g/L (7 mmol/L) after birth.

items.title: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus and Diet: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials Examining the Impact of Modified Dietary Interventions on Maternal Glucose Control and Neonatal Birth Weight
items.summary: This review pooled 18 trials with 1,151 women who had gestational diabetes to see whether changing the type of diet helps. Women on modified diets had slightly bigger drops in blood sugar, were less likely to need medicine, and had babies with slightly lower birth weight and less macrosomia (a very large baby). The quality of the evidence was low to very low, and the studies were small, so the results are uncertain.
keyPoints: Modified diets were linked to larger falls in fasting and after-meal blood sugar than usual diets.
Women on modified diets were less likely to need medication (relative risk 0.65).
Babies were on average about 170 g lighter, and large-baby births (macrosomia) were less common.
The authors say evidence quality was low to very low and the studies were small, but there may be room to improve usual dietary advice.

items.title: Oral anti-diabetic pharmacological therapies for the treatment of women with gestational diabetes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 11 trials (1487 women) of diabetes pills used to treat gestational diabetes, including glibenclamide, metformin and acarbose. For most outcomes, such as caesarean birth, high blood pressure in pregnancy and babies being large for their age, no clear difference was found between the pills and placebo or between the different pills. The evidence was mostly low or very low quality, and many important outcomes were not reported, so the authors could not say whether one pill is better than another.
keyPoints: There was not enough data comparing diabetes pills with placebo or standard care (lifestyle advice) to guide practice.
Metformin and glibenclamide showed no clear differences for caesarean birth, high blood pressure in pregnancy, induction of labour or large babies.
One small study found metformin linked to fewer cases of baby death or serious illness than glibenclamide, based on low-quality evidence.
Choice of pill currently seems to depend on clinical preference, availability and national guidelines; more research is needed.

items.title: Exercise for pregnant women with gestational diabetes for improving maternal and fetal outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 11 trials with 638 women who had gestational diabetes, comparing exercise with usual care. Women who exercised had lower blood sugar both when fasting and after meals. There was no clear difference in caesarean birth, pre-eclampsia, induction of labour or the baby's health outcomes, but many trials were small and the evidence was mixed in quality, so firm conclusions on benefits for babies could not be made.
keyPoints: Exercise was linked to lower fasting blood sugar and lower blood sugar after meals in women with gestational diabetes.
No clear difference was found for caesarean birth, pre-eclampsia, induction of labour or maternal BMI after birth.
No clear difference was found for baby outcomes such as death or illness combined, or low newborn blood sugar, but the data were limited.
Many important outcomes, such as perineal tearing, postnatal depression and later type 2 diabetes, were not reported in the trials.

items.title: Treatments for gestational diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 42 trials of treatments for gestational diabetes (diabetes first found in pregnancy). Packages of care, meaning diet and lifestyle changes plus medicine when needed, lowered the risk of most problems for babies compared with routine care. In indirect comparisons of medicines, metformin looked most likely to work best, but the trials were small, poorly reported and at unclear or high risk of bias, so firm conclusions are hard.
keyPoints: Packages of care (diet, lifestyle and medicine when needed) reduced the risk of most poor outcomes for babies compared with routine care.
Babies were less likely to be large for their gestational age with these packages (relative risk 0.58 across 8 trials and 3462 women).
Metformin had the highest chance of being the most effective medicine compared with insulin or glibenclamide, based on indirect comparisons.
The trials often included few women, were poorly reported and measured few outcomes, so large, well-run trials are urgently needed.

items.title: Different strategies for diagnosing gestational diabetes to improve maternal and infant health
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at seven small trials (1,420 women) comparing different ways of testing for gestational diabetes in pregnancy. The tests, glucose amounts and diagnosis criteria used changed which women were diagnosed, and some drink or food options caused fewer side effects such as nausea. The authors found there is not enough evidence to say which testing strategy is best, and no trial reported on costs.
keyPoints: Different tests and criteria lead to different numbers of women being diagnosed with gestational diabetes.
A two-step approach diagnosed fewer women at 11 to 14 weeks than a one-step approach in one trial of 726 women.
Glucose polymer drinks and glucose in food caused fewer side effects, such as nausea, than glucose monomer drinks or glucose drinks in small trials.
There is insufficient evidence to say which diagnosis strategy is best, and large trials are needed.

items.title: Oral anti-diabetic agents for women with established diabetes/impaired glucose tolerance or previous gestational diabetes planning pregnancy, or pregnant women with pre-existing diabetes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether diabetes tablets, rather than insulin, could be used by women with diabetes who are planning a pregnancy or are already pregnant. Only three small trials (241 women, all with type 2 diabetes) had usable data, and all compared metformin with insulin. Metformin may mean fewer caesarean births, less pregnancy-related high blood pressure and less low blood sugar in newborns. However, the evidence was low or very low quality, so there is not enough data to be sure.
keyPoints: Women taking metformin may be less likely to have a caesarean section than those taking insulin (low-quality evidence).
Pregnancy-induced high blood pressure and newborn low blood sugar may be lower with metformin, but this came from very few trials and the evidence was low or very low quality.
No clear difference was found for pre-eclampsia, induction of labour or babies who were large for their gestational age.
The authors conclude there is not enough trial data and that better-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Different methods and settings for glucose monitoring for gestational diabetes during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 11 trials with 1,272 women who have gestational diabetes, comparing different ways and places to check blood glucose (such as telemedicine, self-testing at home, continuous monitors, and testing before or after meals). For most outcomes for mothers and babies, there were no clear differences between the methods. One small trial found fewer large babies when glucose was checked after meals rather than before meals. The evidence was mostly low or very low quality, so more and better research is needed.
keyPoints: No clear differences were found between telemedicine and standard care, self-monitoring and periodic monitoring, or continuous monitoring and self-monitoring for outcomes like caesarean birth or newborn low blood sugar.
One small trial (66 women) found fewer large-for-gestational-age babies with after-meal glucose checks than with before-meal checks.
The trials were small and of variable quality, and the evidence was mostly low or very low certainty.
More research is needed on how different monitoring methods affect mothers, children and health care use and costs.

items.title: Insulin for the treatment of women with gestational diabetes
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 53 trials (7381 women) to see how insulin compares with oral diabetes medicines for treating gestational diabetes when diet and lifestyle changes are not enough. Insulin and oral medicines had similar effects on most key outcomes for mothers and babies. Women treated with insulin had more hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, but pre-eclampsia and caesarean birth rates were not clearly different. The evidence ranged from very low to moderate quality, and long-term outcomes were poorly reported.
keyPoints: Insulin and oral anti-diabetic medicines had similar effects on key health outcomes for mothers and babies.
Insulin was linked to a higher risk of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (moderate-quality evidence), but no clear difference in pre-eclampsia, caesarean birth or later type 2 diabetes.
No clear differences were found for babies born large, newborn low blood sugar, or later childhood adiposity and neurosensory outcomes.
The choice of treatment may come down to doctor or maternal preference, availability or how severe the gestational diabetes is.

items.title: Hyperglycemia and adverse pregnancy outcomes
items.summary: This large study followed about 25,500 pregnant women from nine countries who had a glucose drink test at 24 to 32 weeks of pregnancy. It looked at whether blood sugar levels lower than those that count as diabetes were still linked to problems for mothers and babies. Higher blood sugar was linked to larger babies and higher insulin-related markers in cord blood, and the risk rose steadily with no clear cut-off point.
keyPoints: Higher blood sugar in pregnancy, even below the level of diabetes, was linked to a higher chance of a baby with a birth weight above the 90th percentile.
Higher blood sugar was also linked to higher cord-blood C-peptide levels (a sign of the baby making extra insulin).
Links with caesarean delivery and newborn low blood sugar were weaker, and the same pattern was seen for other outcomes like early birth, shoulder dystocia and preeclampsia.
The researchers found no obvious blood sugar threshold where risks suddenly increased.

items.title: Creatine and Cognition in Aging: A Systematic Review of Evidence in Older Adults
items.summary: This review looked at whether creatine, a popular dietary supplement, is linked to better thinking skills in people aged 55 and over. It found only six studies, and five of them reported a positive link, especially for memory and attention. Most of the studies were small or of fair to poor quality, so the evidence is limited and more high-quality trials are needed.
keyPoints: Six studies with 1542 participants (55.7% women) were included, mostly healthy older adults living at home.
Five of the six studies found a positive link between creatine and thinking skills, particularly memory and attention.
Only two studies were double-blind supplement trials; four relied on people recalling what they ate.
Study quality was rated good for one study, fair for two and poor for three, so better trials are needed.

items.title: Creatine monohydrate for lean mass, strength, and bone density in postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
items.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
items.summary: This review pooled seven randomised trials (608 postmenopausal women, average age about 62) that compared creatine monohydrate with a placebo. Creatine gave small gains in lean (muscle) mass and leg strength, mainly when taken at 5 g a day or more alongside resistance training. Low doses without exercise showed no measurable effect, and bone density did not change overall. Side effects were mild and similar to placebo, and kidney measures were unchanged.
keyPoints: Lean mass rose by about 0.37 kg more with creatine than with placebo across five trials.
Leg-press strength improved by about 7.5 kg more with creatine across three trials.
Benefits showed up with 5 g a day or more combined with resistance training; 3 g a day or less without exercise showed no effect.
Bone density was unchanged overall, so effects on bone remain unclear, and side effects were mild and similar to placebo.

items.title: Resistance training improves cardiovascular health in postmenopausal women: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 60 studies of strength (resistance) training in women after menopause. Women who did resistance training for at least 4 weeks had small to moderate drops in resting heart rate and blood pressure. Heart rate variability and blood vessel function also improved modestly, and heart scans showed no harmful changes to the heart's structure.
keyPoints: Resistance training lowered resting heart rate and blood pressure in postmenopausal women.
The drop was moderate for systolic blood pressure and mean blood pressure, and small for heart rate and diastolic blood pressure.
Blood vessel function and heart rate variability improved modestly.
Heart scans showed no harmful changes to heart structure.

items.title: Effects and exercise-prescription moderators of Tai Chi on cardiometabolic risk factors in middle-aged and older women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 18 randomized trials of Tai Chi in women aged 45 and older. Tai Chi was linked to lower blood pressure and lower levels of 'bad' cholesterol (LDL), triglycerides and total cholesterol. It did not clearly change 'good' cholesterol (HDL) or fasting blood sugar. Results varied a lot between studies, so how well these findings apply elsewhere is uncertain.
keyPoints: Tai Chi was linked to lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure in middle-aged and older women.
It was also linked to lower LDL cholesterol, triglycerides and total cholesterol, but no clear effect on HDL cholesterol or fasting blood glucose.
Results differed a lot between studies, and the size of the benefit may vary in future settings.
The authors say certainty is limited and larger trials with standardized Tai Chi programmes are needed.

items.title: Home-based exercise in postmenopausal and older women: effects on body composition, physical function, cardiometabolic health, and quality of life-a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 19 trials with 1,128 postmenopausal and older women to see what exercising at home does for the body and mind. Home-based exercise lowered body mass index a little and improved quality of life. Effects on balance, walking, grip strength, body fat and blood fats were unclear. The authors say the evidence for quality of life was very low certainty and more well-designed trials are needed.
keyPoints: Home-based exercise lowered BMI by about 0.57 kg/m2 on average, with moderate certainty evidence.
Quality of life improved, but the certainty of this evidence was very low.
No clear effect was found on walking speed, chair-stand time, handgrip strength, body fat percentage or triglycerides.
Few trials were available for each outcome, so longer and better-standardised studies are needed.

items.title: Effect of different types of exercise on bone mineral density in postmenopausal women: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 49 studies with 3,360 postmenopausal women to compare which types of exercise best protect bone density. Exercise helped bone density overall. Combining aerobic exercise (like walking or cycling) with resistance training (like lifting weights) ranked best at the lower spine and the hip's femoral neck.
keyPoints: Exercise significantly helped bone mineral density in postmenopausal women.
Aerobic plus resistance exercise combined had the best effect, ranking highest at both the lumbar spine and femoral neck.
Aerobic exercise alone and resistance training alone also helped at the lumbar spine.
Whole body vibration and resistance training also showed benefit at the femoral neck.

items.title: Does exercising during peri- or early post-menopause prevent bone and muscle loss: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether exercise can prevent bone and muscle loss around the time of menopause. Only six trials were found, and all were low quality with a high risk of bias. Exercise did not clearly help during perimenopause, but strength training and walking seemed to help bone density in early post-menopause. Because the evidence is so limited, the review could not say which type of exercise works best.
keyPoints: Strength training, endurance training and Tai Chi did not improve bone density or lean mass during perimenopause.
In early post-menopause, strength training and walking improved bone density at several sites, and strength training improved bone density at all sites measured.
Not every strength training study showed a gain in lean (muscle) mass, and walking improved only total hip bone density.
Too few studies and too many different exercise programmes mean the best method remains unclear.

items.title: Effects of exercise on bone metabolism in postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 24 trials (1,067 postmenopausal women) to see how exercise affects blood markers of bone building and bone breakdown. Exercise raised markers linked to new bone formation and lowered markers linked to bone loss. The authors say more high-quality trials are needed to confirm these benefits.
keyPoints: Exercise increased bone-formation markers (ALP, P1NP and osteocalcin) and lowered bone-breakdown marker CTX and parathyroid hormone.
Aerobic exercise lowered CTX, while both aerobic and resistance exercise raised osteocalcin.
Programmes lasting 6 months or less and sessions of 60 minutes or less were particularly effective.
The authors note that more high-quality randomized trials are needed to confirm the findings.

items.title: Interventions for treating urinary incontinence in older women: a network meta-analysis
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 43 trials with 8506 women aged 60 and over who have urinary incontinence (leaking urine). Treatments that train the pelvic floor muscles, with or without education or complementary therapies, looked the most helpful for cure and improvement, with bladder medicines also showing some benefit. However, the evidence was very low to low certainty because trials were small and often had weaknesses, so no firm conclusion about the single best treatment can be drawn.
keyPoints: Physical therapies, mainly pelvic floor muscle training, performed best for 'cure' and for 'cure or improvement' of incontinence in older women.
Adding education or complementary therapies to physical therapy may help further, but this rested on very few studies.

Bladder medicines (β3-adrenergic agonists and antimuscarinic drugs) may also have improved symptoms compared with control, but the evidence is very uncertain, and some medicine trials reported serious side effects.
No serious adverse events were reported for conservative treatments, but the evidence was too limited to say whether any treatment is safer than another.

items.title: Effects of Combined Exercise and Calcium/Vitamin D Supplementation on Bone Mineral Density in Postmenopausal Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 13 randomised trials in postmenopausal women to see whether adding exercise to calcium and vitamin D supplements improves bone density more than supplements alone. Combining the two raised bone density in the lower spine and the neck of the thigh bone compared with supplements alone. Whole-body vibration and gentle mind-body exercises such as Baduanjin showed the clearest benefits, and shorter programmes (6 months or less) gave bigger gains than longer ones. The abstract does not state an overall certainty rating for the evidence.
keyPoints: Exercise plus calcium and vitamin D improved lower spine and femoral neck bone density more than calcium and vitamin D alone.
Whole-body vibration gave the greatest and most consistent benefit at both sites.
Mind-body or traditional Chinese exercises such as Baduanjin improved lower spine bone density.
Programmes of 6 months or less gave larger gains, and longer ones added no extra advantage.

items.title: Effect of resistance training volume on body adiposity, metabolic risk, and inflammation in postmenopausal and older females: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: Journal of Sport and Health Science
items.journal: Journal of Sport and Health Science
items.summary: This review pooled 20 randomized trials of strength (resistance) training in overweight or obese women after menopause and in older women. Both lower-volume and higher-volume training improved body fat, blood fats, blood sugar and a marker of inflammation compared with no training. Higher-volume training showed larger improvements in blood glucose and C-reactive protein (an inflammation marker). The quality of the evidence was low to very low, so the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Strength training improved body fat, metabolic risk markers and inflammation compared with no training in overweight/obese postmenopausal and older women.
Higher-volume training (about 77 sets per week) gave larger improvements in glucose and C-reactive protein than lower-volume training (about 44 sets per week).
The trials had some concerns about risk of bias, and the certainty of the evidence was low to very low.

items.title: Higher volume resistance training enhances whole-body muscle hypertrophy in postmenopausal and older females: A secondary analysis of systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
items.summary: This review combined 14 trials of weight-based strength training in women after menopause and older women. Both lower-volume and higher-volume programmes helped women build muscle compared with women who did not train. Higher-volume training gave a somewhat larger gain (about 1.3 kg versus 0.9 kg of muscle). The authors rate the overall evidence as low certainty, so these results are suggestive rather than firm.
keyPoints: Strength training added muscle in postmenopausal and older women compared with no training.
Higher-volume training built more muscle (about 1.3 kg) than lower-volume training (about 0.9 kg).
The effect size was moderate for higher-volume and small for lower-volume training.
The certainty of the evidence was rated low, and most trials had some concerns about risk of bias.

items.title: Effectiveness of exercise training on arterial stiffness and blood pressure among postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 22 randomised trials with 1,978 postmenopausal women who had raised blood pressure. Women who did exercise training had less stiff arteries and lower blood pressure than those who did not. The best type of exercise for this group is still unclear and needs more research.
keyPoints: Exercise training lowered systolic blood pressure by about 6 points and diastolic by about 3.5 points on average.
Exercise also reduced measures of artery stiffness, including pulse wave velocity and augmentation index.
Starting blood pressure level had a large effect on how much exercise helped.
The best mode of exercise for improving artery stiffness and blood pressure needs further study.

items.title: Efficacy of pelvic floor physiotherapy intervention for stress urinary incontinence in postmenopausal women: systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether pelvic floor physiotherapy helps postmenopausal women who leak urine when they cough, sneeze or exercise (stress urinary incontinence). It pulled together 6 randomized trials with 715 women. Physiotherapy helped in every study, but the treatments were so different that results could not be combined. The authors say it is not yet clear which type works best and that more trials are needed.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor physiotherapy was effective in all 6 trials included, with 715 women in total.
Treatments varied widely: pelvic floor muscle training, vaginal cones, biofeedback, electrical stimulation, radiofrequency and electroacupuncture.
Results could not be pooled because the interventions were so different.
There is no agreement yet on which physiotherapy approach is most effective after menopause.

items.title: Resistance training for postmenopausal women: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 small trials (452 women in total) looking at resistance (strength) training after menopause. Compared with no exercise, strength training of up to 16 weeks seemed to improve everyday physical function and bone density and to reduce hot flashes. No serious side effects were reported. The studies were small and had unclear to high risk of bias, so the evidence is low to very low certainty and better trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Compared with no exercise, resistance training seemed to improve functional capacity and bone mineral density and reduce hot flash frequency.
Compared with aerobic exercise, resistance training may reduce hot flash frequency and fat mass, with no clear difference in quality of life.
No serious adverse events were reported.
The certainty of the evidence was low to very low, so the effects are imprecisely estimated and higher-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Association of exercise, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and cognition among older women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 trials with 994 older women to see how structured exercise affects BDNF, a brain protein used as a stand-in marker for brain health. Exercise was linked to a moderate rise in BDNF levels. There was no clear improvement in a standard memory and thinking test (MMSE). The groups for each exercise type were small, so the results for individual types are uncertain.
keyPoints: Across all trials, exercise gave a moderate increase in BDNF levels in older women.
Aerobic, aquatic and multimodal exercise were each linked to higher BDNF, but sample sizes for each type were small.
The small change in MMSE thinking scores was not statistically significant.
About 10% of participants in the data were men, which the authors note as a limitation.

items.title: The effects of exercise training on body composition in postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 101 trials with about 5,700 postmenopausal women to see how exercise training affects body composition. Exercise increased muscle and lean mass and reduced body fat, waist size and belly (visceral) fat compared with no exercise. Aerobic exercise worked better for losing fat, and resistance (strength) exercise worked better for building muscle. Combining both types of exercise was also a good way to improve body composition.
keyPoints: Exercise training increased muscle mass and fat-free mass in postmenopausal women.
Exercise training reduced fat mass, body fat percentage, waist circumference and visceral fat.
Aerobic training was most helpful for fat loss, while resistance training was most helpful for muscle gain.
Combining aerobic and resistance training may be a useful way to improve body composition.

items.title: Effect of resistance training on lipid profile in postmenopausal women: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 19 randomised trials to see how strength (resistance) training affects blood fats in women after menopause. Strength training lowered total cholesterol, LDL ('bad') cholesterol and triglycerides. The effects were larger in women who already had high cholesterol or obesity, and in shorter programmes. The effect on HDL ('good') cholesterol was small and only seen in women with obesity.
keyPoints: Strength training lowered total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and triglycerides in postmenopausal women.
Effects were stronger in women with high cholesterol or obesity before the trials began.
Shorter programmes (under 16 weeks) showed bigger drops in total cholesterol and triglycerides.
The effect on HDL cholesterol was small and seen only in women with obesity.

items.title: Risk-Reducing Salpingo-Oophorectomy and the Use of Hormone Replacement Therapy Below the Age of Natural Menopause: Scientific Impact Paper No. 66 October 2021: Scientific Impact Paper No. 66
items.source: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
items.organisation: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
items.summary: This Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists paper looks at hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for women who have their ovaries and fallopian tubes removed to prevent ovarian cancer before the natural age of menopause. Removing the ovaries causes early menopause, which brings hot flushes, mood changes, bone thinning and a higher risk of heart disease. HRT is usually advisable up to about age 51 for women who have not had breast cancer. Research suggests HRT in early menopause does not raise breast cancer risk, including for BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers.
keyPoints: HRT is usually advisable up to about age 51 (the average UK age of menopause) for women in early menopause after preventative surgery who have not had breast cancer.
Women with a womb are given estrogen plus progestogen to protect the womb lining; women without a womb are given estrogen only.
Unlike in older women, HRT in early menopause does not appear to increase breast cancer risk, including in BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers after preventative surgery.
Non-hormonal medicines and behavioural therapy are options if HRT cannot be used, but they are less effective; regular exercise and a healthy lifestyle are also advised.

items.title: Effects of physical exercise on bone mineral density in older postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 53 trials with 2,896 women aged 60 and over after menopause to see how exercise affects bone density. Exercise training was linked to small increases in bone density at the neck of the thigh bone, the lower spine and the upper part of the thigh bone. There was no clear difference for total body or total hip bone density. The authors say longer-term studies are needed to confirm these findings.
keyPoints: Exercise training significantly increased bone density at the femoral neck, lumbar spine and trochanter in older postmenopausal women.
The average gains were small, about 0.01 g/cm2 at each of these sites.
There were no significant differences in total body or total hip bone density between exercise and control groups.
Longer-term studies are needed to confirm the results.

items.title: Effects of resistance training on C-reactive protein in menopausal and postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 12 randomized trials (482 women) to see whether strength (resistance) training helps menopausal and postmenopausal women. Women who did resistance training had lower levels of C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation, and better cholesterol (lipid) results than women in control groups. Waist size did not seem to change much. The evidence was rated very low quality, so the authors have little confidence in the results and say the true effect may be quite different.
keyPoints: Resistance training was linked to lower C-reactive protein (an inflammation marker) in postmenopausal women compared with controls.
Cholesterol (lipid) results also improved in the short to long term.
Resistance training may have little to no effect on waist circumference.
Safety data were scarce, and the authors call for better-designed trials.

items.title: Effect of Whey Protein Supplementation in Postmenopausal Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of whey protein supplements in women aged 55 and over. Whey protein helped build leg muscle and arm strength only when women were also doing resistance (strength) training. Without strength training, whey protein did not improve muscle strength or lean mass, and it did not change fat mass or body weight either way.
keyPoints: With resistance training, whey protein improved biceps curl strength and lower-leg lean muscle mass compared with placebo.
Without resistance training, whey protein showed no significant benefit for muscle strength or lean mass.
Whey protein did not significantly change fat mass or weight loss, with or without strength training.
Women taking whey protein without strength training ate less protein from their regular diet.

items.title: The impact of exercise training on endothelial function in postmenopausal women: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 35 studies on whether exercise training improves the health of blood vessel linings (endothelial function) in women after menopause. About two-thirds of the studies found improvement in at least one measure, and the overall effect was moderate. Results varied between studies, and the authors say differences in study designs, training types and participants make them hard to compare.
keyPoints: Two-thirds of studies showed a group-level improvement in at least one measure of blood vessel function after exercise training.
The review found a moderate effect of training on both larger and smaller blood vessel function.
Results were inconsistent; exercise intensity and duration, hormone therapy, clinical status and menopausal status may all play a part.
More research is needed to understand why people respond differently to training.

items.title: Effects of Multicomponent Exercise Training on the Health of Older Women with Osteoporosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review pulled together 14 randomized trials of exercise in older women with osteoporosis (average age about 68). The programs mixed two to four types of exercise, such as strength, aerobic, balance and flexibility work. On average they ran about 27 weeks, with around 2 to 3 sessions a week of about 45 minutes. The authors found improvements in strength, balance, flexibility, bone density, quality of life and everyday physical function, along with a lower risk of falls.
keyPoints: Mixed exercise programs (strength, aerobic, balance, flexibility) improved strength, balance and flexibility in older women with osteoporosis.
Bone mineral density, quality of life and functional fitness also improved.
The programs reduced the risk of falls.
Typical programs lasted about 27 weeks, with roughly 2.6 sessions a week of 45 minutes each.

items.title: The effect of exercise intensity on bone in postmenopausal women (part 2): A meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 53 trials of exercise in healthy women after menopause to see whether harder exercise builds more bone density. Higher-intensity exercise gave a bigger gain in lower-spine bone density than low or moderate intensity. Low and moderate intensity exercise worked about equally well at the hip. Only four trials tested high-intensity exercise, so the evidence for it is still limited.
keyPoints: High-intensity exercise improved lumbar spine bone density more than moderate or low intensity exercise.
Low and moderate intensity exercise had similar effects at the femoral neck (top of the thigh bone); no effect was seen for high intensity, which may be due to too few studies.
Resistance training, possibly combined with impact training, appeared the most effective type of exercise for spine and hip bone.
Adding exercise did not change how well bone medication worked, and few high-intensity trials were available.

items.title: Effect of combined aerobic and resistance exercise on blood pressure in postmenopausal women: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 11 randomized trials to see whether combining aerobic exercise (like walking or cycling) with resistance exercise (like weights) changes blood pressure in women after menopause. Women who did both types of exercise had small but statistically significant drops in blood pressure compared with those who did not. The authors conclude it may be an effective way to help prevent and manage high blood pressure after menopause.
keyPoints: Combined aerobic and resistance exercise lowered systolic blood pressure by about 0.81 mmHg and diastolic by about 0.62 mmHg compared with no exercise.
It also reduced arterial stiffness (pulse wave velocity) and slightly lowered heart rate.
Women aged 60 or older, and those who were overweight or had normal starting blood pressure, seemed to respond more.
Blood pressure fell more with at least 150 minutes of exercise a week, programs lasting 12 weeks, or fewer than 3 sessions a week.

items.title: The Additive Effects of Creatine Supplementation and Exercise Training in an Aging Population: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: This review looked at 17 randomized trials of older adults who did exercise with or without creatine supplements. Any extra benefit for strength, daily function and lean muscle seemed to need low daily doses of creatine plus at least 12 weeks of resistance training. Creatine monohydrate was found to be safe in older adults, and benefits looked more consistent in older women than in men. More long-term studies are still needed, especially for bone and thinking skills.
keyPoints: The authors judged creatine monohydrate safe to use in older adults, based on these trials.
Extra muscle benefits over exercise alone may need continuous low-dose daily creatine plus at least 12 weeks of resistance training.
Possible gains in thigh bone (femur) density may need at least 1 year of creatine with moderate resistance training.
Limited data showed no added effect of creatine on mental health, and benefits were more consistent in older women than in men.

items.title: Effects of dynamic resistance exercise on bone mineral density in postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis with special emphasis on exercise parameters
items.summary: This review combined results from 17 studies of resistance exercise (such as lifting weights) lasting at least 6 months in women after menopause. It found that resistance exercise improved bone density at the lower spine, the neck of the thigh bone and the hip, though the effects were small to moderate. The researchers also looked at how often, how hard and in what way women trained, but could not draw clear advice about the best exercise plan from this.
keyPoints: Resistance exercise gave small-to-moderate improvements in bone density at the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip in postmenopausal women.
Compared with control groups, the bone density gains were statistically significant at all three sites.
Differences in training frequency, intensity, volume and type did not give clear enough results to recommend a best exercise routine.

Fewer sessions per week (under 2) showed bigger gains at the spine and hip than 2 or more, and free weights beat machines at the hip, but the authors say these findings did not allow meaningful recommendations.

items.title: Comparison of the effect of resistance training on the body compositions of different women groups: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness
items.journal: Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness
items.summary: This review pooled 23 randomized trials to see whether resistance training (like weight lifting) changes body composition differently in different groups of women. Benefits were clearest in women after menopause, women with overweight or obesity, and women who were not otherwise active. The authors suggest resistance training is especially worthwhile for these groups.
keyPoints: In postmenopausal women, resistance training reduced body fat percentage and fat mass and increased fat-free mass.
In premenopausal women, it clearly reduced only body fat percentage.
In women with overweight or obesity, it reduced fat mass and body fat percentage and increased fat-free mass, but it had no significant effect in women without overweight or obesity.
In sedentary women it improved fat mass, body fat percentage and fat-free mass, while in non-sedentary women it mainly increased fat-free mass.

items.title: Effect of exercise on bone mineral density and quality of life among postmenopausal women with osteoporosis without fracture: A systematic review
items.source: International Journal of Orthopaedic and Trauma Nursing
items.journal: International Journal of Orthopaedic and Trauma Nursing
items.summary: This review looked at trials testing exercise in postmenopausal women who have osteoporosis but have not had a broken bone. The trials suggest exercise helps improve bone density and quality of life. The exercise types varied a lot, many studies were small or short, and the results could not be combined, so more well-designed trials are needed.
keyPoints: Exercise appeared to improve bone mineral density and quality of life in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.
Programmes studied included Tai Chi, high intensity aerobic exercise, pilates, Eight Section Brocade, slow low-impact loading and closed kinetic exercises.
Four studies had small samples and three had short interventions, and the studies were too different to pool in a meta-analysis.
The authors say better-designed trials are needed to reduce the high risk of bias.

items.title: Vitamin D, Calcium, or Combined Supplementation for the Primary Prevention of Fractures in Community-Dwelling Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force looked at whether vitamin D and calcium supplements stop broken bones in healthy adults living at home. For postmenopausal women, daily low doses (400 IU or less of vitamin D and 1000 mg or less of calcium) were found to give no benefit for preventing fractures. There was not enough evidence to judge benefits or harms for higher doses, or for men and women who have not yet reached menopause. Taking vitamin D and calcium together was linked to more kidney stones.
keyPoints: Daily 400 IU or less of vitamin D with 1000 mg or less of calcium does not prevent first fractures in postmenopausal women, and the Task Force recommends against it (D recommendation).
There is not enough evidence to say whether higher doses help or harm for fracture prevention in postmenopausal women.
There is not enough evidence on fracture prevention for men and premenopausal women.
Vitamin D plus calcium supplements increase the chance of kidney stones.

items.title: Worldwide prevalence of haemorrhoids: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 150 studies, covering almost 9 million people, to estimate how common haemorrhoids (piles) are worldwide. About 1 in 4 people were affected (25.92%), and rates were higher in women (27.33%) than in men. Pregnancy, constipation, obesity, older age, diabetes, high blood pressure and family history were each linked to haemorrhoids in the unadjusted analyses.
keyPoints: About 26% of people worldwide had haemorrhoids at a given time, and around 27% over a lifetime.
Haemorrhoids were more common in women (27.33%) than in men.
Pregnancy and constipation were among the factors linked to a higher chance of haemorrhoids.
Studies using invasive tests (such as examination inside the bowel) found more haemorrhoids, which suggests some cases may go undiagnosed.

items.title: Risk Factors for Gestational Stress Urinary Incontinence: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 20 studies to look at what raises the chance of leaking urine when coughing, sneezing or exercising during pregnancy (gestational stress urinary incontinence). Previous vaginal birth, constipation during pregnancy and having had a baby over 4 kg were key risk factors. Pelvic floor muscle training was linked to a lower chance of leaking. The abstract does not report how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Previous vaginal delivery, constipation during pregnancy and a previous baby over 4 kg were key risk factors for urine leaking in pregnancy.
Age, number of previous births, BMI during pregnancy and gestational age were also linked to leaking in the combined analysis.
Pelvic floor muscle training showed a protective effect.
The authors suggest antenatal care should include ways to prevent this problem.

items.title: AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Treatment of Hemorrhoids: Expert Review
items.summary: This is an expert guidance document from the American Gastroenterological Association on diagnosing and treating haemorrhoids (piles). It notes that haemorrhoids affect up to two-thirds of women during pregnancy. For pregnancy, it advises gentle, conservative care first: fibre, treating constipation, and topical ointments. The advice comes from literature review and expert opinion, so it carries no formal quality-of-evidence rating.
keyPoints: Haemorrhoids occur in up to two-thirds of women during pregnancy.
In pregnancy, treatment should generally be conservative: fibre, treating constipation, and topical ointments.
If symptoms continue after birth, or further pregnancies are planned, office treatments such as banding or infrared coagulation can be considered.
For symptomatic haemorrhoids generally, more fibre and avoiding straining or long times on the toilet are reasonable first steps, though evidence for topical creams is limited.

items.title: Comparison of efficacy and safety between surgical and conservative treatments for hemorrhoids: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled seven studies (760 people) comparing surgery with non-surgical (conservative) treatment for haemorrhoids. Surgery gave more complete symptom relief, less pain in the first few days, and fewer recurrences, but pain was similar after about ten days. Conservative treatment was safer and less invasive but slower to work and more likely to come back. Similar patterns were seen in pregnant women with thrombosed (clotted) external haemorrhoids, where surgery shortened recovery by about a week.
keyPoints: Surgery was about three times as likely as conservative treatment to fully resolve symptoms.
Surgery gave clearly less pain within four days, but pain scores were similar after ten days.
In pregnant women with thrombosed external haemorrhoids, surgery shortened recovery by roughly seven days and reduced recurrence.
Surgery had some specific complications (incontinence 3%, persistent pain 5%, watery discharge 6%), while conservative treatment is safer but slower and recurs more often.

items.title: Global prevalence and risk of gastroesophageal reflux disease symptoms in pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 21 studies of about 9,500 pregnant women to see how common reflux symptoms (heartburn and regurgitation) are in pregnancy. About 4 in 10 women had these symptoms, and they became more common as pregnancy went on. Pregnant women were much more likely to have reflux symptoms than women who were not pregnant. The authors say spotting and managing it early may help comfort and quality of life.
keyPoints: About 41% of pregnant women had reflux symptoms overall, though results varied a lot between studies.
Reflux symptoms rose across pregnancy: about 26% in the first trimester, 33% in the second and 56% in the third.
Heartburn affected about 44% of pregnant women and regurgitation about 38%.
Pregnant women had a much higher risk of reflux symptoms than non-pregnant women (odds ratio 8.37).

items.title: Global prevalence of constipation during pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 13 studies to estimate how common constipation is during pregnancy around the world. About 1 in 3 pregnant women (32.4%) had constipation. It was least common in the first trimester (21.1%) and most common in the second trimester (34%), with 30.3% in the third trimester. The authors say more research is needed on causes and prevention, and suggest education on nutrition and moderate physical activity.
keyPoints: Across 13 studies, about 32.4% of pregnant women had constipation.
Constipation was least common in the first trimester (21.1%).
It was most common in the second trimester (34%), and 30.3% in the third trimester.
The authors suggest nutrition education and moderate physical activity to help reduce constipation, and call for more research on causes and prevention.

items.title: Long-term use of proton pump inhibitors as a risk factor for various adverse manifestations
items.summary: This review looked at the possible harms of taking proton pump inhibitors (PPIs, strong acid-reducing medicines) for a long time. For pregnancy, it notes that long-term PPI use may carry a possible risk of birth defects. Several studies it describes recommend lifestyle changes and antacids first for heartburn in pregnancy, keeping PPIs for severe reflux, with omeprazole named as a safe choice of PPI.
keyPoints: Lifestyle changes and antacids are recommended as the first choice for heartburn in pregnant women.
PPIs are kept for severe reflux disease in pregnancy, and omeprazole is described as a safe PPI choice.
Long-term PPI use in pregnancy may carry a potential risk of congenital malformations.
Long-term PPI use can lead to low vitamin and mineral levels and a higher chance of some infections, so it should be avoided without a proper reason.

items.title: Systematic review with meta-analysis: the risks of proton pump inhibitors during pregnancy
items.summary: This review pooled results from 26 observational studies to look at whether acid-reducing medicines taken in pregnancy are linked to problems for babies. Using proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), a common heartburn treatment, was linked to a somewhat higher chance of birth defects. No link was found with miscarriage, stillbirth, newborn death, preterm birth or low birth weight. The authors note that bias and differences between studies may have affected the results, and there was not enough data to look at specific birth defects or specific drugs.
keyPoints: PPI use in pregnancy was linked to a higher risk of congenital malformations (OR 1.28), with a stronger link in case-control studies (OR 2.04).
No link was found between PPI use and miscarriage, stillbirth, neonatal death, preterm birth or low birth weight.
H2 blockers (another type of acid-reducing medicine) were not linked to birth defects, but may be linked to a slightly higher risk of preterm birth (OR 1.25).
The studies were observational and the authors say bias may be present; there was not enough data to assess specific malformations or drugs.

items.title: Acid-Suppressive Drug Use During Pregnancy and the Risk of Childhood Asthma: A Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 8 population-based observational studies on heartburn-type medicines (acid-suppressing drugs) taken in pregnancy and asthma in children. Children whose mothers used these medicines during pregnancy had a higher chance of asthma, both for proton pump inhibitors and for histamine-2 blockers. The studies did not account for every factor that could affect asthma risk, so this shows a link, not proof that the medicines cause asthma.
keyPoints: Acid-suppressive drug use in pregnancy was linked to a higher risk of childhood asthma (relative risk 1.45).
The link was seen for proton pump inhibitors (relative risk 1.34) and for histamine-2 receptor antagonists (relative risk 1.57).
None of the included studies adjusted for the full set of known confounding factors.
The authors suggest clinicians and parents use caution when deciding whether to take these medicines in pregnancy.

items.title: Less-Restrictive Food Intake During Labor in Low-Risk Singleton Pregnancies: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 trials with almost 4,000 women in low-risk labour to compare eating more freely with being limited to ice chips or sips of water. Women who were allowed to eat or drink more had labours that were about 16 minutes shorter on average. There were no other differences in outcomes for mothers or babies, and vomiting was not more common.
keyPoints: Eating more freely during labour was linked to a labour about 16 minutes shorter on average.
No other benefits or harms were seen for mothers or babies, and rates of operative delivery were similar.
Vomiting was not more common, and no cases of regurgitation during general anaesthesia or Mendelson syndrome occurred in either group.
The findings apply to women with low-risk single-baby pregnancies and no complications that make a caesarean more likely.

items.title: Gum chewing and gastrointestinal function following caesarean delivery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together five randomised trials with 846 women who had a caesarean birth. It compared chewing gum after the operation with not chewing gum. Women who chewed gum got their bowels working again sooner, with earlier bowel sounds, passing gas and opening their bowels. The authors describe gum chewing as a low-cost, non-drug and safe option.
keyPoints: Gum chewing after caesarean birth helped digestion restart, including bowel sounds, passing gas and first bowel movement.
The review combined five randomised trials with 846 women in total.
The authors describe gum chewing as a low-cost, safe, socially acceptable option that does not involve medicine.
It may help reduce stomach and bowel problems after a caesarean.

items.title: Interventions for treating constipation in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at treatments for constipation in pregnancy, but found only a few small studies, so only two (180 women) gave usable results. Stimulant laxatives probably helped constipation more than bulk-forming laxatives, but caused more tummy discomfort and diarrhoea. Fibre supplements may increase how often women pass stools compared with no treatment. Overall, there is not enough evidence to say for sure which treatments work best or are safest.
keyPoints: Stimulant laxatives probably improved constipation more than bulk-forming laxatives, but led to more diarrhoea and abdominal discomfort; women's satisfaction was similar.
Fibre supplements may have increased stool frequency by about 2 times per week compared with no treatment, based on one small study of 40 women.
There was no data on other options such as osmotic laxatives, stool softeners, lubricant laxatives, enemas or suppositories.
The authors conclude the evidence is insufficient and more good-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Interventions for heartburn in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at treatments for heartburn in pregnancy. It found nine small trials, but only four (358 women) had usable data. Women given medicine such as an antacid were more likely to have complete heartburn relief than those given a placebo or no treatment, though the evidence is limited and the trials were small.
keyPoints: Women given pharmaceutical treatment reported complete heartburn relief more often than those given placebo or no treatment (moderate-quality evidence from two trials).
One small trial found sucralfate gave complete relief more often than advice on diet and lifestyle alone.
Side effects did not clearly differ between treatment and placebo or no treatment, but this evidence was very low quality.
There was too little data to judge acupuncture, and no large trials exist, so more research is needed.

items.title: Heavy menstrual bleeding: assessment and management
items.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
items.journal: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
items.summary: This is a NICE guideline on how heavy periods (heavy menstrual bleeding) should be assessed and treated. It is meant to help healthcare professionals find the cause of heavy periods that affect a woman's quality of life and offer suitable treatments. It says treatment choices should take into account the woman's own priorities and preferences. The abstract does not list specific treatments or findings.
keyPoints: The guideline covers assessing and managing heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia).
It aims to help find the cause of heavy periods that are affecting a woman's quality of life.
Treatment should take into account the woman's priorities and preferences.
It is written for healthcare professionals and services, and also for women with heavy periods, their families and carers.

items.title: Etiology and diagnosis of heavy menstrual bleeding among adolescent and adult patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the literature
items.summary: This review pooled results from 53 studies, including over 41,000 patients, to look at what causes heavy periods and how doctors can find the cause. Bleeding disorders were a common finding, affecting about 3 in 10 people with heavy periods overall. They were more common in teenagers (about 39%) than in adults (about 16%). The authors conclude that bleeding disorders should be looked for when the cause of heavy bleeding is not clear.
keyPoints: About 30% of people with heavy menstrual bleeding had an underlying bleeding disorder.
Von Willebrand disease was found in about 8%, platelet function defects in about 9%, and polycystic ovarian syndrome in about 8%.
Bleeding disorders were found in about 39% of adolescents with heavy periods, compared with about 16% of adults.
Causes of heavy bleeding seem to depend on age, so age should be considered when finding the cause.

items.title: Efficacy of GnRH antagonists in the treatment of uterine fibroids: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 11 randomized trials with 4164 premenopausal women who had uterine fibroids and heavy periods. It looked at medicines called GnRH antagonists (relugolix, elagolix, linzagolix and cetrorelix). Compared with placebo, they controlled heavy bleeding much better and shrank fibroids more. The authors say these medicines are an effective option for treating fibroids.
keyPoints: GnRH antagonists controlled heavy uterine bleeding far better than placebo (relative risk 5.09).
Fibroid volume fell more with GnRH antagonists than with placebo (about 27% greater reduction).
Bone density loss was reported as lower in the comparison the authors measured (mean difference -0.35).
The results could not show whether the medicines differ in controlling hot flushes and other vasomotor symptoms.

items.title: Preoperative medical therapy before surgery for uterine fibroids
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 41 trials (3982 women) of medicines given before surgery for uterine fibroids, which are a common cause of heavy periods and anaemia. Medicines called GnRH analogues probably raise blood levels (haemoglobin) before surgery and may shrink the womb and fibroids, but they probably cause more side effects such as hot flushes. Another group of medicines, SPRMs, seemed to offer similar benefits. Most of the evidence is low to moderate certainty, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: GnRH analogues before surgery probably raise haemoglobin by about 0.9 g/dL (moderate-certainty) and may reduce womb and fibroid size (low-certainty).
GnRH analogues probably increase side effects such as hot flushes compared with placebo or no pretreatment.
Before hysterectomy, GnRH analogues may shorten surgery and probably mean fewer blood transfusions and less postoperative illness; before myomectomy the effects were uncertain or small.
SPRMs such as ulipristal acetate probably reduce womb size and raise haemoglobin, but ulipristal acetate use is suspended (March 2025) because of cases of liver failure.

items.title: Genome-wide meta-analysis of heavy menstrual bleeding reveals 36 risk loci
items.summary: Researchers combined genetic data from five large biobanks, covering up to about 85,000 women with heavy periods and nearly 600,000 comparison women. They found 36 spots in the genome linked to heavy menstrual bleeding, 33 of them new. Some of these are near genes involved in hormone production. Heavy bleeding also shared genetic links with fibroids, endometriosis and ovarian cysts.
