The authors say this may help in finding new treatments, but this is genetic research and not a treatment study.
keyPoints: 36 genetic regions were linked to heavy menstrual bleeding, 33 of them newly found.
A common clotting-related gene variant (F5-Leiden) was linked to lower odds of heavy bleeding (odds ratio 0.75).
Some regions sit near genes that help control reproductive hormones (FSHB and LHB/CGB).
Heavy bleeding had strong genetic overlap with uterine fibroids, endometriosis and ovarian cysts.

items.title: Medical treatment of fibroids: FIGO best practice guidance
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This international guidance from FIGO looks at medicines for uterine fibroids, which are common non-cancerous growths in the womb. Only a few drugs are officially approved for fibroids, mainly certain GnRH antagonists, while a related group of medicines (GnRH analogs) is mostly used before surgery because of side effects with long-term use. Other medicines, such as the combined pill, progestin tablets, the hormonal coil (LNG-IUS) and tranexamic acid, are not specifically approved for fibroids but can lighten heavy periods. This can ease symptoms and improve quality of life.
keyPoints: Only a few medicines are officially approved to treat fibroids, including some GnRH antagonists.
GnRH analogs are mainly used before surgery because of their long-term side effects.
Ulipristal acetate was heavily restricted because of safety concerns.
Combined pills, progestins, the LNG-IUS and tranexamic acid can reduce heavy bleeding from fibroids and improve quality of life.

items.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the etiology of heavy menstrual bleeding in 2,770 adolescent females
items.summary: Researchers combined 17 studies covering 2,770 teenagers aged 10-19 with heavy or abnormal periods to see what causes the bleeding. The most common causes were ovary and uterus disorders (about 24%), clotting disorders (about 19%), and platelet disorders (about 6%). For nearly half of the teenagers (about 46%), no clear cause was found. The authors say many different factors can be involved, so a careful check is needed.
keyPoints: Ovary and uterus disorders were the most common cause of heavy periods in teenagers (about 23.7%).
Blood clotting disorders accounted for about 19.4% of cases, and platelet disorders for about 6.2%.
About 45.9% of cases had no clear cause identified.
The authors say several possible causes should be considered when assessing heavy bleeding in teenagers.

items.title: Heavy menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhea in adolescents: A systematic review of self-management strategies, quality of life, and unmet needs
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review looked at 55 studies of young women aged 12-25 with heavy periods or period pain. Many reported physical and emotional problems, and their schoolwork and daily activities were often badly affected. Most used pain medicine or home remedies like heat, massage and herbal tea, but the studies gave no information on how well these worked or what doses were used.
keyPoints: More than 80% of young women with period pain or heavy bleeding reported physical and psychological problems, such as pelvic pain, poor sleep, low mood, diarrhea and nausea.
Quality of life was poorer in those with period pain than in those without it, and school and daily activities were severely affected.
Over 70% used medication for pain and more than half used home remedies, but no studies reported how effective they were or what doses were used.
Most young women got information from their mothers (over 62%) or friends, and limited access to information made symptoms harder to manage.

items.title: Menstrual disorders following COVID-19 vaccination: a review using a systematic search
items.source: Frontiers in Drug Safety and Regulation
items.journal: Frontiers in Drug Safety and Regulation
items.summary: This review pulled together 61 studies on period changes after COVID-19 vaccination. Every study found more people reporting at least one menstrual change in the first cycle after vaccination, across different vaccine types and doses. The authors say the changes are short-lived and mostly mild, but many studies had design weaknesses, so longer-term studies are still needed.
keyPoints: All 61 included studies found a higher share of people with at least one menstrual change in the first cycle after COVID-19 vaccination.
Reported changes included cycle length, amount of bleeding, length of periods, period pain and breakthrough bleeding.
Menstrual changes were described as short-lived and mostly mild.
Many studies had important design limitations, so more longitudinal studies are needed.

items.title: Risk of Recurrence and Reintervention After Uterine-Sparing Interventions for Symptomatic Adenomyosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 42 studies (5,877 women) to see how often symptoms or lesions come back after treatments that keep the womb in place for adenomyosis. Three options were looked at: surgery to remove the adenomyosis (adenomyomectomy), uterine artery embolization (blocking blood flow to the womb), and image-guided heat ablation. These treatments worked well overall and few women needed another procedure, but embolization had higher recurrence and reintervention rates. The women treated with embolization had larger wombs and larger adenomyosis, so the comparison may be unfair, and the authors say more randomized trials are needed.
keyPoints: Recurrence rates were about 12.6% after adenomyomectomy, 29.5% after uterine artery embolization and 10.0% after image-guided thermal ablation.
Reintervention rates were about 2.6% after adenomyomectomy, 12.8% after embolization and 8.2% after thermal ablation.
Embolization had higher recurrence and reintervention rates, but those patients had larger wombs and larger adenomyosis, so selection bias may explain some of the gap.
The included studies were single-arm studies, and larger randomized controlled trials are still needed.

items.title: Risk of thromboembolism in patients with COVID-19 who are using hormonal contraception
items.summary: This review looked for studies on whether hormonal contraception raises the risk of blood clots in people with COVID-19. It found no studies that directly compared clot risk between users and non-users. The few studies available suggest hormonal contraception did not clearly make COVID-19 more severe, but the evidence is very uncertain and of low quality.
keyPoints: No comparative studies were found on blood clot risk in people with COVID-19 who use hormonal contraception.
Combined hormonal contraception may have little to no effect on the odds of death or intubation in COVID-19, based on very low-certainty evidence.
Hospitalization odds may be slightly lower for combined hormonal contraception users with a BMI under 35, but this comes from one study and is very uncertain.
No large increase in COVID-19 severity was seen among hormonal contraception users, but better studies are needed.

items.title: Guideline No. 437: Diagnosis and Management of Adenomyosis
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline describes how adenomyosis (a condition where womb-lining tissue grows into the muscle wall of the uterus) is diagnosed and treated. It says ultrasound or MRI scans can be used to diagnose it. Treatment is matched to symptoms such as heavy periods, pain or trouble getting pregnant, and the guideline notes that options which preserve fertility are available. The abstract lists the options but does not give the detailed recommendations or how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Adenomyosis is common in women of reproductive age.
It can be diagnosed with transvaginal ultrasound or MRI.

Medicines that may be used include anti-inflammatory painkillers, tranexamic acid, combined contraceptive pills, the hormonal coil (levonorgestrel IUS), dienogest and other progestins, and GnRH analogues.
Other options include uterine artery embolization and surgery (endometrial ablation, removing adenomyosis tissue, or hysterectomy), and fertility-preserving options exist.

items.title: A Systematic Review of Minimally Invasive Treatments for Uterine Fibroid-Related Bleeding
items.summary: This review pooled 84 studies of treatments that keep the uterus in place for women before menopause whose fibroids cause heavy bleeding. Myomectomy, uterine artery embolization and radiofrequency ablation all reduced bleeding in many women. The authors say more research is needed to show whether any one treatment is better than the others, and long-term evidence is limited for some newer options.
keyPoints: Myomectomy (surgery to remove fibroids) improved bleeding symptoms in up to 95.9% of patients, with no clear difference between ways of doing it.
Uterine artery embolization (blocking the blood supply to fibroids) improved symptoms in 79 to 98.5% of patients; three studies suggested it may work better than myomectomy for bleeding.
Radiofrequency ablation significantly reduced bleeding severity in 15 studies.
Long-term evidence is limited for focused ultrasound surgery, cryomyolysis, microwave ablation and laser ablation.

items.title: Interventions for heavy menstrual bleeding; overview of Cochrane reviews and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pulled together nine Cochrane reviews to compare treatments for heavy periods, which affect 2 to 5 in every 10 women of reproductive age. Among first-choice treatments, the hormone coil (LNG-IUS) reduced bleeding the most, followed by tranexamic acid and long-cycle progestogen pills. Among second-choice treatments, hysterectomy reduced bleeding the most, followed by endometrial ablation. Much of the evidence was low or very low certainty, so many treatments could not be confidently compared.
keyPoints: The levonorgestrel hormone coil (LNG-IUS) was the best first-line treatment for reducing menstrual blood loss, though the evidence was low certainty.
Tranexamic acid (an antifibrinolytic) probably reduces bleeding (moderate certainty), and long-cycle progestogens also reduced it (low certainty).
For second-line treatment, hysterectomy reduced bleeding the most, followed by endometrial ablation procedures.
No firm conclusions could be drawn on satisfaction with first-line treatments because the evidence was very low certainty.

items.title: Gynaecological management of women with inherited bleeding disorders. A UK Haemophilia Centres Doctors' Organisation Guideline
items.summary: This is a UK guideline for doctors who care for women with inherited bleeding disorders. It explains that heavy periods are very often the first sign of one of these disorders, and that bleeding can range from mild to severe. It sets out how heavy periods should be investigated, and how women who already have a known bleeding disorder should be managed, including around gynaecological surgery.
keyPoints: Heavy menstrual bleeding is very often the first sign of an inherited bleeding disorder and is the most common reason these women come to hospital services.
Bleeding severity varies widely between women with these disorders, so care should be tailored to the individual.
Diagnosis and care need specialist teams, with good communication between gynaecology and haematology.
The guideline covers investigating heavy periods, managing known bleeding disorders, and care around gynaecological surgery and other gynaecological situations.

items.title: Interventions to prevent or treat heavy menstrual bleeding or pain associated with intrauterine-device use
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 21 trials of medicines and other treatments for heavy bleeding or pain linked to using an IUD (coil) for contraception. Most trials were small, and the evidence was mostly low or very low quality, so the authors say the findings should be read with caution. Some treatments, such as vitamin B1 and mefenamic acid, showed possible benefits for heavy bleeding with the copper IUD, but these need more research.
keyPoints: In one trial of copper IUD users, vitamin B1 led to fewer pads used per day and fewer bleeding days than placebo (low-certainty evidence).
Mefenamic acid led to less blood loss than tranexamic acid in copper IUD users, though bleeding duration did not differ (low-certainty evidence).
Tolfenamic acid may help prevent heavy bleeding with a copper IUD (very low-certainty evidence), but may not prevent painful periods.
Ulipristal acetate did not clearly reduce bleeding with the levonorgestrel IUD, and may have increased the percentage of bleeding days when used for prevention.

items.title: Endometrial resection and ablation versus hysterectomy for heavy menstrual bleeding
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 10 trials (1966 women) comparing endometrial resection or ablation (removing or destroying the womb lining) with hysterectomy for heavy periods. Hysterectomy tended to work better for controlling bleeding and meant fewer repeat operations, while ablation usually meant a quicker return to normal activity. Rates of serious complications looked similar overall. Evidence quality ranged from moderate to low.
keyPoints: Women who had ablation were probably less likely to feel their heavy bleeding had improved than those who had open or unspecified-route hysterectomy, but results may be similar to keyhole (minimally invasive) hysterectomy.
Further surgery for treatment failure was probably more likely after ablation than after any type of hysterectomy.
Satisfaction was probably similar with ablation and open or unspecified hysterectomy, but lower than with minimally invasive hysterectomy.
Time to return to normal activity was likely shorter after ablation, though firm conclusions could not be drawn.

items.title: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system and breast cancer risk: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from seven studies on women using the levonorgestrel hormonal coil (LNG-IUS) and breast cancer. It found a small increase in breast cancer risk among users, and the increase looked larger in women aged 50 and over. The authors say the studies had methodological problems and other factors may explain part of the increase. They suggest balancing this against the proven benefits of the coil, such as treating heavy menstrual bleeding.
keyPoints: Pooled results showed a small increase in breast cancer odds in LNG-IUS users (odds ratio 1.16 for all women).
The increase appeared larger in women aged 50 or older (odds ratio 1.52) than in those under 50 (odds ratio 1.12).
The authors found methodological issues in the studies, and other factors may account for some of the increased risk.
The authors say risks should be weighed against proven benefits such as treating heavy menstrual bleeding and avoiding surgery, especially for women with other breast cancer risk factors.

items.title: Progestogens or progestogen-releasing intrauterine systems for uterine fibroids (other than preoperative medical therapy)
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether progestogen pills or progestogen-releasing coils (intrauterine systems) help women before menopause who have uterine fibroids, which can cause heavy periods. Only four small studies (221 women) were found, and the evidence was very low quality, so it is uncertain whether these treatments reduce bleeding or raise haemoglobin compared with the contraceptive pill or other hormone treatments. Hot flushes were reported with goserelin acetate (55% of women) but not with the oral progestogens dienogest or desogestrel.
keyPoints: Four small trials (221 women) were included, and all evidence was very low quality.
It is uncertain whether the progestogen coil (LNG-IUS) reduces heavy bleeding or raises haemoglobin compared with the combined pill or norethisterone acetate.
There was not enough evidence to say whether the coil shrinks fibroids more than the combined pill.
Hot flushes (vasomotor symptoms) occurred in 55% of women on goserelin acetate but not in those on dienogest or desogestrel.

items.title: Endometrial resection and ablation techniques for heavy menstrual bleeding
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 28 trials (4,287 women) comparing different ways of removing or destroying the womb lining (endometrial ablation) to treat heavy periods. Newer techniques that don't need the surgeon to see inside the womb worked about as well as older ones for reducing bleeding and for how satisfied women felt. The newer methods took less time and were more often done with local rather than general anaesthesia. The quality of the evidence ranged from moderate to very low, and it is unclear whether the risk of perforation (a hole in the womb wall) differs between the methods.
keyPoints: Newer (second-generation) ablation methods were about as effective as older hysteroscopic methods for heavy menstrual bleeding.
Rates of periods stopping, improvement in bleeding scores and patient satisfaction were similar between newer and older techniques.
Newer techniques had shorter operating times and were more often done under local anaesthesia.
It is uncertain whether perforation rates differ, and there was little or no difference in needing further surgery such as hysterectomy at 5 years.

items.title: Guideline No. 389-Medical Management of Symptomatic Uterine Leiomyomas - An Addendum
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This is an update to a 2015 Canadian guideline on managing uterine fibroids, which are non-cancerous growths in the womb. It notes that most fibroids cause no symptoms and need no treatment. When fibroids do cause problems such as heavy or long periods, low iron, or pelvic pressure or pain, treatment should aim to ease symptoms and improve quality of life. The abstract does not describe the individual medical treatments or give a certainty rating for the evidence.
keyPoints: Most fibroids cause no symptoms and need no treatment or further tests.
Symptomatic fibroids can cause heavy, irregular or prolonged bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, and pelvic pressure or pain.
Hysterectomy is a definitive solution but is not the preferred choice for women who want to keep their fertility or their uterus.
Treatment choice should aim to improve symptoms and quality of life, weighing risks, benefits and costs.

items.title: No. 292-Abnormal Uterine Bleeding in Pre-Menopausal Women
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looks at abnormal uterine bleeding, including heavy periods, in women who have not yet reached menopause. It says up to 30% of women seek medical help for this problem during their reproductive years. It recommends a clear, step-by-step approach to finding the cause and choosing treatment, starting with medicines and moving to the least invasive surgery only if needed.
keyPoints: Up to 30% of women will seek medical help for abnormal uterine bleeding during their reproductive years.
Abnormal uterine bleeding is common and can sometimes be debilitating.
Care should follow a systematic approach to diagnosis and investigation, using standard terminology.
Treatment should start with medical therapies, followed by the least invasive surgical options that give results the patient is happy with.

items.title: A systematic review of methods to measure menstrual blood loss
items.summary: This review looked at 71 studies on ways to measure how much blood is lost during a period and whether each method can tell normal bleeding from heavy bleeding. Every method has limits. Picture-based charts, where women compare their pads or tampons to drawings, offered a good balance of being easy to use and being reasonably accurate. The authors suggest these could be used alongside questions about how bleeding affects daily life.
keyPoints: Every method for measuring menstrual blood loss has limitations.
Picture-based methods (such as the pictorial blood loss chart and menstrual pictogram) have been tested more thoroughly than questionnaires and models.
Picture-based methods balance ease of use with validated accuracy compared with the lab-based gold standard.
Pictorial methods could be used alongside quality-of-life assessment to evaluate heavy menstrual bleeding in clinics and research.

items.title: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding: American College of Nurse-Midwives
items.summary: This is a clinical guideline from the American College of Nurse-Midwives about abnormal uterine bleeding, meaning bleeding that varies from a typical period. It explains that these changes are common and are often a normal variation with no serious consequences, but they can cause real distress or point to an underlying condition. The guideline describes how midwives tell normal from abnormal bleeding, using a full history and a classification system called PALM-COEIN to guide treatment in a woman-centred way.
keyPoints: Variations in menstrual and perimenstrual bleeding are common and are often normal, with no significant consequences.
Abnormal uterine bleeding can cause significant distress or may signal an underlying condition.
A comprehensive history and the PALM-COEIN classification system help guide evidence-based treatment and an individualised plan of care.
The guideline updates terminology and describes how bleeding is assessed and treated using a woman-centred approach.

items.title: The management of uterine leiomyomas
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline reviews how uterine fibroids (non-cancerous growths in the womb) are assessed and treated. Most fibroids cause no symptoms and need no treatment, but some cause heavy bleeding, anemia or pelvic pressure. Treatment options range from medicines and procedures that keep the womb to hysterectomy, and the best choice depends on symptoms, fibroid size and location, age and whether a woman wants to keep her fertility or uterus.
keyPoints: Fibroids are common (about 70% of women by age 50), but most cause no symptoms and need no treatment; women with symptom-free fibroids can be reassured that there is no evidence for major concern about cancer.

Medicines that help fibroid-related heavy bleeding include the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, GnRH analogues, selective progesterone receptor modulators, oral contraceptives, progestins and danazol.

Hysterectomy is the most effective treatment for symptomatic fibroids but is not preferred for women who want to keep their fertility or uterus; myomectomy and uterine artery embolization are options for those women, with some risk of further treatment or effects on pregnancy.
Treatment should be individual, and anemia should be corrected before planned surgery.

items.title: Progesterone or progestogen-releasing intrauterine systems for heavy menstrual bleeding
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 21 trials (2082 women) on hormone-releasing coils (mostly the levonorgestrel IUS, e.g. Mirena) for heavy periods. The coil reduced bleeding more than tablets and improved quality of life, but caused more minor side effects. Compared with endometrial ablation, results were unclear, and hysterectomy reduced bleeding more than the coil. The quality of the evidence ranged from very low to high depending on the comparison.
keyPoints: The levonorgestrel coil was more effective than oral medicines at reducing heavy bleeding, improved quality of life, and more women stayed on it at two years.
Compared with endometrial ablation, it was unclear whether the coil reduced bleeding more, and satisfaction and quality of life were similar.
Hysterectomy reduced heavy bleeding more than the coil (high quality evidence), though both improved quality of life.
Minor side effects such as pelvic pain, breast tenderness and ovarian cysts were more common with the coil, but it appeared more cost effective than ablation or hysterectomy.

items.title: The two FIGO systems for normal and abnormal uterine bleeding symptoms and classification of causes of abnormal uterine bleeding in the reproductive years: 2018 revisions
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This paper from the FIGO Menstrual Disorders Committee presents the 2018 revisions of FIGO's two systems for abnormal uterine bleeding: one that defines normal and abnormal bleeding symptoms, and one (PALM-COEIN) that classifies their causes. They were first published in 2011 to give doctors and researchers worldwide the same definitions. The revisions came from expert meetings and voting between 2012 and 2017. The abstract does not give the definitions themselves.
keyPoints: FIGO AUB System 1 sets common terms for normal and abnormal menstrual bleeding in the reproductive years.
FIGO AUB System 2 (PALM-COEIN) classifies the causes of abnormal bleeding.
Both systems were reviewed and revised by international experts between 2012 and 2017.

items.title: Hormonal Options for Perimenopause: A Clinician Toolkit
items.summary: This clinical perspective explains that perimenopause, the stage before menopause, looks different for every person and has no specific guidelines. Symptoms can include mood and thinking changes, irregular bleeding, poor sleep, hot flushes and sexual concerns. The article describes how hormonal contraceptives and other hormone-based options may be used, and notes that contraceptives do not suit everyone. It encourages choosing treatment through shared decision making between a patient and their clinician.
keyPoints: Perimenopause is a distinct stage from menopause and is defined in different ways.
It can bring mood and thinking changes, abnormal bleeding, sleep disruption, hot flushes and sexual concerns.
Hormonal contraceptives are often prescribed for perimenopause symptoms but are not always adequate or preferred.
Other hormonal options exist, and treatment can be tailored through shared decision making.

items.title: Pharmacologic Treatments for Females With Menopausal Vasomotor Symptoms: A Clinical Guideline From the American College of Physicians
items.summary: The American College of Physicians reviewed the evidence on medicines for menopausal hot flushes and night sweats and set out a step-by-step order of treatments. Estrogen (with a progestogen if the woman has a uterus) is recommended first. If that cannot be used or is not tolerated, several non-hormonal medicines are suggested as second and third choices. The guideline says the choice should be made together with a clinician, weighing benefits, harms, cost and personal preferences.
keyPoints: First choice: estrogen combined with progestogen for women with a uterus, or estrogen alone for women without a uterus (strong recommendation, high-certainty evidence).
Second choice if first-line treatment is not suitable or not tolerated: the antidepressants desvenlafaxine or venlafaxine (conditional recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence).
Third choice: escitalopram or paroxetine (low-certainty evidence), gabapentin (low-certainty evidence), or elinzanetant or fezolinetant (moderate-certainty evidence).
Treatment should be chosen through shared decision-making that covers benefits, harms, contraindications, other health conditions, preferences, cost and access.

items.title: Non-hormonal management of menopause symptoms-the statement of the European Society of Gynecology
items.summary: The European Society of Gynecology reviewed the evidence on treating menopause symptoms without hormones, such as hot flushes, poor sleep, low mood and vaginal dryness. It found that lifestyle changes are the foundation of care, and that newer medicines called neurokinin receptor antagonists (fezolinetant and elinzanetant) are the most effective non-hormonal drugs for hot flushes. Talking therapies like cognitive behavioral therapy and clinical hypnosis can ease the distress from hot flushes and help sleep. Evidence for complementary approaches such as yoga, acupuncture and black cohosh ranges from moderate to limited.
keyPoints: Healthy diet, regular exercise, weight control, sleep hygiene and behavioral approaches are the foundation of menopause care.

Fezolinetant and elinzanetant are the most effective evidence-based non-hormonal medicines for hot flushes; antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs), gabapentin, clonidine, oxybutynin and pregabalin work to varying degrees.
Cognitive behavioral therapy and clinical hypnosis reduce hot flush distress and improve sleep and quality of life.
For vaginal and urinary symptoms, lubricants, moisturizers, hyaluronic acid products and pelvic floor training help, but evidence does not support routine use of vaginal laser therapy.

items.title: Fezolinetant and Elinzanetant Therapy for Menopausal Women Experiencing Vasomotor Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled seven randomised trials (4,087 women) that compared two non-hormonal medicines, fezolinetant and elinzanetant, with placebo for hot flushes and night sweats in menopause. Both medicines reduced how often and how severe the symptoms were. Elinzanetant showed a larger effect and also improved sleep quality.
keyPoints: Both fezolinetant (30 mg and 45 mg) and elinzanetant (120 mg) reduced how often hot flushes and night sweats happened compared with placebo.
Both medicines also reduced the severity of these symptoms, with elinzanetant showing the largest effect.
Elinzanetant 120 mg improved sleep quality.
The abstract reports results were consistent across trials, and it does not give an overall certainty rating.

items.title: Investigating the effects of probiotics during the menopause transition: A systematic review & meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 39 studies with 3,187 women around the time of menopause to see whether probiotics (supplements with 'friendly' bacteria) help with menopause symptoms. Combining 7 trials that compared probiotics with placebo, probiotics were linked to fewer hot flushes and night sweats, less vaginal dryness and better mood-related symptoms. They did not clearly help physical (somatic) or sexual symptoms. The authors say the studies had a high risk of bias, so more careful research is needed before firm conclusions.
keyPoints: In 7 placebo-controlled trials, probiotics were linked to a large reduction in hot flushes and night sweats (vasomotor symptoms).
Probiotics also improved vaginal dryness, psychological symptoms and vaginal microbiome health, but not somatic or sexual symptoms.
Probiotics may improve how well and how safely estriol and isoflavones work.
The included studies had a high risk of bias, so the findings are promising but need confirming.

items.title: Effects of soy isoflavones on menopausal symptoms in perimenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 trials to see whether soy isoflavones, plant compounds with weak estrogen-like effects, ease symptoms in women going through perimenopause. Overall menopausal symptom scores improved a little, with clearer benefits for headache, palpitations, low mood and psychosocial symptoms. No clear benefit was seen for hot flushes, night sweats, insomnia or fatigue. The authors say the results should be treated with caution because the studies were small and more trials are needed.
keyPoints: Soy isoflavones modestly improved overall menopausal symptom scores in seven studies with 533 women.
They helped with headache, palpitations, psychosocial symptoms and depression.
No significant effect was found for hot flushes, excessive sweating, insomnia, fatigue or vasomotor symptoms overall.
The authors urge caution because of small sample sizes and call for more trials.

items.title: International Menopause Society (IMS) recommendations and key messages on women's midlife health and menopause
items.summary: The International Menopause Society reviewed the research on midlife health and menopause and wrote new guidance for healthcare professionals. It covers hot flushes and night sweats, vaginal and urinary symptoms of menopause, early menopause (premature ovarian insufficiency), bone health, heart health and more. The abstract describes how the guidance was built but does not list the individual recommendations.
keyPoints: The guidance contains 342 recommendations (285 backed by research and 57 good practice points) and 40 key messages.
Topics include hot flushes and night sweats, genitourinary syndrome of menopause, premature ovarian insufficiency, osteoporosis, cardiometabolic health and dementia.
It covers menopause hormone therapy (estrogens, progestogens and combined treatments) and alternatives, and takes account of differences in care between countries.
A new section looks at sarcopenia (loss of muscle), which the authors say needs urgent attention.

items.title: Systematic review and network meta-analysis comparing the efficacy of fezolinetant with hormone and nonhormone therapies for treatment of vasomotor symptoms due to menopause
items.summary: This review pooled results from many trials to compare fezolinetant, a newer non-hormone medicine, with hormone therapy and other non-hormone treatments for moderate to severe hot flushes and night sweats after menopause. Fezolinetant cut the number of daily hot flushes about as well as the hormone therapies studied, and more than the non-hormone options paroxetine, desvenlafaxine and gabapentin. Two hormone options, tibolone and conjugated estrogens with bazedoxifene, worked better on some measures, but neither is available in the United States at the dose studied.
keyPoints: Fezolinetant 45 mg did not differ significantly from any of the 27 hormone therapy regimens in reducing how often hot flushes happened.
Fezolinetant reduced daily hot flush frequency significantly more than paroxetine 7.5 mg, desvenlafaxine, gabapentin ER 1800 mg and placebo.
Tibolone 2.5 mg reduced hot flush severity more than fezolinetant, and tibolone and conjugated estrogens/bazedoxifene had higher rates of a 75% or greater reduction.
The authors say the findings may help guide individual treatment choices for bothersome hot flushes.

items.title: Efficacy of plant-derived dietary supplements in improving overall menopausal symptoms in women: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many placebo-controlled trials of plant-based supplements (such as soy and red clover) in women going through or past menopause. Women taking the supplements had fewer hot flushes and better scores on menopause symptom questionnaires than women taking a placebo. However, the quality of the studies was mixed and they differed a lot from each other, so the authors say more rigorous research is needed.
keyPoints: Plant-derived supplements improved overall menopausal symptom scores compared with placebo.
Daily hot flush frequency was also lower in the supplement groups than in the placebo groups.
About 76% of the studies were of fair or good quality, while 24% were of low quality.
The authors note the evidence is generally of suboptimal quality and varies between studies, so more rigorous trials are needed.

items.title: Effects of nutritional interventions on the severity of depressive and anxiety symptoms of women in the menopausal transition and menopause: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression
items.summary: This review pooled 32 placebo-controlled trials of diet changes, food supplements and nutraceuticals in women going through the menopause transition or after menopause. On average, women taking the nutritional interventions had somewhat lower depression and anxiety scores than those on placebo. However, the studies differed a lot and had a risk of bias, so it is still unclear how well any one approach really works.
keyPoints: Overall, nutritional interventions were linked to lower depressive and anxiety symptoms compared with placebo.
The type and length of the nutritional intervention did not clearly change the size of the effect.
Older age was the only factor that predicted a bigger effect.
Results varied widely and had a risk of bias, so the real effect of different approaches remains unclear.

items.title: Black cohosh extracts in women with menopausal symptoms: an updated pairwise meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 22 randomised trials with 2,310 menopausal women to see whether black cohosh extracts ease menopausal symptoms. Compared with placebo, black cohosh was linked to better overall symptoms, fewer hot flushes and fewer physical symptoms. It did not clearly improve anxiety or low mood. The authors describe the benefits as potential rather than certain.
keyPoints: Black cohosh extracts improved overall menopausal symptoms compared with placebo.
Hot flushes and physical (somatic) symptoms improved with black cohosh.
No clear improvement was found for anxiety or depressive symptoms.
Women stopped taking black cohosh at about the same rate as placebo.

items.title: The Efficacy of Dienogest in Reducing Disease and Pain Recurrence After Endometriosis Surgery: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine studies (1,668 patients) to see whether dienogest, a hormone tablet, helps stop endometriosis coming back after surgery. Dienogest reduced the return of endometriosis cysts compared with placebo and worked about as well as GnRH agonist drugs. Compared with GnRH agonists, dienogest caused fewer hot flashes but more spotting and weight gain.
keyPoints: Dienogest lowered the rate of endometriosis cyst recurrence after surgery compared with placebo.
Dienogest and GnRH agonists had similar recurrence rates.
Pain at 6 months tended to be lower with dienogest than placebo, and individual studies reported a clear reduction.
Compared with GnRH agonists, dienogest caused fewer hot flashes and a trend toward less vaginal dryness, but more spotting and weight gain.

items.title: The Effect of Salvia Officinalis on Hot Flashes in Postmenopausal Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: International Journal of Community Based Nursing and Midwifery
items.journal: International Journal of Community Based Nursing and Midwifery
items.summary: This review pooled four small trials (310 women in total) testing sage (Salvia officinalis), a herbal remedy, for hot flushes after menopause. All four trials reported fewer and milder hot flushes with sage, but when the results were combined, the benefit for how often flushes happened was reported as significant versus placebo, while the effect on severity was not. The authors say sage may help reduce how often hot flushes occur, but more research is needed to confirm this.
keyPoints: Four trials with 310 postmenopausal women were included.
All four trials reported that sage reduced how often and how severe hot flushes were.
Combined results showed an effect on frequency compared with placebo, but not on severity.
The authors suggest wider use of sage only if further studies confirm the findings.

items.title: Effects of Omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids Intake on Vasomotor Symptoms, Sleep Quality and Depression in Postmenopausal Women: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at nine randomized trials of omega-3 fatty acid supplements (such as fish oil) in postmenopausal women. It checked whether they ease hot flashes and night sweats, improve sleep, or lift low mood. Four studies hinted at some benefit for hot flashes and night sweats, but sleep results varied and the depression evidence was inconclusive. Overall, the studies did not provide strong evidence that omega-3 helps, and larger, better-designed trials are needed.
keyPoints: Four of nine studies found possible benefits of omega-3 for hot flashes and night sweats.
Sleep quality results were mixed across the studies.
Evidence on depression was inconclusive.
Overall, there was not enough strong evidence that omega-3 improves hot flashes, sleep or mood; larger trials are needed.

items.title: The role of ovarian hormones in the pathophysiology of perimenopausal sleep disturbances: A systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 86 studies on how ovarian hormones affect sleep around the menopause. Results from good-quality studies suggest that the drop in estrogen and progesterone contributes to sleep problems. Starting estrogen and/or progesterone treatment at the right time improved overall sleep quality. The hormones seem to help both directly in the brain and indirectly, for example by easing hot flushes and night sweats.
keyPoints: The fall in estrogen and progesterone around menopause contributes to sleep disturbances.
Timely treatment with estrogen and/or progesterone therapy improved overall sleep quality.
The hormones may improve sleep directly through the brain and body, and indirectly by reducing vasomotor symptoms like hot flushes.
More studies on the underlying brain pathways are still needed.

items.title: Review & meta-analysis: isopropanolic black cohosh extract iCR for menopausal symptoms - an update on the evidence
items.summary: This review pulled together 35 clinical studies and one earlier meta-analysis, covering 43,759 women, to look at a black cohosh extract (iCR) for menopausal symptoms. Compared with placebo, the extract eased symptoms such as hot flushes and low mood, and higher doses seemed to work better. It worked about as well as low-dose estrogen patches or tibolone, with few mild side effects. The authors conclude it can be an evidence-based option, including for women who cannot use hormones.
keyPoints: iCR beat placebo for physical (neurovegetative) and psychological menopausal symptoms.
Higher doses, or iCR combined with St. John's wort, gave larger benefits; the combination did better for mood symptoms.
Effect was comparable to low-dose transdermal estradiol or tibolone, with better tolerability than tibolone.
Side effects were few and minor, similar to placebo, with no sign of liver harm and no effect on hormone levels, breast or womb lining.

items.title: Efficacy of Micronized Progesterone for Sleep: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trial Data
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This review pooled 9 randomized trials (388 people) testing micronized progesterone, a body-identical form of the hormone, against placebo for sleep. Most trials were in women after menopause. Progesterone improved some sleep measures, such as how quickly people fell asleep, but results were inconsistent across studies. Some trials also gave estrogen or saw hot flushes improve, which makes it harder to know how much of the benefit came from progesterone alone.
keyPoints: Micronized progesterone improved various sleep outcomes compared with placebo in randomized trials, mostly in postmenopausal women.
In a pooled analysis of 4 trials, progesterone helped people fall asleep faster, but total sleep time and sleep efficiency did not clearly improve.
Self-reported sleep improved in most trials, though results varied between studies.
Estrogen use and better hot flushes in some trials limit firm conclusions; larger studies of progesterone alone are needed.

items.title: Evaluation of Clinical Meaningfulness of Red Clover (Trifolium pratense L.) Extract to Relieve Hot Flushes and Menopausal Symptoms in Peri- and Post-Menopausal Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from eight trials (ten comparisons) of red clover extract, which contains plant compounds called isoflavones, in women going through perimenopause or after menopause. Women taking red clover had about 1.7 fewer hot flushes per day than those taking a placebo. The effect looked bigger in postmenopausal women with five or more hot flushes a day, in studies lasting 12 weeks, with doses of 80 mg a day or more, and with products higher in a compound called biochanin A. The authors say more well-designed studies are needed to confirm these findings.
keyPoints: Red clover extract reduced hot flushes by about 1.7 per day compared with placebo.
The benefit was clearer in postmenopausal women with five or more hot flushes daily.
Stronger results were seen with 12-week follow-up, doses of 80 mg/day or more, and higher biochanin A content.
The authors call for further well-designed studies to confirm the effect.

items.title: Exercise and Quality of Life in Women with Menopausal Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review pooled nine randomized trials comparing any type of exercise with no active treatment in women with menopausal symptoms. Exercise improved physical and psychological quality of life scores. There was no clear evidence of benefit for general, social or menopause-specific quality of life, and yoga did not significantly improve hot flush (vasomotor) quality of life scores. The authors say better-designed studies are needed to confirm these findings.
keyPoints: Exercise improved physical and psychological quality of life in women with menopausal symptoms.
No evidence of an effect on general, social or menopause-specific quality of life.
Yoga improved physical quality of life but not general, psychological, sexual or vasomotor symptom scores.
Pelvic floor muscle training did not significantly improve general quality of life.

items.title: Interventions to Address Sexual Problems in People With Cancer: American Society of Clinical Oncology Clinical Practice Guideline Adaptation of Cancer Care Ontario Guideline
items.summary: This guideline from the American Society of Clinical Oncology covers sexual problems that can follow a cancer diagnosis or its treatment. It recommends that the health care team start a conversation about sexual health and offer counselling to everyone with cancer. For women with vaginal dryness or thinning, it suggests trying lubricants and moisturizers first, and it lists other options for some cases. Women and men with hot flushes and night sweats should be offered help, using talking therapies or certain medicines.
keyPoints: A member of the health care team should start a discussion about sexual health with every patient affected by cancer or its treatment.
Counselling should be offered to all patients with cancer to help with sexual response, body image, intimacy and relationships.
For vaginal or vulval dryness and thinning, lubricants plus vaginal moisturizers may be tried first; low-dose vaginal estrogen, lidocaine and DHEA may be considered in some cases.
For hot flushes and night sweats, options include cognitive behavioral therapy, slow breathing, hypnosis, and medicines such as venlafaxine and gabapentin.

items.title: The 2017 hormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society
items.summary: The North American Menopause Society reviewed new research and updated its guidance on menopausal hormone therapy. Hormone therapy is still the most effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats and for vaginal and urinary symptoms of menopause, and it helps prevent bone loss and fractures. The balance of benefits and risks looks best for women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause, and less favourable for those who start later. Risks depend on the type, dose, route and timing of treatment, so choices are tailored to each person.
keyPoints: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for hot flushes, night sweats and genitourinary symptoms of menopause, and it prevents bone loss and fracture.
For women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause with no contraindications, benefits outweigh risks most clearly for bothersome hot flushes and for those at higher risk of bone loss or fracture.
Starting hormone therapy more than 10 years after menopause or at age 60 or older looks less favourable because of higher absolute risks of heart disease, stroke, blood clots and dementia.
For vaginal symptoms not relieved by over-the-counter products, low-dose vaginal estrogen or other therapies are recommended; longer treatment needs a documented reason and regular review.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 698 Summary: Hormone Therapy in Primary Ovarian Insufficiency
items.summary: This guidance from a major obstetrics and gynecology body covers primary ovarian insufficiency, where the ovaries slow down or stop working much earlier than usual. It says hormone therapy is an effective way to ease symptoms like hot flushes and to lower long-term health risks, if there is no reason a woman cannot take it. The abstract notes there is not enough data comparing different hormone regimens in this group.
keyPoints: Primary ovarian insufficiency can lead to hot flushes and night sweats, thinning of vaginal and urinary tissues, bone loss and fractures, heart disease, and a higher risk of death from any cause.
Hormone therapy, taken by mouth or through the skin to reach normal estrogen levels, is recommended as the first approach unless there are contraindications.
Combined hormonal contraceptives prevent pregnancy more reliably than hormone therapy, which matters for women who want to avoid pregnancy, since spontaneous pregnancy is possible but unlikely.
Treatment is recommended until the average age of natural menopause (about 50-51 years), alongside ongoing, comprehensive care.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 698: Hormone Therapy in Primary Ovarian Insufficiency
items.summary: This guidance from a major US obstetrics and gynecology body looks at hormone therapy for women with primary ovarian insufficiency, where the ovaries slow down or stop working much earlier than usual. It says that, unless there is a reason not to, systemic hormone therapy is an effective way to treat symptoms of low estrogen, such as hot flushes, and to lower long-term risks to bones and the heart. The abstract notes that studies comparing different hormone regimens in this group are lacking.
keyPoints: Hormone therapy (by mouth or through the skin) that reaches replacement levels of estrogen is recommended as the first-line approach if there are no contraindications.
Hormone therapy helps treat hot flushes and other low-estrogen symptoms and lowers the risk of osteoporosis, heart disease and urogenital atrophy.
Treatment should continue until the average age of natural menopause, around 50 to 51 years.
Combined hormonal contraceptives prevent pregnancy more reliably than hormone therapy, which matters for women who want to avoid pregnancy.

items.title: Chinese herbal medicine for menopausal symptoms
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 22 trials (2,902 women) of Chinese herbal medicine for menopause symptoms such as hot flushes and night sweats. Compared with placebo (a dummy treatment), the herbs made little or no difference to hot flushes or night sweats in most results. It was also unclear how they compared with hormone therapy, and safety findings were inconclusive. The quality of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate.
keyPoints: There was not enough evidence that Chinese herbal medicine works better or worse than placebo or hormone therapy for hot flushes and night sweats.
Most pooled results against placebo showed little or no difference in daily hot flushes.
Side effects reported with the herbs included mild diarrhoea, breast tenderness, stomach discomfort and an unpleasant taste, but safety results were inconclusive.
The authors say better-designed randomised trials are needed.

items.title: Use of Plant-Based Therapies and Menopausal Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 62 trials with 6,653 women to see whether plant-based therapies ease menopause symptoms. Phytoestrogens (plant compounds that act a little like oestrogen), including soy isoflavones, were linked to modest drops in hot flushes and vaginal dryness, but not night sweats. Most of the trials were of poor quality, so the evidence is not strong and more rigorous studies are needed.
keyPoints: Phytoestrogens were linked to about 1 fewer hot flush per day on average, a modest reduction.
Phytoestrogens were also linked to a small improvement in vaginal dryness scores.
No significant reduction in night sweats was found.
About three in four of the trials (74%) had a high risk of bias in several areas, so the evidence is uncertain.

items.title: Bioidentical hormones for women with vasomotor symptoms
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 23 trials (5779 women) of bioidentical estrogen (17 beta-estradiol, chemically identical to the body's own estrogen) for menopausal hot flushes. Compared with placebo, it reduced hot flushes in patch, gel, oral and nasal forms, but side effects like headache, breast tenderness and vaginal bleeding were more common with some forms. The evidence was mostly low to moderate quality, and no clear difference was found between bioidentical and conjugated equine estrogen.
keyPoints: Bioidentical estradiol worked better than placebo for moderate to severe hot flushes, though the evidence was low to moderate quality.

Side effects such as headache, vaginal bleeding, breast tenderness and skin reactions were more common with patches, gel and nasal forms; oral and topical emulsion showed no clear difference from placebo.
Higher doses may work better but may also cause more side effects.
No good evidence showed bioidentical hormones differ in effectiveness from conjugated equine estrogen, and long-term safety (heart attack, stroke, breast cancer) has not yet been studied.

items.title: Efficacy of phytoestrogens for menopausal symptoms: a meta-analysis and systematic review
items.summary: This review pooled 15 randomized trials of plant-based oestrogen supplements (phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones) taken by the mouth by women going through or past menopause. Women taking phytoestrogens had a small but statistically significant drop in the number of hot flushes each day compared with placebo. Overall menopausal symptom scores did not improve significantly, and side-effects were not significantly different from placebo.
keyPoints: Phytoestrogens reduced daily hot flush frequency more than placebo (10 studies).
Overall menopausal symptom scores (Kupperman index) showed no significant difference from placebo (7 studies).
No significant difference in side-effects between phytoestrogens and placebo (5 studies).
The authors concluded phytoestrogens appear to reduce hot flushes without serious side-effects.

items.title: Add-back therapy with GnRH analogues for uterine fibroids
items.summary: This review looked at women with uterine fibroids who take GnRH analogue medicines, which can cause menopause-like side effects such as hot flushes and bone loss. It checked whether adding a second medicine (add-back therapy) helps. Some add-backs, such as tibolone, seemed to protect bone density and reduce hot flushes, but the evidence was mostly low or moderate quality, trials lasted six months at most, and some add-backs were linked to larger uterine volume.
keyPoints: Tibolone, raloxifene, estriol and ipriflavone may help preserve bone density, based on low or moderate quality evidence.
Four studies reported a large benefit of tibolone on hot flushes and other vasomotor symptoms; the authors also say medroxyprogesterone (MPA) may reduce them.
Larger uterine volume was a side effect linked to some add-backs (MPA, tibolone and conjugated estrogens), and tibolone may have caused more uterine bleeding.
All studies lasted six months or less, which is too short to show effects on bone fractures; for several comparisons the results were unclear or not reported.

items.title: Dehydroepiandrosterone for women in the peri- or postmenopausal phase
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 28 trials with 1273 women in perimenopause or after menopause to see whether DHEA (a hormone precursor) helps menopausal symptoms. DHEA did not improve quality of life and was linked to more acne and other male-hormone-type side effects than placebo. It was unclear whether it eases symptoms like hot flushes, though it may slightly improve sexual function. The overall quality of the studies was moderate to low.
keyPoints: DHEA did not improve quality of life compared with placebo (moderate quality evidence).
DHEA was linked to more androgenic side effects, mainly acne, than placebo (moderate quality evidence).
It is uncertain whether DHEA reduces menopausal symptoms because trial results were inconsistent.
DHEA may slightly improve sexual function compared with placebo.

items.title: Menopause and Common Dermatoses: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 40 studies on how menopause and menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) relate to common skin and hair conditions. Menopause appears to affect when these conditions start and how they behave, with hair loss most strongly linked to the years after menopause. MHT was linked to a higher risk of frontal fibrosing alopecia and rosacea, but results for other skin conditions were mixed or unclear. Most studies used older types of hormone therapy that are less common today, so the evidence is limited.
keyPoints: Hair loss (frontal fibrosing alopecia and female pattern hair loss) showed the strongest links to the time after menopause, with earlier or surgical menopause carrying greater risk.
Acne and rosacea generally improved after menopause, while psoriasis often persisted or worsened and melasma and hidradenitis suppurativa gave mixed or inconsistent results.
MHT was linked to a higher risk of frontal fibrosing alopecia and rosacea; findings for other skin conditions were variable or absent.
Most studies used MHT formulations that are less commonly used now, and more long-term, skin-focused research is needed.

items.title: Relationship between menopausal hormone therapy and incidence risk of breast cancer: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 34 studies to look at whether menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) is linked to breast cancer. Overall, MHT was linked to a modest increase in breast cancer risk. The increase was seen with combined estrogen-progestin therapy, but not with estrogen-only therapy. Results varied a lot between studies and regions.
keyPoints: Overall, MHT was linked to a modest but significant rise in breast cancer risk (OR 1.15).
The higher risk was confined to estrogen-progestin therapy (OR 1.44), while estrogen-only therapy showed no overall link (OR 1.00).
For estrogen-only therapy, randomized trials suggested a protective effect, while observational studies found no effect.
Risk differed by region and was highest among current users in Europe, so local factors may change the risk.

items.title: Long-term hormone therapy for perimenopausal and postmenopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 24 trials (45,660 women) to look at the long-term effects of taking hormone therapy for at least a year after menopause. Most of the results came from one large trial, mainly in women over 60. Combined oestrogen-plus-progestogen therapy probably raised breast cancer risk and may have raised stroke and blood clot risk, while oestrogen-only therapy probably raised stroke and gallbladder surgery risk. Both types probably lowered the risk of broken bones, and neither made much difference to heart attacks or other coronary events.
keyPoints: Combined hormone therapy probably makes little to no difference to coronary events but probably increases breast cancer risk (moderate-certainty evidence).
Combined therapy may increase stroke and venous thromboembolism (blood clots in the veins) risk (low-certainty evidence).
Oestrogen-only therapy probably makes little to no difference to coronary events or breast cancer, but probably increases stroke and gallbladder disease needing surgery.
Both types probably reduce the risk of all clinical fractures; the results come mostly from one trial of oral hormone therapy in mainly older women, so may not reflect current treatments.

items.title: Treatment Preferences in Patients With Hypothyroidism
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 11 randomised trials (1135 adults with hypothyroidism) that compared standard levothyroxine (L-T4) alone with combination treatment containing liothyronine (L-T3) or desiccated thyroid extract. About half of patients (52%) preferred the combination treatments, compared with 24% who preferred levothyroxine alone, and 24% had no preference. The authors conclude that patient preferences should be part of shared decision-making about treatment. The abstract reports preference only, not other outcomes or safety.
keyPoints: 52% of patients preferred combination therapy (L-T4 plus L-T3, or desiccated thyroid extract), 24% preferred levothyroxine alone, and 24% had no preference.
Patients were about twice as likely to prefer combination therapy over levothyroxine alone (relative risk 2.20), and the result held when the studies that differed most were removed.
The preference for combination therapy also held when only crossover studies were analysed.
The authors say patient preferences should be considered in shared decision-making about hypothyroidism treatment.

items.title: Safety of menopause hormone therapy in postmenopausal women at higher risk of venous thromboembolism: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 10 studies on menopause hormone therapy (MHT) in women who already have a higher chance of blood clots (venous thromboembolism). Transdermal estrogen, such as patches or gels, did not raise clot risk in these women. Oral estrogen alone had the next safest profile, and oral estrogen taken with a synthetic progestogen carried the highest clot risk. The studies differed a lot from one another, and the authors say newer data are needed to confirm the findings.
keyPoints: In women with risk factors for blood clots, transdermal estrogen was not linked to an increased clot risk.
Oral estrogen alone had the next safest profile.
Oral estrogen combined with a synthetic progestogen carried the highest increased risk of clots.
The 10 included studies varied in design, dose, route of MHT and type of clot risk factor, so more recent data are needed.

items.title: European society of endocrinology clinical practice guideline for evaluation and management of menopause and the perimenopause
items.summary: This is a clinical practice guideline from the European Society of Endocrinology on how menopause and the perimenopause should be assessed and managed. It covers women who go through menopause in middle age, women with premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) or early menopause, and women for whom hormones are not suitable, including those with or at high risk of breast cancer. It looks at the benefits and risks of hormone therapy, other treatments for symptoms, and whether hormone therapy helps prevent long-term disease. The abstract does not give specific findings or recommendations, so details need to be read in the full guideline.
keyPoints: About 25% of postmenopausal women are reported to have debilitating menopausal symptoms.
The guideline covers evaluation and management for midlife menopause, premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) and early menopause.
It discusses the benefits and risks of hormone therapy and other treatments, including options for women who cannot use hormones, such as those with or at high risk of breast cancer.
It also considers the debated question of whether menopausal hormone therapy can prevent chronic disease.

items.title: Hormone therapy in postmenopausal women and risk of endometrial hyperplasia or endometrial cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 72 trials with about 40,000 postmenopausal women to see how different hormone therapy types affect the lining of the womb (endometrial hyperplasia, a thickening that can sometimes lead to cancer). Estrogen taken alone probably raises the chance of this thickening compared with placebo or with estrogen plus progestogen. Continuous combined therapy may make little or no difference compared with placebo, though the evidence is less certain. There were too few cases of womb cancer to draw any conclusions.
keyPoints: Estrogen on its own probably increases the risk of womb lining thickening compared with placebo, both at one year and after one year (moderate-certainty evidence).
Estrogen alone probably carries a much higher risk of womb lining thickening than estrogen combined with a progestogen taken continuously (moderate-certainty evidence).

Continuous combined estrogen plus progestogen may have little to no effect on this risk compared with placebo, while sequential combined therapy may raise the risk at one year (low-certainty evidence).
Womb cancer was too rare in the trials to draw meaningful conclusions, and evidence on progestogen dose comparisons was too limited to be clear.

items.title: The benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy for the cardiovascular system in postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined 33 randomised trials with about 44,600 postmenopausal women to look at how menopause hormone therapy (MHT) affects the heart and blood vessels. Overall, MHT did not change the risk of death or heart events compared with placebo or no treatment, but it was linked to a higher risk of stroke and blood clots in the veins. Women who started MHT within 10 years of menopause had fewer deaths and heart events than those who started later, though the stroke and clot risks were not lower.
keyPoints: MHT made no significant difference to all-cause death or cardiovascular events overall.
MHT increased the risk of stroke (RR 1.23) and venous thromboembolism, or blood clots in the veins (RR 1.86).
Starting MHT within 10 years of menopause was linked to fewer deaths and heart events than starting later.
Estrogen-only therapy and combined estrogen plus progesterone gave similar heart-related outcomes.

items.title: A systematic review and critical appraisal of menopause guidelines
items.summary: Researchers searched for menopause guidelines published since 2015 and checked how good each one was. Of 26 documents, only five guidelines and one statement on non-hormonal treatments were of at least moderate quality. The best guidelines agreed that menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) is mainly for hot flushes and night sweats, and for low mood linked to menopause. Advice for women in perimenopause was limited.
keyPoints: The five higher-quality guidelines listed hot flushes and night sweats, disturbed sleep, joint and muscle pain, lower sexual desire and low mood as menopause-related symptoms.
Hot flushes and night sweats and menopause-related low mood were the only consistent reasons to use systemic hormone therapy.
No guideline recommended hormone therapy for memory or thinking symptoms, or to prevent other long-term diseases; some supported it for bone health but gave little specific guidance.

Non-hormonal options for hot flushes included a neurokinin 3B antagonist, certain antidepressants (SSRIs/SNRIs) and gabapentin; cognitive behavioural therapy and hypnosis were also seen as possibly helpful.

items.title: The unique risk factor profile of triple-negative breast cancer: a comprehensive meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
items.journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
items.summary: This review pooled results from 33 studies to see which known breast cancer risk factors are linked to triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), a type with a poorer outlook. Family history, longer use of the contraceptive pill and denser breasts were linked to higher TNBC risk. Later first period, later first birth and breastfeeding were linked to lower risk. Menopausal hormone therapy was not significantly linked to TNBC overall.
keyPoints: Family history, longer oral contraceptive use and higher breast density were linked to a higher risk of TNBC.
Later age at first period, later age at first birth and breastfeeding were linked to a lower risk of TNBC.
Menopausal hormone therapy, alcohol, smoking and body mass index were not significantly linked to TNBC overall.
Higher number of births was linked to higher TNBC risk among Black women, but not overall.

items.title: Hormonal Treatments and Vaginal Moisturizers for Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause : A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pooled 46 trials of treatments for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which includes vaginal dryness, painful sex and urinary symptoms. Vaginal estrogen, vaginal DHEA, oral ospemifene and vaginal moisturizers may ease some symptoms in the short term. The evidence is mostly low certainty, and most trials lasted 12 weeks or less. Few long-term data exist, and the studies were too short to rule out rare serious harms.
keyPoints: Vaginal estrogen may improve vaginal dryness, painful sex, the most bothersome symptom and treatment satisfaction.
Vaginal DHEA, oral ospemifene and vaginal moisturizers may also improve dryness and some other symptoms, but the certainty of evidence is low.
Vaginal testosterone, systemic DHEA, vaginal oxytocin, and oral raloxifene or bazedoxifene may give no benefit or have uncertain effects.
Serious harms were not frequently reported, but most studies were short and too small to detect rare serious harms.

items.title: British Gynaecological Cancer Society and British Menopause Society guidelines: Management of menopausal symptoms following treatment of gynaecological cancer
items.source: British Gynaecological Cancer Society and British Menopause Society
items.organisation: British Gynaecological Cancer Society and British Menopause Society
items.summary: Two UK specialist societies wrote joint guidelines on managing menopausal symptoms after treatment for gynaecological cancer. Cancer treatments such as surgery, pelvic radiotherapy, chemotherapy and endocrine therapy can all affect the ovaries and bring on menopausal symptoms. The guidelines look at the benefits and risks of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for each cancer type, including which type to use and when to start after treatment. Vaginal estrogen is described as very effective for urogenital symptoms and safe for most women, and other options besides HRT are also covered.
keyPoints: Surgery, pelvic radiotherapy, chemotherapy and endocrine therapy can all affect ovarian function and cause menopausal symptoms.
The benefits and risks of HRT are considered cancer type by cancer type, with guidance on the type of HRT and the best time to start after treatment.
Vaginal estrogens can be very effective for urogenital symptoms and are safe for most women, including many who cannot use systemic HRT, with rare exceptions.
Alternatives to HRT, both medicines and non-drug approaches, are reviewed.

items.title: Effects of transdermal versus oral hormone replacement therapy in postmenopause: a systematic review
items.summary: This review compared hormone replacement therapy (HRT) taken through the skin (patches or gels) with HRT taken by mouth in women after menopause. It looked at 51 studies covering heart health, blood clots, cholesterol, blood sugar, bone strength and cancer risk. The two routes looked similar for most of these, but blood clot risk was clearly higher with tablets. The authors say the overall evidence is limited and of low quality.
keyPoints: Oral and transdermal HRT looked similar for bone density, blood sugar and cholesterol improvements.
They did not appear different for breast cancer, endometrial disease or cardiovascular risk.
The clearest difference was venous thromboembolism (blood clots in the veins), which was higher with oral HRT.
The authors conclude transdermal HRT may be safer than oral HRT, but the evidence is limited and of low quality.

items.title: The Women's Health Initiative randomized trials of menopausal hormone therapy and breast cancer: findings in context
items.summary: This review looked at how menopausal hormone therapy relates to breast cancer, comparing large observational studies with the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) randomised trials, and responding to criticisms of the WHI findings. In the trials, estrogen taken alone by women who had had a hysterectomy lowered breast cancer cases and deaths. Estrogen combined with a progestin raised breast cancer cases, and the higher risk lasted for about two decades. The authors say women thinking about estrogen plus progestin for hot flushes and night sweats should understand this breast cancer risk.
keyPoints: In the WHI randomised trials, estrogen alone in women with a prior hysterectomy decreased breast cancer incidence and mortality.
Estrogen plus progestin increased breast cancer incidence, and the increase persisted through two decades.
Observational studies linked both estrogen alone and estrogen plus progestin to more breast cancer, which differs from the WHI result for estrogen alone.
Women considering estrogen plus progestin for vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes and night sweats) should understand the breast cancer risk.

items.title: Is Hormone Replacement Therapy a Risk Factor or a Therapeutic Option for Alzheimer's Disease?
items.summary: This systematic review looked at studies in women to see whether hormone replacement therapy (HRT) affects the risk of Alzheimer's disease and memory problems. Two thirds of Alzheimer's cases are in women, and the drop in estrogen at menopause may play a part. The studies gave mixed results, with HRT showing both helpful and harmful effects. Whether HRT helps or harms seems to depend on things like when it is started, a person's genes and heart health, and the dose, type and length of treatment.
keyPoints: Women make up about two thirds of Alzheimer's cases, and menopause may be linked to a higher risk.
Evidence shows HRT can have both a helpful and a harmful effect on dementia risk.
The effect of HRT may depend on the age it is started, genotype, cardiovascular health, dose, formulation and duration.
More research is needed to understand which factors change HRT's effects on the brain.

items.title: Menopause hormone therapy and urinary symptoms: a systematic review
items.summary: This systematic review looked at randomized trials of menopause hormone therapy and urinary symptoms such as burning when peeing, urgency, frequency, leaks and repeat urinary tract infections (UTIs). It found not enough evidence to say that menopause itself causes urinary symptoms. The effect of hormone therapy depended on the type: vaginal estrogen helped urinary symptoms, while systemic hormone therapy (taken through the whole body) may cause leaks or make existing symptoms worse.
keyPoints: There is insufficient evidence to confirm that menopause is linked to urinary symptoms.
Vaginal estrogen improves burning when peeing (dysuria), frequency, urge and stress incontinence, and recurrent UTIs in menopausal women.
Vaginal estrogen decreases the risk of recurrent UTI in postmenopausal women.
Systemic hormone therapy may cause urinary incontinence or worsen existing urinary symptoms.

items.title: Safety of systemic hormone replacement therapy in breast cancer survivors: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled four randomised trials with about 4,050 women who had survived breast cancer. It looked at whether taking systemic hormone replacement therapy (estrogen with progestogen, or tibolone) for menopause symptoms changed the chance of the cancer coming back. Women who took HRT had a higher risk of recurrence than those on placebo or no HRT. The increase was clearer in women whose cancer was hormone receptor-positive.
keyPoints: HRT was linked to a higher risk of breast cancer coming back compared with placebo or no HRT (HR 1.46).
The higher risk was seen in hormone receptor-positive disease (HR 1.8).
No clear increase was found in hormone receptor-negative disease (HR 1.19, not statistically significant).
The authors conclude that other ways to ease menopause symptoms should be offered to breast cancer survivors.

items.title: Eligibility criteria for Menopausal Hormone Therapy (MHT): a position statement from a consortium of scientific societies for the use of MHT in women with medical conditions. MHT Eligibility Criteria Group
items.summary: A group of scientific societies, led by the Spanish Menopause Society, built a set of eligibility criteria for menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) in women with medical conditions. They based it on 14 systematic reviews and 32 meta-analyses, plus an expert panel. The conditions covered included age, time since menopause, past blood clots or heart disease, metabolic syndrome, gut conditions, past cancer and smoking. Each situation is placed in a category from 'no restriction' to 'should not be used', with the quality of the evidence rated.
keyPoints: This is the first MHT eligibility tool built on clinical evidence, modelled on the ones already used for contraception.
Categories follow WHO wording: 1 = no restriction, 2 = benefits outweigh risks, 3 = risks generally outweigh benefits, 4 = should not be used.
Safety was reviewed for age, time since menopause, treatment length, clotting risk, heart disease, metabolic syndrome, gut disease, cancer survivors and smoking.
Evidence quality was graded high, moderate, low or very low; where no direct evidence existed, 'expert opinion' was used.

items.title: Hormone Therapy for the Primary Prevention of Chronic Conditions in Postmenopausal Persons: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force
items.summary: This review pooled results from 20 trials and 3 large cohort studies to look at hormone therapy taken after menopause to try to prevent long-term conditions such as heart disease, bone fractures and cancer. Hormone therapy lowered the risk of some problems, such as fractures and diabetes, but raised the risk of others, such as blood clots, stroke and gallbladder disease. The authors concluded that it brings some benefits and also an increased risk of harms.
keyPoints: Estrogen alone, compared with placebo, was linked to fewer cases of diabetes and fractures.
Estrogen plus progestin was linked to fewer cases of colorectal cancer, diabetes and fractures.
Both types were linked to more gallbladder disease, stroke, blood clots and urinary incontinence; estrogen plus progestin also showed more invasive breast cancer and probable dementia.
Overall, hormone therapy for preventing chronic conditions had some benefits but also increased the risk of harms.

items.title: Menopausal hormone therapy and women's health: An umbrella review
