items.summary: This review pulled together results from 60 earlier systematic reviews on menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), covering many different health outcomes. In trials, MHT clearly reduced how often and how severe hot flushes and night sweats were, and it also lowered the risk of fractures. It was also linked to higher risks of stroke and blood clots, so the overall picture is a mix of benefits and harms. The authors say the quality of the evidence is only moderate to poor, and the review could not show how effects differ by dose, type, or when treatment starts.
keyPoints: In trials, MHT reduced the frequency of hot flushes and night sweats (risk ratio 0.43) and their severity (risk ratio 0.29).
MHT lowered the risk of fractures overall, and was also beneficial for vaginal dryness (vaginal estrogen) and sexual function.
MHT increased the risk of stroke and venous thromboembolism (blood clots), along with some other conditions such as gallbladder disease needing surgery.

Observational studies linked MHT to higher risks of breast and ovarian cancer, and estrogen-alone versus estrogen-plus-progestin therapy had opposite effects on some outcomes such as endometrial cancer.

items.title: Investigation on factors associated with ovarian cancer: an umbrella review of systematic review and meta-analyses
items.summary: This review pulled together results from many earlier reviews and meta-analyses to find what is linked to ovarian cancer. Hormone therapy (estrogen alone, estrogen with progesterone, and overall) was linked to a slightly higher chance of ovarian cancer. Breastfeeding was linked to a lower chance, and several other factors (such as obesity, smoking, and some conditions) were linked to a higher chance. These are links seen in studies, and the abstract does not say how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Estrogen, estrogen-progesterone, and overall hormone therapy were linked to a higher rate of ovarian cancer (reported RR about 1.06 for hormone therapy).
Breastfeeding was linked to a lower risk of ovarian cancer (OR about 0.72).
Diabetes, endometriosis, polycystic ovarian syndrome, obesity, smoking, and perineal talc use were linked to a higher risk.
Coffee, egg, and fat intake were linked to a higher risk, and some gene variations also raised risk.

items.title: Hormone replacement therapy after surgery for epithelial ovarian cancer
items.summary: This review looked at whether hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is safe and helpful for women who had surgery for epithelial ovarian cancer and then went through menopause. It found only three small trials with 350 women in total. HRT may slightly improve overall survival and may make little or no difference to the cancer coming back or progressing. The evidence is low or very low quality, so the results should be treated with caution.
keyPoints: HRT may slightly improve overall survival after surgery for epithelial ovarian cancer (low-certainty evidence).
HRT may make little or no difference to progression-free survival (low-certainty evidence).
Researchers are uncertain about effects on quality of life, breast cancer, stroke, mini-stroke and heart attack because the evidence was very low quality.
The evidence is too limited to say whether or not HRT is very harmful in this group, and better trials are needed.

items.title: Guidelines for the Evaluation and Treatment of Perimenopausal Depression: Summary and Recommendations
items.summary: An expert panel reviewed the published research to create guidelines on spotting and treating depression during perimenopause, the years around the menopause transition. Most women who have a major depressive episode at this stage have had depression before, and low mood often comes alongside hot flushes, sleep problems and life stresses. Standard depression treatments, such as antidepressants and talking therapy, are the first choice. Estrogen may also help mood in some perimenopausal women, especially those with hot flushes, but it is not approved for treating depression.
keyPoints: Most midlife women with a major depressive episode in perimenopause have had depression before.
Depression often appears together with menopause symptoms such as hot flushes and poor sleep, which can overlap and make diagnosis harder.
Antidepressants and psychotherapy are the front-line treatments for perimenopausal depression.
Estrogen therapy shows antidepressant effects in perimenopausal women, particularly those with hot flushes, but data on estrogen plus progestin are sparse and inconclusive.

items.title: Pharmacological Management of Osteoporosis in Postmenopausal Women: An Endocrine Society* Clinical Practice Guideline
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: The Endocrine Society wrote this guideline on using medicines to treat osteoporosis (thinning, fragile bones) after menopause. The writing group looked at clinical trial evidence and real-world experience, and also considered what patients prefer and how well people stick with treatment. They agreed on four main principles for care. Several medicines can lower the chance of broken bones, with acceptable benefits and safety.
keyPoints: A woman's future fracture risk should be worked out using assessment tools suited to her country, to guide treatment decisions.
Patient preferences should be part of treatment planning.
Healthy eating, lifestyle changes and fall prevention should go alongside any osteoporosis medicine to help lower fracture risk.
Several different medicines can reduce fractures in postmenopausal women at risk, with acceptable balance of benefits and risks.

items.title: Safety and efficacy of testosterone for women: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trial data
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 36 randomised trials (8,480 women) of testosterone treatment lasting at least 12 weeks. In postmenopausal women, testosterone improved sexual desire, arousal, orgasm and pleasure, and reduced distress about sex, compared with placebo or other treatment. Testosterone taken by mouth raised LDL ("bad") cholesterol, but this was not seen with patches or creams. Acne and extra hair growth were more common, and no serious side effects were recorded, though long-term safety is still unknown.
keyPoints: Testosterone improved sexual desire, arousal, orgasm, pleasure and satisfying sexual activity, and lowered sexual distress, in postmenopausal women.
Oral testosterone raised LDL cholesterol and lowered HDL cholesterol, but non-oral forms such as patches or creams did not change cholesterol in the same way.
Acne, unwanted hair growth and some weight gain were more common with testosterone; no serious adverse events were recorded.
The authors say non-oral routes are preferred, and that effects on bones, muscles, thinking and long-term safety need more study because few women contributed data.

items.title: Type and timing of menopausal hormone therapy and breast cancer risk: individual participant meta-analysis of the worldwide epidemiological evidence
items.summary: This large analysis pooled data from prospective studies covering 108,647 postmenopausal women who developed breast cancer, to look at how different types of menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) relate to breast cancer risk. Every type except vaginal oestrogens was linked to a higher risk, and the risk rose the longer MHT was used. Risk was higher with oestrogen plus progestagen than with oestrogen alone, and some extra risk lasted for more than 10 years after stopping. The researchers note that these figures apply if the links are largely causal.
keyPoints: All MHT types except vaginal oestrogens were linked to extra breast cancer risk, which grew with longer use and was greater for oestrogen-progestagen than oestrogen-only MHT.

For women of average weight starting at age 50, 5 years of MHT would mean about 1 extra breast cancer per 50 users of oestrogen plus daily progestagen, 1 per 70 with intermittent progestagen, and 1 per 200 with oestrogen-only; 10 years of use would roughly double these excesses.
Some excess risk persisted for over 10 years after stopping, but there was little excess after less than 1 year of use.

items.title: The impact of micronized progesterone on breast cancer risk: a systematic review
items.summary: This systematic review looked at whether menopausal hormone therapy that uses micronized progesterone (a body-identical form of progesterone) affects breast cancer risk. An expert panel found that estrogen combined with micronized progesterone did not raise breast cancer risk for up to 5 years of use. After more than 5 years, there is limited evidence of a possible increase in risk.
keyPoints: Estrogen combined with oral or vaginal micronized progesterone did not increase breast cancer risk for up to 5 years of treatment.
There is limited evidence that using estrogen with oral micronized progesterone for more than 5 years may be linked to a higher breast cancer risk.
Women with a uterus who take estrogen need a progestogen to protect the womb lining.
Counseling on combined hormone therapy should cover breast cancer risk whichever progestogen is used, along with other breast cancer risk factors.

items.title: Hormone replacement therapy for women previously treated for endometrial cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is safe and helpful for women who have been treated for endometrial cancer. Only one trial (1,236 women) could be included, and it closed early, so it was too small to give firm answers. Cancer came back in 2.3% of women taking oestrogen and 1.9% of women taking placebo, a difference that could easily be due to chance. The reviewers say the evidence is very limited and of very low certainty.
keyPoints: Only one randomised trial was found, and it stopped early, so there is not enough high-quality evidence to guide women considering HRT after endometrial cancer.
In that trial, cancer recurrence was 2.3% with oestrogen versus 1.9% with placebo, and new breast cancer was rare in both groups (very low-certainty evidence).
The available evidence, including non-randomised studies, does not suggest significant harm if HRT is used after surgery for early-stage endometrial cancer.
No information exists on HRT after higher-stage (FIGO stage II and above) disease; use should be individualised to a woman's symptoms, preferences and the uncertainty of the evidence.

items.title: Pharmacologic Treatment of Primary Osteoporosis or Low Bone Mass to Prevent Fractures in Adults: A Living Clinical Guideline From the American College of Physicians
items.summary: This 2023 guideline from the American College of Physicians updates its 2017 advice on medicines for weak bones (osteoporosis) and low bone mass to prevent fractures. For women after menopause with osteoporosis, it recommends bisphosphonates as the first medicine (strong recommendation, high-certainty evidence). Denosumab is suggested as a second choice when bisphosphonates are not suitable or cause side effects. For women at very high fracture risk, romosozumab or teriparatide followed by a bisphosphonate may be used. For women over 65 with low bone mass (osteopenia), whether to start a bisphosphonate should be decided individually.
keyPoints: Bisphosphonates are recommended as the first medicine for women after menopause with osteoporosis, to lower fracture risk (strong recommendation, high-certainty evidence).
Denosumab is suggested as a second choice for women who cannot take bisphosphonates or have side effects (conditional recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence).
For women with osteoporosis at very high fracture risk, romosozumab (moderate certainty) or teriparatide (low certainty), followed by a bisphosphonate, is suggested.
For women over 65 with low bone mass (osteopenia), starting a bisphosphonate is an individual decision (conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence).
It replaces the 2017 ACP recommendations.

items.title: Treatment of Low Bone Density or Osteoporosis to Prevent Fractures in Men and Women: A Clinical Practice Guideline Update From the American College of Physicians
items.summary: The American College of Physicians updated its advice on treating weak bones (low bone density and osteoporosis) to prevent fractures. For women with known osteoporosis, it recommends medicines such as alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid or denosumab to lower the risk of hip and spine fractures, and says treatment should last about 5 years. It recommends against using menopausal estrogen (with or without progestogen) or raloxifene to treat osteoporosis. For older women with milder bone thinning (osteopenia) and a high fracture risk, the choice should be made by talking through preferences, risks, benefits and costs.
keyPoints: Alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid or denosumab are recommended for women with known osteoporosis to reduce hip and spine fractures (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence).
Treating osteoporosis with medicine for 5 years is suggested, and bone density monitoring during those 5 years is not recommended (weak recommendations, low-quality evidence).
Menopausal estrogen therapy, estrogen plus progestogen therapy and raloxifene are recommended against for treating osteoporosis (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence).

For women aged 65 or older with osteopenia and high fracture risk, treatment should be decided through a discussion of preferences, fracture risk, benefits, harms and costs (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence).

items.title: AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF CLINICAL ENDOCRINOLOGISTS AND AMERICAN COLLEGE OF ENDOCRINOLOGY POSITION STATEMENT ON MENOPAUSE-2017 UPDATE
items.source: American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and American College of Endocrinology
items.organisation: American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and American College of Endocrinology
items.summary: This 2017 position statement from two US endocrinology societies updates their earlier menopause guidance after reviewing newer trials. None of the earlier recommendations were changed. It covers when hormone therapy may suit symptomatic women, how the type of estrogen and progesterone matters, and what can be used instead of hormones.
keyPoints: Whether to use menopausal hormone therapy should depend on a woman's heart disease risk factors, her age, and how long since her menopause.
Estrogen given through the skin may carry a lower risk of blood clots, and possibly stroke and coronary artery disease, than estrogen taken by mouth.
If progesterone is needed, micronized progesterone is considered the safer choice.
Hormone therapy is not recommended to prevent diabetes, and for women who already have diabetes the decision should be individualized, taking account of age and metabolic and heart risk factors.

items.title: Hormone Therapy for the Primary Prevention of Chronic Conditions in Postmenopausal Women: Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force
items.summary: This review pooled 18 randomized trials (about 40,000 postmenopausal women) that compared hormone therapy with placebo for preventing long-term conditions such as heart disease, bone fractures and cancer. Hormone therapy lowered the risk of fractures and diabetes, but it also raised the risk of blood clots, stroke, gallbladder disease and urinary incontinence. The review concluded that the harms are substantial alongside the benefits, and that evidence about starting hormone therapy early in menopause is inconclusive.
keyPoints: Estrogen-only therapy was linked to fewer fractures (53 fewer cases per 10,000 person-years) and less diabetes (19 fewer cases).
Estrogen-only therapy was linked to more gallbladder disease, stroke, blood clots (venous thromboembolism) and urinary incontinence.

Estrogen plus progestin was linked to fewer fractures, less diabetes and less colorectal cancer, but also more invasive breast cancer, probable dementia, stroke, blood clots, gallbladder disease and urinary incontinence.
Overall, hormone therapy used to prevent chronic conditions has some benefits but a substantial increase in harms, and the evidence on early initiation is inconclusive.

items.title: ESHRE Guideline: management of women with premature ovarian insufficiency
items.summary: This is a European guideline on how to diagnose and care for women with premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), when the ovaries stop working normally before the usual age. Experts reviewed the research up to 2014 and included a patient representative. They produced 99 recommendations, covering diagnosis, long-term health effects, hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and puberty induction. The authors note that many recommendations rest on expert opinion or on studies of post-menopausal women or women with Turner syndrome, because there is little direct data.
keyPoints: The guideline makes 99 recommendations answering 31 key questions on diagnosing and treating POI.
It includes 17 recommendations on diagnosis and assessment, and 46 on the long-term effects of POI and how to monitor and treat them.
It gives 24 recommendations on hormone replacement therapy, 2 on alternative and complementary treatments, and 5 on inducing puberty.
Many recommendations rely on expert opinion or indirect evidence because of limited data, and the group suggests more research.

items.title: Short-term and long-term effects of tibolone in postmenopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 46 randomised trials (about 20,000 women) of tibolone, a synthetic hormone medicine used for menopause symptoms. Tibolone eased hot flushes and night sweats better than placebo but not as well as standard combined hormone therapy. It caused more unscheduled vaginal bleeding than placebo, but less than combined hormone therapy. Much of the evidence on long-term safety was low or very low quality.
keyPoints: Unscheduled vaginal bleeding was more likely with tibolone than placebo: if 18% of women on placebo had bleeding, an estimated 31% to 44% of women on tibolone would (moderate-quality evidence).
Compared with combined hormone therapy, tibolone had less unscheduled bleeding: if 47% on combined therapy had bleeding, an estimated 18% to 27% on tibolone would (moderate-quality evidence).
Tibolone was more effective than placebo but less effective than combined hormone therapy for hot flushes and night sweats.
In women with a history of breast cancer, tibolone raised the risk of the cancer coming back, and it may raise stroke risk in women over 60.

items.title: Hormone Therapy and Other Treatments for Symptoms of Menopause
items.summary: This review looked at hormone therapy and other treatments for menopause symptoms such as hot flushes and vaginal dryness. Combined estrogen and progestogen therapy raises breast cancer risk when used for more than three to five years, so it is advised only for symptoms, at the smallest effective dose for the shortest time. Estrogen works best for hot flushes, but some non-hormonal medicines also help. Most complementary therapies have not been shown to work better than placebo.
keyPoints: Estrogen is the most effective treatment for hot flushes; low-dose paroxetine, venlafaxine and gabapentin are effective non-hormonal alternatives.
Women with a uterus who take estrogen also need a progestogen to lower the risk of womb lining (endometrial) cancer.

There is no high-quality, consistent evidence that yoga, acupuncture, exercise, black cohosh or omega-3 supplements beat placebo; soy may give modest benefit and small studies suggest hypnosis helps hot flushes.
For vaginal symptoms, options include vaginal estrogen, non-hormonal moisturizers, or ospemifene for painful sex due to menopausal changes.

items.title: Hormone therapy for preventing cardiovascular disease in post-menopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 19 trials with over 40,000 post-menopausal women to see whether hormone therapy (taken by mouth) helps prevent heart disease. Overall it found little or no protective benefit for the heart, and a higher risk of stroke and blood clots. Women who started treatment less than 10 years after menopause had lower death and heart disease rates in a smaller analysis, but their clot risk was still higher.
keyPoints: Overall, hormone therapy did not reduce deaths, cardiovascular deaths, heart attacks, angina or the need for heart procedures (high quality evidence).
Hormone therapy raised the risk of stroke (about 6 extra cases per 1000 women) and blood clots in the veins (about 8 extra per 1000 women), plus lung clots (about 4 extra per 1000).
Among women who started less than 10 years after menopause, deaths and coronary heart disease were lower (moderate quality evidence), but blood clot risk was still higher.
Among women who started more than 10 years after menopause, there was little effect on death or heart disease, and higher risks of stroke and blood clots.

items.title: Treatment of Symptoms of the Menopause: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This is a clinical practice guideline from the Endocrine Society on treating menopause symptoms. It found that menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats. For women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause starting, the benefits may outweigh the risks for most who have symptoms. Other options exist for vaginal symptoms and for women who prefer not to use hormones.
keyPoints: Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for hot flushes, night sweats and other menopause symptoms.
Benefits may exceed risks for most symptomatic women under age 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset, and treatment should be tailored to each woman's health and preferences.
Women should be screened for heart disease and breast cancer risk before starting hormone therapy, and it is not recommended to prevent heart disease, breast cancer or dementia.
Low-dose vaginal estrogen and ospemifene treat genitourinary symptoms such as vaginal dryness, while moisturizers and lubricants are options for those avoiding hormones.

items.title: Risks and benefits of estrogen plus progestin in healthy postmenopausal women: principal results From the Women's Health Initiative randomized controlled trial
items.summary: This large trial followed over 16,000 healthy postmenopausal women aged 50-79 with a uterus for an average of 5.2 years. Half took a daily combined estrogen plus progestin pill and half took a placebo. The combined hormones raised the risk of heart disease, stroke, blood clots in the lungs and invasive breast cancer, while lowering the risk of colorectal cancer and hip fracture. The trial was stopped early because overall risks were judged to outweigh benefits, and the authors said this regimen should not be started or continued to prevent heart disease.
keyPoints: Compared with placebo, combined estrogen plus progestin raised the risk of heart disease (HR 1.29), stroke (HR 1.41), lung blood clots (HR 2.13) and invasive breast cancer (HR 1.26).
It lowered the risk of colorectal cancer (HR 0.63) and hip fracture (HR 0.66), and combined fractures overall.

The extra risk was small in absolute terms: per 10,000 women per year, about 7 more heart events, 8 more strokes, 8 more lung clots and 8 more breast cancers, versus 6 fewer colorectal cancers and 5 fewer hip fractures.
Overall risks exceeded benefits, deaths from all causes were not changed, and the regimen should not be used to prevent heart disease.

items.title: The 2022 hormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society
items.summary: This 2022 position statement from the North American Menopause Society updates its 2017 statement on hormone therapy. Hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats and for vaginal and urinary symptoms of menopause, and it prevents bone loss and fractures. For women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause without reasons to avoid it, the benefits generally outweigh the risks; starting later carries greater risks of heart disease, stroke, blood clots and dementia. Risks depend on the type, dose, route and timing, so treatment should be individual and reviewed regularly.
keyPoints: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for hot flushes and genitourinary syndrome of menopause and prevents bone loss and fracture.
Under 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset, without contraindications, the benefit-risk balance is favourable for bothersome hot flushes and bone protection.
Starting more than 10 years after menopause or after 60 carries greater absolute risks of heart disease, stroke, blood clots and dementia.
For vaginal symptoms not helped by over-the-counter products, low-dose vaginal estrogen or other local therapies are recommended.

items.title: Postpartum management of the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 40 trials on treating high blood pressure after birth. Water tablets (diuretics) may help control blood pressure when taken together with a blood pressure medicine, but are not recommended on their own. Evidence on which blood pressure medicine works best is still limited, and the review rated the overall certainty of the evidence as low or very low. No safety concerns were found, and checking and managing your own blood pressure, or making lifestyle changes, was linked to lower blood pressure 8 months after birth.
keyPoints: Diuretics (mostly furosemide) may improve blood pressure control when given alongside a blood pressure medicine, but cannot be recommended as the only treatment.
Evidence on the best choice of blood pressure medicine after birth remains limited; enalapril or amlodipine compared with nifedipine were highlighted as relevant to practice.
Blood pressure self-monitoring or lifestyle change may lead to lower blood pressure 8 months after birth than usual care.
Certainty of the evidence was low or very low, and no safety concerns were found.

items.title: Planned early birth versus expectant management for hypertensive disorders from 34 weeks' gestation to term
items.summary: This review looked at six trials involving 3491 women with high blood pressure in pregnancy (including pre-eclampsia) after 34 weeks. It compared planning an earlier birth with waiting and monitoring closely. Planned early birth lowered the risk of serious complications for the mother and probably lowered the risk of stillbirth. It did not raise the chance of a caesarean birth.
keyPoints: Planned early birth reduced the risk of serious maternal illness or death compared with waiting (high-certainty evidence).
Planned early birth did not increase the chance of caesarean section (high-certainty evidence).
It probably lowered the risk of stillbirth, and probably made little or no difference to baby unit admission (moderate-certainty evidence).

The authors say timing should take into account the woman's preferences, the type of high blood pressure and whether severe features are present; longer-term effects on babies and mothers' heart health still need study.

items.title: Remote blood pressure monitoring in women at risk of or with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pulled together 18 studies (about 28,000 women) on checking blood pressure at home with a care team reviewing the readings, compared with usual care. In pregnancy, home monitoring meant fewer clinic visits and fewer hospital admissions, without more problems for mothers or babies. After birth, it helped more women get their blood pressure checked within 10 days. The authors say the studies differed a lot and few were high quality, so more trials are needed.
keyPoints: Home blood pressure monitoring with clinician review in pregnancy reduced antenatal clinic visits and hospital admissions.
There was no increase in adverse outcomes for mothers or babies, such as caesarean section, growth restriction or NICU admission.
After birth, women with a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy were more likely to have follow-up within 10 days, with no rise in readmissions or unplanned hypertension visits.
Study differences and a lack of high-quality evidence limit the findings, and more randomised trials are needed.

items.title: The Effect of Nursing Interventions in Women With Gestational Hypertension: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 13 studies with 1,458 women who had high blood pressure in pregnancy (gestational hypertension). It looked at nursing-led support such as training programs, home-based care, case management, music therapy and care pathways. Women who received these nursing interventions had lower blood pressure, less anxiety and depression, and shorter hospital stays. Every included study showed a benefit in at least one outcome.
keyPoints: Nursing interventions lowered both systolic and diastolic blood pressure in women with gestational hypertension.
Women receiving nursing interventions had less anxiety and depression.
Hospital stays were shorter with nursing interventions.
The studies were rated as fair to good quality, and all 13 showed a benefit in at least one outcome.

items.title: Pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, and lipid levels during pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from several studies comparing blood fat (lipid) levels in pregnant women with gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia against healthy pregnant women. Women with either condition tended to have lower 'good' cholesterol (HDL) and higher 'bad' cholesterol (LDL), total cholesterol and triglycerides. The authors suggest that tracking lipid levels during pregnancy might help with early prediction and management, though results varied a lot between studies.
keyPoints: Women with gestational hypertension had lower HDL and higher LDL, total cholesterol and triglycerides than healthy pregnant women.
Women with pre-eclampsia showed the same pattern of lower HDL and higher LDL, total cholesterol and triglycerides.
Results differed moderately to a great deal between studies for some measures.
The authors suggest monitoring lipid levels over pregnancy may help with early prediction and management of these conditions.

items.title: Blood pressure-lowering treatment for pregnant women with non-severe hypertension: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of blood pressure-lowering treatment in pregnant women with non-severe high blood pressure (140-159 over 90-109 mmHg). Compared with placebo or no treatment, treatment lowered the chance of developing severe high blood pressure, preeclampsia and preterm birth before 37 weeks. The authors suggest that aiming for a blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg gives the best outcomes for mothers and babies. They also noted moderate differences between studies and signs of publication bias for some outcomes.
keyPoints: Treatment roughly halved the risk of severe hypertension (risk ratio 0.477).
Treatment reduced the risk of preeclampsia (risk ratio 0.819) and preterm birth before 37 weeks (risk ratio 0.856).
Aiming for a blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg was suggested as the best target in non-severe hypertension.
Benefits did not clearly differ between types of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, except for placental abruption.

items.title: How migraine and its associated treatment impact on pregnancy outcomes: Umbrella review with updated systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This study pulled together earlier reviews and newer research on migraine and pregnancy. It found that women with migraine had higher odds of pre-eclampsia (a high blood pressure condition in pregnancy), preterm birth and mental health problems around the time of birth. Women who used triptans (a type of migraine medicine) had higher odds of miscarriage than women without migraine. The authors say more research is needed on some of these links, including low birth weight and triptans.
keyPoints: Migraine was linked to higher odds of pre-eclampsia (pooled OR 2.05 in the updated analysis).
Migraine was also linked to higher odds of preterm birth and mental illness around birth.
Women who used triptans had higher odds of miscarriage than women without migraine, but the authors call for more study of this link.
These are associations, not proof of cause; links to placental abruption, low birth weight and small for gestational age need further investigation.

items.title: Anti-hypertensive therapy for preeclampsia: a network meta-analysis and systematic review
items.summary: This review pooled results from eight randomized trials, covering 1192 women with preeclampsia, to compare blood pressure medicines. Diltiazem lowered blood pressure the most, with labetalol and nicardipine also working well. Dihydralazine was less effective than several of the other drugs. The authors suggest diltiazem as a preferred option for severe preeclampsia with high blood pressure.
keyPoints: Eight randomized trials with 1192 women with preeclampsia were compared; two studies were high quality and six were moderate quality.
Diltiazem ranked as the most effective at lowering blood pressure among the drugs studied.
Labetalol and nicardipine also lowered blood pressure well, and labetalol lowered it more than nicardipine.
Blood pressure stayed higher with dihydralazine than with methyldopa, labetalol, nicardipine or diltiazem.

items.title: Evaluation of antihypertensives for post partum management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of blood pressure medicines taken after birth by women who had high blood pressure in pregnancy or developed it after delivery. Almost all of the medicines studied worked to lower blood pressure after birth. Calcium channel blockers brought blood pressure under steady control faster than the comparison, while women given ACE inhibitors or ARBs more often needed extra blood pressure medicines.
keyPoints: Almost all antihypertensive drugs assessed were effective for treating high blood pressure after birth.
Calcium channel blockers reached sustained blood pressure control faster than the control.
ACE inhibitors or ARBs were more likely to need other blood pressure medicines added.
The authors say treating high blood pressure promptly after birth can be life-saving, and treatment can be tailored to each woman's needs and other health conditions.

items.title: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure Treatment and Hypertensive Adverse Outcomes in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: Some pregnant women have obstructive sleep apnea, a condition where breathing repeatedly pauses during sleep. This review combined six studies with 809 women to see whether using a CPAP machine (a mask that gently keeps the airway open) affects blood pressure problems in pregnancy. Women with sleep apnea who used CPAP had a lower risk of gestational hypertension and preeclampsia than those who did not. The authors say the findings suggest CPAP may reduce these risks.
keyPoints: Women with sleep apnea who used CPAP had about a 35% lower risk of gestational hypertension (RR 0.65).
They also had about a 30% lower risk of preeclampsia (RR 0.70).
The benefit did not appear to depend on the woman's age or body mass index.
The review pooled only six studies, with 809 women in total.

items.title: Hypospadias risk associated with chronic hypertension during pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from several observational studies to see whether long-term (chronic) high blood pressure in the mother is linked to hypospadias in baby boys. Hypospadias is a condition where the opening of the urethra is not at the tip of the penis. The studies found that babies born to mothers with chronic high blood pressure had a higher chance of hypospadias. Because these were observational studies, they show a link, not proof of cause.
keyPoints: Five studies were included in the final analysis after one was excluded for using a different definition of hypospadias.
Maternal chronic high blood pressure was linked to higher odds of hypospadias in male babies (adjusted odds ratio 1.77).
The authors conclude that maternal chronic hypertension increases the risk of hypospadias in male offspring.
They say more research is needed on the biological reasons and on possible effects of blood pressure medicines.

items.title: The impact of antihypertensive treatment of mild to moderate hypertension during pregnancy on maternal and neonatal outcomes: An updated meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 12 randomized trials with 4,461 pregnant women who had mild to moderate high blood pressure. Women who took blood pressure medicine had better outcomes in 7 of the 19 areas checked, including less severe high blood pressure, less preeclampsia and fewer newborn deaths. The medicine did not raise the chance of the baby being small for its age. The authors say this supports treating mild high blood pressure in pregnancy, even though current guidelines do not recommend it.
keyPoints: Treatment lowered the risk of severe high blood pressure, preeclampsia, placental abruption, kidney problems, pulmonary edema and newborn death.
Babies being small for gestational age was not different between treated and untreated groups.
No significant harms to the baby were found.
Guidelines do not currently recommend treating mild hypertension in pregnancy, but recent trials support it.

items.title: Clinical efficacy of low-dose aspirin combined with calcium in preventing preeclampsia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled seven randomized trials in pregnant women at high risk of preeclampsia. It compared low-dose aspirin plus calcium supplements with a control group, and the combination was linked to lower rates of preeclampsia and gestational hypertension. It was also linked to fewer preterm births, less postpartum hemorrhage (heavy bleeding after birth) and fewer cases of poor fetal growth. The abstract does not rate the certainty of the evidence, and the review concludes the combination should be considered for high-risk pregnant women.
keyPoints: Aspirin plus calcium was linked to lower rates of preeclampsia (OR 0.20) and gestational hypertension (OR 0.15) in high-risk pregnant women.
Postpartum hemorrhage was lower in the aspirin plus calcium group (OR 0.15).
Preterm birth (OR 0.26) and fetal growth restriction (OR 0.16) were also lower.
The authors conclude the combination was more effective than aspirin alone and should be considered for high-risk pregnancies.

items.title: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine Special Statement: A quality metric for evaluating timely treatment of severe hypertension
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine says severe high blood pressure in pregnancy is a medical emergency. Treatment within 30 to 60 minutes is recommended to lower the risk of maternal death or serious illness, but it is often delayed by more than an hour. This statement proposes a standard way for hospitals to track how often they treat it on time.
keyPoints: Severe high blood pressure in pregnancy is a medical emergency.
Treatment within 30 to 60 minutes is recommended to reduce the risk of maternal death or severe illness.
Treatment is often delayed by more than 1 hour.
A common quality measure is proposed so hospitals can track and compare timely treatment.

items.title: Optimal blood pressure target to prevent severe hypertension in pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 40 randomized trials with 6,355 pregnant women who had mild to moderate high blood pressure. Treatment that lowered blood pressure cut the risk of developing severe high blood pressure by more than half. It also lowered the risk of preeclampsia, placental abruption and preterm birth, but small-for-gestational-age babies were more common. Reaching a top (systolic) number under 130 mmHg lowered the risk of severe hypertension to about one-third of the risk at 140 or above.
keyPoints: Blood pressure-lowering treatment reduced severe hypertension (risk ratio 0.46) and also reduced preeclampsia, severe preeclampsia, placental abruption and preterm birth before 37 weeks.
The risk of having a small for gestational age baby was higher with treatment (risk ratio 1.25).
An achieved systolic pressure under 130 mmHg cut the risk of severe hypertension to nearly one-third compared with 140 or above.
The authors suggest aiming for a systolic pressure under 130 mmHg with careful monitoring of the baby's growth.

items.title: Maternal Dietary Patterns and Pregnancy Hypertension in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 13 studies from low- and middle-income countries to see whether what women eat in pregnancy is linked to high blood pressure disorders such as pre-eclampsia. Women who ate enough vegetables or fruit had lower odds of pre-eclampsia than women who ate little or none. For meat, grains, a 'Western' diet and alcohol, the studies did not allow firm conclusions. The authors say more research is needed in these countries.
keyPoints: Adequate vegetable intake was linked to lower odds of pre-eclampsia (OR 0.38) compared with no or low intake.
Adequate fruit intake was also linked to lower odds of pre-eclampsia (OR 0.42) compared with no or low intake.
No firm conclusions could be drawn about high meat or grain intake, a Western diet, or alcohol and pre-eclampsia.
More research is needed in low- and middle-income countries, including on how malnutrition and social factors play a part.

items.title: Interpregnancy Weight Change and Hypertension During Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined 12 studies covering about 415,000 women to look at weight change between pregnancies and high blood pressure in the next pregnancy. Women who gained weight between pregnancies had a higher chance of high blood pressure disorders, and the more weight gained, the higher the risk. Women who lost weight between pregnancies had a somewhat lower chance. These are links seen across studies, so they do not prove cause and effect.
keyPoints: Gaining weight between pregnancies was linked to a higher risk of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (odds ratio 1.37).
The more weight gained between pregnancies, the higher the risk of high blood pressure disorders.
Losing weight between pregnancies was linked to a slightly lower risk (odds ratio 0.87).
Weight gain between pregnancies was also linked to higher risk of gestational hypertension and preeclampsia.

items.title: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine Consult Series #50: The role of activity restriction in obstetric management: (Replaces Consult Number 33, August 2014)
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine reviewed the research on activity restriction (such as bed rest or reduced activity) during pregnancy. They found it does not prevent poor pregnancy outcomes, and it carries real physical and emotional risks. They recommend against routine use of activity restriction for preterm birth risk and suggest it not be prescribed for high blood pressure conditions of pregnancy, poor fetal growth, or early waters breaking.
keyPoints: Activity restriction does not prevent adverse pregnancy outcomes but carries significant physical and psychosocial risks.
The Society recommends against routine activity restriction in women at risk of preterm birth from preterm labor symptoms, arrested preterm labor, or a short cervix.
The Society recommends against routine hospital stays and activity restriction to prevent preterm birth in multiple pregnancies such as twins.

The Society suggests activity restriction not be prescribed for hypertensive disease of pregnancy, fetal growth restriction, or preterm premature rupture of membranes, as there is no clear evidence it helps.

items.title: Maternal and Perinatal Outcomes of White Coat Hypertension During Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: White coat hypertension means blood pressure is high in the clinic but normal elsewhere. This review pooled 12 studies to see how it affects pregnancy. Women with it had a higher risk of preeclampsia, smaller babies and preterm birth than women with normal blood pressure. Their outcomes were better than for women with gestational or chronic hypertension.
keyPoints: Women with white coat hypertension seen before 20 weeks had a higher risk of preeclampsia than women with normal blood pressure.
They also had a higher risk of a small-for-gestational-age baby and of preterm birth.
Risks were lower than for women with gestational hypertension, and they delivered about 1 week later than women with chronic hypertension.
The authors say the diagnosis should be confirmed in pregnant women with high readings, and that confirmed cases need monitoring for preeclampsia, small babies and preterm birth.

items.title: Setting and techniques for monitoring blood pressure during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether where and how blood pressure is measured in pregnancy (at home or in clinic, and with different techniques) changes outcomes for mothers and babies. Only three trials were included, and the evidence was low certainty. It is still unclear whether measuring blood pressure at home helps or harms, but using the standard 'disappearance of sound' (K5) method for diastolic pressure is supported.
keyPoints: Home self-monitoring of blood pressure compared with clinic checks: the benefit, if any, remains uncertain because the evidence comes from one small feasibility study of 154 women.

Using K5 (the sound disappearing) to measure the lower blood pressure number is supported for women with high blood pressure in pregnancy; K4 (muffled sound) made little to no difference to pre-eclampsia diagnosis.
The CRADLE device and education package showed little to no difference in maternal deaths versus usual care, but the trial design limitations mean its benefit remains uncertain.
Many important outcomes, such as stillbirth, neonatal death and preterm birth, were not reported or were too uncertain to draw conclusions.

items.title: Antihypertensive drug therapy for mild to moderate hypertension during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled results from randomised trials of blood pressure medicines for women with mild to moderate high blood pressure in pregnancy. Taking these medicines probably halves the chance of the blood pressure rising to a severe level. For other outcomes, such as pre-eclampsia, baby deaths, small babies and preterm birth, the medicines made little or no clear difference, and the evidence for some outcomes was very uncertain. Most trials had a moderate to high risk of bias, so larger, better trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Blood pressure medicines probably halve the risk of developing severe high blood pressure in pregnancy (moderate-certainty evidence).
They may make little or no difference to pre-eclampsia, and probably little or no difference to fetal or neonatal death, small-for-gestational-age babies or preterm birth.
If medicines are used, beta blockers and calcium channel blockers appear more effective than the alternatives at preventing severe high blood pressure.
The effect on other important outcomes, including maternal death, eclampsia and the baby's long-term development, remains unclear because the evidence is very low certainty.

items.title: Oral nifedipine versus intravenous labetalol for severe hypertension during pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled seven small trials (363 women and babies) comparing two medicines used to bring down very high blood pressure in pregnancy: nifedipine taken by mouth and labetalol given into a vein. Nifedipine worked as well as labetalol and was as safe. Women given nifedipine reported fewer side effects, though the finding of less persistent high blood pressure did not hold up in a further check. The authors note the studies were few and small.
keyPoints: Oral nifedipine was as effective and as safe as intravenous labetalol for severe high blood pressure in pregnancy.
Women taking nifedipine reported fewer maternal side effects.
The lower risk of persistent high blood pressure with nifedipine was no longer significant in a sensitivity analysis.
Nifedipine may have an advantage where resources are limited, because it is cheap and easy to give by mouth.

items.title: Effect of folic acid supplementation during pregnancy on gestational hypertension/preeclampsia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 13 studies to see whether taking folic acid during pregnancy lowers the chance of high blood pressure or preeclampsia. The two randomized trials suggested a lower risk, but the larger group of cohort studies did not show a clear effect. The authors concluded that it is still uncertain whether folic acid can prevent these conditions.
keyPoints: The two randomized trials found a lower risk of gestational hypertension/preeclampsia with folic acid compared with placebo (relative risk 0.62).
Cohort studies did not show a clear benefit: the results were compatible with no effect (relative risk 0.92 for gestational hypertension/preeclampsia and 0.88 for preeclampsia alone).
Only 2 of the 13 studies were randomized trials, so the evidence is mixed.
The authors concluded it remains uncertain whether folic acid in pregnancy prevents gestational hypertension or preeclampsia.

items.title: Effect of metformin treatment during pregnancy on women with PCOS: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Clinical and Investigative Medicine. Medecine Clinique et Experimentale
items.journal: Clinical and Investigative Medicine. Medecine Clinique et Experimentale
items.summary: This review pooled results from 11 studies of women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) who kept taking metformin during pregnancy. Early pregnancy loss and preterm birth were lower in the metformin group. Metformin made no clear difference to birth defects or birth weight, and results for gestational diabetes and high blood pressure/preeclampsia were not clear enough to draw a conclusion.
keyPoints: Early pregnancy loss and preterm delivery were significantly lower in women with PCOS who continued metformin.
No significant difference was found in fetal abnormalities or birth weight between metformin and no metformin.
Rates of gestational diabetes and high blood pressure/preeclampsia did not differ significantly, but subgroup results were inconsistent.
The authors say high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to clarify effects on gestational diabetes and hypertension/preeclampsia.

items.title: Italian Advisory Board: sFlt-1/PlGF ratio and preeclampsia, state of the art and developments in diagnostic, therapeutic and clinical management
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: A panel of Italian experts reviewed research on a blood test that measures two placenta-related proteins (the sFlt-1 to PlGF ratio) to help diagnose and predict pre-eclampsia. Recent evidence gives a useful cut-off value that can predict pre-eclampsia in the short term in women who already have signs and symptoms. Across Europe there is no agreement yet on using this test in routine care, and only German guidelines have so far included it as an aid alongside other clinical findings.
keyPoints: The sFlt-1/PlGF ratio test can predict, in the short term, which women with signs and symptoms will go on to develop pre-eclampsia.
Only German guidelines in Europe have so far included the test, as a diagnostic aid alongside other clinical findings.
The panel aims to promote assessing the test's usefulness in Italy, including for women with risk factors, for triage of gestational hypertension and for judging severity.
Possible uses discussed include predicting or ruling out new or repeat pre-eclampsia and predicting poor outcomes for mother and baby.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 623: Emergent therapy for acute-onset, severe hypertension during pregnancy and the postpartum period
items.summary: This committee opinion looks at sudden, very high blood pressure that can happen during pregnancy or after birth. It says that using standard, evidence-based care plans for preeclampsia and eclampsia has been shown to lower the chance of serious problems for mothers. It recommends that hospitals and care teams be ready to give blood pressure medicine quickly in an emergency, then carefully check the health of mother and baby.
keyPoints: Sudden, severe high blood pressure can occur during pregnancy and in the weeks after birth.
Standard, evidence-based care plans for preeclampsia and eclampsia have been shown to reduce serious problems for mothers.
Care teams and hospitals should have systems ready to give medication promptly in a hypertensive emergency.
After the emergency is treated, mother and baby should be fully assessed, including whether more medication is needed and when to deliver.

items.title: Metformin versus insulin for gestational diabetes mellitus: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled eight randomized trials (1,592 women) comparing metformin tablets with insulin for treating gestational diabetes. Women taking metformin had a lower risk of pregnancy-induced high blood pressure. There was no clear difference between the two treatments for baby outcomes such as low blood sugar, large babies, breathing problems, jaundice treatment or perinatal death. The authors say the benefits of metformin are not certain and need to be checked in further trials.
keyPoints: Metformin was linked to a lower risk of pregnancy-induced high blood pressure than insulin (risk ratio 0.54).
No significant differences were found for newborn low blood sugar, large-for-gestational-age babies, respiratory distress, phototherapy or perinatal death.
Overall, there was no clinically relevant difference in efficacy or safety between metformin and insulin.
Metformin's effects on blood sugar control and gestational age at birth are unclear and need more trials.

items.title: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 767: Emergent Therapy for Acute-Onset, Severe Hypertension During Pregnancy and the Postpartum Period
items.summary: This ACOG committee opinion covers urgent treatment of suddenly very high blood pressure during pregnancy or after birth. Women with acute-onset severe high blood pressure need urgent treatment, ideally within 30-60 minutes of it being confirmed, to lower the risk of stroke. Intravenous labetalol and hydralazine are first-line medicines, and immediate-release oral nifedipine may also be used first-line, especially without intravenous access. Standard hospital protocols for pre-eclampsia have been shown to reduce serious complications for mothers.
keyPoints: Acute-onset severe hypertension in pregnancy or after birth needs urgent treatment.
Treatment should start as soon as possible, within 30-60 minutes of confirmed severe hypertension, to reduce the risk of maternal stroke.
Intravenous labetalol and hydralazine are first-line; immediate-release oral nifedipine may also be first-line.
Standardised protocols for pre-eclampsia and eclampsia reduce adverse maternal outcomes.

items.title: Impaired neuromusculoskeletal response to training stimuli associated with low energy availability: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 21 studies of people who were not eating enough to meet their body's energy needs while training (low energy availability). Many of them gained less muscle, strength or performance from training than expected. The studies were quite different from each other, so the results could not be combined into one overall number. The authors say athletes, coaches and clinicians should be aware that low energy availability may blunt how well the body responds to training.
keyPoints: Ten of 21 studies found smaller gains in lean muscle mass with low energy availability (about 1% to 5% less), while ten found no big change.
Six studies found worse sport or functional performance over time with low energy availability (about 4% to 10% lower).
Strength, limb size, cell-level and self-reported measures were all impaired with low energy availability.
Impaired training responses may matter for rehabilitation aimed at building muscle and strength.

items.title: Relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) in elite adult team ball sport athletes: a systematic review
items.source: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
items.journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
items.summary: This review looked at how common Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) is in elite adult team ball sport athletes. REDs happens when the body does not get enough energy for training and everyday needs. Across 14 studies of 265 athletes in 12 sports, estimates ranged widely, from 0 to 80 percent, depending on the method used. The authors say the problem seems common in these sports, but research is limited and there is no agreed way to measure it.
keyPoints: Fourteen studies covering 265 elite athletes in 12 team ball sports were included.
Estimates of REDs or low energy availability ranged from 0 to 80 percent, because six different methods were used.
Studies using energy availability calculations found low energy availability in 26.3 to 63.6 percent of athletes.
The authors conclude REDs appears common in elite team ball sports, but research is limited and a consistent way to measure it is needed.

items.title: Pharmacological interventions to improve bone density in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This review pooled 13 randomized trials of medicines to protect bone density in women whose periods stopped because of stress, low weight or heavy exercise (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea). Skin-patch hormone replacement therapy improved bone density in the lower spine and the neck of the thigh bone compared with placebo or no treatment. Hormone pills and the combined contraceptive pill did not show a clear benefit. Teriparatide, a bone-building medicine, improved lower spine density more than the patch or the contraceptive pill, but not at the hip sites.
keyPoints: Transdermal (skin patch) hormone replacement therapy improved bone density in the lower spine and the femoral neck compared with placebo or no treatment.
Oral hormone replacement therapy and the combined oral contraceptive pill showed no significant bone benefit at any site.
Teriparatide improved lower spine bone density more than transdermal hormone therapy or the contraceptive pill, but not at the femoral neck or total hip.
These options are considered when lifestyle changes have not brought periods back.

items.title: Biochemical Responses to Experimentally Induced Short-Term Low Energy Availability in Athletes: A Systematic Review
items.source: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
items.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
items.summary: This review pooled 13 small experiments (145 athletes) in which athletes were deliberately given too little food energy for their training for a short time. Within days, markers of bone breakdown rose and bone building fell in about half of the studies, leptin (a hormone linked to energy stores) dropped, and testosterone fell in half. No consistent changes were seen in estradiol, progesterone, inflammation or iron. The authors note that low carbohydrate intake often went along with low energy, so it may have added to these effects.
keyPoints: Short-term low energy availability shifted bone markers in about half of the studies, suggesting more bone breakdown and less bone building.
Leptin consistently fell, and testosterone fell in half of the interventions.
No consistent changes were seen in estradiol, progesterone, calcium metabolism, inflammation or iron status.
The authors call for standardized, sex-specific research and for monitoring key markers when athletes are at risk of low energy availability.

items.title: Exploring the associations between low energy availability and mental health among university athletes: A systematic literature review
items.summary: This review looked at 18 studies of university athletes to see whether not eating enough for the energy they use (low energy availability) is linked to mental health problems. Low energy availability was very common, and it often went along with disordered eating, such as strict control over food and a strong drive to be thin. Athletes with menstrual problems, such as missed periods, had higher disordered eating scores. There was early evidence that anxiety and depression were more common with low energy availability, but only a few studies looked at these, and almost all were snapshot studies that cannot show cause and effect.
keyPoints: Low energy availability was very common in university athletes, found in 41.7% to 100% of those studied.
Low energy availability and disordered eating often occurred together, especially strict dietary restraint and a drive for thinness.
Athletes with menstrual dysfunction had significantly higher disordered eating scores.
Early evidence from a small number of studies suggested more anxiety and depression with low energy availability.

items.title: Bone Mineral Density in Women with Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled studies of bone density (measured by DXA scan) in women whose periods stopped because of low energy intake, stress or heavy exercise (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea), compared with women with regular periods. Women with this condition tended to have lower bone density, especially at the hip, and the loss was much larger in women with anorexia nervosa. Some results changed depending on how the data were analysed, and the studies differed a lot from each other, so larger studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Women with functional hypothalamic amenorrhea had lower hip bone density than women with regular periods; the lower-back result was less certain.
Women with anorexia nervosa had much bigger bone density deficits at both the lower back and the hip.
Bone health checks are recommended after 6 or more months without periods, or sooner with severe energy deficiency or past fractures.
Restoring energy intake, gaining weight and getting periods back is the main treatment; combined pills, bisphosphonates and denosumab are not recommended for routine use.

items.title: Low Energy Availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 59 studies to see how common low energy availability (not eating enough for the energy used in training) is among athletes, and what it does. About 45% of athletes had low energy availability, with similar rates in women (44.2%) and men (49.4%). Athletes with it tended to perform worse, miss more training through illness, and have weaker bones and more bone stress injuries. The review notes that spotting and correcting it early may prevent the wider problems of relative energy deficiency in sport, which can include changes to menstrual function.
keyPoints: 44.7% of athletes across 46 studies had low energy availability, including 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes.
63.0% of athletes in eight studies were at risk of relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs), a condition that can affect menstrual function, bone health and immunity.
Low energy availability was linked to poorer endurance, run performance and training response, and more training days missed through illness.
Most studies found impaired bone health and a higher risk of bone stress injuries; results on injury risk in general were mixed.

items.title: Risk Factors for Running-Related Injury in High School and Collegiate Cross-country Runners: A Systematic Review
items.source: Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy
items.journal: Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy
items.summary: This review pulled together 24 studies of high school and college cross-country runners to see what raises the chance of a running injury. Being female, having had an injury before, and having signs of relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S, when the body doesn't get enough fuel for its training) were linked to more injuries. Evidence was moderate that RED-S risk factors raised injury risk, especially bone stress injuries. Evidence on training changes and poor sleep was weaker, but pointed toward possible extra risk.
keyPoints: Female runners and runners with a past running injury were most at risk of getting injured.
There was moderate certainty that RED-S risk factors increased injury risk, particularly bone stress injuries.
Weak thigh muscles were linked to more knee pain at the front of the knee.
Evidence was limited that bigger changes in training, poorer sleep and focusing on one sport raise injury risk.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone therapy among patients with idiopathic and functional hypothalamic amenorrhea: a systematic review of the literature and a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 35 studies of about 1,000 women who had missed periods because of a problem in the brain's hormone signalling (hypothalamic amenorrhea, which can be linked to stress, low weight or heavy exercise). It looked at pulsed GnRH treatment, a medicine given in small regular doses to trigger ovulation. The treatment appeared to help many women ovulate, with a trend toward pregnancies and live births, and serious side effects were uncommon. Only three of the studies were randomized trials; the rest were observational.
keyPoints: Pulsed GnRH treatment appeared to achieve high ovulation rates in women with hypothalamic amenorrhea.
There was a trend toward high pregnancy and live birth rates per ovulatory cycle.
Giving the medicine under the skin worked about as well as giving it into a vein.
Ovarian overstimulation was uncommon and mild, and twin or multiple pregnancies were slightly more likely than in the general population.

items.title: Exclusive breastfeeding and infant colic: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 15 observational studies covering about 216,000 babies under 12 months old. It looked at whether babies who were exclusively breastfed had less colic than babies fed in other ways. Exclusively breastfed babies had about 19% lower odds of colic overall. The difference was clearer when compared with mixed feeding, but not clear when compared with formula feeding alone. The studies varied a lot, and the authors say better-quality research is still needed.
keyPoints: Exclusively breastfed babies had 19% lower odds of colic than babies who were not exclusively breastfed.
Compared with mixed feeding, exclusive breastfeeding was linked to lower odds of colic (OR 0.72).
Compared with formula feeding, the difference was smaller and could have been due to chance.
Results differed a lot between studies, and the authors call for further high-quality studies.

items.title: Safety and efficacy of adding postbiotics in infant formula: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine randomized trials with 2,065 infants to see whether adding postbiotics to infant formula is safe and helpful. Postbiotics did not increase serious side effects, colic, gas, diarrhea, vomiting or tummy pain, and babies grew normally. The only benefit found was a higher level of an antibody (SIgA) in stool, but the certainty of that evidence was very low. The authors conclude that postbiotics in formula appear safe but did not clearly show a useful effect.
keyPoints: Adding postbiotics to infant formula did not increase serious adverse events, infantile colic, flatulence, diarrhea, vomiting or abdominal pain.
Weight gain, length gain and head growth were not significantly different from regular formula.
Stool SIgA (an immune-related antibody) was higher with postbiotics, but certainty of this evidence was very low.
The authors describe postbiotic formula as safe but not shown to be effective.

items.title: Effect of lactase supplementation on infant colic: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials
items.source: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.journal: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.summary: Researchers reviewed five trials with 391 babies under 6 months old who had colic, comparing lactase drops (an enzyme that helps digest milk sugar) with placebo or no treatment. Three trials reported shorter crying times, but when two trials were combined there was no clear difference in crying or fussing time after one week. Most of the trials had a high risk of bias, so the overall evidence is inconclusive. The authors say better-designed trials are needed.
keyPoints: Five randomized trials with 391 infants under 6 months were included.
Three trials reported less crying, but one found this only in babies whose parents followed the treatment closely.
Combining two trials showed no clear difference in crying or fussing time after one week of lactase.
Only one trial had a low risk of bias, so evidence that lactase helps colic remains inconclusive.

items.title: Lactase for infantile colic: A systematic review of randomized clinical trials
items.source: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.journal: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.summary: This review looked at six randomized trials, covering 394 babies up to 6 months old with colic, to see if lactase drops help reduce crying. Lactase is an enzyme that helps break down milk sugar. Three trials found babies cried for less time with lactase than with a placebo, while the other three found no clear difference. The authors say it is still unclear whether lactase helps and that better-designed studies are needed.
keyPoints: Six trials with 394 babies were reviewed; results were mixed.
Three trials found shorter crying time with lactase than placebo, and three found no significant difference.
Only one of the two studies that measured breath hydrogen found a significant drop in levels.
The authors conclude that drug treatment for colic remains debatable and more standardized studies are needed.

items.title: Parental perceptions and experiences of infant crying: A systematic review and synthesis of qualitative research
items.summary: This review pulled together 22 qualitative studies, covering 376 parents and carers in eight countries, about what it is like to live with a crying baby. Excessive crying had a big emotional impact on parents and often strained relationships. Parents tried many ways to soothe their baby and cope, but many felt support was lacking and wanted more information and help.
keyPoints: Excessive infant crying has a substantial emotional impact on parents and carers and often affects their relationships.
Parents used a range of soothing and coping strategies but were often desperate for an effective treatment or cure.
Support from health professionals was often seen as lacking.
Crying and beliefs about maternal diet affecting breastmilk could shake parents' confidence in breastfeeding, making them feel their milk was not enough or was harmful.

items.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis showed that complementary and alternative medicines were not effective for infantile colic
items.summary: Researchers combined the results of five trials (422 babies) to see whether osteopathy or chiropractic treatment helps babies with colic cry less or sleep more. Compared with no extra treatment, these approaches did not clearly reduce crying time or increase sleeping time. The authors rated the quality of the evidence as very low, so the findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: Osteopathy and chiropractic treatment did not clearly reduce crying time in babies with colic compared with no extra treatment.
They also did not clearly increase sleeping time.
Results varied a lot between the five studies, and the evidence quality was rated very low.

items.title: Probiotics in the treatment of infantile colic: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled nine randomized trials covering 587 babies with colic to see whether probiotics (live 'good' bacteria supplements) help. Babies given probiotics were more likely to respond to treatment than babies given a placebo. The authors say probiotics may help with treating and preventing colic, especially in the first four weeks of use. They also note that research on this topic has been disputed until now.
keyPoints: Nine randomized trials in 587 infants with colic were combined in the analysis.
Probiotics had a higher overall effective rate than placebo (RR 1.88, 95% CI 1.61 to 2.19).
Benefits seemed strongest within four weeks of starting probiotics.
The authors conclude probiotics may improve both treatment and prevention of colic.

items.title: Complementary and Alternative Therapies for Infantile Colic: A Systematic Review of the Literature
items.source: Alternative Therapies in Health and Medicine
items.journal: Alternative Therapies in Health and Medicine
items.summary: This review looked at complementary therapies for infant colic, which is unexplained, uncontrollable crying in the first three months of life. It found 13 studies of acupuncture, aromatic oils and massage. Most reported that these approaches helped colic symptoms, with no serious side effects reported, but the authors say more research is needed to firm up the evidence.
keyPoints: Acupuncture was found helpful in two randomized trials, but one study found it did not work.
Aromatic oils (given by mouth, inhaled or applied to the skin) were reported as effective with no serious side effects.
Massage was found to effectively reduce colic symptoms.
The authors conclude that further study is needed to strengthen the evidence for these therapies.

items.title: Probiotics for the Management of Infantile Colic: A Systematic Review
items.source: MCN. The American Journal of Maternal Child Nursing
items.journal: MCN. The American Journal of Maternal Child Nursing
items.summary: This review looked at 20 studies (15 randomised trials and 5 meta-analyses) on whether probiotics help babies with colic. In breastfed babies with colic, probiotics given by mouth cut crying time by at least half compared with placebo. For formula-fed babies, and for preventing colic in the first place, the evidence was not clear enough to say either way.
keyPoints: In breastfed babies with colic, oral probiotics reduced crying time by at least 50% compared with placebo.
Whether probiotics help formula-fed babies with colic needs more study.
There was no evidence to support or rule out probiotics for preventing colic.
The authors say probiotics, especially the strain Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938, can safely be recommended if parents want a treatment option.

items.title: Comparison of common interventions for the treatment of infantile colic: a systematic review of reviews and guidelines
items.summary: This review looked at earlier reviews and national guidelines on four common treatments for infant colic: manual therapy, probiotics, acid-reducing medicines (proton pump inhibitors) and simethicone. Probiotics had the strongest evidence for cutting crying time in breastfed babies. Manual therapy (such as hands-on treatment) also reduced crying, but the evidence was weaker. Simethicone showed no benefit, and acid-reducing medicines did not help with crying or fussing.
keyPoints: Probiotics had the strongest evidence, reducing crying time in breastfed infants by about 25 to 65 minutes over 24 hours.
Manual therapies reduced crying time by about 33 to 76 minutes per 24 hours, but the evidence was moderate to low quality.
Simethicone showed no benefit or a negative effect, and proton pump inhibitors did not reduce crying and fussing.
All three national guidelines agreed on education, reassurance, advice and checking mother and baby, but did not agree on other treatments.

items.title: A systematic review of prevention and treatment of infantile colic
items.summary: This review looked at trials from 2007 to 2017 testing ways to prevent or treat colic (long, hard-to-soothe crying) in babies. There was moderately strong evidence that a probiotic called Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 shortened crying time. Acupuncture had little or no effect on crying. In all the studies that followed babies to three months or beyond, crying dropped steeply over time in both treated and untreated groups.
keyPoints: Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 shortened crying duration, with moderately strong evidence and positive results in three of four national settings.
Four trials of acupuncture found no or minimal effect on how long babies cried.
Crying declined steeply over time by around three months of age, even without treatment.
More studies in more populations are needed, and support strategies for parents of colicky babies are a major knowledge gap.

items.title: Parent training programmes for managing infantile colic
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether training programmes for parents can help babies under four months with colic. Programmes teach things like soothing techniques, feeding advice and stress reduction. Pooling results from three small studies, parent training may reduce how long babies cry compared with usual care or reassurance, but the evidence is low quality. Evidence for other comparisons was too limited to draw conclusions.
keyPoints: Parent training may reduce babies' daily crying time compared with reassurance or routine care, based on three studies with 157 babies.
The certainty of this evidence was low because the studies were small and had some risk of bias.
No side effects were reported, but none of the studies clearly measured them.
The authors say more and better-designed trials are needed to know how well these programmes work.

items.title: Probiotics for the Treatment of Infantile Colic: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together five randomized trials of a probiotic called Lactobacillus reuteri in infants with colic, most of whom were breastfed. Babies given the probiotic were more likely to have their crying or fussing time cut by half or more than babies given a control. No side effects were linked to the probiotic.
