The authors say more research is needed for formula-fed babies.
keyPoints: Infants given L. reuteri were about 2.3 times more likely to have at least a 50% drop in crying or fussing time than controls.
The five trials looked at two different strains of L. reuteri, mostly in breastfed infants.
No adverse events were linked to probiotic supplementation.
More research is needed to know whether probiotics help formula-fed infants with colic.

items.title: Infant Colic-What works: A Systematic Review of Interventions for Breast-fed Infants
items.source: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.journal: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.summary: This review looked at treatments for colic in breast-fed and mixed-fed babies under 6 months old, combining results from 17 randomised trials. Probiotics (especially L. reuteri) and preparations containing fennel oil appeared to cut daily crying time. The authors note there are limits to these findings. Evidence for changing the mother's diet, lactase, sugar solutions and simethicone was weak, and better trials are needed.
keyPoints: Probiotics, especially L. reuteri, appeared to reduce crying by about 56 minutes a day by day 21.
Preparations containing fennel oil appeared to reduce crying by about 72 minutes a day, though the range of results was wide.
Evidence for mothers changing their diet, lactase, sucrose, glucose and simethicone was weak.
The authors say more well-designed trials are needed for all of these treatments.

items.title: The relationship between migraine and infant colic: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from three studies that looked at whether infant colic and migraine go together. Migraine was linked to higher odds of infant colic, meaning children and adults with migraine were more likely to have had colic as babies. The authors note that only a small number of studies were included, so the finding is limited. It shows a link, not a proven cause.
keyPoints: Infant colic was associated with increased odds of migraine across the studies pooled.
The odds ratio was about 6.5 in one analysis and 5.6 in a more cautious analysis.
Removing the study with the largest effect still showed a link, with an odds ratio of 3.6.
The main limitation was the small number of studies included.

items.title: Probiotics in infants for prevention of allergic disease
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 24 trials (about 7,000 mother-infant pairs) that tested whether giving babies probiotics, or probiotics plus prebiotics, prevents allergic conditions. Probiotics made little to no difference to asthma, hay fever or cow's milk allergy by age two, and may slightly reduce eczema, but this small effect disappeared in the most reliable trials. No serious side effects were reported. Overall the authors say the evidence is not strong enough to draw firm conclusions.
keyPoints: Probiotics may make little to no difference to asthma, allergic rhinitis (hay fever) or IgE-mediated cow's milk allergy by age two (low-certainty evidence).
Probiotics may slightly reduce eczema by age two, but in the trials at lowest risk of bias there was little or no difference.
The evidence on probiotics or synbiotics and food allergy is very uncertain or shows little to no difference.
No serious adverse events related to probiotics or synbiotics were reported, but there is insufficient evidence to support routine use for preventing allergies.

items.title: A Systematic Review of the Relation between Complementary Feeding and Children's Development
items.summary: This review looked at whether the quality of babies' diets when they start solid foods, and the way they are fed, relate to how children develop. Several studies linked a better-quality diet with better thinking skills, language, social understanding and general development. Two studies linked the feeding approach with language development. Many other findings showed no clear link, so the authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Better diet quality during complementary feeding was linked to better cognitive (thinking) development in five studies.
Diet quality was also linked to language development (six studies), social cognition (three studies) and general development (six studies).
The feeding approach was linked to language development in two studies.
About 20 findings showed a significant link, but 17 did not, so the evidence is mixed and more research is needed.

items.title: Interventions with pregnant women, new mothers and other primary caregivers for preventing early childhood caries
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 23 trials with almost 26,000 caregivers, testing ways to prevent tooth decay in young children. Giving pregnant women, mothers and other caregivers advice on baby diet and feeding probably leads to a slightly lower risk of early childhood tooth decay. For most other approaches, such as breastfeeding support, oral hygiene advice, vitamin D in pregnancy or dental treatment for mothers, the evidence was too weak to say whether they help.
keyPoints: Advice on diet and feeding for babies up to age one probably reduces the risk of tooth decay in baby teeth by about 15 per cent (moderate-certainty evidence).
Breastfeeding promotion and support made little or no difference to tooth decay (low-certainty evidence).
Evidence on oral hygiene advice, vitamin D in pregnancy and dental treatments for mothers was low or very low certainty, so no firm conclusions can be drawn.
The authors call for larger, high-quality trials, and 13 studies are already under way.

items.title: Infant formulas for the treatment of functional gastrointestinal disorders: A position paper of the ESPGHAN Nutrition Committee
items.journal: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.summary: The European paediatric gastroenterology and nutrition society (ESPGHAN) reviewed the evidence on special infant formulas sold for spit-up, colic and constipation in babies. These problems are common, usually normal in the early months, and often need no treatment. The evidence that special formulas help is limited, and the group says they should only be used on medical advice.
keyPoints: Spit-up, colic and constipation are common and usually normal in young babies, and typically do not need treatment or a switch to a special formula.
Breastfed babies with these problems should not be moved from breastfeeding to commercial formula.
Specialized formulas are not advised for colic because there is a lack of clinical evidence that they work.
Thickened formulas may be considered in specific cases of spit-up, and formulas with high β-palmitate and extra magnesium may be considered to soften stools in constipation.

items.title: Complementary feeding approaches and risk of choking: A systematic review
items.source: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.journal: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.summary: This review looked at whether the way parents introduce solid foods changes a baby's risk of choking. It compared baby-led weaning (babies feed themselves finger foods) with traditional spoon-feeding, using 7 studies. No study found a statistically significant difference in choking between the approaches. The authors suggest choking risk may depend more on how familiar a baby is with a food texture and how well parents understand how to make foods safer.
keyPoints: No included study found a statistically significant difference in choking risk between baby-led weaning, baby-led introduction to solids and spoon-feeding.
In five studies, spoon-fed babies had more choking episodes than baby-led babies, though the differences were not statistically significant.
Choking risk may relate more to a baby's familiarity with a texture and to parents knowing how to reduce the risk than to the feeding approach.
The authors say advice on making foods safer needs to be clearer and reinforced for all parents.

items.title: Indications for extensively hydrolyzed cow's milk protein in the neonatal period
items.summary: This French practice guideline looked at when newborns really need a special 'extensively hydrolyzed' cow's milk formula, where the milk proteins are broken down into tiny pieces. The authors say many prescriptions for it are based on old habits rather than good evidence. They sort situations into those with good evidence, those with weaker evidence, and those where it is not justified.
keyPoints: Good evidence supports extensively hydrolyzed formula for newborns with a proven cow's milk protein allergy, and for occasional supplements alongside breastfeeding.

Some uses, such as restarting feeds after necrotizing enterocolitis, short bowel syndrome or intestinal surgery when mother's own milk or donor milk is unavailable, are not backed by high-level evidence.
The formula is not justified for newborns just at risk of allergy (atopy), premature babies, or those with severe neurological problems, unstable circulation or congenital heart disease.
Each baby's situation should be considered individually, and how well the milk is tolerated and works should be rechecked over time.

items.title: Donor human milk for preventing necrotising enterocolitis in very preterm or very low-birthweight infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at very preterm or very low-birthweight babies who could not get enough of their own mother's milk. It compared feeding with donated human milk against formula. Donor milk roughly halved the risk of necrotising enterocolitis (NEC), a serious bowel condition in premature babies. It probably made little or no difference to serious infections or to deaths before leaving hospital.
keyPoints: Donor human milk reduced the risk of NEC by about half compared with formula (high certainty evidence, 11 trials, 2261 infants).
Donor human milk probably has little or no effect on late-onset invasive infection (moderate certainty).
Donor human milk probably has little or no effect on death from any cause before hospital discharge (moderate certainty).
The review covered 12 trials with 2296 infants, all in neonatal units in Europe or North America.

items.title: Vitamin D for the management of asthma
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 20 placebo-controlled trials of vitamin D in children and adults with asthma, mostly mild to moderate asthma. Vitamin D did not reduce asthma attacks needing steroid tablets, and it did not improve asthma control or lung function. It also did not raise the rate of serious side effects. People with severe asthma or very low vitamin D levels were poorly represented, so those groups are still unclear.
keyPoints: Vitamin D did not reduce or increase the number of people having asthma attacks needing steroid treatment (high-quality evidence).
No benefit was found for asthma control scores, emergency visits or lung function, and results did not differ by age, dose or starting vitamin D level.
No effect on serious side effects was seen; reported reactions such as high urine calcium or stomach upset occurred in both vitamin D and placebo groups.
Too few people with severe asthma or very low vitamin D were studied, and one trial of a different form (calcidiol) showed benefit, so more research is needed.

items.title: The Volume of Breast Milk Intake in Infants and Young Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 167 studies to estimate how much breast milk babies and young children take in each day. Across all studies the average was about 670 mL a day. Intake changed with the baby's age, weight and feeding pattern, and the way it was measured also affected the numbers.
keyPoints: Average daily breast milk intake across all studies was 670 mL per day (117 mL/kg per day).
For healthy term babies exclusively breastfed up to 6 months, intake was about 624 mL/day at 1 month, 735 mL/day at 3 months, 729 mL/day at 6 months and 593 mL/day at 12 months.
Intake per kilogram of body weight fell as babies grew, from 135 mL/kg per day at 1 month to 61 mL/kg per day at 12 months.
Estimates differed by region and by measurement method, with the deuterium dilution method tending to give higher numbers than test-weighing.

items.title: WHO Guideline for complementary feeding of infants and young children 6–23 months of age
items.summary: This is a World Health Organization guideline on feeding babies and young children from 6 to 23 months, the time when foods are added alongside milk. It gives evidence-based recommendations for both breastfed and non-breastfed children, in countries of all income levels. It replaces two older WHO sets of guiding principles on complementary feeding.
keyPoints: Complementary feeding means giving foods in addition to milk once breast milk or formula alone no longer meets a baby's nutritional needs, usually from about 6 months.
Between 6 and 23 months children learn to accept healthy foods and set long-term eating patterns.
This is also the period of highest risk for slowed growth and nutrient deficiencies.
The guideline covers the needs of both breastfed and non-breastfed children.

items.title: Supplementation of Infant Formula and Neurodevelopmental Outcomes: a Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at clinical trials and long-term studies of infant formulas with added ingredients, to see whether they affect children's thinking and learning. Adding fatty acids (LC-PUFA) sometimes helped certain skills but often made no difference, with no consistent benefit overall. Changing the amount of protein did not change children's test results, and milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) showed short-term benefits but no lasting effect.
keyPoints: Added LC-PUFA fatty acids gave some positive effects on specific skills or none, with no consistent benefit for thinking and learning.
Changing the protein amount in formula did not affect children's neuropsychological test results.
Added MFGM was linked to better cognitive development in the short term, but no effect was seen in the long term.
More studies are needed to confirm the safety of these added ingredients for children's cognitive development.

items.title: Impact of prelacteal feeds and neonatal introduction of breast milk substitutes on breastfeeding outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from prospective studies (which follow babies forward in time) on giving babies fluids other than breast milk in the first days or weeks of life. Babies given these early fluids, called prelacteal feeds, were more likely to stop exclusive breastfeeding and to stop breastfeeding altogether before 6 months. Introducing formula (breast milk substitutes) in the first month was also linked to a shorter time breastfeeding. The authors call for support to prevent unnecessary early milk-based feeds and formula in the newborn period.
keyPoints: Prelacteal feeds were linked to a higher chance of stopping exclusive breastfeeding in babies under 6 months (RR 1.44).
Prelacteal feeds were also linked to a higher chance of stopping any breastfeeding in babies under 6 months (RR 2.23).
Nine studies found that giving formula in the newborn period was linked to a shorter breastfeeding duration.
The authors say effective interventions are needed to prevent unnecessary milk-based prelacteals and formula early on.

items.title: Prevalence of ankyloglossia according to different assessment tools: A meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of the American Dental Association
items.journal: Journal of the American Dental Association
items.summary: This review pooled results from 71 studies to estimate how common ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) is. Overall about 5 in 100 people were found to have it, and it was more common in infants, at about 7 in 100. The rate changed a lot depending on which assessment tool was used, from 2% to 20%. Boys seemed more affected than girls, but the evidence for this was very low certainty, so it is unclear.
keyPoints: Overall prevalence of tongue-tie was about 5% across 71 studies.
It was more common in infants, at about 7%.
Reported rates ranged from 2% to 20% depending on the assessment tool used.
Whether boys are more affected than girls is uncertain (very low certainty evidence).

items.title: Preventing food allergy in infancy and childhood: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials
items.summary: This review pulled together 46 trials on ways to prevent food allergy in babies and young children. Introducing well-cooked egg from 4 to 6 months probably lowers the risk of egg allergy, and regular peanut from 4 to 11 months probably lowers peanut allergy risk in babies at higher risk. For most other approaches, such as avoiding allergen foods, vitamins, fish oil, probiotics and skin emollients, the evidence is very uncertain and they may make little or no difference.
keyPoints: Well-cooked egg (not pasteurised raw egg) introduced from 4 to 6 months probably reduces the risk of hen's egg allergy.

Regular peanut eaten from 4 to 11 months probably cuts peanut allergy a lot in higher-risk infants in countries where it is common; this rests on moderate certainty evidence from single trials in high-income countries.
Avoiding allergy foods, vitamin supplements, fish oil, probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics and emollients may have little to no effect, but the evidence is very uncertain.
Breastfeeding and hydrolysed formulas may not reduce cow's milk allergy, and short-term cow's milk formula top-ups in the first week of life may raise the risk.

items.title: Protein supplementation of human milk for promoting growth in preterm infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether adding extra protein to breast milk helps premature babies grow while they are in hospital. It pooled six small trials with 204 babies. Low-quality evidence suggests the extra protein may increase short-term growth in weight, length and head size. The effects on hospital stay, feeding problems and a serious bowel condition (necrotising enterocolitis) are uncertain because the evidence was very weak, and there was no information on longer-term outcomes.
keyPoints: Low-quality evidence found that adding protein to human milk may increase in-hospital growth in weight, length and head circumference in preterm babies.
It is uncertain whether protein supplementation leads to longer hospital stays, as this came from one small trial and the evidence was very low quality.
The effect on feeding intolerance and necrotising enterocolitis is uncertain.
No data were available on brain development or on outcomes after leaving hospital.

items.title: Early full enteral feeding for preterm or low birth weight infants
items.summary: This review looked at whether giving preterm or low birth weight babies full milk feeds very early, rather than starting small and building up slowly, affects growth or a serious bowel problem called necrotising enterocolitis. It combined six trials from India with 526 babies, most born very preterm. The trials did not give enough information to say how early full feeding affects growth. It is also unclear whether it changes the risk of necrotising enterocolitis, because the evidence is very uncertain.
keyPoints: Six trials (526 babies, mostly very preterm) compared early full milk feeds with slowly increased feeds plus intravenous fluids.
There was not enough data to tell how early full feeding affects growth; the two trials that reported weight gain pointed in opposite directions (very low-certainty evidence).
One trial found a slightly higher weight score at hospital discharge with early full feeding (low-certainty evidence).
No clear effect on necrotising enterocolitis was found, but the evidence was very low certainty.

items.title: Formula versus donor breast milk for feeding preterm or low birth weight infants
items.summary: This review pooled 12 trials with 1,879 preterm or low birth weight babies to compare formula with donor breast milk when a mother's own milk is not enough. Babies fed formula gained weight and grew faster in hospital. They also had a higher risk of necrotising enterocolitis, a serious bowel condition. No effect was found on death, long-term growth or later development. The trials had some weaknesses, and most were funded by formula makers.
keyPoints: Formula-fed babies had faster weight gain, length growth and head growth while in hospital.
Formula feeding raised the risk of necrotising enterocolitis (about 3 more cases per 100 babies; roughly 1 extra case for every 33 babies fed formula).
No effect was found on all-cause mortality, long-term growth or neurodevelopment.
The trials had methodological weaknesses, and most were funded by companies that made the study formula.

items.title: Recommendations for Prevention and Control of Influenza in Children, 2019-2020
items.summary: This statement from the American Academy of Pediatrics updates its advice on flu vaccines and flu medicines for children for the 2019-2020 season. It recommends a yearly flu vaccine for all children from 6 months of age who have no medical reason to avoid it. Flu antiviral medicine is recommended for children with suspected or confirmed flu, especially those who are very unwell or at higher risk of complications.
keyPoints: All children without medical contraindications should get a flu vaccine every year, starting at 6 months of age.
Any licensed, recommended vaccine suited to the child's age can be used, with no preference for one product over another.
Antiviral treatment is recommended for children with suspected or confirmed flu.
Antivirals are especially important for children who are in hospital, have severe or worsening illness, or have conditions that raise their risk of flu complications.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation guidelines
items.source: Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
items.journal: Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
items.summary: This review compares vitamin D supplement guidelines from different agencies and scientific groups. Guidelines focused on bone health suggest aiming for a blood level of 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) with daily doses of 400-800 IU depending on age. Guidelines that also consider vitamin D's wider effects suggest a higher target of 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L) and doses of 400-2000 IU a day. Side effects from taking supplements are described as rare and usually linked to extremely high doses taken for a long time.
keyPoints: Bone-focused guidelines suggest a blood level of 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) and 400-800 IU a day, depending on age.
Guidelines focused on wider effects suggest 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L) and 400-2000 IU a day, depending on age, body weight, health status and ethnicity.
Food and sunlight alone are generally not enough to keep levels in the 30-50 ng/mL range all year round.
Harmful effects such as high blood calcium are rare and usually come from very high doses taken for a long time.

items.title: Prevention and Management of Procedural Pain in the Neonate: An Update
items.summary: This is a practice guideline on preventing and treating pain in newborn babies during medical procedures, especially in the NICU. It says that preventing pain in newborns is important because repeated painful experiences may have lasting harmful effects. The smallest and sickest premature babies go through the most painful procedures and are at the greatest risk. The guideline notes there are gaps in knowledge about the best methods, but says safe and proven pain relief is currently underused for routine minor procedures.
keyPoints: Repeated painful exposures in newborns may have harmful consequences, so preventing pain is an ethical goal for all neonatal health care professionals.
The smallest and sickest preterm babies face the most painful procedures and the greatest risk of neurodevelopmental problems.
Proven and safe pain-relief methods are underused for routine minor painful procedures, even though there are still gaps in knowledge about the most effective approaches.
Every facility caring for newborns should have a pain-prevention program and a plan for assessing and managing pain, using both medicine-based and non-medicine approaches.

items.title: Prevention of Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding in Newborn Infants: A Position Paper by the ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition
items.journal: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.summary: This position paper from a European children's nutrition committee looks at vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a serious bleeding risk in newborns and young babies because they naturally have low vitamin K levels. It says the condition can largely be prevented by giving vitamin K. All healthy newborns should receive it, either as one injection at birth or as oral doses over the first weeks to months. The injection is the preferred route because it is the most reliable.
keyPoints: All newborn infants should receive vitamin K prophylaxis, and the date, dose and method should be recorded.
Options for healthy newborns are 1 mg vitamin K1 by injection at birth, or oral vitamin K1 given in repeated doses (3 x 2 mg, or 2 mg at birth then 1 mg weekly for 3 months).
Injection is the preferred route for efficiency and reliability; oral dosing depends on families sticking to the schedule.
Oral vitamin K is not appropriate for preterm babies, babies who are too unwell or have poor gut absorption, or those whose mothers took medicines that interfere with vitamin K.

items.title: Nutrient-enriched formula versus standard formula for preterm infants following hospital discharge
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 16 trials with 1251 preterm babies to see whether nutrient-enriched formula after leaving hospital helps them grow and develop better than standard term formula. 'Postdischarge formula' did not show consistent effects on growth up to 12 to 18 months after the due date. 'Preterm formula', which is normally only used in hospital, was linked to faster growth, but few trials looked at development and none found differences at 18 months.
keyPoints: Postdischarge formula versus standard term formula: no consistent effect on growth up to 12 to 18 months post term (moderate-quality evidence).
Preterm formula versus term formula: higher growth through infancy, about 500 g more weight and 5 to 10 mm more length at 12 to 18 months post term.
The few trials that checked development found no differences at 18 months post term.
Recommendations to prescribe postdischarge formula are not supported by the available evidence, and no data cover later childhood.

items.title: Breastfeeding and intelligence: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 17 studies to see whether breastfed children score differently on intelligence tests. Breastfed children scored about 3.4 IQ points higher on average. The gap was smaller (about 2.6 points) in studies that took mother's IQ into account. The authors say a randomised trial also found a benefit and suggest the link may be causal.
keyPoints: Breastfed children scored about 3.4 IQ points higher on average (range 2.30 to 4.58).
In studies that adjusted for mother's IQ, the difference was smaller at about 2.6 points.
The review found no sign of publication bias.
The authors conclude breastfeeding is linked to better performance on intelligence tests and that the link may be causal.

items.title: Nutritional Management of Low Birth Weight and Preterm Infants in Low- and Low Middle-Income Countries
items.summary: This review pulled together 15 earlier reviews on how to feed preterm and low birth weight babies, with a focus on low- and lower-middle-income countries. It found that breastfeeding support, breast milk fortification and some vitamin and mineral supplements helped babies grow and stay healthier. Formula milk was linked with a higher risk of a serious bowel condition and, in these settings, a higher risk of newborn death. The authors say larger trials are still needed to strengthen the evidence.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding promotion increased early and exclusive breastfeeding at 3 and 6 months in lower-income settings.
Breast milk fortification and nutrient-enriched formula improved growth; formula milk raised the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis overall and neonatal death in low- and lower-middle-income settings.
Iron supplements reduced anemia and vitamin A reduced deaths (in lower-middle-income countries), with little to no harm seen from zinc, calcium/phosphorus or vitamin D supplements.
When breast milk is not available, fortified feeds or nutrient-enriched formula can support better growth.

items.title: Interventions to Support Breastfeeding: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force
items.summary: This large review pooled 90 randomized trials (about 49,600 people) of support aimed at helping mothers breastfeed, such as counselling and education in primary care. Support increased the share of babies who were breastfed, and especially exclusively breastfed, up to and at 6 months. Evidence on infant health and on mothers' anxiety, depression and well-being was limited and mixed. Support did not change whether breastfeeding started or whether it was still going at 12 months.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding support increased any breastfeeding up to and at 6 months (risk ratio 1.13).
Support had a larger effect on exclusive breastfeeding up to and at 6 months (risk ratio 1.46).
No relationship was found with starting breastfeeding or with breastfeeding at 12 months.
Evidence on infant health outcomes and maternal anxiety, depression and well-being was limited and mixed.

items.title: Effect of Neonatal Unit Interventions Designed to Increase Breastfeeding in Preterm Infants: An Overview of Systematic Reviews
items.summary: This review looked at what neonatal units can do to help premature babies breastfeed more. It pulled together results from earlier systematic reviews. Skin-to-skin 'kangaroo' care, avoiding bottles while breastfeeding is being established, cup feeding and unit-wide improvement programmes were linked with more babies being breastfed. Starting kangaroo care within 24 hours of birth, oral stimulation and giving colostrum by mouth swab showed no clear benefit.
keyPoints: Kangaroo mother care (skin-to-skin contact) was linked to more babies having any and exclusive breastfeeding at discharge.
Avoiding bottles while breastfeeding was being established was linked to more babies breastfeeding at discharge and exclusively breastfeeding 3 months later.
Cup feeding and quality improvement programmes in neonatal units showed possible benefit for breastfeeding rates.
Very early kangaroo care (within 24 hours), oral stimulation and oropharyngeal colostrum showed no evidence of benefit; effects by gestational age or birthweight were not reported.

items.title: A Systematic Review Supporting the Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guidelines on Vitamin D
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This review pulled together 151 studies to see whether taking vitamin D helps prevent disease, to support Endocrine Society guidelines. In children, vitamin D may slightly reduce breathing infections, and in pregnancy it may help with some mother and baby outcomes, but the evidence for both is low quality. The review found no trials on whether routine vitamin D blood testing is helpful or harmful.
keyPoints: In children and adolescents, low-certainty evidence suggested vitamin D may reduce respiratory tract infections.
In pregnant women, low-certainty evidence suggested possible benefits for maternal, fetal and newborn outcomes.
High-dose vitamin D taken intermittently may increase falls compared with lower daily doses.
No trials were found on the benefits and harms of screening with a vitamin D blood test.

items.title: Bovine Milk Fat Globule Membrane Supplementation and Neurocognitive Development: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled eight randomized trials (1352 healthy babies and young children up to 2 years) to see whether adding bovine milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) to infant formula helps brain development. Formula with MFGM was linked to better scores for cognitive development and executive function, but not for language, motor or social-emotional development. Cognitive scores were not significantly different from those of breastfed babies. The authors also note that the evidence is limited and there is no conclusive proof of benefit.
keyPoints: Formula with added MFGM was linked to improved cognitive development compared with standard formula.
Executive function improved, but language, motor and social-emotional development did not.
Cognitive development did not differ significantly from breastfed babies.
The authors say the evidence is limited and not conclusive.

items.title: Maternal Lifestyle Factors Affecting Breast Milk Composition and Infant Health: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 20 studies on how a mother's diet and lifestyle can change the make-up of her breast milk and her baby's health. Mum's weight, what she eats and her intake of nutrients such as iodine, omega-3 fats and vitamins were linked to differences in milk and in infant growth and brain development. Smoking was linked to changes in milk, including lower osteopontin, which may matter for a baby's immunity and growth. The abstract does not report how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Maternal body mass index and the amount of fat, protein and carbohydrate eaten were linked to the fatty acids in breast milk, which relate to infant growth, thinking skills and metabolic health.
Iodine, omega-3 fatty acids and vitamins in the mother's intake were linked to better neurodevelopment and lower risk of allergic (atopic) conditions in babies.
Maternal diet and supplements improved the nutrient content of breast milk and infant outcomes in the studies reviewed.
Smoking was linked to altered milk, including lower osteopontin, and exposure to the toxin ochratoxin A raised concerns.

items.title: The rates and factors of perceived insufficient milk supply: A systematic review
items.summary: This review pooled 27 studies on 'perceived insufficient milk supply', which is when a mother feels she isn't making enough milk. About half of mothers who stopped breastfeeding said this was the reason, and 10% to 25% of mothers who were still breastfeeding reported it. Feeling more confident about breastfeeding went along with less worry about supply, and breastfeeding knowledge was also linked to it. The authors say support is needed to help mothers at risk keep breastfeeding.
keyPoints: About 50% of mothers who stopped breastfeeding gave perceived low milk supply as the reason.
Among mothers still breastfeeding, 10% to 25% reported perceived low milk supply.
Higher breastfeeding confidence and a baby who sucks well were linked to less perceived low supply, while using formula top-ups was linked to more.
Baby crying was often taken as a sign of low supply, and not taking in enough energy or fluids was a reported cause.

items.title: Nutraceuticals and polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review of the literature
items.summary: This review looked at randomized trials of supplements used by women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), including inositols, vitamin D, vitamin E and probiotics. Inositol, a vitamin-like compound, worked best for blood sugar control and fertility, including more regular periods and ovulation. Some combinations helped with high male-type hormones, inflammation and oxidative stress. The authors say larger, more consistent studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Inositols (myo- and D-chiro-inositol at a 40:1 ratio) were the most effective for improving glucose handling and fertility, with restored ovulation and more regular periods.
Vitamin D with probiotics, vitamin E with coenzyme Q10, and inositol with B vitamins showed promising results for lowering high androgen (male-type hormone) levels.
Probiotics with selenium, or vitamin E with omega 3, improved inflammation and antioxidant status.
Larger studies with more consistent ways of measuring results are still needed.

items.title: Vitamin D requirements in infancy: an updated systematic review
items.source: Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care
items.journal: Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care
items.summary: This review looked at recent randomized trials (published since 2017) on how much vitamin D healthy babies need. The trials did not show any extra benefit from giving more than the usual 400 IU a day. Higher amounts may push blood vitamin D levels to a range that has been linked to possible harms, and 1200 IU a day may even raise the risk of allergic sensitization. Whether larger amounts could help long-term health, such as bone strength, allergies or cancer later in life, is still not known.
keyPoints: No new trial evidence shows that giving more than the usual 400 IU of vitamin D daily improves any important outcome in healthy babies.
Larger amounts may lead to blood vitamin D levels that have been reported as possibly linked to harm.
A daily dose of 1200 IU may increase the risk of allergic sensitization.
It is still unclear whether more generous doses affect long-term outcomes like osteoporosis, allergies or cancer.

items.title: Choline, Neurological Development and Brain Function: A Systematic Review Focusing on the First 1000 Days
items.summary: This review pulled together animal and human studies on choline, a nutrient involved in brain development, during pregnancy and the first two years of a child's life. It found that getting more choline, through the mother's diet or the child's, may support normal brain development and may help protect the brain when a baby is exposed to alcohol before birth. Benefits for thinking skills were mainly seen in animal studies. The authors suggest most children would benefit from more choline and that health guidelines may need to be re-evaluated.
keyPoints: Extra choline in the maternal or child's diet in the first 1000 days may support normal brain development (animal and human evidence).
Choline may help protect against brain and metabolic harm, particularly when a baby is exposed to alcohol in the womb (animal and human evidence).
Improved brain and thinking function was seen mainly in animal studies.
The authors suggest health guidelines should be re-evaluated to communicate choline's potential benefits through food and/or supplements.

items.title: Fat supplementation of human milk for promoting growth in preterm infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether adding extra fat to human milk helps premature babies grow better in hospital. Only one very small trial, with 14 babies, was found. It showed no clear difference in weight, length or head growth, and no clear increase in feeding problems. The evidence is very low quality, so it is not possible to say whether fat supplementation helps or harms.
keyPoints: Only one small trial (14 preterm babies) met the review's criteria.
No clear difference in short-term growth in weight, length or head size between fat-supplemented and unsupplemented human milk.
No clear evidence that adding fat caused more feeding intolerance, but the evidence was very low quality.
No information was available on long-term growth, brain development or heart and metabolic health.

items.title: Carbohydrate supplementation of human milk to promote growth in preterm infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether adding extra carbohydrate to breast milk helps premature babies grow. Only one small trial of 75 preterm babies was found, and the quality of its evidence was very low. Babies given a prebiotic carbohydrate weighed more at 30 days and went home sooner, but the review concludes there is not enough evidence to know the real short- or long-term effects.
keyPoints: Only one small, unblinded trial (75 preterm infants) met the review's criteria.
At 30 days, babies given a prebiotic carbohydrate weighed about 160 grams more than babies given unsupplemented milk, but this was very low-quality evidence.
No clear difference was found in feeding intolerance or necrotising enterocolitis between the groups.
The review found insufficient evidence on carbohydrate supplementation of human milk for preterm infants, and no data on long-term growth or development.

items.title: Relationship between vitamin D deficiency and both gestational and postpartum depression
items.summary: This review looked at eight studies with 8,583 women from seven countries to see whether low vitamin D is linked to depression during pregnancy and after birth. Six of the eight studies found a link. The authors concluded there is a probable relationship between vitamin D deficiency and a higher chance of depression in these periods, and that vitamin D supplements look like a promising way to lower the risk of depressive symptoms.
keyPoints: Six of eight studies found an association between low vitamin D and depression in pregnancy or after birth.
The authors conclude there is a probable relationship between vitamin D deficiency and a higher chance of gestational and postpartum depression.
Vitamin D supplementation appears to be a promising way to reduce the risk of depressive symptoms.
The review covered 8,583 women from seven countries.

items.title: A systematic review of vitamin D status in southern European countries
items.summary: Researchers pulled together 107 studies covering about 630,000 people in Southern Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean to see how common low vitamin D is. Despite plenty of sunshine, low vitamin D was common, with more than a third of studies reporting average levels below 50 nmol/L. Women, newborns and infants, and teenagers were more likely to have poor vitamin D status. Results varied a lot between studies and countries.
keyPoints: More than one-third of studies reported average vitamin D levels below 50 nmol/L, and about 10% reported averages below 25 nmol/L.
Females, newborns/infants and adolescents had the highest rates of poor vitamin D status.
Rates of low vitamin D in different studies ranged from 6.8% to 97.9% (the highest was in Italian newborns).
The authors call for tailored approaches such as vitamin D food fortification and/or supplements for higher-risk groups.

items.title: Prenatal Primary Prevention of Mental Illness by Micronutrient Supplements in Pregnancy
items.summary: This review looked at whether vitamins and other nutrients taken in pregnancy could lower a child's later risk of mental illness. Folic acid and phosphatidylcholine supplements showed signs of helping children's emotional development. Vitamins A and D were linked to lower risk of schizophrenia and autism in looking-back (retrospective) studies. Omega-3 results were mixed: early-pregnancy use was linked to higher risk of schizophrenia and ADHD symptoms, while later-pregnancy use was linked to less childhood wheezing and fewer premature births.
keyPoints: Folic acid and phosphatidylcholine supplements showed evidence of improving childhood emotional development linked to later mental illness.
Vitamins A and D were linked to lower risk of schizophrenia and autism, but only in retrospective observations.
Omega-3 in early pregnancy was linked to higher schizophrenia risk and more ADHD symptoms, but in later pregnancy to less childhood wheezing and premature birth.
Studies are hard to do because mental illnesses like schizophrenia appear many years after birth.

items.title: Maternal and Neonatal Metabolic Outcomes of Vitamin D Supplementation in Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined five randomized trials with 310 women who had gestational diabetes. It looked at whether taking vitamin D supplements changed their blood sugar and cholesterol, and how their babies did. Women who took vitamin D had better fasting blood sugar, cholesterol and inflammation markers, and their newborns were less likely to have high bilirubin (a cause of newborn jaundice). The review is small and the abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplements in women with gestational diabetes were linked to lower fasting blood sugar.
Total and LDL ("bad") cholesterol were lower and HDL ("good") cholesterol was higher with vitamin D.
A marker of inflammation (hs-CRP) was lower in women who took vitamin D.
Newborns of women who took vitamin D were less likely to have hyperbilirubinemia (high bilirubin, linked to jaundice).

items.title: Glutamine supplementation to prevent morbidity and mortality in preterm infants
items.summary: This review pooled 12 randomised trials involving 2,877 preterm babies to see whether glutamine supplements, an amino acid given by mouth or through a drip, improve outcomes. It found no effect on deaths, serious infections or a bowel condition called necrotising enterocolitis. Follow-up of children aged 18 to 24 months and beyond also showed no differences. The trials were generally of good quality.
keyPoints: No effect of glutamine supplementation on death in preterm infants was found.
No effect was found on serious infection or necrotising enterocolitis.
Three trials that followed children to 18 to 24 months and beyond found no effects on neurodevelopment.
The review concluded there is no evidence that glutamine gives important benefits to preterm babies.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation for preventing infections in children under five years of age
items.summary: This review looked at whether giving vitamin D supplements to children under five prevents infections such as pneumonia and diarrhoea. It found four trials with over 3,000 children. The main evidence, mostly from one large trial, did not show that vitamin D lowered the number of pneumonia or diarrhoea episodes. No trials looked at TB or malaria.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplements made little difference to first episodes of pneumonia (moderate quality evidence) or to episodes of diarrhoea.
Whether supplements affect deaths or hospital stays is unclear, because there were too few events and the evidence was low or very low quality.
Blood vitamin D levels were higher in supplemented children, but the evidence was low quality and levels were not always higher at the end of the trials.
No trials were found on whether vitamin D prevents TB, malaria or fever illness.

items.title: Pharmacologic and Nutritional Therapies in Idiopathic Male Infertility: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 41 randomized trials (3,615 men) testing medicines and nutritional supplements in men whose infertility has no clear cause. Antioxidants were linked to better sperm concentration, movement and shape. However, the certainty of the evidence was very low, and results varied a lot between studies, so it is unclear how much any one man would benefit. Other treatments showed possible small gains, but the results could not rule out no effect.
keyPoints: Antioxidants were associated with higher sperm concentration, motility and normal shape in men with idiopathic infertility.
Certainty of the evidence was very low and the range of likely individual effects was wide.
PDE inhibitors and methyl donors showed possible benefits, but the results were also consistent with no effect.
Larger trials that report live births are needed.

items.title: Guideline No. 447: Diagnosis and Management of Endometrial Polyps
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline explains how womb (endometrial) polyps should be diagnosed and managed. Polyps are common and can cause abnormal bleeding, difficulty getting pregnant, or bleeding after menopause. Options are watching and waiting, medication, or surgery, depending on symptoms, the chance of cancer and the patient's own choice. The abstract does not give the individual recommendations or how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Endometrial polyps are common and can cause abnormal bleeding, infertility or bleeding after menopause.
Polyps without symptoms often do not need treatment.
Management options are expectant (watchful waiting), medical or surgical, depending on symptoms, cancer risk and patient choice.
Medication can be used, but surgery is often needed.

items.title: Probiotics supplementation in the treatment of male infertility: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at four randomized trials of probiotic supplements in men with infertility where no clear cause was found. The studies reported improvements in sperm quality, especially how well sperm move. The authors suggest probiotics may help by reducing oxidative damage to sperm DNA. Only four studies were included, so more research is needed to be sure.
keyPoints: Four randomized clinical studies in men with unexplained (idiopathic) infertility were reviewed.
Probiotics showed antioxidant effects that may protect sperm DNA from damage.
Improvements were seen in all sperm measures, with the biggest gain in sperm motility.
The authors describe probiotics as a possible treatment option for idiopathic male infertility.

items.title: Intramural Leiomyomas and Fertility: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 13 studies to look at how fibroids inside the muscle wall of the womb (intramural fibroids) relate to the chance of getting pregnant. Women with these fibroids, even small ones, had lower pregnancy and live-birth rates than women without fibroids. Women with more than one fibroid did worse than women with a single fibroid, who showed no difference. Having the fibroids removed did not improve the chance of pregnancy compared with leaving them in place.
keyPoints: Even small intramural fibroids (under 3 cm) were linked to lower clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy or live-birth rates.
Women with more than one fibroid had lower pregnancy and live-birth rates, while women with a single fibroid had no difference in outcomes.
Pregnancy rates after surgery to remove intramural fibroids were no different from those with fibroids left in place.
The authors conclude that removing intramural fibroids does not confer a fertility benefit.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of acupuncture for polycystic ovary syndrome: An overview of systematic reviews
items.summary: This study looked at 11 existing reviews of trials on acupuncture for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a common cause of infertility from irregular ovulation. Some reviews suggested acupuncture, especially alongside medicines, may improve pregnancy and ovulation rates and help with weight and menstrual cycles. However, most of the reviews were of low or very low quality, and the evidence was inconsistent. The authors concluded that how well acupuncture works and how safe it is for PCOS is still uncertain.
keyPoints: Some reviews found acupuncture combined with medicines may improve clinical pregnancy and ovulation rates in PCOS.
Acupuncture alone was reported to improve pregnancy rates compared with medicine alone, and to help menstrual cycle recovery and BMI compared with no treatment.
Acupuncture was reported to cause no adverse events or only events without serious harm.
Most of the reviews were of low or very low quality, so the true benefit and safety remain uncertain and better studies are needed.

items.title: Prevalence of adenomyosis in women with subfertility: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 21 studies covering about 25,600 women who were having trouble getting pregnant. They found that about 1 in 10 of these women had adenomyosis on its own, meaning a condition where the womb lining grows into the womb wall. The rate was lower when adenomyosis occurred together with fibroids or endometriosis. Results differed a lot between studies, regions and ways of diagnosing it.
keyPoints: About 10% of women with subfertility had isolated adenomyosis (95% CI 6-15%).
Adenomyosis alongside endometriosis was found in about 6% of women, and alongside fibroids in about 1%.
The reported rate varied by country, for example about 19% in Australia versus about 5% in Asia.
The rate depended on how it was diagnosed: about 11% when several ultrasound features were used, and under 1% in the one study using only an indirect feature.

items.title: The influence of lead exposure on male semen parameters: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from ten observational studies comparing semen quality in healthy men exposed to lead (through the environment or work) with men who were not exposed. Men exposed to lead had lower semen volume, sperm concentration, total sperm count, sperm vitality and total sperm motility. No difference was found in normal sperm shape, progressive motility or semen thickness. The authors say lead exposure is widespread and that exposed workers should have their semen assessed.
keyPoints: Lead exposure was linked to lower semen volume, sperm concentration and total sperm count.
Sperm vitality and total sperm motility were also lower in exposed men.
No difference was seen in normal sperm shape, progressive motility or semen viscosity.
The authors suggest public health attention to lead exposure and semen checks for exposed workers.

items.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility†
items.summary: This European guideline looked at how to diagnose and treat couples whose fertility tests all come back normal (unexplained infertility). It makes 52 recommendations. The first treatment suggested is intrauterine insemination (IUI) combined with ovarian stimulation (medicines that help the ovaries release eggs). Most recommendations rest on very low or low quality evidence, so advice may change as better studies appear.
keyPoints: Unexplained infertility is diagnosed only after standard checks of both partners find no clear problem.
First-line treatment is IUI combined with ovarian stimulation.
Of 40 evidence-based recommendations, none had high-quality evidence, one had moderate, nine low and 31 very low quality evidence.
Many extra tests and treatments have not been properly tested, and recommendations may be revised as new studies appear.

items.title: The Effect of Uterine Adenomyosis on IVF Outcomes: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled earlier studies to see how adenomyosis (a condition where womb lining tissue grows into the womb muscle) affects IVF and ICSI results. Women with adenomyosis had lower live birth, clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy rates, and a higher miscarriage rate, than women without it. Surgery may help natural conception, but only two studies looked at this. Long-term GnRH agonist treatment before IVF did not clearly improve results, based on only three studies.
keyPoints: Women with adenomyosis had lower live birth rates after IVF/ICSI than women without it (OR 0.59).
Clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy rates were lower, and miscarriage was more common (OR 2.11).
Surgery was linked to more natural conceptions, but data came from only two studies.
Pretreatment with long-term GnRH agonists did not improve IVF outcomes, though only three studies were included.

items.title: Fertility, pregnancy and neonatal outcomes of patients with adenomyosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 17 observational studies to see how adenomyosis relates to fertility, pregnancy and newborn outcomes. In women having assisted reproductive technology (ART), adenomyosis was linked to lower clinical pregnancy rates and more miscarriages. It was also linked to more pregnancy complications, including pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, Caesarean section and postpartum bleeding. These links held after accounting for age and how the pregnancy was conceived. Because the studies were observational, they show associations rather than proving cause.
keyPoints: After ART, adenomyosis was linked to a lower clinical pregnancy rate (OR 0.69) and a higher miscarriage rate (OR 2.17).
Adenomyosis was linked to a higher risk of pre-eclampsia, preterm delivery, Caesarean section, baby in an unusual position, small-for-gestational-age babies and postpartum haemorrhage.
The associations remained after adjusting for age and mode of conception.
The authors suggest counselling before ART and close monitoring during pregnancy, and say ultra-long down-regulation protocols need testing in randomised trials.

items.title: Diagnosis and treatment of infertility in men: AUA/ASRM guideline part I
items.summary: This guideline from two medical societies sets out how a man should be checked when a couple is struggling to conceive. It covers taking a health history, a physical exam and further tests when needed. It also notes that male infertility can be linked to other health conditions, so being checked matters for the man's own health too.
keyPoints: Evaluating the male partner is a recommended part of investigating an infertile couple.
The check starts with a medical history and physical exam, followed by diagnostic tests where indicated.
Finding male infertility can raise the chance of other health problems developing later in a man's life.
Some medical conditions are linked to particular causes of male infertility.

items.title: Granulocyte-colony stimulating factor administration for subfertile women undergoing assisted reproduction
items.summary: This review pooled 15 trials (about 1,250 women) testing G-CSF, a growth-factor drug, given during IVF to see if it helps women get pregnant. No trial reported live births, and the evidence on ongoing pregnancy and miscarriage was very low quality, so it is unclear whether G-CSF helps. It may improve clinical pregnancy rates in women with two or more previous failed IVF cycles, but this finding is low quality and the studies had weaknesses. Few trials reported side effects, and none reported major ones.
keyPoints: No trial reported live-birth rate, the main outcome of interest.
It is uncertain whether G-CSF improves ongoing pregnancy or lowers miscarriage, based on very low-quality evidence.
Low-quality evidence suggests G-CSF may raise clinical pregnancy rates in women with two or more previous IVF failures.
Only four trials reported side effects, and none found major adverse events.

items.title: Regular (ICSI) versus ultra-high magnification (IMSI) sperm selection for assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review compared two ways of choosing sperm for ICSI in fertility treatment: the usual method and IMSI, which looks at sperm under very high magnification. It pooled 13 trials with 2775 couples. The evidence was all of very low quality, so it is not clear whether IMSI improves live birth or pregnancy rates or changes the risk of miscarriage. No trials reported on birth defects.
keyPoints: It is uncertain whether IMSI improves live birth rates or changes miscarriage rates compared with standard ICSI.
IMSI may increase the chance of a clinical pregnancy, but the evidence is very low quality, so any real difference is very uncertain.
None of the included trials reported on congenital abnormalities (birth defects).
The authors say the evidence neither supports nor rules out using IMSI, and better-designed, larger trials are still needed.

items.title: Evidence-based treatments for couples with unexplained infertility: a guideline
items.summary: The American Society for Reproductive Medicine reviewed 88 studies to guide treatment for couples whose infertility has no clear cause. Because the cause is unknown, treatment is based on trial and experience rather than a targeted fix. For most couples, the best first step is about 3 or 4 cycles of ovarian stimulation with oral medications plus intrauterine insemination (IUI), followed by IVF if that does not work.
keyPoints: Treatment of unexplained infertility is empiric, meaning it is based on what has worked in practice rather than on a known cause.
For most couples, the best initial treatment is typically 3 or 4 cycles of ovarian stimulation with oral medications and IUI.
IVF is recommended for couples who do not conceive with ovarian stimulation and IUI.
The guideline covers options such as clomiphene citrate, letrozole (an aromatase inhibitor), gonadotropins, timing of IUI, and IVF.

items.title: Vitamins combined with traditional Chinese medicine for male infertility: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 randomized trials with 1488 men who had fertility problems. It compared traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) plus vitamins with vitamin E or vitamin E plus C alone. The combination improved sperm numbers, movement and the pregnancy rate, with no increase in side effects. The authors say longer, larger, better-designed trials are still needed before firm guidance can be given.
keyPoints: TCM plus vitamins beat vitamin E or vitamin E + C alone for sperm concentration, motility and viability.
The combination also improved pregnancy rates in couples where the man had infertility.
Three TCM capsules (Shengjing, Huanshao and compound Xuanju) showed benefit for pregnancy rate, sperm concentration or sperm motility.
Side effects were not higher with the combination; more long-term, multicenter, double-blind trials are needed.

items.title: Fluid and pharmacological agents for adhesion prevention after gynaecological surgery
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 32 trials (3492 women) of fluids, gels and drugs used during gynaecological surgery to stop scar-like bands called adhesions from forming. Gels and fluids reduced the number of women with adhesions when doctors looked again by camera surgery. But the review found no evidence that they improved pregnancy, live birth or pelvic pain, and steroids showed no clear benefit for pregnancy outcomes.
keyPoints: Fluid (hydroflotation) agents reduced adhesions at a second look-laparoscopy compared with no treatment (high-quality evidence).
Gel agents also reduced adhesions compared with no treatment (high-quality evidence), and probably did so more than fluid agents (moderate-quality evidence).
No clear effect was seen on pelvic pain, live birth or clinical pregnancy; the evidence on these was low or very low quality, and harm could not be ruled out for some comparisons.
Steroids showed no clear effect on live birth or pregnancy rates (low-quality evidence), and no adverse events from the treatments were reported.

items.title: Infertility and teratogenicity after paternal exposure to systemic dermatologic medications: A systematic review
items.source: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
items.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
items.summary: This review looked at whether skin medications taken as tablets or injections by men can affect their fertility or cause birth defects in a pregnancy. It checked 13 medications that were once flagged as risky in pregnancy. Studies on a man's use were found for 10 of them, and 6 showed a negative effect. The authors say better-quality research is needed, especially on possible birth defects.
keyPoints: 13 systemic skin medications were reviewed; studies on fathers' use existed for 10 of them.
Evidence of a negative effect on male fertility was found for 6 medications.
Many medications once rated as risky in pregnancy also seem to affect male fertility.
More and better studies are needed, particularly on whether a father's use could cause birth defects.

items.title: Screening hysteroscopy in subfertile women and women undergoing assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether a camera check of the womb (screening hysteroscopy) helps women who have trouble conceiving, or who are about to have IVF, when ultrasound looks normal. In women having IVF, the pooled results hinted at more live births, but the two most reliable trials showed no benefit. For women with unexplained infertility trying to conceive naturally, only one small trial exists and its evidence is very low quality. Overall, there is not enough good evidence to say routine screening hysteroscopy improves success.
keyPoints: No high-quality evidence supports routine screening hysteroscopy for subfertile women with a normal ultrasound or hysterosalpingogram.
Before IVF, low-quality evidence suggests it may raise live birth and clinical pregnancy rates, but the two trials at low risk of bias showed no benefit.
Miscarriage rates may be little different after screening hysteroscopy before IVF (low-quality evidence).
There is too little data to draw conclusions about safety, and no trials looked at hysteroscopy before IUI.

items.title: Influence of oral vitamin and mineral supplementation on male infertility: a meta-analysis and systematic review
items.summary: This review pooled 18 placebo-controlled trials to see whether vitamin and mineral supplements improve male fertility. Some supplements, including selenium, co-enzyme Q10, carnitine, and zinc with folic acid, were linked to better semen quality. Few trials looked at pregnancy rates, and the studies were small, so the authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Selenium, co-enzyme Q10, and L-carnitine with acetyl-L-carnitine improved semen measures in the pooled analysis.
Zinc combined with folic acid, and the omega-3 fats EPA and DHA, showed promising results in the systematic review.
Only a few trials measured pregnancy rate, so the effect on actually conceiving is less clear.
The authors note small numbers of studies and participants and call for better-designed trials.

items.title: Interventions for unexplained infertility: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 27 trials (4,349 couples) to compare ways of managing unexplained infertility: waiting and trying naturally, ovarian stimulation (OS), intrauterine insemination (IUI), OS with IUI, and IVF/ICSI. Across all couples, there was not enough evidence to show that any treatment gave more live births than waiting. In couples with a poor chance of conceiving naturally, OS with IUI and IVF/ICSI probably increased live births. Ovarian stimulation, with or without IUI, may raise the chance of multiple pregnancy, though the overall chances stayed low.
keyPoints: Across all couples with unexplained infertility, there was insufficient evidence that OS, IUI, OS-IUI or IVF/ICSI gave more live births than expectant management (low-certainty evidence).
In couples with a poor chance of natural conception, OS-IUI and IVF/ICSI increased live birth compared with waiting (moderate-certainty evidence), with no clear difference between the two.
Compared with expectant management or IUI, OS may increase multiple pregnancy and OS-IUI probably does; evidence for IVF/ICSI was insufficient.
There was insufficient evidence of a difference in moderate or severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) between IVF/ICSI and OS-IUI.

items.title: Withania somnifera (Indian ginseng) in male infertility: An evidence-based systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether ashwagandha (Withania somnifera, also called Indian ginseng) helps men with fertility problems. It pooled four small clinical trials, only one of which was a randomized trial. Sperm numbers, semen volume and sperm movement improved after treatment, but the authors say there are too few studies to call the evidence robust. No side effects were reported.
keyPoints: Only four clinical trials were found, and just one was a randomized controlled trial.
In men with low sperm counts, sperm concentration, semen volume and sperm motility rose after 90 days of treatment compared with before treatment.
Testosterone and luteinizing hormone levels also improved, and 14% of normal-sperm-count men achieved a pregnancy outcome.
The authors call the data promising but too limited, and say larger, high-quality randomized trials are needed.

items.title: Anti-adhesion therapy following operative hysteroscopy for treatment of female subfertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at treatments used after hysteroscopy (a procedure to treat problems inside the womb) to stop scar tissue forming, in women having fertility problems. Treatments included intrauterine devices, hormones and barrier gels. They may reduce scar tissue seen at a follow-up check, but no study measured live births and the evidence was low to very low quality. Whether these treatments improve pregnancy outcomes remains uncertain.
keyPoints: No study reported live birth, so the effect on having a baby is unknown.
Devices, hormones or gels may lead to fewer womb adhesions (scar tissue) at second-look hysteroscopy than no treatment or placebo (low-quality evidence).
There was not enough evidence to say whether these treatments change term delivery or ongoing pregnancy rates (very-low-quality evidence).
The authors conclude that the benefit of anti-adhesion treatment for reproductive outcomes remains uncertain and more research is needed.

items.title: Tubal flushing for subfertility
items.summary: This review looked at whether flushing the fallopian tubes with a dye-like liquid (used to check the tubes are open) might also help women with fertility problems get pregnant. It combined 13 trials with about 2,900 women. Flushing with an oil-based liquid may raise the chance of pregnancy and live birth compared with no treatment, though the evidence is low quality. Results for water-based liquid and other comparisons were unclear, and side effects were not well reported.
keyPoints: Oil-based contrast flushing was linked to more live births and ongoing pregnancies than no treatment, based on low quality evidence.
For women with a 17% chance of ongoing pregnancy without treatment, the estimate with oil-based flushing was between 29% and 55%.
Water-based contrast flushing showed no clear difference from no treatment, and the evidence was very low quality.
Evidence on side effects was too limited to draw firm conclusions, and more good trials are needed.

items.title: Fertility evaluation of infertile women: a committee opinion
items.summary: This 2026 committee opinion from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine reviews how women with infertility should be assessed. It says the evaluation should be systematic, quick and cost-effective, looking for all relevant factors and starting with the least invasive tests for the most common causes. It replaces the 2021 version of the same document. The abstract does not list the specific tests or timings.
keyPoints: Infertility evaluation in women should be systematic, prompt and cost-effective.
It should look for all relevant factors, starting with the least invasive methods for the most common causes.
Replaces the 2021 ASRM committee opinion of the same name.
keywords: when to see a fertility doctor
trying to conceive for a year

items.title: Blastocyst-stage versus cleavage-stage embryo transfer in assisted reproductive technology
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 36 trials (8,389 women) comparing IVF embryos transferred at the blastocyst stage (day 5 to 6) with embryos transferred earlier at the cleavage stage (day 2 to 3). Blastocyst transfer probably gives more live births per fresh transfer and may give more over the first 12 months, but it probably also raises the chance of preterm birth. Evidence for most results was low certainty, and the findings mainly apply to women with a good chance of pregnancy.
keyPoints: Live birth per fresh transfer was probably higher with blastocyst transfer: if 32% had a live birth with cleavage-stage transfer, about 37% to 43% would with blastocyst transfer (moderate certainty).
Over 12 months, including frozen transfers, blastocyst transfer may increase live births, but it is unclear whether this holds once all embryos are used (low certainty).
Preterm birth was probably higher with blastocyst transfer: if 3.5% had a preterm birth with cleavage-stage transfer, between 3.9% and 8.5% would with blastocyst transfer (moderate certainty).
Blastocyst transfer may leave fewer spare embryos to freeze and may more often end with no embryo to transfer; miscarriage rates may differ little.

items.title: Does the use of letrozole in infertility treatment increase the risk of foetal malformations? A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled 20 randomized trials (6,679 patients) to check whether letrozole, a fertility medicine, raises the chance of birth defects or pregnancy loss. It found no clear increase in birth defects or pregnancy loss compared with clomiphene, natural conception, gonadotropins or berberine, including when used with timed intercourse. The authors call the results somewhat reassuring, but the certainty of the evidence is low to very low, so the true effect is still uncertain.
keyPoints: No increase in congenital malformations was found with letrozole compared with clomiphene, natural conception, gonadotropins or berberine.
No increased risk was seen when letrozole was used for timed intercourse, intrauterine insemination or frozen embryo transfer.
Pregnancy loss rates were not significantly different from clomiphene or natural conception.
Certainty of the evidence was very low to low, and the authors say more randomized trials are needed.

items.title: Association between preconception body mass index and fertility in adult female: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 18 studies to look at how a woman's body mass index (BMI) before pregnancy relates to how easily she conceives. Women with overweight or obesity took longer to become pregnant and were more likely to have trouble conceiving. Being underweight was also linked to a slightly longer time to pregnancy. The authors suggest that a healthy BMI before trying to conceive may support fertility.
keyPoints: Overweight and obesity were linked to a longer time to pregnancy (reduced fecundability), with obesity showing the stronger effect.
Overweight or obesity was linked to higher odds of subfecundity (OR 1.44) and infertility (OR 1.60).
Being underweight was moderately linked to a longer time to pregnancy.
The authors say managing BMI before pregnancy may improve fertility.

items.title: Indoor and outdoor air pollution and couple fecundability: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 33 articles from 28 studies on air pollution and how quickly couples conceive. Outdoor air pollution from traffic, including nitrogen oxides and fine particles, was linked to reduced chances of conceiving each cycle. Secondhand smoke and formaldehyde were linked to this too, while there was little evidence that volatile solvents had an effect. The studies measured exposure in very different ways, so the picture is not fully settled.
keyPoints: Outdoor air pollution, including traffic-related pollution, nitrogen oxides and fine particles (PM2.5), was linked to reduced fecundability (the chance of conceiving each cycle).
Secondhand smoke and formaldehyde exposure were also linked to reduced fecundability.
There was little evidence that exposure to volatile solvents reduces fecundability.
Studies differed a lot in when and how exposure was measured, so better indoor air monitoring is needed in future research.

items.title: Letrozole Compared With Clomiphene Citrate for Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 29 randomised trials (3,952 women) comparing two fertility medicines, letrozole and clomiphene citrate, in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and infertility. Women taking letrozole were more likely to ovulate, become pregnant and have a live birth. The authors recommend letrozole over clomiphene, but note the quality of the evidence is mixed.
keyPoints: Letrozole led to higher ovulation rates than clomiphene citrate (RR 1.14).
Clinical pregnancy was more likely with letrozole (RR 1.48).
Live birth was more likely with letrozole (RR 1.49), based on eight trials.
The authors recommend letrozole as the ovulation induction drug of choice in PCOS, though the evidence quality is mixed.

items.title: Aromatase inhibitors (letrozole) for ovulation induction in infertile women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 41 randomised trials (6522 women) of letrozole for helping women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) ovulate. Compared with clomiphene-type drugs, letrozole led to more live births and more pregnancies when followed by timed intercourse. Rates of ovarian overstimulation, miscarriage and multiple pregnancy were similar between the treatments. Compared with a surgical option called laparoscopic ovarian drilling, the evidence was too weak to say which works better.
keyPoints: Live birth was more likely with letrozole than with clomiphene-type drugs (high-certainty evidence); for a woman with a 20% chance using clomiphene, the estimate with letrozole is 27% to 35%.
Clinical pregnancy rates were also higher with letrozole (high-certainty evidence).
Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, miscarriage and multiple pregnancy rates were similar between letrozole and clomiphene-type drugs (high-certainty evidence).
It is uncertain whether letrozole beats laparoscopic ovarian drilling for live birth, as the evidence was low or very low certainty.

items.title: Persistent organic pollutants and couple fecundability: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 28 papers from 19 studies on whether long-lasting environmental chemicals (called persistent organic pollutants, or POPs) affect how long it takes a couple to conceive. The strongest evidence was that a woman's exposure to PCBs is linked to a longer time to pregnancy, with some support for links to flame-retardant chemicals (PBDEs) and PFAS. There was little or no evidence that exposure to older pesticides in women, or any of these chemicals in men, affected time to pregnancy. The studies measured exposure in very different ways, so the results could not be combined into one overall number.
keyPoints: Female exposure to polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) had the strongest link to a longer time to conceive.
Female exposure to flame retardants (PBDEs) and PFAS had some support for a link to longer time to pregnancy.
Little or no link was found for female exposure to organochlorine pesticides or for male exposure to any of the chemical groups.
Many of these chemicals are no longer made but are still found in people's bodies, and newer replacement chemicals may have similar effects.

items.title: Fresh versus frozen embryo transfers in assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled randomised trials comparing a 'freeze all' approach (freezing every embryo and transferring later) with the usual IVF/ICSI approach that includes a fresh embryo transfer. Overall chances of a live birth were probably about the same with either approach. Freezing all embryos may lower the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), but may raise the risk of high blood pressure in pregnancy and of larger babies.
