The evidence was moderate to low quality, so findings should be read with some caution.
keyPoints: Cumulative live birth rate is probably little or no different between 'freeze all' and conventional fresh-transfer IVF/ICSI (moderate-quality evidence).
OHSS may be less common with 'freeze all' (about 1% versus 3%), based on low-quality evidence.
'Freeze all' may increase the risk of high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy, large-for-gestational-age babies and higher birth weight.
Time to pregnancy is likely shorter with a fresh transfer, since 'freeze all' delays embryo transfer; the evidence on miscarriage and multiple pregnancy was too uncertain to draw conclusions.

items.title: Immediate versus postponed frozen embryo transfer after IVF/ICSI: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether it is better to have a frozen embryo transfer straight away or to wait at least one menstrual cycle after a failed fresh transfer or a freeze-all cycle. Pooling 15 studies, immediate transfer was linked to a slightly higher chance of a live birth and of a clinical pregnancy. All the studies were looking back at past records rather than randomly assigning patients, so the evidence is considered low quality and the result may be biased.
keyPoints: Pooled results showed slightly higher live birth odds with immediate versus postponed frozen embryo transfer (adjusted odds ratio 1.20).
Clinical pregnancy odds were also slightly higher with immediate transfer (adjusted odds ratio 1.22).
Twelve of the 15 studies found no difference in live birth rate between the two approaches.
The usual practice of waiting at least one cycle may not be the best approach, but randomised trials are needed to confirm this.

items.title: Fibroids and natural fertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether fibroids (non-cancerous growths in the womb) make it harder to get pregnant without fertility treatment. Studies on IVF suggest some fibroids reduce the chance of an embryo implanting, but those results may not apply to natural conception. Looking at the studies on natural fertility, the reviewers found fibroids might interfere with getting pregnant, but the evidence is not strong enough to prove it.
keyPoints: Only a few studies have properly looked at fibroids and natural fertility, so the link between them has been insufficiently investigated.
Combining four studies, women who had trouble conceiving were more likely to have fibroids (odds ratio 3.54, 95% CI 1.55 to 8.11).
In the two most informative studies comparing time to pregnancy, the result was not clearly significant (odds ratio 1.93, 95% CI 0.89 to 4.18).
The authors say the evidence suggests, but does not demonstrate, that fibroids may interfere with natural fertility, and more research is urgently needed.

items.title: Preconception lifestyle advice for people with infertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at seven trials (2,130 people) testing whether lifestyle advice before conception helps people with infertility have a baby. Advice covering several topics may make little to no difference to the number of live births. The evidence was low to very low quality, so the review could not give clear guidance on what advice to offer.
keyPoints: Advice on a mix of lifestyle topics may make little to no difference to live births, based on low-quality evidence from one trial.
In women with infertility and obesity, weight advice may slightly lower BMI, but effects on live birth, miscarriage and pregnancy complications are uncertain.
Combined advice may make little to no difference to folic acid use, alcohol abstinence or smoking cessation in women.
No studies reported on adverse events or miscarriage for combined advice, and the evidence on safety was too weak for conclusions.

items.title: Intra-uterine insemination for unexplained subfertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 15 trials (2068 women) of intra-uterine insemination (IUI) for couples with unexplained difficulty conceiving. IUI was compared with timed intercourse or waiting, with and without ovary-stimulating medicine. In many comparisons it is uncertain whether IUI helps, because the evidence was limited. IUI with stimulation probably gives more live births than waiting in couples with a low chance of natural conception, but the risk of multiple pregnancy remains unclear.
keyPoints: Overall evidence was of very low to moderate quality, mainly because there were too few participants to be sure of the results.
In couples with a low predicted chance of natural conception, IUI with stimulation (clomiphene citrate or letrozole) probably results in more live births than waiting in a natural cycle.
IUI in a natural cycle probably results in more live births than expectant management with stimulation, and IUI with stimulation may give more live births than IUI in a natural cycle.
It is uncertain whether IUI changes the chance of multiple pregnancy, as the trials were too small to tell.

items.title: A systematic review on the effect of DMARDs on fertility in rheumatoid arthritis
items.summary: This review looked at whether disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) used for rheumatoid arthritis affect fertility. Only four studies, all in women, were good enough to include. They found no harmful effects of methotrexate, certolizumab pegol, etanercept or sulfasalazine on time to pregnancy, a hormone linked to egg supply (AMH), or history of infertility. The authors say there is little evidence overall, especially for men, and more research is needed.
keyPoints: Four studies, all in women, were included after screening more than 9,000 references.
No harmful effects were found on time to pregnancy, anti-Müllerian hormone levels or history of infertility.
The authors suggest better-controlled disease activity may explain why these drugs did not appear to harm fertility.
There is a clear gap in knowledge, especially for men with rheumatoid arthritis, and more research is needed.

items.title: Exposure to non-persistent chemicals in consumer products and fecundability: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether everyday chemicals found in consumer products, such as phthalates, parabens and bisphenol A, affect how long it takes a couple to conceive. It found 15 papers from 12 studies. Overall the evidence is limited and results were mixed, though a few chemicals showed early hints of a link with longer time to pregnancy. The authors suggest that people trying to conceive may wish to reduce their exposure as a common-sense step.
keyPoints: Results for phthalates (in men or women) and time to pregnancy were mixed and unclear.
There was early, preliminary support that some parabens and glycol ethers in women, and benzophenone in men, were linked to longer time to conceive, but this needs more research.
Little to no link was seen between bisphenol A, triclocarban or triclosan and time to pregnancy.
The authors advise both women and men trying to conceive to minimise exposure to these chemicals as a common-sense measure.

items.title: Should home-based ovulation predictor kits be offered as an additional approach for fertility management for women and couples desiring pregnancy? A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether home ovulation predictor kits (the urine test strips that signal your fertile window) help women who are trying to get pregnant. It found only four studies, and the quality of the evidence was low. Two trials found no difference in how long it took to get pregnant, while two more recent trials found higher self-reported pregnancy rates among kit users. Most women said they felt satisfied and confident using the kits, and stress did not rise in the one trial that measured it.
keyPoints: Two randomised trials found no difference in time to pregnancy with ovulation kits.

Two more recent trials found higher self-reported pregnancy rates in kit users (pooled relative risk 1.40), but an older trial in couples with unexplained or male-factor infertility found no difference in clinical pregnancy.
One trial found no increase in stress or anxiety after two cycles of use, apart from a drop in positive mood.
Almost all women reported feeling satisfied, comfortable and confident using the kits; no studies measured live birth or harms.

items.title: Influence of increased paternal BMI on pregnancy and child health outcomes independent of maternal effects: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 17 studies to look at whether a father's body weight affects conception, pregnancy and the child's health, separately from the mother's weight. Infertility was more common in men who were overweight or obese. Individual studies also linked higher paternal BMI to some differences in birth size and childhood growth. The authors conclude that a father's weight can affect pregnancy and child outcomes, though only the infertility result could be pooled in a meta-analysis.
keyPoints: Infertility was more common in obese men (odds ratio 1.49) and overweight men (odds ratio 1.18).
Individual studies found higher paternal BMI linked to small-for-gestational-age babies and larger-than-expected babies (macrosomia).
Most studies found higher paternal BMI linked to different growth patterns and higher BMI in childhood; one study found a higher likelihood of autism spectrum disorder.
The authors say research should account for fathers' contributions, not only mothers' factors.

items.title: Coffee and caffeine intake and male infertility: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 28 observational studies, covering almost 20,000 men, on coffee and caffeine and male fertility. Coffee, tea and cocoa drinks did not seem to change semen quality in most studies, though cola and caffeinated soft drinks were linked to lower semen volume and sperm count in some. Caffeine was linked to some sperm DNA changes, and coffee drinking was tied to a longer time to pregnancy in some studies but not others. Overall the evidence was inconsistent and inconclusive.
keyPoints: Most studies found no effect of caffeine from coffee, tea or cocoa on semen quality.
Some studies linked cola and caffeinated soft drinks to lower semen volume, count and concentration.
Caffeine was linked to sperm aneuploidy and DNA breaks, but not to other markers of DNA damage.
Male coffee drinking was linked to a longer time to pregnancy in some studies but not all; better-designed studies are needed.

items.title: How effective are weight-loss interventions for improving fertility in women and men who are overweight or obese? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the evidence
items.summary: This review pooled 40 studies (14 randomised trials) of non-surgical weight-loss programmes in overweight or obese women, men and couples who were trying to conceive. In women, programmes using a reduced-calorie diet plus exercise were more likely to lead to pregnancy than no programme. These programmes also helped with weight loss and, where reported, improved ovulation. Miscarriage rates did not go down with any programme, and there were few studies in men and couples.
keyPoints: In women, reduced-calorie diet and exercise programmes made pregnancy more likely than control programmes (risk ratio 1.59, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.50).
The programmes led to weight loss and better ovulation, where these were measured.
None of the interventions reduced miscarriage rates.
The authors suggest a diet lower in fat and refined carbohydrates plus more aerobic exercise as the basis for such programmes, and note a lack of randomised studies in men and couples.

items.title: Perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances and measures of human fertility: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 16 studies in men and 11 in women on whether PFAS, long-lasting chemicals found widely in the environment, affect fertility. In men, results were inconsistent and there is little evidence of a link with semen quality or reproductive hormones, though small effects of PFOS cannot be ruled out. In women, some studies found it took longer to become pregnant with higher PFOS or PFOA levels, but the authors think this is most likely not a true cause-and-effect link.
keyPoints: In men, there is little evidence that PFAS exposure affects semen quality or reproductive hormone levels.
Subtle links between higher PFOS and lower testosterone or abnormal sperm shape cannot be excluded.
Four of eight studies in women found longer time to pregnancy with higher PFOS or PFOA.
The link in women was seen mainly in women who had already given birth and is most likely not causal.

items.title: Dairy Intake and Iodine Status in Pregnant and Lactating Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 51 studies, mostly of pregnant women, to see whether eating dairy foods is linked to better iodine levels. Women who ate more dairy tended to have higher iodine levels in their urine and were less likely to be iodine deficient. Almost all the studies were observational, so they show a link rather than proof that dairy causes the difference. Findings on iodine in breast milk were mixed.
keyPoints: Higher dairy intake was linked to higher urinary iodine levels (low-certainty evidence).
Higher dairy intake was linked to lower odds of iodine deficiency (odds ratio 0.58, moderate-certainty evidence).
The link was stronger in later pregnancy and when the dairy food was milk.
Dairy provided about 27% of iodine intake from foods.

items.title: Iodine status during child development and hearing ability: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether iodine intake during pregnancy or childhood affects children's hearing. Iodine helps make thyroid hormones, which are needed for the ear and hearing parts of the brain to develop. Thirteen studies were found, but only three were of good quality, so firm conclusions can't be drawn. Overall, the evidence is limited and more good-quality research is needed.
keyPoints: One trial of iodine supplements in mildly iodine-deficient pregnant women found no effect on their babies' hearing, though hearing was only a secondary outcome.
In severely iodine-deficient children, iodine supplementation improved hearing thresholds in two non-randomised studies.
Five of six cross-sectional studies found that better iodine status in children went with better hearing.
Only three of the thirteen studies were of good quality, so the evidence is limited.

items.title: Maternal Iodine Status and Birth Outcomes: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 23 studies with over 42,000 pregnant women to see whether iodine levels in pregnancy are linked to babies' birth outcomes. Women with higher urinary iodine had babies who were slightly higher on birth weight centiles and had a somewhat lower risk of being small for their gestational age. The links were modest in size, and the studies varied in how they measured iodine and accounted for other factors. The authors suggest keeping iodine sufficient in the population, especially for women of childbearing age on restricted diets low in iodide.
keyPoints: Urinary iodine of 150 μg/L or more was linked to a lower risk of a baby being small for gestational age (RR 0.85).
Raw birth weight did not differ clearly between higher and lower iodine groups, but birth weight centile was about 2 centiles higher with higher urinary iodine.
The main weakness was how studies adjusted for other factors, and they differed in how urine samples were collected and iodine status was defined.
The authors recommend maintaining iodine sufficiency, especially for women of childbearing age on diets low in iodide.

items.title: Effects of iodine supplementation on thyroid function parameter: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Trace Elements in Medicine and Biology
items.journal: Journal of Trace Elements in Medicine and Biology
items.summary: This review pulled together 11 studies of pregnant women who took iodine supplements by mouth. Taking 200 micrograms of iodine a day raised urinary iodine levels, a sign of getting enough iodine, and the review found helpful effects on iodine status and mother's thyroid hormones overall. Starting before pregnancy or early in pregnancy looked like the best timing. A few studies found no effect from the 200 microgram dose, so results were not completely consistent.
keyPoints: 200 micrograms of iodine a day raised urinary iodine levels during pregnancy, supporting adequate intake.
Daily iodine supplements had satisfactory effects on iodine status and on the mother's thyroid hormone levels.
The best time to start appeared to be before pregnancy or in early pregnancy.
Some individual studies showed no effect from the 200 microgram dose.

items.title: Prevalence of insufficient iodine intake in pregnancy worldwide: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 61 studies covering about 163,000 pregnant women around the world. It found that about half (53%) did not get enough iodine. In countries with low iodine levels overall, the figure was much higher (86%), but even in countries counted as having enough iodine, about 51% of pregnant women fell short. The authors say iodised salt alone may not be enough to meet pregnant women's needs.
keyPoints: Overall, 53% of pregnant women worldwide had insufficient iodine intake.
In countries with insufficient iodine status, 86% of pregnant women had inadequate iodine, compared with 51% in countries considered sufficient.
Iodine deficiency in pregnancy is linked to impaired foetal growth and development.
Salt iodisation alone may not give pregnant women enough iodine, so other actions may be needed.

items.title: The prevalence of insufficient iodine intake in pregnancy in Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled studies from across Africa to see how much iodine pregnant women were getting, before and after iodine was added to foods such as salt. Before 1995, severe iodine deficiency was common in pregnancy. Things improved after fortification began, but by 2005 to 2020 most countries still had mildly low iodine levels in pregnancy, and a few had severely low levels. The authors conclude that the improvement is not enough, leaving many pregnant women at risk of iodine deficiency.
keyPoints: Before 1995, severe iodine deficiency was common in pregnant women across Africa (pooled median urinary iodine 28.6 μg/L).
After iodine fortification of foods such as salt began, iodine levels in pregnancy improved.
Between 2005 and 2020, few African countries had enough iodine in pregnancy, most were mildly low and some were severely low (pooled median 145 μg/L).
The authors say the improvement is sub-optimal and leaves many pregnant women at risk of iodine deficiency.

items.title: Iodine contrast prior to or during pregnancy and neonatal thyroid function: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pooled 26 studies on babies whose mothers had iodine-based contrast dye for imaging (such as HSG, CT or urography) before or during pregnancy. Thyroid problems in newborns were rare, with none reported after HSG or CT in the pooled results, and a slightly higher rate after amniofetography. There was a tendency toward more thyroid problems when larger amounts of contrast were used. The authors suggest exposure may raise the risk of thyroid dysfunction in babies and recommend using as little contrast as possible.
keyPoints: Newborn thyroid dysfunction was rare overall: 0% after hysterosalpingography and CT, and about 2% after amniofetography in pooled results.
There was a tendency toward higher risk of thyroid problems with larger amounts of contrast.
The studies had low to high risk of bias, and some estimates came from only a few studies.
The authors recommend keeping the amount of contrast as low as possible.

items.title: Implications of iodine deficiency by gestational trimester: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 11 studies on what happens when pregnant women do not get enough iodine, and whether the effects differ by trimester. Low iodine was linked to problems such as a larger thyroid gland, thyroid nodules, an underactive thyroid (subclinical hypothyroidism) and pre-eclampsia. The authors say the harm from low iodine in the first or second trimester may still be reversible if it is found early. The abstract is partly unclear and does not give a certainty rating for the evidence.
keyPoints: Pregnant women are sensitive to changes in iodine, which can affect the mother's thyroid and the baby's brain development.
Low iodine was linked to a bigger thyroid, thyroid nodules, subclinical hypothyroidism and pre-eclampsia, among other problems.
Damage from low iodine in the first or second trimester may still be reversible.
The authors say low iodine needs to be found early to protect both mother and baby.

items.title: Iodine Status of Women and Infants in Russia: A Systematic Review
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review pulled together 19 studies on iodine levels in women and infants across 25 regions of Russia. Iodine was measured using urine tests. The results suggest that pregnant women and infants in Russia are not getting as much iodine as recommended. The authors say iodine deficiency is becoming a public health problem again there and call for action.
keyPoints: 19 studies from 25 Russian regions were included in the review.
Iodine levels varied a lot between regions, with no clear geographic pattern.
Pregnant women and infants in Russia appeared to have iodine levels below recommended amounts.
The authors call for urgent public health measures at national, regional and individual levels.

items.title: Iodine fortification of foods and condiments, other than salt, for preventing iodine deficiency disorders
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at adding iodine to foods and drinks other than salt (such as milk, biscuits, yoghourt, fish sauce and water) to prevent iodine deficiency. Eleven studies were included, mostly in school children, with three in women of reproductive age. Iodine fortification likely raised the amount of iodine in urine, which is a sign of better iodine intake. Whether it reduces goitre or helps growth is uncertain, because very little good-quality evidence was found.
keyPoints: Iodine-fortified foods likely increase urinary iodine levels (moderate-quality evidence from randomised trials).
Effects on goitre (swelling of the thyroid) and on growth measures are uncertain (very low-quality evidence).
One study reported no adverse events, but this evidence was low quality.
The authors say more high-quality studies are needed on benefits and safety.

items.title: Multiple micronutrient powders for home (point-of-use) fortification of foods in pregnant women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at vitamin and mineral powders that can be sprinkled onto food during pregnancy, as an alternative to taking tablets. Only two small trials (1172 women) were found, and the evidence was very low quality. The powders did not clearly differ from tablets with the same nutrients for anaemia or haemoglobin, and women were less likely to keep using the powders than iron and folic acid tablets. There was no evidence on most outcomes, such as birth weight or preterm birth.
keyPoints: Only two trials were included, and both had a moderate to high risk of bias.
Powders and tablets with the same seven nutrients (including iodine) showed no clear difference in maternal anaemia or haemoglobin near term.
Women were less likely to keep using powders than iron and folic acid tablets.
No evidence was found for most outcomes, including low birthweight and preterm birth, so more research is needed.

items.title: American Society of Hematology 2026 guidelines for diagnosis of iron deficiency
items.summary: The American Society of Hematology wrote new guidelines on how to diagnose iron deficiency, which is the most common vitamin and mineral deficiency and can lead to anemia if left untreated. A panel that included a patient representative reviewed the evidence and made 5 recommendations. These include blood ferritin (iron store) cut-offs for specific groups of people, aiming to spot iron deficiency even when anemia is not yet present, plus advice for people with inflammation. The authors also point out gaps in the research.
keyPoints: Iron deficiency is the most common micronutrient deficiency and can progress to anemia if untreated.
The guidelines recommend serum ferritin thresholds for specific populations to diagnose iron deficiency.
The goal is to diagnose iron deficiency whether or not anemia is present.
The guidelines give advice on diagnosing iron deficiency in people with inflammation.

items.title: Daily iron supplementation for prevention or treatment of iron-deficiency anaemia in infants, children, and adolescents
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 101 trials (over 50,000 children and teenagers aged 0-19) to see what happens when they take iron by mouth every day. Daily iron probably lowers the chance of iron-deficiency anaemia, and it made little to no difference to growth, coughs, fevers or breathing illness. Iron may darken stools, and in some groups it probably or possibly increases vomiting. For many outcomes the evidence was rated low or very low certainty, so those results are uncertain.
keyPoints: Iron alone probably reduces iron-deficiency anaemia (moderate-certainty evidence).
Iron makes little to no difference to growth, cough, fever or respiratory illness (high-certainty evidence).
Iron may cause darker stools, and iron combined with other vitamins and minerals probably increases vomiting, though some of this evidence is low or very low certainty.
The authors conclude daily iron may significantly reduce iron-deficiency anaemia in this age group with little difference in illness.

items.title: Iron deficiency, supplementation, and sports performance in female athletes: A systematic review
items.source: Journal of Sport and Health Science
items.journal: Journal of Sport and Health Science
items.summary: This review looked at 23 studies of 669 high-level female athletes to see how low iron affects sports performance and whether iron supplements help. Low iron was linked to about 3-4% poorer endurance performance. Endurance improved by 2-20% when iron-deficient athletes took about 100 mg of elemental iron a day by mouth for up to 56 days, or iron given by injection or drip over 8-10 days. Study quality was moderate, and most studies were small, which makes it harder to be sure of the results.
keyPoints: Up to 60% of female athletes may have iron deficiency, and it was linked to a 3-4% drop in endurance performance.
Taking about 100 mg of elemental iron per day (or iron given by injection or drip over 8-10 days) improved endurance performance by 2-20% in iron-deficient athletes.
Maximal aerobic capacity improved by 6-15% after iron supplements, but effects on strength and anaerobic power varied a lot.
Study quality was moderate and most studies had 20 or fewer athletes, limiting how firmly effects could be detected.

items.title: The benefits and harms of oral iron supplementation in non-anaemic pregnant women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 23 studies of 4,492 pregnant women who did not have anaemia, comparing iron supplements taken by mouth with placebo or no supplement. Women who took iron had higher haemoglobin and iron stores (ferritin) and were about half as likely to develop anaemia during pregnancy. Iron did not change birth weight, preterm birth or caesarean rates. Information on side effects was patchy and poor quality, so the review could not say whether iron causes any harm in this group.
keyPoints: Iron supplements cut the risk of anaemia in pregnancy by about half (relative risk 0.50, high certainty).
About 10 non-anaemic women would need to take iron to prevent one case of anaemia.
No difference was found in birth weight, preterm birth or caesarean section.
Evidence on harms such as stomach upset or iron overload was inconsistent and too poor to draw conclusions.

items.title: Effect of probiotic and prebiotics supplementation on hemoglobin levels and iron absorption among women of reproductive age and children: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 29 trials of probiotics (helpful gut bacteria) and prebiotics (fibres that feed them) in women of reproductive age and children, looking at iron absorption, ferritin (iron stores) and haemoglobin. In women, these supplements, with or without iron, slightly raised ferritin and may have improved how much iron the body absorbs. They made little or no difference to haemoglobin in women, and had no clear effect on any measure in children. The evidence for iron absorption was low certainty, and for ferritin it was moderate.
keyPoints: In women, probiotics and/or prebiotics raised ferritin by about 2.45 ng/ml on average (moderate certainty of evidence).
Iron absorption may have improved slightly in women, but the evidence for this was low certainty.
Little or no effect on haemoglobin was seen in women.
In children, there was no significant change in haemoglobin, ferritin or iron absorption (low or very low certainty).

items.title: Optimal dose and duration of iron supplementation for treating iron deficiency anaemia in children and adolescents: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 28 studies with 8,829 children and teenagers (19 or younger) who had iron deficiency anaemia, to see what iron dose and length of treatment raised haemoglobin (the oxygen-carrying protein in blood) the most. Iron supplements raised haemoglobin by about 2 g/dL overall. Lower daily doses (under 5 mg per kg of body weight) worked well, especially for those starting with lower haemoglobin, and treatment lasting under 3 months or over 6 months did best. The review did not rate how certain the evidence is, and it excluded pregnant women.
keyPoints: Iron supplements raised haemoglobin by about 2 g/dL on average in children and adolescents with iron deficiency anaemia.
Low-dose iron (under 5 mg/kg/day) showed favourable results, particularly for those with lower starting haemoglobin.
Treatment shorter than 3 months or longer than 6 months worked better than 3 to 6 months.
The authors say treatment should be tailored to starting haemoglobin and how severe the anaemia is.

items.title: Clinical outcome post treatment of anemia in pregnancy with intravenous versus oral iron therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 34 trials of pregnant women with anaemia to compare iron given through a drip (intravenous) with iron tablets. Women who had intravenous iron were somewhat less likely to have maternal complications and were much less likely to have side effects. Their haemoglobin (the blood's oxygen-carrying protein) also rose more, and faster. No clear difference was seen in complications for newborns, and the evidence for individual outcomes was not conclusive.
keyPoints: Maternal complications were about 21% less likely with intravenous iron than oral iron (moderate quality evidence).
Adverse events were less likely with intravenous iron (odds ratio 0.39), based on 34 studies and 13,909 women (low quality evidence).
Intravenous iron raised haemoglobin more, and at a higher pace, than oral iron.
No significant difference was found in newborn complications (low quality evidence).

items.title: Clinical effectiveness of ferric carboxymaltose (iv) versus iron sucrose (iv) in treatment of iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 18 studies of pregnant women in the second and third trimesters with moderate-to-severe iron deficiency anaemia. It compared two iron treatments given through a drip into a vein: ferric carboxymaltose and iron sucrose. Ferric carboxymaltose raised haemoglobin a little more in the first four weeks and was linked to fewer side effects. There was little evidence on how either treatment affects the pregnancy or the baby.
keyPoints: Haemoglobin rose by about 0.57 g/dl more with ferric carboxymaltose than with iron sucrose in the first four weeks.
Ferric carboxymaltose was linked to fewer adverse events than iron sucrose (pooled odds ratio 0.5).
The review concluded that ferric carboxymaltose is effective and safer than iron sucrose for blood measures in pregnancy.
Evidence on pregnancy and newborn outcomes after intravenous iron was limited, so more research is needed.

items.title: Efficacy of different doses of daily prophylactic iron supplementation in pregnant women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 15 randomized trials with 2,726 pregnant women to compare different daily doses of iron supplements for preventing anemia. Taking 60 mg of elemental iron a day worked better than 30 mg a day. Doses above 60 mg a day did not raise hemoglobin (the blood's oxygen-carrying protein) more than 60 mg or less, although some iron stores in the blood were higher. The authors rated the certainty of these findings as moderate.
keyPoints: 60 mg of elemental iron daily was more effective than 30 mg daily for preventing anemia in pregnancy.
Doses of 60 mg or less worked about as well as doses above 60 mg for preventing anemia.
Hemoglobin change was similar between the two groups, though iron and ferritin levels rose more with doses above 60 mg.
The authors rated the certainty of evidence as moderate for both comparisons.

items.title: Role of iron in the reduction of anemia among women of reproductive age in low-middle income countries: insights from systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of iron treatment in women of reproductive age in low- and middle-income countries. Iron therapy in any form improved haemoglobin and ferritin levels, which points to better iron-deficiency anaemia. Results varied a lot between studies, so the size of the benefit is uncertain. More research is needed on side effects, work performance, mental health and how well women stick with iron treatment.
keyPoints: Iron therapy in any form may reduce anaemia and improve haemoglobin and ferritin levels.
Results differed widely between the included studies (very high heterogeneity).
More evidence is needed on side effects, work performance, mental health, costs and adherence.
Women who are not pregnant but planning a pregnancy soon were highlighted as needing more study.

items.title: Fortification of condiments and seasonings with iron for preventing anaemia and improving health
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 16 studies of adding iron to everyday seasonings such as salt, fish sauce and soy sauce, to see if it prevents anaemia and iron deficiency. Most of the studies were in children and teenagers, and three involved only women. The authors are unsure whether iron-fortified seasonings reduce anaemia or raise haemoglobin, but they may reduce iron deficiency. Every study had a high risk of bias, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Iron-fortified condiments probably slightly reduce iron deficiency (moderate-certainty evidence).
Whether iron-only fortified condiments reduce anaemia or raise haemoglobin is uncertain (very low-certainty evidence).
Condiments fortified with iron plus other micronutrients may reduce anaemia and iron deficiency (low-certainty evidence).
All 16 studies had a high risk of bias, and none reported side effects.

items.title: Fortification of salt with iron and iodine versus fortification of salt with iodine alone for improving iron and iodine status
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 18 studies (over 8,800 people) comparing salt fortified with both iron and iodine to salt with iodine alone. Iron-and-iodine salt may slightly raise haemoglobin and may lower the chance of having anaemia. Both kinds of salt kept iodine levels above the level that counts as deficient. Most of the evidence was low certainty, and many studies had some risk of bias.
keyPoints: Iron-and-iodine salt may slightly improve haemoglobin (about 0.43 g/dL higher) compared with iodised salt (low-certainty evidence).
It may reduce the risk of anaemia by 21% (moderate-certainty evidence) and of iron deficiency anaemia by 65% (low-certainty evidence).
It may make little to no difference to ferritin or transferrin receptor levels, though body iron stores may rise slightly.
Urinary iodine was lower with the double-fortified salt, but both salts raised it above the deficiency cut-off.

items.title: Wheat flour fortification with iron and other micronutrients for reducing anaemia and improving iron status in populations
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 10 trials (3,319 people aged two and over) that tested wheat flour with added iron, with or without other vitamins and minerals. Iron-fortified flour may lower the chance of anaemia, but the evidence is low certainty. Effects on iron deficiency and haemoglobin were mostly uncertain, and almost no trials reported side effects. Only two trials studied women as a group of their own.
keyPoints: Iron-fortified wheat flour may reduce the risk of anaemia by about 27% (low-certainty evidence).
Compared with unfortified flour, flour fortified with iron plus other micronutrients probably reduces iron deficiency (moderate-certainty evidence).
Effects on haemoglobin levels and on iron deficiency in other comparisons are uncertain (very low-certainty evidence).
Most trials did not report side effects, apart from infection or inflammation, which probably changed little.

items.title: Iron Deficiency, a Risk Factor of Thyroid Disorders in Reproductive-Age and Pregnant Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to look at whether low iron is linked to thyroid problems in women. Women of reproductive age with iron deficiency were more likely to have thyroid antibodies, which can signal thyroid autoimmunity. Pregnant women with iron deficiency had higher TSH, lower free thyroxine (FT4), and were more likely to have an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism). The authors say iron levels may be worth monitoring and low iron treated early in these groups.
keyPoints: In women of reproductive age, iron deficiency was linked to a higher chance of positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies (OR 1.89).
Pregnant women with iron deficiency had higher TSH and lower free thyroxine (FT4) levels.
Pregnant women with iron deficiency were more likely to have overt hypothyroidism (OR 1.60) and subclinical hypothyroidism (OR 1.37).
The authors conclude that monitoring iron status and treating iron deficiency early is important for these women.

items.title: British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines for the management of iron deficiency anaemia in adults
items.summary: This is a clinical guideline from the British Society of Gastroenterology on managing iron deficiency anaemia in adults. Iron deficiency anaemia can usually be found with a blood test and treated with iron, taken by mouth or through a vein. It can come from a poor diet, trouble absorbing iron, or ongoing blood loss, including heavy periods or bleeding in the gut. About a third of men and postmenopausal women with the condition have an underlying problem, most often in the digestive tract, so looking for the cause matters as well as replacing the iron.
keyPoints: Iron deficiency anaemia is usually diagnosed by blood testing and treated with iron replacement, by mouth or intravenously.
Common causes include poor dietary intake, poor absorption of iron, and chronic blood loss such as from periods or the gut.
About a third of men and postmenopausal women with iron deficiency anaemia have an underlying abnormality, most often in the gut.
Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in at-risk people is a reason for fast-track specialist referral in the UK, since gut cancers can show up this way without clear symptoms.

items.title: Adherence to iron-folic acid supplementation among pregnant women in Ethiopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 15 studies of 5,808 pregnant women in Ethiopia to see how many take their iron-folic acid supplements as advised. About 4 in 10 women (41%) took them as recommended, which is lower than the WHO target. Women were more likely to take them if they had more schooling, started antenatal care early, attended four or more visits, and had good knowledge and health education about iron and anemia.
keyPoints: About 41% of pregnant women in Ethiopia took iron-folic acid supplements as recommended, below the WHO target.
Starting antenatal care by 16 weeks and attending four or more visits were linked to better adherence.
Good knowledge about anemia and the supplements, and receiving health education on their benefits, were linked to better adherence.
Women with secondary or higher education and women who had anemia in the current pregnancy were more likely to adhere.

items.title: Wheat flour fortification with iron for reducing anaemia and improving iron status in populations
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled nine trials (3,166 people aged two and over) that tested wheat flour with added iron, alone or with other vitamins and minerals. Iron-fortified flour may make little or no difference to anaemia and probably makes little or no difference to iron deficiency. Whether it raises haemoglobin (the oxygen-carrying protein in blood) is uncertain, as the evidence is very low quality. No trials reported side effects such as constipation, nausea or diarrhoea.
keyPoints: Flour fortified with iron alone may have little or no effect on anaemia (low-certainty evidence).
It probably makes little or no difference to iron deficiency (moderate-certainty evidence).
Effects on haemoglobin are uncertain when iron is added alone (very low-certainty evidence).
Only two of the nine trials included women, and none reported other side effects.

items.title: Effect of vitamin A supplementation on iron status in humans: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
items.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
items.summary: This review pooled 23 studies (mostly clinical trials) in children, teenagers, and pregnant or breastfeeding women to see whether vitamin A supplements alone affect iron status and anemia. Supplements lowered the risk of anemia by 26% and raised hemoglobin, whatever the life stage. In pregnant and breastfeeding women, ferritin (a marker of the body's iron stores) also went up. The authors conclude this may help people who have low vitamin A levels in their blood.
keyPoints: Vitamin A supplements reduced the risk of anemia by 26% and raised hemoglobin compared with no treatment.
In pregnant and breastfeeding women, ferritin levels rose by about 6.6 μg/L on average.
In children and teenagers, vitamin A supplements did not clearly change how common iron deficiency was.
Benefits were suggested mainly for people with low vitamin A (retinol) levels in their blood.

items.title: Intermittent iron supplementation for reducing anaemia and its associated impairments in adolescent and adult menstruating women
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 25 trials with almost 11,000 menstruating women to see whether taking iron supplements only once to three times a week helps with anaemia. Compared with no treatment or a placebo, weekly-style iron lowered the chance of anaemia and raised haemoglobin and iron stores. Compared with daily iron, it worked about as well for anaemia and caused fewer side effects, though iron stores (ferritin) were a little lower. The quality of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate, so there is still uncertainty.
keyPoints: Intermittent iron (one to three times a week) reduced the risk of anaemia compared with no treatment or placebo (low-quality evidence).
Compared with daily iron, intermittent iron had similar effects on anaemia (moderate-quality evidence) but slightly lower ferritin levels on average (low-quality evidence).
Women taking iron intermittently were less likely to report side effects than those taking it daily (moderate-quality evidence).
More research is needed on side effects, work performance, depression and how well women stick to the regimen.

items.title: Intravenous or oral iron for treating iron deficiency anaemia during pregnancy: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 15 trials (1,938 pregnant women) that compared iron given through a vein (intravenous) with iron tablets as first treatment for iron deficiency anaemia. Intravenous iron raised the mother's blood measures more at delivery, but babies' blood measures were similar with both treatments. A few small differences favoured intravenous iron, such as fewer blood transfusions at delivery and slightly higher birthweight, but this evidence was low or very low quality. The authors found no strong evidence that intravenous iron is better than iron tablets as a first treatment.
keyPoints: Intravenous iron improved the mother's blood measures at delivery more than oral iron.
Babies' blood measures were similar whether the mother had intravenous or oral iron.
Intravenous iron was linked to fewer blood transfusions at delivery and a small rise in birthweight (about 58 g), but the evidence was low or very low quality.
All 15 trials had a high risk of bias in at least one area, so there is no strong evidence that intravenous iron is better as a first treatment.

items.title: Food fortification with multiple micronutrients: impact on health outcomes in general population
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 43 studies of foods with extra vitamins and minerals added, such as rice, flour, milk and biscuits. Most of the studies (36 of 43) were in children, so the findings may not apply directly to women. Compared with no fortification, fortified foods may lower rates of anaemia, iron deficiency and some vitamin deficiencies. The evidence was low to very low quality, so no firm conclusions can be drawn.
keyPoints: Fortified foods may reduce anaemia by about 32% and iron deficiency anaemia by about 72% compared with no intervention.
They may also reduce iron deficiency and vitamin A, B2, B6 and B12 deficiencies.
The effect on zinc deficiency and on children's growth measures is uncertain.
No studies reported side effects, illness or deaths, and most evidence was low or very low quality.

items.title: Adherence of iron and folic acid supplementation and determinants among pregnant women in Ethiopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 20 studies of about 16,800 pregnant women in Ethiopia to see how many keep taking their iron and folic acid supplements. Fewer than half (about 46%) took them as advised. Women were more likely to keep taking them if they had been given information about the supplements, understood why they matter, and started antenatal care early and attended often. Fear of side effects and forgetting were the main reasons for not taking them.
keyPoints: About 46% of pregnant women in Ethiopia took their iron and folic acid supplements as advised.
Women who received counselling, had good knowledge of the supplement, began antenatal care before 16 weeks, or had 4 or more visits were more likely to keep taking them.
Fear of side effects (about 46%) and forgetfulness (about 31%) were the main barriers.
The authors suggest better counselling, managing side effects, and family or partner support to help women remember their tablets.

items.title: Impact of Double-Fortified Salt with Iron and Iodine on Hemoglobin, Anemia, and Iron Deficiency Anemia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 14 trials in lower- and middle-income countries that tested salt fortified with both iron and iodine. In the more tightly controlled trials, people using this salt had higher hemoglobin levels and a lower risk of anemia and iron deficiency anemia. The abstract reports positive effects in women and school-age children. Real-world (effectiveness) studies showed a much smaller benefit, and the authors say more of these studies are needed.
keyPoints: In controlled efficacy trials, double-fortified salt raised hemoglobin and lowered the risk of anemia (RR 0.59) and iron deficiency anemia (RR 0.37).
Positive effects were seen in women and school-age children.
In real-world effectiveness studies, the hemoglobin increase was smaller but still statistically significant.
All studies were in lower- and middle-income countries, and more effectiveness studies are needed.

items.title: Fortification of maize flour with iron for controlling anaemia and iron deficiency in populations
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether adding iron (plus other vitamins and minerals) to maize flour, a staple food in many countries, helps prevent anaemia and low iron. It found only a few studies, covering children over 2 and women. The evidence was of very low quality, so it is not clear whether fortified maize flour makes any difference to anaemia, iron levels or haemoglobin. None of the studies reported side effects.
keyPoints: It is uncertain whether iron-fortified maize flour reduces anaemia or iron deficiency.
Only 3 studies contributed data, and the evidence was judged very low certainty.
No change in haemoglobin or ferritin (iron store) levels could be confirmed.
No studies reported on any side effects.

items.title: Daily iron supplementation for improving anaemia, iron status and health in menstruating women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 67 trials with 8,506 menstruating women to see what daily iron supplements do. Women taking iron were much less likely to have anaemia or iron deficiency, and had higher haemoglobin and iron stores. They also did better on exercise tests and felt less tired, but had more stomach and bowel side effects. Evidence on thinking and memory was uncertain.
keyPoints: Daily iron supplements reduced the risk of anaemia (moderate quality evidence) and of iron deficiency (moderate quality evidence).
Iron raised haemoglobin levels (high quality evidence) and improved exercise performance and symptomatic fatigue.
Iron increased constipation and loose stools or diarrhoea (high quality evidence), and gastrointestinal side effects overall (low quality evidence).
Whether iron improves cognitive performance is uncertain because trials gave conflicting results.

items.title: Menstrual irregularities and cardiometabolic risk: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled results from eight observational studies covering about 354,000 women. It compared heart and metabolic health in women with irregular periods and women with regular periods. Women with irregular cycles had higher risks of heart disease, stroke, high blood pressure, diabetes and high cholesterol. Because these were observational studies, they show an association, not that irregular periods cause these conditions.
keyPoints: Women with irregular cycles had a higher overall risk of cardiovascular disease (RR 1.43) than women with regular cycles.
Risks were higher for coronary artery disease, high blood pressure, heart failure and stroke or other cerebrovascular disease.
Risks were also higher for diabetes (RR 1.75) and high cholesterol (RR 1.33).
The authors conclude that regular check-ups are important for women with menstrual irregularities.

items.title: Association of psychosocial factors at work with fertility and menstrual disorders: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether stress and conditions at work are linked to fertility and menstrual problems in working women. It found nine studies. Some suggested that women with very demanding jobs and little control over their work were less likely to conceive, and that long hours, heavy lifting and rotating night shifts were linked to earlier menopause. The authors say there is not enough high-level evidence to draw firm conclusions.
keyPoints: Women with high job demands and low job control were less likely to conceive in some studies.
Working over 40 hours a week, frequent heavy lifting and rotating night shifts were linked to earlier menopause.
Studies of night shift or rotating work and fertility outcomes found no significant differences.
The review concludes that high-level evidence is insufficient and better-designed studies are needed.

items.title: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea and dietary intervention: A systematic review to guide further research in amenorrheic women without overt eating disorder
items.summary: This review looked at whether changes to diet help women whose periods have stopped because of stress, low energy intake, weight loss or heavy exercise (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea), without an eating disorder. Eleven articles were included. Periods came back in 1 to 12 months with dietary changes, and one article suggested about 350 extra calories a day helped. How well diet alone works in the long term is still unclear.
keyPoints: Eating enough to correct an energy shortfall is the main treatment for this type of missed period.
Across the studies, periods returned within 1 to 12 months.
One article pointed to an extra 350 kcal per day to restore periods.
The long-term effect of diet changes alone is unclear and more research is needed.

items.title: Prevalence and determinants of pregnancy termination in Ethiopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies in Ethiopia to see how common pregnancy termination is and what factors are linked to it. About one in five women (21.5%) had terminated a pregnancy, which is higher than in other sub-Saharan African countries. Irregular menstrual bleeding, being a student, starting sex before age 18 and having multiple partners were linked to higher odds of termination. These are associations, not proof of cause.
keyPoints: The pooled prevalence of pregnancy termination in Ethiopia was 21.52%, or about one in five women.
Women with irregular menstrual bleeding had higher odds of pregnancy termination (OR 1.86).
Being a student, first sex before age 18, and having multiple sexual partners were also linked to termination.
The authors call for attention to delaying early sexual initiation and reducing sexual risk behaviours.

items.title: Bloody stressed! A systematic review of the associations between adulthood psychological stress and menstrual cycle irregularity
items.summary: This review pulled together 41 studies on whether psychological stress is linked to irregular periods in healthy adult women. The stressors studied included the COVID-19 pandemic, school or university pressure, and work stress. Most studies found a link between stress and period problems, most often irregular cycles and unusual bleeding amounts. The authors note that studies defined period problems in different ways, which makes them harder to compare.
keyPoints: Most of the 41 studies found an association between psychological stress and menstrual problems.
The most common problems were irregular periods and abnormal menstrual flow.
Stressors studied included COVID-19 pandemic stress, academic stress and work stress.
Studies used different definitions of menstrual disorders, so results are hard to compare.

items.title: Study on the influencing factors of primary dysmenorrhea in female college students: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 23 studies of about 18,000 female college students to look at what is linked with painful periods that have no underlying disease (primary dysmenorrhea). About 7 in 10 students had this kind of period pain. Getting enough sleep was linked with less pain, while family history, an early first period, irregular cycles, cold drinks, lots of caffeine and stress were linked with more. These are links seen across studies, not proof that one thing causes another.
keyPoints: About 70% of female college students in the pooled studies had primary dysmenorrhea.
Adequate sleep was linked with lower odds of period pain (a protective factor).
Family history of period pain, early age at first period, irregular menstrual cycles, drinking cold drinks, high caffeine intake and stress were each linked with higher odds.
Studying a medical specialty was also linked with higher odds of period pain.

items.title: Anti-Müllerian hormone for the diagnosis and prediction of menopause: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 41 studies (over 28,000 women) to see whether a blood test for anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), which reflects how many egg follicles remain in the ovaries, can help diagnose or predict menopause. Lower AMH for a woman's age was linked with menopause coming earlier, but the test could not pinpoint when menopause would happen, especially in younger women. Very low or undetectable AMH may help spot premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) earlier in young women with a family history or missing periods.
keyPoints: Lower age-specific AMH levels were generally linked with an earlier age at menopause.
AMH alone could not predict age at menopause precisely; estimates for women under 40 ranged from 2 to 12 years.
The test predicted menopause better as women got older and menopause was closer.
Undetectable or extremely low AMH may help with early diagnosis of POI in young women with a family history of POI or with absent periods.

items.title: Psychological factors in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together eight studies comparing women who have functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (periods that stop because of stress, low weight or heavy exercise) with women who have regular periods. Women with FHA tended to have higher levels of depression and a stronger drive for thinness. They also showed more anxiety, sleep problems and difficulty recognising their own feelings. The authors say these factors seem linked to the condition continuing, and suggest care that includes gynecologists, psychologists and psychiatrists.
keyPoints: Depression and a strong drive for thinness were the psychological factors most linked to FHA.
Women with FHA also had higher anxiety, sleep disorders, dysfunctional attitudes and difficulty identifying feelings (alexithymia).
The pooled results for drive for thinness and depression were statistically significant.
The authors recommend teamwork between gynecologists, clinical psychologists and psychiatrists, and call for longer-term studies with comparison groups.

items.title: COVID-19 vaccination and menstrual disorders among women: Findings from a meta-analysis study
items.source: Journal of Infection and Public Health
items.journal: Journal of Infection and Public Health
items.summary: This review pooled results from 16 studies to estimate how often women reported period changes after a COVID-19 vaccine. Heavy periods, infrequent periods and more frequent periods were the most commonly reported changes. The authors say this does not prove the vaccine caused them, and that longer-term studies are needed to confirm any link.
keyPoints: Pooled estimates of reported changes after vaccination: heavy periods about 24%, infrequent periods about 23%, more frequent periods about 16%.
Changes in cycle length were reported less often, at about 7%.
A fairly high share of women reported some menstrual irregularity after vaccination.
Further longitudinal studies are needed to confirm whether the vaccine causes these changes.

items.title: Giant prolactinomas, a detailed analysis of 196 adult cases
items.summary: Researchers pooled 196 published adult cases of giant prolactinomas, which are very rare pituitary tumours that make a lot of prolactin. In women, the most common first sign was missed periods (amenorrhea), while men more often had vision problems and headaches. Dopamine agonist medicines were the main treatment and shrank the tumour in most people, but prolactin levels returned to normal in only about half.
keyPoints: Giant prolactinomas are rare, and about 5% of all prolactinomas are this large.
Amenorrhea (absent periods) was the most common presenting symptom in women, reported in 58%.
Dopamine agonist medicines were the treatment of choice: tumours shrank in 88% of cases, but prolactin normalised in only 51%.
Women had smaller tumours and lower prolactin at diagnosis, yet more pituitary hormone deficiencies and worse outcomes than men.

items.title: Traditional Chinese herbal medicine in treating amenorrhea caused by antipsychotic drugs: Meta-analysis and systematic review
items.summary: This review pooled results from 18 studies on traditional Chinese herbal medicine for periods that stopped because of antipsychotic medicines. Across the studies, about 91% of women were reported to respond to treatment. Most studies needed more than three months of treatment to see a clear improvement in periods. The authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Overall reported effectiveness of Chinese herbal medicine was 0.91 (95% confidence interval 0.89-0.93).
In most studies it took longer than three months to reach this level of effect.
Commonly used herbs included Danggui, Chuanxiong, Taoren, Honghua and Gancao.
The authors conclude the herbs can be effective but call for more research.

items.title: Hormone therapy for uterine and endometrial development in women with premature ovarian insufficiency
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at which hormone treatments best support the growth of the womb and womb lining in women whose ovaries stopped working before age 40 (premature ovarian insufficiency). Only three small trials, with 52 women in total, could be included. The evidence was very low quality, so the review could not say which hormone type, dose or route (oral or vaginal) works best.
keyPoints: Premature ovarian insufficiency means the ovaries lose function before age 40, often causing absent or irregular periods and low oestrogen.
Three small trials (52 women) compared oral versus patch oestrogen, low versus high oestradiol dose, and oral versus vaginal oestradiol with dydrogesterone.
The evidence was very low certainty, mainly because the studies were so small, so no clear conclusions could be drawn.
The authors call for larger, well-designed trials, including looking at pregnancy outcomes after donated eggs or embryos.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of traditional Chinese medicine on treating oligomenorrhea: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 26 randomised trials with 2,389 women who had oligomenorrhea (infrequent periods) to see whether traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) helps. Adding TCM to standard medical treatment was linked to heavier menstrual flow, longer periods, a thicker womb lining and higher estradiol and progesterone levels. Side effects did not differ between the groups. The authors say the quality of the evidence was relatively low, so more rigorous trials are needed.
keyPoints: TCM added to standard medical treatment was linked to increased menstrual blood volume and longer periods.
TCM plus standard treatment also showed possible improvements in endometrial thickness and estradiol and progesterone levels.
No significant difference in adverse events was found between the groups.
The quality of the evidence was relatively low, so better-designed trials are needed.

items.title: DHEA and polycystic ovarian syndrome: Meta-analysis of case-control studies
items.summary: This study pooled results from earlier case-control studies that compared DHEA, a hormone often used as a marker of stress, in women with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and in healthy women. DHEA levels were higher on average in women with PCOS. The results varied a lot between the studies, so the findings should be read with caution. The authors suggest stress may play a part in how PCOS develops.
keyPoints: Women with PCOS had higher DHEA levels than healthy women (SMD 1.15, 95% CI 0.59-1.71).
Results differed greatly between the studies included (heterogeneity of 95%).
The authors conclude the findings point to stress being involved in how PCOS develops.
PCOS is described as causing irregular periods, excess hair growth and polycystic ovaries.

items.title: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system associated amenorrhea: a systematic review and metaanalysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 9 clinical studies to work out how many women using a levonorgestrel hormonal coil (the 20 microgram type) stop having periods in the first year. About 1 in 5 users (around 20%) had at least one 90-day stretch with no bleeding by the end of the first year. Most users did not stop having periods in that time. The authors note that some of the later estimates were less reliable because the studies differed from each other.
keyPoints: Almost no users (0.2%) had no periods during the first 90 days after insertion.
About 8% had no periods on days 91-180, rising to roughly 14% and then 20% by later in the first year.
About 18% had at least one 90-day period with no bleeding during the first year.
Most users do not stop having periods in the first year, which matches the product labeling.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of ulipristal acetate for symptomatic uterine fibroids
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pooled six randomised trials (1121 women) of ulipristal acetate, a tablet taken by mouth, for uterine fibroids that cause symptoms. Compared with placebo, it made periods stop far more often, reduced heavy bleeding and improved quality of life. There was not enough trial evidence to judge side effects, or to say whether it works better than leuprolide acetate, another fibroid medicine.
keyPoints: Compared with placebo, ulipristal acetate made periods stop (amenorrhea) much more often in women with symptomatic fibroids.
It reduced heavy menstrual bleeding and improved quality of life.
Trial evidence on side effects was insufficient.
There was not enough evidence to show better results than leuprolide acetate.

items.title: Turner Syndrome Systematic Review: Spontaneous Thelarche and Menarche Stratified by Karyotype
items.summary: This review pooled results from 43 studies of girls with Turner syndrome, a genetic condition where the ovaries often stop working early. It looked at how often breast development and a first period start on their own, without hormone treatment. About 1 in 3 girls had spontaneous breast development and about 1 in 5 had a spontaneous first period, but rates varied a lot depending on the type of chromosome change.
keyPoints: Overall, 32% of girls with Turner syndrome had spontaneous breast development and 20.8% had a spontaneous first period.
Girls with X monosomy (45,X) had the lowest rates: 13% for breast development and 9.1% for a first period.
Girls with the 45,X/47,XXX pattern had the highest rates: 88.1% for breast development and 66.2% for a first period.
The authors conclude that karyotype (chromosome pattern) should strongly shape conversations about puberty and future fertility.

items.title: Herbal Medicine for Oligomenorrhea and Amenorrhea: A Systematic Review of Ancient and Conventional Medicine
items.summary: This review looked at herbs used for infrequent or absent periods, first in old Traditional Persian medicine books and then in modern studies. Of 198 plants listed in the old texts, 87 were judged more effective, but only 12 modern studies covering 8 plants were found. The authors say just a few plants have been shown to help with period irregularities, so the evidence is limited.
keyPoints: Traditional Persian medicine lists 198 plants for bringing on periods, and 87 were rated more effective.
Only 12 modern studies were found, covering 8 plants including chaste tree (Vitex agnus-castus), fenugreek, fennel, cinnamon and nettle.
Few plants have actually been proven effective for irregular periods.
The findings are meant as a starting point for future research, not proof that these herbs work.

items.title: Understanding variation in prevalence estimates of polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 21 studies to see how common polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is, and why estimates differ. About 7% of women had PCOS using the older NIH criteria, compared with about 12% using the Rotterdam criteria, which also count how the ovaries look on scan. The authors say the uncertainty around diagnosing PCOS needs to be addressed so women get more certain diagnoses and are less likely to be wrongly labelled.
keyPoints: Pooled PCOS prevalence was 7% with NIH criteria, 12% with Rotterdam criteria and 10% with Androgen Excess Society criteria.
Including ovarian appearance in the criteria gave significantly higher prevalence estimates.
Different definitions of missed or irregular periods and of excess hair growth did not significantly change prevalence, but few studies were available to compare.
The authors call for clearer diagnostic standards to reduce misdiagnosis and the psychological harm it can cause.

items.title: Menstrual Patterns in the First Gynecological Year: A Systematic Review
items.source: Journal of Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology
items.journal: Journal of Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 22 studies of more than 2000 healthy teenagers to describe periods and ovulation in the first year after a first period. Cycles in this first year were often long and varied, and they got shorter as the year went on. Irregular cycles, painful periods and even ovulation were all common. The authors note that high-quality evidence on this topic is limited.
keyPoints: Average cycle length ranged from 32 to 61 days in the first gynecological year and became shorter over the year.
Average period length was about 5 days (4.9 to 5.4 days), and painful periods were reported by 30% to 89% of teens.
Ovulatory cycles were found in 0 to 45% of cycles and became more common as the year went on.
Because ovulation and irregular cycles are both common, the authors advise promoting safe sexual practice and keeping prompt medical care available.

items.title: Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This is a clinical guideline from the Endocrine Society on functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA), where periods stop because the brain's signals to the ovaries slow down. It is often linked to stress, weight loss, too much exercise, or a mix of these. The guideline says other causes must be ruled out first, and that care works best when doctors, dietitians and mental health professionals work together. Treatments for problems like bone loss and infertility are still being debated and studied.
keyPoints: FHA is a type of ongoing missed ovulation with no identifiable organic cause, often linked to stress, weight loss, excessive exercise, or a combination.
FHA is a diagnosis of exclusion, so doctors should check for other hormonal and body-wide causes first.
A team approach is needed, including medical care, dietary support and mental health support.
Bone loss and infertility are possible complications, and the best treatments for them are still under debate and investigation.

items.title: Selective progesterone receptor modulators (SPRMs) for uterine fibroids
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 14 trials of medicines called selective progesterone receptor modulators (SPRMs) for premenopausal women with uterine fibroids. Compared with placebo, short-term SPRM treatment improved fibroid symptoms and quality of life, reduced menstrual bleeding and made periods stop in many women. One trial found no clear difference between an SPRM and another drug, leuprolide acetate. The medicines caused more changes to the womb lining, which the review says are benign, not cancer and not precancerous.
keyPoints: Compared with placebo, SPRMs improved fibroid symptom scores and quality of life (moderate-quality evidence).
SPRMs reduced menstrual blood loss and led to far higher rates of amenorrhoea (periods stopping) than placebo.
One trial found no clear difference between an SPRM and leuprolide acetate for quality of life, bleeding or pelvic pain.
Womb lining changes were more common with SPRMs, but the review describes them as benign and not related to cancer; the evidence on this was low quality compared with placebo.

items.title: Breastfeeding and maternal health outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to see how breastfeeding relates to the mother's own health. Breastfeeding for more than 12 months was linked to a lower risk of breast and ovarian cancer, and breastfeeding in general to a lower risk of type 2 diabetes. Exclusive or mostly-exclusive breastfeeding was linked to a longer time without periods after birth. The review found no clear link with bone density, depression or weight change after birth.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding for more than 12 months was linked to a 26% lower risk of breast cancer and a 37% lower risk of ovarian cancer.
Breastfeeding was linked to a 32% lower risk of type 2 diabetes.
Exclusive and predominant breastfeeding were linked to a longer duration of lactational amenorrhoea (no periods while breastfeeding).
No clear evidence was found of a link between breastfeeding and bone mineral density, postpartum depression or postpartum weight change.

items.title: Current evaluation of amenorrhea: a committee opinion
items.summary: This 2024 committee opinion from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine gives clinicians principles and strategies for working out why someone has no periods, either never having started them (primary amenorrhoea) or having stopped (secondary amenorrhoea). It replaces the 2008 version. The abstract does not list the specific tests.
keyPoints: Covers the diagnostic evaluation of both primary and secondary amenorrhoea.
Replaces the ASRM document of the same name from 2008.

items.title: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 651: Menstruation in Girls and Adolescents: Using the Menstrual Cycle as a Vital Sign
items.summary: This ACOG committee opinion explains what is normal for periods in girls and teenagers. The usual age of the first period has stayed between 12 and 13 years in well-nourished populations. Clinicians should explain what to expect from the first period and the normal range of cycle length afterwards, because spotting unusual patterns early may help find health problems. It suggests treating the menstrual cycle as a vital sign of overall health.
keyPoints: The median age at the first period is between 12 and 13 years in well-nourished populations.
Several medical conditions can cause abnormal bleeding with unpredictable timing and flow.
Clinicians should explain the normal range of cycle length after the first period.
Assessing the menstrual cycle as a vital sign helps judge overall health.

items.title: Lactational amenorrhoea method for family planning
items.summary: This review looked at the lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM), where a mother uses full breastfeeding and the absence of periods as a form of birth control after having a baby. Across the studies, pregnancy rates at six months were low, ranging from about 0% to 7.5%. Women who were fully breastfeeding and had no periods but used no method had similarly low rates, and the review found no clear difference between the two groups. It is uncertain whether LAM support actually makes periods stay away for longer.
keyPoints: In controlled studies of LAM users, pregnancy rates at six months were 0.45% and 2.45%, and one study reported 5%.
Fully breastfeeding women with no periods who used no contraception had pregnancy rates of about 0.9% to 1.2% at six months.
No clear difference in pregnancy rates was found between women supported to use LAM and similar women using no method.
How long periods stayed away varied a lot between populations, so it is uncertain whether LAM extends this time.
keywords: can i get pregnant while breastfeeding
when will my period come back

items.title: Management of bleeding irregularities during contraceptive implant use: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 21 trials of treatments for irregular bleeding in people using a contraceptive implant. Some treatments, such as the anti-inflammatory drugs celecoxib and mefenamic acid, tamoxifen and ulipristal acetate, generally improved bleeding during and after treatment compared with placebo. Others, such as tranexamic acid and some hormone treatments, helped only while being taken, and several options were not consistently effective. The strength of the evidence ranged from high to very low depending on the treatment, and more research is needed.
keyPoints: Celecoxib, mefenamic acid, tamoxifen and ulipristal acetate generally improved bleeding patterns during and after treatment compared with placebo.
Tranexamic acid, oral ethinyl estradiol (50 mcg), combined oral contraceptives and mifepristone with ethinyl estradiol or doxycycline improved bleeding only during treatment.
Ibuprofen, aspirin, vitamin E, the estradiol patch and oral levonorgestrel were not consistently effective.
Satisfaction with bleeding patterns improved with tamoxifen and ulipristal acetate, and satisfaction with treatment improved with celecoxib, tamoxifen and mifepristone.
keywords: how to stop bleeding on implant

items.title: Comparison of levonorgestrel in different forms and copper intrauterine devices for emergency contraception: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled five studies (1,510 women) comparing the copper coil with levonorgestrel emergency contraception (such as the morning-after pill) after unprotected sex. The copper coil was more effective at preventing pregnancy, and women who had one were more likely to be using an effective ongoing contraceptive afterwards. Even so, more women preferred levonorgestrel, which is taken by mouth.
keyPoints: The copper coil prevented pregnancy after unprotected sex better than levonorgestrel-containing methods.
Women who got a copper coil as emergency contraception were more likely to be using an effective contraceptive method afterwards.
Women more often preferred levonorgestrel methods over the copper coil.
The copper coil also gives long-term contraception, lasting over a decade.
