items.title: Extended duration of use of long-acting reversible contraceptives: Systematic review
items.source: Canadian Family Physician Medecin de Famille Canadien
items.journal: Canadian Family Physician Medecin de Famille Canadien
items.summary: This review looked at 25 studies of what happens when long-acting contraceptives (the etonogestrel implant, hormonal coils and copper IUDs) are kept in beyond their approved time. Almost no pregnancies were reported during the extra time, and other side effects were uncommon. The risk of the coil slipping out (expulsion) continued during extended use. The authors conclude that prolonged use is safe and much more effective than short-acting methods.
keyPoints: No pregnancies were reported when the etonogestrel implant was used for 1 or 2 extra years beyond the recommended limit.
No pregnancies were reported with the copper TCu380A IUD in years 8 to 16 across several studies.
The hormonal coil (LNG-IUS) had no pregnancies in 9 studies following women for 6 to 15 years, with a few pregnancies reported in years 6 and 7 in other studies.
The risk of expulsion continued during prolonged use of the copper IUD and the 52-mg hormonal coil, while other adverse events were rare.

items.title: Misoprostol for intrauterine device placement
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 14 trials with 1,972 women to see whether misoprostol, a medicine that softens the cervix, makes getting an IUD (coil) fitted less painful or easier. For routine IUD placement it made little to no difference to pain or to whether the IUD was placed successfully. It did cause more cramping and diarrhoea before the procedure. It may help women who have had a recent failed placement attempt.
keyPoints: Misoprostol made little to no difference to pain after IUD placement, and may make little to no difference to pain during placement, compared with placebo or no treatment.
It probably made little to no difference to placement success, except in women with a recent failed attempt, where success probably increased slightly (based on one trial of 90 women).
Misoprostol probably increases cramping or abdominal pain before placement and slightly increases diarrhoea.
Evidence that it improves satisfaction is very uncertain, and it may make little difference to how easy placement is for providers.

items.title: Diabetes Group Prenatal Care: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 8 studies (1,701 pregnant people with type 2 diabetes or gestational diabetes) comparing diabetes group prenatal care with usual one-to-one care. Rates of preterm birth, large babies and most other pregnancy outcomes were similar between the two types of care. People in group care were more likely to get a long-acting reversible contraceptive (LARC, such as an IUD or implant) after birth, and those with gestational diabetes were more likely to complete their postpartum glucose test.
keyPoints: Preterm birth and large-for-gestational-age babies were similar with group care and individual care.
Postpartum LARC uptake was higher with group care: 46.1% vs 34.1% (three studies).
Among people with gestational diabetes, 74.0% in group care completed the postpartum glucose test vs 49.4% in individual care.
Attendance at the 6-week postpartum visit did not differ between the two types of care.

items.title: Chinese guidelines on the management of endometrial hyperplasia
items.source: Group for Chinese Guidelines On The Management Of Endometrial Hyperplasia
items.organisation: Group for Chinese Guidelines On The Management Of Endometrial Hyperplasia
items.summary: These Chinese clinical guidelines cover how to diagnose and treat endometrial hyperplasia, a thickening of the womb lining that often causes abnormal bleeding. For hyperplasia without atypia, a hormone-releasing coil (the levonorgestrel IUS) is suggested as an initial treatment because it was linked to higher regression, lower recurrence and fewer side effects than oral progestins. For atypical hyperplasia, surgery is usually advised, but the coil is the preferred medical option for those who cannot have surgery, want a pregnancy or are under 45.
keyPoints: Abnormal uterine bleeding is the most common symptom, and a biopsy is used to confirm the diagnosis.
For hyperplasia without atypia, progesterone is the preferred medicine, and the LNG-IUS (hormonal coil) can be the first treatment, with higher regression and lower recurrence than oral progestins.
For atypical hyperplasia, minimally invasive hysterectomy is advised, but the LNG-IUS is the preferred medical treatment when surgery is not suitable, fertility is wanted or the woman is under 45.
Treatment continues until two biopsies in a row show no abnormal changes, and long-term follow-up and patient education are recommended.

items.title: Comparison of the effectiveness of levonorgestrel intrauterine system and dienogest in the management of adenomyosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled six clinical trials (707 women, all from Asia) comparing two hormone treatments for adenomyosis, a condition where the womb lining grows into the womb muscle. Dienogest, a progestin pill, reduced pelvic pain and shrank the womb more than the levonorgestrel coil (LNG-IUS). Women with the coil had higher haemoglobin (blood iron) levels. Side effects were similar for both treatments. The authors say few studies were available, so more well-designed trials are needed.
keyPoints: Dienogest reduced pelvic pain more than the LNG-IUS (hormonal coil).
Dienogest also reduced womb size more than the LNG-IUS.
Women using the LNG-IUS had higher haemoglobin levels than those taking dienogest.
Side effects such as weight gain, headache, mood changes, acne and reduced libido were similar in both groups.

items.title: Fertility-preserving treatment for stage IA endometrial cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 754 young women with early-stage (stage IA) endometrial cancer who wanted to keep their fertility and were treated with progestin hormones. About 66% of those taking oral progestin had their cancer fully clear within a year, compared with about 86% of those using a levonorgestrel hormonal coil (LNG-IUD). Pregnancy rates after treatment were 58% with oral progestin and 44% with the coil, but the range of results for the coil was very wide, so that number is uncertain.
keyPoints: Complete response within 12 months was about 66% with oral progestin and about 86% with the LNG-IUD.
Among studies of grade 1 tumours only, response was about 66% with oral progestin and about 83% with the LNG-IUD, though the coil estimate was imprecise.
Pooled pregnancy rates were about 58% after oral progestin and 44% after the LNG-IUD, with a very wide range for the coil.
The authors say these findings may help patients and doctors make personalised treatment decisions.

items.title: Influence of the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system on the risk of breast cancer: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 10 studies on whether the hormonal coil (levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system) is linked to breast cancer. Six studies found a link to higher breast cancer risk, while three found no sign of higher risk. The authors say the studies differed a lot and many other factors could affect the results, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Six of 10 studies found a positive association between the hormonal coil and breast cancer; three found no higher risk.
The results point to a possible increased risk, especially in postmenopausal women and with longer use.
One study found increased risk of invasive breast cancer only in women aged 40-45.
The authors suggest advice based on each person's own risk profile, and hormone-free options may be considered for women with a history of breast cancer.

items.title: Immediate versus delayed postabortal insertion of contraceptive implant
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at three trials with 1,162 women to compare getting a contraceptive implant right at the time of an abortion with getting it later. Getting the implant straight away probably means more women end up with an implant and fewer have an unintended pregnancy in the next six months. For medical abortion, having the implant put in at the same time probably makes little or no difference to whether the abortion works. The certainty of the evidence ranged from moderate to very low.
keyPoints: Immediate implant insertion probably lowers unintended pregnancy within six months after abortion (moderate certainty).
Women are probably more likely to start an implant if it is placed immediately, after both medical and surgical abortion.
Placing the implant at the same time as medical abortion medicines probably has little or no effect on abortion failure (moderate certainty).
There may be no difference in abnormal bleeding at one month between immediate and delayed insertion (low certainty).

items.title: Awareness, knowledge, and misconceptions of adolescents and young people regarding long-acting reversible contraceptives: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 40 studies of about 10,470 young people (aged 12-25) to see what they know about long-acting contraception such as coils (IUDs) and implants. Only about 65% had heard of at least one type. Many held mistaken beliefs, for example that these methods cannot be used by people who have never had a baby, or that they can cause infertility. The authors conclude that clinicians should specifically address these points when giving advice.
keyPoints: Only about 65% of young people were aware of at least one type of long-acting reversible contraceptive (LARC).
About 62% did not realise LARCs can be used by people who have never had a baby.
About 37% believed LARCs could cause infertility.
The authors say clinicians should counsel young people that LARCs suit those who have not had children and do not cause infertility.

items.title: A systematic review on clinical effectiveness, side-effect profile and meta-analysis on continuation rate of etonogestrel contraceptive implant
items.summary: This review pulled together 51 studies on the etonogestrel contraceptive implant (the small rod placed under the skin of the arm). It found the implant to be very effective at preventing pregnancy and generally safe. However, fewer women kept using it for a year compared with those who had a hormonal coil (LNG-IUS) or copper coil, mostly because of changes to their periods.
keyPoints: The implant was very effective: eight of 15 studies reported 100% effectiveness, and the Pearl Index (pregnancies per 100 women-years) ranged from 0 to 1.4.
Abnormal bleeding or period changes were the most commonly reported side effect and were the main reason women stopped using it.
Continuing to use the implant ranged from 57-97% at one year, 44-95% at two years and 25-78% at three years.
One-year continuation was higher for the hormonal coil and the copper coil than for the implant, and bone mineral density showed no significant difference at one year.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 419: Coercion Free Contraceptive Care
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian committee opinion gives guidance to health care providers on how to talk about birth control without pressure or coercion. It says people should be supported to choose the method that suits them, including the right to decline contraception, use a less effective method, or stop a method at any time. The aim is better patient autonomy and a better experience in health care settings, especially for people who may be more vulnerable to feeling pressured.
keyPoints: Contraception counselling should respect a person's beliefs, culture, preferences and ability to use the method they choose.
People have the right to access the contraceptive method they want, to decline contraception or use less effective methods, and to stop a method freely.
People have the right to unbiased, non-coercive counselling and evidence-based information from their provider.
Following these recommendations should reduce real or perceived coercive care, particularly among vulnerable populations.

items.title: Self-administered subcutaneous medroxyprogesterone acetate for improving contraceptive outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled three randomized trials (1,264 participants) comparing women injecting themselves with subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (a contraceptive injection) against having a provider give it. Women who self-injected were more likely to keep using the contraceptive. The benefit seemed larger for women under 25 and for women in low- and middle-income countries. The effects on other outcomes are uncertain because the evidence for them was very low quality.
keyPoints: Self-injection probably increases continuation of contraceptive use compared with provider-given injections (risk ratio 1.35, moderate-certainty evidence).
The effect on continuation appeared larger for younger women (under 25) and for women in low- and middle-income countries.
There was no difference depending on whether the provider was a community health worker or clinic-based.
Effects on other outcomes remain uncertain because the certainty of evidence was very low.

items.title: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM) Consult Series #49: Cesarean scar pregnancy
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This guideline from the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine covers cesarean scar pregnancy, where an early pregnancy implants in the scar from a past cesarean birth. It can lead to serious complications, and it can be hard to diagnose quickly. The best treatment is not known, but the guideline makes recommendations on managing it and on contraception afterwards, including long-acting options such as IUDs and implants.
keyPoints: Waiting and watching (expectant management) is recommended against because of the risk of severe complications.
Surgical removal or ultrasound-guided vacuum aspiration may be considered, while sharp curettage alone should be avoided.
Methotrexate injected into the pregnancy sac may be used for medical treatment, but methotrexate given through the body alone should not be used.

Women who have had a cesarean scar pregnancy should be told about the risks of another pregnancy and counselled on effective contraception, including long-acting reversible contraception and permanent contraception.

items.title: Long-acting reversible contraception immediately after medical abortion: systematic review with meta-analyses
items.summary: This review pooled randomised trials on starting long-acting contraception right after a medical abortion (mifepristone plus misoprostol). Having the contraceptive implant or injection on the same day as mifepristone did not make the abortion less effective, and the implant was linked to fewer later unintended pregnancies and higher satisfaction. Putting in an intrauterine device soon after the pregnancy passes was also found to be reasonable. The quality of the evidence ranged from very low to high, mainly because of few events, people dropping out and no blinding.
keyPoints: Implant or injection given on the same day as mifepristone did not change how well the abortion worked.
Same-day implant was linked to fewer later unintended pregnancies and higher patient satisfaction; same-day injection was linked to higher satisfaction.
Early or immediate IUD insertion after the pregnancy passed gave higher uptake and continuation than delayed insertion in some groups.
The authors conclude that implants or injections should be offered on the day of mifepristone and intrauterine methods as soon as possible after expulsion.

items.title: Update to U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, 2016: Updated Recommendations for the Use of Contraception Among Women at High Risk for HIV Infection
items.source: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.journal: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.summary: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) updated its contraception guidance for women at high risk of getting HIV. After reviewing the evidence and the World Health Organization's 2019 guidance, it now says progestin-only injections (such as DMPA) and IUDs, both hormonal and copper, can be used without restriction in these women. Other hormonal methods, including implants, the pill and progestin-only pills, were already considered safe to use without restriction.
keyPoints: Progestin-only injectables (including DMPA) and IUDs (hormonal and copper) are now rated category 1, safe to use without restriction, for women at high risk of HIV; they were previously category 2.
Women at high risk of HIV may also be at risk of other sexually transmitted infections, so STD screening guidance applies before IUD insertion.
Combined hormonal methods, implants and progestin-only pills remain category 1, with no restriction for women at high risk of HIV.
Advice on using hormonal contraception or IUDs alongside HIV treatment medicines also applies to medicines taken to prevent HIV (PrEP).

items.title: Progestogen-releasing intrauterine systems for heavy menstrual bleeding
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 25 trials (2,511 women) on hormone-releasing coils (the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, or LNG-IUS) for heavy periods. Compared with other medicines such as the pill or tranexamic acid, the coil may reduce bleeding more and probably gives slightly better quality of life, with fewer women stopping treatment. Compared with endometrial ablation it is probably similar for bleeding but more likely to cause side effects, and the evidence versus hysterectomy is too uncertain to draw conclusions. Much of the evidence is low or very low certainty.
keyPoints: Compared with other medical treatments, the LNG-IUS may lower menstrual blood loss more (low-certainty evidence) and probably improves quality of life slightly (moderate-certainty evidence).
Serious side effects are probably similar between the LNG-IUS and other medical treatments, and women on other medicines are probably more likely to stop treatment or have treatment failure.
Compared with endometrial ablation, bleeding results were inconsistent, the LNG-IUS probably causes more side effects, and it may have higher treatment failure and need for hysterectomy.
It is uncertain whether the LNG-IUS is better or worse than hysterectomy for heavy bleeding, satisfaction or quality of life.

items.title: Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system for endometrial hyperplasia
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 13 trials of women with endometrial hyperplasia (a thickening of the womb lining that can sometimes turn into cancer). It compared the hormone coil (levonorgestrel IUD) with progestogen taken by other routes, such as tablets, and with no treatment. The coil probably works better than other progestogen treatments at reversing the thickening, based on moderate-quality evidence. Side effects, especially device-related ones, were poorly reported, so the evidence on safety is limited.
keyPoints: The hormone coil probably clears endometrial hyperplasia more often than non-coil progestogens in the short term (up to six months), based on moderate-quality evidence.
Low-quality evidence suggests the coil may mean fewer hysterectomies, and very low-quality evidence suggests higher satisfaction with treatment.
The coil may cause more bleeding or spotting but less nausea than other progestogen treatments.
There was not enough evidence to judge device-related side effects, such as expulsion, or cost.

items.title: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system for endometrial protection in women with breast cancer on adjuvant tamoxifen
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether a hormone coil (the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, or LNG-IUS) protects the womb lining in women with breast cancer who take tamoxifen, a drug that can cause womb lining problems and bleeding after menopause. Across four trials with 543 women, the coil probably lowered the chance of womb polyps and overgrowth of the womb lining (hyperplasia). It also probably increased unexpected bleeding or spotting in the first one to two years. There was not enough evidence to say whether it prevents womb cancer.
keyPoints: The LNG-IUS probably reduces womb polyps and, slightly, womb lining overgrowth (hyperplasia) in women taking tamoxifen.
It probably increases abnormal vaginal bleeding or spotting at 12 and 24 months, though no cases were reported by 60 months.
There was not enough evidence to know whether it prevents womb cancer, as no studies reported cases.
No clear difference was seen in breast cancer coming back or in breast cancer deaths, but larger studies are needed.

items.title: Systematic review of efficacy with extending contraceptive implant duration
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review looked for studies on how well hormonal contraceptive implants prevent pregnancy when left in longer than the approved time. Out of nearly 3,000 articles, only six were good enough to include. These studies were of poor to fair quality and had limits such as not applying to everyone and not accounting for other factors. The authors conclude that there is only limited data on using implants beyond their approved duration.
keyPoints: Only six studies met the review's criteria out of 2951 articles found.
Five studies looked at the etonogestrel implant (Implanon) and one at the levonorgestrel implant (Jadelle).
All studies were rated poor to fair quality, with limits in generalizability and control of confounders.
The review concluded that data on extended-duration implant use are limited.

items.title: Cyclical progestogens for heavy menstrual bleeding
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 15 trials (1071 women) of progestogen tablets taken for part of the menstrual cycle to treat heavy periods. Short-course tablets (taken for 7 to 10 days mid-cycle) and longer-course tablets (days 5 to 26) may both reduce bleeding less than other treatments such as tranexamic acid or the levonorgestrel hormonal coil (LNG-IUS). The evidence was low or very low quality, so the authors are uncertain about the findings and they could change with new trials.
keyPoints: Short-course progestogen tablets may reduce menstrual blood loss less than tranexamic acid, danazol or a progesterone-releasing coil.
Long-course progestogen tablets may reduce bleeding less than the LNG-IUS, tranexamic acid or ormeloxifene, but may work similarly to the combined vaginal ring.
Breast tenderness and bleeding between periods were more likely with the LNG-IUS than with long-course progestogen tablets.
Evidence quality was low or very low, partly because most women knew which treatment they were getting.

items.title: Antifibrinolytics for heavy menstrual bleeding
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 13 trials (about 1,300 women) of tranexamic acid and similar medicines for heavy periods. Compared with a placebo, these medicines reduced blood loss and more women said their bleeding improved. They also seemed to work better than some other tablets, but may work less well than the hormonal coil (levonorgestrel IUS). The evidence ranged from very low to moderate quality, and there was too little data to be sure about side effects such as blood clots.
keyPoints: Compared with placebo, antifibrinolytics cut blood loss by about 53 mL per cycle and more women improved (moderate-quality evidence).
TXA may be more likely to bring improvement than progestogen tablets or NSAIDs, with fewer side effects than progestogens (low-quality evidence).
In one small trial, the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (hormonal coil) may have worked better than TXA, with 85% of women improving versus 20% to 65% (very low-quality evidence).
Few blood clot events were reported, but most studies did not specifically look for them, so safety data are limited.

items.title: Barriers to implementation of long-acting reversible contraception: A systematic review
items.source: Journal of the American Association of Nurse Practitioners
items.journal: Journal of the American Association of Nurse Practitioners
items.summary: This review looked at 14 studies to understand why long-acting reversible contraception (LARC), such as coils and implants, is used less often than health organisations recommend. LARC is one of the most effective forms of birth control. The review found that the main barriers sit with the health care system and professionals, including gaps in provider education, little hands-on training, and practical barriers in clinics. The authors suggest better LARC training for nurse practitioners.
keyPoints: LARC is one of the most effective forms of contraception, but it is still used less than major health organisations recommend.
Three groups of barriers were found: gaps in provider education and competency, a lack of hands-on training, and barriers to practice.
The authors say LARC training should be part of advanced practice nursing education and continuing education.

items.title: Oral and intrauterine progestogens for atypical endometrial hyperplasia
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for trials comparing a hormone coil (the levonorgestrel IUS) with oral progestogen tablets for treating atypical endometrial hyperplasia, a pre-cancer change in the womb lining. It found only one trial, and just 19 of its women had this exact condition. In that small group there was not enough evidence to say whether the coil or the tablets worked better. Across all 153 women in the trial, vaginal bleeding was more common with the coil, while nausea rates were similar. The evidence was low or very low quality.
keyPoints: No trials were found that were done only in women with atypical endometrial hyperplasia; results came from a 19-woman subgroup of one larger trial.
All 6 women using the hormone coil had their atypical hyperplasia regress, versus 10 of 13 on oral progestogen, but this was too little evidence to say which works better.
Vaginal bleeding was more common with the coil than with oral progestogen (low-quality evidence).
There was no clear difference in nausea between the coil and tablets (very low-quality evidence).

items.title: Long-acting reversible contraception in adolescents: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pulled together 12 studies of 4,886 women under 25 who used a hormonal or copper coil (IUD) or the contraceptive implant. Most kept their method for at least a year: about 84 out of 100 kept any long-acting method, about 74 out of 100 kept an IUD, and about 84 out of 100 kept the implant. The authors conclude that IUDs and implants should be offered to all adolescents as first-line options.
keyPoints: 12-month continuation of any long-acting reversible contraceptive was 84% in adolescents and young women.
IUD continuation at 12 months was 74% and implant continuation was 84%.
Among postpartum adolescents, 12-month continuation was 84%.
About 8% of IUDs were expelled (came out), based on pooled results.

items.title: Practice Bulletin No. 186 Summary: Long-Acting Reversible Contraception: Implants and Intrauterine Devices
items.summary: This is a practice guideline on long-acting reversible contraception (LARC), which means intrauterine devices (IUDs, or coils) and contraceptive implants. It describes them as the most effective reversible birth control methods. Because they work over the long term without daily or monthly effort, they are easy to use correctly, and fertility returns quickly once the device is removed.
keyPoints: IUDs and contraceptive implants are the most effective reversible contraceptive methods.
They do not need ongoing effort from the patient to work well over the long term.
Fertility returns rapidly after the device is removed.
The guideline gives advice on choosing suitable patients and on starting and managing LARC.

items.title: Practice Bulletin No. 186: Long-Acting Reversible Contraception: Implants and Intrauterine Devices
items.summary: This guideline from US obstetrician-gynecologists looks at long-acting reversible contraception (LARC), which means contraceptive implants and intrauterine devices (IUDs or coils). It describes them as the most effective reversible birth control methods. Because they do not need ongoing effort from the user, they work well over the long term, and fertility returns quickly once the device is removed.
keyPoints: Implants and IUDs (LARC) are the most effective reversible contraceptive methods.
Unlike many other methods, LARC does not require ongoing effort from the patient to work well long term.
Fertility returns rapidly after the device is removed.
The bulletin gives evidence-based recommendations on choosing patients for LARC and on starting and managing these methods.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 668: Menstrual Manipulation for Adolescents With Physical and Developmental Disabilities
items.summary: This opinion from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists looks at managing periods for teenagers with physical or developmental disabilities. If the teen, her family and her doctor agree that treatment is needed after an evaluation, hormonal methods can be considered, with pros and cons reviewed for each person. The goal is to reduce how heavy periods are and how many days they last, rather than to stop them completely.
keyPoints: Hormonal methods should be reviewed with the teen and her caregivers, weighing advantages and disadvantages for her specific needs.
Complete absence of periods may be hard to achieve, so expectations should be realistic; the aim is optimal suppression (less flow and fewer days of bleeding).
Suppressing periods before they start (before menarche) and endometrial ablation are not recommended as treatments.
Good care for these teens is comprehensive, confidential and respectful, supports the teen's own choices, avoids harm, and covers puberty, periods, sexuality, safety and consent.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 670: Immediate Postpartum Long-Acting Reversible Contraception
items.source: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
items.organisation: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
items.summary: This guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists looks at starting a long-acting birth control method, such as an IUD (coil) or implant, right after giving birth. It says this can help prevent unplanned pregnancies and pregnancies that come too close together. It notes there are few reasons why a woman could not have a coil or implant placed straight after birth. It also says women should be told about all their postpartum birth control choices so they can make their own informed decision.
keyPoints: Immediate postpartum LARC (IUDs and implants) could reduce unintended pregnancies and pregnancies that follow too soon after a birth.
There are few reasons why a woman could not have an IUD or implant placed right after birth.
Women should be counseled about all postpartum contraception options, including immediate LARC, ideally during pregnancy.
Hospitals need education and protocols so that immediate postpartum LARC is easier to access.

items.title: Progestin-only contraceptives: effects on weight
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 22 studies of about 11,450 women to see whether progestin-only contraceptives (injections, hormonal coils, implants and mini-pills) change body weight. In most studies, users and non-users did not differ significantly in weight or body composition. Average weight gain at 6 or 12 months was under 2 kg (4.4 lb) in most studies. The overall quality of the evidence was low, so the findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: In 15 of the 22 studies, weight change and body composition did not differ significantly between groups.
Mean weight gain at 6 or 12 months was less than 2 kg (4.4 lb) in most studies, and about twice as much at two to four years.
Some studies found more weight or body fat gain with the DMPA injection compared with a copper IUD or no hormonal method.
Overall evidence quality was low, and the authors suggest counselling about typical weight gain may help reduce stopping contraception because of weight worries.

items.title: Theory-based interventions for contraception
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 25 randomized trials of counselling and education programs built on health behaviour theories to help people choose and use contraception. In nine higher-quality trials, programs based on social cognitive theory (mostly for teenagers) and motivational interviewing (a supportive counselling style) were linked to more effective contraceptive use. In one trial, motivational interviewing also led to more people starting and using long-acting methods like implants and IUDs than non-standard counselling. The review rated the overall evidence as moderate.
keyPoints: Teen-focused programs based on social cognitive theory led to more effective contraceptive and condom use, and in one trial adolescent mothers had fewer second births within two years.
Motivational interviewing groups more often reported using effective contraception and less often reported using ineffective methods than groups given handouts.
In one trial, motivational interviewing led to more people starting long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) by one month and using it at three months than non-standard counselling.
The review calls for effective programs adapted to low-resource settings and clearer reporting of how theory was used.

items.title: Steroidal contraceptives and bone fractures in women: evidence from observational studies
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 14 observational studies on whether hormonal contraceptives affect the chance of broken bones later in life. The studies did not show an overall link between the pill and fractures, though a few found higher risk in certain groups. Women who used the DMPA injection may have a higher fracture risk, while one study suggested the hormonal IUD may be linked to a lower risk. Because these studies only observe people, they cannot prove cause and effect.
keyPoints: Observational studies do not show an overall link between oral contraceptive use and fracture risk, although some found higher risk in specific subgroups.
DMPA (the progestin injection) users may have an increased fracture risk, with higher risk reported for longer use.
One study found the levonorgestrel hormonal IUD may be linked to a lower fracture risk.
Comparison groups in observational studies usually differ, so results need careful adjustment for other factors.

items.title: Gonadotropins for ovulation induction in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at FSH injections (gonadotropins) used to trigger ovulation in women with PCOS who did not ovulate or get pregnant on clomiphene or letrozole. It pooled 15 trials with 2,348 women. Different types of FSH injections seemed to work about equally well, though the evidence was low or very low quality. In one larger trial, FSH injections probably led to more live births than carrying on with clomiphene, but may also raise the chance of miscarriage.
keyPoints: There may be little or no difference in live birth, multiple pregnancy, clinical pregnancy or miscarriage between recombinant FSH and urinary-derived FSH (low-certainty evidence).

For women who did not respond to clomiphene, FSH injections probably gave more live births (RR 1.24) and clinical pregnancies than continuing clomiphene (moderate-certainty evidence, one trial of 661 women), without more multiple pregnancies.
FSH injections may increase the miscarriage rate compared with continued clomiphene (low-certainty evidence).
It is uncertain whether any treatment differs in ectopic pregnancy or ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) risk; no women in the clomiphene comparison developed OHSS.

items.title: Interventions for fertility preservation in women with cancer undergoing chemotherapy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at two ways to protect fertility in women having chemotherapy for cancer, mostly breast cancer: stimulating the ovaries to freeze eggs or embryos, and using GnRH agonist medicines to temporarily switch the ovaries off. GnRH agonists may greatly lower the chance that chemotherapy causes ovarian insufficiency (the ovaries stopping working properly), but the evidence is low certainty. For egg or embryo freezing with added protective drugs (letrozole or tamoxifen), there was no evidence on live births, ovarian insufficiency or survival. No studies compared the two approaches directly.
keyPoints: GnRH agonists may result in a large reduction in chemotherapy-related ovarian insufficiency in women with breast cancer (low-certainty evidence).
The effect of GnRH agonists on live birth is very uncertain, and they may make little or no difference to survival over 10 years (low certainty).
For ovarian stimulation with letrozole or tamoxifen, there was no evidence on live birth or survival; there is probably little to no difference between the two drugs in the number of eggs retrieved.
No studies compared egg or embryo freezing directly with GnRH agonist suppression, and evidence for cancers other than breast cancer was too limited to draw conclusions.

items.title: Effects of letrozole combined with clomiphene in the treatment of polycystic ovary syndrome: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 randomised trials with 931 women who have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and are trying to get pregnant. It looked at taking letrozole and clomiphene together to help trigger ovulation, compared with a control group. The combination was linked to higher ovulation and pregnancy rates. It did not clearly change side effects, follicle numbers or womb lining thickness.
keyPoints: Letrozole plus clomiphene was linked to higher pregnancy rates (RR 1.50) than the comparison treatment.
Ovulation rates were also higher with the combination (RR 1.29).
No clear difference was found in adverse effects, womb lining thickness or number of mature follicles.
The authors conclude the combination helps improve ovulation, pregnancy rates and hormone levels in PCOS.

items.title: Ovulation triggers in unassisted reproduction, an old question still unanswered: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether an ovulation trigger shot (hCG) helps women with unexplained or anovulatory infertility get pregnant when they use ovulation-inducing medicines with natural intercourse or IUI. Six trials with 1,218 women were included. The results did not show a clear benefit or harm for pregnancy, live birth, miscarriage or multiple pregnancy. The authors say the evidence is not strong enough to recommend for or against using a trigger.
keyPoints: Six trials (1,218 women) were included, and all used hCG as the trigger.
Clinical pregnancy was not clearly different with a trigger (odds ratio 1.23, range 0.91-1.66).
hCG may increase ovulation, but the result was not clear-cut (odds ratio 1.70, range 0.84-3.43).
Evidence is insufficient to recommend or refute ovulation triggers; effects on pregnancy outcomes remain uncertain.

items.title: Trends in acupuncture for infertility: a scoping review with bibliometric and visual analysis
items.summary: This review mapped out research on acupuncture for infertility where the goal is natural conception. It found most studies looked at women with polycystic ovary syndrome, ovulation problems, or a condition where the egg is not released from the follicle. A pooled analysis of small trials suggested acupuncture did better than an hCG trigger injection alone, but the authors say clearer, better-designed studies are still needed because most studies had unclear research aims.
keyPoints: The review covered 310 articles; most were studies of female infertility, mainly from polycystic ovary syndrome, ovulation disorders and luteinized unruptured follicle syndrome.
In pooled trials, acupuncture worked better than hCG alone (11 trials, 662 participants).
Adding acupuncture to hCG plus letrozole showed no clear difference compared with hCG plus letrozole alone (one small trial of 84 participants).
Reported side effects included mild ovarian irritation and early signs of miscarriage; the authors call for well-designed confirmatory studies.

items.title: Therapeutic donor insemination for LGBTQ+ families: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at the evidence on therapeutic donor insemination (using donor sperm to try to get pregnant) for LGBTQ+ families. The authors note that high quality, prospective studies in this group are limited. Even so, they found that a simple, low-intervention approach for people who ovulate had equal or higher success rates than routine infertility care protocols, without raising risk. They conclude this care can be provided in community, primary care and fertility clinic settings with support and training.
keyPoints: A low-tech, low-intervention approach for people who ovulate had equal or higher success rates than routine infertility care protocols.
This approach did not increase risk compared with routine protocols.
Donor insemination for LGBTQ+ families can be provided appropriately in community-based settings, primary care and fertility clinics, with support and training.
High quality, prospective studies specific to this group are limited, so more research is needed.

items.title: Ovulation induction drug and ovarian cancer: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 34 studies to see whether fertility drugs used to trigger ovulation are linked to ovarian cancer. Overall, women who had these treatments did not have a higher rate of invasive ovarian cancer or borderline ovarian tumours (growths that are usually less aggressive) than other women. The risk did not rise with more treatment cycles or with any particular drug. Women who had never given birth appeared to have a higher risk of borderline tumours, so the authors suggest closer follow-up for this group.
keyPoints: Overall, ovulation induction was not linked to more invasive ovarian cancer or borderline ovarian tumours.
The risk did not increase with the number of treatment cycles or with specific ovulation induction drugs.
In women who had never given birth, the risk of borderline tumours appeared higher with ovulation induction.
The authors recommend careful monitoring and follow-up for women who have not had children and are treated with ovulation induction.

items.title: Intrauterine Insemination After Human Chorionic Gonadotropin Trigger or Luteinizing Hormone Surge: A Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 13 studies to compare two ways of timing intrauterine insemination (IUI): an hCG trigger shot given after ultrasound monitoring, or waiting for the body's own natural LH surge, which can be tracked at home. Pregnancy rates were not meaningfully different between the two approaches. This was true for natural cycles and for cycles using clomid or letrozole tablets. The studies differed from one another quite a bit, which makes the result less certain.
keyPoints: No significant difference in chance of pregnancy between hCG trigger timing and LH surge timing for IUI.
The same result held in natural cycle IUI and in cycles using oral medicines (clomid or letrozole).
The authors concluded that at-home LH monitoring gave similar pregnancy outcomes to hCG-timed IUI.
The included studies varied noticeably, and most were not randomised trials.

items.title: Double versus single intrauterine insemination (IUI) in stimulated cycles for subfertile couples
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at nine trials of couples having intrauterine insemination (IUI) with fertility medication, comparing one insemination per cycle with two. It is unclear whether a second insemination leads to more live births, and the evidence was low quality. Clinical pregnancy rates may be higher with double IUI, but this should be read with caution. The review could not tell whether double IUI changes the chance of miscarriage, multiple pregnancy or ectopic pregnancy.
keyPoints: It is uncertain whether double IUI improves live birth rate compared with single IUI (low quality evidence).
Clinical pregnancy rate may be higher with double IUI: about 14% with single IUI versus roughly 16% to 23% with double IUI.
It is uncertain whether double IUI affects miscarriage, multiple pregnancy or ectopic pregnancy rates.
All findings were rated low quality because of small trials, unclear bias and inconsistent results.

items.title: Acupuncture and clomiphene citrate for anovulatory infertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine trials with 1441 women who had trouble ovulating and compared acupuncture, with or without the fertility drug clomiphene citrate, against clomiphene alone. Adding acupuncture to clomiphene did not clearly change pregnancy, ovulation or pregnancy loss rates. Acupuncture used on its own was linked to higher pregnancy rates and fewer pregnancy losses than clomiphene alone, but the authors say these results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Acupuncture added to clomiphene showed no significant difference in pregnancy, ovulation or pregnancy loss rates.
Acupuncture alone did not raise the ovulation rate compared with clomiphene alone.
Acupuncture alone was linked to a higher pregnancy rate (odds ratio 2.34) and lower pregnancy loss (odds ratio 0.19) than clomiphene alone.
The authors advise that results be interpreted with caution in real clinical practice.

items.title: Gonadotropins versus oral ovarian stimulation agents for unexplained infertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled eight trials (nearly 3,000 people) of women with unexplained infertility having intrauterine insemination (IUI) with ovarian stimulation. It compared oral tablets (clomiphene or letrozole) with injectable hormones called gonadotropins. Gonadotropins gave slightly more live births, but they also raised the chance of multiple pregnancies such as twins by a similar amount. The authors concluded the trial data do not support using gonadotropins for IUI in unexplained infertility.
keyPoints: Gonadotropins were linked to a small increase in live birth (relative risk 1.09) compared with oral medicines.
They were also linked to a similar small increase in multiple pregnancy (relative risk 1.06).
The number of singleton (one baby) births per patient was similar in both groups.
The authors concluded the randomized data do not support gonadotropins for IUI in women with unexplained infertility.

items.title: Gonadotrophins for ovulation induction in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This review pooled 15 trials (2,387 women) of fertility injections called gonadotrophins, used to trigger ovulation in women with PCOS who did not ovulate or conceive on clomiphene. The different types of gonadotrophin (lab-made versus urine-derived) seemed to give similar results, though much of the evidence was low or very low quality. In one large trial, gonadotrophins led to more live births than continuing clomiphene, with more miscarriages but no extra multiple pregnancies.
keyPoints: Lab-made (recombinant) FSH and urine-derived gonadotrophins may make little or no difference to live birth, multiple pregnancy, clinical pregnancy or miscarriage (low-quality evidence).
For the other urine-derived types (HMG or HP-HMG) compared with uFSH, the evidence was too weak (very low quality) to say whether one is better.
After clomiphene failure, gonadotrophins gave more live births than continuing clomiphene (moderate-quality evidence, one trial of 661 women), without more multiple pregnancies.
The authors suggest weighing cost and convenience when choosing between gonadotrophin types; it is uncertain whether any type lowers the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

items.title: Letrozole Compared With Clomiphene Citrate for Unexplained Infertility: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled eight randomized trials with 2,647 women who have unexplained infertility. It compared two fertility tablets, letrozole and clomiphene citrate, used to stimulate the ovaries. Pregnancy rates, live births, miscarriages and twin pregnancies were similar with both medicines. The trials differed from one another quite a bit, which limits how firm the conclusion is.
keyPoints: Positive pregnancy tests were similar with letrozole and clomiphene (24% vs 23%).
No clear differences were found in clinical pregnancy, live birth, miscarriage or twin pregnancy.
Blood estradiol (an oestrogen hormone) levels were lower with letrozole than with clomiphene.
The studies varied noticeably, which limits how certain the result is.

items.title: Clomiphene citrate and neural tube defects: a meta-analysis of controlled observational studies
items.summary: Researchers combined 13 studies covering about 218,000 pregnancies to see whether taking clomiphene citrate, a common fertility drug used to trigger ovulation, around the time of conception raises the chance of neural tube defects in the baby. The pooled result showed a small increase in risk (about 21%), but this was not statistically significant, meaning it could be due to chance. The authors concluded that clomiphene exposure was not significantly linked to neural tube defects.
keyPoints: Thirteen studies with 218,819 pregnancies were pooled in this meta-analysis.
Clomiphene use around conception was not significantly linked to neural tube defects (odds ratio 1.21, 95% CI 0.88-1.66).
The studies agreed fairly well with each other, and there was no sign of publication bias.
The result is in line with an earlier 1995 meta-analysis that also found no significant link.

items.title: First-line ovulation induction for polycystic ovary syndrome: an individual participant data meta-analysis
items.summary: This study pooled the original data from 20 trials with almost 4,000 women who have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and trouble getting pregnant because they do not ovulate. It compared medicines used to trigger ovulation. Letrozole probably led to more live births and pregnancies, and to faster pregnancy, than clomiphene citrate (CC). CC plus metformin may help a little with pregnancy rates, but the evidence did not show a clear difference in live births.
keyPoints: Compared with clomiphene, letrozole probably improved live birth rates (risk ratio 1.43) and clinical pregnancy rates (risk ratio 1.45), with moderate-certainty evidence.
Letrozole also probably shortened the time to pregnancy compared with clomiphene.

Clomiphene plus metformin might improve pregnancy rates and shorten time to pregnancy compared with clomiphene alone, but the evidence was low certainty and there was insufficient evidence of a difference in live births.

The authors concluded letrozole can be recommended as the preferred first-line treatment for women with PCOS and infertility, and that blood levels of testosterone and insulin may influence which treatment works best.

items.title: Metformin for ovulation induction (excluding gonadotrophins) in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 41 trials (4,552 women) to see whether metformin helps women with PCOS ovulate and become pregnant. Compared with placebo, metformin may improve live birth rates and probably raises pregnancy rates and may raise ovulation rates, but stomach and bowel side effects are probably more common. Adding metformin to clomiphene did not clearly improve live births over clomiphene alone. When metformin was compared with clomiphene, results were unclear and differed by body weight, and the evidence was of very low quality.
keyPoints: Versus placebo, metformin may improve live birth rates (low-quality evidence) and probably increases clinical pregnancy (moderate-quality evidence).
Gastrointestinal side effects are probably more common with metformin: about 10% with placebo versus roughly 22% to 40% with metformin.
It is uncertain whether metformin plus clomiphene improves live birth compared with clomiphene alone, although clinical pregnancy was probably higher with the combination.
Metformin versus clomiphene gave inconclusive live birth results that differed by BMI, and the effect on miscarriage is uncertain in all comparisons.

items.title: Tamoxifen versus clomiphene citrate for ovulation induction in infertile women
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled 12 studies (1,302 women) comparing two fertility tablets, tamoxifen and clomiphene citrate, for women who do not ovulate. Overall, the two drugs did not differ in ovulation or pregnancy rates, and the best-designed trials (RCTs) also found no difference. Some other study types hinted that tamoxifen might work better, but the authors say the true effect still needs to be confirmed.
keyPoints: Across all studies, tamoxifen and clomiphene citrate gave similar ovulation and pregnancy rates.
In case-control studies only, tamoxifen was linked to higher ovulation and pregnancy rates, but this was not seen in randomised trials.
No clear differences were found in womb lining thickness or miscarriage rate.
The authors say the exact effectiveness of tamoxifen versus clomiphene needs further confirmation.

items.title: Risk of endometrial cancer in women treated with ovary-stimulating drugs for subfertility
items.summary: This review pooled 19 studies to see whether fertility drugs that stimulate the ovaries are linked to cancer of the womb lining (endometrial cancer). Some analyses showed a higher risk, especially with clomiphene at high doses or many cycles, but others showed no difference. The evidence was very low quality, so no firm conclusions can be drawn, and the higher risk may be due to the underlying fertility problem (such as PCOS) rather than the drugs themselves.
keyPoints: When subfertile women were compared with other subfertile women, any ovary-stimulating drug was not linked to a higher risk of endometrial cancer; when compared with the general population, a higher risk was seen.
Clomiphene citrate was linked to a higher risk in subfertile women, but only at high total doses (over 2000 mg) and with more than 7 cycles.
The clomiphene link may be largely due to underlying risk factors such as polycystic ovary syndrome rather than the drug itself.
Evidence on gonadotropins was inconclusive, and all evidence was rated very low quality.

items.title: Hysteroscopic polypectomy prior to infertility treatment: A cost analysis and systematic review
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This study looked at whether removing womb-lining polyps with a camera procedure (hysteroscopy) before fertility treatment saves money. Researchers combined published pregnancy rates with treatment costs in a cost model. They found that removing polyps first lowered the average cost of each pregnancy for women having intrauterine insemination (IUI) or IVF/ICSI. The office-based procedure saved more than the operating-room version.
keyPoints: Polyp removal before four cycles of IUI saved about €6658 per clinical pregnancy with office polypectomy and €728 with operative polypectomy.
Before IVF/ICSI, office polypectomy saved about €15,854 and operative polypectomy about €6644 per ongoing pregnancy.
Polypectomy before IUI stayed cost-effective if the clinical pregnancy rate was above 30.2% (office) or 52.6% (operative), and the procedure cost was under €4414.
Polypectomy before IVF/ICSI stayed cost-effective if the ongoing pregnancy rate was above 26.4% (office) or 31.7% (operative), and the procedure cost was under €6376.

items.title: Gonadotrophins for ovulation induction in women with polycystic ovarian syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 14 trials (1,726 women) of injectable fertility hormones called gonadotrophins, used to trigger ovulation in women with PCOS who did not respond to clomiphene. It compared the lab-made (recombinant) form of FSH with hormones made from urine, and different urine-based types against each other. No clear difference was found in live births, pregnancies, or a complication called ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS). The evidence was low or very low quality, so the authors suggest cost and convenience may guide the choice.
keyPoints: No evidence of a difference in live birth between lab-made FSH and urine-derived gonadotrophins (low-quality evidence).
No evidence of a difference in clinical pregnancy rates between the two types.
No clear difference in OHSS rates, though the evidence was very low quality.
Authors suggest weighing costs and convenience when choosing between types.

items.title: Letrozole versus clomiphene citrate in polycystic ovary syndrome: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together seven randomized trials that compared two fertility medicines, letrozole and clomiphene citrate, for triggering ovulation in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). In total it covered 1833 women. Women who took letrozole had more live births and more pregnancies than women who took clomiphene. The two medicines did not differ in rates of multiple pregnancy, miscarriage or ovulation.
keyPoints: Live birth rates were higher with letrozole than with clomiphene (relative risk 1.55).
Pregnancy rates were also higher with letrozole (relative risk 1.38).
Multiple pregnancy, miscarriage and ovulation rates were similar between the two medicines.
The authors concluded letrozole is better than clomiphene for live birth and pregnancy in women with PCOS.

items.title: AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF CLINICAL ENDOCRINOLOGISTS, AMERICAN COLLEGE OF ENDOCRINOLOGY, AND ANDROGEN EXCESS AND PCOS SOCIETY DISEASE STATE CLINICAL REVIEW: GUIDE TO THE BEST PRACTICES IN THE EVALUATION AND TREATMENT OF POLYCYSTIC OVARY SYNDROME - PART 2
items.summary: This is a 2014 best-practice guide from US endocrine societies on polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), the most common hormone condition in women of reproductive age. It says weight loss is the main first treatment, and losing as little as 5% of body weight can bring back regular periods and help ovulation and fertility medicines work better. Women with PCOS who want a baby should be checked for diabetes and high blood pressure beforehand, and the guide notes that the clinical trial evidence for weight-loss counselling before conception is limited.
keyPoints: Losing as little as 5% of body weight can restore regular periods and improve the response to ovulation-inducing and fertility medicines.
Women with PCOS should be screened and treated for high blood pressure and diabetes before trying to conceive, because of higher risks of gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia and placental abruption.
For infertility caused by lack of ovulation, treatment should start with a tablet such as clomiphene citrate or letrozole.
Women should be counselled about weight loss before trying to conceive, although there is limited trial evidence showing a benefit.

items.title: To discard or not to discard 1PNs? A systematic review and meta-analysis on 291,474 embryos
items.summary: Some embryos made in IVF show only one pronucleus (a small structure seen soon after fertilisation) instead of the usual two, and are often thrown away. This review pooled 24 studies to compare these 1PN embryos with usual 2PN embryos. 1PN embryos were less likely to grow to the blastocyst stage and had lower live birth rates when untested. But when they were confirmed to have the normal number of chromosomes, live birth rates looked similar, so these embryos can sometimes be viable.
keyPoints: 1PN embryos reached the blastocyst stage about half as often as 2PN embryos.
Untested 1PN blastocysts had a lower live birth rate than 2PN blastocysts, but after chromosome testing (PGT-A) the live birth rate was similar.
The rate of normal chromosome numbers (euploidy) was comparable between 1PN and 2PN embryos.
In untested embryos, 1PN blastocysts made by ICSI had a much lower live birth rate, while those made by standard IVF showed no clear difference.

items.title: Advanced sperm selection techniques for assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at special lab methods for picking sperm during IVF or ICSI, to see whether they improve the chance of a baby. It combined five trials with 3752 women. Choosing sperm that bind to hyaluronic acid (HA-ICSI) may make little or no difference to live birth, but probably slightly lowers miscarriage. For the other methods, the evidence was too weak to say whether they help.
keyPoints: HA-ICSI may make no difference to live birth or slightly increase it (25% with standard ICSI versus 24% to 31% with HA-ICSI; low-certainty evidence).
HA-ICSI probably slightly reduces miscarriage (about 7% with ICSI versus 3% to 6% with HA-ICSI; moderate-certainty evidence).
The effects of zeta potential selection, microfluidic sorting and SpermSlow are uncertain because the evidence is very low certainty.
The review says more high-quality studies are needed before any of these techniques can be recommended for routine use.

items.title: Preimplantation Genetic Testing for Monogenic Disorders: A Health Technology Assessment
items.summary: This review looked at preimplantation genetic testing for single-gene disorders (PGT-M), where embryos made through IVF are tested before transfer for an inherited condition a parent is at risk of passing on. The researchers found four systematic reviews, all of low or critically low quality, and no studies comparing PGT-M with other options such as natural conception followed by prenatal testing. The evidence is very uncertain about effects on live births, pregnancy and pregnancy loss. Overall, how well PGT-M works could not be determined.
keyPoints: Four systematic reviews were included, and all were rated low or critically low quality.
No studies compared PGT-M with relevant alternatives, such as conceiving and then having prenatal diagnostic testing.
The evidence is very uncertain about live births, clinical pregnancy, ongoing pregnancy and pregnancy loss.
False-negative results appear to be low, but the evidence is very uncertain, and effects on parents' emotional wellbeing and quality of life are unknown.

items.title: Clinical outcomes following preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic conditions: a systematic review of observational studies
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 51 observational studies of IVF with preimplantation genetic testing for single-gene (monogenic) conditions, covering over 5,000 cycles. About 3 in 10 cycles ended in a live birth (29.7%). Studies that also screened embryos for chromosome numbers (aneuploidy) reported higher rates than those that did not, but these were comparisons across different studies, not a direct trial.
keyPoints: Across 5,305 cycles, clinical pregnancy was 34.0% and birth was 29.7% per cycle.
Per embryo transfer, clinical pregnancy was 24.8% and birth was 21.7%.
With added chromosome screening, birth rates were 37.6% per cycle and 31.8% per transfer.
Without chromosome screening, birth rates were 28.1% per cycle and 18.6% per transfer.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of double trophectoderm biopsy and/or cryopreservation in PGT: balancing the need for a diagnosis against the risk of harm
items.summary: This review pooled 10 studies of embryos that had to be warmed, biopsied again and/or frozen again during genetic testing (PGT), for example after an unclear first result. Compared with embryos biopsied and frozen only once, live birth and pregnancy rates per transfer were lower, and miscarriage was higher among pregnancies. The certainty of the evidence ranged from low to moderate. The authors say the extra handling may still be worthwhile to avoid transferring embryos with a genetic or chromosome problem, so the risks and benefits need weighing for each couple.
keyPoints: Live birth per embryo transfer was lower with double cryopreservation (OR 0.56) and with double biopsy plus double cryopreservation (OR 0.51) than with a single biopsy and single freeze.
Clinical pregnancy rates per transfer were also lower, and miscarriage per pregnancy was higher in both repeat-handling groups.
Embryo survival after warming, and pregnancy and newborn outcomes, were within expected ranges in the studies that reported them.
The authors say the risks should be weighed against the benefit of avoiding affected or aneuploid embryos for each couple.

items.title: Preimplantation genetic testing and disorders of placental implantation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review pooled 8 studies to see whether taking a small biopsy from an embryo for genetic testing (PGT) during IVF raises the risk of problems with how the placenta attaches. It found no clear increase in placenta accreta spectrum, where the placenta grows too deeply into the womb wall. The waters broke early (before labour, before term) a little more often after PGT, but this result came mostly from a single study and needs more research. Placental abruption, placenta previa and high blood pressure disorders showed no clear differences.
keyPoints: Embryo biopsy for PGT was not linked to a higher risk of placenta accreta spectrum.
Early rupture of the waters before term (PPROM) was somewhat more common after PGT, mainly driven by one study.
Placental abruption, placenta previa and high blood pressure disorders of pregnancy did not differ clearly between groups.
People who had PGT tended to have a slightly lower BMI, so the groups may not be fully comparable.

items.title: Live birth and other reproductive outcomes of mosaic and euploid embryos: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review pooled studies comparing pregnancy results after transferring 'mosaic' embryos (which have a mix of normal and abnormal cells) with fully normal (euploid) embryos in IVF. Mosaic embryos were less likely to implant and led to fewer live births. Once a pregnancy was established, miscarriage rates were similar, and babies' health outcomes were as favorable, though birth weight tended to be a little lower. The studies used different testing and reporting methods, so more standardized research is needed.
keyPoints: Mosaic embryos had significantly lower implantation and live birth rates than euploid embryos.
Once implantation happened, pregnancy loss and miscarriage rates were similar between mosaic and euploid embryos.
Segmental mosaicism seemed to have better outcomes than whole-chromosome mosaicism.
Babies from mosaic embryos tended toward lower birth weight, but neonatal health outcomes were as favorable as with euploid embryos.

items.title: Economic evaluations of assisted reproductive technologies in high-income countries: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 40 studies from high-income countries that weighed the costs of fertility treatments against how well they work. Several high-cost add-ons, including genetic testing of embryos (PGT-A) for the general population and ICSI when infertility is unexplained, were unlikely to be good value because they added little or no benefit. Cheaper medicines for ovarian stimulation, such as biosimilars or HMG, cost less but did not work as well. The authors note the evidence has gaps, and no studies looked at what patients themselves prefer.
keyPoints: It is uncertain whether PGT-A improves pregnancy rates compared with IVF without it, so it could not be shown to be cost-effective.
ICSI for infertility not caused by male factors appears no more effective than standard IVF fertilization, so it is not cost-effective.
Biosimilars or HMG for ovarian stimulation are cheaper but compromise clinical effectiveness.
Limits include inconsistent outcome measures, some studies not based on high-quality trials, and no studies measuring patient preferences.

items.title: Effect of different treatment protocols on in vitro fertilisation/intracytoplasmic sperm injection (IVF/ICSI) outcomes in adenomyosis women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies of women with adenomyosis who had IVF or ICSI. Women with adenomyosis had lower pregnancy and live birth rates and more miscarriages than women without it. Frozen embryo transfer, especially after pre-treatment with a GnRH agonist, may be a better choice than fresh transfer. In fresh transfer cycles, the ultralong protocol had better pregnancy results than the long, short or antagonist protocols.
keyPoints: Adenomyosis was linked to a 26% lower clinical pregnancy rate and a 35% lower live birth rate in IVF/ICSI.
Miscarriage was almost twice as likely with adenomyosis (27.8% vs 13.9%).
In frozen embryo transfer cycles, the differences between women with and without adenomyosis were not statistically significant.
In fresh transfer cycles, the ultralong protocol gave better pregnancy rates than the long, short or antagonist protocols.

items.title: Causes of embryo implantation failure: A systematic review and metaanalysis of procedures to increase embryo implantation potential
items.summary: This review pooled 11 studies to look at why embryos sometimes fail to implant during IVF. It found that testing embryos for the correct number of chromosomes (PGT-A) raised the odds of implantation. The review concluded that implantation success depends mostly on the embryo having the right chromosomes, while factors in the womb had a small effect. Older women had a harder time reaching several healthy embryos.
keyPoints: Genetic testing of embryos for chromosome problems (PGT-A) significantly increased the odds of implantation.
Success in assisted reproduction largely depends on the embryo having the normal number of chromosomes (being euploid).
Having three euploid embryos greatly increases success rates, but this is hard to achieve in older women.
Factors outside the embryo, such as the womb lining, were present but had only a marginal impact.

items.title: Personalized versus standard frozen-thawed embryo transfer in IVF/ICSI cycles: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review pooled 10 studies (one randomized trial and nine cohort studies) to see whether timing an embryo transfer using an endometrial receptivity array (ERA) test improves IVF/ICSI results compared with standard timing. Overall, there was no clear difference in pregnancy rates or live birth rates between the two approaches. Some small subgroup differences appeared, but the authors concluded the test seems to offer limited guidance and that better-quality trials are needed.
keyPoints: Personalized transfer timing guided by ERA did not significantly change clinical pregnancy rate compared with standard timing in unselected patients.
No significant differences were found in secondary outcomes such as live birth rate between the two groups.
Some subgroup results varied, for example fewer miscarriages in poor-prognosis patients but lower pregnancy rates in donor cycles.
The authors say ERA appears to have limited value for guiding embryo transfer and more high-quality randomized trials are needed.

items.title: Evaluation of non-invasive gene detection in preimplantation embryos: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review pooled 20 studies on non-invasive genetic testing of embryos during IVF. This test checks the fluid the embryo grows in, rather than removing cells from the embryo. Across the studies, the test found genetic problems about 84% of the time and correctly ruled them out about 85% of the time. The authors say it may be an alternative way to test embryos, but larger studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Across 20 studies, non-invasive embryo testing had a pooled sensitivity of 0.84 and specificity of 0.85.
The authors conclude it may have high detection accuracy and could serve as an alternative way to analyse embryos.
Adding fluid from inside the embryo to the culture fluid did not improve accuracy.
Results varied between studies, and the authors say large-scale studies are needed to confirm its value.

items.title: Spontaneous collapse as a prognostic marker for human blastocysts: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether a blastocyst (a 5-6 day old embryo) that spontaneously shrinks and re-expands, called collapse, is linked to IVF outcomes. Collapse is seen with time-lapse cameras in the lab. Pooling seven studies, collapsed blastocysts were less likely to be chromosomally normal and led to fewer clinical and ongoing pregnancies. Live birth and miscarriage rates did not clearly differ, and all the studies were retrospective with varying results, so the findings should be read with caution.
keyPoints: About 37% of blastocysts in the seven studies showed spontaneous collapse.
Collapse was linked to lower clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy rates and to fewer chromosomally normal (euploid) embryos.
Live birth and miscarriage rates were not clearly different with or without collapse.
The authors suggest collapsed blastocysts could be ranked lower when choosing which embryo to transfer.

items.title: Factors associated with embryo mosaicism: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review pooled results from seven earlier studies plus data from one fertility clinic to look at what is linked to mosaic embryos, which contain a mix of normal and abnormal cells. Embryos tested on day 6 or 7 and embryos from women under 34 had slightly higher rates of mosaicism. Embryo quality, sperm quality and the father's age were not linked to mosaicism. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Embryos biopsied on day 6 or 7 had a slightly higher rate of mosaicism than those biopsied earlier.
Mosaicism was higher in women under 34 than in women 34 or older, unlike aneuploidy (embryos with the wrong number of chromosomes), which rises with age.
Embryo quality, sperm quality and paternal age were not linked to mosaic embryo rates.
The authors say knowing these factors may help improve results of fertility treatment.

items.title: The role of endometrial scratching prior to in vitro fertilization: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled randomized trials to see whether endometrial scratching (a small procedure that gently injures the womb lining) before an embryo transfer improves the chance of pregnancy. Overall, live birth and clinical pregnancy were somewhat more likely after scratching, though the certainty of this evidence was low. The benefit was seen when scratching was done in the menstrual cycle before the transfer cycle, and mainly in women who had already had failed IVF attempts.
keyPoints: Overall, live birth was more likely after scratching than after sham or no procedure (relative risk 1.12), but certainty was low.
Scratching done in the menstrual cycle before the transfer cycle was linked to more live births (moderate certainty); scratching during the transfer cycle showed no effect.
A higher chance of live birth was seen only in women with previous IVF failures (moderate certainty), and more past failures meant a greater likely benefit.
The number of scratches and the type of instrument did not seem to change the chance of live birth.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis: clinical outcomes of recurrent pregnancy failure resulting from preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy
items.summary: This review pooled 13 studies of people with recurrent pregnancy failure who were having IVF. It compared those who had embryos tested for chromosome problems (PGT-A) with those who did not. The tested group had higher rates of implantation, pregnancy and live birth, and a lower miscarriage rate. The better pregnancy and live birth results were seen both in women under 35 and in women 35 or older.
keyPoints: PGT-A was linked to a higher live birth rate (RR 1.75) than standard IVF/ICSI in people with recurrent pregnancy failure.
Implantation, clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy rates were also higher with PGT-A.
The clinical miscarriage rate was lower with PGT-A (RR 0.74).
Pregnancy and live birth rates were better with PGT-A in both age groups, under 35 and 35 or older.

items.title: Interventions to optimize embryo transfer in women undergoing assisted conception: a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analyses
items.summary: This review pulled together 188 randomized trials (nearly 60,000 women) testing things done around the time of embryo transfer in IVF/ICSI. Ultrasound guidance, a soft catheter and hyaluronic acid in the transfer medium were linked to more clinical pregnancies. Bed rest after transfer was linked to fewer clinical pregnancies. The quality of the trials was moderate and there was a significant risk of publication bias, and results for miscarriage and live birth were limited by inconsistent reporting.
keyPoints: Ultrasound-guided transfer, soft catheters and hyaluronic acid were linked to higher clinical pregnancy rates.
Atosiban, G-CSF and hCG showed a trend towards higher clinical pregnancy rates, but larger trials are needed before they are adopted.
Bed rest after transfer was linked to a lower clinical pregnancy rate and should not be recommended.
NSAIDs, preventive antibiotics, acupuncture and cervical mucus removal showed no significant benefit.

items.title: Morphological and morphokinetic associations with aneuploidy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 58 studies (over 40,000 embryos) to see whether time-lapse imaging of embryos in IVF can show which embryos have the wrong number of chromosomes (aneuploid).
