Embryos with chromosome problems tended to reach some growth stages a little later, by roughly 1 to 2.5 hours. But there was a lot of overlap between healthy and affected embryos, so time-lapse alone cannot reliably tell them apart. The authors say the evidence is of poor quality and more research is needed.
keyPoints: Embryos with chromosome abnormalities were slightly delayed in reaching stages such as 8 cells, 9 cells and the expanded blastocyst (about 1 to 2.5 hours).
The overlap between normal and abnormal embryos was large, so it is not possible to definitively classify an embryo by timing alone.
Other visible features, such as fragmentation, were inconsistent and based on poor-quality, varied evidence.
Time-lapse data might help decide which embryos to prioritise for genetic testing, but it is not a replacement for it based on this review.

items.title: Impact of endometrial scratching on reproductive outcome in patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 randomized trials of endometrial scratching, a minor procedure that lightly scratches the womb lining, in women who had at least one failed fertility treatment cycle (IVF, ICSI or IUI). Women who had scratching had higher rates of clinical pregnancy, embryo implantation and live birth than those who did not. There was no clear difference in miscarriage or multiple pregnancy. The authors say more trials are needed to work out the best timing and who it helps before it becomes routine.
keyPoints: Clinical pregnancy, implantation and live birth rates were higher with endometrial scratching than without.
Miscarriage and multiple pregnancy rates did not differ significantly between the two groups.
The review pooled 16 randomized trials, with about 1,770 women in the scratching group and 1,934 in the control group.
The authors call for more trials to find the right timing and the right group of women before it is used routinely.

items.title: Day 5 versus day 3 embryo biopsy for preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic/single gene defects
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether testing an embryo on day 5 or on day 3 of its development works better when couples use IVF to avoid passing on a single-gene condition (called PGT-M). Only one small trial of 20 women was found. The evidence was very low quality, so it is uncertain whether either timing leads to more live births or fewer miscarriages.
keyPoints: Only one trial, with 20 women, met the review's criteria.
It is uncertain whether day 5 or day 3 biopsy changes live births or miscarriages.
Other outcomes, such as ectopic pregnancy and stillbirth, also could not be compared with any confidence.
No studies reported on birthweight, gestational age at birth, or major birth defects.

items.title: Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy: A Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society Guideline
items.summary: The Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society reviewed the evidence on PGT-A, an IVF add-on that tests embryos for the wrong number of chromosomes before transfer. In trials of good-prognosis patients who had two or more embryos to test, PGT-A increased implantation and ongoing pregnancy or birth rates per embryo transfer. It is hard to apply these results to the wider group of people with infertility, so the guideline says use of PGT-A should be individualised. Benefits need to be weighed against costs and technical limits.
keyPoints: Trials so far only included good-prognosis patients who could produce two or more blastocysts for biopsy.
In that group, PGT-A raised the implantation rate and the ongoing pregnancy or delivery rate per transfer.
Results cannot easily be generalised to the wider infertility population, so use should be individualised by factors such as age and ability to make embryos.
Counselling and informed consent are needed, as limits include possible embryo damage, false positives, false negatives and mosaicism.

items.title: Impact of preimplantation genetic testing on obstetric and neonatal outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies covering about 785,000 pregnancies, comparing those that followed preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) with those from standard IVF or ICSI. PGT pregnancies had lower rates of low birth weight, very low birth weight and very early (very preterm) birth, but a higher rate of high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy. Most other outcomes were no different. The authors concluded that PGT did not increase the risk of adverse obstetric outcomes overall, though a possible link with slower baby growth in the womb needs more study.
keyPoints: PGT pregnancies had lower rates of low birth weight, very low birth weight and very preterm birth than standard IVF/ICSI pregnancies.
PGT pregnancies had a higher rate of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (risk ratio 1.30).
No increase was found in birth defects, gestational diabetes, placenta problems or cesarean section overall.
With frozen-thawed embryo transfer, PGT was linked to more preterm birth and slower growth in the womb (IUGR), which the authors say needs further investigation.

items.title: Does theFMR1 gene affect IVF success?
items.summary: This review looked at whether the FMR1 gene, specifically the length of a repeating section called the CGG repeat, affects the chance of success with IVF. For women with normal or intermediate repeat lengths, the effect on IVF outcomes such as pregnancy rates was minimal. Women who carry a premutation (55-200 repeats) may get fewer eggs from IVF stimulation, but the findings were inconsistent. Repeat length can also affect the risk of passing on Fragile X syndrome, so counselling and genetic testing options may be relevant for some patients.
keyPoints: For normal (under 45) or intermediate (45-54) CGG repeat lengths, the effect on IVF outcomes including pregnancy rates was minimal.
A meta-analysis found no link between normal repeat length and IVF pregnancy rates (summary odds ratio 1.0).
Premutation carriers (55-200 repeats) may have lower egg yields with IVF, though findings were inconsistent.
Patients with longer repeat lengths may benefit from clinical and psychological counselling and may want to consider preimplantation genetic testing.

items.title: Time-lapse systems for embryo incubation and assessment in assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at time-lapse systems, which take pictures of embryos in the incubator during IVF, compared with the usual method of taking embryos out each day to check them under a microscope. It pooled nine trials with 2,955 couples. The review found not enough good-quality evidence to say whether time-lapse systems improve live birth, miscarriage or pregnancy rates. The evidence was low or very low quality, so the results should be read with caution. Time-lapse systems often add significant extra cost to treatment.
keyPoints: Nine trials with 2,955 couples were included, and the evidence was low to very low quality.
It is unclear whether time-lapse systems change live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates compared with conventional incubation.
One comparison suggested fewer miscarriages with time-lapse plus selection software, but this was very low-quality evidence.
The authors found too little good evidence to choose between time-lapse systems and conventional incubation.

items.title: Can time-lapse parameters predict embryo ploidy? A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether time-lapse imaging, which films embryos as they grow in the lab, can show if an embryo has the right number of chromosomes. Researchers pooled 13 studies, but the studies were very different from each other. No timing or growth measure was reliably able to predict chromosome status. The authors conclude that time-lapse measures should not yet replace genetic screening of embryos.
keyPoints: 13 studies were included, but they differed a lot in design, patients, biopsy day and how results were measured.
No single or combined time-lapse measure was consistently able to predict whether an embryo had the right number of chromosomes.
The evidence is too mixed to draw firm conclusions about time-lapse for chromosome screening.
Time-lapse measures should not yet be used in place of preimplantation genetic screening (PGS).

items.title: The use of preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A): a committee opinion
items.summary: This committee opinion from two US fertility societies looked at preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A), which checks embryos for the wrong number of chromosomes during IVF. It says the value of PGT-A as a screening test for IVF patients has not yet been determined. Some studies show higher birth rates when testing is paired with transferring a single embryo, but these studies have important limitations.
keyPoints: The value of PGT-A as a screening test for IVF patients has yet to be determined.
Several studies show higher birth rates after aneuploidy testing combined with elective single-embryo transfer.
This suggests testing might lower the chance of twins or other multiple pregnancies.
The studies behind these findings have important limitations.

items.title: Gonadotrophin dose in expected low responders undergoing ovarian stimulation for in-vitro fertilization/intracytoplasmic sperm injection: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled six randomized trials (2,262 women) of IVF or ICSI treatment in women expected to respond poorly to ovarian stimulation. It compared higher versus lower starting doses of the fertility drugs called gonadotrophins. Live birth, ongoing pregnancy and clinical pregnancy rates did not differ clearly between the two approaches, though lower doses gave slightly fewer usable embryos. The authors say the evidence is not yet enough to say whether a higher starting dose helps.
keyPoints: No significant difference in live birth, ongoing pregnancy or clinical pregnancy rates between higher and lower starting doses.
The number of eggs retrieved did not differ significantly between the groups.
A lower starting dose was linked to slightly fewer usable embryos.
The authors concluded the evidence is insufficient to show that a higher starting dose improves live birth rates in expected low responders.

items.title: Efficiency versus efficacy: a systematic review and meta-analysis of preimplantation genetic diagnosis versus natural conception for carriers of chromosomal translocations
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review pooled results from 49 studies of 7,026 couples where one partner carries a chromosomal translocation (a rearrangement of chromosome pieces). It compared IVF with embryo genetic testing (PGD) to trying naturally. Each attempt with PGD led to more live births (32.0% vs 18.5%), but over time the total live birth rate was about the same as for couples with a good outlook trying naturally (36.0% vs 36.6%). PGD may therefore speed things up rather than raise the final chance of a baby.
keyPoints: Per attempt, PGD gave a higher live birth rate than natural conception (32.0% vs 18.5%).
Cumulative live birth rate with PGD (36.0%) was not significantly different from good-prognosis couples conceiving naturally (36.6%).
Carriers of Robertsonian translocations had more normal or balanced embryos than carriers of reciprocal translocations (38.3% vs 22.5%).
Translocation type predicted PGD success, but the carrier's sex did not; advice should fit each couple's goals for time to pregnancy.

items.title: Frozen versus fresh embryo transfer in low responders: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at women who produce only a few eggs during IVF (called low responders). It compared freezing all embryos and transferring them later with transferring a fresh embryo straight away. Freezing all embryos did not give better results, and in the one randomized trial it led to fewer live births. The authors say more randomized trials are needed.
keyPoints: One randomized trial (rated high certainty) found frozen transfer gave fewer live births than fresh transfer (RR 0.79), as well as fewer clinical pregnancies and lower cumulative live birth.
Non-randomized studies found no clear difference in live birth, but this evidence was very uncertain.
In women meeting the POSEIDON low-responder criteria, miscarriage was lower with fresh transfer.
The authors conclude that a 'freeze-all' approach did not improve outcomes for low responders and that fresh transfer may be as good or better.

items.title: Does intracytoplasmic sperm injection outperform conventional in vitro fertilization in couples without severe male factor infertility? A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled six randomised trials comparing ICSI (injecting a single sperm into an egg) with conventional IVF in couples who did not have severe male factor infertility. ICSI did not give a higher chance of a live birth, either per embryo transfer or across all transfers from one egg collection. The authors rated this as high-quality evidence and concluded that ICSI should not be routinely recommended unless there is severe male infertility.
keyPoints: Live birth rate was about 33% with ICSI and 35% with conventional IVF, with no meaningful difference (four studies, 1,438 couples).
Cumulative live birth rate was about 43% with ICSI and 47% with conventional IVF, again with no clear benefit from ICSI (three studies, 1,911 couples).
ICSI was linked to a slightly lower preterm birth rate, based on a small number of studies (222 couples).
The authors advise against routine ICSI for reasons other than severe male infertility, while noting that few high-quality trials reported live birth data.

items.title: Culture media for human pre-implantation embryos in assisted reproductive technology cycles
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether the liquid used to grow embryos in the lab (culture medium) affects the chance of having a baby after IVF or ICSI. It included 26 trials, but no two well-designed trials compared the same media, so results could not be combined. One study suggested a medium called G5 probably gives a somewhat higher chance of live birth than another called HTF, but the overall evidence was limited and often very low quality. The authors conclude there is not enough evidence to say any one culture medium is better.
keyPoints: No two well-designed trials compared the same culture media, so the results could not be pooled.
One study suggested G5 medium probably increases cumulative live birth compared with HTF (44.1% versus 37.9%), with moderate-certainty evidence.
For other comparisons, it is unclear whether live birth rates differ, and the evidence was very low certainty.
The authors conclude there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the use of any specific embryo culture medium.

items.title: Impact of artificial intelligence in embryo selection to improve pregnancy rates per transfer in IVF cycles: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review looked at whether artificial intelligence (AI) tools that help pick which embryo to transfer during IVF lead to more pregnancies than the usual method of judging embryos by how they look. Ten studies were included, but only two had data that could be combined. There was no clear difference in clinical pregnancy rates between AI-assisted and standard selection. AI may help make embryo grading more consistent, but it has not been shown to work better.
keyPoints: Pooled results from two studies showed no significant difference in clinical pregnancy rate per transfer between AI-assisted and morphology-based embryo selection.
The AI tools predicted outcomes well in lab-style testing, but this did not consistently lead to better results per cycle.
AI may offer more standardized and consistent embryo scoring between different embryologists.
Live birth, miscarriage and time to pregnancy were not reported in the available studies, so larger trials are needed.

items.title: Optimizing intrauterine insemination and spontaneous conception in women with unilateral hydrosalpinx or tubal pathology: A systematic review and narrative synthesis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review looked at women with a blocked or damaged fallopian tube on one side (such as hydrosalpinx, a fluid-filled tube) who want to conceive naturally or with intrauterine insemination (IUI), where IVF is not possible. Treating a hydrosalpinx by removing or blocking the tube seemed to improve the chance of pregnancy. Women with a blockage near the womb end of the tube did about as well with IUI as women with open tubes, while those with a blockage at the far end did less well per cycle. The authors say the evidence is limited and more studies are needed.
keyPoints: Removing or blocking a tube with hydrosalpinx (salpingectomy or tubal occlusion) appeared to improve the chance of natural or IUI pregnancy, though more prospective studies are needed.
Women with a blockage at the womb end of one tube (proximal) had similar IUI pregnancy rates to women with open tubes.
Women with a blockage at the far end of one tube (distal) had lower pregnancy rates per IUI cycle, and extra IUI cycles added little benefit.
The studies varied a lot and were mostly retrospective, so the evidence guiding care for this group has significant gaps.

items.title: Using serum anti-Müllerian hormone levels to predict the chance of live birth after spontaneous or assisted conception: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 32 studies to see whether a blood test for anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), a marker of egg reserve, can predict the chance of having a baby after IVF/ICSI, IUI or trying naturally. Higher AMH was linked to a higher chance of a live birth after IVF/ICSI, but no cut-off level could be found below which a live birth was not possible. There was not enough data to say whether AMH predicts success after IUI or when trying to conceive without fertility treatment. The authors note the studies had limitations and differed in how they were done.
keyPoints: Higher AMH levels were linked to a higher chance of live birth after IVF/ICSI, in a non-linear way.
No AMH threshold was found below which live birth could not be achieved after IVF/ICSI.
A low AMH level should not be the only reason to rule out IVF treatment, especially in young patients.
There was not enough data to judge AMH as a predictor after IUI or when trying to conceive without fertility treatment.

items.title: The clinical value of progestin-primed ovarian stimulation protocol for women with diminished ovarian reserve undergoing IVF/ICSI: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies with 4,182 women who have a low egg supply (diminished ovarian reserve) and are having IVF or ICSI. It compared a progestin-primed stimulation protocol (PPOS) with clomiphene or letrozole plus gonadotropin injections. PPOS was linked to higher pregnancy rates, fewer cancelled cycles and far fewer early LH surges, though it needed more gonadotropin medication for longer. The authors say larger, well-designed studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Clinical pregnancy and cumulative pregnancy rates were higher with PPOS (odds ratios 1.39 and 1.73).
More good-quality embryos were produced and fewer cycles were cancelled with PPOS.
Premature LH surges were much less common with PPOS.
PPOS needed a longer duration and larger amount of gonadotropin, and the authors call for larger, more rigorous studies.

items.title: Live birth rate of gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonist versus luteal phase gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist protocol in IVF/ICSI: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 52 studies, covering about 10,000 women, to compare two common medicine plans used to stimulate the ovaries during IVF or ICSI. The two plans were the antagonist protocol and the long agonist protocol. Live birth rates were similar for both. The antagonist plan was linked to a lower risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), especially in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
keyPoints: Live birth rates were comparable between the antagonist and long agonist protocols.
The antagonist protocol was linked to a lower rate of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), especially in women with PCOS.
Women in the antagonist group had a lower clinical pregnancy rate, fewer eggs retrieved or fewer high-grade embryos in some groups, including poor responders.
More research is needed on cumulative live birth rates (across several transfers) for the general and poor-response groups.

items.title: Intrauterine insemination + controlled ovarian hyperstimulation versus in vitro fertilisation in unexplained infertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled eight randomised trials comparing IUI with ovary-stimulating medicine against IVF for couples with unexplained infertility. Overall, IVF gave a higher live birth rate, with no clear difference in multiple pregnancies or ovarian over-stimulation. For treatment-naive women under 38, there was no clear difference in live births, but in women over 38 IVF did better (based on one trial). The evidence quality was moderate to low, and the authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Across eight trials, IVF was linked to a higher live birth rate than IUI with ovary stimulation (RR 1.53), though results varied a lot between trials.
There was no significant difference in multiple pregnancy or ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) rates.
In treatment-naive women under 38, live birth rates did not differ significantly between the two approaches.
In women over 38, live birth rates were significantly higher with IVF, based on a single trial.

items.title: Association of ovarian stimulation and embryonic aneuploidy in in vitro fertilization cycles with preimplantation genetic testing: A narrative systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 14 studies covering 4,805 IVF cycles in which embryos were genetically tested. It asked whether the strength of ovarian stimulation (the fertility drugs used to produce more eggs) affects how many embryos have the wrong number of chromosomes. Stronger stimulation seemed linked to a higher share of these abnormal embryos. But a stronger response also gave more healthy embryos to transfer, which may mean more transfer attempts and a higher chance of a live birth overall. The authors say more research is needed to know whether stimulation itself causes harm.
keyPoints: More robust ovarian stimulation seemed to be associated with a higher proportion of embryos with chromosome abnormalities (aneuploidy).
A higher response to stimulation was linked to more chromosomally normal embryos available for transfer.
More normal embryos can mean more transfer cycles and potentially a higher cumulative live birth rate.
Further evidence is needed to know whether stimulation has a negative effect, especially at the cellular level.

items.title: A systematic review of the quality of clinical prediction models in in vitro fertilisation
items.summary: Researchers reviewed 33 studies describing 35 tools that estimate a person's chance of pregnancy or live birth with IVF. Model quality has improved over time, but accuracy varied a lot. The review recommends the McLernon post-treatment model, which estimates the chance of a live birth over up to six complete IVF cycles. The authors say it still needs testing in countries with different IVF practices.
keyPoints: Most IVF prediction models only estimate the chance of success for a single fresh cycle.
The McLernon post-treatment model estimates the cumulative chance of live birth over up to six complete cycles, including fresh and frozen embryo transfers.
It was built on UK national data and performed best when tested on other data sets.
It needs further testing in countries with different IVF practices and policies.

items.title: Clomiphene citrate and letrozole to reduce follicle-stimulating hormone consumption during ovarian stimulation: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 22 trials of women having IVF to see whether adding a pill (clomiphene citrate or letrozole) could reduce the amount of FSH injections needed during ovarian stimulation. Live birth and pregnancy rates were similar with and without clomiphene. In women who were not expected to respond poorly, clomiphene probably lowered the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome but also meant fewer eggs were collected. Evidence for letrozole was limited and more studies are needed.
keyPoints: Using clomiphene to cut down FSH gave similar live birth and clinical pregnancy rates, based on moderate- to high-quality evidence.
In women expected to respond poorly, clomiphene gave similar results with lower medication costs.
In other women, clomiphene probably reduced the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) but also reduced the number of eggs retrieved.
More studies are needed on letrozole, and on outcomes such as total pregnancies per egg collection and whether women would agree to repeat a cycle.

items.title: Corifollitropin alfa compared to daily FSH in controlled ovarian stimulation for in vitro fertilization: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This study pooled the results of seven randomized trials comparing two IVF stimulation medicines: corifollitropin alfa (a long-lasting FSH given less often) and daily FSH injections. Live birth, ongoing pregnancy and clinical pregnancy rates were similar with both. The long-lasting medicine gave more mature eggs and more embryos, but more cycles were cancelled because of overstimulation, so it should be used cautiously in women who tend to respond strongly.
keyPoints: Live birth, ongoing pregnancy and clinical pregnancy rates were comparable between corifollitropin alfa and daily FSH.
Corifollitropin alfa led to more mature (metaphase II) eggs collected and more embryos formed.
Cycle cancellation due to overstimulation was significantly more common with corifollitropin alfa.
Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) rates were statistically similar between the two approaches.

items.title: A Systematic Review on GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Reproductive Health: Integrating IVF Data, Ovarian Physiology and Molecular Mechanisms
items.summary: This review looked at how GLP-1 medicines (such as liraglutide and exenatide), often used for weight and blood sugar, may affect the ovaries and fertility, especially in women with PCOS. In overweight women with PCOS, trials showed more regular periods, weight loss and lower free testosterone, and some signs of higher pregnancy rates in IVF and natural cycles. Animal studies showed both helpful and harmful effects on the ovaries and womb lining. The authors say more controlled human research is needed to confirm reproductive safety.
keyPoints: In overweight or obese women with PCOS, GLP-1 medicines improved menstrual regularity, reduced body weight and lowered free testosterone.
Liraglutide combined with metformin improved IVF pregnancy rates, and exenatide increased natural conception rates.
Animal studies showed both benefits (better follicle growth) and harms (oxidative stress, egg-supporting cell death, womb inflammation), depending on context and dose.
Controlled human studies are still needed on reproductive safety, especially in women without PCOS and in IVF settings.

items.title: Infertility treatment and offspring blood pressure-a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to see whether children conceived through fertility treatment such as IVF or ICSI have higher blood pressure than children conceived naturally. Across the studies, there was no clear difference in blood pressure between the two groups, even after accounting for factors like mother's age, smoking and the child's birth weight. The studies varied quite a lot from one to another, so the results are not perfectly consistent. The authors say couples considering these treatments can take some reassurance from the findings.
keyPoints: No meaningful difference in systolic or diastolic blood pressure was found between children conceived with fertility treatment and those conceived naturally.
Results stayed the same after adjusting for maternal, child and birth factors.
Type of treatment (IVF vs ICSI), birth year, child's age group and study location did not change the findings.
The studies differed considerably from each other, so some uncertainty remains.

items.title: Association of bisphenol A exposure with in vitro fertilization outcomes: A meta-analysis and systematic review
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies to see whether bisphenol A (BPA), a chemical found in some plastics, is linked to IVF and ICSI results. Higher BPA levels in urine, blood, follicular fluid or semen were linked to lower rates of normal fertilization and fewer high-quality embryos. No clear link was found with clinical pregnancy, blastocyst formation or implantation, but there were few studies and they differed a lot. The authors say more research is needed to confirm the findings.
keyPoints: Higher BPA exposure was linked to a lower normal fertilization rate in IVF/ICSI.
BPA exposure was also linked to fewer high-quality embryos.
The drop in fertilization was larger in groups with higher BPA levels (above 1.55 ng/ml).
No significant link was seen with clinical pregnancy, blastocyst formation or implantation, possibly because few studies were available.

items.title: Melatonin improves fertilization rate in assisted reproduction: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from 17 studies to see whether taking melatonin, a hormone with antioxidant properties, helps during assisted reproduction such as IVF. Women who took melatonin had more mature eggs, a higher antral follicle count and a higher fertilization rate. However, there was no clear difference in clinical pregnancy rates.
keyPoints: Melatonin was linked to a higher fertilization rate in assisted reproduction.
Melatonin was also linked to more mature eggs (MII) and a higher antral follicle count.
No statistically significant difference was found in clinical pregnancy rates.

items.title: Comparative efficacy and safety of metformin, anti-obesity agents, and myoinositol in improving IVF/ICSI outcomes and reducing ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 20 randomised trials (1,827 women with PCOS having IVF or ICSI) to compare metformin, weight-loss medicines and myoinositol. None of these treatments clearly improved pregnancy outcomes. Both metformin and myoinositol appeared to lower the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), but metformin caused more side effects while myoinositol caused fewer. The authors say more robust trials are needed to confirm these findings.
keyPoints: Metformin and myoinositol may reduce the risk of OHSS in women with PCOS having IVF/ICSI, but neither clearly improved pregnancy outcomes.
Metformin was linked to more side effects, lower estrogen (E2) levels on trigger day and more mature eggs.
Myoinositol was linked to a shorter time on gonadotropin (stimulation) medicines and fewer side effects than controls.
No studies reported an increased risk of fetal abnormalities.

items.title: Vitamin D and in vitro fertilization: a systematic review
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review looked at 18 studies on whether vitamin D levels in the blood are linked to how well IVF works. Most studies (12) found no link, 5 found a positive link, and 1 found a negative link. The authors conclude the link between vitamin D and pregnancy rates after IVF is uncertain.
keyPoints: Of 18 studies, 5 found higher vitamin D linked to better IVF results, 12 found no link, and 1 found a negative link.
The link between vitamin D levels and pregnancy rates after IVF is uncertain.
Vitamin D might matter more for White than Asian patients, and for the number of follicles collected, but this is not settled.
Vitamin D may affect the immune system, which could play a role in embryo implantation and pregnancy.

items.title: Systematic review of acupuncture to improve ovarian function in women with poor ovarian response
items.summary: This review pooled seven small trials (516 women) of acupuncture added to standard ovarian stimulation in women with poor ovarian response having IVF. Acupuncture was linked to more eggs retrieved, a higher implantation rate and some hormone changes. It did not clearly improve clinical pregnancy rate, fertilisation rate or embryo quality. The studies were generally low or very low quality, so the authors call the benefit for pregnancy outcomes doubtful and say more trials are needed.
keyPoints: Acupuncture plus standard stimulation was linked to a higher implantation rate and about one more egg retrieved on average.
It was also linked to a thicker womb lining, a higher antral follicle count and lower FSH levels.
No clear difference was seen in clinical pregnancy rate, fertilisation rate, high-quality embryo rate or AMH.
The authors say the evidence is of low or very low quality and that benefit for pregnancy outcomes is doubtful.

items.title: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection versus conventional in vitro fertilisation in couples with males presenting with normal total sperm count and motility
items.summary: This Cochrane review compared two IVF methods, ICSI (a single sperm is injected into the egg) and conventional IVF (sperm and eggs are mixed in a dish), for couples where the male partner has a normal sperm count and motility. It combined three trials with 1539 couples. Neither method was better for live birth, pregnancy, miscarriage or the safety outcomes studied, though the evidence for live birth was low-certainty.
keyPoints: ICSI and conventional IVF showed no clear difference in live birth rates, but this evidence was low-certainty.
There was probably little or no difference in multiple pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, prematurity or miscarriage.
Viable pregnancy rates were probably similar between the two methods (moderate-certainty evidence).
The authors concluded that neither method was superior when sperm count and motility are normal.

items.title: Pregnancy Benefit of Acupuncture on in vitro Fertilization: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 58 randomised trials with nearly 11,000 women having IVF to see whether acupuncture improves pregnancy results. Overall, acupuncture was linked to higher clinical pregnancy and live birth rates than comparison groups. However, the quality of the evidence was low or extremely low, and the studies varied a lot in how they were done, so the findings should be treated with caution.
keyPoints: Acupuncture was linked to a higher clinical pregnancy rate (relative risk 1.19) and live birth rate (relative risk 1.11) than control groups, but the evidence was rated extremely low and low quality.
Only transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation, a type of acupuncture using mild electrical pulses, showed a benefit for both pregnancy and live birth rates.
No studies were graded as high-quality evidence, and results differed across studies.
The authors concluded that the evidence linking acupuncture to better IVF outcomes is relatively weak.

items.title: Effect of female body mass index on intrauterine insemination outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 11 studies covering over 23,000 intrauterine insemination (IUI) treatments. It compared women with a BMI under 25 to women with a BMI of 25 or higher. There was no clear difference between the two groups in live births, clinical pregnancies, miscarriages or ectopic pregnancies. The authors still suggest that weight loss counselling be offered to women with a raised BMI having IUI, to lower the risk of problems later in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Live birth and clinical pregnancy rates after IUI did not differ significantly between women with a BMI under 25 and those with a BMI of 25 or more.
Miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy rates also showed no statistically significant difference.
The authors concluded that a raised female BMI did not affect IUI treatment outcomes.
Weight loss counselling should still be offered to women with a raised BMI undergoing IUI, to reduce related obstetric complications.

items.title: Acupuncture effects on in-vitro fertilization pregnancy outcomes: A meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 29 studies with over 6,600 women having IVF to see whether acupuncture around embryo transfer improves pregnancy results. Compared with no extra treatment, women who had acupuncture had higher rates of pregnancy and live birth. But when acupuncture was compared with sham (fake) acupuncture, there was no clear difference in any outcome, so the benefit seen may not be due to the needles themselves. The authors say more studies comparing acupuncture with sham acupuncture are needed.
keyPoints: Compared with no extra treatment, acupuncture was linked to higher biochemical, clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates and live birth rates.
Compared with sham acupuncture, there was no significant difference in pregnancy, live birth or miscarriage.
Miscarriage rates did not differ between acupuncture and no extra treatment.
The authors call for further studies comparing acupuncture with sham acupuncture.

items.title: Effect of acupuncture on IVF-related anxiety: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from eight trials (2253 people) to see whether acupuncture eases anxiety during IVF. Acupuncture was linked to a small drop in anxiety around embryo transfer or egg collection compared with control groups. The certainty of this evidence was very low, and the studies had problems that limit how far the results can be trusted. The authors say more research is needed to confirm the benefit.
keyPoints: Acupuncture was associated with a small but statistically significant reduction in IVF-related anxiety compared with any control.
The evidence was rated very low certainty, with a high risk of performance bias and large differences between trials.
The authors describe acupuncture as a drug-free and safe treatment that may help people burdened by IVF anxiety.
More investigation is needed to confirm the findings.

items.title: Acupuncture versus placebo acupuncture for in vitro fertilisation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled eight randomised trials with 3607 women having IVF to see whether acupuncture around the time of embryo transfer helps, compared with a fake (placebo) acupuncture device. Acupuncture did not make a statistically significant difference to pregnancy, miscarriage or live birth rates. Side effects such as discomfort and bruising were mild to moderate.
keyPoints: Acupuncture around embryo transfer did not significantly change clinical pregnancy rates compared with placebo acupuncture (moderate certainty).
Live birth and miscarriage rates were also not significantly different (high certainty).
Placebo acupuncture did not differ significantly from usual care.
Side effects of acupuncture, such as discomfort and bruising, were mild to moderate.

items.title: Acupuncture performed around the time of embryo transfer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 20 trials with 5130 women to see whether acupuncture around the time of embryo transfer improves IVF results. Compared with no extra treatment, acupuncture was linked to more pregnancies, more live births and fewer miscarriages. But when it was compared with sham (fake) acupuncture, there was no clear difference, so some of the benefit may come from non-specific effects such as the care and attention involved. The results varied a lot between studies, and the authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Compared with no extra treatment, acupuncture was linked to more clinical pregnancies (RR 1.32) and live births (RR 1.30).
Miscarriage was lower with acupuncture than with no extra treatment (RR 1.43 as reported).
There was no significant difference between real acupuncture and sham acupuncture.
Benefit for pregnancy rates may be greater in women with several previous IVF cycles or low baseline pregnancy rates, and there was significant variation between studies.

items.title: The effects of acupuncture on pregnancy outcomes of in vitro fertilization with embryo transfer: An interdisciplinary systematic review
items.source: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.journal: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.summary: This review pulled together 31 randomized trials with 4,450 women to look at whether acupuncture during IVF with embryo transfer improves pregnancy outcomes. The authors did not reach a conclusion about whether it helps. They say larger, better-designed, standardized trials are needed first.
keyPoints: The review included 31 randomized trials and 4,450 women, comparing acupuncture with no acupuncture or sham (placebo) acupuncture.
No conclusion could be drawn on whether acupuncture or Traditional Chinese Medicine improves IVF outcomes.
The authors call for larger, standardized, multicenter randomized trials before any conclusions are made.

items.title: Whether vitamin D was associated with clinical outcome after IVF/ICSI: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from several studies looking at vitamin D levels in women having IVF or ICSI. Women with low vitamin D had a lower chance of a live birth than women with enough vitamin D. Differences in clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy were small and not clearly meaningful. The authors concluded that women with low vitamin D should be given vitamin D.
keyPoints: Low vitamin D was linked to a lower chance of live birth after IVF/ICSI (RR 0.74).
Clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy showed only small trends that were not clear-cut.
The review included 9 cohort studies, but only 2 to 3 looked at ongoing pregnancy and live birth.
The authors suggest vitamin D should be supplied to women with low levels.

items.title: Pain relief for women undergoing oocyte retrieval for assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 24 trials (3,160 women) comparing different ways of easing pain during egg retrieval for IVF, including sedation, pain-relief drugs, a numbing injection near the cervix, acupuncture and general anaesthesia. No single method was clearly better than the others. Combining approaches, such as sedation with opioid pain relief plus a paracervical block or acupuncture, seemed to relieve pain better than one method alone. Most of the evidence was low or very low quality, and it was not enough to say whether any method changes pregnancy rates.
keyPoints: No single method or technique was shown to be better than the others for pain relief during and after egg retrieval.
Combining sedation and pain medicine with a paracervical block or acupuncture gave better pain relief than one approach alone.
There was not enough evidence to say whether any pain-relief method affects pregnancy rates.
All the methods reviewed were linked with high satisfaction, and women's preferences and local resources are worth considering.

items.title: Air pollution and female fertility: a systematic review of literature
items.summary: This review looked at 11 studies on whether air pollution affects female fertility. In people having IVF, higher nitrogen dioxide and ozone were linked to fewer live births, and larger airborne particles were linked to more miscarriage. In the general population, fine particles were linked to lower chances of conceiving, and some gases may be linked to miscarriage and stillbirth. The studies were observational and varied a lot, so the authors say larger trials are needed before firm conclusions.
keyPoints: In IVF patients, nitrogen dioxide and ozone were linked to a lower live birth rate.
Particulate matter (PM10) was linked to more miscarriage in the IVF group.
In the general population, fine particulate matter was linked to reduced chances of conceiving each cycle.
Studies were observational, retrospective and varied widely, so definitive conclusions can't yet be drawn.

items.title: Psychological consequences of IVF fertilization - Review of research
items.source: Annals of Agricultural and Environmental Medicine
items.journal: Annals of Agricultural and Environmental Medicine
items.summary: This review looked at research on the emotional and psychological effects of IVF on individuals, couples and families. It found that some partners going through IVF may not get enough support from the people closest to them. The authors argue that unsupportive social interactions can affect well-being, may make conceiving harder, and are one reason people drop out of IVF. They say more research is needed on how supportive relationships help couples during IVF.
keyPoints: IVF can be a source of psychological and emotional difficulty for couples trying to have a child.
Some partners going through IVF may not have enough support from their closest social circle.
Unsupportive social interactions are argued to affect well-being and to be one reason people stop IVF treatment.
More studies are needed on how supportive social interactions help couples during IVF.

items.title: Gender differences in emotional reactions to in vitro fertilization treatment: a systematic review
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review pulled together 26 studies on how men and women feel emotionally during IVF treatment. Both partners had psychological distress, but in different patterns. The authors concluded that couples would benefit from support programs designed for both partners.
keyPoints: Women had raised anxiety and depression before treatment, and these rose further on egg retrieval day, around embryo transfer, and while waiting for the pregnancy test.
Men reported raised depression scores before treatment, which usually increased while waiting for the IVF result.
Both men and women had lower positive feelings before the pregnancy test.
A failed IVF cycle had long-term negative emotional effects for both partners.

items.title: Serum vitamin D status and in vitro fertilization outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from five studies of women having IVF to see whether vitamin D levels in the blood were linked to treatment outcomes. Women with low vitamin D (below 20 ng/ml) were not significantly less likely to get a clinical pregnancy. They were, however, less likely to have a live birth. The review shows an association only, so it cannot say that low vitamin D caused the difference.
keyPoints: Five studies were included in the analysis.
Low vitamin D was not significantly linked to a lower clinical pregnancy rate (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.69-1.11).
Low vitamin D was linked to a lower live birth rate (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.61-0.93).

items.title: The role of vitamin D in reproductive dysfunction in women - a systematic review
items.source: Annals of Agricultural and Environmental Medicine
items.journal: Annals of Agricultural and Environmental Medicine
items.summary: This review looked at published studies on vitamin D and conditions that can affect women's fertility, including PCOS, uterine fibroids and endometriosis, as well as IVF outcomes. Vitamin D appears to play a part in how the female reproductive system works and has been linked to all of these. The authors say larger studies are still needed to understand what role vitamin D has in treating infertility.
keyPoints: Vitamin D is linked to the working of the female reproductive system.
Vitamin D has been associated with PCOS, uterine fibroids, endometriosis and IVF outcomes.
Larger studies are needed to know what role vitamin D plays in treating female infertility.

items.title: The role of acupuncture in in vitro fertilization: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials to see whether acupuncture during IVF improves the chance of a clinical pregnancy. When acupuncture was given only around the time of embryo transfer, it did not significantly improve pregnancy rates, whether compared with no acupuncture or with sham (fake) acupuncture. Some benefit was seen in a few specific timing patterns, such as during the follicle phase plus around transfer, or 30 minutes after transfer and in the implantation phase. The abstract does not rate the certainty of the evidence.
keyPoints: Acupuncture given only at the time of embryo transfer did not significantly improve IVF clinical pregnancy rates.
There was no clear difference when acupuncture was compared with sham acupuncture around embryo transfer.
A pooled benefit was found when acupuncture was given at the follicle phase and 25 minutes before and after transfer (RR 1.56).
A pooled benefit was also found when given 30 minutes after transfer and in the implantation phase (RR 1.76).

items.title: Psychological adjustment in adolescents conceived by assisted reproduction techniques: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 17 studies of teenagers (aged 11 to 18) who were conceived through assisted reproduction such as IVF, egg donation or donor insemination. Compared with naturally conceived teenagers, they seemed to be equally well adjusted and to have positive relationships with their parents. Some small differences depended on the type of treatment, and the authors note that small studies and low rates of telling teens about their conception limit how far the findings can be applied.
keyPoints: Teenagers conceived by IVF, egg donation or donor insemination seemed as well adjusted as naturally conceived teenagers.
Parent-teen relationships were positive in families created through assisted reproduction.
With donor insemination, the sex of the parent and child, and when and how the teen was told about their conception, affected parent-teen relationships.
Studies were small, often involved single births, and many teens had not been told how they were conceived, so results may not apply to everyone.

items.title: ESHRE guideline: ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI: an update in 2025†
items.summary: This is the 2025 update of the ESHRE guideline on ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI. It gives 121 recommendations on every step of stimulation, from pre-treatment checks to preventing a complication called ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), and also covers fertility preservation and egg freezing. The authors say much of the evidence behind the recommendations is of low or very low quality, and several newer treatments are not well studied yet.
keyPoints: The guideline covers pre-stimulation evaluation, pituitary suppression and stimulation, monitoring, triggering egg maturation, luteal support and OHSS prevention.
It includes 17 recommendations on fertility preservation, including elective egg freezing and egg donation.
Of the evidence-based recommendations, none rested on high-quality evidence, 6 on moderate, 36 on low and 148 on very low-quality evidence.
For several newer treatments the evidence was too limited, so the guideline advises against them or says they should only be used in research.

items.title: Approaches to frozen embryo transfer: a Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society guideline
items.summary: This Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society guideline reviewed recent randomized trials on how frozen embryo transfers (FET) are done during IVF. Freezing all embryos can help prevent a complication called ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, but the evidence does not show it improves live birth rates or pregnancy outcomes for most people having IVF. Using your own ovulation or an artificial (medicated) cycle for the transfer gave similar live birth and pregnancy loss results. The guideline says the approach should be tailored to each person.
keyPoints: Freeze-all cycles in Canada rose from 24.0% to 78.4% over the last decade.

A freeze-all strategy helps prevent ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, but routine use is not supported for better live birth rates, fewer pregnancy losses or better obstetric outcomes in the general IVF population.
Ovulatory FET cycles offer no advantage over artificial FET cycles for live birth or pregnancy loss, and evidence on obstetric and perinatal outcomes is conflicting.
The route of progesterone given in artificial FET cycles does not significantly change live birth or pregnancy loss rates.

items.title: Hydrosalpinx treatment before in-vitro fertilization: systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from nine randomized trials (plus 17 observational studies) on treating hydrosalpinx, a fluid-filled blocked fallopian tube, before IVF embryo transfer. No treatment was shown to clearly improve live birth rates compared with the others or with no treatment. Removing the tube (salpingectomy), blocking it (laparoscopic tubal occlusion) or draining it with ultrasound-guided aspiration did raise ongoing or clinical pregnancy rates compared with no treatment. Sclerotherapy looked helpful in the wider analysis that included observational studies.
keyPoints: No hydrosalpinx treatment was shown to improve live birth rate after IVF in the trial-only analysis.
Salpingectomy and ultrasound-guided aspiration increased ongoing pregnancy rates compared with no treatment.
Salpingectomy and laparoscopic tubal occlusion increased clinical pregnancy rates compared with no treatment.
In the wider analysis, sclerotherapy may be an effective alternative to standard laparoscopic surgery, with a favorable safety profile.

items.title: In vitro maturation in subfertile women with polycystic ovarian syndrome undergoing assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review compared in vitro maturation (IVM), where eggs are collected early and matured in the lab, with standard IVF or ICSI in women with PCOS. It found four trials with 810 women. IVM greatly lowered the risk of moderate or severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) but raised the chance of miscarriage in pregnancies that were confirmed. The effect on live birth and pregnancy rates is very uncertain.
keyPoints: IVM greatly reduced moderate or severe OHSS compared with standard IVF (high-certainty evidence); about 3.5% with IVF versus roughly 0% to 2.4% with IVM.
IVM increased miscarriage per clinical pregnancy compared with IVF (high-certainty evidence); about 20.1% with IVF versus roughly 20.4% to 40.4% with IVM.
The effect on live birth and clinical pregnancy is very uncertain (very low-certainty evidence).
There was probably little to no difference in preterm birth, and the effect on birth defects was uncertain (low-certainty evidence).

items.title: ESHRE guideline: number of embryos to transfer during IVF/ICSI†
items.summary: This European guideline looked at when it might make sense to transfer two embryos instead of one during IVF or ICSI. It found that no single clinical or embryo factor on its own justifies choosing a double embryo transfer over an elective single embryo transfer. Double transfer raises the chance of twins or more, which brings higher risks such as preterm birth and low birthweight. Much of the evidence behind the recommendations is low or very low quality, so the guideline also lists areas that need more research.
keyPoints: No clinical or embryological factor alone justifies a double embryo transfer instead of an elective single embryo transfer.
Double embryo transfer is linked to more multiple pregnancies, which raises the risk of preterm birth, low birthweight and other problems for mother and babies.
Single embryo transfer is the approach preferred by international and national professional organisations to reduce these risks.
Of the evidence-based recommendations, 28% rest on moderate-quality evidence and the rest on low (12%) or very low-quality (60%) evidence.

items.title: The use of preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy: a committee opinion
items.summary: This committee opinion looks at preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A), a test that checks embryos for the wrong number of chromosomes during IVF. The committee says the value of PGT-A as a routine test for everyone having IVF has not been shown. Recent large randomized trials found that pregnancy outcomes after frozen embryo transfer were similar with or without PGT-A. Whether it lowers the chance of miscarriage is still unclear, and the studies have important limitations.
keyPoints: The value of PGT-A as a routine screening test for all IVF patients has not been demonstrated.
Some earlier single-center studies reported higher live-birth rates after PGT-A in patients with a favorable outlook.
Recent multicenter randomized trials in women with available blastocysts found similar overall pregnancy outcomes with frozen embryo transfer, with or without PGT-A.
Whether PGT-A reduces the risk of clinical miscarriage is unclear, and the studies have important limitations.

items.title: Oocyte activation for women following intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI)
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at artificial oocyte activation (AOA), an extra lab step sometimes used during ICSI to help eggs fertilise. It included 20 trials, but the main findings came from four trials with 743 women, and only one trial with 343 women met the review's quality standard. The evidence is very uncertain about whether AOA improves live birth or changes miscarriage rates. For couples with a past history of low or no fertilisation, AOA may help live birth rates, but this evidence is low certainty.
keyPoints: Overall, the evidence is very uncertain about AOA's effect on live birth and miscarriage in women having ICSI.
In couples with a history of low or no fertilisation, AOA may increase live birth rates with little or no difference in miscarriage, based on low-certainty evidence.
None of the trials reported birth defects, so short- and long-term safety data are lacking.
Chemical AOA methods varied a lot between trials, so results should be interpreted with caution.

items.title: Efficacy of atosiban for repeated embryo implantation failure: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled seven studies of women who had repeated embryo implantation failure during IVF and compared those given atosiban around embryo transfer with those who were not. Atosiban was linked to a higher clinical pregnancy rate, and this held across study types and for women with 2 or with 3 previous failed transfers. Rates of ectopic pregnancy, multiple pregnancy and miscarriage were not clearly different. Only two of the studies were randomized trials, so the authors say larger, better-designed trials are needed to confirm the result.
keyPoints: Atosiban was linked to a higher clinical pregnancy rate in women with repeated implantation failure (RR 1.54).
The benefit appeared in randomized trials, cohort studies, and in women with 2 or 3 previous failed transfers.
Ectopic pregnancy, multiple pregnancy and miscarriage rates did not differ significantly between groups.
Most included studies were not randomized trials, and larger well-designed trials are needed to confirm the finding.

items.title: Impact of FIGO type 3 uterine fibroids on in vitro fertilization outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies of 1020 women having IVF, comparing 324 women with FIGO type 3 fibroids (fibroids that touch the inner lining of the womb but sit in the muscle wall) with 696 women without fibroids. Women with untreated type 3 fibroids had lower live birth, pregnancy and implantation rates. The effect looked worse with larger and more numerous fibroids. The review could not say whether removing these fibroids by surgery improves IVF results.
keyPoints: Women with untreated FIGO type 3 fibroids had lower live birth rates than women without fibroids.
Clinical pregnancy and implantation rates were also lower in women with these fibroids.
Larger fibroids and a higher number of fibroids were linked to worse IVF outcomes.
No firm conclusions could be drawn about whether surgery for these fibroids helps IVF outcomes.

items.title: Endometrial scratching in women undergoing IVF/ICSI: an individual participant data meta-analysis
items.summary: This study pooled the original data from 13 trials (4,112 women) to see whether endometrial scratching, a small procedure that gently scratches the womb lining before IVF/ICSI, improves the chance of a live birth. Overall, scratching may improve live birth rates, but the benefit was modest and several analyses were borderline. No particular group of women, by age, past failed transfers, treatment type or cause of infertility, was found to benefit more or less. The authors say it should be used with caution and that patients should be counselled about the uncertainties.
keyPoints: Live birth was more likely with scratching than with no scratch or a sham procedure (odds ratio 1.29, 95% CI 1.02-1.64).
Some other analyses gave similar results, but a few had ranges that included no effect.
No subgroup (age, number of previous failed embryo transfers, treatment type, infertility cause) was found to benefit more or less.
Patients should be counselled on the level of evidence and the uncertainties, and the timing of the scratch may matter.

items.title: TEAS, DHEA, CoQ10, and GH for poor ovarian response undergoing IVF-ET: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 randomized trials (2,323 women) of women with poor ovarian response having IVF. It compared add-on treatments (CoQ10, DHEA, growth hormone and TEAS, a type of electrical acupoint stimulation) with standard ovarian stimulation alone. CoQ10 and DHEA were linked to higher pregnancy rates, and CoQ10 ranked best for live birth. The authors say larger trials that compare the treatments directly are still needed to confirm this.
keyPoints: CoQ10 and DHEA improved clinical pregnancy rates compared with standard stimulation alone.
CoQ10 ranked best for live birth rate; DHEA improved embryo implantation, embryo quality and number of eggs retrieved.
Growth hormone ranked second for some outcomes, and TEAS was the least effective of the four add-ons.
Several of the add-ons did not clearly reduce the chance of an IVF cycle being cancelled.

items.title: Efficacy of progestin-primed ovarian stimulation in women with polycystic ovary syndrome undergoing in vitro fertilization: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine studies (3 randomised trials and 6 cohort studies, 2,289 women) comparing progestin-primed ovarian stimulation (PPOS) with standard GnRH analogue protocols for women with PCOS having IVF or ICSI. The trials found no clear difference in the risk of moderate or severe OHSS, the number of mature eggs, or live birth rates. The certainty of the evidence was generally low. The authors say PPOS could still be a practical, patient-friendly option, especially when embryos will be frozen and transferred later.
keyPoints: No significant difference in OHSS risk, mature egg numbers or live birth rate between PPOS and GnRH analogue protocols in the randomised trials.
In cohort studies, PPOS needed a higher dose of gonadotropin and tended to improve implantation and pregnancy rates.
There is currently no evidence that PPOS lowers OHSS risk or improves pregnancy outcomes in women with PCOS.
PPOS may be a viable alternative, especially when frozen-thawed embryo transfer is planned; better trials and long-term safety data on children are still needed.

items.title: Overweight, obesity and assisted reproduction: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 53 studies covering more than 1.4 million fertility treatment cycles (IVF or ICSI). It looked at how being overweight or having obesity relates to treatment outcomes. A higher body mass index was linked to weak negative effects on pregnancy, live birth and miscarriage rates. The authors say more robust studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Being overweight or obese had a weak negative link with clinical pregnancy and live birth rates after IVF or ICSI.
A higher body mass index was also weakly linked to higher miscarriage rates, fewer mature eggs, longer ovarian stimulation and higher gonadotropin doses.
The review included 53 studies of generally good quality with low or moderate heterogeneity.
The authors say more robust studies are needed to understand other aspects of exposure and outcomes.

items.title: The role of assisted hatching in in vitro fertilization: a guideline
items.summary: This guideline from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine looked at assisted hatching, a lab step in IVF where a small opening is made in the outer shell of an embryo before transfer. It found moderate evidence that this step does not meaningfully raise live birth rates in fresh IVF cycles. There is not enough evidence to say whether it helps people with a poor outlook or those having frozen embryo transfers.
keyPoints: Moderate evidence shows assisted hatching does not significantly improve live birth rates in fresh IVF cycles.
Evidence is insufficient to show a benefit for patients with a poor prognosis.
Evidence is also insufficient to show a benefit in frozen embryo transfer cycles.
This guideline replaces the 2014 version.

items.title: Follicular flushing during oocyte retrieval in assisted reproductive techniques
items.summary: This review looked at whether flushing the follicles with fluid during egg collection for IVF gives better results than simply drawing the fluid out. It combined 15 trials with 1643 women. The review could not show that flushing changes the chance of a live birth or miscarriage. Flushing may make the egg collection take a little longer, and there was not enough evidence to judge safety.
keyPoints: It is uncertain whether flushing follicles changes the live birth rate compared with aspiration alone (moderate-certainty evidence).
It is also uncertain whether flushing changes miscarriage rate, number of eggs, number of embryos or clinical pregnancy rate (low to very low certainty).
The egg retrieval procedure may take longer with flushing.
There was not enough evidence to draw firm conclusions about adverse events or safety.

items.title: Assisted hatching on assisted conception (in vitro fertilisation (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI))
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 39 trials (7,249 women) of assisted hatching, where the outer shell of an embryo is thinned or opened before it is placed back during IVF or ICSI. It is not clear whether assisted hatching increases the chance of a live birth. It may slightly raise the chance of a multiple pregnancy (such as twins). The quality of the evidence was low to very low, so the findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: Researchers are uncertain whether assisted hatching improves live birth rates compared with no assisted hatching (low-quality evidence).
Assisted hatching may slightly increase the chance of a multiple pregnancy, from about 9% to between 10% and 14%.
Clinical pregnancy rates may be slightly higher with assisted hatching overall, but the data quality was low and results varied between studies.
It is uncertain whether assisted hatching affects miscarriage rates (very low-quality evidence).

items.title: Monitoring of stimulated cycles in assisted reproduction (IVF and ICSI)
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at two ways of monitoring the ovaries during IVF or ICSI stimulation: vaginal ultrasound alone, or ultrasound plus blood tests for estradiol. Six trials with 781 women found no clear difference in pregnancy rates, number of eggs collected, or ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS). None of the trials measured live birth. The evidence was low quality, so the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Ultrasound-only monitoring was not shown to be better or worse than ultrasound plus estradiol blood tests for clinical pregnancy or OHSS.
The number of eggs collected looked similar with both monitoring methods.
None of the six trials reported live birth rates.
All the evidence was low quality, and the authors suggest the choice may depend on convenience and cost.

items.title: PGT-A: who and when? Α systematic review and network meta-analysis of RCTs
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review pooled 11 randomized trials of PGT-A, a test that checks embryos for the wrong number of chromosomes before transfer in IVF. For the general IVF population, it did not raise the chance of a live birth per patient, though it did lower miscarriage rates. Live births improved only in women over 35, and only when the test was done on day-5 (blastocyst-stage) embryos. It did not appear to help younger women.
keyPoints: PGT-A did not improve live-birth rates per patient in the general IVF population.
PGT-A lowered the miscarriage rate in the general population.
In women over 35, PGT-A improved live-birth rates; in younger women it appeared ineffective.
Only day-5 (blastocyst-stage) biopsy showed improved live-birth rates per embryo transfer.

items.title: Evidence-based outcomes after oocyte cryopreservation for donor oocyte in vitro fertilization and planned oocyte cryopreservation: a guideline
items.summary: This American Society for Reproductive Medicine guideline reviewed 30 studies on freezing eggs, both for planned (elective) egg freezing and for donor egg IVF. There is not enough evidence to predict how likely a live birth is after planned egg freezing. Limited data suggest that freezing eggs at a younger age gives better chances of ongoing pregnancy and live birth than freezing at an older age. Babies born from frozen eggs appear to have similar health outcomes to babies born from fresh eggs.
keyPoints: There is insufficient evidence to predict live birth rates after planned egg freezing.
On limited data, ongoing and live birth rates appear better when eggs are frozen at a younger age than at an older age.
Pregnancy rates per embryo transfer were not significantly different with frozen versus fresh donor eggs, but there is not enough evidence to say live birth rates are the same.
Neonatal outcomes appear similar with frozen and fresh eggs; more studies of cumulative live birth rates are needed.

items.title: Progestin-Primed Ovarian Stimulation Protocol for Patients in Assisted Reproductive Technology: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of progestin-primed ovarian stimulation (PPOS), an IVF protocol that uses progesterone-type medicine instead of the usual drugs to stop an early egg-release hormone surge. Pregnancy and live birth rates were not different from the standard protocols. PPOS was linked to a lower rate of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), and to more eggs and usable embryos in women with both low and normal ovarian reserve. The authors say larger trials are needed to confirm these results.
keyPoints: Clinical pregnancy and live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates with PPOS were not different from standard protocols.
PPOS was linked to a lower rate of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).
In women with diminished ovarian reserve, PPOS had a lower rate of premature LH surge.
More eggs, mature eggs and viable embryos were seen with PPOS in women with low and normal ovarian reserve; larger trials are needed to confirm this.

items.title: Metformin treatment before and during IVF or ICSI in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 13 trials (1,132 women with polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS) to see whether taking metformin before and during IVF or ICSI helps. It found no clear evidence that metformin improves the chance of a live birth. Metformin may lower the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) but may cause more side effects. The evidence was low or very low quality, so the results are uncertain.
keyPoints: No conclusive evidence that metformin improves live birth rates; with a long GnRH-agonist protocol the effect on live births is uncertain, and one small trial using a short GnRH-antagonist protocol suggested metformin may lower live births.
Metformin may reduce the risk of OHSS (for example, from about 20% to roughly 6-14%).
With a long GnRH-agonist protocol, metformin may increase the clinical pregnancy rate, but the effect on miscarriage is uncertain.
Metformin may cause more side effects than placebo or no treatment.

items.title: Conventional and modern markers of endometrial receptivity: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 163 studies of 88,834 women to see whether tests of the womb lining (the endometrium) can predict who will get pregnant. Things like lining thickness, ultrasound pattern and blood flow were linked to pregnancy, but none could predict it well enough to be used in routine care. Some newer molecular tests look promising, but more data are needed.
keyPoints: Lining thickness, ultrasound pattern, blood flow measures and some molecules were linked to clinical pregnancy.
These markers were poor at predicting who would get pregnant, so they are not recommended for clinical use yet.
Some modern molecular tests look promising, and further data are awaited.
The results may help manage couples' expectations during IUI and IVF.

items.title: Glucocorticoid supplementation during ovarian stimulation for IVF or ICSI
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether taking steroid medicines called glucocorticoids during ovarian stimulation for IVF or ICSI helps women have a baby. Only four small trials were found, and results from just two (310 women) could be used. There was not enough evidence to say whether the steroids make any difference to live birth rates, and the quality of the evidence was low or very low.
keyPoints: It is unclear whether glucocorticoids given during ovarian stimulation improve live birth rates; the evidence was low quality.
Steroids may possibly raise the clinical pregnancy rate, but the result was not conclusive.
Neither usable trial reported on ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) or side-effects, so safety is unclear.
The review concluded that more research is needed.

items.title: Volume expanders for the prevention of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
items.summary: This review looked at nine trials (1867 women) testing fluids called volume expanders (albumin, HES and mannitol) to prevent ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), a serious complication of fertility treatment, in women at high risk. All three fluids appeared to lower rates of moderate or severe OHSS, but the evidence was low to very low quality. Albumin also seemed to lower pregnancy rates, while HES and mannitol showed no clear effect on pregnancy. The authors say larger trials are needed before these treatments are used routinely.
keyPoints: Albumin, HES and mannitol were each linked to fewer cases of moderate or severe OHSS in high-risk women.
Albumin appeared to reduce pregnancy rates, for example from about 40% to about 32% in one estimate.
HES and mannitol showed no clear effect on pregnancy rates, but this rests on very few trials.
No studies reported live birth, and side effects were too poorly reported to draw firm conclusions.

items.title: Acute pain management after vaginal delivery with perineal tears or episiotomy
items.summary: This review looked at 79 studies on how to ease pain after a vaginal birth with a perineal tear or an episiotomy (a cut made to widen the birth opening). The authors judged the evidence to be of good quality. They recommend paracetamol (acetaminophen), anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) and ice or cold packs as the main first steps. Some other options, such as numbing creams and injections, did not have enough evidence to recommend.
keyPoints: Acetaminophen and NSAIDs are recommended as first-line pain treatment, along with ice or chemical cold packs.
Epidural morphine (2 mg or less) is suggested only for women who had a labour epidural and a severe tear, with breathing monitored.
Local anaesthetic infiltration, numbing creams or sprays, ointments and pudendal nerve block are not recommended because evidence is lacking or insufficient.

For stitches, a continuous suture is recommended over interrupted stitches for episiotomy or second-degree tears when pain is the outcome, and for first- or second-degree tears, no stitches or glue may be better for pain than suturing.

items.title: Care of late intrauterine fetal death and stillbirth: Green-top Guideline No. 55
items.source: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
items.organisation: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
items.summary: This is a UK guideline on caring for women and families when a baby dies in the womb late in pregnancy. It recommends that most women are offered a medicine-assisted induction of labour and a vaginal birth, with caesarean birth considered for some. It also covers tests to find out why the baby died and the importance of emotional support and informed choice. Some advice, such as medicine doses for women with previous caesareans, rests on limited evidence.
keyPoints: A combination of mifepristone and a prostaglandin medicine (misoprostol) is usually recommended first to induce labour.
Vaginal birth is recommended for most women, but caesarean birth may need to be considered for some; parents should have a detailed discussion of both the physical and emotional sides of each option.
With full investigation, including postmortem and placenta examination, a possible or probable cause can be found in up to three-quarters of late stillbirths.

There is not enough evidence to recommend a specific misoprostol regimen after 28 weeks for women with a previous caesarean or uterine scar, and for women with more than two caesareans or atypical scars the safety of induction is unknown.

items.title: Global and regional causes of maternal deaths 2009-20: a WHO systematic analysis
