items.summary: This WHO review looked at what causes women to die during pregnancy, birth and the weeks after, using data from 2009-20 around the world. The most common cause was severe bleeding (haemorrhage), followed by existing health problems made worse by pregnancy and high blood pressure disorders. Most deaths from bleeding and infection happened after the baby was born. The authors say effective treatments exist, so better access to quality care is the key need.
keyPoints: Worldwide, severe bleeding was the leading cause of maternal death (27%), followed by indirect causes (23%) and high blood pressure disorders (16%).
Bleeding deaths were most common in sub-Saharan Africa and in Western Asia and Northern Africa; high blood pressure deaths were highest in Latin America and the Caribbean.
Most deaths from bleeding and infection (sepsis) happened in the postpartum period, so care after birth matters as well as care during labour.
Data on maternal suicide and deaths after 42 days postpartum were very limited, with only 12 countries recording any maternal suicides.

items.title: Effectiveness of breathing exercise on the duration of labour: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together trials that tested whether breathing exercises change how long labour lasts. It included 1418 women and found that those who did breathing exercises had a shorter second stage of labour (the pushing stage) than those who did not. The authors describe breathing exercises as a helpful way to shorten this stage. The abstract does not rate the overall certainty of the evidence.
keyPoints: Breathing exercises shortened the second stage of labour compared with no breathing exercises.
The review combined trials with 1418 participants in total, with an average of about 38.9 weeks of pregnancy.
The authors conclude breathing exercises are a beneficial preventive step for shortening second stage labour.
Other outcomes such as anxiety, pain duration, episiotomy and mode of birth were also looked at, but the abstract reports no results for them.

items.title: Comparison of Maternal Labor-Related Complications and Neonatal Outcomes Following Elective Induction of Labor at 39 Weeks of Gestation vs Expectant Management: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies covering about 1.6 million women with a single baby to compare planned induction of labour at 39 weeks with waiting for labour to start naturally. Induction was linked to fewer serious tears, fewer assisted vaginal births, fewer very large babies and fewer low newborn Apgar scores. Among women who had given birth before, it was also linked to fewer emergency caesareans. Among first-time mothers, induction was linked to a slightly higher chance of shoulder dystocia, where the baby's shoulder gets stuck during birth.
keyPoints: Induction at 39 weeks was linked to 37% lower odds of third- or fourth-degree perineal tears.
It was also linked to fewer assisted vaginal births, fewer babies with macrosomia (very large babies) and fewer low 5-minute Apgar scores.
In women who had given birth before, induction was linked to fewer emergency caesarean sections.
In first-time mothers, induction was linked to higher odds of shoulder dystocia, so the authors suggest discussing this risk.

items.title: The Effects of Music-Based Interventions for Pain and Anxiety Management during Vaginal Labour and Caesarean Delivery: A Systematic Review and Narrative Synthesis of Randomised Controlled Trials
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review looked at 28 randomised trials (2,835 women) testing whether listening to music eases pain and anxiety during vaginal birth and caesarean delivery. Most, but not all, of the trials found less pain and anxiety with music. It seemed to help most with light to moderate pain and anxiety, particularly when women chose their own music, or when it was relaxing instrumental music or used alongside another therapy. The long-term effects are not clear.
keyPoints: Most, but not all, trials found music reduced pain and anxiety during vaginal birth and caesarean delivery.
Music was especially useful for light to moderate pain and anxiety.
Helpful approaches included music chosen by the woman, relaxing or instrumental music, and music combined with another therapy or a wider care plan.
The long-term effects of music-based interventions are unclear.

items.title: Birthing ball for reducing labor pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled seven randomized trials with 533 women to see whether sitting and moving on a birthing ball (an exercise ball) eases pain in labour. Women who used a birthing ball reported pain about 1.7 points lower than women who did not. Using the ball made no clear difference to the type of birth (vaginal, assisted or caesarean) or to perineal tears. The authors concluded it is an effective way to reduce pain for women labouring without an epidural.
keyPoints: Labour pain was 1.70 points lower with a birthing ball than without (95% CI -2.20 to -1.20).
No significant difference in spontaneous vaginal birth, assisted vaginal birth, caesarean birth or perineal tears.
The findings apply to women labouring without an epidural, with a single baby head-down.
The authors conclude the birthing ball is an effective pain-reduction method in labour.

items.title: Aromatherapy intervention on anxiety and pain during first stage labour in nulliparous women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together nine randomised trials that tested aromatherapy (scented essential oils) as extra support for pain and anxiety during the first stage of labour. The combined results suggested aromatherapy lowered both pain and anxiety. The authors describe the evidence as more credible than before, though the abstract does not give a formal certainty rating.
keyPoints: Nine randomised trials were included in the review.
Aromatherapy significantly reduced pain and anxiety in the first stage of labour.
Pain was lower in both the early active and late active phases of labour.
The authors note earlier evidence for non-drug pain relief was limited by a lack of high quality studies.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of non-pharmacological interventions for labour pain management: A systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 43 studies of nine non-drug ways to ease pain in labour. Acupressure, aromatherapy and massage lowered labour pain scores compared with usual care or placebo, with aromatherapy ranking highest. Yoga and acupressure were linked to shorter labour stages, and the methods did not change newborn Apgar scores or the use of pain medicines. The authors say these methods look effective and safe for low-risk pregnant women, but better-designed studies are still needed to confirm this.
keyPoints: Acupressure, aromatherapy and massage significantly reduced labour pain, with aromatherapy ranking as the most effective.
Yoga was linked to a shorter first stage of labour and acupressure to a shorter second stage.
No significant differences were found in newborn 5-minute Apgar scores or in the use of pharmacological pain relief compared with usual care or placebo.
The authors suggest choosing these options according to the woman's own preferences and values.

items.title: Low-dose oral misoprostol for induction of labour
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 61 trials (over 20,000 women) on low-dose misoprostol tablets taken by mouth to start labour. Compared with other induction methods, it was probably linked to fewer caesarean births, though it may take longer, so fewer women gave birth within 24 hours. It also seemed to cause less over-strong contraction with changes in the baby's heart rate than vaginal misoprostol or vaginal dinoprostone. The certainty of the evidence ranged from moderate to very low, and the authors say more trials are needed to find the best regimen.
keyPoints: Compared with vaginal dinoprostone, oral low-dose misoprostol probably led to fewer caesarean sections and less hyperstimulation with baby heart rate changes (moderate to low certainty).
Fewer women gave birth within 24 hours with oral misoprostol than with dinoprostone or vaginal misoprostol, so labour may take longer (low certainty).
Compared with a Foley catheter or intravenous oxytocin, oral misoprostol probably led to fewer caesarean sections (moderate certainty).
The authors suggest a starting dose of 25 µg may balance effectiveness and safety, but the best regimen still needs more trials.

items.title: Interventions for fear of childbirth including tocophobia
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at seven trials (1357 women) testing non-drug approaches such as education, cognitive behavioural therapy, group discussion, peer education and art therapy for high or severe fear of childbirth, including tocophobia. These approaches may lower fear scores slightly, but the drop may be too small to make a real difference. They probably reduce caesarean births and the number of women preferring a caesarean, and made little or no difference to depression scores. The evidence is limited, so the effect on fear itself is uncertain.
keyPoints: Non-drug interventions may reduce fear of childbirth scores, but the reduction may not be clinically meaningful (low-certainty evidence).
They probably reduce the number of women having a caesarean section (moderate-certainty evidence).
They probably mean fewer women prefer a caesarean birth (moderate-certainty evidence).
There may be little or no difference in depression scores, and epidural use may increase slightly (low-certainty evidence).

items.title: Acupuncture or acupressure for pain management during labour
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 28 trials with 3960 women to see whether acupuncture or acupressure helps with pain in labour. Compared with sham (fake) acupuncture, real acupuncture may increase satisfaction with pain relief and probably reduces the use of pain-relief medicines, though it may make little difference to how strong the pain feels. Acupressure may slightly reduce pain compared with other comparison groups. For many other comparisons the evidence was very low quality, so the effects are uncertain.
keyPoints: Acupuncture versus sham acupuncture: it may make little or no difference to pain intensity, but may increase satisfaction with pain relief (moderate-certainty) and probably reduces use of pain-relief medicines (moderate-certainty).

Acupressure probably slightly reduces labour pain compared with a combined control group (moderate-certainty), and probably lowers the caesarean rate compared with a sham control (moderate-certainty).
Acupuncture may have little to no effect on caesarean or assisted vaginal birth rates.
For many comparisons the evidence was very low certainty, and no trial was at low risk of bias on all domains; the authors call for better research.

items.title: Induction of labour at or beyond 37 weeks' gestation
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 34 trials (over 21,000 women and babies) comparing a policy of inducing labour at or after 37 weeks with waiting for labour to start naturally. All women had low-risk pregnancies. Induction was linked to fewer baby deaths around the time of birth, fewer stillbirths, fewer NICU admissions and probably slightly fewer caesarean births. The overall chance of a baby dying was small either way (about 0.4 versus 3 per 1000).
keyPoints: Induction was linked to fewer deaths around birth (0.4 versus 3 per 1000) and fewer stillbirths, with high-certainty evidence.
Caesarean births were probably slightly fewer with induction, and operative vaginal births (forceps or vacuum) were probably no different.
NICU admissions were lower with induction; postpartum bleeding and breastfeeding at discharge probably made little or no difference.
The best timing for induction still needs more research, and tailored counselling may help women choose between induction and waiting, especially beyond 41 weeks.

items.title: The Effectiveness of Aromatherapy in the Management of Labor Pain and Anxiety: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 33 studies on using aromatherapy (scented essential oils) during labour. The oils were used in different ways, such as breathing them in, massage, footbaths, birthing pools and compresses, and lavender was the most common. Most of the studies found that aromatherapy reduced labour pain and anxiety. The authors conclude it may help as a complementary option alongside usual care.
keyPoints: 33 studies were included, most of them from Iran.
Aromatherapy was given by inhalation, massage, footbath, birthing pool, acupressure or compress.
Lavender was the most commonly used essential oil (13 studies).
Most studies found less labour pain and anxiety with aromatherapy.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 209: Obstetric Analgesia and Anesthesia
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) about pain relief and anesthesia during labor and delivery. It states that labor causes severe pain for many women, and that a woman's request for pain relief is a sufficient medical reason to provide it when there is no medical reason against it. It also says access to pain relief such as an epidural should not depend on a woman's health insurance or ability to pay.
keyPoints: Unless there is a medical reason not to, a woman's own request is enough of a reason to receive pain relief in labor.
A woman who asks for an epidural should not be denied it because of her health insurance status, and the methods a hospital offers should not depend on ability to pay.
Anesthesia services should be available to provide labor pain relief and surgical anesthesia in all hospitals that offer maternity care.
Trained labor nurses, under appropriate physician supervision, can help manage epidural pain relief so more women can benefit.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 212: Pregnancy and Heart Disease
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists looks at heart disease in pregnancy and the weeks after birth. In the United States, heart and blood vessel disease is now the leading cause of death in pregnant and postpartum women, and rates are higher in nonwhite and lower-income women. The guideline explains how to spot heart risk factors early, how to care for women with heart disease during and after pregnancy, and how to plan care between pregnancies.
keyPoints: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in pregnant and postpartum women in the US, and accounts for 26.5% of pregnancy-related deaths.
Nonwhite and lower-income women have higher rates of illness and death from heart disease in pregnancy.
Contributing factors include missed chances to find heart risk factors during prenatal care and delays in recognising heart symptoms after birth.
The guideline covers risk checks before and after pregnancy, care for women with existing or new heart disease, and a care plan between pregnancies.

items.title: Women's experiences of pharmacological and non-pharmacological pain relief methods for labour and childbirth: a qualitative systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 24 studies of what women said about pain relief in labour, including epidurals, opioid pain medicines, relaxation and massage. Women had mixed experiences with every method. Medicines such as epidurals can reduce pain but may cause side-effects, while relaxation and massage may not reduce pain much but can help women feel supported and connected to their birth companions and midwives. The studies were all from high- and upper-middle-income countries.
keyPoints: Women report mixed experiences of different labour pain relief methods.
Pharmacological methods (such as epidural and opioids) can reduce pain but have negative side-effects.
Non-pharmacological methods (such as relaxation and massage) may not reduce labour pain but can help bonding with professionals and birth supporters.
Women need information on the risks and benefits of all available pain relief methods.

items.title: Massage, reflexology and other manual methods for pain management in labour
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 14 trials of hands-on methods such as massage and warm packs for easing pain during labour. Massage appeared to lower pain during the first stage of labour compared with usual care, and warm or thermal packs may also help with pain and labour length. However, the quality of the evidence was low to very low, and few trials looked at safety, so the results are uncertain.
keyPoints: Massage reduced self-reported pain in the first stage of labour compared with usual care (low-quality evidence from six trials).
Massage showed no clear difference in labour length, use of pain medicine, assisted vaginal birth or caesarean section (very low-quality evidence).
Single trials found massage gave women a greater sense of control and less anxiety, and two trials found more satisfaction with birth.
Warm packs and thermal methods may reduce pain and shorten labour, but the evidence was very low quality; no trials of reflexology were found.

items.title: Relaxation techniques for pain management in labour
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 19 trials (2,519 women) of relaxation methods such as relaxation, yoga, music and mindfulness for pain in labour. Relaxation, yoga and music may reduce pain and increase satisfaction with pain relief, but the evidence was low to very low quality, so the results should be treated with caution. There was not enough evidence to say whether mindfulness or audio analgesia help. Most trials did not report on safety.
keyPoints: Relaxation lowered pain intensity in early (latent) labour, but showed no clear difference in pain during active labour.
Yoga and music may reduce pain, and yoga was linked to greater satisfaction with pain relief and childbirth experience, based on low-quality evidence from small numbers of trials.
No clear effect was seen on assisted vaginal birth or caesarean rates, and most trials did not report on safety.
Evidence for mindfulness and audio analgesia was too limited to draw conclusions.

items.title: Immersion in water during labour and birth
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 15 trials (3,663 healthy, low-risk women) to see what happens when women spend time in a bath or pool during labour or birth. Being in water during the first stage of labour probably makes little difference to the type of birth or to serious perineal tears, and may slightly reduce the use of epidurals or similar regional pain relief. The review found no evidence of extra harm to mothers or babies, but the evidence for the second stage and for rare outcomes is limited and mostly low quality. No trial took place in a midwife-led setting.
keyPoints: Water immersion in the first stage of labour probably makes little or no difference to spontaneous vaginal birth, instrumental birth or caesarean section.
Fewer women who used water needed regional analgesia (about 39% versus 43%), based on moderate-quality evidence.
Rates of third- or fourth-degree tears were similar with and without immersion, and the review found no evidence of increased harm to women or babies.
Evidence on the second stage of labour, newborn infection, intensive care admission and early versus late entry into water was too limited to show clear differences.

items.title: Epidural versus non-epidural or no analgesia for pain management in labour
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 40 trials with over 11,000 women to compare epidural pain relief in labour with other options, mostly opioid injections. Epidurals gave better pain relief and higher satisfaction, though the evidence for this was low quality. Epidurals probably did not change caesarean rates or long-term backache, and there was no clear effect on babies' Apgar scores or neonatal intensive care admissions. Epidurals were linked to more low blood pressure, fever, difficulty passing urine and longer labours.
keyPoints: Epidural analgesia may reduce labour pain more than opioids and more women rated their pain relief as excellent or very good (low-quality evidence).
Assisted vaginal birth may have been more common with epidurals overall, but this difference was not seen in trials done after 2005.
No difference was found in caesarean section rates or long-term backache, and no clear differences in Apgar scores or neonatal intensive care admission.
Epidurals were linked to more low blood pressure, fever, urinary retention and longer labours, but less nausea, vomiting and breathing depression than opioids.

items.title: WHO recommendations: Intrapartum care for a positive childbirth experience
items.summary: The World Health Organization (WHO) brought together new and existing recommendations on care during labour and birth into one guideline. When delivered as a package, they are meant to give good-quality, evidence-based care in any setting or level of health service. The guideline puts the woman at the centre and takes a human rights-based approach to make labour and birth a better experience for mothers and babies.
keyPoints: The guideline combines new and existing WHO recommendations on essential care during labour and birth.
It is designed to apply in any country or health care setting, whatever level of services is available.
It stresses woman-centred, holistic, human rights-based care to improve the experience of labour and birth for women and babies.
It is meant to guide national and local health policies and clinical protocols, rather than speak to individual patients directly.

items.title: Labor Induction versus Expectant Management in Low-Risk Nulliparous Women
items.summary: This large trial looked at low-risk women having a first baby. Some were randomly chosen to have labour induced at 39 weeks, and others waited for labour to start on its own. Induction did not significantly reduce the chance of death or serious complications for the baby. It did lead to fewer caesarean births, 18.6% compared with 22.2%.
keyPoints: About 6,100 low-risk first-time mothers were randomly assigned to induction at 39 weeks or to waiting for labour to start naturally.
Serious problems for babies were 4.3% with induction and 5.4% with waiting, which was not a statistically significant difference.
Caesarean delivery was significantly lower with induction (18.6%) than with waiting (22.2%).

items.title: Maternal position in the second stage of labour for women with epidural anaesthesia
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether being upright or lying down (for example on your side or semi-reclined) during the pushing stage of labour changes outcomes for women with an epidural. Across eight trials with 4464 women, there may be little or no difference in the overall chance of caesarean or instrumental birth. When only the most reliable studies were analysed, upright positions led to more operative births and more caesareans, and women were slightly more satisfied in the recumbent group. Many of the other findings were uncertain because the evidence was low or very low quality.
keyPoints: Across all trials, there may be little or no difference in operative birth (caesarean or instrumental) between upright and recumbent positions (low-quality evidence).
In the three studies at lowest risk of bias, upright positions meant about 63 more operative births per 1000 women, including about 25 more caesareans per 1000 (high-quality evidence).
Satisfaction with the childbirth experience was slightly lower in the upright group, and probably fewer babies had low cord pH in the upright group (moderate-quality evidence).
Position probably makes little or no difference to postpartum haemorrhage requiring transfusion (moderate-quality evidence).

items.title: Midwife-led continuity models versus other models of care for childbearing women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 15 trials with over 17,000 women to compare midwife-led continuity care (seeing the same midwife or small team through pregnancy and birth) with other models of care. Women in midwife-led continuity care were less likely to have an epidural or spinal, an instrumental birth (forceps or vacuum), or an episiotomy, and more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth. They were also less likely to have a preterm birth or to lose a baby, and most studies found they were more satisfied with their care. The review found no worse outcomes for women or babies, and the main findings were graded as high quality.
keyPoints: Midwife-led continuity care meant fewer epidurals or spinals (RR 0.85), fewer instrumental births (RR 0.90) and fewer episiotomies (RR 0.84).
Women were slightly more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth (RR 1.05) and more likely to have no pain relief or anaesthesia during labour (RR 1.21).
There were fewer preterm births (RR 0.76) and fewer fetal losses and neonatal deaths overall (RR 0.84); the authors say these findings need further research.

There was no difference in caesarean births, intact perineum, postpartum haemorrhage or breastfeeding initiation; most studies reported higher satisfaction, and labour was about 30 minutes longer on average.

items.title: ASCIA Guideline: Infant Feeding for Food Allergy Prevention
items.summary: The Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy (ASCIA) updated its guideline on feeding babies to help prevent food allergy. It makes 16 recommendations, half based on published evidence and half on expert agreement. The main advice is to start solid foods when a baby shows signs of being ready, and to include well cooked egg and suitable forms of peanut soon after starting.
keyPoints: Start solid foods when the baby shows developmental readiness, usually around 6 months and not before 4 months.
Include well cooked egg and appropriate forms of peanut soon after solids begin, and offer other common allergen foods from the family diet; once introduced, offer them about once a week.
Breastfeeding is encouraged with no changes to the mother's diet; special formulas (hydrolysed milk, soy or other proteins) are not recommended for allergy prevention.
Mild rashes around the mouth after eating, with no other allergy symptoms, may not be an allergic reaction, and the food should be offered again.

items.title: Inositol for infertile women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether myo-inositol, a widely used supplement, helps women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) who are struggling to conceive. It pulled together 21 trials with 1634 women. The evidence was low or very low quality, so researchers are mostly unsure whether myo-inositol changes live birth, miscarriage or other outcomes. For women having IVF, it may slightly raise the chance of clinical pregnancy compared with no treatment, but this finding is also low certainty.
keyPoints: The review included 21 trials with 1634 women with PCOS and infertility; all trials with usable data tested myo-inositol.

For women having ovulation induction or intrauterine insemination, the evidence came from one small study and was too uncertain to say whether myo-inositol affects live birth, miscarriage or other outcomes.
For women having IVF, myo-inositol may slightly increase clinical pregnancy rates compared with no treatment (low-certainty evidence), but its effect on live birth and miscarriage is unclear.
Compared with metformin in IVF, it is unclear whether myo-inositol makes a difference, based on one study with very low-certainty evidence.

items.title: When Weight Matters: How Obesity Impacts Reproductive Health and Pregnancy-A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 35 studies on how obesity affects fertility in both women and men, IVF outcomes, and pregnancy. It found that obesity is linked to hormone changes, insulin resistance and inflammation, which can make it take longer to get pregnant and lower IVF success. In pregnancy, obesity was linked to higher risks of gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, caesarean birth and some newborn complications. The authors say managing weight before pregnancy and tailored care during IVF and pregnancy may help.
keyPoints: Obesity is linked to longer time to pregnancy, lower IVF success and a higher risk of miscarriage.
Obesity affects hormones, ovarian function, womb lining receptivity and sperm quality, in both women and men.
In pregnancy, obesity raises the risk of gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, caesarean delivery, large babies and NICU admission.
The review supports weight management before pregnancy and individualised IVF and antenatal care.

items.title: Progestogen for preventing miscarriage in women with recurrent miscarriage of unclear etiology
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether taking progestogen (a progesterone-type medicine) early in pregnancy helps women with repeated miscarriages of unknown cause. It combined nine trials with 1426 women. Progestogen probably made little to no difference to miscarriage rates or to the number of babies born alive. Evidence on preterm birth and other outcomes was very limited or missing.
keyPoints: Progestogen probably makes little to no difference to the miscarriage rate compared with placebo or no treatment (moderate-certainty evidence).
Live birth rates were probably similar with progestogen and placebo (moderate-certainty evidence).
The effect on preterm birth is uncertain because the evidence is very low certainty.
Few trials reported on harms such as maternal side effects, so less is known about these.

items.title: Fertility-sparing treatment for atypical endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at ways to treat atypical endometrial hyperplasia (an overgrowth of the womb lining) and early womb cancer without removing the womb, for women who hope to have children. It found 12 studies with 904 women, but the evidence was low certainty and the studies had a high risk of bias. Adding metformin to progestin tablets may slightly improve how often the condition fully clears. A hormonal coil (levonorgestrel IUS) seemed about as effective as progestin tablets and may cause slightly less weight gain.
keyPoints: It is unclear which treatment, route or dose of progestin works best for fertility-sparing care, because the evidence is low certainty.
Adding metformin to progestin may slightly increase the chance of complete response, but may make little to no difference to live birth rate.
The levonorgestrel IUS (hormonal coil) may work about as well as oral progestin for complete response and may reduce severe weight gain slightly.
No studies gave evidence on overall survival, progression-free survival or quality of life.

items.title: Prevention of cardiovascular diseases in women planning pregnancy and during pregnancy. Expert opinion of the Section of Prevention and Epidemiology of the Polish Cardiac Society, the Polish Society of Gynecologists and Obstetricians, the Polish Society of Family Medicine, the Polish Lipid Association, and the Polish Lifestyle Medicine Society
items.summary: This expert opinion from several Polish medical societies looks at how to prevent heart and blood vessel disease in women who are planning a pregnancy or are pregnant. It recommends healthy lifestyle habits, spotting and treating risk factors early, and good care after the birth. It also covers high blood pressure and lipid (blood fat) problems in pregnancy. The abstract does not rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Preventing heart disease around pregnancy needs several steps: lifestyle changes, early detection and treatment of risk factors, and full postpartum care.
Key lifestyle strategies are a proper diet, regular physical activity, a healthy weight, stress management, enough sleep and avoiding smoking.
Pregnancy-related high blood pressure can harm mother and baby if not treated properly, and treating lipid disorders in pregnancy is a challenge for doctors.
The document also stresses mental health care in pregnancy and the role family doctors can play in prevention.

items.title: Acupuncture for polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether acupuncture helps women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) who ovulate rarely or not at all. It combined nine trials with 1606 women. Compared with fake (sham) acupuncture, real acupuncture may make little or no difference to live births, pregnancies, ovulation or miscarriage, though this evidence is low certainty. Side effects were probably more common with acupuncture.
keyPoints: Compared with sham acupuncture, acupuncture may make little to no difference to live birth, clinical pregnancy, ovulation, multiple pregnancy or miscarriage (low-certainty evidence).
Adverse events are probably more common with acupuncture than sham acupuncture (moderate-certainty evidence).
It is unclear whether acupuncture improves ovulation compared with relaxation or Diane-35, because the evidence is very uncertain.
Only a few trials were found and they reported different outcomes, so larger, well-designed trials are needed.

items.title: Metformin for endometrial hyperplasia
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether metformin, a diabetes medicine, can help treat endometrial hyperplasia, a thickening of the womb lining that can lead to womb cancer if left untreated. It pooled seven trials with 387 women. Adding metformin to the hormone treatment megestrol may help the womb lining return to normal more often than megestrol alone, but the evidence is low quality. Overall, the authors found not enough evidence to say whether metformin should or should not be used.
keyPoints: Seven randomised trials with 387 women were included; most outcomes were rated very low certainty.
Metformin plus megestrol may improve regression of hyperplasia compared with megestrol alone (low-certainty evidence).
It is uncertain whether metformin alone beats megestrol, or whether it adds anything to a levonorgestrel intrauterine system.
The authors found insufficient evidence to support or refute metformin and call for larger, well-designed long-term trials.

items.title: Early versus delayed oral feeding after major gynaecologic surgery
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether women can safely eat and drink within 24 hours after major gynaecologic surgery, rather than waiting until bowel function returns. It combined seven trials with 902 women. The reviewers found no evidence that early eating causes harm, such as bowel blockage, nausea, vomiting or a swollen belly. Early eating may bring small benefits, though much of the evidence is low certainty.
keyPoints: No evidence of harm from early eating after major gynaecologic surgery, measured as bowel slowdown (ileus), nausea, vomiting or abdominal swelling.
Early feeding probably means a slightly sooner first bowel movement, with moderate-certainty evidence.
Early feeding may mean a slightly sooner return to solid food and a slightly shorter hospital stay, based on low-certainty evidence.
Infections after surgery were probably less common with early feeding (moderate certainty), and satisfaction may be higher.

items.title: Opening the black box: why do euploid blastocysts fail to implant? A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Even when an embryo has the right number of chromosomes (found through PGT-A genetic testing), only about 50-60% implant. This large review pooled results from hundreds of studies to look at what else might explain why some of these embryos do not lead to a pregnancy. Lower embryo quality, slower development, older age, obesity and earlier repeated implantation failure were linked to poorer outcomes. Most studies were small or looked back at past cases, so the review rates the quality of the evidence as low or very low.
keyPoints: Lower embryo quality (such as a reduced inner cell mass or outer layer quality) and slower development were linked to lower chances of a live birth.
Women aged 38 or older had slightly lower live birth rates even with genetically tested embryos, and obesity was linked to lower live birth rates and more miscarriages.
Transferring a frozen-thawed embryo was linked to better results than a fresh transfer after PGT-A, while repeated freezing and warming cycles may slightly lower success.
Most included studies were retrospective or small, so the evidence is low or very low quality and many causes of implantation failure remain unexplained.

items.title: Can Dietary Patterns Impact Fertility Outcomes? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 11 studies on whether overall eating patterns affect the chance of pregnancy and live birth, both for people conceiving naturally and for those having fertility treatment (ART). Closer following of a Mediterranean-style diet was linked to better live birth or pregnancy rates in fertility treatment, based on only two studies. Some other healthy eating patterns were also linked to better outcomes, but the studies were too different to combine. Overall, the evidence is early, and it is still unclear which diet pattern helps most.
keyPoints: After removing high risk-of-bias studies, higher Mediterranean diet adherence was linked to better live birth or pregnancy rates in ART (odds ratio 1.91, based on two studies).
Several healthy diets (ProFertility diet, Dutch Dietary Guidelines, Fertility diet) were linked to better ART or natural conception outcomes, but results could not be pooled.
The authors describe the evidence as preliminary because the studies varied a lot.
It is currently unclear which diet patterns are linked to better fertility and ART outcomes.

items.title: Adipose Tissue Dysfunction in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This systematic review looked at how body fat tissue works in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), which affects about 5% to 15% of women of reproductive age. It found that fat tissue in PCOS often does not work as it should, for example in how it responds to insulin and how it handles stored fat, and this appears to be true even in women who do not carry extra weight. The authors conclude that this poorly working fat tissue contributes to the metabolic and inflammation problems seen in PCOS. Many of the studies gave contradictory, unclear or limited results, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Fat tissue does not work as it should in PCOS, including in women without excess body fat.
Fat cells in PCOS take up less sugar in response to insulin, partly because of lower levels of a sugar transporter called GLUT4.
How well fat tissue functions seems to matter more for metabolic and inflammation problems in PCOS than where fat sits on the body or how much there is.
Many studies had contradictory, unclear or limited data, so more research is urgently needed.

items.title: Chronic kidney disease, female infertility, and medically assisted reproduction: a best practice position statement by the Kidney and Pregnancy Group of the Italian Society of Nephrology
items.summary: Women with chronic kidney disease are more likely to have fertility problems, and some will need help to conceive, such as IVF. An Italian group of kidney specialists wrote a best practice statement based on a literature review and expert experience, noting that there is little research in this area. They say fertility treatment is an option for women with kidney disease, but it needs extra caution and close monitoring.
keyPoints: All medically assisted reproduction techniques can be used by women with chronic kidney disease, but caution is needed.
Twin pregnancy should be avoided, and risks of bleeding, blood clots and infection should be considered.
Severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome carries a high risk of kidney damage, so it should be carefully avoided.
Egg freezing should be considered for women with autoimmune diseases who need cytotoxic (cell-killing) treatment.

items.title: Mediterranean diet and female reproductive health over lifespan: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pulled together 32 studies, covering over 100,000 women, to see how following a Mediterranean diet relates to female reproductive health across life. In pregnancy, the diet was linked to lower chances of gestational diabetes, preterm birth and high blood pressure. Evidence for fertility and other life stages was limited and only suggestive. Most women in the studies were White, so the findings may not apply equally to everyone.
keyPoints: In trials, a Mediterranean diet was linked to lower risk of gestational diabetes, preterm birth and gestational high blood pressure.
The effect on preterm birth was bigger when the diet started in the first trimester.
Evidence of benefit for fertility and healthy weight gain in pregnancy is suggestive but limited.
Data on menarche, menopausal hot flushes, PCOS and pregnancy loss is sparse; no link was seen for PCOS-like features or pregnancy loss.

items.title: The impact of obesity and metabolic health on male fertility: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 112 studies from 2013 to 2023 on how a man's weight and metabolic health affect his fertility. Obesity, diabetes and metabolic syndrome were linked to poorer semen quality and sperm DNA integrity. Higher male body weight was also linked to fewer live births, both with natural conception and with fertility treatment. Exercise generally seemed to help fertility markers, while weight-loss medicines and surgery had mixed results.
keyPoints: Obesity, diabetes and metabolic syndrome in men were linked to poorer semen quality and sperm DNA integrity.
Male obesity was linked to fewer live births, both with natural conception and assisted reproduction.
Physical exercise generally appeared to improve male fertility markers, though the type and intensity of exercise may matter.
Weight-loss medicines such as metformin and GLP-1 agonists, and gastric bypass surgery, showed mixed effects on male reproductive health, so more research is needed.

items.title: Pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies for obese women with subfertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 10 trials of weight-loss strategies, such as diet and lifestyle programmes or medicines like metformin, for women with obesity who were having trouble getting pregnant. The evidence was low to very low quality, so it could not show whether any of these strategies changes the chance of live birth, pregnancy or miscarriage. Lifestyle programmes may lower body mass index (BMI). No trials compared medicines directly with lifestyle changes.
keyPoints: Evidence was too limited to say whether diet or lifestyle programmes change the chance of live birth or pregnancy in women with obesity and subfertility.
Lifestyle programmes may lower BMI, though the evidence was low or very low quality.
It was unclear whether medicines such as metformin affect live birth, miscarriage or side effects.
No studies compared medicines with lifestyle changes, and the authors call for trials combining the two.

items.title: Barrier agents for adhesion prevention after gynaecological surgery
items.summary: This review looked at 19 trials of barrier materials placed inside the pelvis during gynaecological surgery to stop scar-like tissue (adhesions) from forming. Some barriers, such as a collagen membrane or oxidised regenerated cellulose, may reduce adhesions at a follow-up look inside the pelvis, but the evidence is low or very low quality. No trial measured pelvic pain or live birth, so it is not known whether these barriers help with pain or fertility. No harmful events were linked to the barriers.
keyPoints: No trial reported pelvic pain or live birth rate, so effects on these outcomes are unknown.
Low-quality evidence suggests a collagen membrane may reduce adhesions compared with no treatment.
Low-quality evidence suggests oxidised regenerated cellulose may reduce adhesions re-forming after open surgery.
No adverse events were directly attributed to the barrier agents, but most studies were commercially funded and poorly reported.

items.title: Metabolic syndrome in polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to look at metabolic syndrome (a cluster of problems such as extra belly fat, high blood pressure, and abnormal blood fats and sugar) in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Women with PCOS were found to be about three times as likely to have metabolic syndrome. The higher risk was seen in women with PCOS who were overweight or obese, but not clearly in lean women. It was linked to weight and metabolic features such as insulin resistance, not to male-type hormone levels.
keyPoints: Women with PCOS had about 3.35 times the odds of metabolic syndrome compared with women without PCOS.
The higher risk was seen in overweight or obese women with PCOS, but not clearly in lean women with PCOS.
Waist size, BMI, blood fats, blood pressure, glucose tolerance and insulin resistance were linked to differences in metabolic syndrome rates between studies.
Hormone measures such as testosterone and the type of PCOS were not linked to metabolic syndrome.

items.title: Epidemiology of uterine fibroids: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 60 studies to find out how common uterine fibroids are and which factors are linked to getting them. Fibroids are very common non-cancerous growths in the womb that can cause problems and may affect fertility. Black women had two to three times the risk compared with white women, and this was the factor with the strongest evidence. The authors say better-quality studies that follow women over time are still needed.
keyPoints: Reported rates varied widely: 4.5% to 68.6% of women had fibroids, depending on who was studied and how fibroids were detected.
Black race was the only factor repeatedly linked to higher risk, at two to three times that of white race.
Age, being before menopause, high blood pressure, family history, and more time since last birth were linked to higher risk.
Oral contraceptives, the contraceptive injection (depot medroxyprogesterone acetate) and having given birth were linked to lower risk.

items.title: Association of Gestational Weight Gain With Maternal and Infant Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 23 studies covering more than 1.3 million pregnancies to see how weight gain in pregnancy, compared with Institute of Medicine (IOM) guideline ranges, relates to outcomes for mothers and babies. About 23% of women gained less than recommended and 47% gained more. Gaining less than recommended was linked to more small babies and preterm births, while gaining more was linked to more large babies and caesareans. These are associations from observational studies, so they do not prove cause.
keyPoints: Gaining less weight than the IOM guidelines was linked to a higher risk of a small-for-gestational-age baby (about 5 percentage points higher) and of preterm birth (about 5 points higher).

Gaining more than the guidelines was linked to a higher risk of a large-for-gestational-age baby (about 4 points higher), macrosomia (about 6 points higher) and caesarean birth (about 4 points higher).
Gaining less than recommended was linked to fewer large babies and less macrosomia, and gaining more was linked to fewer small babies and preterm births.
Gestational diabetes could not be assessed because of the way the available data were reported.

items.title: Comparison of Luteal Support Protocols in Frozen IVF/ICSI Cycles: A Network Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies (8 of them randomised trials) with 4,688 women having frozen embryo transfer as part of IVF/ICSI, comparing 12 ways of giving luteal support (hormone support after the embryo is transferred). Adding a small 0.1 mg injection of a GnRH agonist under the skin to vaginal progesterone, taken until week 12, appeared to improve clinical pregnancy rates. This held whether the injection was given once (day 3 after transfer) or twice (days 3 and 6). The abstract does not report live birth results, and the overall risk of bias in the studies was moderate.
keyPoints: Vaginal progesterone plus a single or double dose of subcutaneous GnRH agonist significantly improved clinical pregnancy (risk ratio 1.86, 95% credibility interval 1.18 to 2.93).
The helpful regimen was 0.1 mg GnRH agonist on day 3, or days 3 and 6, after embryo transfer, added to vaginal progesterone until week 12.
Fourteen studies including eight randomised trials and 4,688 women were compared across 12 luteal support strategies.
Overall risk of bias was moderate and the comparisons across studies were consistent with each other.

items.title: Retrospective cohort study and meta-analysis of individualized luteal phase support with additional oral dydrogesterone in artificially prepared frozen embryo transfer cycles
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: Some women having a frozen embryo transfer with hormone replacement have low progesterone levels in their blood after starting vaginal progesterone. This study looked at 550 cycles and found that adding oral dydrogesterone for women with low levels gave similar live birth rates to women whose levels were already sufficient. A combined analysis of earlier studies also found similar ongoing pregnancy rates with extra dydrogesterone.
keyPoints: About 29% of cycles (159 of 550) had low progesterone (below 11 ng/mL) after two days of vaginal progesterone.
Live birth rates were similar: 24.2% with routine support and 27.2% with added dydrogesterone for low levels.
Adding dydrogesterone was not linked to a different chance of live birth after adjusting for other factors.
The meta-analysis also found similar ongoing pregnancy rates between groups.

items.title: Oral dydrogesterone versus micronized vaginal progesterone for luteal phase support: a double-blind crossover study investigating pharmacokinetics and impact on the endometrium
items.summary: This small study compared two ways of giving progesterone support after egg collection in IVF: a tablet taken by mouth (dydrogesterone) and a vaginal progesterone. Researchers looked at hormone levels in the blood and at tissue samples from the womb lining a week later. The womb lining looked very similar with both treatments, with only subtle differences in some immune cells. The authors say this supports earlier trials showing the tablet works about as well as vaginal progesterone, but the study was small.
keyPoints: All 42 womb lining samples showed a normal secretory (post-ovulation) pattern, and gene activity did not differ significantly between the two treatments.
After a dose of the oral tablet, drug levels peaked within about 1.5 hours and cleared quickly, so how often it is taken may matter as well as the dose.
Immune cell patterns differed slightly: vaginal progesterone was linked to fewer T cells and B cells and more natural killer cells than the oral tablet.
The authors say the findings support earlier results that oral dydrogesterone works about as well as vaginal progesterone, but more research is needed.

items.title: Optimizing intrauterine insemination: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effectiveness and safety of clinical treatment add-ons
items.summary: This review pooled 66 randomised trials (over 16,000 participants) of extra treatments added to standard intrauterine insemination (IUI). Using vaginal progesterone after insemination in cycles with fertility medication appeared to improve the chance of an ongoing pregnancy or live birth. Endometrial scratch and ovarian stimulation in the first half of the cycle also showed possible benefit, but the evidence for these is weaker. Most other add-ons made no clear difference, and the authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Vaginal progesterone for luteal phase support in stimulated IUI cycles significantly increased ongoing pregnancy or live birth (RR 1.37), with moderate to low certainty.
Endometrial scratch may increase pregnancy or live birth (RR 1.44), but the evidence is very uncertain.
Ovarian stimulation in the follicular phase (two studies) may increase success (RR 1.39), with low certainty.
The other add-ons studied showed no significant difference in the main outcomes.

items.title: Luteal phase support for natural cycle frozen embryo transfer: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from 9 studies to see whether extra hormone support after ovulation (luteal phase support) helps pregnancy outcomes in natural cycle frozen embryo transfer. Support was linked to a higher clinical pregnancy rate, but it did not change the chemical pregnancy rate or the miscarriage rate overall. The benefit looked clearer in people who used an hCG trigger shot to prompt ovulation.
keyPoints: Luteal phase support was linked to a higher clinical pregnancy rate (RR 1.23) compared with no support.
No significant difference was found in chemical pregnancy rate or miscarriage rate overall.
An hCG trigger for ovulation may cause luteal phase deficiency, and support improved pregnancy rates for people who had an hCG trigger.
The authors conclude that luteal phase support might improve clinical pregnancy rate in natural cycle frozen embryo transfer.

items.title: Low Luteal Serum Progesterone Levels Are Associated With Lower Ongoing Pregnancy and Live Birth Rates in ART: Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses
items.summary: This review pooled 32 studies of fertility treatment (assisted reproductive technology) to see whether progesterone levels in the blood after embryo transfer relate to pregnancy outcomes. In cycles without a corpus luteum (the structure that normally makes progesterone after ovulation), pregnancy and live birth were less likely when progesterone fell below a certain level, and miscarriage was more likely. In stimulated cycles, women who did not have an ongoing pregnancy or live birth had lower average progesterone levels. The authors suggest that checking progesterone levels could help tailor how much progesterone is given.
keyPoints: In cycles with no corpus luteum, low luteal progesterone was linked to fewer ongoing pregnancies (RR 0.72) and fewer live births (RR 0.73).
Miscarriage was more common when progesterone levels were low in cycles with no corpus luteum (RR 1.48).
In stimulated cycles, average progesterone was lower in women without an ongoing pregnancy or live birth.
The authors say monitoring progesterone could help individualise progesterone treatment, especially in cycles without a corpus luteum.

items.title: Progestogens in the management of miscarriage and preterm birth
items.summary: An expert panel in Malaysia reviewed the research on progestogens (hormones related to progesterone) for miscarriage and preterm birth. They recommend progestogens in some situations: threatened miscarriage in women who have had a miscarriage before, luteal phase support during assisted reproduction, and a short cervix in the middle of pregnancy. It may also be considered for recurrent miscarriage when no other cause is found.
keyPoints: Progestogens are recommended for women with a threatened miscarriage who have had a previous miscarriage.
They are recommended as luteal phase support for women having assisted reproduction.
They are recommended for women with a short cervix (under 25mm) in the middle of pregnancy.
They can be considered for recurrent miscarriage when no other cause is found.

items.title: Luteal phase support for women trying to conceive by intrauterine insemination or sexual intercourse
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 25 trials (5,111 women) testing luteal phase support, extra hormones given after ovulation, for women trying to conceive by intrauterine insemination (IUI) or intercourse. It is unclear whether vaginal progesterone raises the chance of a live birth or ongoing pregnancy. It may raise the clinical pregnancy rate, but the evidence is low quality and the effect on miscarriage is unclear. Other hormones and routes (oral, injected, GnRH agonist, hCG) did not clearly improve pregnancy outcomes, and the evidence for them is very uncertain.
keyPoints: Unclear whether vaginal progesterone increases live birth or ongoing pregnancy (low-certainty evidence).
Vaginal progesterone may increase clinical pregnancy rates in cycles with ovarian stimulation, but low-certainty evidence means this is not firm.
Effects on miscarriage and multiple pregnancy are uncertain for progesterone and the other treatments studied.
No trial tested luteal support in natural cycles, and oral progesterone, GnRH agonist and hCG showed no clear benefit (very low-certainty evidence).

items.title: Should women receive luteal support following natural cycle frozen embryo transfer? A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from eight studies on whether extra hormone support after a natural-cycle frozen embryo transfer helps. Adding progesterone was linked to more clinical pregnancies and more live births. Adding hCG did not increase pregnancy rates. The authors say larger trials are still needed to confirm these findings.
keyPoints: Progesterone support after natural-cycle frozen embryo transfer was linked to a higher clinical pregnancy rate and a higher live birth rate.
The link between progesterone and live birth stayed significant when only randomised trials were counted.
hCG used for luteal support did not increase clinical pregnancy rates.
The authors say more large randomised trials are needed to improve the quality of the evidence.

items.title: Luteal phase support for in vitro fertilization/intracytoplasmic sperm injection fresh cycles: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 89 trials with nearly 30,000 women to compare ways of supporting the luteal phase (the time after egg collection when the womb lining needs hormone support) in fresh IVF/ICSI cycles. Most active treatments, including vaginal and intramuscular progesterone, gave more ongoing pregnancies than placebo or no support. The differences between the active treatments were small and very uncertain, so several options may work about equally well. Starting progesterone up to 96 hours after egg retrieval did not change pregnancy outcomes compared with starting within 48 hours.
keyPoints: Most active luteal support options (except rectal or subcutaneous progesterone) led to more ongoing pregnancies than placebo or no support.
Starting progesterone up to 96 hours after egg retrieval did not affect pregnancy outcomes compared with starting within 48 hours.
Adding a GnRH agonist to vaginal progesterone pessaries was linked to more live births, but its safety in this phase still needs to be studied.
Differences between the active treatments were small and very uncertain, so there may be several reasonable options.

items.title: Luteal Phase Support Using Subcutaneous Progesterone: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at progesterone given as an injection under the skin to support the second half of the cycle (the luteal phase) during fertility treatment. In women with a good outlook having a fresh IVF cycle, the under-the-skin route worked about as well as vaginal progesterone. For frozen embryo transfers the results were mixed, and one group of egg-donor recipients had more miscarriages with the under-the-skin route. The best protocol is still not known, and cost has not yet been studied.
keyPoints: In women with a good outlook having fresh IVF, subcutaneous progesterone was not inferior to vaginal progesterone.
In frozen embryo transfer cycles, results were mixed, with more miscarriages seen in egg-donor recipients using the subcutaneous route.
Women's acceptance of the subcutaneous route compared with the vaginal route looked encouraging, though studies used different questionnaires.
No cost-effectiveness analysis has been done yet, and an optimal luteal support protocol has not been identified.

items.title: Fresh versus elective frozen embryo transfer in IVF/ICSI cycles: a systematic review and meta-analysis of reproductive outcomes
items.summary: This review pooled 11 randomized trials (5,379 people) comparing fresh embryo transfer with freezing all embryos and transferring them in a later cycle during IVF/ICSI. Overall, live birth rates were somewhat higher with frozen transfer, but the benefit appeared only in women who respond very strongly to ovarian stimulation and in cycles using genetic testing of embryos. Frozen transfer lowered the risk of moderate or severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) but was linked to a higher risk of pre-eclampsia.
keyPoints: Live birth rate was higher with frozen transfer overall (RR 1.12), but the gain was seen only in hyper-responders and in cycles with embryo genetic testing (PGT-A).
No difference in live birth rate for normal responders, and cumulative live birth rate was not significantly different overall.
Moderate or severe OHSS was less likely with frozen transfer (RR 0.42).
Pre-eclampsia was more likely after frozen transfer (RR 1.79); other outcomes showed no significant differences.

items.title: The role of luteal support during IVF: a qualitative systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at how progesterone support after egg collection (luteal support) affects pregnancy outcomes in women having IVF or ICSI. It found that support should probably start 24-72 hours after egg retrieval and continue at least until a positive pregnancy test. Newer options, oral dydrogesterone and progesterone injected under the skin, gave similar pregnancy and pregnancy loss rates to vaginal or muscle-injected progesterone, and patients seemed to find them easier to accept and tolerate.
keyPoints: The best time to start luteal support seems to be 24-72 hours after egg retrieval, continuing at least until a positive pregnancy test.
Most IVF centres worldwide give progesterone support up to 8 weeks of pregnancy.
Oral dydrogesterone and subcutaneous progesterone had pregnancy and pregnancy loss rates comparable to vaginal and intramuscular progesterone, with possibly better patient acceptance.
In frozen-thawed embryo transfer, dydrogesterone and vaginal progesterone were not effective on their own, but there is no reason to avoid either when they are combined.

items.title: Evaluation of progestogen supplementation for luteal phase support in fresh in vitro fertilization cycles
items.summary: This review pooled results from 82 studies covering 26,726 women having fresh IVF cycles. It looked at whether giving progesterone-type medicine (progestogen) after egg collection improves pregnancy rates, and how best to give it. Progestogen supplements clearly raised clinical pregnancy rates compared with no treatment, whichever way they were given. Adding estrogen did not help, and carrying on beyond about 3 weeks made no difference.
keyPoints: Progestogen supplements (injection into muscle, vaginal, under the skin or oral) all increased clinical pregnancy rates compared with no treatment.
Injections into the muscle gave the highest pregnancy rates, about 1.4 times the odds of vaginal use.
Starting between egg retrieval and embryo transfer worked best, with 1 day after egg retrieval the most beneficial.
Adding estrogen showed no benefit, and stopping after 3 weeks or less gave similar results to continuing for up to 12 weeks.

items.title: Systematic review of the clinical efficacy of vaginal progesterone for luteal phase support in assisted reproductive technology cycles
items.summary: This review looked at 18 trials that directly compared different vaginal progesterone products (Crinone, Cyclogest, Lutigest and Utrogestan Vaginal) used to support the second half of the cycle during fertility treatment such as IVF. Pregnancy rates were not meaningfully different between the products, and side effects like irritation were similar. The authors concluded these products appear to be equally safe and effective choices, and noted that further analyses could strengthen the findings.
keyPoints: No significant difference in clinical pregnancy rate was found between Utrogestan Vaginal and Crinone.
Utrogestan Vaginal and Lutigest were non-inferior to Crinone for ongoing pregnancy rates.
Patient-reported perineal irritation with Crinone and Lutigest was not significantly different from Cyclogest.
Changing the timing or dose of Utrogestan Vaginal or Crinone made no significant difference.

items.title: Progestogens and pregnancy loss
items.summary: This review looked at progestogens, which are hormones similar to progesterone, and whether they help prevent pregnancy loss. It covered their use before pregnancy as luteal support, for threatened miscarriage, for repeated miscarriages, and to prevent early labor. Across these uses, the studies it summarised generally pointed to a benefit, such as more live births. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: As luteal support, progestogens were linked to more live births or ongoing pregnancies (odds ratio 1.77) in a Cochrane review.
For threatened miscarriage, a Cochrane review linked progestogens to lower odds of pregnancy loss (odds ratio 0.53).
For recurrent miscarriage, a meta-analysis found a 28% increase in the live birth rate.
Recent meta-analyses also report benefits for preventing preterm labor.

items.title: Interventions for the prevention of OHSS in ART cycles: an overview of Cochrane reviews
items.summary: This overview pulled together 27 Cochrane reviews on ways to lower the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), a treatment-related complication, during assisted reproduction (IVF and similar treatments). Seven reviews found interventions that reduced OHSS, and most of these did not harm pregnancy outcomes. The strength of the evidence ranged from very low to high, and some reviews are out of date. Progesterone for luteal phase support was among the options linked to less OHSS, but this evidence was low quality.
keyPoints: Moderate-quality evidence supports metformin for women with PCOS, GnRH antagonist protocols, and a GnRH agonist trigger in donor oocyte or freeze-all programmes to reduce OHSS.
Low-quality evidence suggests clomiphene citrate, cabergoline and progesterone for luteal phase support may also reduce OHSS; evidence for intravenous fluids was very low quality.
Coasting (withholding gonadotrophins) looks promising but needs more research.
Evidence is currently insufficient to support the widespread practice of embryo cryopreservation.

items.title: Progesterone luteal support after ovulation induction and intrauterine insemination: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined 11 trials (2,842 patients, 4,065 cycles) to see whether progesterone support after ovulation induction and intrauterine insemination (IUI) helps. When gonadotropin injections were used to trigger ovulation, adding progesterone made pregnancy and live birth more likely. When clomiphene citrate was used, with or without gonadotropins, progesterone did not improve pregnancy rates.
keyPoints: With gonadotropin ovulation induction, progesterone support raised the chance of clinical pregnancy (RR 1.56) and live birth (RR 1.77).
About 11 patients need progesterone support to get one extra live birth in gonadotropin IUI cycles.
With clomiphene citrate, or clomiphene plus gonadotropins, progesterone showed no benefit for clinical pregnancy.
There was no live birth data for clomiphene-based cycles.

items.title: GnRH agonist during luteal phase in women undergoing assisted reproductive techniques: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled eight trials (2776 women) of adding a GnRH agonist medicine during the luteal phase, the weeks after egg collection or ovulation, for women having fertility treatment. Overall it seemed to raise the chance of ongoing pregnancy, but when only the more reliable studies were counted, no clear benefit remained. The authors rated the evidence as very low quality and no trial reported on birth outcomes or birth defects. They concluded that using it in routine care would be premature.
keyPoints: Combining eight trials, adding a GnRH agonist in the luteal phase was linked to a higher chance of live birth or ongoing pregnancy.
When studies at high risk of bias or without live birth data were removed, the benefit was no longer clear.
The quality of evidence was very low because of study limitations, imprecise and inconsistent results, and suspected publication bias.
No included study reported adverse perinatal outcomes or congenital malformations, so safety remains unclear.

items.title: Dydrogesterone vs progesterone for luteal-phase support: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from eight randomized trials comparing two ways of giving progesterone-type support after fertility treatment (ART/IVF): a pill called dydrogesterone and vaginal progesterone. Pregnancy rates and miscarriage rates were not meaningfully different between the two. Two of three studies found fewer women were dissatisfied with the pill than with vaginal progesterone, while the third found no difference.
keyPoints: Oral dydrogesterone and vaginal progesterone gave similar ongoing pregnancy rates (7 trials, 3134 women).
Clinical pregnancy and miscarriage rates also showed no relevant difference between the two.
Two of three studies reporting dissatisfaction found it lower with oral dydrogesterone (for example 4.6% vs 18.0% against vaginal gel).
The authors conclude oral dydrogesterone seems as effective as vaginal progesterone and appears better tolerated.

items.title: Meta-analysis of estradiol for luteal phase support in in vitro fertilization/intracytoplasmic sperm injection
items.summary: This review pooled 15 randomized trials with 2,406 women having IVF or ICSI. It looked at whether adding estradiol to progesterone for luteal phase support (hormone support after egg transfer) improves pregnancy outcomes. Adding estradiol made no clear difference to pregnancy rates compared with progesterone alone, whether taken by mouth, vaginally or through the skin, and at different daily doses.
keyPoints: Adding estradiol to progesterone did not improve clinical pregnancy rates in IVF/ICSI.
No difference was seen for other outcomes such as implantation, ongoing pregnancy, miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy.
Different routes (oral, vaginal, skin patch) and doses (2, 4 and 6 mg daily) showed no significant effect.
The authors say more trials are needed on other ways of giving estradiol.

items.title: Timing luteal support in assisted reproductive technology: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at five randomized trials (872 women) of when to start progesterone after egg retrieval during IVF. Starting on the day of egg retrieval, or up to about 3 days after, seemed to work about equally well. Starting before retrieval gave lower pregnancy rates, and starting as late as day 6 looked worse in one trial. The trials were too different to combine, and the authors say more studies are needed.
keyPoints: Starting progesterone before egg retrieval gave pregnancy rates 5%-12% lower than starting on the day of retrieval in two studies.
One study found a 16% drop in pregnancy when progesterone started on day 6 after retrieval compared with day 3.
Starting on the day of retrieval versus 2 or 3 days afterward showed no significant difference in pregnancy.
The authors suggest a window from the evening of egg retrieval to day 3 afterward, but say more trials are needed to define the best start time.

items.title: Luteal phase support for assisted reproduction cycles
items.summary: This large review pooled 94 trials (26,198 women) of medicines used to support the second half of the cycle (the luteal phase) after fertility treatment such as IVF. Giving progesterone or hCG was linked with higher rates of live birth or ongoing pregnancy than placebo or no treatment, and adding a GnRH agonist to progesterone seemed to help further. Adding oestrogen did not seem to improve results, and the way progesterone was given (injection, vaginal, oral) made little clear difference. Most of the evidence was low or very low quality because of poor reporting and small studies.
keyPoints: Progesterone was linked with higher live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates than placebo or no treatment, but the evidence was very low quality.
hCG did not clearly improve live birth rates and raised the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) in one study.
Adding a GnRH agonist to progesterone was linked with better pregnancy outcomes, based on low-quality evidence.
Adding oestrogen did not seem to help, and the route of progesterone (injection, vaginal, rectal or oral) was not clearly linked to better outcomes.

items.title: European Association of Urology Guidelines on Male Sexual and Reproductive Health: 2025 Update on Male Infertility
items.summary: The European Association of Urology updated its 2025 guidelines on male infertility, covering how it is diagnosed, treated and followed up. The guidelines advise that every man seeking help for fertility problems should have a full urological check. They also recommend looking at the female partner at the same time, so a couple can decide together on timing and treatment.
keyPoints: All men seeking medical help for fertility problems should have a thorough urological assessment.
The female partner should be investigated in parallel, so couples can share decisions about timing and treatment.
Men with infertility or abnormal semen results should be counselled about the associated health risks.
The 2025 update adds new sections on exome sequencing (a genetic test) and probiotic treatment, and updates advice on diagnostic work-up.

items.title: The Effect of Dietary Supplements on Male Infertility in Terms of Pregnancy, Live Birth, and Sperm Parameters: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 50 randomised trials of dietary supplements taken for at least 12 weeks by men with fertility problems, compared with placebo. Supplements did not increase pregnancy or live birth rates. Some supplements improved single sperm measures, such as zinc and folic acid for sperm concentration and selenium, carnitine and coenzyme Q10 for motility. The studies were mostly of limited quality and the certainty of the evidence was low or very low, so the authors found no convincing evidence that any supplement helps male infertility.
keyPoints: No effect of dietary supplements on pregnancy or live birth was found.

Zinc, folic acid and combination supplements (3 or more ingredients) improved sperm concentration; selenium, carnitine and coenzyme Q10 improved motility; alpha-lipoic acid improved normal sperm shape.
Vitamin D, vitamin E and omega-3 fatty acids did not improve sperm parameters.
Most studies had some concerns or high risk of bias, and certainty of evidence was generally low or very low.

items.title: Summary of the Clinical Practice Guidelines for Male Infertility by the Japanese Urological Association With the Support of the Japan Society for Reproductive Medicine
items.summary: These 2024 Japanese guidelines set out how male infertility should be assessed and treated. Male factors play a part in about half of infertility cases, and the most common cause is poor sperm production. Checks include a medical history, physical exam, semen analysis and hormone tests, with genetic tests for severe cases. Treatments range from medicines to surgery, and the guidelines rate how strong the evidence is for each one.
keyPoints: Male factors contribute to about 50% of infertility cases, and poor sperm production is the most common cause (82.4%).
Diagnosis includes medical history, physical exam, semen analysis, hormone testing, genetic testing for severe cases, and imaging when needed.

Strongly supported treatments (grade A) include gonadotropin therapy for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, surgery for palpable varicoceles, and micro-TESE sperm retrieval for nonobstructive azoospermia.
Evidence for antioxidant therapy is limited (grade C), and the guidelines also cover fertility preservation before cancer treatment and treating sexual dysfunction.

items.title: Association between body mass index and semen quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 50 studies of about 71,000 men to see how body weight relates to semen quality. Men with obesity had lower semen volume, fewer sperm, and sperm that moved less well and looked less normal than men with a BMI under 25. Men who were overweight also showed some reductions, though smaller. The authors suggest that keeping a normal weight may help protect semen quality.
keyPoints: Men with obesity had lower semen volume, total sperm number, sperm movement and normal sperm shape than men with BMI under 25.
Men who were overweight had smaller reductions, in semen volume and progressive motility (sperm moving forward).
The effect was larger with higher obesity classes (BMI 35 or more) than with class I obesity (BMI 30 to 34.9).
Semen quality reductions were seen in men from the general population and in infertile or subfertile men.

items.title: Pharmacological non-hormonal treatment options for male infertility: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 randomised trials in 1,342 men with infertility to compare non-hormonal medicines (clomiphene, tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors and antioxidants) for improving sperm quality. Clomiphene looked best for sperm concentration compared with the other treatments, but it was not clearly better than placebo. The trials were of low quality, so the authors concluded there is not enough evidence to support routine use of these medicines.
keyPoints: Clomiphene raised sperm concentration more than antioxidants, aromatase inhibitors or tamoxifen, but not more than placebo.
All treatments had similar effects on sperm motility, semen volume and normal sperm shape.
The overall quality of the 14 included trials was low.
There is not enough evidence to support routine use of clomiphene, tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors to improve semen results; more trials are needed.

items.title: The Association Between Male Viral Infections and Infertility: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 135 studies of 30,298 men of reproductive age to see how viral infections relate to male infertility. Men with HPV had more sperm DNA damage and lower sperm count, concentration, viability and normal shape than men without HPV.
