Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV and COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) were also linked to poorer semen quality. HPV and hepatitis B may also affect the results of fertility treatments such as IVF.
keyPoints: Men with HPV had higher sperm DNA fragmentation and lower sperm count, concentration, viability and normal morphology.
Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV and SARS-CoV-2 were also linked to poorer semen quality.
Hepatitis B was linked to a lower fertilization rate in assisted reproduction.
HPV was linked to a lower clinical pregnancy rate and a higher miscarriage rate; HPV and adeno-associated virus were more common in men in fertility treatment.

items.title: Clomiphene citrate for male infertility: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 15 small studies of men with fertility problems who took clomiphene citrate, a medicine that acts on hormone signals to boost sperm production. Sperm concentration and movement (motility) were higher during treatment than before it. Sperm shape (morphology) did not change. No serious side effects were reported, and pregnancy rates varied widely between studies.
keyPoints: Sperm concentration was on average 8.38 million per ml higher during clomiphene treatment.
Sperm motility was on average 8.14% higher during treatment, but sperm shape did not change.
No serious side effects were reported during follow-up.
Where pregnancy was reported (10 studies), the average rate was 17%, ranging from 0% to 40%.

items.title: H19 Sperm Methylation in Male Infertility: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 11 studies to compare a chemical tag (methylation) on a gene called H19 in sperm from men with abnormal sperm and men with normal sperm. Methylation was lower in infertile men than in fertile men. The drop was larger in men with a low sperm count and in men whose partners had repeated pregnancy loss. The authors suggest checking H19 methylation in couples having fertility treatment, as it may give clues about treatment outcome and the health of children born.
keyPoints: H19 methylation in sperm was significantly lower in infertile men than in fertile controls.
The reduction was more marked in men with low sperm count (oligozoospermia) and in those linked to recurrent pregnancy loss.
The results did not depend on the man's age or sperm concentration.
The authors suggest H19 methylation could be evaluated in couples using assisted reproductive techniques for information on treatment outcome and offspring health.

items.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 90 trials with over 10,000 men who had fertility problems to see whether antioxidant supplements help couples have a baby. Antioxidants may slightly raise the chances of pregnancy and live birth, but the evidence is low to very low certainty. When weaker studies were removed, the live birth benefit was no longer seen. The authors say the evidence is inconclusive and larger, better trials are needed.
keyPoints: Antioxidants may increase live birth rates, but this is based on very low-certainty evidence and disappeared when high-risk-of-bias studies were removed.
Antioxidants may increase clinical pregnancy rates, based on low-certainty evidence.
No clear difference in miscarriage was found, though few studies reported it.
Antioxidants may cause more mild stomach discomfort (about 2% on placebo versus roughly 2% to 7% on antioxidants).

items.title: The semen microbiome and its impact on sperm function and male fertility: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 55 observational studies (over 51,000 men) to see how bacteria in semen relate to sperm quality and male fertility. Several bacteria were linked to poorer sperm measures, while Lactobacillus appeared to be linked to better sperm quality. The authors say the evidence on fertility itself is inconclusive and more studies are needed.
keyPoints: Semen contains a rich and varied mix of bacteria in both fertile and infertile men.
Ureaplasma urealyticum was more common in infertile men and was linked to lower sperm concentration and poorer sperm shape.
Enterococcus faecalis, Mycoplasma hominis and Prevotella were linked to worse sperm measures, while Lactobacillus appeared protective.
Chlamydia trachomatis was not more common in infertile men and did not significantly affect semen parameters.

items.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Infertility in Men: AUA/ASRM Guideline PART II
items.summary: This is Part II of a guideline from two US medical societies on how to manage the male partner when a couple is struggling to conceive. It covers medication, surgery, and assisted options like IUI, IVF and ICSI. The authors conclude that male factors are a common contributor to infertility and that specific treatments and assisted reproduction can be effective. The abstract does not list the individual recommendations.
keyPoints: Male factors are a common contributor to couples' infertility.
Specific treatments, including medical therapy and surgery, can help manage male infertility.
Assisted reproductive techniques such as IUI, IVF and ICSI are effective options for managing male infertility.
The guideline will be updated as knowledge about current and future treatments grows.

items.title: The Association between Mortality and Male Infertility: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled six studies to see whether men with fertility problems have a higher risk of early death. Compared with fertile men, infertile men had a somewhat higher risk of death, and the risk went up as sperm quality got worse. However, infertile men still had a lower risk of death than the general population, which suggests that social and lifestyle factors also matter.
keyPoints: Compared with fertile men, infertile men had a higher risk of death (pooled hazard ratio 1.26).
Men with very low or no sperm had a higher risk of death than men with normal sperm counts, and the risk rose as semen quality got worse.
Compared with men in the general population, infertile men had a lower risk of death.
The authors suggest social determinants of health also play an important role.

items.title: Surgical or radiological treatment for varicoceles in subfertile men
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 48 trials (5,384 people) of surgery or radiology treatments for varicoceles, which are enlarged veins in the scrotum linked to male infertility. It is unclear whether treatment increases live births, but treatment may improve the chance of pregnancy compared with delayed or no treatment. There was not enough evidence to say whether surgery or radiology is better. Among surgical options, microscopic subinguinal surgery probably gives slightly better pregnancy rates and fewer recurrences than other operations.
keyPoints: Treatment may raise pregnancy rates compared with delayed or no treatment (about 21% with no or delayed treatment versus 22% to 48% after treatment), but this evidence is low certainty.
It is uncertain whether treatment improves live birth rates, because the evidence is very low certainty.
There was not enough evidence to say whether surgery or radiological treatment works better, or how their side effects compare.
Microscopic subinguinal surgery probably slightly improves pregnancy rates and reduces varicocele recurrence compared with other surgical methods (moderate-certainty evidence).

items.title: European Academy of Andrology guideline Management of oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia
items.summary: This European guideline looks at how doctors should assess and manage men whose semen shows low sperm numbers, reduced movement and abnormal shape (oligo-astheno-teratozoospermia), which is common in couples having trouble conceiving. The cause is often unknown. It recommends a set of checks, including physical exams, two semen tests, hormone tests and a scrotal ultrasound, and gives advice on which treatments may or may not help.
keyPoints: Two semen analyses, a general and scrotal physical exam, hormone tests and a scrotal ultrasound are recommended as part of the investigation.
Chromosome and Yq microdeletion testing is advised when sperm concentration is very low (5 million per mL or less), and cystic fibrosis gene testing if a blockage in the genital tract is suspected.
Men are not advised to stop physical activity, and testosterone (androgen) replacement is not advised to improve the chance of pregnancy.

Assisted reproduction is suggested when other treatments are not available or not working; testosterone replacement is only for men with signs of low testosterone, after fertility treatment is finished.

items.title: Semen quality and alcohol intake: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 15 studies covering 16,395 men to see whether alcohol intake affects semen quality. Drinking alcohol was linked to slightly lower semen volume and fewer sperm with normal shape. The differences were clearer for daily drinkers than for occasional drinkers, and moderate drinking did not seem to harm semen results. The authors say more research is needed before giving advice beyond avoiding heavy drinking.
keyPoints: Alcohol intake was linked to lower semen volume and a lower share of sperm with normal shape.
The effect was larger when comparing daily drinkers with occasional drinkers than when comparing never-drinkers with occasional drinkers.
Moderate drinking did not appear to harm semen parameters.
The only advice the authors support for now is to avoid heavy drinking, until studies show how changes in semen results affect pregnancy outcomes.

items.title: Safety of psychotropic medications in pregnancy: an umbrella review
items.summary: This study pulled together 21 earlier reviews covering more than 17 million people to look at whether psychotropic medicines (such as antidepressants) taken in pregnancy are linked to health problems for mothers or babies. Some links, such as preterm birth with antidepressants and heart malformations with paroxetine in the first trimester, had only 'suggestive' evidence. No link reached the 'convincing' or 'highly suggestive' level. Most of the reviews it drew on were of low or critically low quality, so the findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: Antidepressant use in pregnancy was linked to preterm birth with suggestive evidence, in people with depression or any mental disorder.
SSRI use in people with depression was linked to babies being small for gestational age, again with suggestive evidence.
Paroxetine in the first trimester was linked to a small increase in major and heart malformations in babies, with suggestive evidence.
No link to adverse outcomes reached convincing or highly suggestive evidence, and most included reviews were low quality.

items.title: Antirheumatic drugs in reproduction, pregnancy, and lactation: a systematic literature review informing the 2024 update of the EULAR recommendations
items.summary: This review looked at 255 studies on medicines used for rheumatic conditions (such as inflammatory arthritis) around conception, during pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Biologic medicines, including TNF inhibitors, were not linked to pregnancy complications or serious infant infections, and the breastfeeding data were reassuring. Oral steroids were linked to a higher chance of preterm birth in a dose-dependent way, and anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) may temporarily lower the chance of conceiving.
keyPoints: TNF inhibitors were not linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes or serious infant infections, and other biologic medicines raised no concerns.
Oral glucocorticoids (steroids) were linked to a higher risk of preterm birth, rising with dose.
NSAID use could reversibly reduce fecundability (the monthly chance of conceiving).
Data on biologic medicines during breastfeeding were reassuring.

items.title: EULAR recommendations for use of antirheumatic drugs in reproduction, pregnancy, and lactation: 2024 update
items.summary: European rheumatology experts updated their guidance on which arthritis and autoimmune medicines can be used when trying for a baby, during pregnancy and while breastfeeding. They reviewed the research and agreed 5 main principles and 12 recommendations. Several older medicines and all biologic medicines were judged compatible with breastfeeding, and some are considered compatible with pregnancy after an individual risk-benefit check.
keyPoints: Antimalarials, azathioprine, colchicine, cyclosporine, sulfasalazine and tacrolimus are considered compatible with pregnancy.
NSAIDs (anti-inflammatory painkillers) and glucocorticoids (steroids) should be used more cautiously during pregnancy.
All TNF inhibitor biologics can be used throughout pregnancy after an individual risk-benefit assessment, and other biologics may be used if needed.

For breastfeeding, compatible drugs include antimalarials, azathioprine, colchicine, cyclosporine, glucocorticoids, IVIG, NSAIDs, sulfasalazine and tacrolimus, and all biologics are considered compatible.

items.title: Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for prevention, screening and treatment of peripartum depression
items.summary: This guideline pulled together 145 systematic reviews to make recommendations on preventing, screening for and treating depression during pregnancy and after birth. It recommends talking-based support for prevention, screening for depression in pregnancy and postpartum, and cognitive-behavioural therapy for treatment. Antidepressant medication is recommended for severe depression in pregnancy. Treatment choices should weigh severity, past history, risks and benefits for mother and baby, and the woman's own preferences.
keyPoints: Psychological and psychosocial support is strongly recommended to prevent depression in women with no symptoms and in women at higher risk.
Depression screening is strongly recommended during pregnancy and after birth.
Cognitive-behavioural therapy is strongly recommended for treating mild to severe peripartum depression.
Antidepressant medication is strongly recommended for severe depression in pregnancy, and electroconvulsive therapy for treatment-resistant or life-threatening severe depression.

items.title: Evaluation of the evidence on acetaminophen use and neurodevelopmental disorders using the Navigation Guide methodology
items.summary: This systematic review looked at 46 studies on paracetamol (acetaminophen) use in pregnancy and later neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism and ADHD in children. Most of the studies (27) found a link between use in pregnancy and these conditions, 9 found no link and 4 found a possible protective effect. The authors concluded the evidence is consistent with an association and suggested pregnant women be advised to limit use. The abstract does not say that paracetamol causes these conditions, and the studies varied a lot, so results were summarised in words rather than combined into one number.
keyPoints: Of 46 studies, 27 reported a link between paracetamol use in pregnancy and autism, ADHD or other neurodevelopmental conditions, 9 found no link and 4 found a protective effect.
Higher-quality studies were more likely to report a link.
The studies differed a lot, so the authors summarised them in words rather than pooling the results.
The authors conclude the evidence is consistent with an association and recommend advising pregnant women to limit paracetamol use.

items.title: Maternal paracetamol (acetaminophen) use during pregnancy and risk of autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder in offspring: umbrella review of systematic reviews
items.summary: This review looked at nine earlier systematic reviews (covering 40 studies) on whether taking paracetamol (acetaminophen) in pregnancy is linked to autism or ADHD in children. The reviews reported possible to strong links, but most warned that bias and other factors could explain them, and confidence in their findings was low to critically low. In the two studies that compared siblings, which better account for family factors, the small increased risks seen in the wider groups disappeared. The authors concluded that existing evidence does not clearly link paracetamol use in pregnancy with autism or ADHD.
keyPoints: Nine systematic reviews were assessed; seven of them advised caution because of possible bias and confounding.
Confidence in the reviews' findings was low (two reviews) or critically low (seven reviews).
In sibling-controlled studies, the small increased risks for autism and ADHD seen in whole-group analyses did not persist.
Overall, existing evidence does not clearly link paracetamol use in pregnancy with autism or ADHD.

items.title: Benefits and Risks of Antidepressant Drugs During Pregnancy: A Systematic Review of Meta-analyses
items.summary: This review looked at 51 meta-analyses (studies that combine the results of many other studies) on antidepressant use during pregnancy. It found some increased risks, including birth defects with certain antidepressants, preterm birth and short-term problems in newborns, but the effects were mostly small. The quality of the underlying evidence was low, partly because it is hard to separate the effect of the medicine from the effect of the depression itself. Almost no studies looked at the benefits of taking antidepressants.
keyPoints: Evidence showed higher risks of major birth defects with some antidepressants (paroxetine and fluoxetine), but not with sertraline, and of heart defects, preterm birth, newborn adaptation symptoms and a lung condition in newborns.
For stillbirth, miscarriage, low birthweight and autism, the evidence was limited or inconclusive, and no increased risk was found for gestational hypertension, preeclampsia or ADHD.
Only one analysis looked at benefits, finding limited evidence that antidepressants help prevent relapse in severe or recurrent depression.
The authors suggest antidepressants be a second-line option in pregnancy after psychotherapy, and that paroxetine and fluoxetine be avoided where guidelines advise.

items.title: Analgesic drug use in pregnancy and neurodevelopment outcomes: an umbrella review
items.summary: This study pulled together five existing systematic reviews on painkiller use in pregnancy and later autism and ADHD in children. All five found that taking acetaminophen (paracetamol) in pregnancy was linked to a slightly higher chance of ADHD in the child, and the link may grow with higher doses. The reviews could not show that the medicine itself causes ADHD, and results varied depending on when and how much was taken. The authors suggest keeping use during pregnancy to a minimum.
keyPoints: All five reviews found a link between acetaminophen use in pregnancy and ADHD in children, with risk ratios from 1.08 to 1.34.
There may be a dose-dependent pattern, meaning more use was linked to higher risk.
Differences in timing and dose of use may explain some variation between studies.
The authors suggest minimising acetaminophen exposure in pregnancy and call for more research on how it might affect development.

items.title: Pain management for medical abortion before 14 weeks' gestation
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at ways to ease pain during medical abortion (mifepristone plus misoprostol) before 14 weeks. It found five studies, which were too different to combine. One study found that a high dose of ibuprofen probably reduced pain more than paracetamol. Most other findings came from small studies with low or very low certainty.
keyPoints: In one trial of 108 women, ibuprofen 1600 mg probably lowered pain scores by about 2 points out of 10 more than paracetamol 2000 mg (moderate-certainty evidence).
Paracetamol did not appear to cause more side effects or make the abortion less likely to be complete, but it eased pain less than ibuprofen 1600 mg.
Pregabalin 300 mg and ibuprofen 800 mg showed little to no clear pain benefit over placebo, and walking around or resting made little difference to pain (low to very low certainty).
Most results were low or very low certainty because studies were small and two had a high risk of bias; larger, high-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (single dose) for perineal pain in the early postpartum period
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether a single dose of an anti-inflammatory painkiller (NSAID, such as ibuprofen-type medicines) helps with perineal pain in the first days after birth. It combined 35 trials with over 5,000 women, none of whom were breastfeeding. NSAIDs may give better pain relief than a placebo or paracetamol, and fewer women needed extra pain medicine. The evidence is mostly low or very low certainty, so the findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: Compared with placebo, more women had adequate pain relief at four hours with a single NSAID dose (low-certainty evidence).
Fewer women needed extra pain relief after an NSAID than after placebo (moderate-certainty at four hours).
NSAIDs may give more pain relief than paracetamol at four hours (low-certainty evidence).
Side effects were not clearly different from placebo, but many studies did not check them, and effects on babies and breastfeeding were not studied.

items.title: Paracetamol/acetaminophen (single administration) for perineal pain in the early postpartum period
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether a single dose of paracetamol (acetaminophen) eases pain around the vaginal opening and perineum in the first days after childbirth. It pooled 10 placebo-controlled trials, using data from 1301 women. More women had pain relief with paracetamol than with placebo, and fewer needed extra pain medicine. The trials were old (1970s to early 1990s) and the evidence was rated low certainty.
keyPoints: A single dose of paracetamol may give more women pain relief after vaginal birth than placebo.
Fewer women taking paracetamol may need additional pain relief.
There may be little or no difference in nausea or sleepiness, but this came from only one trial.
Side effects in babies were not studied, and the evidence is low certainty because the trials were old and varied.

items.title: Associations Between Maternal Depression, Antidepressant Use During Pregnancy, and Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes: An Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled data on more than 400,000 women to look at depression and antidepressant use in pregnancy. Depression itself was linked to a higher chance of preterm birth and low Apgar scores (a quick health check of newborns), even in women who took no antidepressants. SSRIs, a common type of antidepressant, may also be linked to preterm birth and low Apgar scores on their own. The study shows associations, so it cannot prove that depression or SSRIs caused these outcomes.
keyPoints: Depression or a depression diagnosis during pregnancy was linked to preterm birth, even without antidepressant use.
Women with depression who did not use antidepressants had higher odds of preterm birth (OR 2.2).
SSRI use was linked to preterm birth and, in some groups, low Apgar scores.
The authors conclude SSRIs may be independently associated with these outcomes.

items.title: Environmental risk factors, protective factors, and peripheral biomarkers for ADHD: an umbrella review
items.summary: This review pulled together results from 35 earlier reviews to see which environmental factors and blood markers are linked to ADHD in children. Several pregnancy-related factors were linked to a higher chance of ADHD, including paracetamol (acetaminophen) use during pregnancy. These are links seen in observational studies, which cannot show cause and effect, and the authors say more high-quality studies are needed to work out causality.
keyPoints: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) use during pregnancy was linked to a modestly higher chance of ADHD (relative risk 1.25), and this evidence was rated convincing for an association.
Other factors linked to ADHD included maternal pre-pregnancy obesity, high blood pressure in pregnancy, pre-eclampsia and smoking during pregnancy.
Earlier family studies suggest that links for pre-pregnancy obesity, overweight and smoking may be partly explained by shared family or genetic factors.
The authors conclude that further high-quality studies are needed to establish whether these factors actually cause ADHD.

items.title: Relief of pain due to uterine cramping/involution after birth
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 28 trials (2749 women) testing pain relief for cramping pains after a vaginal birth, which happen as the womb shrinks back to its usual size. Anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen-type medicines) probably worked better than a dummy pill and better than opioid painkillers for pain relief. The evidence for paracetamol, herbal remedies and TENS (a nerve-stimulation device) was too weak to draw conclusions. Many trials left out breastfeeding women, so the results may not apply to everyone.
keyPoints: NSAIDs probably give better pain relief than placebo and than opioids (moderate-certainty evidence).
NSAIDs may reduce the need for extra pain relief compared with placebo, with a similar risk of side effects for the mother.
Opioids may work better than placebo but may cause more side effects.
Paracetamol, herbal remedies and TENS could not be judged because the evidence was very low certainty.

items.title: Depression, Antidepressants and Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 20 studies to see whether depression, or taking antidepressants, is linked to high blood pressure conditions in pregnancy (such as gestational hypertension and preeclampsia). Most studies found some link for both depression and antidepressant use. The authors say this is only a possible association and that more research is needed, so it cannot show that either one causes high blood pressure.
keyPoints: Of 10 studies on depression and pregnancy-related high blood pressure, 8 found a significant association.
Of 10 studies on antidepressant medicines, 9 found an association with high blood pressure in pregnancy, to varying degrees.
The authors conclude there is a possible association, but further studies are needed.

items.title: Environmental risk factors and biomarkers for autism spectrum disorder: an umbrella review of the evidence
items.summary: This review pulled together many studies to see which factors before and during pregnancy are linked to autism in children. Several maternal factors were convincingly linked, including age 35 or over, high blood pressure, pre-eclampsia, being overweight, and antidepressant use. SSRI antidepressant use in pregnancy was linked to higher autism risk, but the authors say other factors may explain this. Antidepressant use before pregnancy was also linked, which suggests the mother's underlying mental health condition may play a part.
keyPoints: Maternal age 35 or over, chronic or gestational high blood pressure, pre-eclampsia and being overweight were convincingly linked to autism in children.
SSRI use during pregnancy was linked to higher autism risk (odds ratio 1.84), as was antidepressant use before pregnancy (relative risk 1.48).
The authors say the SSRI link could be affected by confounding factors, such as the mother's underlying psychiatric disorder.
These are observational findings, so they show links, not proof of cause.

items.title: Recommendations of the Polish Psychiatric Association for treatment of affective disorders in women of childbearing age. Part I: Treatment of depression
items.summary: This is a clinical guideline from the Polish Psychiatric Association on treating depression in women who could become pregnant. It covers common situations: being on antidepressants and planning or discovering a pregnancy, becoming depressed during pregnancy, postpartum depression, and taking antidepressants while breastfeeding. It is based on current international standards and expert agreement, and it includes information on how safe different antidepressants are.
keyPoints: Doctors treating depression in women of childbearing age should openly discuss sexuality and the chance of becoming pregnant.
The guideline covers antidepressant use when planning pregnancy, during pregnancy, after birth and while breastfeeding.
Recommendations are based on worldwide standards and expert consensus, not a single trial.
It includes data on the safety of antidepressants to help guide treatment choices.

items.title: International Society for Nutritional Psychiatry Research Practice Guidelines for Omega-3 Fatty Acids in the Treatment of Major Depressive Disorder
items.source: International Society for Nutritional Psychiatry Research
items.organisation: International Society for Nutritional Psychiatry Research
items.summary: An international expert panel reviewed the research and used a consensus process to write practice guidelines for using omega-3 fatty acids to treat major depression. They found that omega-3 products high in EPA (rather than DHA) are considered effective, at about 1-2 g of EPA a day. The panel agreed omega-3s can be used for depression in pregnant women, children and older adults, and for prevention in people at high risk. This is expert consensus guidance, and the abstract does not give a certainty rating for the evidence.
keyPoints: Omega-3 products that are pure EPA, or EPA/DHA with more than twice as much EPA as DHA, are considered effective for depression.
The recommended dose is 1-2 g of EPA per day.
Product quality may affect how well omega-3s work, and side effects such as stomach or skin problems should be monitored.
The panel agreed omega-3s can be used to treat depression in pregnant women, as well as children and the elderly.

items.title: Prenatal Exposure to Acetaminophen and Risk for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder and Autistic Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression Analysis of Cohort Studies
items.summary: This review pooled seven large observational studies covering about 132,000 mother-child pairs to look at paracetamol (acetaminophen) use in pregnancy and later ADHD and autism in children. Children whose mothers took paracetamol in pregnancy had a somewhat higher chance of ADHD, autism and hyperactivity symptoms. The authors stress that these studies only show an association, not that paracetamol caused the conditions, and the results could be affected by bias.
keyPoints: Pooled risk was about 34% higher for ADHD, 19% higher for autism and 24% higher for hyperactivity symptoms in children exposed before birth.
The link with ADHD looked stronger with longer follow-up of the child and with longer duration of paracetamol use.
All the studies were observational, and they measured exposure and outcomes in very different ways.
The authors say the findings are concerning but should be read with caution because of possible bias.

items.title: Screening for Depression in Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence on screening adults for depression, including pregnant and postpartum women. It recommends that all adults 18 and over be screened for depression, including during pregnancy and after birth. Screening works best when there are systems in place to confirm the diagnosis, offer effective treatment and follow up.
keyPoints: Screening for depression is recommended for the general adult population (B recommendation).
The recommendation specifically includes pregnant and postpartum women.
Screening should come with systems for accurate diagnosis, effective treatment and follow-up.

items.title: Safety of GLP-1 and Dual GLP-1/GIP Receptor Agonists in Preconception, Pregnancy, and Lactation: A Systematic Review of Maternal, Fetal, and Neonatal Outcomes
items.summary: This review pooled 36 human studies on GLP-1 medicines (such as semaglutide) used before pregnancy, during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Large studies did not consistently show more birth defects, poor fetal growth, stillbirth or newborn deaths compared with women using insulin or with similar health conditions. Information on breastfeeding is very limited: one small study found no semaglutide in breast milk. Data on using these medicines throughout the whole pregnancy are still limited.
keyPoints: Exposure around conception or in early pregnancy was not consistently linked to more major birth defects, poor fetal growth, stillbirth or newborn death.
Maternal outcomes such as gestational diabetes, high blood pressure in pregnancy, preterm birth and weight gain varied between studies, with no repeatable safety warning.
Lactation data were sparse; one study found no detectable semaglutide in human milk.
Evidence on continued use throughout pregnancy remains limited.

items.title: Hidradenitis Suppurativa Treatment During Pregnancy and Lactation: Navigating Challenges
items.summary: This systematic review looked at how to treat hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), a painful, long-term skin condition affecting skin folds, during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Several treatments have some evidence suggesting they are relatively safe in pregnancy and while breastfeeding. The review found very little research in this group, so more studies are needed on safety and how well treatments work.
keyPoints: Topical clindamycin, oral clindamycin-rifampicin, adalimumab, metformin, antiseptic washes and certolizumab pegol have evidence supporting relative safety in pregnant and breastfeeding women.
Certolizumab pegol has promising safety data among biologics, but more data is needed on how well it works for HS.
Newer HS medicines secukinumab and bimekizumab show promise in the general population, but their safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding still needs study.
HS flares are widely reported during pregnancy and after birth, and there is little research on managing it in these times.

items.title: Performance of Diagnostic Breast Imaging in Symptomatic Pregnant and Lactating Patients: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 25 studies (1,681 women) to see how well breast imaging finds cancer in pregnant or breastfeeding women who have breast symptoms. Ultrasound, mammography and breast MRI all performed well. Only a few studies had complete data for each test, so the exact numbers are uncertain.
keyPoints: Ultrasound correctly picked up about 81% of cancers and correctly cleared about 85% of women without cancer.
Mammography picked up about 72% of cancers and correctly cleared about 93% of women without cancer.
Breast MRI picked up about 91% of cancers and correctly cleared about 88% of women without cancer.
The authors concluded that all three tests showed high diagnostic performance in symptomatic pregnant or lactating women.

items.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Therapeutic Interventions in Pregnancy and Lactation-Associated Osteoporosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This review looked at treatments for pregnancy and lactation-associated osteoporosis, a rare condition where bones become weak during pregnancy or breastfeeding. It gathered 66 studies covering 451 women. Bone density went up with calcium and vitamin D, with bisphosphonates and with teriparatide. In two trials teriparatide raised bone density more than calcium and vitamin D, but the studies differed a lot and there was little direct comparison, so the best treatment is still unclear.
keyPoints: Bone density in the lower spine rose by about 2% to 7.5% with calcium and vitamin D, 5% to 41.5% with bisphosphonates, and 8% to 24.4% with teriparatide after 12 months.
In two trials, teriparatide raised spine and hip bone density more than calcium and vitamin D.
The studies were very different from each other and had few direct comparisons between treatments.
The authors conclude that no safe conclusions can be made about the best treatment for these women.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of domperidone and metoclopramide on human milk production in postpartum mothers: a bayesian network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This study pooled results from 17 randomized trials to compare two medicines, domperidone and metoclopramide, that are sometimes used to boost breast milk supply after birth. In mothers of preterm babies, domperidone increased daily milk volume more than metoclopramide or placebo (a dummy pill). In mothers who gave birth at term, domperidone did not show a clear benefit, and metoclopramide was no better than placebo in either group. The studies were small, so the findings are limited.
keyPoints: Domperidone increased daily breast milk volume in mothers of preterm infants compared with metoclopramide or placebo.
In mothers who delivered at term, domperidone showed no clear benefit over metoclopramide or placebo.
Metoclopramide was no better than placebo for milk volume in either preterm or term mothers.
Rates of drug-related side effects were similar for domperidone, metoclopramide and placebo.

items.title: Effects of maternal probiotic supplementation on breast milk microbiome and infant gut microbiome and health: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology MFM
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology MFM
items.summary: This review pooled 24 randomised trials (2,761 mothers and 1,756 babies) to see whether probiotic supplements taken by mothers during pregnancy or breastfeeding change the bacteria in breast milk and in the baby's gut. Probiotics increased helpful bacteria and reduced harmful bacteria in breast milk, and increased helpful bacteria in babies' guts. Babies whose mothers took probiotics also had less infant colic and slightly lower weight gain. The authors concluded probiotics were safe and beneficial, but results varied a lot between studies.
keyPoints: Maternal probiotics raised the detection and amount of beneficial bacteria in breast milk and lowered pathogenic bacteria.
Babies had more beneficial bacteria in their gut when mothers took probiotics.
Infant colic was less likely (risk ratio 0.30) and weight gain was somewhat lower.
The authors say Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Streptococcus thermophilus and S. boulardii could be used as maternal supplements to promote infant health.

items.title: Breastfeeding and Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) Vaccination: Position Statement of Indian Academy of Pediatrics Advisory Committee on Vaccination and Immunization Practices
items.summary: The Indian Academy of Pediatrics reviewed the evidence on COVID-19 vaccines for women who are breastfeeding. They recommend that all breastfeeding women can have a COVID-19 vaccine. They also support the Indian government's decision to treat breastfeeding women as eligible for vaccination.
keyPoints: The Indian Academy of Pediatrics recommends COVID-19 vaccines for all breastfeeding women.
Breastfeeding women are now considered eligible for COVID-19 vaccination in India.
The advice is based on a review of studies on vaccine safety and efficacy in breastfeeding women and on other national and international recommendations.
The statement was agreed by consensus among the academy's vaccination committee members.

items.title: Pregnancy- and lactation-associated osteoporosis with vertebral fractures: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 338 reported cases of a rare condition in which bones weaken and the spine fractures during pregnancy or breastfeeding. It found the condition is rare and seems more likely in older and thinner women. Back pain was the main symptom, usually starting in the last 3 months of pregnancy or the first 3 months after birth. Bisphosphonates were the most widely used medicine, but the review says more research is needed before clear treatment advice can be given.
keyPoints: Pregnancy- and lactation-associated osteoporosis with spinal fractures is rare and more likely in older and thinner pregnant women.
Back pain was the main symptom, and up to 91.5% of cases began in the last 3 months of pregnancy or first 3 months after delivery.
Most cases had several spinal fractures (about 4 on average), mainly in the lower back and mid-to-lower spine, and most happened in a first pregnancy.
Bisphosphonates were the most commonly used treatment, but many factors affect drug choice and clearer recommendations need more studies.

items.title: Maternal plasma levels of oxytocin during breastfeeding-A systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 29 small studies (601 women) on how the hormone oxytocin rises when a mother breastfeeds. Oxytocin is released in short bursts during feeding, helps milk flow, and is linked to lower stress and anxiety. Stress and some birth interventions, such as emergency caesarean section and epidural pain relief, were linked to weaker hormone responses, which may affect how breastfeeding gets started.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding triggers a short release of oxytocin lasting about 20 minutes, which causes milk ejection.
More oxytocin pulses early on were linked to more milk and longer breastfeeding, and stress reduced the pulses.
Emergency caesarean section reduced oxytocin and prolactin release, and epidural pain relief reduced prolactin and the mother's mental adaptation.
Synthetic oxytocin infusions increased prolactin and mental adaptation and restored the negative effects linked to caesarean section and epidural.

items.title: The effect of mother-infant skin to skin contact on success and duration of first breastfeeding: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine trials (about 1,150 mothers and babies) to see whether holding the baby skin to skin right after birth helps the first breastfeed. Babies who had skin to skin contact were more likely to breastfeed successfully the first time, and the first feed lasted longer. The authors say healthcare providers can use these results when thinking about ways to support breastfeeding.
keyPoints: Skin to skin contact right after birth made a successful first breastfeed more likely.
The first breastfeeding session lasted longer with skin to skin contact.
The review combined nine randomized trials with 1,150 mothers and babies in total.
Starting breastfeeding within the first half hour after birth is a World Health Organization recommendation.

items.title: European task force on atopic dermatitis position paper: treatment of parental atopic dermatitis during preconception, pregnancy and lactation period
items.source: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology
items.journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology
items.summary: A group of European skin specialists wrote a position paper on treating atopic dermatitis (eczema) in adults who are planning a baby, pregnant or breastfeeding. They based it on published research and expert opinion, using safety data that often comes from people with other inflammatory conditions or from transplant medicine. They judged moisturisers, steroid creams, tacrolimus, certain antiseptic washes and UV light therapy to be safe options. Tablets or injections that act on the whole body should only be started after careful thought.
keyPoints: Moisturizers, topical corticosteroids and tacrolimus are considered safe for future parents and for pregnant and breastfeeding women with atopic dermatitis.
Antiseptics such as chlorhexidine, octenidine, potassium permanganate and bleach (sodium hypochlorite) are also considered safe.
Ultraviolet (UV) therapy may be used.
Treatments that work on the whole body should be prescribed only after careful consideration, and limited to systemic corticosteroids, cyclosporine A and, in selected cases, azathioprine.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 723 Summary: Guidelines for Diagnostic Imaging During Pregnancy and Lactation
items.summary: This guideline looks at whether imaging tests such as ultrasound, MRI, X-ray, CT scans and nuclear medicine scans are safe during pregnancy and while breastfeeding. It says confusion about safety often leads to useful tests being avoided or breastfeeding being stopped without need. Ultrasound and MRI are not linked to risk and are the first choices in pregnancy, and the radiation dose from most other scans is much lower than the level linked to harm to a baby.
keyPoints: Ultrasound and MRI are not associated with risk and are the imaging techniques of choice in pregnancy, used only when they help answer a medical question.
With few exceptions, X-ray, CT and nuclear medicine scans use radiation doses far below those linked to fetal harm, so they should not be withheld if needed.
Breastfeeding should not be interrupted after gadolinium (MRI contrast) is given.
Worry about safety often causes unnecessary avoidance of tests or unnecessary pauses in breastfeeding.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 656: Guidelines for Diagnostic Imaging During Pregnancy and Lactation
items.summary: This guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists looks at how safe medical imaging is during pregnancy and breastfeeding. It says ultrasound and MRI are not linked to risk and are the first choices in pregnancy. X-rays, CT scans and nuclear medicine scans usually use a dose far below the level linked to harm to a baby, so they should not be withheld when needed. Breastfeeding does not need to stop after gadolinium contrast is given.
keyPoints: Ultrasound and MRI are not associated with risk and are the imaging methods of choice in pregnancy, used only when they help answer a medical question.
With few exceptions, radiation from X-ray, CT or nuclear medicine imaging is much lower than the dose linked to fetal harm, so these tests should not be withheld if needed.
Breastfeeding should not be interrupted after gadolinium contrast is given.
Confusion about safety often leads to unnecessary avoidance of useful tests or unnecessary stopping of breastfeeding.

items.title: Effect of restricted pacifier use in breastfeeding term infants for increasing duration of breastfeeding
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether limiting dummy (pacifier) use helps healthy full-term babies keep breastfeeding for longer. Two trials with 1,302 babies suggest that using a pacifier probably makes no real difference to how many babies were exclusively or partly breastfed at three or four months. There was not enough evidence on breastfeeding problems like sore nipples or on longer-term effects on baby's health.
keyPoints: Pacifier use did not significantly change the share of babies exclusively breastfed at 3 or 4 months.
Pacifier use did not change the share of babies partly breastfed at 3 or 4 months.
This held whether the pacifier was started from birth or after breastfeeding was well established.
Evidence on breastfeeding difficulties and long-term infant health effects is lacking.

items.title: Sertraline and breastfeeding: review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at published studies and some new data on sertraline, an antidepressant, taken by breastfeeding mothers. In most breastfed babies tested, sertraline could not be detected in the blood at all. The authors conclude sertraline is a first-line medicine for breastfeeding women because babies are exposed to very little and few side effects have been reported.
keyPoints: Of 167 infant blood tests for sertraline, 146 (87.4%) were below the level that can be detected.
Most infant blood levels of its breakdown product, desmethylsertraline, were also undetectable (70.0%), and this product has only a fraction of sertraline's activity.
Sertraline is described as a first-line drug for breastfeeding women, with very few adverse events reported in case reports.
Routine blood tests or genetic testing for mothers or infants are not needed; routine pediatric care is enough monitoring for babies of mothers taking sertraline alone.

items.title: Methods of milk expression for lactating women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 34 trials of different ways to express (pump or hand-express) breast milk, though only 17 trials gave usable data. The best method seems to depend on the mother and baby and how long since birth. Some low-cost approaches, like starting early, relaxation music, breast massage, warming the breasts and hand expression, may work as well as or better than large electric pumps for some outcomes. The authors urge caution because the studies were small and very different from one another.
keyPoints: Starting to pump within 60 minutes of birth of a very low birthweight baby gave more milk in the first week than starting later.
Relaxation tapes or music, warming the breasts before pumping, and massage during pumping were linked to greater milk volume for mothers of babies in neonatal units.
No difference was found in milk contamination or in breast or nipple pain between the methods compared.
Small studies, wide variation and manufacturer support for many pump trials mean the results should be applied with caution.

items.title: Ibuprofen — Drugs and Lactation Database (LactMed®)
items.source: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
items.journal: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
items.summary: This entry from LactMed, the US National Library of Medicine's database on medicines and breastfeeding, covers ibuprofen. Very little ibuprofen passes into breast milk, it leaves the body quickly, and babies are safely given much higher doses than they could get through milk, so it is a preferred painkiller and anti-inflammatory for breastfeeding mothers. Taking ibuprofen and paracetamol (acetaminophen) on a fixed schedule for 24 hours after a vaginal birth appears to increase breastfeeding rates.
keyPoints: Ibuprofen levels in breast milk are extremely low and it has a short half-life.
Ibuprofen is a preferred choice for pain or inflammation while breastfeeding.
Fixed-schedule ibuprofen plus paracetamol for 24 hours after vaginal birth appears to increase the breastfeeding rate.
Breastfeeding initiation did not differ between ibuprofen alone and paracetamol alone.

items.title: Acetaminophen — Drugs and Lactation Database (LactMed®)
items.source: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
items.journal: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
items.summary: This entry from LactMed, the US National Library of Medicine's database on medicines and breastfeeding, covers paracetamol (acetaminophen). It is described as a good choice for pain relief and fever in breastfeeding mothers. The amounts that reach breast milk are much smaller than the doses usually given to babies, and side effects in breastfed babies appear to be rare.
keyPoints: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is a good choice for pain and fever while breastfeeding.
Amounts in milk are much less than doses usually given to infants.
Adverse effects in breastfed infants appear to be rare.
Fixed-schedule paracetamol plus ibuprofen for 24 hours after vaginal birth appears to increase the breastfeeding rate.

items.title: Naproxen — Drugs and Lactation Database (LactMed®)
items.source: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
items.journal: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
items.summary: This entry from LactMed, the US National Library of Medicine's database on medicines and breastfeeding, covers naproxen. Limited information shows that naproxen levels in breast milk are low and side effects in breastfed babies seem uncommon. Because naproxen stays in the body a long time and one serious reaction was reported in a breastfed newborn, other painkillers may be preferred while feeding a newborn or premature baby.
keyPoints: Limited information indicates naproxen levels in breast milk are low.
Adverse effects in breastfed infants are apparently uncommon.
Because of its long half-life and a reported serious reaction in a newborn, other medicines may be preferred while nursing a newborn or preterm baby.

items.title: Cognitive Training During Midlife: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 19 studies (7,765 people) on brain-training exercises in healthy middle-aged adults, including women going through the menopause transition. In the combined analysis of eight studies, brain training was linked to better executive function, verbal memory and working memory straight after training. The authors suggest it may help support thinking skills in midlife, including during menopause. The abstract does not say how long the benefits last or rate the quality of the evidence.
keyPoints: Brain training was linked to improved executive function (planning and mental flexibility) in middle-aged adults.
Verbal memory and working memory also improved, though by smaller amounts.
The review covered 19 studies with 7,765 people; eight studies went into the combined analysis.
The authors suggest brain training may help thinking skills in midlife, including in women during the menopause transition.

items.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of menopause hormone therapy on cognition
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 34 randomized trials (about 27,000 women) to see whether menopause hormone therapy affects memory and thinking. Overall, hormone therapy did not change cognitive scores, but some effects depended on the type of hormones, when treatment started and how long it lasted. The authors say results were mixed and more research with larger, more consistent studies is needed.
keyPoints: Overall, menopause hormone therapy had no effect on cognitive domain scores.
Women who had surgical menopause and took mostly estrogen-only therapy showed better global cognition than those on placebo.
Estrogen started in midlife or near menopause was linked to better verbal memory, while starting in late life had no effect.
Estrogen-progestogen therapy for spontaneous menopause was linked to lower MMSE scores, mostly in studies of older women, and treatment longer than 1 year was linked to worse visual memory.

items.title: Association between testosterone and cognitive performance in postmenopausal women: a systematic review of observational studies
items.summary: This review looked at whether natural testosterone levels in the blood are linked to thinking and memory in women after menopause. It pulled together 10 observational studies of women living in the community. Most found no link, but some found positive links and some found negative ones. The authors say the results are inconclusive because testosterone was measured imprecisely and the studies used very different methods.
keyPoints: Ten observational studies of postmenopausal women were included.
Most studies found no link between total or free testosterone and cognitive performance.
A few studies reported positive links and others negative links, for example with overall thinking ability and word recall.
The findings are inconclusive because testosterone tests were imprecise and the studies differed a lot in design and cognitive tests.

items.title: Effect of dehydroepiandrosterone therapy on cognitive performance among postmenopausal women: a systematic review of randomized clinical trial data
items.summary: This review looked at whether taking DHEA supplements, which are sold over the counter in some countries, improves thinking and memory in women after menopause. Only four small randomized trials met the criteria, all using 50 mg by mouth each day. Only one short trial found a benefit, in some visual-spatial tests, and the others found none. Overall, the review does not support DHEA as a way to improve thinking skills, and the studies had a high risk of bias.
keyPoints: Four randomized trials of 50 mg daily DHEA were included.
Only one 4-week trial of 24 women showed better visual-spatial test results than placebo.
No other study showed a cognitive benefit from DHEA compared with placebo.
The studies were different from each other and had a high risk of bias, so results could not be pooled.

items.title: Systematic review and narrative synthesis of cognition in perimenopause: The role of risk factors and menopausal symptoms
items.summary: This review pulled together 33 studies on thinking and memory during perimenopause, the years leading up to the final period. It looked at how thinking skills relate to menopause symptoms and to other factors such as lifestyle, income and reproductive history. Many factors were linked to memory and thinking, and hot flushes, mood changes and poor sleep were also linked to thinking difficulties. The authors describe the picture as complex rather than a single simple cause.
keyPoints: Many women report memory and thinking concerns during the menopause transition, and tests show declines in some thinking skills for some women.
The review found links between thinking skills and demographic, socio-economic, lifestyle and reproductive factors.
Hot flushes and night sweats, mood symptoms and sleep problems were each linked to thinking difficulties.
The authors describe a complex relationship, with both direct and indirect effects of risk and protective factors on thinking during menopause.

items.title: The effect of hormone replacement therapy on cognitive function in healthy postmenopausal women: a meta-analysis of 23 randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from 23 randomized trials of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in healthy women after menopause, looking at thinking and memory. Overall, HRT was linked to a very small decline in global cognition. The small decline was seen mainly in women older than 60 and in those who used HRT for more than 6 months. The authors say more trials are needed in younger women and with short-term HRT use.
keyPoints: Across 23 randomized trials, HRT had a small negative effect on global cognition (SMD -0.04).
The effect was clearer in women older than 60 and in those taking HRT for more than 6 months.
After adjusting for age or length of treatment, the link between HRT and cognition was no longer significant.
More trials in younger women and with short-term HRT are needed to clarify the effects.

items.title: Mediterranean diet and health: A systematic review of epidemiological studies and intervention trials
items.summary: This review looked at studies on the Mediterranean diet and long-term health, including observational studies and randomised trials. It found the diet generally had a favourable effect on heart health, blood pressure, cholesterol, weight, diabetes and some cancers. It also showed benefits for brain function, including thinking skills (cognition) and mood. The authors note the quality of the evidence was mostly moderate or low, so more good-quality research is needed.
keyPoints: The Mediterranean diet showed a general protective effect against cardiovascular disease and related risk factors such as blood pressure, lipids, obesity and diabetes.
Benefits were also found for several types of cancer and for overall mortality.
Brain benefits were seen for cognition and mood, and to a lesser extent Parkinson's disease.
The quality of the published evidence was generally moderate or low, and more high-quality research is needed.

items.title: Surgical menopause in association with cognitive function and risk of dementia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 11 studies (almost 19,000 women) on menopause caused by surgically removing both ovaries before natural menopause. Women who had this surgery at 45 or younger had a higher risk of dementia and faster memory decline later in life. Surgery at any age was not clearly linked to dementia, though it was linked to faster decline in some memory and thinking-speed skills. The authors say the evidence is limited and more large studies are needed.
keyPoints: Surgical menopause at any age was not clearly linked to dementia risk overall.
Surgical menopause at age 45 or younger was linked to a higher dementia risk (based on 2 studies).
Surgical menopause was linked to faster decline in verbal memory, semantic memory and processing speed.
Among women who had the surgery, a younger age at surgery went with faster cognitive decline.

items.title: Prevalence of aromatase inhibitor-induced arthralgia in breast cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 21 studies (13,177 women) to see how often joint pain happens with aromatase inhibitors, hormone-blocking medicines used after menopause for hormone-sensitive breast cancer. About 46 in 100 women (pooled estimate 45.9%) had this joint pain, though results varied a lot between studies. Some factors were linked to higher or lower risk, such as earlier taxane chemotherapy and body weight. The authors say more research is needed on treatments like exercise.
keyPoints: Joint pain (arthralgia) was reported by about 46% of women taking aromatase inhibitors, with individual studies ranging from 20% to 74%.
Results differed a great deal between studies (very high heterogeneity), so the true rate may vary.
Taxane-based chemotherapy was linked to higher risk of joint pain, while a body mass index of 25-30 and stage III cancer were linked to lower risk.
Joint pain is linked to women not sticking with treatment, and more research is needed on options such as exercise therapy.

items.title: Incidence of menopausal symptoms in postmenopausal breast cancer patients treated with aromatase inhibitors
items.summary: This study pooled results from many trials of postmenopausal women with breast cancer who took aromatase inhibitors, a common hormone-lowering treatment. Women on these drugs had a higher risk of joint pain and trouble sleeping than comparison groups. Hot flashes were the most common symptom, affecting roughly 3 in 10 women. The authors suggest that spotting and managing these symptoms early could make the treatment safer to use.
keyPoints: Women taking aromatase inhibitors had a higher risk of joint pain (risk ratio 1.63) and insomnia (risk ratio 1.24).
About 30% of women on these drugs had hot flashes, about 18% had joint pain, about 17% had insomnia, about 17% had fatigue and about 15% had sweating.
Joint pain and sweating differed between women with early-stage and advanced-stage breast cancer.
Early detection and management of menopausal symptoms may lead to safer use of these drugs.

items.title: Do soy isoflavones improve cognitive function in postmenopausal women? A meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 10 placebo-controlled trials (1,024 postmenopausal women) testing soy isoflavone supplements for thinking and memory. Overall, the supplements were linked to a small improvement in combined cognitive test scores and in visual memory. The benefit seemed larger in women under 60 and in treatment lasting under 12 months. The authors say longer follow-up and reporting of side effects are still needed.
keyPoints: Soy isoflavone supplements were linked to a small but statistically significant improvement in overall cognitive test scores (0.08) and visual memory (0.10).
Effects were clearer in women younger than 60 and in studies lasting less than 12 months.
Where studies were done and how long treatment lasted seemed to influence the results.
The authors call for follow-up of dementia rates and for future studies to report adverse effects.

items.title: Impact of sleep disturbances on health-related quality of life in postmenopausal women: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 57 studies published between 2013 and 2023 on sleep problems in women during and after the menopause transition. It found that sleep problems are very common after menopause, even in women who do not have hot flushes or night sweats. Poor sleep was linked to lower quality of life, including depression, anxiety and muscle and joint pain, and to less ability to work and do daily activities.
keyPoints: Sleep disturbances are highly common in postmenopausal women, including those without hot flushes or night sweats.
Risk factors included menopausal status, depression, vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes and night sweats), high glycemic index diets, and age.
Poor sleep was linked to worse quality of life, including depression, anxiety and musculoskeletal pain.
Poor sleep was also linked to reduced work productivity and difficulty with daily activities.

items.title: The effect of hormone replacement therapy on musculoskeletal pain in menopausal women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 57 studies and almost 4 million women to see whether hormone replacement therapy (HRT) eases muscle and joint pain around menopause. Overall, women who had ever used HRT had about the same amount of general muscle and joint pain as women who never had. For osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, the studies were too different to combine, and their results conflicted. The authors say more purpose-built studies are needed before firm conclusions can guide care.
keyPoints: Up to 70% of menopausal women report muscle and joint pain, and low oestrogen may play a role.
Ever using HRT versus never using it made no significant difference to general musculoskeletal pain (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.96-1.04).
Results for osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis were conflicting, and the studies varied too much to pool.
The authors conclude that specially designed studies are needed to say whether HRT helps musculoskeletal pain.

items.title: Integrative Lifestyle Strategies for Osteoarthritis Management in Post- Menopausal Women: Insights on Exercise and Diet
items.summary: This review looked at how exercise and diet might help manage osteoarthritis (joint wear-and-tear) in women after menopause. It found that aerobic and strength exercise can improve joint function and reduce pain, and that nutrients such as omega-3 fats, calcium and vitamin D may help ease inflammation. The authors describe a combined approach of targeted exercise, diet changes and hormonal balance as a promising, low-risk option. They also note gaps in public awareness and in how these approaches are put into practice.
keyPoints: Aerobic and resistance exercise improved joint function, reduced pain and affected inflammation markers.
Moderate-intensity exercise was described as especially effective for advanced osteoarthritis, while high-intensity exercise helped in early-stage disease.
Omega-3 fatty acids, calcium and vitamin D may help reduce inflammation and slow disease progression.
Awareness is low: 87% of women did not know about the link between menopause and osteoarthritis.

items.title: The effectiveness of psychosocial interventions on physiological symptoms of menopause: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 28 randomised trials (2,887 women) testing talking and behavioural approaches, such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), for menopause symptoms. These approaches made hot flushes and night sweats much less bothersome and clearly improved sleep and insomnia. They did not improve sexual functioning or urogenital symptoms. The abstract does not report a separate result for muscle or joint pain.
keyPoints: Psychosocial approaches, especially CBT, lowered how bothersome hot flushes and night sweats felt, with smaller effects on how often they happened or how severe they were.
Sleep quality and insomnia improved, with the largest effects seen for insomnia.
No improvement was found for sexual functioning or urogenital symptoms.
Women stayed in the programmes well (average retention about 87%), and the authors see these approaches as options alone or alongside medicines.

items.title: Long-Term Side Effects of Breast Cancer Treatments: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at studies of breast cancer survivors to see which side effects of treatment last at least a year or more. It found many long-term effects, including joint pain, bone thinning, tiredness, swelling in the arm, menopausal symptoms and low mood. Joint pain and osteoporosis were linked to endocrine (hormone-blocking) therapy. The authors call for ongoing monitoring, rehabilitation, lifestyle support and emotional support after treatment.
keyPoints: Endocrine therapy was linked to joint pain, osteoporosis and metabolic changes in survivors.
Menopausal symptoms, persistent fatigue, cognitive problems and psychological distress were also common long after treatment.
Chemotherapy was linked to nerve damage (peripheral neuropathy) and memory or thinking decline; surgery to remove lymph nodes was a main cause of lymphedema.
The authors recommend routine monitoring, personalised rehabilitation, lifestyle changes and psychosocial support in survivorship care.

items.title: Are there gender-specific differences in hip and knee cartilage composition and degeneration? A systematic literature review
items.source: European Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery & Traumatology
items.journal: European Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery & Traumatology
items.summary: This review pulled together 11 studies comparing knee and hip cartilage in women and men, mostly using MRI scans. Women generally had less cartilage than men, and the gap grew after menopause, when women lost cartilage faster. This helps explain why osteoarthritis (joint wear) affects women more often and more severely. The studies used quite different methods, so the findings come with some caution.
keyPoints: Men had significantly more knee and hip cartilage than women, and differences were seen from childhood onward.
After menopause, women had lower cartilage volume and greater cartilage loss.
Differences are partly explained by body and bone size, but also by differences in cartilage makeup and how fast it breaks down after menopause.
Women have a significantly higher risk of developing osteoarthritis than men.

items.title: Effects of physical exercise on muscle function of the knee, pain and quality of life in postmenopausal women with knee osteoarthritis: A systematic review with meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from five randomized trials of exercise in postmenopausal women with knee osteoarthritis. Exercise improved physical function, such as walking ability and the physical function score on a common knee questionnaire, compared with no exercise. It did not clearly reduce pain or stiffness. There was not enough data to judge effects on knee muscle function or quality of life, and the studies used very different tests, which made comparing them hard.
keyPoints: Exercise improved physical function in postmenopausal women with knee osteoarthritis, measured by the Six-Minute Walk Test and the WOMAC physical function score.
No significant differences in pain or stiffness were seen between exercise and comparison groups.
There was not enough data to combine results for knee muscle function or quality of life.
Only five trials were included, and differences in assessment tools limited the analysis.

items.title: Musculoskeletal Pain during the Menopausal Transition: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from 16 studies to look at how common muscle and joint pain is around the time of menopause. About 7 in 10 women in the menopausal transition (perimenopause) reported this kind of pain. Women in perimenopause were more likely to have it than women who had not yet started the transition, and about as likely as women after menopause. Moderate to severe pain was more likely after menopause than before it.
keyPoints: About 71% of perimenopausal women reported musculoskeletal (muscle and joint) pain across the studies reviewed.
Perimenopausal women had higher odds of this pain than premenopausal women, but similar odds to postmenopausal women.
Moderate to severe pain was more likely in postmenopausal women than in premenopausal or perimenopausal women.
The authors conclude perimenopause is a time when women are especially prone to developing this pain.

items.title: Are aquatic exercises efficacious in postmenopausal women with knee osteoarthritis? A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness
items.journal: Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness
items.summary: This review pooled six trials with 432 postmenopausal women who have knee osteoarthritis, comparing water-based exercise with no water exercise. Water exercise improved overall knee symptoms. It did not clearly improve pain, stiffness, physical function, daily activities, sport or quality of life. The authors say more research is needed because there is limited data.
keyPoints: Water-based exercise improved overall knee osteoarthritis symptoms in postmenopausal women.
No clear difference from the control group was found for pain, stiffness, function, daily activities, sport or quality of life.
This result differs from earlier reviews, which had suggested benefits.
Only six trials were included, so the authors say further research is needed.

items.title: Cognitive functioning in perimenopause: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 26 studies with 9,428 women to see how thinking and memory change around perimenopause. Women in perimenopause did worse on cognitive tests than women before menopause, but this was only seen in studies that used a standard method for sorting women into reproductive stages. Perimenopausal and postmenopausal women did not differ overall, and the researchers say results have been inconsistent because studies were set up differently.
keyPoints: Perimenopausal women had poorer cognitive results than premenopausal women, a moderate-sized difference.
This difference only appeared in studies that used the standard STRAW+10 staging criteria.
Overall, there was no difference between perimenopausal and postmenopausal women.
Compared with postmenopausal women, perimenopausal women did better on objective tasks (accuracy, reaction time) but tended to report slightly worse thinking themselves.

items.title: FIGO best practice recommendations for the mental health of women at menopausal age
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) reviewed the evidence on mental health around the menopause and issued best practice recommendations. Anxiety and low mood are common during perimenopause, and they can affect quality of life. Treatment can be tailored to the person and may include lifestyle changes, talking therapy, or medicines such as hormone therapy. Experts rated eight of the 13 questions as strong recommendations.
keyPoints: Symptoms of anxiety and depression are common during perimenopause, but menopause-related mental health problems are often overlooked, especially in low- and middle-income countries.
Primary care providers need training to spot symptoms early, and psychological support should be part of menopause care.

Treatment should be individualised and may include lifestyle changes, cognitive-behavioural therapy and hormone therapy; transdermal estradiol is preferred for mood swings, particularly in women with metabolic risks.
Escitalopram and venlafaxine help depressive symptoms and hot flushes in women with major depressive disorder, and mindfulness, exercise and therapy have shown benefits.

items.title: Testosterone therapy for cognition in menopause: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether testosterone treatment improves thinking and memory in women during and after menopause. Only five small studies were found, and three of them (244 postmenopausal women) could be combined. The combined results showed no clear effect on planning, verbal memory or visual memory. The authors say this means there isn't enough evidence to tell, rather than proof that testosterone has no effect.
keyPoints: Only five studies were eligible, and three (244 postmenopausal women) were pooled in the analysis.
No statistically significant effect of testosterone on executive function, verbal learning and memory, or visuospatial learning and memory; effects were mostly close to zero.
No studies looked at how women themselves felt about their thinking and memory, or at women in perimenopause.
The evidence is too limited to say either way, and larger trials are needed, especially during the menopause transition.

items.title: Epilepsy and menopausal health: A European Menopause and Andropause Society (EMAS) and Centre for Global Epilepsy clinical guide
items.summary: This clinical guide from a European menopause society and an epilepsy centre looks at how to care for women who have both epilepsy and menopause. Women with epilepsy may reach menopause earlier and are more likely to develop heart disease, weak bones and memory or thinking problems. There is very little research on the best treatments for this group, because women with epilepsy are often left out of studies. The guide, based on a literature review and expert agreement, says care should be personalised.
keyPoints: Women with epilepsy may be at higher risk of early menopause, heart disease, osteoporosis and cognitive problems than women without epilepsy.
Menopausal hormone therapy can be considered if the likely benefits outweigh the risks, and transdermal (skin) estrogen may be preferred to limit swings in hormone levels.
Seizure medicines and hormone therapy can interact, so seizure medicine doses may need to change.
Healthcare providers should be trained in epilepsy care at menopause, with multidisciplinary teams.

items.title: Effects of physical activity on depressive and anxiety symptoms of women in the menopausal transition and menopause: a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity
items.journal: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity
items.summary: This review pooled results from 21 randomised trials with about 2,000 women in the menopausal transition or after menopause. Women who took part in physical activity had fewer depressive and anxiety symptoms than women in comparison groups. Low and moderate intensity exercise both seemed to help, and the amount of effort did not clearly change the results. Results varied a lot between studies, so the size of the benefit is uncertain.
keyPoints: Physical activity lowered depressive symptoms in women during the menopausal transition and after menopause compared with controls.
Anxiety symptoms also improved overall, but in the subgroup analysis the benefit was seen only in postmenopausal women.
Low and moderate intensity exercise both helped, with no clear difference between intensities.
The authors conclude that low to moderate intensity activity can help manage depression and anxiety in menopausal women.

items.title: Women's experiences and expectations during the menopause transition: a systematic qualitative narrative review
items.summary: This review pulled together 12 qualitative studies (2014-24) in which women aged 45-60 described what menopause is like for them.
