Many saw menopause as a natural, normal part of ageing, and some found positives such as new beginnings and a higher status as elders. Others found it hard alongside other midlife pressures, with poor access to information about symptoms and mood changes that affected their sense of identity and their relationships. The authors say the quality of this kind of research needs to improve.
keyPoints: Many women viewed menopause as a natural, normal part of ageing, with positives like new beginnings and elder status.
Some women struggled with menopause on top of other midlife pressures, and lacked information about their symptoms.
Mood changes were a specific challenge, affecting women's identity and social connections.
Negative experiences were shaped by stigma and gendered stereotypes about ageing.

items.title: Comparative efficacy of acupuncture-related interventions for perimenopausal depression and anxiety: A systematic review and frequentist meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 54 trials with 4,406 women to compare different acupuncture-based treatments for low mood and anxiety around perimenopause. Acupuncture-related treatments worked better than Western medicine alone on depression and anxiety scores, menopausal symptoms and response rates. Combinations such as acupuncture with Western medicine or with Chinese herbal medicine ranked among the best, but the quality of the evidence was only low to moderate, so more high-quality trials are needed.
keyPoints: Acupuncture-related treatments beat Western medicine alone for depression, anxiety, menopausal complaints and clinical response.
Electroacupuncture plus Western medicine, and manual acupuncture plus Chinese herbal medicine, ranked among the most effective options.
Electroacupuncture alone lowered anxiety scores on the Hamilton Anxiety Scale.
Evidence certainty was mostly low to moderate, so the findings need confirming in better trials.

items.title: Subjective versus objective cognition during menopause: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society
items.journal: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society
items.summary: Many women notice "brain fog" around menopause, but it has been unclear whether how thinking feels matches how it tests. This review pooled 24 studies (5,629 women) and compared women's own ratings of their thinking with memory and thinking tests. It found only a small link with learning efficiency, and no clear link in other areas of thinking. The authors say we need better ways to measure menopausal brain fog.
keyPoints: Women's own sense of their thinking was only weakly linked to test results for learning efficiency (r = .12).
No significant links were found between self-rated and tested performance in other thinking areas.
Twelve different questionnaires were used to measure self-rated thinking, and none was specific to menopause.
The authors call for a reliable measure of menopause-related thinking symptoms and a clearer picture of what brain fog involves.

items.title: Effects of melatonin intake on depression and anxiety in postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled five randomised trials (441 women in total) to see whether melatonin supplements help depression and anxiety after menopause. Across the trials, melatonin was linked to lower depression and anxiety scores, with a small effect on depression and a larger one on anxiety. The authors call melatonin promising but say more high-quality studies are needed, especially to check its safety.
keyPoints: Five randomised trials with 441 women were included.
Melatonin was linked to a significant, small reduction in depression scores in postmenopausal women.
Melatonin was linked to a significant, larger improvement in anxiety scores.
More high-quality studies are needed to determine safety.

items.title: The effectiveness of psychosocial interventions on non-physiological symptoms of menopause: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 30 trials with 3,501 women to see whether talking and mind-based therapies help with mood and wellbeing during menopause. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and mindfulness-based programmes both eased anxiety and depression. These approaches also improved thinking skills and quality of life, though results varied between studies and longer-term effects were not looked at.
keyPoints: CBT and mindfulness-based interventions both significantly reduced anxiety and depression symptoms in menopause.
Psychosocial interventions also improved cognition (thinking and memory) and quality of life, with the biggest benefit seen for quality of life.
CBT needed fewer therapy hours on average (11.3) than mindfulness programmes (18.6), suggesting less cost and burden for women.
The authors note that findings varied between studies, and the review could not say when in menopause these approaches work best.

items.title: The risk of depression in the menopausal stages: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies that followed women over time to see how often depression or low mood showed up at different stages of menopause. Women in perimenopause (the transition years) had a higher risk of depressive symptoms and depression than women who had not yet started the transition. Women after menopause did not have a clearly higher risk than women before it. The studies measured menopause stages and depression in different ways, which makes the comparisons less exact.
keyPoints: Perimenopausal women had a higher risk of depressive symptoms and diagnoses than premenopausal women (odds ratio 1.40).
No clearly higher risk was found in postmenopausal women compared with premenopausal women.
The findings came from an ethnically diverse group of women across 17 studies, with 7 studies used in the pooled analysis.
The authors say screening and support for mood in perimenopause is needed.

items.title: Global prevalence of depression in menopausal women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 55 studies covering about 76,800 women to estimate how common depression is around and after menopause. They found that roughly 1 in 3 women (35.6%) had depression, with similar rates in perimenopause and after menopause. The studies differed a lot from one another, and there were signs of publication bias, so the exact figure is uncertain. The authors say regular screening and access to prevention and treatment should be available.
keyPoints: Pooled depression prevalence in menopausal women was 35.6% across 55 studies.
Rates were similar in perimenopausal (33.9%) and postmenopausal (34.9%) women.
Results varied by region, screening tool, study design and setting, and the studies were very different from each other.
The authors recommend regular screening and access to effective prevention and treatment.

items.title: Guideline No. 451: Asymptomatic Endometrial Thickening in Postmenopausal Women
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looks at what to do when an ultrasound shows a thickened womb lining in a woman after menopause who has no bleeding. It aims to avoid unnecessary tests and procedures while still checking women who may be at risk of womb cancer. The guideline's public summary says that without bleeding, a lining thinner than 11 mm is rarely a serious problem, but it should still be looked at by a health care provider.
keyPoints: A thickened womb lining is often found on ultrasound in postmenopausal women who have no bleeding.
Without bleeding, a lining under 11 mm is rarely a serious problem but should still be evaluated by a health care provider.
The aim is to avoid unnecessary invasive tests while selectively investigating women at risk of endometrial cancer.
Fewer unnecessary procedures could mean less anxiety, pain and risk of complications.

items.title: A systematic review on the impact of nutrition and possible supplementation on the deficiency of vitamin complexes, iron, omega-3-fatty acids, and lycopene in relation to increased morbidity in women after menopause
items.summary: This review looked at 90 observational studies on nutrient shortfalls in women after menopause, including vitamins B6, B12 and D, iron, omega-3 fats and lycopene. It found that women with low levels of these nutrients seemed more likely to have problems such as heart disease, osteoporosis, depression and memory decline. Because the studies were observational and too different to combine, the review cannot prove that the deficiencies cause these problems. The authors say newer studies are needed before firm recommendations can be made.
keyPoints: Women after menopause may be more likely to have shortfalls in several vitamins and nutrients.
Low levels of these nutrients were linked in the studies to heart and brain-blood-vessel events, metabolic disease, osteoporosis, obesity, depression and cognitive decline.
Keeping nutrient levels healthy through a balanced diet of fresh fruits, vegetables and healthy fats, or through suitable supplements, is suggested to support quality of life.
The studies were too varied to pool, and more recent research is needed before firm recommendations.

items.title: Ovarian suppression for adjuvant treatment of hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 15 trials of 11,538 premenopausal women with early hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. It looked at what happens when ovarian suppression (switching off the ovaries' oestrogen production) is added to other treatment. Adding it lowered the risk of dying and of the cancer coming back, and probably lowered the risk of cancer in the other breast. It also brought menopause-type side effects, including more hot flushes and possibly more low mood or anxiety, and may raise the risk of bone thinning.
keyPoints: Adding ovarian suppression reduced deaths (high-certainty evidence) and improved disease-free survival (high-certainty evidence).
The survival benefit was seen when it was added to observation, to tamoxifen, or to chemotherapy plus tamoxifen, but not when added to chemotherapy alone.
Hot flushes were more common with ovarian suppression (low-certainty evidence), and some studies reported more depression, anxiety or neuropsychiatric symptoms while others found no difference.
One study suggested a higher risk of osteoporosis (low-certainty evidence), and some women reported worse quality of life, such as vaginal dryness and night sweats.

items.title: Effects of Different Types of Exercise on Bone Mineral Density in Postmenopausal Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from controlled trials of exercise lasting at least 6 months in women after menopause. It looked at bone density in the lower spine, the neck of the thigh bone and the hip. All three types of exercise studied (weight-bearing, resistance training, or a mix of both) improved bone density at all three sites. The authors say the benefit looks largely similar whatever the type of exercise, but that this kind of analysis is too rough to set exact exercise guidelines.
keyPoints: Weight-bearing exercise, resistance training and mixed programmes all significantly improved bone density at the lumbar spine, femoral neck and total hip.
The benefit was largely independent of the type of exercise.
The review covered 84 exercise groups from controlled trials lasting 6 months or more.
The authors note that a meta-analysis may be too rough a tool to produce specific exercise recommendations.

items.title: Supplementation of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) in pre- and postmenopausal women - position statement of expert panel of Polish Menopause and Andropause Society
items.summary: An expert panel from the Polish Menopause and Andropause Society reviewed trials and meta-analyses on DHEA, a hormone that falls with age, taken as a supplement by women before and after menopause. They concluded it is effective for some conditions, such as low bone density, low libido and vaginal dryness from menopause. It is probably effective for depression and anxiety, but the panel noted its use is still debated. No serious side effects were reported.
keyPoints: DHEA supplements were judged effective for women with low bone density or osteoporosis after menopause.
They were also judged effective for menopausal vaginal atrophy and for women before menopause with low libido.
Trials suggest DHEA is probably effective for depression and anxiety, as well as for low sexual desire after menopause.
No serious adverse effects have been reported, although use of DHEA is still described as controversial.

items.title: Adjuvant gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced premature ovarian failure in premenopausal women
items.summary: This review pooled 12 trials of about 1,369 women having chemotherapy for cancers such as breast cancer, ovarian cancer or Hodgkin's lymphoma. It looked at whether taking a GnRH agonist (a hormone-suppressing medicine) alongside chemotherapy helps protect the ovaries from early menopause. Women who also took the medicine were less likely to develop premature ovarian failure, and more likely to get their periods back or keep them. The trials were at high or unclear risk of bias, and evidence on protecting fertility was not strong enough to draw conclusions.
keyPoints: Premature ovarian failure occurred in about 11% of women using a GnRH agonist with chemotherapy, versus about 25% with chemotherapy alone (moderate-certainty evidence).
Periods returned or continued more often with the agonist within 12 months, but there was no clear difference after 12 months (low-certainty evidence).
Pregnancy rates did not clearly differ between groups, and evidence on protecting fertility was insufficient.
Common side effects of GnRH analogues included hot flushes, vaginal dryness and mood swings, with no overall difference in side effects between groups.

items.title: Isoflavone Supplements for Menopausal Women: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 68 studies of isoflavone supplements (plant compounds found in soy) used for menopause symptoms. It found they reduce hot flashes beyond the placebo effect, may slow bone loss in the lower spine, and may help blood pressure in early menopause. There was no clear benefit for vaginal or urinary symptoms or for thinking and memory. Studies varied a lot in dose, ingredients and length, so firm conclusions are hard to reach.
keyPoints: Isoflavones reduced hot flashes even after accounting for the placebo effect.
They reduced loss of bone density in the lumbar spine and showed benefits for systolic blood pressure in early menopause.
No conclusive benefit was found for urogenital symptoms or cognition (thinking and memory).
Differences in doses, ingredients, outcomes and trial length make conclusions difficult; the authors say evidence so far favours use because of a good safety profile.

items.title: Clinical Updates in Women's Health Care Summary: Mood and Anxiety Disorders: Primary and Preventive Care Review
items.summary: This practice guideline review looks at how mood and anxiety disorders are managed in women. It explains that depression and anxiety can start or get worse during times of hormonal change, such as the premenstrual period, after having a baby, and perimenopause. Pregnancy and breastfeeding make choosing medicines more complicated, so care needs to be planned around each woman's situation. The abstract does not give specific treatment results or rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Mood and anxiety problems can begin or worsen during hormonal changes like menarche, the premenstrual period, postpartum and perimenopause.
Treatment during pregnancy and breastfeeding is more complex, which makes choosing psychiatric medicines harder.
Care for women with mood or anxiety disorders should be thorough and tailored to the individual.

items.title: Association of Age at Menopause and Duration of Reproductive Period With Depression After Menopause: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 observational studies covering about 67,700 women who went through natural menopause. It found that going through menopause later, and having a longer reproductive period, were linked to a lower chance of depression after menopause. Women who reached menopause at 40 or older had about half the risk of depression compared with women who had premature menopause. These are links seen in observational studies, so they do not prove cause and effect.
keyPoints: Each 2-year increase in age at menopause was linked to slightly lower odds of depression after menopause (odds ratio 0.98).
A longer reproductive period was linked to a similar small drop in depression risk (odds ratio 0.98).
Menopause at age 40 or older was linked to a 50% lower risk of depression than premature menopause.
The authors suggest women with early menopause may be at higher risk and could benefit from support or estrogen-based treatments.

items.title: Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments (CANMAT) 2016 Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Adults with Major Depressive Disorder: Section 6. Special Populations: Youth, Women, and the Elderly
items.source: Canadian Journal of Psychiatry. Revue Canadienne de Psychiatrie
items.journal: Canadian Journal of Psychiatry. Revue Canadienne de Psychiatrie
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looked at how to treat major depression in special groups, including pregnant and breastfeeding women and women in perimenopause or menopause. The evidence for treatment in these groups is more limited than for other adults, and the risks of treatment are often poorly studied and reported. Even so, the available data and clinical experience suggest these women can benefit from following standard depression treatment guidelines.
keyPoints: Recent studies inform depression treatment in pregnant and breastfeeding women and in women in perimenopause or menopause.
Evidence for how well treatments work in these groups is more limited than in the general adult population.
Risks of treatment in these groups are often poorly studied and reported.
Despite limited evidence, women in these groups can benefit from systematic use of depression treatment guidelines.

items.title: Women's experience of menopause: a systematic review of qualitative evidence
items.source: JBI Database of Systematic Reviews and Implementation Reports
items.journal: JBI Database of Systematic Reviews and Implementation Reports
items.summary: This review pulled together 24 qualitative studies about how women around the world experience natural menopause. It found that menopause is lived in many different ways, with physical and emotional changes that strongly affect women, along with both gains and losses. Women also reported growing resilience and used coping strategies to support their physical and emotional wellbeing. The review notes that health care providers often pay little attention to how women themselves see menopause.
keyPoints: Menopause is experienced differently from woman to woman, shaped by personal, family and cultural background.
Physical and emotional changes strongly affect women, and hot flushes and night sweats were the strongest reported symptoms.
Women described menopause as a time of both gains and losses, and resilience and coping strategies often grew during this time.
The authors conclude that care should be tailored to each woman's needs, preferences and expectations, as women can feel vulnerable at this stage.

items.title: Cognitive-behavioral, acceptance-based, and mindfulness-based interventions for psychological and sleep-related symptoms during menopause: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 12 studies of talking and mind-based therapies for women going through menopause. The therapies were cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT, including a version for insomnia) and mindfulness- or acceptance-based programs. Most were linked to less depression and anxiety and better sleep, with CBT showing the most consistent effects for insomnia. The studies differed a lot from one another and the results could not be combined statistically, so the conclusions are limited.
keyPoints: Most of the therapies were linked to fewer depression and anxiety symptoms and better sleep.
CBT, including CBT for insomnia, had the most consistent effects, especially for insomnia.
Mindfulness- and acceptance-based programs looked promising but gave more mixed results.
The studies varied in format, measures and follow-up time, so firm conclusions are limited.

items.title: Effect of Soy Isoflavones on Measures of Estrogenicity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: This review pooled 40 randomized trials (3,285 postmenopausal women) to see whether soy isoflavones act like the hormone estrogen in the body. Women took a median of 75 mg a day for about 24 weeks. Soy isoflavones made no significant difference to womb lining thickness, vaginal cell maturation, or blood levels of FSH and estradiol compared with non-isoflavone comparison groups. The authors rated the certainty of the evidence as high to moderate.
keyPoints: Soy isoflavones had no significant effect on womb lining (endometrial) thickness in postmenopausal women.
They also had no significant effect on vaginal maturation index, FSH or estradiol levels.
The authors conclude soy isoflavones do not appear to have estrogen-like effects on these four measures and likely act as selective estrogen receptor modulators.
Evidence certainty was high to moderate across all outcomes.

items.title: Safety of Fezolinetant for Treatment of Moderate to Severe Vasomotor Symptoms Due to Menopause: Pooled Analysis of Three Randomized Phase 3 Studies
items.summary: This study pooled results from three year-long trials of fezolinetant, a non-hormonal daily pill for moderate to severe hot flushes and night sweats during menopause. Over 3,100 women took part, and about 55% of those on placebo and 63-65% of those on fezolinetant reported some side effect. Serious drug-related problems were uncommon, and the authors concluded the drug was safe and well tolerated over 52 weeks.
keyPoints: Common side effects with fezolinetant included upper respiratory infections, headache, back pain, joint pain, diarrhoea, urinary tract infection and trouble sleeping.

Liver test increases happened in about 1.5-2.3% of women taking fezolinetant; they were usually without symptoms, temporary, and settled with continued treatment or stopping, with no severe liver injury seen.
Womb lining (endometrial) safety results were within US FDA criteria, and there was no increased risk of growths compared with placebo.
Serious drug-related side effects and stopping treatment because of them were uncommon.

items.title: Effects of resveratrol on the lipid profile of post-menopause women: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether resveratrol, a plant compound sold as a supplement, changes blood fats such as cholesterol in women after menopause. It pooled results from randomised trials and found no significant difference in total cholesterol, HDL, LDL or triglycerides. Only two small studies were included and the evidence was low quality, so the authors say there is too little evidence to make recommendations.
keyPoints: No significant difference was found in total cholesterol, HDL ("good" cholesterol), LDL or triglycerides between resveratrol and comparison groups.
Only two studies were available for each outcome, and the evidence was rated low quality.
The authors conclude evidence is limited and call for studies with higher doses, longer supplementation and more outcomes.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of fezolinetant and elinzanetant for vasomotor symptoms in postmenopausal women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from ten trials (4,663 women) of two non-hormonal medicines, fezolinetant and elinzanetant, for hot flushes and night sweats after menopause. Both medicines reduced how often and how severe these symptoms were, and elinzanetant also improved menopause-related quality of life. Higher doses of both medicines were linked to more side effects. The authors say the two medicines have not been compared head to head and long-term safety still needs study.
keyPoints: Both fezolinetant and elinzanetant reduced the frequency and severity of hot flushes and night sweats.
Elinzanetant showed a greater reduction in symptom frequency and improved menopause-specific quality of life.
Higher doses of both medicines were linked to more side effects, with elinzanetant having a more favourable side-effect profile than fezolinetant.
More research is needed to compare the two directly and to check long-term safety.

items.title: The state of evidence in acupuncture: A review of metaanalyses and systematic reviews of acupuncture evidence (update 2017-2022)
items.summary: This review looked at 862 earlier reviews of acupuncture published between 2017 and 2022, covering 184 health conditions. Menopausal symptoms were one of ten conditions where the reviews found evidence of a positive effect. The authors note that a lack of high-quality trials sometimes makes the reviews hard to compare.
keyPoints: Of 184 conditions studied, ten showed evidence of a positive effect from acupuncture, including menopausal symptoms and female infertility (alongside medical fertility treatment).
Another 82 conditions showed evidence of a potential positive effect, while 86 had unclear or insufficient evidence.
The amount and quality of acupuncture evidence has grown since earlier reviews covering up to 2017.
Too few high-quality trials in some areas limits how firmly conclusions can be drawn.

items.title: Pharmacological Treatments for Menopausal Vasomotor Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis of Efficacy and Safety
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 41 randomized trials (about 14,700 postmenopausal women) comparing drug treatments for moderate to severe hot flushes and night sweats. Estrogen-based treatments were the most effective at reducing how often and how badly symptoms occurred. Fezolinetant and elinzanetant, which are non-hormonal medicines, showed moderate benefit. Most treatments had safety similar to placebo, and no clear differences in serious side effects were found.
keyPoints: Synthetic conjugated estrogens 1.25 mg gave the biggest drop in how often hot flushes occurred.
Drospirenone 0.5 mg plus estradiol 0.5 mg was most effective for reducing how severe symptoms were.
Fezolinetant and elinzanetant, both non-hormonal, showed moderate effectiveness.
Most treatments had safety similar to placebo, though estradiol 0.5 mg plus dydrogesterone 2.5 mg was linked to more side effects overall; serious side effects did not differ significantly.

items.title: Acupuncture for mood disorders in perimenopausal women: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 49 randomized trials looking at acupuncture for low mood and anxiety in women going through perimenopause. Women who had acupuncture had lower depression and anxiety scores, and better overall menopause symptom scores than those taking drugs. The authors say the studies had some weaknesses in design and quality, so larger, better-run trials are still needed to be sure.
keyPoints: Acupuncture was linked to lower depression scores (Hamilton Depression Scale) and lower anxiety scores in perimenopausal women.
Compared with drugs, acupuncture gave better menopause symptom scores (Kupperman Index) and lower follicle-stimulating hormone levels.
No clear difference was seen in luteinizing hormone or estradiol levels.
Results varied a lot between studies, and the authors call for larger, more rigorous multicenter trials.

items.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for perimenopausal insomnia
items.summary: This review pooled nine randomized trials (968 women) testing acupuncture alone for trouble sleeping around menopause. Women who had acupuncture did better than comparison groups on sleep quality scores, overall treatment response and menopause quality-of-life scores. The authors say larger, longer, multi-center trials are still needed to give more reliable results.
keyPoints: Acupuncture alone improved sleep quality scores (PSQI) and the overall effective rate compared with control groups.
Acupuncture also improved menopause symptom and quality-of-life scores, and some hormone and brain-chemical measures.
Estrogen (E2) levels did not differ significantly between the acupuncture and control groups.
The authors call for larger, multi-center trials with long-term follow-up to confirm the results.

items.title: Cognitive behavioural therapy for menopausal symptoms: a systematic review of efficacy in improving quality of life
items.summary: This review looked at 16 studies with 910 women to see whether cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), a talking therapy, helps with menopause symptoms. It found that CBT improved quality of life and eased hot flushes, night sweats, low mood, anxiety and sleep problems. Group CBT gave the biggest benefits, and self-help CBT gave smaller but still meaningful improvements. CBT may be a useful option for women who cannot or choose not to take hormone replacement therapy.
keyPoints: CBT significantly improved health-related quality of life during menopause.
It eased hot flushes and night sweats as well as psychological and sleep-related symptoms.
Group-based CBT gave the most benefit, while self-help CBT gave moderate but meaningful improvements.
CBT is a non-drug option, especially where hormone replacement therapy is not suitable or is declined.

items.title: Bone mineral density in patients with primary ovarian insufficiency: A systematic review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled ten studies comparing bone density in 578 women with primary ovarian insufficiency (early loss of normal ovary function, also called premature menopause) and 480 women without it. Bone density was lower in women with the condition at the femur neck (top of the thigh bone) and in the non-dominant forearm. No differences were found at the lumbar spine, total hip or hip neck. The authors suggest hormone replacement therapy may help reduce fracture risk linked to bone thinning in these women.
keyPoints: Women with primary ovarian insufficiency had significantly lower bone density at the femur neck and non-dominant forearm.
No differences in bone density were seen at the lumbar spine, total hip or hip neck.
The authors raise the possibility that hormone replacement therapy could lower fracture risk linked to bone thinning in these women.

items.title: Acupuncture-adjuvant therapies for treating perimenopausal depression: A network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 27 trials with 2,269 women who had depression during perimenopause (the years around menopause). It compared different acupuncture-based treatments with each other and with the antidepressant fluoxetine plus menopausal hormone treatment. Several acupuncture types, especially warm acupuncture, scored better than fluoxetine plus hormone treatment, and warm acupuncture ranked best on depression scores. The authors suggest the findings could help patients and therapists choose among acupuncture options, but the abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Warm acupuncture, electroacupuncture and common acupuncture were more effective than fluoxetine plus menopausal hormone treatment, though some confidence ranges were close to showing no difference.
Warm acupuncture was ranked the best treatment for perimenopausal depression and beat the other four acupuncture-related treatments on depression scores.
The analysis covered 27 randomised trials, 2,269 women and 8 treatment approaches.

items.title: Influence of phytoestrogens on endometrial thickness: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 10 randomized trials (1,476 postmenopausal women) to see whether plant-based estrogen-like compounds (phytoestrogens) thicken the lining of the womb. Women taking phytoestrogens did not show a meaningful change in womb lining thickness compared with control groups, at 3, 6, 12 or 24 months. The authors say the evidence is still uncertain because the studies differed from one another and most reported results only up to 3 to 6 months.
keyPoints: No significant difference in womb lining (endometrial) thickness between phytoestrogen users and controls at 3, 6, 12 or 24 months.
The review covered 10 randomized trials with 1,476 postmenopausal women.
Evidence is still uncertain because the studies varied a lot and most followed women for only 3 to 6 months.

items.title: Efficacy of cognitive therapy and behavior therapy for menopausal symptoms: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 14 randomised trials (1618 women) testing cognitive and behavioural therapy for menopause symptoms. The therapy reduced hot flushes, night sweats, low mood, anxiety, fatigue and improved quality of life, mostly by small to moderate amounts. The benefit lasted over time but faded somewhat. It worked better for symptoms of natural menopause than for menopause caused by treatment.
keyPoints: Cognitive and behaviour therapy reduced hot flushes, night sweats, depression, anxiety and fatigue, and improved quality of life.
Effects were mostly small to moderate.
Benefits were sustained long-term but declined somewhat over time.
Effects were stronger for natural menopause symptoms than for treatment-induced menopause symptoms.

items.title: Soy Isoflavones and Breast Cancer Risk: A Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies that looked at how much soy and isoflavones women eat and whether they went on to develop breast cancer. In studies that followed women over time, eating more soy isoflavones was linked to fewer breast cancers, in both pre-menopausal and post-menopausal women. The authors concluded that soy isoflavones can reduce breast cancer risk. The abstract does not report how certain the evidence is, and these were observational links rather than proof of cause.
keyPoints: Soy contains isoflavones, plant compounds with a structure similar to the hormone estrogen.
Higher isoflavone intake was linked to lower breast cancer occurrence in forward-looking (prospective) studies.
The link was seen in both pre-menopausal and post-menopausal women.
The authors concluded that soy isoflavone consumption can reduce breast cancer risk.

items.title: Lipid Profile in Patients With Primary Ovarian Insufficiency: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 studies of women with primary ovarian insufficiency (POI, when the ovaries stop working normally early) and compared them with healthy women. Women with POI had higher total cholesterol, triglycerides and LDL ("bad") cholesterol. HDL ("good") cholesterol did not clearly differ. The authors suggest early medical treatment such as hormone replacement therapy to lower heart disease risk, but this is not a non-hormonal option.
keyPoints: Women with POI had higher total cholesterol, triglycerides and LDL cholesterol than healthy women.
HDL cholesterol showed no significant difference between the groups.
Results varied between studies, possibly due to region, sample size, body mass index and age.
The authors recommend early medical intervention, such as hormone replacement therapy, to reduce heart disease risk linked to abnormal blood fats.

items.title: Behavioral interventions for improving sleep outcomes in menopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 randomized trials with 2,108 women in perimenopause or after menopause to see whether non-drug approaches improve sleep. Cognitive behavioral therapy, physical exercise, and mindfulness or relaxation all improved sleep, and no serious side effects were reported. However, the studies varied a lot and had some risk of bias, so the overall certainty of the evidence was very low.
keyPoints: Behavioral interventions overall improved sleep outcomes in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women.
Cognitive behavioral therapy, physical exercise, and mindfulness/relaxation each improved sleep on both self-reported and objective measures.
Low- and moderate-intensity exercise also improved sleep.
No serious adverse events were reported, but the certainty of the evidence was very low.

items.title: Acupuncture for cancer-related conditions: An overview of systematic reviews
items.summary: This overview looked at 51 systematic reviews of studies on acupuncture for symptoms linked to cancer and its treatment. Acupuncture appeared helpful for several problems, including hot flashes and menopause symptoms after breast cancer, joint pain, pain, fatigue and poor sleep. No serious side effects were reported. However, most of the reviews were rated very low quality or at high risk of bias, so the results should be treated with caution.
keyPoints: Acupuncture appeared to help hot flashes and menopause symptoms in women with breast cancer, and also joint pain, cancer-related pain, fatigue and insomnia.
Results for depression, anxiety and nerve damage from chemotherapy were mixed, so acupuncture is described as an option depending on the person.
No severe side effects linked to acupuncture were reported, and it was regarded as relatively safe.
Quality was a concern: 45 of 51 reviews were rated very low quality and 35 had a high risk of bias, and the authors call for better-designed trials.

items.title: Acupuncture for Breast Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Patient-Reported Outcomes
items.summary: This review pooled 29 randomized trials of acupuncture in women with breast cancer who had symptoms from their cancer treatment. Women who had acupuncture reported better quality of life and less pain, fatigue, hot flashes, sleep problems and anxiety than comparison groups. Depression improved about the same in both groups. The authors say some subgroups had limited data and that larger, better-designed trials are needed to confirm the results.
keyPoints: Acupuncture was linked to better quality of life and lower pain scores in women with breast cancer.
Women who had acupuncture were more likely to report improvements in hot flashes, fatigue, sleep problems and anxiety.
Depression improved by a similar amount with and without acupuncture.
The authors say more rigorous, larger trials are needed to confirm these results.

items.title: Acupuncture Improves Multiple Treatment-Related Symptoms in Breast Cancer Survivors: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine
items.journal: Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine
items.summary: This review pooled 20 trials (1,709 breast cancer survivors) to see whether acupuncture eases symptoms linked to cancer treatment, including hot flashes. Acupuncture reduced pain, tiredness and hot flash severity compared with control groups. When it was compared only with sham (fake) acupuncture, the benefits were not statistically significant. Some trials had a high risk of bias, so the authors say more rigorous studies are needed.
keyPoints: Acupuncture was more effective than control groups for pain, fatigue and hot flash severity.
Compared with waitlist or usual care, acupuncture also reduced depression and neuropathy.
Against sham acupuncture, effects showed trends but were not significant.
No serious side effects were reported; mild ones such as bruising, pain and headache occurred in 11 studies, and safety reporting was incomplete.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of gabapentin and pregabalin in patients with vasomotor symptoms: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 21 randomized trials (3519 women) to see whether gabapentin and pregabalin, two non-hormonal medicines, ease hot flashes and night sweats. Gabapentin reduced how often hot flashes happened and lowered overall symptom scores compared with placebo, in both menopausal women and women with breast cancer. It caused more dizziness and sleepiness, and it worked less well than estrogen. There was not enough evidence to say whether pregabalin helps.
keyPoints: Gabapentin reduced hot flash frequency compared with placebo at 4 and 12 weeks.
Dizziness and somnolence (sleepiness) were more common with gabapentin than with placebo.
Estrogen reduced hot flash frequency more than gabapentin; gabapentin and antidepressants did not differ significantly in hot flash severity.
Evidence for pregabalin is still lacking, and trials comparing it with other treatments were too limited to draw conclusions.

items.title: Gabapentin for the treatment of hot flushes in menopause: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled seven randomized trials comparing gabapentin with a placebo for hot flushes in women after menopause. Women taking gabapentin reported fewer hot flushes, shorter flushes and lower overall flush scores. They also had more side effects, such as dizziness and unsteadiness. The authors say gabapentin could be an option for women who cannot use hormone therapy.
keyPoints: Gabapentin reduced how often hot flushes happened compared with placebo.
Gabapentin also shortened hot flushes and lowered their combined severity score.
Dizziness and unsteadiness were more common with gabapentin than with placebo.
The authors suggest gabapentin may suit women who cannot take hormone therapy, and that future studies should look for the lowest effective dose.

items.title: Management of Menopause Symptoms with Acupuncture: An Umbrella Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine
items.journal: Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine
items.summary: This review pulled together earlier reviews and newer trials to see whether acupuncture helps hot flushes and night sweats around the menopause. Women who had acupuncture had fewer and less severe symptoms and better quality of life than women who had no acupuncture. The benefit was smaller or not clearly there when acupuncture was compared with sham (fake) acupuncture, so some of the effect may come from non-specific effects such as the experience of treatment itself. Safety has not been studied rigorously, but no clear sign of harm was found.
keyPoints: Acupuncture reduced how often and how severe hot flushes were, and improved quality of life, compared with no acupuncture.
Compared with sham acupuncture, the benefits were smaller or not statistically significant.
Some or all of the benefit may be due to non-specific effects rather than the needling itself.
Safety has not been rigorously examined, but there was no clear signal of significant harm.

items.title: Effect of phytoestrogens on sexual function in menopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled earlier studies to see whether plant-based oestrogen-like compounds (phytoestrogens) help sexual problems in menopausal women. Soy, red clover, genistein and flaxseed did not show clear benefits for sexual function. Maritime pine bark, fenugreek and fennel appeared to help, and fenugreek improved libido. The abstract does not rate the overall certainty of the evidence, and only a few trials were available for some products.
keyPoints: Soy and red clover had no significant effect on sexual function in the pooled results.
Genistein, flaxseed and Korean red ginseng did not significantly improve sexual function.
Maritime pine bark, fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum) and fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) improved sexual function in the published reports.
Fenugreek had a positive effect on libido (sex drive).

items.title: Acupuncture for hot flashes in women with breast cancer: A systematic review
items.source: Journal of Cancer Research and Therapeutics
items.journal: Journal of Cancer Research and Therapeutics
items.summary: This review pooled 12 randomized trials of acupuncture for hot flashes in women who have had breast cancer. Combined results showed fewer hot flashes and lower symptom scores after treatment and at follow-up compared with controls. But only some individual trials found a clear benefit, and two trials found acupuncture did worse than hormone therapy. The authors say the studies were few and of poor quality, so the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Across 12 trials, acupuncture seemed helpful for hot flashes in women with breast cancer.
Pooled results showed fewer hot flashes and better Kupperman index scores than controls, after treatment and at follow-up.
Only three trials found a clear difference from controls, and six found no difference.
The authors say there is not enough evidence to prove acupuncture works, because the studies were small and of poor quality.

items.title: Effectiveness of Traditional Chinese Acupuncture versus Sham Acupuncture: a Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at whether traditional Chinese acupuncture eases hot flashes better than 'sham' acupuncture (a fake version used as a comparison) in menopausal women who have had breast cancer. The researchers found five randomized trials. Traditional acupuncture did slightly better than sham, but the difference was not statistically strong. The authors concluded the evidence was not enough to say acupuncture works better than sham.
keyPoints: Five randomized trials were analyzed out of 272 studies found.
Traditional acupuncture showed a slight edge over sham acupuncture for hot flashes.
The differences were not strong statistically.
The evidence was not enough to confirm that traditional acupuncture is more effective than sham.

items.title: Effects of traditional Chinese medicine on symptom clusters during the menopausal transition
items.summary: This review looked at controlled trials of traditional Chinese medicine (acupuncture, Chinese herbal medicine and moxibustion) for hot flushes that occur together with other menopause symptoms such as poor sleep, low mood or pain. Eleven trials were included. Results for acupuncture were mixed, while the herbal and moxibustion trials mostly reported benefits. The authors call the results promising but say larger, better-reported trials are needed. No serious side effects were reported in any trial.
keyPoints: Five of eight acupuncture trials significantly reduced hot flushes, and some also showed benefit for mood, sleep or pain.
All three Chinese herbal medicine trials had significant findings, including for hot flushes with mood, pain or sleep symptoms.
One trial of moxibustion plus counseling reduced hot flushes, mood symptoms and pain.
None of the trials reported serious adverse events, but few trials reported results for individual symptoms and larger studies are needed.

items.title: Systematic review of acupuncture to control hot flashes in cancer patients
items.summary: This review looked at eight trials of acupuncture for hot flashes in women with cancer, all of them women with breast cancer. Women who got real acupuncture improved compared with their own starting point. But when real acupuncture was compared with fake (sham) acupuncture, only a few studies found a clear benefit, and none of the studies were at low risk of bias. The authors concluded the evidence is not strong enough to say whether acupuncture helps or not.
keyPoints: Eight randomized trials were included, all in women with breast cancer.
Hot flashes improved from the starting point in every real acupuncture group.
Only three studies showed real acupuncture beating sham acupuncture or no treatment, and one of those was for night-time hot flashes only.
No study had a low risk of bias, so the evidence cannot support or rule out a benefit.

items.title: Nonhormonal management of menopause-associated vasomotor symptoms: 2015 position statement of The North American Menopause Society
items.summary: The North American Menopause Society reviewed the evidence on treatments for hot flushes and night sweats that do not use hormones. These options matter for women who cannot or prefer not to take hormone therapy. Cognitive-behavioural therapy and, to a lesser extent, hypnosis were found to help, as were certain prescription medicines. Many popular remedies, such as herbal supplements, acupuncture and exercise, did not have enough good evidence to be recommended as proven.
keyPoints: Cognitive-behavioural therapy and, to a lesser extent, clinical hypnosis are recommended as effective for reducing hot flushes and night sweats.
Paroxetine is the only non-hormonal medicine approved by the US FDA for these symptoms; other antidepressants, gabapentinoids and clonidine also show evidence of benefit.
Weight loss, mindfulness-based stress reduction, S-equol (a soy isoflavone derivative) and stellate ganglion block may help but need more study.

Cooling techniques, avoiding triggers, exercise, yoga, paced breathing, over-the-counter and herbal supplements, acupuncture and chiropractic care are not recommended as proven treatments at this time.

items.title: The 2023 nonhormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society
items.summary: This 2023 position statement from the North American Menopause Society updates its 2015 review of non-hormone treatments for hot flushes and night sweats. Recommended options include cognitive behavioural therapy, clinical hypnosis, SSRI/SNRI antidepressants, gabapentin and fezolinetant, with oxybutynin, weight loss and stellate ganglion block also supported by more limited evidence. Paced breathing, supplements and herbal remedies, soy, cooling techniques, avoiding triggers, exercise, yoga and acupuncture are not recommended for hot flushes. Hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment, but these options matter for women who cannot or prefer not to use it.
keyPoints: Recommended with good evidence: cognitive behavioural therapy, clinical hypnosis, SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin and fezolinetant.
Also recommended on more limited evidence: oxybutynin, weight loss and stellate ganglion block.
Not recommended for hot flushes: paced breathing, supplements and herbal remedies, soy products, cannabinoids, acupuncture, exercise, yoga, cooling techniques and avoiding triggers.
Hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment and should be considered within 10 years of the final period.

items.title: Acupuncture as an independent or adjuvant therapy to standard management for menopausal insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 28 randomised trials to see whether acupuncture helps with sleep problems during menopause. Acupuncture improved sleep scores compared with fake (sham) acupuncture, and also compared with standard care such as sleeping pills or menopausal hormone therapy. The reviewers rated the overall evidence as very low to moderate quality, because many studies were poorly designed and results varied a lot between studies. They concluded acupuncture may help women with menopausal insomnia.
keyPoints: Six higher-quality trials found real acupuncture beat sham acupuncture on sleep scores, total sleep time and sleep efficiency, and cut time awake after falling asleep.
The benefit over sham acupuncture was still seen at a 4-week follow-up.
Acupuncture lowered sleep scores more than standard care, but after more than 8 weeks of treatment there was no clear difference from western medication.
Acupuncture added to standard care reduced sleep scores more than standard care alone.

items.title: Effect of physical activity on sleep in women experiencing vasomotor symptoms during menopause: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine trials (1,579 women) testing whether exercise improves sleep in women with hot flashes and night sweats during menopause. Exercise did not clearly improve overall sleep quality or insomnia, though it gave a small improvement in general sleep problems. Results varied between studies, likely because the type, amount and timing of exercise differed.
keyPoints: Exercise did not significantly improve sleep quality or insomnia in women with hot flashes and night sweats.
There was a small improvement in sleep problems overall.
Effects differed between studies, possibly due to the type, frequency, intensity, timing and length of exercise.
None of the studies were rated as high risk of bias, though there were some concerns.

items.title: A Meta-Analysis: Anti-Inflammatory Medicinal Plants for Age-Related Menopause-Like Symptoms and Psychological Problems in Breast Cancer and Healthy Perimenopausal Women
items.summary: This review pooled 27 randomised trials of plant-based supplements with anti-inflammatory properties. It looked at menopause-like symptoms in healthy perimenopausal women (2,104 women) and in women with breast cancer (917 women). The supplements improved symptom scores and response rates compared with the comparison treatments, and women had fewer psychological problems. Women with breast cancer also had less anxiety and insomnia. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Plant-based supplements improved menopause symptom scores (Kupperman's Index and Menopause Rating Scale) compared with comparators.
Women with breast cancer had a bigger drop in symptom scores than healthy perimenopausal women, and a bigger drop in Kupperman's Index than women on hormone therapy.
In both groups, more women responded to treatment and fewer had psychological problems.
Women with breast cancer reported less anxiety and insomnia with the supplements.

items.title: Menopause and movement: exercise for better sleep and psychological well-being-a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 13 randomized trials with 1,470 women going through perimenopause or after menopause. It looked at whether exercise helps sleep and emotional well-being. The authors found that several kinds of exercise, including aerobic exercise, yoga, Pilates, resistance training, stretching and relaxation, were linked to better sleep and better psychological well-being. Hormone therapy can help symptoms but its side effects limit long-term use, so exercise is one non-hormone option.
keyPoints: Thirteen randomized trials (1,470 women) were included in the review.
Aerobic, yoga, Pilates, resistance, stretching and relaxation exercise were all linked to better sleep quality.
The same types of exercise were linked to better psychological well-being in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women.
Earlier research on exercise for these symptoms was not consistent, which is why this review was done.

items.title: Effectiveness of nonpharmacological interventions for menopause-related insomnia: A systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 44 randomised trials to compare non-drug treatments for sleep problems in women going through menopause. Compared with no treatment or usual care, relaxation, cognitive behavioural therapy, mindfulness, aromatherapy, acupuncture, massage, yoga and exercise all improved sleep quality. Mindfulness ranked as the most effective option, and exercise showed the smallest benefit.
keyPoints: Eight non-drug approaches each improved sleep quality compared with a control condition.
The approaches were relaxation, cognitive behavioural therapy, mindfulness, aromatherapy, acupuncture, massage, yoga and exercise.
Mindfulness had the largest improvement and ranked most effective; exercise had the smallest.
The review combined 44 randomised controlled trials out of 1925 studies screened.

items.title: The role of lifestyle medicine in menopausal health: a review of non-pharmacologic interventions
items.summary: This systematic review looked at studies from 2000 to 2024 on lifestyle approaches (healthy eating, physical activity, mental well-being, avoiding risky substances, good sleep and healthy relationships) for women going through menopause. These approaches were linked to fewer hot flushes and night sweats, better sleep, better mental well-being, healthier weight, and lower risk of heart, metabolic and bone problems. The authors suggest lifestyle medicine is a useful, low-cost foundation for menopause care alongside other options. The abstract does not rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Lifestyle changes were associated with fewer vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes and night sweats) and better sleep quality.
Lifestyle approaches were linked to better mental well-being and healthier weight regulation.
They were also associated with lower cardiometabolic and osteoporosis risk.
Person-centred, team-based care helped women stick with changes and improved their own reports of how they felt.

items.title: Effects of cognitive behavioral therapy on sleep quality and insomnia severity index in women with menopausal insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 11 randomized trials (973 women) of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) in menopausal women. CBT-I clearly improved sleep quality and lowered insomnia severity. It worked whether it was delivered face to face or remotely, and regardless of how bad the insomnia was at the start. The authors suggest it is a useful non-drug option, and say longer-term results still need more study.
keyPoints: CBT-I significantly improved sleep quality in menopausal women.
CBT-I significantly reduced insomnia severity scores.
Benefits were seen with face-to-face, telephone and internet-based programs.
More research is needed on long-term effects and on how well it works across different cultures.

items.title: Nutritional interventions in treating menopause-related sleep disturbances: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 59 studies on whether changing what you eat or drink, or taking nutritional supplements, can help sleep problems linked to menopause. Most studies (37) found some sleep benefit, while 22 found none. The studies were quite different from each other and most were of low quality, so it is hard to draw firm conclusions. The authors say better-designed trials are needed.
keyPoints: 37 of 59 studies reported that a nutritional intervention improved some aspect of sleep; 22 found no benefit.
The improvements were mainly in sleep that women rated themselves (subjective sleep).
Most studies were of low methodological quality and varied widely in the interventions tested.
The authors call for more high-quality, adequately sized randomized controlled trials.

items.title: Mapping global prevalence of menopausal symptoms among middle-aged women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 321 studies covering about 482,000 middle-aged women to see how common 19 menopausal symptoms are around the world. Symptoms were very common overall, with joint and muscle discomfort the most frequent (about 65%). How common symptoms were varied by region, country income, menopausal stage and body mass index (BMI).
keyPoints: Joint and muscle discomfort was the most common symptom (about 65%); formication (a crawling-skin feeling) was the least common (about 20%).
Vaginal dryness was about twice as common after menopause (about 45%) as before it (about 21%).
Hot flashes were less common in high-income countries (about 50%) than in low-income countries (about 66%).
Sleep problems, depression, anxiety and urinary problems differed by BMI, and depression was especially common in South America.

items.title: Global prevalence of sleep disorders during menopause: a meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined the results of many studies from around the world to estimate how common sleep problems are during menopause. They found that about half of women (51.6%) had some kind of sleep disorder. Restless legs syndrome had the highest reported rate, though that estimate was very uncertain. The authors conclude that sleep problems in menopause are common and deserve attention from health services.
keyPoints: About 51.6% of women in menopause had a sleep disorder (95% CI 44.6-58.5%).
Among postmenopausal women, the reported rate was 54.7% (95% CI 47.2-62.1%).
Restless legs syndrome had the highest reported rate at 63.8%, but the range was very wide (10.6-96.3%), so this figure is uncertain.
The authors recommend that health policymakers offer interventions to support sleep health in menopausal women.

items.title: Does menopause elevate the risk for developing depression and anxiety? Results from a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 22 studies to ask whether menopause raises the risk of depression and anxiety. It found that depression and anxiety are common during menopause and afterwards. Hot flushes and night sweats, a past history of major depression, and stressful life events or social factors seemed to raise the risk. The authors suggest changing estrogen levels may play a part, but the studies cannot prove this.
keyPoints: Depression and anxiety are common during menopause and after it.
Hot flushes and night sweats (vasomotor symptoms) and a past history of major depression were linked with higher risk of depression.
Stressful life events, social factors and a more anxious personality style were also linked with higher risk.
The authors suggest estrogen changes affecting brain chemicals such as serotonin and GABA may help explain the link.

items.title: Effects of different physiotherapy modalities on insomnia and depression in perimenopausal, menopausal, and post-menopausal women: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 31 studies on physiotherapy-type treatments for sleep problems and low mood in women around and after menopause. Reflexology, yoga, walking and aromatherapy massage were linked to less insomnia and depression. Exercise and stretching mostly improved sleep, but results for depression were mixed. There was not enough evidence for craniofacial massage, footbaths or acupressure.
keyPoints: Reflexology, yoga, walking and aromatherapy massage reduced insomnia and depression in menopausal women.
Most exercise and stretching programmes improved sleep quality, but findings on depression were inconsistent.
Evidence was insufficient for craniofacial massage, footbaths and acupressure.
Overall, non-drug physiotherapy approaches had a positive effect on insomnia and depression.

items.title: Hormone therapy for sexual function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 36 trials (over 23,000 women, nearly all postmenopausal) that compared hormone therapy with placebo or no treatment for sexual function. Estrogen on its own probably gives a small improvement in sexual function, especially for lubrication, pain and satisfaction. For estrogen with progestogen, tibolone-type drugs and SERMs, the evidence is too weak to say whether they help. Many of the trials had a high risk of bias, and results varied a lot between studies.
keyPoints: Estrogen alone probably slightly improves overall sexual function in women with menopausal symptoms or early postmenopause, and in postmenopausal women generally (moderate-quality evidence).
The benefit was seen especially in lubrication, pain and satisfaction.
It is uncertain whether estrogen combined with progestogens helps, based on one small study with very low-quality evidence.
Evidence for synthetic steroids such as tibolone and for SERMs is very low quality, and current evidence does not suggest they improve sexual function.

items.title: Acupuncture combined with Chinese herbal medicine in the treatment of perimenopausal insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 15 randomized trials with 1188 women who had insomnia around the time of perimenopause. It compared acupuncture combined with Chinese herbal medicine against Western medicine alone. The combined approach seemed to improve sleep and anxiety scores more than Western medicine alone. The authors note that the included studies had a higher risk of bias, so better-quality trials are needed to confirm the results.
keyPoints: Acupuncture plus Chinese herbal medicine seemed more effective than Western medicine alone for perimenopausal insomnia.
Sleep quality scores (PSQI) and anxiety scores (HAMA) improved more with the combined treatment.
Follicle-stimulating hormone levels were lower with the combined treatment, but estradiol and LH levels did not differ.
The included studies had a higher risk of bias, so more rigorous trials are needed.

items.title: Different regimens of menopausal hormone therapy for improving sleep quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 15 randomized trials to see whether menopausal hormone therapy (HT) improves sleep. Compared with placebo, HT improved sleep that women reported themselves, but did not change sleep measured by overnight sleep tests (polysomnography). The size of the benefit depended on the type of hormone and how it was taken, with skin patches or gels looking more helpful than tablets. The authors conclude HT helps sleep problems 'to some extent'.
keyPoints: HT improved self-reported sleep compared with placebo, but not sleep measured by polysomnography.
17β-estradiol and conjugated equine estrogens both improved sleep quality.
Transdermal (through the skin) HT showed a larger benefit than oral HT.
Estrogen combined with progesterone helped sleep, while estrogen alone did not show a clear benefit.

items.title: Dietary intake and menopausal symptoms in postmenopausal women: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 19 studies on how what postmenopausal women eat relates to menopausal symptoms, including sleep problems, hot flushes and mood. Eating more vegetables, whole grains and unprocessed foods was linked to milder symptoms, while processed foods, saturated fats and sugars were linked to stronger symptoms. Caffeine and the type of fat eaten were also linked to symptom intensity. The authors say the evidence is inconsistent, inconclusive and based on a small number of studies.
keyPoints: Diets higher in vegetables, whole grains and unprocessed foods were linked to milder psychological, sleep, hot flush, urogenital and body symptoms.
Highly processed foods, saturated fats and sugars were linked to more intense symptoms.
Caffeine intake and the type of fat eaten were linked to how strong menopausal symptoms were.
The evidence is inconsistent and inconclusive, and comes from only a small number of studies.

items.title: Italian Association of Sleep Medicine (AIMS) position statement and guideline on the treatment of menopausal sleep disorders
items.summary: An Italian sleep medicine group reviewed the research on sleep problems after menopause, including hot flushes, insomnia, sleep apnea and restless legs. They found that menopausal hormone therapy helps hot flushes, insomnia and mood, and that some antidepressants can also improve sleep. Non-drug approaches like cognitive behavioral therapy and aerobic exercise may give long-term benefits for insomnia. For restless legs syndrome, the results on hormone therapy were conflicting.
keyPoints: Menopausal hormone therapy improves hot flushes and night sweats, insomnia and mood.
Some antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs and mirtazapine) can improve insomnia, alone or alongside hormone therapy.
Cognitive behavioral therapy and aerobic exercise may bring long-term benefits for postmenopausal insomnia.
CPAP and mandibular advancement devices lower blood pressure and cortisol in postmenopausal women with sleep apnea, while data on hormone therapy for restless legs are conflicting.

items.title: Managing vulvovaginal atrophy after breast cancer
items.summary: This guideline looks at vaginal dryness and pain (vulvovaginal atrophy) in women who have had breast cancer. Cancer treatment can cause sudden menopause, which often brings stronger symptoms such as hot flushes, night sweats and poor sleep. In women without breast cancer, vaginal estrogen and simple lubricants or moisturisers can usually treat vaginal dryness and pain safely. For women with breast cancer, long-term trials of vaginal estrogen have not been done, so the advice rests on expert agreement rather than trial evidence.
keyPoints: Cancer treatment can cause an early, sudden menopause, with more severe symptoms than natural menopause.
Vaginal dryness and pain can happen whether or not a woman has a sexual partner.
In women without breast cancer, vaginal estrogen (cream, pessary or ring) and lubricants or moisturisers can usually be used safely.
Safe use of vaginal estrogen after breast cancer has not been tested in long randomised trials, so the guidance reflects clinical consensus.

items.title: Global, regional, and national burden of cardiovascular diseases among postmenopausal women, 1990-2040: a systematic analysis for the global burden of disease study 2021
items.summary: This study used worldwide health data to look at heart and blood vessel disease in women aged 55 and over, from 1990 to 2021, and projected trends to 2040. Rates of new cases and deaths (adjusted for age) fell around the world, but the total number of cases and deaths nearly doubled because populations are growing and ageing. Richer regions saw the biggest improvements, while poorer regions improved more slowly or got worse. High blood pressure was the main risk factor that can be changed.
keyPoints: Age-adjusted rates of heart disease and deaths in women 55 and over fell globally, but total cases and deaths nearly doubled as populations grew and aged.
Ischemic heart disease and stroke were the biggest contributors to the burden.
The gap between high-income and low-income regions widened, with slower progress or worsening trends in low-income settings.
High systolic blood pressure was the leading risk factor that can be changed, and the authors call for better blood pressure control and prevention.

items.title: Age at Iatrogenic Menopause and Cardiovascular Morbidity and Mortality: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 36 studies of over 2.6 million women to look at menopause caused by medical treatment, such as surgery to remove the ovaries, and later heart health. Women with this kind of menopause had a higher risk of heart disease, stroke and death from any cause than comparison groups. The extra risk of dying was seen mainly when menopause happened before age 45. Later age at menopause was linked with lower risk. The studies were observational, so they show links rather than proof of cause.
keyPoints: Menopause caused by medical treatment was linked to higher risk of cardiovascular events (about 25% higher), coronary heart disease and stroke.
Higher risk of cardiovascular and all-cause death was seen only when this menopause happened before age 45.
At age 45 or older, there was no clear extra risk of death.
Each 5 years later at menopause was linked to lower risk of heart problems and death.

items.title: The association of menopause with cardiometabolic disease risk factors in low- and middle-income countries: a systematic review and meta-analyses
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies in low- and middle-income countries to compare women before and after menopause. After menopause, women were more likely to have heart and metabolism risk factors such as metabolic syndrome, high blood pressure, high triglycerides (a type of blood fat) and high blood sugar. The authors say early monitoring and prevention for midlife women in these countries is needed.
keyPoints: Postmenopausal women had higher odds of metabolic syndrome than premenopausal women (OR 1.18).
They also had higher odds of high blood pressure (OR 1.10), raised triglycerides (OR 1.16) and raised blood glucose (OR 1.21).
A higher waist-to-hip ratio was more common after menopause (OR 1.22).
The authors call for early monitoring and interventions to reduce heart and metabolic risk in midlife women.

items.title: Effects of five types of exercise on vascular function in postmenopausal women: a network meta-analysis and systematic review of 32 randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 32 randomized trials (1,427 postmenopausal women) to compare five types of exercise for blood vessel health. Most types of exercise improved how well blood vessels widen and how stiff the arteries are. Interval training (short bursts of harder effort) and combined aerobic plus resistance training ranked as the most effective overall. None of the exercise types significantly reduced the thickness of the carotid artery wall.
keyPoints: Steady endurance, interval, resistance and hybrid training all significantly improved blood vessel widening (flow-mediated dilatation).
All five exercise types significantly reduced artery stiffness (pulse wave velocity).
Interval training and hybrid training significantly reduced the augmentation index, another measure of artery stiffness.
The authors suggest prioritizing interval training and combined aerobic plus resistance training, and found no significant change in carotid artery wall thickness with any exercise.

items.title: Cardiovascular risk of hormone replacement therapy in menopausal women with diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical trials and observational studies
items.summary: This review pulled together 19 studies on whether hormone replacement therapy (HRT) affects heart disease risk in menopausal women who have diabetes. Across nine observational studies, women with diabetes who used HRT did not have a higher risk of heart attack than those who did not use it. The review notes that data were limited for other heart outcomes and that more robust research is needed to confirm this.
keyPoints: Observational studies did not suggest a higher heart attack risk for menopausal women with diabetes who used HRT.
The pooled result for heart attack risk was 0.83, but the range of uncertainty included both a lower and a slightly higher risk.
There was too little data to combine results from the clinical trials or for other heart outcomes.
Most studies had a moderate risk of bias, and the authors call for more robust research to validate the finding.

items.title: Evidence for the cardiovascular effects of osteoporosis treatments in randomized trials of post-menopausal women: A systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 27 randomized trials (about 68,700 postmenopausal women) to see whether osteoporosis medicines affect the risk of heart attack, stroke and other serious heart problems. Overall, they found no solid evidence that any of the osteoporosis treatments raised the risk of heart problems compared with placebo. Romosozumab ranked as more likely than placebo to carry increased risk, though this was not a statistically significant finding. Abaloparatide looked linked to fewer heart events, but this came from just one trial.
keyPoints: No osteoporosis treatment was shown to significantly increase cardiovascular events compared with placebo.
Abaloparatide was linked to lower odds of major heart events, but this came from a single trial of 1,642 women.
Romosozumab ranked as more likely than placebo to have increased risk of cardiovascular events.
When all parathyroid-hormone-type drugs were grouped, the direction of effect was similar but no longer statistically significant.

items.title: Effects of exercise training on metabolic syndrome risk factors in post-menopausal women - A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 39 randomised trials with 2,132 post-menopausal women to see how exercise training affects the risk factors for metabolic syndrome. Exercise lasting more than 8 weeks improved waist size, triglycerides, HDL ("good") cholesterol, fasting blood sugar and blood pressure. Moderate-intensity exercise and combined exercise (more than one type) worked best, with combined exercise the most effective.
keyPoints: Exercise training improved all metabolic syndrome risk factors: waist circumference fell by about 2.6 cm, and systolic and diastolic blood pressure fell by about 6 and 4 mmHg.
Triglycerides and fasting blood glucose went down and HDL cholesterol went up in the exercise groups compared with controls.
Moderate-intensity and combined exercise helped most, and combined exercise was the most effective.
Training of 12 weeks or longer improved most risk factors, and benefits were also seen in interventions lasting 8-10 weeks.

items.title: Supplementation of vitamin D isolated or calcium-associated with bone remodeling and fracture risk in postmenopausal women without osteoporosis: A systematic review of randomized clinical trials
items.summary: This review pulled together nine randomized trials of vitamin D supplements, taken alone or with calcium, in postmenopausal women who did not have osteoporosis. Supplements raised vitamin D blood levels and improved some markers of bone turnover. But the review could not confirm that they lowered the risk of broken bones. Only one study found fewer fractures, using 800 IU of vitamin D plus 1200 mg of calcium.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplements raised blood vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D) levels and lowered parathyroid hormone, depending on starting levels.
800 to 1000 IU of vitamin D combined with calcium reduced, improved or maintained bone mineral density.
A very high dose of 500,000 IU once a year for 5 years did not reduce fractures or falls.
Only one of the nine studies showed fewer fractures, so a fracture benefit could not be confirmed.

items.title: Relationship between metabolic syndrome and follicle-stimulating hormone in postmenopausal women
items.summary: This study looked at 219 women after menopause to see how follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), a hormone that rises after menopause, relates to metabolic syndrome. Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of problems such as excess body fat, raised blood sugar and abnormal blood fats that raise heart and diabetes risk. Women with metabolic syndrome had lower FSH levels than women without it. Lower FSH was linked to more body fat and more insulin resistance, so FSH may one day help flag metabolic risk, though this is an early finding.
keyPoints: Women with metabolic syndrome had lower FSH and estradiol levels than women without it.
Lower FSH was linked to more body fat mass and higher insulin resistance (HOMA-IR).
Higher FSH was linked to higher adiponectin, a hormone that helps the body respond to insulin.
