Women in the lowest FSH group had higher odds of metabolic syndrome than those in the highest group (odds ratio 1.32).

items.title: Exercise training and vascular function in postmenopausal individuals: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine small studies (182 postmenopausal women in total) to see whether aerobic exercise improves blood vessel function. Vessel function was measured by flow-mediated dilation (FMD), a marker linked to heart disease risk. Exercise training improved FMD overall, and the gain was larger in studies with a comparison group than in before-and-after studies. The results varied a lot between studies, so the size of the benefit is uncertain.
keyPoints: Aerobic exercise training significantly improved blood vessel function (FMD) in postmenopausal women.
The improvement was greater in controlled studies than in before-and-after studies.
Larger gains were seen in people with higher resting blood pressure and in those whose fitness (maximal oxygen uptake) rose the most.
Results differed widely between studies, and only nine studies with 182 people were included.

items.title: Metabolic differences in women with premature ovarian insufficiency: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 21 studies, covering 1,573 women with premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) and 1,762 women with normal ovarian function. Women with POI had higher waist size, cholesterol, triglycerides and fasting blood sugar than the comparison group, and slightly higher insulin. Blood pressure did not differ significantly between the groups. The authors say this shows why early checks and lifelong attention to metabolic health matter for women with POI.
keyPoints: Women with POI had a larger waist circumference than women with normal ovarian function.
Total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides and fasting glucose were all higher in women with POI.
Insulin levels were marginally higher, but blood pressure differences were not significant.
The authors point to early screening and lifelong management of metabolic health for women with POI.

items.title: Cardiovascular Changes in Menopause
items.summary: This review looked at published research from 1986 to 2019 on how menopause affects the heart and blood vessels. It found that menopause is linked to changes similar to cardiovascular ageing. Changes such as unhealthy blood fats, insulin resistance, fat redistribution and high blood pressure appear to add to the risk of heart and blood vessel disease. The abstract does not rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Menopause is associated with changes consistent with cardiovascular aging.
Dyslipidemia (unhealthy blood fats), insulin resistance, fat redistribution and high blood pressure contribute to higher cardiovascular risk.
Atherosclerosis (artery narrowing) appears to result from risk factors becoming stronger around the perimenopausal period.
Oxidative stress and levels of L-arginine and ADMA may also affect blood vessel function in menopause.

items.title: Meta-analysis: Early Age at Natural Menopause and Risk for All-Cause and Cardiovascular Mortality
items.summary: Researchers combined 16 studies covering more than 320,000 women to see whether going through menopause at a younger age is linked to a higher risk of dying. Reaching natural menopause early was linked to a small increase in the risk of death from any cause. Menopause before age 40 stood out most, and it was also linked to a slightly higher risk of death from heart disease in some analyses. These studies show a link, not proof that early menopause causes these outcomes.
keyPoints: Early natural menopause was linked to a small rise in the risk of death from any cause.
The link was clearest for premature menopause (before age 40).
Early menopause overall was not clearly linked to heart-related death, but premature menopause showed a borderline link in some analyses.
The authors conclude premature menopause may be an independent risk factor for death from any cause and from heart disease.

items.title: Effect of long-term weight gain on the risk of breast cancer across women's whole adulthood as well as hormone-changed menopause stages: A systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together many studies to see whether gaining weight over adulthood or after menopause is linked to breast cancer. Women who gained the most weight as adults, or who gained weight after menopause, had about a 55-59% higher risk of breast cancer after menopause than women who gained the least. No link was seen in women before menopause. The authors say more studies are needed to confirm how strong the link is.
keyPoints: After menopause, the highest adult weight gain group had about 55% higher breast cancer risk than the lowest group.
Weight gain since menopause was linked to about 59% higher risk of breast cancer after menopause.
Each 5 kg of adult weight gain was linked to about 8% higher risk after menopause, with a stronger link in Asian women.
No significant link was found between weight gain and breast cancer in women before menopause.

items.title: Association between serum lipids and breast cancer risk in premenopausal women: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 13 studies to see whether blood fats (lipids) differ in women with breast cancer before menopause compared with women without it. Triglycerides and LDL ('bad') cholesterol were higher in the women with breast cancer, while total cholesterol and HDL ('good') cholesterol did not differ. The studies varied a lot from one another, and there was signs of publication bias in the triglyceride results, so the findings should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Triglycerides were higher in premenopausal women with breast cancer than in women without.
LDL cholesterol was also higher in premenopausal women with breast cancer.
Total cholesterol and HDL cholesterol showed no significant difference between the groups.
The included studies were highly varied, and publication bias was found in the triglyceride analysis.

items.title: Menopause symptom management in women with dyslipidemias: An EMAS clinical guide
items.summary: This clinical guide from a menopause society (based on a literature review and expert agreement) looks at how menopause symptom treatments affect cholesterol and blood fats in postmenopausal women. Menopause tends to push blood fats in an unhealthy direction, so the choice of treatment can matter for women who already have high cholesterol. The guide describes which hormone and non-hormone options have helpful, neutral or less favourable effects on blood fats.
keyPoints: Menopause is linked to higher total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, and lower HDL ("good") cholesterol.
Oral and other systemic estrogens lower LDL cholesterol and raise HDL, and skin-patch (transdermal) estrogen is preferred over tablets for women with high triglycerides.
Micronized progesterone or dydrogesterone are the preferred progestogens because they have a neutral effect on blood fats; low-dose vaginal estrogen and ospemifene have favourable effects.
Fluoxetine and citalopram affect blood fats more favourably than sertraline, paroxetine or venlafaxine, and non-oral testosterone for low sexual desire has little or no effect on blood fats.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of effects of menopausal hormone therapy on cardiovascular diseases
items.summary: This review pooled results from 26 randomised trials and 47 observational studies to look at how menopausal hormone therapy relates to heart and blood vessel disease. Both kinds of study found a higher risk of blood clots in the veins. Trials also found a slightly higher risk of stroke, while observational studies found a lower risk of heart attack. Effects differed by when treatment was started, existing health conditions, type of regimen and how it was taken.
keyPoints: Both trials and observational studies found a higher risk of venous blood clots with hormone therapy.
Trials found a higher stroke risk, while observational studies found a lower heart attack risk.
Results varied by timing of starting, underlying disease, regimen type and route of administration.
The authors suggest underlying disease and timing of starting should be carefully considered before beginning therapy after menopause.

items.title: The route of administration, timing, duration and dose of postmenopausal hormone therapy and cardiovascular outcomes in women: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 33 studies (6 trials and 27 observational studies, covering over 2.5 million women) to see how the dose, type, timing and length of menopausal hormone therapy relate to heart disease risk. Overall, low-dose oral or skin-patch (transdermal) hormone therapy did not appear to raise heart disease risk, especially when started around menopause or in the first 10 years after. Hormone therapy may raise the risk of blood clots and stroke in a dose-related way, and transdermal estrogen at a low dose with micronized progesterone looked like the safer option. The evidence was mostly observational and rated low to moderate quality, so the findings are not certain.
keyPoints: Evidence did not support concerns that oral or transdermal hormone therapy increases heart disease risk, but no trials have shown it protects the heart.
Hormone therapy may increase blood clot and stroke risk in a dose-dependent way; low-dose transdermal estrogen (under 50 µg/day) with micronized progesterone appears safer for clot and stroke risk.
Low-dose oral hormone therapy appears safe for heart health in the menopause transition and within about 10 years of menopause onset.

If started more than 10 years after menopause (over about 60), risks are higher, so the shortest time, lowest dose and ideally a transdermal route are advised, with treatment tailored to each woman's heart risk.

items.title: Lipid profile differences during menopause: a review with meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 66 studies of over 114,000 women to compare blood fat (lipid) levels before and after menopause. Women who had gone through menopause had higher triglycerides, total cholesterol and LDL ('bad') cholesterol than women who had not. HDL ('good') cholesterol did not differ. Part of the difference was explained by postmenopausal women being older on average.
keyPoints: Postmenopausal women had higher triglycerides, total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol than premenopausal women.
HDL cholesterol showed no difference between the two groups.
Some of the difference in lipid levels was linked to age, not menopause alone.
The authors say this less favourable lipid profile may raise the risk of heart disease and stroke if lifestyle or medication measures are not used.

items.title: Metabolic syndrome in menopause and associated factors: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to look at how menopause relates to metabolic syndrome, a group of risk factors for heart disease and diabetes. After menopause, almost all measured risk factors were worse than before menopause. Women who had surgical menopause had a higher risk than those who went through menopause naturally. Different types of hormone therapy affected the risk factors in different ways.
keyPoints: Nearly all metabolic syndrome measures were less favourable in postmenopausal women than in premenopausal women, except HDL ('good') cholesterol.
Women with surgical menopause had a 1.51-fold higher risk of metabolic syndrome than women with natural menopause.
Hormone therapy with estradiol showed more benefit for triglycerides and diastolic blood pressure.
Hormone therapy with conjugated equine estrogen showed a better effect on both HDL and LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Association of Age at Onset of Menopause and Time Since Onset of Menopause With Cardiovascular Outcomes, Intermediate Vascular Traits, and All-Cause Mortality: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 32 studies covering over 310,000 women to see whether the age at which menopause starts is linked to heart disease and early death. Women who went through menopause before age 45 had a higher risk of coronary heart disease, death from heart disease, and death from any cause than women who reached menopause at 45 or older. Women whose menopause began between 50 and 54 had a lower risk of fatal coronary heart disease than those who were younger than 50. These studies show links, not proof of cause, and results on time since menopause were inconsistent.
keyPoints: Menopause before age 45 was linked to about 50% higher risk of coronary heart disease (relative risk 1.50) compared with menopause at 45 or older.
Early menopause was also linked to higher risk of death from heart disease (1.19) and death from any cause (1.12).
Menopause at 50 to 54 was linked to a lower risk of fatal coronary heart disease than menopause before 50 (0.87).
Evidence on stroke was less clear, and four studies on time since menopause gave inconsistent results.

items.title: Menopausal Hormone Therapy and Mortality: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This review pooled results from 43 randomized trials to see whether menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) changes the risk of dying. Overall, MHT did not change the risk of death from any cause, from heart problems, or from stroke or cancer. Combined estrogen-plus-progesterone therapy was linked to a likely increase in breast cancer deaths, while estrogen alone was not. In a small group of 5 trials where women started MHT younger, death rates were lower.
keyPoints: Across 43 trials, MHT made no difference to the overall risk of death, including in women with existing heart disease.
No link was found between MHT and death from heart problems or stroke.
Estrogen plus progesterone was linked to a likely increase in breast cancer deaths, but estrogen alone was not.
In 5 trials where MHT likely started at a younger age or soon after menopause, death rates were lower.

items.title: Sex-specific management of migraine a systematic review and consensus statement from the European Headache Federation (EHF)
items.summary: The European Headache Federation reviewed 37 studies and combined them with expert consensus to look at how migraine and its treatment differ between women and men, including around periods, pregnancy and breastfeeding. Newer anti-CGRP migraine medicines seem to work similarly in both sexes. Several common migraine treatments were judged generally safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding, though some have trimester-specific limits. The authors say the evidence is limited, especially on safety around pregnancy.
keyPoints: Acute and preventive anti-CGRP therapies seem to work similarly in women and men, and anti-CGRP antibodies work equally well before and after menopause.
For migraine linked to periods, triptans and lasmiditan are effective; frovatriptan is recommended for short-term prevention, and topiramate or anti-CGRP antibodies for long-term prevention.
In pregnancy, triptans, greater occipital nerve blocks and onabotulinumtoxinA are considered safe; during breastfeeding, triptans appear safe.
Expert consensus supports acetaminophen, antiemetics, magnesium and some other drugs as generally safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding, with some trimester-specific limits.

items.title: Pharmacologic Treatment for Migraine Prevention in Adults Practice Guideline Recommendations: Report of the AAN Guidelines Subcommittee and the American Headache Society
items.summary: This is an updated guideline from the American Academy of Neurology and the American Headache Society on medicines taken regularly to prevent migraine in adults. A expert panel reviewed studies published up to June 2024 and wrote recommendations on when to start a preventive medicine and how to choose one. It also covers special situations, including treatment during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and sex-related factors in choosing medicines.
keyPoints: The guideline gives advice on how to decide when to start a preventive migraine medicine and which one to start.
It includes recommendations on choosing medicines during pregnancy and lactation.
It addresses sex-related factors when choosing a migraine preventive medicine.
It covers choices for people with fibromyalgia, obesity, high blood pressure or medication overuse, and for older adults, plus how to judge benefits, side effects and stopping treatment.

items.title: Association between migraine, migraine subtype, and adverse pregnancy outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 19 studies covering more than 1.4 million deliveries to see whether migraine is linked to problems in pregnancy. Women with migraine had a higher chance of preeclampsia (a pregnancy blood pressure condition) and preterm birth than women without migraine. Links with low birth weight and small babies were less consistent. The authors say more studies are needed to strengthen these findings.
keyPoints: Pregnant women with migraine had a higher risk of preeclampsia and preterm birth than women without migraine.
Both migraine with aura and migraine without aura were linked to higher risk of preeclampsia and preterm birth.
Migraine may be linked to low birth weight and small-for-gestational-age babies, but the results were inconsistent.
The authors say additional studies are needed to strengthen these findings.

items.title: International Headache society evidence-based guidelines on the use of non-invasive neuromodulation devices for the acute and preventive treatment of migraine
items.summary: The International Headache Society reviewed trials of non-invasive devices that use gentle electrical or magnetic stimulation to treat migraine. Only 15 studies were good enough to use, and the quality of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate. Weak recommendations were made for a few specific devices, either for treating an attack or for preventing migraines. The devices were found to be safe, generally well tolerated and free of drug interactions.
keyPoints: Weak recommendations were given for SAVI Dual, Cefaly, Relivion and Nerivio to treat acute migraine attacks.
Weak recommendations were given for gammaCore Sapphire, Cefaly and Nerivio to prevent migraine.
The devices are safe, generally well tolerated and have no drug interactions, making them a possible alternative to medication.
For situations without enough trial evidence, including menstrual migraine, the group gave expert consensus advice instead, and more research is needed.

items.title: Acute and preventive treatment of menstrual migraine: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 26 randomized trials of treatments for menstrual migraine, a type of migraine linked to the monthly cycle that is often more severe and harder to treat. Triptans, with or without other pain relievers, worked better than placebo for relieving attacks and for prevention. Sumatriptan and lasmiditan gave the best pain relief during an attack, while frovatriptan and two newer injectable drugs (galcanezumab and erenumab) helped most with prevention.
keyPoints: Sumatriptan and lasmiditan were the most effective first-line treatments for an acute menstrual migraine attack, with better pain relief at 2 and 24 hours.
Frovatriptan was the more effective triptan for preventing menstrual migraine from coming back.
The CGRP antibody drugs erenumab and galcanezumab reduced the number of headache days per month more than triptans.

items.title: Migraine treatment: Position paper of the French Headache Society
items.summary: The French Headache Society updated its migraine treatment advice to reflect new drugs and new safety data. Newer preventive medicines that block a pain-related protein called CGRP can now be offered as a first choice, although national reimbursement is limited to people with severe migraine. The paper also says topiramate should no longer be a first-choice preventive for women who could become pregnant, because of possible harm to a baby's brain development if exposed in the womb.
keyPoints: CGRP-targeting preventive treatments (monoclonal antibodies and gepants) can be offered as first-line treatment, based on efficacy and safety.
French reimbursement covers these only for severe migraine, at least eight headache days a month, after two earlier preventive treatments have failed.
Topiramate is formally contraindicated in pregnancy because pharmacovigilance data suggest a possible effect on neurodevelopment in children exposed in utero.
In women of childbearing age topiramate needs extreme caution: effective contraception, no alternative available and annual follow-up, as with valproate.

items.title: Erenumab efficacy in migraine headache prophylaxis: A systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 53 studies on erenumab, a monthly injection approved to help prevent migraines. Both the 70 mg and 140 mg doses cut the number of migraine days each month and the days when migraine-specific medicine was needed. The reviewers also found it helped people with menstrual migraine, aura, medication overuse headache, and migraine that had not responded to earlier preventive treatments.
keyPoints: Both the 70 mg and 140 mg doses reduced monthly migraine days and days of migraine-specific medicine use.
More people had at least a 50%, 75% or 100% drop in monthly migraine days compared with before treatment.
Benefit began in the first week and lasted during and after treatment.
It also worked in menstrual migraine, migraine with aura, medication overuse headache and hard-to-treat migraine, and with Onabotulinumtoxin-A.

items.title: Comparative efficacy of different treatments for menstrual migraine: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 14 randomized trials (4,601 people) to compare treatments for menstrual migraine, a type of migraine linked to the menstrual cycle that is often harder to treat. For short-term prevention, frovatriptan 2.5 mg twice daily worked best compared with placebo. For treating an attack once it started, sumatriptan 100 mg worked best compared with placebo. The authors say more high-quality trials are needed to be sure which treatment is most effective.
keyPoints: Frovatriptan 2.5 mg twice daily had the highest chance of working for short-term prevention compared with placebo.
Sumatriptan 100 mg was the most effective option for treating an attack compared with placebo.
The review covered 14 randomized trials with 4,601 patients.
More high-quality randomized trials are needed to find the most effective treatment.

items.title: Review of migraine incidence and management in obstetrics and gynaecology
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This systematic review looked at how common migraines are in women's health care, including gynaecology, pregnancy and contraception use, and how they are managed. It found that women who have migraines and take combined hormonal contraception have about a six-fold higher average risk of stroke. Migraines in pregnancy were linked with higher risks of high blood pressure conditions, low birth weight and preterm birth. The authors advise that women with migraines avoid combined hormonal contraception and use progesterone-only pills instead.
keyPoints: Women with migraines who take combined hormonal contraception have an average six-fold increase in stroke risk.
Desogestrel 75mcg/day, a progesterone-only pill, reduced migraine intensity compared with combined hormonal contraceptives.
Migraines in pregnancy were linked with a higher risk of gestational hypertension, pre-eclampsia, low birth weight and preterm birth.
Authors advise asking about migraines at appointments and avoiding combined hormonal contraception in women with migraines.

items.title: Associations Between Migraine and Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 14 studies to see whether a history of migraine is linked to problems in pregnancy. Women with migraine had a higher chance of preeclampsia (a pregnancy condition involving high blood pressure) and of having a baby with low birth weight. No clear link was found with preterm birth or babies being small for their gestational age. The authors suggest shared underlying heart and blood vessel risk may play a role.
keyPoints: Women with a history of migraine had about twice the odds of preeclampsia (OR 2.07).
Migraine history was linked to a slightly higher chance of low birth weight (OR 1.18).
No significant link was found between migraine and preterm birth or small-for-gestational-age babies.
The authors suggest women with migraine history be informed and monitored in pregnancy.

items.title: Effectiveness of the progestin-only pill for migraine treatment in women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled four studies on whether a progestin-only contraceptive pill (desogestrel 75 mcg a day) helps women with migraine. The pill modestly reduced the number of migraine attacks and migraine days, and also eased pain intensity, duration and the need for pain medicines. The quality of the evidence was low to very low, because the studies were small and observational and tested only one type of pill. Larger randomized trials are still needed to confirm these results.
keyPoints: The desogestrel progestin-only pill significantly but modestly reduced migraine attacks and migraine days.
Migraine intensity and duration, use of pain relief and triptans, and headache-related quality of life also improved.
Fewer than 10% of participants stopped treatment because of side effects.
Two studies found similar migraine outcomes for the desogestrel pill and a combined oral contraceptive.

items.title: Latest clinical recommendations on valproate use for migraine prophylaxis in women of childbearing age: overview from European Medicines Agency and European Headache Federation
items.summary: Valproate is a medicine that has been widely used to prevent migraine attacks. This 2018 European review looked at its use in women who could become pregnant, because the harm it can cause to babies exposed in the womb is well documented. The review found that earlier 2014 advice to limit its use in this group did not work well enough, and newer studies suggest an even greater risk to a child's brain development. European regulators and the European Headache Federation called for stricter prescribing rules and better education for women with migraine.
keyPoints: Valproate can cause birth defects and harm to a baby's development when taken during pregnancy.
More recent studies show an even greater risk of neurodevelopmental problems in children exposed in the womb.
The 2014 European recommendations did not succeed in limiting valproate use in women of childbearing age.
The 2018 review called for tighter prescribing conditions, more public awareness and better education for women with migraine.

items.title: Medical Treatment Guidelines for Preventive Treatment of Migraine
items.summary: The Taiwan Headache Society reviewed the medicines used to prevent migraine and updated its 2008 guideline. It names propranolol as the first choice for preventing episodic migraine, with several other medicines as second-line options. It advises against preventive migraine medicines during pregnancy or breastfeeding. For migraine linked to periods, some pain relievers and triptans can be used around the menstrual period.
keyPoints: Propranolol has the best evidence and fewer side effects, so it is the first-line choice for preventing episodic migraine.
Valproic acid, topiramate, flunarizine and amitriptyline are suggested as second-line options; OnabotulinumtoxinA and topiramate are recommended for chronic migraine.
Preventive migraine medicines are not recommended during pregnancy or lactation.
For menstrual migraine, nonsteroid anti-inflammatory drugs and triptans can be used for prevention during the menstrual period.

items.title: Migraine, cardiovascular disease, and stroke during pregnancy: systematic review of the literature
items.summary: This review pulled together 17 studies on migraine and blood-vessel problems during pregnancy. Women with migraine had higher chances of high blood pressure in pregnancy, preeclampsia, stroke, heart attack and blood clots than women without migraine. The authors note there is not much data, so more research is needed to work out which women with migraine may be at risk.
keyPoints: Women with migraine had a higher risk of gestational hypertension and preeclampsia than women without migraine.
Ischemic stroke in pregnancy was linked to migraine, especially active migraine.
Migraine was also linked to higher risk of heart attack, heart disease and blood clots (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolus) in pregnancy.
The authors say the amount of data is limited and more research is needed.

items.title: Migraine and breast cancer risk: a prospective cohort study and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
items.journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
items.summary: Researchers followed over 115,000 nurses for 20 years to see whether having migraine changes the chance of getting breast cancer. Women with migraine did not have a higher or lower risk of breast cancer, and their natural sex hormone levels were no different from women without migraine. A pooled review of earlier studies found a lower risk only in case-control studies, not in the stronger long-term cohort studies, so the overall evidence does not support a link.
keyPoints: In a large 20-year study, migraine was not linked to breast cancer risk, whether in situ or invasive.
Natural sex hormone levels did not differ between women with and without migraine.
Pooled case-control studies suggested a lower breast cancer risk with migraine, but pooled cohort studies showed no link.
Overall, long-term cohort evidence does not support an association between migraine and breast cancer.

items.title: Pregnancy outcome following prenatal exposure to triptan medications: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined six studies covering over 4,000 babies whose mothers took triptan migraine medicines during pregnancy, and compared them with women who did not take triptans. Triptan use did not appear to raise the rates of major birth defects or early birth. Miscarriage rates were higher in triptan users than in healthy women, but not higher than in women with migraine who did not take triptans. Women with migraine who did not use triptans had slightly more birth defects than healthy women, and both findings need more research.
keyPoints: Triptan use in pregnancy did not appear to increase major birth defects or premature birth.
Compared with women who have migraine but did not take triptans, triptan users showed no significant increase in birth defects, early birth or miscarriage.
Compared with healthy women, triptan users had a higher rate of miscarriage, which the authors say needs further research.
Women with migraine who did not take triptans had more major birth defects than healthy women, which also needs further research.

items.title: Systematic Review of Preventive and Acute Treatment of Menstrual Migraine
items.summary: This review looked at trials of treatments for menstrual migraine, which are migraine attacks linked to the menstrual cycle. Menstrual migraine attacks tend to be more disabling, last longer, come back more often and respond less well to treatment than other migraines. The researchers found that triptans have the strongest evidence, both for treating an attack and for short-term prevention. Other treatments have less research behind them and need more trials.
keyPoints: Menstrual migraine is common, and about half of women have a higher risk of migraine linked to their cycle.
Menstrual migraine attacks are usually more disabling, longer and more likely to return than non-menstrual attacks.
Triptans have the most research and strong evidence for both acute treatment and short-term prevention.
Other options, such as hormonal, anti-inflammatory, supplement and non-drug approaches, need more randomized trials.

items.title: Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy in unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled earlier studies to ask whether testing embryos for the wrong number of chromosomes (PGT-A) helps people who have had two or more unexplained pregnancy losses. In these studies, PGT-A was linked to fewer pregnancy losses and more live births per embryo transfer and per patient. The authors say the evidence is low quality, so the results are uncertain, and they call for better-designed randomised trials.
keyPoints: PGT-A was linked to fewer clinical pregnancy losses and more live births per transfer and per patient in people with unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss.
Euploid (chromosomally typical) embryos gave similar live birth and pregnancy loss rates in people with and without recurrent loss.
Whether couples with unexplained recurrent loss have more chromosomally abnormal embryos remains unclear.
The authors describe the evidence as low quality and say randomised trials comparing IVF with PGT-A against expectant management are needed.

items.title: Safety of Dupilumab Therapy for Atopic Dermatitis during Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 15 small observational studies of 115 pregnant women with atopic dermatitis (eczema) who used dupilumab, a biologic medicine, before or during pregnancy. About 19 in 100 pregnancies ended in miscarriage, though the range was wide, and no birth defects were reported. The authors say dupilumab looks probably safe in pregnancy, with no clear rise in miscarriage or malformation risk compared with the general population. They also say the results are inconclusive because there are few large, well-designed studies.
keyPoints: Fifteen observational studies covering 115 pregnant women were included, and all looked at dupilumab.
The pooled miscarriage rate was 18.9%, with a wide confidence range (5.3% to 38.2%).
No congenital malformations (birth defects) were reported in newborns.
Evidence is limited and inconclusive because of the small number of large, well-designed studies.

items.title: Antiphospholipid syndrome in pregnancy: a comprehensive literature review
items.summary: This review looked at antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), an autoimmune condition that can cause blood clots and problems in pregnancy, including repeated miscarriage. It brought together studies on how APS works, how it is diagnosed and how it is treated in pregnancy. The review found that low-dose aspirin and heparin help reduce miscarriage rates, and that hydroxychloroquine may help in higher-risk cases. The authors say treatment should be tailored to each person and that more research is needed.
keyPoints: APS affects about 0.5% of people and is a leading contributor to recurrent pregnancy loss, preeclampsia and poor fetal growth.
Evidence supports low-dose aspirin and heparin to reduce miscarriage rates.
Hydroxychloroquine has shown promise for improving live birth rates and reducing preterm delivery in high-risk cases.
Newer treatments, such as TNF-alpha inhibitors and nitric oxide modulators, may help in cases that do not respond to usual treatment, but more research is needed.

items.title: Controlled ovarian stimulation protocols for assisted reproduction: a network meta-analysis
items.summary: This large Cochrane review looked at 338 trials (59,086 women) comparing different drug combinations used to stimulate the ovaries before assisted conception such as IVF. For women expected to respond normally, the newer 'short antagonist' approach probably gave about the same chance of a live birth as the older 'long agonist' approach, and it may lower the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), a condition where the ovaries over-react. Stimulating without any drug to hold back natural ovulation may lower the chance of a live birth. Most of the evidence was low certainty, and many trials could not be included because of bias or missing data.
keyPoints: In women expected to respond normally, short antagonist protocols probably give little to no difference in live birth or ongoing pregnancy compared with long agonist protocols (moderate-certainty evidence).
Short antagonist protocols may reduce OHSS compared with long agonist protocols (low-certainty evidence).
Stimulation without pituitary suppression may lower live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates compared with antagonist or flare protocols (low-certainty evidence).
In women expected to respond strongly, hMG may lower OHSS compared with rFSH but may increase cycle cancellation (low-certainty evidence, one study).

items.title: Guideline No. 464: Recurrent Pregnancy Loss
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline explains how doctors should assess and care for people who have had two or more pregnancy losses. Causes can be chromosomal, structural, hormonal, immune, infectious or linked to lifestyle, but most cases have no clear cause. Some tests and treatments may help, but the evidence for many treatments varies, so doctors are advised to use unproven ones cautiously. Emotional support and trauma-informed care are described as essential.
keyPoints: Recurrent pregnancy loss is defined as two or more pregnancy losses, including non-consecutive and very early (biochemical) losses.
Suggested checks include thyroid problems, diabetes, antiphospholipid syndrome, uterine shape problems, and genetic testing of pregnancy tissue or parents' chromosomes.
Possible helpful steps include cutting back on caffeine, smoking and alcohol, addressing obesity, antibiotics for chronic endometritis, and progesterone, especially if started in the luteal phase.
Early pregnancy clinic access, emotional support, close monitoring and shared decision-making are considered essential, and tests carry a high chance of finding no cause.

items.title: Vitamin B12 supplementation during pregnancy for maternal and child health outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at five trials with 984 pregnant women, mostly in low- and middle-income countries, to see whether taking vitamin B12 by mouth in pregnancy helps mothers and babies. B12 supplements may lower the chance of mothers being B12 deficient and may raise B12 levels in both mothers and babies, but the evidence is very uncertain. There was little clear evidence on anaemia, preterm birth, low birthweight or child development, and miscarriage could not be properly assessed.
keyPoints: Supplements may reduce maternal B12 deficiency (about 26% versus 68% in the two trials that measured it), but the evidence is very uncertain.
Mothers and babies in the supplement groups had higher B12 blood levels.
The evidence is uncertain for anaemia, preterm birth and low birthweight, with no clear difference found.
Miscarriage data could not be combined because the trials gave no usable numbers or clear definition, and no trials looked at neural tube defects.

items.title: Effects of Levothyroxine Treatment on Fertility and Pregnancy Outcomes in Subclinical Hypothyroidism: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of levothyroxine (thyroid hormone medicine) in women with subclinical hypothyroidism, where thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is raised but thyroid hormone levels are normal. Treatment before pregnancy did not clearly improve pregnancy or live birth rates or reduce miscarriage, and treatment during pregnancy also made no clear difference to live births or miscarriage. Preterm birth may be lower with treatment in women whose TSH was above 4.0 mU/L, but not in those with TSH between 2.5 and 4.0 mU/L. The authors say more well-designed studies are needed, especially for TSH above 4.0.
keyPoints: Levothyroxine before pregnancy did not significantly improve live birth or pregnancy rates, or reduce miscarriage, in subclinical hypothyroidism.
Levothyroxine during pregnancy did not significantly change live birth or miscarriage rates.
The effect on preterm birth differed by TSH level: a possible benefit when TSH was above 4.0 mU/L, but none seen at 2.5-4.0 mU/L.
The authors call for further well-designed studies, especially for pre-conception treatment when TSH is above 4.0 mU/L.

items.title: Progestogens in women with threatened miscarriage or recurrent miscarriage: A meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined 15 randomised trials (about 6,600 pregnancies) of progesterone given to women with bleeding in early pregnancy (threatened miscarriage) or a history of repeated miscarriage. Progesterone probably led to slightly more live births, about 3 more per 100 pregnancies overall. It probably made little or no difference to birth defects or other serious pregnancy problems. The benefit may be mostly in women who have had a miscarriage before.
keyPoints: Progesterone probably increases live births slightly overall (about 3.1% more), with moderate certainty.
For women with at least one prior miscarriage, live births probably rose by about 5%, with moderate certainty.
For threatened miscarriage with no prior miscarriage, the effect is very uncertain (very low certainty).
Progesterone probably has little or no effect on congenital anomalies or other serious adverse pregnancy events.

items.title: Autologous platelet-rich plasma for assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether putting a woman's own platelet-rich plasma (PRP) into the womb or ovaries helps IVF or ICSI treatment work better. It combined 12 trials with 1069 women. The evidence was very low quality, so it is not clear whether PRP improves live birth or reduces miscarriage. One small trial also hinted at a higher chance of preterm birth.
keyPoints: The review is uncertain whether PRP in the womb or ovaries improves outcomes of assisted reproduction.
Only 1 of 12 trials was at low risk of bias, and that trial found no clear effect on live birth or miscarriage.
When all trials were pooled, womb PRP looked linked to more live births and clinical pregnancies, but the certainty was very low.
One trial of 120 women suggested womb PRP may increase the risk of preterm delivery (low-certainty evidence), and most trials gave little or no safety data.

items.title: Chronic endometritis and recurrent reproductive failure: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled earlier studies, covering 1,038 women, to see whether chronic endometritis (long-lasting low-level inflammation of the womb lining) is linked to fertility problems. Chronic endometritis was found more often in women with recurrent pregnancy loss and in women with infertility than in comparison groups. It was not clearly linked to repeated failure of embryos to implant. The review shows an association, not that chronic endometritis causes these problems.
keyPoints: Chronic endometritis was found in 37.6% of women with recurrent pregnancy loss, compared with 16.4% of controls.
Chronic endometritis was found in 19.46% of infertile women, compared with 7.7% of controls.
No significant link was found between chronic endometritis and recurrent implantation failure (6.35% vs 5.8%).
The authors conclude chronic endometritis appears to be associated with infertility and recurrent pregnancy loss.

items.title: Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management
items.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
items.journal: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
items.summary: This is a NICE guideline on how ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage are diagnosed and first managed in women with pain or bleeding in early pregnancy, up to 13 completed weeks. It aims to improve how early pregnancy loss is diagnosed and to give women better support so the emotional impact of their loss is limited. It is written for healthcare professionals, and also for women, families and carers. The abstract does not list the specific recommendations or rate the strength of the evidence.
keyPoints: Covers diagnosing and initially managing ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage in early pregnancy, up to 13 completed weeks.
Aims to improve how early pregnancy loss is diagnosed.
Aims to improve the support women are given, to limit the psychological impact of their loss.
Intended for healthcare professionals, commissioners, and women with early pregnancy complications, their families and carers.

items.title: Recurrent MiscarriageGreen-top Guideline No. 17
items.source: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
items.organisation: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
items.summary: This is a UK guideline from the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists on recurrent miscarriage, which it defines as three or more first trimester miscarriages. It says doctors may start tests after two miscarriages if they suspect a cause. It lists which tests are worth offering, which are not, and which treatments may help.
keyPoints: Women with recurrent miscarriage should be offered tests for antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin), a uterine scan (ideally 3D ultrasound) for shape differences, and thyroid tests including TPO antibodies.
Chromosome testing of pregnancy tissue is advised after a third or later miscarriage and after any second trimester miscarriage; parental blood chromosome tests are offered in certain cases.
Aspirin and heparin are recommended for antiphospholipid syndrome but not for unexplained recurrent miscarriage; progesterone should be considered if there is bleeding in early pregnancy.
Immune, infection and sperm DNA tests are not routinely recommended outside research; the guideline advises a BMI of 19-25, no smoking, limited alcohol and caffeine under 200 mg a day.

items.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome and recurrent pregnancy loss, a review of literature
items.summary: This review looked at 37 studies on whether polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is linked to repeated miscarriages. It found that the studies are few in number and give inconsistent results, so the link is still unclear. The authors say more research is needed to understand which factors, such as weight, insulin resistance and hormone levels, may raise the risk of miscarriage in women with PCOS.
keyPoints: Studies on PCOS and recurrent pregnancy loss are few and inconsistent.
The review included 37 articles, mostly case-control and cohort studies, with only a small number of trials.
Factors worth further study include PCOS type, BMI and obesity, insulin resistance, high androgen levels, AMH and clotting disorders (thrombophilia).
More research is needed to give better medical guidance during pregnancy for women with PCOS.

items.title: Cleavage-stage versus blastocyst-stage embryo transfer in assisted reproductive technology
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 32 trials (5,821 women or couples) comparing IVF embryo transfer on day 5 to 6 (blastocyst stage) with transfer on day 2 to 3 (cleavage stage). In fresh transfers, blastocyst transfer was linked to higher live birth and clinical pregnancy rates. It was also linked to a higher chance that no embryo was available to transfer and to fewer spare embryos being frozen. The evidence for live birth was low quality, and it is still unclear whether the benefit holds when frozen embryo transfers are counted too.
keyPoints: Live birth after a fresh transfer was higher with blastocyst transfer: if 31% of women had a live birth with cleavage-stage transfer, about 32% to 41% would with blastocyst transfer (low-quality evidence).
Clinical pregnancy was also higher with blastocyst transfer, about 42% to 47% compared with 39% (moderate-quality evidence).
Having no embryo to transfer was more likely with blastocyst transfer (about 2% to 4% compared with 1%), and fewer women had spare embryos frozen (moderate and low-quality evidence).
The review is uncertain whether blastocyst transfer changes miscarriage or multiple pregnancy rates, or the total pregnancy rate across fresh and frozen transfers; more research is needed.

items.title: Vitamin D and miscarriage: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 studies (about 7,700 women) to see whether vitamin D levels are linked to miscarriage. Women with low vitamin D had a higher chance of miscarriage than women with healthy levels. It is still unknown whether treating low vitamin D before pregnancy prevents miscarriage. The overall quality of the evidence was low or very low.
keyPoints: Women with vitamin D deficiency (below 50 nmol/L) had higher odds of miscarriage than women with healthy levels (above 75 nmol/L).
Women with either insufficient or deficient vitamin D also had higher odds of miscarriage than women with healthy levels.
Four trials tested vitamin D treatment, but differences between them and weak data meant their results could not be combined.
It remains unknown whether treating vitamin D deficiency before pregnancy lowers the risk of pregnancy loss.

items.title: Diagnosis and treatment of luteal phase deficiency: a committee opinion
items.summary: This committee opinion from two major fertility societies looks at luteal phase deficiency (LPD), a suspected problem with the second half of the menstrual cycle, when the body is thought to make too little progesterone or respond poorly to it. The committee found that LPD has not been proven to be a separate cause of infertility or repeated pregnancy loss. There is also disagreement about how to diagnose it and whether treating it improves outcomes.
keyPoints: LPD is a clinical diagnosis linked to a luteal phase of 10 days or less.
Possible causes include progesterone that does not last long enough, progesterone levels that are too low, or the womb lining not responding well to progesterone.
LPD has been seen with some medical conditions and also in fertile women with normal periods.
LPD has not been proven to cause infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss on its own, and it is unclear whether treatment improves outcomes.

items.title: Progestogens for preventing miscarriage: a network meta-analysis
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined seven randomised trials (5,682 women) to see whether progesterone-type medicines (progestogens) help prevent miscarriage. For most women with early pregnancy bleeding or a history of repeated miscarriages, these medicines probably make little or no difference to the chance of a live birth. The exception was vaginal progesterone for women with early bleeding who had already had one or more miscarriages, where live births increased slightly, with no clear rise in side effects. Evidence on other progestogens, such as dydrogesterone, is still too limited to be sure.
keyPoints: Progestogens probably make little or no difference to live birth rates for women with early pregnancy bleeding (threatened miscarriage) or recurrent miscarriage.
Vaginal micronized progesterone increased live births for women with early pregnancy bleeding and one or more previous miscarriages (high-certainty evidence).
Vaginal progesterone showed likely no difference in congenital abnormalities or adverse drug events compared with placebo.
Effects of dydrogesterone, oral progesterone and 17-α-hydroxyprogesterone remain uncertain because of limited or very low-certainty evidence.

items.title: Obesity in Pregnancy: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 230
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) on obesity in pregnancy. It notes that obesity is the most common medical condition in women of reproductive age, and that its effects on pregnancy are often overlooked. It says care should start before pregnancy and continue through the postpartum period, and can involve other professionals such as nutritionists.
keyPoints: Obesity is the most common medical condition in women of reproductive age.
Managing obesity takes long-term approaches, from public health measures to individual nutrition, behavior or surgical options.
Care should begin before pregnancy and continue through the postpartum period.
Nutritionists and other health professionals can support the obstetric care team.

items.title: Methods for managing miscarriage: a network meta-analysis
items.summary: This large Cochrane review pooled 78 trials with nearly 18,000 women to compare ways of managing an early miscarriage (up to 14 weeks): waiting, medicine, or surgery. Surgical and medical methods may be more likely than waiting (or placebo) to fully clear the pregnancy. Waiting had the highest chance of serious complications, including unplanned or emergency surgery. Most of the evidence was low certainty, and the authors say the main results may be unreliable because missed and incomplete miscarriage behaved differently.
keyPoints: Surgical methods ranked highest for completing a miscarriage, then medical methods (misoprostol, or mifepristone plus misoprostol), then waiting or placebo.
Mifepristone plus misoprostol was the best-ranked non-surgical option, and suction aspiration after cervical preparation was the best-ranked surgical option.
Waiting or placebo had the highest chance of serious complications, such as blood transfusion or the need for unplanned or emergency surgery; no deaths were reported in the studies.
Surgical and medical methods may work better for missed miscarriage than for incomplete miscarriage.

items.title: Toxoplasma gondii infection and spontaneous abortion: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to see whether infection with Toxoplasma gondii, a common parasite, is linked to miscarriage. Women who had a miscarriage were more likely to have signs of past infection, and even more likely to have signs of a recent infection. The authors conclude that recent infection is associated with a higher risk of miscarriage, though an association does not prove cause, and they call for more research.
keyPoints: About 10% of women with a miscarriage tested positive for T. gondii by PCR (a test for the parasite's DNA).
Signs of past (latent) infection were linked to higher odds of miscarriage (odds ratio 1.84).
Signs of recent infection were linked to even higher odds of miscarriage (odds ratio 3.72).
The authors call for more studies of toxoplasmosis risk factors and for confirmatory testing at the time of miscarriage.

items.title: Interventions for endometriosis-related infertility: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 26 randomized trials covering 2,245 women who had endometriosis confirmed by laparoscopy and were having trouble getting pregnant. Compared with placebo, laparoscopic surgery alone or a GnRH agonist medicine alone was linked to higher odds of becoming pregnant. There was not enough evidence on other treatments, or on live birth, miscarriage and side effects, to draw conclusions. The authors say more trials are needed.
keyPoints: Laparoscopic surgery alone gave higher odds of pregnancy than placebo (odds ratio 1.63).
GnRH agonist treatment alone also gave higher odds of pregnancy than placebo (odds ratio 1.68).
Evidence on other treatments, and on live birth, miscarriage and adverse events, was insufficient.
More trials are needed, including ones comparing IVF and IUI with other treatments.

items.title: Aspirin or heparin or both for improving pregnancy outcomes in women with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies and recurrent pregnancy loss
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at aspirin and heparin (blood thinners) for women who have lasting antiphospholipid antibodies and have lost two or more pregnancies. It found that taking heparin plus low-dose aspirin may lead to more live births and fewer pregnancy losses than aspirin alone. The evidence is low to very low certainty because the studies were small or had a risk of bias, and one large study drove most of the benefit. Safety information such as bleeding was often not reported well.
keyPoints: Heparin plus aspirin may increase live births compared with aspirin alone (low-certainty evidence from 5 studies, 1295 women).
Heparin plus aspirin may reduce pregnancy loss compared with aspirin alone (low-certainty evidence).
It is very uncertain whether aspirin alone makes any difference to live birth compared with placebo, based on one small trial of 40 women.
Side effects, including bleeding, were often not reported, so more research is needed on risks and benefits.

items.title: Evaluation of human papilloma virus in semen as a risk factor for low sperm quality and poor in vitro fertilization outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 studies to see whether human papillomavirus (HPV) found in semen affects sperm quality and the results of IVF. Men with HPV in their semen tended to have lower sperm concentration, motility (movement) and normal shape. Couples where the sperm carried HPV had lower pregnancy rates and a higher miscarriage rate. Most studies had a moderate risk of bias, so the authors say larger, better-designed studies are needed before any clinical advice is given.
keyPoints: HPV in semen was linked to lower sperm concentration, motility and morphology (shape).
Couples with HPV-infected sperm had lower pregnancy rates in assisted reproduction.
The link with higher miscarriage rates was even stronger than the link with lower pregnancy rates.
Most studies had a moderate risk of bias, so more large, well-designed studies are needed before management recommendations.

items.title: Antioxidants for female subfertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 63 trials with 7760 women who were having trouble getting pregnant, to see whether antioxidant supplements taken by mouth help. Some results suggested higher live birth and pregnancy rates, but the quality of the evidence was low to very low, so we cannot be sure. No increase in miscarriage, multiple pregnancy, stomach upset or ectopic pregnancy was seen, though that evidence was also of low quality. A 2026 editorial note says nine included studies were retracted or flagged, but the editors found this did not meaningfully change the conclusions.
keyPoints: Antioxidants may improve live birth and clinical pregnancy rates compared with placebo or no treatment, but the evidence is very low to low quality.
No difference was found in miscarriage, multiple pregnancy, gastrointestinal problems or ectopic pregnancy, based on low-quality evidence.
Comparisons between different antioxidants, such as lower versus higher melatonin doses, showed no clear difference.
Overall, evidence supporting oral antioxidant supplements for subfertile women is limited.

items.title: Multiple-micronutrient supplementation for women during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 20 trials (about 141,800 women), mostly in low- and middle-income countries, comparing multiple-micronutrient supplements (with iron and folic acid) to iron with or without folic acid. The multiple-micronutrient supplements led to fewer low birthweight babies and probably fewer small-for-gestational-age and very preterm births. They made no important difference to miscarriage, stillbirth or newborn deaths. The authors say the findings may support swapping iron and folic acid alone for these supplements in low- and middle-income countries.
keyPoints: Multiple-micronutrient supplements reduced the number of low birthweight babies (high-quality evidence).
They probably slightly reduced small-for-gestational-age babies (moderate-quality evidence) and very preterm births.
Little or no difference was seen for miscarriage, stillbirth, perinatal or newborn deaths, or maternal death.
One UK trial against placebo found less maternal anaemia in the third trimester but no clear effect on preterm birth or birthweight.

items.title: Alcohol Use in Pregnancy and Miscarriage: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 24 studies covering about 231,808 pregnant women to look at alcohol use and miscarriage. Women who drank alcohol during pregnancy had a somewhat higher risk of miscarriage than women who did not drink. The risk went up a little with each extra drink per week, even at low amounts. The authors note it is hard to measure early miscarriage and to record how much people really drink.
keyPoints: Pregnant women who drank alcohol had higher odds of miscarriage than those who abstained (odds ratio 1.19).
For 5 or fewer drinks per week, each extra weekly drink was linked to a 6% increase in miscarriage risk.
Results were similar across study designs, countries and ways of measuring alcohol use.
Studies had limits, such as recruiting people early enough and measuring alcohol use accurately; more research is needed on drinking before pregnancy is recognised.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 200: Early Pregnancy Loss
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists covers early pregnancy loss, which is the loss of a pregnancy inside the womb during the first trimester. It reviews how doctors can tell whether an early pregnancy is viable or not. It also describes the options for managing a loss, which are waiting for it to pass naturally, taking medicine, or having a surgical procedure.
keyPoints: Early pregnancy loss means losing a pregnancy in the womb during the first trimester, and it is common in clinical practice.
Doctors use a range of diagnostic tools to tell a viable pregnancy from a nonviable one.
Patients should be offered the full range of management options: expectant, medical and surgical.

items.title: Surgery for tubal infertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for trials comparing surgery on blocked or damaged fallopian tubes with no treatment or with IVF, to see which gives more live births. The researchers found no suitable randomised trials. So it is still unknown whether tubal surgery works better or worse than IVF or waiting for women with tubal infertility.
keyPoints: No suitable randomised controlled trials were found, so no conclusions could be drawn.
How well tubal surgery works compared with IVF or no treatment, in terms of live births, remains unknown.
Estimated live birth rates after surgery range from 9% for severe tubal disease to 69% for mild disease, but these have not been tested rigorously against other options.
Large, well-designed trials are needed that also compare side effects and costs, and consider factors like age and how long a woman has been trying to conceive.

items.title: Non-pharmaceutical Chinese Medical Therapies for Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy: An Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: This review pulled together 22 earlier reviews of non-drug Chinese medicine treatments, such as acupuncture, for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. Acupuncture, in particular, was linked with lower nausea and vomiting scores and with fewer signs of ketones in urine. Much of the underlying research was low quality, so the authors say acupuncture may help but the evidence is limited and better studies are needed.
keyPoints: Acupuncture lowered nausea and vomiting scores (PUQE) compared with controls, based on moderate-certainty evidence.
Acupuncture raised the rate of negative urine ketone tests, also with moderate-certainty evidence.
Of the 22 reviews, only 6 were rated high quality, and most evidence ratings were low or very low.
The authors conclude acupuncture may have potential benefits but stronger, larger trials are needed.

items.title: What are the costs associated with nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum? A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at what nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, and its severe form hyperemesis gravidarum, cost patients and health systems. Seven studies were included, and all found a significant financial burden, including costs to the patient outside of medical bills. Costs rose as the illness became more severe, and care in outpatient or day-stay units cost less than other models. The studies were quite different from each other, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: All seven studies found a significant economic burden from nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum.
Costs went up as the severity of the illness increased.
Outpatient or day-stay care models were more cost-effective, partly by reducing how severe the illness became.
The studies differed in methods and outcomes measured, so further research with agreed outcome measures is needed.

items.title: Efficacy of acupoint-related therapies for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy: a Bayesian network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 38 randomised trials (1,164 pregnant women) comparing different acupoint-based treatments, such as acupressure, acupuncture and moxibustion, for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. Most of these treatments worked better than usual care, with Thunder Fire Moxibustion, ginger moxibustion and acupressure ranking among the most effective for symptom scores. Acupuncture-based treatments also ranked best for quality of life. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is, and the comparisons are statistical rankings across many small trials.
keyPoints: Thunder Fire Moxibustion ranked highest for improving nausea and vomiting scores, followed by ginger moxibustion acupoint application and acupressure.
Acupoint application worked better than usual care, but not as well as acupoint application with warming additions or acupuncture.
Traditional Chinese medicine acupuncture ranked best for improving quality of life, and usual care ranked lowest across all measures.
Overall, acupuncture-based treatments performed better than other approaches for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy.

items.title: Treatments for hyperemesis gravidarum: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 25 studies covering 20 different treatments for hyperemesis gravidarum, a severe form of pregnancy sickness. For almost all treatments, the evidence was too weak to draw firm conclusions. Acupressure added to standard care may reduce nausea and vomiting somewhat, but even that evidence is low quality. The authors say bigger, better-designed studies are needed.
keyPoints: Hyperemesis gravidarum affects 0.3%-3% of pregnant women and is the leading cause of hospital stays in early pregnancy.
The certainty of evidence was very low for all 20 treatments reviewed, except acupressure.
Acupressure alongside standard care showed a possible moderate decrease in nausea and vomiting, but the certainty of evidence was low.
Few studies exist, and larger studies using validated scoring and agreed diagnostic criteria are needed.

items.title: The Management of Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum (Green-top Guideline No. 69)
items.source: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
items.organisation: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
items.summary: This is a 2024 guideline from the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists on managing nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and the severe form called hyperemesis gravidarum. It recommends starting with well-studied first-line anti-sickness medicines, with other medicines added if these do not work. It also covers how severity is measured, how fluids are given in hospital, and vitamin B1 (thiamine) supplements for women who are vomiting a lot.
keyPoints: Validated scoring tools such as PUQE and HELP can be used to judge how severe the nausea and vomiting is; ketones in the urine should not be used to judge dehydration or severity.
First-line medicines (antihistamines, phenothiazines, and doxylamine/pyridoxine) have good safety and effectiveness data and should be offered first when medicine is needed.

If first-line medicines do not work, ondansetron or metoclopramide can be used as second-line options; ondansetron is linked to a very small increase in the absolute risk of cleft lip or palate when used in the first trimester, which should be weighed against the risks of poorly controlled hyperemesis.
Women admitted with vomiting or very low food intake should be given thiamine, and combinations of anti-sickness drugs can be used if one drug is not enough.

items.title: Acupuncture for nausea and vomiting during pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 24 randomised trials with 2,390 women to see whether acupuncture helps with nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. Acupuncture added to usual medicine worked better than medicine alone, and acupuncture on its own seemed about as effective as medicine. Serious side effects were not more common with acupuncture. The quality of the evidence ranged from moderate to very low, and the authors say larger, stronger studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Acupuncture plus usual medicine reduced nausea and vomiting scores and the rate of treatment not working, compared with medicine alone.
Acupuncture alone worked better than medicine alone for the rate of treatment not working, and the two were similar for symptom scores.
Serious side effects were not significantly different between acupuncture and medicine or sham (fake) acupuncture.
The effect of acupuncture on depression and anxiety was unclear, and evidence certainty ranged from moderate to very low.

items.title: Prevalence and determinants of hyperemesis gravidarum among pregnant women in Ethiopia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 11 studies from Ethiopia, covering 3,510 pregnant women, to see how common severe pregnancy sickness (hyperemesis gravidarum) is and what is linked to it. About 7 in 100 women (7.12%) had it, though results varied a lot between studies and regions. Having had it in an earlier pregnancy, being in the first trimester, and having a Helicobacter pylori stomach infection were all linked to higher odds of having it.
keyPoints: The pooled rate of hyperemesis gravidarum in Ethiopia was 7.12%, with high variation between studies.
Rates ranged from 3.4% in Oromia to 11.3% in the Amhara region.
A previous history of hyperemesis gravidarum, being in the first trimester, and H. pylori infection were each linked to higher odds.
The authors suggest these groups be a focus of prenatal counseling on managing and reducing the condition.

items.title: Perinatal outcomes of infants born to mothers with hyperemesis gravidarum: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 61 studies to see how babies fare when their mothers had hyperemesis gravidarum, the severe form of pregnancy nausea and vomiting. It found links with some less favourable outcomes, such as very early birth, very low birth weight and more newborn intensive care admissions. Babies were also less likely to be very large or stillborn. The review could not tell why these links exist.
keyPoints: Hyperemesis gravidarum was linked with preterm birth before 34 weeks and birth weight under 1500 g.
It was also linked with more neonatal intensive care admissions, newborn resuscitation and placental abruption.
It was linked with fewer babies weighing over 4000 g and fewer stillbirths.
No link was found with low Apgar scores, fetal loss, perinatal deaths or neonatal deaths, and the reasons behind the findings could not be studied.

items.title: Is hyperemesis gravidarum associated with transient hyperthyroidism? A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 29 studies, with 28 in the meta-analysis, to see whether severe pregnancy sickness (hyperemesis gravidarum) is linked to a temporary overactive thyroid. Women with hyperemesis had higher levels of thyroid hormones (fT3 and fT4) and lower TSH than women without it. The authors conclude that hyperemesis is significantly associated with this temporary thyroid change, called gestational transient thyrotoxicosis. The studies were observational, so the review shows a link rather than proving cause.
keyPoints: Women with hyperemesis gravidarum had higher fT3 and fT4 thyroid hormone levels than women without it.
TSH was significantly lower in women with hyperemesis gravidarum.
HCG levels were also higher in women with hyperemesis gravidarum.
The authors conclude hyperemesis is significantly associated with gestational transient thyrotoxicosis, a temporary thyroid overactivity.

items.title: Hyperemesis gravidarum and vitamin K deficiency: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at what is known about vitamin K deficiency in women with hyperemesis gravidarum, which is severe nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. It found 15 studies, mostly small case reports, and some women had signs of poor blood clotting. A few women had bleeding problems and some babies had complications, including bleeding in the brain and changes in how the face and bones formed. Because the evidence is mostly individual cases, the review could not say how often this happens.
keyPoints: Vitamin K deficiency and related complications can occur in women with hyperemesis gravidarum.
In the one cohort study, 10 of 39 women with HG who were tested (26%) had a prolonged clotting time.
Reported complications included bleeding in mothers and, in babies, brain bleeding and developmental changes affecting the face and bones.
The review could not work out how common vitamin K deficiency is in HG.

items.title: Long-term health outcomes of children born to mothers with hyperemesis gravidarum: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review looked at 19 studies of children whose mothers had hyperemesis gravidarum, a severe form of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. It found small increases in some mental health and brain development problems, and possibly testicular cancer in sons. The authors say this evidence comes from few studies of low quality, so the findings are uncertain and show a link, not a cause.
keyPoints: Children of mothers with hyperemesis gravidarum had higher odds of anxiety disorder and sleep problems, based on two small studies.
All 6 studies on ADHD and autism found more cases among exposed children, but results varied too much to combine into one number.
Hyperemesis gravidarum was linked to testicular cancer in male offspring up to age 40, though the range of possible results was wide.
The authors conclude the increases in adverse outcomes are small and the evidence is based on few studies of low quality.

items.title: Hyperemesis gravidarum and neonatal outcomes: A systematic review of observational studies
items.summary: This review pulled together 15 observational studies, covering over 112,000 women with severe pregnancy sickness (hyperemesis gravidarum), to see whether it affects newborns' health. The studies disagreed with each other, partly because they defined the condition differently and looked at different groups of women. The authors concluded it is still uncertain whether hyperemesis gravidarum harms neonatal outcomes, and that more research is needed.
keyPoints: 15 observational studies were included, covering more than 112,000 women with hyperemesis gravidarum.
Most of the studies were of moderate quality, and they differed in how they defined hyperemesis gravidarum.
It remains uncertain whether hyperemesis gravidarum has a negative effect on newborn outcomes.
The authors say more studies are needed.

items.title: Adverse pregnancy outcomes and Helicobacter pylori infection: A meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 31 studies covering about 16,900 pregnant women to see whether infection with Helicobacter pylori (a stomach bacterium) is linked to problems in pregnancy. Women who tested positive had higher rates of preeclampsia, slower baby growth in the womb, gestational diabetes and severe pregnancy sickness (hyperemesis gravidarum). The link with severe sickness was especially strong. Infection was not linked to when labour started. The studies show an association, not proof that the infection causes these problems.
keyPoints: H pylori infection in pregnancy was linked to higher rates of preeclampsia, foetal growth restriction and gestational diabetes.
The link with hyperemesis gravidarum (severe nausea and vomiting) was the strongest, with about 14 times higher odds in infected women.
H pylori infection was not linked to spontaneous onset of labour.
The authors recommend screening and treating women for H pylori before and during pregnancy to help avoid complications.

items.title: Ondansetron in Pregnancy and the Risk of Congenital Malformations: A Systematic Review
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This review looked at ten studies on whether taking ondansetron (an anti-sickness medicine) during pregnancy raises the chance of birth defects. One study linked it to cleft palate and another to heart defects, but the other studies did not find the same results. The authors say there is little evidence of a link, but more research is needed to confirm whether it is a safe option for pregnancy sickness.
keyPoints: Ondansetron is not approved for use in pregnancy, yet it is increasingly prescribed for nausea, vomiting and hyperemesis gravidarum.
One case-control study found a link with cleft palate and one cohort study found a higher risk of heart defects.
These findings were not repeated in the other studies reviewed.
The authors conclude there is little evidence linking ondansetron to birth defects, but more studies are needed to confirm its safety.

items.title: Psychological interventions for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at psychological approaches used to treat nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, such as behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, hypnosis and progressive muscle relaxation. Only six clinical trials were found, and all were rated as poor in methodological quality. Because of this, the review could not show whether these approaches work, and the authors say stronger studies are needed.
keyPoints: Four types of psychological intervention have been tested: behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, hypnosis and progressive muscle relaxation.
Only six clinical trials were included in the review.
All six trials were rated as poor quality using the Jadad scale.
Better studies are needed before we know how well these approaches work for pregnancy nausea and vomiting.
