items.title: Psychological morbidity associated with hyperemesis gravidarum: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 59 studies on mental health in women with hyperemesis gravidarum (HG), the severe form of pregnancy sickness. In the 12 studies that could be compared directly, women with HG scored much higher on depression and anxiety scales than women without significant nausea and vomiting. The results varied a lot between studies, so the exact size of the difference is uncertain. The authors say care for HG should include psychological support.
keyPoints: Women with HG had much higher depression scale scores than women without significant pregnancy nausea and vomiting.
Women with HG also had higher anxiety scale scores.
The studies differed widely from one another, so the size of the effect is uncertain.
The authors conclude that services for women with HG should include psychological care and support.

items.title: Effect of acustimulation on nausea and vomiting and on hyperemesis in pregnancy: a systematic review of Western and Chinese literature
items.summary: This review pulled together 29 trials (3,519 women) testing acustimulation, such as acupressure or acupuncture, for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and severe pregnancy sickness (hyperemesis). When results were counted as 'improved or not', acustimulation looked helpful. But when symptoms were measured on a scale, there was no clear sign of relief. The authors say the evidence is not conclusive and better, larger trials are needed.
keyPoints: Across trials, acustimulation was linked to more women improving when results were counted as improved or not (pooled relative risk 1.73).
Studies that measured nausea and vomiting on a scale did not show clear evidence of symptom relief.
The authors conclude there is some evidence of benefit, but it is not conclusive.
Larger, well-designed trials are needed to check how well these treatments work and how safe they are.

items.title: Ondansetron Use in Pregnancy and Birth Defects: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at eight studies of women who took ondansetron, an anti-sickness medicine, in early pregnancy for nausea and vomiting or hyperemesis gravidarum. The three largest studies found no clear rise in birth defects overall. Two of them did find a small rise in heart defects, but other studies did not find this, so the results conflict. The authors say ondansetron should be kept for women whose symptoms are not controlled by other methods.
keyPoints: Overall risk of birth defects after ondansetron in early pregnancy appears to be low.
The three largest studies showed no clear increase in birth defects as a whole.
Two studies found a small increase in heart defects, mostly septal defects (holes between heart chambers), but this was not seen in other studies.
Ondansetron should be reserved for women whose symptoms have not been adequately controlled by other methods.

items.title: Interventions for treating hyperemesis gravidarum
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 25 trials (2052 women) of treatments for hyperemesis gravidarum, the severe form of pregnancy sickness. Most comparisons came from single small studies, and the evidence was mostly low or very low quality. No one treatment stood out as clearly better than the others, though some medicines differed in side effects such as drowsiness.
keyPoints: There is little high-quality, consistent evidence supporting any one treatment for hyperemesis gravidarum.
Metoclopramide caused more drowsiness and dry mouth than ondansetron, with no clear difference in how well they eased nausea or vomiting.
Promethazine caused more drowsiness, dizziness and dystonia than metoclopramide in one study.
Corticosteroids did not clearly shorten hospital stays, but fewer women needed to be readmitted in four studies.

items.title: Treatments for Hyperemesis Gravidarum and Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 78 studies (about 8,900 women) on treatments for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, including the severe form called hyperemesis gravidarum. Several options may help more than a dummy treatment (placebo), including ginger, vitamin B6, antihistamines, metoclopramide, a vitamin B6 and doxylamine combination, and ondansetron. Corticosteroids may help in severe cases. The reviewers say the overall quality of the evidence was low.
keyPoints: For mild symptoms, ginger, vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), antihistamines and metoclopramide may work better than placebo.
For moderate symptoms, pyridoxine-doxylamine, promethazine and metoclopramide may work better than placebo; ondansetron helped across a range of severity.
Corticosteroids may help in severe cases.

One small trial found psychotherapy improved moderate symptoms, and another found taking pyridoxine-doxylamine early lowered the chance of symptoms getting worse again; evidence for other treatments was limited.

items.title: Treatments for hyperemesis gravidarum and nausea and vomiting in pregnancy: a systematic review and economic assessment
items.summary: This large review pulled together 73 studies on treatments for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, including the severe form called hyperemesis gravidarum. Some treatments showed better results than a dummy treatment, including ginger, vitamin B6, antihistamines and some anti-sickness medicines. For many other treatments the evidence was unclear, and the reviewers said the amount and quality of the studies was limited, so bigger and better trials are needed.
keyPoints: Ginger, antihistamines, metoclopramide (for mild illness) and vitamin B6 (mild to severe illness) worked better than placebo.
Diclectin (doxylamine plus pyridoxine) was more effective than placebo, and taking it before symptoms start helped women at high risk of severe nausea that returned in a later pregnancy.
For severe illness, ondansetron was more effective than metoclopramide, and intravenous fluids helped correct dehydration and improve symptoms.
Day case care for moderate to severe symptoms was found to be as effective as staying in hospital, while tube feeding was seen as an extreme option for very severe cases.

items.title: Interventions for nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 41 trials (5449 women) of treatments for nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy, including acupressure, acupuncture, ginger and vitamin B6. The authors found a lack of high-quality evidence to support any one treatment. Ginger may help, and three recent studies favoured ginger over placebo, but results were limited and not consistent. This does not mean the treatments don't work, only that the evidence is not strong enough to be sure.
keyPoints: No single treatment for early-pregnancy nausea and vomiting has strong, high-quality evidence behind it.
Ginger products may be helpful, but the evidence was limited and not consistent.
Acupuncture showed no significant benefit, and evidence for acupressure was limited.
Evidence for vitamin B6, doxylamine-pyridoxine and other anti-sickness drugs in mild or moderate cases was limited, and there was little information on side effects.

items.title: Antispasmodic and analgesic strategies for renal colic in pregnancy: a comprehensive analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from ten randomised trials (936 pregnant women) comparing antispasmodic and pain-relief medicines for kidney stone pain (renal colic) in pregnancy. Phloroglucinol worked best for pain relief within one hour and caused the fewest side effects like nausea and dizziness. Progesterone came second, and anisodamine did worst. The authors say more high-quality research is needed to confirm these findings.
keyPoints: Phloroglucinol was the most effective at easing pain within 1 hour and had the fewest side effects.
Progesterone ranked second for pain relief; anisodamine was the least effective.
Phloroglucinol had lower pain recurrence at 6 hours and fewer side effects such as blurred vision and palpitations than anisodamine.
The authors conclude phloroglucinol is preferred, can be combined with progesterone, and anisodamine is not advised, but more high-quality research is needed.

items.title: Pregnancy outcomes and birth defects in offspring following Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs exposure during pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies on NSAID painkillers (such as ibuprofen) taken during pregnancy. Babies exposed in early pregnancy had a higher chance of birth defects than unexposed babies, and NSAID use was also linked to preterm birth. Miscarriage risk looked a little higher too, but that result could be due to chance. The authors say pregnant women should weigh the possible benefits and risks before using NSAIDs.
keyPoints: Early-pregnancy NSAID exposure was linked to a 28% higher risk of congenital anomalies overall (OR 1.28).
The risk of major birth defects was 19% higher (OR 1.19) compared with babies not exposed.
Miscarriage risk trended higher (OR 1.20), but the finding was not statistically significant.
NSAID use in pregnancy was linked to a negative impact on preterm birth, and the authors advise weighing benefits and risks.

items.title: Opioid analgesic exposure during the first trimester of pregnancy and the risk of major congenital malformations in infants: a systematic review and meta-analysis†
items.summary: This review pooled results from 12 studies on prescribed opioid painkillers taken in the first three months of pregnancy and the chance of major birth defects in babies. Overall, babies exposed to opioids were not found to have a higher chance of major birth defects than unexposed babies. However, most of the studies had serious problems in how they were done, so the true risk is still uncertain.
keyPoints: Opioid painkiller use in the first trimester was not linked to a higher overall risk of major birth defects (relative risk 1.04).
No clear increase was seen for heart or brain and spine malformations.
A small increase in atrial septal defects (a type of heart defect) was seen with codeine, and higher but very uncertain estimates were seen for gut malformations and cleft palate.
Eleven of the 12 studies were at high risk of bias, so the findings remain uncertain.

items.title: Maternal non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug exposure during pregnancy and risk of miscarriage: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined ten studies covering about 207,000 pregnant women to see whether NSAID painkillers (such as ibuprofen) are linked to miscarriage. Overall, NSAID use during pregnancy was not clearly linked to a higher chance of miscarriage. However, women who took NSAIDs around the time of conception did have a higher chance of miscarriage. The authors say more research is needed on whether the type, dose or timing of the medicine matters.
keyPoints: Across all ten studies, NSAID use during pregnancy was not statistically significantly linked to miscarriage.
NSAID use around the time of conception was linked to a higher risk of miscarriage (odds ratio 2.32).
No significant link was seen for NSAID use in the first trimester, though the sample may have been too small to tell.
More studies are needed to see whether the risk differs by NSAID type, dose or timing.

items.title: Symptomatic treatment (using NSAIDS) versus antibiotics in uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection: a meta-analysis and systematic review of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled four randomized trials with 1165 non-pregnant adult women who had an uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection (UTI, such as a bladder infection). It compared treating with anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs, like ibuprofen) against treating with antibiotics. Antibiotics probably worked better: more women had their symptoms clear by day 3 or 4, and fewer developed a kidney or other upper urinary tract infection. The study did not include pregnant women, so it does not tell us about NSAID use in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Women taking NSAIDs were less likely to have their UTI symptoms resolve by day 3 or 4 than women taking antibiotics (moderate certainty).
Upper urinary tract infection complications were more likely with NSAIDs than with antibiotics (moderate certainty).
A positive urine culture was more likely to persist with NSAIDs, and these women were about three times more likely to need a rescue antibiotic (low certainty for the rescue antibiotic finding).
The authors concluded antibiotics were more effective than NSAIDs for acute uncomplicated lower UTI; the review covered non-pregnant women only.

items.title: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for assisted reproductive technology
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) taken alongside fertility treatment such as IVF help women get pregnant or avoid miscarriage. It pooled 11 trials with 1,884 women. The researchers could not tell whether NSAIDs make any difference to ongoing pregnancy or miscarriage, and the evidence was of very low quality. No trial reported live birth rates.
keyPoints: It is uncertain whether NSAIDs given during assisted reproduction change ongoing pregnancy or miscarriage rates; the evidence was very low quality.
None of the trials reported live birth per woman, the main outcome of interest.
Evidence on clinical pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, multiple pregnancy and side effects was also uncertain (low to very low quality).
The authors say larger, well-designed placebo-controlled trials that report live births are needed.

items.title: Effect of fish-oil supplementation on the glycemic and lipidemic profiles of pregnant women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 15 studies of pregnant women taking fish-oil capsules or a placebo. It looked at blood sugar, insulin and blood fat levels. Overall, fish oil made no difference compared with placebo. Small benefits for insulin and insulin resistance showed up only in some subgroups, such as women with diabetes and those taking lower EPA doses.
keyPoints: Across all 15 studies, fish-oil capsules had no overall effect on blood sugar or blood fat measures compared with placebo.
In pregnant women with diabetes, fish oil was linked to lower insulin and lower insulin resistance (HOMA-IR).
Women taking less than 200 mg of EPA also showed a reduction in insulin resistance.
The benefits were found in subgroup analyses, not in the overall results.

items.title: Docosahexaenoic Acid and Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Association with Improved Maternal and Fetal Health
items.summary: This review pooled nine randomized trials (5,710 women) that compared DHA, an omega-3 fatty acid, taken in the second half of pregnancy with a placebo or no supplement. Babies of women taking DHA (450-800 mg a day) weighed about 100 grams more at birth on average, and fewer were born with low birth weight. Fewer preterm births were seen, but this result was not statistically significant, and DHA did not change how long pregnancy lasted.
keyPoints: DHA supplements (450-800 mg/day) were linked to higher infant birth weight, by about 100 grams on average.
Low birth weight was less common in the DHA groups than in the placebo groups.
The drop in preterm births was small and not statistically significant, though the authors say DHA may reduce preterm birth risk.
DHA had no effect on the length of pregnancy.

items.title: Impact of n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid intake in pregnancy on maternal health and birth outcomes: systematic review and meta-analysis from randomized controlled trails
items.summary: This review combined results from 59 randomized trials of omega-3 supplements (DHA, EPA and/or ALA) taken during pregnancy. Women who took omega-3 had a lower risk of preeclampsia and of preterm birth, and their pregnancies lasted slightly longer on average. Babies also had a slightly higher average birth weight, and there was a borderline reduction in low birth weight. The authors conclude that omega-3 supplementation in pregnancy may help prevent these problems.
keyPoints: Omega-3 supplements were linked to a lower risk of preeclampsia (about 16% lower in the pooled results).
Preterm birth before 37 weeks was less likely (about 14% lower), and birth before 34 weeks was also less likely (about 23% lower).
Pregnancy lasted about 1.35 days longer on average, and babies weighed about 49 grams more at birth.
The drop in low birth weight was borderline, so that result is less clear.

items.title: Effect of Prenatal Omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acid Supplementation on Childhood Eczema: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: International Archives of Allergy and Immunology
items.journal: International Archives of Allergy and Immunology
items.summary: This review combined six randomised trials (1,646 mothers and babies) to see whether taking omega-3 supplements in pregnancy lowers the chance of eczema in children. Overall, it found no clear drop in eczema or in IgE-associated eczema (eczema linked to allergy). In children aged 3 or younger, there was a possible reduction in IgE-associated eczema, but this came from a subgroup analysis and should be treated cautiously.
keyPoints: Across all children, omega-3 supplements in pregnancy did not clearly reduce eczema (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.46).
IgE-associated eczema was also not clearly reduced overall (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.29 to 1.57).
In children aged 3 or younger, IgE-associated eczema was lower in the omega-3 group (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.96).
The authors say the effect of omega-3 in pregnancy on childhood eczema was uncertain before this review.

items.title: Association between omega-3 fatty acid supplementation and lower risk of preterm delivery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 26 trials with about 20,000 pregnant women to see whether omega-3 supplements lower the chance of a baby being born early. Overall, supplements were not clearly linked to fewer preterm births compared with placebo or no treatment. Some subgroup results hinted at a benefit with mixed DHA and EPA products and with doses above 1 g, but these were secondary findings.
keyPoints: Across 26 trials (20,124 women), omega-3 supplements were not associated with a lower risk of preterm delivery (risk ratio 0.92, confidence interval 0.85 to 1.01).
Supplements made little difference to how long pregnancy lasted.
In subgroup analyses, lower preterm birth rates were seen with mixed DHA and EPA supplements rather than DHA alone, and with doses above 1 g.
The authors say more evidence is needed on other pregnancy outcomes.

items.title: The effects of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids supplementation in pregnancy, lactation, and infancy: An umbrella review of meta-analyses of randomized trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from 28 earlier reviews of randomized trials, covering 672 trials and over 270,000 people, to see what omega-3 fatty acid supplements do in pregnancy, breastfeeding and infancy. Moderate to high certainty evidence showed omega-3 supplements in pregnancy lowered the risk of pre-eclampsia and low birth weight and improved babies' head size. Other possible benefits, such as for preterm birth and depression before and after birth, were backed by lower certainty evidence.
keyPoints: Omega-3 supplements in pregnancy reduced pre-eclampsia and low birth weight and improved head circumference (moderate to high certainty).
In infants, omega-3 reduced severe retinopathy of prematurity and cholestasis (moderate to high certainty).
Favorable effects on preterm delivery, depression before and after birth, blood sugar control and inflammation were seen, but the evidence was low certainty.
Infant benefits such as language development, visual acuity and peanut sensitization were also suggested, again with low certainty.

items.title: Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (n-3 PUFA) supplementation for prevention and treatment of perinatal depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized-controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 11 randomized trials of omega-3 supplements (fish-oil type fatty acids) taken around pregnancy and after birth to prevent or treat depression. Overall, women taking omega-3 did not have meaningfully different depression scores from those taking a placebo. No trial reported any serious side effects. The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to say whether omega-3 helps with perinatal depression.
keyPoints: Omega-3 supplements did not reduce depression scores more than placebo, either for prevention or for treatment.
Results did not depend on the daily dose of DHA, EPA, or both.
No trial reported any serious adverse effects from omega-3 supplements.
The authors say omega-3 may help other maternal and infant outcomes, but evidence for perinatal depression is insufficient.

items.title: Omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid and sleep: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and longitudinal studies
items.summary: This review pooled 20 studies (12 clinical trials and 8 longitudinal studies) to see whether omega-3 fatty acids affect sleep. In infants, omega-3 seemed to make sleep patterns more mature, and in children with sleep problems it lowered a sleep disturbance score. No effect was found on sleep in healthy children or in adults. The authors say more robust studies are needed to confirm these links.
keyPoints: Omega-3 may improve infants' sleep organization and maturity, with less active sleep and more wakefulness.
In children with clinical-level sleep problems, omega-3 lowered the total sleep disturbance score.
No effect was found on sleep duration, sleep latency or sleep efficiency in healthy children.
No effect was found on adults' sleep duration, sleep quality or insomnia severity.

items.title: Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis of the Relationship Between Polyunsaturated and Trans Fatty Acids During Pregnancy and Offspring Weight Development
items.summary: This review pooled 27 trials and 14 observational studies to see whether omega-3 fats (DHA and EPA) and trans fats during pregnancy affect a child's weight. Higher-dose DHA and/or EPA supplements (over 650 mg a day) were linked to slightly higher birth weight and slightly higher BMI at ages 5 to 10. High trans fat levels in pregnancy seemed to go with lower birth weight. The observational studies were mostly inconsistent, and the authors say more high-quality long-term studies are needed.
keyPoints: DHA and/or EPA doses over 650 mg a day were linked to a slightly higher birth weight (about 88 g on average).
The same higher doses were linked to a small rise in BMI at 5 to 10 years, rated as moderate quality evidence.
High trans fat levels during pregnancy seemed to be linked to lower birth weight.
Results from observational studies were generally inconsistent, and more long-term, high-quality studies are needed.

items.title: Supplementation of Omega 3 during Pregnancy and the Risk of Preterm Birth: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 37 trials that compared omega-3 supplements with placebo (dummy pills) in pregnancy to see if they lower the chance of preterm birth. At first the results looked like a benefit, with about 11% fewer preterm births and 27% fewer early preterm births. But after more careful checks of the data, these differences were no longer statistically significant. The authors concluded that omega-3 supplements in pregnancy do not reduce the risk of preterm birth, and that more studies are needed.
keyPoints: Across 37 trials, omega-3 supplements first appeared to cut preterm birth risk by 11% and early preterm birth risk by 27%.
After sensitivity analyses, the differences were no longer significant for preterm birth or early preterm birth.
The authors conclude omega-3 supplements do not reduce the risk of preterm birth or early preterm birth.
More studies are needed on omega-3 supplements and other harmful outcomes for the baby.

items.title: The impact of omega-3 fatty acid supplementation on glycemic control in patients with gestational diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled studies
items.summary: This review pooled seven randomized trials of omega-3 fatty acid supplements versus placebo in women with gestational diabetes. Women taking omega-3 had lower fasting blood sugar, lower insulin resistance and lower levels of an inflammation marker. The supplements did not clearly change birth outcomes such as large babies, newborn jaundice, early delivery or preeclampsia.
keyPoints: Omega-3 supplements lowered fasting blood glucose compared with placebo in gestational diabetes.
Insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) and the inflammation marker hs-CRP were also lower with omega-3.
No clear effect was seen on macrosomia, newborn jaundice, preterm delivery, preeclampsia or nitric oxide.
The authors concluded omega-3 may help blood sugar control and inflammation in gestational diabetes.

items.title: Risk factors for postpartum depression: An evidence-based systematic review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses
items.summary: This review gathered findings from earlier systematic reviews and meta-analyses to see what raises or lowers the chance of postpartum depression. Things linked with higher risk included past depression, abuse, lack of social support, poor sleep, caesarean birth and vitamin D deficiency. Skin-to-skin care and some nutrition factors, such as eating more fish and seafood, were linked with lower risk. The authors say the evidence on some other factors is not strong enough to draw conclusions.
keyPoints: Thirteen risk factors were identified, including depression history, abuse or violence, lack of social support, poor postpartum sleep, gestational diabetes, caesarean section and a negative birth experience.
Skin-to-skin care was linked with lower risk of postpartum depression.
Greater seafood consumption, fish and omega-3 (PUFA) intake, higher DHA in breast milk, multivitamin use, and calcium, vitamin D, zinc and possibly selenium were linked with lower risk.
Five factors, such as cortisol levels and traditional confinement practices, remain controversial because the evidence is insufficient.

items.title: Fish intake during pregnancy or infancy and allergic outcomes in children: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled one randomised trial and many cohort studies to see whether eating fish in pregnancy or infancy affects a child's risk of allergies. Eating fish during pregnancy was not linked to a lower risk of any allergic condition in the child. Babies who ate fish in their first year had a lower risk of eczema and allergic rhinitis (hay fever). The authors say better-quality trials are needed to confirm this.
keyPoints: Maternal fish intake during pregnancy was not linked to lower risk of any allergic outcome in children, in both the trial and the observational studies.
Fish eaten in the first year of life was linked to lower risk of eczema (RR 0.61) and allergic rhinitis (RR 0.54).
The protective effect in infancy may come from fish itself rather than specifically from omega-3 fats.
High-quality, adequately powered randomised trials are needed to confirm the findings.

items.title: Long chain polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation in infants born at term
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 15 trials (1,889 babies) that compared formula milk with added omega-3 and omega-6 fats (DHA and AA) to ordinary formula in full-term babies. Most trials found no clear benefit for thinking and movement development, and results for eyesight were mixed. Growth was mostly similar between groups, though one pooled analysis found slightly lower weight at one year in babies given the added fats. The reviewers rated the overall evidence as low quality.
keyPoints: Most trials found no benefit of added DHA and AA for babies' mental or movement development, including at 18 months and in follow-up to age 9.
Eyesight results were mixed: one type of test showed a benefit at 12 months, while another type showed none.
No study found clear benefit or harm for growth, though one pooled analysis showed slightly lower weight scores at one year in supplemented babies.
The authors concluded that routine addition of these fats to full-term infant formula cannot be recommended at this time.

items.title: Omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids and fish oil supplementation during pregnancy: which evidence?
items.summary: This review pulled together 34 randomized trials of omega-3 or fish oil supplements taken during pregnancy, covering over 16,000 pregnancies. The supplements did not prevent preterm birth, pre-eclampsia, poor growth in the womb, gestational diabetes, small babies, postpartum depression, or improve children's development. The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to support routine omega-3 supplements in pregnancy, though some early signals need more research.
keyPoints: Across 34 trials, omega-3 supplements were not linked to preventing preterm birth, pre-eclampsia, poor fetal growth, gestational diabetes, small-for-gestational-age babies or postpartum depression.
There was not enough evidence to support routine use of omega-3 supplements during pregnancy.
In women with gestational diabetes, omega-3 was linked to lower inflammation markers, less newborn jaundice (hyperbilirubinemia) and fewer newborn hospital stays.
Starting omega-3 by 20 weeks was linked to fewer perinatal deaths in single pregnancies, but this needs more research; data on birth weight and childhood thinking skills were limited.

items.title: Omega-3 long-chain PUFA intake during pregnancy and allergic disease outcomes in the offspring: a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies and randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pulled together studies on whether eating more fish or omega-3 fats during pregnancy affects allergies in children. Most of the studies found a protective link, and a pooled analysis of three trials showed fewer cases of eczema and food sensitisation in babies' first year. However, the results were not consistent across studies, so the authors say the link cannot be confirmed or ruled out.
keyPoints: Nine of 13 observational study publications and 5 of 7 trial publications found that more omega-3 or fish intake in pregnancy was linked to fewer allergy symptoms in the child.
Pooled results from three trials showed lower rates of atopic eczema, a positive skin-prick test, egg sensitisation and any food sensitisation in the first 12 months of life.
The trials differed a lot from each other, which limited the meta-analysis.
Because results were inconsistent, the link between maternal omega-3 intake and childhood allergy cannot be firmly confirmed or rejected.

items.title: Omega-3 supplementation during pregnancy to prevent recurrent intrauterine growth restriction: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled three randomized trials of 575 women who had a healthy single pregnancy but had previously had a baby with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR, when a baby grows slower than expected in the womb). Women who took omega-3 supplements had about the same rate of IUGR as women who did not (22.8% vs 20.2%). Birth weight and perinatal deaths were also similar between the groups. The authors concluded that omega-3 supplements do not prevent IUGR from happening again.
keyPoints: Omega-3 supplements did not lower the chance of IUGR recurring in women who had a previous IUGR pregnancy.
IUGR occurred in 22.8% of women taking omega-3 and 20.2% of controls, which was not a meaningful difference.
Birth weight and perinatal death rates were similar with and without omega-3.
Women taking omega-3 delivered about 1.4 weeks later on average.

items.title: Supplementation with long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFA) to breastfeeding mothers for improving child growth and development
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 8 randomised trials (1567 women, all in high-income countries) that tested omega-3 (LCPUFA/DHA) supplements taken by breastfeeding mothers. Overall, the supplements did not clearly improve children's brain development, eyesight or growth. One small study found better attention scores at age five, but this evidence is weak. The evidence quality ranged from low to moderate, and no harmful effects were reported.
keyPoints: No clear difference in children's language, problem-solving, movement or visual development at follow-up beyond 24 months.
No significant differences in children's length, weight, head size or body fat.
One study found better attention scores at five years, but the authors call this weak evidence; one small study also reported less infant allergy in the short term only.
Evidence is inconclusive for or against giving omega-3 supplements to breastfeeding mothers, and no adverse effects were reported.

items.title: Alendronate for the primary and secondary prevention of osteoporotic fractures in postmenopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled randomized trials of alendronate, a common bone-strengthening drug, in postmenopausal women. It looked at women at lower risk of fracture (primary prevention) and women at higher risk, such as those with osteoporosis or a past spine fracture (secondary prevention). Alendronate probably lowers the chance of spine fractures in higher-risk women and may lower it in lower-risk women, though most of the evidence was low certainty. Gastrointestinal side effects were little different from placebo, and no cases of jaw bone damage or unusual thigh bone fractures were seen in these trials.
keyPoints: In higher-risk women, alendronate probably reduces clinical spine fractures (moderate-certainty evidence).
In higher-risk women, it may also reduce non-spine, hip and wrist fractures and serious adverse events (low-certainty evidence).
In lower-risk women, it may reduce clinical spine and non-spine fractures but may make little or no difference to hip or wrist fractures (low-certainty evidence).
Gastrointestinal side effects were little different from placebo, and no jaw osteonecrosis or atypical femoral fractures were observed.

items.title: Assessing the Efficacy of Romosozumab in Postmenopausal Osteoporosis: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 randomized trials with about 15,500 postmenopausal women who have osteoporosis. It looked at romosozumab, a bone-building antibody medicine, compared with placebo and other osteoporosis treatments. Romosozumab raised bone density in the lower spine more than the comparison treatments and cut new spinal fractures. Safety was similar to the other treatments, though the authors say longer-term safety data are still needed.
keyPoints: Romosozumab improved lower spine bone density more than placebo, denosumab, teriparatide and alendronate.
It reduced the risk of new spinal (vertebral) fractures about 4-fold compared with placebo.
It raised a marker of bone formation more than denosumab and alendronate.
Safety was comparable to the other treatments, but long-term safety data are still needed.

items.title: Guidelines for fracture risk assessment and management of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and men above the age of 50 in Qatar
items.summary: The Qatar Osteoporosis Association, a panel of six local rheumatologists, wrote national guidelines for finding and treating osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and in men over 50. They reviewed published studies and other guidelines to build their advice. The guidelines suggest using a risk tool that takes age into account to decide who needs screening and treatment. The abstract does not rate how strong the underlying evidence is.
keyPoints: The guidelines recommend the age-dependent Qatar fracture risk assessment tool to screen for osteoporosis and sort people into risk groups.
Treatment choices are recommended based on a person's fracture risk level.
Bone density (DEXA) scans are discouraged for people who have no risk factors.
The guidelines also cover investigations and monitoring of people with osteoporosis.

items.title: Effects of exercise on bone density and physical performance in postmenopausal women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 19 trials with 1,249 postmenopausal women to see whether adding exercise to medicine or supplements helps more than medicine or supplements alone. Exercise did not clearly improve bone density overall, though combining several types of exercise improved lower spine bone density. Adding exercise did improve leg strength, balance, fear of falling and quality of life. The authors note the quality of the evidence was low to very low, so results should be treated with caution.
keyPoints: Adding exercise did not significantly improve bone density at the lower spine or hip overall compared with medicine or supplements alone.
Combining multiple types of exercise training did show a significant improvement in lower spine bone density.
Added exercise improved leg strength, balance, walking-and-standing speed (Timed Up and Go), fear of falling and quality of life.
The authors recommend combining exercise with medicine or supplements to further improve physical function and some areas of bone density.

items.title: Effects of probiotic supplementation on bone health in postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 randomized trials with 1,183 postmenopausal women to see whether probiotic supplements affect bone health. Women taking probiotics had higher bone density in the lower spine and hip than comparison groups, and lower levels of two bone breakdown markers. The effect looked stronger in women with osteopenia (thinner bones) than in women with osteoporosis. The authors say more trials are needed to confirm these findings.
keyPoints: Probiotic supplementation was linked to higher bone mineral density in both the lumbar spine and the hip in postmenopausal women.
Probiotics were associated with lower levels of CTX and BALP, which are markers of bone turnover.
The bone density benefit was greater in women with osteopenia than in women with osteoporosis.
The authors conclude that probiotics may increase bone density, and that more trials are needed to confirm this.

items.title: Quality of life in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 13 studies of 2897 postmenopausal women to compare quality of life across three groups: normal bone density, osteoporosis, and osteoporotic fractures. Women with osteoporosis reported worse overall quality of life than women with normal bone density. Women who had broken a bone due to osteoporosis reported worse quality of life still, especially for physical wellbeing.
keyPoints: Postmenopausal women with osteoporosis had worse overall quality of life than those with normal bone density.
Women with osteoporotic fractures had worse quality of life than women with osteoporosis without fractures, especially in physical health.
Higher bone mineral density was linked to better quality of life.
More severe fragility fractures were linked to worse quality of life.

items.title: GRADE-ADOLOPMENT of clinical practice guideline for postmenopausal osteoporosis management-a Pakistani context
items.summary: This study adapted an American guideline on postmenopausal osteoporosis (thinning of the bones after menopause) for use in Pakistan, where about one in five postmenopausal women is affected. Most of the original 51 recommendations were kept as they were, while a few were changed because some drugs are not available locally. One notable change is a higher vitamin D dose of 2000-4000 IU for people who are older, obese, or have trouble absorbing nutrients, because lower doses were found to be not enough in these groups.
keyPoints: The Pakistani guideline has 50 recommendations, adapted from the 2020 American Association of Clinical Endocrinology guideline.
45 of the 51 original recommendations were adopted unchanged; 4 were adopted with minor changes because some drugs are unavailable, and 1 was left out.
A Pakistan-specific version of the FRAX fracture risk tool was added.
Vitamin D 2000-4000 IU is recommended for older people, people with obesity, or those with malabsorption, alongside baseline vitamin D and calcium checks.

items.title: Predictors of osteoporotic fracture in postmenopausal women: a meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research
items.journal: Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research
items.summary: This review pooled results from 10 studies of more than 1.2 million women after menopause to look for factors linked to broken bones from osteoporosis. Several factors were linked to fracture, including age, body mass index, having three or more children, high blood pressure, diabetes, alcohol intake, and when periods started and stopped. Estrogen use and vitamin D supplements were also linked to fracture risk. The authors say the findings may help spot higher-risk women earlier, but the abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Age, BMI, parity of 3 or more, history of high blood pressure, history of diabetes and alcohol intake were linked to osteoporotic fracture after menopause.
Starting periods at age 15 or later, and menopause before 40 or after 50, were also linked to fracture.
Estrogen use and vitamin D supplements were linked to fracture risk, and so was education level (senior high school and above).
The authors suggest these factors could help identify high-risk women early and support prevention.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of efficacy and safety of Romosozumab in postmenopausal osteoporosis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 randomised trials of romosozumab, a bone-building injection, in women with osteoporosis after menopause. Compared with control treatment, it lowered the risk of spine fractures, other bone fractures and falls, and it raised bone density at the spine, hip and femoral neck. Overall side effects were similar to the control groups. The authors recommend romosozumab for postmenopausal osteoporosis.
keyPoints: Romosozumab lowered spine fracture risk (odds ratio 0.43), other non-spine fractures (0.78) and clinical fractures (0.70) at 24 months, rated high-quality evidence.
Falls were less common with romosozumab (odds ratio 0.87), rated high-quality evidence.
Bone mineral density rose at the lumbar spine, total hip and femoral neck at 12 months.
Total and serious side effects were similar to the control group, rated moderate-quality evidence.

items.title: Time to Benefit of Bisphosphonate Therapy for the Prevention of Fractures Among Postmenopausal Women With Osteoporosis: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
items.summary: This study pooled results from 10 randomized trials of about 23,000 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. It looked at how long bisphosphonate medicines (alendronate, risedronate and zoledronic acid) need to be taken before they prevent fractures. About 12 months of treatment was needed to prevent 1 non-spine fracture for every 100 women treated.
keyPoints: About 12.4 months of bisphosphonate treatment was needed to avoid 1 non-spine fracture per 100 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.
About 20.3 months was needed to avoid 1 hip fracture per 200 women treated.
About 12.1 months was needed to avoid 1 clinical spine fracture per 200 women treated.
The authors conclude treatment is most likely to help women with a life expectancy longer than about 12.4 months.
keywords: how long does it take to work

items.title: Efficacy and safety of vitamin K2 for postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at a long-term follow-up: meta-analysis and systematic review
items.source: Journal of Bone and Mineral Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Bone and Mineral Metabolism
items.summary: This review pooled nine randomised trials with 6,853 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis to see whether vitamin K2 supplements help bones over the long term. Women taking vitamin K2 had bigger gains in bone density in the lower spine and forearm, and their bone-related blood markers changed in a favourable direction. Side effects were reported more often with vitamin K2, but none of the serious problems were linked to it. The authors concluded that vitamin K2 appears beneficial and safe, though the abstract does not report how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Vitamin K2 was linked to a larger increase in bone mineral density in the lumbar spine and forearm.
Vitamin K2 lowered undercarboxylated osteocalcin and raised osteocalcin, which are blood markers related to bone health.
Adverse reactions were somewhat more common with vitamin K2, but no serious adverse events were related to it.
The authors concluded vitamin K2 supplementation is beneficial and safe for treating osteoporosis after menopause.

items.title: Efficacy of vitamin K2 in the prevention and treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 16 randomised trials with 6,425 postmenopausal women to see whether vitamin K2 supplements help bone health. Vitamin K2 was linked with better bone density in the lower spine. Overall, fracture rates did not differ between groups, but they were lower after one study that differed from the others was left out. Side effects were similar to the comparison groups.
keyPoints: Vitamin K2 was linked with maintained or improved bone density in the lower spine (lumbar spine) in postmenopausal women.
Across six trials there was no clear difference in fractures overall; removing one very different study showed fewer fractures with vitamin K2.
Vitamin K2 lowered blood levels of undercarboxylated osteocalcin, a marker of vitamin K status in bone.
Side effects did not differ significantly between the vitamin K2 and control groups.

items.title: Effects of thyroid-stimulating hormone suppression after thyroidectomy for thyroid cancer on bone mineral density in postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 studies of postmenopausal women who had thyroid surgery for thyroid cancer and took levothyroxine to lower their thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), and compared their bone density with women without thyroid cancer. Strong TSH lowering (TSH below 0.10 mIU/L) was linked to lower bone density in the lower spine. Milder TSH lowering was not linked to a clear difference. The authors say more research is needed to learn whether this leads to more broken bones.
keyPoints: Stringent TSH suppression (below 0.10 mIU/L) after thyroidectomy was linked to lower lumbar spine bone density in postmenopausal women.
Moderate TSH suppression (0.10-0.49 mIU/L) showed no significant difference in bone density.
TSH suppression was not significantly linked to lower bone density at the femoral neck (top of the thigh bone) overall.
It is not yet known whether strong TSH suppression raises fracture risk; further studies are needed.

items.title: Swimming as Treatment for Osteoporosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from five randomized trials (263 women) to see whether swimming improves bone density in women with osteoporosis. Swimming may improve bone density in postmenopausal women, but only when the swimming time was between 3 and 6 hours, and especially for long-term swimmers. Less than 3 hours showed no effect on bone density. The authors say more research is needed to confirm how well swimming works.
keyPoints: Swimmers had better lumbar spine bone density than non-swimmers in the pooled analysis.
Swimming for 3 to 6 hours was linked to higher bone density, while under 3 hours showed no effect.
The benefit appeared greatest in long-term swimmers.
Only five trials were included, so the authors say the effectiveness of swimming needs further investigation.

items.title: Executive summary of European guidance for the diagnosis and management of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women
items.summary: This is a short summary of updated European guidance on how to assess and treat postmenopausal women who are at risk of bone fractures from osteoporosis. It updates a 2013 guideline and was written by osteoporosis expert groups from a European perspective. The abstract describes the guidance in general terms and does not list the specific recommendations or rate the strength of the evidence.
keyPoints: Updated European guidance covers the diagnosis and management of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women.
It focuses on assessing and treating women at risk of fractures caused by osteoporosis.
It replaces the previous guideline published in 2013.
Written by the International Osteoporosis Foundation and the European Society for Clinical and Economic Aspects of Osteoporosis and Osteoarthritis.

items.title: Denosumab compared to bisphosphonates to treat postmenopausal osteoporosis: a meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research
items.journal: Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research
items.summary: This study pooled results from 11 randomized trials, covering 5,446 people, to compare two common osteoporosis medicines: denosumab and bisphosphonates. Denosumab led to bigger gains in bone density at the hip, spine and forearm. However, the number of broken bones and the rate of side effects were not meaningfully different between the two. The authors say longer trials are needed to learn about possible complications of denosumab.
keyPoints: Denosumab increased bone mineral density more than bisphosphonates at the total hip, femoral neck, lumbar spine and one-third radius.
There was no significant difference in fracture risk between denosumab and bisphosphonates.
Rates of adverse events, and of stopping treatment because of them, were not significantly different.
The authors call for longer-term trials to identify possible complications of denosumab.

items.title: Efficacy of N-Acetylcysteine in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 22 studies with 2,515 women who have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) to see how N-acetylcysteine (NAC), an antioxidant supplement, affects reproductive outcomes. NAC was linked to higher progesterone levels and a thicker womb lining compared with placebo or other drugs. It also raised LH levels compared with metformin, but made no clear difference to estradiol, SHBG or FSH. The authors say NAC may be a potential treatment option for PCOS.
keyPoints: NAC was linked to a significant rise in progesterone and in endometrial (womb lining) thickness compared with placebo and other drugs.
NAC raised LH levels more than metformin did.
No significant differences were seen in estradiol, SHBG or FSH levels.
The authors conclude NAC may be a potential treatment option for women with PCOS.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists on weight management and metabolic parameters in PCOS women: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of GLP-1 medicines (drugs that affect appetite and blood sugar) in adult women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), compared with metformin or placebo. The medicines lowered body weight, BMI, waist measurements and insulin resistance. They also caused more nausea, vomiting and dizziness. The authors say longer-term effects on blood sugar and blood fats still need to be studied.
keyPoints: GLP-1 medicines significantly reduced body weight, BMI, waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and abdominal girth in women with PCOS.
They also lowered fasting insulin, blood sugar 2 hours after a glucose test, and insulin resistance (HOMA-IR).
Hormone levels such as testosterone were unchanged, and HDL ("good") cholesterol went down.
Side effects were more common: nausea, vomiting and dizziness.

items.title: European Paediatric Surgeons' Association Consensus Statement on the Management of Neonatal Ovarian Simple Cysts
items.summary: European paediatric surgeons reviewed the evidence and agreed on how to manage simple ovarian cysts found in newborn girls. They advise that babies with cysts larger than 4 cm be offered keyhole surgery within the first 2 weeks of life, while smaller cysts can be watched with repeat ultrasound scans. The statement notes there is still limited data on the benefits and risks of draining a cyst before birth.
keyPoints: Newborns with simple ovarian cysts larger than 4 cm should be offered surgery within the first 2 weeks of life.
The preferred surgery is keyhole (laparoscopic) draining and opening of the cyst using bipolar instruments.
After surgery, ultrasound follow-up is advised at 3 months; if surgery is not done, scans are advised every 3 to 4 months until 1 year.
Data on the benefits and complications of draining a cyst with ultrasound before birth are still limited; babies who had this should be followed for 6 months.

items.title: The Effect of Hormonal Treatment on Ovarian Endometriomas: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 studies of 888 women to see whether hormone treatment for endometriosis shrinks endometriomas (ovarian cysts caused by endometriosis). On average, cysts were about 55% smaller after at least 6 months of treatment. Results differed a lot between studies, and most studies were at risk of bias, so the exact amount of shrinkage a person might see is uncertain.
keyPoints: Hormonal suppression for at least 6 months reduced endometrioma volume by about 55% on average.
The biggest reductions were seen with dienogest and with norethindrone acetate plus letrozole, followed by relugolix and leuprolide acetate.
Combined hormonal contraceptives and other progestins did not show a statistically significant reduction in cyst size.
Results varied widely between studies and most were at risk of selection bias, so the exact reduction is uncertain.

items.title: Ranking the dietary interventions by their effectiveness in the management of polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 19 trials with 727 women who have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) to compare different diets, and metformin, on weight, hormones, blood sugar and blood fats. The DASH diet (a heart-healthy eating pattern) ranked best for insulin resistance, fasting blood sugar, fasting insulin and triglycerides. A low-calorie diet ranked best for body mass index, and metformin ranked best for lowering testosterone and LDL cholesterol. The authors conclude that diets differ in their effects and that DASH looks most effective overall.
keyPoints: The DASH diet ranked highest for improving insulin resistance, fasting blood glucose, fasting insulin and triglycerides in women with PCOS.
A low-calorie diet ranked best for BMI, and a low-calorie diet combined with metformin ranked best for weight loss.
Metformin ranked best for lowering total testosterone and LDL cholesterol.
The low-carb diet ranked best for reducing cholesterol, and different diets affect different measures.

items.title: A systematic review of GLP-1 on anthropometrics, metabolic and endocrine parameters in patients with PCOS
items.summary: This review looked at eight studies with 486 women who have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) to see how GLP-1 medicines affect weight and hormone and metabolic measures. GLP-1 medicines reduced body weight and improved some hormone and metabolic measures. Using a GLP-1 medicine together with metformin gave larger benefits for weight loss than the comparison treatment. The authors say more research is needed on the long-term safety of the combined treatment.
keyPoints: GLP-1 receptor agonists effectively reduced body weight in women with PCOS.
They also improved some hormone and metabolic measures.
Combining a GLP-1 medicine with metformin had a greater effect on weight loss and gave favorable hormone and metabolic results.
Long-term safety of combined treatment in women with PCOS and overweight or obesity still needs study.

items.title: Effect of cinnamon as a Chinese herbal medicine on markers of cardiovascular risk in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 12 randomized trials of cinnamon supplements in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Cinnamon was linked to small improvements in body weight, fasting blood sugar, insulin resistance, total cholesterol and LDL ('bad') cholesterol. The studies differed a lot from one another, so the authors say larger, better-standardized trials are needed.
keyPoints: Cinnamon was linked to a small average weight loss of about 0.47 kg.
Women taking cinnamon had lower insulin resistance and lower fasting blood sugar (about 7.7 mg/dL lower on average).
Total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol also tended to be lower, by about 11 mg/dL each.
Results varied considerably between studies, so more research with larger groups is needed.

items.title: The Association Between Obesity and Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: An Epidemiologic Study of Observational Data
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This review pooled 58 studies covering about 86,000 adults in 24 countries to see whether places with more obesity also have more polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). It found a modest link: when obesity was more common in a population, PCOS was somewhat more common too. The data cannot show that obesity causes PCOS. The link was clearest in the higher-quality studies.
keyPoints: Populations with higher average BMI or obesity rates tended to have higher PCOS rates, though the link was modest.
Using the Rotterdam criteria, a 1% rise in obesity was linked to about a 0.4% rise in PCOS.
The study cannot establish that obesity causes PCOS.
The link was stronger when only high-quality studies were included.

items.title: Inositol is an effective and safe treatment in polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 26 randomized trials with 1,691 women who have PCOS, comparing inositol with placebo or with metformin. Women taking inositol were more likely to have regular periods than those on placebo, and inositol worked about as well as metformin for this. Inositol also lowered body mass index, blood sugar and some male-type hormones compared with placebo. The authors concluded inositol is an effective and safe treatment for PCOS.
keyPoints: Women taking inositol were about 1.8 times more likely to have regular menstrual cycles than those on placebo.
Inositol was non-inferior to metformin for getting cycles back to regular.
Compared with placebo, inositol lowered BMI, glucose, insulin response and testosterone-related hormones, and raised sex-hormone-binding globulin.
The authors concluded inositol is an effective and safe treatment in PCOS.

items.title: Comparison of dietary and physical activity behaviors in women with and without polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 39 471 women
items.summary: This review pooled 54 observational studies (about 39,000 women) to compare eating and activity habits in women with and without polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Women with PCOS tended to have lower overall diet quality, to eat more cholesterol and less magnesium and zinc, and to be less physically active, although they drank less alcohol. Total calories, carbohydrates, fat, protein and fibre were similar between the groups. The studies differed a lot from one another, so the reasons behind these differences are still unclear.
keyPoints: Women with PCOS had higher cholesterol intake and lower magnesium intake than women without PCOS, with a tendency toward lower zinc.
Women with PCOS were less physically active overall and had lower alcohol intake.
Total energy, carbohydrate, fat, protein, fibre, glycemic index and glycemic load were similar between the groups.
Most studies found poorer adherence to healthy eating patterns in women with PCOS, but the studies varied widely, so other factors may play a role.

items.title: Effect of yoga on polycystic ovarian syndrome: A systematic review
items.source: Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies
items.journal: Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies
items.summary: This review looked at published research on whether yoga helps women with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). Out of about 74 papers, 16 were judged most relevant. The studies concluded that different parts of yoga were used successfully to manage PCOS, either on their own or alongside medicine. The abstract does not rate how strong or certain this evidence is.
keyPoints: 16 relevant studies published between 2012 and 2019 were reviewed.
The studies measured things like blood fats, blood sugar handling, hormones, quality of life, anxiety and depression.
The studies concluded that yoga was used successfully to manage PCOS, with or without medication.
The review describes yoga as helping reduce and manage symptoms more effectively when used along with medicine.

items.title: Long-term cardiometabolic disease risk in women with PCOS: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 23 studies that followed women with and without polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) over several years. Women with PCOS had higher risks of high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes, and a higher risk of non-fatal stroke-type events. The authors say this should be taken into account when doctors assess heart disease risk in women with PCOS.
keyPoints: Women with PCOS had about 3 times the risk of type 2 diabetes compared with women without PCOS.
Risk of high blood pressure was about 1.75 times higher, and non-fatal cerebrovascular (stroke-type) events were about 1.4 times higher.

Total cholesterol was slightly higher and HDL ("good") cholesterol slightly lower in women with PCOS; no clear differences were found for LDL cholesterol, triglycerides or coronary heart disease events.
There was too little data on deaths from heart disease to draw conclusions, and trials are still needed to show whether screening and treatment reduce future heart disease.

items.title: Psychiatric disorders in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 57 studies covering over 172,000 people to look at mental health in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Women with PCOS were more likely to have a diagnosis of depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder than women without PCOS. Their symptoms on mental health scales were also worse. The studies were of fair quality, but most results were not adjusted for other factors that could affect them.
keyPoints: Women with PCOS had higher odds of a depression diagnosis (about 2.8 times) and an anxiety diagnosis (about 2.8 times).
Bipolar disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder were also more common in women with PCOS.
No clear link was found with social phobia or panic disorder.
Symptoms of depression, anxiety, OCD and somatization (physical symptoms linked to stress) were more severe in women with PCOS.

items.title: Effects of orlistat vs. metformin on weight loss-related clinical variables in women with PCOS: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine studies of orlistat, a weight-loss medicine, in overweight or obese women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). The data suggest orlistat lowers weight and BMI, and most studies also saw better testosterone levels, and some saw better insulin resistance and cholesterol. In a small comparison of three trials (121 women), orlistat and metformin had similar effects on BMI, insulin and testosterone.
keyPoints: Orlistat significantly reduced BMI and body weight in overweight or obese women with PCOS.
Seven of eight studies reported lower testosterone, and five of eight reported improved insulin resistance with orlistat.
In three randomised trials (121 women), orlistat and metformin had similar effects on BMI, insulin resistance, testosterone and insulin.
The comparison with metformin rests on a small number of women and wide uncertainty ranges.

items.title: Management of moderate and severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome: a Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society clinical practice guideline
items.summary: This guideline from the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society looks at how to diagnose and manage moderate and severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), a possible complication of ovarian stimulation for fertility treatment. OHSS is mainly diagnosed from symptoms, with scans and blood tests used to judge how severe it is. Care for moderate and severe cases is mostly supportive, either at home or in hospital, and may include draining fluid from the abdomen. Critical OHSS needs hospital care with a team of specialists.
keyPoints: OHSS is a potentially serious complication of ovarian stimulation used in assisted reproduction.
Diagnosis is mostly clinical, and scans or lab tests help work out how severe it is.
Moderate and severe OHSS is managed mainly with supportive care, as an outpatient or inpatient, and may include paracentesis (fluid drainage).
Critical OHSS requires hospital admission and multidisciplinary care.

items.title: Development and validation of a gonadotropin dose selection model for optimized ovarian stimulation in IVF/ICSI: an individual participant data meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled individual patient data from 14 randomised trials (2,907 women under 39 having IVF/ICSI) to build a model for choosing the starting dose of fertility stimulation drugs. The model could not predict live birth well, so changing the starting dose is not a good way to improve the chance of a baby. It did a reasonably good job of predicting treatment risks, such as ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), using simple details like age and AMH.
keyPoints: The model predicted live birth poorly (AUC about 0.55), so the starting dose did not reliably change the chance of a live birth.
The model predicted combined treatment risks, including OHSS, adequately (AUC about 0.75 to 0.77).
The models use easily obtained details such as age, AMH, starting dose and the type of GnRH analog.
Choosing a dose for each patient may lower treatment risks and could reduce treatment costs.

items.title: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist protocols for pituitary suppression in assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 40 trials (4148 women) comparing different ways of using GnRH agonist medicines to stop the body releasing eggs too early during IVF or ICSI stimulation. The long and short protocols gave little or no difference in live births or ongoing pregnancies, though the long protocol may improve clinical pregnancy rates. The evidence was low to very low certainty, and very few studies reported on ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) or miscarriage, so no clear conclusions could be drawn on these.
keyPoints: Long versus short protocols: little or no difference in live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates (low-certainty evidence).
The long protocol may improve clinical pregnancy rates compared with the short protocol (low-certainty evidence).
It is uncertain whether any protocol changes OHSS or miscarriage rates, as only a few studies reported them.
No studies reported on cost or how acceptable the protocols were to women, and many trials were old.

items.title: Administration of dehydroepiandrosterone improves endometrial thickness in women undergoing IVF/ICSI: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 randomised trials with 1,973 women having IVF or ICSI to see whether taking DHEA, a hormone supplement, helps. DHEA was linked to a thicker womb lining and a higher clinical pregnancy rate, plus slightly more eggs and good-quality embryos. The evidence was low to very low quality, and there was not enough evidence to say whether it changes live birth or miscarriage rates. The authors say more research is needed before DHEA is used in routine care.
keyPoints: DHEA was linked to a thicker womb lining (about 0.93 mm more on average) and a higher clinical pregnancy rate.
It was also linked to slightly more eggs retrieved and fertilised, and more high-quality embryos.
There was not enough evidence to reach a conclusion on live birth, ongoing pregnancy or miscarriage rates.
No severe side effects were seen, but the authors say results should be read with caution and need more research.

items.title: Oral GnRH antagonists for ovulation suppression during ovarian stimulation protocols: systemic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review pulled together four studies of 813 women having IVF to compare oral GnRH antagonist pills with the usual injected version. These medicines stop the body from releasing eggs too early during ovarian stimulation. The pills and injections gave similar results for cycle cancellation, number of eggs retrieved, fertilization and blastocyst rates. The quality of the evidence was moderate, and the authors say more research is needed to confirm how well the pills work and how safe they are.
keyPoints: No clear differences were found between oral and injected GnRH antagonists in cycle cancellation, eggs retrieved, fertilization or blastulation rates.
The review included four studies with 813 women in total.
Evidence quality was rated moderate using GRADE.
The authors suggest oral GnRH antagonists may be useful, but say effectiveness and safety still need to be firmly established.

items.title: Cycle regimens for endometrial preparation prior to frozen embryo transfer
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 32 trials (6,352 women) comparing different ways to prepare the womb lining for a frozen embryo transfer: natural cycles, hormone therapy cycles, and cycles using drugs to trigger ovulation. Across the comparisons, no approach clearly gave more live births or fewer miscarriages than another. Much of the evidence was low or very low quality, so the results are uncertain.
keyPoints: No cycle regimen was clearly better or safer than another for live birth or miscarriage rates.
Natural cycle versus hormone therapy with GnRHa suppression probably made little or no difference to live birth or multiple pregnancy (moderate-certainty evidence).
Most other comparisons were low or very low certainty, with wide ranges consistent with possible benefit or harm.
The review notes that important outcomes were often not reported and studies were small.

items.title: Venous thromboembolism associated with medically assisted reproduction (MAR): British fertility society policy and practice guidance for assessment and prevention
items.summary: This is a guidance document from the British Fertility Society on blood clots (venous thromboembolism, or VTE) linked to fertility treatment such as ovarian stimulation and embryo transfer. Clots are not thought to be common with this treatment, but they can cause serious harm and are often preventable. Because they usually happen after treatment ends and are often managed outside the fertility clinic, they may be underreported. The guidance aims to help clinicians spot who is at risk and use steps to lower that risk.
keyPoints: Blood clots are not thought to be a common complication of fertility treatment, but they can cause serious illness and are often preventable.
Clots usually appear after treatment finishes and may be treated outside the fertility unit, so they are probably underreported.
Fertility cycles are rising, especially in women over 40 and for fertility preservation, so the number of clots may rise too.
The guidance covers risk factors, how to assess clot risk, and best-practice ways to reduce risk during ovarian stimulation and embryo transfer cycles.

items.title: Androgens (dehydroepiandrosterone or testosterone) for women undergoing assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 28 trials (about 3,000 women, mostly 'poor responders' to standard IVF) to see whether adding DHEA or testosterone before or during IVF helps. DHEA likely makes little to no difference to live birth or pregnancy rates. Testosterone pre-treatment likely improves live birth and clinical pregnancy rates, though the evidence is only of moderate certainty. Reported side effects were minor but data on them were sparse.
keyPoints: DHEA pre-treatment likely makes little to no difference to live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates (moderate certainty).
Testosterone pre-treatment likely improves live birth rates (for example, from about 10% to between 15% and 30%) and clinical pregnancy rates (moderate certainty).
Neither DHEA nor testosterone is likely to lower miscarriage rates.
The effect on multiple pregnancy is very uncertain, and the evidence for testosterone versus estradiol is also uncertain.

items.title: Utility and Outcomes of Ovarian Tissue Cryopreservation and Transplantation for Gynecologic Cancers: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 23 studies on freezing ovarian tissue and later putting it back (autologous transplantation) to protect fertility in women with gynecologic cancers. About 1 in 4 women with gynecologic cancer who then had ovarian stimulation had at least one child, and hormone function returned in most women after transplantation. The procedure is still used rarely for these cancers, and the authors say longer-term results are still needed.
keyPoints: Only about 7.5% of women having ovarian tissue freezing, and 9.6% having transplantation, had gynecologic cancers; blood cancers and breast cancer made up about 66%.
Among women with gynecologic cancer who had ovarian stimulation after transplantation, 27.3% had at least one child.
Ovarian hormone function was restored in 78.1% of women after transplantation, and grafts lasted a median of 32 months.
No cancer recurrence at the graft site was reported in women with gynecologic cancer.

items.title: Progesterone level in assisted reproductive technology: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 64 studies (nearly 58,000 women) to see whether progesterone levels during IVF/ICSI treatment affect pregnancy outcomes. In fresh cycles, a raised progesterone level at the start of stimulation made no clear difference to live birth rates. A raised level on the day of the ovulation trigger was linked to lower live birth and pregnancy rates when day 3 embryos were transferred, but not when day 5 embryos were transferred. For frozen embryo transfer cycles, the studies were too different from each other to combine into a clear answer.
keyPoints: Raised progesterone at baseline in fresh cycles did not clearly affect live birth rate.
Raised progesterone at the ovulation trigger was linked to a lower live birth rate with day 3 embryo transfer, but not with day 5 transfer.
No firm conclusions could be drawn for frozen embryo transfer cycles because the studies varied too much.
The authors note possible publication bias and uncontrolled confounding factors.

items.title: Association between the number of oocytes and cumulative live birth rate: A systematic review
items.source: Best Practice & Research. Clinical Obstetrics & Gynaecology
items.journal: Best Practice & Research. Clinical Obstetrics & Gynaecology
items.summary: This systematic review looked at how the number of eggs collected during IVF relates to the chance of having a baby over all fresh and frozen embryo transfers from one egg collection. More eggs were linked to a higher chance of a live birth. How much this matters depends on age: under 35, collecting more than about 25-30 eggs added little benefit, while over 35 more eggs seemed to keep helping.
keyPoints: Collecting more eggs was linked to a higher cumulative live birth rate.
In women under 35, there was little extra benefit above about 25-30 eggs.
In women over 35, more eggs seemed to improve the chance of a live birth until the very end of reproductive age.
In women aged 44 or older, the chance of a live birth stayed low no matter how many eggs were collected.

items.title: Glucocorticoid supplementation during ovulation induction for assisted reproductive technology: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of women having IVF or ICSI to see whether adding a steroid medicine (glucocorticoids such as prednisolone) during ovarian stimulation helps pregnancy outcomes. It found no clear effect on live birth, miscarriage or implantation. Clinical pregnancy rates per cycle seemed slightly higher, but this result depended on the cause of infertility, the dose and how long the treatment lasted, so the authors say it should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Adding prednisolone during ovarian stimulation did not significantly change live birth rate in IVF/ICSI.
Miscarriage and implantation rates were also not significantly different from the control group.
Clinical pregnancy rate per cycle tended to be higher with glucocorticoids, but this varied by infertility cause, dose schedule and treatment length.
Overall, the authors conclude that glucocorticoid therapy does not significantly improve clinical outcomes and results should be interpreted cautiously.

items.title: In vitro fertilisation for unexplained subfertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether IVF helps couples with unexplained subfertility compared with waiting, or with IUI (with or without fertility medicines). IVF may give a better chance of a live birth than IUI without medicines. In women who had not had treatment before, there may be little or no difference in live births between IVF and IUI with medicines such as gonadotropins or clomiphene. The authors say the overall evidence is low quality, so results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: IVF may improve live birth rates compared with unstimulated IUI (low-quality evidence).
In treatment-naive women, there may be little or no difference in live birth, multiple pregnancy or OHSS between IVF and IUI with gonadotropins or clomiphene (low-quality evidence).
In women already treated with IUI plus clomiphene, IVF may improve live birth rates compared with IUI plus gonadotropins (low-quality evidence).
We are uncertain whether IVF beats expectant management, as the evidence is very low quality and side effects were not reported.

items.title: Female dietary patterns and outcomes of in vitro fertilization (IVF): a systematic literature review
