items.summary: This review looked at whether the way a woman eats before IVF is linked to getting pregnant or having a baby. Seven studies were found. Some linked eating a Mediterranean-style, 'profertility' or Dutch 'preconception' diet with better results, but the studies had weaknesses and could not show that diet was the cause. The review does not support recommending any one diet to improve IVF success.
keyPoints: Seven prospective cohort studies of nine dietary patterns were included.
Higher adherence to a Mediterranean, 'profertility' or Dutch 'preconception' diet was linked to pregnancy or live birth in at least one study, but this does not prove cause.
The studies had methodological problems and risk of bias, and the Mediterranean diet studies gave very mixed results.
The review does not support recommending any single dietary pattern to improve pregnancy or live birth rates during IVF.

items.title: Endometrial injury for pregnancy following sexual intercourse or intrauterine insemination
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether deliberately scratching or injuring the womb lining (endometrial injury) helps women get pregnant through sex or intrauterine insemination (IUI). It combined 22 trials with 3,703 women, most with unexplained infertility. The evidence was too weak to show whether it increases live birth, because most studies had a high risk of bias. Pain during the procedure was usually reported as mild to moderate.
keyPoints: It is uncertain whether endometrial injury improves live birth; the one lowest-risk-of-bias study found no clear effect.
When all studies were pooled, results looked more positive, but the evidence was very low quality and should be read with caution.
Most women reported mild to moderate pain during the procedure (very low-quality evidence).
The authors say current evidence does not support routine use of endometrial injury in women having IUI or trying to conceive naturally.

items.title: Fertility treatment and cancers-the eternal conundrum: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 29 studies to ask whether fertility treatment raises the risk of breast, ovarian, womb lining (endometrial) or cervical cancer. Overall, fertility treatment did not significantly raise the risk of breast, ovarian or endometrial cancer, and cervical cancer was less common in treated women. Ovarian cancer was more common in women who had IVF or clomiphene citrate, and borderline ovarian tumours were also more common. The authors say the studies varied a lot, so results should be read with caution and the ovarian link needs more research.
keyPoints: Overall, fertility treatment did not significantly change the incidence of breast, ovarian or endometrial cancer.
Cervical cancer was significantly less common in the fertility treatment group (OR 0.68).
Ovarian cancer was more common in women who had IVF (OR 1.32) or clomiphene citrate (OR 1.40), and borderline ovarian tumours were also more common (OR 1.69).
Breast cancer was less common in the IVF subgroup (OR 0.75); the authors call the overall results reassuring but urge caution because the studies differed widely.

items.title: GnRH agonist and hCG (dual trigger) versus hCG trigger for follicular maturation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of women having IVF. It compared a 'dual trigger' (a GnRH agonist plus hCG) with the usual hCG-only trigger shot that finishes egg maturation. Women who had the dual trigger were more likely to have a live birth per started cycle, and the evidence for this was rated moderate. Several other results also favoured the dual trigger, but those were rated low evidence.
keyPoints: Dual trigger was linked to a higher live birth rate per started cycle than hCG alone (moderate evidence).
Clinical pregnancy rate was also higher with dual trigger (low evidence).
More eggs, mature eggs, fertilized eggs and usable embryos were collected with dual trigger (low evidence).
Ongoing pregnancy and implantation rates showed a trend towards improvement but were not clearly different (low evidence).

items.title: Recombinant human luteinizing hormone co-treatment in ovarian stimulation for assisted reproductive technology in women of advanced reproductive age: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 12 randomized trials of women aged 35 and over having fresh IVF cycles. It compared stimulation with FSH alone against FSH plus added luteinizing hormone (LH). In women aged 35-40, adding LH was linked to higher clinical pregnancy and implantation rates, but fewer eggs were collected. Live birth and miscarriage rates were not different between the two approaches, and the authors say more trials are needed to confirm the findings.
keyPoints: In women aged 35-40, FSH plus LH was linked to higher clinical pregnancy rates than FSH alone (OR 1.45).
Implantation rates were also higher with FSH plus LH in women aged 35-40 (OR 1.49).
Slightly fewer eggs were retrieved with FSH plus LH than with FSH alone.
Live birth rates, miscarriage rates and the number of mature (metaphase II) eggs did not differ between the two groups.

items.title: Ovarian stimulation for freeze-all IVF cycles: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at how ovarian stimulation (the fertility medicines used to grow eggs) should be planned when all embryos are frozen and transferred later, instead of a fresh transfer. It found good-quality evidence that more eggs retrieved means a higher chance of a live birth overall, but very large numbers carry their own risks, so a target of 15 to 20 eggs is suggested. The authors also report that some approaches, like a GnRH antagonist protocol and a GnRH agonist trigger, make treatment safer in freeze-all cycles. For several other questions, the evidence is limited or conflicting.
keyPoints: Good-quality evidence shows the chance of a live birth over a full treatment course rises as more eggs are retrieved, but stimulation is advised to aim for 15 to 20 eggs because retrieving very large numbers has risks.

The risk of severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is virtually eliminated in freeze-all cycles, and a GnRH antagonist protocol with a GnRH agonist trigger is the preferred approach for safety.
Moderate-quality evidence suggests delaying the trigger injection by 2-3 days may give more mature eggs without lowering pregnancy rates.
Evidence is conflicting or lacking on raised progesterone late in stimulation and on very high estradiol levels, though no significant harms from high estradiol have been described.

items.title: Adjuvant treatment strategies in ovarian stimulation for poor responders undergoing IVF: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of add-on treatments given alongside IVF stimulation to women with poor ovarian response (few eggs collected). Compared with stimulation alone, adding DHEA or coenzyme Q10 was linked to a higher chance of clinical pregnancy. Growth hormone, letrozole and clomiphene were linked to lower gonadotrophin doses, and coenzyme Q10 to fewer cancelled cycles. The authors note that more high-quality trials using the same definition of poor response are still needed.
keyPoints: DHEA and coenzyme Q10 were each linked to a higher chance of clinical pregnancy than stimulation without an add-on.
hCG, oestradiol and growth hormone were linked to more eggs retrieved; testosterone and growth hormone to more embryos transferred.
Clomiphene citrate, letrozole and growth hormone were linked to lower gonadotrophin doses, and coenzyme Q10 to the lowest cycle cancellation rate.
The authors call for more high-quality trials using uniform standards for defining poor ovarian response.

items.title: Ovarian stimulation and endometriosis progression or recurrence: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 16 studies to see whether the hormone medicines used to stimulate the ovaries (alone, with IUI, or with IVF) make endometriosis worse or bring it back. Early case reports described some severe problems, but later observational studies were more reassuring. For IVF, the evidence suggests it does not worsen pain or raise the chance of endometriosis coming back. The evidence for IUI and for deep endometriosis is weaker and less certain.
keyPoints: IVF does not appear to worsen endometriosis-related pain (moderate quality evidence).
IVF does not appear to increase the risk of endometriosis recurrence (moderate quality evidence).
Any effect of IVF on ovarian endometriomas is mild, if present at all (low quality evidence).
IUI may increase the risk of recurrence (low quality evidence), and deep invasive endometriosis might progress with stimulation (very low quality evidence).

items.title: Management of thin endometrium in assisted reproduction: a clinical practice guideline from the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society
items.summary: This is a clinical guideline from the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society on thin endometrium (a thin womb lining) in assisted reproduction such as IVF. It looks at how lining thickness relates to pregnancy and live birth in ovarian stimulation, fresh IVF cycles and frozen embryo transfer cycles. It also gives recommendations on add-on treatments that aim to thicken the lining and improve pregnancy outcomes. The abstract does not give the specific findings or recommendations.
keyPoints: Thin endometrium is a common challenge for people having assisted reproduction.
The guideline reviews how endometrial thickness affects pregnancy and live birth in ovarian stimulation and IVF, both fresh and frozen cycles.
It gives evidence-based recommendations, using the GRADE framework, on assessing and managing thin endometrium.
It also covers whether add-on treatments (adjuvants) can improve lining thickness and pregnancy outcomes.

items.title: The management of unexplained infertility: an evidence-based guideline from the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society
items.summary: This guideline from the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society looks at how to treat unexplained infertility, which affects as many as half of couples seeking fertility care. It reviews options from waiting and watching, through lower-intervention treatments like IUI and ovarian stimulation, up to IVF. The authors say treatment should be tailored to each person's age and how long they have been trying, and should focus on approaches most likely to lead to a healthy live birth.
keyPoints: Unexplained infertility is a diagnosis of exclusion, so treatment has often been based on experience rather than firm proof.
The guideline covers expectant management, laparoscopy, IUI, ovarian stimulation with oral medicines or gonadotropins, stimulation plus IUI, and IVF.
Treatment should be individualized based on age and duration of infertility.
Recommendations prioritize strategies most likely to result in a healthy live birth.

items.title: No. 362-Ovulation Induction in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looks at ways to help women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) ovulate and get pregnant. It recommends weight loss and exercise first for those who need it, followed by ovulation-inducing medicines such as aromatase inhibitors or selective estrogen receptor modulators. If these do not work, referral to a fertility specialist is suggested to consider injectable hormones or IVF.
keyPoints: First step for infertility with PCOS should include weight loss and exercise, aiming for a BMI below 35 where this applies.
Aromatase inhibitors (now considered safe and effective) and selective estrogen receptor modulators are the first-line medicines for inducing ovulation.
Insulin sensitizers should not be the first treatment but can be added as helpers when appropriate.
If these approaches fail or do not work, referral to a reproductive endocrinologist should be considered for gonadotropins or IVF.

items.title: Oocyte, embryo and blastocyst cryopreservation in ART: systematic review and meta-analysis comparing slow-freezing versus vitrification to produce evidence for the development of global guidance
items.summary: This review pooled results from trials comparing two ways of freezing eggs and embryos in fertility treatment: slow-freezing and vitrification (ultra-fast freezing into a glass-like state). Vitrification led to more eggs and embryos surviving the freeze-thaw process and was linked to better pregnancy outcomes. The evidence for pregnancy outcomes was low quality, while the evidence for survival was moderate quality. Frozen-then-warmed eggs gave similar pregnancy rates to fresh eggs in the one trial that compared them.
keyPoints: Embryos survived freezing and warming more often with vitrification than with slow-freezing (moderate quality evidence).
Pregnancy rates were higher with vitrification for eggs and embryos, but the evidence was low quality and based on few trials.
In one trial, vitrified eggs gave about the same ongoing pregnancy rate as fresh eggs.
The authors suggest clinics still using slow-freezing should consider switching to vitrification.

items.title: Human chorionic gonadotrophin priming for fertility treatment with in vitro maturation
items.summary: This review looked at whether giving an hCG hormone injection before egg collection helps in in vitro maturation (IVM), a fertility treatment where immature eggs are collected and matured in the lab. IVM avoids the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), which is higher in women with polycystic ovaries. Across four small trials with 522 women, there was no clear evidence that hCG priming changed live birth, pregnancy or miscarriage rates. The evidence was low quality, and there was a hint that priming might lower pregnancy rates, but this is uncertain.
keyPoints: No clear difference in live birth or miscarriage rates was found between hCG priming and no priming.
Low quality evidence suggested hCG priming may lower clinical pregnancy rates, but the result was inconclusive.
No studies reported side effects other than miscarriage, so safety could not be properly judged.
Better designed trials are needed to settle whether hCG priming helps and what dose and timing work best.

items.title: Long-acting FSH versus daily FSH for women undergoing assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether one weekly injection of a long-acting FSH hormone works as well as daily FSH injections for women having IVF or ICSI. It combined six randomised trials with 3,753 women and rated the study quality as moderate. Overall, live birth rates and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) rates were not different between the two approaches. A medium dose worked as well as daily injections, while a low dose was linked to fewer live births.
keyPoints: Overall, long-acting FSH and daily FSH gave similar live birth rates and similar OHSS rates.
A medium dose (150 to 180 μg) of long-acting FSH was as effective and safe as daily FSH in women with unexplained subfertility.
A low dose (60 to 120 μg) of long-acting FSH was linked to fewer live births than daily FSH.

Pregnancy, miscarriage, multiple pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy and birth defect rates did not differ between the groups, and more research is needed in women who respond very strongly or poorly to stimulation.

items.title: Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone agonist protocols for pituitary suppression in assisted reproduction
items.summary: This review pooled 37 trials (3,872 women) comparing different ways of using GnRH agonist medicines during IVF or ICSI. These medicines stop the body releasing an egg too early during ovarian stimulation. Long and short protocols showed no clear difference in live birth or ongoing pregnancy, although long protocols gave more clinical pregnancies. The evidence was low to moderate quality, and there was too little data to judge side effects.
keyPoints: No clear difference in live birth or ongoing pregnancy between long and short GnRH agonist protocols (low quality evidence).
Clinical pregnancy rates were higher with a long protocol than a short one (moderate quality evidence).
No clear difference in cycle cancellation between long and short protocols (low quality evidence).

Other protocol comparisons, such as stopping versus continuing the medicine or lowering the dose, showed no clear difference in birth or pregnancy outcomes, and there was too little data to judge side effects.

items.title: Optimizing IUI: evidence-based guidance for use of add-ons and variations in IUI treatment, a British Fertility Society policy and practice guideline
items.summary: The British Fertility Society reviewed 154 randomised trials (34,825 participants) on 25 add-ons and variations used in intrauterine insemination (IUI), including LH surge detection, follicle monitoring, and the timing of ovulation triggering. Many of these extras are offered without strong proof that they help. The review found that most of the evidence is low quality and many trials were too small, so most recommendations are uncertain.
keyPoints: The guideline looked at 25 IUI add-ons and variations, including follicular monitoring, LH surge detection, and ovulation triggering and timing.
It was based on 154 randomised controlled trials with 34,825 participants.
Most of the evidence is low quality, which limits how certain the recommendations are.
The guideline says this uncertainty should be clearly explained to patients during counselling.

items.title: Synchronised approach for intrauterine insemination in subfertile couples
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 42 trials (6603 couples) of ways to time intrauterine insemination (IUI) with ovulation, such as using urine LH tests, hCG trigger injections, or different waiting times after the injection. For most comparisons, the evidence was low certainty and too imprecise to show whether one method works better than another. One small study suggested live birth or ongoing pregnancy may be lower with hCG alone than with hCG plus FSH, but this rests on low-certainty evidence. No clear differences were seen in clinical pregnancy or in side effects such as miscarriage or multiple pregnancy.
keyPoints: There is not enough evidence to say whether any method of timing insemination with ovulation is better than another.
Comparing insemination 0 to 33 hours, 34 to 40 hours, or over 40 hours after the hCG injection gave results too imprecise to be useful.
Using a urine LH surge versus an hCG trigger, and recombinant versus urinary hCG, showed no clear difference in live birth or ongoing pregnancy (low-certainty evidence).
hCG alone may give lower live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates than hCG plus FSH, based on one small study of low-certainty evidence.

items.title: Progestogens for prevention of luteinising hormone (LH) surge in women undergoing controlled ovarian hyperstimulation as part of an assisted reproductive technology (ART) cycle
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 14 trials of women having fertility treatment (IVF-type cycles). It asked whether progestogen medicines taken by mouth can stop the body releasing an egg too early, as an alternative to the usual injected GnRH medicines. Progestogens may work about as well as GnRH antagonists at keeping egg collection cycles from being cancelled, but much of the evidence is low or very low quality and the results are uncertain. No firm conclusions could be drawn on live birth rates or most other outcomes.
keyPoints: There may be little or no difference in egg-collection cancellation between progestogens and GnRH antagonists, but the evidence is low certainty.
One study in poor responders was very uncertain about live birth rates with medroxyprogesterone compared with a GnRH antagonist (very low certainty).
Micronised progesterone may give 2 to 6 more mature (MII) eggs than GnRH antagonists in normal responders (low-quality evidence).
When comparing progestogens, dydrogesterone suggested slightly fewer cancelled collections than medroxyprogesterone or micronised progesterone, but most results were uncertain.

items.title: Remifentanil patient-controlled analgesia for labour analgesia: guidance from the obstetric anaesthetists' association: Recommendations for well tolerated provision of remifentanil PCA for labour analgesia
items.summary: An expert group from the Obstetric Anaesthetists' Association wrote guidance on remifentanil PCA, a pain relief option in labour where the woman presses a button to give herself small doses of a strong painkiller through a drip. The guidance says it can work well, especially for women who cannot or choose not to have an epidural or spinal. It has some risks, but when used within set limits there is a record of it being effective and safe. Most recommendations are based on low or moderate certainty evidence, and there is little data for higher-risk pregnancies.
keyPoints: Remifentanil PCA can give effective pain relief in labour, particularly when an epidural or spinal is not possible or is declined.
When used within defined limits, there is now an established record of effectiveness and safety, though some risks remain.
Labour wards need clear protocols for giving and monitoring it, and staff trained to spot and manage complications.
There is little data on its use in higher-risk mothers and babies, which is a research priority.

items.title: Automated mandatory bolus versus basal infusion for maintenance of epidural analgesia in labour
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 18 trials (4,590 healthy women at term) comparing two ways of topping up labour epidurals: small doses given automatically at set times (automated bolus) versus a continuous drip. Automated bolus was linked to less breakthrough pain needing an anaesthetist and to less numbing medicine being used per hour. There was no clear difference in caesarean births, instrumental births (forceps or vacuum), length of epidural pain relief, or babies' Apgar scores. The authors say larger studies are still needed on caesarean and instrumental birth rates.
keyPoints: Automated bolus lowered the chance of breakthrough pain needing anaesthetist help compared with continuous infusion (moderate certainty).
It also used less local anaesthetic per hour (moderate certainty).
No clear difference in caesarean or instrumental delivery, or in how long epidural analgesia lasted (moderate certainty).
Maternal satisfaction may be higher with automated bolus, and no study found a difference in Apgar scores.

items.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis to examine intrapartum interventions, and maternal and neonatal outcomes following immersion in water during labour and waterbirth
items.summary: This review pooled 36 studies (over 157,000 women) comparing labour or birth in a birthing pool with usual care without water. It looked mainly at healthy women with straightforward pregnancies. Water immersion was linked to less pain, less use of epidurals and injected opioid pain relief, fewer episiotomies, less postpartum haemorrhage, and higher maternal satisfaction. Waterbirth was linked to a slightly higher chance of the umbilical cord snapping (cord avulsion), though this stayed rare, and no other differences in newborn outcomes were found.
keyPoints: Water immersion was linked to lower use of epidurals and injected opioids, and to lower reported maternal pain.
Women who used water had fewer episiotomies, more intact perineums and less postpartum haemorrhage.
Maternal satisfaction was higher with water immersion.
Cord avulsion was more common with waterbirth (4.3 vs 1.3 per 1000), but the absolute risk stayed low, and no other newborn differences were found.

items.title: Causes and outcomes in studies of fear of childbirth: A systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 21 studies on why some women fear childbirth and what follows from it. Stress, anxiety, depression and low social support were linked to more fear during pregnancy. Fear was also linked to longer labours, use of epidural pain relief and obstetric complications. The studies defined fear differently, so results were hard to combine, and these were observational studies that show links, not proof of cause.
keyPoints: Stress, anxiety, depression and lack of social support were linked to fear of childbirth in pregnancy.
Reported outcomes included needing psychiatric care, traumatic stress symptoms, longer labour, epidural use and obstetric complications.
First-time and previous mothers had similar levels of fear but for different reasons.
In women who had given birth before, the strongest predictor of fear was a previous negative or operative birth.

items.title: Perceptions and experiences of labour companionship: a qualitative evidence synthesis
items.summary: This review pulled together 51 studies on what labour companionship is like for women, partners, doulas and health workers. Companions helped by giving information, speaking up for the woman, offering hands-on help such as massage and encouraging movement, and giving emotional support. Women said having a compassionate, trustworthy companion helped them have a positive birth experience, while those without one could see their birth as more negative. The authors had high or moderate confidence in many findings, and low confidence in others, such as views about male partners.
keyPoints: Companions gave four kinds of support: information (including help with non-drug pain relief), advocacy, practical help like massage and hand-holding, and emotional support.
Women wanted a companion who was compassionate and trustworthy; having one helped them feel in control and confident and supported a positive birth experience.
Male partners often felt their presence helped, though some felt anxious seeing labour pain or felt left out of the care team (low confidence).
Barriers to companionship included lack of space and privacy, providers not recognising the benefits, and gaps between policy and practice.

items.title: Naloxone for opioid-exposed newborn infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether giving naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid effects, helps newborns who may have been exposed to opioid pain relief given to their mothers during labour. It found nine small trials with 316 babies in total. There was some evidence that naloxone improves how well babies breathe in the first hours, but the trials did not look at neonatal unit stays or breastfeeding. The authors concluded the evidence is not strong enough to say whether naloxone gives important benefits.
keyPoints: Nine trials (316 babies) compared naloxone with placebo or no drug in newborns exposed to opioid pain relief before delivery.
There is some evidence that naloxone increases alveolar ventilation (how much fresh air reaches the lungs).
The trials did not measure neonatal unit admission or breastfeeding success, and none recruited babies who were clearly struggling to breathe or respond.
The authors say the evidence is insufficient and, given safety concerns, suggest naloxone use may be best limited to further clinical trials.

items.title: Position in the second stage of labour for women with epidural anaesthesia
items.summary: This review pooled five trials (879 women) comparing upright positions with lying-down positions during the pushing stage of labour for women who had an epidural. It found no clear difference in the chance of a caesarean or instrumental (forceps or vacuum) birth, or in how long pushing lasted. The evidence was mostly very low quality and the results were uncertain, so important differences have not been ruled out. The authors say women with an epidural should be encouraged to use whatever position feels comfortable.
keyPoints: No clear difference was found between upright and lying-down positions in operative birth (caesarean or instrumental), based on moderate-quality evidence.
No clear differences were found for length of the second stage, tearing needing stitches, or baby outcomes, but the evidence was mostly very low quality.
There were not enough data to reach firm conclusions, and more and larger studies are needed.
The authors say women with an epidural should be encouraged to use whatever position they find comfortable in the second stage of labour.

items.title: Practice Bulletin No. 177 Summary: Obstetric Analgesia and Anesthesia
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on pain relief during labour and anaesthesia for common procedures around delivery. It says labour is severely painful for many women and that a woman's request for pain relief is, by itself, a good enough medical reason to provide it when there is no medical reason against it. It also says access to epidural pain relief should not depend on a woman's health insurance or ability to pay.
keyPoints: Maternal request is a sufficient medical reason for pain relief in labour when there is no medical contraindication.
A woman who asks for an epidural should not be denied it because of her health insurance status.
Anaesthesia services should be available for labour pain relief and surgical anaesthesia in all hospitals that offer maternity care.
Non-drug options such as massage, water immersion, acupuncture, relaxation and hypnotherapy are not covered but may help as add-ons or alternatives.

items.title: Patient-controlled analgesia with remifentanil versus alternative parenteral methods for pain management in labour
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at remifentanil, a short-acting opioid that women can give themselves through a drip during labour (patient-controlled analgesia). It pooled 20 trials with 3569 women, comparing it with other opioid injections and with epidurals. Remifentanil worked better than other opioid injections but not as well as an epidural. Most of the evidence is low or very low quality, and information on safety for mothers and babies is limited.
keyPoints: Women using remifentanil had stronger pain relief at one hour than with other opioids given by injection or drip, but more pain and less satisfaction than with an epidural.
Women using remifentanil were much more likely to need extra pain relief than women with an epidural, but less likely than women given other opioid injections.
The chance of caesarean birth was no different between remifentanil and epidural or other injected opioids; a possible increase versus another patient-controlled opioid was very uncertain.
Safety data for mothers (breathing problems) and babies (Apgar scores) were limited, so no firm conclusions could be drawn.

items.title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Acetaminophen Use During Pregnancy and the Risk of Neurodevelopmental Disorders in Childhood
items.source: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
items.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
items.summary: This review pooled results from 16 studies to see whether taking paracetamol (acetaminophen) in pregnancy is linked to neurodevelopmental conditions in children. It found a small increased risk of ADHD, but the authors say this may be partly explained by other factors that were not measured or by reporting errors. No link was found with autism or other conditions. The authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Paracetamol use in pregnancy was linked to a small increase in ADHD risk (pooled odds ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.08-1.27).
The link got weaker in extra checks, and the authors say it may be partly due to unmeasured factors.
No significant link was found with autism when based on a doctor's diagnosis (OR 1.10, 95% CI 0.98-1.24).
No significant increase in risk was seen for other neurodevelopmental conditions, and the authors call for further, more robust studies.

items.title: Association between in utero exposure to acetaminophen and external genital tract malformations in boys and girls: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 10 observational studies to see whether taking acetaminophen (paracetamol) in pregnancy is linked to birth differences in the external genitals of boys or girls. For boys, they found no link to undescended testicles or hypospadias, and no difference in a measure called anogenital distance. For girls, there was not enough data to draw any conclusion. The evidence was low to very low certainty, because the studies did not fully account for other factors that could affect results.
keyPoints: No significant link was found between acetaminophen in pregnancy and undescended testicles (cryptorchidism) or hypospadias in boys.
No meta-analysis was possible for girls because there was too little data.
All included studies had a serious or critical risk of bias, and the certainty of the evidence was low to very low.
The authors note that acetaminophen remains an important medicine, and that going without pain or fever treatment in pregnancy may harm the developing baby.

items.title: Prenatal exposure to paracetamol and risk of autism spectrum disorder: systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies
items.source: Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia E Obstetricia
items.journal: Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia E Obstetricia
items.summary: This review pooled eight observational studies covering over 2.5 million people to look at whether paracetamol (acetaminophen) taken in pregnancy is linked to autism in children. It found a modest link: about an 18% higher chance of an autism diagnosis in exposed children, but no clear link for autism symptoms. The studies had some concerns about bias and family-related factors that could affect results, so the link does not show that paracetamol causes autism. The authors suggest pregnant women and their care teams talk through the benefits and risks of treating pain and fever.
keyPoints: Pooled results showed an 18% higher risk of an autism diagnosis in children exposed to paracetamol before birth.
The increase for autism symptoms was not statistically significant.
Included studies had 'some concerns' to 'high' risk of bias, and family-related confounding was identified.
The authors call for careful benefit-risk discussions with expectant mothers about managing pain and fever.

items.title: Medication use during pregnancy and the risk of gastroschisis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies
items.summary: This review pooled 18 observational studies covering about 750,000 pregnancies to see whether medicines taken in pregnancy are linked to gastroschisis, a birth defect where a baby's bowel develops outside the belly. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) was not linked to gastroschisis. Aspirin, ibuprofen, decongestants such as pseudoephedrine, and oral contraceptives were linked to a higher risk, but only in some subgroups of studies, so the authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: No association was found between paracetamol use in pregnancy and gastroschisis (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.96-1.41).
First-trimester use of aspirin, ibuprofen, pseudoephedrine/phenylpropanolamine and oral contraceptives was associated with a higher risk of gastroschisis.
These links were significant only in certain subgroups, defined by location, adjustment variables and type of control group.
The authors call for more research to confirm these medicines as risk factors and to assess their safety in pregnancy.

items.title: Non-prescribed drug use and predictors among pregnant women in Ethiopia: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 11 studies of 4,492 pregnant women in Ethiopia to see how often they take medicines without a prescription. About 3 in 10 women (30%) did so, and the rate differed by region. Paracetamol was the most common non-prescribed medicine, taken by about 34% of those who used any. The study measured how common this is, not whether the medicines caused harm.
keyPoints: About 30% of pregnant women in Ethiopia used non-prescribed medicines, ranging from about 10% in Tigray to about 37% in Amhara.
Paracetamol was the most frequently used non-prescribed medicine (34%), followed by amoxicillin (15%), aspirin (4%), metronidazole (3%) and ciprofloxacin (3%).
Past self-medication, illness during pregnancy and marital status were linked to taking non-prescribed medicines.
The authors call for more awareness of possible side effects of non-prescribed medicines in pregnancy.

items.title: Effect of Acetaminophen use during pregnancy on adverse pregnancy outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled six studies (four cohort, two case-control) to see whether taking acetaminophen (paracetamol) in pregnancy is linked to preterm birth, low birth weight or babies being small for their gestational age. It found no increased risk of preterm birth, and lower risks of low birth weight and small-for-gestational-age babies in those who took it. The authors conclude it does not appear to raise the risk of these outcomes, but the studies lacked information on dose and how often it was taken.
keyPoints: No increased risk of preterm birth was found (RR 0.97; 95% CI 0.59-1.58).
Acetaminophen use was linked to lower risks of low birth weight (RR 0.65) and small-for-gestational-age babies (RR 0.69).
Use in the third trimester showed no significant effect on these outcomes.
There is little information on the dose and how often acetaminophen was used.

items.title: Long-Term Safety of Prenatal and Neonatal Exposure to Paracetamol: A Systematic Review
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review looked at 30 studies on whether paracetamol (acetaminophen) taken during pregnancy, or given to newborns, is linked to later health problems in children. Studies on use during pregnancy reported possible links with problems in brain development, allergic conditions such as asthma and eczema, and reproductive outcomes. Only one study found a possible link with newborn use. The authors say the evidence is limited and that better-quality data are urgently needed.
keyPoints: 30 studies were included; 27 looked at use during pregnancy, 2 at use in newborns and 1 at both.
Studies of use in pregnancy reported possible links with later brain development, allergic (atopic) and reproductive problems.
Only one study found a possible link between newborn paracetamol and long-term problems.
The authors describe the evidence as limited and call for stronger research on long-term safety.

items.title: Paracetamol overdose in the newborn and infant: a life-threatening event
items.summary: This review looked at published reports of newborns and infants who were given too much paracetamol (acetaminophen). In some cases the baby was exposed before birth after the mother took an overdose, and in others the cause was a dosing mistake. A single overdose with blood levels under a set safety limit carried a low risk of serious liver damage, but repeated high doses need careful handling. The antidote N-acetylcysteine reduces liver harm. The review is based on case reports, not large trials.
keyPoints: Paracetamol is the only drug recommended for fever in newborns, and at recommended doses it has not been linked to liver injury in neonates.
Newborn poisoning came from a mother's overdose passing across the placenta in some cases, and from medication errors in others.
Babies with a single overdose and blood levels below the Rumack-Matthew nomogram limits are at low risk of serious liver damage; those with more than one high dose need cautious management.
N-acetylcysteine is the treatment of choice for paracetamol poisoning and is given by weight-based dosing tables.

items.title: Acetaminophen use during pregnancy and the risk of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: A causal association or bias?
items.summary: This review pooled seven observational studies on paracetamol (acetaminophen) use in pregnancy and ADHD in children. Taken at face value, the studies linked paracetamol use to a modestly higher chance of ADHD. When the authors tested for hidden factors such as parental ADHD, the link got smaller in most studies. They conclude the association may be due to unmeasured confounding, and that a causal link cannot be confirmed.
keyPoints: Pooled adjusted results from seven observational studies showed a risk ratio of 1.35 for ADHD with paracetamol use in pregnancy.
Bias analysis lowered the estimated risk in five of the seven studies, suggesting parental ADHD could explain part of the link.
The authors say the association may be due to unmeasured confounding.
Their ability to conclude that paracetamol causes ADHD is limited.

items.title: Association of maternal prenatal acetaminophen use with the risk of attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder in offspring: A meta-analysis
items.source: Australian and New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry
items.journal: Australian and New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry
items.summary: This review pooled eight cohort studies covering about 245,000 participants to look at paracetamol (acetaminophen) use in pregnancy and ADHD in children. It found an association: children whose mothers used it in pregnancy had a somewhat higher risk of ADHD. The link looked stronger with use in the third trimester and with longer use, about 28 days or more. Because the studies only observed groups of people, the abstract describes an association rather than proof of cause.
keyPoints: Pooled results from eight cohort studies showed a 25% higher relative risk of ADHD in children exposed to paracetamol before birth.
Use in the third trimester was linked to a 26% higher relative risk.
Using paracetamol for 28 or more days in pregnancy was linked to a 63% higher relative risk.
The authors conclude there is an association, and that timing and duration of use may matter.

items.title: Prenatal paracetamol use and asthma in childhood: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 13 studies, covering over one million people, to see whether taking paracetamol (acetaminophen) during pregnancy is linked to asthma in children. It found a small but statistically significant link: children whose mothers took paracetamol in pregnancy were somewhat more likely to have asthma. The link appeared for use in the first trimester and in the second and third trimesters. The review shows an association only, and the abstract does not say whether paracetamol itself causes asthma.
keyPoints: Prenatal paracetamol use was linked to a higher risk of childhood asthma (OR 1.19, 95% CI 1.12-1.27) across 13 studies.
Use in the first trimester was linked to increased asthma risk (OR 1.21, 95% CI 1.14-1.28).
Use in the second and third trimesters was also linked to increased asthma risk (OR 1.13, 95% CI 1.04-1.23).
The authors concluded that prenatal paracetamol exposure was significantly associated with increased child asthma risk.

items.title: Analgesia use during pregnancy and risk of cryptorchidism: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined 10 earlier studies to see whether pain relief medicines (such as paracetamol) taken in pregnancy are linked to cryptorchidism, where a baby boy's testicle has not moved down into the scrotum. They found only weak evidence of a small link, and the result was borderline. The authors say any strong link seems unlikely, but more detailed research is needed.
keyPoints: Pooled results from 10 studies showed only weak evidence of an association between any pain relief use in pregnancy and cryptorchidism (odds ratio 1.11, 95% CI 1.00-1.23).
Evidence for effects of how long or when in pregnancy the medicine was used was also weak, and there was too little data to combine results for these questions.
The authors conclude that analgesia use in pregnancy is not strongly linked to cryptorchidism but that further detailed research is needed.
Limitations include mothers' self-reported use possibly not matching real exposure, grouping different medicines together, and most studies being from Europe or the USA.

items.title: Paracetamol exposure in pregnancy and early childhood and development of childhood asthma: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 11 observational studies to see whether paracetamol use in pregnancy or infancy is linked to asthma in children aged 5 and older. Using paracetamol in the first trimester was linked to somewhat higher odds of childhood asthma, but results varied a lot between studies and only one accounted for the mother's respiratory infections. In infancy, the link got weaker and was no longer clear once respiratory infections were taken into account. The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to change guidelines on early-life paracetamol use.
keyPoints: First-trimester paracetamol use was linked to higher odds of childhood asthma (pooled odds ratio 1.39, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.91), but results differed a lot between studies.
Only one of the five pregnancy studies adjusted for the mother's respiratory tract infections, which could be an alternative explanation.
In infancy, more days of paracetamol use was linked to asthma, but the link shrank and became unclear after adjusting for respiratory infections.
The authors found insufficient evidence to warrant changing current guidelines on early-life paracetamol exposure.

items.title: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) for patent ductus arteriosus in preterm or low-birth-weight infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether paracetamol can help close a patent ductus arteriosus (a blood vessel near the heart that stays open) in babies born early. Only two small trials were found, covering 250 premature babies, and both compared oral paracetamol with oral ibuprofen. Paracetamol may work about as well as ibuprofen at closing the vessel, but the quality of the evidence was low to moderate. The authors say longer-term follow-up of these babies is needed before any recommendations can be made, partly because of reports linking paracetamol in pregnancy to autism and of brain effects in mice.
keyPoints: Oral paracetamol appeared to close a patent ductus arteriosus about as well as oral ibuprofen in preterm babies.
Babies given paracetamol needed supplemental oxygen for fewer days and had less high bilirubin (jaundice) in the studies where this was measured.
Evidence quality was low for closure of the vessel and moderate for other outcomes, and only two trials were included.
The authors say trials must follow babies to at least 18 to 24 months before paracetamol can be recommended for newborns.

items.title: Recurrent pregnancy loss: a male crucial factor-A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to look at the male side of recurrent pregnancy loss (two or more failed pregnancies). Men whose partners had repeated losses had more sperm DNA damage and some weaker semen results than men in control groups. The man's age, body mass index, smoking and alcohol intake were not linked to sperm DNA damage in these studies. The authors say the findings show an association, not proof of cause.
keyPoints: Sperm DNA fragmentation was higher in partners of women with recurrent pregnancy loss than in controls.
Semen volume, total sperm number, sperm movement and normal sperm shape were lower in the recurrent loss group.
Age, body mass index, smoking and alcohol intake were not associated with sperm DNA fragmentation.
The authors suggest gynecologists and urologists should talk to each other when investigating recurrent loss.

items.title: The Relationship Between Paternal Smoking and Overweight/Obesity with Childhood Overweight/Obesity: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at whether a father's smoking and weight during pregnancy and the baby's first year are linked to the child being overweight or obese up to age 12. Fathers with overweight or obesity were consistently linked to a higher risk of childhood overweight or obesity. Findings on fathers' smoking were less consistent: most studies found a higher risk, but one found no link. These are associations, so they do not prove that the father's habits caused the child's weight.
keyPoints: Paternal overweight or obesity was consistently associated with a higher risk of childhood overweight or obesity.
Five of six studies found that paternal smoking during pregnancy may be linked to higher child overweight or obesity risk, while one found no association.
Evidence on paternal smoking was less consistent than evidence on paternal weight.
The authors suggest overweight and obesity patterns pass across generations and may need wider changes that address social and economic causes.

items.title: Epidemiological characteristics and risk factors of reproductive dysfunction in male infertility: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This study combined results from 28 articles, covering over 23,000 infertile men and about 41,000 healthy men, to look for factors linked to male reproductive problems such as poor semen quality and sexual dysfunction. Smoking and alcohol use were both linked to a higher chance of these problems, along with older age, higher body weight, high blood pressure, diabetes, depression and anxiety. These are links found in observational data, and results varied a lot between the studies combined.
keyPoints: Smoking was linked to a higher likelihood of male reproductive dysfunction (odds ratio 1.33).
Alcohol use was also linked to a higher likelihood (odds ratio 1.36), though the range of possible values was wide.
Older age, higher BMI and obesity were associated with male reproductive dysfunction.
Hypertension, diabetes, depression and anxiety were also linked to male reproductive dysfunction.

items.title: Parental Smoking and the Risk of Birth Defects in Offspring in China: A Systematic Review and meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined 62 studies from China, covering over 8.9 million births, to look at parents' smoking and birth defects in babies. Babies whose mothers smoked, or were exposed to smoke while pregnant, had a higher chance of birth defects. A father's smoking was also linked to a higher chance, though the link was smaller. The authors conclude that parents should be encouraged to quit smoking around pregnancy.
keyPoints: Maternal active smoking was linked to roughly double the odds of birth defects (OR 2.19).
Maternal passive (secondhand) smoke exposure was linked to higher odds too (OR 2.59).
Paternal smoking was linked to higher odds of birth defects (OR 1.47).
Congenital heart disease risk was higher with both paternal and maternal active smoking.

items.title: Addiction and human male fertility: A systematic review and a critical appraisal
items.summary: This review pulled together 65 studies on how addiction to different substances affects male fertility. The substances covered were opioids, cannabis, alcohol, cocaine, anabolic steroids, tobacco and caffeine. Most studies found a negative effect on male fertility, but the strength of the evidence varied. The authors say better-designed future studies are needed to pin down the effect of each specific substance.
keyPoints: Most of the 65 studies reviewed found that the substances studied had a negative impact on male fertility.
Substances covered were opioids and cannabis, alcohol, cocaine, anabolic steroids, tobacco and caffeine.
The level of evidence varied between studies and substances.
The authors concluded that addiction harms male fertility and call for more carefully designed future studies.

items.title: Maternal smoking during pregnancy and the risk of congenital urogenital malformations: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 52 studies to see whether smoking during pregnancy is linked to birth defects of the urinary and genital organs. Babies born to mothers who smoked had a somewhat higher chance of these conditions, including undescended testes, hypospadias and kidney malformations. Paternal smoking during the mother's pregnancy was also linked to a higher risk. The authors suggest that quitting tobacco may help lower this risk.
keyPoints: Maternal smoking in pregnancy was linked to a higher risk of urogenital birth defects overall (odds ratio 1.13).
Risks were also higher for cryptorchidism (undescended testes), hypospadias and kidney malformations.
Paternal smoking during the mother's pregnancy was also significantly associated with these defects (odds ratio 1.26).
The link with smoking more than 10 cigarettes a day was not statistically significant.

items.title: The association between cannabis use and testicular function in men: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine studies of men to see whether using cannabis is linked to poorer sperm quality or changes in reproductive hormones. Men who used cannabis had more sperm problems in the raw numbers, but after combining the studies the difference was not statistically clear. The authors say the evidence does not point to a clinically important link, but they cannot rule out an effect because the studies were few and varied.
keyPoints: Nine studies were pooled, covering 4014 men with semen data and 4787 with hormone data.
About 45% of cannabis users had impaired semen parameters versus about 25% of non-users, but the pooled risk difference was not statistically significant.
Testosterone and LH levels did not differ clearly between users and non-users; FSH was slightly lower in users.
The authors conclude there is no evidence of a clinically significant link, but better-designed studies are needed.

items.title: Paternal Smoking Before Conception and During Pregnancy Is Associated With an Increased Risk of Childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of 17 Case-Control Studies
items.summary: This review pooled results from 17 case-control studies to look at whether a father's smoking is linked to childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), a type of blood cancer. Children whose fathers smoked before conception or during the pregnancy had a somewhat higher risk of ALL. The more fathers smoked, the higher the risk tended to be. These studies can show a link but not prove cause, so the authors say the finding needs confirming in prospective studies.
keyPoints: Paternal smoking before conception was linked to a 15% higher risk of childhood ALL (risk ratio 1.15).
Paternal smoking during pregnancy was linked to a 20% higher risk (risk ratio 1.20).
Heavier smoking was associated with higher risk in the dose-response analysis.
The evidence comes from observational studies and needs confirmation in prospective studies.

items.title: Tobacco smoking and semen quality in infertile males: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 studies of 10,823 men attending infertility clinics, about half of them smokers, to see how tobacco smoking relates to semen quality. Smokers were more likely to have a low sperm count and had more sperm with an abnormal shape (head, neck and tail). Smoking was not linked to changes in sperm motility, semen pH or reproductive hormone levels in these men.
keyPoints: Low sperm count (oligozoospermia) was more common in smokers than non-smokers (risk ratio 1.29).
Smokers had more sperm with shape defects in the head, neck and tail.
Sperm motility, semen pH and reproductive hormones were not clearly affected by smoking.
The findings come from men who were already attending infertility clinics.

items.title: The relationship between cannabis and male infertility, sexual health, and neoplasm: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 91 studies on how cannabis (marijuana) affects men's fertility, sexual health and cancers of the urinary and reproductive organs. Using sperm measures as a stand-in for fertility, the authors concluded that cannabis compounds likely have a harmful, inhibiting effect on male fertility. Findings on sexual function and cancer were mixed, and the authors say long-term studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Cannabis compounds likely have an inhibiting effect on male fertility, judged by semen measures.
Evidence on sexual function is mixed: cannabis may make sex feel better but may contribute to erectile dysfunction at higher doses.
Cannabis use appears to be an independent risk factor for testicular cancer, while bladder cancer data conflict and prostate cancer data suggest possible anti-cancer effects.
The authors call for long-term prospective studies to understand these effects better.

items.title: Tobacco smoke exposure and the risk of childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia and acute myeloid leukemia: A meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 19 studies from 9 countries to see whether tobacco smoke exposure is linked to childhood leukemia (ALL and AML). Mothers' smoking before, during or after pregnancy was not linked to either type. A father's smoking was linked to a higher risk of childhood ALL, and the risk was higher the more he smoked.
keyPoints: Maternal smoking before, during or after pregnancy was not associated with childhood ALL or AML.
Paternal smoking was linked to a significantly higher risk of childhood ALL (OR 1.15), but not clearly to AML when grouped as smoker versus non-smoker.
Heavier paternal smoking (more than 10 cigarettes a day) was linked to higher risk of childhood ALL.
Paternal daily cigarette consumption was also related to AML (OR 1.242).

items.title: Prenatal exposure to maternal smoking during pregnancy and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in offspring: A meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined 27 studies with over 3 million people to look at smoking during pregnancy and ADHD in children. Smoking during pregnancy was linked to a higher chance of ADHD in the child, even after accounting for parents' mental health history and family income. Stopping smoking before pregnancy was not linked to ADHD. Results on passive smoke from a partner's smoking were mixed, so no clear conclusion could be drawn.
keyPoints: Smoking during pregnancy was linked to childhood ADHD after adjusting for parental psychiatric history and socioeconomic status.
Stopping smoking during the first trimester was still associated with childhood ADHD.
Stopping smoking before pregnancy was not significantly linked to childhood ADHD, and quitting before conceiving is strongly recommended for women who smoke.
Results on passive smoking from a partner's smoking during pregnancy were inconsistent, and the risk varied across world regions.

items.title: Environmental tobacco smoke exposure and risk of habitual snoring in children: a meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health
items.journal: Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health
items.summary: This review pooled 24 studies with nearly 88,000 children to look at whether breathing in other people's tobacco smoke is linked to habitual snoring in children. Children exposed to smoke at home were more likely to snore regularly, and the link was strongest for smoke exposure during pregnancy and for a mother's smoking. The studies were observational, so they show a link rather than proving cause.
keyPoints: Children exposed to household smoking had about 46% higher odds of habitual snoring than unexposed children.
The link was stronger for maternal smoking (OR 1.87) and smoke exposure during pregnancy (OR 1.95) than for paternal smoking (OR 1.45).
Each extra cigarette per day smoked by people living with the child was linked to about a 2.1% higher risk of habitual snoring.
The findings come from observational studies, which can show an association but not prove cause.

items.title: The Effect of Nutrients and Dietary Supplements on Sperm Quality Parameters: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials that tested whether nutrients and dietary supplements change sperm quality in men. Selenium, zinc, omega-3 fatty acids, coenzyme Q10 and carnitines improved some measures, such as sperm concentration, movement and shape. The authors say the results should be read cautiously because the studies were small and differed a lot from one another.
keyPoints: Selenium, zinc, omega-3 fatty acids and coenzyme Q10 increased sperm concentration.
Selenium, zinc, omega-3, coenzyme Q10 and carnitines improved how well sperm move (total motility).
Selenium, omega-3, coenzyme Q10 and carnitine supplements improved sperm shape (morphology).
Results need careful interpretation because the studies were small and varied considerably.

items.title: Evidence for decreasing sperm count in African population from 1965 to 2015
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies of sperm concentration in African men between 1965 and 2015. It found that average sperm concentration fell over time, by about 72.6% across the 50 years. The current average is close to the WHO lower cut-off value for normal sperm concentration. The authors list infections, pesticides, heavy metals, tobacco and alcohol as likely contributing factors, but the abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Average sperm concentration in African men fell by about 72.6% between 1965 and 2015.
The latest average (about 20.38 million per ml) is close to the WHO cut-off of 15 million per ml.
Regular tobacco and alcohol use are named as likely contributing factors, alongside infections, pesticides and heavy metals.
The review is based on 14 studies, and the abstract does not state how certain the evidence is.

items.title: Fathers' Role in Alcohol-Exposed Pregnancies: Systematic Review of Human Studies
items.summary: This review pulled together 11 studies (over 41,000 people) to look at how a father's drinking before conception and during his partner's pregnancy relates to health. The studies found that a father's alcohol use was linked to the mother's drinking and health in pregnancy, as well as to outcomes for the baby before and after birth. The authors say paternal health care around alcohol should get more attention in reproductive and pregnancy policy.
keyPoints: Paternal alcohol use before conception or during pregnancy was linked to the mother's health and her drinking during pregnancy.
Paternal alcohol use was also linked to fetal and infant health outcomes.
The review combined 11 human studies with a total of 41,062 participants.
The authors conclude that preconception health care for fathers about alcohol is an important future focus.

items.title: Cigarette Smoking and Semen Quality: A New Meta-analysis Examining the Effect of the 2010 World Health Organization Laboratory Methods for the Examination of Human Semen
items.summary: This review pooled results from 20 studies of 5,865 men to see whether cigarette smoking affects semen quality. Men who smoked had lower sperm counts, less sperm movement (motility) and a smaller share of normally shaped sperm. The effects were bigger in men who were already infertile and in moderate or heavy smokers than in light smokers. The newer 2010 WHO lab methods changed the picture very little.
keyPoints: Smoking was linked to lower sperm count, motility and normal sperm shape.
Effects were larger in infertile men and in moderate or heavy smokers than in mild smokers.
Using the 2010 WHO semen-testing methods did not much change the size of the effects, apart from sperm shape where the effect was smaller.
The authors conclude smoking has an overall negative effect on semen quality.

items.title: Parental Tobacco Smoking and Acute Myeloid Leukemia: The Childhood Leukemia International Consortium
items.summary: Researchers pooled data from 12 studies, including 1,330 children with acute myeloid leukemia (a rare childhood blood cancer) and 13,169 comparison children, to look at parents' smoking. Overall, a mother's smoking before, during or after pregnancy was not linked to the disease, though a higher risk was seen in Hispanic children. A father's smoking was linked to a modestly higher risk, with larger increases for heavy smokers. The authors note that differences between ethnic groups and possible biases in the studies need more investigation.
keyPoints: Maternal smoking before, during or after pregnancy was not linked to childhood acute myeloid leukemia overall.
Smoking during pregnancy was linked to higher risk in Hispanic children only (odds ratio 2.08), not in other ethnic groups.
Paternal smoking was linked to a roughly 1.2- to 1.3-fold higher risk, with higher risks for heavy smokers.
The link with paternal smoking differed by the specific type of leukemia.

items.title: Prevalence of polycystic ovary syndrome: a global and regional systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 92 studies with over 157,000 participants to estimate how common polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is around the world. About 12 in 100 adult women had PCOS when the Rotterdam criteria were used, but the figure changed depending on which diagnostic criteria were applied. Rates were highest in the Eastern Mediterranean and South-East Asian regions. The certainty of the evidence was low to very low, and there was no data from Africa.
keyPoints: Global PCOS prevalence among adult women was 12.1% using Rotterdam criteria, 7.9% using the original NIH criteria, 12.7% using AE-PCOS criteria, and 7.8% by self-report.

By region (Rotterdam criteria), prevalence was highest in the Eastern Mediterranean (15.1%) and South-East Asia (14.3%), and lower in Europe (11.7%), the Americas (10.5%) and the Western Pacific (9.1%).
Including adolescents gave slightly lower figures, for example 11.4% by Rotterdam criteria.
Studies used inconsistent diagnostic criteria, and the authors stress the need for early, accurate diagnosis.

items.title: GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment in women with polycystic ovary syndrome-a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 11 randomised trials of GLP-1 receptor agonist medicines in women with PCOS. When added to other treatment, these medicines may lead to a small drop in body mass index (BMI) in the short term. The evidence on blood sugar, insulin, excess hair growth, period regularity, mood and quality of life is too limited or low in quality to draw conclusions.
keyPoints: GLP-1 receptor agonists were linked to modest short-term weight loss in women with PCOS and overweight or obesity (BMI about 1.4 points lower, low certainty).
No difference was seen in LDL cholesterol or triglycerides (low certainty).
Evidence was too limited to say whether they help with glucose, insulin, hirsutism or menstrual regularity.
No studies looked at quality of life, mental health or cost-effectiveness.

items.title: Impact of lifestyle interventions on reproductive and psychological outcomes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 24 studies (1,373 women) testing whether diet, exercise and behaviour changes help women with PCOS. Eating changes, alone or with exercise, were linked to about 5% weight loss, more regular periods, higher pregnancy rates and lower testosterone. Structured exercise programmes also improved ovulation and period regularity. The authors conclude that combined lifestyle approaches can help reproductive health and well-being, but longer-term studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Diet changes, alone or with exercise, were linked to about 5% weight loss, more regular periods, higher pregnancy rates and lower testosterone.
A 20-week exercise programme improved ovulation rates by 49.1% and lowered testosterone and free androgen index.
Structured exercise increased menstrual regularity by 60% and reduced body mass index.
The authors say long-term studies and personalised approaches are needed, as PCOS varies a lot between women.

items.title: The Role of Lifestyle Interventions in PCOS Management: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This systematic review looked at how lifestyle changes affect women with PCOS. It covered eating patterns, exercise and behavioural support. The review reports that these changes improved insulin sensitivity, hormone balance and body measures, and may lower long-term risks of metabolic and heart disease. The abstract does not rate the quality of the evidence.
keyPoints: Several eating patterns, including low glycemic index, Mediterranean, high-fibre and anti-inflammatory diets, improved insulin sensitivity and hormonal balance.
Aerobic and resistance exercise improved insulin sensitivity, helped weight loss and improved metabolic and reproductive outcomes.
Behavioural and education programmes can improve awareness, adherence to treatment and help with the mental health side of PCOS.
Lifestyle changes may also reduce long-term risks of metabolic and cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Society for Endocrinology Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation of Androgen Excess in Women
items.summary: This guideline from the Society for Endocrinology covers how doctors should investigate women who have high levels of androgens (male-type hormones such as testosterone). Most cases are linked to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), but very high levels can sometimes point to other causes, such as growth in the adrenal glands or ovaries, genetic conditions or severe insulin resistance. The guideline gives doctors a step-by-step approach to checking for these causes, using the best available evidence.
keyPoints: Androgen excess is common in women and is linked to PCOS in most cases.
Severe androgen excess is less common and may signal other causes, including adrenal or ovarian tumours, genetic disorders or severe insulin resistance.
The guideline makes recommendations on clinical assessment, blood tests, dynamic testing and imaging.
It was written by specialists in several fields and includes a patient perspective.

items.title: Inositol for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis to Inform the 2023 Update of the International Evidence-based PCOS Guidelines
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This review pooled 30 trials (over 2,000 women) to see whether inositol, a supplement that may help the body respond to insulin, helps with PCOS. It found some possible benefits for certain blood sugar and metabolic measures, and possibly for ovulation with D-chiro-inositol, but little or no effect on other outcomes. Overall the authors say the evidence is limited and inconclusive.
keyPoints: Myo-inositol or D-chiro-inositol may help some metabolic measures, and D-chiro-inositol may help ovulation, but inositol may have no effect on other outcomes.
Metformin may improve waist-hip ratio and hirsutism more than inositol, with likely no difference in reproductive outcomes.
Myo-inositol likely causes fewer stomach and gut side effects than metformin, and these are usually mild and short-lived.
The evidence is limited and inconclusive, so decisions about inositol should weigh the uncertainty alongside personal values and preferences.

items.title: Association between polycystic ovarian syndrome and incompetent uterine cervix: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.journal: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.summary: This review pooled three observational studies covering about 3,800 pregnant women with PCOS and about 9,400 without. Cervical incompetence (a cervix that opens too early in pregnancy) was found in 3.7% of women with PCOS compared with 0.6% of women without PCOS. The authors say this suggests a higher risk in pregnancies with PCOS. Only three studies were included, and their results varied a lot, so the exact size of the risk is uncertain.
keyPoints: Cervical incompetence occurred in 3.7% of pregnant women with PCOS versus 0.6% of those without PCOS.
The pooled risk ratio was 5.3, with a wide range of uncertainty (1.9 to 14.6).
The results differed a lot between the three studies (heterogeneity 89%).
The authors call for guidelines on spotting cervical incompetence early in pregnant women with PCOS to help prevent problems linked to preterm labour.

items.title: Global prevalence of polycystic ovary syndrome in women worldwide: a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 35 studies covering more than 12 million people to estimate how common polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is worldwide. About 9 in 100 women were found to have PCOS. The number changed depending on which diagnostic criteria were used, and the authors noted the condition appeared especially common in Africa.
keyPoints: Worldwide, about 9.2% of women had PCOS (range 6.8-12.5%).
The estimate was 5.5% using NIH criteria, 11.5% using Rotterdam criteria and 7.1% using AES criteria.
In studies where women reported their own diagnosis, prevalence was about 11%.
The authors say PCOS is common, especially in Africa, and health systems should act on timely prevention and treatment.

items.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of pregnancy outcomes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 104 studies covering over 106,000 pregnancies to compare women with and without PCOS. Women with PCOS had higher odds of miscarriage, gestational diabetes, high blood pressure in pregnancy, pre-eclampsia and caesarean birth. These higher odds remained even when women were matched for age and BMI, and when only high-quality studies were counted. The authors say PCOS status should be recorded for anyone planning pregnancy or recently pregnant, so complications can be prevented.
keyPoints: Women with PCOS had higher odds of miscarriage, gestational diabetes, gestational hypertension, pre-eclampsia and caesarean section.
The higher odds stayed significant after matching for age and BMI and when looking only at high-quality studies.
Women with PCOS were younger, had a higher BMI around conception and gained more weight in pregnancy.
The findings fed into the 2023 international PCOS guideline, which recommends recording PCOS status in all women planning or in early pregnancy.

items.title: 2023 International Evidence-Based Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Guideline Update: Insights From a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on Elevated Clinical Cardiovascular Disease in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
items.source: Journal of the American Heart Association
items.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
items.summary: This review pooled 20 studies of about 1.06 million women to see whether polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is linked to heart and blood vessel disease. Women with PCOS had higher odds of heart disease events, heart attack and stroke than women without PCOS. The link with death from heart disease was less clear. The findings informed the 2023 International PCOS Guideline, which now recommends awareness of this higher risk and a full risk assessment.
keyPoints: Women with PCOS had higher odds of combined cardiovascular disease (OR 1.68), heart attack (OR 2.50) and stroke (OR 1.71) than women without PCOS.
The link between PCOS and death from cardiovascular disease was less clear.
Some results were limited by few studies and large differences between studies.
The 2023 International Guideline now recommends awareness of increased cardiovascular risk and a comprehensive risk assessment in PCOS.

items.title: Statins for women with polycystic ovary syndrome not actively trying to conceive
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether statins (cholesterol-lowering medicines) help women with PCOS who are not trying to get pregnant. It found six small trials with 396 women in total, using simvastatin or atorvastatin for six weeks to six months. The evidence was of very low certainty, so researchers could not say whether statins improve periods, excess hair growth, acne or testosterone levels. The trials that checked for side effects reported no significant differences between groups.
keyPoints: Six small trials (396 women) tested statins in PCOS, and all main results were very low-certainty evidence.
It is uncertain whether statins improve menstrual regularity, hirsutism (excess hair), acne or testosterone levels compared with placebo, metformin or the pill.
No trials reported whether statins restore spontaneous ovulation.
Trials that recorded side effects found no significant differences between groups.

items.title: Recommendations from the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
items.summary: This is the 2023 international guideline on how polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) should be diagnosed and managed. It was built from systematic reviews, expert input and the views of women with PCOS. Key updates include using an AMH blood test as an alternative to ultrasound for diagnosis in adults, and continued emphasis on healthy lifestyle and emotional wellbeing. The evidence behind the recommendations is generally low to moderate quality, so more research is still needed.
keyPoints: AMH blood levels can now be used instead of an ultrasound to help diagnose PCOS in adults only.
PCOS is recognised as affecting more than periods and fertility, including metabolic health, heart disease risk, sleep apnea, mental health and a higher risk of problems in pregnancy.
Healthy lifestyle, emotional wellbeing and quality of life remain a focus, with awareness of weight stigma.
The guideline favours evidence-based medical treatment and cheaper, safer fertility management, with shared decision making between patients and clinicians.

items.title: Life Modifications and PCOS: Old Story But New Tales
items.summary: This systematic review looked at 10 randomized controlled trials on lifestyle changes (diet, exercise and behavior changes) for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). It reports that these changes appear to ease the metabolic problems and improve the reproductive problems linked to PCOS, particularly in women with obesity. Lifestyle changes are now widely accepted as the first treatment step. The review notes that the best diet makeup and the best type of exercise for different groups of women are not yet well studied.
keyPoints: Diet, exercise and behavior changes appear to ease metabolic problems and improve reproductive problems in women with PCOS, especially those with obesity.
Lifestyle changes are increasingly recognised as the first-line management for PCOS.
How lifestyle changes work in PCOS, the best diet makeup and the best type of exercise for specific groups are rarely reported.
The review links lifestyle changes to PCOS features such as high androgen levels, insulin resistance and obesity, and points to priorities for future research.

items.title: Chinese herbal medicine for subfertile women with polycystic ovarian syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether Chinese herbal medicine helps women with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) who are struggling to get pregnant.
