It pooled eight small trials with 609 women. The evidence was mostly very low quality, so it is not possible to say whether the herbs help or whether they are safe. None of the trials measured live birth.
keyPoints: There is not enough evidence to support using Chinese herbal medicine for subfertile women with PCOS.
None of the trials reported live birth rates, and very few reported side effects, so safety is unclear.
Adding herbal medicine to clomiphene may improve pregnancy rates, but this finding rests on limited, low certainty evidence.
The review calls for better-designed trials that measure live birth and safety.

items.title: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling for ovulation induction in women with anovulatory polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at laparoscopic ovarian drilling, a keyhole surgery, compared with fertility medicines for women with PCOS who do not ovulate and did not respond to clomiphene. It combined 38 trials with 3,326 women. Surgery may lead to slightly fewer live births than medicines, but when only the most reliable trials were checked, it was unclear whether there was any difference. Surgery probably leads to fewer multiple pregnancies. Most of the evidence was low quality.
keyPoints: Ovarian drilling may slightly lower the chance of a live birth compared with medicines alone, based on low-quality evidence; in the most reliable trials the difference was uncertain.
Ovarian drilling probably reduces the chance of a multiple pregnancy such as twins (moderate-quality evidence).
There may be little or no difference in clinical pregnancy rates, and the effect on miscarriage is uncertain.
Ovarian drilling may lower the rare risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome; evidence on drilling one ovary versus both was too weak to draw conclusions.

items.title: Lifestyle changes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 15 small trials (498 women) of lifestyle changes such as exercise, diet and behavioural support in women with PCOS, compared with little or no treatment. Lifestyle changes may lower a hormone measure called the free androgen index, and may lead to small drops in weight and body mass index. The review is unsure about effects on glucose tolerance. No trials looked at live birth, miscarriage or menstrual regularity, and most of the evidence was low quality.
keyPoints: Lifestyle intervention may improve the free androgen index (a measure of male-type hormones) in women with PCOS.
It may reduce weight by about 1.7 kg and BMI by about 0.3 kg/m2 on average.
The effect on glucose tolerance is uncertain.
No studies reported live birth, miscarriage or menstrual regularity, and most trials were at risk of bias.

items.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists versus metformin in PCOS: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from eight randomized trials comparing GLP-1 receptor agonists (a type of diabetes and weight-loss medicine) with metformin in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). GLP-1 medicines did better than metformin at improving insulin sensitivity, lowering body mass index and reducing waist size. They also caused more nausea and headache. The authors say the evidence is of moderate to low quality, so the findings are not conclusive and better research is needed.
keyPoints: Compared with metformin, GLP-1 receptor agonists improved insulin sensitivity, body mass index and abdominal girth more.
GLP-1 receptor agonists were linked to more nausea and headache than metformin.
The authors suggest GLP-1 medicines might suit women with PCOS who have obesity, especially with insulin resistance.
The evidence was of moderate to low quality, and more high-quality studies are needed.

items.title: Acupuncture for polycystic ovarian syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at eight trials with 1546 women who have PCOS and irregular or absent ovulation, testing whether acupuncture helps fertility and symptoms. Compared with sham (fake) acupuncture, real acupuncture did not clearly change live birth, pregnancy, ovulation or miscarriage rates, though the evidence was low quality. Real acupuncture probably caused more side effects than sham acupuncture; in other comparisons, reported side effects included dizziness, nausea and bruising. Overall the evidence was very low to moderate quality, and there were too few trials to say if acupuncture works for PCOS.
keyPoints: Real acupuncture did not clearly improve live birth, clinical pregnancy, ovulation or miscarriage rates compared with sham acupuncture (low-quality evidence).
Women receiving real acupuncture may have had fewer days between periods than those given sham acupuncture (low-quality evidence).
Real acupuncture probably leads to more adverse events than sham acupuncture (moderate-quality evidence); in other comparisons, reported events included dizziness, nausea and bruising under the skin.
It is uncertain whether acupuncture improves ovulation compared with relaxation or Diane-35, because the evidence was very low quality.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 194 Summary: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from ACOG, a US professional body for obstetricians and gynecologists. It looks at the best available evidence on how polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is diagnosed and treated. PCOS involves higher levels of male-type hormones, irregular or absent ovulation, and polycystic ovaries. The cause is still unknown, and treatment mostly focuses on easing symptoms. The guideline notes that PCOS can raise the risk of diabetes and heart disease over time.
keyPoints: PCOS is defined by high androgen (male-type hormone) levels, problems with ovulation, and polycystic ovaries.
The cause of PCOS is not known, and treatment is mainly based on managing symptoms.
PCOS can lead to metabolic problems, including a higher risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
Long-term treatment plans should take these metabolic risks into account.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 194: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
items.summary: This is a clinical guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). It describes PCOS as a condition with high levels of male-type hormones, irregular or absent ovulation, and polycystic ovaries. The cause is still unknown, so treatment mostly targets symptoms. The guideline also notes that PCOS can lead to longer-term health effects, which should be considered when planning treatment.
keyPoints: PCOS is defined by high androgen (male-type hormone) levels, ovulation problems, and polycystic ovaries.
The cause of PCOS is not known, and treatment is mostly based on symptoms and experience.
PCOS can raise the risk of diabetes and heart disease over time.
These long-term metabolic risks should be taken into account when choosing long-term treatment.

items.title: Aromatase inhibitors (letrozole) for subfertile women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 42 randomised trials (7,935 women) of letrozole, a fertility medicine, in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) who do not ovulate regularly. Compared with clomiphene citrate, the usual first-choice drug, letrozole led to more live births and more pregnancies when followed by timed intercourse. Rates of miscarriage, twin or multiple pregnancy, and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) were similar between the two drugs. Letrozole and laparoscopic ovarian drilling (a keyhole surgery) looked similar, but only a few studies compared them.
keyPoints: Live birth was more likely with letrozole than clomiphene (moderate-quality evidence); about 1 extra live birth for every 10 women treated.
Pregnancy rates were also higher with letrozole than clomiphene (moderate-quality evidence).
Miscarriage, multiple pregnancy and OHSS rates were similar for letrozole and clomiphene (high-quality evidence).
Letrozole and laparoscopic ovarian drilling showed no clear difference in live birth or pregnancy rates, but the evidence was low quality.

items.title: Recommendations from the international evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This is an international guideline on how polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) should be diagnosed and managed. It was built from the best available evidence, expert input from many specialties, and the views of women with PCOS. The guideline gives 166 recommendations and practice points. The authors say the evidence behind them is generally low to moderate in quality, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: The guideline refines the criteria used to diagnose PCOS, aiming to make diagnosis more accurate.
It aims to reduce unnecessary testing.
It puts more focus on education, healthy lifestyle changes, emotional wellbeing and quality of life.
It emphasises evidence-based medical treatment and cheaper, safer fertility management.

items.title: The polycystic ovary syndrome: a position statement from the Polish Society of Endocrinology, the Polish Society of Gynaecologists and Obstetricians, and the Polish Society of Gynaecological Endocrinology
items.summary: Three Polish medical societies put together this position statement on how PCOS should be diagnosed and treated. In adults, PCOS is still diagnosed using the Rotterdam criteria, which means having two out of three features: irregular ovulation, high levels of male-type hormones (shown by symptoms or blood tests), and polycystic-looking ovaries. In teenagers, the criteria are different, and treatment is tailored to the main type of PCOS a person has.
keyPoints: In adult women, PCOS is diagnosed when two of three features are present: ovulation problems, signs or blood-test evidence of high androgens (male-type hormones), and polycystic ovaries.
In teenagers, diagnosis needs period problems two years after the first period plus signs or blood-test evidence of high androgens; polycystic-looking ovaries are not required.
The statement warns that the current tests for high androgens and ovary ultrasound are imperfect and can lead to problems in diagnosis.
Treatment should be personalised to the main PCOS type: metabolic, high-androgen, or reproductive.

items.title: Translation and implementation of the Australian-led PCOS guideline: clinical summary and translation resources from the International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
items.summary: This is the first international, evidence-based guideline for diagnosing and managing polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), developed over two years by health professionals and women with PCOS. It covers diagnosis, health screening, emotional wellbeing, lifestyle, medicines and fertility treatment. Key changes include simpler diagnosis without an ovarian ultrasound in most cases, and letrozole as the first-choice medicine for infertility.
keyPoints: In adult women with both high androgen signs (like excess hair growth) and irregular or absent ovulation, an ovarian ultrasound is not needed to diagnose PCOS.

In young women within 8 years of their first period, diagnosis needs both signs and ultrasound is not recommended, because normal ovaries in this age group can look similar. Teens with some features but no clear diagnosis are treated as 'at risk' and followed up.
Screening for metabolic problems now takes into account both PCOS status and other metabolic risk factors.
Letrozole is now first-line treatment for infertility in PCOS because it improves live birth rates and lowers the chance of multiple pregnancies compared with clomiphene citrate.

items.title: Inositol for subfertile women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether myo-inositol, a popular supplement, helps women with PCOS who are having trouble getting pregnant. It pooled 13 trials with 1,472 women, mostly taking it before IVF. The evidence was low to very low quality, so researchers are uncertain whether it improves live birth or pregnancy rates. Despite widespread use, no high-quality evidence supports it.
keyPoints: Researchers are uncertain whether myo-inositol improves live birth rates compared with standard treatment in women with PCOS having IVF.
Researchers are also uncertain whether myo-inositol increases the clinical pregnancy rate, as the evidence is very low quality.
An apparent drop in miscarriage depended mainly on one trial with an unusually high miscarriage rate in the control group, and it disappeared when that trial was removed.
Myo-inositol may make little or no difference to multiple pregnancy rates, based on low-quality evidence.

items.title: Metformin during ovulation induction with gonadotrophins followed by timed intercourse or intrauterine insemination for subfertility associated with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether adding metformin to FSH injections (a second-line fertility treatment) helps women with PCOS who have trouble ovulating. Across five small trials (264 women), adding metformin was linked to more live births and pregnancies. The evidence was low quality, so the findings are preliminary. There was not enough data to say whether metformin changes the chance of twins or other multiple pregnancies, or to judge side effects.
keyPoints: Metformin plus FSH was linked to a higher live birth rate than FSH alone (about 32% to 60% versus an assumed 27%), based on two trials.
Clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates were also higher with metformin.
No clear difference was found in multiple pregnancy, miscarriage or ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).
Evidence on side effects was very limited, and the authors say more trials are needed.

items.title: No. 350-Hirsutism: Evaluation and Treatment
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline reviews the causes, assessment and treatment of hirsutism, which is excess, coarse hair growth in a male-like pattern. It says a careful history, physical exam and selected lab tests confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment. Hirsutism can improve slowly but markedly with a three-part approach: mechanical hair removal, medicines that lower androgen (male-type hormone) production, and medicines that block androgen receptors. Improvement usually takes at least 6 to 9 months of therapy.
keyPoints: Treatment works best with three parts together: mechanical hair removal, suppressing androgen production, and blocking androgen receptors.
At least 6 to 9 months of therapy are needed before hirsutism improves.
In people with PCOS, weight loss and exercise lower androgen levels and improve self-esteem.
Patients should be told about health problems linked to high androgens, including irregular periods, infertility, diabetes and heart disease.

items.title: Ovarian surgery for symptom relief in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 22 trials (2278 women) of a keyhole operation called laparoscopic ovarian drilling for women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) who have irregular periods, unwanted hair growth or acne. The operation did not clearly improve period regularity or hair growth and acne compared with most medicines tested, such as metformin, clomiphene and letrozole. It caused fewer stomach side effects than metformin plus clomiphene. The quality of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate.
keyPoints: No clear evidence that ovarian drilling improves period regularity or hair growth and acne compared with most medical treatments.
Ovarian drilling caused fewer stomach side effects than metformin plus clomiphene (moderate-quality evidence).
Four to five punctures per ovary may work better for period regularity than two or fewer (low-quality evidence).
One small study found a benefit over gonadotrophin injections for regulating periods, but these are rarely used for this purpose.

items.title: Insulin-sensitising drugs (metformin, rosiglitazone, pioglitazone, D-chiro-inositol) for women with polycystic ovary syndrome, oligo amenorrhoea and subfertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 48 trials (4451 women) of insulin-sensitising drugs, mostly metformin, for women with PCOS who ovulate rarely or not at all and want to conceive. Metformin alone may improve live birth compared with placebo, but the evidence is low quality. Adding metformin to clomiphene raised pregnancy and ovulation rates, though it was unclear whether this means more live births. Metformin caused more stomach and gut side effects, and in obese women clomiphene worked better than metformin alone.
keyPoints: Metformin alone may improve live birth rates compared with placebo or no treatment (low-quality evidence), and also raised ovulation and clinical pregnancy rates.
Metformin plus clomiphene gave more pregnancies and ovulation than clomiphene alone, but no clear difference in live births (low-quality evidence).
In obese women with PCOS, clomiphene appears preferable to metformin alone for inducing ovulation; results differed by body mass index (BMI).
Gastrointestinal side effects were much more likely with metformin, and there was no clear evidence of increased miscarriage rates in women taking metformin alone.

items.title: The prevalence and phenotypic features of polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 24 studies to estimate how common polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is among women of reproductive age. Depending on which diagnostic criteria were used, about 6% to 10% of women were found to have PCOS. The authors note that studies defined PCOS in different ways and often recruited participants in ways that could skew results, so the numbers should be read with some caution.
keyPoints: Using NIH criteria, about 6% of women had PCOS; using Rotterdam or AE-PCOS Society criteria, about 10%.
In studies of unselected general populations, estimates were similar: 6% (NIH), 9% (Rotterdam) and 10% (AE-PCOS Society).
Among the features of PCOS, polycystic-looking ovaries were found in 28% of women, irregular or absent ovulation in 15%, excess hair growth (hirsutism) in 13% and high androgen levels in 11%.
Studies defined PCOS differently and often had selection bias, and ethnic differences may affect features such as hirsutism.

items.title: AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF CLINICAL ENDOCRINOLOGISTS, AMERICAN COLLEGE OF ENDOCRINOLOGY, AND ANDROGEN EXCESS AND PCOS SOCIETY DISEASE STATE CLINICAL REVIEW: GUIDE TO THE BEST PRACTICES IN THE EVALUATION AND TREATMENT OF POLYCYSTIC OVARY SYNDROME--PART 1
items.source: American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists, American College of Endocrinology, and Androgen Excess and PCOS Society
items.organisation: American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists, American College of Endocrinology, and Androgen Excess and PCOS Society
items.summary: This 2015 US clinical guide from endocrine specialist societies sums up best practice for diagnosing and treating polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), which is the most common hormone condition in women of reproductive age. PCOS is diagnosed when at least two of three features are present: irregular or absent ovulation, high androgen (male-type hormone) levels, and polycystic-looking ovaries. Care should cover periods, fertility, extra hair growth, hair loss and acne, and the guide describes medicines that can help with these. Diagnosing PCOS in teenagers is harder, because many PCOS-like features are common in normal puberty.
keyPoints: PCOS is diagnosed when at least two of three features are present: chronic anovulation, high androgens (from symptoms or blood tests), and polycystic ovaries.
Cycles longer than 35 days suggest chronic anovulation, and ovulation problems are linked to a higher chance of infertility and of thickening or cancer of the womb lining.
Birth control pills, anti-androgen medicines and (in teenagers) metformin are described as treatment options, chosen according to symptoms.
In teenagers, irregular cycles are common in the first 2 to 3 years after periods start, and ultrasound is not a first-line test under age 17.

items.title: Consensus statement on prevention and detection of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
items.source: Australasian CREI Consensus Expert Panel on Trial evidence (ACCEPT) group
items.journal: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology
items.organisation: Australasian CREI Consensus Expert Panel on Trial evidence (ACCEPT) group
items.summary: An Australian and New Zealand expert group reviewed the evidence on preventing and spotting ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), a serious reaction that can follow fertility treatment that stimulates the ovaries. They found several approaches that can lower the risk, including metformin in women with PCOS and certain medicine choices in the treatment cycle. The group also agreed that using a lower dose of stimulating hormone, freezing all embryos and transferring a single embryo are sensible ways to reduce OHSS. They could not agree on some questions, and they said OHSS needs a standard definition and more research.
keyPoints: Evidence shows lower OHSS risk with metformin in women with PCOS, with GnRH antagonist rather than GnRH agonist, and with a GnRH agonist trigger in antagonist cycles.
The experts agreed that reducing the FSH dose, freezing all embryos and transferring a single embryo are appropriate ways to reduce OHSS.
No agreement was reached on coasting, the lowest egg number at which to freeze all embryos, or care after egg collection is cancelled.
OHSS needs one universally agreed definition so prevention and early detection can improve.

items.title: Effect of pelvic floor muscle training on urinary incontinence symptoms in postmenopausal women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled five randomized trials to see whether pelvic floor muscle training helps bladder leaks in women after menopause. Women who did the training had clearly fewer and milder leakage symptoms than women in the comparison groups. The results were similar when trials that added electrical stimulation or biofeedback were left out. The trials varied a lot from one to another, and only five were included.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training significantly reduced urinary incontinence symptoms in postmenopausal women compared with controls.
The authors estimate a 92% chance of meaningful improvement for women receiving the training.
Results stayed similar when studies that combined training with electrostimulation or biofeedback were removed.
Future studies should look at women who also have genitourinary symptoms of menopause.

items.title: Impact of postpartum exercise on pelvic floor disorders and diastasis recti abdominis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 65 studies (about 21,000 women) to see how exercise in the first year after birth affects pelvic floor problems and the gap between the tummy muscles (diastasis recti). Pelvic floor muscle training lowered the odds of urinary leaking and pelvic organ prolapse compared with no training. Tummy muscle exercises reduced the gap between the abdominal muscles, though this evidence was lower quality. For other outcomes, such as bowel leakage and sexual function, the evidence was limited.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training reduced the odds of urinary incontinence by 37% (moderate certainty evidence, 7 trials).
Pelvic floor muscle training reduced the odds of pelvic organ prolapse by 56%, based on one trial of 123 women (moderate certainty).
Abdominal muscle training reduced the distance between the tummy muscles more than no exercise (low certainty evidence).
Evidence on anal incontinence, sexual function and the risk of diastasis recti was limited.

items.title: Pelvic floor muscle training with feedback or biofeedback for urinary incontinence in women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 41 trials with 3483 women who leak urine. It compared pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) on its own with PFMT plus biofeedback, which gives extra information about how well the muscles are working. Adding biofeedback made little or no difference to quality of life, and only a small leakage reduction that may not matter in daily life. Women using biofeedback may be slightly more satisfied with their treatment, though that evidence is low certainty.
keyPoints: Adding biofeedback to pelvic floor training made little or no difference to incontinence-related quality of life (high-certainty evidence).
Women with biofeedback had about 0.29 fewer leakage episodes in 24 hours, a difference that may not be clinically important (moderate-certainty evidence).
Women probably reported little to no difference in cure or improvement, but may be slightly more satisfied with biofeedback (low-certainty evidence).
No severe adverse events were reported; milder issues such as discomfort or vaginal discharge seemed linked to using a vaginal or rectal device.

items.title: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training Interventions in Female Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from several studies of young women who play sports and had never given birth. It looked at whether pelvic floor muscle training helps with bladder leaks. Training made the pelvic floor muscles stronger and reduced the amount of urine leaked. It did not change the resting pressure inside the vagina.
keyPoints: Athletes are almost 3 times more likely to have urinary incontinence than women who are not active.
Pelvic floor muscle training increased the strength of the pelvic floor muscles in female athletes.
Pelvic floor muscle training reduced the amount of urine leaked.
Training had no effect on vaginal resting pressure.

items.title: Pelvic floor training to prevent stress urinary incontinence: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at seven randomised trials with 1,401 pregnant women to see whether pelvic floor muscle training can prevent leaking urine when coughing, sneezing or exercising (stress urinary incontinence). The authors found that, when done with a suitable method, this training can prevent or help cure the problem. Starting early in pregnancy seemed to help bladder control after birth. The abstract does not rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Stress urinary incontinence is common after birth, affecting 30 to 47% of women in the first 12 months.
Pelvic floor muscle training, applied with the appropriate method, can prevent or cure stress urinary incontinence.
Starting the training early in pregnancy had positive effects on bladder control after delivery.
The review covered 7 randomised trials with 1,401 pregnant women.

items.title: Clinical practice guideline for acupuncture and moxibustion: Female urinary incontinence
items.summary: This is a clinical practice guideline from the World Federation of Acupuncture-moxibustion Societies on using acupuncture and moxibustion (heat treatment with burning herbs) for urinary incontinence in women. The group made ten recommendations, and nearly all were 'conditional', which generally means the supporting evidence is not strong enough for firm advice. The guideline also describes treatment protocols taken from randomized trials.
keyPoints: Urinary incontinence is common in women but often under-reported and under-treated, and it can seriously affect quality of life.
The guideline made ten recommendations on acupuncture and moxibustion; nine were conditional for the treatment and one was conditional for either the treatment or the comparison.
It describes one conventional needle protocol, two deep-needling protocols on lower back acupoints, and four moxibustion protocols.
The recommendations were developed using GRADE methods and an expert panel vote (modified Delphi).

items.title: Comparisons of approaches to pelvic floor muscle training for urinary incontinence in women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 63 trials with 4,920 women to compare different ways of doing pelvic floor muscle training for bladder leaks. It compared the type of exercise, how often or how hard women trained, and how the training was taught. Some approaches seemed a little better than others, but for many comparisons there was little or no difference. Much of the evidence is low or very low quality, so the findings are uncertain. The trials did not include women who were pregnant or recently postpartum.
keyPoints: Direct pelvic floor training (repeated, isolated squeezes of the pelvic floor muscles) may improve quality of life a bit more than indirect exercises that are not pelvic floor contractions.
Training in a group or one-to-one with a clinician probably makes little to no difference to quality of life (moderate-certainty evidence).
Clinic supervision versus home training, and clinic versus app-based support, showed little clear difference, but the evidence is very uncertain.
About 6% of women in trials that recorded side effects had one, almost all linked to vaginal or rectal training devices (discharge, spotting or discomfort).

items.title: Pelvic floor physical therapy and mindfulness: approaches for chronic pelvic pain in women-a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from small trials of pelvic floor physical therapy and mindfulness for women with long-lasting pelvic pain. It found that these approaches were linked to lower scores on a scale measuring how much people dwell on and feel overwhelmed by their pain, both after treatment and later on. Sexual function scores also differed during follow-up. Only a few small studies were available, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Seven trials (279 women) were reviewed, and five were combined in the meta-analysis.
Pain catastrophizing scores were lower after mindfulness and pelvic floor physical therapy, and this held at follow-up.
Sexual function scores differed significantly during follow-up between pelvic floor physical therapy and mindfulness.
The authors say few studies used both approaches, and a team-based, multidisciplinary approach to care is likely needed.

items.title: The effect of pelvic floor muscle-strengthening exercises on low back pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis on randomized clinical trials
items.summary: This review pooled 19 randomized trials (about 900 people) testing whether pelvic floor muscle-strengthening exercises, often called Kegel exercises, ease low back pain. People doing the exercises had lower back pain than those in the comparison groups, including postpartum and pregnant women. The results varied a lot between studies, so the authors say they should be read with caution. The exercises seemed to help more when done for more weeks.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle-strengthening exercises significantly reduced low back pain intensity compared with control groups.
The pain reduction was seen in postpartum women and in pregnant women.
Results differed a lot between studies (high heterogeneity), so the findings should be treated with caution.
The authors suggest these exercises could be part of a low back pain management plan, with longer programmes showing larger effects.

items.title: Technical Update No. 433: eHealth Solutions for Urinary Incontinence Among Women
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline update looked at websites, phone apps and telemedicine (online or remote care) for women over 18 with urinary incontinence, also called bladder leaks. It found that these tools can be useful alongside usual non-surgical care, especially apps that use motivational ideas to help people change habits. The strength of the evidence ranges from weak to strong depending on the tool, and research in this area is changing quickly. These options carry little or no harm and may lower costs and make care easier to reach.
keyPoints: Websites and mobile apps are useful as extra tools in non-surgical care for urinary incontinence.
Apps that use motivational principles for behaviour change are of particular interest.
Telemedicine is an effective way to deliver non-surgical incontinence care and may improve access and reduce costs.
Evidence for these tools ranges from weak to strong, and they have minimal or no harm.

items.title: Surgery for women with apical vaginal prolapse
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 59 trials (6705 women) comparing different operations for apical prolapse, where the uterus or the top of the vagina after hysterectomy slips down. Compared with several vaginal operations, sacral colpopexy (a surgery done through the abdomen that lifts the vagina using mesh) led to less awareness of prolapse, less repeat prolapse surgery and fewer bladder leaks with coughing or sneezing. Several other operations seemed to work about equally well, and mesh placed through the vagina offered no advantage over repair with the woman's own tissue. Evidence quality ranged from very low to moderate.
keyPoints: Sacral colpopexy had lower rates of prolapse awareness, repeat surgery, prolapse on examination and stress urinary incontinence than a variety of vaginal operations (mostly moderate-certainty evidence).
Transvaginal mesh gave no advantage over native tissue repair, and about 17.5% of women had mesh exposure.
No clear differences were found between vaginal hysterectomy and vaginal or abdominal hysteropexy (uterus-preserving surgery) for the main outcomes.
Laparoscopic sacral colpopexy meant a shorter hospital stay than open surgery and a shorter operating time than robotic surgery.

items.title: Bladder training for treating overactive bladder in adults
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at bladder training (scheduled toilet visits and gradually stretching the time between them) for overactive bladder in adults, mostly women. Across 15 trials with 2007 people, bladder training may help cure or improve symptoms compared with no treatment, and may work better than anticholinergic medicines with fewer side effects. It did not seem to differ from pelvic floor muscle training. Most of the evidence was low or very low quality, so firm conclusions can't yet be drawn.
keyPoints: Bladder training may cure or improve overactive bladder compared with no treatment, but the evidence is low to very low certainty.
Bladder training may work better than anticholinergic medicines and may cause fewer side effects, based on low or very low certainty evidence.
There may be no difference in benefit or safety between bladder training and pelvic floor muscle training.
The authors say more well-designed trials are needed to reach a firm conclusion.

items.title: Prevalence and factors of urinary incontinence among postpartum: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 32 studies covering 28,303 women to see how common urinary leaks are after having a baby and what raises the risk. About 1 in 4 women (26%) had urinary incontinence after birth. Risk was higher with vaginal birth, older age, a larger baby and several other factors, while cesarean birth was linked to a lower risk.
keyPoints: About 26% of women (95% CI 21% to 30%) had urinary incontinence after childbirth.
Twelve factors were linked to postpartum incontinence, including age 35 or older, two or more deliveries, a baby over 4 kg, perineal tearing, instrumental delivery and a long second stage of labor.
Earlier urinary incontinence-related problems, vaginal birth and a baby over 4 kg were highlighted as significant risk factors.
Cesarean delivery was linked to a lower risk of postpartum urinary incontinence.

items.title: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training for Urinary Incontinence with or without Biofeedback or Electrostimulation in Women: A Systematic Review
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review looked at 15 randomised trials with 2,441 non-pregnant women who had bladder leaks. Pelvic floor muscle training reduced leaking more than doing nothing, especially for stress and mixed incontinence. Adding biofeedback, electrical stimulation or other physio methods did not clearly work better than the exercises alone. The authors note that future trials should measure outcomes in the same way.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training reduced urinary leakage and improved pelvic floor muscle contraction compared with control groups.
About half of women doing the training (50.5%) improved, and about 1 in 5 (21.8%) became dry on a pad test.
Biofeedback, vaginal cones, electrical stimulation and whole body vibration also reduced leaks, but none was clearly better than the exercises alone.
Trials measured results in different ways, so more consistent studies are needed.

items.title: Conservative interventions for treating urinary incontinence in women: an Overview of Cochrane systematic reviews
items.summary: This overview pulled together 29 Cochrane reviews (112 trials, about 9,000 women) on non-surgical treatments for urinary leaks in women. Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) was better than no treatment for all types of leaking, for cure or improvement and for quality of life. Weight loss also led to more cure and improvement than no treatment in women with any type of urinary incontinence. The authors note that most of the evidence inside the reviews is of low certainty.
keyPoints: There is high certainty that pelvic floor muscle training works better than no treatment for all types of urinary incontinence, for both cure or improvement and quality of life.
Training that is more intense, more frequent or individually supervised probably works better (moderate certainty).
Weight loss gave more cure and improvement than no treatment for women with any type of urinary incontinence.
Electrical stimulation helped women with urgency leaks, and cones helped women with stress leaks (cones were better than no treatment, but not better than PFMT).

items.title: Management of urinary incontinence in postmenopausal women: An EMAS clinical guide
items.summary: This is a clinical guide from the European Menopause and Andropause Society (EMAS) on managing urinary incontinence (bladder leakage) after the menopause. Leakage becomes more common with age, affecting 38% to 55% of women over 60, yet few women seek help. The guide, based on a literature review and expert consensus, says treatment usually starts with lifestyle changes, pelvic floor exercises and bladder training, with other options available if these are not enough.
keyPoints: Urinary incontinence affects 38% to 55% of women over 60, but few seek care.
First-line management is lifestyle and behavior changes, pelvic floor exercises and bladder training.
Estrogens and other medicines can help urgency incontinence that does not improve with these measures.
Surgery, including midurethral slings, is described as safe and effective for stress incontinence in postmenopausal women.

items.title: Guideline No. 411: Vaginal Pessary Use
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline reviews how vaginal pessaries (removable support devices worn in the vagina) are fitted and cared for. They can be used for pelvic organ prolapse and for stress urinary incontinence (leaks when coughing or exercising). Most women can be fitted successfully and have good symptom relief and high satisfaction. Serious problems were seen only when a pessary was neglected, and minor issues like discharge or odour can usually be treated.
keyPoints: Most women with prolapse or stress urinary incontinence can be successfully fitted with a pessary.
Pessaries bring excellent symptom relief and high satisfaction with minimal complications.
Women may choose a pessary instead of surgery or while waiting for surgery.
Major complications were seen only when pessaries were neglected; minor ones such as discharge, odour and erosions can usually be treated.

items.title: Prevalence and factors related to urinary incontinence in older adults women worldwide: a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies
items.summary: This review pooled results from 29 studies covering over 500,000 older women (aged 55 to 106) to estimate how common bladder leaks are. About 37 in 100 older women were affected, with the highest rate in Asia (about 45 in 100). Several factors were linked with leaks, including older age, obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, smoking, urinary tract infections, number of births and education level.
keyPoints: About 37.1% of older women worldwide were found to have urinary incontinence.
The highest rate was seen in Asia, at about 45.1%.
Factors linked with bladder leaks included older age, obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, smoking, urinary tract infections, delivery rank (birth order) and education.
The authors say diagnosis and treatment of incontinence in older women should be prioritised.

items.title: Physical activity and urinary incontinence during pregnancy and postpartum: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled seven studies of over 12,000 women to see whether physical activity in pregnancy or after birth is linked to urinary incontinence (leaking urine). It found no clear link either way, so being active did not appear to cause or prevent leaking. The authors describe the evidence as low quality, and there was not enough data to look at recovery from incontinence. They suggest moderate activity should still be encouraged for its other proven benefits in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Physical activity during pregnancy was not associated with urinary incontinence (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.69-1.18).
Physical activity after birth was also not associated with urinary incontinence (OR 1.31, 95% CI 0.74-2.34).
There was not enough data to assess whether activity helps women recover from incontinence.
The authors say moderate physical activity should be encouraged because of its other evidence-based benefits for pregnancy outcomes.

items.title: No. 397 - Conservative Care of Urinary Incontinence in Women
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looked at the evidence for non-surgical care of urine leaks in women over 18. It covered how leaks are assessed and which conservative treatments help, including lifestyle changes, pelvic floor muscle training, behavioural approaches and mechanical devices. The guideline reports that the evidence for these options is strong, that they carry little or no harm, and that they are cost-effective.
keyPoints: Evidence that conservative care works for urinary incontinence in women is described as strong.
Conservative options include lifestyle changes, pelvic floor muscle training, behavioural management and mechanical devices.
These options carry minimal or no harm.
They also offer an established cost benefit.

items.title: Pelvic floor muscle training for preventing and treating urinary and faecal incontinence in antenatal and postnatal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 46 trials (10,832 women) to see whether pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) prevents or treats leaking urine or stool during pregnancy and after birth. Women who were not leaking at the start and did structured PFMT in pregnancy were less likely to report urine leakage in late pregnancy and in the months after birth. For women who already had leakage, and for leakage of stool, the evidence was too uncertain to say whether PFMT helps. Many trials were small or at risk of bias, and few followed women beyond 12 months.
keyPoints: Women without leakage who did PFMT in pregnancy probably had less urine leakage in late pregnancy (moderate-quality evidence) and slightly less at 3 to 6 months after birth (high-quality evidence).
For women who already leaked urine, there was no clear evidence that PFMT reduced leakage, and the evidence was low or very low quality.
There was no clear evidence that PFMT changed stool (faecal) incontinence, and starting PFMT only after birth for all women was not likely to reduce urine leakage.
Almost no side effects were reported; two women in one small trial stopped because of pelvic floor pain.

items.title: Pessaries (mechanical devices) for managing pelvic organ prolapse in women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at vaginal pessaries (soft devices that support the vagina and hold prolapsed organs in place) for pelvic organ prolapse. It found only four small trials with 478 women in total. It is unclear whether pessaries work better than no treatment or pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) on their own, but using a pessary together with PFMT probably improves symptoms and quality of life compared with PFMT alone. Pessaries may also cause more side effects than PFMT.
keyPoints: Four small trials (478 women) were included, so the evidence is limited and could not be combined.
It is uncertain whether a pessary improves prolapse symptoms compared with no treatment or with PFMT alone.
A pessary plus PFMT probably gives more symptom improvement and better prolapse-specific quality of life than PFMT alone (moderate-certainty evidence).
Pessaries may cause more side effects than PFMT, such as increased vaginal discharge, more urinary incontinence, or irritation of the vaginal walls (low-certainty evidence).

items.title: Pelvic Organ Prolapse: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 214
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from ACOG and the American Urogynecologic Society on pelvic organ prolapse, a common and non-cancerous condition in women. Prolapse can cause a vaginal bulge or pressure and problems with passing urine, bowel movements or sex, which may affect quality of life. The guideline reviews what is known about prolapse and sets out how it should be diagnosed and managed based on the best available evidence. The abstract does not list the specific treatment recommendations or rate the certainty of the evidence.
keyPoints: Pelvic organ prolapse is a common, benign condition in women.
It can cause vaginal bulge and pressure, bladder and bowel problems, and sexual difficulties.
Women in the US have a 13% lifetime risk of having surgery for prolapse.
Symptoms are most common at ages 70-79, and cases are expected to rise by about 50% by 2050.

items.title: Screening for Urinary Incontinence in Women: A Recommendation From the Women's Preventive Services Initiative
items.summary: The Women's Preventive Services Initiative, a coalition of women's health organisations, reviewed the evidence on screening women for bladder leaks (urinary incontinence). It recommends that women are asked about urinary incontinence every year. The questions should cover whether leaks happen and whether they affect daily activities and quality of life. Women who need it should be referred for further assessment and treatment.
keyPoints: Women of all ages, including adolescents, should be screened for urinary incontinence once a year.
Screening should ask whether leaks happen and whether they affect activities and quality of life.
Women should be referred for further evaluation and treatment if indicated.
The recommendation drew on a systematic review of screening tools and treatments, plus indirect evidence linking screening to health outcomes.

items.title: Pelvic floor muscle training versus no treatment, or inactive control treatments, for urinary incontinence in women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 31 trials with 1817 women to see whether pelvic floor muscle training helps with leaking urine, compared with no treatment or inactive treatments. Women who did the training were much more likely to report being cured or improved, and they leaked less often and lost less urine. Side effects were rare and minor. Most trials were small, with follow-up mostly under 12 months, so long-term benefits are still unclear.
keyPoints: Women with stress incontinence who did pelvic floor training were about 8 times more likely to report cure (56% versus 6%), rated high-quality evidence.
Training probably reduced leakage by about one episode in 24 hours and led to less urine lost on short pad tests.
Women who did the training were also more satisfied and had better sexual outcomes; adverse events were rare and minor.
The authors suggest pelvic floor training could be part of first-line, non-surgical care, but long-term effects need more research.

items.title: Selective versus routine use of episiotomy for vaginal birth
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 12 trials (6177 women) comparing episiotomy only when needed with episiotomy as routine for vaginal birth. When no instrument-assisted birth was planned, using episiotomy selectively may mean about 30% fewer women have severe tears of the perineum or vagina. There was no clear sign of harm from the selective approach for mothers or babies, though the quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate depending on the outcome.
keyPoints: A policy of selective episiotomy may result in 30% fewer women with severe perineal or vaginal trauma (low-certainty evidence).
There was probably little or no difference in painful sex six months or more after birth, and possibly little or no difference in long-term urinary incontinence.
The belief that routine episiotomy prevents perineal or vaginal trauma is not supported by current evidence.
Evidence is limited for births where instruments (forceps or vacuum) are planned, and pain and women's preferences were not well measured.

items.title: Pelvic floor muscle training for prevention and treatment of urinary and faecal incontinence in antenatal and postnatal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 38 trials with nearly 9,900 women to see whether pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) helps prevent or treat leaking urine or stool around pregnancy and birth. For women who were not leaking before, starting a structured PFMT programme early in pregnancy may lower the chance of urine leakage in late pregnancy and in the months after birth. It is still unclear whether PFMT works as a treatment once leaking has started, or whether it helps with leaking stool. Many trials were small or had weaknesses, so much of the evidence is low or very low quality.
keyPoints: Women who were continent and did PFMT in pregnancy may have about 62% less urinary incontinence in late pregnancy (low-quality evidence) and about 29% less at 3 to 6 months after birth (moderate-quality evidence).
Whether PFMT treats urinary incontinence that has already started, in pregnancy or after birth, is uncertain (very low-quality evidence).
For faecal incontinence, antenatal PFMT made little or no difference in late pregnancy, and effects after birth are uncertain.
Apart from two reports of pelvic floor pain, trials reported no harmful effects of PFMT.

items.title: Postpartum practice: guidelines for clinical practice from the French College of Gynaecologists and Obstetricians (CNGOF)
items.source: French College of Gynaecologists and Obstetricians (CNGOF)
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.organisation: French College of Gynaecologists and Obstetricians (CNGOF)
items.summary: The French College of Gynaecologists and Obstetricians reviewed the research to make recommendations for care after birth, for mothers and babies. It recommends breastfeeding for at least 4-6 months, starting effective contraception by 21 days after birth, and avoiding combined hormonal contraception (containing oestrogen) before six weeks because of clot risk. It also covers pelvic floor exercises and notes that the months after birth can be emotionally hard, with postpartum depression the most common difficulty.
keyPoints: Exclusive and extended breastfeeding is recommended for at least 4-6 months, as it is linked to fewer illnesses and better cognitive development in children.
Effective contraception should start no later than 21 days after birth for women who do not want a closely spaced pregnancy.
Combined hormonal contraception is not recommended before six weeks after birth because of the higher risk of venous blood clots.
Pelvic floor exercises are recommended for urinary incontinence that persists at 3 months after birth, but not routinely for women without symptoms.

items.title: Associations between hysterectomy and pelvic floor disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 60 studies (over 3.5 million women) to see whether having a hysterectomy for a non-cancer reason is linked to pelvic floor problems later. Women who had a hysterectomy were more likely to have urinary leakage and overactive bladder in the first 10 years. After 10 years, they were more likely to have pelvic organ prolapse and stress urinary incontinence. The authors suggest these possible risks be talked through when planning a hysterectomy, along with non-surgical options where suitable.
keyPoints: Within 10 years of hysterectomy, urinary incontinence of all types was more likely, including stress, mixed and overactive bladder symptoms.
More than 10 years after hysterectomy, pelvic organ prolapse was more likely (effect size 1.56).
More than 10 years after hysterectomy, stress urinary incontinence was also more likely (effect size 2.40).
The authors say these risks should be discussed during counselling, with medical or non-hysterectomy options considered if clinically acceptable.

items.title: Perioperative interventions in pelvic organ prolapse surgery
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 49 trials (5,657 women) testing extra steps around the time of prolapse surgery, such as pelvic floor muscle training and how long a urinary catheter stays in. For most of these steps, no clear benefit or harm was found, and the evidence was mostly low to moderate certainty. The main exception was catheter timing: keeping a catheter in for more than 24 hours may greatly raise the chance of a urinary tract infection.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training around prolapse surgery may make no clinically relevant difference to awareness of prolapse, repeat surgery, surgical failure or symptom scores (low-certainty evidence).
Removing the catheter before 24 hours versus at 24 hours probably made no clinically relevant difference to urinary tract infections (moderate-certainty evidence).
Keeping the catheter in for longer than 24 hours may greatly increase urinary tract infection risk (low-certainty evidence) and probably lengthens hospital stay (moderate-certainty evidence).
There is little data overall, so most other measures, like bowel preparation, vaginal oestrogen or cranberry supplements, showed no clinically meaningful difference.

items.title: Pelvic floor muscle training for urinary symptoms, vaginal prolapse, sexual function, pelvic floor muscle strength, and quality of life after hysterectomy: a systematic review with meta-analyses
items.summary: This review pooled six randomized trials with 776 women to see whether pelvic floor muscle training helps after a hysterectomy. Moderate-quality evidence showed it improves sexual function compared with no training. For urinary symptoms, muscle strength and quality of life, the results were too imprecise to say, and it made little or no difference to vaginal prolapse. Whether any benefits last after the training ends is not known.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training improved sexual function by about 5 points on the Female Sexual Function Index compared with no intervention (moderate-quality evidence).
Effects on urinary symptoms, pelvic floor strength and quality of life were unclear because the estimates were too imprecise.
Training had no or negligible effect on vaginal prolapse.
Long-term effects after the training period remain uncertain.

items.title: Management of female pelvic organ prolapse-Summary of the 2021 HAS guidelines
items.journal: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.summary: This is a summary of the 2021 French national health authority (HAS) guidelines on managing pelvic organ prolapse, when pelvic organs such as the bladder or womb drop down into the vagina. The guidelines say prolapse is diagnosed by examination, and that pelvic floor muscle training and pessaries (devices placed in the vagina for support) are the recommended first treatments. Surgery is suggested if these do not meet a woman's goals and symptoms are disabling and caused by the prolapse.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training and pessaries are recommended as first-line treatment, alone or together, along with managing risk factors that can be changed.
Surgery should be offered if conservative options fall short and symptoms are disabling, caused by the prolapse, and the prolapse is significant (stage 2 or more).
Laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy is recommended for apical and anterior prolapse, and vaginal surgery using the woman's own tissue is a recommended option for elderly and frail patients.
Decisions about using mesh should be made with a multidisciplinary team, and patients should be reassessed by their surgeon after surgery, even without symptoms.

items.title: Pelvic floor reconstructive surgery under local anesthesia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined 19 studies of women who had pelvic floor surgery (such as prolapse or stress urinary incontinence repair) under local anaesthetic, with or without sedation. Women who had local anaesthetic reported less pain than those who had general or regional anaesthetic for up to about 18 hours after surgery, and less nausea compared with regional anaesthetic at 8 hours. Pain after 24 hours and the amount of morphine used were similar between the groups. The authors conclude local anaesthetic is a safe and workable option that can allow quicker recovery.
keyPoints: Local anaesthetic gave lower pain scores than general or regional anaesthetic at 4-6 hours and 8-18 hours after surgery.
Pain scores after 24 hours did not differ between the groups.
Morphine use during and after prolapse surgery was similar with local or general anaesthetic.
Nausea 8 hours after surgery was lower with local than with regional anaesthetic.

items.title: Pelvic Organ Prolapse
items.source: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the American Urogynecologic Society
items.organisation: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the American Urogynecologic Society
items.summary: This is a joint guideline from two US medical groups about pelvic organ prolapse, a common, non-cancerous condition where pelvic organs press down into or out of the vagina. It can cause a vaginal bulge or pressure, bladder or bowel problems, and sexual difficulties that affect quality of life. The guideline reviews current understanding and sets out how the condition is diagnosed and managed based on the best available evidence. An update notes that the US FDA ordered the sale of transvaginal synthetic mesh products for prolapse repair to stop.
keyPoints: Prolapse is a common, benign condition that can cause vaginal bulge, pressure, bladder or bowel problems and sexual difficulties.
US women have about a 13% lifetime risk of having surgery for prolapse.
Symptoms are most common in women aged 70 to 79, though younger women can be affected.
The number of women with prolapse in the US is expected to rise by about 50% by 2050.

items.title: Prolapse surgery with or without incontinence procedure: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled ten randomised trials that compared prolapse surgery with and without an added operation for stress urinary incontinence (leaking when coughing or exercising). In women who already leaked, or who leaked when tested before surgery, adding a midurethral sling during vaginal prolapse repair meant far fewer needed a later operation for leaking. Serious complications were more common with the sling (14% versus 8%). Adding the extra procedure did not increase overactive bladder symptoms, urgency leaking or surgery for trouble emptying the bladder.
keyPoints: In women with stress leaking symptoms or hidden leaking found on testing, adding a sling to vaginal prolapse surgery cut later incontinence surgery (0% versus 40% in one group, 1% versus 15% in another).
The benefit was not significant in women who were dry and had no hidden leaking, or who were not tested.
Serious adverse events were more frequent after vaginal prolapse repair with a sling (14% versus 8%), but not after sacrocolpopexy with Burch colposuspension.
Combined surgery did not raise the risk of overactive bladder symptoms, urgency incontinence or surgery for voiding problems.

items.title: Surgery for women with pelvic organ prolapse with or without stress urinary incontinence
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 19 trials (2,717 women) of surgery for pelvic organ prolapse, looking at what happens to bladder leakage on effort (stress urinary incontinence, SUI) afterwards. In women who already have SUI, or who leak only when the prolapse is pushed back, adding a mid-urethral sling during vaginal repair probably lowers the chance of leaking after surgery. In women with no leaking, the benefit of a sling was less clear. The evidence was mostly low to moderate quality.
keyPoints: In women with prolapse and SUI, a mid-urethral sling added to vaginal repair probably reduces leaking after surgery (moderate-quality evidence).
In women who leak only with the prolapse pushed back (occult SUI), a sling also probably reduces leaking after surgery.
In women who do not leak, there was no conclusive evidence that a sling helps, and results for adding a Burch colposuspension during abdominal prolapse surgery were uncertain.
Anterior mesh repair may slightly raise new leaking compared with native tissue repair but may lower prolapse coming back (low-quality evidence).

items.title: Management of apical compartment prolapse (uterine and vault prolapse): A FIGO Working Group report
items.summary: This international expert report reviewed the treatment options for apical prolapse, where the uterus or the top of the vagina drops down. It looked at non-surgical and surgical choices, weighing the evidence, cost and difficulty. Pessaries, vaginal surgeries and sacrocolpopexy (surgery done through the abdomen) all had good results. Long-term data on mesh use are still awaited.
keyPoints: Women have an estimated 11-19% lifetime risk of having surgery for pelvic organ prolapse, and this is expected to rise.
Pessaries have been used for centuries and are the most successful non-surgical option, with low complication rates and low cost.
Two vaginal operations, sacrospinous ligament fixation and uterosacral ligament suspension, give similar results with low complication rates and good value for money.

Sacrocolpopexy lasts well and improves quality of life; keyhole and robotic methods work as well as open surgery with no difference in mesh exposure, but mesh costs more and long-term mesh complications need further study.

items.title: Anterior vaginal repair for urinary incontinence in women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at anterior vaginal repair, an operation sometimes used for stress urinary incontinence (leaking when coughing, sneezing or exercising). Ten trials were included. Open abdominal surgery to lift the bladder neck (such as the Burch procedure) worked better than anterior vaginal repair based on women's own reports of cure, and fewer women needed repeat incontinence surgery. There was not enough evidence to compare vaginal repair with physical therapy or needle suspension, and little information on complications.
keyPoints: Women reported more failures after anterior vaginal repair than after open abdominal retropubic suspension, both within one to five years (38% versus 17%) and after five years (38% versus 21%).
Repeat surgery for incontinence was needed more often after anterior repair (23% versus 2%) in three of the trials.
Open abdominal surgery appeared better even in women who also had prolapse, although fewer women had prolapse after anterior repair.
There was not enough evidence to compare anterior repair with physical therapy or needle suspension, and too little information on complications.

items.title: Transvaginal mesh or grafts compared with native tissue repair for vaginal prolapse
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 37 trials (4023 women) comparing prolapse repairs that use mesh or grafts with repairs using the woman's own tissue. Permanent vaginal mesh lowered the chance of feeling prolapse, needing repeat surgery for prolapse, and prolapse showing on examination. But it also caused more problems, including bladder injury during surgery, new stress urinary incontinence, and mesh exposure needing repeat surgery. The authors concluded mesh has limited use for a first prolapse operation. Evidence for absorbable mesh and biological grafts was too limited to draw conclusions.
keyPoints: Permanent mesh meant fewer women were aware of prolapse (moderate-quality evidence) and fewer needed repeat surgery for prolapse than with native tissue repair.
Permanent mesh had more harms: bladder injury at surgery, new stress urinary incontinence, and mesh exposure; 8% of mesh group women needed repeat surgery for mesh exposure.
Overall repeat surgery (for prolapse, incontinence or mesh exposure) was more common with mesh, so the authors say it has limited use in first-time prolapse surgery.
There was not enough evidence to judge absorbable mesh or biological grafts against native tissue repair.

items.title: Effects of Traditional Chinese Exercise on Menopausal Symptoms, Bone Health and Mental Health in Perimenopausal and Postmenopausal Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 randomized trials with 1,023 women in perimenopause or after menopause to see how traditional Chinese exercise (such as tai chi or qigong) affects symptoms, bones and mood. Women who did these exercises had fewer menopausal symptoms, less depression and slightly better spine bone density. Effects on other bone sites and on overall quality of life were unclear, partly because few studies looked at them. The authors say larger, high-quality trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Traditional Chinese exercise significantly reduced menopausal symptoms and depression.
It improved spine bone mineral density.
Effects on bone density at other sites (such as thigh, pelvis and whole body) were uncertain because few studies measured them.
Three studies found no clear improvement in quality of life scores.

items.title: The Effectiveness of Lifestyle Interventions, Including Exercise, Diet, and Health Education on Symptoms Experienced During Perimenopause: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.source: Journal of Aging and Physical Activity
items.journal: Journal of Aging and Physical Activity
items.summary: This review pulled together 25 randomized trials that tested lifestyle changes for perimenopause symptoms, including exercise, health education, and combinations of the two. Both exercise and health education might help with symptoms. However, the studies varied a lot and had inconsistent methods, so firm guidelines cannot yet be made. No trial looked at diet changes on their own.
keyPoints: 25 randomized trials were included: 9 on exercise only, 12 on combined approaches, and 5 on health education only.
Exercise and health education might offer benefits for managing perimenopausal symptoms.
No studies looked at diet-only interventions.
Large differences between studies and inconsistent methods mean evidence-based guidelines are not yet possible; better research is needed.

items.title: Complementary therapies for management of menopausal symptoms: a systematic review to inform the update of the International Menopause Society recommendations on women's midlife health
items.summary: This review looked at 158 studies on complementary therapies (such as herbs, supplements, acupuncture and mind-body approaches) for menopause symptoms. Some therapies showed promising results, but most of the evidence was low or very low certainty. Moderate-certainty evidence supported black cohosh, Chinese herbal medicine, and acupuncture combined with Chinese herbal medicine for some symptoms. Most complementary therapies appeared safe, but the authors say better research is still needed.
keyPoints: Most evidence for acupuncture, Chinese herbal medicine, herbs, nutrients and mind-body therapies was low or very low certainty.
Moderate-certainty evidence supported black cohosh for hot flushes and menopausal symptoms, and Chinese herbal medicine for menopausal symptoms, sleep and blood pressure.
Acupuncture plus Chinese herbal medicine showed moderate-certainty benefit for sleep, and vitamin D for lowering fracture risk.
High-certainty evidence supported the safety of vitamin D, and most complementary therapies appeared safe.

items.title: Prevalence and incidence of depressive, anxiety, and insomnia symptoms in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 102 studies, covering over 1.1 million women, to estimate how common low mood, anxiety and trouble sleeping are around the menopause. Roughly one in three women had depressive, anxiety or insomnia symptoms during the transition. Rates were higher when symptoms were measured with screening questionnaires and in early menopause. Most of the studies were judged to have a low or moderate risk of bias.
keyPoints: About 32% of perimenopausal and 30% of postmenopausal women had depressive symptoms at a given point in time.
Anxiety symptoms were found in about 29% of perimenopausal and 39% of postmenopausal women.
Insomnia symptoms affected about 27% of perimenopausal and 42% of postmenopausal women.
The authors conclude that routine mental health screening and joined-up care across different specialists are needed.

items.title: A systematic review of heart rate variability and menopausal vasomotor symptoms
items.summary: This review looked at whether heart rate variability, a simple measure of how the body's automatic nervous system is working, differs between women who have hot flushes or night sweats and women who do not. Only three studies could be combined, and they did not show a clear difference between the two groups. The results varied a lot from study to study, so the authors say larger, more standardised studies are needed.
keyPoints: Three studies were suitable for pooling; women with and without hot flushes or night sweats showed no clear difference in heart rate variability.
The results differed widely between studies (very high heterogeneity), which limits how firmly conclusions can be drawn.
The menopausal transition is linked with higher heart disease risk, but this review could not confirm a link through heart rate variability.
Larger, standardised studies are needed to understand how nervous system function, hot flushes and heart disease risk are connected.

items.title: Estrogens and human brain networks: A systematic review of structural and functional neuroimaging studies
items.summary: This review pulled together brain-scan studies looking at how estrogen relates to the structure and activity of the human brain. It covered 54 studies on the body's own estrogen and 28 on estrogen given as medicine, such as in contraception or menopausal hormone therapy. Estrogen-related changes were reported in brain networks for emotion, reward and memory, and in some areas of grey and white matter. The hippocampus and amygdala seemed especially adaptable. The abstract does not rate how certain these findings are.
keyPoints: Estrogen changes during the menstrual cycle, puberty, postpartum and the menopause transition are linked to effects on thinking, mood and behavior.
The review included 54 studies (2,494 people) on natural estrogen and 28 studies (1,740 people) on estrogen taken as medicine.
Estrogen-related changes were found in emotion, reward, memory and resting-state brain networks, and in regional grey and white matter.
The hippocampus and amygdala showed particular neural plasticity, meaning they can change in response to estrogen.

items.title: Exploring symptom clusters across the menopausal stages - systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 14 studies (about 14,760 women) to look at how menopause symptoms group together in perimenopause and after menopause. They found four main groups of symptoms: body (somatic), hot flushes and night sweats (vasomotor), mood and thinking (psychological), and sexual. Only body symptoms showed a clear difference between the stages, and symptoms varied a lot from woman to woman. The authors say care should be tailored to the person and that longer-term studies are needed.
keyPoints: Menopause symptoms tend to fall into four groups: somatic (body), vasomotor, psychological and sexual.
Body (somatic) symptoms differed significantly between menopausal stages.
No clear differences between stages were found for hot flush, sexual or psychological symptoms.
Symptoms varied a lot between women, so the authors call for person-centred care and long-term studies.

items.title: Executive Summary: The AUA/SUFU/AUGS Guideline on Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause
items.summary: This guideline from three US urology and urogynecology societies covers genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), which is bothersome vaginal and urinary symptoms caused by falling estrogen during the menopause transition. It reviewed dozens of studies on how GSM is diagnosed and treated. Doctors diagnose GSM from symptoms, with or without physical findings, after checking for other causes. Many hormonal and non-hormonal treatments have been studied, and low-dose vaginal estrogen has the strongest evidence.
keyPoints: GSM is diagnosed from symptoms, with or without physical findings, after other causes or co-existing conditions are ruled out.
Many hormonal and non-hormonal treatments have been studied for GSM symptoms.
Low-dose vaginal estrogen has the most robust evidence of the options reviewed.
There is not enough evidence to recommend one hormonal therapy over another, so treatment choices should be made together with the clinician based on personal goals and preferences.

items.title: A systematic review of community pharmacy interventions to improve peri- and post-menopausal health
items.summary: This review looked for studies on whether community pharmacies can improve health for women going through perimenopause or menopause. Out of 915 articles, only two small studies qualified. One used ultrasound screening in pharmacies to spot post-menopausal women at risk of weak bones, and the other tested a pharmacy menopause education programme. Both studies were of low quality, so it is not yet clear how well pharmacy-led care works.
keyPoints: Only two studies were found on pharmacy-led care for peri- and post-menopausal women.
In one study, pharmacy ultrasound screening found 11 out of 100 post-menopausal women at risk of osteoporosis, and they were referred to their doctor.
In the other study, women in a pharmacy education programme reported access to personalised menopause counselling and better knowledge of menopause topics.
Both studies were low quality, and the authors say better research is needed to know if pharmacy-led interventions are feasible, effective and acceptable.

items.title: Socioecological factors influencing physical activity engagement for women across the menopausal transition: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 20 studies to understand what helps or gets in the way of women staying physically active during the menopausal transition. Existing health complaints were a common barrier, while knowing the health benefits of exercise, feeling safe and confident, and having social support helped. The authors note that few studies used a clear theory to explore these influences, so the picture may be incomplete.
keyPoints: Existing health complaints were a common barrier to being active during the menopausal transition.
Knowing the health benefits of physical activity during menopause helped women stay active.
Feeling safe, avoiding injury and having confidence in exercising were important parts of successful programs.
Social support was an important helper for taking part in activity.

items.title: EMAS position statement: Thyroid disease and menopause
items.summary: This is a position statement from the European Menopause and Andropause Society, based on a literature review and expert agreement. It looks at how thyroid disease and menopause can occur together in midlife. Both can cause a wide range of symptoms, which can make it harder to diagnose either one and can delay diagnosis. The experts say treatment decisions for both conditions should be made carefully, with a personalised approach.
keyPoints: Thyroid disease is common in women in their late reproductive years, so it can exist alongside menopause.
Thyroid disease and menopause can both cause a wide range of symptoms, which can make diagnosis difficult and delayed.
Treatment decisions for both conditions should be made with caution and take this age group's specific characteristics into account.
A personalised approach should include family history, involve the woman in decisions, and respect her preferences.

items.title: Disordered eating behaviours during the menopausal transition: a systematic review
items.source: Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism = Physiologie Appliquee, Nutrition et Metabolisme
items.journal: Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism = Physiologie Appliquee, Nutrition et Metabolisme
items.summary: This review looked at whether disordered eating (unhealthy eating habits and attitudes toward food and weight) changes during the menopausal transition. It found only 10 studies, and most were one-time snapshots rather than following women over time. Binge eating may be higher in perimenopause, and restrictive eating may be more common after menopause than before it. Results were mixed and the quality of the studies was limited, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Binge eating may be higher during perimenopause.
Restrictive eating appeared more common after menopause than before it.
Both studies that looked at menopausal symptoms found strong links between symptoms and disordered eating.
Findings were mixed and the studies were of limited quality, so firm conclusions cannot be drawn yet.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis investigating differences in chronic inflammation and adiposity before and after menopause
