items.summary: This review pooled studies comparing women before and after menopause to see if body fat and signs of low-level inflammation differ. After menopause, women had higher levels of two fat-related hormones (leptin and adiponectin) and a larger waist, waist-to-hip ratio and body mass index. Other inflammation markers, such as C-reactive protein and interleukin-6, did not clearly differ. The authors say the certainty of the evidence is low, so more long-term studies following women through the menopause transition are needed.
keyPoints: Postmenopausal women had higher leptin and adiponectin levels than premenopausal women.
Postmenopausal women had greater waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and body mass index.
No clear differences were found for interleukin-6 or C-reactive protein, and tumour necrosis factor-α showed only a possible trend.
The evidence was of low certainty, and studies following women over the menopausal transition are still needed.

items.title: PCOS during the menopausal transition and after menopause: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 37 studies of women with PCOS who were in the menopause transition or past menopause, and compared them with women without PCOS. Women with PCOS had higher androgen (male-type hormone) levels, more weight around the middle, higher blood sugar and insulin, and more diabetes, high blood pressure, heart attack and stroke. Most of these differences faded when women had a similar body weight, which suggests extra weight drives much of the extra risk. The authors say the evidence is of low quality and mixed, so firm conclusions can't yet be drawn.
keyPoints: After menopause, women with PCOS still had higher androgen levels than other women, even when body weight was similar.
Women with PCOS had higher rates of diabetes and high blood pressure, and more heart attack and stroke, than women without PCOS.
When women had a similar BMI, the main difference left was lower HDL ('good') cholesterol in women with PCOS.
The authors say most heart and metabolic problems seem linked to excess weight, so targeting obesity matters; the evidence quality is low.

items.title: Associations between menopause and body image: A systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 18 studies on how menopause relates to the way women feel about their bodies. Women with more frequent, stronger or more numerous menopausal symptoms tended to have a more negative body image. Differences between menopausal stages were inconsistent, and there was little evidence linking hormone levels to body image. Most studies were a single snapshot in time, so they cannot show what causes what.
keyPoints: All 6 studies on menopausal symptoms found some link between more symptoms and greater body image concern.
Body image differences between menopausal stages were inconsistent across 12 studies.
Only 2 studies looked at reproductive hormones and body image, and the evidence was minimal.
17 of 18 studies were cross-sectional and not all adjusted for other factors, so results should be read with caution.

items.title: Use of hormonal contraceptives in perimenopause: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 15 studies on using hormonal contraceptives during perimenopause, the years leading up to menopause. Most studies that measured symptoms found hormonal contraceptives helped more than no treatment, and most studies that looked at long-term effects, such as bone loss and metabolic health, also found benefits. The authors note the data are limited and there are few studies comparing one method with another, so the best option for each woman is still unclear.
keyPoints: Six of nine studies on symptoms found hormonal contraceptives gave statistically significant improvement compared with no treatment.
Six of seven studies on long-term outcomes, including bone loss and metabolic measures, showed significant improvements.
A levonorgestrel intrauterine device with added low-dose menopausal estrogen showed positive results for disruptive symptoms and long-term outcomes, based on limited data.
Benefits apply if a woman has no contraindications; choice should reflect her risk factors, symptoms, long-term risks and benefits, and preferences.

items.title: Prevalence of Psychosomatic and Genitourinary Syndrome Among Menopausal Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 29 studies to see how common body-related (somatic), emotional (psychological) and genitourinary symptoms are before, during and after menopause. Symptoms were generally more common after menopause, especially genitourinary ones such as vaginal and urinary problems. The authors suggest health professionals should check for these symptoms so women can have a better quality of life.
keyPoints: Somatic (body) symptoms were reported by about 52.6% of post-menopausal women, compared with 34.6% before menopause and 39.5% in perimenopause.
Genitourinary syndrome affected about 55.1% of post-menopausal women, 31.9% of perimenopausal women and 19.2% of premenopausal women.
Psychological symptoms were less common in premenopausal women (about 28.4%).
The authors conclude that post-menopausal women are at higher risk of menopausal symptoms, so health professionals should evaluate them.

items.title: n-3 PUFA Improve Emotion and Cognition during Menopause: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at whether omega-3 fats (n-3 PUFA, found in fish oil) affect mood and thinking during the menopause transition. It found 17 studies, 11 in people and 6 in animals. Most studies reported fewer depression symptoms with omega-3 intake, while results for anxiety and thinking skills in people were mixed. The authors say more research is needed to be sure how well omega-3 works.
keyPoints: Most studies reported milder depressive symptoms with omega-3 intake during the menopause transition.
Results for anxiety and thinking skills (cognition) in women were mixed.
In animal studies, omega-3 consistently reduced anxiety and improved thinking.
The authors conclude omega-3 may help mood and cognition but say more research is needed.

items.title: Hormone Therapy for the Primary Prevention of Chronic Conditions in Postmenopausal Persons: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed whether taking hormone therapy (estrogen with progestin, or estrogen alone after a hysterectomy) can prevent long-term conditions like heart disease, cancer, osteoporosis and fractures in women after menopause. It found, with moderate certainty, that there is no net benefit overall. It recommends against using hormone therapy for this purpose. This advice applies to women without menopause symptoms who are considering hormones only to prevent disease, not to treat symptoms such as hot flushes.
keyPoints: The Task Force recommends against combined estrogen and progestin to prevent chronic conditions in postmenopausal women (D recommendation).
It also recommends against estrogen alone to prevent chronic conditions in women who have had a hysterectomy (D recommendation).
For both types of hormone therapy, the evidence showed no net benefit, with moderate certainty.
The advice is for women without symptoms who are considering hormones purely for prevention.

items.title: Antidepressants during and after Menopausal Transition: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from seven randomized trials (1,676 women, average age about 53) that compared antidepressants with placebo in women with depression during and after the menopausal transition. Antidepressants improved depressive symptoms more than placebo, and more women responded to treatment or reached remission. Women taking antidepressants were more likely to stop treatment because of side effects, although overall dropout rates were similar to placebo.
keyPoints: Antidepressants reduced depressive symptoms more than placebo in women during and after menopausal transition.
Response and remission rates were higher with antidepressants than with placebo.
Antidepressants also helped depressive symptoms in women who did not have a formal diagnosis of major depression.
Stopping treatment because of side effects was more common with antidepressants, while overall dropout rates did not differ.

items.title: Menopause, lung function and obstructive lung disease outcomes: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at ten population-based studies to see how menopause affects breathing and lung health. Studies on asthma gave mixed results, and there were few studies on COPD. Overall, menopause seemed linked to a meaningful drop in lung function, but not in a way that points to obstructive lung disease. It is hard to tell menopause's effect apart from ageing, hormone therapy use, and a higher risk of metabolic syndrome at this time of life.
keyPoints: Findings on menopause and asthma were conflicting across studies.
Few studies looked at menopause and COPD, so little can be said.
Menopause was generally linked to clinically significant reductions in lung function, in a non-obstructive pattern.
Ageing, hormone therapy use and metabolic syndrome risk make the effect of menopause hard to separate out.

items.title: Bioidentical Estrogen for Menopausal Depressive Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 trials (1,208 women) that compared bioidentical estrogen with placebo for low mood in women going through or past menopause. On average, bioidentical estrogen did not clearly improve depressive symptoms. The studies differed a lot from each other, so the authors say firm conclusions are not possible. There may be some benefit for perimenopausal women taking estradiol alone, but this was not confirmed.
keyPoints: Across 10 trials, bioidentical estrogen had no clinically significant effect on depressive symptoms compared with placebo.
Results did not differ by whether progestogen was added, or by perimenopausal versus postmenopausal status.
The trials were very different from one another, which limits what can be concluded.
A possible benefit in perimenopausal women taking estradiol alone may have been hidden by studies of older postmenopausal women whose low mood was not linked to menopause.

items.title: Improving vasomotor symptoms; psychological symptoms; and health-related quality of life in peri- or post-menopausal women through yoga: An umbrella systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together earlier research on yoga, tai chi and qigong for women going through the menopause transition or after menopause. Only yoga studies were found. Compared with control groups, yoga lowered hot flushes and night sweats and also eased psychological symptoms, although the effects were small. The authors say yoga may be a useful option for these symptoms, but side effects were rarely reported and the studies measured outcomes in different ways.
keyPoints: Yoga reduced hot flushes and night sweats compared with controls (5 trials).
Yoga also reduced psychological symptoms such as low mood and anxiety (6 trials).
No studies of tai chi or qigong were found, and quality-of-life effects were rarely reported.
Side effects were rarely reported and outcome measures were not standardised.

items.title: Effect and safety of paroxetine for vasomotor symptoms: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled six randomised trials (1,571 women) of paroxetine, a non-hormone medicine, for moderate-to-severe hot flushes and night sweats in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women. Paroxetine cut hot flushes by about 9 per week after 4 weeks and about 7 per week after 12 weeks compared with placebo or no treatment. The quality of the evidence was rated moderate. The medicine caused side effects, including nausea and dizziness.
keyPoints: Paroxetine reduced hot flush frequency by 8.86 per week at week 4 and 7.36 per week at week 12.
The review included six randomised trials with 1,571 perimenopausal and postmenopausal women.
The quality of the evidence for the effect on hot flushes was moderate.
Paroxetine causes nausea and dizziness in some women.

items.title: Positive well-being during the menopausal transition: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 19 studies to see how the menopause transition relates to positive well-being, such as good mood and satisfaction with life, rather than distress. Most studies found no clear link between menopausal stage and well-being. Symptoms like hot flushes were linked to lower well-being in only one study. The authors suggest positive well-being may be largely unaffected by menopause.
keyPoints: Only 2 of 18 studies found a significant link between menopausal stage and well-being.
One study found hot flushes and night sweats were linked to lower well-being.
Four studies found that overall symptom scales were linked to lower well-being, mainly because those scales include psychological symptoms like crying spells.
Positive well-being may be largely unaffected by menopause and could help women cope with the challenges of midlife.

items.title: Identification of depression and anxiety during pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis of test accuracy
items.summary: This review pooled 16 studies to see how well common questionnaires pick up depression and anxiety during pregnancy. Most evidence was about the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). At a score of 10 or more, it correctly flagged about 84 in 100 women with major depression and correctly cleared about 87 in 100 without it. The authors say the EPDS alone is not perfectly suited for spotting depression in pregnancy, and evidence for other tools is very uncertain.
keyPoints: The EPDS at a cutoff of 10 or more had a combined sensitivity of 0.84 and specificity of 0.87 for major depression in pregnancy.
Most of the studies had a moderate to high risk of bias.
Only one study each looked at the GAD-2, PHQ-9, PHQ-2, Matthey mood question and Whooley questions, so their usefulness remains very uncertain.
Screening questionnaires may work best as a complement to a broader conversation between women and their healthcare professionals.

items.title: Predictive validity of the Edinburgh postnatal depression scale and other tools for screening depression in pregnant and postpartum women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 17 studies to see how well the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), a short questionnaire, picks up depression in pregnant and postpartum women. The EPDS correctly identified most women with depression and most women without it, both during pregnancy and after birth. It performed better than the PHQ-9 and about as well as some other tools. The authors concluded it can be used in preference to other tools in primary care or midwifery settings.
keyPoints: In pregnancy, the EPDS correctly flagged about 81% of women with depression and correctly cleared about 87% of those without.
After birth, the EPDS correctly flagged about 79% of women with depression and correctly cleared about 92% of those without.
The EPDS scored better than the PHQ-9 and similarly to the Beck Depression Inventory and the Kessler scale.
The authors concluded the EPDS performed excellently and can be used in preference to other tools in primary care or midwifery centres.

items.title: Prevalence and correlates of perinatal depression
items.summary: This study pulled together 128 earlier reviews to give a global picture of depression during pregnancy and after birth. On average, about 1 in 4 women (26-29%) were affected, whether during pregnancy or after the baby arrived. Rates looked higher when women filled in questionnaires than when they had a structured interview, and higher in some vulnerable groups. The included reviews were all of medium-to-high quality, but the authors say the original research behind them could still be improved.
keyPoints: Average prevalence was 26.3% for perinatal depression, 28.5% for depression in pregnancy and 27.6% for postnatal depression.
Rates were higher with self-report questionnaires (27.4%) than with structured interviews (17.0%), and higher in potentially vulnerable groups (32.5%) than in the general population (24.5%).

Factors linked with perinatal depression included past mental illness, stressful life events, low social support, a history of abuse, relationship conflict, the baby blues, child care stress, long-term health conditions, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, second-hand smoke and poor sleep.
The authors call for more standardised ways of assessing and diagnosing perinatal depression and for better-designed studies.

items.title: Screening for Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence on checking adults for depression and suicide risk in primary care, including pregnant and postpartum women. It recommends screening for depression, finding moderate certainty that screening has a moderate overall benefit. For suicide risk screening, it found there is not enough evidence to say whether the benefits outweigh the harms.
keyPoints: Screening adults for depression is recommended, including pregnant and postpartum women (B recommendation).
The Task Force has moderate certainty that depression screening gives a moderate net benefit.
Evidence is insufficient to judge the benefits and harms of screening for suicide risk in adults, including pregnant and postpartum women.
Untreated major depression can interfere with daily life and is linked to higher risks of heart problems and death.

items.title: Screening and Diagnosis of Mental Health Conditions During Pregnancy and Postpartum: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 4
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) on how mental health conditions should be screened for and diagnosed during pregnancy and the first year after birth. It covers depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, thoughts of suicide and postpartum psychosis. The conditions may start before pregnancy, appear for the first time during pregnancy or after birth, or get worse in that time. The abstract does not list the individual recommendations, but says each is rated by strength and quality of evidence.
keyPoints: The guideline covers screening and diagnosis of depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, suicidality and postpartum psychosis in pregnancy and postpartum.
It applies to people whose mental health conditions began before pregnancy, started in pregnancy or the first year after birth, or got worse during that time.
Recommendations are graded by strength and evidence quality, with Good Practice Points where evidence was lacking.
Treatment with medicines is covered in a separate ACOG guideline (No. 5).

items.title: Treatment and Management of Mental Health Conditions During Pregnancy and Postpartum: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 5
items.summary: This is a clinical practice guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG). It looked at the evidence on how safe and how well psychiatric medicines work for depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder and acute psychosis during pregnancy and breastfeeding. It gives recommendations on treating and managing these conditions, with a focus on medication, and rates each recommendation by strength and evidence quality. Where evidence was missing or too limited, it gives good practice points instead of formal recommendations.
keyPoints: The guideline covers treatment of depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder and acute postpartum psychosis in pregnancy and the first year after birth.
It reviews the safety and effectiveness of psychiatric medicines during pregnancy and lactation.
Each recommendation is classified by strength and quality of evidence.
Where evidence was inadequate or absent, ungraded good practice points give guidance instead.

items.title: Consensus statement on Singapore Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines on Depression and Anxiety
items.source: Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore
items.journal: Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore
items.summary: Experts in Singapore reviewed research from 2001 to 2022 and agreed on ten guideline statements to support women with depression and anxiety around pregnancy and after birth. Depression and anxiety in this period affect about 1 in 10 women in Singapore and are linked to outcomes such as low birthweight, preterm birth and effects on a baby's development and behaviour. The statements cover mental health advice before pregnancy, screening and assessment, and care and treatment.
keyPoints: Perinatal depression and anxiety affect about 1 in 10 women in Singapore and are linked to low birthweight, preterm birth and effects on infant development, temperament and behaviour.
Ten consensus statements cover preconception mental health advice, screening and assessment, and optimising care and treatment.
Special care is recommended for women who had severe maternal events, for adolescents and for women with special needs.
The guidelines also address the mental health needs of the infant.

items.title: Screening for depression among the general adult population and in women during pregnancy or the first-year postpartum: two systematic reviews to inform a guideline of the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care
items.source: Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care
items.organisation: Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care
items.summary: Two reviews looked for good-quality trials testing whether screening for depression in primary care (compared with no screening) leads to better outcomes. Only three trials were found, and just one involved pregnant or postpartum women. That trial of 462 postpartum women found fewer screened women were flagged as possibly depressed at 6 months, but the authors had serious concerns about how it was done. Overall, the evidence on screening in pregnancy and after birth is very uncertain, and better trials are needed.
keyPoints: Only one trial, of 462 postpartum women, looked at screening in pregnant or postpartum women.
In that trial, fewer screened women were identified as possibly depressed at 6 months postpartum (RR 0.59), and their average depression scores were lower.
The authors had serious concerns about the questionnaire cut-offs, diagnostic confirmation, selective outcome reporting and the size of the reported effects.
The evidence on screening in pregnant or postpartum women is described as very uncertain; for general adults, one trial gave moderate certainty that screening likely makes little to no difference.

items.title: Mapping global prevalence of depression among postpartum women
items.summary: This large review pulled together 565 studies from 80 countries to find out how common depression is after childbirth. About 17% of women worldwide were found to have postpartum depression, though rates varied a lot between regions. It was lower in wealthier, more developed countries and highest in Southern Africa.
keyPoints: Around 17% of women worldwide had postpartum depression, and the authors say this is roughly one in five women.
Rates were much higher in some regions, such as Southern Africa (about 40%), and lower in high-income countries.
Rates differed with factors like social support, partner care, violence, financial difficulties, life stress, smoking, alcohol and living conditions.
The authors say the many causes call for attention and action from health professionals, health authorities and the wider community.

items.title: Association Between Maternal Perinatal Depression and Anxiety and Child and Adolescent Development: A Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 191 studies covering almost 196,000 mother-child pairs. It looked at whether depression and anxiety around pregnancy and birth were linked to how children develop from infancy to age 18. Maternal depression and anxiety were linked to poorer social-emotional, thinking (cognitive) and adaptive behaviour outcomes in children, and the links continued into childhood and adolescence. The authors say these links are not proof of cause, and for language and motor development the results were less clear.
keyPoints: Depression and anxiety in pregnancy and after birth were linked to poorer social-emotional development in children.
Links with thinking (cognitive) skills and adaptive behaviour were also found, and they extended beyond infancy into childhood and adolescence.
Results for language and motor development were less clear, with some ranges that included no link.
The authors conclude that perinatal depression and anxiety are important targets for prevention and early support for mothers.

items.title: Non-clinical interventions for reducing unnecessary caesarean section
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 29 studies of non-clinical approaches (such as childbirth classes, relaxation training, and changes to how hospitals and doctors work) meant to reduce unnecessary caesarean sections. For women, some programmes, like childbirth training workshops and nurse-led relaxation training, may lower caesarean rates, but the evidence was low certainty and based on small studies. The strongest evidence was for approaches aimed at doctors, such as guidelines combined with second opinions or audit and feedback, which slightly lowered caesarean rates without clear harm. Many other interventions made little or no difference, and most studies were in high-income countries.
keyPoints: Childbirth training workshops, nurse-led relaxation training and couple-based psychosocial programmes may reduce caesarean section, but the evidence was low certainty and came from small studies.
Guidelines combined with a mandatory second opinion or with audit and feedback slightly reduced caesarean rates, with little or no difference in maternal or newborn outcomes (high certainty).
Education of doctors by a local opinion leader reduced elective caesarean section from 66.8% to 53.7%.
Antenatal education programmes and decision aids made little or no difference to caesarean rates, and the effect of many other interventions was very uncertain.

items.title: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 757: Screening for Perinatal Depression
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on checking for depression during pregnancy and after birth. Perinatal depression happens during pregnancy or in the first 12 months after delivery and affects about one in seven women. The guideline recommends that care providers screen for depression and anxiety at least once in the perinatal period using a standard, validated questionnaire, and check mood again at the postpartum visit.
keyPoints: Perinatal depression affects about one in seven women, during pregnancy or in the first 12 months after delivery.
Care providers are advised to screen for depression and anxiety symptoms at least once during pregnancy or after birth using a validated tool.
A full check of mood and emotional well-being, including screening for postpartum depression and anxiety, is recommended at the postpartum visit.
Screening alone can help, but starting treatment or referral to mental health care gives the most benefit.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-regression of the prevalence and incidence of perinatal depression
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 96 studies to estimate how common depression is during pregnancy and after birth (the perinatal period). About 12 in every 100 women (11.9%) were affected. Rates were higher in women living in low- and middle-income countries than in high-income countries. The review notes there was too little data to work out how many new cases appear over time, and few studies came from low-income countries.
keyPoints: The pooled estimate was that 11.9% of women experience depression in the perinatal period.
Rates were higher in women from low- and middle-income countries than in high-income countries (odds ratio 1.8).
Studies using symptom questionnaires found higher rates than those using formal diagnostic interviews.
Not enough data were available to estimate how many new cases occur (incidence).

items.title: Identifying the women at risk of antenatal anxiety and depression: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 97 studies to find out which factors make anxiety and depression more likely during pregnancy. The most common risk factors were having little partner or social support, a history of abuse or domestic violence, past mental illness, an unplanned or unwanted pregnancy, high stress, pregnancy complications and pregnancy loss. The authors say the causes are complex and that screening for anxiety and depression should be offered to all pregnant women.
keyPoints: Risk factors linked to anxiety and depression in pregnancy included lack of partner or social support, and a history of abuse or domestic violence.
Other factors were a personal history of mental illness, an unplanned or unwanted pregnancy, adverse life events and high perceived stress.
Current or past pregnancy complications and pregnancy loss were also linked to higher risk.
The authors conclude that screening for anxiety and depression should be universal practice in pregnancy.

items.title: Psychological and educational interventions for subfertile men and women
items.summary: This review looked at 39 trials (4,925 people) testing counselling, therapy or education programmes for people having fertility treatment. It asked whether these help with anxiety, depression and distress, and whether they improve the chance of a pregnancy or live birth. Many trials suggested small to moderate drops in anxiety and depression with psychological support, but the studies were poorly designed, so the results cannot be trusted. The review concludes that it is uncertain whether these programmes help with mental health or pregnancy rates.
keyPoints: About one in five couples seeking fertility treatment have clinically relevant anxiety, depression or distress.
Psychological interventions often showed lower anxiety and depression scores than usual care, but the studies were too different and too flawed to combine reliably.
Very few trials measured live birth or ongoing pregnancy, and those that did lost many participants along the way.
The authors call for better-designed trials, including comparison groups that receive similar time and attention.

items.title: Debriefing interventions for the prevention of psychological trauma in women following childbirth
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether a debriefing session after birth, where a woman talks through her birth experience, helps prevent psychological trauma. It pooled seven trials from the UK, Australia and Sweden. The trials showed no clear benefit or harm from debriefing, but the evidence was mostly low or very low quality.
keyPoints: No clear difference in trauma symptoms or PTSD between women who had a debriefing session and those who had standard postnatal care alone.
The evidence was mostly low or very low quality, with few studies and a high risk of bias.
The authors found no evidence to support routine debriefing for women who felt their birth was traumatic.
The authors suggest that better emotional care from health professionals during birth may help reduce the risk of birth feeling traumatic.

items.title: Advocacy interventions to reduce or eliminate violence and promote the physical and psychosocial well-being of women who experience intimate partner abuse
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 13 trials (2141 women) testing advocacy, meaning informal counselling, safety planning and help reaching services, for women who have experienced abuse by a partner. Advocacy seemed to bring some benefits, but most studies were small, so it is unclear how large the benefits are. Brief advocacy may help with depression and abuse, especially in pregnancy, while intensive advocacy may help women leaving shelters over the following one to two years.
keyPoints: Brief advocacy (under 12 hours) may give small short-term mental health benefits: fewer women developed depression in two healthcare studies.
In pregnancy, brief advocacy was linked to less minor physical abuse and less emotional abuse at about one year in one study.
Intensive advocacy for women leaving shelters may slightly improve quality of life and reduce severe physical abuse at 24 months, but did not clearly reduce depression.
Advocacy showed no clear effect on sexual abuse, and the authors say the size of benefit is uncertain because most studies were small.

items.title: Guideline No. 465: Obstetrical Anal Sphincter Injuries (OASIs) Part II: Long-Term Management and Counselling Regarding Subsequent Mode of Delivery
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline covers long-term care for women who had a severe perineal tear involving the anal sphincter during birth (called an OASI). It says dedicated follow-up clinics and pelvic health physiotherapy play a key role in recovery and long-term outcomes. It also offers new tools to help women and their care providers decide together how to give birth next time. The abstract does not give a certainty rating for its recommendations.
keyPoints: Dedicated follow-up clinics and pelvic health physiotherapy play a critical role in recovery and long-term outcomes after a severe tear.
Women should be told about the possible benefits of referral to specialized centers, including a possibly better long-term outlook.
The guideline gives new algorithms to support shared decision-making about the mode of delivery after an earlier OASI.
Access to these services should not depend on where a woman lives or what she can afford, and telehealth and local provider training are suggested to help.

items.title: The effects of warm perineal compress on perineal trauma and postpartum pain: a systematic review with meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies (10 randomised trials and 4 non-randomised) to see whether a warm compress held against the perineum during the pushing stage of labour helps protect against tearing and pain. Women who had a warm compress had less perineal pain, fewer second-, third- and fourth-degree tears, and fewer episiotomies. They were also more likely to have an intact perineum. There was no clear difference in first-degree tears, the length of the pushing stage, or babies' Apgar scores.
keyPoints: Warm perineal compress during the second stage of labour reduced postpartum perineal pain.
It lowered the rate of second-, third- and fourth-degree tears and of episiotomy.
Women using it were about three times as likely to have an intact perineum.
No clear difference was found for first-degree tears, length of the second stage, or Apgar scores at 1 and 5 minutes.

items.title: Perineal techniques during the second stage of labour for reducing perineal trauma and postpartum complications
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 17 trials with about 13,700 women to see whether techniques used by midwives in the pushing stage of labour reduce perineal tears and heavy bleeding after birth. A warm compress on the perineum probably lowers serious (third- or fourth-degree) tears and perineal pain. For most other techniques, such as hands-off birth, massage and vocalisation, the evidence was low quality or very uncertain. Overall, the authors say the evidence is very uncertain and very few studies measured bleeding after birth.
keyPoints: A warm compress on the perineum likely reduces third- or fourth-degree tears and probably reduces perineal pain (moderate-certainty evidence).
Warm compress combined with massage likely reduces second-degree tears compared with no technique, and probably increases maternal satisfaction (moderate-certainty evidence).
Perineal massage alone, hands-off (poised) birth and vocalisation showed little clear effect on tears, and the evidence was low or very low certainty.
Few studies reported postpartum haemorrhage, so effects on bleeding after birth remain unclear.

items.title: Hyaluronidase for reducing perineal trauma
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether an injection of hyaluronidase (an enzyme) into the perineum during the second stage of labour can reduce tearing, episiotomy and swelling for women having a first vaginal birth. It combined five trials with 747 women. Compared with a placebo injection, it made little or no difference to tears or episiotomy, but it probably reduced swelling 24 hours after birth. Compared with no injection, it may have lowered tears or episiotomy, but the evidence was low quality, so it is still uncertain whether it truly works.
keyPoints: Versus placebo injection, hyaluronidase may make no difference to perineal tears, episiotomy or third and fourth degree tears (low-certainty evidence).
Versus placebo, it likely reduced perineal swelling 24 hours after birth (moderate-certainty evidence).
Versus no injection, it may lower the chance of tears or episiotomy (low-certainty evidence), but results for episiotomy and milder tears were very uncertain.
No side effects were reported in the trials, but the authors say there are too few high-quality trials to judge effectiveness and safety.

items.title: Guideline No. 457: Obstetrical Anal Sphincter Injuries (OASIS) Part I: Prevention, Recognition, and Immediate Management
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looks at severe vaginal tears that involve the muscle around the anus (called obstetrical anal sphincter injuries, or OASIS). It covers how to lower the chance of these tears, how to spot them, and how to treat them right after birth. Some birth practices and good early care are linked to fewer tears and fewer lasting problems. The abstract does not give specific certainty ratings for each recommendation.
keyPoints: Some birth practices are linked to lower rates of severe tears, such as controlling and flexing the baby's head and using a cut called a mediolateral episiotomy when appropriate.
Correct diagnosis and repair of these tears can reduce short- and long-term complications.
Giving antibiotics to prevent infection and managing bowel and bladder function after the tear are part of recommended immediate care.
Better detection and a standard way of classifying these injuries should help limit long-term problems and improve research.

items.title: Predictive factors for obstetric anal sphincter injury in primiparous women: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 21 studies of first-time mothers to see what is linked to damage to the anal sphincter muscle (a deeper type of perineal tear) found on ultrasound after a first vaginal birth. About 1 in 4 women (26%) had ultrasound signs of sphincter damage, and about 1 in 5 had damage that was not noticed at the birth itself. Several factors were linked to it, including forceps delivery, shoulder dystocia, labor augmentation and episiotomy. Most of the studies had some risk of bias, so the results should be read with care.
keyPoints: 26% of women had ultrasound evidence of anal sphincter damage after a first vaginal birth.
20% of women had sphincter damage on ultrasound that was not reported clinically at the birth.
Forceps delivery, shoulder dystocia, labor augmentation, episiotomy and a shorter perineal body before birth were linked to higher odds of damage.
Antenatal perineal massage and a pelvic floor muscle dilator in labor did not change the odds; age, BMI, induced labor, epidural and baby's birth weight showed no difference.

items.title: Predictors for sexual dysfunction in the first year postpartum: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies looking at what raises the chance of sexual problems and painful sex in the first year after giving birth. Women who had a tear involving the anal sphincter had higher odds of both sexual problems and painful sex. Having an episiotomy was linked to painful sex, and instrument-assisted vaginal birth was linked to sexual problems. The authors conclude that injury to the perineum, rather than how the baby is born, matters most.
keyPoints: Anal sphincter injury was linked to higher odds of sexual dysfunction (OR 3.00) and painful sex (OR 1.92).
Episiotomy was linked to painful sex (OR 1.64) but not clearly to sexual dysfunction overall.
Caesarean birth was linked to lower odds of painful sex compared with spontaneous vaginal birth, but did not clearly change the odds of sexual dysfunction.
Instrument-assisted vaginal birth was linked to sexual dysfunction (OR 1.70), with no clear difference for painful sex.

items.title: Hands-on versus hands-off techniques for the prevention of perineal trauma during vaginal delivery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled five randomized trials (7,287 women) comparing two ways of delivering the baby's head: a 'hands-on' technique, where the midwife or doctor presses on the baby's head and the perineum, and a 'hands-off' technique. Overall rates of severe tearing (third- or fourth-degree) were similar between the two approaches. Hands-on delivery was linked to more third-degree tears and more episiotomies. The abstract does not give a certainty rating for the evidence.
keyPoints: Severe perineal trauma (third- or fourth-degree tears) was similar with hands-on and hands-off techniques (1.5% vs 1.3%).
Third-degree tears were more common with hands-on delivery (2.6% vs 0.7%).
Episiotomy was more common with hands-on delivery (13.6% vs 9.8%).
No clear difference was found in intact perineum or in first-, second- or fourth-degree tears.

items.title: Antibiotic prophylaxis for operative vaginal delivery
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether giving antibiotics through a drip right after a vacuum or forceps birth lowers the chance of infection. Two trials with 3813 women were included. Antibiotics reduced infections of the tear or stitches in the perineum (the area between the vagina and anus), probably reduced wound breakdown, and slightly eased perineal pain. For some outcomes, such as womb infection (endometritis) and side effects, the evidence was too weak to tell, and most of the evidence came from one large study in a high-income country.
keyPoints: Antibiotics given after a vacuum or forceps birth reduced superficial and deep perineal wound infections (high-certainty evidence).
They probably reduced wound breakdown and serious infectious complications.
They slightly improved perineal pain, and may slightly reduce hospital readmission.
The effect on womb infection, side effects and length of hospital stay is unclear because the evidence was low-certainty.

items.title: Systematic review of pelvic floor interventions during pregnancy
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pulled together 22 randomized trials of healthy pregnant women to see whether pelvic floor exercises during pregnancy help with childbirth and pelvic floor problems. Pelvic floor muscle training shortened the second stage of labour in the largest study and reduced urinary incontinence (bladder leaks). Perineal massage was linked to less perineal pain in some trials. The EPI-NO perineal dilator device showed no benefit in most studies.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training reduced urinary incontinence, based on 10 trials.
The largest training study found a shorter second stage of labour.
Two of six perineal massage trials reported less perineal pain.
Two of three EPI-NO dilator studies showed no benefit.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 198: Prevention and Management of Obstetric Lacerations at Vaginal Delivery
items.summary: This is an ACOG practice guideline on tears (lacerations) that happen during vaginal birth. It explains that tears are common and that most do not cause lasting problems. Severe tears that reach the anal sphincter muscles are less common but can lead to pelvic floor injury, leaking of urine or stool, pain and sexual difficulties that may last for years. The guideline aims to give evidence-based advice on preventing, spotting and repairing tears, and on episiotomy.
keyPoints: Tears to the cervix, vagina, vulva and perineum are common after vaginal birth.
Most tears do not cause long-term problems with how the body works.
Severe tears into or through the anal sphincter are less frequent but are linked to pelvic floor injury, incontinence, pain and sexual dysfunction.
Symptoms from severe tears can persist or appear many years after birth.

items.title: Pushing/bearing down methods for the second stage of labour
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 21 trials (about 3,700 women) that compared different ways of pushing in the second stage of labour. It looked at spontaneous versus directed pushing, and at delaying pushing versus pushing straight away when a woman has an epidural. Neither approach clearly changed serious perineal tears or episiotomy rates. The evidence ranged from moderate to very low quality, so the authors could not name a best method.
keyPoints: Spontaneous and directed pushing showed no clear difference in third or fourth degree tears, episiotomy, or the length of the second stage of labour.
With an epidural, delayed pushing meant less time actually pushing (about 19 minutes less) and slightly more spontaneous vaginal births, but the second stage lasted about 56 minutes longer overall.

Delayed pushing was linked to a higher chance of low umbilical cord blood pH, based on four studies, while newborn intensive care admissions and low five-minute Apgar scores showed no clear difference.
There is no conclusive evidence for any one pushing style, so the woman's preference, comfort and clinical situation should guide the choice.

items.title: Perineal techniques during the second stage of labour for reducing perineal trauma
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 22 trials (about 15,000 women) testing things a midwife or doctor might do around the perineum (the skin between the vagina and anus) in the pushing stage of labour to reduce tearing. Warm compresses and perineal massage may lead to fewer serious (third- and fourth-degree) tears. For most other outcomes and techniques, the results were unclear, inconsistent or based on too few studies. The trials were generally at moderate to high risk of bias.
keyPoints: Warm compresses probably reduce third- and fourth-degree tears (moderate-quality evidence), but did not clearly change other outcomes.
Perineal massage probably reduces third- and fourth-degree tears (moderate-quality evidence) and may increase the chance of an intact perineum, though results varied a lot between studies.
Hands-on versus hands-off made no clear difference to tearing; hands-off may mean fewer episiotomies, but this evidence was poor quality.
There was not enough evidence on Ritgen's manoeuvre, cold compresses, oils or perineal protection devices to draw conclusions.

items.title: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis after normal vaginal birth for reducing maternal infectious morbidity
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether giving antibiotics to every woman after an uncomplicated vaginal birth, compared with placebo or no antibiotics, prevents infections. Only three older trials (1,779 women) were found, and the evidence was low to very low quality. Antibiotics may lower the chance of endometritis (infection of the womb lining), but made little or no difference to urinary tract infections, wound infection after episiotomy, or length of hospital stay. The authors say the evidence is too limited to guide routine practice.
keyPoints: Routine antibiotics may reduce the risk of endometritis after an uncomplicated vaginal birth, but the evidence is very low quality.
Antibiotics made little or no difference to urinary tract infections, wound infection after episiotomy, or hospital stay.
Only three trials from the 1960s and 1990s were included, and most had a high risk of bias.
Antibiotics are not a substitute for infection prevention measures around childbirth, and wider use can add to antibiotic resistance.

items.title: Practice Bulletin No. 165: Prevention and Management of Obstetric Lacerations at Vaginal Delivery
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists looks at tears that can happen during vaginal birth and how they are prevented, found and repaired. It explains that tears are common and that most do not cause lasting problems. Severe tears that reach the anal sphincter happen less often but are more likely to cause pelvic floor injury, leaks of urine or stool, pain and sexual difficulties, sometimes for many years. The abstract does not give details of the specific recommendations or the certainty of the evidence.
keyPoints: Tears of the cervix, vagina, vulva and perineum are common after vaginal birth.
Most tears do not lead to problems with how the body works afterwards.
Severe tears into or through the anal sphincter are less common but linked to a higher risk of incontinence, pain and sexual difficulties.
Symptoms from severe tears can last or appear many years after birth.

items.title: Obstetrical Anal Sphincter Injuries (OASIS): Prevention, Recognition, and Repair
items.source: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.organisation: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline reviews the evidence on serious childbirth tears that involve the anal muscle (OASIS): how to prevent them, spot them, repair them, and plan future births. These tears can cause lasting problems such as leaking from the bowel, pain and fistulas. After a successful repair, most women can safely have a vaginal birth next time, and the chance of the same injury happening again is about 4-8%.
keyPoints: Every woman should be carefully checked for tears after birth, and deeper tears should get a rectal examination before repair to look for anal sphincter injury.
Using episiotomy only when needed (rather than routinely) lowers the rate of these tears, and slowing the baby's head as it emerges also helps.

After repair, a single dose of IV antibiotics, laxatives, and pain relief with anti-inflammatories and paracetamol are recommended; women with ongoing bowel leakage should be referred to pelvic floor physiotherapy.
The risk of this injury happening again in a later birth is 4-8%, and about 2.3 planned caesareans would be needed to prevent one case of bowel leakage, which also adds maternal risks.

items.title: Worldwide prevalence of dysmenorrhea: a systematic review and meta-analysis across 70 countries
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 336 studies across 70 countries to estimate how common period pain (dysmenorrhoea) is. About 7 in 10 women (71.3%) reported period pain, and it was more common in some places and groups, such as university students. The studies varied a lot from one to the next, and the authors rated the certainty of the evidence as very low, so the exact numbers should be treated as rough estimates.
keyPoints: The pooled worldwide prevalence of period pain was 71.3%.
Pain with no underlying cause (primary dysmenorrhoea) was estimated at 73%, and pain linked to another condition (secondary dysmenorrhoea) at 35%.
Period pain was reported more often in Central America (89.6%), Sri Lanka (97.7%), among adults (73.3%) and at universities (78.4%).
Results differed greatly between studies and the certainty of evidence was very low.

items.title: Progesterone receptor modulators for endometriosis
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at drugs called progesterone receptor modulators (mifepristone and gestrinone) as treatment for endometriosis. Nine trials with 922 women were included, and no new trials were found in this update. Mifepristone may ease period pain but may cause hot flushes, while gestrinone had mixed results compared with other medicines. The evidence was low to very low certainty, so firm conclusions are not possible.
keyPoints: Mifepristone may reduce period pain (dysmenorrhoea) in women with endometriosis after three months, based on low-certainty evidence from one study.
Mifepristone may cause more hot flushes, and its effect on painful sex is very uncertain.
Gestrinone may be less effective than leuprorelin for period pain but may help painful sex more and cause fewer hot flushes.
The effects of gestrinone compared with danazol are uncertain, and there is not enough evidence for other drugs in this group.

items.title: Noninvasive Diagnosis of Endometriosis in Adolescents and Young Female Adults: A Systematic Review
items.source: Journal of Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology
items.journal: Journal of Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology
items.summary: This review looked at 26 studies, covering 2,299 girls and young women aged 8 to 25, to see how endometriosis can be found without surgery. Period pain was the most common symptom, followed by long-lasting pelvic pain. Ultrasound and MRI scans both helped find signs of the condition, though they are not perfect. MRI may pick up signs even when an earlier ultrasound looked normal.
keyPoints: Period pain (dysmenorrhoea) and chronic pelvic pain were the key symptoms of endometriosis in adolescents.
Among adolescents suspected of having endometriosis, 32.8% showed at least one sign on ultrasound.
Ultrasound can miss subtle lesions, while MRI showed promise, even after a normal ultrasound.
The authors say early recognition and proactive diagnosis are important for managing endometriosis in adolescents.

items.title: Aerobic exercise to alleviate primary dysmenorrhea in adolescents and young women: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 16 randomized trials with 918 adolescents and young women who have period pain with no underlying disease (primary dysmenorrhea). Aerobic exercise, done for at least one menstrual cycle, reduced both how strong the pain was and how long it lasted. Results varied a lot between studies, and the authors rate the evidence for the best exercise types and doses as moderate quality. More trials in younger teens are still needed.
keyPoints: Aerobic exercise lowered period pain intensity and shortened pain duration by about 12.5 hours on average.
Pilates, low-intensity exercise, up to two sessions a week, and two menstrual cycles of exercise showed the biggest effects.
Results differed widely between studies, so the size of the benefit is uncertain.
The authors call for more trials in younger age groups to guide advice for adolescents.

items.title: Guideline No. 345: Primary Dysmenorrhea
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline reviews how to assess and treat primary dysmenorrhea, which is period pain with no underlying cause found. It says this pain is common but often undertreated, even though effective, low-cost treatments exist. Treatments include anti-inflammatory pain medicines (NSAIDs) and hormonal contraceptives, and they can be started without a pelvic exam or waiting for a firm diagnosis.
keyPoints: Primary dysmenorrhea is common and often undertreated or dismissed, despite effective treatment being widely available at minimal cost.
Treatment includes non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and hormonal contraceptives.
Treatment can be provided without a pelvic examination or invasive procedures and should not be delayed pending a definitive diagnosis.
Treating the pain may improve quality of life and reduce time away from school or work; untreated persistent pain may develop into a chronic pain syndrome.

items.title: Pharmacologic Interventions for Endometriosis-Related Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 31 randomised trials (8,665 people) to compare medicines for pain caused by endometriosis. Several treatments worked better than placebo, including leuprolide combined with the combined pill, dienogest, leuprolide alone and the combined pill alone. The authors suggest some options may suit particular pain types better, and call for larger, better-designed trials to confirm the results.
keyPoints: Four treatments beat placebo for endometriosis-related pelvic pain: leuprolide plus the combined pill, dienogest, leuprolide alone, and the combined pill.
Leuprolide combined with the combined pill was the most effective for overall pelvic pain.
Elagolix and vitamin C plus vitamin E were the most effective for period pain and pain during sex.
Gestrinone worked best for pelvic pain that is not linked to periods.

items.title: Efficacy of non-pharmacological interventions for primary dysmenorrhoea: a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 33 randomised trials testing eight non-drug treatments for period pain with no known cause (primary dysmenorrhoea). All eight, including exercise, herbs, acupuncture, aromatherapy, TENS, topical heat, acupressure and yoga, may reduce pain compared with placebo or no treatment. Exercise, acupuncture and topical heat showed the biggest drops in pain scores. The authors say these may help in the short term, but larger and better-quality studies are needed.
keyPoints: Eight non-drug approaches may all reduce period pain compared with placebo or no treatment.
Exercise, acupuncture and topical heat probably gave the largest reduction in pain scores.
Exercise and acupuncture are considered potentially effective for short-term treatment.
Larger, higher-quality research is still needed.

items.title: Ginger for Pain Management in Primary Dysmenorrhea: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: Journal of Integrative and Complementary Medicine
items.journal: Journal of Integrative and Complementary Medicine
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies testing ginger for period pain in women with no underlying condition causing it (primary dysmenorrhoea). Ginger reduced both how strong the pain was and how long it lasted compared with a placebo. It worked about as well as anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) and exercise for pain strength. The authors say the findings are limited because many studies had a risk of bias and little safety information was reported.
keyPoints: Ginger reduced period pain intensity and pain duration more than placebo.
Ginger and NSAIDs showed no difference in pain intensity.
Ginger and exercise also showed no difference in pain intensity.
Safety data were rarely reported, so the balance of risks and benefits is unclear.

items.title: Vitamin C and E antioxidant supplementation may significantly reduce pain symptoms in endometriosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled five randomised trials of women with endometriosis who took vitamin C and vitamin E together or a placebo. More of the women taking the vitamins reported less chronic pelvic pain, less period pain and less pain during sex than those on placebo. The authors say this suggests the vitamins may help with endometriosis pain, but they describe it as a possible benefit.
keyPoints: Vitamin C and E together were linked to more women reporting less chronic pelvic pain than placebo.
More women on the vitamins also reported relief from period pain (dysmenorrhoea).
Pain during sex (dyspareunia) was also reported as improved more often with the vitamins.
The authors conclude vitamins C and E have a potential ability to ease endometriosis pain.

items.title: Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) for pain control in women with primary dysmenorrhoea
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at TENS, a small device that sends gentle electrical pulses through the skin, as a way to ease period pain. It combined 20 trials with 585 women. Both high-frequency and low-frequency TENS may reduce pain compared with a placebo or no treatment, but the evidence is low quality, so the true effect is uncertain. Very few side effects were reported, though many trials did not report on them.
keyPoints: High-frequency TENS may reduce period pain compared with placebo or no treatment (low-certainty evidence).
Low-frequency TENS may reduce period pain compared with placebo or no treatment (low-certainty evidence).
It is uncertain whether TENS works better or worse than paracetamol, acupressure or other therapies, because the evidence is low or very low quality.
Few adverse effects were reported, but many trials did not report on them, so safety is not well established.

items.title: Comparative effectiveness of exercise interventions for primary dysmenorrhea: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 49 trials (3,129 women) to compare different kinds of exercise for period pain with no known underlying cause (primary dysmenorrhoea). All six types of exercise were linked to less menstrual pain. Resistance exercise and multi-component exercise (a mix of exercise types) showed the clearest drops in pain intensity. How well exercise worked also depended on how long, how often and for how long each session women trained.
keyPoints: All six exercise types studied were linked to reduced period pain.
Resistance exercise and multi-component exercise showed statistically significant reductions in pain intensity.
Meaningful pain relief appeared with 4 to 8 weeks of exercise training; resistance exercise worked best beyond 8 weeks.
Multi-component exercise and stretching ranked best for menstrual symptoms, and core-strengthening and multi-component exercise ranked best for shortening pain duration.

items.title: Efficacy of Zinc Supplementation in the Management of Primary Dysmenorrhea: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled six randomised trials with 739 women who had period pain without an underlying condition (primary dysmenorrhoea). Women taking zinc supplements reported less pain than those taking a placebo. Taking zinc for 8 weeks or longer was linked with greater pain relief, and side effects were not significantly different from placebo. The review authors concluded zinc looks effective and well tolerated, though the abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Zinc supplements reduced period pain more than placebo across six trials (739 women).
Taking zinc for 8 weeks or longer was linked with greater pain reduction.
Doses as low as 7 mg/day of elemental zinc gave significant relief; higher doses added only a small extra benefit.
Side effects did not differ significantly between zinc and placebo, suggesting good tolerability.

items.title: Effect of Vitamin D Supplementation on Primary Dysmenorrhea: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from 8 randomized trials with 695 women who had period pain with no underlying condition (primary dysmenorrhea). Women who took vitamin D by mouth reported less pain than those given a placebo. The pain relief was seen when the average weekly dose was over 50,000 IU. The authors conclude vitamin D could be an alternative way to ease period pain.
keyPoints: Eight randomized trials (695 participants) were combined in the analysis.
Vitamin D lowered period pain scores compared with placebo.
Pain eased when the average weekly dose was over 50,000 IU, whether taken for fewer or more than 70 days.
The authors suggest vitamin D supplementation is an alternative treatment for period pain.

items.title: Combined oral contraceptive pill for primary dysmenorrhoea
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 21 trials (3723 women) to see how well combined birth control pills treat period pain that has no underlying pelvic cause. The pills reduced pain more than placebo, with a moderate size of benefit. They also caused more side effects, especially irregular bleeding, headaches and nausea. It was unclear whether the pills work better than anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs), because only one small study compared them.
keyPoints: Combined pills reduce period pain more than placebo or no treatment (high-quality evidence for the size of the pain reduction).
About 28% of women improved on placebo, versus roughly 37% to 60% of women using the pill.
Side effects were more common with the pill: irregular bleeding (high-quality evidence), plus headaches and nausea (moderate-quality evidence).
Taking the pill continuously (no break) may ease pain more than the standard regimen, but the evidence is low quality and long-term safety data are needed.

items.title: Prevalence and Risk Factors of Primary Dysmenorrhea in Students: A Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 96 studies covering about 78,000 students (mostly university students, average age 19) to see how common period pain without an underlying disease (primary dysmenorrhoea) is. About two in three students (66.1%) reported period pain, and the share seemed to rise over the last decade. Several lifestyle and health factors were linked to having period pain, though a link does not prove cause.
keyPoints: Overall, 66.1% of students reported primary dysmenorrhoea: about 31% mild, 26% moderate and 8% severe.
Reported prevalence rose from 58.8% before 2010 to 71.5% in 2015 to 2021.
Linked factors included being underweight, skipping breakfast, poor sleep, staying up late, little exercise, and eating cold or spicy foods or being exposed to cold during periods.
Family history of period pain, irregular cycles, heavy stress, anxiety and negative mood during periods were also linked to period pain.

items.title: Effects of vitamin D supplementation in endometriosis: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether vitamin D supplements help women with endometriosis. Lab and animal studies suggested vitamin D might shrink endometriosis tissue and slow its growth. But when the human studies were combined, vitamin D did not clearly help period pain, ongoing pelvic pain, or the results of IVF. The studies were small and varied a lot, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Pooled results from two small human studies found no clear benefit of vitamin D for period pain in endometriosis.
Vitamin D also showed no clear effect on non-cyclic pelvic pain, and the one IVF study found no difference compared with placebo.
Animal and lab studies suggested vitamin D reduced endometriosis tissue growth and invasion, but this was not seen in human results.
The authors say the studies were few and varied, so more research is needed.

items.title: Efficacy of Physiotherapy Treatment in Primary Dysmenorrhea: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review pooled nine randomised trials (692 women) of physiotherapy for period pain with no known underlying cause. Treatments included exercise, massage, yoga, electrotherapy, stretching, kinesio tape and relaxation. Overall, physiotherapy reduced pain scores more than no treatment or a placebo, by about 1 point on a 10-point scale. The authors describe the evidence as low quality, and results varied a lot between studies.
keyPoints: Physiotherapy lowered period pain more than no treatment or placebo (about 1.1 points on the pain scale).
Techniques studied included exercise, massage, yoga, electrotherapy, stretching, kinesio tape and relaxation.
Few side effects were reported.
The authors say women may consider physiotherapy alone or alongside other treatments, but the evidence is low quality.

items.title: Nifedipine for primary dysmenorrhoea
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether nifedipine, a drug normally used to calm uterine contractions in preterm labour, can ease period pain. Only three small, older trials were found, and data from two of them (66 women) could be used. Nifedipine may have relieved pain better than placebo, but the evidence was of very low quality, so no firm conclusion can be drawn.
keyPoints: Nifedipine may give more pain relief than placebo in primary period pain, but the evidence is very low quality.
Side effects looked similar between nifedipine and placebo, though the data were too limited to be sure.
Participants said they would choose nifedipine over their previous painkiller if it were available.
Larger, better-run trials are needed before nifedipine can be considered a proven treatment.

items.title: Efficacy of herbal medicine (cinnamon/fennel/ginger) for primary dysmenorrhea: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled nine randomised trials with 647 women who had period pain with no underlying disease (primary dysmenorrhoea). Women taking cinnamon, fennel or ginger reported less pain than those taking a placebo, and cinnamon also shortened how long the pain lasted. The authors say more studies are needed to confirm these results.
keyPoints: Cinnamon, fennel and ginger each reduced period pain intensity compared with placebo.
Cinnamon also shortened how long the pain lasted.
The pain benefit was seen over one cycle and in the higher-quality studies.
The authors note that further studies are needed to confirm the findings.

items.title: An update and systematic review on the treatment of primary dysmenorrhea
items.summary: This review looked at 17 studies on treatments for period pain that is not caused by another condition (primary dysmenorrhoea). The treatments included herbal remedies, medicines, and acupuncture or acupressure. The authors suggest these may ease pain in several ways, such as lowering chemicals called prostaglandins, but say more trials are needed to confirm the benefits and check for side effects.
keyPoints: The review covered 17 papers: 10 on complementary medicine, 3 on drug treatments, and 4 on acupuncture or acupressure.
Herbal remedies, medicines and acupressure seem to reduce pain, possibly by lowering prostaglandins, raising beta-endorphins and improving blood flow to the womb.
Reported side effects included nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and liver and kidney problems.
The authors say further trials are needed to confirm the benefits and make sure the treatments are safe.

items.title: The Prevalence and Academic Impact of Dysmenorrhea in 21,573 Young Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined 38 studies of 21,573 young women to see how common period pain is and how it affects school and university life. About 7 in 10 young women reported period pain, no matter which country they lived in. Around 1 in 5 had missed school or university because of it, and about 4 in 10 said it hurt their concentration or performance in class.
keyPoints: About 71% of young women reported period pain, with similar rates in high-income and lower-income countries.
Rates were similar for school students (about 72.5%) and university students (about 74.9%).
About 20% reported missing school or university because of period pain.
About 41% said period pain negatively affected classroom performance or concentration.

items.title: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for heavy menstrual bleeding
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 19 trials (759 women) of anti-inflammatory painkillers such as naproxen and mefenamic acid for heavy periods. These drugs reduced heavy bleeding better than a dummy treatment (placebo), but not as well as tranexamic acid, danazol or the hormone coil (LNG IUS). Compared with the combined pill and some other treatments, there was no clear difference, but the studies were small. The evidence quality was low to moderate.
keyPoints: NSAIDs reduced heavy period bleeding more than placebo.
NSAIDs were less effective than tranexamic acid, danazol or the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG IUS).
Danazol caused more side effects than NSAIDs, and it is not a usual treatment for heavy periods today.
No clear difference was found between NSAIDs and the combined pill, luteal progestogen or ethamsylate, but most studies were too small to be sure.

items.title: Exercise for dysmenorrhoea
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether regular exercise eases period pain (primary dysmenorrhoea) in women with moderate-to-severe pain. It found 12 trials with 854 women. Low-quality evidence suggests exercise may reduce period pain by a noticeable amount, around 25 points on a 100-point pain scale. The evidence is low quality, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Exercise may reduce period pain intensity by about 25 mm on a 100 mm pain scale compared with no treatment (low-quality evidence).
The benefit was seen with exercise of about 45 to 60 minutes, three or more times a week, whatever the intensity (stretching, yoga, core work, Zumba or aerobic training).
Evidence on side effects, overall period symptoms, quality of life and exercise compared with anti-inflammatory painkillers was too limited to draw conclusions.
It is unclear if the benefits last after exercise stops or whether they apply to women over 25.

items.title: Physical activity for primary dysmenorrhea: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 15 randomized trials (1,681 women) to see whether regular physical activity helps period pain that is not caused by another condition. Regular exercise probably lowers period pain and may shorten how long it lasts, compared with not exercising. The trials were mostly of low or moderate quality and their results varied a lot, so researchers say better trials are needed to confirm this.
keyPoints: Physical activity was linked to lower pain intensity, about 1.89 cm less on a 10 cm pain scale.
Pain may have lasted about 3.92 hours less in women who were physically active.
Evidence quality was moderate for pain intensity and low for pain duration.
The authors say physical activity may be an effective treatment, but high-quality trials are needed to confirm it.

items.title: Heat therapy for primary dysmenorrhea: A systematic review and meta-analysis of its effects on pain relief and quality of life
items.summary: This review pulled together six trials of heat therapy, such as heating pads, for period pain that has no underlying pelvic condition. Heat eased period pain more than unheated placebo, more than pain medicine in two of the trials that could be combined, and more than no treatment. The results come from only a few small trials, so the evidence is suggestive rather than firm, and better quality trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Two trials found heat helped period pain more than an unheated placebo.
Three trials found heating pads relieved period pain more than pain medication.
One trial found heat reduced period pain compared with no treatment.
The results rest on few trials with small numbers of participants, so stronger trials are needed.

items.title: No. 345-Primary Dysmenorrhea Consensus Guideline
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This is a Canadian clinical guideline on primary dysmenorrhea, which means period pain with no underlying cause found. It reviewed trials and studies published between 2005 and 2016 to update advice on how the pain is investigated and treated. The guideline notes that this pain is common and often undertreated, and that effective treatment is widely available at low cost. Treating it may improve quality of life and reduce time lost from school or work.
keyPoints: Primary dysmenorrhea is period pain with no identified underlying cause, and it is common.
It is frequently undertreated, even though effective therapy is widely available at minimal cost.
Treatment can improve quality of life and reduce time lost from school or work.
The guideline updates the 2005 advice using evidence from 2005 to 2016.

items.title: Dietary supplements for dysmenorrhoea
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 27 trials (3,101 women, mostly students in their late teens or early twenties) testing dietary supplements for painful periods. Some supplements, such as ginger, fenugreek, zinc, vitamin B1 and a few herbs, showed signs of reducing pain, but nearly all findings came from single, small trials. All the evidence was low or very low quality, and very little information on side effects was reported, so safety is unclear.
keyPoints: There is no high quality evidence that any dietary supplement works for painful periods.
Some supplements (for example ginger, fenugreek, zinc sulphate, vitamin B1 and zataria) showed possible pain reduction, but the evidence was very limited and low quality.
Vitamin E showed no benefit compared with placebo or no treatment.
Only 4 of 27 studies reported side effects in both groups, so evidence of safety is lacking.

items.title: Acupuncture for dysmenorrhoea
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 42 trials (4640 women) testing acupuncture and acupressure for primary period pain, the cramping pain that has no underlying disease. Some trials found less pain with acupuncture than with no treatment or anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs), but the evidence was low or very low quality. The one trial at low risk of bias found no difference between real and sham acupuncture. Overall, there is not enough evidence to say whether acupuncture or acupressure works.
keyPoints: The authors concluded there is insufficient evidence to show whether acupuncture or acupressure helps primary period pain.
Compared with NSAIDs, acupuncture trials reported more pain relief and fewer side effects, but the evidence was low quality.
The only trial at low risk of bias found no difference between acupuncture and sham acupuncture.
Most trials did not report side effects, and evidence quality was low or very low for every comparison.

items.title: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for dysmenorrhoea
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 80 trials (5,820 women) of anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) for period pain with no underlying cause. NSAIDs relieved pain much better than placebo and appeared to work better than paracetamol. They also caused more side effects, such as stomach and nervous system effects. The evidence was mostly low quality, and it is not clear whether any one NSAID is best or safest.
keyPoints: NSAIDs were more effective than placebo for period pain: if 18% of women on placebo got moderate or excellent relief, about 45% to 53% on NSAIDs would.
NSAIDs caused more side effects than placebo: if 10% on placebo had side effects, about 11% to 14% on NSAIDs would, with more stomach and neurological effects.
