NSAIDs appeared to work better than paracetamol, though only three trials were available.
There was not enough evidence to say which individual NSAID is safest or most effective, and COX-2-specific NSAIDs showed no clear advantage.

items.title: The effectiveness and safety of physical activity and exercise on women with endometriosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together six randomised trials with 251 women who have endometriosis to see whether exercise helps with symptoms. Exercise appeared to improve quality of life and pain, and possibly mental health, pelvic floor problems and bone density. The studies were small, short and measured things in different ways, so only two could be combined in a meta-analysis. The authors say better, longer trials are needed to confirm the benefits.
keyPoints: Physical activity and exercise had beneficial effects on endometriosis symptoms, especially quality of life and pain relief.
The combined analysis of two studies showed improvements in quality of life related to pain, sense of control, and emotional well-being.
Benefits were also reported for mental health, pelvic floor problems and bone density across the included trials.
Study quality was limited and treatment periods were short, so higher-quality, longer trials are needed.

items.title: Exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation for adults with heart failure
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 60 trials (8,728 adults) of exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation for people with heart failure. Compared with no exercise, it probably lowers the chance of being admitted to hospital and probably improves quality of life, but there was no clear difference in deaths. Home-based and digitally supported programmes seemed to work about as well as centre-based ones. Women were under-represented in the trials, so the authors call for more research in women.
keyPoints: Exercise-based rehabilitation likely reduced hospital admissions from any cause (about 16% versus 24%, moderate-certainty evidence).
It likely improved quality of life on the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure questionnaire by an amount large enough to matter (moderate-certainty evidence).
There was no clear difference in deaths in the short term (low-certainty evidence).
Benefits looked similar whether programmes were home-based or centre-based, and with different types or amounts of exercise.

items.title: Prehabilitation for Patients Undergoing Orthopedic Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 48 trials (about 3,500 people, 61.5% women, average age 64) that compared exercise-based 'prehabilitation' before orthopedic surgery with usual care. Before knee or hip replacement, prehab improved function, muscle strength or quality of life, and before lumbar (lower spine) surgery it reduced back pain. Some benefits lasted after surgery, such as better function 6 weeks after knee replacement and 6 months after lumbar surgery. Many other results were of low or very low quality because of risk of bias and differences between studies.
keyPoints: Before knee replacement, prehabilitation improved function and muscle strength (moderate-certainty evidence).
Before hip replacement, it improved quality of life and muscle strength (moderate-certainty evidence).
Before lumbar surgery, it reduced back pain (high-certainty evidence) and improved quality of life (moderate-certainty evidence).
Other benefits were promising but based on low to very low quality evidence, so better trials are needed.

items.title: Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts
items.summary: This study pooled data from 15 groups that followed 47,471 adults for about 7 years to see how daily step counts relate to the chance of dying from any cause. People who took more steps each day had a lower risk of death. The benefit grew with more steps, then levelled off at roughly 6,000-8,000 steps a day for adults 60 and older and 8,000-10,000 steps a day for younger adults. The study shows an association, so it cannot prove that steps alone caused the lower risk.
keyPoints: Compared with the least active group (about 3,500 steps a day), the most active group (about 10,900 steps a day) had around half the risk of death from any cause.
Risk kept falling as steps increased, up to about 6,000-8,000 steps a day in adults 60 and older and 8,000-10,000 in those under 60.
Walking pace seemed to matter less once total daily steps were taken into account.
The authors say the findings can help set step guidelines for promoting physical activity.

items.title: Comparison of Power Training vs Traditional Strength Training on Physical Function in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 20 trials of healthy older adults (aged 60 and over, about two-thirds women) to compare power training, where weights are lifted as fast as possible, with traditional strength training. Power training was linked to a small improvement in physical function compared with traditional strength training. The evidence was low certainty because of risk of bias and small trial sizes, so larger, better-quality trials are needed.
keyPoints: Power training (lifting fast, lowering under control) was linked to a modest improvement in physical function compared with traditional strength training.
The result for self-reported physical function was uncertain, with a wide range that included no benefit.
Certainty of the evidence was low, mainly due to high risk of bias and imprecision.
The authors say larger, high-quality trials are needed for firmer conclusions.

items.title: Summarizing the effects of different exercise types in chronic low back pain - a systematic review of systematic reviews
items.summary: This review looked at 45 earlier reviews of exercise for long-lasting low back pain in adults aged 18 to 70. It compared nine types of exercise, such as yoga, Pilates, resistance training and walking. Several types gave small, mostly short-term improvements in pain and disability compared with no or minimal treatment, with no major difference between types. Many of the studies behind these reviews were of limited quality, so the certainty of the results is low to moderate.
keyPoints: Motor control exercises, Pilates, resistance training, traditional Chinese exercises and yoga gave small, mostly short-term benefits for pain and disability.
There was no major difference in effect between the exercise types.
Many of the included reviews were of low-to-moderate quality and based on trials with high risk of bias.
Conflicting results lowered the certainty of the evidence to very low to moderate.

items.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour
items.summary: These World Health Organization guidelines set out how much physical activity people of different ages need to get real health benefits and lower health risks. They cover children, adults and older adults, and look at time spent sitting as well as exercise. For the first time they also give specific advice for pregnant and postpartum women. The abstract does not give the exact amounts or a certainty rating.
keyPoints: The guidelines give evidence-based advice on how often, how hard and how long to be active for health benefits.
They cover children, adolescents, adults and older adults.
For the first time, they link sedentary behaviour (sitting time) with health outcomes.
They include recommendations for pregnant and postpartum women, and for people with chronic conditions or disability.

items.title: Dose-response associations between accelerometry measured physical activity and sedentary time and all cause mortality: systematic review and harmonised meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined data from eight studies of about 36,000 middle-aged and older adults (nearly three-quarters were women) whose movement was measured with activity trackers called accelerometers. People who did more physical activity of any kind, including light activity, had a lower risk of dying during follow-up than the least active people. People who spent more time sitting had a higher risk. These are links seen in observational studies, which cannot prove cause and effect.
keyPoints: Any physical activity, even light activity, was linked to a lower risk of death, with the biggest drop seen when moving from the least active group to the next.
The most active quarter of people had about 73% lower risk of death than the least active quarter (hazard ratio 0.27).
More time spent sitting was linked to higher risk of death, with the most sedentary quarter at about 2.6 times the risk of the least sedentary.
The findings apply to middle-aged and older adults, and the pattern was non-linear, with benefits levelling off at higher activity levels.

items.title: Physical activity for women with breast cancer after adjuvant therapy
items.summary: This review pooled 63 trials with 5,761 women who had finished chemotherapy or radiation for breast cancer. Physical activity programmes (aerobic exercise, resistance training, or both) gave small-to-moderate improvements in quality of life, emotional and physical function, anxiety and fitness. Few minor side effects were reported. The evidence was very low to moderate quality, so the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Physical activity gave small-to-moderate gains in quality of life, emotional function, perceived physical function, anxiety and cardiorespiratory fitness.
Some benefits, such as less fatigue, better fitness and more self-reported activity, lasted three months or longer after programmes ended.
No data were available on breast cancer deaths, deaths from any cause, or cancer coming back, so no conclusions were possible on these.
Trials varied a lot in the type, amount and length of activity and had a high risk of bias, so the best type of exercise is still unclear.

items.title: Interventions for promoting habitual exercise in people living with and beyond cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 23 trials with 1372 people who had had breast, prostate, colorectal or lung cancer and were not very active. It asked which approaches help people start and keep up regular exercise. Programmes that used goal setting, step-by-step increases in activity and instruction on how to exercise did best at helping people stick to guideline-level exercise, and they all included some supervision. Exercise programmes improved aerobic fitness at 8 to 12 weeks and at 6 months, but the evidence was low quality, and most studies were in white women with breast cancer.
keyPoints: Programmes that set goals, built up activity in graded steps and taught how to exercise were most common among those where 75% or more of people stuck to guideline-level exercise.
Exercise programmes improved aerobic fitness at 8 to 12 weeks and at 6 months compared with usual care (low-quality evidence).
Very few serious adverse effects were reported, which the authors say is reassuring that exercise is safe for people with cancer.
Long-term follow-up data are limited, and many studies had a high risk of bias or poor reporting.

items.title: Yoga for improving health-related quality of life, mental health and cancer-related symptoms in women diagnosed with breast cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 24 trials (2166 women) to see whether yoga helps women with breast cancer, during or after treatment. Compared with no therapy, yoga improved quality of life, eased fatigue and helped sleep in the short term, with moderate-quality evidence. Compared with psychosocial or educational programmes, yoga reduced depression, anxiety and fatigue. The evidence for yoga versus other exercise was very low quality and showed no clear difference.
keyPoints: Versus no therapy, yoga improved quality of life, reduced fatigue and reduced sleep problems in the short term (moderate-quality evidence).
Versus psychosocial or educational programmes, yoga reduced depression, anxiety and fatigue in the short term (moderate-quality evidence).
Yoga did not clearly reduce depression or anxiety versus no therapy, and had no clear medium-term effects on quality of life or fatigue.
Yoga may work about as well as other exercise, but this evidence is very low quality; no serious adverse events were reported.

items.title: Non-pharmacological interventions for cognitive impairment due to systemic cancer treatment
items.summary: This review looked at non-drug approaches, such as computer-based brain training, memory strategy training, meditation and physical activity, for memory and thinking problems after cancer treatment. Only five small trials were found, all in breast cancer survivors, and all had a high risk of bias. Brain training and memory strategy training showed some benefits for thinking skills, but the evidence was low quality. The effect of physical activity on thinking was unclear.
keyPoints: Only five small trials (235 people in total) were found, all in breast cancer survivors.
Computer-based cognitive training and compensatory strategy training showed some benefits for memory and self-reported thinking skills.
Evidence for physical activity and meditation on thinking skills was unclear, with just one small physical activity trial of 19 people.
The evidence was low quality, so the authors say findings should be read with caution and larger studies are needed.

items.title: Comparison of premenstrual dysphoric disorder treatment with antidepressants and combined oral contraceptives: a systematic review with network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 16 studies (5 in the combined analysis) on treating premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) with antidepressants called SSRIs or combined birth control pills. Both types of treatment helped. Taking paroxetine continuously worked best among the antidepressants, and a drospirenone and ethinylestradiol pill taken in a 24/4 schedule worked best among the pills. The authors say more studies directly comparing the two treatment types are still needed.
keyPoints: Both SSRI antidepressants and combined oral contraceptives were effective for managing PMDD.
Continuous paroxetine showed the greatest effect across all symptom areas measured.
The 24/4 drospirenone/ethinylestradiol pill was the most effective pill, helping both physical and emotional symptoms.
Choosing a treatment should take into account main symptoms, how well it is tolerated, and plans for pregnancy; head-to-head trials are still needed.

items.title: Prevalence, Risk Factors, and Treatments for Suicidality in People Living with Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD): A Systematic Review
items.source: Administration and Policy in Mental Health
items.journal: Administration and Policy in Mental Health
items.summary: This review pulled together 18 studies on suicidal thoughts and behaviours in people with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a severe mood condition linked to the menstrual cycle. The studies consistently found that people with PMDD are at higher risk of suicidality, though the reported rates varied a lot between studies. No studies tested treatments for suicidality in people with PMDD. Many of the studies had quality problems, so exact numbers should be read with care.
keyPoints: Evidence is clear that people with PMDD are at increased risk of suicidality, even though studies differed in methods and definitions.
Reported rates varied widely: 26%-86% for suicidal ideation, 11.5%-41.5% for suicide planning, and 7.1%-60.7% for suicide attempts.
Risk factors included other psychiatric conditions, high impulsivity, aggression and hopelessness scores, and hormonal factors.
No studies were found that tested treatments for suicidality in people with PMDD, and about 70% of studies had quality concerns.

items.title: Functional MRI evidence of brain alterations in premenstrual dysphoric disorder: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together brain-scan (fMRI) studies of women with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), covering 294 women with PMDD and 304 without. It found differences in how brain areas involved in controlling emotions are activated and connected. The authors say this suggests PMDD involves wide brain networks, not one single spot, and may help guide new treatments, since about 40 percent of women do not respond to SSRIs.
keyPoints: PMDD affects about 1.6% of women of reproductive age, and around 40% do not respond to SSRIs, the usual first treatment.
Women with PMDD showed less activation in some control and regulation areas of the brain, such as the anterior cingulate and prefrontal cortex.
They also showed more activation in the amygdala and insula, and weaker connections between emotion and control areas.
The authors suggest these brain differences could help in developing new treatments, but no treatment was tested.

items.title: The impact of menstruation-related symptoms on women's quality of life, work productivity, and economic burden: a structured narrative review
items.summary: This review pulled together 86 studies on painful periods, PMS/PMDD and heavy periods. It found these conditions are linked to lower quality of life, emotional distress and trouble coping at school or work. Most of the lost productivity came from people working while unwell rather than taking time off. Treatment often eased symptoms, but day-to-day functioning did not always improve to the same degree.
keyPoints: Painful periods, PMS/PMDD and heavy periods were all linked to lower quality of life, psychological distress and impaired school or work functioning.
Lost productivity was mainly from presenteeism (working while unwell) rather than absence, so counting sick days underestimates the impact.
Anxiety, low mood, emotional ups and downs and poor sleep were key contributors to reduced quality of life.
Treatment and medical consultations often improved symptoms, but gains in productivity were inconsistent, and the authors call for approaches that address both clinical and psychosocial needs.

items.title: Cognition and behaviour across the menstrual cycle in individuals with premenstrual dysphoric disorder - A systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 21 studies (1,222 people) that looked at thinking and behaviour at different points in the menstrual cycle in people with and without premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Tests of thinking skills, like memory and concentration, showed few and inconsistent differences linked to PMDD. Studies of how people process information suggest a tendency to focus on negative things may be central to the PMDD experience. The authors noted weaknesses in the studies, and the results could not be combined statistically.
keyPoints: Evidence that PMDD changes thinking performance (cognitive abilities) was limited and inconsistent.
Studies suggest a negative attentional bias, meaning attention drawn to negative things, is central to how PMDD is experienced.
How people process and think about information, and how they behave, may tell us more about PMDD than their absolute thinking abilities.
Many studies had risk of bias, such as no power calculation and unsuitable statistical methods, and the results could not be combined.

items.title: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and quality of life: a meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials comparing SSRI antidepressants with placebo, looking at whether they improve quality of life. SSRIs gave small-to-moderate improvements in quality of life for several conditions, including premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) and menopausal symptoms. The authors note that small studies, many people dropping out, and uneven participant groups limit how strongly SSRIs can be recommended for this purpose.
keyPoints: Compared with placebo, SSRIs improved quality of life in premenstrual dysphoric disorder (effect size 0.38) and menopausal symptoms (0.40).
Improvements were also seen in major depression, persistent depressive disorder, cancer and type 2 diabetes, but not clearly in COPD, heart failure or irritable bowel syndrome.
Paroxetine showed the largest effect among the SSRIs studied, and quality of life improved as depressive symptoms eased.
Small-study effects, high dropout rates and demographic imbalances limit how firmly SSRIs can be recommended to improve quality of life.

items.title: Intermittent selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for premenstrual syndromes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
items.summary: This review pooled eight randomised trials (460 women) comparing two ways of taking SSRI antidepressants for premenstrual syndromes such as PMDD: only in the second half of the cycle (intermittent) versus every day (continuous). It found no clear difference between the two in how many women improved, how many dropped out, or how much symptoms changed. All the studies had a moderate or high risk of bias, so the results should be read with caution. Because intermittent dosing avoids the risk of antidepressant withdrawal symptoms, the authors suggest it should be considered more often.
keyPoints: Eight trials with 460 women found no statistically significant difference between intermittent and continuous SSRI dosing for response rates.
Dropout rates and changes in symptom scores were also not meaningfully different between the two approaches.
All included studies had a moderate or high risk of bias.
Intermittent (luteal phase) dosing avoids withdrawal symptoms linked to long-term daily use, so the authors say it should be considered more commonly.

items.title: Short report: cognitive behavioral therapy - a primary mode for premenstrual syndrome management: systematic literature review
items.summary: This review looked at 32 studies of non-drug treatments for premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and premenstrual dysphoric disorder, mainly cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and psychoeducation (learning about PMS and how to manage it). All the studies found symptoms improved, in some cases to complete remission, with no side effects reported. Self-help packages seemed enough for most women, while the most severe cases needed one-to-one CBT. The authors say better-quality research is still needed.
keyPoints: All 32 studies found that non-drug approaches such as CBT and psychoeducation reduced PMS symptoms, from significant improvement to complete remission.
No side effects were reported, and the benefits lasted over time.
Self-help packages, including ones delivered through modern technology, appeared to be enough for most women.
The most severe forms of PMS needed one-to-one CBT.

items.title: Efficacy of combined oral contraceptives for depressive symptoms and overall symptomatology in premenstrual syndrome: pairwise and network meta-analysis of randomized trials
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: Researchers pooled the results of 9 randomized trials covering 1,205 women with premenstrual syndrome (PMS) or premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) to see whether combined birth control pills help. The pills worked better than placebo for overall premenstrual symptoms. They did not clearly help low mood or depressive symptoms in particular, and no one type of pill was shown to work better than another.
keyPoints: Combined oral contraceptives were more effective than placebo for overall premenstrual symptoms in PMS or PMDD.
They did not show a clear benefit over placebo for premenstrual depressive symptoms specifically.
No combined oral contraceptive was found to be more effective than any other.
The authors note that evidence for this treatment has been scarce.

items.title: Association Between Smoking and Premenstrual Syndrome: A Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from 13 studies with about 25,800 participants to look at whether smoking is linked to premenstrual syndrome (PMS). People who smoked were more likely to have PMS, and the link was stronger for the severe form, premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). The studies show an association only, so they cannot prove that smoking causes PMS. The authors suggest the link may run both ways: smoking may be used to ease low mood, or it may make symptoms worse.
keyPoints: Smoking was linked to a higher chance of PMS overall (odds ratio 1.56).
The link was stronger for PMDD (odds ratio 3.15) than for PMS (odds ratio 1.27).
The authors suggest nicotine may be used to relieve low mood, but may also worsen symptoms by affecting the brain's stress response.
Having both PMS or PMDD and tobacco use can make treatment more complicated.

items.title: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder Without Comorbid Psychiatric Conditions: A Systematic Review of Therapeutic Options
items.summary: This review looked at 55 studies on treating premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) in adult women who had no other mental health conditions. It found that the best-supported options were a type of antidepressant called SSRIs (especially paroxetine and fluoxetine) and low-dose combined hormonal pills. Other approaches such as light therapy, talking therapy, supplements and herbal medicines looked promising, but more research is needed to confirm they work.
keyPoints: PMDD affects about 2% to 8% of women during their reproductive years.
SSRI antidepressants, especially paroxetine and fluoxetine, were among the best options for PMDD.
Low doses of oral estrogen-progestin (combined hormonal) pills were also among the best options.
Light therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, supplements and herbal medicines showed promise but need more research.

items.title: Effect of nutritional interventions on the psychological symptoms of premenstrual syndrome in women of reproductive age: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review looked at 31 randomized trials (3,254 women aged 15 to 50) testing diet changes and supplements for the mood and emotional symptoms of premenstrual syndrome (PMS). Vitamin B6, calcium and zinc were the ones that most consistently helped. For many other options, such as vitamin D, magnesium and soy, there was not enough evidence to say either way. Almost all of the trials had a risk of bias, so the findings are not yet conclusive.
keyPoints: Vitamin B6, calcium and zinc consistently showed positive effects on psychological PMS symptoms.
There was not enough evidence for vitamin B1, vitamin D, whole grains, soy isoflavones, fatty acids, magnesium, multivitamins or PMS-specific diets.
Only 1 of the 31 trials had a low risk of bias.
More consistent, better-designed and clearly reported research is needed before firm nutrition advice can be given.

items.title: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues for premenstrual syndrome (PMS)
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 11 small trials (275 women) of GnRH agonists, medicines that switch off ovulation, for premenstrual syndrome (PMS), including the severe form called PMDD. GnRH agonists without add-back hormones clearly eased overall PMS symptoms compared with placebo. But they can cause menopause-like side effects, and more women stopped treatment because of side effects. It is still unclear whether adding back oestrogen or progestogen reduces side effects without weakening the benefit.
keyPoints: GnRH agonists without add-back improved overall PMS symptoms compared with placebo (high-certainty evidence).
Women on GnRH agonists were more likely to stop treatment because of side effects than women on placebo (high-certainty evidence).
GnRH agonists may increase menopausal side effects such as hot flushes, though this evidence was low certainty.
There was not enough evidence to show that add-back hormones reduce side effects without lowering benefit; the authors say these medicines can give a short-term break from PMS symptoms.

items.title: Effect of zinc supplementation on premenstrual symptoms: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from small trials testing zinc supplements for premenstrual symptoms (PMS) in women of reproductive age. Zinc reduced overall PMS scores and emotional symptoms, with moderate certainty, and physical symptoms, with low certainty. The authors say it shows promise but that only a few trials were included and they varied in how they were done, so more and better studies are needed.
keyPoints: Zinc supplements reduced total PMS scores and emotional symptoms, with moderate certainty of evidence.
Physical symptoms also improved, but the evidence was low certainty.
Only five trials were reviewed, and all had some concerns about risk of bias.
More large, well-run trials are needed to confirm benefit and work out the right dose.

items.title: Physical Activity and Menstrual Health Symptoms and Characteristics: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies
items.summary: This review pooled results from 82 observational studies (over 100,000 women) to see whether being more physically active is linked to better menstrual health. Women with lower activity levels had higher odds of period pain and premenstrual syndrome (PMS). Links with cycle length, bleed length and flow were mixed. Most studies were low quality, so these are links, not proof that exercise causes the difference.
keyPoints: Lower physical activity was linked to higher odds of menstrual pain (odds ratio 1.67) and PMS (odds ratio 1.22).
Lower activity was also linked to cycle irregularity, but this result was less certain.
Findings for cycle length, bleed length and flow were mixed.
Study quality was low: most studies were cross-sectional and relied on self-reported activity.

items.title: The prevalence of premenstrual dysphoric disorder: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 44 studies (about 50,000 people) to estimate how common premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is. When PMDD was confirmed by tracking symptoms daily over two cycles, about 3.2% of people had it. When it was only a provisional diagnosis, the figure was higher at 7.7%. The authors say studies using provisional diagnosis probably overestimate how common PMDD is.
keyPoints: Confirmed PMDD (symptoms tracked prospectively over two cycles) had a pooled prevalence of 3.2%.
Provisional PMDD diagnosis gave a higher estimate of 7.7%, which is likely to be artificially high.
In community-based samples with confirmed diagnosis, prevalence was 1.6%.
Results varied a lot between studies, by region, type of sample, and how PMDD was diagnosed.

items.title: Functional and structural neuroimaging in premenstrual dysphoric disorder: A systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 24 brain-imaging studies of women with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) and compared them with women without it. The results were not consistent across studies. Still, several brain areas involved in mood, emotion and thinking were linked to PMDD, and some changes seemed to match symptom strength and the stage of the menstrual cycle.
keyPoints: Studies looked at 608 women with PMDD and 418 healthy comparison women using different brain scanning methods.
Results were not consistent, but areas such as the prefrontal cortex, amygdala, hippocampus, insula, basal ganglia and cerebellum were implicated.
Some brain differences were tied to how severe symptoms were and to the cycle phase.
In the luteal phase (the days before a period), depressive symptoms were linked to higher serotonin transporter binding in the midbrain.

items.title: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 34 randomised trials comparing SSRI antidepressants (such as fluoxetine, sertraline and paroxetine) with placebo in women with PMS or PMDD. SSRIs probably reduce premenstrual symptoms, and seem to work better when taken every day than when taken only in the two weeks before a period. They also probably cause more side effects than placebo, most commonly nausea, weakness or low energy, and sleepiness. About two thirds of the studies were funded by drug companies and publication bias is suspected, so the results should be read with some caution.
keyPoints: SSRIs probably reduce overall self-rated premenstrual symptoms compared with placebo (moderate-certainty evidence).
Taking SSRIs continuously was probably more effective than taking them only in the luteal phase (the two weeks before a period).
SSRIs probably increase side effects, including nausea, weakness or low energy, sleepiness, insomnia, sexual problems and dry mouth.
68% of included studies were pharmaceutical-funded and publication bias is suspected, so findings should be interpreted with caution.

items.title: Biological rhythms in premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 25 studies on body rhythms, such as sleep and hormone patterns, in women with premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Some studies found that these women had lower melatonin, a higher body temperature at night, and felt they slept worse than women without PMS or PMDD. Other measures, such as cortisol, prolactin and objectively measured sleep, gave mixed results. The authors say research in this area is still growing.
keyPoints: Women with PMS/PMDD showed lower melatonin levels in some studies.
Nighttime core body temperature was higher in some women with PMS/PMDD.
Women with PMS/PMDD reported worse sleep quality than women without these conditions.
Results for cortisol, prolactin, thyroid stimulating hormone and objective sleep measures were conflicting, and wrist activity tracking showed no difference.

items.title: Premenstrual syndrome prevalence in Turkey: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 18 studies in Turkey, covering 6,890 women of reproductive age, to see how common premenstrual syndrome (PMS) is. They found that about half of the women (52.2%) had PMS. The authors say PMS is common in this group and that women could benefit from training on how to manage symptoms.
keyPoints: Overall, 52.2% of women in the 18 studies had premenstrual syndrome.
PMS was reported in 59% of high school students, 50.3% of university students and 66% of women in the general population.
Average age of participants was not significantly linked to how common PMS was.
The authors suggest health professionals offer training to help women manage PMS symptoms, and call for more studies on ways to cope with PMS.

items.title: Oral contraceptives containing drospirenone for premenstrual syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled five trials (858 women, mostly with PMDD, the severe form of PMS) testing combined pills with drospirenone and ethinylestradiol against placebo. The pill may ease overall premenstrual symptoms and reduce the effect of symptoms on work, social life and relationships, with small to moderate benefits. It may also cause more side effects than placebo, such as breast pain and nausea. The evidence was mostly low quality, and the placebo also helped many women.
keyPoints: Drospirenone pills may improve overall premenstrual symptoms and day-to-day functioning (productivity, social activities, relationships) in women with PMDD, with small to moderate effects.
The pill may lead to more side effects overall and more people stopping because of them; it probably causes more breast pain and may cause more nausea and bleeding between periods.
The effect on premenstrual mood symptoms is uncertain, and no serious rare side effects such as blood clots were reported in the trials.
It is not known whether benefits last beyond three cycles, whether the pill helps women with milder symptoms, or whether it beats other combined pills.

items.title: The Prevalence of Menstrual Cycle Disorders and Menstrual Cycle-Related Symptoms in Female Athletes: A Systematic Literature Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 60 studies of 6,380 female athletes not using hormonal contraceptives to see how common period problems and period-related symptoms are. Period problems were common, and painful periods (dysmenorrhoea) were the most frequent at about 1 in 3 athletes, though results varied a lot between studies. Most studies relied on athletes remembering their symptoms, and the authors say better, standardised ways of measuring problems like heavy bleeding are needed.
keyPoints: Painful periods were the most common period problem, affecting about 32% of athletes (range 7.8% to 85.6%).
Prevalence varied widely for every type of period disorder, including heavy menstrual bleeding, and little data existed on anovulation or luteal phase deficiency.
Mood-related symptoms appeared more common than physical ones, and more athletes reported symptoms in the first days of a period than before it.
Nine in ten studies relied on athletes recalling symptoms, and most studies were of moderate quality; the authors call for standard definitions and prospective tracking of cycles and symptoms.

items.title: A scoping review of hormonal clinical trials in menstrual cycle-related brain disorders: Studies in premenstrual mood disorder, menstrual migraine, and catamenial epilepsy
items.summary: This review looked at 85 studies of hormone treatments for three conditions linked to the menstrual cycle: premenstrual mood disorder, menstrual migraine and cycle-related epilepsy. Hormone treatments have been tested most often for premenstrual mood disorder and least for epilepsy. Combined birth control pills containing drospirenone showed promising results for both premenstrual mood disorder and menstrual migraine. The review did not give an overall certainty rating.
keyPoints: Hormone treatments were tested in 56 trials for premenstrual mood disorder, 21 for menstrual migraine and 8 for cycle-related epilepsy.
Combined oral contraceptives containing drospirenone showed promising results for both premenstrual mood disorder (PMDD) and menstrual migraine.
Drugs that switch off ovulation (GnRH agonists) were supported by a meta-analysis for premenstrual mood disorder, but were tested in only two menstrual migraine trials.
Menstrual migraine research has focused heavily on estrogen-based treatments, while epilepsy research has focused on progesterone in the second half of the cycle.

items.title: Menstrual disturbances and its association with sleep disturbances: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 35 studies on how sleep relates to menstrual problems, including premenstrual syndrome (PMS), painful periods and abnormal or heavy periods. Women with these problems were more likely to report poor sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, trouble falling or staying asleep, and short sleep. The studies show a link rather than proving cause, and the authors say longer-term studies using objective sleep measures are still needed.
keyPoints: PMS and painful periods were linked to poor sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, difficulty falling or staying asleep, and short sleep.
Abnormal cycles and heavy bleeding were linked to poorer sleep satisfaction, less efficient sleep and shorter sleep.
No studies looked at the timing of sleep.
The authors suggest that helping women with period problems improve their sleep could be worthwhile.

items.title: Association between premenstrual dysphoric disorder and perinatal depression: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at seven studies to see whether premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a severe form of premenstrual mood symptoms, is linked to depression around pregnancy and after birth. Most of the studies found a link between PMDD and depression, especially depression after the baby is born. One study found no link when depression was checked at 4 weeks after birth. The authors note that the research is limited and varies a lot in how it was done.
keyPoints: Six of seven studies found a positive link between PMDD and postpartum depression.
Only one study looked at depression during pregnancy, and it also found a positive link.
One study found no significant link when depression was checked at 4 weeks after birth.
The authors suggest health professionals check for PMDD when monitoring women during the perinatal period.

items.title: Risk factors of postpartum depression and depressive symptoms: umbrella review of current evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses of observational studies
items.summary: This review pulled together 11 systematic reviews (185 studies, over 3 million women) to see which factors are linked to postpartum depression. The strongest links were with premenstrual syndrome, violent experiences and unintended pregnancy. No link was found with epidural pain relief during labour or with medically assisted conception. The certainty of the evidence was low or very low, and these are links seen in observational studies, not proof of cause.
keyPoints: Premenstrual syndrome, violent experiences and unintended pregnancy had the strongest links to postpartum depression (rated highly suggestive).
Caesarean section and gestational diabetes showed suggestive links; preterm delivery, anaemia and vitamin D deficiency showed weaker links.
No significant association was found for epidural pain relief in labour or for medically assisted conception.
No risk factor reached 'convincing' evidence, and certainty was low or very low; the authors suggest using these factors to help assess postpartum depression risk.

items.title: Effect of omega-3 fatty acids on premenstrual syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials to see whether omega-3 fatty acids (the fats found in fish oil) help with premenstrual syndrome (PMS). Overall, omega-3 reduced PMS severity, including both body symptoms and mood-related symptoms. The trials differed a lot from one another, so the authors say the benefit should be stated with caution.
keyPoints: Omega-3 fatty acids reduced overall PMS severity across the pooled trials.
They also reduced both physical (somatic) and psychological PMS symptoms.
The benefit appeared larger when the treatment was taken for longer.
The studies varied widely in their results, so the authors urge caution about firm conclusions.

items.title: Premenstrual exacerbation of mental health disorders: a systematic review of prospective studies
items.summary: This review looked at 35 studies that tracked mental health symptoms day by day across the menstrual cycle in people who already had a mental health condition. It found clear evidence that symptoms got worse around the time of the period for psychotic disorders, panic disorder, eating disorders, depression and borderline personality disorder. Evidence was less consistent for anxiety, and bipolar disorder showed a different pattern. The studies varied a lot in size and methods, so the overall evidence was mixed, but some people seem to be sensitive to hormone changes.
keyPoints: Symptoms clearly got worse around the period for psychotic disorders, panic disorder, eating disorders, depression and borderline personality disorder.
Evidence for anxiety was less consistent, and bipolar disorder showed a different pattern of symptom change.
Studies differed widely in size and methods, which may explain some of the mixed results.
Hormone changes across the cycle may worsen symptoms in a subgroup of people who are hormone sensitive.

items.title: Relationship of Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder With Bipolar Disorder: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at how often premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) and bipolar disorder occur together. Only five studies were found. They suggest each condition is more common in people who have the other than in the general population. The studies were limited because they did not track symptoms day by day over time, which is needed to confirm PMDD.
keyPoints: Among people with PMDD, 10% to 15% were also diagnosed with bipolar disorder.
Among people with bipolar disorder, 27% to 76% received a PMDD diagnosis.
Few studies exist, and most did not monitor symptoms prospectively, which makes it hard to tell PMDD apart from premenstrual worsening of bipolar disorder.
The authors call for more prospective studies to improve detection, diagnosis and treatment.

items.title: Factors Associated with the Prevalence and Severity of Menstrual-Related Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review pooled results from 77 studies to find which factors are linked to period pain (primary dysmenorrhea) and premenstrual syndrome (PMS). Period pain was more common with a family history of it, stress, low body weight, irregular cycles, short sleep and late bedtimes. Smoking was linked to more severe period pain and to PMS. These are links between factors and symptoms, so they do not prove one causes the other.
keyPoints: Having a family history of period pain was linked to much higher odds of period pain (OR 3.80).
Stress, sleeping under 7 hours, going to bed after 23:01, irregular cycles and a BMI under 18.5 were each linked to more period pain.
Low BMI (under 18.5) and smoking were linked to more severe period pain.
Smoking was linked to a higher chance of premenstrual syndrome (OR 1.86).

items.title: Suicidality in women with Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder: a systematic literature review
items.summary: This review looked at ten studies on suicidal thoughts and suicide attempts in women with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a condition with severe physical and emotional changes in the second half of the menstrual cycle. Suicidal thoughts, plans and attempts were strongly linked to PMDD, even after accounting for other mental health conditions. The authors conclude that women with PMDD are a higher-risk group and that spotting and treating PMDD symptoms is important.
keyPoints: Suicidal thoughts, plans and attempts were strongly linked to PMDD in the ten studies reviewed.
This link held even when other psychiatric conditions were taken into account.
Women with PMDD who attempted suicide did not have more severe attempts, or more attempts in the luteal phase, than attempters without PMDD.
The authors say identifying and treating PMDD symptoms is vital for reducing suicide attempts.

items.title: Suicidality in patients with premenstrual dysphoric disorder-A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled six studies with about 8,500 participants to see whether premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is linked to suicidal thoughts and behaviour. People with PMDD were about twice as likely to report suicidal thoughts, suicide attempts and suicide plans. The authors note that PMDD was only a provisional diagnosis in all the included studies, and they conclude that clinicians treating PMDD should watch for signs of suicidal thoughts and behaviour.
keyPoints: PMDD was linked to higher odds of suicidal ideation (odds ratio 2.34).
PMDD was linked to higher odds of a suicide attempt (odds ratio 2.13) and of a suicide plan (odds ratio 2.24).
PMDD diagnoses in all the included studies were provisional, which limits the findings.
The authors say clinicians should be alert to suicidal thoughts and behaviour in people with PMDD.

items.title: Neuroimaging premenstrual dysphoric disorder: A systematic and critical review
items.summary: This review pulled together 18 brain imaging studies (361 people in total) on premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a severe, hormone-linked mood condition. Studies found differences in the brains of people with PMDD, such as a larger cerebellum and changes in how the brain's emotion circuits respond to emotional images. The authors say this research is still limited and somewhat inconsistent, so clear, repeatable brain features have not yet been established.
keyPoints: Brain imaging studies of PMDD found greater cerebellar grey matter volume and metabolism, along with altered serotonin and GABA signalling.
In response to emotional stimuli, people with PMDD showed stronger activity in the amygdala and weaker activity in frontal brain areas.
These findings suggest PMDD involves real structural, chemical and functional brain differences, though the research is sparse and not always consistent.
The authors say clearer, well-replicated brain features are needed to help earlier diagnosis and to guide prevention and treatment.

items.title: Vitex agnus-castus in premenstrual syndrome: A meta-analysis of double-blind randomised controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from well-reported, placebo-controlled trials of chasteberry (Vitex agnus-castus) for premenstrual syndrome (PMS). Out of 21 trials found, only three (520 women) reported their herbal products well enough to be included. In these, women taking chasteberry extracts were about 2.6 times more likely to see their PMS symptoms improve than women taking a placebo. The authors say most other chasteberry trials could not be counted as evidence because of incomplete reporting, so more well-reported trials are needed.
keyPoints: Women taking chasteberry were 2.57 times more likely to have their PMS symptoms improve than those taking a placebo (95% CI 1.52-4.35).
Only 3 of 21 trials (520 women) met the quality criteria, and they tested two specific extracts, Ze 440 and BNO 1095.
Most chasteberry trials could not be used as evidence because the herbal product was not described well enough.
The authors call for more well-reported trials to confirm how well chasteberry extracts work.

items.title: Premenstrual syndrome and alcohol consumption: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 19 studies to see whether drinking alcohol is linked to premenstrual syndrome (PMS). Women who drank alcohol had a moderately higher chance of having PMS than women who did not. The link was stronger for heavy drinking than for any drinking. This type of study shows an association, not proof that alcohol causes PMS.
keyPoints: Any alcohol intake was linked to a moderate increase in PMS risk (odds ratio 1.45).
Heavy drinking was linked to a larger increase in risk (odds ratio 1.79).
The authors say future studies should avoid cross-sectional designs.
It is not yet known whether a low level of drinking exists below which there is no effect on PMS.

items.title: Acupuncture and acupressure for premenstrual syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether acupuncture or acupressure helps with premenstrual syndrome (PMS). It found five small trials with 277 women in total. The limited evidence suggests both may ease physical and mood symptoms compared with a sham (fake) treatment, but the quality of the evidence was low to very low, so the results are uncertain.
keyPoints: Compared with sham acupuncture, real acupuncture may reduce mood and physical PMS symptoms and may improve quality of life, based on low-quality evidence from one trial of 67 women.
Acupressure may reduce the number of women with moderate to severe PMS symptoms compared with sham acupressure, based on low-quality evidence from one trial of 90 women.
There was not enough evidence to say whether side effects differ between acupuncture and sham acupuncture.
No trials compared acupuncture or acupressure with standard treatments such as SSRIs, so it is unknown how they compare.

items.title: Risk factors for premenstrual asthma: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 20 studies to look at who is more likely to have asthma that gets worse just before a period (premenstrual asthma). Women with this pattern tended to be older, have more severe and longer-standing asthma, and have a higher body-mass index. They were also more likely to have painful periods and premenstrual syndrome. Why it happens, including the role of hormone levels and inflammation, is still unclear.
keyPoints: Women with premenstrual asthma were older, had more severe asthma, a longer history of asthma and a higher body-mass index.
They were more likely to have aspirin-sensitive asthma.
They more often had painful periods, premenstrual syndrome, shorter cycles and longer menstrual bleeding.
The role of hormone levels and body-wide inflammation remains unclear.

items.title: The treatment of premenstrual syndrome with preparations of Vitex agnus castus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 17 randomized trials of Vitex agnus castus (chasteberry), a herbal remedy, for premenstrual syndrome (PMS). Most trials reported that it reduced PMS symptoms, and the combined result looked large. However, the trials were mostly of poor quality and the results varied a lot, so the true benefit is probably smaller than it looks and no firm conclusion can be drawn.
keyPoints: 13 of 14 trials comparing Vitex with placebo, supplements or other herbs reported positive effects on overall PMS symptoms.
Most trials had a high risk of bias, results varied widely between studies, and there were signs of publication bias.
The authors say the pooled effect should be seen as exploratory and likely overestimates the real benefit.
Better-quality trials are needed, comparing standardized Vitex extracts with placebo, SSRIs and oral contraceptives.

items.title: Non-contraceptive oestrogen-containing preparations for controlling symptoms of premenstrual syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at five trials (305 women) of hormone-therapy-strength oestrogen, given by patch, implant or tablet, for premenstrual syndrome (PMS). Continuous oestrogen (patches or implants) taken with a progestogen seemed to give a small to moderate improvement in overall symptoms. Oestrogen tablets taken only in the second half of the cycle looked ineffective and might make symptoms worse, but this came from one tiny study. All the evidence was very low quality, and long-term safety was not studied.
keyPoints: Continuous oestrogen (patch or implant) plus progestogen gave a small to moderate improvement in overall PMS symptoms, but the evidence was very low quality.
Oestrogen tablets taken only in the second half of the cycle were probably ineffective and possibly harmful, based on one study of 11 women.
A lower patch dose (100 micrograms) may cause fewer side effects than a higher dose (200 micrograms), though the evidence was very uncertain and effectiveness did not clearly differ.
The trials were too small and short (2 to 8 months) to say anything about long-term risks such as endometrial or breast cancer.

items.title: Vitex agnus castus for premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at eight randomized trials of Vitex agnus castus (chasteberry) for premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). All eight trials found a benefit, and the herb was generally well tolerated. The studies used different diagnostic criteria, different ways of measuring symptoms and different extracts, so the results are hard to compare. The authors conclude it may be a safe and effective option to consider for PMS or PMDD symptoms.
keyPoints: All eight randomized trials reported a positive effect of Vitex agnus castus on PMS or PMDD symptoms.
The herb was overall well tolerated.
Most trials studied PMS rather than PMDD.
Different extracts, diagnostic criteria and outcome measures limit how well the studies can be compared.

items.title: Visually Directed Hysteroscopic Biopsy in the Evaluation of Abnormal Uterine Bleeding and Postmenopausal Bleeding: A Joint Society Practice Guideline
items.summary: A joint guideline from three gynaecology societies looked at the best way to check the womb lining when someone has abnormal bleeding or bleeding after menopause. It compared hysteroscopy (looking inside the womb with a thin camera, with or without taking a small tissue sample) against blind sampling, where tissue is taken without looking first. Hysteroscopy was more accurate at finding or ruling out cancer, pre-cancerous changes, polyps and fibroids inside the womb. The guideline recommends that sampling be done together with hysteroscopy when possible.
keyPoints: Hysteroscopy, with or without a tissue sample, was more accurate than blind womb-lining biopsy for finding or excluding cancer, pre-cancerous changes, hyperplasia, polyps and submucous fibroids.
It was generally better at detecting these problems than at ruling them out.
When a tissue sample is needed for abnormal or postmenopausal bleeding, a sample taken with a camera view is favoured over blind sampling.
Hysteroscopy is especially useful when scans or sampling are inconclusive or a focal problem in the womb is suspected.

items.title: The optimal endometrial thickness threshold for prediction of endometrial cancer in postmenopausal women without bleeding remains uncertain-Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.journal: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.summary: Sometimes an ultrasound scan after menopause shows a thicker womb lining (more than 4 mm) in a woman who has had no bleeding. This review pulled together 16 studies of 4088 women to find the best lining thickness for spotting womb cancer or pre-cancer in this situation. The studies were too different to combine, and many were looked back on after the fact, which can bias results. The review found no clear thickness cut-off, so there is not enough evidence yet to say what is best.
keyPoints: A womb lining over 4 mm found by chance in women with no postmenopausal bleeding is a common reason for referral to a specialist.
Up to 15% of womb cancers are estimated to happen in women who have no postmenopausal bleeding.
Studies used widely different thresholds, and no clear link was found between lining thickness and the rate of hyperplasia or cancer.
The authors conclude there is a lack of evidence to guide care and call for a well-designed prospective study.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of fezolinetant, a neurokinin-3 antagonist, in treating vasomotor symptoms in postmenopausal women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from several trials of fezolinetant, a non-hormonal medicine, for hot flashes and night sweats after menopause. Women taking it had fewer and less severe hot flashes and night sweats, and their quality-of-life scores improved. Side effects and drop-out rates were similar to the comparison group, and uterine bleeding was less common. The authors note a possible rise in womb-lining overgrowth or tumours, and say the trials were small, short and varied, so more safety research is needed.
keyPoints: Fezolinetant significantly reduced how often hot flashes and night sweats happened, and how severe they were, at weeks 4 and 12.
Menopause quality-of-life and symptom-interference scores improved with treatment.
Overall side effects and drug-related drop-outs were similar to the comparison group, and uterine bleeding was less common.
The authors warn of a possible increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia or tumours, and note small, short, varied trials as limitations.

items.title: Can a higher endometrial thickness threshold exclude endometrial cancer and atypical hyperplasia in asymptomatic postmenopausal women? A systematic review
items.source: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology
items.journal: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology
items.summary: This review looked at women past menopause who have no bleeding but whose ultrasound happens to show a thickened womb lining. Today, a lining of 4 mm or more often leads to further tests, even though the chance of cancer is low. The review found that higher cut-offs of around 11 to 12 mm may work better, but the evidence is not strong enough to be sure. The authors suggest that watching and waiting may be reasonable for women with no symptoms or risk factors and a lining under 10 mm.
keyPoints: Better-quality studies pointed to 11 to 12 mm as a more useful cut-off than 4 mm for finding womb cancer or pre-cancer in women without bleeding.
The review says the evidence for these higher cut-offs is not rigorous, and evidence that they improve outcomes is inadequate.
Observation may be reasonable for women with no symptoms, no risk factors and a womb lining under 10 mm.

items.title: Is There a Survival Advantage in Diagnosing Endometrial Cancer in Asymptomatic Patients? A Systemic Review and Meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This review pooled six studies covering 2,961 women with endometrial (womb lining) cancer. It compared women whose cancer was found before any symptoms with women whose cancer was found after postmenopausal bleeding began. Cancers found in women without symptoms were more often at an early stage (stage I). But overall survival and the chance of the cancer coming back were not clearly better for these women.
keyPoints: Women diagnosed without symptoms were more likely to have stage I tumours (relative risk 1.19).
The share of high-grade (more aggressive) tumours was similar in both groups.
Overall survival and recurrence-free survival did not differ significantly between women with and without symptoms.
The authors suggest that invasive tests after an incidental ultrasound finding in women with no symptoms should be weighed carefully, since no survival benefit is expected.

items.title: Ultrasound detection of endometrial cancer in women with postmenopausal bleeding: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 44 studies of about 17,000 women who had bleeding after menopause, to see how well an ultrasound scan of the womb lining can pick up womb (endometrial) cancer. Cancer was found in about 8 in 100 of these women. The womb lining was much thicker in women with cancer (about 16 mm) than in those without (about 4 mm). Using a lining thickness of 5 mm or more as the cut-off found nearly all cancers while helping reduce invasive follow-up tests by 17%.
keyPoints: About 7.7% of women with bleeding after menopause in these studies had endometrial cancer.
Average womb lining thickness was 16.4 mm in women with cancer and 4.1 mm in women without.
A cut-off of 5 mm or more found about 96% of cancers and cut invasive workups by 17% compared with a 3 or 4 mm cut-off.
Other ultrasound measures such as lining volume and blood flow were linked to cancer, but there was too little data to judge specific cut-offs.

items.title: Diagnostic accuracy of saline contrast sonohysterography in detecting endometrial polyps in women with postmenopausal bleeding: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Polyps in the lining of the womb are common in women who bleed after menopause, and up to 6% may contain abnormal or early cancer cells. This review pooled five studies on saline contrast sonohysterography, an ultrasound scan where salty water is placed in the womb to show up polyps. The scan found roughly 85-90% of polyps and correctly ruled them out in roughly 85-90% of women without them. Results were better when the scan was of good quality.
keyPoints: Pooled across five studies, the scan correctly found about 85-87% of polyps and correctly cleared about 85-91% of women without polyps, depending on the comparison used.
Accuracy improved (about 91% of polyps found) when a study with poor-quality scans was left out.
If the scan shows no sign of a polyp and a sample of the womb lining is benign, watchful waiting without further procedures could be considered.
If the scan is of good quality, it can help decide which women need a follow-up camera examination of the womb (hysteroscopy).

items.title: No. 385-Indications for Pelvic Examination
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline explains when a pelvic exam is needed. It recommends a pelvic exam for any woman with gynaecologic symptoms, including bleeding after menopause, so treatable conditions are not missed or delayed. For women with no symptoms, the evidence is limited, so most advice is optional and based on expert opinion and low-quality evidence.
keyPoints: Women with symptoms such as bleeding after menopause, vaginal discharge, pelvic pain or painful sex should have the appropriate parts of a pelvic exam (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence).
Cervical screening should follow provincial or territorial guidelines in women without symptoms (strong recommendation).

There is not enough evidence to say whether routine pelvic exams in healthy women without symptoms find other cancers or conditions; an exam alongside cervical screening may be considered (weak recommendation, very low-quality evidence).
No pelvic exam is needed before prescribing hormonal contraception to a healthy woman without symptoms (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence).

items.title: Association of Endometrial Cancer Risk With Postmenopausal Bleeding in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 129 studies to look at how often bleeding after menopause is linked to womb (endometrial) cancer. Around 9 in 10 women with endometrial cancer had bleeding after menopause. But only about 1 in 11 women with bleeding after menopause were found to have the cancer, so most cases have other, non-cancer causes.
keyPoints: About 91% of women with endometrial cancer had bleeding after menopause, whatever the stage of the cancer.
About 9% of women with bleeding after menopause were found to have endometrial cancer.
The risk ranged from 7% to 12% depending on hormone therapy use, and from 5% in North America to 13% in Western Europe.
Checking women who have bleeding after menopause could catch as many as 90% of endometrial cancers, but most of these women will not have cancer.

items.title: The accuracy of endometrial sampling in women with postmenopausal bleeding: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pooled 12 studies of 1029 women with bleeding after menopause to see how well an endometrial sample (a small tissue sample from the womb lining) finds problems such as cancer. The sample was good at finding cancer, but it missed more cases of atypical hyperplasia and other womb lining problems like polyps than was previously thought. The sample also failed or was too small to use fairly often. The authors conclude that further tests may be needed even when a sample result is benign.
keyPoints: Compared with D&C, endometrial sampling found 100% of endometrial cancers and 92% of atypical hyperplasia.
Compared with hysteroscopy, it found 90% of cancers, 82% of atypical hyperplasia and only 39% of all womb lining problems, including polyps.
Samples failed in about 11% of women and were insufficient in about 31%.
The authors say that because sampling can miss problems, further checks for focal (localised) changes are warranted after a benign result.

items.title: Impact of postpartum physical activity on maternal depression and anxiety: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 35 studies (about 4,000 postpartum women) to see whether exercise after birth affects depression and anxiety. Exercise-only programmes lowered the severity of depression and anxiety symptoms and reduced the chance of postpartum depression compared with no exercise. The authors rated the certainty of this evidence from randomised trials as moderate.
keyPoints: Exercise reduced the severity of postpartum depressive symptoms, with a moderate-sized effect (19 trials).
Exercise reduced anxiety symptoms, with a small effect, and lowered the odds of postpartum depression by 45% (4 trials).

A moderate reduction in depressive symptoms needed at least 350 MET-min/week, for example about 80 minutes a week of moderate exercise like brisk walking, water aerobics, stationary cycling or resistance training.
No included studies looked at whether exercise changes the chance of developing postpartum anxiety.

items.title: Prenatal exercise and its effects on postpartum mental health: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether staying active during pregnancy affects mental health after birth. Across 19 studies, more physical activity in pregnancy was linked to fewer depressive symptoms, less anxiety and better overall well-being after birth. Gentle activities like yoga seemed especially helpful, while results for moderate-intensity exercise were mixed. A combined analysis of four trials found a meaningful drop in depression and anxiety scores among postpartum women in exercise programmes.
keyPoints: Higher physical activity in pregnancy was consistently linked to better mental health after birth.
Low-intensity exercise such as yoga was particularly effective at reducing postpartum depressive symptoms.
Moderate-intensity exercise had mixed results, with some studies finding no significant effect.
Four trials using the EPDS showed reduced depression and anxiety symptoms with physical activity programmes.

items.title: Impact of sleep on postpartum health outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 60 studies of more than 20,000 women in the first year after birth to see how sleep affects their health. Sleep programmes led to a small drop in how severe depression symptoms were, and the evidence for this was rated high certainty. The programmes did not change the chance of developing depression, and they had no clear effect on anxiety, blood pressure, weight or breastfeeding, though much of that evidence was low certainty. Observational studies suggested that better sleep goes with fewer anxiety and depression symptoms and that shorter sleep goes with more weight kept after birth, but this evidence was low or very low certainty.
keyPoints: Sleep interventions after birth gave a small reduction in depression symptom severity (high certainty evidence).
Sleep interventions did not change the odds of developing depression (moderate certainty) or anxiety (low certainty).
No effect was found on blood pressure, weight, BMI or exclusive breastfeeding (low certainty).
Observational studies linked good sleep with fewer anxiety and depression symptoms, and shorter sleep with more postpartum weight retention (low to very low certainty).

items.title: Brexanolone, zuranolone and related neurosteroid GABAA receptor positive allosteric modulators for postnatal depression
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at six placebo-controlled trials (674 women) of newer medicines for postnatal depression that work differently from usual antidepressants: intravenous brexanolone and ganaxolone, and oral zuranolone. Zuranolone probably improved depression and led to more remission than placebo at 45 days, but it also probably caused more side effects, most often sleepiness. The intravenous medicines may have made little or no difference to depression compared with placebo. No trials compared these medicines with other treatments such as talking therapy or standard antidepressants.
keyPoints: Oral zuranolone probably improves depression response and remission at 45 days compared with placebo (moderate-certainty evidence).
Zuranolone probably increases side effects for the mother, with sleepiness the most common.

Intravenous medicines such as brexanolone may make little or no difference to depression response or remission (low-certainty evidence) and probably do not change the number of side effects; more women stopped treatment than with placebo.
No studies compared these medicines with other active treatments, so firm recommendations are hard to make; the authors suggest an individual discussion of benefits and risks.

items.title: Risk factors for postpartum depression: an umbrella review
items.summary: This review pulled together 77 earlier meta-analyses to look at what raises or lowers the chance of postpartum depression. Forty of 53 factors studied were linked to it. The strongest links were a history of depression, poor social support, intimate partner violence, sleep disorders and an unintended pregnancy. Most of the evidence was rated low or very low certainty, so these links should be read with caution.
keyPoints: The strongest risk factors were poor social support, a history of depression, intimate partner violence, sleep disorders and unintended pregnancy.
Factors linked to lower risk included physical activity after birth, doula support, breastfeeding support and parenting interventions.
Most of the evidence was low or very low certainty; only a few findings from randomised trials were moderate to high quality.
The authors suggest screening and prevention should focus on higher-risk groups and call for better-quality studies.

items.title: The effect of digital health interventions on postpartum depression or anxiety: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 31 randomized trials (over 11,000 women) comparing digital health tools, such as apps and online programs, with usual care for postpartum depression and anxiety. Women using digital tools had modestly lower depression and anxiety symptom scores. However, the studies differed a lot from each other, and the few that looked at how many women screened positive found no clear difference. More research is needed to find which digital tools work best.
keyPoints: Digital health interventions modestly but significantly reduced postpartum depression symptom scores compared with usual care (29 studies).
They also modestly reduced postpartum anxiety symptom scores (17 studies).
In the few studies that checked screen-positive rates for depression (4) or anxiety (1), there was no significant difference from usual care.
Women using digital tools were more likely to drop out of the studies overall, but app-based tools had similar drop-out rates to usual care.

items.title: Urinary incontinence increases risk of postpartum depression: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 11 studies to see whether bladder leaks (urinary incontinence) after childbirth are linked to postpartum depression. Women with urinary incontinence had somewhat higher odds of postpartum depression, and the link was similar whether measured before or after 6 months. The authors say incontinence may be a possible predictor of postpartum depression, but the studies varied and this shows an association rather than proof of cause.
keyPoints: Across 11 studies, women with urinary incontinence had higher odds of postpartum depression (odds ratio 1.45).
The link was a little stronger in the 7 cohort studies (odds ratio 1.63).
The association did not weaken at 6 months or later after birth.
The authors suggest health professionals offer support and treatment to women who have these conditions.

items.title: Association between postpartum depression and breastfeeding self-efficacy in mothers: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled earlier studies to look at how postpartum depression relates to a mother's confidence in breastfeeding (called breastfeeding self-efficacy). Mothers with depression had lower breastfeeding confidence on both the first and third days after birth. The authors say depression may be linked to lower confidence and less attention to the mother's role, and that mothers need good support. The abstract does not rate the quality of the evidence and shows only an association, not a cause.
keyPoints: Postpartum depression was linked to lower breastfeeding self-efficacy on the first day after birth.
The same link was seen on the third day after birth.
The authors found no sign of publication bias in the studies reviewed.
Healthcare providers are encouraged to offer support that fits mothers' needs and to develop screening and treatment protocols.

items.title: Comparison of Patient Health Questionnaire-9, Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and Hospital Anxiety and Depression - Depression subscale scores by administration mode: An individual participant data differential item functioning meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled data from tens of thousands of people who completed three depression questionnaires, including the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). They checked whether the way a questionnaire is given (on paper or on a screen, alone or with an interviewer, in person or by phone) changes the answers. Some small differences were found for individual questions, but total scores did not differ in any meaningful way. The authors conclude the method can be chosen based on preference, practicality or cost.
keyPoints: Total scores on the EPDS, PHQ-9 and HADS-D did not differ materially by how the questionnaire was given.
Some individual questions showed statistically significant differences, but the effect on total scores was negligible.
The study compared self-completion versus interview, private versus clinic or research settings, paper versus electronic, and in-person versus phone.
Clinicians and researchers can pick a method based on patient preference, feasibility or cost.

items.title: Is Serum Vitamin D Associated with Depression or Anxiety in Ante- and Postnatal Adult Women? A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 25 studies to see whether vitamin D levels in the blood are linked to depression or anxiety during pregnancy and after birth. Women with depression, both during pregnancy and after birth, tended to have lower vitamin D levels than women without depression. Only one study found a link between low vitamin D and anxiety in pregnancy. The authors say the evidence is very low to low quality, and that these studies show a link but cannot show that low vitamin D causes depression.
keyPoints: Women with depression in pregnancy had lower vitamin D levels on average (about 4.6 ng/mL lower) than women without depression.
Women with postnatal depression had vitamin D levels about 2.4 ng/mL lower on average than women without it.
Low vitamin D may not be related to anxiety symptoms before childbirth; only one study found a link.
Better-designed studies that follow women over time are needed to understand these links.

items.title: Zuranolone for postpartum depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis of two randomized studies
