items.source: Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia E Obstetricia
items.journal: Revista Brasileira de Ginecologia E Obstetricia
items.summary: This review pooled two randomized trials of zuranolone, an oral medicine for postpartum depression, in 346 women. Women taking zuranolone had better depression scores and more symptom remission than those given a placebo. Sleepiness (sedation) was more common with zuranolone and may depend on the dose, while other side effects were not clearly different. The authors say the medicine may be safe and effective, but sedation needs more study.
keyPoints: Zuranolone was linked to better depression response and symptom remission than placebo at several time points, including 3, 15 and 45 days.
Women on zuranolone also needed lower doses of antidepressants.
Sedation (sleepiness) was more likely with zuranolone and may be dose related.
No clear differences were found for other side effects.

items.title: Global Prevalence of Perinatal Depression and Its Determinants Among Rural Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 86 studies to estimate how common depression during pregnancy and after birth is among women in rural areas worldwide. About 22 in 100 rural women were affected, with higher rates in low-income and lower middle-income countries. Violence, mental health problems during pregnancy, low family income and food insecurity were linked to more depression, while good social support and more education were linked to less.
keyPoints: The pooled rate of perinatal depression in rural areas was 22.1%, which is higher than global figures.
Rates were higher in low-income (24.5%) and lower middle-income countries (22.8%).
Self-reported screening questionnaires found more depression (22.8%) than diagnostic interviews (17.6%).
Risk factors included violence, antenatal psychiatric disorder, low family income, male-child preference and food insecurity; social support and higher education were protective.

items.title: Associations between maternal psychological distress and mother-infant bonding: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 133 studies to look at how a mother's emotional distress relates to her bond with her baby. In the first year after birth, feeling depressed, anxious or stressed was linked to more bonding difficulties. Distress during pregnancy and before pregnancy was also linked to later bonding problems, though the link was usually weaker. The authors say distress and bonding problems often go together but should not be assumed to, and suggest bonding could be checked alongside routine perinatal screening.
keyPoints: Depression, anxiety and stress in the first year after birth were each linked to bonding problems between mother and baby.
Distress during pregnancy was linked to later bonding problems, but the links were mostly weaker and less certain.
Depression and anxiety before pregnancy were also associated with postpartum bonding problems.
Distress and bonding problems often occur together, but this should not be assumed; the authors suggest adding validated bonding measures to perinatal screening.

items.title: Epidemiology of perinatal depression in Italy: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies in Italy to estimate how common depression is during pregnancy and after birth. About 1 in 5 women were at risk of depression during pregnancy, and the share after birth depended on the screening cut-off used on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). The authors say these rates are similar to those in other countries, and they noted some bias in the studies reviewed.
keyPoints: About 20% of women in Italy were at risk of depression during pregnancy.
After birth, about 27.5% scored at risk using an EPDS cut-off of 9 or more, and about 11% using a cut-off of 12 or more.
These rates are similar to those reported in other countries.
The authors suggest specific prevention actions are needed during pregnancy, and they found significant publication bias in the studies.

items.title: The effect of prenatal education on fear of childbirth, pain intensity during labour and childbirth experience: a scoping review using systematic approach and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether antenatal classes, on top of routine pregnancy care, help with fear of childbirth, labour pain and mood after birth. Combining 18 studies, education plus routine care may reduce fear of childbirth, postpartum depression and labour pain compared with routine care alone. However, the studies were not good enough to draw firm conclusions, and none looked at the childbirth experience itself.
keyPoints: Antenatal education plus routine care may lower fear of childbirth, postpartum depression and labour pain compared with routine care alone.
The existing studies lack enough quality to make definitive conclusions.
No study examined childbirth experience, and there was very little evidence on postpartum anxiety and mother-baby attachment.
Larger, high-quality randomised trials are needed.

items.title: Prevalence of Postpartum Depression Based on Diagnostic Interviews: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 54 studies (about 15,600 women) that used diagnostic interviews, which are considered the most reliable way to identify depression, to estimate how common postpartum depression is. About 12% of women had some form of depression in the first year after birth, and about 7% had major depression. These rates were lower than earlier estimates that relied on self-reported questionnaires. The studies varied a lot from one to the next.
keyPoints: About 1 in 8 women (12.1%) experienced a depressive condition within one year after giving birth.
About 1 in 15 women (7.0%) had major depression in the first year postpartum.
Depression was most common in the first 6 months, especially around 2-3 weeks and 6-8 weeks after birth.
Rates of major depression were higher in low- and middle-income countries than in high-income countries.

items.title: The Association of Breastfeeding with a Reduced Risk of Postpartum Depression: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to look at whether breastfeeding is linked to postpartum depression. Women who did not exclusively breastfeed had about 89% higher odds of postpartum depression than those who did. The review found exclusive breastfeeding is associated with a lower risk of postpartum depression. This shows a link only, so it cannot show that breastfeeding itself prevents depression.
keyPoints: Mothers who did not exclusively breastfeed had 89% higher odds of postpartum depression (OR 1.89, 95% CI 1.50-2.39).
The link held whichever depression score cutoff (9/10 or 12) the studies used, though it looked somewhat stronger with the lower cutoff.
The review concluded that exclusive breastfeeding is associated with a reduced risk of postpartum depression.

items.title: Prevalence of Perinatal Depression and Anxiety in Both Parents: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 23 studies covering about 29,000 couples to see how often both parents have depression around the time of a baby's birth. Both parents were depressed in roughly 2 in 100 couples during pregnancy and the first 12 weeks after birth, and in about 3 in 100 couples between 3 and 12 months after birth. Too few studies looked at anxiety in both parents to give a number. The authors say perinatal care should consider the mental health needs of both parents.
keyPoints: Both parents had depression at the same time in about 1.7% of couples during pregnancy.
Both parents had depression in about 2.4% of couples in the first 12 weeks after birth, and about 3.2% of couples from 3 to 12 months after birth.
Only 3 studies reported on anxiety in both parents, so no combined figure could be calculated.
Perinatal care should consider parents' mental health both as individuals and as a couple.

items.title: Family History of Psychiatric Disorders as a Risk Factor for Maternal Postpartum Depression: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 26 studies covering about 100,000 women to see whether a family history of psychiatric disorders is linked to postpartum depression. Mothers with a family history of any psychiatric disorder had roughly twice the odds of developing postpartum depression within 12 months of giving birth. The authors rated the certainty of this evidence as moderate.
keyPoints: 26 studies with 100,877 women were pooled in the analysis.
A family history of psychiatric disorders was linked to about 2 times the odds of postpartum depression (OR 2.08).
Assuming 15% of mothers in the general population develop postpartum depression, this equals a risk ratio of about 1.79.
The overall certainty of the evidence was moderate according to GRADE.

items.title: Associations of Unintended Pregnancy With Maternal and Infant Health Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 36 studies from the US (over 524,000 women) to see how unplanned pregnancies compare with planned ones. Unplanned pregnancies were linked to higher rates of depression during pregnancy and after birth, more interpersonal violence, and slightly higher rates of preterm birth and low birth weight. These are associations from observational studies, so they do not prove that unplanned pregnancy causes these outcomes. The studies also varied in how they measured things and gave limited background information on participants.
keyPoints: Depression after birth was more common with unintended pregnancy (15.7% vs 9.6%), with odds about 1.5 times higher.
Depression during pregnancy was also more common (23.3% vs 13.9%).
Interpersonal violence was reported more often (14.6% vs 5.5%) after unintended pregnancy.
Preterm birth (9.4% vs 7.7%) and infant low birth weight (7.3% vs 5.2%) were slightly more common, and results held up when history of depression was taken into account.

items.title: Antidepressant treatment for postnatal depression
items.summary: This Cochrane review pulled together 11 trials (1016 women) of antidepressant treatment for depression in the first year after birth. Most trials tested SSRIs, a common type of antidepressant, for 4 to 12 weeks. SSRIs may work better than placebo (dummy pills) for improving or clearing depression, but the evidence is low or very low certainty because the trials were small and many women dropped out. No harm to children, including breastfed babies, was noted, but information on this was limited.
keyPoints: SSRIs may help more than placebo: 55% versus 43% responded and 42% versus 27% reached remission, though these gains were not firmly certain.
Women taking SSRIs and placebo stopped treatment at similar rates (27% in both groups).
Many women had side effects, but no trial found a difference in side effects between treatment groups.
Evidence is too limited to compare antidepressants with talking therapies or other treatments, or to judge safety for babies; the authors call for larger, longer trials.

items.title: Early postnatal discharge from hospital for healthy mothers and term infants
items.summary: This review pulled together 17 trials (9,409 women) comparing going home from hospital early after birth with standard hospital stays, for healthy mothers and full-term babies. Early discharge probably leads to slightly more babies being readmitted to hospital within 28 days, for problems like jaundice, dehydration or infection. For mothers, it probably made little to no difference to readmission, breastfeeding, or contact with health professionals, and may make little difference to depression in the first six months, though that evidence was low quality. The meaning of 'early discharge' varied a lot between trials, which makes results harder to interpret.
keyPoints: Early discharge probably slightly increases baby readmission within 28 days: about 69 per 1000 babies versus 43 per 1000 with standard care (moderate-certainty evidence).
Early discharge probably makes little to no difference to mothers' readmission within six weeks or to breastfeeding at six weeks (moderate-certainty evidence).
Early discharge may make little to no difference to depression within six months after birth, but the evidence is low certainty and the true effect could go either way.
Early discharge may slightly reduce hospital costs up to discharge but may not change costs of care after going home (low-certainty evidence).

items.title: Schedules for home visits in the early postpartum period
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 16 trials with about 12,000 women to compare different schedules of home visits in the first weeks after birth. Individualised midwife care at home probably lowered the number of women with high depression scores at four months. More home visits may mean fewer infant healthcare visits and slightly more exclusive breastfeeding, and women may be more satisfied with home visits than with check-ups at a facility. Overall the evidence was low quality and results were not consistent, so the best visit schedule is still unclear.
keyPoints: Individualised midwife care with home visits probably reduced the number of women with EPDS scores of 13 or more at four months (one study, 1295 women).
More home visits may reduce infant healthcare use and slightly increase exclusive breastfeeding at six weeks, but the evidence is low certainty.
Women may be more satisfied with home visits than with facility-based postnatal care.
The evidence is very uncertain about any effect on maternal or newborn death, and the best visit schedule needs further research.

items.title: Early psychological interventions for prevention and treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and post-traumatic stress symptoms in post-partum women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether talking-based support given soon after a traumatic birth can reduce post-traumatic stress symptoms. It pooled 11 studies of different early psychological interventions. Support led by a midwife or other clinician within 72 hours of a traumatic birth worked better than usual care at 4-6 weeks. The authors say more high-quality studies with longer follow-up (6-12 months) are needed before this becomes routine care.
keyPoints: Eleven studies of early psychological interventions after a traumatic birth were reviewed.
Midwife- or clinician-led support within 72 hours was more effective than usual care at reducing traumatic stress symptoms at 4-6 weeks.
Longer follow-up of 6-12 months and higher-quality studies are still needed.
It is not yet clear which specific face-to-face or online approaches work best.

items.title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Prevalence of the Maternity Blues in the Postpartum Period
items.source: Journal of Obstetric, Gynecologic, and Neonatal Nursing
items.journal: Journal of Obstetric, Gynecologic, and Neonatal Nursing
items.summary: This review pooled results from 26 studies including 5,667 women to find out how common the 'baby blues' (maternity blues) are after childbirth. About 4 in 10 women (39%) had them, but individual studies ranged widely, from about 14% to 76%. The authors say it is important for health care providers and mothers to know the key symptoms.
keyPoints: Pooled across studies, about 39% of women experienced maternity blues after childbirth (95% confidence interval 32.3 to 45.6).
Results varied a lot between studies, from 13.7% to 76.0%.
The highest rate was in African studies, at 49.6%.
The authors recommend attention to key symptoms and education programs for health care providers and mothers after birth.

items.title: Maternal Postpartum Diet and Postpartum Depression: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at whether what a mother eats after giving birth is linked to postpartum depression (PPD) symptoms. Only six studies met the criteria, and most found that women who followed a healthier diet had fewer PPD symptoms. The studies mostly could not show cause and effect, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Six studies were included: four cross-sectional and two cohort studies.
All but one study found that a healthier postpartum diet went with fewer PPD symptoms.
Healthy patterns included fruits, vegetables, fish, grains, legumes and herbs.
The authors say longitudinal and intervention studies are still needed to confirm any effect.

items.title: Prevalence of perinatal depression and its determinants in Mainland China: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together many studies from Mainland China to estimate how common depression is during pregnancy and after birth. About 1 in 6 women (16.3%) had perinatal depression, with 19.7% affected during pregnancy and 14.8% after birth. Lower income, poor physical health, worry about the pregnancy and less social support were linked to higher risk, while better living conditions and more education were linked to lower risk. The authors note the studies varied a lot and some publication bias was found.
keyPoints: Perinatal depression affected 16.3% of women in Mainland China overall.
Depression was found in 19.7% of women during pregnancy and 14.8% after birth.
Lower socioeconomic status, poor physical health, pregnancy anxiety and low social support raised risk.
Better living conditions and higher education were linked to lower risk, and rates have risen over the last decade.

items.title: Accuracy of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) for screening to detect major depression among pregnant and postpartum women: systematic review and meta-analysis of individual participant data
items.summary: This large review pooled data from 58 studies to see how well the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), a short questionnaire, picks up major depression in pregnant and postpartum women. A score of 11 or higher gave the best balance between correctly spotting depression and correctly ruling it out. A higher cut-off of 13 or more missed more women with depression but was better at avoiding false alarms. Results were similar for pregnant and postpartum women.
keyPoints: A cut-off score of 11 or higher gave the best balance of sensitivity and specificity.
At a cut-off of 11 or higher, about 81% of women with major depression were identified and about 88% of women without depression were correctly screened out.
A cut-off of 13 or higher was less sensitive (about 66%) but more specific (about 95%), and could be used to find women with higher symptom levels.
Lower cut-offs could be used if the aim is to avoid missing women who meet diagnostic criteria.

items.title: Postpartum fatigue and depression: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 35 studies (34 on mothers, 1 on fathers) to see how tiredness and low mood are linked in the first two years after birth. They found a strong link: mothers who were more tired also tended to have more symptoms of depression. The size of the link varied a lot between studies, and the reasons for this were not clear. The authors suggest that checking for both tiredness and depression when either is reported could help in working out what is going on and what help is needed.
keyPoints: Fatigue and depressive symptoms are strongly linked in women in the first two years after childbirth (correlation of about 0.52).
The strength of the link varied a lot between studies, and factors like infant age, maternal age and how fatigue was measured did not explain this.
Assessing both fatigue and depression when either one is reported could help with accurate diagnosis and prioritising treatment.
Only one study looked at fathers, so little can be said about them.

items.title: Maternal posttraumatic stress disorder during the perinatal period and child outcomes: A systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 21 studies on mothers who have post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) during pregnancy or in the first year after birth, and how their children fared. PTSD after birth was linked with lower birth weight and less breastfeeding. For many other outcomes, such as preterm birth and child development, the studies disagreed, and the studies were generally of poor to medium quality. The authors suggest that screening for PTSD around the time of birth may be worthwhile, with referral for treatment where needed.
keyPoints: Postpartum PTSD was linked with low birth weight and lower rates of breastfeeding.
Results on preterm birth, fetal growth, mother-infant relationship and child development were contradictory.
Findings on infant cortisol levels and eating or sleeping difficulties came from single studies and need confirming.
The authors say early screening for PTSD in the perinatal period may be advisable, with referral for effective treatment if appropriate.

items.title: Antidepressants for preventing postnatal depression
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether taking antidepressants can prevent postnatal depression in women who are not currently depressed. Only two small trials (81 women in total) were found, and all the women had had postnatal depression before. The review could not reach any clear conclusion about whether antidepressants prevent postnatal depression, because the evidence was very limited and of very low quality.
keyPoints: Only two small trials with 81 women in total met the review's criteria, so results could not be combined.
In one trial, nortriptyline did not prevent postnatal depression compared with placebo (about 23% vs 24% developed it).
In the other trial, sertraline may have lowered the chance of postnatal depression, but the result was uncertain because of the very small numbers.
The authors say larger trials are needed, including comparisons with other prevention approaches such as psychological therapies, and checks for effects on babies.

items.title: Prevalence and incidence of postpartum depression among healthy mothers: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 58 studies of about 37,000 healthy mothers who had no earlier history of depression and had healthy full-term babies. About 17 in 100 of these mothers had postpartum depression, and about 12 in 100 developed it newly after birth. Rates were similar to those reported for mothers with a past history of depression, and they varied by region. The authors say healthy mothers are often left out of intervention studies.
keyPoints: Overall prevalence of postpartum depression was 17% among healthy mothers with no prior depression.
The incidence (new cases) was 12% in this group.
Prevalence was lowest in Europe (8%) and highest in the Middle-East (26%).
Prevalence did not differ by screening time point, but it rose beyond six months after birth.

items.title: The prevalence of posttraumatic stress disorder in pregnancy and after birth: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 59 studies covering more than 24,000 women to find out how common post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is during pregnancy and after birth. In community samples, about 3 in 100 women had PTSD in pregnancy and about 4 in 100 after birth. Rates were much higher, around 19 in 100, for women in high-risk groups. The authors say PTSD may increase after birth if it is not identified and treated, and recommend that maternity services assess and treat it.
keyPoints: In community samples, the average rate of PTSD was 3.3% in pregnancy and 4.0% after birth.
Women in high-risk groups had much higher rates: about 19% in pregnancy and about 18.5% after birth.
PTSD may increase after birth if it is not identified and treated.
The authors recommend assessment and treatment of PTSD within maternity services.

items.title: The aetiology of post-traumatic stress following childbirth: a meta-analysis and theoretical framework
items.summary: This review pooled 50 studies of more than 21,000 women to look at what is linked to post-traumatic stress after childbirth, which affects about 3% of women. Before birth, depression in pregnancy, fear of childbirth, health problems in pregnancy and a past history of PTSD were most strongly linked to it. During birth, a bad personal experience of the birth, an operative birth (assisted vaginal birth or caesarean) and lack of support were the main links. After birth, PTSD often occurred together with depression. These are links, not proof of cause, and the findings may help maternity services with screening and support.
keyPoints: About 3.17% of women report post-traumatic stress after childbirth.
Depression in pregnancy, fear of childbirth, pregnancy complications and a history of PTSD were the strongest links before birth.
A negative birth experience, operative birth and lack of support were the strongest links during birth.
Birth-related PTSD was highly linked with postnatal depression (r = 0.60).

items.title: Breastfeeding and depression: a systematic review of the literature
items.summary: This review pulled together 48 studies on how breastfeeding and depression are linked during pregnancy and after birth. Depression in pregnancy was linked to breastfeeding for a shorter time, though not to whether a mother planned to breastfeed or started. Shorter breastfeeding and postnatal depression were linked in almost all studies, and each seemed to predict the other. The authors say more research, especially studies that follow women over time, is needed to untangle these links.
keyPoints: Depression in pregnancy predicts a shorter breastfeeding duration, but not breastfeeding intention or initiation.
Breastfeeding duration is associated with postpartum depression in almost all the studies reviewed.
Postpartum depression and stopping breastfeeding predicted each other in several studies.
The authors suggest help for depressed pregnant women should aim to support both breastfeeding and emotional adjustment after birth.

items.title: FIGO position statement on postpartum intrauterine devices (PPIUD)
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This position statement from FIGO, an international group of obstetricians and gynaecologists, looks at fitting an intrauterine device (IUD or coil) soon after childbirth. It describes the postpartum IUD as a non-hormonal, long-acting, reversible method that works well, costs little and can be inserted safely right after a vaginal or caesarean birth. FIGO says short gaps between pregnancies are linked to more health problems for mothers and babies, so contraception soon after birth matters. It calls for postpartum contraception, including the IUD, to be part of routine maternity care, with good counselling so women can make their own informed choices.
keyPoints: A postpartum IUD is a non-hormonal, long-acting reversible method with a low failure rate.
It can be safely inserted immediately after a vaginal or caesarean delivery.
Short gaps between pregnancies are linked to more illness and death in mothers and newborns.
FIGO recommends including postpartum contraception in routine maternity care, supported by comprehensive counselling.

items.title: Progestogen-only contraception use during breastfeeding: an updated systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 61 studies on whether progestogen-only birth control (pills, injections, implants and hormonal coils) affects breastfeeding or babies' health. It also looked at whether starting these methods before 6 weeks after birth makes any difference. The studies kept finding no consistent harm to breastfeeding or to infant growth and illness. The strength of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate, and many of the newer studies had a high risk of bias.
keyPoints: Using progestogen-only contraception while breastfeeding was not linked to consistent harm to breastfeeding, such as continuing, supplementing or how long it lasted.
Infant outcomes such as growth and illness also showed no consistent adverse effects.
Starting the implant earlier (before 6 weeks after birth) versus later was not found to cause problems in the newer randomised studies.
New evidence included preterm babies, and the review concluded it adds support for the safety of these methods during breastfeeding.

items.title: Antenatal Care Interventions to Increase Contraceptive Use Following Birth in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: Systematic Review and Narrative Synthesis
items.summary: This review looked at programs in low- and middle-income countries that reached women during pregnancy to help them use family planning after birth. Of 24 studies that measured contraceptive use in the first year after birth, 18 found that women who got the program used contraception more than those who did not. The programs varied a lot, but those that combined several different approaches seemed most likely to work.
keyPoints: 31 different programs were reviewed, mostly from sub-Saharan Africa, and about half were randomized trials.
18 of 24 studies reporting on contraceptive use found more use in the first year after birth among women who received the program.
Programs that used a multifaceted package of activities appeared most likely to have a positive effect.
The programs were very different from one another, so results are hard to compare directly.

items.title: Toward person-centred measures of contraceptive demand: a systematic review of the relationship between intentions to use and actual use of contraception
items.summary: This review looked at whether women who say they plan to use contraception actually go on to use it. It pulled together 10 studies that followed women over time, many of them pregnant or postpartum women. In 6 of the 10 studies, women who said they intended to use contraception were more likely to use it later. The authors say there were too few studies and too many differences between them to combine the results fully, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: 6 of 10 studies found that women who intended to use contraception were significantly more likely to use it later.
3 studies still found this link after accounting for other factors such as differences between groups of women.
Few studies directly looked at intention and later use, and most recruited pregnant or postpartum women.
The authors conclude that asking women about their intention to use contraception may be a strong way to predict later use.

items.title: A systematic review of randomised controlled trials of the effects of digital health interventions on postpartum contraception use
items.summary: This review pooled 12 randomised trials (5,527 women) of digital tools, such as videos, text messages and phone counselling, aimed at helping women use contraception after birth. Videos may moderately increase contraception use and text messages probably increase it a little. Phone counselling probably increased use of long-acting methods like implants and coils, but the effect on repeat pregnancy is uncertain because the evidence is very limited.
keyPoints: Video-based education may moderately increase contraception use after birth (low certainty).
Text message (SMS) education probably modestly increases contraception use (moderate certainty).
Phone counselling probably increased use of long-acting reversible contraception (moderate certainty), but its effect on overall contraception use was uncertain (very low certainty).
The effects of digital tools on repeat pregnancy are uncertain, and more high-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Utilisation, effectiveness, and safety of immediate postpartum intrauterine device insertion: a systematic literature review
items.summary: This review pulled together 133 studies from around the world on getting an IUD (a small device placed in the womb to prevent pregnancy) fitted right after giving birth. It found that these 'postpartum IUDs' are safe and work well. Pregnancies were rare, but the device can sometimes slip out, mostly in the first weeks at home. Long-term follow-up data are limited.
keyPoints: Postpartum IUDs are safe and effective, according to the review's conclusion.
Pregnancies were rare: 96 among 12,191 women, and mostly happened in women who were no longer using the IUD.
The IUD can come out (expulsion), mainly early after going home; rates within 3 months ranged widely, from 0% to 41%.
Abnormal bleeding, infections and perforations were rare, and few studies had long-term follow-up.

items.title: Factors Influencing Contraceptive Choice During the Postpartum Period: A Qualitative Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 34 studies published between 2000 and 2021 to find out what shapes the choice of contraception after having a baby. It found four groups of influences: personal and financial background, health and pregnancy history, the care a woman receives, and cultural beliefs. The authors conclude that the choice comes from a mix of social surroundings and medical factors. They suggest clinicians talk about the most common influences during consultations.
keyPoints: Four groups of factors shape postpartum contraception choice: demographic and economic, clinical, health care delivery, and sociocultural.
Clinical factors include number of previous births, how the pregnancy and birth went, past contraception use and whether the pregnancy was planned.
Counselling sessions about contraception, place of delivery and the health care system also play a role.
The main influences are number of births, education level, knowledge and beliefs about contraception, and family influence, and clinicians should address these in consultations.

items.title: Strategies for Improving Postpartum Contraception Compared With Routine Maternal Care: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 16 studies (about 14,000 women) to see whether extra support services help women start contraception after giving birth, compared with usual care. The extra support helped more women use contraception and led to fewer repeat pregnancies in the first 6 months after birth. The benefit was not clear at 12 months, and the overall certainty of the evidence was low to moderate.
keyPoints: Service interventions increased contraceptive use and lowered repeat pregnancy for up to 6 months after birth.
No clear benefit was found for contraceptive use at 12 months, repeat pregnancy over the year, or induced abortions in the first year.
Overall certainty of the evidence was low to moderate.
The authors say more studies are needed to combine the helpful interventions into practical strategies.

items.title: Implementation strategies, facilitators, and barriers to scaling up and sustaining post pregnancy family planning, a mixed-methods systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 29 studies on ways to help women use contraception after a pregnancy ends, whether after birth or after an abortion. Programmes that reached women and their partners directly, such as counselling, were linked to more women using contraception afterwards. Success depended on good counselling, offering family planning as part of routine postnatal or post-abortion care, and on religious and social attitudes. About 60% of the studies had an unclear risk of bias, so the findings should be read with some care.
keyPoints: Programmes to scale up family planning after pregnancy were linked to more women using contraception afterwards.
Strategies aimed at women and their partners were part of 26 of the 29 reports and increased uptake and coverage of contraceptive methods.
Counselling and offering family planning within postnatal or post-abortion care helped these programmes work.
Religious and social norms also affected how well programmes worked.

items.title: Effectiveness and Harms of Contraceptive Counseling and Provision Interventions for Women : A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 38 randomized trials (about 25,000 women) to see whether extra contraceptive counseling or providing contraception improves contraceptive use. Women who got extra counseling, advance supplies of emergency contraception, or contraceptive services right after birth or at the time of abortion were more likely to use contraception than those who got usual care. These services did not raise rates of sexually transmitted infections or reduce condom use. Pregnancy rates were generally lower with the interventions, but most trials were too small to show this clearly.
keyPoints: Contraceptive use was higher with enhanced counseling (RR 1.39) than with usual care.
Having emergency contraception provided in advance roughly doubled its use (RR 2.12).
Counseling or contraception provided right after birth or at the time of abortion increased contraceptive use.
Interventions did not increase sexually transmitted infections or reduce condom use.

items.title: Immediate versus delayed postpartum insertion of contraceptive implant and IUD for contraception
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether getting a contraceptive implant or an IUD (a small device placed in the womb) right after birth works better than waiting until a later visit. It combined 16 trials: 5 on implants and 11 on IUDs. More people ended up with an implant or IUD when it was offered right after birth. However, IUDs placed straight after birth may be more likely to come out on their own, and immediate implants may be linked with more bleeding and other side effects in the first six weeks.
keyPoints: Immediate insertion probably means more people start an implant (moderate-certainty evidence) or an IUD (moderate-certainty evidence) than waiting for a later visit.
IUDs placed immediately after birth may be more likely to be expelled (come out) by six months than IUDs placed later (low-certainty evidence).
Immediate implants may be linked with more prolonged bleeding and other side effects in the first six weeks (low-certainty evidence).
Hormonal implants and IUDs placed right after birth may have little or no negative effect on breastfeeding.

items.title: Acceptability of immediate postpartum and post-abortion long-acting reversible contraception provision to adolescents: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at what teenagers (aged 10-19) think about having a long-acting contraceptive, such as an implant or coil, fitted straight after giving birth or after an abortion. Ten studies were found, and only three covered the post-abortion period. Fitting straight after birth seemed acceptable to teenagers who had no side effects and who could make their own choices. The authors say there is very little research on this topic, so more is needed.
keyPoints: Having long-acting contraception available straight after birth was important for teenagers to be able to get it.
Teenagers liked that these methods last a long time, but poor counselling, side effects, safety myths and pressure from partners or community led some to avoid or stop them.
Limited evidence suggests teenagers may prefer implants over intrauterine devices, and may face more barriers to post-abortion fitting than adults.
Almost no evidence was found on teenagers' decisions about fitting straight after an abortion.

items.title: Postpartum intrauterine contraceptive device use and its associated factors in Ethiopia: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 12 studies in Ethiopia to see how many women use an intrauterine device (IUD, or coil) after giving birth, and what makes use more likely. About 22 in 100 women (21.63%) used one, which the authors describe as low. Use was more common among women with more education, those who went to antenatal care, those who had counselling or good knowledge of the IUD, and those whose husbands were supportive.
keyPoints: The pooled rate of postpartum IUD use among women in Ethiopia was 21.63%, described as significantly low.
Higher education, antenatal care visits, counselling, good knowledge and awareness of the IUD were linked to greater use.
Husband support showed the strongest link (odds about 11 times higher), and age and occupation were also associated with use.
The authors suggest health education and more focus on women's education and antenatal care use could raise postpartum IUD use.

items.title: Patients and providers' knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs regarding immediate postpartum long-acting reversible contraception: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at what women and healthcare providers in the US know and believe about getting a long-acting reversible contraceptive, such as an IUD, right after giving birth. It found 18 US studies: 6 on women's preferences and 12 on providers. Providers' knowledge of immediate postpartum LARC varied, and many said they lacked training and felt uncomfortable with counselling and insertion. The authors say more work is needed to understand what patients and providers need so this option can be offered well.
keyPoints: The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends LARC right after birth to help prevent unintended pregnancy.
Providers' knowledge about immediate postpartum LARC varied between studies.
Lack of training and discomfort with counselling and insertion were reported by providers as barriers to postpartum IUDs.
More research is needed on patients' and providers' needs and preferences for offering LARC counselling after birth.

items.title: Unintended pregnancy prevention in women using psychoactive substances: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 22 studies of programs meant to prevent unplanned pregnancy in women who use alcohol, drugs or other psychoactive substances. Programs built on behavior change theory helped more women start effective contraception than giving out written information alone. Results were strongest when counseling and free birth control were offered on site. Most studies had weaknesses and a high risk of bias, and it is unclear whether the benefits last or lower unplanned pregnancy rates over time.
keyPoints: Behavior-change-based programs led more women to start effective contraception than written information alone.
Results were stronger when programs offered on-site contraceptive counseling and free birth control.
Financial incentives also seemed to increase contraception use.
Programs for pregnant and postpartum women with heavy substance use helped women start contraception, but unplanned pregnancy rates stayed high over long follow-up.

items.title: Postpartum modern contraception utilization and its determinants in Ethiopia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 19 studies in Ethiopia to see how many women use modern contraception after giving birth, and what makes it more likely. About 46 in 100 women (45.79%) used a modern method after birth, which the authors describe as low. Women who went to more antenatal visits, had a postnatal check, had some formal education, had used family planning before, or had received family planning counselling were more likely to use contraception.
keyPoints: Pooled across 19 studies, about 45.79% of Ethiopian women used modern contraception after birth, which the authors call low.
More than four antenatal visits, attending a postnatal visit, formal education, past family planning use and family planning counselling were linked to higher use.
Having more than four living children was also linked to higher use.
The authors conclude that strengthening antenatal and postnatal care services is needed to encourage contraception use after birth.

items.title: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM) Consult Series #48: Immediate postpartum long-acting reversible contraception for women at high risk for medical complications
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM) issued guidance on placing long-acting reversible contraception (LARC, such as an IUD or implant) right after birth, especially for women whose health conditions make another pregnancy riskier. It recommends offering LARC to these women and discussing immediate postpartum options with all pregnant women during prenatal care. Immediate IUD placement has a higher chance of the device coming out than placement later, but people tend to keep using it for longer, so the benefits appear to outweigh this risk. Current evidence suggests these methods do not harm breastfeeding.
keyPoints: LARC should be offered to women at highest risk of health problems from a future pregnancy (graded strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence).
IUDs placed right after birth are more likely to be expelled than those placed later, but long-term continuation is higher, so benefits appear to outweigh the risk.
Women are encouraged to breastfeed, as current evidence suggests LARC methods do not negatively affect lactation.
Counseling should be patient-centered and based on shared decision-making to avoid coercion.

items.title: Postpartum hormonal contraception use and incidence of postpartum depression: a systematic review
items.source: European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care
items.journal: European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care
items.summary: This review looked at whether using hormonal birth control after having a baby is linked to postpartum depression. Only four studies met the criteria, and they gave mixed results. Overall, the evidence was limited and did not show a consistent link between hormonal contraception and postpartum depression.
keyPoints: Two studies found no difference in postpartum depression rates between women using the depot medroxyprogesterone injection and women using no hormonal contraception.
One study of an injectable (norethisterone enanthate) given right after birth found a 2-3-fold higher risk of depression at 6 weeks, but not at 3 months.
One study found a 35-44% lower risk of postpartum depression with progestin-only pills and levonorgestrel IUDs compared with no hormonal contraception.
The same study saw a small rise in antidepressant use with the etonogestrel implant and vaginal ring, and a lower rate with progestin-only pills.

items.title: Society of Family Planning Guidelines: Postplacental insertion of intrauterine devices
items.summary: This guideline reviewed the evidence on having an intrauterine device (IUD) fitted within 10 minutes after the placenta is delivered, after either a vaginal or cesarean birth. It found this is safe and does not cause more complications than having an IUD fitted later. The IUD is more likely to come out on its own (expulsion) when fitted straight after birth, especially after a vaginal birth, though rates vary widely between studies.
keyPoints: Fitting an IUD within 10 minutes of delivering the placenta is safe and has no higher risk of complications than fitting it later.
Most studies find the IUD is more likely to be expelled after fitting straight after birth than after later fitting.
Expulsion is more common after vaginal delivery than after cesarean delivery, but rates vary widely and the reasons are unclear.
It is most likely to help people who are unlikely to come back for a postpartum visit, if a replacement is available when an IUD comes out and the risks and benefits are explained.

items.title: The relationship between progestin hormonal contraception and depression: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 26 studies on whether progestin-only birth control (implants, hormonal coils, injections and mini-pills) is linked to depression. Most studies found little or no link when depression was measured with validated tools. A few studies did report an association, including one good-quality study of progestin-only pills and the intrauterine device. Overall, the evidence did not support the common belief that these methods raise depression risk.
keyPoints: 26 studies were reviewed, including 5 randomized trials, 11 cohort studies and 10 cross-sectional studies.
Studies of implants and injections found no link with depression, and most hormonal coil studies found none either.
Two progestin-only pill studies showed no increase in depression scores, but one good-quality study found an association with progestin-only pills and the intrauterine device.
The authors concluded that most of the evidence does not support an association between progestin contraceptives and depression.

items.title: Clinic-Based Programs to Prevent Repeat Teen Pregnancy: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at clinic-based programs meant to prevent a second pregnancy in teenagers. Out of over 27,000 papers found, only five described this kind of program. Two showed a positive effect, two showed no effect, and one described ways to help teen mothers stay connected to care. The authors say few programs seem to help, and that getting contraception right after birth or home visits may be good ways to reach teen mothers.
keyPoints: Only five studies of clinic-based programs aimed at preventing repeat teen pregnancy were found.
Of four studies measuring outcomes, two found positive effects and two found no effect on repeat teen pregnancy.
Few programs positively changed the factors that may reduce repeat teen pregnancy.
Contraception offered immediately after birth and home visiting programs may be good opportunities to support teen mothers.

items.title: Immediate versus delayed postpartum insertion of contraceptive implant for contraception
items.summary: This review pooled three trials (410 women) comparing getting a contraceptive implant straight after birth, before leaving hospital, with getting it later. Women offered the implant right after birth were more likely to actually have one by their first postpartum check-up. Early insertion led to more days of abnormal bleeding and more side effects in the first six weeks, but the groups looked similar in how many kept the implant at six months. The evidence quality ranged from very low to moderate.
keyPoints: More women had an implant by the first postpartum check-up when it was inserted immediately after birth (moderate quality evidence).
Immediate insertion meant about 6 more days of abnormal bleeding and more side effects in the first six weeks (low quality evidence).
There was little or no difference in keeping the implant at six months (low quality evidence).
It was unclear whether unintended pregnancy rates, satisfaction or breastfeeding at six months differed, because the evidence was very limited.

items.title: Immediate postpartum insertion of intrauterine device for contraception
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 15 trials of having a coil (intrauterine device or system) fitted within 10 minutes of the placenta being delivered, compared with fitting it later in the hospital stay or at the postpartum check-up. Women who had the coil fitted straight after birth were more likely to still be using it at six months, but the coil was also more likely to fall out (be expelled). The review authors say the evidence is limited because most full trial reports were small, though overall quality was moderate.
keyPoints: Fitting a coil straight after the placenta is delivered meant women were more likely to be using it at six months than those fitted at the postpartum visit.
The coil was more likely to be expelled by six months with immediate fitting, but the estimate was imprecise.
The authors say the benefit of effective contraception right after birth may outweigh the higher risk of expulsion.
Follow-up visits and teaching women the signs of expulsion can help catch a coil that has come out early.

items.title: Education for contraceptive use by women after childbirth
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 12 trials (4145 women) testing whether education about contraception after childbirth helps women use contraception or avoid another pregnancy. Most programs showed no clear effect, though a home-based mentoring program for teenage mothers led to fewer second births within two years. A few lower-quality studies also found benefits. Overall, the evidence was moderate to low quality, and the authors say programs need better design and better ways of measuring results.
keyPoints: Among the higher-quality trials, only one showed a clear benefit: teenage mothers with home-based mentoring had fewer second births within two years.
Five other higher-quality interventions had no effect.
Lower-quality studies in Nepal (education right after birth) and Australia (structured home visits for teenagers) found more contraceptive use at six months.
Many trials did not use objective outcome measures, so the overall evidence of effectiveness was mostly low quality.

items.title: Obstetric Care Consensus No. 8: Interpregnancy Care
items.source: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
items.organisation: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
items.summary: This consensus from ACOG and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine describes care between pregnancies. All women who have been pregnant, whatever the outcome, should get interpregnancy care continuing on from postpartum care. It starts with planning whether and when to have more children, depression screening, vaccines, managing diabetes or high blood pressure and planning long-term care. For women with long-term conditions it is a chance to improve health before another pregnancy.
keyPoints: Everyone who has been pregnant, including after miscarriage or abortion, should receive interpregnancy care.
Early components include reproductive life planning, depression screening, vaccination and managing diabetes or hypertension.
Women with chronic conditions can use this time to optimise health before a next pregnancy.
For women not planning more pregnancies it supports long-term health.
keywords: how soon to get pregnant again

items.title: Physical activity postpartum: A systematic review and quality appraisal of clinical guidelines
items.summary: Researchers reviewed 18 guidelines from health organisations on exercise after having a baby and checked how well each was made. Most guidelines suggest at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, while a 2025 Canadian guideline supports a minimum of 120 minutes. They also commonly suggest pelvic floor muscle training and strengthening exercises. Only 7 of the 18 guidelines met the standard for good methods, so the evidence behind some advice is still limited.
keyPoints: Guidelines agree that postpartum women should aim for at least 120-150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity each week.
Pelvic floor muscle training and strengthening exercises are commonly recommended.
Women with special health conditions are advised to seek guidance from a healthcare provider.
Only 7 of 18 guidelines (39%) had satisfactory methodological quality; more research is needed on specific types of activity and delivery mode.

items.title: Physical activity programmes for promoting bone mineralisation and growth in preterm infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether daily exercise programmes (gentle stretching and movement of the limbs) help the bones and growth of babies born early. It pooled 15 small trials with 434 preterm babies, mostly in hospital for a few weeks. The exercises may increase bone density and weight gain, but the evidence is low or very low quality. It is very uncertain whether they change fractures or total bone mineral content.
keyPoints: Exercise programmes for preterm babies may increase whole-body bone density (low-certainty evidence).
They may also increase weight gain, but may make little to no difference to length gain (low-certainty evidence).
It is very uncertain whether they affect fracture risk or whole-body bone mineral content.
No usable data were available on bone health at 12 to 24 months, and larger, better trials are needed.

items.title: Impact of postpartum physical activity on maternal anthropometrics: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 64 randomised trials of exercise after birth, with over 12,000 women and people taking part. Exercise on its own led to modest drops in body weight, body mass index (BMI) and body fat compared with no exercise. The evidence for these changes was moderate to high certainty. Exercise did not seem to change lean body mass, but that evidence was low certainty.
keyPoints: Exercise alone reduced weight by about 1.3 kg, BMI by about 0.7 and fat mass by about 1.5 kg compared with no exercise.
Around 120 minutes a week of brisk walking was linked to a 1-point drop in BMI.
Exercise showed no clear effect on lean body mass, though the evidence was low certainty.
The authors conclude physical activity helps improve body measurements and reduce weight kept after pregnancy.

items.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength Training to Prevent and Treat Urinary Incontinence in Postpartum Primiparous Women: A Systematic Review
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This review looked at five trials with 444 women after their first birth, comparing active pelvic floor exercise programs with usual care. The results varied a lot between studies: two found no clear difference between groups, while others found improvements. Overall, the authors concluded that pelvic floor muscle training helps prevent and treat urinary leakage after birth and improves pelvic floor strength.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training was concluded to be effective for preventing and treating urinary incontinence after a first birth.
Urinary symptoms improved in the groups that did the training.
Muscle strength did not clearly differ between groups, but adding biofeedback gave a clear improvement.
Results were very mixed across the five studies, which included 444 women in total.

items.title: Precision medicine exploration of postpartum rectus abdominis muscle separation: from basic research to clinical practice
items.summary: This review looked at diastasis recti, where the two sides of the tummy muscles stay separated after pregnancy. It affects roughly 30-60% of women, and in many it lasts beyond 6 months after birth. The review describes why it happens and newer ways to measure and treat it, including AI-assisted ultrasound, keyhole surgery and sensor-guided rehabilitation exercises. It also notes there are no agreed diagnostic criteria and little long-term follow-up (beyond 5 years) of the newer methods.
keyPoints: Muscle separation after birth affects about 30-60% of women, and many cases last longer than 6 months.
It is linked to pregnancy hormones, changes in connective tissue and mechanical strain on the abdomen, so care may need to be individualised.
Keyhole (laparoscopic) repair had lower recurrence rates (under 10%) and quicker recovery than open surgery.
Rehab systems with real-time muscle feedback helped reduce the gap between the muscles, but standard diagnostic criteria and long-term results are still lacking.

items.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Type 2 Diabetes Prevention Through Lifestyle Interventions in Women with a History of Gestational Diabetes-A Summary of Participant and Intervention Characteristics
items.summary: This review pooled 30 randomised trials of lifestyle programmes (such as diet and activity support) for women who had gestational diabetes, to see how well they prevent type 2 diabetes and help with weight. Programmes worked better when they started within a year after birth, were based on behaviour-change theory, and involved women with overweight or obesity. Delivery by text message, web or phone call was linked to greater weight loss.
keyPoints: Programmes that began within one year after birth reduced type 2 diabetes risk more.
Greater benefit was seen in women with an average BMI of 30 or more and in programmes based on behaviour-change theory.
For weight loss, programmes worked better in women with an average BMI of 25 or more.
Programmes using text messages, web or phone calls were more effective for weight loss.

items.title: Does Walking Reduce Postpartum Depressive Symptoms? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: This review pooled five small trials (242 mothers with mild-to-moderate postpartum depression) to see whether walking helps depression symptoms. On average, mothers who walked had lower scores on a standard depression questionnaire (the EPDS) than those who did not, and the drop was large enough to matter in everyday life. The authors note the number of studies was small and results varied quite a lot between studies, so the finding is preliminary.
keyPoints: Walking was linked to a clinically meaningful drop in depression scores (about 4 points on the EPDS) compared with controls.
Supervised, group-based, walking-only programmes with 90-120+ minutes a week of moderate walking may give bigger improvements.
Only five studies were included and results differed between them, so the evidence is limited.
The authors suggest walking may help mothers manage postpartum depression and fits around many barriers new mothers face.

items.title: Effectiveness of nonpharmacological interventions for reducing postpartum fatigue: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from ten small trials (1,194 women) testing non-drug ways to ease tiredness after birth. Exercise and drinking tea were linked to less fatigue, and tea was also linked to lower depression scores. Talking-based education programmes did not show a benefit. The authors say the findings should be read with caution because the studies were few, small and varied in quality.
keyPoints: Exercise was linked to a clear reduction in postpartum fatigue after the intervention.
Drinking tea was linked to less fatigue and may also help with low mood.
Psychoeducational (education and counselling) programmes did not show benefits for fatigue or depression.
Skin-to-skin contact, warm showers and lavender aroma were also tried, but the abstract does not report firm results for them.

items.title: Postnatal exercise interventions: a systematic review of adherence and effect
items.summary: This review pulled together 25 small trials of exercise programmes for women in the first year after birth (1466 women in total). Women stuck with supervised programmes better than unsupervised ones. Across studies, exercise improved physical fitness and reduced tiredness, and three studies found no harm to breastfeeding. The overall quality of the studies was low, so the results are not very firm.
keyPoints: Women followed supervised exercise programmes more closely than unsupervised ones (86% vs 73.6% adherence), and fewer dropped out (10% vs 14.5%).
Studies agreed that exercise improved physical fitness and reduced fatigue after birth.
Three studies showed no negative effect of exercise on breastfeeding.
Most studies were small with low quality and a high risk of bias, and the exercise programmes varied a lot, so better research is needed.

items.title: Why can't I exercise during pregnancy? Time to revisit medical 'absolute' and 'relative' contraindications: systematic review of evidence of harm and a call to action
items.summary: This review looked at 44 studies on medical conditions that have traditionally been listed as reasons not to exercise in pregnancy. It found that most of these 'no exercise' rules were based on expert opinion, with little direct evidence that exercise causes harm. For 11 conditions, such as gestational hypertension and twin pregnancy, women may actually benefit from regular activity, sometimes with changes. A smaller group of serious conditions did show strong potential for harm.
keyPoints: Most listed contraindications to exercise in pregnancy rest on expert opinion, with minimal evidence that exercise is harmful or that restricting activity helps.
Eleven conditions previously seen as contraindications, including gestational hypertension and twin pregnancy, may allow beneficial regular activity with or without modifications.

Severe cardiorespiratory disease, placental abruption, vasa previa, uncontrolled type 1 diabetes, intrauterine growth restriction, active preterm labour, severe pre-eclampsia and cervical insufficiency were linked to strong potential for harm.
The authors call for clinical guidelines to be re-evaluated, as removing barriers to activity may benefit mother and baby.

items.title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
items.summary: The World Health Organization updated its guidelines on physical activity and sitting time for all ages. For the first time, it includes specific recommendations for pregnant and postpartum women. For adults, it recommends 150-300 minutes of moderate activity (or 75-150 minutes of vigorous activity) each week, plus regular muscle-strengthening activity.
keyPoints: Adults should do 150-300 minutes of moderate-intensity activity, or 75-150 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity, or an equivalent mix, each week.
Regular muscle-strengthening activity is recommended for all age groups.
The guidelines include specific recommendations for pregnant and postpartum women for the first time.
Some physical activity is better than none, and more is better for health; reducing sedentary behaviour is also recommended, though evidence was too limited to set a specific sitting-time limit.

items.title: Physical activity during pregnancy and postpartum depression: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 21 studies (17 in the main analysis, covering about 93,000 women) to see whether being physically active during pregnancy affects depression after birth. Women who were active in pregnancy had lower postpartum depression scores than women who were not, and the effect looked stronger in studies where women were assigned an exercise programme. The studies measured activity in very different ways, so results varied a lot, and the authors say better-quality studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Women who were physically active during pregnancy had lower postpartum depression scores than women who were not active.
The link was stronger in intervention studies, where women were given an exercise programme.
Results varied widely between studies because activity was measured in different ways, such as how hard, how often, or what type.
The authors conclude that activity in pregnancy appears to reduce the risk of postpartum depression symptoms, but high-quality studies are still needed.

items.title: Physical Activity and the Occurrence of Postnatal Depression-A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 16 studies on whether being physically active during pregnancy or after birth is linked to postnatal depression. Women who were regularly active, compared with those who were inactive, had a lower risk of developing depression during pregnancy and after the baby arrived. The authors conclude that physical activity may be an important way to help prevent postnatal depression.
keyPoints: Regular physical activity during pregnancy and after birth was linked to a lower risk of depression, compared with inactivity.
The review included 16 studies found by searching one database for English-language papers from 2000 to 2018.
Postpartum depression can start within a month of birth and last up to a year, and it can affect both mother and baby.
The authors conclude that physical activity can be an important factor in preventing postnatal depression.

items.title: Systematic Review of Expected Weight Changes After Birth for Full-Term, Breastfed Newborns
items.source: Journal of Obstetric, Gynecologic, and Neonatal Nursing
items.journal: Journal of Obstetric, Gynecologic, and Neonatal Nursing
items.summary: This review looked at 11 recent studies of how much weight healthy, full-term, breastfed newborns lose in their first weeks. Most babies lose about 6-7% of their birth weight by day 2 and 7-8% by day 3, and some lose 10% or more. Most babies are back to their birth weight by 10 to 14 days. Note that this is about the baby's weight, not the mother's weight after birth.
keyPoints: By day 3, breastfed newborns usually lose about 7-8% of their birth weight.
The lowest weight usually happens on day 2, 3 or 4 after birth.
Some breastfed newborns lose 10% or more of their birth weight.
Most babies regain their birth weight by 10 to 14 days, and rates of exclusive breastfeeding were lower when babies lost more weight.

items.title: Lifestyle interventions to maternal weight loss after birth: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at eight randomised trials of technology-based programmes (such as apps, text messages or online support) to help women lose weight after having a baby. Most of the trials found that women using the programmes lost more weight than women who did not. However, the studies were small and short, and in half of them women found it hard to keep up with the programme over time.
keyPoints: Most of the eight trials found more weight loss in the technology-support group than in the comparison group.
Five studies followed women for only 40 days to 16 weeks, and six had between 18 and 66 women, so the results are limited.
Half of the studies reported that women found it hard to stick with the programmes over time.
The authors concluded that technology-based support can help postpartum women reach a healthy lifestyle and weight control, but larger and longer studies are needed.

items.title: Does aerobic exercise reduce postpartum depressive symptoms? a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from 13 randomised trials with 1,734 mothers in the first year after birth. It looked at whether aerobic exercise lowers symptoms of depression. Exercise was linked to fewer depressive symptoms overall. The authors say the results should be read with caution because the studies differed a lot and had some risk of bias.
keyPoints: Across all 13 trials combined, exercise significantly reduced depressive symptoms after birth.
The benefit did not differ significantly between women who might have depression and women in the general postpartum population.
Group exercise, exercise chosen by the mother, and exercise combined with other support may all be helpful.
The authors urge caution because the trials varied widely and had risk of bias.

items.title: Diagnosis and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage: a race against time
items.summary: This review looks at how to spot and treat heavy bleeding after birth (postpartum haemorrhage) quickly. It reports that the bleeding happens in about 13% of vaginal births and 31% of caesarean births. Judging blood loss by eye misses about half of cases, so international guidelines recommend measuring blood loss objectively, for example with a calibrated collection drape. Acting fast at each step can make the difference between life and death.
keyPoints: Postpartum haemorrhage affects an estimated 13% of women after vaginal birth and 31% after caesarean birth.
Estimating blood loss by eye misses 52% of diagnoses at vaginal birth, so guidelines recommend measuring it objectively, such as with a calibrated blood collection drape.
Measuring blood loss and monitoring vital signs, together with a standard first-response treatment bundle, has been shown to diagnose bleeding earlier and improve outcomes.
Six delays to avoid include late diagnosis, late first treatment, late escalation of care, and late access to blood and blood products.

items.title: Tranexamic acid for preventing postpartum haemorrhage after vaginal birth
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether giving tranexamic acid (a drug that helps blood clot) to every woman during a vaginal birth prevents heavy bleeding afterwards. It combined three trials with almost 19,000 women. Adding the drug to usual care made little to no difference to how many women lost 500 mL or more of blood, and likely made little to no difference to losses of 1000 mL or more. The evidence is too limited to say whether it affects rare serious events such as death or blood clots.
keyPoints: Tranexamic acid given routinely to prevent bleeding made little to no difference to blood loss of 500 mL or more (high-certainty evidence).
It likely made little to no difference to blood loss of 1000 mL or more, severe illness, or satisfaction, and made no difference to blood transfusions.
In women without anaemia, one trial found slightly fewer needed extra medicines to help the womb contract; no difference was seen in women with anaemia.
Evidence on maternal death, blood clots, hysterectomy and seizures is too uncertain to draw conclusions.

items.title: Causes of and risk factors for postpartum haemorrhage: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pooled results from 327 studies covering over 847 million women to find out why heavy bleeding after birth (postpartum haemorrhage) happens and who is more likely to have it. The most common cause was the womb not tightening properly after birth (uterine atony), found in about 7 in 10 cases. Several factors raised the chance of heavy bleeding, with some linked more strongly than others. The authors say most of the studies were of high methodological quality.
keyPoints: Uterine atony (the womb not contracting well after birth) was the most common cause, at about 70.6% of cases, followed by genital tract trauma (16.9%) and retained placenta (16.4%).

Strongly linked risk factors included anaemia, previous heavy bleeding after birth, caesarean birth, multiple pregnancy, placenta praevia, assisted reproductive technology use, a baby over 4500 g, and shoulder dystocia.
Moderately linked factors included BMI of 30 or more, gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, polyhydramnios, antepartum haemorrhage and COVID-19 infection.

The authors say the findings support the WHO recommendation that all women giving birth be offered medicines to help the womb contract, and support using treatment bundles because some women have more than one cause.

items.title: Uterotonic agents for preventing postpartum haemorrhage: a network meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pooled 122 trials (almost 122,000 women) comparing medicines given after birth to help the womb contract and prevent heavy bleeding. Most of the medicines worked better than no treatment. Adding ergometrine or misoprostol to oxytocin, the current standard, may lower the chance of heavy bleeding further, but these combinations were linked to more side effects such as nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Carbetocin worked about as well as oxytocin and did not raise the risk of side effects.
keyPoints: Most uterotonic medicines prevent heavy bleeding after birth (500 mL or more) better than placebo or no treatment.
Ergometrine plus oxytocin lowers the risk of bleeding of 500 mL or more compared with oxytocin alone (high-certainty evidence); misoprostol plus oxytocin probably does too (moderate-certainty).
Carbetocin has similar effects to oxytocin and was the only agent not linked to more side effects.
Other agents raised the risk of side effects such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or fever compared with oxytocin, and ergometrine may raise blood pressure and cause headache.

items.title: FIGO recommendations on objective measurement of blood loss after birth for early detection of postpartum hemorrhage
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This guideline from FIGO looks at how blood loss after birth is measured. Postpartum haemorrhage (heavy bleeding after birth) is the leading cause of maternal death worldwide, and judging blood loss by eye is often inaccurate and can miss it. Measuring blood loss objectively, for example with calibrated drapes, gives a more reliable estimate and helps care teams act sooner. The paper also describes barriers, such as cost and training, to making this routine in all settings.
keyPoints: Visual estimation of blood loss after birth is widely used but highly inaccurate and often leads to missed or delayed diagnosis of heavy bleeding.
Objective measurement, such as calibrated drapes and cumulative measurement, is not perfectly precise but is far more reliable than estimating by eye.
Combining objective measurement with early warning systems has been effective in reducing complications and deaths from postpartum haemorrhage.
Low-cost, reusable, locally made devices could help bring objective measurement to settings with limited resources.

items.title: Effectiveness of care bundles for prevention and treatment of postpartum hemorrhage: a systematic review
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review looked at 'care bundles', which are sets of three or more steps that hospitals carry out together to prevent or treat heavy bleeding after birth. It pooled 22 studies. One bundle used to treat bleeding, called E-MOTIVE, clearly improved outcomes for women giving birth vaginally, and the evidence for it was rated high certainty. A California bundle that covers both prevention and treatment may lower severe complications, but the evidence for that is weaker.
keyPoints: The E-MOTIVE treatment bundle cut the risk of severe complications from bleeding (risk ratio 0.40) and also reduced blood transfusions, severe bleeding and average blood loss, based on high-certainty evidence.
The California Maternal Quality Care Collaborative bundle, which covers prevention and treatment, may reduce severe maternal complications (risk ratio 0.64), but this evidence is low certainty.
Prevention-only bundles may reduce blood loss and the length of hospital and intensive care stays, but only 2 studies were found and certainty is low.
Most other bundles need more research before they are widely adopted, and many studies were not designed in a way that gives reliable answers.

items.title: Influence of maternal body mass index on pregnancy complications and outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled many studies to see how a mother's weight before or early in pregnancy relates to complications. Women with overweight or obesity had higher odds of gestational diabetes, high blood pressure in pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, caesarean birth, induced labour and heavy bleeding after birth than women of normal weight. The risks were higher with obesity than with overweight, which the authors describe as a dose-dependent effect. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Overweight and obesity were linked to higher odds of heavy bleeding after birth (postpartum haemorrhage), with odds ratios of 1.67 and 1.88 compared with normal weight.
Gestational diabetes, gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia were all more likely with higher body mass index.
Caesarean birth and induction of labour were also more common in women with overweight or obesity.
Risks rose step by step from overweight to obesity.

items.title: Prophylactic antibiotics for manual removal of retained placenta in vaginal birth
