items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether giving antibiotics as a precaution helps when a placenta that has not come out on its own after a vaginal birth is removed by hand. It found four older studies of 974 women, and it is not clear whether the antibiotics lower the risk of a womb infection (endometritis). They also seemed to make little or no difference to heavy bleeding after birth or to the baby being admitted to intensive care. The evidence is weak, and the authors say better trials are needed.
keyPoints: Four retrospective studies with 974 women were included, all comparing antibiotics with no antibiotics.
It is very uncertain whether preventive antibiotics reduce womb infection after manual removal of the placenta (very low-certainty evidence).
Antibiotics may make little to no difference to postpartum haemorrhage or to newborn intensive care admission (low-certainty evidence).
No data were found on many other outcomes, such as sepsis, hospital stay, side effects or women's satisfaction.

items.title: Perceptions and experiences of the prevention, detection, and management of postpartum haemorrhage: a qualitative evidence synthesis
items.summary: This review pulled together 43 studies of what women, families and health workers say about heavy bleeding after birth (postpartum haemorrhage, or PPH), mostly in low- and middle-income countries. It found that beliefs about bleeding, who decides to seek help, and shortages of staff and supplies all shape how quickly PPH is spotted and treated. Confidence in the findings ranged from very low to high, and the review did not test any treatments.
keyPoints: In many communities, bleeding after birth is seen as normal or as cleansing, and some people believe PPH is caused by spirits or punishment (moderate to high confidence).
For home births, female family members or traditional birth attendants usually notice heavy bleeding first, and family members often decide whether and when to seek care (high confidence).
Women who had PPH in health facilities described it as painful, embarrassing and traumatic, and partners and family found it stressful too (moderate confidence).
Shortages of drugs, supplies, blood and staff delay care, while team simulation training can help different health workers work together well in an emergency (high to moderate confidence).

items.title: Aspirin Use to Prevent Preeclampsia and Related Morbidity and Mortality: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force
items.summary: This review pulled together 23 randomised trials (nearly 27,000 people) on taking daily low-dose aspirin during pregnancy. For people at increased risk of preeclampsia, aspirin was linked to a lower chance of preeclampsia, preterm birth, poor growth of the baby in the womb, and death of the baby around the time of birth. It did not raise the risk of heavy bleeding after birth (postpartum hemorrhage) or other bleeding problems, and no harms were seen for babies.
keyPoints: Low-dose aspirin was linked to a lower risk of preeclampsia (about 15% lower) in people at increased risk.
It was also linked to lower risks of preterm birth, poor fetal growth and perinatal death.
There was no significant increase in postpartum hemorrhage or other bleeding-related harms.
No rare perinatal or longer-term harms were found; most trials enrolled mainly White populations.

items.title: Uterine balloon tamponade for the treatment of postpartum hemorrhage: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review looked at uterine balloon tamponade, a balloon placed inside the womb to press on the lining and help stop heavy bleeding after birth. It pooled 91 studies covering 4729 women. The balloon worked in about 86 out of 100 women treated, and complications were uncommon. However, trials and observational studies disagreed on whether using the balloon actually improves outcomes, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Across 91 studies, the balloon stopped severe bleeding after birth in about 85.9% of women treated.
Success was highest when bleeding was due to a weak womb muscle (87.1%) or placenta previa (86.8%), and lowest with placenta accreta spectrum (66.7%).
It worked somewhat less often after cesarean births (81.7%) than vaginal births (87.0%).
Complications linked to the balloon were low (6.5% or less), but trials and observational studies gave conflicting results on its overall benefit.

items.title: Quantitative Blood Loss in Obstetric Hemorrhage: ACOG COMMITTEE OPINION SUMMARY, Number 794
items.summary: This ACOG opinion looks at how blood loss is measured after birth. Heavy bleeding after birth (postpartum hemorrhage) causes about 11% of maternal deaths in the United States, and many of these deaths may be preventable. Guessing blood loss by eye is often inaccurate, which can delay care. Measuring it, for example by weighing materials or using graduated drapes, gives a more accurate picture, though it has not yet been shown to improve health outcomes.
keyPoints: Postpartum hemorrhage causes about 11% of US maternal deaths, and 54-93% of deaths from obstetric hemorrhage may be preventable.
Estimating blood loss by eye is imprecise and is a leading cause of delayed response to heavy bleeding.
Measuring blood loss (graduated drapes or weighing) is more accurate than visual estimation, but no one method is shown to be best.
Using a full hemorrhage care bundle is linked to better outcomes, but more research is needed on the effect of measuring blood loss alone.

items.title: Intramuscular versus intravenous prophylactic oxytocin for the third stage of labour
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether oxytocin, a medicine given just after a vaginal birth to help prevent heavy bleeding, works differently when given as a shot into the muscle or through a drip into a vein. It combined three trials with 1306 women. The evidence was very low quality, and no clear difference in benefits or risks was found between the two routes. The authors say better-designed, larger trials are needed.
keyPoints: Three trials with 1306 women compared oxytocin into the muscle with oxytocin into a vein after vaginal birth.
There was no clear difference between the two routes for severe bleeding (1000 mL or more), blood transfusion, or other bleeding outcomes.
The evidence was very low quality because of study design limits and small numbers of events.
Maternal death, low blood pressure and how satisfied women were were not reported, so larger, better trials are needed.

items.title: Practice Bulletin No. 183: Postpartum Hemorrhage
items.summary: This is a clinical guideline from US obstetricians about heavy bleeding after birth, called postpartum hemorrhage. It describes how common and serious it is, and covers risk factors, how it is checked for, how it is prevented and how it is treated. It also encourages maternity teams to use standard, step-by-step plans of care so bleeding is handled quickly and consistently.
keyPoints: Postpartum hemorrhage means losing 1,000 mL or more of blood, or losing blood with signs of low blood volume, within 24 hours of birth.
It is the leading cause of maternal death worldwide and the leading cause of severe illness for mothers in the United States.
In the US, rates of postpartum hemorrhage rose 26% between 1994 and 2006, mainly because the uterus did not contract well after birth (atony), while deaths from it have fallen since the late 1980s.
Maternity providers are encouraged to use standardized care bundles, such as shared policies, guidelines and algorithms, to manage postpartum hemorrhage.

items.title: Effect of exercise on depression and anxiety symptoms: systematic umbrella review with meta-meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pulled together 63 earlier reviews of trials, covering about 79,500 people, to see how exercise affects depression and anxiety symptoms. Exercise reduced both, and aerobic exercise (like brisk walking, jogging or cycling) had the biggest effect. Among the groups studied, postnatal women were one of the two groups who gained the most for depression. Depression benefits were larger with group and supervised exercise.
keyPoints: Exercise reduced depression and anxiety symptoms across all groups studied.
Postnatal women, along with adults aged 18-30, showed the greatest depression benefit.
Aerobic exercise had the strongest effect on both depression and anxiety.
Group and supervised exercise was linked to larger reductions in depression; shorter, lower-intensity exercise was linked to larger reductions in anxiety.

items.title: The effect of postpartum interventions on healing and pain in women with perineal trauma: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 19 studies with 1899 women to see which care methods help healing and pain after a perineal tear or episiotomy. Treatments given in the first 24 hours did not reduce pain, but by day two cold application worked best. Treatments sped up healing by at least two days, with perineal education (diet, Kegel exercises, spotting infection signs, hygiene) helping most. Healing began around days 7 to 10 even without any treatment, and the authors say more research is needed on herbal creams and hygiene advice.
keyPoints: Interventions in the first 24 hours after an episiotomy did not reduce pain.
Cold application on the second day was the most effective way to ease perineal pain.
Interventions started healing at least two days earlier, and perineal education was the most effective method.
Healing began around days 7 to 10 even without intervention.

items.title: Comparative Efficacy and Acceptability of Non-surgical Treatments with or without Exercise for Diastasis Recti Abdominis in Postpartum Women: A Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: This review pooled 21 randomised trials (1,195 women) to compare non-surgical treatments for diastasis recti, the gap that can open between the stomach muscles after birth. Exercise alone, a support corset, acupuncture and exercise combined with muscle stimulation all narrowed the gap compared with no treatment. Combining exercise with neuromuscular electrical stimulation ranked best. The authors say the results need careful reading because the studies varied and some data were sparse.
keyPoints: Exercise alone, a corset, acupuncture and exercise plus electrical muscle stimulation all reduced the gap between the stomach muscles compared with no treatment.
Exercise combined with neuromuscular electrical stimulation ranked as the best treatment tested, followed by acupuncture with exercise.
Treatments combined with exercise ranked better than treatments used without exercise.
Women found the different treatments similarly acceptable.

items.title: Impact of exercise on musculoskeletal pain and disability in the postpartum period: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 37 studies of nearly 3,800 women in the first year after birth to see whether exercise eases back and pelvic pain. Exercise programmes, especially strengthening of the trunk muscles, were linked to less low back and pelvic pain and less related disability compared with no exercise. The evidence for these results was of moderate certainty. Evidence on whether exercise affects fear of movement was limited and inconclusive.
keyPoints: Trunk-strengthening exercise after birth was linked to a greater drop in low back and pelvic pain than no exercise (about 2 points on a 0-10 scale).
Exercise also reduced pain-related disability, with a large effect, and similar results were seen for general bodily pain.
The authors rated the evidence for these findings as moderate certainty.
It was unclear whether exercise changes fear of movement (kinesiophobia), because the evidence was limited.

items.title: Comparative Efficacy of Abdominal Exercises and Abdominal Binding on Diastasis Recti Abdominis Reduction in Postpartum Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: This review pooled 13 randomised trials of women with diastasis recti (a separation of the tummy muscles that often happens in pregnancy) after birth. It compared abdominal exercises, abdominal binding and no treatment. Abdominal exercises narrowed the gap below the belly button more than binding or no treatment, but results above the belly button were unclear. Back-related disability and pelvic floor scores did not clearly improve, and the authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Abdominal exercises reduced the muscle gap below the belly button more than binding or no intervention.
Exercises did not clearly help close the gap above the belly button.
No significant improvement was found in back-related disability (ODI) or pelvic floor symptom (PFDI) scores.
The authors call for more research using standard criteria and more diverse groups of women.

items.title: Effects of conservative approaches for treating diastasis recti abdominis in postpartum women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 34 trials of non-surgical treatments for diastasis recti (a gap between the two belly muscles) after birth. Abdominal exercises narrowed the gap more than no treatment, and adding other treatments, especially electrical stimulation, helped a little more. The evidence is very low certainty, so the results should be treated with caution.
keyPoints: Abdominal exercises reduced the muscle gap by about 6.8 mm compared with no treatment.
Only isotonic abdominal exercises (where the muscle moves through its range) gave a clear reduction in the gap.
Adding electrical stimulation to abdominal exercises gave the biggest extra benefit, about 4.4 mm.
The evidence is very low certainty, and better-designed trials are needed to confirm these findings.

items.title: An evidence-based comparison of rehabilitation strategies for diastasis recti abdominis in postpartum women: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 27 trials with 1,340 women to compare treatments for diastasis recti, the gap that can open between the stomach muscles after pregnancy. Programs that trained both the deep and the surface tummy muscles, especially with gentle electrical muscle stimulation and breathing techniques, narrowed the gap the most. Kinesio-taping and abdominal binders helped less. The quality of the evidence ranged from low to high, so the authors advise caution and say more studies are needed.
keyPoints: Exercise programs working both deep and surface abdominal muscles reduced the gap between the muscles more than single-muscle or non-exercise approaches.
The best results came when exercise was combined with neuromuscular electrical stimulation and breathing techniques.
Kinesio-taping and abdominal binders showed low to moderate effectiveness.
Evidence quality varied from low to high, and few treatments were compared directly, so results should be read cautiously.

items.title: Effects of perineal massage at different stages on perineal and postpartum pelvic floor function in primiparous women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 trials covering 1057 first-time mothers to see when perineal massage works best: in late pregnancy or during the pushing stage of labour. Massage at either time helped reduce injury to the perineum (the area between the vagina and anus). Massage during the pushing stage was linked to less perineal pain right after birth, while massage in pregnancy was linked to less bowel and wind leakage three months after birth.
keyPoints: Perineal massage in pregnancy or during the second stage of labour can help reduce perineal injuries in first-time mothers.
Massage during the second stage of labour was linked to less perineal pain right after birth than massage in pregnancy.
Only massage in pregnancy was linked to less faecal (bowel) and flatus (wind) incontinence at three months after birth.
Neither timing made a significant difference to urinary incontinence at three months postpartum.

items.title: Update on Physiotherapy in Postpartum Urinary Incontinence. A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at eight randomized trials of physiotherapy for urinary leakage after birth. All of them tested pelvic floor muscle training, and six of the eight found significant benefits, including for strength, endurance, quality of life and sexual function. The authors conclude that this training helps, and recommend supervised exercise combined with a home routine. It is not clear whether the benefits last over time.
keyPoints: All eight included trials used pelvic floor muscle training as the treatment.
Six of the eight studies reported significant improvements, such as in muscle strength, quality of life and sexual function.
Supervised, controlled exercise combined with a home training routine is recommended.
It is not clear whether the benefits are maintained over time.

items.title: Effect of different interventions on the efficacy of postpartum urinary incontinence in China: A systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review compared 13 different treatments for urinary leakage after childbirth (postpartum stress urinary incontinence) by pooling results from earlier studies, mostly from China. Treatments that combined approaches ranked highest, and acupressure together with pelvic floor muscle training ranked as most effective. Pelvic floor muscle training alone, biofeedback electrical stimulation alone and health coaching ranked lowest. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Acupressure plus pelvic floor muscle training ranked as the most effective of 13 treatments for postpartum urinary leakage.
Combined treatments, such as pelvic floor training with acupuncture or electrical stimulation, generally ranked higher than single treatments.
Pelvic floor muscle training alone, biofeedback electrical stimulation alone and health coaching ranked lowest.
Improvement in clinical measures was seen in women with postpartum stress urinary incontinence.

items.title: Effectiveness of physiotherapy for lower urinary tract symptoms in postpartum women: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 17 randomised trials of women with bladder symptoms after childbirth, such as leaking urine. It compared pelvic floor muscle training alone with training plus electrical stimulation, with or without biofeedback. Adding electrical stimulation worked better than training alone for early postpartum bladder symptoms, and the authors describe it as safe.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training plus electrical stimulation (with or without biofeedback) worked better than training alone for early postpartum bladder symptoms.
Women who had both stimulation and biofeedback on top of training had better incontinence quality of life scores and stronger pelvic floor muscles.
Urine leakage over one hour was lower, and bladder pressure and flow measurements improved, with the combined treatment.
The authors concluded the combined approach was both more effective and safe in the early postpartum period.

items.title: Does perinatal period pelvic floor muscle exercises affect sexuality and pelvic muscle strength? A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials to see whether pelvic floor muscle exercises during pregnancy and after birth change sexual function and pelvic floor strength. The authors found the exercises had a small effect on sexual function in first-time mothers, both during pregnancy and after birth. They describe the exercises as a safe approach that may help improve sexual function after birth.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor exercises showed a small positive effect on sexual function during pregnancy and after birth in first-time mothers.
The effect on sexual function after birth was smaller and less certain than the effect seen during pregnancy.
The authors describe pelvic floor muscle training as a safe strategy that can improve sexual function after birth.

items.title: Prenatal anemia and postpartum hemorrhage risk: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research
items.summary: This review pooled results from 13 studies to see whether having anemia (low iron or low red blood cells) during pregnancy is linked to heavy bleeding after birth, known as postpartum hemorrhage. Severe anemia in pregnancy was linked to a higher chance of heavy bleeding after birth. Mild and moderate anemia did not show a clear link. The authors say severe anemia needs close management during pregnancy.
keyPoints: Severe anemia in pregnancy was linked to about 3.5 times higher odds of postpartum hemorrhage.
No clear link was found between mild anemia and postpartum hemorrhage.
No clear link was found between moderate anemia and postpartum hemorrhage.
The authors conclude that severe anemia in pregnancy warrants intensive management.

items.title: What is the evidence for abdominal and pelvic floor muscle training to treat diastasis recti abdominis postpartum? A systematic review with meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether abdominal and pelvic floor muscle exercises help treat diastasis recti, a separation of the tummy muscles that is common after birth. It pooled seven trials with 381 women. Deep tummy muscle training (transversus abdominis) may have narrowed the gap slightly, but the evidence was very low quality. The authors conclude there is not yet enough good evidence to recommend any specific exercise programme.
keyPoints: Seven randomised trials with 381 women were included.
Deep tummy muscle (transversus abdominis) training may have reduced the gap between the muscles by about 0.6 cm, but the evidence was very low quality.
Curl-up exercises showed very low quality evidence of benefit, based on single trials at high risk of bias.
Pelvic floor muscle training was not shown to be better than minimal intervention for diastasis recti, based on low to very low quality evidence.

items.title: Antenatal perineal massage benefits in reducing perineal trauma and postpartum morbidities: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 11 randomized trials with 3,467 women to see whether massaging the perineum (the area between the vagina and anus) during late pregnancy helps protect against tearing in birth. Women who did antenatal perineal massage had fewer episiotomies and fewer perineal tears, including fewer severe (third- and fourth-degree) tears. They also had less perineal pain, better wound healing, and less anal incontinence afterwards.
keyPoints: Antenatal perineal massage was linked to fewer episiotomies (about 21% lower risk) and fewer perineal tears (about 21% lower risk).
The risk of severe third- and fourth-degree tears was lower in the massage group.
Women who did massage had less perineal pain, better wound healing and less anal incontinence after birth.
The second stage of labor (pushing) was shorter, and Apgar scores for babies at 1 and 5 minutes were better.

items.title: Aspirin (single dose) for perineal pain in the early postpartum period
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether a single dose of aspirin eases pain in the perineum (the area between the vagina and anus) in the first days after birth. It combined 17 trials, mostly from 1967 to 1997, in women who had had an episiotomy (a surgical cut) and were not breastfeeding. Aspirin may help more women get adequate pain relief four to eight hours later than a placebo (dummy pill), but the evidence is low quality. It is uncertain whether aspirin changes the need for extra pain relief or the chance of side effects.
keyPoints: Aspirin may give more women adequate pain relief four to eight hours after a dose than placebo, based on low-certainty evidence.
It is uncertain whether aspirin reduces the need for extra pain relief or changes side effects, because the evidence is very low certainty.
No clear differences were found between aspirin doses of 300 mg, 600 mg and 1200 mg.
All trials involved women with episiotomy pain who were not breastfeeding, so there is no evidence on breastfeeding or effects on babies.

items.title: Interventions for preventing postpartum constipation
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at ways to prevent constipation after giving birth, mostly laxatives. It found only five small, mostly old trials, and the evidence was low to very low quality. One trial suggested senna may bring on the first bowel movement sooner but may also cause more tummy cramps. Overall, there isn't enough good evidence to say whether laxatives work or are safe for preventing constipation after birth.
keyPoints: There is not enough evidence to draw general conclusions about whether laxatives prevent postpartum constipation.
In one trial of 471 women, senna may increase the chance of a first bowel movement within 24 hours of birth (low-certainty evidence).
In the same trial, senna may increase abdominal cramps; it may make little or no difference to loose stools or diarrhoea in breastfed babies, but that evidence is very uncertain.
No trials tested diet, fluids, education or behaviour changes, and none looked at pain or straining or quality of life.

items.title: Effects of exercise on pregnancy and postpartum fatigue: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review pulled together seven trials (five in the main analysis) on whether exercise eases tiredness during pregnancy and after birth. Overall, exercise may have a small helpful effect on fatigue. The benefit was clearest for supervised exercise programmes after birth that lasted more than eight weeks. The authors say larger, high-quality trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Exercise during pregnancy and after birth may modestly reduce fatigue.
Postpartum exercise, supervised exercise and longer programmes showed clearer improvements than the comparison groups.
Supervised programmes lasting more than eight weeks after birth may be helpful for postpartum fatigue.
Only a few small studies were available, so more large, high-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Local cooling for relieving pain from perineal trauma sustained during childbirth
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 10 trials (1,233 women) testing cooling treatments such as ice packs and cold gel pads on the perineum to ease pain after childbirth. There is limited, very low-certainty evidence that cooling may reduce perineal pain in the first two days after birth. No harmful effects were noted, but the studies were small and the evidence is weak, so the authors say the results should be viewed with caution.
keyPoints: Ice packs or cold gel pads may reduce perineal pain in the first two days after birth, but the evidence is very low certainty.
Cooling was used for 10 to 20 minutes in the trials, and no adverse effects on wound healing were noted, though this came from small studies or was not reported.
Several treatments together, including prescription and non-prescription pain relief, are likely needed to manage perineal pain well.
The authors call for further well-designed trials because high-certainty evidence is still lacking.

items.title: The effectiveness of exercise-based interventions for preventing or treating postpartum depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 18 trials that tested exercise programs, mostly aerobic exercise or coaching, for preventing or treating low mood and depression in women between 4 and 52 weeks after birth. Exercise gave a small reduction in depressive symptoms overall. The quality of the evidence was low, so the real benefit is still uncertain and needs better testing.
keyPoints: Exercise-based programs were linked to a small reduction in postpartum depressive symptoms across the 18 trials.
The quality of evidence was low across the individual studies.
Exercise may offer another way to help prevent major depression in women with mild, below-threshold depressive symptoms after birth.
More rigorous trials against active comparison groups are needed, and cost-effectiveness is not yet clear.

items.title: Perineal prevention and protection in obstetrics: CNGOF clinical practice guidelines
items.journal: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.summary: These French clinical guidelines reviewed what can be done in pregnancy and childbirth to prevent serious tears involving the anal sphincter (OASIS) and later pelvic floor problems. They recommend perineal massage in pregnancy for women who want it, and a careful check for tears right after birth. Routine episiotomy (a cut to widen the opening) is not recommended in normal births, and a caesarean is not advised just to prevent later incontinence.
keyPoints: Perineal massage during pregnancy should be encouraged for women who want it (Grade B).

An episiotomy is not recommended in normal deliveries to reduce the risk of anal sphincter injury (Grade A); if one is done, a mediolateral cut is recommended and the reason should be explained and consent given.
The baby's head should be manually controlled as it crowns and the perineum supported to reduce the risk of serious tears (Grade C).
A perineal examination just after birth is recommended to check for anal sphincter injury (Grade B), and caesarean is not recommended solely to prevent later urinary or anal incontinence (Grade B).

items.title: Active versus expectant management for women in the third stage of labour
items.summary: This Cochrane review compared two ways of delivering the placenta after birth. In active management, a medicine is given to help the womb contract, the cord is clamped early and gently pulled to deliver the placenta. In expectant management, the placenta is allowed to come out on its own. Active management may reduce blood loss and anaemia after birth, but it may also cause side effects such as vomiting, afterpains and higher blood pressure. The evidence comes from only eight studies and is low or very low quality, so the findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: Active management may lower the number of women with anaemia (haemoglobin below 9 g/dL) after birth, and probably reduces blood loss over 500 mL and the need for extra medicines to help the womb contract.
It is uncertain whether active management lowers the risk of severe bleeding over 1000 mL, because the evidence is very low quality.
Possible downsides include higher blood pressure, vomiting, afterpains, more pain relief use and more women returning to hospital with bleeding.
The authors suggest women could be given information on the benefits and harms of both methods to support informed choice.

items.title: Quantitative Blood Loss in Obstetric Hemorrhage: ACOG COMMITTEE OPINION, Number 794
items.summary: This opinion from ACOG looks at how blood loss is measured after birth. Heavy bleeding after birth is a leading cause of maternal death in the US, and many of these deaths may be preventable. Measuring blood loss with tools like graduated drapes or weighing is more accurate than guessing by eye, but it has not yet been shown to improve health outcomes. More research is needed.
keyPoints: Postpartum hemorrhage causes about 11% of maternal deaths in the US, and 54-93% of deaths from obstetric hemorrhage may be preventable.
Guessing blood loss by eye is often inaccurate, and this is a leading cause of delayed response to heavy bleeding.
Measuring blood loss (for example with graduated drapes or by weighing) is more accurate than visual estimates, but no one method is shown to be best.
Hospital hemorrhage bundles (sets of care steps) are linked to better outcomes, but the specific effect of measuring blood loss still needs more research.

items.title: Planned birth at or near term for improving health outcomes for pregnant women with gestational diabetes and their infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether planning the birth at or near term (by induction or caesarean) is better than waiting for labour to start naturally in women with gestational diabetes. Only one trial of 425 women was found. There were no clear differences in caesarean birth, postpartum bleeding, an intact perineum or serious complications, but babies in the induction group were more likely to have jaundice. The evidence was low to very low quality, so no firm conclusions can be drawn.
keyPoints: Only one trial (425 women) was available, so the evidence is limited.
No clear differences were seen between induction and waiting for labour in caesarean section, instrumental vaginal birth, postpartum haemorrhage or intact perineum.
Babies of women who were induced had higher rates of neonatal jaundice (hyperbilirubinaemia).
The authors say better-quality trials are urgently needed.

items.title: Use of endoanal ultrasound for reducing the risk of complications related to anal sphincter injury after vaginal birth
items.summary: This review looked at whether a quick ultrasound scan of the back passage, done after birth but before a tear is stitched, could help prevent bowel control problems. Only one trial was found, with 752 first-time mothers who had second-degree tears. Women who had the scan first had less severe loss of bowel control later on, but more perineal pain at three months. The authors say the evidence is limited and more good-quality research is needed before this could be recommended routinely.
keyPoints: One trial of 752 first-time mothers with second-degree tears was included.
Having an endoanal ultrasound before the repair was linked to a lower rate of severe anal incontinence (loss of stool or wind causing social or hygiene problems).
Perineal pain at three months was higher in the ultrasound group.
The authors say more high-quality trials are needed before routine use on the labour ward could be supported.

items.title: Optimal types and doses of exercise for improving sleep quality in perinatal women: a systematic review and network meta-analysis based on randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pulled together 23 randomised trials (1,862 women) from pregnancy through the first year after birth to see which kinds of exercise best improve sleep quality. Relaxation exercises ranked highest among aerobic exercise, aerobic plus resistance training, yoga and Pilates. The best-ranked pattern was relaxation exercise for 4 weeks or less, 1-2 times a week, for 30-60 minutes per session. The abstract does not report an overall certainty rating, and the authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Relaxation exercises ranked best for improving sleep quality, ahead of aerobic exercise, aerobic plus resistance training, yoga and Pilates.
Programmes lasting 4 weeks or less ranked best for program length.
Sessions 1-2 times per week and lasting 30-60 minutes ranked best for frequency and session length.
The authors suggest prioritising this regimen in perinatal care and call for further research on exercise types and doses.

items.title: Cognitive and emotional correlates of sleep in the peripartum period: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 33 studies of 16,563 women to look at how sleep relates to thinking and emotions during pregnancy and after birth. Poor sleep was consistently linked with lower mood, harder emotion control, and more rumination and worry (going over the same thoughts again and again). Results for memory and concentration were mixed. Most of the evidence was a one-time snapshot, with only limited follow-up over time, so it shows a link rather than proving cause.
keyPoints: Poor sleep was consistently linked with worse mood and emotion regulation in the peripartum period.
Poor sleep was also linked with more rumination and worry.
Findings for memory and other thinking skills were mixed.
The limited follow-up evidence suggested poor sleep may contribute to changes in mood, anger and worry from pregnancy into the postpartum period.

items.title: Trajectories of sleep health during the perinatal period: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 17 studies that followed women's sleep from pregnancy through the first year after birth. Sleep patterns varied a lot from woman to woman. About 36% of women had a poorer-than-ideal sleep quality pattern, and about 22% had a poorer-than-ideal sleep duration pattern. Poorer sleep patterns were linked to higher risks of problems for mothers and babies, and to factors such as lower income, higher pre-pregnancy weight, and early fatigue, anxiety or low mood.
keyPoints: About 36% of women had a nonoptimal sleep quality pattern and about 22% had a nonoptimal sleep duration pattern across pregnancy and the first year postpartum.
Around 13% of women followed a clinical insomnia pattern, and about 15% had a poor sleep efficiency pattern.
When sleep quality patterns were regrouped, 38.9% of women had consistently good sleep, 37.6% had sleep that got worse, and 23.5% had sleep that improved from poor.
Low socioeconomic status, high pre-pregnancy BMI, poor baseline sleep and health, and high early fatigue, anxiety and depressive symptoms were linked to poorer sleep patterns.

items.title: The effects of aromatherapy on anxiety and sleep quality in maternal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 13 studies looking at aromatherapy (scented oils or inhaled scents) for anxiety and sleep in pregnant and postpartum women. Overall, aromatherapy was linked to lower anxiety and better sleep quality. The effects looked stronger when used during pregnancy. The authors say there were only a few studies, so more high-quality research is needed before the findings can be considered reliable.
keyPoints: Across 13 studies, aromatherapy was linked to lower anxiety in women around pregnancy and after birth.
Aromatherapy was also linked to better sleep quality.
The benefits were larger in the pregnancy (prenatal) group than overall.
The number of studies was limited, so the authors call for more high-quality research to confirm the results.

items.title: Sleep, circadian activity patterns and postpartum depression: A systematic review and meta-analysis of actigraphy studies
items.summary: This review pooled 19 studies that measured sleep with wrist-worn activity trackers (actigraphy) in women during pregnancy or after birth. It looked at how sleep and daily activity patterns relate to mental health after the baby arrives. The amount of sleep a mother got at night was most closely linked to how she felt psychologically, especially fatigue and postpartum depression. The authors say more studies are needed, particularly on sleep-wake rhythms during pregnancy.
keyPoints: Total night-time sleep after birth was the sleep measure most closely linked to mothers' mental wellbeing.
The review found night-time sleep was related to postpartum fatigue.
The combined analysis suggested night-time sleep was most strongly linked with postpartum depression.
More studies are needed on sleep-wake rhythms in pregnancy and after birth.

items.title: Dreaming for two: A systematic review of mental sleep activity during pregnancy
items.summary: This review looked at 17 studies on how pregnancy affects dreams and nightmares. Women tend to dream and have nightmares a lot during pregnancy, and remembering many dreams was linked to poorer sleep quality. Dreams often reflect pregnancy-related worries and experiences, and the authors suggest dreaming may help women prepare mentally for life after birth.
keyPoints: Women tend to have many dreams and nightmares during pregnancy.
Remembering lots of dreams was linked to poorer sleep quality in some studies.
Most dream content related to pregnancy, likely reflecting daytime experiences and concerns.
Dreaming may help with psychological preparation and coping with changes after childbirth.

items.title: Infant feeding type and maternal sleep during the postpartum period: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from seven studies of 6,472 mothers to compare night-time sleep in breastfeeding and non-breastfeeding mothers after birth. Breastfeeding mothers slept a little longer at night on average, by about a quarter of an hour. Mothers who shared sleeping space with their baby also slept longer if they were breastfeeding. The authors say more research is needed to understand how feeding choices and mothers' own sleep are linked.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding mothers had slightly longer night-time sleep than non-breastfeeding mothers (about 0.24 hours more on average).
Co-sleeping with the baby at night was linked to longer sleep in breastfeeding mothers.
The authors found no sign of publication bias, but say breastfeeding may be associated with longer sleep rather than proven to cause it.
More research is needed on how mothers' feeding decisions affect their sleep.

items.title: Changes in parental sleep from pregnancy to postpartum: A meta-analytic review of actigraphy studies
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 16 studies that used wrist-worn sleep trackers (actigraphy) to measure how parents' sleep changes from pregnancy through the first year after a baby is born. Parents slept less overall, slept less efficiently, and spent more time awake during the night after the birth. These changes were biggest in the first four weeks, and by about 16 weeks sleep was starting to move back toward pre-birth levels.
keyPoints: Total sleep time and sleep efficiency dropped after a baby was born, while time awake after first falling asleep went up.
The biggest changes in sleep were seen in the first four weeks after birth.
Up to 16 weeks after birth sleep was still different from before, but starting to return toward pre-birth levels.
The authors say future studies should include fathers as well as mothers and report a wider range of sleep measures.

items.title: Effect of postpartum anaemia on maternal health-related quality of life: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 27 studies to see how low iron or anaemia after birth affects how mothers feel day to day. Women who were anaemic or low in iron were more likely to have symptoms of depression than women with enough iron. In three trials, mothers given iron supplements had lower fatigue scores than those who were not. It was still unclear whether postpartum anaemia affects how mothers bond or interact with their babies.
keyPoints: Iron-deficient or anaemic women were about 1.66 times more likely to have symptoms of depression after birth than women who were not anaemic.
In three randomised trials, iron supplements lowered fatigue scores compared with the control group.
Two of four studies found anaemic mothers were less responsive and had more negative feelings towards their children, but overall the effect on mother-child interaction is unclear.
The review concluded that postpartum anaemia lowers quality of life and that replacing iron improves tiredness and depression symptoms.

items.title: The Efficacy of Digital Cognitive-Behavioral Interventions in Supporting the Psychological Adjustment and Sleep Quality of Pregnant Women with Sub-Clinical Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review pooled seven trials with 1,873 pregnant women who had mild, sub-clinical mood symptoms. It looked at online or app-based programs using cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which helps people change unhelpful thoughts and habits. The programs reduced depression and anxiety symptoms by the end of the program, but the depression benefit did not last into the postpartum follow-up. They did not improve sleep quality. The authors say no firm conclusions can be drawn about which type of program works best.
keyPoints: Digital CBT programs reduced mild depression symptoms in pregnancy by the end of the program.
The depression benefit was not maintained at follow-up after birth.
The programs reduced anxiety symptoms but had no effect on sleep quality.
The programs were well accepted, and no firm conclusions could be drawn about which type works best.

items.title: Risk factors for lactation mastitis in China: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined 14 studies of about 8,000 Chinese women to find what raises the chance of lactation mastitis, a painful breast inflammation during breastfeeding. Several factors were linked to higher risk, including improper milking method, repeated milk stasis (milk building up in the breast), nipple problems, short postpartum rest time and sleeping on the stomach after birth. The authors suggest that changing some of these, such as feeding posture, milking method and sleeping position, could lower how often mastitis happens.
keyPoints: Mastitis affects roughly 3% to 33% of women after birth, and risk was highest in the first six months postpartum.
Improper milking method and repeated milk stasis were linked to much higher odds of mastitis.
Postpartum rest time of less than 3 months and sleeping on the stomach were linked to higher odds.
Modifiable factors include breastfeeding posture, milking method, nipple cleaning, breast massage by non-medical staff and sleeping position.

items.title: The Effects of Aromatherapy on Postpartum Women: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 15 randomised trials (2,131 women in total) that tested aromatherapy after birth. Most of the studies found it helped with physical and emotional wellbeing, including sleep quality, fatigue, anxiety, mood and pain. Most studies reported no serious side effects. The authors suggest aromatherapy may be used as a gentle extra option alongside usual care, but the abstract does not rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Most of the 15 trials found aromatherapy improved physical and emotional health after birth.
Benefits were seen for sleep quality, fatigue, anxiety, depression, stress and mood.
Aromatherapy also helped with several kinds of pain, such as pain after a caesarean, after an episiotomy and from sore nipples.
Most studies reported no serious side effects, and the best length of treatment varied by essential oil.

items.title: Interventions for sleep problems during pregnancy: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 16 studies with 1,252 pregnant women to see whether treatments can improve poor sleep and insomnia in pregnancy. The treatments included talking therapies for insomnia, relaxation, mindfulness and yoga, acupuncture, herbal products and medication. Every approach showed some early promise, but few of the studies were high quality, so it is still unclear how well any of them work.
keyPoints: Sleep problems are common in pregnancy but are often not diagnosed or treated.
The 16 studies tested cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, relaxation, mindfulness and yoga, herbal products, acupuncture and medication.
All of the treatments showed preliminary support, but only six studies were randomised controlled trials and only four followed women over time.
The authors call for better-quality trials and for effective sleep programmes to be built into routine pregnancy care.

items.title: Postpartum stress and infant outcome: A review of current literature
items.summary: This review looked at 74 studies on how stress after birth (including depression and anxiety symptoms) is linked to babies' health and development. It found that ongoing stress in new mothers is associated with slower infant growth, delays in language, thinking and movement, and poorer infant sleep. The authors describe the evidence linking postpartum stress to infant outcomes as strong, but note that many outside factors play a part and not all articles were reviewed.
keyPoints: Postpartum stress was linked to poorer infant growth and development, including language, cognitive and motor skills.
Postpartum stress was linked to poorer infant sleep, which can have a knock-on 'ripple effect'.
Postpartum depression was inversely related to breastfeeding, and breastfeeding success helped support good infant feeding outcomes.
The link between postpartum stress and infant outcomes works through many outside factors, and more research is needed on factors that could be changed.

items.title: Sleep in parents of preterm infants: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 18 reports from 16 studies on how well parents of babies born early sleep, both while the baby is in hospital and after going home. It found that sleep amount and sleep quality were often poor. Parental stress was the factor most often linked with worse sleep. The authors say more research is needed to find which parents are most at risk and to guide advice.
keyPoints: Most studies that measured sleep quality found it was poor, mostly based on parents' own reports, and two studies that measured sleep objectively also found poor quality.
One study of mothers of preterm babies found they averaged 6.3 hours of sleep a day in the first 5-10 days.
Parental stress was the factor most consistently linked with poorer sleep quality.
The authors conclude that sleep for parents of preterm infants is inadequate and may affect family health, and that more research is needed to guide targeted support.

items.title: Consequences of maternal postpartum depression: A systematic review of maternal and infant outcomes
items.summary: This review pulled together 122 studies on what happens when postpartum depression goes untreated. It looked at effects on mothers, on babies, and on how mothers and babies relate to each other. The authors conclude that postpartum depression can make it harder for mothers to thrive and for children to develop well, so spotting and treating it early seems important.
keyPoints: The review covered 122 studies on the effects of untreated postpartum depression.
Maternal effects included physical health, psychological health, relationships and risky behaviors.
Infant effects included growth, physical health, sleep, and motor, cognitive, language, emotional, social and behavioral development.
The authors say detecting and treating depression early in the postnatal period may help avoid harmful consequences.

items.title: Safe Sleep and Skin-to-Skin Care in the Neonatal Period for Healthy Term Newborns
items.summary: This clinical report looks at skin-to-skin care and rooming-in (keeping baby in the mother's room) for healthy newborns in the hospital. These practices are linked to more breastfeeding, safer and healthier transitions after birth, and better bonding. The report also notes case reports of rare but serious events, such as sudden unexpected collapse, suffocation, and falls from hospital beds, when a baby is not being watched during skin-to-skin time or sleep. It is written to help hospitals set up policies that keep both practices going safely.
keyPoints: Skin-to-skin care and rooming-in are supported by evidence for more breastfeeding, safer transitions, and better mother-baby bonding.
There are case reports of sudden unexpected newborn collapse, suffocation and falls from adult hospital beds, mostly during unobserved skin-to-skin care or rooming-in.
Sleep habits modeled in hospital, such as baby's sleep position, are likely to shape sleep practices at home after discharge.
The report aims to help hospitals and birthing centers create safe skin-to-skin and safe sleep policies.

items.title: Long-term risk of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events in women with gestational diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 9 large studies covering about 4.2 million women to see how having gestational diabetes (diabetes first found in pregnancy) relates to long-term health. Women who had gestational diabetes were more likely to later have heart failure, heart attack, stroke, or to die from any cause than women who did not. The authors say long-term monitoring and prevention matter, even if blood sugar returned to normal after the birth.
keyPoints: Women with past gestational diabetes had a higher risk of death from any cause (HR 1.29); absolute rates were 3.2% versus 2.5%.
Risks were also higher for acute heart failure (HR 1.74), heart attack (HR 1.63) and ischemic stroke (HR 1.70).
Results held up in sensitivity analyses, and no significant publication bias was found, though results varied between studies for most outcomes.
The authors say long-term monitoring and preventive steps are needed, even after blood sugar normalises after pregnancy.

items.title: Anxiety in pregnancy complicated by gestational and pre-gestational diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 34 studies to look at anxiety in women with diabetes during pregnancy. Women with gestational diabetes were more likely to have anxiety during pregnancy than women without diabetes. After birth, anxiety levels in women who had gestational diabetes were about the same as in other women. There was too little evidence to say anything firm about diabetes that was present before pregnancy.
keyPoints: Women with gestational diabetes had higher odds of anxiety during pregnancy than healthy women (OR 1.69).
About 36% of women with gestational diabetes screened positive for anxiety in eight Asian studies, but results varied hugely between studies, so this number is very uncertain.
Anxiety after birth did not differ significantly between women who had gestational diabetes and healthy women.
Evidence on pre-existing diabetes came from only two studies and is preliminary; more research is needed before routine anxiety screening can be recommended.

items.title: Maternity versus non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether being screened for gestational diabetes in a maternity setting (a service focused on pregnancy care) works better than being screened in a general medical setting. Only one trial, with 781 pregnant women, was found. It suggests screening in a maternity setting may mean more women complete screening and follow-up, and may shorten the wait to reach antenatal diabetes care by about 4.7 days, though this evidence is low certainty. For most other outcomes, such as diagnosis rates, pre-eclampsia and baby outcomes, the evidence was too weak to say whether the setting makes a difference.
keyPoints: Screening in a maternity setting may increase the number of women who follow screening and follow-up guidelines (low-certainty evidence).
Maternity settings may also cut the time to reach antenatal diabetes care by about 4.7 days (low-certainty evidence).
The reviewers were very uncertain whether the setting changes diagnosis of gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, or outcomes for babies.
Only one trial was found, and its analysis weakened the protection that randomisation normally gives, so more research is needed.

items.title: Postpartum diabetes mellitus among patients with early gestational diabetes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Diabetes and Its Complications
items.journal: Journal of Diabetes and Its Complications
items.summary: This review pooled 11 studies to compare women diagnosed with gestational diabetes early in pregnancy (before 24 weeks) with women diagnosed later (24 weeks or after). After birth, diabetes was found more often in the early group (12.8% vs 6.1%). Impaired glucose tolerance, a stage between normal blood sugar and diabetes, was also more common (24.7% vs 13.0%).
keyPoints: Diabetes diagnosed after birth was more common in women with early gestational diabetes than in those diagnosed later (12.8% vs 6.1%).
Impaired glucose tolerance after birth was also higher in the early group (24.7% vs 13.0%).
The review included 11 studies covering 1,573 women with early and 3,340 with standard gestational diabetes.
Most studies checked blood sugar handling 5 to 12 weeks after birth.

items.title: Calcium Supplementation in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review of Clinical Studies
items.summary: This review pulled together 34 clinical studies on taking calcium supplements during pregnancy. Calcium was linked to less high blood pressure and preeclampsia, a lower chance of preterm birth, and better bone density after birth. The benefits seemed biggest for women who don't get enough calcium from food or who are at high risk of blood pressure problems. The authors say bigger, high-quality trials are still needed to confirm these results.
keyPoints: Calcium supplements were linked to less frequent and less severe gestational hypertension and preeclampsia.
Supplementation was linked to lower risk of preterm birth, longer pregnancy, higher birth weight and better maternal bone density after birth.
Benefits were strongest with high-dose regimens (1.5-2 g/day) split into smaller doses.
The right daily dose may depend on a woman's diet, needs and general health, and larger randomized trials are needed.

items.title: The efficacy of interventions to prevent type 2 diabetes among women with recent gestational diabetes mellitus-A living systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Women who have had gestational diabetes are more likely to develop type 2 diabetes, especially in the first few years after giving birth. This review pooled 17 trials (3 using medicines and 14 using lifestyle changes) in women within 5 years of a gestational diabetes pregnancy. Overall, the programmes did not clearly lower the number of women who developed type 2 diabetes, though one way of analysing four of the studies hinted at a reduction. The authors call the evidence unclear and say more studies are needed.
keyPoints: Gestational diabetes is now recognised as a risk factor for later type 2 diabetes, with risk especially high in the first few years after childbirth.
Across 17 trials, interventions did not significantly reduce type 2 diabetes compared with usual care or placebo.
An analysis of four studies that reported hazard ratios suggested diabetes incidence may be reduced (hazard ratio 0.68).
The review describes the evidence as equivocal and calls for more studies, including ones testing medicines.

items.title: The effect of previous history of Pre-Eclampsia on subclinical carotid atherosclerosis up to 20 years Postpartum: A systematic review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: Researchers combined 12 studies (583 women who had pre-eclampsia and 610 who had uncomplicated pregnancies) to see whether pre-eclampsia leads to early thickening of the neck (carotid) artery walls, a sign of artery disease. On average the women were checked about 8.5 years after giving birth, and up to 20 years. Overall, artery thickness was not meaningfully different between the two groups, though the studies varied a lot in their results. The authors note that women with a past history of pre-eclampsia do carry more heart disease risk factors.
keyPoints: Overall, carotid artery wall thickness was not significantly different in women with past pre-eclampsia compared with women with uncomplicated pregnancies.
Only 5 of the 12 studies found thicker artery walls in women with past pre-eclampsia; the rest found no difference or even thinner walls.
Results did not differ meaningfully between early-onset and late-onset pre-eclampsia.
Women with past pre-eclampsia have more cardiovascular risk factors, even though significant artery changes were not seen up to 20 years after birth.

items.title: Comparing the detection rate of postpartum diabetes in early and 4-12 week postpartum screening tests in women with gestational diabetes mellitus: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Women who had gestational diabetes are at higher risk of developing diabetes later, but many miss the usual blood sugar test at 4-12 weeks after birth. This review combined four studies to see how well a sugar tolerance test done in the first few days after birth, before leaving hospital, picks up abnormal results. The early test caught about 74% of abnormal cases but wrongly flagged about 44% of women whose results were actually normal. The authors suggest an early test before discharge is a practical option, though more research is needed.
keyPoints: An early postpartum glucose tolerance test had a sensitivity of 74% and a specificity of 56%.
The early test could help tell normal results from abnormal ones, including diabetes and glucose intolerance.
The authors say an early test before hospital discharge can be advised for women with gestational diabetes.
More studies are needed to see how well the early test detects diabetes and glucose intolerance separately.

items.title: Incidence of postpartum hypertension within 2 years of a pregnancy complicated by pre-eclampsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled studies that followed women for up to 2 years after a pregnancy with high blood pressure, including pre-eclampsia. About 28% of these women were diagnosed with high blood pressure in that time, compared with about 9% of women who had normal blood pressure in pregnancy. The extra risk was biggest in the first 6 months after birth. The authors suggest that checks and heart-health support may need to start soon after delivery.
keyPoints: High blood pressure was diagnosed within 2 years of birth in 28.4% of women who had hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, versus 9.1% of those who did not.
Overall, the odds of high blood pressure were about six times higher after a pregnancy with high blood pressure or pre-eclampsia.
The raised risk was highest in the first 6 months after delivery.
The authors say diagnosis and heart-health measures may need to begin in the early postpartum period.

items.title: Cardiovascular risk factors in women with previous gestational diabetes mellitus: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 93 studies to compare heart-disease risk factors in women who had gestational diabetes with women who did not. Women with past gestational diabetes had higher blood pressure, weight (BMI), blood sugar, insulin, total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, and lower HDL ('good') cholesterol. Some of these differences showed up within a year after the birth. The authors suggest early screening could help find risk factors that can be changed.
keyPoints: Women with previous gestational diabetes had higher blood pressure, BMI, blood glucose, insulin, total and LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, and lower HDL cholesterol.
Higher blood pressure, total cholesterol, triglycerides and glucose were seen as early as less than 1 year after the birth.
The authors conclude these women have a higher risk of cardiovascular disease based on these conventional risk factors.
Women with previous gestational diabetes may benefit from early screening to find risk factors that can be modified.

items.title: Physiological track-and-trigger/early warning systems for use in maternity care
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at early warning systems that midwives and doctors use to spot when a pregnant or recently delivered woman is getting sicker, using checks like blood pressure, heart rate and temperature. Only two trials were found, both in low-resource settings. The systems may reduce bleeding and shorten hospital stays, but made little to no difference to deaths of mothers or babies. The evidence ranged from very low to moderate certainty, and it may not apply to wealthier settings.
keyPoints: Early warning systems probably make little to no difference to maternal death and may make little to no difference to newborn death.
They may reduce haemorrhage (heavy bleeding) and shorten a woman's hospital stay (low-certainty evidence).
There may be little to no difference in sepsis, eclampsia or HELLP, and probably little to no difference in intensive care admission.
Both trials were in low-resource settings, so results may differ elsewhere; more high-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus after gestational diabetes mellitus: A systematic review & meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 39 studies of about 2.8 million women to see how often type 2 diabetes is diagnosed after gestational diabetes (diabetes first found in pregnancy). Women who had gestational diabetes were roughly nine times more likely to be diagnosed with type 2 diabetes six weeks or more after birth than women who did not. The risk was higher in older women, women with a family history of diabetes, and Black and non-Hispanic White women. The authors say screening after birth is often missed and that providers may want to give extra attention to these groups.
keyPoints: Women with gestational diabetes had a pooled risk of type 2 diabetes about 8.9 times higher than women without it.
The risk was higher in older women and in women with a family history of diabetes.
Black and non-Hispanic White women, and women living in Europe and South-East Asia, had a higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes after gestational diabetes.
Screening for type 2 diabetes after birth is often not done, and the authors suggest providers focus on higher-risk groups.

items.title: Peripartum management of hypertension: a position paper of the ESC Council on Hypertension and the European Society of Hypertension
items.source: ESC Council on Hypertension and the European Society of Hypertension
items.organisation: ESC Council on Hypertension and the European Society of Hypertension
items.summary: This position paper from two European heart and blood pressure societies sets out how high blood pressure should be managed around the time of birth. High blood pressure is the most common medical problem in this period and raises the risk of serious illness. The advice is largely based on expert opinion, because there is little strong trial evidence for treating severe high blood pressure in this setting.
keyPoints: For women with severe high blood pressure, treatment is recommended, even though this is based on expert opinion rather than strong trial data.
Labetalol given into a vein and methyldopa taken by mouth are the two most often used medicines.
Short-acting nifedipine by mouth is suggested only if the other medicines or a drip are not available.
Inducing labour at 37 weeks is linked to better outcomes for mothers with gestational hypertension or mild pre-eclampsia.

items.title: Progression to type 2 diabetes in women with a known history of gestational diabetes: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 20 studies covering over 1.3 million people, including nearly 68,000 women who had gestational diabetes (diabetes first found in pregnancy). It compared how often these women later developed type 2 diabetes with women who had a normal-sugar pregnancy. Women with a history of gestational diabetes had almost 10 times the risk of type 2 diabetes. The authors say this shows how important it is to try to prevent type 2 diabetes, especially in the early years after pregnancy.
keyPoints: Women with past gestational diabetes had about a 10-fold higher risk of type 2 diabetes than women with a normal-sugar pregnancy (relative risk 9.51).

Among women who had gestational diabetes, around 16% in mixed-ethnicity and 16% in mostly non-white groups, and about 10% in white groups, went on to develop type 2 diabetes. The differences between these groups were not statistically significant.
The size of the risk was not significantly linked to age, body mass index, publication year or length of follow-up.
The authors highlight the importance of prevention, particularly in the early years after pregnancy.

items.title: Incidence Rate of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus after Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of 170,139 Women
items.summary: This review pooled 28 large studies covering 170,139 women who had gestational diabetes (diabetes first found in pregnancy) to see how often they later develop type 2 diabetes. About 26 in every 1000 women developed type 2 diabetes each year, and the risk kept rising the longer they were followed. The authors say these findings may encourage more women with past gestational diabetes to be screened for type 2 diabetes.
keyPoints: The pooled rate of type 2 diabetes after gestational diabetes was about 26 per 1000 person-years.
Estimated risk was about 20% at 10 years, 29% at 20 years and 58% at 50 years after gestational diabetes.
Women from Asia, older women and women with a higher body mass index seemed to have a higher risk.
The authors suggest the high long-term risk could motivate more women with past gestational diabetes to get screened for type 2 diabetes.

items.title: A systematic review on costs and cost-effectiveness of screening and prevention of type 2 diabetes in women with prior gestational diabetes: Exploring uncharted territory
items.summary: Women who had gestational diabetes are more likely to develop type 2 diabetes later. This review looked at studies of what it costs, and whether it is good value, to screen for and prevent type 2 diabetes in these women after pregnancy. Only four studies were found, and their quality was poor. Even so, repeat glucose testing every three years had the lowest cost per case found, and prevention programmes looked potentially cost-effective or cost-saving.
keyPoints: Women with prior gestational diabetes are more likely to develop type 2 diabetes than women with normal blood sugar in pregnancy.
An oral glucose tolerance test every three years gave the lowest cost per case detected.
Prevention programmes (diet and behaviour changes, counselling, dietary consultation) were potentially cost-effective or cost-saving.
The studies were of poor quality, so more good economic studies are needed.

items.title: Gestational diabetes and the risk of cardiovascular disease in women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine studies covering over 5 million women to see whether gestational diabetes (diabetes first found in pregnancy) is linked to later heart and blood vessel disease. Women who had gestational diabetes had about twice the risk of future cardiovascular events compared with women who did not. The higher risk was still seen in women who never went on to develop type 2 diabetes. The studies were observational, so they show a link rather than proof of cause.
keyPoints: Women with gestational diabetes had about twice the risk of future cardiovascular events (RR 1.98) compared with women without it.
The higher risk remained (56% higher) even among women who did not develop type 2 diabetes.
The risk was already raised in the first decade after pregnancy (about 2.3 times higher).
The authors say these women are an at-risk group and may benefit from early checks and steps to lower heart risk.

items.title: Preclinical atherosclerosis at the time of pre-eclamptic pregnancy and up to 10 years postpartum: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined 14 studies that used a neck (carotid artery) ultrasound to measure artery wall thickness, an early sign of hardening of the arteries. Women who had pre-eclampsia had thicker artery walls than women who did not, both during the pregnancy and in the first 10 years after birth. The authors suggest this scan might help spot women with early artery changes after a pre-eclampsia pregnancy.
keyPoints: Women with pre-eclampsia had thicker carotid artery walls than women without it, at the time of diagnosis.
The difference was still there in the first 10 years after the pregnancy, though smaller.
Signs of early artery hardening may be present at the time of pre-eclampsia.
Carotid ultrasound may offer a way to identify women with artery changes after a pre-eclampsia pregnancy.

items.title: Different types of dietary advice for women with gestational diabetes mellitus
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 19 small trials (1,398 women) comparing different types of dietary advice for women with gestational diabetes, such as low glycaemic index, low-carbohydrate, energy-restricted and DASH diets. For most diets, there were no clear differences in outcomes for mothers or babies, such as caesarean birth, pre-eclampsia or larger-than-expected babies. The DASH diet may have lowered caesarean births, but this came from only two small trials. The evidence was mostly low or very low quality, and long-term health outcomes were largely not reported.
keyPoints: No clear differences in main outcomes were found between most types of dietary advice for gestational diabetes.
The DASH diet was linked to fewer caesarean sections than a control diet (two trials, 86 women).
Most of the evidence was low or very low quality because trials were small and varied in quality.
More and larger trials are needed, including ones that follow long-term health outcomes.

items.title: A best practice position statement on the role of the nephrologist in the prevention and follow-up of preeclampsia: the Italian study group on kidney and pregnancy
items.summary: This position statement from Italian kidney specialists reviews what is known about preeclampsia, a pregnancy condition with high blood pressure and protein in the urine that usually clears up after birth. It notes that preeclampsia is linked to a higher chance of kidney disease later in life, and that kidney disease itself affects up to 3 in 100 pregnancies. The authors suggest long-term follow-up after preeclampsia and aim to guide how kidney specialists help with prevention and with care after delivery. The abstract does not rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Preeclampsia is estimated to affect about 3 to 5 in 100 pregnancies, or up to 10 in 100 if related conditions such as pregnancy-induced hypertension and HELLP syndrome are counted.
Having preeclampsia is linked to a higher risk of developing chronic kidney disease later in life.
Chronic kidney disease complicates up to 3% of pregnancies, so kidney specialists are now more involved in pregnancy care.
The statement supports long-term follow-up after preeclampsia, with attention to preventing it in women who had it before or who already have kidney disease.

items.title: Postpartum screening practices, progression to abnormal glucose tolerance and its related risk factors in Asian women with a known history of gestational diabetes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 27 studies of Asian women who had gestational diabetes (diabetes first found in pregnancy). It looked at how many had a blood sugar check after the birth and how many went on to have raised blood sugar or diabetes. Many women were not tested, even though a lot of them developed pre-diabetes or diabetes later.
keyPoints: The share of women who had a blood sugar test after pregnancy ranged widely, from 13.1% to 81.9%, and was low in most Asian countries.
Between 3.9% and 50.9% of women developed pre-diabetes, and 2.8% to 58% developed diabetes, depending on how long they were followed.
Diabetes after pregnancy was linked to a family history of diabetes, being diagnosed earlier in pregnancy, needing insulin in pregnancy, and a higher weight before pregnancy.
These risk factors are similar to those seen in developed countries.

items.title: Firsttrimester Diagnosis and Therapy @ 11-13+6 Weeks of Gestation - Part 2
items.summary: This German guideline reviewed the evidence on the ultrasound and screening visit done at 11 to 13+6 weeks of pregnancy. It says this visit is the best time to check for several pregnancy problems, including pre-eclampsia (high blood pressure with protein in the urine) and poor baby growth. Finding these risks early means parents can be counselled and follow-up and prevention can be planned, which can delay or lower the chance of the problem appearing later. In most cases no further tests are needed and parents can be reassured.
keyPoints: Screening for pregnancy complications works best at 11 to 13+6 weeks of gestation.
Identifying risk of pre-eclampsia (high blood pressure and protein in the urine) and slow baby growth is described as a solved problem at this stage.
Early screening helps plan prevention and how often follow-up checks are needed, which can delay and reduce later complications.
Finding glucose problems and preterm birth risk early is still described as unsolved; a repeat scan around week 20 is recommended to complete the check for malformations.

items.title: Firsttrimester Diagnosis and Therapy @ 11-13+6 Weeks of Gestation - Part 1
items.summary: This German guideline reviewed the evidence on the ultrasound scan done at 11 to 13+6 weeks of pregnancy. It looks at checking for physical differences in the baby, chromosome conditions, and pregnancy problems such as pre-eclampsia (high blood pressure and protein in the urine) and poor baby growth. The guideline says this early scan is the best time to screen for many complications, which lets parents be counselled early and lets care be planned.
keyPoints: Screening for complications of pregnancy can best be done at 11 to 13+6 weeks.
Finding women at risk of high blood pressure with protein in the urine, and of poor baby growth, is described as a solved problem at this stage.
Finding problems with blood sugar handling and preterm birth is still described as unsolved.
A repeat scan at around 20 weeks is recommended to finish checking for physical differences in the baby.

items.title: L-Arginine and L-Citrulline for Prevention and Treatment of Pre-Eclampsia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 20 randomised trials (2,028 women) and 3 non-randomised trials of L-arginine and L-citrulline supplements in pregnancy. When taken to prevent pre-eclampsia, L-arginine was linked to a lower risk of pre-eclampsia and of severe pre-eclampsia, and in women already affected it may have lowered systolic blood pressure and fetal growth restriction. The evidence was low or very low certainty and many trials had a high risk of bias, so the results should be read with caution. The authors say more trials are needed to find the best dose and timing.
keyPoints: In prevention trials, L-arginine was linked to a lower risk of pre-eclampsia (relative risk 0.52) and severe pre-eclampsia (relative risk 0.23), based on low-certainty evidence.
In treatment trials, L-arginine may reduce systolic blood pressure by about 5.6 mmHg (very low-certainty evidence) and fetal growth restriction (low-certainty evidence).
Only one small study (36 women) looked at L-citrulline and found no effect on pre-eclampsia or blood pressure.
