The authors say L-arginine looks promising but the findings should be interpreted cautiously, and the best dose and start time are still unknown.

items.title: Polyphenols for the Prevention or Management of Preeclampsia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 trials of plant-based polyphenol products (such as EGCG from green tea and resveratrol) taken during pregnancy, looking at pre-eclampsia outcomes. In women who already had pre-eclampsia, adding EGCG or resveratrol to the blood pressure drug nifedipine may have helped bring blood pressure down faster and delayed the next hypertensive crisis. These results came from just one trial of 349 women and the certainty was low. For the other products studied, no differences were seen, and overall the evidence on benefits and harms is limited and uncertain.
keyPoints: EGCG added to nifedipine may shorten the time to blood pressure control by about 14 minutes (1 trial, low certainty).
Resveratrol added to nifedipine may shorten the time to blood pressure control by about 15 minutes (1 trial, low certainty).
No differences were seen for Salvia miltiorrhiza, Bryophyllum pinnatum, raspberry or cranberry extracts.
Evidence on the benefits and side effects of polyphenols in pregnancy is limited and uncertain.

items.title: Prenatal lead exposure and risk of Pregnancy-Induced hypertension: A systematic review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from many studies to look at whether lead in a pregnant woman's blood is linked to high blood pressure in pregnancy, including pre-eclampsia. Women with pre-eclampsia had clearly higher average blood lead levels than women with normal blood pressure. The studies differed a lot from one another, and the authors found signs of publication bias, but the link still held when extreme results were removed. This shows an association, not proof that lead causes pre-eclampsia.
keyPoints: Women with pre-eclampsia had higher average blood lead levels (18.4 µg/dL) than women with normal blood pressure (7.4 µg/dL).
The authors conclude that lead exposure in pregnancy is associated with a higher risk of pre-eclampsia and gestational hypertension.
The studies varied a lot in design and results, and publication bias was found, so the findings should be read with care.
The authors highlight the value of monitoring environmental lead and taking steps to reduce lead exposure during pregnancy.

items.title: Maternal Hemodynamics from Preconception to Delivery: Research and Potential Diagnostic and Therapeutic Implications: Position Statement by Italian Association of Preeclampsia and Italian Society of Perinatal Medicine
items.summary: Two Italian medical societies reviewed research on how a mother's blood circulation works during pregnancy and how it relates to high blood pressure and slow baby growth. They suggest that measuring a woman's circulation pattern (such as how tight or relaxed her blood vessels are) could help doctors understand her condition and choose a better treatment. The authors say the evidence is not conclusive because there are no large randomized trials yet.
keyPoints: Unusual maternal circulation is linked to slow growth of the baby in the womb (fetal growth restriction).
Unusual maternal circulation is also linked to complicated high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy.
Circulation patterns might help doctors pick a more suitable treatment for high blood pressure in pregnancy.
Women's heart and circulation profiles may also help guide follow-up care, because cardiovascular risk is higher later in life.

items.title: A summary of the 2023 Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand (SOMANZ) hypertension in pregnancy guideline
items.summary: This is a summary of the 2023 Australian and New Zealand guideline on high blood pressure in pregnancy, which affects up to 1 in 10 pregnancies. It updates the 2014 version and gives 39 recommendations on screening, preventing, diagnosing and managing these conditions, especially pre-eclampsia. It also covers long-term care for women who have had high blood pressure in pregnancy, and includes patient infographics in several languages.
keyPoints: High blood pressure disorders of pregnancy affect up to 10% of pregnancies and raise the risk of problems for mothers and babies.
The guideline gives 39 recommendations on screening, preventing, diagnosing and managing these conditions, especially pre-eclampsia.

New content includes combined first trimester screening to find women at higher risk of pre-eclampsia, preventive treatments, blood tests called angiogenic biomarkers, and long-term care after high blood pressure in pregnancy.
Where evidence was limited, the guideline gives expert-based practice points instead of firm recommendations.

items.title: Pregnancy outcome predictors in systemic lupus erythematosus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 72 studies covering over 10,000 pregnancies in women with lupus (SLE) to find out which factors before pregnancy are linked to problems like pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and pregnancy loss. Earlier lupus kidney disease (lupus nephritis), long-term high blood pressure, active lupus around the time of conception, and secondary antiphospholipid syndrome were each linked to a higher chance of adverse outcomes. The authors note that many of the included studies had considerable risk of bias, so the results should be read with some caution. The findings may help doctors tailor advice to each woman before she becomes pregnant.
keyPoints: Previous lupus nephritis was linked to a lower chance of live birth and higher risks of preterm birth and pre-eclampsia.
Chronic high blood pressure was linked to higher risks of lupus flare, preterm birth and pre-eclampsia.
Active lupus at or before conception was linked to higher risks of preterm birth and pre-eclampsia.
Secondary antiphospholipid syndrome was linked to fewer live births and more pregnancy loss after 20 weeks and preterm birth.

items.title: Low-dose aspirin for the prevention of superimposed preeclampsia in women with chronic hypertension: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled nine studies of 2,150 pregnant women who already had chronic high blood pressure. It looked at whether taking low-dose aspirin lowered the chance of superimposed pre-eclampsia (pre-eclampsia developing on top of existing high blood pressure). Aspirin did not clearly reduce pre-eclampsia, but it probably reduced preterm birth. The evidence for pre-eclampsia was low to very low quality, so firm conclusions are hard to draw.
keyPoints: Low-dose aspirin did not significantly reduce superimposed pre-eclampsia in randomized trials (low-quality evidence) or in observational studies (very low-quality evidence).
Aspirin made no significant difference to preterm pre-eclampsia, small-for-gestational-age babies or perinatal death, and starting it early did not change this.
Aspirin was linked to a significant reduction in preterm birth (moderate-quality evidence).
The authors say the preterm birth benefit justifies continued use of aspirin prophylaxis, though the evidence is limited by differences between studies and risk of bias.

items.title: Pre-eclampsia during pregnancy and risk of endometrial cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from seven studies to see whether having pre-eclampsia in pregnancy is linked to a higher chance of later developing endometrial cancer (cancer of the womb lining). Overall, no link was found. When the researchers also counted early pre-cancer changes in the womb lining, there was some sign of a small increase in risk, and the authors say more large studies are needed.
keyPoints: Across seven studies covering 11,724 endometrial cancer cases, pre-eclampsia was not linked to a higher risk of endometrial cancer.
When pre-cancer changes and cancer were counted together, there was some evidence of a higher risk (HR 1.34).
The authors call for more large studies that look at pre-eclampsia sub-types and early pre-cancer conditions.

items.title: Polygenic prediction of preeclampsia and gestational hypertension
items.summary: Researchers compared the DNA of over 20,000 women who had pre-eclampsia and over 11,000 who had gestational hypertension with hundreds of thousands of women who did not. They found 18 regions of DNA linked to these conditions, 12 of them newly identified. A genetic risk score built from this work predicted who developed these conditions, even after accounting for usual clinical risk factors. It also changed which women would qualify for low-dose aspirin to help prevent pre-eclampsia. This is early research that may help doctors judge pregnancy risk more precisely in future.
keyPoints: 18 DNA regions were linked to pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension, and 12 of them were new findings.
The regions point to blood pressure signaling, blood vessel growth, kidney function, placenta development and immune system problems.
A genetic risk score predicted both conditions in separate groups of women, independent of clinical risk factors.
The score changed which women would be eligible for low-dose aspirin to prevent pre-eclampsia.

items.title: Alternative magnesium sulphate regimens for women with pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 16 trials (3,020 women) comparing different ways of giving magnesium sulphate, the main drug used to prevent and treat seizures (eclampsia) in pre-eclampsia. The trials compared different doses, giving the drug into a vein or a muscle, and shorter or longer treatment after birth. The reviewers found no clear evidence that any one regimen works better than another, and most of the evidence was low or very low certainty. Most trials were small, so more well-designed research is needed.
keyPoints: No compelling evidence shows that one magnesium sulphate regimen is more effective than another for preventing or treating eclampsia.
In women with eclampsia, a shorter maintenance course may reduce flushing compared with 24 hours of treatment (low-certainty evidence).

Shorter treatment after birth versus 24 hours showed an uncertain effect on eclampsia and may make little or no difference to severe illness or side effects such as slowed breathing (low-certainty evidence).
Most trials were small and many important outcomes were not reported, so well-designed trials are needed.

items.title: Association Between Low-Dose Aspirin and Development of Gestational Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This review looked at whether taking low-dose aspirin in pregnancy to help prevent pre-eclampsia is linked to a higher chance of developing gestational diabetes. Across 9 studies, aspirin did not appear to raise the risk of gestational diabetes. However, there were few studies and many were of poor quality, so the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Low-dose aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention was not associated with a greater risk of gestational diabetes.
The review pooled 9 studies: 6 randomized trials (1932 patients) and 3 cohort studies (over 313,000 patients).
No studies reported data on newborn low blood sugar, large babies, birth injury or shoulder dystocia.
The small number and poor quality of studies limit how far the results can be trusted.

items.title: Periodontitis and Preeclampsia in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 30 studies to see whether gum disease (periodontitis) during pregnancy is linked to pre-eclampsia, a pregnancy condition involving high blood pressure. Women with periodontitis had about three times the odds of pre-eclampsia, and the link looked stronger in lower-middle-income countries. These were observational studies, so they show a link but cannot prove that gum disease causes pre-eclampsia. It is not yet known whether treating gum disease would prevent it.
keyPoints: Periodontitis was significantly linked to a higher risk of pre-eclampsia (odds ratio 3.18) across 30 studies.
The link was stronger in the cohort studies (odds ratio 4.19) and in lower-middle-income countries (odds ratio 6.70).
The authors say future studies should test whether treating gum disease in pregnancy prevents pre-eclampsia.

items.title: Aspirin Use to Prevent Preeclampsia and Related Morbidity and Mortality: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence on taking daily low-dose aspirin to prevent preeclampsia, a serious pregnancy complication affecting about 4% of pregnancies in the US. It concluded, with moderate certainty, that daily low-dose aspirin brings a substantial net benefit for pregnant people at high risk. Benefits include a lower risk of preeclampsia, preterm birth, poor baby growth and death around the time of birth. It recommends 81 mg a day, started after 12 weeks of pregnancy, for those at high risk.
keyPoints: Preeclampsia affects about 4% of US pregnancies and accounts for 6% of preterm births and 19% of medically indicated preterm births.
The Task Force recommends low-dose aspirin (81 mg a day) after 12 weeks of pregnancy for people at high risk of preeclampsia (a B recommendation).
Moderate-certainty evidence shows daily low-dose aspirin lowers the risk of preeclampsia, preterm birth, small for gestational age/growth restriction and perinatal death.
The advice applies to people with no past bad reactions to, or reasons to avoid, low-dose aspirin.

items.title: Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 222
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) on high blood pressure in pregnancy, including gestational hypertension and preeclampsia. The abstract explains how common and serious these conditions are worldwide. It states that the guideline covers how they are diagnosed and managed, but the abstract does not give the specific recommendations.
keyPoints: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are one of the leading causes of maternal and perinatal death worldwide.
Preeclampsia is estimated to affect 2-8% of pregnancies globally.
In the United States, preeclampsia rates rose by 25% between 1987 and 2004, and it is costly, with much of the cost linked to premature births.
The bulletin provides guidelines for diagnosing and managing gestational hypertension and preeclampsia.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 202 Summary: Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia
items.summary: This is a summary of an American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) guideline on high blood pressure in pregnancy, including gestational hypertension and preeclampsia. The abstract describes how common and serious these conditions are: preeclampsia affects about 2-8% of pregnancies worldwide and is a leading cause of death for mothers and babies. The guideline is meant to guide diagnosis and management, but the abstract itself does not list the specific recommendations.
keyPoints: Preeclampsia is estimated to complicate 2-8% of pregnancies worldwide.
High blood pressure disorders cause about 26% of maternal deaths in Latin America and the Caribbean, 9% in Africa and Asia, and 16% in high-income countries.
In the United States, preeclampsia rates rose by 25% between 1987 and 2004.
The guideline covers how gestational hypertension and preeclampsia are diagnosed and managed.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 202: Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on gestational hypertension and preeclampsia. The abstract describes how common and serious these conditions are: preeclampsia affects about 2-8% of pregnancies worldwide, and high blood pressure disorders are a leading cause of death for mothers and babies. The guideline is meant to guide how doctors diagnose and manage these conditions. The abstract does not give the specific diagnosis or treatment recommendations.
keyPoints: Preeclampsia is estimated to affect 2-8% of pregnancies worldwide.
High blood pressure disorders cause about 16% of maternal deaths in high-income countries and about 26% in Latin America and the Caribbean.
In the US, the rate of preeclampsia rose by 25% between 1987 and 2004.
The condition is costly: an estimated $2.18 billion in the US in 2012 within the first year after delivery, with much of the cost tied to premature births.

items.title: Calcium supplementation commencing before or early in pregnancy, for preventing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether taking calcium supplements before pregnancy or in early pregnancy helps prevent high blood pressure disorders such as pre-eclampsia. Only one trial qualified, in women who had pre-eclampsia before. Calcium may make little or no difference to pre-eclampsia, and the evidence is low quality. The review concludes that current evidence neither supports nor rules out routine calcium use before conception and in early pregnancy.
keyPoints: Only one trial (1355 women with previous pre-eclampsia) was included, so the evidence is limited.
Calcium started before conception may make little or no difference to the risk of pre-eclampsia (low-quality evidence).
Calcium may slightly reduce the combined risk of pre-eclampsia or pregnancy loss, but the result was borderline and inconclusive.
Results were inconclusive for most other outcomes for mothers and babies, such as preterm birth, birthweight and caesarean section.

items.title: Antiplatelet agents for preventing pre-eclampsia and its complications
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 77 trials (about 40,000 pregnant women) that tested antiplatelet medicines, mostly low-dose aspirin, in women at risk of pre-eclampsia. Aspirin led to small-to-moderate benefits: fewer cases of pre-eclampsia, fewer preterm births, fewer small babies and fewer baby deaths. It probably slightly raised the chance of heavy bleeding after birth and may marginally raise the chance of placental abruption. Overall the authors concluded that outcomes improved and the medicine appears safe at these doses.
keyPoints: Antiplatelet agents reduced pre-eclampsia by 18% (about 16 fewer cases per 1000 women treated), with high-quality evidence.
Preterm birth before 37 weeks fell by 9% (about 16 fewer per 1000 treated), and fetal or neonatal death fell by 14% (about 5 fewer per 1000 treated).
Aspirin probably slightly increased postpartum bleeding over 500 mL and may marginally increase placental abruption (moderate-quality evidence).
Almost all women started treatment after 12 weeks, so it is unclear if starting earlier would help more.

items.title: Interventionist versus expectant care for severe pre-eclampsia between 24 and 34 weeks' gestation
items.summary: This review looked at six trials (748 women) comparing two ways of caring for women with severe pre-eclampsia between 24 and 34 weeks: delivering early, or delaying delivery with careful monitoring. Women in the trials had no urgent reason for immediate delivery. Babies of women who were monitored and delivered later tended to have fewer breathing and brain-bleed problems. There was not enough evidence to be sure how each approach affects the mother's safety.
keyPoints: Early delivery was linked to more bleeding in the baby's brain (intraventricular haemorrhage), more breathing problems from hyaline membrane disease, and more need for ventilation.
Babies in the early delivery group were born at a lower gestational age, but were not more likely to be admitted to neonatal intensive care.
There was little or no difference in caesarean section rates between the two approaches.
Evidence on maternal outcomes such as eclampsia was too limited to draw reliable conclusions, and larger high-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Planned early delivery versus expectant management for hypertensive disorders from 34 weeks gestation to term
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled five trials (1,819 women) comparing planned early delivery with waiting (expectant management) for women with high blood pressure disorders from 34 weeks of pregnancy. Planned early delivery was linked to fewer serious problems for the mother, but babies born early had more breathing difficulties and more NICU admissions. There was not enough reliable information to say whether overall serious outcomes for babies differed.
keyPoints: Planned early delivery lowered the combined risk of maternal death and severe illness (risk ratio 0.69, high-certainty evidence).
It was also linked to lower risk of HELLP syndrome and severe kidney problems in the mother.
Early delivery was linked to more respiratory distress syndrome and more NICU admissions for babies.
There was no clear difference in caesarean section rates or in hospital stay for mothers or babies; more research is needed on different types of hypertensive disease and the best timing.

items.title: Preeclampsia and Future Cardiovascular Health: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 22 studies covering over 6.4 million women, including more than 258,000 who had pre-eclampsia. It looked at whether having pre-eclampsia in pregnancy is linked to heart and blood vessel problems later in life. Women who had pre-eclampsia had a higher risk of heart failure, coronary heart disease, stroke and death from heart disease. The link remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index and diabetes.
keyPoints: Pre-eclampsia was linked to about a 4-fold higher risk of later heart failure.
Risk of coronary heart disease, stroke and death from heart disease was roughly 2-fold higher after pre-eclampsia.
The higher risks remained after adjusting for age, body mass index and diabetes.
The authors highlight the importance of lifelong monitoring of heart risk factors in women who have had pre-eclampsia.

items.title: Screening for Preeclampsia: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence on screening for preeclampsia, a pregnancy condition with high blood pressure that can harm both mother and baby. They found that checking blood pressure is accurate and that treating preeclampsia once found can reduce serious problems for mother and baby. The harms of screening and treatment were judged to be small at most. They recommend that pregnant women have their blood pressure measured throughout pregnancy.
keyPoints: Preeclampsia affects about 4% of pregnancies in the US and can cause stroke, seizures (eclampsia), organ failure, poor fetal growth, low birth weight and stillbirth.
The Task Force recommends screening all pregnant women with blood pressure measurements throughout pregnancy (a B recommendation).
Treatment of preeclampsia that is found through screening can reduce illness and death for mothers and babies, and harms of screening and treatment were judged to be no greater than small.
Preeclampsia is more common, and more often fatal, among African American women, and unequal access to prenatal care may play a part.

items.title: Treating periodontal disease for preventing adverse birth outcomes in pregnant women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pulled together 15 trials with over 7,000 pregnant women to see whether treating gum disease during pregnancy improves birth outcomes. Treatment showed no clear effect on preterm birth, and no clear effect on pre-eclampsia. It may lower the chance of a low birth weight baby, but the evidence is low quality and confidence in that result is limited. All the trials had a high risk of bias, and no harms from the gum treatments were reported.
keyPoints: It is not clear whether treating gum disease in pregnancy changes the chance of preterm birth (low-quality evidence).
Treatment may reduce low birth weight (under 2500 g), from about 12.6% to 9.7%, but confidence in this result is limited.
Pre-eclampsia, perinatal death and small-for-gestational-age babies showed no clear difference with treatment, and the evidence was low to very low quality.
There was not enough evidence to say which type of gum treatment works best.

items.title: Aspirin versus Placebo in Pregnancies at High Risk for Preterm Preeclampsia
items.summary: This trial looked at whether taking low-dose aspirin during pregnancy lowers the chance of preterm pre-eclampsia (pre-eclampsia leading to delivery before 37 weeks) in women at high risk. Over 1,700 women were randomly given either 150 mg of aspirin a day or a placebo, from 11-14 weeks until 36 weeks of pregnancy. Preterm pre-eclampsia happened in 1.6% of the aspirin group compared with 4.3% of the placebo group. There were no significant differences in newborn problems or other side effects between the groups.
keyPoints: Preterm pre-eclampsia occurred in 1.6% of women taking aspirin versus 4.3% of those taking placebo.
The women studied were at high risk and took 150 mg of aspirin daily from 11-14 weeks until 36 weeks of pregnancy.
No significant differences were found between groups in newborn adverse outcomes or other adverse events.
Most women took their tablets as planned, and the results held up when women who dropped out were accounted for.

items.title: Clinical risk factors for pre-eclampsia determined in early pregnancy: systematic review and meta-analysis of large cohort studies
items.summary: Researchers pooled 92 large studies covering over 25 million pregnancies to find which things known by 16 weeks of pregnancy raise the chance of pre-eclampsia. Having had pre-eclampsia before, chronic high blood pressure, pregestational diabetes, a BMI above 30 before pregnancy, and fertility treatment were all linked with higher risk. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome had the highest rate of pre-eclampsia. The authors say these factors, alone or together, might help identify women at high risk early in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Prior pre-eclampsia carried the biggest increase in relative risk (about 8 times higher).
Chronic high blood pressure was second: about 16% developed pre-eclampsia, with about 5 times the relative risk.
Pregestational diabetes (about 11%), prepregnancy BMI over 30 (about 7%) and assisted reproductive technology (about 6%) were also clear risk factors.
These findings can help build tools to predict pre-eclampsia and guide who is offered aspirin in pregnancy.

items.title: Inter-pregnancy interval and risk of recurrent pre-eclampsia: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether the gap between pregnancies affects the chance of pre-eclampsia coming back in women who had it before. It combined results from observational studies that included over 77,000 women. Shorter gaps (under 2 years) were not linked to a higher risk compared with gaps of 2 to 4 years, but gaps longer than 4 years were linked to a slightly higher risk. The authors say the results should be read with caution because the studies were observational and could be affected by other factors.
keyPoints: Gaps of less than 2 years between pregnancies were not linked to a higher risk of pre-eclampsia coming back, compared with gaps of 2 to 4 years.
Gaps longer than 4 years were linked to a small increase in the risk of recurrent pre-eclampsia (adjusted odds ratio 1.10).
The findings come from observational studies, so other factors may have influenced the results.

items.title: Calcium supplementation (other than for preventing or treating hypertension) for improving pregnancy and infant outcomes
items.summary: This review pooled 23 trials with about 18,600 pregnant women to see whether calcium supplements, taken for reasons other than blood pressure problems, improve pregnancy and baby outcomes. Overall, calcium did not clearly reduce preterm birth or low birthweight. Babies were on average about 56 grams heavier in the calcium group, but the results varied between studies and it is unclear whether this small difference matters in practice.
keyPoints: No clear difference in preterm birth before 37 weeks or before 34 weeks between women who took calcium and those who did not.
No clear difference in the number of babies born with low birthweight.
Babies in the calcium group were on average about 56 g heavier, but the studies varied a lot and the clinical importance is uncertain.
The authors found no clear extra benefit of calcium supplements for preventing preterm birth or low birthweight.

items.title: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation during pregnancy or labour for maternal and neonatal outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether taking vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) during pregnancy or labour helps mothers and babies. It found only four small trials with 1,646 women, and the quality of the trials was mostly unclear. There was no clear difference in pre-eclampsia, eclampsia or newborn Apgar scores. One trial suggested less dental decay, but the evidence was low quality.
keyPoints: No statistically significant difference was found in the risk of pre-eclampsia or eclampsia between women who took vitamin B6 and those who did not.
Vitamin B6 capsules or lozenges were linked to a lower risk of dental decay in pregnancy, but this evidence was low quality and based on single trials.
One very small trial (33 women) found lower average birthweights with vitamin B6.
The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to show clinical benefits of vitamin B6 in pregnancy or labour, and more trials are needed.

items.title: Vitamin E supplementation in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 21 trials with over 22,000 pregnant women to see whether vitamin E supplements, mostly taken together with vitamin C or other agents, improve pregnancy outcomes. Vitamin E did not clearly lower the risk of pre-eclampsia, stillbirth, preterm birth or poor baby growth. It may lower the risk of placental abruption, but it was linked to more abdominal pain and more waters breaking early at term. The authors concluded the data do not support routine vitamin E supplements in pregnancy.
keyPoints: No clear difference in pre-eclampsia risk with vitamin E combined with other supplements compared with placebo (moderate quality evidence).
No clear difference in stillbirth, neonatal death, preterm birth or poor fetal growth.
Placental abruption was less likely with supplementation (high quality evidence), but more research is needed on this.
Supplementation was linked to more self-reported abdominal pain and more term waters breaking before labour starts.

items.title: Early Pregnancy Biomarkers in Pre-Eclampsia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from many studies to see how well blood tests in early pregnancy can predict pre-eclampsia, a blood pressure condition that affects 2% to 8% of pregnancies. Single blood markers were not very good at picking out who would go on to develop it. Combining several markers worked better, but results varied a lot between studies. The authors say larger, high quality studies are needed before the best test can be identified.
keyPoints: Pre-eclampsia affects 2% to 8% of pregnancies and is an important cause of illness and death around the time of birth.
Single early-pregnancy blood markers predicted pre-eclampsia poorly, catching about 40% of cases at a 10% false positive rate.
Using a combination of markers improved prediction compared with single markers.
Results were inconsistent between studies, so large, high quality research is still needed.

items.title: Vitamin C supplementation in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 29 trials with about 24,300 pregnant women to see whether vitamin C supplements, alone or with other supplements, improve pregnancy outcomes. Vitamin C made no clear difference to stillbirth, newborn death, poor baby growth, preterm birth or pre-eclampsia. It may lower the risk of placental abruption, but the authors say more research is needed. The review concludes the evidence does not support routine vitamin C supplements in pregnancy.
keyPoints: No clear difference in stillbirth, neonatal death, poor fetal growth, preterm birth or pre-eclampsia, with moderate to high quality evidence for most of these.
Women taking vitamin C had a lower risk of placental abruption (high quality evidence) and a small increase in gestational age at birth.
Vitamin C taken with vitamin E was linked to a higher risk of term prelabour rupture of membranes, while vitamin C alone was linked to a lower risk; evidence on this was limited.
The authors conclude the data do not support routine vitamin C supplementation to prevent these complications.

items.title: American Thyroid Association 2026 Guidelines for Thyroid Disease in Preconception, Pregnancy, and Postpartum
items.summary: The American Thyroid Association updated its guidelines on thyroid disease before, during and after pregnancy, replacing the 2017 version. The guidelines cover thyroid testing, iodine, thyroid antibodies, underactive and overactive thyroid, thyroid nodules and cancer, and thyroid problems after birth. The authors say much of the evidence is low-to-moderate quality, so the guidelines reflect current best practice and expert agreement rather than certainty.
keyPoints: The guidelines give evidence-based advice on thyroid care for women with infertility, in pregnancy, and after birth or while breastfeeding.

Topics include thyroid function testing, iodine supplements, thyroid autoimmunity, hypothyroidism, hypothyroxinemia, hyperthyroidism and Graves' disease, thyroid nodules and cancer, and postpartum thyroid problems.
Where research was limited, the task force wrote Good Practice Statements based on expert consensus.
The authors note that much of the underlying evidence is of low-to-moderate quality and that care should be individualised.

items.title: Preconception and first-trimester metformin on pregnancy outcomes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 12 trials (1,708 women with PCOS) that looked at taking metformin before pregnancy and into the first trimester. Women who took metformin before conception and kept taking it through early pregnancy were more likely to have a clinical pregnancy, and may have had fewer miscarriages and more live births. Stopping metformin once pregnant did not show the same pattern. The studies were low to moderate quality and most results were uncertain, so more high-quality research is needed.
keyPoints: Metformin started before conception and continued through the first trimester was linked to higher clinical pregnancy rates in women with PCOS.
Continuing metformin may reduce miscarriage and increase live births, but these results were not clear-cut statistically.
Stopping metformin after a positive pregnancy test showed a possible rise in miscarriage compared with placebo or no treatment.
The authors conclude that continuing metformin seems to have greater benefit than stopping it, but better-quality research is needed.

items.title: Preexisting Diabetes and Pregnancy: An Endocrine Society and European Society of Endocrinology Joint Clinical Practice Guideline
items.source: Endocrine Society and European Society of Endocrinology
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.organisation: Endocrine Society and European Society of Endocrinology
items.summary: This joint guideline from the Endocrine Society and the European Society of Endocrinology gives advice for women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes who are planning pregnancy, pregnant or recently postpartum. It suggests asking about pregnancy plans at health visits, using contraception when pregnancy is not wanted, and keeping blood sugar as close to target as possible. Most of the evidence behind the advice was low or very low quality, so many recommendations are cautious suggestions rather than firm rules.
keyPoints: Women with diabetes who could become pregnant are asked about pregnancy intentions at every reproductive, diabetes and primary care visit, because preconception care is linked to lower HbA1c and fewer congenital malformations.
Contraception is suggested when pregnancy is not desired, and for women with type 2 diabetes, stopping a GLP-1 receptor agonist before conception is suggested rather than during early pregnancy.

In pregnancy, standard glucose targets still apply (fasting under 95 mg/dL, 1-hour after meals under 140, 2-hour under 120); either a continuous glucose monitor or finger-prick testing is suggested for type 2 diabetes, and a hybrid closed-loop pump for type 1.
Delivery timing based on individual risk assessment is suggested rather than waiting, and diabetes care is suggested after birth, including after pregnancy loss or termination.

items.title: FIGO good practice recommendations on preconception care: A strategy to prevent preterm birth
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: FIGO, an international body of obstetricians and gynaecologists, issued good practice recommendations on care before pregnancy as a way to help prevent preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks). More than half of pregnancies worldwide are unplanned, which limits the chances to act early. The recommendations suggest moving from care focused only on pregnancy to care centred on the woman, and including a check on the future baby's health risks. The aim is to spot and manage risk factors that can be changed before pregnancy begins.
keyPoints: Preterm birth is a leading cause of newborn death and long-term health problems worldwide, and progress in reducing it has been small, especially in low-resource settings.
Preconception care is recognised as an effective way to prevent preterm birth, but unplanned pregnancies (over half globally) limit its reach.
Care before pregnancy can help find and manage changeable risk factors, including medical, previous pregnancy, nutrition, infection, mental health, and social or environmental factors.
The guidance calls for policies and advocacy so that everyone has fair access to preconception services.

items.title: Effectiveness of preconception weight loss interventions on fertility in women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of weight loss programs (lifestyle changes and/or medication) in women with overweight or obesity who were planning pregnancy. Women in weight loss programs were more likely to become pregnant than women in comparison groups. However, this did not translate into more live births, and miscarriage rates were not clearly different overall. The authors say the findings do not support a one-size-fits-all recommendation to lose weight right before conception.
keyPoints: Women in weight loss programs were more likely to become pregnant (risk ratio 1.24) than women in control groups.
There was no clear difference in live birth or miscarriage rates overall.
The pregnancy benefit was seen in programs lasting 12 weeks or fewer and in women with a BMI of 35 or higher.
Miscarriage was higher in the intervention groups among women who were having fertility treatment.

items.title: Indian Academy of Pediatrics Consensus Guidelines on Preconception Care
items.summary: The Indian Academy of Pediatrics issued consensus guidelines on health care before pregnancy, aimed at adolescents and young adults. The guidance says the time before conception is an early chance to improve pregnancy and childbirth outcomes. It recommends that couples planning a pregnancy focus on healthy habits and get certain checks and vaccines beforehand.
keyPoints: Every woman planning a pregnancy should aim to reach and keep a healthy metabolic state.
Couples are advised to follow a healthy lifestyle, including a nutritious diet and avoiding substance abuse.
Timely screening for genetic disorders and for sexually transmitted infections in both men and women is recommended.
Appropriate vaccination and attention to mental health concerns are also recommended.

items.title: AGA Clinical Practice Update on Pregnancy-Related Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease: Expert Review
items.summary: This American Gastroenterological Association expert review gives practical advice on stomach, bowel and liver conditions in pregnancy. For nausea and vomiting, it says treating symptoms early may help stop them turning into hyperemesis gravidarum (severe pregnancy sickness). The advice comes from published studies and expert opinion, not a formal systematic review, so the statements are not rated for evidence quality.
keyPoints: Early treatment of nausea and vomiting of pregnancy may reduce progression to hyperemesis gravidarum.
Treatment starts with diet and lifestyle measures, then vitamin B6 and doxylamine, hydration and adequate nutrition.
Ondansetron, metoclopramide, promethazine and intravenous glucocorticoids may be needed in moderate to severe cases.
For constipation in pregnancy, options include dietary fiber, lactulose and polyethylene glycol-based laxatives.

items.title: A Systematic Review of Clinical Guidelines for Preconception Care
items.summary: Researchers reviewed 11 freely available international guidelines on preconception care, which covers steps to improve health before pregnancy. Ten of the guidelines were of moderate quality and only one was of very high quality. The strongest evidence behind the recommendations was for taking folic acid to lower the risk of neural tube defects and for antiviral medication to prevent HIV transmission. For many other areas, the evidence was weaker.
keyPoints: Only 1 of 11 preconception care guidelines was rated very high quality; 10 were moderate quality.
The evidence behind recommendations ranged from the lowest level to the highest level.
The best evidence is for folic acid to reduce neural tube defects and for antiviral medication to prevent HIV transmission.
High-quality guidelines on preconception care are lacking, and few areas are backed by high-quality evidence.

items.title: Dietary guideline adherence during preconception and pregnancy: A systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 18 studies that looked at how well people trying to conceive and pregnant women follow dietary guidelines. Most studies found that women did not meet recommendations for vegetables, cereal grains or folate. Pregnant women often fell short on iron and calcium and often ate more fat than recommended. The authors note this could affect pregnancy, birth and the baby's later health, and that little is known about men's diets before conception.
keyPoints: Most studies found women before and during pregnancy did not meet recommendations for vegetables, cereal grains or folate.
Pregnant women missed iron targets in 91% of studies and calcium targets in 55% of studies, and exceeded fat recommendations in 55%.
Higher education, older age and not smoking were linked to better adherence to dietary guidelines.
Men's diets before conception and the reasons behind adherence are still poorly studied.

items.title: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 762: Prepregnancy Counseling
items.summary: This guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists explains why talking with a health professional before pregnancy is useful. The aim is to improve health before conception and lower risks for the woman, the baby and the newborn. It suggests this kind of counseling should be offered to anyone who may want to become pregnant and repeated at several points during the reproductive years.
keyPoints: Anyone planning a pregnancy should be offered counseling, whatever their sexual orientation or gender identity, and whether or not they are using contraception.
Long-term conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure, mental health conditions and thyroid disease should be well managed before pregnancy.
Counseling can cover use of alcohol, nicotine and drugs, screening for sexually transmitted infections, genetic conditions and intimate partner violence, and the best gap between pregnancies.
Taking folic acid before pregnancy is encouraged to reduce the risk of neural tube defects.

items.title: EULAR recommendations for women's health and the management of family planning, assisted reproduction, pregnancy and menopause in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and/or antiphospholipid syndrome
items.summary: European rheumatology experts reviewed the evidence and agreed on advice for women with lupus (SLE) and/or antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) about family planning, pregnancy, fertility treatment and menopause. They say menopause hormone therapy and hormonal contraception can be used when the disease is stable or inactive and the risk of blood clots is low. Most women with these conditions can have successful pregnancies, and steps can be taken to lower the risks.
keyPoints: Menopause hormone replacement therapy can be used in patients with stable or inactive disease and a low risk of blood clots.
Family planning should be discussed as early as possible after diagnosis, and most women can have successful pregnancies.
Assisted reproduction can be used safely when disease is stable or inactive; those with antiphospholipid antibodies/APS should receive blood thinners and/or low-dose aspirin.
Cervical screening is similar to the general population, with extra care if taking immune-suppressing drugs, and HPV vaccination can be used when disease is stable.

items.title: Iodine supplementation for women during the preconception, pregnancy and postpartum period
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 11 trials with over 2,700 women to see whether iodine supplements before, during or after pregnancy help mothers and babies. Iodine supplements were linked to less postpartum hyperthyroidism (an overactive thyroid after birth) and to more digestive upset in pregnancy, but the evidence was low or very low quality. For most other outcomes, such as preterm birth, low birthweight and thyroid problems in babies, no clear differences were seen. The authors say there is not enough data to reach firm conclusions about routine iodine supplements.
keyPoints: Iodine supplements were linked to a lower chance of postpartum hyperthyroidism, based on low-quality evidence from three trials.
Digestive intolerance was more likely with iodine in pregnancy, based on one small trial and very low-quality evidence.
No clear differences were found for preterm birth, low birthweight, hypothyroidism or thyroid antibodies in mothers or newborns.
Almost all evidence came from areas with mild or moderate iodine deficiency, so it may not apply to areas with severe deficiency; more high-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Preconception care for diabetic women for improving maternal and infant health
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for good-quality trials testing whether preparing for pregnancy (preconception care) helps women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes and their babies. It found only three small trials, all in adolescent girls with diabetes at US clinics, testing an education programme. None of them reported on the main health outcomes for mothers or babies, so the review could not say whether preconception care improves health. The authors say more high-quality research is needed.
keyPoints: Only three trials (254 adolescent girls with diabetes) were found, with unclear to high risk of bias.
The trials did not report on main outcomes such as birth complications, caesarean section, or birth defects in babies.
One trial found a slightly higher score for starting preconception conversations with healthcare providers, but the result was uncertain.
There is not enough trial evidence to judge the effects of preconception care for women with diabetes on mothers and infants.

items.title: The EULAR points to consider for use of antirheumatic drugs before pregnancy, and during pregnancy and lactation
items.summary: A European rheumatology group reviewed the research on medicines for conditions like rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, before and during pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Several commonly used medicines were found compatible with pregnancy and breastfeeding. A few others should be stopped before trying to conceive, and many have too little safety data to be sure. The group concluded that active disease can usually be treated with reasonable safety for the baby.
keyPoints: Antimalarials, sulfasalazine, azathioprine, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, colchicine, intravenous immunoglobulin and glucocorticoids were found compatible with pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil and cyclophosphamide need to be stopped before conception because they are proven to harm a developing baby.
Leflunomide, tofacitinib, abatacept, rituximab, belimumab, tocilizumab, ustekinumab and anakinra lack enough safety data, so stopping before a planned pregnancy is advised.
Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors are the best-studied biologics and appear reasonably safe when used in the first and second trimester.

items.title: Risks associated with obesity in pregnancy, for the mother and baby: a systematic review of reviews
items.summary: This review pulled together 22 earlier reviews that compared pregnant women with obesity to pregnant women of healthy weight. Women with obesity were more likely to have problems such as gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, high blood pressure in pregnancy, depression, caesarean or instrumental birth, and wound infection. Their babies had higher chances of preterm birth, being large for gestational age, birth defects and perinatal death. The authors conclude that women with obesity need support to lose weight before conceiving and to limit weight gain in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Obesity in pregnancy is linked with higher chances of gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, depression, caesarean or instrumental birth and surgical site infection.
Babies of mothers with obesity had greater risk of preterm birth, being large for gestational age, foetal defects, congenital anomalies and perinatal death.
Breastfeeding was less likely to start, and more likely to stop early, in women with obesity.
The authors say women with obesity need support to lose weight before conception and to minimise weight gain in pregnancy.

items.title: Screening and subsequent management for thyroid dysfunction pre-pregnancy and during pregnancy for improving maternal and infant health
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether testing all pregnant women for thyroid problems, instead of only those thought to be at higher risk or no one, leads to better health for mothers and babies. Two large trials (26,408 women) were included. Testing everyone found and treated more women with an underactive thyroid, but it did not clearly change rates of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, miscarriage, or children's IQ at age three. The authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Testing all pregnant women found about three times as many cases of underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) as testing only higher-risk women, and more women received thyroid medication.
No clear differences were seen in pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, miscarriage, or fetal and newborn death between screening approaches.
Screening everyone for hypothyroidism did not clearly change the chance of a child having an IQ below 85 at three years.
Data were missing for several outcomes, including side effects of screening and treatment, so more trials are needed.

items.title: The Dietary Reference Intakes for Japanese (2025): Overview and Future Directions for the Pregnant and Lactating Women's Section
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research
items.summary: This commentary reviews the 2025 Japanese national nutrition guidelines for pregnant and breastfeeding women and compares them with recent Japanese research. The guidelines give extra energy and nutrient targets for each trimester. Studies show many women in Japan eat less than recommended of several nutrients, and folate awareness and intake remain low. The authors say there are still important gaps in the evidence, such as how much energy women of different body sizes need for healthy weight gain.
keyPoints: The 2025 Japanese guidelines set extra energy and nutrient targets for each trimester of pregnancy.
Japanese studies show many pregnant women eat less than recommended of energy and several nutrients, and few know about or get enough folate.
Anemia in pregnancy (hemoglobin below 11 g/dL) is linked to worse outcomes, and low vitamin D and calcium can affect the mother's bone health.
Evidence gaps remain on energy needs by body mass index, diet and fetal growth, and advice for breastfeeding and the time before pregnancy.

items.title: Choline in Pregnancy and Lactation: Essential Knowledge for Clinical Practice
items.summary: This review looked at recent human research on choline, an essential nutrient, during pregnancy and breastfeeding. It found promising links between choline and a baby's brain development, liver function and a lower risk of neural tube defects, as well as possible benefits for pregnancy outcomes. Most pregnant and breastfeeding women do not get as much choline as is recommended, and the gap may grow as more people eat plant-based diets. The authors suggest choline supplements should be considered alongside folic acid advice.
keyPoints: Most pregnant and breastfeeding women do not meet recommended choline intakes.
Choline shows promising links to baby's brain development, liver function and a lower neural tube defect risk.
Plant-based diets tend to be lower in choline, so the intake gap may widen.
The authors suggest clinicians consider choline supplementation alongside folic acid during pregnancy and lactation.

items.title: Calcium supplementation during pregnancy for preventing hypertensive disorders and related problems
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 10 trials with about 37,500 pregnant women to see whether calcium supplements prevent pre-eclampsia and related problems. Overall, calcium made little to no difference to pre-eclampsia or preterm birth, especially in the largest trials, where the evidence was high certainty. Low and high doses of calcium also gave similar results. Some outcomes, such as maternal death and side effects, were too rare or too poorly measured to say much.
keyPoints: Compared with placebo, calcium may make little to no difference to pre-eclampsia (low-certainty evidence overall, high-certainty when only large trials were counted).
Large trials showed little to no difference in preterm birth before 37 weeks, and calcium probably makes little to no difference to stillbirth.
Evidence on maternal death, side effects and newborn death is very uncertain because these events were rare or rarely measured.
Low-dose and high-dose calcium gave similar results for pre-eclampsia, perinatal loss and stillbirth in women at high risk in low-calcium-intake populations.

items.title: Probiotics for infantile colic: Is there evidence beyond doubt? A meta-analysis and systematic review
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomised trials of probiotics (friendly bacteria) given to babies under 3 months old with colic. On average, babies given probiotics cried about 51 minutes less per day. The benefit looked larger in exclusively breastfed babies, while evidence for formula-fed babies and babies born by caesarean is limited.
keyPoints: Probiotics were linked to an average of 51 fewer minutes of crying per day in babies with colic.
Exclusively breastfed babies had the biggest drop in crying time, about 74 minutes per day.
Reductions were also seen with Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 and with other probiotic strains.
Evidence is limited for formula-fed babies and babies born by caesarean.

items.title: Effects of vitamin D in pregnancy on maternal and offspring health-related outcomes: An umbrella review of systematic review and meta-analyses
items.summary: This review pulled together 16 earlier systematic reviews and meta-analyses, covering about 250,000 women, on vitamin D in pregnancy. Low vitamin D was linked with higher risks of preterm birth, smaller babies, recurrent miscarriage, bacterial vaginosis and gestational diabetes. Taking vitamin D supplements in pregnancy was linked with higher birth weight and lower risks of pre-eclampsia, miscarriage and some childhood conditions. The authors suggest vitamin D levels be monitored, especially in women at high risk of deficiency.
keyPoints: Vitamin D deficiency in pregnancy was associated with preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age or low birth weight babies, recurrent miscarriage, bacterial vaginosis and gestational diabetes.
Vitamin D supplements in pregnancy were linked with higher birth weight and lower risks of pre-eclampsia, miscarriage, fetal or newborn death, and ADHD and autism spectrum disorder in childhood.
In women with gestational diabetes, supplements were linked with lower risks of macrosomia (a very large baby), fetal distress, polyhydramnios and neonatal hospitalization.
The authors suggest vitamin D status be monitored in pregnancy, and that a dose above 400 IU/day may help prevent certain adverse outcomes.

items.title: Vitamin D for the Prevention of Disease: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: The Endocrine Society reviewed trials of vitamin D given to people without a known need for it, to see whether it lowers disease risk. For pregnant people, it suggests vitamin D supplements because of their potential to lower the risk of pre-eclampsia, stillbirth, preterm birth, small babies and newborn death. It also suggests against routine blood testing of vitamin D in most people, and says the best dose is still unclear.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplements are suggested in pregnancy because they may lower the risk of preeclampsia, intra-uterine mortality, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth and neonatal mortality.
Vitamin D is also suggested for children aged 1 to 18 (rickets and respiratory infections), adults over 75, and people with high-risk prediabetes.
Routine blood testing of 25(OH)D is not suggested for the general population, including people with obesity or dark skin, because no trial evidence supports it.
The best dose is unclear because the trials used very different doses, and food alone rarely supplies enough, so fortified foods plus supplements can be used.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation for women during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether taking vitamin D during pregnancy, alone or with calcium and other vitamins, improves health for mothers and babies. After a stricter check of study trustworthiness, only 10 studies remained, so most findings are very uncertain. Vitamin D alone may lower the risk of severe bleeding after birth and of low birthweight, but each of these rests on few studies and the evidence is low quality.
keyPoints: For pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm birth, the evidence on vitamin D alone is very uncertain.
Vitamin D alone may reduce severe bleeding after birth, but only one study reported this (low-certainty evidence).
Vitamin D alone may reduce low birthweight, but a possible increase in risk cannot be ruled out (low-certainty evidence).
Vitamin D with calcium, or with other vitamins and minerals, gave very uncertain or uncertain results; the authors call for larger, higher-quality trials.

items.title: Daily oral iron supplementation during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 57 trials with almost 49,000 pregnant women to see what daily iron tablets do during pregnancy. Iron probably or possibly lowers the chance of anaemia and iron deficiency by the end of pregnancy. Babies were probably a little less likely to be born with low birthweight. For most other outcomes there was little or no difference, or the evidence was too uncertain to say.
keyPoints: Daily iron may reduce anaemia (4.0% vs 7.4%) and iron deficiency at term (44% vs 66%), based on low-certainty evidence.
Iron probably reduces iron-deficiency anaemia at term (5.0% vs 18.4%), based on moderate-certainty evidence.
Iron probably lowers the chance of a low-birthweight baby (5.2% vs 6.1%), but there was probably little to no difference in preterm birth.
The evidence on side effects and on severe anaemia was very uncertain, and no trials reported malaria or infection during pregnancy.

items.title: Screening and Supplementation for Iron Deficiency and Iron Deficiency Anemia During Pregnancy: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force looked at whether routine screening for low iron, and routine iron supplements, help pregnant people without symptoms and their babies. It found the current evidence is not strong enough to say whether the benefits outweigh the harms for either one. This does not mean these steps are harmful or useless, only that the research cannot yet settle the question.
keyPoints: Iron deficiency is the leading cause of anemia in pregnancy; about 18% of pregnant people have iron deficiency and about 5% have iron deficiency anemia.
Iron deficiency becomes more common as pregnancy goes on, from about 7% in the first trimester to about 28% in the third.
The Task Force found the evidence insufficient to judge the balance of benefits and harms of screening for iron deficiency or iron deficiency anemia in pregnant people without symptoms.
The Task Force also found the evidence insufficient to judge the balance of benefits and harms of routine iron supplementation in pregnant people without symptoms.

items.title: Italian Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders: epidemiology
items.summary: This Italian guideline reviews how common fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD) are and why they are hard to diagnose. About 10% of women worldwide keep drinking during pregnancy, with high rates in Europe. Heavy drinking is common in young adults aged 20-24, the same age group with many unplanned pregnancies. The guideline says preventing alcohol use in pregnancy matters for both mother and baby, and recommends more education and early diagnosis centers.
keyPoints: About 10% of women worldwide continue to drink alcohol during pregnancy, with notably high rates in Europe.
Risky drinking is common in young adults aged 20-24, which overlaps with high rates of unplanned pregnancy and raises the risk of FASD.
Research on alcohol's risks in pregnancy varies, so more education on the issue is needed.

The guideline recommends education campaigns, especially in schools and universities, and early diagnosis centers; urine testing for ethylglucuronide (EtG) each trimester is suggested as a way to monitor alcohol intake.

items.title: The Impact of Minerals on Female Fertility: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This systematic review pulled together 39 studies on how minerals relate to female fertility, including in women using IVF. It found that minerals such as selenium, zinc and copper appear important for reproductive health, while exposure to toxic metals like cadmium and lead appears harmful. The authors say more research is needed before firm guidelines on supplement doses or blood levels can be set.
keyPoints: Selenium, zinc and copper were found to be important for maintaining reproductive health.
Exposure to toxic metals such as cadmium and lead was linked to harm to fertility.
The review looked at outcomes including egg quality, ovulation, embryo development, miscarriage and IVF results.
Further research is needed to refine guidelines for mineral supplementation and blood levels in women with fertility problems.

items.title: The effects of oral ferrous bisglycinate supplementation on hemoglobin and ferritin concentrations in adults and children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 17 randomised trials comparing a type of iron supplement called ferrous bisglycinate with other iron supplements. In pregnant women, taking it for 4 to 20 weeks led to higher haemoglobin levels and fewer reported stomach and gut side effects. There was no clear difference in children, and the authors say more trials are needed in other groups.
keyPoints: In pregnant women, ferrous bisglycinate raised haemoglobin more than other iron supplements.
Pregnant women taking it reported fewer gastrointestinal side effects than those taking other iron supplements.
Ferritin levels showed a trend towards being higher in pregnancy, but the difference was not statistically significant.
No significant differences in haemoglobin or ferritin were found in children.

items.title: Antenatal dietary supplementation with myo-inositol for preventing gestational diabetes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at seven trials (1319 pregnant women) of myo-inositol, a natural sugar-like supplement, to see if it helps prevent gestational diabetes. The trials suggest it may lower the chance of gestational diabetes, high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy and preterm birth. However, the studies were small, mostly done in Italy, and the certainty of the evidence was low to very low, so the results are uncertain.
keyPoints: Myo-inositol may reduce gestational diabetes (risk ratio 0.53) and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (risk ratio 0.34).
It may also be linked to fewer preterm births, and may make little to no difference to caesarean section rates.
The effect on large-for-gestational-age babies, weight gain in pregnancy and newborn low blood sugar was unclear.
The authors call for larger studies in more diverse groups of women, with long-term follow-up and checks for harms.

items.title: Iron supplements in pregnant women with normal iron status: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled eight randomised trials (2,822 women) of daily iron tablets in pregnant women who were not anaemic and had normal iron levels. Compared with no iron, daily iron probably lowered the chance of iron deficiency anaemia at term and of having a low birthweight baby. It may also lower iron deficiency at term and small-for-gestational-age babies, but the evidence for those findings is less certain.
keyPoints: Daily iron probably reduces iron deficiency anaemia at term (moderate-certainty evidence).
Daily iron probably reduces the chance of a low birthweight baby (moderate-certainty evidence).
Daily iron may reduce iron deficiency at term and small-for-gestational-age babies (low-certainty evidence).
The review included only randomised trials; no observational studies met the criteria.

items.title: Calcium for pre-eclampsia prevention: A systematic review and network meta-analysis to guide personalised antenatal care
items.summary: This review pooled results from 30 trials with over 20,000 women to look at calcium supplements for preventing pre-eclampsia, a pregnancy condition involving high blood pressure. Calcium roughly halved the risk of pre-eclampsia, and a lower dose (under 1 g a day) worked about as well as a higher dose (1 g or more a day). The benefit was seen in women who did not get much calcium from their diet, but not in women whose usual calcium intake was already adequate.
keyPoints: Calcium supplements lowered the risk of pre-eclampsia, with a similar effect for high doses (RR 0.49) and low doses (RR 0.49).
Direct comparison found no clear difference between high-dose and low-dose calcium.
The benefit did not depend on baseline pre-eclampsia risk, taking vitamin D as well, or when calcium was started.
Calcium did not help women whose average calcium intake was already adequate.

items.title: Effectiveness of Dietary Interventions in Prevention and Treatment of Iron-Deficiency Anemia in Pregnant Women: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.summary: This review looked at seven randomized trials testing whether changing what pregnant women eat can prevent or treat iron-deficiency anaemia. The diet-based approaches included iron-fortified foods, foods with extra nutrients, and general dietary counselling. All of them were found to be effective at improving blood haemoglobin levels. However, many studies had a medium or high risk of bias, so the authors say more carefully run trials are needed to confirm the results.
keyPoints: Diet-based approaches (more iron, more of several nutrients, or counselling alone) were all effective in the seven included trials.
The main measure of success was haemoglobin, a blood marker used to check for anaemia.
Most studies had a medium risk of bias and some had a high risk, so confidence in the results is limited.
The authors call for more rigorous randomized trials to confirm these findings.

items.title: 2021 Canadian Cardiovascular Society Guidelines for the Management of Dyslipidemia for the Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease in Adults
items.summary: These Canadian guidelines update advice on managing cholesterol and other blood fats to help prevent heart disease in adults. They keep recommending statin medicine for people at higher risk, and suggest checking a blood fat called lipoprotein(a) once in a lifetime. They also add new advice on caring for the long-term heart health of women who had high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy. Regular exercise and a heart-healthy diet remain the foundation of prevention.
keyPoints: Statins are still recommended for people with clinical atherosclerosis, most people with diabetes or chronic kidney disease, and those with LDL cholesterol of 5 mmol/L or higher.
Lipoprotein(a) should be measured once in a person's lifetime as part of first cholesterol screening.
There are new recommendations for preventive care of women who had hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
Regular exercise and a heart-healthy diet remain the cornerstone of preventing cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Omega-3 Fatty Acid Dietary Supplements Consumed During Pregnancy and Lactation and Child Neurodevelopment: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This systematic review looked at whether taking omega-3 supplements during pregnancy or breastfeeding affects a child's brain development. It pulled together 15 randomized trials and one cohort study. Some trials found small improvements in thinking skills in babies and children when mothers took omega-3 in pregnancy, but every trial also had results that were not significant. The evidence is limited, and there was not enough to say whether omega-3 helps other areas such as language, behaviour or vision.
keyPoints: Limited evidence suggests omega-3 supplements in pregnancy may support better cognitive (thinking) development in children.
5 of 8 pregnancy-only trials found cognitive gains of 6%-11% on at least one measure, but all 8 also had non-significant results.
Evidence was inconsistent or insufficient for language, motor, visual and social-emotional development, and for conditions like ADHD, autism, anxiety or depression.
There was not enough evidence on supplements taken during breastfeeding, and teenagers and lower-income groups were underrepresented.

items.title: Nutrition-specific interventions for preventing and controlling anaemia throughout the life cycle: an overview of systematic reviews
items.summary: This large review pulled together 75 earlier reviews on ways to prevent or treat anaemia (low haemoglobin, often from low iron) at every age. Daily iron supplements may raise haemoglobin and lower the risk of anaemia and iron deficiency anaemia in babies, children, and pregnant and non-pregnant women. Iron-fortified foods also helped in several groups. Very few reviews looked at improving diet variety and quality, and the quality of evidence ranged from high to very low.
keyPoints: Daily iron supplements may raise haemoglobin and reduce anaemia and iron deficiency anaemia in infants, children, and pregnant and non-pregnant women.
In pregnancy, daily iron (with or without folic acid) raised haemoglobin and cut the risk of anaemia, while intermittent iron raised the risk of anaemia near term but caused fewer side effects.
Adding iron to foods such as flour, rice, salt and soy sauce raised haemoglobin and lowered anaemia risk in several reviews.
Few reviews tested diet-based approaches, and none looked at women aged 50 and over or at fortification or diet changes in non-pregnant women of reproductive age.

items.title: Vitamin and Mineral Supplementation During Pregnancy on Maternal, Birth, Child Health and Development Outcomes in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 72 studies (about 450,000 women) from low- and middle-income countries to see how vitamin and mineral supplements in pregnancy affect mothers and babies. Supplements that combine many micronutrients improved some birth outcomes compared with iron-folic acid alone, including fewer preterm births, small-for-gestational-age babies and low birthweight. Single supplements helped in only a few areas, and supplements made little difference to deaths of mothers or babies.
keyPoints: Multiple micronutrient supplements, compared with iron-folic acid, improved preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age and low birthweight outcomes, and also child diarrhea and retinol levels.
Iron-folic acid improved maternal anemia and reduced low birthweight.
Single supplements helped a few outcomes: calcium for pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, iron for maternal anemia, vitamin D for preterm births, and zinc for maternal zinc levels.
Across all comparisons, supplements had little to no effect on maternal, newborn, perinatal or infant deaths; lipid-based supplements showed no apparent effect.

items.title: The Role of Iron in Brain Development: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at whether low iron, or taking iron supplements, in pregnancy and the first four years of a child's life affects brain development. Iron is known to matter for how the brain grows, but the studies did not show a clear link between iron status and development in young children. Many of the studies were low quality and designed very differently, so the picture is uncertain. There was very little research on pregnancy and early infancy.
keyPoints: No clear relationship was found between iron status and developmental outcomes in any age window or area of development.
Most of the studies found were low quality and varied a lot in how they were designed.
Few studies looked at iron during pregnancy or in early infancy.
The authors call for more high-quality research, especially in pregnancy and early infancy.

items.title: Effect of Probiotic Supplementation on Newborn Birth Weight for Mother with Gestational Diabetes Mellitus or Overweight/Obesity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled seven randomised trials (1,093 women) to see whether taking probiotics during pregnancy changes newborn birth weight in women with gestational diabetes or overweight. Overall, probiotics made little difference compared with placebo. The effects pointed in different directions in different groups, so there is no evidence that probiotics can be used to control a baby's birth weight in these situations.
keyPoints: Across seven trials, probiotics had little effect on newborn birth weight compared with placebo.
In women with gestational diabetes, probiotic use was linked to lower birth weight in a subgroup analysis.
In women with obesity, probiotic use was linked to higher birth weight in a subgroup analysis.
The authors conclude there is no evidence that probiotics can control newborn birth weight in women with gestational diabetes or overweight.

items.title: Probiotics to prevent infantile colic
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether giving probiotics (helpful live bacteria) to newborns, or to mothers in pregnancy and then babies, can prevent infant colic. Six trials with 1886 babies compared probiotics with a placebo. There was no clear evidence that probiotics prevent colic from starting, but babies who had probiotics cried about 33 minutes less per day on average. The evidence was low certainty, so these results could change with more research.
keyPoints: No clear evidence that probiotics are better than placebo at preventing infant colic from developing.
Daily crying time was about 33 minutes shorter with probiotics, and about 44 minutes shorter with Lactobacillus reuteri.
No clear difference in serious side effects between probiotics and placebo.
All results were low-certainty, so the findings may change with further research.

items.title: Lipid-based nutrient supplements for maternal, birth, and infant developmental outcomes
items.summary: This review looked at lipid-based nutrient supplements (nutrient-rich ready-to-use pastes) taken in pregnancy, using four trials with about 8,000 women in lower-income countries. Compared with standard iron and folic acid tablets, the supplements made little or no difference to weekly weight gain in pregnancy. Babies in the supplement groups were slightly heavier and longer at birth, but women had more anaemia than with iron-folic acid or multiple micronutrient tablets. The authors say the effects are small and the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Weekly weight gain in pregnancy was no different with the supplements than with iron-folic acid tablets or multiple micronutrient tablets.

Compared with iron-folic acid, the supplements were linked to slightly higher birth weight (about 53 g) and birth length (about 0.24 cm), and fewer small-for-gestational-age babies and stunted newborns.
Supplements were similar to multiple micronutrient tablets for all maternal, birth and infant outcomes studied.
Iron-folic acid and multiple micronutrients were better than the supplements at reducing maternal anaemia.

items.title: Omega-3 fatty acid addition during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 70 trials with nearly 20,000 pregnant women to see what happens when omega-3 fatty acids (from supplements or food, such as fish oil) are added during pregnancy. Women who took omega-3 had fewer babies born before 37 weeks and fewer born before 34 weeks, based on high-quality evidence. Pregnancies were probably more likely to go past 42 weeks, and babies were slightly less likely to have low birthweight. Evidence on pre-eclampsia and on longer-term outcomes for mothers and children was weaker.
keyPoints: Preterm birth before 37 weeks was lower with omega-3 (11.9% vs 13.4% without), and birth before 34 weeks was also lower (2.7% vs 4.6% without), both with high-quality evidence.
Pregnancies going past 42 weeks were probably more common with omega-3 (2.6% vs 1.6% without), and there may be a small increase in larger-than-expected babies.
Low birthweight was less common, and perinatal death and neonatal care admissions were possibly reduced.
