Pre-eclampsia may be slightly reduced, but this evidence was low quality; few differences were seen in children's development, mostly based on low or very low quality evidence.

items.title: Position paper on vegetarian diets from the working group of the Italian Society of Human Nutrition
items.summary: Italian nutrition experts reviewed 295 studies on key nutrients in vegetarian diets. They concluded that well-planned vegetarian diets with plenty of variety and a reliable source of vitamin B12 can give enough of the nutrients people need. The paper gives practical tips on B12, protein, calcium, iron, zinc and omega-3 fats. The abstract does not look specifically at pregnancy or babies.
keyPoints: Vegetarians should get vitamin B12 from fortified foods or supplements.
Plant protein is digested less well than animal protein, so vegetarians may need to eat somewhat more protein.

Good sources of calcium, iron and zinc include low-oxalate vegetables like Brassicaceae, nuts, seeds and calcium-rich mineral water; soaking, germinating and sour-dough leavening help the body absorb minerals from pulses and cereals.
Omega-3 status can be kept up with walnuts, flaxseeds, chia seeds and their oils, while limiting corn and sunflower oils.

items.title: Impact of maternal nutrition on breast-milk composition: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 36 studies of 1,977 breastfeeding women to see how much a mother's diet changes the nutrients in her breast milk. Some links were found, such as eating fish going with more DHA (an omega-3 fat) in milk, and dietary vitamin C going with more vitamin C in milk. Overall the authors say the evidence is scarce and varied, and many recommendations rest on studies that only show indirect links.
keyPoints: Three studies linked eating fish with higher DHA (an omega-3 fat) in breast milk.
Two studies found that more vitamin C in the diet went with more vitamin C in breast milk.
Seventeen of the 36 studies looked at fatty acids in breast milk; the rest covered many different nutrients.
Available evidence is scarce and varied, and current advice often relies on indirect associations.

items.title: Screening for Iron Deficiency Anemia and Iron Supplementation in Pregnant Women to Improve Maternal Health and Birth Outcomes: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force reviewed whether checking pregnant women for iron deficiency anaemia, or giving everyone iron supplements, leads to better health for mothers and babies. It found the current evidence is not strong enough to say whether the benefits outweigh the harms for either approach. This applies to pregnant women and teenagers in the U.S. without symptoms of iron deficiency anaemia.
keyPoints: Evidence is insufficient to judge the benefits and harms of screening symptom-free pregnant women for iron deficiency anaemia.
Evidence is insufficient to judge the benefits and harms of routine iron supplements for pregnant women to prevent poor maternal or birth outcomes.
The advice does not cover women who are malnourished, have symptoms of iron deficiency anaemia, or have blood conditions or special nutritional needs.
This is an update of the Task Force's 2006 recommendation.

items.title: Fertility preservation in patients with medical indications: a committee opinion
items.summary: This is a committee opinion from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine. It says people who are about to have treatments that could harm their fertility, or who are at risk of premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), should be offered counseling about fertility preservation options quickly. It also says care is best given by comprehensive programs set up for these patients' particular challenges. It replaces the group's 2019 guidance.
keyPoints: Patients about to have treatments that risk their fertility should get prompt counseling about fertility preservation options.
People at risk of premature ovarian insufficiency should also be offered this counseling.
Fertility preservation is best provided by comprehensive programs designed for these patients' unique challenges.
This opinion replaces the 2019 committee opinion on fertility preservation.

items.title: Primary ovarian insufficiency in Classic Galactosemia: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at the research on primary ovarian insufficiency (POI, when the ovaries stop working normally early in life) in women with classic galactosemia, a rare inherited condition. Even with diet treatment from birth, POI is a common long-term problem. The exact cause is still unclear, and how the ovaries are affected varies from person to person. Some women with the condition do still manage to conceive.
keyPoints: The exact cause of POI in classic galactosemia is still unclear, and links between genotype, galactose levels and ovarian function vary between studies.
Checking AMH (a hormone marker of ovarian reserve) before puberty may help predict POI.
Early estrogen replacement, calcium and strategies to improve galactosylation should be considered to protect bone health.
The course of POI is unpredictable: nearly 30% of women trying to conceive succeeded within a year, rising to almost 50% after two years.

items.title: Menopause hormone therapy and risk of mild cognitive impairment or dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from ten studies (one trial and nine observational studies, over one million women) to see whether menopause hormone therapy (MHT) changes the chance of mild cognitive impairment or dementia. It found no clear link either way, and this held when results were split by timing, duration and type of MHT. The certainty of the evidence ranged from moderate to very low, and no studies looked at women with premature ovarian insufficiency.
keyPoints: No significant association was found between MHT use and risk of mild cognitive impairment or dementia.
Results did not differ significantly by when MHT was started, how long it was used, or its type.
No included studies looked at testosterone or at MHT use in premature ovarian insufficiency.
The authors say MHT decisions should rest on other benefits and risks, not on preventing dementia.

items.title: Practice guideline on ovarian tissue cryopreservation and transplantation in the prevention and treatment of iatrogenic premature ovarian insufficiency
items.summary: This practice guideline looks at freezing and later re-transplanting ovarian tissue to protect fertility and ovarian function in girls and women facing chemotherapy or radiotherapy. These treatments can cause premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), where the ovaries stop working properly before age 40. International and national guidelines see this approach as the most promising option for those who cannot delay cancer treatment. The Chinese guideline group set out 18 recommendations to guide doctors in using it.
keyPoints: Premature ovarian insufficiency means ovarian function declines before age 40, which can reduce fertility and cause menopausal symptoms.
POI is linked to a higher risk of chronic diseases related to early menopause and can affect quality of life.
Chemotherapy and radiotherapy put many girls and women at risk of POI.
Freezing ovarian tissue and transplanting it later is considered the most promising way to preserve ovarian function and fertility when cancer treatment cannot be delayed.

items.title: Birth weight and premature ovarian insufficiency: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from five studies covering over 2 million women to see whether birth weight is linked to premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), when the ovaries stop working normally before age 40. Women who were born with low birth weight had a slightly higher chance of developing POI as adults than women born at a normal weight. Being born very large (macrosomia) showed no link to POI. This type of study shows an association, not that low birth weight directly causes POI.
keyPoints: Low birth weight was linked to a higher risk of POI in adulthood (OR 1.15, 95% CI 1.09-1.22) compared with normal birth weight.
No link was found between macrosomia (very high birth weight) and POI.
The review combined five cohort and case-control studies with about 2.2 million women, of whom about 1% had POI.
The authors describe the evidence for the low birth weight link as strong and suggest preventing low birth weight where possible.

items.title: Society for endocrinology guideline for understanding, diagnosing and treating female hypogonadism
items.summary: The Society for Endocrinology has issued new guidance on female hypogonadism, which means the ovaries make too little estrogen before the usual age of menopause. It covers premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) and also causes linked to the brain's hormone-controlling glands. Earlier guidelines mostly looked at POI alone and often borrowed evidence from women who had gone through menopause at the usual age. This guidance was written with specialists from several fields plus expert patients and a patient support group.
keyPoints: Female hypogonadism is a fairly common hormone condition in women who have not yet reached menopause age.
Care has varied a lot, and many past guidelines covered only POI and relied on evidence from postmenopausal women.
The new guidance covers all forms of female hypogonadism, including POI and causes in the hypothalamus or pituitary gland, whether organic or functional.
It was developed by endocrinology, primary care, gynaecology and reproductive health experts, with input from patients.

items.title: The effects of acupuncture on patients with premature ovarian insufficiency and polycystic ovary syndrome: an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses
items.summary: This review pulled together results from 38 earlier meta-analyses on acupuncture for women with premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). In women with PCOS, acupuncture was linked to higher pregnancy and ovulation rates and better hormone and metabolic measures. In women with POI, acupuncture was linked to improvements in blood hormone levels, including estradiol, FSH and LH. The abstract does not rate the quality of the underlying evidence, and it notes that earlier meta-analyses had given inconclusive results.
keyPoints: In PCOS, acupuncture was linked to higher pregnancy and ovulation rates.
In PCOS, acupuncture was linked to lower LH, testosterone, insulin resistance and BMI.
In POI, acupuncture improved blood levels of LH, FSH, the LH/FSH ratio and estradiol.
The authors conclude acupuncture-related therapies improve pregnancy rate and hormonal and metabolic imbalances in POI and PCOS.

items.title: Environmental Exposure to Per- and Polyfluorylalkyl Substances (PFASs) and Reproductive Outcomes in the General Population: A Systematic Review of Epidemiological Studies
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review pulled together 30 studies (about 27,900 people) on everyday background exposure to PFAS, the 'forever chemicals' found in some drinking water and products. It found no effect on fertility, and weak to moderate links to higher odds of preterm birth (with PFOS) and miscarriage (with PFOA). There was limited but suggestive evidence linking PFAS to early menopause and primary ovarian insufficiency. Findings on menstrual cycles and fetal growth were inconsistent, and the authors say larger studies are needed.
keyPoints: No effect of background PFAS levels on fertility was found.
Higher PFOS levels were linked to weakly to moderately higher odds of preterm birth, and higher PFOA levels to miscarriage.
Evidence linking PFAS to early menopause and primary ovarian insufficiency was limited but suggestive.
Findings on menstrual cycle changes and fetal growth were inconsistent.

items.title: The global prevalence of premature ovarian insufficiency: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to estimate how common premature ovarian insufficiency (POI, when the ovaries stop working normally before age 40) is around the world. It found that about 3.5% of women are affected. Rates were higher in some groups and regions, and the authors recommend more public awareness and health education about POI.
keyPoints: The global overall prevalence of POI among women was 3.5%.
POI was most common after medical treatment causes (11.2%) and with autoimmune causes (10.5%).
By region, prevalence was highest in North America (11.3%), then South America (5.4%).
It was higher in developing countries (5.3%) than in developed countries (3.1%), and the trend over 20 years was upward, though not statistically significant.

items.title: Male- and female-specific reproductive risk factors across the lifespan for dementia or cognitive decline: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pooled results from 94 studies, covering millions of women and men, to see whether reproductive factors across life are linked to dementia or memory decline. Several female factors were linked to a higher risk, including early menopause (22% higher), late first period, having no children, and having had both ovaries removed. The authors say these links may reflect the role of sex hormones in the brain. These are associations, so they do not show that one thing causes the other.
keyPoints: Early menopause was linked to a 22% higher risk of dementia or cognitive decline.

Other female factors linked to higher risk were late first period (15%), never having had children (11%), having five or more children (32%), having both ovaries removed (8%) and a short reproductive period (14%).
Higher estradiol levels were linked to a 46% higher risk.
In men, androgen deprivation therapy (18%) and higher sex hormone-binding globulin (22%) were linked to higher risk.

items.title: Fresh and cryopreserved ovarian tissue transplantation for preserving reproductive and endocrine function: a systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 20 studies of women who had frozen ovarian tissue thawed and put back, to see whether it restores fertility and hormone function. After the transplant, about 37 in 100 women became pregnant and about 28 in 100 had a live birth. Hormone levels also moved toward normal, with oestrogen rising and FSH falling. The evidence mostly comes from case reports and case series, and the authors say larger, better-described studies are still needed.
keyPoints: After frozen ovarian tissue transplantation, pooled rates were 37% for pregnancy, 28% for live birth and 37% for miscarriage.
Oestrogen rose and FSH fell after transplant, showing the ovaries were working again.
FSH took a median of 19 weeks to drop below 25 IU/l, and grafts worked for a median of 2.5 years.
The authors conclude the procedure can restore reproductive and hormonal function, but larger studies are needed to work out the best methods.

items.title: Dietary factors and onset of natural menopause: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 15 studies of women to see whether what we eat affects the age at which natural menopause starts. A few foods were linked to the timing: more green and yellow vegetables went with earlier menopause, while some low-fat dairy and low alcohol intake went with later menopause. Most other nutrients and diet patterns showed no consistent link. The studies were observational and few in number, so the overall evidence is still unclear.
keyPoints: Higher intake of green and yellow vegetables was linked to earlier natural menopause.
Higher intake of some dairy products, such as low-fat and skimmed milk, and low alcohol intake were linked to later menopause.
A vegetarian diet might be linked to earlier menopause, but no other diet pattern showed a consistent effect.
Overall, the evidence on diet and menopause timing remains controversial because the studies were observational, few, and mostly at medium risk of bias.

items.title: Impact of unilateral versus bilateral ovarian endometriotic cystectomy on ovarian reserve: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 studies of 783 women who had surgery to remove endometriomas (cysts on the ovary caused by endometriosis). Before surgery, women with cysts on one or both ovaries had similar levels of AMH, a blood marker of egg supply. After surgery, AMH was lower in women who had both ovaries operated on, and AMH fell in both groups, by about 39.5% with one ovary and 57.0% with both. The authors suggest the surgery, rather than the cyst itself, is what reduces ovarian reserve, so removal should be considered carefully, especially when both ovaries are affected.
keyPoints: Before surgery, AMH levels were not significantly different between women with one-sided and two-sided endometriomas.
After cyst removal, AMH was significantly lower in women who had both ovaries operated on than in those who had one.
AMH dropped by 39.5% after one-sided surgery and 57.0% after two-sided surgery, and the drop was sustained.

The authors say AMH seems a better marker of ovarian reserve than antral follicle count (AFC) in women with endometrioma, and that removal should be cautiously considered, especially in bilateral cases.

items.title: The global prevalence of primary ovarian insufficiency and early menopause: a meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 31 studies worldwide to estimate how common primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) and early menopause are. They found POI affects about 3.7% of women, and early menopause about 12.2%. POI was more common in countries with medium or low human development levels. The authors say these conditions are common enough that health systems should plan for them.
keyPoints: About 3.7% of women have primary ovarian insufficiency (POI).
About 12.2% of women have early menopause.
POI was more common in medium and low Human Development Index countries.
The rates did not change over time, and the authors call for health policy-makers to prioritise prevention and treatment.

items.title: Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone Agonists During Chemotherapy for Preservation of Ovarian Function and Fertility in Premenopausal Patients With Early Breast Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Individual Patient-Level Data
items.summary: This review combined data from five trials of 873 premenopausal women with early breast cancer. It looked at whether a temporary ovary-suppressing medicine (a GnRH agonist) given during chemotherapy protects the ovaries and future fertility. Fewer women who had the medicine developed premature ovarian insufficiency (14.1% vs 30.9%), and more went on to have a pregnancy afterwards (10.3% vs 5.5%). Cancer outcomes were not significantly different between the two groups.
keyPoints: Premature ovarian insufficiency occurred in 14.1% of women given the medicine during chemotherapy, compared with 30.9% of those given chemotherapy alone.
At least one pregnancy after treatment happened in 10.3% of the medicine group and 5.5% of the chemotherapy-only group.
No significant differences were seen in disease-free survival or overall survival between the groups.
The authors conclude this is an available option to lower the chance of chemotherapy-induced early menopause and possibly improve future fertility.

items.title: Menopause: Full Guideline
items.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
items.journal: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
items.summary: This is a UK national guideline on menopause. It notes that many women have menopausal symptoms that can affect quality of life, and that symptoms often last 7 years or more. Because of this, telling women the symptoms will simply get better with time is described as inappropriate, and help should be offered where possible. The guideline covers diagnosis and treatment, including hormonal and non-hormonal options, for women who go through menopause in middle age and for those with premature ovarian insufficiency (POI).
keyPoints: Symptoms may continue for 7 years or more, so advice that they will just improve with time is inappropriate.
Women should be told about the available options, with their risks and benefits, and take part in decisions about their care.
The guideline covers diagnosis and management of menopause symptoms, including hormonal and non-hormonal treatments.
It also covers women with premature ovarian insufficiency and women for whom hormones are not appropriate, including those with or at high risk of breast cancer.

items.title: Outcome of fetuses with early increased nuchal translucency: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at what happens in pregnancies where the nuchal translucency (NT) measurement, a fluid-filled space at the back of the baby's neck, is increased very early, before 11 weeks. It combined five small studies covering 401 pregnancies. About 4 in 10 of these pregnancies had a complication such as a chromosomal or genetic condition, a structural anomaly or pregnancy loss. Risk was lower when the measurement returned to normal at the 11-14 week scan, but it was still raised.
keyPoints: About 42% of pregnancies with early increased NT had an adverse outcome, such as a chromosomal, genetic or structural anomaly or perinatal loss.
The increased NT went back to normal by the 11-14 week scan in about half of cases (48.8%).
Adverse outcomes occurred in 64.2% of pregnancies where the increase persisted, compared with 19.4% where it resolved.
The thicker the NT, the higher the risk: 31.9% at 2.5-3.4 mm, 50.4% at 3.5-4.4 mm and 70.2% at 4.5 mm or more.

items.title: Diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound screening for fetal structural abnormalities during the first and second trimester of pregnancy in low-risk and unselected populations
items.summary: This large review pooled 87 studies covering over 7 million pregnancies to see how well ultrasound scans find structural problems in the baby (such as problems with the heart, spine or organs). A scan at 11 to 14 weeks found most lethal problems but only about 4 in 10 problems overall. Having a scan in both the first and second trimesters found more problems than a single second-trimester scan, but this comparison is based on very low-certainty evidence because no studies compared the two approaches directly.
keyPoints: A first-trimester scan found about 91% of lethal anomalies (moderate-certainty evidence) but only about 38% of all structural anomalies (low-certainty evidence).
Scanning in both trimesters found about 84% of structural anomalies, compared with about 51% for a single second-trimester scan.
False alarms were rare with all approaches, roughly 0.1% to 0.2% of pregnancies without an anomaly.
Most of the evidence on first-trimester and two-stage scanning comes from single specialist hospitals, so results may not apply to everyone.

items.title: Diagnostic yield of exome sequencing in isolated fetal growth restriction: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at babies in the womb who were growing slowly with no other visible problems, and whose standard genetic tests (chromosomal microarray or karyotype) had come back normal. When researchers added a deeper genetic test called exome sequencing, they found a single-gene (monogenic) condition linked to the poor growth in about 12% of these pregnancies. Most of the pregnancies were tested before 32 weeks. The review pooled eight studies covering 146 babies, so the numbers are fairly small.
keyPoints: Eight studies with 146 fetuses with isolated fetal growth restriction and normal microarray or karyotype results were pooled.
Exome sequencing found a likely pathogenic or pathogenic variant causing the growth problem in 17 cases, about 12% (95% CI 7% to 18%).
This means a single-gene condition was found in roughly 1 in 8 of these apparently isolated cases.
Most fetuses were tested before 32 weeks of pregnancy.

items.title: Gastroschisis: a systematic review of diagnosis, prognosis and treatment
items.summary: This review pooled results from 44 studies covering 3,770 babies diagnosed with gastroschisis, a condition where a baby's bowel sits outside the belly wall at birth. Most babies survived (about 91 in 100), and most had surgery soon after birth. Babies with the more complicated form needed much longer hospital stays than those with the simple form. The authors say the data can help in counselling families who receive this diagnosis before birth.
keyPoints: Neonatal survival was about 91%, and fetal death before birth was under 1%.
About 23% of babies were born preterm and about 55% were born by cesarean section.
Around 80% had immediate surgical repair, most often with primary closure.
Average hospital stay was 38 days for simple gastroschisis and 89 days for complex gastroschisis.

items.title: First-trimester ultrasound detection of fetal heart anomalies: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 63 studies covering over 328,000 pregnancies to see how well an ultrasound at 11-14 weeks can spot major heart problems in the baby. It found the scan picks up a little over half of major heart anomalies in lower-risk pregnancies and about two thirds in higher-risk pregnancies. When the scan did flag a problem, it was right about 94-95% of the time. Scans that looked at the heart's outflow tracts or used colour-flow Doppler found more problems, and some types of heart anomaly are easier to spot early than others.
keyPoints: In lower-risk pregnancies, the early scan detected about 56% of major heart anomalies; in higher-risk pregnancies, about 68%.
A positive result was correct roughly 95% of the time, and a normal result was very rarely wrong about what it showed (specificity above 99.7%).
Detection was significantly better when the scan included an outflow-tract view or colour-flow Doppler.
The authors conclude that first-trimester heart scans can identify over half of affected babies, and that screening programmes should use structured protocols.

items.title: Predicting risk of postpartum haemorrhage: a systematic review
items.summary: Researchers reviewed 14 studies that built tools to predict who is at risk of heavy bleeding after birth (postpartum haemorrhage). Every study had a high risk of bias, for example small numbers of women or no proper testing of the tool. Only three tools, for caesarean birth, placenta accreta spectrum and placenta praevia, showed some potential for use in care. There is still no reliable tool for women having a general vaginal or labouring birth.
keyPoints: 14 studies of tools predicting heavy bleeding after birth were found, and all were at high risk of bias.
Three tools show some potential for clinical use: for caesarean birth, placenta accreta spectrum (with MRI) and placenta praevia.
No tool yet exists for the general population of women giving birth, including those in labour.
The tools need stronger testing in other groups of women before they can be relied on.

items.title: Ultrasound for diagnosis of birth weight discordance in twin pregnancies
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at how well ultrasound can spot a big difference in weight between twins before birth, compared with their actual weights after birth. Across 39 studies, ultrasound often missed true weight differences, but when it did flag a difference it was usually correct. The evidence was very low certainty, so ultrasound alone may not be a reliable basis for big decisions about twin pregnancies.
keyPoints: Ultrasound caught only about half of true weight differences between twins (sensitivity about 51% at a 20% cut-off and 46% at a 25% cut-off).
Ultrasound was good at ruling out a difference when there wasn't one (specificity about 91% to 93%).
The evidence was very low certainty, and the authors say it is not enough to rely on ultrasound weight estimates alone for clinical decisions.
Other measures, such as amniotic fluid and umbilical artery Doppler, need further study alongside ultrasound.

items.title: Antepartum Fetal Surveillance: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 229
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) on checking a baby's wellbeing before birth. The aim of these checks is to lower the risk of stillbirth. They use tracing of the baby's heart rate, ultrasound and Doppler blood-flow scans. They are routinely used when a pregnancy has an existing health condition such as diabetes, or when a problem such as poor baby growth develops.
keyPoints: The goal of antepartum fetal surveillance is to reduce the risk of stillbirth.
Heart rate pattern tests have been used for almost four decades, alongside ultrasound and umbilical artery Doppler scans.
These checks are routinely used in pregnancies with existing conditions like diabetes or new complications like fetal growth restriction.
The guideline reviews when and how to use these tests, based on the best scientific evidence.

items.title: Routine ultrasound for fetal assessment before 24 weeks' gestation
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 13 trials with about 85,000 women to see what routine ultrasound scans before 24 weeks of pregnancy do, compared with scans only when needed or no scans. Early scans probably lower short-term worry about the pregnancy. Scans in the second trimester may mean fewer inductions for a baby thought to be overdue, and may help spot major fetal abnormalities and twin pregnancies. The scans did not seem to change other major outcomes, though the trials were mostly older and the evidence is often low in certainty.
keyPoints: First trimester scans probably reduce short-term maternal anxiety about the pregnancy (moderate-certainty evidence).
Second trimester scans may reduce induction of labour for post-maturity, probably through more accurate dating (low-certainty evidence).
Routine second trimester scans may improve detection of twin pregnancy and major fetal abnormality, and probably increase the number of women who end a pregnancy for a major abnormality.
Scans did not appear to change perinatal loss, and long-term follow-up of children showed no sign of harm to physical or intellectual development.

items.title: Screening for Fetal Chromosomal Abnormalities: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 226
items.summary: This ACOG guideline explains the tests available to check for chromosomal conditions in a pregnancy. It says no single test is best for everyone, so each person should be given clear information about the benefits and limits of each option. Testing is a personal choice, and every patient can accept or decline it after counseling.
keyPoints: Every patient should be counseled about testing for fetal chromosomal abnormalities in each pregnancy.
All patients should be offered both screening tests and diagnostic tests.
No one screening test is better than the others in every situation, so the choice depends on the person's clinical context, values and goals.
Patients have the right to accept or decline testing after counseling.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 203: Chronic Hypertension in Pregnancy
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from ACOG, a US group of obstetricians and gynecologists, on chronic high blood pressure that is present before or early in pregnancy. It explains how this condition is defined and diagnosed, how it can affect a pregnancy and how pregnancy can affect it. It also reviews the evidence on ways to manage it. The abstract notes the condition is becoming more common and can raise health risks for mother and baby.
keyPoints: Chronic hypertension is present in about 0.9-1.5% of pregnant women and may cause significant health problems for the mother, baby and newborn.
The rate rose by 67% from 2000 to 2009, with the biggest rise (87%) among African American women.
The rise is largely linked to obesity and women being older at pregnancy, and the trend is expected to continue.
The guideline sets out criteria for diagnosing chronic hypertension and appraises the evidence for management options.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 196: Thromboembolism in Pregnancy
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists covers blood clots (thromboembolism) in pregnancy. Pregnant and postpartum women have a four to five times higher risk of clots than women who are not pregnant, and most of these clots are in the veins. Clots in the veins are one of the leading causes of maternal death in the United States. The guideline covers risk factors, diagnosis, treatment and prevention, and has been updated on screening for clot risk and on managing blood-thinning medicine around delivery.
keyPoints: Pregnant and postpartum women have a fourfold to fivefold higher risk of thromboembolism than nonpregnant women.
About 80% of clots in pregnancy are venous, affecting 0.5 to 2.0 per 1,000 pregnant women.
Venous thromboembolism accounts for 9.3% of maternal deaths in the United States.
The bulletin covers risk factors, diagnosis, treatment and prevention, including screening for clot risk and anticoagulation around delivery.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 197: Inherited Thrombophilias in Pregnancy
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists about inherited thrombophilias, which are conditions passed down in families that raise the risk of blood clots. It reviews how these conditions relate to blood clots and to problems in pregnancy. It also covers who may need testing and how these conditions can be managed during pregnancy and after birth. The guideline notes there is limited evidence to guide testing and treatment.
keyPoints: Inherited thrombophilias are linked to a higher risk of blood clots (venous thromboembolism) and to some adverse pregnancy outcomes.
Evidence to guide screening for and management of these conditions in pregnancy is limited.
The guideline covers who may be candidates for thrombophilia testing.
It gives updated consensus advice on blood-clot prevention (prophylaxis) during pregnancy and after birth, including considerations around epidural-type (neuraxial) anesthesia.

items.title: First and second trimester serum tests with and without first trimester ultrasound tests for Down's syndrome screening
items.summary: This large review pooled 22 studies of 228,615 pregnancies to compare screening tests for Down's syndrome that combine blood markers from the first and second trimesters, with or without an early ultrasound. Combining a first-trimester ultrasound (nuchal translucency) with blood markers from both trimesters and the mother's age worked better than tests without the ultrasound. The best-performing combination found about nine in ten Down's syndrome pregnancies, with 5% of unaffected pregnancies getting a false alarm. Because few studies tested this combination, the authors could not recommend one single screening strategy.
keyPoints: Tests that add first-trimester ultrasound to first and second trimester blood markers plus maternal age were significantly better than tests without the ultrasound.
The best combination detected about 9 in 10 Down's syndrome pregnancies at a 5% false positive rate.
False positive results can lead to invasive diagnostic testing, and false negatives mean a pregnancy with Down's syndrome is missed.
Too few studies were available to recommend one specific screening strategy.

items.title: Analysis of cell-free DNA in maternal blood in screening for aneuploidies: updated meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 35 studies of a blood test that looks at fetal DNA in a pregnant woman's blood (cell-free DNA, or NIPT) to screen for Down syndrome and some other chromosome conditions. In single-baby pregnancies, the test picked up more than 99% of babies with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), about 98% with trisomy 18 and about 99% with trisomy 13, with very few false alarms. There were too few cases of sex chromosome conditions, and too few twin pregnancies, to judge how well the test works for those.
keyPoints: In single-baby pregnancies, the test detected more than 99% of trisomy 21, about 98% of trisomy 18 and about 99% of trisomy 13.
The combined false-positive rate for these three conditions was about 0.13%.
Too few cases of sex chromosome conditions were reported to judge how well screening works for them.
For twin pregnancies the results for trisomy 21 look encouraging, but only a small number of cases were studied.

items.title: Regimens of ultrasound surveillance for twin pregnancies for improving outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for trials comparing different ultrasound check-up schedules for twin pregnancies. It found only one small trial of 526 women. Adding Doppler scans (which check blood flow) at 25, 30 and 35 weeks to regular growth scans made no clear difference to baby deaths, birth timing, caesarean births or hospital stays. The trial was too small to pick up rare outcomes, so there is not enough evidence to say which ultrasound schedule is best for twins.
keyPoints: Only one trial (526 women with twins) met the review's criteria.
Growth plus Doppler scans at 25, 30 and 35 weeks showed no clear difference from growth scans alone for baby deaths, stillbirth, caesarean birth or hospital admission.
The trial was too small to detect rare outcomes such as stillbirth or newborn death.
There is not enough trial evidence to say which ultrasound surveillance schedule is best for twin pregnancies, and more studies are needed.

items.title: Practice Bulletin No. 162: Prenatal Diagnostic Testing for Genetic Disorders
items.summary: This guideline explains the difference between prenatal genetic screening, which estimates the chance of a genetic condition, and diagnostic testing, which aims to confirm whether a condition is present. Definitive diagnosis for most genetic conditions needs amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling (CVS), though imaging such as ultrasound can sometimes point to a condition. Testing cannot find every problem, and results cannot predict all outcomes, so choices should fit each person's own risks, goals and preferences.
keyPoints: Screening shows whether the chance of a genetic condition is raised; diagnostic testing aims to say whether a specific condition is present.
Amniocentesis or CVS is needed to definitively diagnose most genetic disorders, although ultrasound, echocardiography or MRI may sometimes be diagnostic of a structural abnormality.
Testing cannot find all problems, and many genetic conditions vary widely in how they show up, so results cannot predict every outcome.
Benefits include reassurance when results are normal, finding conditions that may be treated before birth, planning the right place and team for delivery, and the option of ending a pregnancy.

items.title: Routine ultrasound in late pregnancy (after 24 weeks' gestation)
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 13 trials with almost 35,000 women to see whether routine ultrasound scans after 24 weeks help women with low-risk or unselected pregnancies. Women who had a routine late scan did not have better outcomes than those who did not. There were no clear differences in baby deaths around birth, preterm birth, induction of labour or caesarean section. Little is known about long-term effects on children or about how the scans affect mothers' emotional wellbeing.
keyPoints: Routine ultrasound after 24 weeks did not improve outcomes for mothers or babies in low-risk or unselected pregnancies.
No difference was found in perinatal death, preterm birth before 37 weeks, induction of labour or caesarean section.
There is little or no data on mothers' psychological effects, preterm birth before 34 weeks, or child neurodevelopment at age two.
The evidence for the main outcomes was rated moderate or high quality.

items.title: Ultrasound for fetal assessment in early pregnancy
items.summary: This large review combined 11 trials with over 37,000 women to see what routine ultrasound scans in early pregnancy (before 24 weeks) actually achieve, compared with scans only when there is a specific reason. Routine early scans were better at spotting twins or other multiple pregnancies and major fetal abnormalities, and were linked to fewer inductions for 'post term' pregnancy. They did not reduce deaths around the time of birth or other poor outcomes for babies. Follow-up of children scanned before birth found no harm to their physical or thinking development.
keyPoints: Routine early ultrasound greatly reduced the chance that a multiple pregnancy (such as twins) was missed by 24 weeks (moderate quality evidence).
Routine scans found more major fetal abnormalities before 24 weeks (moderate quality evidence).
Routine scans were linked to fewer inductions of labour for 'post term' pregnancy, but this evidence is low quality, and better dating may explain it.
Routine scans did not change the rate of perinatal death, and long-term follow-up showed no harmful effect on children's development.

items.title: Symphysial fundal height (SFH) measurement in pregnancy for detecting abnormal fetal growth
items.summary: Doctors and midwives often measure the distance from the pubic bone to the top of the womb (symphysial fundal height) to check whether a baby is growing too slowly. This Cochrane review looked for trials comparing this tape measurement with ultrasound or with feeling the belly by hand, and found only one trial of 1639 women. That trial showed no clear difference in small babies, baby deaths, caesarean section or other outcomes, but the evidence was low quality. The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to say whether the tape measurement works well for spotting slow growth.
keyPoints: Only one trial (1639 women) met the review's criteria, comparing the tape measurement with feeling the belly by hand.
No clear difference was found in babies born small for their age or in perinatal deaths, though the evidence was low quality.
No clear difference was found in neonatal nursery admission, induction of labour or caesarean section.
The authors say there is insufficient evidence to recommend any change to current practice and that more trials are needed.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of heat exposure impacts on maternal, fetal and neonatal health
items.summary: This review pooled results from 198 studies across 66 countries to see how hot weather affects pregnancy and newborns. Higher heat exposure was linked to higher odds of preterm birth, with a bigger increase during heat waves. Heat was also linked to higher risks of stillbirth, congenital anomalies, gestational diabetes and other pregnancy complications. The authors note that studies measured heat and were designed in very different ways, which limits how firm the findings are.
keyPoints: Each 1 °C rise in heat exposure was linked to about 4% higher odds of preterm birth, and heat waves to about 26% higher odds.
High heat exposure was linked to higher risks of congenital anomalies and gestational diabetes; stillbirth showed a possible increase, but the range of results was wide.
Any obstetric complication was about 25% more likely during heat waves.
The timing of greatest risk during pregnancy differed by condition, and results were limited by differences in how studies measured heat.

items.title: Oral antihypertensive treatment during pregnancy: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 23 trials (3989 women) comparing three blood pressure medicines used in pregnancy: methyldopa, labetalol and nifedipine. Labetalol and methyldopa lowered the chance of severe high blood pressure compared with no treatment or placebo. Labetalol was linked to less preeclampsia and fewer preterm births than nifedipine, so it was modestly favoured. The trials were of low-to-moderate quality, so the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Labetalol and methyldopa reduced severe high blood pressure compared with placebo or no treatment.
Labetalol was linked to less preeclampsia and fewer preterm births than nifedipine.
For most other outcomes, the three medicines showed no significant differences.
The included studies were of low overall quality, so caution is advised.

items.title: Effects of relaxation interventions during pregnancy on maternal mental health, and pregnancy and newborn outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 32 studies of 3,979 pregnant women who tried relaxation methods such as yoga, music, breathing exercises, muscle relaxation, mindfulness and hypnosis. Relaxation lowered stress, anxiety and depression symptoms, and babies were born slightly heavier on average. Effects on other birth outcomes, such as delivery mode, Apgar score and gestational age, were mixed. The authors say better-quality, larger trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Relaxation reduced maternal stress, anxiety and depressive symptoms in the pooled results.
Babies were about 80 g heavier on average, with the clearest gain seen with progressive muscle relaxation.
Four trials found shorter labour, and two of six trials found more spontaneous vaginal births and fewer instrumental or caesarean deliveries.
Effects on Apgar score, birth length and gestational age were inconsistent across trials.

items.title: Magnesium sulphate for women at risk of preterm birth for neuroprotection of the fetus
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled six trials (about 5,900 women) of magnesium sulphate given to women at risk of preterm birth before 34 weeks, to protect the baby's brain. Babies whose mothers had magnesium sulphate were less likely to have cerebral palsy up to age two. The treatment also probably caused more side effects in mothers that were bad enough to stop it. By early school age, the review found little to no difference in outcomes for children.
keyPoints: Up to age two, magnesium sulphate reduced cerebral palsy and the combined outcome of death or cerebral palsy (high-certainty evidence).
It probably reduced severe bleeding in the baby's brain (severe intraventricular haemorrhage).
It probably increased maternal side effects severe enough to stop treatment, though serious outcomes like death or cardiac arrest were rare and showed little difference.
At early school age there was little to no difference in outcomes, and more research on long-term effects is needed.

items.title: SMFM Consult Series #70: Management of short cervix in individuals without a history of spontaneous preterm birth
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This guideline from the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine covers what to do when a mid-pregnancy ultrasound shows a short cervix in someone who has never had a preterm birth. Most births before 34 weeks happen in people with no earlier preterm birth, and cervical length measured by vaginal ultrasound is one of the best predictors. The guideline recommends vaginal progesterone for a very short cervix and advises against cerclage, pessary and 17-alpha hydroxyprogesterone caproate in this group.
keyPoints: A short cervix is defined as 25 mm or less on a mid-pregnancy transvaginal ultrasound in a singleton pregnancy with no previous spontaneous preterm birth.
Vaginal progesterone is recommended when the cervix is 20 mm or less before 24 weeks, and can be considered at 21 to 25 mm after shared decision-making.
Cerclage (a stitch in the cervix) is not recommended for a short cervix without dilation, and a cervical pessary is not recommended for singleton pregnancies.
17-alpha hydroxyprogesterone caproate should not be used to treat a short cervix, and progesterone, pessary or cerclage are not routinely recommended for twins outside clinical trials.

items.title: Magnesium Sulfate Before Preterm Birth for Neuroprotection: An Updated Cochrane Systematic Review
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled six trials (about 5,900 pregnant people) testing magnesium sulfate given to people at risk of giving birth before 34 weeks. Babies whose mothers received it had a lower risk of cerebral palsy, and of death or cerebral palsy, up to 2 years of age compared with placebo. The treatment caused more side effects in pregnant people, sometimes enough that treatment was stopped. All trials were in high-income countries, and longer-term effects are still unclear.
keyPoints: Magnesium sulfate before preterm birth reduced cerebral palsy in children (high-certainty evidence).
It also lowered the risk of severe bleeding in the baby's brain (moderate-certainty evidence).
It made little or no difference to death up to 2 years of age.
Side effects severe enough to stop treatment were about three times more common in those who received it (moderate-certainty evidence).

items.title: Relationship between periodontal disease and preterm birth. A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Medicina Oral, Patologia Oral Y Cirugia Bucal
items.journal: Medicina Oral, Patologia Oral Y Cirugia Bucal
items.summary: This review pooled five randomized trials with 1,984 pregnant women who had gum (periodontal) disease. About half had non-surgical gum treatment during pregnancy and half did not. The review found no proven link between gum disease in pregnancy and preterm birth. Treatment showed a slight trend toward fewer preterm births, but the result was not statistically significant, so it could be due to chance.
keyPoints: No demonstrated association was found between gum disease in pregnancy and preterm birth.
Four of five trials leaned toward non-surgical gum treatment lowering preterm birth, but none of the results were statistically significant.
The authors say more trials with similar designs are needed for a definitive answer.

items.title: Technical Update No. 439: Antenatal Corticosteroids at Late Preterm Gestation
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline update looked at giving one course of steroid medicine (antenatal corticosteroids) to pregnant people at risk of giving birth between 34 and 36 weeks and 6 days. The steroids lower the chance of the baby having breathing problems (respiratory distress) but raise the chance of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) in the newborn. The long-term effects on children from steroids given this late are not known.
keyPoints: Steroids given at 34+0 to 36+6 weeks lower the risk of breathing problems in newborns.
They also raise the risk of low blood sugar in newborns.
The long-term effects of steroids given at this stage are uncertain, and there is no direct evidence on brain development.
The guideline is for maternity care providers, including midwives, family doctors and obstetricians.

items.title: Management of preterm labor: Clinical practice guideline and recommendation by the WAPM-World Association of Perinatal Medicine and the PMF-Perinatal Medicine Foundation
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from two international perinatal medicine groups on how preterm labor (labor starting too early in pregnancy) should be managed. It aims to help health professionals diagnose preterm labor more accurately. It also covers giving the right treatments at the right time, and avoiding unnecessary or excessive interventions. The abstract does not give specific recommendations or rate the strength of the evidence.
keyPoints: The guideline aims to improve how accurately preterm labor is diagnosed.
It supports timely, appropriate use of tocolytics (medicines that slow contractions), antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulphate.
It aims to help avoid unnecessary or excessive interventions.
It is based on expert consensus and the scientific literature, and is not meant to set a legal standard of care.

items.title: Different corticosteroids and regimens for accelerating fetal lung maturation for babies at risk of preterm birth
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 11 trials of steroid injections given to women at risk of early birth to help baby's lungs mature. It compared two steroids, dexamethasone and betamethasone, and different ways of giving them. For most outcomes in babies and young children, the two drugs may make little or no difference, but for some outcomes the evidence was not clear enough to rule out benefits or harms. There was not enough good evidence to say that one dosing plan is better than another.
keyPoints: Dexamethasone and betamethasone probably make little or no difference to breathing problems (respiratory distress syndrome) in newborns, based on high-certainty evidence.
Evidence was unclear for baby death, cerebral palsy, bleeding in the brain and a bowel condition called necrotising enterocolitis, so important benefits or harms could not be ruled out.
Neurodevelopment at about two years probably did not differ between the two drugs, but no trials followed children beyond early childhood.
Evidence on different doses, timing and forms of the steroids was sparse and very low certainty, so no particular regimen is supported over another.

items.title: Tocolytics for delaying preterm birth: a network meta-analysis (0924)
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 122 trials (13,697 women) of drugs that aim to slow early labour (tocolytics). Compared with placebo or no treatment, all the drug types studied probably or possibly delayed birth by 48 hours and by 7 days, which can give time for other treatments such as steroids for the baby's lungs. The drugs caused a range of side effects, from mild to potentially serious. Effects on newborn deaths and on infection were uncertain, and the certainty of much of the evidence was low.
keyPoints: Betamimetics, calcium channel blockers, magnesium sulphate, oxytocin receptor antagonists, nitric oxide donors and combinations were probably or possibly effective at delaying birth for 48 hours and 7 days.
Nitric oxide donors ranked highest for delaying birth, followed by calcium channel blockers, oxytocin receptor antagonists and combinations.

Side effects included breathlessness, palpitations and vomiting with betamimetics, and headache with calcium channel blockers and nitric oxide donors; betamimetics and combinations were more likely to lead to treatment being stopped.
Effects on newborn and perinatal deaths and on maternal or newborn infection were uncertain.

items.title: Cervical pessary for preventing preterm birth in singleton pregnancies
items.summary: This review pooled eight trials (almost 3,000 women) of a cervical pessary, a soft ring placed around the cervix to support it, for preventing early birth in single-baby pregnancies. Compared with no treatment or with vaginal progesterone, a pessary may lower the chance of birth before 34 or 37 weeks. However, the results are uncertain because the possible range of effects includes both benefit and no benefit. The evidence was mostly low to moderate certainty, and there was too little data to compare a pessary with cervical cerclage (a stitch in the cervix).
keyPoints: A pessary may reduce birth before 34 weeks or before 37 weeks compared with no treatment, but this is low-certainty evidence and the results could also mean no effect.
Compared with vaginal progesterone, a pessary may reduce early birth, but the moderate-certainty results are still uncertain because they could mean no difference.
A pessary probably makes little or no difference to maternal infection or inflammation.
Evidence on pessary versus cerclage was too limited to draw conclusions, and more good-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Evaluating Progestogens for Preventing Preterm birth International Collaborative (EPPPIC): meta-analysis of individual participant data from randomised controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled individual data from 31 trials (11,644 women) testing progesterone-type medicines to prevent preterm birth in women at higher risk. In single-baby pregnancies with a past early birth or a short cervix, vaginal progesterone and 17-OHPC injections reduced births before 34 weeks. For twins and triplets, progesterone treatment did not reduce early birth, and 17-OHPC was linked to more early waters breaking. Some other benefits looked favourable but were less certain, and a possible rise in maternal complications was also uncertain.
keyPoints: In high-risk single-baby pregnancies, vaginal progesterone reduced birth before 34 weeks (relative risk 0.78) and 17-OHPC showed a similar trend (0.83).
The benefit may be greatest for women with a short cervix, because their underlying risk is higher.
Evidence for oral progesterone was too limited to support its use.
For twin and triplet pregnancies without other risk factors, progesterone treatment was not supported, and 17-OHPC raised the risk of early rupture of membranes before 34 weeks.

items.title: Chorioamnionitis and Risk for Maternal and Neonatal Sepsis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 55 studies to see whether chorioamnionitis (an infection of the membranes around the baby during pregnancy) is linked to sepsis, a serious blood infection, in newborns and mothers. Babies exposed to chorioamnionitis had higher odds of both early- and late-onset sepsis, though most results were not adjusted for other factors. There was not enough evidence to say whether chorioamnionitis is linked to sepsis in mothers. The authors say the findings support current guidelines for preventative care of newborns.
keyPoints: Both histologic (found on lab examination) and clinical chorioamnionitis were linked to higher odds of early-onset sepsis in newborns.
Both types were also linked to higher odds of late-onset sepsis in preterm babies.
Confirmed sepsis occurred in about 6-7% of exposed babies early on and about 22-26% later on.
Three studies on maternal sepsis were inconclusive, so no link could be confirmed.

items.title: Multifetal Gestations: Twin, Triplet, and Higher-Order Multifetal Pregnancies: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 231
items.summary: This ACOG practice bulletin reviews twin, triplet and higher-order pregnancies and how they are managed. Multiple pregnancies have become more common over recent decades, linked to women conceiving at older ages and to fertility treatment. Preterm birth is described as one of the most serious complications, and the abstract says that none of the interventions tried so far to prolong these pregnancies has made a substantial difference.
keyPoints: Twin births in the US rose 76% from 1980 to 2009, then fell 4% between 2014 and 2018.
Older maternal age at conception and assisted reproductive technology are the two main reasons multiple pregnancies have become more common.
Multiple pregnancies carry higher risks of fetal anomalies, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm birth.
Preterm birth is one of the most consequential complications, and no tested intervention has substantially prolonged these pregnancies.

items.title: Guideline No. 398: Progesterone for Prevention of Spontaneous Preterm Birth
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looked at whether progesterone treatment during pregnancy helps women who are at higher risk of spontaneous preterm birth (going into labour early without a medical reason). It found that progesterone significantly lowers the risk of early birth in a particular group of higher-risk women. Using it can cost money and may be uncomfortable, but no other harms to the mother or baby were found. The abstract does not list the specific recommendations or their evidence ratings.
keyPoints: Progesterone therapy significantly reduces the risk of spontaneous preterm birth in a subgroup of women at increased risk.
The treatment has a cost and some discomfort for the woman.
No other harmful effects on mothers or babies have been identified.
The guideline is aimed at pregnant women at increased risk, such as those with a previous preterm birth or a short cervix.

items.title: Associations between high temperatures in pregnancy and risk of preterm birth, low birth weight, and stillbirths: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 70 studies in 27 countries to see whether hot weather during pregnancy is linked to preterm birth, low birth weight and stillbirth. Preterm births were more common at higher temperatures in most studies. The increases in risk were relatively small for each person, but heat exposure is common, and the link appeared stronger for women in lower socioeconomic groups and at younger or older ages.
keyPoints: Odds of preterm birth rose about 5% for every 1°C increase in temperature and about 16% during heatwaves.
Higher temperature was linked to lower birth weight in 18 of 28 studies, though results varied a lot between studies.
Stillbirths rose about 5% for every 1°C rise in temperature, and all eight studies on this found an association.
Links were largest among women in lower socioeconomic groups and at age extremes, so risks may be greatest in low and middle income countries.

items.title: Antenatal corticosteroids for accelerating fetal lung maturation for women at risk of preterm birth
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 27 trials (over 11,000 women) of steroid injections given before an expected preterm birth to help the baby's lungs mature. Babies of women who received a single course were less likely to die around the time of birth or to develop breathing problems (respiratory distress syndrome). The steroids probably also lowered the risk of bleeding in the baby's brain and of developmental delay in childhood. The review found little to no difference in serious maternal outcomes such as infection of the womb lining, though the evidence there is less precise.
keyPoints: Antenatal corticosteroids reduced perinatal death (about 15% lower risk) and neonatal death (about 22% lower risk), based on high-certainty evidence.
They reduced respiratory distress syndrome in newborns by about 29%, also high-certainty evidence.
They probably reduce bleeding in the baby's brain (IVH) and developmental delay in childhood, with moderate-certainty evidence.
There was probably little to no difference in maternal death, chorioamnionitis or endometritis, but the wide margins of error leave possible benefit or harm open.

items.title: Antibiotics for asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 15 trials with over 2000 pregnant women who had a urine infection with no symptoms (asymptomatic bacteriuria). Women given antibiotics may have fewer kidney infections (pyelonephritis), fewer preterm births and fewer low birthweight babies than those given a placebo or no treatment. However, the evidence was low certainty, because most of the trials had problems in how they were done, so confidence in these results is limited.
keyPoints: Antibiotics may reduce the risk of kidney infection (pyelonephritis) in pregnancy; this was low-certainty evidence.
Antibiotics may reduce preterm birth and low birthweight babies, also based on low-certainty evidence.
Results were inconclusive for serious newborn problems, and side effects for mothers were rarely described.
Only one of the 15 trials was at low risk of bias; more research is needed on who is most likely to benefit.

items.title: No. 211-Screening and Management of Bacterial Vaginosis in Pregnancy
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline reviewed the research on checking for and treating bacterial vaginosis (BV) during pregnancy. The aim was to see whether treating BV helps prevent problems like preterm labour, preterm birth and early waters breaking. The guideline found there is currently no agreement on whether all pregnant women should be screened for or treated for BV to prevent preterm birth.
keyPoints: There is currently no consensus on screening all pregnant women for bacterial vaginosis to prevent problems such as preterm birth.
There is also no consensus on treating bacterial vaginosis in the general pregnant population to prevent adverse outcomes.
The guideline looked at antibiotic treatment success and effects on preterm labour, preterm birth and preterm premature rupture of membranes.

items.title: Adolescent Pregnancy Guidelines
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline sets out how to care for pregnant teenagers before, during and after birth. For the period after birth, it recommends that contraception be discussed before delivery, with a focus on long-acting reversible methods, to reduce the high rate of repeat pregnancy in this group. It also recommends breastfeeding support and postpartum programs, including screening for postpartum depression.
keyPoints: Postpartum care should include a focus on contraception, especially long-acting reversible methods, to lower high repeat-pregnancy rates in adolescents.
Talking about contraception should begin before delivery.
Postpartum programs should support young parents, increase breastfeeding, screen for postpartum depression and lengthen the time between pregnancies.
STI testing is recommended after birth, and breastfeeding should be recommended with enough support to help teens keep going.

items.title: Progestin-only contraception and thrombosis: An updated systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 33 studies on whether progestin-only birth control is linked to blood clots. The DMPA injection (Depo-Provera) was generally linked to a higher risk of clots in the veins (VTE), but not clots in the arteries such as heart attack or stroke. Other progestin-only methods, including hormonal coils (levonorgestrel IUDs), implants and progestin-only pills, did not generally show a higher risk. The certainty of the evidence was low or very low, so these findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: Risk of vein clots (VTE) was generally higher with DMPA than with no use, both in the general population and in women with conditions linked to clotting.
DMPA was not generally linked to arterial clots such as heart attack or stroke.
Levonorgestrel IUDs, implants and progestin-only pills were generally not linked to higher clot risk.
Evidence was limited for many individual conditions, and certainty was low or very low for all outcomes.

items.title: Effect of Medical Therapies for Endometriosis on Bone Health: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 37 studies on how hormone treatments for endometriosis affect bone mineral density (a measure of bone strength). GnRH agonists (with add-back therapy), dienogest and GnRH antagonists were each linked to small drops in bone density over 6 to 12 months. Data on the injection DMPA could not be combined. The authors say it is still unclear how much these small changes matter in real life.
keyPoints: GnRH agonists with add-back therapy lowered bone density by about 0.9% at 6 months and 1.5% at 12 months.
Dienogest was linked to lower bone density at 6 months (about 0.8%) and 12 months (about 1.9%), though results varied a lot between studies.
GnRH antagonists lowered bone density by about 2.2% at 6 months, and most of those studies did not use add-back therapy.
The clinical significance of these bone changes is uncertain, and the authors call for expert guidance on bone health during long-term hormonal treatment.

items.title: Society of Family Planning Clinical Recommendation: Contraceptive considerations for individuals with cancer and cancer survivors part 3 - Skin, blood, gastrointestinal, liver, lung, central nervous system, and other cancers: Joint with the Society of Gynecologic Oncology
items.summary: This guideline from the Society of Family Planning and the Society of Gynecologic Oncology covers birth control choices for people who have or have had skin, blood, digestive, liver, lung, brain and some other cancers. For most of these cancers, it recommends that all contraceptive methods be available. For a few situations (melanoma, follicular lymphoma, meningioma, and severely reduced liver function) it advises a more careful, shared decision or specific method choices.
keyPoints: For most listed cancers (nonmelanoma skin, blood and lymphatic, colorectal, pancreatic, esophageal, gastric, glioma, bladder, kidney, thyroid, head and neck, soft tissue sarcoma), clinicians should offer all contraceptive methods.
After melanoma, follicular lymphoma, or meningioma, people who want hormonal contraception are advised to decide together with their doctor and oncologist.
With severely altered liver function after liver cancer, nonhormonal and progestin-only methods are recommended first.
For liver cancer with normal liver function, all methods are recommended as options.

items.title: Consensus conference results on contraception in women beyond 40 years of age
items.source: European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care
items.journal: European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care
items.summary: Italian experts reviewed the research on hormonal birth control for women over 40 and voted on seven shared statements, which 95 to 99 percent of participants backed. They found that heart and blood vessel safety is the most important factor when choosing a method. Progestogen-only methods are considered safe for cardiovascular risk and have a neutral effect on bone density. The abstract does not report how strong the underlying evidence is.
keyPoints: Cardiovascular safety is the main factor when choosing a contraceptive after age 40.
Progestogen-only methods are considered safe for cardiovascular risk and have a neutral effect on bone density.
The levonorgestrel intrauterine device, estradiol valerate/dienogest pill and the combined vaginal ring are seen as the most effective options for managing menstrual bleeding.
Implants and vaginal rings may have positive effects on sexual function, while combined methods help protect bone density.

items.title: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate and breast cancer: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at ten studies on whether the contraceptive injection (DMPA, or depot medroxyprogesterone acetate) is linked to breast cancer. Most studies found no overall increase in breast cancer among women who use it, though a few found a small or significant rise. There may be a possible increase in current or recent users, especially women under 35, but the evidence is limited and more research is needed.
keyPoints: Most of the ten included studies found no overall higher breast cancer rate in DMPA users; one found a slightly higher risk and two found a significant increase.
The authors say there is little evidence that DMPA increases overall breast cancer risk.
Breast cancer may be possibly more common in current and recent users, especially women younger than 35.
Long-term use did not lead to a higher risk, and further studies are needed to confirm the findings.

items.title: Symptoms of mental disorders and oral contraception use: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 22 studies to look at whether taking the birth control pill is linked to symptoms of mental health problems, such as low mood. Most studies found no clear effect, though a few suggested the pill might be a risk for some people. It is still unclear whether progestin-only pills differ from combined pills in this way. There were some signs of a higher risk of depressive symptoms in teenage pill users.
keyPoints: Most of the 22 studies found no significant effect of oral contraceptive use on mental health symptoms.
Evidence on whether progestin-only pills carry more risk of mental symptoms than combined pills is inconclusive.
There are some indications of increased depressive symptoms in adolescent pill users.
The decision to use the pill should depend on a person's medical history and be reviewed regularly.

items.title: Prevalence and risk factors for type 2 diabetes mellitus in women with gestational diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 46 studies of nearly 200,000 women who had gestational diabetes to see which factors go with later type 2 diabetes. Several factors were linked to a higher chance, including using progestin-only contraceptives, having gestational diabetes again, needing insulin in pregnancy, higher body weight before and after pregnancy, high blood pressure, a large baby, and a family history of diabetes. These are links seen in studies, not proof that any one factor causes diabetes.
keyPoints: Progestin-only contraceptive use was linked to about twice the odds of later type 2 diabetes, though the range of results was wide and only just reached statistical significance (OR 2.12, 95% CI 1.00-4.45).

Other strongly linked factors were recurrent gestational diabetes, insulin use in pregnancy, higher BMI before pregnancy and after delivery, a large baby (macrosomia), high blood pressure, and higher HbA1c.
Older age, family history of diabetes, and higher fasting and oral glucose tolerance test results were linked to a moderate increase in risk.
The authors suggest these findings could help doctors plan early prevention and tailored care for women who have had gestational diabetes.

items.title: Hormonal contraceptive use and the risk of sexually transmitted infections: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 37 studies to see whether using hormonal birth control is linked to catching sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or bacterial vaginosis. The link was not the same for every infection. Hormonal contraception was linked to a higher risk of chlamydia and herpes, and to a lower risk of trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis. For gonorrhoea, the link was slightly lower but not statistically significant. The authors say the findings should be read carefully, since the effect went in different directions depending on the infection.
keyPoints: Hormonal contraceptive use was linked to a higher risk of chlamydia and herpes.
It was linked to a lower risk of trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis.
The link with gonorrhoea was negative but not statistically significant.
Because results differed by infection, the authors advise careful interpretation when making guidelines and policy.

items.title: Update to U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use: Self-Administration of Subcutaneous Depot Medroxyprogesterone Acetate
items.source: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.journal: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.summary: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) updated its contraception guidance to say that people can give themselves the DMPA-SC contraceptive injection. The update follows a World Health Organization recommendation and is based on moderate-certainty evidence that self-injecting is safe and effective, and that people stay on the method longer than when a provider gives the shot. Injections given by a provider stay available. The guidance says self-injection should be offered through shared decision-making, never pressure.
keyPoints: Self-administered DMPA-SC should be available as an additional way to get injectable contraception.
Moderate-certainty evidence shows self-injection is safe and effective, with higher continuation rates than provider-administered DMPA.
Provider-administered DMPA should remain available.
Self-injection should be offered without coercion, through shared decision-making that respects patient preferences.

items.title: Drug-Induced Intracranial Hypertension: A Systematic Review and Critical Assessment of Drug-Induced Causes
items.summary: Researchers reviewed published case reports of raised pressure inside the skull (intracranial hypertension) that may have been caused by medicines. They found 259 verifiable cases. Vitamin A-type drugs, tetracycline antibiotics, growth hormone and lithium were most strongly linked, while progestin-only contraceptives and combined pills were only weakly linked. The authors describe the condition as uncommon but sight-threatening.
keyPoints: Out of 5117 articles screened, 259 verifiable cases of drug-induced intracranial hypertension were found.
Vitamin A derivatives, tetracycline-class antibiotics, recombinant growth hormone and lithium had the strongest links.
Progestin-only contraceptives and combined oral contraceptives were weakly associated with the condition.
The condition is described as uncommon but can threaten sight, so knowing its symptoms (persistent headache, pulsatile tinnitus, visual obscuration) may help.

items.title: Gynecologic Considerations for Adolescents and Young Women With Cardiac Conditions: ACOG Committee Opinion Summary, Number 813
items.summary: This ACOG guidance looks at birth control and pregnancy planning for teenagers and young women who have heart conditions. Because pregnancy can carry serious health risks for people with heart disease, it advises that starting birth control should not be put off over safety worries. For some heart conditions, a progestin-only method is a reasonable starting choice while the safety of estrogen-containing methods is checked with the patient's heart doctor.
keyPoints: Starting contraception should not be delayed because of worries about possible contraindications, since pregnancy can cause serious health problems in people with heart conditions.

For valvular heart disease, cardiomyopathy or hypertension, ACOG says it is reasonable to start a progestin-only method until an estrogen-containing method is confirmed safe with the patient's cardiologist.
Contraceptive counseling should be patient-centered, free of coercion, and suited to the person's age and health literacy.
Future pregnancies should be planned with maternal-fetal medicine and cardiology specialists, and anyone continuing a pregnancy should be referred to a pregnancy heart team.

items.title: Side Effects and Health Benefits of Depot Medroxyprogesterone Acetate: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 24 studies on the side effects and health benefits of the DMPA contraceptive injection. The studies suggest it is linked to weight gain, more body fat, irregular bleeding and missed periods. Evidence on mood and sex drive changes was mixed, and evidence on lower cancer risk and lower risk of infertility from blocked tubes was limited. The authors say better-quality research is needed and that counselling should be honest about these limits and value women's own experiences.
keyPoints: Studies suggest DMPA is associated with weight gain, increased body fat, irregular bleeding and amenorrhea (no periods).
Evidence for links with mood or libido changes was inconsistent.
