Evidence for a lower risk of some cancers and tubal infertility was limited.
None of the 24 studies were randomized trials, so higher-quality research is needed.

items.title: Association between progestin-only contraceptive use and cardiometabolic outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 19 observational studies to see whether progestin-only contraceptives (pills, injections and hormonal coils) are linked to heart and metabolic problems such as blood clots, heart attack, stroke, high blood pressure and diabetes. Progestin-only pills were not linked to a higher risk of clots, heart attack or stroke. Injectable contraceptives were linked to a higher risk of venous blood clots, while the hormonal coil (levonorgestrel intrauterine device) was linked to a lower risk. The evidence comes from observational studies, which cannot prove cause and effect.
keyPoints: Oral progestin-only pills showed no increased risk of venous thromboembolism, heart attack or stroke compared with non-users.
Injectable progestin-only contraceptives were associated with a higher risk of venous thromboembolism (relative risk 2.62).
Women using a levonorgestrel intrauterine device had a lower risk of venous thromboembolism (relative risk 0.53).
No effect on blood pressure was found, and a possible increase in diabetes risk with injectables was not statistically significant.

items.title: Update to CDC's U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, 2016: Revised Recommendations for the Use of Hormonal Contraception Among Women at High Risk for HIV Infection
items.journal: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.summary: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) updated its guidance on hormonal birth control for women at high risk of HIV. For progestin-only injections such as DMPA, the benefits are judged to outweigh the possible risks. There may be a slightly higher chance of getting HIV with the injection, but it is unclear whether this is a real effect or a problem with how the studies were done. Other hormonal methods have no restrictions for women at high risk of HIV.
keyPoints: CDC rates progestin-only injectables (including DMPA) as category 2 for women at high risk of HIV, meaning the advantages outweigh the theoretical or proven risks.
There is evidence of a possible increased risk of getting HIV with progestin-only injections, but it is uncertain whether this is a real biological effect or due to study methods.
Women should not be denied the injection because of this concern, but should be told about the uncertainty and how to lower their HIV risk.
Combined hormonal methods, implants and progestin-only pills have no restrictions (category 1) for women at high risk of HIV.

items.title: Hormonal contraception and pelvic floor function: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 13 studies to see whether hormonal contraception affects bladder, bowel, vaginal and sexual symptoms in women who have not yet reached menopause. It found links between oral contraceptive use and two painful conditions: interstitial cystitis (painful bladder syndrome) and vulvar vestibulitis (pain at the vaginal opening). For other symptoms the evidence was unclear, and the authors say better-designed prospective studies are needed to show whether the pill actually causes these problems.
keyPoints: Ever using oral contraceptives was linked to interstitial cystitis (OR 2.31, 95% CI 1.03-5.16).
Current oral contraceptive use was linked to vulvar vestibulitis (OR 2.10, 95% CI 1.26-3.49).
The effect on painful sex (dyspareunia) was inconsistent across studies, and evidence was unclear for other symptoms.
The authors say these are associations only and that prospective studies are needed to establish cause.

items.title: Intrauterine Contraception Continuation in Adolescents and Young Women: A Systematic Review
items.source: Journal of Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology
items.journal: Journal of Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 9 studies of women aged 25 and younger to see how many kept using their birth control after 12 months. About 86% of IUD users were still using the IUD at one year. That was much higher than for the pill, the injection, the vaginal ring or the patch, which were all around 40-49%. IUD continuation was similar to that of the implant.
keyPoints: 12-month continuation was 86.5% for IUDs, compared with 39.6% for the pill, 39.8% for the Depo-Provera injection, 48.9% for the vaginal ring and 39.8% for the patch.
There was no significant difference in 12-month continuation between IUDs and the etonogestrel implant (85.3%).
The authors conclude that IUD use should be encouraged in young women, given high rates of unintended pregnancy and imperfect use of other methods.

items.title: Guideline No. 460: Diagnosis and Management of Intrauterine Early Pregnancy Loss
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline explains how early pregnancy loss (miscarriage) inside the womb should be diagnosed and managed. It stresses that a wrong diagnosis could harm a healthy pregnancy, while long waits for confirmation can add anxiety and delay care. It supports caring conversations that help patients understand their options, with time off for grief and mental health support. It does not cover recurrent pregnancy loss (2 or more losses), ectopic pregnancy or pregnancy of unknown location.
keyPoints: Early pregnancy loss is common and can be a traumatic experience.
A wrongly diagnosed loss can put a healthy, normally placed pregnancy at risk, so diagnosis needs care.
Waiting a long time for a confirmed diagnosis can increase anxiety and delay treatment.
Patient-centred care, such as in an Early Pregnancy Assessment Clinic, helps patients make informed choices about management and follow-up, including bereavement leave and mental health support.

items.title: Should a repeat cervical cerclage be inserted when the primary cerclage fails, to prevent pregnancy loss and preterm birth? A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at what happens when a stitch placed in the cervix (a cerclage) to help prevent early birth fails during a pregnancy. It compared putting in a second stitch with simply waiting and watching. Across six small studies, there was no clear difference in pregnancy loss or preterm birth between the two approaches. The authors say the evidence is poor and limited, and that people should be told this when making decisions.
keyPoints: No clear difference in pregnancy loss, or in birth before 34 or 37 weeks, between a repeat cerclage and expectant management.
There was a trend towards better outcomes with expectant management, but it was not statistically significant.
Only six retrospective studies were suitable, and the overall quality and amount of evidence is poor.
More research is needed to help patients and clinicians make informed decisions.

items.title: Septum resection for women of reproductive age with a septate uterus
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether surgery to remove the wall of tissue inside the uterus (a septate uterus) improves pregnancy outcomes compared with waiting and watching. In the one randomised trial (79 women), surgery made little or no difference to live birth, ongoing pregnancy or clinical pregnancy. Miscarriage may have been slightly higher after surgery, but the result could also be due to chance. Results from the other, non-randomised studies were too uncertain to draw conclusions.
keyPoints: One randomised trial found little or no difference in live birth between septum resection and expectant management (low-certainty evidence).
In that trial, miscarriage may have been slightly higher after surgery, but the range of results included no effect.
Reported surgical complications included uterine perforation, bleeding, and a residual septum that needed repeat surgery.
Non-randomised studies gave very low-certainty evidence, so it is unclear whether surgery changes pregnancy outcomes.

items.title: Subsequent pregnancy outcomes after second trimester miscarriage or termination for medical/fetal reason: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies
items.summary: This review pulled together ten studies on what happens in the next pregnancy after a miscarriage in the second trimester (the middle three months). About 8 in 10 of these next pregnancies ended in a live birth. There may be a higher chance of preterm birth next time, but the evidence was rated very low quality, so this is uncertain. No studies were found on pregnancies after a termination for medical or fetal reasons.
keyPoints: Across ten studies covering 12,004 later pregnancies, an estimated 81% ended in a live birth after a second trimester miscarriage.
Estimated rates were 15% for another miscarriage and 13% for preterm birth in the next pregnancy.
Case-control studies suggested higher odds of preterm birth after a second trimester loss (odds ratio 4.52).
The authors say larger, better quality studies are needed, and no studies looked at termination for medical or fetal reasons.

items.title: Evidence-based diagnosis and treatment for uterine septum: a guideline
items.summary: This guideline from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine looked at how a uterine septum (a band of tissue dividing the inside of the womb) is diagnosed and treated with surgery. It found that removing the septum has been shown to improve outcomes for people with recurrent pregnancy loss and to make it less likely that a baby is in an unusual position at birth. For people with infertility, the guideline suggests talking through the options with a doctor and deciding together whether to have the surgery.
keyPoints: Removing a uterine septum has been shown to improve outcomes in people with recurrent pregnancy loss.
Septum removal can lower the chance of malpresentation, where the baby is not head-down at birth.
For infertility, the guideline recommends shared decision-making after counseling to decide whether to have the septum removed.

items.title: Prior Spontaneous or Induced Abortion Is a Risk Factor for Cervical Dysfunction in Pregnant Women: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled six studies covering over 2.5 million pregnancies to see whether a past miscarriage or induced abortion is linked to cervical problems in a later pregnancy, such as a short cervix or cervical insufficiency (when the cervix opens too early). Women with a history of abortion had higher odds of cervical dysfunction, and the odds rose with the number of previous abortions. The link was seen for both spontaneous and induced abortions, and it was strongest in studies of surgical abortion. This type of study shows an association, not that abortion directly causes the problem.
keyPoints: A history of spontaneous or induced abortion was linked to about 2.7 times higher odds of cervical dysfunction in the current pregnancy.
For induced abortions alone the odds were about 2.5 times higher, and about 4 times higher in studies limited to surgical abortions.
The risk of cervical dysfunction was also related to the number of previous abortions.
The analysis combined six studies, and cervical dysfunction was defined as cervical insufficiency in four and short cervix in the others.

items.title: Hold your needles in women with recurrent pregnancy losses with or without hereditary thrombophilia: Meta-analysis and review of the literature
items.source: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.journal: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.summary: This review pooled 12 randomised trials with 2,298 women who had repeated pregnancy losses. It compared low molecular weight heparin (a blood-thinning injection) with no heparin. In women without an inherited clotting disorder, heparin made no clear difference to the chance of a live birth. In women with an inherited clotting disorder the result was also not clear, and the trials differed a lot, though heparin may help in some specific types.
keyPoints: Heparin injections did not clearly improve live birth rates in women with recurrent pregnancy loss.
In women without an inherited clotting disorder, there was no benefit, and the studies agreed fairly well.
In women with an inherited clotting disorder, the result was not significant and the studies varied widely.
The authors suggest heparin might help in some specific inherited clotting defects.

items.title: Male sperm quality and risk of recurrent spontaneous abortion in Chinese couples: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 24 studies of Chinese couples to see whether a male partner's sperm quality is linked to recurrent miscarriage (two or more pregnancy losses). Partners of women with recurrent miscarriage had lower sperm numbers, lower sperm viability and movement, fewer normally shaped sperm, and more sperm DNA damage than partners of women with no history of miscarriage. Semen volume and pH did not differ. The studies varied a lot and lacked detailed data, so larger studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Male partners of women with recurrent miscarriage had lower sperm density, viability, progressive motility and normal shape.
They also had higher rates of misshapen sperm and higher sperm DNA fragmentation.
Semen volume and semen pH showed no significant difference between the groups.
The authors note high variation between studies and call for larger prospective studies.

items.title: The effectiveness of IVIG therapy in pregnancy and live birth rate of women with recurrent implantation failure (RIF): A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled five studies of women who had repeated failed embryo implantation (usually during fertility treatment) and were given IVIG, an immune-system treatment given through a drip. Women who received IVIG had higher pregnancy and live birth rates than women who did not, but miscarriage rates were not different. The studies were not randomised trials, so the authors say firm conclusions must wait for larger, better-designed trials.
keyPoints: Pregnancy and live birth rates were higher in women who received IVIG than in comparison groups.
There was no significant difference in miscarriage rates between the IVIG and comparison groups.
IVIG may help women with repeated implantation failure who have specific immune-system problems.
The review included only five non-randomised studies, so larger randomised trials are needed before final conclusions.

items.title: Antiplatelet and anticoagulant agents for primary prevention of thrombosis in individuals with antiphospholipid antibodies
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether blood-thinning medicines (aspirin, heparin and similar drugs) can prevent a first blood clot in people who have antiphospholipid antibodies but have never had a clot. It included nine trials with 1044 people, many of them women with a history of pregnancy loss. There was not enough evidence to show that any of these treatments help or harm for preventing clots. Adding a stronger blood thinner to aspirin did seem to cause more minor bleeding, such as nosebleeds and heavy periods, in one study.
keyPoints: Evidence was too limited to show whether blood thinners prevent a first blood clot in people with antiphospholipid antibodies.
No clear difference in clot risk was found between a blood thinner (with or without aspirin) and aspirin alone, or between aspirin and placebo.
Minor bleeding (nosebleeds, heavy periods) was higher with a blood thinner plus aspirin than with aspirin alone in one study.
The review did not look at pregnancy outcomes, and larger trials focused on clots are needed.

items.title: Supplementation with progestogens in the first trimester of pregnancy to prevent miscarriage in women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized, controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 10 randomized trials (1,586 women) of progestogen hormone treatment in early pregnancy for women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage. Women given progestogens had a lower risk of another miscarriage and a slightly higher live birth rate than those who were not. No clear differences were seen in preterm birth, newborn deaths or genital abnormalities in babies. The authors note limits in the included studies, so the best type, dose and route of treatment remain unclear.
keyPoints: Progestogens in the first trimester were linked to a lower risk of miscarriage (RR 0.72) and a higher live birth rate (RR 1.07).
Synthetic progestogens, including weekly 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate injections, were linked to lower miscarriage risk, but natural progesterone was not.

No statistically significant differences were found for preterm birth, neonatal death or fetal genital abnormalities, though the authors say it seems safe for babies, the results were too imprecise to rule out harm.
Because of study limitations, the best type, dose and route of progestogen cannot yet be recommended.

items.title: Chinese herbal medicines for unexplained recurrent miscarriage
items.summary: This review looked at nine small trials (861 women) of Chinese herbal medicines for unexplained recurrent miscarriage. Herbal medicine alone did not give a different live birth rate than other medicines alone. Herbal medicine combined with Western medicines may have led to more continuing pregnancies and live births than Western medicines alone, but the trials were of poor quality, so the evidence is limited. There was almost no information on safety for the mother or baby.
keyPoints: Herbal medicine alone gave no clear difference in live births compared with other medicines alone (one trial, 80 women).
Herbal medicine plus Western medicines may improve continuing pregnancy and live birth rates compared with Western medicines alone.
Herbal medicine plus psychotherapy had a higher live birth rate than psychotherapy alone (one trial, 90 women).
Trials were small and poor quality, and safety for mothers and babies was mostly not reported, so more high-quality studies are needed.

items.title: Pregnancy loss: French clinical practice guidelines
items.source: Collège National des Gynécologues Obstétriciens Français
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.organisation: Collège National des Gynécologues Obstétriciens Français
items.summary: These French clinical guidelines set out how doctors should confirm, investigate and treat pregnancy loss. They suggest waiting for a repeat scan before confirming a suspected loss, and testing women with recurrent miscarriage for conditions such as diabetes, thyroid problems and antiphospholipid syndrome. Low-dose aspirin plus a preventive dose of heparin is recommended for women with obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome. Each recommendation is graded A, B or C, with A the strongest.
keyPoints: A suspected early pregnancy loss should only be confirmed after a follow-up scan 7 to 14 days later, depending on the scan findings (Grade C).
Women with recurrent pregnancy loss should be checked for diabetes, antiphospholipid syndrome, thyroid problems and other causes, including uterine abnormalities (Grades A to C).
Low-dose aspirin and low-molecular-weight heparin at a preventive dose are recommended for women with obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome (Grade A).
Delaying a new pregnancy after an early miscarriage is not recommended (Grade A), and blood sugar should be controlled before conception in women with diabetes (Grade A).

items.title: Uterine septum: a guideline
items.summary: This guideline from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine reviewed the research on a septate uterus, where a wall of tissue divides the inside of the womb. A septate uterus has been linked to a higher risk of miscarriage, early delivery, and the baby lying in an unusual position. Studies suggest that removing the septum may improve live-birth rates in women who have had pregnancy losses or fertility problems. There is not enough evidence to say which surgical method works best.
keyPoints: A septate uterus is associated with a higher risk of miscarriage, premature delivery, and malpresentation (baby in an unusual position).
There is not enough evidence that a uterine septum causes infertility.
Treating the septum is linked to better live-birth rates in women with prior pregnancy loss, recurrent pregnancy loss, or infertility.
For women with no infertility or pregnancy loss, septum incision may be considered after counseling about risks and benefits; no single surgical method is shown to be better.

items.title: Dopamine agonists for preventing future miscarriage in women with idiopathic hyperprolactinemia and recurrent miscarriage history
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether dopamine agonists, medicines that lower the hormone prolactin, can prevent miscarriage in women with unexplained high prolactin and a history of repeated miscarriages. Only one small trial of 48 women qualified. It suggested the medicine bromocriptine lowered the chance of miscarriage compared with no treatment, but the evidence was low quality and the trial had a high risk of bias. The review concluded there is not enough evidence to say whether these medicines really work, and side effects for mothers and babies were not reported.
keyPoints: Only one small trial (48 women) met the review's criteria, and it was judged at high risk of bias.
In that trial, bromocriptine was linked to fewer miscarriages than no treatment (low-quality evidence).
There was no clear difference in live births or in how many women became pregnant (very low-quality evidence).
No information was reported on side effects for mothers or babies, and larger, better-designed trials are needed.

items.title: Association of VEGF genetic polymorphisms with recurrent spontaneous abortion risk: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 10 studies, covering 1,832 women with recurrent miscarriage and 2,271 healthy women, to look at whether small natural variations in a gene called VEGF are linked to repeated pregnancy loss. Four of these variations were linked to a higher chance of recurrent miscarriage. Two of them appeared to matter differently in Asian and non-Asian groups. The abstract does not rate how certain this evidence is.
keyPoints: Four VEGF gene variations (rs1570360, rs3025039, rs2010963 and rs3025020) were linked to higher risk of recurrent miscarriage.
The rs1570360 variation was linked to risk in non-Asian groups.
The rs3025039 variation was linked to risk in Asian groups.
Earlier studies had given conflicting results, so the authors pooled 10 studies to get a clearer picture.

items.title: Association of skewed X chromosome inactivation and idiopathic recurrent spontaneous abortion: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 studies, covering 1594 women with recurrent miscarriage and 1924 comparison women, to see whether skewed X chromosome inactivation is linked to unexplained recurrent miscarriage. No link was found when skewing was defined at 80% or 90%. A link did appear with extreme skewing (95% or more) and in women who had three or more losses, but not when recurrent miscarriage was defined as two or more losses. The authors say more studies are needed to confirm a possible genetic cause.
keyPoints: No significant link between skewed X inactivation and recurrent miscarriage when skewing was defined at 80% or 90%.
Extreme skewing (95% or more) was more common in women with recurrent miscarriage than in comparison women.
The link was seen in women with three or more pregnancy losses, but faded when two or more losses were counted.
More studies are needed to confirm a possible genetic mechanism.

items.title: Vaginismus treatment: a systematic review and meta-analysis of contemporary therapeutic approaches
items.summary: This review pulled together 18 studies of 863 women with vaginismus, a condition where the pelvic floor muscles tighten involuntarily and make penetration painful or impossible. Several treatments helped most women, with success rates of roughly 78% to 86%. Treatments that combined psychological and physical approaches did best. The studies used different ways of diagnosing vaginismus and measuring success, so the results are not perfectly consistent.
keyPoints: Combined psychosexual treatments had the highest success rate (86%).
Cognitive-behavioral therapy (82%), botulinum toxin injections (85%) and pelvic floor physiotherapy (85%) also helped most women.
Vaginal dilator therapy had the lowest success rate (78%).
Studies differed in how they defined vaginismus and success, and longer-term results are still needed.

items.title: Role of flibanserin in managing hypoactive sexual desire disorder in women: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 8 randomised trials involving about 7,900 women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD), a condition of persistently low sexual desire that causes distress. Women taking flibanserin 100 mg had slightly more satisfying sexual events each month, higher desire scores and less sexual distress than women taking a placebo. This was seen in women before and after menopause. Side effects such as dizziness, tiredness, nausea, sleepiness and trouble sleeping were more common with flibanserin, and the authors note these may overshadow its benefits.
keyPoints: Flibanserin 100 mg was better than placebo for satisfying sexual events, sexual desire and sexual distress in premenopausal women.
Postmenopausal women taking flibanserin 100 mg also had improvements in satisfying sexual events, desire and distress scores.
Dizziness, fatigue, nausea, sleepiness and insomnia were more common with flibanserin, but were mild.
Serious and severe side effects were similar between flibanserin and placebo groups.

items.title: Testosterone use for hypoactive sexual desire disorder in postmenopausal women
items.summary: This short practice article looks at using testosterone to treat hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD), meaning a lasting low sex drive that causes distress, in women after menopause. It draws on clinical guidelines built from a large meta-analysis of the benefits and risks of testosterone therapy. The guidelines say HSDD in postmenopausal women is the only evidence-based reason to use testosterone. The article also covers how to identify patients, dosing, monitoring and follow-up.
keyPoints: Testosterone is described as an evidence-based therapy for HSDD in postmenopausal women.
Guidelines based on the most comprehensive meta-analysis to date name HSDD in postmenopausal women as the sole evidence-based indication for testosterone.
The guidelines give recommendations on identifying patients, dosing, monitoring and follow-up.

items.title: Antenatal perineal massage - risk of perineal injuries, pain, urinary incontinence and dyspereunia - a systematic review
items.source: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.journal: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.summary: This review pulled together 18 studies on massaging the perineum (the area between the vagina and anus) during late pregnancy. It looked at whether this massage affects tearing, episiotomy, pain, bladder or bowel leakage, and painful sex after birth. The authors concluded that massage may protect the perineum from injury during labour and may lower the chance of gas and fecal incontinence after birth. Studies used different techniques and timings, and only 2 looked at painful sex, so that part is less clear.
keyPoints: Most studies started the massage from about 34 weeks of pregnancy until delivery.
Antenatal perineal massage may protect the perineum from injury during labour.
It may also reduce the risk of gas and fecal incontinence after birth.
Studies varied in massage timing, frequency and how women were taught, which may affect the results; only 2 studies looked at painful sex.

items.title: Effectiveness of physical therapy interventions in women with dyspareunia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 19 studies of physical therapy for women with painful sex (dyspareunia). Treatments included electrical nerve stimulation, pelvic floor muscle training, massage and combined programs. Electrotherapy, alone or with pelvic floor training, improved pain and quality of life, but did not clearly improve sexual function. The abstract does not rate the certainty of the evidence.
keyPoints: Electrotherapy, and electrotherapy combined with pelvic floor muscle training, significantly reduced pain and improved quality of life.
These treatments did not show significant improvement in sexual function.
The authors highlight strengthening the pelvic floor muscles and TENS (a gentle electrical nerve stimulation) as especially useful.
Manual trigger point release and Thiele massage were also reported to help reduce pain intensity.

items.title: Single-incision sling operations for urinary incontinence in women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 62 trials (8051 women) of single-incision sling surgery for stress urinary incontinence (leaking when coughing, sneezing or exercising). These slings worked about as well as transobturator slings for improving leakage at 12 months, and may work as well as retropubic slings. Whether they cause more or less painful sex (dyspareunia) than other slings is uncertain. The authors say longer-term safety and effectiveness are still unclear.
keyPoints: Single-incision slings improved leakage about as well as transobturator slings at 12 months (high-certainty evidence) and may do so for retropubic slings (low-certainty evidence).
Painful sex after surgery: the effect compared with transobturator slings is uncertain, because results were consistent with both benefit and harm (moderate-certainty evidence).
Compared with transobturator slings, single-incision slings probably caused less pain at 24 months, but women may report lower quality of life at 12 months.
Longer-term data are needed to clarify the safety and long-term effectiveness of these slings.

items.title: Lichen Sclerosus and Sexual Dysfunction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 23 earlier studies, covering 486 women with vulvar lichen sclerosus, a long-term autoimmune skin condition. They found that about 6 in 10 of these women (59%) had some kind of sexual difficulty. Pain during sex was the most commonly reported problem. Only a small number of studies met the review's criteria, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: About 59% of women with lichen sclerosus had some form of sexual dysfunction (range 48-70%).
Pain during intercourse, or general pain with sex, was the most common problem reported.
Talking about sexual concerns with women who have lichen sclerosus could help them seek treatment.
Few studies were included, and more research is needed using biopsy-confirmed diagnoses and validated sexual function questionnaires.

items.title: International Society for the Study of Women's Sexual Health Clinical Practice Guideline for the Use of Systemic Testosterone for Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder in Women
items.source: International Society for the Study of Women's Sexual Health
items.organisation: International Society for the Study of Women's Sexual Health
items.summary: This guideline from a women's sexual health society explains when and how testosterone might be used for women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD), a persistent low sex drive that causes distress. It recommends skin-applied (transdermal) testosterone for women whose low desire is not mainly caused by things like relationship or mental health problems. Research suggests a moderate benefit, and no serious side effects were seen with doses that keep hormone levels in the normal range, but long-term safety is not known. Testosterone is not approved for women in most countries, so it is prescribed off-label.
keyPoints: Skin-applied testosterone is recommended for women with HSDD that is not mainly linked to modifiable factors such as relationship or mental health problems.
Current research supports a moderate benefit; no serious adverse events were seen at physiologic doses, but long-term safety has not been established.
A blood testosterone level cannot diagnose HSDD, but is used as a starting point so levels can be monitored to stay in the normal premenopausal range.
Compounded testosterone products are not recommended because there is not enough evidence on whether they work or are safe.

items.title: Selective oestrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) for endometriosis
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether SERMs, medicines that act on oestrogen receptors, help treat endometriosis, a condition that can cause pelvic pain and pain during sex. Only one small trial of 93 women was found, testing raloxifene against placebo after surgery to remove endometriosis. The evidence was very low quality, so the effects on pain, side effects and recurrence are uncertain. The trial was stopped early because women taking raloxifene had higher pain scores than those on placebo.
keyPoints: Only one small trial (93 women) met the review's criteria, and it tested raloxifene after surgery.
Pain came back sooner in the raloxifene group, and the trial was stopped early because of higher pain scores.
The review could not tell whether raloxifene changes side effects or the chance of endometriosis returning.
The authors say more research is needed to understand any role for SERMs in endometriosis.

items.title: Pine bark (Pinus spp.) extract for treating chronic disorders
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at pine bark extract supplements for long-term health conditions, including one small study in women with sexual dysfunction. That study reported better sexual satisfaction and lower pain scores, but the evidence was rated very low certainty, so we cannot tell whether the supplement truly works. The authors concluded that no firm conclusions about benefits or safety are possible because the studies were small and poorly reported.
keyPoints: Only one study (75 women) looked at pine bark extract for female sexual dysfunction; it reported higher satisfaction and lower pain scores.
The evidence for women's sexual function and pain was rated very low certainty.
Across all 27 trials, small sizes and poor reporting meant no definitive conclusions on whether the supplement works or is safe.
Most studies did not report serious side effects or hospital admissions.

items.title: Female Sexual Dysfunction: ACOG Practice Bulletin Clinical Management Guidelines for Obstetrician-Gynecologists, Number 213
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on female sexual dysfunction. This is when a woman feels personal distress about her desire, arousal, orgasm, or pain during sex. It is fairly common, but many women do not bring it up unless a doctor asks, and many doctors feel unsure about raising it. The guideline gives an overview, updated ways to diagnose it, and management approaches based on the best available evidence.
keyPoints: Female sexual dysfunction means distress about desire, arousal, orgasm, or pain.
It is relatively common, but women are unlikely to discuss it with their provider unless asked.
Providers may not ask because of limited training, little clinical time, or underestimating how common it is.
The guideline outlines updated diagnostic criteria and currently recommended management strategies.

items.title: INFERTILITY AND SEXUAL DYSFUNCTIONS: A SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW
items.summary: This review looked at published studies from 2012 to 2017 to see whether infertility and its treatment affect a couple's sex life. It found that sexual problems were common in couples facing infertility, affecting about 43% to 90% of women and 48% to 58% of men. Couples also reported being less satisfied with their sex lives. The authors suggest that sexual therapy and support during infertility treatment may help.
keyPoints: Infertility was linked to worse sexual health in couples.
Sexual dysfunction was reported by 43%-90% of women and 48%-58% of men with infertility.
Couples reported lower satisfaction with their sex lives.
Sexual therapy and support during infertility treatment might benefit couples.

items.title: Interventions for sexual dysfunction following treatments for cancer in women
items.summary: This review looked at treatments for sexual problems in women after cancer treatment, such as low desire or painful sex. It found 11 trials with 1509 women, all after gynaecological or breast cancer. Results were mixed and most trials were small, so the review could not give clear answers about what works. Only a pH-balanced vaginal gel clearly improved sexual function.
keyPoints: Eight of the 11 trials tested talking-based or educational support; three found benefit on some measures and five found none.
Only the trial of a pH-balanced vaginal gel showed significant improvement in sexual function.
Eight trials were at high risk of bias because they had fewer than 50 women per group.
Most trials did not measure harm; the two drug trials that did reported none.

items.title: Cyproterone acetate for hirsutism
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 23 small trials of cyproterone acetate (an anti-androgen, usually taken with ethinylestradiol) for women with excess unwanted hair growth (hirsutism). For most comparisons with other medicines, such as spironolactone and ketoconazole, hair scores were similar. There were small differences against flutamide, and mixed results against finasteride and spironolactone plus the pill. The studies were small and the evidence ranged from very low to high quality, so firm conclusions are hard to draw.
keyPoints: Cyproterone acetate plus ethinylestradiol may make little to no difference in hair scores (moderate- or low-certainty evidence, depending on the comparison) compared with most other treatments tested, including spironolactone, ketoconazole and finasteride.
It may improve hirsutism slightly more than flutamide, based on one small trial of 28 women.
Higher and lower doses of cyproterone acetate with ethinylestradiol were not clearly different in hair scores (very low-certainty evidence).
There was not enough data to compare side effects, and larger, better-designed studies are needed.

items.title: Polycystic ovaries and herbal remedies: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at earlier studies on herbal remedies for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a hormone condition that can cause acne, extra hair growth and fertility problems. The authors report that some plants, such as Vitex agnus-castus, may lower male hormone levels and reduce unwanted hair growth. Others, like cinnamon, liquorice and ginseng, were linked to lower blood sugar and fats. The review concludes herbal medicines may ease PCOS symptoms with few side effects but need a longer treatment time. The abstract does not rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Vitex agnus-castus was reported to reduce unwanted hair growth by lowering testosterone and other male hormones.
Aloe vera and chamomile were reported to improve fertility by increasing the number of ovarian follicles.
Liquorice, ginseng, cinnamon and d-chiro inositol were reported to lower blood sugar and fats in PCOS.
Herbal medicines may improve PCOS symptoms with minimal side effects but a longer treatment cycle.

items.title: Evaluation of the Safety and Effectiveness of Nutritional Supplements for Treating Hair Loss: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 30 studies of vitamins, supplements and food-based products used to treat hair loss in people who were not known to be low in any nutrient. Several products, including Viviscal, Nutrafol, zinc and pumpkin seed oil, showed possible benefit in the best-quality studies, while a few others had only low-quality evidence. Side effects were rare and mild. The authors say results should be read with each study's design in mind, and larger, better trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Studies with the best evidence suggested possible benefit from products such as Viviscal, Nourkrin, Nutrafol, zinc, tocotrienol and pumpkin seed oil.
Kimchi and cheonggukjang, vitamin D3 and Forti5 had only low-quality evidence for improving hair loss.
Side effects were rare and mild for all the treatments reviewed.
The authors suggest doctors discuss possible benefits and risks of supplements with patients, and call for larger trials with active comparators.

items.title: Human Stem Cell Use in Androgenetic Alopecia: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at whether stem cell treatments can help with androgenetic alopecia, a common type of hair loss that affects both women and men. It pulled together 14 studies and mainly looked at hair density. No major side effects were reported, and stem cells seemed promising either on their own or alongside standard treatment. The authors say the results should be treated with caution until larger, more representative studies confirm them.
keyPoints: Fourteen studies on stem cell use in androgenetic alopecia were included in the review.
No major side effects were reported during or after stem cell treatment.
Stem cells seem a promising alternative or add-on to standard hair loss treatment.
Results need to be repeated in larger and more representative groups before firm conclusions can be drawn.

items.title: Treatments for alopecia areata: a network meta-analysis
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 63 trials (4,817 people, children and adults) testing treatments for alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition that causes patchy hair loss. The only treatment with strong evidence was baricitinib, which increased hair regrowth compared with placebo, both in the short and long term. For most other treatments, the evidence is very uncertain, and very little was reported on quality of life.
keyPoints: Baricitinib increased short-term hair regrowth of 75% or more compared with placebo (high-certainty evidence).
Baricitinib also increased long-term hair regrowth compared with placebo (high-certainty evidence).
Serious side effects with baricitinib were uncommon and results on this were inconclusive; the authors say this small risk should be weighed against the expected benefit.
For most other treatments, including steroids, topical minoxidil and contact immunotherapy, the effect on hair regrowth is very uncertain, and evidence on quality of life is scant.

items.title: Safety and Effectiveness of Oral Nutraceuticals for Treating Acne: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 42 randomized trials (3,346 people) of supplements taken by mouth for acne, such as vitamins, green tea extract, probiotics and omega-3 fats. Studies of fair or good quality suggested possible benefit from vitamins B5 and D, green tea extract, probiotics and omega-3s, often with fewer pimples or better doctor ratings. Side effects were rare, though zinc sometimes caused stomach and gut problems. Many of the studies were small, so larger trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Vitamins B5 and D, green tea extract, probiotics and omega-3 fatty acids showed possible benefit for acne in fair or good quality studies.
Benefits were mostly fewer acne lesions or better investigator global assessment scores.
Side effects were rare for most supplements, but zinc was linked to stomach and gut side effects.
Many studies were small, and the authors call for larger randomized trials.

items.title: Guideline No. 444: Hirsutism: Evaluation and Treatment
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline reviews how hirsutism (excess dark, coarse hair growth in women, often in a male-like pattern) is diagnosed and treated. It describes three main ways to manage it: removing hair mechanically, lowering the body's production of androgen hormones, and blocking the effect of androgens on the body. The main downsides of treatment are side effects, how long treatment can take, and cost.
keyPoints: Hirsutism can be managed in three ways: mechanical hair removal, suppressing androgen production, and androgen receptor blockade.
The main limitations of treatment are side effects, cost, and a potentially long duration of treatment.
The guideline is meant for women with hirsutism and for the doctors who care for them, including family doctors, gynaecologists and hormone specialists.

items.title: Androgenetic alopecia in women and men: Italian guidelines adapted from European Dermatology Forum/European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology guidelines
items.source: Giornale Italiano Di Dermatologia E Venereologia
items.journal: Giornale Italiano Di Dermatologia E Venereologia
items.summary: This is an Italian clinical guideline, adapted from European dermatology guidelines, on androgenetic alopecia (hormone-related hair thinning). It affects up to 80% of men and 50% of women over a lifetime and is driven by the hormone DHT acting on sensitive hair follicles. The guideline covers how it is diagnosed and the medical treatments available, including topical minoxidil, antiandrogen medicines and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors. The abstract does not report how strong the evidence is for each treatment.
keyPoints: Androgenetic alopecia is the most common form of hair loss, affecting up to 50% of women in their lifetime.
It is caused by the hormone DHT gradually shrinking and lightening hair on androgen-sensitive follicles.
It looks different in women and men, and trichoscopy (a close scalp exam) helps diagnose it and track treatment response.
Treatment options include topical minoxidil, antiandrogen agents and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors.

items.title: Female Pattern Hair Loss and Androgen Excess: A Report From the Multidisciplinary Androgen Excess and PCOS Committee
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: An expert group from dermatology and endocrinology reviewed the research on female pattern hair loss, a common type of thinning on the central scalp in women. They agreed that it is mainly diagnosed by examining the patient, and that hair loss alone does not mean high androgen (male-type hormone) levels if blood tests are normal. They recommend checking for possible androgen excess in every patient, and starting treatment with 5% minoxidil.
keyPoints: Isolated female pattern hair loss should not be treated as a sign of high androgens when androgen levels are normal.
Every patient with this type of hair loss should be assessed for possible androgen excess.
Tests for vitamin D, iron, zinc, thyroid hormones and prolactin are optional but recommended.
Treatment should begin with 5% minoxidil; 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors or antiandrogens can be added when hair loss is severe or androgen levels are high.

items.title: Japanese Dermatological Association Guidelines: Guidelines for the treatment of acne vulgaris 2017
items.summary: These are national acne treatment guidelines from the Japanese Dermatological Association, updated in 2016 and 2017. They now recommend combination treatments, especially gels that combine benzoyl peroxide with other ingredients, rather than antibiotics used on their own. They also suggest keeping antibiotic treatment short, to about 3 months, so that acne bacteria do not become resistant to antibiotics. The guidelines also cover rosacea, which can look like acne but needs a different treatment plan.
keyPoints: Combination treatments, especially fixed-dose gels containing benzoyl peroxide, are recommended over antibiotics used alone during a flare of inflamed acne.
Antibiotic treatment for acute inflammatory acne should be limited to about 3 months to help avoid antibiotic-resistant acne bacteria.
For keeping acne under control afterwards, benzoyl peroxide, adapalene, or a gel combining 0.1% adapalene and 2.5% benzoyl peroxide are recommended.
Rosacea needs to be told apart from acne because it is treated differently.

items.title: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of male-pattern and female-pattern hair loss, 2017 version
items.summary: This is a 2017 Japanese guideline on treating male-pattern and female-pattern hair loss. For women, it recommends 1% minoxidil applied to the scalp twice daily as a first-line treatment. It says oral finasteride and dutasteride should not be used for female-pattern hair loss. The abstract does not describe how strong the evidence was.
keyPoints: Topical 1% minoxidil twice daily is recommended as a first-line treatment for female-pattern hair loss.
Oral finasteride and dutasteride are contraindicated (not to be used) for female-pattern hair loss.
Oral minoxidil and prosthetic hair transplantation are recommended against.
Other options such as light-emitting diode or low-level laser treatment, wigs, and topical products were also reviewed.

items.title: The effectiveness of treatments for androgenetic alopecia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
items.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
items.summary: This review pooled results from good or fair quality randomized trials of non-surgical treatments for androgenetic alopecia, a hormone-linked pattern of hair loss. Minoxidil, finasteride and low-level laser light therapy all worked better than placebo in men. For women, 2% minoxidil also worked better than placebo. The studies varied a lot from one to the next, so results should be read with some care.
keyPoints: 2% minoxidil was more effective than placebo for promoting hair growth in women with androgenetic alopecia.
In men, 2% and 5% minoxidil, 1 mg finasteride and low-level laser light therapy were all more effective than placebo.
Other treatments could not be assessed because the data were lacking.
The authors noted high heterogeneity (differences between studies) in most of the trials.

items.title: Interventions for acne scars
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 24 trials (789 adults) testing treatments for acne scars, mostly the dented kind on the face, such as lasers, chemical peels, skin needling and injectable fillers. Most of the evidence was very low quality, so it is hard to say which treatments work best. The only moderate-quality finding was that injectable fillers may improve dented acne scars compared with a placebo, but nobody was followed for longer than 48 weeks.
keyPoints: Overall there is a lack of high-quality evidence on treatments for acne scars, because the studies were small and varied in how they measured improvement.
Injectable fillers probably gave better scar improvement than placebo at 24 weeks (moderate-quality evidence), but long-term effects have not been studied.
Lasers, chemical peels and skin needling often looked similar to each other, but this evidence was very low quality and may mean none of them clearly works.
Pain was common with most treatments, and chemical peeling was linked to more skin darkening (hyperpigmentation) than skin needling in one small study.

items.title: Interventions for female pattern hair loss
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 47 trials (5,290 women) testing treatments for female pattern hair loss, the most common type of hair loss in women. Topical minoxidil helped more women regrow hair than placebo, and the 2% and 5% strengths worked about equally. Finasteride was no better than placebo, and results for laser devices were mixed. Many of the trials were at unclear or high risk of bias, and much of the evidence was moderate to low quality.
keyPoints: Minoxidil 2% or 1% led to moderate to marked hair regrowth in more women than placebo (157/593 vs 77/555), based on moderate quality evidence.
Minoxidil 2% and 5% showed no clear difference in regrowth, and adverse events were similar to placebo and between strengths (low quality evidence).
Finasteride 1 mg was no more effective than placebo (low quality evidence).
Laser combs gave inconsistent results: women did not rate them better than a sham device, but hair counts rose from baseline.

items.title: Combination treatment for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline
items.summary: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine reviewed the research on treating long-term insomnia with cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) together with sleep medication. It suggests that CBT-I plus medication is better than medication alone. It also suggests that adding medication to CBT-I does not offer enough extra benefit over CBT-I by itself. The evidence behind both suggestions is low certainty.
keyPoints: For adults with chronic insomnia, the guideline suggests CBT-I plus insomnia medication over medication alone (conditional recommendation, low certainty).
The guideline suggests against using CBT-I plus medication over CBT-I alone (conditional recommendation, low certainty).
People who care most about sleeping longer early in treatment, or who care less about daytime symptoms, may reasonably choose combination treatment instead of CBT-I alone.
Conditional recommendations mean the choice should take a person's own values and preferences into account.

items.title: Effects of exercise on sleep quality in women - A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
items.journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
items.summary: This review pooled results from 16 randomised trials to see whether exercise improves sleep in adult women with insomnia symptoms. Exercise significantly lowered scores on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, meaning sleep quality got better. Shorter programmes (under 12 weeks) did better for overall sleep quality and daytime tiredness, while longer ones (12 weeks or more) were linked to less use of sleep medication. The authors say more studies are needed to learn how age, type of exercise and time of day matter.
keyPoints: Exercise significantly improved sleep quality scores in adult women, based on 16 trials.
Programmes shorter than 12 weeks worked better for sleep quality and daytime dysfunction.
Programmes of 12 weeks or longer reduced the use of sleep medication.
Exercise may be a useful non-drug option for sleep problems in women.

items.title: Effects of cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia compared with controls among cancer survivors: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials
items.summary: This review combined 19 trials (1,803 people, 94% women, mostly breast cancer survivors) testing cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) against usual care, waiting lists or sleep education alone. CBT-I improved insomnia scores by about 4.4 points on average, which helped an appreciable number of people but fell short of the 6-point change that would suggest many people benefited in a clearly important way. Sleep, fatigue and quality of life also improved a little, though not enough on average to count as clearly important. The evidence was low to very low certainty, so the true effect could differ.
keyPoints: CBT-I improved insomnia severity by an average of 4.4 points compared with controls, below the 6-point threshold for clearly important benefit.
Sleep diary measures, fatigue and quality of life also improved, but on average not enough to reach clinically important thresholds.
Results did not meaningfully differ by treatment type or cancer-related characteristics.
The authors say new strategies are needed, especially for people who do not respond to CBT-I.

items.title: Components and Delivery Formats of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Chronic Insomnia in Adults: A Systematic Review and Component Network Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This large review pooled 241 trials (about 31,000 adults, two-thirds of them women) to see which parts of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) work best for long-term sleep problems. Changing unhelpful thoughts about sleep, limiting time in bed (sleep restriction), and using the bed only for sleep (stimulus control) seemed to help most. Sleep hygiene tips were not essential, and relaxation exercises did not seem to add benefit. Sessions with a therapist in person worked best, though the authors note hidden interactions could affect these conclusions and larger trials are needed.
keyPoints: Helpful CBT-I parts included cognitive restructuring, third-wave components, sleep restriction and stimulus control.
Sleep hygiene education was not essential, and relaxation procedures may be counterproductive.
In-person therapist-led programs were the most beneficial format.
The best combination in person raised remission rates by 33 percentage points versus in-person education alone (number needed to treat of 3).

items.title: Sleep-related adverse events of smoking cessation drugs: A network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 79 trials with about 36,700 smokers (without psychiatric conditions) to compare sleep-related side effects of different quit-smoking medicines. People taking bupropion, alone or combined with other treatments, were more likely to report insomnia than those using nicotine replacement alone. Other sleep effects, such as odd dreams, nightmares and sleepiness, varied by medicine. The authors advise healthcare providers to be careful when prescribing these drugs because of possible sleep side effects.
keyPoints: Bupropion, bupropion with a nicotinic receptor agonist, and bupropion with nicotine replacement were linked to more insomnia than nicotine replacement alone.
Bupropion plus a nicotinic receptor agonist ranked highest for insomnia risk; placebo ranked lowest.
A nicotinic receptor agonist plus nicotine replacement ranked first for abnormal dreams, the agonist alone for nightmares, and nortriptyline for sleepiness.
Providers are advised to consider sleep-related side effects when prescribing smoking cessation drugs.

items.title: Dietary patterns and insomnia symptoms: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 37 observational studies (over 591,000 people) to look at how eating patterns relate to insomnia symptoms. People who followed a Mediterranean-style or other healthy diet had a lower chance of insomnia symptoms. Diets with a high glycemic index or glycemic load, or an unhealthy pattern, were linked to a higher chance. The studies were mostly well done, but the certainty of the evidence was very low, and this kind of study shows links, not cause and effect.
keyPoints: Mediterranean, high-quality and healthy diets were linked to a lower risk of insomnia symptoms.
High glycemic index, high glycemic load and unhealthy diet patterns were linked to a higher risk of insomnia symptoms.
Most studies were of good quality, but the certainty of the evidence was very low.
The review covered the general population, not women only.

items.title: Initial treatment choices for long-term remission of chronic insomnia disorder in adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 13 trials (823 adults, about 60% women) comparing three ways to start treating long-term insomnia: cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), sleep medicines, or both together. Starting with CBT-I gave better long-term results than medicine alone, with high-certainty evidence. Adding medicine to CBT-I did not clearly help more than CBT-I alone.
keyPoints: CBT-I led to more long-term remission of insomnia than medication alone (odds ratio 1.82, high certainty).
About 41% of people starting with CBT-I were in long-term remission, compared with 28% of those starting with medication.
Fewer people dropped out of CBT-I than out of medication treatment.
Combining CBT-I with medicine may beat medicine alone, but there was no clear gain over CBT-I alone, so it may not be worth the extra burden.

items.title: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia to treat major depressive disorder with comorbid insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 19 randomized trials (4,808 adults, about 73% women) of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) in people with major depression and insomnia. CBT-I worked better than comparison conditions for easing depression and for clearing insomnia. About 32% of people in the CBT-I groups had a depression response, compared with 17% in the comparison groups after a median of 8 weeks. CBT-I may lead to more people dropping out of treatment, but the evidence on that is lower quality.
keyPoints: CBT-I made a depression response more likely than control conditions (moderate certainty evidence).
CBT-I made insomnia remission more likely than control conditions (moderate certainty evidence).
Depression symptoms improved beyond sleep problems alone.
Dropout may be higher with CBT-I, though this finding was low certainty.

items.title: Efficacy of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia in breast cancer: A meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 14 randomized trials (1,363 people) of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) in patients and survivors of breast cancer. CBT-I reduced insomnia and improved sleep quality, with medium-to-large effects right after treatment. The benefit was smaller but still present at 12 months. The authors note that the CBT-I programs tested varied, so the best mix of components is still unclear.
keyPoints: CBT-I reduced insomnia and improved sleep quality in women treated for breast cancer.
Effects were medium to large right after treatment and at follow-up within six months.
A smaller benefit was still seen at 12 months after treatment ended.
Results were similar however the therapy was delivered or compared, but the exact components of CBT-I varied between trials.

items.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline
items.summary: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine reviewed the research on non-drug treatments for long-term (chronic) insomnia in adults. It strongly recommends cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), which combines several techniques. It makes weaker, conditional suggestions for some other talking and behavior-based therapies, and suggests sleep hygiene tips alone are not a good single treatment.
keyPoints: Multicomponent cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is strongly recommended for chronic insomnia in adults.
Brief multicomponent therapies, stimulus control, sleep restriction therapy and relaxation therapy are each conditionally suggested.
Sleep hygiene advice used on its own is conditionally suggested against.
A conditional recommendation means the choice should take into account the person's own values and preferences.

items.title: The effect of yoga on sleep quality and insomnia in women with sleep problems: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 19 trials with 1,832 women who had sleep problems to see if yoga helps sleep. Overall, yoga improved sleep quality compared with groups that did no active treatment. The benefit was not clearly seen for insomnia scores, or in women with breast cancer or women going through menopause. No serious side effects were linked to yoga.
keyPoints: Across 19 trials, yoga led to a significant overall improvement in sleep in women.
Sleep quality (PSQI scores) improved with yoga in 16 trials, but 3 trials found no clear effect on insomnia severity (ISI).
No clear benefit on sleep quality was found in women with breast cancer or in peri/postmenopausal women.
Yoga was not associated with any serious adverse events.

items.title: Natural Products from Single Plants as Sleep Aids: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 79 human studies of 21 single-plant products taken by mouth as sleep aids. Valerian was the most studied, but its results conflicted from study to study. Most other plants had not been tested well in people. Overall, the evidence is limited and inconclusive, so researchers say more studies are needed.
keyPoints: 79 studies covering 21 plants were included in the review.
Valerian was studied most often, but results were conflicting.
Other plants were not tested as rigorously in human studies.
Evidence that single-plant products improve sleep is limited and inconclusive.

items.title: Deprescribing antipsychotics for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia and insomnia: Evidence-based clinical practice guideline
items.source: Canadian Family Physician Medecin de Famille Canadien
items.journal: Canadian Family Physician Medecin de Famille Canadien
items.summary: This guideline looked at when it is safe to slowly reduce and stop antipsychotic medicines used for dementia-related behaviour symptoms and for insomnia. The team used published evidence and a formal rating process to make its recommendations. It recommends deprescribing (tapering off) antipsychotics in adults with primary insomnia, or with secondary insomnia once underlying conditions are managed. The guideline says antipsychotics are linked to harms and can be safely tapered, and it is meant to support, not replace, decisions made with patients and families.
keyPoints: Deprescribing antipsychotics is recommended for adults with primary insomnia treated for any length of time.
It is also recommended for secondary insomnia when the underlying health conditions are being managed.
Antipsychotics are associated with harms and can be safely tapered.
People may be more open to stopping if they understand the reason, help plan the taper, and are offered behavioural advice.

items.title: Mindfulness-based interventions for women with breast cancer: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 randomised trials with 1709 women who had breast cancer to see whether mindfulness-based programmes (MBSR and MBCT) help. Compared with usual care, women had small improvements right after the programme in quality of life, fatigue, sleep, stress, anxiety and depression. The average benefits were smaller than the level considered clearly meaningful in daily life, so how much they matter is unclear. Side effects were not well reported, and the authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Compared with usual care, mindfulness programmes gave small improvements in sleep, fatigue, stress, anxiety, depression and quality of life right after the programme.
Benefits for anxiety and depression lasted up to 6 months, and for anxiety up to 12 months.
Against other active treatments, only anxiety and depression improved, and only right after the programme.
Average effects were below the threshold for a clearly meaningful difference, and side effects were not well reported.

items.title: Home-based multidimensional survivorship programmes for breast cancer survivors
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 26 trials (2,272 women) of home-based programmes for breast cancer survivors that combined education, exercise and/or psychological support. The programmes appeared to give a short-term lift in quality of life and to ease anxiety, fatigue and insomnia right after the programme ended. Most benefits were not seen at four to six months or later. Evidence for insomnia, anxiety and fatigue was low quality, so these results are uncertain.
keyPoints: Home-based programmes may improve breast cancer-specific and overall quality of life straight after the programme, with moderate-quality evidence.
They may reduce insomnia, fatigue and anxiety immediately after the programme, but this evidence is low quality.
Anxiety benefits did not last to four to six months, and there was no clear difference in quality of life at four to six or 12 months.
No studies reported on healthcare use or cost, so those effects are unknown.

items.title: Pharmacotherapy Treatment Options for Insomnia: A Primer for Clinicians
items.summary: This review looks at the medicines used to treat insomnia, including FDA-approved sleep medicines and others that are often prescribed off-label. It notes that chronic insomnia often lasts longer than 2 years, and that the FDA no longer limits how long newer sleep medicines can be used. It also describes FDA safety changes: a warning about sleep-related complex behaviours such as sleep-driving, and lower doses of most zolpidem products for women because blood levels can stay high into the morning and cause daytime drowsiness.
keyPoints: Insomnia is common and can lower quality of life and raise the chance of some psychiatric conditions.
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is referenced alongside medicine options.
The FDA now requires lower doses of most zolpidem products for women because of high morning drug levels that can cause daytime carry-over effects.
All sleep medicines now carry an FDA warning about sleep-related complex behaviours, such as sleep-driving.

items.title: Sleep During Pregnancy and Offspring Outcomes From Infancy to Childhood: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 34 studies on how a mother's sleep during pregnancy relates to her child's health and development after birth. Studies consistently linked poor sleep in pregnancy with poorer sleep in the child, higher body mass index, more physical health conditions, poorer overall development and more behavioural problems. Early evidence also suggests links to differences in children's brain structure and function. These studies show associations, so they cannot prove that poor sleep itself causes these outcomes.
keyPoints: Poor sleep in pregnancy was consistently linked to poorer sleep in the child.
It was also linked to higher child body mass index, more physical health conditions, poorer development and more behavioural problems.
Emerging evidence links sleep in pregnancy to differences in children's brain structure and function.
The authors say more research is needed to understand the long-lasting effects of sleep across pregnancy.

items.title: Impact of postpartum physical activity on maternal sleep: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 studies of about 3,100 women in the first year after birth to see whether being physically active affects sleep. Exercise programmes were linked to better sleep quality and less daytime tiredness compared with no exercise. No clear effect was found on how long women slept, how quickly they fell asleep, sleep efficiency, or sleep disturbance.
keyPoints: Exercise-only programmes improved sleep quality after birth compared with no exercise (moderate certainty of evidence).
Exercise reduced daytime and general fatigue compared with no exercise (high certainty of evidence).
No effect was found on sleep duration, time to fall asleep, sleep efficiency or sleep disturbance.
The authors conclude that postpartum physical activity improves maternal sleep quality and fatigue.

items.title: The impact of maternal sleep during pregnancy on childhood health: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 24 population-based studies on how a mother's sleep during pregnancy relates to her child's later health. Poor sleep and sleep disturbance in pregnancy were linked with worse outcomes across several areas of childhood health. The authors say the quality of the studies should be improved, so the findings should be read with some caution.
keyPoints: 24 studies were included, covering childhood metabolism, neurocognition, sleep and allergy.
Poor sleep and sleep disturbance during pregnancy were linked to negative effects on multiple aspects of children's health.
The authors note the quality of the studies should be improved.
Future studies are needed with longer follow-up and more specific ways of measuring maternal sleep and children's health.

items.title: Maternal sleep disordered breathing and offspring growth outcome: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 63 studies of pregnant women to see whether breathing problems during sleep, such as snoring and sleep apnea, are linked to the baby's growth. Habitual snoring and obstructive sleep apnea were linked to a higher chance of the baby being larger than expected for their age in the womb. In studies that identified sleep apnea using medical codes, it was linked to a higher chance of a smaller than expected baby. The authors say more research is needed to understand why, and whether treating sleep problems helps baby growth.
keyPoints: Habitual snoring (based on self-report) was linked to a higher chance of a large-for-gestational-age baby.
Obstructive sleep apnea diagnosed by objective testing was linked to a higher chance of a large-for-gestational-age baby.
Sleep apnea identified through medical codes was linked to a higher chance of a small-for-gestational-age baby.
Results differed by type of sleep breathing disorder and how it was diagnosed; it is not yet known whether treatment improves baby growth.

items.title: A systematic review of behaviour change techniques used in the context of stillbirth prevention
items.summary: This review looked at programmes designed to prevent stillbirth by helping pregnant women change behaviours such as smoking, sleep position, tracking baby's movements and going to antenatal appointments. Nine programmes from high-income countries were included. Most mainly gave information about health risks. The programmes so far have had limited effects on stillbirth rates, though some did lead to changes like less smoking, more knowledge or less time sleeping on the back.
keyPoints: Nine stillbirth prevention programmes were reviewed, covering smoking, baby movement monitoring, sleep position and antenatal care attendance.
Of eight programmes tested for effect, three showed lower stillbirth rates and four changed behaviour, including less time sleeping on the back.
Most programmes relied on giving information about health consequences, and used a limited range of behaviour change methods.
The authors conclude that programmes so far have limited effects on stillbirth and that better-designed approaches are needed.

items.title: The effect of prone positioning on maternal haemodynamics and fetal wellbeing in the third trimester-A primary cohort study with a scoping review
items.summary: Researchers studied 21 women past 28 weeks of pregnancy as they lay on their left side, then on their front (prone), then on their left side again. Lying on the front lowered the amount of blood the heart pumps each minute and raised blood pressure, and fetal accelerations in heart rate were slightly less common. Baby's overall heart rate was not changed. The authors say the effect on baby's wellbeing is uncertain and that more work is needed to make prone positioning safe in pregnancy.
keyPoints: In late pregnancy, lying prone reduced cardiac output (5.7 vs 7.1 in left lateral) and raised blood pressure compared with lying on the left side.
Fetal heart rate, variability and decelerations did not change, but fetal accelerations were less common when prone (86% vs 95%).
A computer model suggested the drop in cardiac output could be due to the main vein (inferior vena cava) being compressed.
A review of 47 case reports found outcomes were generally favourable, but the authors conclude the effect on fetal wellbeing is uncertain.

items.title: Association between sleep duration during pregnancy and preterm birth: a dose-response meta-analysis
items.summary: This study combined results from nine earlier studies to see whether how long a woman sleeps in pregnancy is linked to preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks). Very short and very long sleep were both linked to a slightly higher chance of preterm birth compared with normal sleep. The risk looked lowest at around 7 hours and rose for women sleeping about 4 hours a day. These studies show a link only, so they cannot prove that sleep length causes preterm birth.
keyPoints: Extreme sleep duration, either short or long, in pregnancy was linked to a higher chance of preterm birth compared with normal sleep (summarized relative risk 1.13).
Short sleepers had about a 20% higher relative risk of preterm birth than women with normal sleep.
Using 7 hours of sleep as the reference, women sleeping 4 hours a day had a higher predicted risk of preterm birth.
The relationship was U-shaped: risk was higher at both the short and the long ends of sleep duration.

items.title: Maternal sleep during pregnancy and adverse pregnancy outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 41 studies to see whether how long pregnant women sleep is linked to pregnancy complications. Women who slept for a short time had a higher risk of gestational diabetes, and long sleep was also linked to gestational diabetes and caesarean birth. Short or long sleep was not clearly linked to high blood pressure in pregnancy, preterm birth, low birthweight or small babies. These studies show an association, which does not prove that sleep itself causes these outcomes.
keyPoints: Short sleep in pregnancy was linked to about 1.8 times the risk of gestational diabetes.
Long sleep was also linked to a higher risk of gestational diabetes and of caesarean section.
No significant link was found between short or long sleep and gestational hypertension, preterm birth, low birthweight or small for gestational age.
The authors suggest sleep should be routinely screened in pregnancy care.

items.title: Sleep-disordered breathing in pregnancy: a developmental origin of offspring obesity?
items.source: Journal of Developmental Origins of Health and Disease
items.journal: Journal of Developmental Origins of Health and Disease
items.summary: This review looked at animal and human studies on sleep-disordered breathing (such as sleep apnea and heavy snoring) during pregnancy. It found that these breathing problems are common in pregnancy and are linked to babies being born smaller or larger than expected, which may raise the chance of obesity later in life. The authors say bigger, forward-looking human studies are needed to understand the effects properly.
keyPoints: Sleep-disordered breathing tends to get worse over the course of pregnancy and is common.
Human studies link it to babies being born both small and large for their gestational age, which may raise later obesity risk.
Evidence suggests inflammation and oxidative stress may play a role, possibly affecting the mother's metabolism and the placenta.
The authors call for larger, prospective human studies to confirm the effects on children's metabolic health.

items.title: Women's sleep position during pregnancy in low- and middle-income countries: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked for studies on how pregnant women sleep in lower- and middle-income countries and whether sleep position is linked to stillbirth.
