Out of 3,480 records screened, only two studies (from Ghana and India) qualified, so very little is known. In Ghana, about 1 in 10 women (9.7% of 220) slept on their back. The Indian study could not show a link to stillbirth because it only reported sleep position for women who had a stillbirth.
keyPoints: Only two studies from lower- and middle-income countries met the review's criteria.
In Ghana, 9.7% of 220 pregnant women reported sleeping on their back (supine).
The review could not answer whether sleep position is linked to stillbirth in these countries.
The authors say more research is needed on how pregnant women sleep in these settings, since sleep position may be something that can be changed.

items.title: Sleep disorders during pregnancy and postpartum depression: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 13 observational studies covering about 36,900 women to look at whether sleep problems in pregnancy are linked to postpartum depression. Women who had sleep disorders during pregnancy had around three times the odds of developing postpartum depression. The studies differed a lot from one another, so the exact size of the link is uncertain. The authors suggest that screening pregnant women for sleep problems may be worthwhile.
keyPoints: Sleep disorders during pregnancy were linked to higher odds of postpartum depression (odds ratio about 3.3).
The studies varied greatly in their results (high heterogeneity), so the exact strength of the link is uncertain.
The authors say their findings support screening pregnant women for sleep disturbances.
The review also reported that older age in pregnancy was associated with higher risk of postpartum depression.

items.title: Associations between symptoms of sleep-disordered breathing and maternal sleep patterns with late stillbirth: Findings from an individual participant data meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined data from five case-control studies (851 women whose baby was stillborn at 28 weeks or later, and 2,257 comparison women) to see whether sleep patterns and snoring symptoms were linked to late stillbirth. A positive Berlin Questionnaire (a screening tool for sleep-disordered breathing), sleeping more than 9 hours, and taking daily daytime naps in the last month were linked to higher odds of late stillbirth. Sleep that was more restless than average was linked to lower odds. Snoring on its own, sleep quality and daytime sleepiness were not linked. This type of study shows associations, not cause and effect.
keyPoints: A positive Berlin Questionnaire, sleep over 9 hours, and daily daytime naps in the last month were each linked to higher odds of late stillbirth.
Sleep that was more restless than average was linked to lower odds of late stillbirth.
Any snoring, habitual snoring, sleep quality and daytime sleepiness were not linked to late stillbirth.
The authors suggest the restless sleep common in late pregnancy may be normal and is not linked to higher risk.

items.title: Association of Supine Going-to-Sleep Position in Late Pregnancy With Reduced Birth Weight: A Secondary Analysis of an Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis
items.summary: This study looked at 1,760 women in late pregnancy (28 weeks or more) and asked which position they usually went to sleep in. Babies born to the 57 women who usually went to sleep on their back were about 144 g lighter on average than babies of women who did not. Going to sleep on the back was also linked to a higher chance of the baby being small for gestational age by one growth standard. The authors say the link is plausible and could be changed, but this type of study shows an association, not proof of cause.
keyPoints: Women who usually went to sleep on their back in the last 1 to 4 weeks had babies about 144 g lighter on average (3410 g vs 3554 g).

Going to sleep on the back was linked to about a 3-fold higher chance of a small-for-gestational-age baby by INTERGROWTH-21st standards, but the result was not statistically significant by customized standards.
Only 3.2% of the women reported usually going to sleep on their back.
The authors suggest encouraging women in the third trimester to settle to sleep on their side could help optimise birth weight.

items.title: The intrapartum and perinatal risks of sleep-disordered breathing in pregnancy: a systematic review and metaanalysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 33 studies to see whether pregnant women with sleep-disordered breathing (breathing problems during sleep, such as sleep apnoea) had different labour and baby outcomes than women without it. Women with sleep-disordered breathing were more likely to have a preterm birth, a low-birthweight baby, and a caesarean or assisted vaginal birth. Their babies were also more likely to have a low 5-minute Apgar score, need nursery admission, or die around the time of birth. These are links seen across studies, and the abstract does not say they prove cause and effect.
keyPoints: Sleep-disordered breathing in pregnancy was linked to preterm birth (odds ratio 1.86) and low birthweight (odds ratio 1.67).
Affected women were less likely to have a vaginal birth and more likely to have an assisted vaginal birth or a caesarean, both planned and emergency.
Their babies had higher odds of a low 5-minute Apgar score, neonatal nursery admission, and stillbirth or perinatal death.
Women with sleep-disordered breathing tended to be older and to have a higher body mass index.

items.title: Maternal sleep during pregnancy and poor fetal outcomes: A scoping review of the literature with meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at research on how a mother's sleep during pregnancy relates to the baby's health. It covered sleep apnea (breathing pauses during sleep), poor sleep quality, sleep length and sleeping on the back, and linked them to birth weight, growth, preterm birth and stillbirth. Some studies suggest these sleep problems may affect the baby's growth, how long the pregnancy lasts, and in some cases survival. The authors say the evidence is limited and often conflicting, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Obstructive sleep apnea, disrupted sleep and sleep position may have a negative effect on the baby, including altered growth and length of pregnancy.
These effects are described as biologically and physically plausible.
Evidence on maternal sleep and baby outcomes is limited and often conflicting.
The authors call for more research in this area.

items.title: Do psychosocial sleep interventions improve infant sleep or maternal mood in the postnatal period? A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled nine trials (1,656 mothers) of sleep-focused support programs offered to new parents. Mothers reported their babies slept a little longer at night after these programs, but the babies still woke up just as often. Mothers' mood improved slightly, but this result may have been affected by publication bias, so it needs more research to confirm.
keyPoints: Sleep-focused programs were linked to a small increase in the amount of night-time sleep mothers reported for their babies.
There was no clear evidence that the programs reduced how often babies woke at night.
Maternal mood improved slightly, but this finding could be influenced by publication bias.
More research is needed to know whether better infant sleep leads to better maternal mood.

items.title: Guideline No. 470: Nicotine and Pregnancy
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline from the SOGC gives recommendations on how nicotine use should be handled during pregnancy and after birth. It covers cigarettes, e-cigarettes (vapes) and smokeless tobacco, and calls nicotine use in pregnancy a major preventable cause of poor outcomes for mothers and babies. The guideline recommends that care providers routinely ask about nicotine use, offer counselling first, and consider nicotine replacement or other medicines carefully when needed.
keyPoints: Everyone who is pregnant or planning pregnancy should be routinely screened for nicotine use.
Behavioural counselling is recommended as the first-line approach to quitting.
Nicotine replacement therapy or other medicines can be used cautiously when needed.
Support should continue after the baby is born to help prevent a return to smoking or vaping.

items.title: Incentives for smoking cessation
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled many trials to see whether rewards such as money or vouchers help people stop smoking. In pregnant people who smoke, those offered incentives were about twice as likely to have quit at the longest follow-up, which ran up to 48 weeks after birth. The review rates this evidence as high certainty. Benefits in the wider population also continued for at least six months after the rewards ended.
keyPoints: In 13 trials with 3,942 pregnant people, incentives roughly doubled the chance of having quit smoking (risk ratio 2.13) at the longest follow-up, up to 48 weeks postpartum.
The evidence for pregnant people is now rated high certainty, up from moderate in the previous review.
In 39 studies of mixed populations (18,303 people), incentives raised quit rates by about half (risk ratio 1.52) at six months or longer.
The benefit lasted even when the final follow-up came after the rewards had stopped, and larger rewards did not clearly work better than smaller ones.

items.title: Maternal vaping and pregnancy adverse outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine studies covering about 423,000 pregnant women to look at vaping and pregnancy outcomes. Compared with women who did not smoke, those who vaped had higher chances of preterm birth, low birth weight and a baby that was small for its age. Vaping was not clearly different from smoking tobacco for preterm birth or low birth weight, though the risk of a small-for-age baby was lower than with smoking or with using both together.
keyPoints: Vaping in pregnancy was linked to a 40% higher chance of preterm birth compared with not smoking or vaping.
It was also linked to a 49% higher chance of low birth weight and a 32% higher chance of a baby small for gestational age.
Compared with tobacco smokers, vaping showed no clear difference in preterm birth or low birth weight, but a lower chance of a small-for-age baby.
The authors concluded that vaping in pregnancy is linked to worse outcomes than using no nicotine.

items.title: Vaping and Smoking in Pregnancy-A Meta-Analysis of Neurobehavioural Development in Prenatally Exposed Offspring
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies on what happens to children whose mothers used nicotine or cannabis in pregnancy, by smoking or vaping. In humans, exposure was linked to more difficulty with thinking, emotional and behavioural self-control, and with movement and motor development. Animal studies also point to effects on offspring development. Almost all the human evidence was about regular cigarettes, and only one human study looked at vaping, so we know much less about vaping itself.
keyPoints: Prenatal nicotine or cannabis exposure was linked to poorer self-regulation (thinking, emotions, behaviour) in children.
Exposure was also linked to weaker motor function and neuromotor development.
Only one human study included electronic cigarettes, so the evidence on vaping in pregnancy is very limited.
Animal studies suggest e-cigarette exposure can affect offspring development, and the authors call for more human research.

items.title: Cannabis Use in Pregnancy and Neonatal Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 53 studies to see whether using cannabis during pregnancy is linked to problems for babies around the time of birth. Cannabis use was linked to higher odds of preterm birth, babies being smaller than expected for their age, and death around the time of birth, even after allowing for tobacco use. Average birthweight did not differ in a clear way. The authors say their confidence in these findings is limited because the evidence quality was low or very low.
keyPoints: Cannabis use in pregnancy was linked to higher odds of preterm birth (adjusted odds ratio 1.42).
It was also linked to higher odds of a baby being small for gestational age (1.76) and of perinatal death (1.5).
There was no clear difference in average birthweight.
Most studies did not record when or how much cannabis was used, so confidence in the findings is limited.

items.title: Vaping during pregnancy: a systematic review of health outcomes
items.summary: This review pulled together 26 studies, covering over 765,000 women, on vaping during pregnancy. Most studies found no clear extra risk from vaping compared with using no nicotine, and risks that looked similar to smoking. But most of the studies were of poor quality, so firm conclusions can't be drawn.
keyPoints: More studies found no increased risk from exclusive vaping than compared with using no nicotine or tobacco.
When vaping was compared with smoking, most studies found a similar level of risk.
One trial comparing vaping with nicotine replacement therapy for quitting smoking found no evidence of risk for either.
Most studies did not measure vaping and smoking exposure well, so results can't be reliably linked to vaping alone.

items.title: Clinical Practice Guideline of Spanish Society of Pneumology and Thoracic Surgery (SEPAR) on Pharmacological Treatment of Tobacco Dependence 2023
items.source: Spanish Society of Pneumology and Thoracic Surgery (SEPAR)
items.organisation: Spanish Society of Pneumology and Thoracic Surgery (SEPAR)
items.summary: A Spanish lung specialists' society reviewed the evidence on medicines used to help people stop smoking and turned it into practice recommendations. Varenicline, nicotine replacement, bupropion and cytisine all worked better than placebo, with varenicline and combined nicotine therapy doing best. For pregnancy, the guideline says to put talking-based (behavioral) support first.
keyPoints: Varenicline, nicotine replacement therapy, bupropion and cytisine are more effective than placebo for quitting smoking.
Varenicline and combined nicotine therapy were better than the other treatments.
In pregnancy, behavioral treatment (counselling and support) is the priority.
There is no scientific evidence that quit-smoking medicines work in adolescents.

items.title: S3 Guideline "Smoking and Tobacco Dependence: Screening, Diagnosis, and Treatment" - Short Version
items.summary: This is a German national guideline on helping people stop smoking, written by 63 experts and agreed by 50 professional societies. It recommends starting with brief counselling and phone or app-based support, and moving to behavioural therapy with or without medication if those are not enough. For pregnant women, the guideline says medication should be limited to a few well-defined exceptions and nicotine replacement.
keyPoints: Brief counselling, phone counselling and internet or smartphone support are recommended first-step options for quitting smoking.
If these are not enough, individual or group behavioural therapy is advised, possibly with medication.
If nicotine replacement does not work, varenicline or bupropion should be offered in the general adult population.
In pregnant women and adolescents, medication use should be limited to well-specified exceptions and nicotine replacement.

items.title: Interventions for Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence on ways to help adults, including pregnant people, stop smoking. It found with high certainty that behavioural support, such as counselling, helps pregnant people quit and improves pregnancy outcomes. There was not enough evidence to judge whether stop-smoking medicines or e-cigarettes are safe and helpful for quitting during pregnancy.
keyPoints: Smoking in pregnancy raises the risk of miscarriage, birth defects, sudden infant death syndrome and weaker lung function in childhood.
Behavioural support to quit smoking has a substantial benefit for pregnant people, with high certainty.
Evidence on stop-smoking medicines in pregnancy is insufficient because few studies exist, so benefits and harms cannot be balanced.
Evidence on e-cigarettes as a way to quit is insufficient for adults, including pregnant people, because well-designed trials are missing.

items.title: Pharmacological interventions for promoting smoking cessation during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 11 trials with 2,412 pregnant women who smoked, testing nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) and bupropion alongside behavioural support. NRT may help more women stop smoking by late pregnancy, but the evidence is low certainty and the benefit was not clear in the better-designed placebo-controlled trials. No harm to birth outcomes was found, though the evidence was also limited. Bupropion did not show a benefit, and no trials tested varenicline or e-cigarettes.
keyPoints: NRT may increase the chance of not smoking in late pregnancy, but this evidence is low certainty.
The benefit was unclear in placebo-controlled trials, so future studies may change this conclusion.

No difference was found between NRT and control groups in miscarriage, stillbirth, premature birth, birthweight or other birth outcomes; side effects were mild, such as headache, nausea and skin irritation from patches.
Bupropion showed no benefit for quitting, and there was little safety evidence; no trials tested varenicline or e-cigarettes.

items.title: Factors influencing the uptake and use of nicotine replacement therapy and e-cigarettes in pregnant women who smoke: a qualitative evidence synthesis
items.summary: This review pulled together 21 studies in which pregnant women who smoked shared their views on nicotine replacement therapy (NRT, such as patches or gum) and e-cigarettes. Women said wanting to protect their baby was a main reason for using these products. Advice from health professionals strongly shaped their choices: clear messages that NRT or e-cigarettes are safer than smoking made women feel more confident, while being told they were just as dangerous made them less confident. Most findings were of moderate certainty, with less data on e-cigarettes than on NRT.
keyPoints: Wanting to protect their unborn baby was one of the main reasons women used NRT or e-cigarettes.
Women felt more confident using these products when health professionals said they were safer than smoking and okay to use in pregnancy.
Past experiences with NRT, good or bad, affected whether women were willing to use it again in pregnancy.
The authors suggest consistent, evidence-based messages from health professionals could help women use NRT and e-cigarettes as recommended and stay smoke-free.

items.title: Smoking and smoking cessation in pregnancy. Synthesis of a systematic review
items.source: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.journal: Journal of Gynecology Obstetrics and Human Reproduction
items.summary: This review looked at international research from 2003 to 2019 to work out the best ways to help women stop smoking during pregnancy and after birth. Counselling and other non-drug support had a moderate benefit for quitting, birth weight and premature birth. Nicotine replacement products may be an option for pregnant women who could not quit with non-drug support alone. Smoking after the baby is born matters too, and the same treatment options can be used then.
keyPoints: Counselling and other non-drug support had a moderate benefit for quitting smoking, birth weight and premature birth.
Self-help programmes and health education are recommended to help pregnant smokers quit and should be advised by healthcare professionals.
Nicotine replacement therapy may be prescribed to pregnant women who have not managed to quit with non-drug support.
Smoking in the postpartum period needs attention, and the same treatment options as in pregnancy can be used.

items.title: Telephone counselling for smoking cessation
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 104 trials with over 111,000 people, mostly adult smokers from the general population, to see whether telephone counselling helps people quit smoking. Smokers who got proactive phone counselling (where the counsellor calls them) were more likely to quit than those given self-help materials or a single brief call. The review also covers some trials that included pregnant women, but it does not report results for pregnancy separately. The evidence is moderate in certainty, and many trials had a high risk of bias.
keyPoints: Among people who called a quitline, multiple proactive counselling sessions led to higher quit rates than self-help materials or one brief call.
Among smokers who did not call a helpline, being offered telephone counselling also raised quit rates.
Telephone support worked better for people motivated to quit, and when added to self-help materials or a brief talk with a health professional.
Evidence on reactive counselling (where the smoker makes the call) was inconclusive because few studies looked at it.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 721 Summary: Smoking Cessation During Pregnancy
items.summary: This guidance from US obstetricians explains that smoking is one of the most important changeable causes of poor pregnancy outcomes, linked to health problems and deaths in mothers, babies and infants. Quitting is hard because cigarettes are powerfully addictive, but caring support from a pregnancy care provider can make a big difference. Short counselling sessions with pregnancy-specific materials and a referral to a quit line help people stop smoking. There is little data on the health effects of e-cigarettes and vaping, including in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Smoking is one of the most important modifiable causes of poor pregnancy outcomes and is linked to maternal, fetal and infant illness and death.
Clinics that routinely identify pregnant women who smoke and offer treatment or referral see higher quit rates.
A short counselling session with pregnancy-specific materials plus referral to a smokers' quit line is an effective way to help quit.
Little is known about the health effects of e-cigarettes and vaping, in the general population or in pregnancy.

items.title: Committee Opinion Summary NO. 722: Marijuana Use During Pregnancy and Lactation
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from an obstetrics and gynecology committee about marijuana (cannabis) use before and during pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Because of concerns about a baby's brain development and the harms of smoking, women who are pregnant or planning pregnancy are encouraged to stop using marijuana. There is not enough research to know how marijuana affects breastfed babies, so use during breastfeeding is discouraged.
keyPoints: Women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy should be encouraged to stop using marijuana, because of concerns about impaired neurodevelopment and the effects of smoking.
Doctors are discouraged from prescribing or suggesting medical marijuana before pregnancy, during pregnancy, and while breastfeeding.
Women using marijuana for medical reasons are encouraged to switch to an alternative treatment that has better pregnancy safety data.
There are not enough data on how marijuana affects breastfed infants, so use during breastfeeding is discouraged.

items.title: Behavioral and Pharmacotherapy Interventions for Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Women: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force updated its advice on helping adults, including pregnant women, stop smoking tobacco. It recommends that health professionals ask about tobacco use, advise quitting, and offer counselling-based support. For pregnant women, there is not enough evidence to judge the benefits and harms of stop-smoking medicines, or of e-cigarettes as a way to quit.
keyPoints: All adults, including pregnant women, should be asked about tobacco use and advised to stop (an 'A' recommendation, the Task Force's strongest grade).
Pregnant women who smoke should be offered behavioral support (counselling-type help) to quit.
Evidence is insufficient to judge the balance of benefits and harms of stop-smoking medicines in pregnant women.
Evidence is insufficient to recommend e-cigarettes (electronic nicotine delivery systems) for quitting smoking in adults, including pregnant women.

items.title: Lenacapavir as pre-exposure prophylaxis for HIV prevention
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at lenacapavir, a long-acting injection taken twice a year to prevent HIV (PrEP), and compared it with daily PrEP pills. It combined two large trials with 8660 people, including young women aged 16 to 25 in South Africa and Uganda. Lenacapavir led to far fewer new HIV infections than daily pills over 52 weeks, with high-certainty evidence. Injection site reactions were more common, but stopping because of them was rare.
keyPoints: Lenacapavir cut new HIV infections by a large amount compared with daily oral PrEP at 52 weeks (about 14 fewer infections per 1000 people), with high-certainty evidence.
Serious side effects were slightly less common with lenacapavir, and overall side effects were about the same as with oral PrEP.
Injection site reactions were likely more common with lenacapavir (moderate-certainty evidence), but few people stopped because of them.
No trials compared lenacapavir with the other long-acting injection (cabotegravir), placebo or no PrEP.

items.title: Antiretroviral Drugs for Treatment and Prevention of HIV in Adults: 2024 Recommendations of the International Antiviral Society-USA Panel
items.summary: An expert panel updated its guidance on HIV treatment and prevention for adults, based on new research and new drugs. It recommends antiretroviral therapy for everyone with HIV, with most people starting a regimen built around bictegravir or dolutegravir. For prevention, daily or as-needed pills and long-acting injections are effective options for people more likely to be exposed to HIV. The panel notes that ending the HIV epidemic also depends on fixing unequal access to care.
keyPoints: Antiretroviral therapy is recommended for all people with HIV.
Most people start with an integrase inhibitor (bictegravir or dolutegravir) plus 1 or 2 other HIV medicines, with specific advice for situations such as pregnancy.
Long-acting injectable treatment is available for people who prefer not to take daily pills or who find daily treatment hard.
Pills (daily or intermittent) and long-acting injections are effective ways to prevent HIV, and doxycycline taken after sex is recommended to help prevent other sexually transmitted infections.

items.title: Recent Guidelines on Anal Cancer Screening: A Systematic Review
items.source: Journal of Lower Genital Tract Disease
items.journal: Journal of Lower Genital Tract Disease
items.summary: This review looked at six recent medical society recommendations on screening for anal cancer, all published after a major trial called ANCHOR. The societies agree on some points, such as testing with a cell sample (anal cytology) and treating precancerous changes, but differ on who to screen and when to follow up. Some groups cover only people living with HIV, while others also cover women with vulvar cancer or precancerous vulvar changes and female transplant recipients.
keyPoints: Six society recommendations published since July 2022 were reviewed; three covered only people living with HIV and three also covered other higher-risk groups, including women with vulvar cancer or high-grade vulvar lesions and female transplant recipients.
Four societies recommended anal cytology, with or without HPV testing, as the first screening method; one offered several options and one suggested HPV type 16 testing.
Societies recommended a closer examination called high-resolution anoscopy after abnormal results, but the point at which to refer varied between them.
All societies that mentioned treating precancerous anal lesions recommended it, and four also advised quitting smoking and/or HPV vaccination.

items.title: Estimating the effect of maternal viral load on perinatal and postnatal HIV transmission: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pooled 147 studies covering 82,723 mother-baby pairs to see how a mother's HIV viral load relates to passing HIV to her baby around birth and while breastfeeding. Transmission around birth was very rare (0.2% or less) when the viral load was undetectable (under 50 copies per mL), and rose as the viral load went up. No transmissions were seen among women who started HIV treatment before pregnancy and were undetectable near birth. The risk during breastfeeding was very low but not zero, and the data are not yet enough to say whether 'undetectable equals untransmittable' applies to breastfeeding.
keyPoints: Risk of passing HIV to the baby around birth was 0.2% with a viral load under 50 copies per mL, 1.3% at 50-999, and 5.1% at 1000 or more.
Among 4,675 women on treatment before pregnancy who were undetectable near birth, there were zero transmissions, supporting 'undetectable equals untransmittable' in pregnancy and birth.
Monthly risk during breastfeeding was 0.1% with a recent undetectable viral load and 0.5% with a viral load of 50 or more.
Current breastfeeding data are limited, often lacking frequent viral load checks or modern treatment, so they cannot confirm 'undetectable equals untransmittable' during breastfeeding.

items.title: Probability of vertical HIV transmission: a systematic review and meta-regression
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 110 studies to estimate how likely HIV is to pass from a mother to her baby, and what changes that chance. The chance of passing on HIV was lower when the mother had a higher CD4 count (a measure of immune health) and when she had been on HIV medicine for longer before delivery. Starting treatment earlier in pregnancy also made it more likely that the virus was undetectable at delivery. The authors say more evidence is needed on how newer treatments affect transmission.
keyPoints: For women not on HIV treatment, a higher CD4 count was linked to lower odds of passing HIV to the baby around birth.
For women on treatment, each extra week on HIV medicine before delivery lowered the odds of transmission by 5.6%.
Starting HIV treatment late in pregnancy was linked to lower odds of an undetectable viral load at delivery.
Integrase inhibitor-based treatment looked better than another type, but the authors note this was confounded by study region.

items.title: CDC Clinical Guidelines on the Use of Doxycycline Postexposure Prophylaxis for Bacterial Sexually Transmitted Infection Prevention, United States, 2024
items.summary: This is a US CDC guideline on taking the antibiotic doxycycline after sex to help prevent syphilis, chlamydia and gonorrhea. In three large trials, a 200 mg dose taken within 72 hours after sex cut syphilis and chlamydia infections by more than 70% and gonorrhea by about half. The CDC recommends offering it to gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men and to transgender women who had one of these infections in the past 12 months, after a shared decision with their provider.
keyPoints: Doxycycline 200 mg taken within 72 hours after oral, vaginal or anal sex reduced syphilis and chlamydia by over 70% and gonorrhea by about 50% in three randomized trials.
The CDC recommends counseling and a prescription for men who have sex with men and transgender women who had syphilis, chlamydia or gonorrhea in the past 12 months.
The dose should not exceed 200 mg in 24 hours, and it should be part of wider sexual health care including STI testing, vaccination and HIV prevention or care.
People using it should be tested for STIs at baseline and every 3-6 months, and their ongoing need should be reviewed at the same times.

items.title: [Translated article] AEDV Expert Consensus for the Management of Syphilis
items.summary: This is an expert consensus statement from Spanish dermatology and venereology specialists on managing syphilis, an infection that is becoming more common again in Western countries. It covers how syphilis can look, how it is diagnosed and followed up, and how it is treated. Penicillin is the treatment of choice for every form of syphilis, including in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Penicillin is the treatment of choice for all forms of syphilis, including in pregnant women and people living with HIV; macrolide antibiotics are not advised because of possible resistance.
Anyone diagnosed with syphilis should also be offered HIV testing and screening for other sexually transmitted infections, and their sexual contacts should be assessed and treated as appropriate.
Pregnant women should be screened for syphilis in the first trimester, and all women who have a pregnancy loss after week 20 should be tested.
Follow-up blood tests after treatment, using the same non-treponemal test each time, check that the infection has healed and help detect reinfection.

items.title: Doxycycline prophylaxis for the prevention of sexually transmitted infections: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled results from six randomized trials testing whether taking the antibiotic doxycycline around the time of sex lowers the chance of bacterial sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Taking doxycycline after sex cut new chlamydia and syphilis cases substantially in men who have sex with men and transgender women, and may help against gonorrhea too. No serious side effects were reported. Most of the evidence is from men who have sex with men and transgender women, so it says less about other groups.
keyPoints: Doxycycline taken before or after sex reduced overall STI cases by about 56% across the pooled trials.
Taking it after sex (doxy-PEP) lowered chlamydia and syphilis cases a lot and gonorrhea cases to a smaller degree.
How well it works against gonorrhea may depend on local antibiotic resistance patterns.
No serious adverse events were reported, and the evidence for doxy-PEP in men who have sex with men and transgender women was rated high certainty.

items.title: Intermittent preventive treatment regimens for malaria in HIV-positive pregnant women
items.summary: This review pooled 14 trials of nearly 5,000 pregnant women with HIV in areas where malaria is common. It looked at whether adding another anti-malaria drug (mefloquine or dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine) to daily cotrimoxazole protects better than cotrimoxazole alone. Adding either drug seemed to lower malaria infection in the mother and placenta. Dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine did not appear to raise the risk of passing HIV to the baby and was well tolerated, while mefloquine had a possible higher HIV transmission risk and tolerability problems.
keyPoints: Adding mefloquine or dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine to daily cotrimoxazole probably lowers malaria parasites in the mother's blood at delivery and malaria in the placenta (moderate-certainty evidence).
Dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine plus cotrimoxazole led to fewer women with placental malaria on tissue testing (high-certainty evidence).
Neither approach made much difference to anaemia, low birth weight, pregnancy loss or newborn deaths.

Mefloquine may raise the risk of HIV passing to the baby and was poorly tolerated, whereas dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine showed no clear increase in HIV transmission or side effects (low-certainty evidence).

items.title: DNA methylation as a triage marker for colposcopy referral in HPV-based cervical cancer screening: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Cervical screening now often starts with a test for high-risk HPV, which finds most cases but also flags many women who do not need treatment. This review pooled 23 studies of DNA methylation tests, which look for chemical changes in cervical cells, as a second step for HPV-positive women. The tests picked up high-grade cell changes reasonably well, and a negative result was fairly reassuring. The authors say the tests show great potential, but they need standardising and better validation before wider use.
keyPoints: Pooled across 23 studies, methylation tests detected CIN2+ with 68% sensitivity and 75% specificity.
For the more serious CIN3+ changes, sensitivity was 78% and specificity 74%.
A negative result was fairly reassuring: negative predictive value was 86% for CIN2+ and 94% for CIN3+.
These tests may be a good alternative to cytology and genotyping for deciding who needs colposcopy, and could make screening more cost-effective.

items.title: 2021 European guideline on the management of Mycoplasma genitalium infections
items.source: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology
items.journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology
items.summary: This European guideline explains how Mycoplasma genitalium, a sexually transmitted infection, should be diagnosed and treated. Many infections cause no symptoms, so testing is now mainly for people who have symptoms. Treatment depends on whether the infection is resistant to macrolide antibiotics, so testing for resistance is important. Because resistance is rising, the guideline narrows who should be tested and treated.
keyPoints: In women, M. genitalium is linked to cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease in 10-25% of cases, and many infections cause no symptoms.
Diagnosis needs a special lab test (nucleic acid amplification) that also checks for macrolide resistance.
Azithromycin cures 85-95% of infections that are not macrolide-resistant, while doxycycline alone cures only 30-40%.
Moxifloxacin is the second-line treatment and is used for longer in complicated infections such as pelvic inflammatory disease, but resistance to it is increasing.

items.title: Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to prevent HIV: a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical effectiveness, safety, adherence and risk compensation in all populations
items.summary: This review pulled together 15 randomised trials with over 25,000 people to see whether taking daily HIV prevention pills (oral PrEP) works and is safe. PrEP clearly lowered HIV infections in men who have sex with men, in couples where one partner has HIV, and in people who inject drugs. It did not show a clear benefit in heterosexual participants, so more research is needed there. It worked best in people who took the pills as prescribed, and no increase in risky behaviour or other sexually transmitted infections was found.
keyPoints: PrEP cut HIV infection rates in men who have sex with men, serodiscordant couples and people who inject drugs.
No clear benefit was seen in heterosexual participants, and the authors say more research is needed before recommending it for this group.
How well PrEP worked was strongly linked to how consistently people took it.
PrEP was found to be safe, but starting it with an unrecognised HIV infection raised the risk of drug-resistant virus.

items.title: Accuracy and effectiveness of HPV mRNA testing in cervical cancer screening: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at a type of cervical screening test that detects the activity (mRNA) of high-risk HPV, and compared it with the more common HPV DNA tests. The mRNA test studied (called APTIMA) found precancerous changes about as well as DNA tests and was slightly better at correctly ruling out women without them. It could be suitable for routine screening on samples taken by a clinician at around 5-year intervals. It was less sensitive on samples women collected themselves than on clinician-collected samples.
keyPoints: On clinician-collected samples, the APTIMA mRNA test was similarly sensitive to validated HPV DNA tests for CIN2+ and CIN3+ (precancerous cervical changes) and slightly more specific.

Over 4-7 years of follow-up, safety results after a negative mRNA test versus a negative DNA test were varied, and one study with up to 10 years of follow-up showed no difference in later detection of CIN3+.
The authors say APTIMA could be accepted for primary cervical screening on clinician-collected samples at intervals of around 5 years.
On self-collected samples, APTIMA was less sensitive for CIN2+ than on clinician-collected samples, with similar specificity.

items.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021
items.summary: This is the CDC's updated guideline on how to treat and prevent sexually transmitted infections (STIs), replacing the 2015 version. It was updated after experts met in 2019. It covers changes to treatment for gonorrhea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis, plus pelvic inflammatory disease, bacterial vaginosis and other infections. It is written to help health care providers, and the abstract does not rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Treatment recommendations were updated for gonorrhea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis.
Metronidazole was added to the recommended treatment for pelvic inflammatory disease, and there are new alternative options for bacterial vaginosis.
More risk factors now count for syphilis testing in pregnant women, and one-time testing for hepatitis C is recommended.
The guideline also updates advice on HPV vaccination, Mycoplasma genitalium, and two-step blood testing for genital herpes.

items.title: Management of Genital Herpes in Pregnancy: ACOG Practice Bulletinacog Practice Bulletin, Number 220
items.summary: This guideline from ACOG covers how to manage genital herpes during pregnancy. Genital herpes is common, so many women of childbearing age are infected or may become infected, and the virus can pass to the baby during pregnancy or birth. The update says that for women whose first-ever herpes episode happens in the third trimester, cesarean delivery may be offered because the virus can keep shedding for a long time.
keyPoints: Genital herpes during pregnancy can pose a risk to the developing baby and newborn.
About 15.9% of females aged 14 to 49 in the United States have HSV-2 infection, and the total with genital herpes is higher because HSV-1 also causes it.
Passing the virus from mother to baby is a major health concern because so many women of childbearing age are infected or will be.
For a first-episode infection in the third trimester, cesarean delivery may be offered because of possible prolonged viral shedding.

items.title: Antibiotics for treating urogenital Chlamydia trachomatis infection in men and non-pregnant women
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 14 trials (about 2,700 people, mostly men) comparing antibiotics for genital chlamydia infection. In men, a single dose of azithromycin was probably less likely to clear the infection than a week of doxycycline, though there may be little difference in symptoms. For women, the evidence was too limited to say which antibiotic works better.
keyPoints: In men, azithromycin probably fails to clear the chlamydia infection more often than doxycycline (moderate-quality evidence).
For women, it is uncertain whether azithromycin or doxycycline works better, because few women were studied and the evidence was very low quality.
Azithromycin probably causes slightly fewer side effects than doxycycline overall, and the side effects reported were mostly mild and stomach-related.
Doxycycline versus ofloxacin could not be reliably compared, and no studies looked at antibiotic resistance or reinfection.

items.title: Rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy for people living with HIV
items.summary: This review pulled together seven trials with about 18,000 adults living with HIV in low- and middle-income countries. It compared starting HIV treatment (antiretroviral therapy, or ART) within seven days of diagnosis with standard care. Starting quickly probably led to more people having an undetectable virus level and staying on treatment after 12 months. The effect on deaths was uncertain, and there was not enough evidence to judge side effects.
keyPoints: Starting ART within 7 days of diagnosis probably increases viral suppression at 12 months (moderate-certainty evidence).
Rapid starts probably improve ART uptake at 12 months (moderate-certainty) and may improve staying in care (low-certainty).
Deaths were lower with rapid ART, but the result could be due to chance (very low-certainty evidence).
The benefits came from rapid ART delivered with extra supports, and there was not enough evidence on adverse events.

items.title: Psychosocial group interventions to improve psychological well-being in adults living with HIV
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 16 trials with about 2,500 adults living with HIV to see whether group-based support programmes improve mental well-being. Groups using cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) may lower depression slightly, and the benefit may last up to 15 months. There was little or no effect on anxiety, stress or coping, and mindfulness groups showed no clear benefit. The evidence is low or very low quality, so it is not clear how much difference these groups make in daily life.
keyPoints: CBT-based group programmes may have a small effect on depression, lasting up to 15 months (low certainty evidence).
The average depression score was only about 1.4 points lower on a 63-point scale, and the review says the clinical importance is unclear.
There may be little or no effect on anxiety, stress or coping.
Mindfulness-based groups did not show clear effects on depression, anxiety or stress (very low certainty evidence).

items.title: Interventions for treating genital Chlamydia trachomatis infection in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 15 trials (1754 women) on treating genital chlamydia infection during pregnancy. Erythromycin, and possibly clindamycin, cleared the infection more often than placebo. The antibiotics compared (amoxicillin, erythromycin, clindamycin, azithromycin) worked about equally well. Azithromycin and clindamycin caused fewer side effects, such as nausea and stomach cramps, than erythromycin.
keyPoints: Treating chlamydia in pregnancy with antibiotics clears the infection; erythromycin and clindamycin worked better than placebo.
No clear difference in cure or repeat infection was found between amoxicillin, erythromycin, clindamycin and azithromycin.
Azithromycin, clindamycin and amoxicillin had fewer side effects than erythromycin, mostly stomach-related.
No clear differences were seen in preterm birth, early waters breaking or low birthweight, but few trials reported these outcomes.

items.title: Iodine supplementation for preventing iodine deficiency disorders in children and adolescents
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled eight trials with 2,528 children and teenagers to see whether iodine supplements, compared with placebo, help prevent problems caused by low iodine. Iodine gave a slight boost in thinking skills and likely lowered the risk of an underactive thyroid and of death in infants. It probably made little or no difference to weight. Evidence on goitre (a swollen thyroid) was very uncertain, and none of the trials reported side effects.
keyPoints: Iodine supplements slightly improved cognitive (thinking) function compared with placebo, based on high-certainty evidence from one study.
Iodine likely greatly reduced hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) and lowered infant deaths, both with moderate-certainty evidence from single studies.
Iodine may make little or no difference to children's weight (low-certainty evidence).
The effect on goitre is very uncertain overall, and no trial reported side effects or quality of life.

items.title: Efficacy and Safety of Teprotumumab in Thyroid Eye Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from 10 studies of teprotumumab, a medicine approved in the US for thyroid eye disease (the eye problems linked to Graves' disease). Compared with placebo, it reduced bulging of the eyes, improved double vision and lowered disease activity. Side effects and serious side effects were more common with teprotumumab. The authors say it could become an important first-line treatment.
keyPoints: Teprotumumab improved eye bulging (proptosis), double vision and disease activity score compared with placebo in randomised trials.
In observational studies, 82% of patients had a proptosis response, with an average reduction of about 3.3 mm.
Adverse events and serious adverse events were more common with teprotumumab than with placebo.
The benefits were seen regardless of previous treatments, disease severity or dose.

items.title: ETA guidelines for the use of levothyroxine sodium preparations in monotherapy to optimize the treatment of hypothyroidism
items.summary: The European Thyroid Association (ETA) expert group looked at how levothyroxine, the standard medicine for an underactive thyroid, is used in everyday life. Many people on it still do not reach their goals of feeling better and having a well-controlled TSH level. The group made suggestions to get more out of treatment, stressing that the plan should be tailored to each person. They also discuss food, medicines and health conditions that can raise the amount of levothyroxine needed, including liquid and softgel forms of the medicine.
keyPoints: Levothyroxine on its own is the mainstay treatment for hypothyroidism, but many people do not reach symptom relief and target TSH levels.
The guideline stresses that treatment should be individualized to each person.
Food, other medicines and certain health conditions can increase how much levothyroxine a person needs.
The guideline gives specific attention to liquid and softgel versions of levothyroxine.

items.title: Efficiency and Safety of Tocilizumab for the Treatment of Thyroid Eye Disease: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at 29 studies of tocilizumab, a medicine used for thyroid eye disease, mostly in people whose condition did not respond to steroids or kept coming back. It found the medicine often reduced eye inflammation during the active phase and often reduced bulging of the eyes. No severe side effects were reported. Most studies were case reports or small case series and only one randomized trial was found, so more direct comparisons with other treatments are still needed.
keyPoints: Tocilizumab has mainly been used in thyroid eye disease that resisted glucocorticoids or relapsed.
It was mostly effective at reducing inflammatory signs, with an overall relapse rate of 8.2%.
Many studies showed less eye bulging (proptosis), though the only randomized trial found a non-significant improvement at 6 months.
No severe side effects were reported with intravenous or subcutaneous use.

items.title: Association between primary hypothyroidism and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: an updated meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 28 observational studies covering about 76.5 million people to see whether an underactive thyroid (primary hypothyroidism) is linked to fatty liver disease, now called MASLD. People with hypothyroidism were more likely to have MASLD, and much more likely to have its more serious forms, such as steatohepatitis or advanced scarring. Because these studies only observe people, they show a link rather than proving that hypothyroidism causes liver disease.
keyPoints: Primary hypothyroidism was linked to a higher chance of having fatty liver disease (MASLD), with an odds ratio of 1.43.
The link was stronger for the more severe forms (steatohepatitis or advanced fibrosis), with an odds ratio of 2.84.
Over about 4.5 years of follow-up, the link to developing new MASLD was borderline and not statistically significant.
The authors conclude that hypothyroidism is associated with both having MASLD and its severity.

items.title: Comparison of the safety between propylthiouracil and methimazole with hyperthyroidism in pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 13 studies to compare two anti-thyroid medicines, propylthiouracil (PTU) and methimazole (MMI), for an overactive thyroid during pregnancy. Women treated with MMI had a higher risk of babies born with congenital anomalies than those treated with PTU. The two medicines did not differ clearly in liver damage or miscarriage. The authors concluded PTU is the safer choice in the first trimester, but it is unclear whether switching between the two medicines helps.
keyPoints: Methimazole was linked to a higher risk of congenital anomalies than propylthiouracil.
No clear difference was found between the two medicines for liver toxicity or miscarriage.
Switching between the two medicines during pregnancy did not clearly lower birth defect risk compared with PTU alone.
The authors say PTU is appropriate for treating maternal thyroid disease in the first trimester.

items.title: Effect of physical exercise in people with hypothyroidism: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: Scandinavian Journal of Clinical and Laboratory Investigation
items.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Clinical and Laboratory Investigation
items.summary: This review pulled together 10 studies on exercise programmes in people with an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism), mostly women with the mild, subclinical form. Exercise appeared safe, and aerobic and resistance training seemed to help physical and mental health. It did not significantly change thyroid hormone levels such as TSH, FT3 or FT4. The studies were of low to moderate quality, so the results are uncertain.
keyPoints: Exercise seemed safe for people with hypothyroidism.
Aerobic and resistance training were linked to improvements in physical and mental health outcomes.
Exercise did not have a significant effect on thyroid function (TSH, FT3 and FT4 levels).
The 10 studies were of low to moderate quality and most involved women with subclinical hypothyroidism.

items.title: Rituximab for thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at rituximab, an antibody medicine given through a drip, for active thyroid eye disease linked to Graves' disease. Only two small trials (56 people in total) were found, and both stopped early. The review concludes there is not enough evidence to support using rituximab for this condition. Side effects, such as infusion reactions, were more common with rituximab.
keyPoints: Only two small trials met the review's criteria, and both were stopped early.
Compared with steroid treatment, rituximab may improve eye inflammation scores at 24 weeks, but the evidence is low certainty; evidence for other outcomes was very low certainty.
Compared with placebo, rituximab showed no clear benefit, and the evidence was very low certainty.
Side effects were more common with rituximab, including mild infusion reactions in most people and two major reactions in one trial.

items.title: Congenital Hypothyroidism: A 2020-2021 Consensus Guidelines Update-An ENDO-European Reference Network Initiative Endorsed by the European Society for Pediatric Endocrinology and the European Society for Endocrinology
items.summary: This is an updated set of European expert guidelines on congenital hypothyroidism, a condition where a baby is born with an underactive thyroid. The experts reviewed the research on newborn screening, diagnosis and treatment. They recommend starting the right dose of levothyroxine (thyroid hormone medicine) straight away once the condition is found, with regular follow-up checks.
keyPoints: Newborn screening helps find congenital hypothyroidism early, and the guidelines support its benefits.
Once diagnosed, treatment with correctly dosed levothyroxine should start immediately.
Frequent follow-up and blood tests keep thyroid hormone levels in the target range, with attention to brain development and senses such as hearing and vision.
People with the condition should have a well-planned move from children's to adult care.

items.title: Evidence-Based Use of Levothyroxine/Liothyronine Combinations in Treating Hypothyroidism: A Consensus Document
items.summary: Three major thyroid societies (American, British and European) looked at whether adding liothyronine (LT3) to standard levothyroxine (LT4) helps people with hypothyroidism. Fourteen earlier trials have not shown a consistent benefit, yet many patients say they feel better on the combination. The experts agreed a new, better-designed trial is justified and set out how it should be run. This paper does not recommend combination treatment for routine use.
keyPoints: Fourteen earlier clinical trials did not show a consistent benefit of LT4/LT3 combination therapy, though it is widely used and some patients report feeling better.
Experts agreed there is enough uncertainty to justify a new clinical trial of combination therapy.
Future trials should include people who are unhappy with their current treatment, use patient-reported outcomes as the main measure, and use a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind design.
Trials should also look at whether gene differences affecting thyroid hormone handling change who benefits.

items.title: The 2021 European Group on Graves' orbitopathy (EUGOGO) clinical practice guidelines for the medical management of Graves' orbitopathy
items.summary: These are 2021 European expert guidelines on how to treat Graves' orbitopathy, an eye condition linked to Graves' disease (an overactive thyroid). Treatment depends on how active and how severe the eye disease is, and early referral to a specialist centre is advised for most people. The guidelines cover mild, moderate-to-severe and sight-threatening disease, and surgery for lasting changes once the disease has settled.
keyPoints: Risk factors include smoking, thyroid dysfunction, high levels of thyrotropin receptor antibodies, radioactive iodine treatment and high cholesterol.

In mild, active disease, controlling risk factors, local treatments and selenium (in areas where selenium is low) are usually enough; low-dose oral prednisone is needed alongside radioactive iodine, especially if risk factors are present.

For active moderate-to-severe disease, glucocorticoids given into a vein work better and are better tolerated than tablets, and are recommended together with mycophenolate sodium as first-line treatment.
Sight-threatening disease is treated with high doses of intravenous methylprednisolone and, if there is no response, urgent surgery to relieve pressure around the eye.

items.title: Association Between Gut Microbiota and Autoimmune Thyroid Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together eight studies, covering 196 people with autoimmune thyroid disease (such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis and Graves' disease), and compared their gut bacteria with people without the condition. The mix of bacteria in the gut was different in people with thyroid disease. This shows a link, but the abstract does not say that gut bacteria cause thyroid disease or that changing them would help.
keyPoints: Gut bacteria differed between people with autoimmune thyroid disease and people without it.
Variety of gut bacteria was higher in Hashimoto's thyroiditis and lower in Graves' disease compared with controls.
Helpful bacteria such as Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus were lower in autoimmune thyroid disease, while Bacteroides fragilis was higher.
The authors describe an association only, based on a small number of studies.

items.title: Thyroid hormones treatment for subclinical hypothyroidism: a clinical practice guideline
items.summary: This guideline looked at whether thyroid hormone tablets help adults with subclinical hypothyroidism, where TSH is raised but thyroxine (free T4) is normal. A review of 21 trials with 2192 people found no clinically meaningful benefit for quality of life, tiredness, depressive symptoms or weight. The panel strongly recommends against treatment for most adults and suggests monitoring the thyroid over time instead. It does not apply to women trying to become pregnant or to people with very high TSH, and may not apply to people with severe symptoms or those aged 30 or under.
keyPoints: Strong recommendation against thyroid hormones for adults with subclinical hypothyroidism (raised TSH, normal free T4).
Moderate to high quality evidence shows no clinically relevant benefit for quality of life, thyroid-related symptoms, depressive symptoms, fatigue or body mass index.
Low quality evidence suggests little or no effect on cardiovascular events or death; harms were measured in only one trial.
The recommendation does not apply to women trying to become pregnant or to people with TSH above 20 mIU/L; instead, thyroid function should be monitored.

items.title: Radioiodine therapy versus antithyroid medications for Graves' disease
items.summary: This Cochrane review compared radioiodine treatment with the antithyroid drug methimazole for Graves' disease, the most common cause of an overactive thyroid. It found only two trials with 425 adults. Eye problems linked to Graves' disease developed or got worse more often after radioiodine (38%) than after methimazole (19%). Radioiodine may lower the chance of the overactive thyroid coming back, but the evidence is very uncertain, and quality was low or very low for most results.
keyPoints: Eye problems (Graves' ophthalmopathy) developed or worsened in 38% of people given radioiodine versus 19% given methimazole (low quality evidence).
Radioiodine may reduce the chance of the overactive thyroid coming back, but the size of this benefit is uncertain (very low quality evidence).

Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) was very common after radioiodine, but thyroid hormone replacement was not started early in that trial; about 11% on methimazole had likely drug-related side effects.
Quality of life looked similar between the two treatments, but no numbers were reported, and only methimazole was tested among antithyroid drugs.

items.title: 2016 American Thyroid Association Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
items.summary: The American Thyroid Association updated its 2011 guidelines on diagnosing and treating an overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism) and other causes of too much thyroid hormone (thyrotoxicosis). An expert panel reviewed the research and rated how strong each recommendation is and how good the evidence behind it is. The guideline covers treatment options such as radioactive iodine, antithyroid medicines and surgery, and includes advice for pregnant patients, children and teenagers.
keyPoints: The guideline gives 124 evidence-based recommendations for caring for people with thyrotoxicosis.
It covers Graves' disease treatment with radioactive iodine, antithyroid drugs or surgery, and treatment of toxic nodules and goiter.
It includes updated advice on managing hyperthyroidism in pregnancy, as well as in children, adolescents and people with Graves' eye disease.
Choosing a treatment depends on the exact cause, other health conditions and patient preference.

items.title: 2016 Guidelines for the management of thyroid storm from The Japan Thyroid Association and Japan Endocrine Society (First edition)
items.source: Japan Thyroid Association and Japan Endocrine Society
items.organisation: Japan Thyroid Association and Japan Endocrine Society
items.summary: This is a clinical guideline from Japanese thyroid and endocrine societies on thyroid storm, a rare emergency where severe overactive thyroid causes multiple organs to fail. Looking at 356 patients in Japan, about 11% still died, most often from multiple organ failure or acute heart failure. The guideline sets out 15 recommendations for treatment, intensive care admission and prevention, based on national surveys and literature searches.
keyPoints: Thyroid storm is an endocrine emergency; early suspicion, prompt diagnosis and intensive treatment improve survival.
In 356 patients in Japan, mortality was about 11%, with multiple organ failure and acute heart failure the common causes of death.
Combined treatment with antithyroid drugs, inorganic iodide, corticosteroids and beta-blockers has been suggested to improve survival.
The guideline gives 15 recommendations covering treatment, ICU admission criteria, prognosis and preventive approaches.

items.title: Chinese herbal medicines for hypothyroidism
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for good-quality trials testing Chinese herbal medicines as a treatment for hypothyroidism (an underactive thyroid). The reviewers searched major medical and Chinese databases up to September 2014 and found no randomised trials, so they could not say whether these herbal medicines work. No ongoing registered trials were found either.
keyPoints: No randomised trials of Chinese herbal medicines for hypothyroidism were found.
Because of this, the effects of these herbs on hypothyroidism could not be established.
No ongoing registered trials on the topic were found.

items.title: Thyroid surgery for Graves' disease and Graves' ophthalmopathy
items.summary: This review looked at five trials (886 people) comparing different types of thyroid surgery for Graves' disease, an autoimmune condition that causes an overactive thyroid. Removing the whole thyroid was better at stopping the overactive thyroid from coming back than leaving part of it in place. However, whole-thyroid removal carried a higher chance of permanently low calcium levels, which is linked to the parathyroid glands. The overall quality of the evidence was low to moderate, and no study looked at quality of life.
keyPoints: Total thyroidectomy was better than partial (subtotal) surgery at preventing hyperthyroidism from returning, based on moderate quality evidence.
Total thyroidectomy carried a greater risk of permanent low calcium or parathyroid problems than subtotal surgery, based on low quality evidence.
The type of surgery did not change how Graves' eye disease (ophthalmopathy) improved, and did not seem to affect permanent voice-nerve palsy.
No trial measured quality of life or costs, so these are still unknown.

items.title: Association of gestational thyroid function and thyroid autoimmunity with gestational diabetes: a systematic review and individual participant meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled individual data from about 63,500 pregnant people in 25 studies to see whether thyroid blood tests and thyroid antibodies were linked to gestational diabetes. Lower levels of the thyroid hormone free T4, and a pattern called isolated hypothyroxinaemia (low free T4 with normal TSH), were linked to a higher chance of gestational diabetes. Subclinical hypothyroidism and thyroid antibodies were not linked to it, which goes against what was long believed. These studies show links, not proof of cause, and more research is needed on whether treating low thyroid hormone changes diabetes risk.
keyPoints: Isolated hypothyroxinaemia was linked to more gestational diabetes: 6.5% compared with 3.5% in people with normal thyroid function.
Lower free T4 was linked to a higher risk of gestational diabetes, and higher free T3 and a higher free T3-to-free T4 ratio were also linked to higher risk.
No link was found between gestational diabetes and TSH, thyroid antibodies, or subclinical hypothyroidism.
Follow-up studies are needed to learn whether starting or adjusting levothyroxine affects insulin resistance and diabetes treatment in pregnancy.

items.title: The risk of developing gestational diabetes mellitus in maternal subclinical hypothyroidism: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 16 studies to see whether pregnant women with subclinical hypothyroidism (a mildly underactive thyroid with few or no symptoms) are more likely to develop gestational diabetes. Overall, women with subclinical hypothyroidism had a somewhat higher chance of gestational diabetes than women with normal thyroid function. The link was not clear when thyroid antibodies were absent, or when the thyroid problem was found in the first trimester.
keyPoints: Across 16 studies, pregnant women with subclinical hypothyroidism had about a 34% higher odds of gestational diabetes than women with normal thyroid function.
Women with subclinical hypothyroidism who had no thyroid antibodies did not show a clear increase in gestational diabetes risk.
Women with subclinical hypothyroidism in the first trimester did not show a clear increase in risk, whether or not antibodies were present.
The authors conclude that subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy is related to a higher risk of gestational diabetes.

items.title: Pregnancy and the disease recurrence of patients previously treated for differentiated thyroid cancer: A systematic review and meta analysis
items.summary: This review pooled ten studies to ask whether pregnancy makes thyroid cancer more likely to come back in women who were already treated for differentiated thyroid cancer. About 13 in 100 pregnant women had a recurrence, and the risk was no different from women who were not pregnant. Women whose cancer had not fully responded to earlier treatment had a higher chance of recurrence, so the authors say these women need closer watching during pregnancy.
keyPoints: Pregnancy showed little or no link to the cancer coming back in women previously treated for differentiated thyroid cancer.
Pooled recurrence was about 13% in pregnant women, with no significant difference compared with women who were not pregnant.
Recurrence risk rose as the response to earlier treatment got worse, from excellent to structurally incomplete.
Clinicians should pay more attention to pregnant women whose cancer shows ongoing signs in blood tests or scans.

items.title: Best practices in the laboratory diagnosis, prognostication, prediction, and monitoring of Graves' disease: role of TRAbs
items.summary: This paper is a practice guideline from South Asian endocrinologists about a blood test called TRAbs (TSH receptor antibodies) in Graves' disease, an autoimmune cause of an overactive thyroid. The test can help confirm the diagnosis, guide treatment choices and predict how the illness may go. It is also useful for checking thyroid function around pregnancy, before conception and in newborns. The panel reviewed the existing research and agreed 21 recommendations for healthcare providers.
keyPoints: TRAbs are antibodies that switch on the thyroid and drive Graves' disease.
Measuring TRAbs has a role in diagnosis, choosing treatment, predicting outcome and monitoring.
The test is also helpful for thyroid checks during pregnancy, before conception and in newborns.
Adding TRAbs to the diagnostic pathway can make Graves' disease care more cost-effective.

items.title: Relationship between Iron Deficiency and Thyroid Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled ten studies that compared thyroid hormone levels in people with and without iron deficiency. People with iron deficiency had lower levels of thyroid hormones (FT4 and FT3) and lower TSH, and this was seen in pregnant women too. Iron deficiency was also linked to more thyroid antibodies, which can point to thyroid autoimmunity. The studies only looked at one point in time, so they cannot show that iron deficiency causes these changes, and more research is needed.
keyPoints: People with iron deficiency had lower TSH, FT4 and FT3 levels than people without it.
Pregnant women with iron deficiency showed lower TSH, FT4 and FT3; non-pregnant women showed lower FT4 and FT3 but no TSH difference.
Lower ferritin (iron stores) went along with lower TSH and FT4 levels.
Iron deficiency was linked to more positive thyroid antibody tests, suggesting a possible link with thyroid autoimmunity.

items.title: Association between maternal thyroid function and risk of gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia: a systematic review and individual-participant data meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled data from 19 studies covering about 46,500 pregnant women to see whether thyroid blood test results were linked to high blood pressure in pregnancy. Women with subclinical hypothyroidism (a mildly underactive thyroid) had a higher chance of pre-eclampsia, 3.6% compared with 2.1% in women with normal thyroid function. TSH levels that were either higher or lower than usual were linked to more pre-eclampsia. This type of study shows links, not cause and effect.
keyPoints: Subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy was linked to a higher risk of pre-eclampsia (3.6% vs 2.1%).
Both higher and lower TSH levels were associated with a higher risk of pre-eclampsia.
Subclinical hyperthyroidism, isolated low thyroxine (hypothyroxinaemia) and TPO antibody positivity were not linked to gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia.
Whether treating thyroid levels to a certain target lowers the risk still needs to be tested in future trials.

items.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the efficacy and pregnancy outcomes of levothyroxine sodium tablet administration in pregnant women complicated with hypothyroidism
items.summary: This review pooled nine studies with 2,873 pregnant women who had an underactive thyroid (mostly subclinical hypothyroidism). It compared women treated with levothyroxine tablets to women who were not. Treated women had lower rates of preterm birth, miscarriage, heavy bleeding after birth and low birth weight babies. The authors note there were too few studies to say whether treatment changes the chance of high blood pressure in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Women treated with levothyroxine had fewer preterm births and fewer miscarriages than the comparison group.
Treated women also had less postpartum hemorrhage and fewer low birth weight babies.
The review found nine studies with 2,873 pregnant women in total.
There were too few studies to know if levothyroxine affects gestational hypertension.

items.title: Indications for Outpatient Antenatal Fetal Surveillance: ACOG Committee Opinion, Number 828
items.summary: This American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) opinion gives guidance on when checks on a baby's wellbeing, such as monitoring in clinic, may be offered during pregnancy. These checks aim to lower the risk of stillbirth. Guidance covers conditions where stillbirth happens more often than 0.8 per 1,000 and where the risk is more than double that of pregnancies without the condition. The advice is a set of suggestions, not strict rules, and each plan should be tailored to the person.
keyPoints: Antenatal fetal surveillance is done to reduce the risk of stillbirth.
Surveillance is suggested for conditions where stillbirth is reported more often than 0.8 per 1,000 and the relative risk or odds ratio is above 2.0.
It has not been shown to improve outcomes for every condition linked to stillbirth, so there is no complete list of indications.
Shared decision making between the pregnant person and the clinician is important, and whether and when to offer testing should be individualised.

items.title: Recurrent pregnancy loss: diagnostic workup after two or three pregnancy losses? A systematic review of the literature and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether couples who have had two pregnancy losses are just as likely to have abnormal test results as couples who have had three or more. For uterine abnormalities and antiphospholipid syndrome, rates were about the same in both groups, though the evidence was low quality. For chromosomal problems, inherited clotting disorders and thyroid disorders, there was not enough evidence to say either way. The authors say the findings may support testing after two losses, but more research is needed and few abnormal results currently have an evidence-based treatment.
keyPoints: Uterine abnormalities and antiphospholipid syndrome were about equally common after two losses versus three or more (low quality evidence).
Evidence was insufficient to compare thyroid disorders, chromosomal abnormalities and inherited thrombophilia between the two groups; only two studies looked at thyroid disorders.
The results may support testing after two pregnancy losses, but better studies of what test results mean for future pregnancies are urgently needed.
For most cases with abnormal test results, no evidence-based treatment is currently available.

items.title: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 223
items.summary: This is a clinical guideline from ACOG, a major US group of obstetricians and gynecologists, on thyroid disease in pregnancy. It explains that both an overactive thyroid (thyrotoxicosis) and an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) are linked to poorer pregnancy outcomes. It also notes concern about how overt thyroid disease in the mother may affect the baby's development, and that some thyroid medicines can cross the placenta and reach the baby's thyroid. The updated guidance covers how thyroid disease is diagnosed and managed in pregnancy, and adds a new management flowchart.
keyPoints: Both overactive and underactive thyroid are linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes.
Overt maternal thyroid disease raises concern about fetal development.
Medicines that act on the mother's thyroid can cross the placenta and affect the baby's thyroid.
The updated bulletin covers diagnosis and management and includes a new clinical algorithm.

items.title: Association of maternal thyroid function with birthweight: a systematic review and individual-participant data meta-analysis
items.summary: This study pooled data from about 48,000 mother-baby pairs across many studies to see how a mother's thyroid levels during pregnancy relate to her baby's birthweight. Mild underactivity of the thyroid (subclinical hypothyroidism) was linked to a higher chance of the baby being smaller than expected for their age and a slightly lower birthweight. A different pattern, isolated hypothyroxinaemia (low thyroid hormone with normal TSH), was linked to a lower chance of a small baby and a slightly higher birthweight. These are associations, and the authors say the results should prompt careful thought about the risks and benefits of levothyroxine treatment in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy was linked to more small-for-gestational-age babies (11.8% vs 10.0%) and an average birthweight about 38 g lower.
Isolated hypothyroxinaemia was linked to fewer small-for-gestational-age babies (7.3% vs 10.0%) and an average birthweight about 45 g higher.
Higher maternal TSH and free thyroxine levels, even within the normal range, were each linked to slightly lower birthweight.
The authors say the findings should prompt careful consideration of the benefits and risks of levothyroxine therapy during pregnancy.

items.title: Maternal Thyroid Dysfunction During Pregnancy and the Risk of Adverse Outcomes in the Offspring: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
