items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This review pooled results from 29 studies to look at whether a mother's thyroid problems during pregnancy are linked to health and development problems in her children. Both an overactive thyroid and an underactive thyroid were linked to a small increase in the chance of ADHD and epilepsy in children, and an underactive thyroid was also linked to autism. These are links found in studies, so they do not prove the thyroid problem caused the outcomes. The authors say checking thyroid function and treating problems promptly should be considered in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Maternal hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid) was linked to slightly higher odds of ADHD (OR 1.18) and epilepsy (OR 1.19) in children.
Maternal hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) was linked to higher odds of ADHD (OR 1.14), autism spectrum disorder (OR 1.41) and epilepsy (OR 1.21).
The authors conclude that routine thyroid function measurement and timely treatment should be considered for pregnant women.

items.title: Differences in Diagnostic Criteria Mask the True Prevalence of Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 63 studies to work out how common thyroid problems really are in pregnancy. Reported rates vary a lot because studies use different blood-test cutoffs, test at different times and come from places with different iodine levels. Using trimester-specific TSH cutoffs gave the most accurate estimates, and the authors call these the best estimate to date.
keyPoints: Using the 97.5th percentile TSH cutoff, about 0.50% of pregnant women had overt hypothyroidism, 3.47% had subclinical hypothyroidism and 2.05% had isolated hypothyroxinemia.
Overt hyperthyroidism affected about 0.91% of women in the first trimester and 0.65% in the second; subclinical hyperthyroidism affected about 2.18% and 0.98%.
How common hyperthyroidism appears to be depends on when in pregnancy women are tested.
Population-based, trimester-specific TSH cutoffs give more accurate diagnosis of an underactive thyroid in pregnancy.

items.title: Thyroxine replacement for subfertile women with euthyroid autoimmune thyroid disease or subclinical hypothyroidism
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether levothyroxine (thyroid hormone) helps women having fertility treatment who have mildly underactive thyroid (subclinical hypothyroidism) or thyroid antibodies with normal thyroid levels. It combined four trials with 820 women. In women with thyroid antibodies but normal thyroid function, thyroxine may make little difference to live birth or miscarriage rates. The evidence was low or very low quality, so the authors could draw no clear conclusions.
keyPoints: In women with subclinical hypothyroidism, one small trial (64 women) suggested thyroxine may improve live birth rates, but the evidence was low quality.
In women with thyroid antibodies and normal thyroid function, thyroxine may make little difference to live birth or miscarriage rates (two trials, 686 women, low-quality evidence).
Side effects and pregnancy complications were rarely reported, and preterm births were similar between groups where they were reported.
The authors could draw no clear conclusions because the evidence was of very low to low quality.

items.title: Association of Thyroid Function Test Abnormalities and Thyroid Autoimmunity With Preterm Birth: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined data from 19 studies covering about 47,000 pregnant women who did not have overt thyroid disease and were not treated for thyroid test results. Women with mildly underactive thyroid function (subclinical hypothyroidism), low thyroxine with normal TSH (isolated hypothyroxinemia), or thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies had a somewhat higher chance of preterm birth (before 37 weeks). The extra risk was small in absolute terms, and most women in these groups still delivered at term.
keyPoints: Preterm birth occurred in 6.1% of women with subclinical hypothyroidism vs 5.0% of women with normal thyroid function.
Preterm birth occurred in 7.1% of women with isolated hypothyroxinemia vs 5.0% of women with normal thyroid function.
Women with TPO antibodies had preterm birth in 6.6% of cases vs 4.9% of women without them.
The authors say these findings should inform decisions about thyroid screening and levothyroxine treatment in pregnancy, weighing possible harms and benefits.

items.title: Maternal thyroid hormone insufficiency during pregnancy and risk of neurodevelopmental disorders in offspring: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 39 studies to see whether mild thyroid hormone shortfalls in pregnancy are linked to neurodevelopmental conditions in children. Mildly underactive thyroid (subclinical hypothyroidism) and low thyroxine with normal TSH (hypothyroxinaemia) were linked to higher odds of indicators of intellectual disability in children. No link was found with ADHD, and the link with autism was unclear. Two trials found no evidence that treating mild thyroid insufficiency with levothyroxine from about 8 to 20 weeks reduced the chance of a low IQ in children.
keyPoints: Maternal subclinical hypothyroidism and hypothyroxinaemia were associated with indicators of intellectual disability in children (odds ratios about 2.1 and 1.6).
No association was found with ADHD, and the effect on autism risk was unclear.
Trials showed no evidence that levothyroxine for mild thyroid insufficiency, started at 8 to 20 weeks of pregnancy, reduces low IQ in children.
The observational studies varied a lot from one another, which limits how firm the findings are.

items.title: Graves' disease and pregnancy
items.summary: This guideline section explains how Graves' disease (an overactive thyroid condition) is managed during pregnancy. Although serious problems are rare, the disease can affect the baby and the mother, so care is shared by several specialists. Treatment in pregnancy uses antithyroid medicines on their own. Monitoring continues through pregnancy, around the birth, and in the weeks after delivery.
keyPoints: Graves' disease can rarely but seriously cause fetal or newborn thyroid problems, premature birth and pre-eclampsia.
Pregnancy treatment relies on antithyroid drugs alone, without adding levothyroxine.

Women with a history of Graves' disease and persistent thyroid antibodies need fetal monitoring, and their newborns need monitoring too if antibodies remain at the end of pregnancy or the mother took antithyroid treatment.
Hyperthyroidism can come back in the weeks after delivery, so the mother needs monitoring; long-term effects on children's brain development are poorly known.

items.title: Effect of levothyroxine supplementation on pregnancy outcomes in women with subclinical hypothyroidism and thyroid autoimmuneity undergoing in vitro fertilization/intracytoplasmic sperm injection: an updated meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled four randomized trials covering 787 couples having IVF or ICSI, where the woman had mild underactive thyroid (subclinical hypothyroidism) and/or thyroid antibodies. Taking levothyroxine (thyroid hormone) did not clearly change clinical pregnancy, live birth or preterm birth rates. It was linked to fewer miscarriages overall, but the benefit was not clear when mild underactive thyroid or thyroid antibodies were looked at separately. The authors say more large trials are needed to confirm this.
keyPoints: No significant effect of levothyroxine on clinical pregnancy rate, live birth rate or preterm birth rate.
Levothyroxine was linked to a lower miscarriage rate than placebo or no treatment (RR 0.51).
The miscarriage benefit was not significant when subclinical hypothyroidism or thyroid antibodies were analysed separately.
The authors recommend levothyroxine for these women during IVF/ICSI but say more randomized trials are needed to confirm this.

items.title: The impact of maternal hypothyroidism during pregnancy on neonatal outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine studies to see how an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) in pregnancy relates to the baby's health at birth. Babies born to mothers with hypothyroidism weighed slightly more on average, and there was a trend toward more preterm birth and low birth weight, though these results were borderline. The authors suggest levothyroxine (L-T4) thyroid hormone treatment should be recommended. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Babies of mothers with hypothyroidism in pregnancy had a slightly higher average birth weight.
There was a trend toward more preterm birth and low birth weight, but the results were borderline rather than clear-cut.
No significant increase in babies born small for their gestational age was found.
The authors suggest L-T4 (levothyroxine) supplementation should be recommended for hypothyroidism in pregnancy.

items.title: The Effect of Subclinical Maternal Thyroid Dysfunction and Autoimmunity on Intrauterine Growth Restriction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from 13 cohort studies to see whether mild thyroid problems in pregnancy are linked to a baby not growing as expected in the womb (intrauterine growth restriction, or IUGR). Mildly underactive thyroid (subclinical hypothyroidism) was linked to a higher chance of IUGR. Mildly overactive thyroid, thyroid antibodies (TPOAb) and low thyroxine alone (isolated hypothyroxinemia) showed no clear link to IUGR. The abstract does not rate how certain the evidence is.
keyPoints: Subclinical hypothyroidism was associated with a higher risk of IUGR (odds ratio 1.54).
Subclinical hyperthyroidism showed no clear effect on IUGR risk.
Positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPOAb) showed no clear effect on IUGR risk.
Isolated hypothyroxinemia showed no clear effect on IUGR risk.

items.title: Reproductive Factors but Not Hormonal Factors Associated with Thyroid Cancer Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled 25 studies to see whether hormone-related and reproductive factors change the chance of getting thyroid cancer. Birth control pills and hormone replacement therapy did not change the risk. Longer breastfeeding was linked to a lower risk, while having had children and being older at menopause were linked to a higher risk. The authors say more studies are needed, as earlier findings were mixed.
keyPoints: Oral contraceptives and hormone replacement therapy did not change thyroid cancer risk overall.
Longer breastfeeding was linked to a moderately lower thyroid cancer risk in the pooled cohort studies.
Women who had given birth had a higher risk than women who had not in hospital-based case-control studies.
Older age at menopause was linked to a weakly higher risk, and the authors call for more research.

items.title: Impact of travel time to health facilities on perinatal outcomes: a systematic review with narrative synthesis and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at 37 studies on how the time it takes to travel to a health facility affects the chances that a baby survives around the time of birth. Shorter journeys were consistently linked to better outcomes, with the best survival seen for trips of under 30 minutes to a hospital. The authors say the combined numbers are only illustrative because the studies differed a lot in how they were done. This is about reaching care for birth or newborn transfer, not about travelling or flying during pregnancy.
keyPoints: Across studies, shorter travel times to health facilities were linked to better survival for babies around birth.
Journeys of under 30 minutes to a hospital had the highest survival rates.
Pooled estimates showed more than 2-fold higher odds of survival for journeys to hospital at 30 minute, 1 hour and 2 hour limits, but results varied widely between studies.
The authors suggest a 30-minute or 1-hour travel norm is preferable to the 2-hour limit used in many low- and middle-income countries, alongside good quality of care.

items.title: Costs of medical evacuation and transportation of First Nations Peoples and Inuit who travel for medical care in Canada: A systematic review
items.source: Canadian Journal of Public Health = Revue Canadienne de Sante Publique
items.journal: Canadian Journal of Public Health = Revue Canadienne de Sante Publique
items.summary: This review looked at what it costs when First Nations and Inuit women in remote Canadian communities must travel to a city to wait for labour and birth, usually from 36-38 weeks of pregnancy. Across 19 studies, medical evacuation cost between about CAD $7,714 and $31,794. Families also faced lost income and a lack of respect for cultural practices. The review says it was unclear who pays for what, and more research is needed.
keyPoints: A guideline asks First Nations and Inuit women in rural and remote areas to travel to urban centres at 36-38 weeks of pregnancy to await labour and birth.
Medical evacuation was the most expensive direct cost, ranging from CAD $7,714 to CAD $31,794.
Indirect and intangible costs included lost income and lack of respect for cultural practices.
Information on how this travel is funded was unclear, and more research is needed across Canada.

items.title: Are all vaccines safe for the pregnant traveller? A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together published studies on whether common travel vaccines are safe during pregnancy. Flu and Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria, whooping cough) vaccines have the strongest safety evidence, and meningococcal, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rabies and yellow fever vaccines also looked safe in the studies available. For several other travel vaccines, there was little or no safety data in pregnancy.
keyPoints: The safety of the flu vaccine in pregnancy is supported by high-quality evidence.
Tdap showed no evidence of harm in trials; a small rise in chorioamnionitis (womb infection) was seen in 3 of 12 observational studies, but the review says the benefit to babies is much larger.
Meningococcal vaccines are probably safe, and observational data support hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rabies and live yellow fever vaccines.
Little or no data exist for polio, typhoid, Japanese encephalitis, tick-borne encephalitis and MMR vaccines in pregnancy.

items.title: Treatment of soil-transmitted helminth infections in pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis of maternal outcomes
items.summary: This review pooled 23 studies on treating intestinal worm infections (soil-transmitted helminths) during pregnancy, which can be picked up through travel or migration. Albendazole cured up to 90% of hookworm and Ascaris infections and about 50% of Trichuris infections, and no serious side effects were linked to any drug studied. The authors conclude albendazole is effective and safe for the mother.
keyPoints: Albendazole had cure rates up to 90% for hookworm and Ascaris, but only about 50% for Trichuris.
Mebendazole cured 70% or fewer cases, and ivermectin cured 29% of hookworm and 56% of Trichuris infections in pregnant women.
Pregnancy loss, haemoglobin levels and pre-term delivery rates did not differ between albendazole or mebendazole and placebo or controls.
No serious adverse events were attributable to any drug studied.

items.title: The safety of atovaquone-proguanil for the prevention and treatment of malaria in pregnancy: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at what happens to pregnancies when women take atovaquone-proguanil, a malaria medicine, during pregnancy. It pooled results from 16 studies, including 446 women who took the medicine. Rates of miscarriage, stillbirth and birth defects looked similar to what is expected in comparable groups of women. The authors say the available data are limited and more safety data are needed.
keyPoints: Malaria in pregnancy is a significant risk, and the choice of preventive medicines for pregnant women is limited.
Among 446 women exposed to atovaquone-proguanil, about 8% had a miscarriage, about 1% had a stillbirth and about 2.6% had a baby with a congenital anomaly.
Outcomes were similar to expected rates in similar populations.
The authors say it may be a promising option but more data on safety in pregnancy are needed.

items.title: Dengue and Zika Virus Diagnostic Testing for Patients with a Clinically Compatible Illness and Risk for Infection with Both Viruses
items.summary: This CDC guidance explains how doctors should test for dengue and Zika virus in people who have symptoms and live in or have recently travelled to areas where both viruses occur. Pregnant women with symptoms should have blood and urine tests taken as soon as possible, within 12 weeks of symptoms starting. Women who may have had Zika during pregnancy, and their babies, should be checked and followed up for possible problems.
keyPoints: For symptomatic non-pregnant people, virus-detecting (NAAT) tests should be done on blood taken within 7 days of symptoms starting; antibody (IgM) tests are used on later samples or when NAAT is negative.
For symptomatic pregnant women, blood and urine samples should be collected as soon as possible within 12 weeks of symptom onset for both NAAT and IgM antibody testing.
Antibody tests can cross-react between dengue and Zika, so positive antibody results with a negative NAAT should be confirmed with neutralizing antibody tests, including for all pregnant women.

Women with lab evidence of possible Zika infection in pregnancy and their infants should be evaluated and managed for possible adverse outcomes; screening advice for pregnant women without symptoms is unchanged.

items.title: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 746 Summary: Air Travel During Pregnancy
items.summary: This guidance from ACOG looks at air travel during pregnancy. It says that when there are no pregnancy or medical complications, occasional flying is safe for pregnant women, with the same precautions as anyone else. It also gives simple tips for staying comfortable and lowering the chance of swelling or blood clots.
keyPoints: Occasional air travel is safe for pregnant women who have no obstetric or medical complications.
Seat belts should be worn the whole time seated, because sudden severe turbulence cannot be predicted and could cause injury.

Support stockings, moving the legs regularly, loose clothing, short walks and staying hydrated can help reduce leg swelling and clot risk, although evidence linking flying in pregnancy to these problems is lacking.
Cosmic radiation exposure is negligible for most travellers, but aircrew and frequent flyers may exceed recommended limits and should be informed about the risks.

items.title: Update: Interim Guidance for Preconception Counseling and Prevention of Sexual Transmission of Zika Virus for Men with Possible Zika Virus Exposure - United States, August 2018
items.source: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.journal: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.summary: This 2018 update from the US CDC gives advice for men who may have been exposed to Zika virus, for example by travelling to or living in an area where it spreads. Zika can pass through mosquito bites or sex, and infection during pregnancy can cause serious birth defects. The CDC now advises men planning to conceive to wait at least 3 months before having unprotected sex.
keyPoints: Men with possible Zika exposure who are planning to conceive are advised to wait at least 3 months before unprotected sex, counted from symptom onset or from their last possible exposure if they had no symptoms.
Couples who are not trying to conceive can consider condoms or abstaining from sex for at least 3 months after symptom onset or last possible exposure.
Possible exposure includes travel to or living in an area with Zika risk, or sex without a condom with a partner who has done so.
Zika infection during pregnancy can cause fetal brain abnormalities and other serious birth defects.

items.title: Antenatal Corticosteroid Use in Twin Pregnancies: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 studies of about 18,000 babies from twin pregnancies to see whether steroid injections given before birth (to help babies' lungs mature) help or harm. Overall, the steroids were not clearly linked to fewer baby deaths or less breathing distress syndrome. They were linked to more low blood sugar, more need for extra oxygen, and more admissions to neonatal intensive care or special care. The evidence was of moderate to low certainty, so the authors say the results should be read cautiously.
keyPoints: Antenatal corticosteroids were not significantly linked to fewer neonatal deaths or less respiratory distress syndrome in twin pregnancies.
Babies exposed to the steroids had higher rates of low blood sugar, needing supplemental oxygen, and NICU or special care admission.
The higher risk of low blood sugar was seen at all gestational ages studied.
Certainty of the evidence was moderate to low, so findings should be interpreted cautiously.

items.title: Selective fetal growth restriction in dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy: systematic review and meta-analysis of pregnancy and perinatal outcomes
items.summary: This review pooled 13 studies of twin pregnancies where each baby has its own placenta and sac (dichorionic diamniotic) and one twin is growing much smaller than expected (selective fetal growth restriction). Compared with similar twin pregnancies without this problem, babies had a higher chance of dying before birth and a higher chance of illness or needing newborn intensive care. The authors say these pregnancies are at high risk, and that counselling should use twin-specific data rather than singleton data.
keyPoints: Death of a baby before birth happened in about 2.6% of babies in twin pregnancies with selective growth restriction, compared with about 0.6% without it (odds ratio 5.2).
Illness or admission to newborn intensive care was about three times more likely when selective growth restriction was present (odds ratio 3.2).
Within a twin pair, the smaller twin had higher rates of newborn illness (39.0% vs 29.9%) and perinatal death (3.0% vs 1.6%) than the better-grown twin.
There was no clear difference in risk of birth before 34 weeks or of pre-eclampsia or gestational high blood pressure.

items.title: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine Consult Series #72: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome and twin anemia-polycythemia sequence
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This is a guideline from the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine about two complications that can happen when identical twins share one placenta: twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) and twin anemia-polycythemia sequence (TAPS). It recommends an early scan to find out whether twins share a placenta, regular ultrasound checks from 16 weeks, and laser surgery for more serious TTTS. It also gives advice on timing of birth after treatment.
keyPoints: A first-trimester ultrasound is recommended to work out whether twins share a placenta and amniotic sac.
Twins who share a placenta but have separate sacs should have ultrasound checks every 2 weeks from 16 weeks until delivery, more often if there is concern.
Fetoscopic laser surgery is the standard treatment for stage II to IV TTTS found between 16 and 26 weeks, and referral to a fetal intervention center is recommended.
After successful laser treatment, delivery of both surviving twins is recommended at 34 to 36 weeks, and laser surgery should not change the way the babies are delivered.

items.title: Chorionicity and neurodevelopmental outcomes in twin pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 studies to see whether the type of twin pregnancy affects how children develop later. Twins who share a placenta (monochorionic) had higher odds of developmental problems and cerebral palsy than twins with separate placentas (dichorionic). The difference disappeared when babies affected by twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) were left out, and also after laser surgery for TTTS.
keyPoints: Twins sharing a placenta (monochorionic) had higher odds of neurodevelopmental impairment and cerebral palsy than twins with separate placentas.
The difference between the two groups disappeared when babies with twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) were excluded.
Monochorionic twins with TTTS were at high risk of neurologic disability.
After fetoscopic laser surgery for monochorionic twins, there was no difference in outcomes, and the surgery was seen as an acceptable treatment.

items.title: Clinical practice guidelines on the use of aspirin in pregnancy: Systematic review
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This review compared 16 clinical guidelines on taking aspirin during pregnancy. The guidelines largely agree on who should be offered it: women at higher risk of preeclampsia, such as those who have had preeclampsia before or who have long-term conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes. They disagree on the dose, when to start, and when to stop.
keyPoints: Aspirin is commonly recommended in pregnancy for women at high risk of preeclampsia or poor baby growth (fetal growth restriction).
15 of 16 guidelines listed previous preeclampsia, chronic high blood pressure, autoimmune disease and type 1 or 2 diabetes as major risk factors for using aspirin.
Guidelines differed on the dose, the pregnancy week to start, and when to stop aspirin.

items.title: Guideline No. 440: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancies
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline from the SOGC explains how pregnancies with monochorionic twins (identical twins who share one placenta) should be monitored and managed. It covers both straightforward pregnancies and ones with complications. The aim is to catch problems early and so lower the risk of illness or death around the time of birth. The abstract does not list the individual recommendations or give an overall certainty rating.
keyPoints: Monochorionic twins (sharing one placenta) are advised to have more frequent ultrasound monitoring than dichorionic twins.
The guideline covers complications such as TTTS, TAPS, selective fetal growth restriction, acardiac (TRAP) twins, monoamniotic twins and loss of one twin.
Careful monitoring and timely management aim to reduce illness and death for babies around birth.
Recommendations were rated with the GRADE approach for quality of evidence and strength.

items.title: Neonatal Morbidity of Monoamniotic Twin Pregnancies: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies of 685 monoamniotic twin pregnancies (identical twins sharing one placenta and one amniotic sac) with no fetal anomalies. It looked at how often newborns had health problems depending on how early they were born. Problems, mostly breathing difficulties, were common after early births and became less frequent as pregnancy continued, with a clear drop for babies born at 33 to 34 weeks. Babies did not do differently whether the mother was monitored in hospital or as an outpatient.
keyPoints: Monoamniotic twin pregnancies carry a high risk of newborn health problems, mainly breathing (respiratory) problems.
Overall newborn problems occurred in 75.4% of births at 24-30 weeks, 65.5% at 31-32 weeks, 37.6% at 33-34 weeks and 18.5% at 35-36 weeks.
Problems fell gradually the later the babies were born, with a notable reduction for births at 33 to 34 weeks.
No difference in newborn problems was found between hospital (inpatient) and outpatient monitoring; the 35-36 week figures rest on very few cases.

items.title: Fetal reduction from twin to singleton gestation: A meta-analysis
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pooled six studies of 2,867 women with twin pregnancies, comparing those who had one baby reduced to a singleton pregnancy with those who continued with twins. Women who had the reduction had lower odds of preterm birth, high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy and cesarean delivery. The authors say larger, well-powered prospective studies are still needed to confirm these findings.
keyPoints: Odds of birth before 34 weeks were 36% lower after reduction to a singleton pregnancy.
Odds of birth before 37 weeks were 77% lower after reduction.
Odds of hypertensive disorders were 75% lower and odds of cesarean delivery 65% lower.
The authors call for sufficiently powered prospective studies to support these findings.

items.title: Bed rest with and without hospitalisation in multiple pregnancy for improving perinatal outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether bed rest, in hospital or at home, improves outcomes for women expecting twins or triplets. It pulled together six trials with 636 women. Bed rest in hospital did not clearly reduce very early birth, baby deaths or low birthweight, and the evidence was low quality. The authors conclude there is not enough evidence to support routine bed rest in multiple pregnancy.
keyPoints: Strict bed rest in hospital made no clear difference to very preterm birth, perinatal death or low birthweight compared with normal activity at home (low-quality evidence).
Strict bed rest in hospital was linked to a slightly higher chance of labour starting on its own and a higher average birthweight (about 137 g).
One trial found partial bed rest in hospital was linked to less gestational hypertension, but showed no clear difference in other outcomes.
None of the trials reported costs or possible harms such as blood clots or effects on emotional wellbeing.

items.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Multiple Gestations
items.source: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Radiology looks at ultrasound scans in twin and higher-order pregnancies. Women expecting twins usually have more scans than those with one baby, including early scans, a nuchal translucency scan, an anatomy scan at 18 to 22 weeks, and growth scans later on. Twin pregnancies carry higher risks of early birth, birth defects, slow growth, and problems with the placenta or umbilical cord. Working out early whether twins share a placenta helps decide how closely the pregnancy should be watched.
keyPoints: Women with twins typically have more ultrasound scans than women with one baby, including growth scans in the third trimester.
Twin pregnancies have higher risks of preterm delivery, birth defects, slow fetal growth, placenta previa, vasa previa and unusual cord attachment.
Whether twins share a placenta (chorionicity) should be worked out as early as possible so that those sharing one can be watched more closely.
Twins who share a placenta are more likely to have heart problems and special complications such as twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, so heart screening is warranted.

items.title: Planned early delivery versus expectant management for monoamniotic twins
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for trials comparing planned early delivery (32 to 34 weeks) with waiting for spontaneous labour or later planned delivery in monoamniotic twin pregnancies, where twins share one amniotic sac. No trials were found, so there is not enough evidence to say which approach is best. The authors point to older case series and expert opinion in the meantime, and say the choice should involve women and their families.
keyPoints: Monoamniotic twins are rare, about 1 in 10,000 pregnancies, and the best time for delivery is not known.
No randomised trials were found, so no strong conclusions can be drawn about early versus later delivery.
Plans should consider whether high-quality newborn care is available if early delivery is chosen.
Women and families should be involved in decisions about these high-risk pregnancies.

items.title: Specialised antenatal clinics for women with a multiple pregnancy for improving maternal and infant outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for trials comparing specialised antenatal clinics for twin or other multiple pregnancies with standard antenatal care. Only one small study of 162 women was found, and it had some design limitations. It is unclear whether specialised clinics change the risk of baby death around birth, but women in the specialised clinic were more likely to have a caesarean birth. Overall, there is too little evidence to say whether specialised clinics improve health for mothers or babies.
keyPoints: Only one study (162 women) met the review's criteria, so the evidence is very limited.
It is uncertain whether specialised clinics make any difference to deaths of babies around the time of birth (very low quality evidence).
Women in specialised clinics were more likely to have a caesarean birth (moderate quality evidence).
No clear differences were found for postnatal depression, breastfeeding, stillbirth or newborn death, but the evidence was very low quality.

items.title: Planned caesarean section for women with a twin pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether planning a caesarean section is better than planning a vaginal birth for women expecting twins. It combined two trials, mostly one large study of 2,804 women, and found no clear difference in serious problems for mothers or babies. The evidence was rated moderate quality. The authors say there is not enough evidence to support routine planned caesarean for twin pregnancies at term when the first baby is head-down.
keyPoints: No clear difference between planned caesarean and planned vaginal birth for maternal death or serious illness, or for baby death or serious illness.
About 43% of women who planned a vaginal birth still had a caesarean for at least one twin, compared with about 91% in the planned caesarean group.
No clear differences were found in breastfeeding difficulties or in scores for postnatal depression.

Authors conclude there is insufficient evidence to support routine planned caesarean for term twins when the first baby is head-down, and that women should be told the possible risks and benefits of each option.

items.title: Recommendations from the WHO guideline for the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of infertility
items.summary: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a guideline on preventing, diagnosing and treating infertility, which affects about one in six people in their lifetime. A multidisciplinary group, including patient representatives, reviewed the evidence and made 40 recommendations and six good practice statements. These cover prevention, diagnosis and treatment, including a recommendation on diagnosing unexplained infertility and six on treating it. Most recommendations are conditional because the evidence was missing, or of low or very low certainty.
keyPoints: WHO made 40 recommendations and six good practice statements on preventing, diagnosing and treating infertility.
Good practice statements include listening to people with infertility and involving them in treatment decisions.
Prevention advice covers fertility information, reducing risk from sexually transmitted infections, lifestyle factors and tobacco use.
There is one recommendation on diagnosing unexplained infertility and six on treating it.

items.title: Effects of Tribulus (Tribulus terrestris L.) Supplementation on Erectile Dysfunction and Testosterone Levels in Men-A Systematic Review of Clinical Trials
items.summary: This review looked at 10 small studies (483 men in total) of Tribulus terrestris, a plant supplement often claimed to raise testosterone and improve sexual function. At doses of 400 to 750 mg a day for 1 to 3 months, it helped erectile problems in 3 of the 5 studies that measured this. Most studies found no real change in testosterone, and the evidence overall was weak, with half of the studies of low methodological quality.
keyPoints: Tribulus improved erectile dysfunction in 3 of the 5 studies that assessed it, but the level of evidence is low.
8 of 10 studies found no significant change in testosterone; men in those studies did not have low testosterone to start with.
Only 2 studies, in men with low testosterone (hypogonadism), showed small rises of about 60 to 70 ng/dL.
Only one of the 10 studies involved men with unexplained infertility, so little can be said for that group.

items.title: Effects of Carnitine and Coenzyme Q10 on Sperm Quality and Pregnancy Rates in Men with Unexplained Infertility: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 studies to look at whether the antioxidants carnitine and coenzyme Q10 improve sperm quality in men with unexplained infertility. Both supplements, and L-carnitine combined with acetyl-L-carnitine, improved sperm measures compared with placebo. Coenzyme Q10 raised sperm concentration the most, and L-carnitine did most for sperm movement. The authors say larger, higher-quality studies are still needed to confirm these results.
keyPoints: L-carnitine, coenzyme Q10 and L-carnitine plus acetyl-L-carnitine improved sperm quality compared with placebo.
Coenzyme Q10 gave the largest increase in sperm concentration.
L-carnitine gave the largest improvement in progressive sperm motility (how well sperm swim forward).
More high-quality, large studies are needed to confirm that antioxidants work for male infertility.

items.title: IVF versus IUI with ovarian stimulation for unexplained infertility: a collaborative individual participant data meta-analysis
items.summary: This study pooled the original data from four trials (934 women) that compared IVF with IUI plus ovarian stimulation for couples with unexplained infertility. It looked at how many couples had a live birth over the same time period. IVF did not lead to clearly more live births or to a faster pregnancy, and the rate of multiple pregnancy was not clearly different. The authors say both treatments are reasonable options.
keyPoints: Cumulative live birth rates were 50.3% with IVF and 43.2% with IUI with ovarian stimulation, a difference that was not statistically significant.
Multiple pregnancy rates were 3.8% with IVF and 5.2% with IUI with ovarian stimulation, also not a significant difference.
There is no robust evidence that IVF gets couples to a live birth faster than IUI with ovarian stimulation.
The authors say cost and the couple's preferences should be weighed when choosing between the two treatments.

items.title: Association of abstinence time with semen quality and fertility outcomes: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 85 studies to look at how long a man waits between ejaculations (abstinence time) affects sperm quality and fertility treatment results. Shorter abstinence was linked to some improvements in sperm quality, with possibly more benefit for men with fertility problems, including unexplained infertility, than for healthy men. Any benefit may be mainly within the first 4 days. The authors say the link may not be causal because other factors could be involved.
keyPoints: In healthy men, shorter abstinence gave only limited improvements in semen quality, such as a lower DNA fragmentation index.
In men with unexplained infertility, shorter abstinence was linked to lower DNA fragmentation and better sperm viability.
Shorter abstinence may be more helpful for infertile men, especially within the first 4 days.
The authors urge caution about cause and effect because of possible confounding factors.

items.title: The prevalence of endometriosis in unexplained infertility: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pooled studies of couples with unexplained infertility who had a keyhole surgery (laparoscopy) to look inside the pelvis. It found endometriosis in about 44% of them, and most cases were minimal or mild. Other problems, such as blocked or damaged tubes and scar-like adhesions, were also found fairly often. The authors say this matters most for people who also have pain that could point to endometriosis.
keyPoints: Endometriosis was found in 44% of people with unexplained infertility who had a laparoscopy, and 74% of cases were minimal or mild.
Tubal problems were found in 20% and adhesions in 16%.
Pelvic abnormalities were found more often in women who had already had fertility treatment (75%) than in those who had not (53%).
The high rate of endometriosis may help decisions for people who also have pain symptoms suggestive of endometriosis.

items.title: Economic evaluation of lifestyle interventions in infertility management: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at the cost side of lifestyle programmes for couples having infertility treatment, including those with unexplained infertility. It found only five studies, all from high-income countries (the Netherlands, Australia and Japan). Programmes that added things like coaching, diet changes, exercise, weight management, quitting smoking and mindfulness seemed to improve pregnancy and live birth outcomes. They were also likely to cost less per outcome than standard infertility care.
keyPoints: Five studies met the review's criteria, all from high-income countries.
Adding lifestyle programmes to infertility treatment tended to improve pregnancy and live birth outcomes.
Programmes covered coaching, nutrition, exercise, weight management, smoking cessation and mindfulness.
Lifestyle programmes were likely to be more cost-effective than standard infertility care.

items.title: Recommendations from the 2024 Australian evidence-based guideline for unexplained infertility: ADAPTE process from the ESHRE evidence-based guideline on unexplained infertility
items.summary: This is the 2024 Australian guideline on unexplained infertility, adapted from a European guideline from 2023. It sets out recommendations for how couples should be tested and what treatments may be offered when no clear cause of infertility is found. None of the recommendations rest on high quality evidence, and most rest on low or very low quality evidence, so the guideline also lists areas needing more research.
keyPoints: The guideline has 40 evidence-based recommendations, 21 practice points and three research recommendations.
It covers how infertility is defined, which tests are used to reach a diagnosis of unexplained infertility, and treatment options including waiting, active treatment and surgical procedures.
It refines the definition of unexplained infertility and covers basic diagnostic steps that earlier guidelines did not address.
No recommendation was based on high quality evidence; most were based on low or very low quality evidence.

items.title: Prevalence of thyroid autoantibody positivity in women with infertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled many studies to see how common thyroid antibodies (a sign the immune system is targeting the thyroid) are in women with infertility compared with healthy women. About 1 in 5 women overall had these antibodies, and they were found more often in women with infertility, including those with unexplained infertility, endometriosis, ovulation problems and blocked tubes. The authors suggest that checking women with infertility for thyroid antibodies is clinically important. The review shows the antibodies are more common in women with infertility, not that they cause it.
keyPoints: The pooled rate of thyroid antibody positivity was 20% worldwide.
Women with infertility were about 1.5 times as likely to have thyroid antibodies as healthy controls.
Antibodies were more common in unexplained infertility, endometriosis, ovulation disorders and fallopian tube causes.
The higher rates were also seen in women with normal thyroid hormone levels, and in women with recurrent pregnancy loss.

items.title: Kisspeptin as a predictor of miscarriage: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether kisspeptin, a hormone made in the body, could help predict miscarriage. It pulled together seven small case-control studies, which suggested kisspeptin levels might signal whether a pregnancy is likely to continue. Two studies also linked changes in kisspeptin to unexplained infertility and to low embryo implantation rates in women having fertility treatment. The authors say better-quality studies are needed before it can be used as a test.
keyPoints: Seven case-control studies suggested kisspeptin may be a marker of pregnancy loss.
Two studies linked kisspeptin changes to unexplained infertility and low embryo implantation in assisted reproduction.
Kisspeptin might become a way to check pregnancy viability in the future.
Stronger studies are needed before it can be used for diagnosis or prediction.

items.title: Ovarian stimulation strategies for intrauterine insemination in couples with unexplained infertility: a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled individual data from 7 trials (about 2,400 couples with unexplained infertility) having intrauterine insemination (IUI) with medicines to stimulate the ovaries. Injectable hormones (gonadotrophins) gave more live births and a shorter time to conception than clomiphene citrate, but also more multiple pregnancies (twins or more). When lower starting doses and stricter cancellation rules were used, the differences in live birth and multiple pregnancy were no longer clear. Letrozole was compared in only one trial, so little can be said about it yet.
keyPoints: Gonadotrophins increased live birth compared with clomiphene (moderate-certainty evidence) and shortened the time to a live birth.
Gonadotrophins may raise the chance of multiple pregnancy compared with clomiphene (low-certainty evidence).
With low starting doses and stricter cancellation criteria, effectiveness and safety of the different medicines looked acceptable, so cost, availability and patient preference can guide the choice.
Effects did not seem to differ by age, BMI or whether infertility was primary or secondary; more trials of letrozole are needed.

items.title: Global epidemiology of Neisseria gonorrhoeae in infertile populations: systematic review, meta-analysis and metaregression
items.summary: This review pooled results from 147 studies in 56 countries to see how common gonorrhoea is among people being checked or treated for infertility. About 2.2% of them had a current gonorrhoea infection, which is several times higher than in the general population. The rate was higher in women with blocked or damaged tubes, in those with secondary infertility, and in Africa. The authors say this supports a possible role for gonorrhoea in infertility, and that some infertility may be preventable by controlling its spread.
keyPoints: Around 2.2% of people in infertile populations had current gonorrhoea worldwide, and 5.0% in Africa.
Rates were higher with tubal factor infertility (3.6%) and mixed or unexplained infertility (3.6%), compared with ovarian and non-tubal infertility (0.1%).
Secondary infertility had a higher rate (2.5%) than primary infertility (0.5%).
The authors suggest some infertility may be preventable by controlling gonorrhoea transmission.

items.title: Agents for ovarian stimulation for intrauterine insemination (IUI) in ovulatory women with infertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 82 trials with 12,614 women to compare different fertility medicines used to stimulate the ovaries before intrauterine insemination (IUI) in women who ovulate, including couples with unexplained infertility. Gonadotropin injections probably give a higher chance of live birth than anti-oestrogen tablets. There was no clear evidence that aromatase inhibitors beat anti-oestrogens, and no agent clearly raised the chance of multiple pregnancy. Much of the evidence was low or very low certainty, so many comparisons remain uncertain.
keyPoints: Gonadotropins probably improve cumulative live birth rates compared with anti-oestrogens (moderate-certainty evidence).
Gonadotropins may also give more live births than aromatase inhibitors (low-certainty evidence).
There was no convincing evidence that aromatase inhibitors lead to more live births than anti-oestrogens.
None of the agents compared clearly increased multiple pregnancy rates, and adding GnRH agonists or antagonists did not appear to help (low-certainty evidence).

items.title: The impact of nutrition and lifestyle on male fertility
items.summary: This review gathered studies on how diet and everyday exposures relate to male fertility, especially when no cause for infertility is found. Better sperm quality was seen in men eating a healthy diet, while poorer sperm quality went with more red and processed meat and full-fat dairy. The authors say the overall quality of evidence is still weak and needs to improve.
keyPoints: Higher intake of red meat, processed and organ meat and full-fat dairy was linked to lower-quality sperm.
A diet rich in fruit, vegetables, whole grains and fish was linked to better semen parameters.
Exposure to pollutants such as pesticides, phthalates from food and water containers, and water disinfection by-products has been reported to harm male fertility.
Trials of micronutrient supplements look encouraging for sperm quality and assisted fertilization outcomes, but the best way to use them is not yet established.

items.title: Chinese herbal medicine for female infertility: an updated meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 40 randomized trials with 4,247 women who had infertility, including unexplained infertility, and compared Chinese herbal medicine with Western fertility drugs. The authors found higher pregnancy rates with the herbal treatment: about 60% versus 33% on average. They also reported better ovulation rates and other fertility signs. The abstract does not rate the quality of the evidence, so these results should be read with care.
keyPoints: Across 40 trials, women given Chinese herbal medicine were about 1.74 times as likely to become pregnant as women given Western medical drug treatment alone.
Average pregnancy rates were 60% with Chinese herbal medicine and 33% with Western medical treatment.
The authors report that pregnancy rates improved about 2-fold within 3-6 months.
Ovulation rates, cervical mucus score, basal body temperature pattern and womb lining thickness were also positively influenced.

items.title: The management of uterine fibroids in women with otherwise unexplained infertility
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looks at how to manage uterine fibroids (non-cancerous growths in the womb) in women whose infertility has no other clear cause. It says that fibroids growing into the womb cavity (submucosal) should be removed to improve the chances of pregnancy. Fibroids on the outside of the womb (subserosal) do not appear to affect fertility, and removing fibroids within the womb wall (intramural) is generally not recommended when the womb lining is intact. Uterine artery embolization is generally not advised for women who want to become pregnant.
keyPoints: Submucosal fibroids (those pressing into the womb cavity) should be removed in women with otherwise unexplained infertility to improve conception and pregnancy rates.
Subserosal fibroids do not appear to affect fertility, and removing them is not recommended.
Surgery to remove intramural fibroids is generally not recommended when the womb lining is intact, though care can be individualised if there are no other options.
Uterine artery embolization is linked with lower pregnancy rates, more miscarriages and loss of ovarian reserve, so it is generally not offered to women seeking pregnancy.

items.title: Prevalence, Diagnosis, and Management of Stress Urinary Incontinence in Women: A Collaborative Review
items.summary: This review looked at recent research and guidelines on stress urinary incontinence, which is leaking urine during activity such as coughing or exercise. It found the condition is often missed and under-treated. Pelvic floor muscle training is the first-line approach, and surgery is a second option with higher risks. For complicated or severe cases, high-quality data are still lacking.
keyPoints: Stress urinary incontinence is underdiagnosed and undertreated, and many women with it do not seek care.
Pelvic floor muscle training is a first-line treatment and helps symptoms when it comes with good instruction and supervision.
Sling surgery is a second-line option, but worries about mesh-related complications have reduced its use and made some patients hesitant.
Other surgical options such as bulking agents, colposuspension and fascial slings have robust evidence but different side-effect profiles, and data for severe cases remain limited.

items.title: Why should we stop implanting transobturator sling?
items.summary: This French urology position paper looked at two common mesh sling operations for stress urinary incontinence (leaks when coughing, sneezing or exercising): the retropubic type (TVT) and the transobturator type (TOT). It reports that synthetic slings, especially TVT, are safe and work well, with low long-term complication and repeat-surgery rates. TOT has fewer injuries to the bladder during surgery but more chronic groin and pelvic pain, and the mesh is harder to remove if problems occur. The authors argue TOT should be stopped in favour of TVT; this is an expert opinion based on level 3 evidence.
keyPoints: Synthetic slings, especially TVT, are reported to be safe and effective with low long-term complication and revision rates.
Slings work about as well as older Burch colposuspension surgery but cause fewer voiding (urination) problems.
TOT carries a lower risk of bladder perforation but a significantly higher rate of chronic groin and pelvic pain.
The authors recommend discontinuing TOT, and focusing on surgeon training, patient selection and aftercare.

items.title: Practice bulletin on the management of female stress urinary incontinence in France from the Committee of female urology (CUROPF) of the French Association of Urology (AFU)
items.summary: This is a French urology society's interim guidance on treating stress urinary incontinence, which is leaking urine when coughing, sneezing or exercising. It recommends that women are told about all their options and share in the decision. Lifestyle changes and supervised pelvic floor muscle training come first, while some newer energy-based treatments do not yet have enough evidence. Sling surgery is still considered the gold standard in selected cases but is tightly regulated in France.
keyPoints: First-line care includes lifestyle changes, physical activity and weight loss, which may reduce leaks, especially in women who are overweight or obese.
Pelvic floor muscle training supervised by trained professionals is the cornerstone of non-surgical treatment, with strong evidence that it prevents and treats stress leaks.

Vaginal pessaries may be considered, particularly alongside pelvic floor training; laser, radiofrequency and electromagnetic treatments lack enough evidence and should only be used in clinical trials.
Duloxetine has modest benefit with frequent side effects, topical estrogens may help after menopause, and mid-urethral sling surgery remains the gold standard in selected cases.

items.title: Practice bulletin on the diagnosis of female stress urinary incontinence in France from the Committee of Female Urology (CUROPF) of the French Association of Urology (AFU)
items.summary: French urology specialists published a practice bulletin on how doctors should assess stress urinary incontinence, which is leaking urine when coughing, sneezing or exercising. It sets out a step-by-step way to work out whether leaks are stress-type or another kind. This includes talking through symptoms, filling in questionnaires and a physical exam with a cough test. The abstract does not rate the strength of the evidence, and national guidelines are still to come.
keyPoints: A structured assessment starts with a detailed interview, symptom and quality-of-life questionnaires, and a physical exam including a cough stress test.
Risk factors reviewed include age, number of births, mode of delivery, obesity and menopausal status; hysterectomy, radiotherapy and constipation are more debated.
Tools such as bladder diaries, pad tests and non-invasive urodynamic tests can help, while invasive urodynamics and imaging are kept for selected, complex cases.
Doctors distinguish between a bladder-neck/urethra that moves too much and a weak urethral sphincter, which helps guide treatment choices.

items.title: Transvaginal mesh or grafts or native tissue repair for vaginal prolapse
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 51 trials (7846 women) comparing surgery for vaginal prolapse using permanent mesh, absorbable mesh or biological grafts against traditional repair with the woman's own tissue. Permanent mesh lowered the chance of being aware of prolapse, needing repeat prolapse surgery, or having prolapse found on examination. But it also meant more women needing repeat surgery overall (for prolapse, stress incontinence or mesh exposure), more bladder injuries, and more new bladder leaks with coughing or sneezing. Absorbable mesh and biological grafts showed no clear benefit over repair with the woman's own tissue.
keyPoints: Permanent mesh lowered awareness of prolapse and repeat prolapse surgery compared with native tissue repair, based on moderate-certainty evidence.
About 11.8% of women with mesh had mesh exposure, and 6.1% needed surgery for it.
Permanent mesh was linked to more total repeat surgery, bladder injury and new stress urinary incontinence; painful sex (dyspareunia) did not differ clearly.
The authors conclude transvaginal mesh has limited use in first-time prolapse surgery, and that absorbable meshes and biological grafts are not supported.

items.title: Conservative Interventions for Urinary Incontinence on Postpartum Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 17 randomized trials on non-surgical treatments for bladder leaks after childbirth. Pelvic floor exercises done with supervision, or with a vaginal cone, reduced leaking more than exercises done alone. Adding other therapies such as acupuncture or core training seemed to help further. The authors say more research is needed to confirm how well these treatments work.
keyPoints: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training plus a vaginal cone cut rates of postpartum leaking more than pelvic floor exercises done on your own.
Combining pelvic floor training, or electrical stimulation and biofeedback, with other therapies (for example acupuncture or core training) improved symptom severity.
Supervised pelvic floor training, and electrical stimulation and biofeedback plus core training, gave the biggest gains in incontinence-related quality of life.
All 17 studies had low to moderate risk of bias, but the authors say more evidence is needed.

items.title: The Urogynecology Section of the Polish Society of Gynecologists and Obstetricians Guideline for the diagnostic assessment of stress urinary incontinence in women
items.summary: A Polish guideline group updated its advice on how doctors should assess stress urinary incontinence, which is leaking urine when coughing, sneezing or exercising. It describes a two-step process: an initial assessment, then specialized testing only for women who need it. For many women, the initial assessment is enough to plan the best treatment.
keyPoints: Assessment is split into initial diagnostics and specialized diagnostics.
For a number of women, the initial assessment is enough to choose the best treatment plan.
The initial assessment also helps identify who needs further specialized testing.

The extent of specialized testing is tailored to each woman and depends on how complex her symptoms are, any past surgery, the treatment plan, the doctor's experience, available equipment and cost-effectiveness.

items.title: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training In Women Practicing High-impact Sports: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at whether pelvic floor muscle training helps women who leak urine while doing high-impact sports. It pooled five small studies with 104 women in total. Training reduced how often and how much women leaked, and some studies also found stronger pelvic floor muscles. The two studies that measured quality of life found no difference after training.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training improved urine leakage symptoms in female athletes, reducing both how often and how much they leaked.
Two of three studies that measured pelvic floor function found stronger maximal muscle contraction, and one found better vaginal resting pressure.
Neither of the two studies that measured quality of life found a difference after training.
The review included only five small studies (104 women), so the evidence base is limited.

items.title: Can you breathe yourself to a better pelvic floor? A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether breathing exercises can help bladder leaks or pelvic organ prolapse, either on their own or alongside pelvic floor muscle training. It pooled 18 studies, including nine randomised trials. Training the pelvic floor muscles worked better than breathing exercises, and adding breathing exercises gave no extra benefit. The authors say the evidence for using breathing exercises instead of, or on top of, pelvic floor training is scant or non-existent.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training was more effective than breathing exercises for bladder leaks and prolapse.
Adding breathing exercises to pelvic floor training had no additional effect.
Pelvic floor muscles were activated much less when breathing out than during a deliberate pelvic floor contraction.
The studies were small and varied, so the evidence for breathing exercises is scant.

items.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training on Quality of Life in Women with Urinary Incontinence: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from recent studies on pelvic floor muscle training (exercises that strengthen the muscles supporting the bladder) in women with bladder leaks. Quality of life improved moderately overall, with a small effect in studies that had a comparison group and a moderate effect in studies that tracked one group before and after. Benefits were seen in areas like social activities and general health, mainly for women with stress urinary incontinence (leaks when coughing, sneezing or exercising).
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training moderately improved quality of life in women with urinary incontinence.
The effect was small in controlled studies and moderate in before-and-after studies of a single group.
Social activities and general health were among the areas that improved.
Benefits were seen mainly in women with stress urinary incontinence.

items.title: Prophylactic antibiotics for preventing infection after continence surgery in women with stress urinary incontinence
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether giving antibiotics around the time of surgery for stress urinary incontinence (leaking when coughing, sneezing or exercising) lowers the chance of infection afterwards. Only three small trials with 390 women were found. The evidence was of very low quality, so it is not possible to say whether the antibiotics help or not. None of the trials reported on side effects of the antibiotics.
keyPoints: Three trials (390 women) were found; the review authors rated the evidence as very low certainty.
It is very uncertain whether antibiotics (cefazolin) change the risk of wound infections, urinary tract infections, fever or mesh exposure.
The trials studied different operations and different antibiotic doses, which makes results hard to compare.
There was not enough evidence to support or rule out routine antibiotics, and more trials are needed.

items.title: The Urogynecology Section of the Polish Society of Gynecologists and Obstetricians Guideline on the use of urodynamic testing in gynecological practice
items.summary: This guideline from Polish gynecology specialists explains when urodynamic testing, a set of tests that measure how the bladder stores and empties urine, is useful for women with bladder symptoms. The tests give a first diagnosis that doctors then check against a woman's history, physical exam and other test results. The guideline says the tests are not needed before first-time surgery for simple stress urinary incontinence (leaks when coughing or exercising), but can help guide treatment when the problem is more complicated.
keyPoints: Urodynamic testing gives a preliminary diagnosis, which doctors combine with medical history, examination and other test results.
Testing before surgery for stress urinary incontinence is allowed, but the decision is left to the doctor.
It is not necessary before first surgery for uncomplicated stress urinary incontinence, but it can improve treatment choices in complicated cases.
How much testing is done should match each woman's symptoms and needs.

items.title: Traditional suburethral sling operations for urinary incontinence in women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 34 trials with 3,244 women to see how well traditional sling operations work for stress urinary incontinence (leaking when coughing, sneezing or exercising). Compared with another open operation called colposuspension, traditional slings probably left more women dry in the medium term (one to five years) and fewer needed repeat surgery. Compared with newer mid-urethral slings, traditional slings were probably no better and may be less effective, and may cause more complications. Most trials did not follow women for long, so the long-term picture is unclear.
keyPoints: Versus colposuspension, traditional slings probably led to more women being dry at one to five years (69% vs 59%, moderate-quality evidence).
Women were less likely to need repeat continence surgery after a traditional sling than after colposuspension (high-quality evidence).
Versus mid-urethral slings, traditional slings were probably no better and may be less effective at one to five years; mid-urethral slings may have fewer complications (low-quality evidence).
Evidence is too limited to say whether traditional slings are better or worse than drugs, injectables or other treatments, and long-term follow-up data are lacking.

items.title: Mid-urethral sling operations for stress urinary incontinence in women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 81 trials with over 12,000 women to look at mid-urethral sling surgery, a small tape placed under the urethra to treat stress urinary incontinence (leaks when coughing, sneezing or exercising). The surgery worked well in the short and medium term, whichever route the tape took. The two main routes (through the groin area or behind the pubic bone) had similar cure rates but different side effects. Evidence quality was mostly moderate, and longer-term data are still limited.
keyPoints: Slings are highly effective in the short and medium term, and growing evidence suggests they keep working in the long term.
Cure rates were similar for the transobturator (groin) route and the retropubic route, with short-term subjective cure ranging from about 62% to 98% and 71% to 97% respectively.
The transobturator route had fewer bladder perforations (0.6% versus 4.5%) and less voiding difficulty, but more groin pain (6.4% versus 1.3%).
Repeat incontinence surgery in the long term was more likely after the transobturator route, though this is based on limited, low quality evidence.

items.title: 2014 consensus statement on improving pelvic floor muscle training adherence: International Continence Society 2011 State-of-the-Science Seminar
items.summary: This is an expert consensus statement from the International Continence Society on why people find it hard to keep up pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), the exercises often used for bladder leaks. The panel found few high-quality studies, so its conclusions rely partly on expert opinion. It found that sticking with the exercises matters for both short-term and longer-term benefit, and that belief in your own ability and intention to keep going predict who sticks with them.
keyPoints: Few high-quality studies on sticking with pelvic floor exercises were found, so conclusions draw on expert opinion.
Sticking with the exercises is central to short- and longer-term benefit from PFMT.
Confidence in being able to do the exercises (self-efficacy) and intention to keep going predicted adherence.
Patient-related factors were the biggest barrier to sticking with PFMT in an online survey of health professionals and the public.

items.title: Lifestyle interventions for the treatment of urinary incontinence in adults
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 11 trials of everyday lifestyle changes for bladder leaks in adults, such as weight loss, drinking less fluid and cutting down on caffeine. The best sign of benefit was for weight loss, where more women reported fewer leaks after six months, though the evidence was low quality. For fluid intake, caffeine and soy diets, the studies were too weak to say whether they help. The authors conclude there isn't enough evidence yet to say reliably whether lifestyle changes treat bladder leaks.
keyPoints: In one trial, 76% of women on a weight loss programme reported improved leaks at six months versus 54% of controls, and the effect was still seen at 18 months (low quality evidence).
Drinking less fluid may improve quality of life related to leaks, but the evidence was very low quality and some people had headaches, constipation or thirst.
No firm conclusions could be reached about cutting caffeine or eating a soy-rich diet because the trials were weak.
Side effects seemed uncommon, but there were no trials on alcohol, constipation, smoking or physical activity.

items.title: Updates to Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline (2025)
items.summary: This is a 2025 update to a urology guideline on women who get repeat urinary tract infections (UTIs) that are not caused by other health problems. It aims to cut unneeded antibiotic use, lower antibiotic resistance and side effects, and improve women's quality of life. The update adds more non-antibiotic options for preventing UTIs and shows that a negative urine test can help rule out a UTI. It also shifts away from relying on germ detection alone toward a clinician's judgement about the risks and benefits of antibiotics for each woman.
keyPoints: There are now more non-antibiotic options to help prevent repeat UTIs.
A negative urinalysis (urine test) is better understood as a way to rule out a UTI.
Decisions about antibiotics rely less on detecting germs and more on a clinician weighing each woman's individual risks and benefits.
The guideline aims to reduce inappropriate antibiotic use, antibiotic resistance and antibiotic side effects.

items.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines by Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA): 2025 Guidelines on Management and Treatment of Complicated Urinary Tract Infections--Duration of Antibiotics for Complicated UTI
items.summary: This guideline looked at how long antibiotics are needed for complicated urinary tract infections (UTIs), including those with bacteria in the blood. It suggests that people who are getting better on effective antibiotics can use a shorter course instead of a longer one. Shorter courses worked about as well as longer ones, except in men with fever where a prostate infection is suspected, who may need longer treatment.
keyPoints: For complicated UTI in people who are improving, 5-7 days of a fluoroquinolone or 7 days of a non-fluoroquinolone antibiotic is suggested instead of longer courses.
This applies whether or not Gram-negative bacteria are also found in the blood.
Men with fever and a suspected acute prostate infection may benefit from 10-14 days of treatment.
Short courses of oral beta-lactam antibiotics may need higher doses to work well.

items.title: Bacterial Vaccines for the Management of Recurrent Urinary Tract Infections: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 studies (2,822 adults) on bacterial vaccines to prevent urinary tract infections (UTIs) that keep coming back. In placebo-controlled trials, more people who had the vaccine stayed UTI-free over 6 to 12 months. The authors say the evidence is limited and low quality, so longer, larger trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Vaccines may help adult women stay free of repeat UTIs in the short term (6-12 months).
In placebo-controlled studies, about 6 to 7 people would need to be vaccinated for one extra person to stay UTI-free, though this estimate was very uncertain.
The studies varied a lot, and there was a slight risk that unpublished results were missing.
Long-term benefit is not yet known and needs larger, longer trials.

items.title: Cranberry Juice, Cranberry Tablets, or Liquid Therapies for Urinary Tract Infection: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 20 trials with 3,091 people to compare cranberry juice, cranberry tablets and simply drinking more fluids for urinary tract infections (UTIs). Cranberry juice was linked to fewer UTIs and less antibiotic use than placebo drinks or no treatment. Drinking more fluids also lowered UTI rates compared with no treatment, but cranberry juice did better. The authors rate the certainty of this evidence as moderate to low.
keyPoints: Cranberry juice was linked to a 54% lower rate of UTIs than no treatment and a 27% lower rate than a placebo drink.
Cranberry juice was linked to 49% less antibiotic use than a placebo drink and 59% less than no treatment.
Cranberry products also reduced UTI-related symptoms.
Increased fluid intake lowered UTI rates compared with no treatment, though cranberry in liquid form gave better results.

items.title: Prophylaxis Options in Children With a History of Recurrent Urinary Tract Infections: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pooled 23 trials with 3,335 children who kept getting urinary tract infections (UTIs) to compare ways of preventing new infections. Cranberry products and the antibiotic nitrofurantoin were linked to fewer UTIs while children were taking them. Nitrofurantoin looked like the best option for cutting the number of infections. None of the options were shown to reduce kidney scarring.
keyPoints: Cranberry products lowered the odds of symptomatic UTIs during prophylaxis compared with no treatment.
Nitrofurantoin lowered the odds of UTIs compared with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or trimethoprim, and may be the best option overall for reducing UTIs.
No prevention option was shown to reduce kidney scarring.
More trials of non-antibiotic options are needed, especially looking at kidney scarring risk.

items.title: Global prevalence of urinary tract infection in pregnant mothers: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 27 studies covering 30,641 pregnant women to estimate how common urinary tract infections (UTIs) are in pregnancy worldwide. About 24 in 100 pregnant women had a UTI, counting both infections with symptoms and those without. Larger and more recent studies tended to report lower rates. The authors recommend regular UTI screening in pregnancy and prompt treatment if an infection is found.
keyPoints: The overall global prevalence of UTI in pregnancy was 23.9% (95% confidence interval 16.2-33.8), including symptomatic and asymptomatic infections.
Larger studies and more recent studies reported lower UTI rates.
The authors recommend that all pregnant women have regular UTI screening tests and prompt treatment if diagnosed.
Early detection and treatment are described as important to prevent complications for both mother and baby.

items.title: Cranberries for preventing urinary tract infections
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 50 trials with nearly 9,000 people to see whether cranberry products prevent urinary tract infections (UTIs). Cranberry products probably lowered the chance of a UTI in women who get them repeatedly, in children, and in people prone to UTIs after a medical procedure. There was little or no benefit in pregnant women, older people in care homes, or adults who cannot empty their bladder fully. Stomach side effects were probably no different from placebo.
keyPoints: Overall, cranberry products reduced the risk of symptomatic UTIs confirmed by a urine culture (moderate certainty evidence).
They probably helped women with recurrent UTIs, children, and people prone to UTIs after a medical intervention.
Little or no benefit was seen in pregnant women, elderly people in institutions, and adults with bladder emptying problems.
Compared with antibiotics, cranberry made little or no difference to UTI risk, and stomach side effects probably did not differ from placebo.

items.title: Cranberries for treating urinary tract infections
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for good-quality trials testing whether cranberry juice or cranberry products can treat a urinary tract infection (UTI) that is already present. It found no trials that met its standards. This means there is currently no good-quality evidence showing that cranberries treat UTIs, and the review calls for properly designed studies.
keyPoints: No randomised trials of cranberries for treating UTIs met the review's inclusion criteria.
Seven studies were excluded because of the wrong design, mixed treatments or no relevant results; one study is ongoing with unknown status.
There is no good-quality evidence that cranberry juice or products are effective for treating UTIs.
Future studies should compare cranberry products with placebo and measure symptoms, urine clearing, side effects, dose and duration.

items.title: D-mannose for preventing and treating urinary tract infections
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether D-mannose, a sugar sold as a supplement, can prevent or treat urinary tract infections (UTIs). It found seven small trials with 719 adults, but the studies were too different to combine and were of poor quality. The review found little to no evidence either for or against D-mannose, and side effects were few and mild, mostly diarrhoea and vaginal burning.
keyPoints: Seven trials (719 adults) were included, but no two were similar enough to pool their results.
Effects of D-mannose on UTIs were uncertain compared with no treatment or with antibiotics, based on very low certainty evidence.
Few side effects were reported and none were serious; the most common were diarrhoea and vaginal burning.
The authors call for a larger, well-designed trial comparing D-mannose with a placebo.
