items.title: Estrogen for the prevention of recurrent urinary tract infections in postmenopausal women: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled eight randomized trials (4,702 postmenopausal women) comparing estrogen with placebo for preventing repeated urinary tract infections. Vaginal estrogen cut the number of infections and lowered vaginal pH. Oral estrogen made no clear difference to infection rates. Side effects like vaginal irritation or itching were reported with vaginal estrogen, but were not significantly more common than with placebo.
keyPoints: Vaginal estrogen significantly reduced recurrent UTIs compared with placebo (relative risk 0.42).
Oral estrogen showed no significant difference in recurrent UTIs compared with placebo.
Vaginal estrogen lowered vaginal pH in postmenopausal women.
Vaginal discomfort, irritation, burning and itching were reported, with no significant increase versus placebo.

items.title: Consumption of cranberry as adjuvant therapy for urinary tract infections in susceptible populations: A systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 23 trials with nearly 4,000 people who are prone to urinary tract infections (UTIs) to see whether cranberry products help prevent them. Overall, people taking cranberry had about 30% fewer UTIs than those who did not. The authors say cranberry can be considered as an extra way to help prevent UTIs, but because of limits in the studies included, the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Across 23 trials (3,979 people), cranberry products lowered the risk of UTIs by about 30% (risk ratio 0.70).
Risk dropped by about 32% in women with recurrent UTIs, 45% in children and 51% in people using indwelling catheters.
Cranberry juice appeared to work better than capsules or tablets in the subgroup comparison (35% lower risk).
The authors conclude cranberry may be considered as an add-on for prevention, but the studies had limitations.

items.title: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Asymptomatic Bacteriuria: 2019 Update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America
items.summary: Asymptomatic bacteriuria means bacteria are found in the urine but there are no symptoms of a urinary tract infection. It is common, including in healthy women. This updated guideline from the Infectious Diseases Society of America builds on its 2005 advice, which was to screen for and treat it only in pregnant women or before invasive urologic procedures. The update notes that treating it with antibiotics adds to inappropriate antibiotic use and the spread of antibiotic resistance.
keyPoints: The 2005 guideline advised screening and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnant women or before invasive urologic procedures.
Treatment was not recommended for healthy women, older women or men, or people with diabetes, indwelling catheters or spinal cord injury.
Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria with antibiotics contributes to inappropriate antibiotic use, which promotes antibiotic resistance.
The update adds recommendations for groups not covered before and addresses how to interpret vague symptoms in groups where this condition is common.

items.title: Cranberry Reduces the Risk of Urinary Tract Infection Recurrence in Otherwise Healthy Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 7 randomized trials involving about 1,500 generally healthy women who had had a urinary tract infection (UTI) before. Women who took cranberry had about a 26% lower risk of getting another UTI than those given a placebo or no treatment. The studies were fairly small, and the authors say larger, high-quality studies are needed to confirm the result.
keyPoints: Across 7 trials (1,498 women), cranberry lowered the risk of UTI coming back by 26% (risk ratio 0.74).
The results suggest cranberry may help prevent repeat UTIs in generally healthy women.
The studies were relatively small, and two had problems such as many people dropping out or selective reporting of results.
The authors call for larger, high-quality studies to confirm the findings.

items.title: Urinary alkalisation for symptomatic uncomplicated urinary tract infection in women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for trials testing urinary alkalisers (products that make urine less acidic) for easing symptoms of simple urinary tract infections in women. The reviewers screened 172 possible studies and none met the criteria. So there is no trial evidence yet on whether these products work or are safe for this use.
keyPoints: No randomised trials were found that tested urinary alkalisers for symptoms of uncomplicated UTI in women.
Urinary alkalisers are widely used in some countries and recommended in some national formularies, but some guidelines advise against them.
Until trials are done, whether these products are safe and effective for UTI symptoms is unknown.

items.title: Probiotics for preventing urinary tract infections in adults and children
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether probiotics can prevent urinary tract infections (UTIs) in adults and children. It combined nine small trials with 735 people in total. Probiotics did not clearly reduce repeat UTIs compared with placebo or no treatment, but the studies were small and of poor quality, so a benefit or a harm cannot be ruled out.
keyPoints: No significant reduction in repeat symptomatic UTIs was found with probiotics compared with placebo (6 studies, 352 people).
One study found no clear difference between probiotics and antibiotics, but one trial is too little evidence to draw a conclusion.
The studies were small with a high risk of bias, so any apparent effects may be misleading or overestimated.
Reported side effects included diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, constipation and vaginal symptoms; information on serious harms was limited.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 717: Sulfonamides, Nitrofurantoin, and Risk of Birth Defects
items.summary: This ACOG committee opinion looks at whether two groups of antibiotics, sulfonamides and nitrofurantoin, are linked to birth defects. The evidence is mixed. In the second and third trimesters both can still be used as first-choice treatments for urinary tract infections. In the first trimester they are still considered appropriate when no other suitable antibiotic is available, because untreated infections can cause serious problems for mother and baby.
keyPoints: Evidence linking sulfonamides and nitrofurantoin to birth defects is mixed.
In the second and third trimesters both may continue to be used as first-line treatment for urinary tract infections.
In the first trimester they are considered appropriate when no suitable alternative antibiotic is available.
Pregnant women should not be denied treatment for infections, because untreated infections can lead to serious complications.

items.title: RSV-Pre-F Vaccination During Pregnancy and Neonatal Outcomes-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled seven studies on whether the RSV vaccine given in pregnancy raises the chance of preterm birth or a baby needing neonatal intensive care (NICU). Across all studies combined, no link to preterm birth or NICU admission was found. The three randomised trials alone did suggest a higher chance of preterm birth, while the four observational studies did not. The authors rate the evidence as low to very low certainty, so firm conclusions can't be drawn yet.
keyPoints: Combined results from all seven studies showed no overall link between maternal RSV vaccination and preterm birth.
The three randomised trials alone showed a higher risk of preterm birth (RR 1.26), but the four observational studies showed no association.
NICU admission was not significantly affected by the vaccine.
The authors call for continued surveillance and long-term safety monitoring as the vaccine is rolled out more widely.

items.title: Recommendations for Prevention and Control of Influenza in Children, 2025-2026: Technical Report
items.summary: This technical report from the American Academy of Pediatrics explains why all children without medical reasons to avoid it should get a flu vaccine every year from 6 months of age. It reviews recent flu seasons, how serious flu is for children, how well the vaccines work, and how many children are vaccinated. It also covers the types of flu vaccine available for 2025-2026, vaccination during pregnancy and breastfeeding, flu testing, and antiviral medicines for treatment and prevention.
keyPoints: The AAP recommends yearly flu vaccination for all children from 6 months of age who have no medical contraindications.
Flu vaccination protects both children and the wider community.
The report includes guidance on flu vaccination during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Antiviral medicines can be used to treat flu and to prevent it after exposure.

items.title: Prevention and Control of Seasonal Influenza with Vaccines: Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices - United States, 2025-26 Influenza Season
items.source: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.journal: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.summary: This US report sets out the 2025-26 flu vaccine recommendations from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. It recommends a yearly flu vaccine for everyone aged 6 months and older who has no reason to avoid it. A new recommendation for the 2025-26 season is that children up to age 18, pregnant women and all adults receive only single-dose flu vaccines that are free of the preservative thimerosal.
keyPoints: Yearly flu vaccination is recommended for everyone aged 6 months and older without a contraindication.
New for 2025-26: children aged 18 or under, pregnant women and all adults should receive only single-dose vaccines free of thimerosal as a preservative.
Several vaccine types are expected to be available, including inactivated, recombinant and live attenuated (nasal) vaccines.
The report also notes the approval of FluMist for self- or caregiver administration and Flublok for ages 9 and up.

items.title: Use of Clesrovimab for Prevention of Severe Respiratory Syncytial Virus-Associated Lower Respiratory Tract Infections in Infants: Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices - United States, 2025
items.source: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.journal: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.summary: This US guideline covers three ways to protect babies from severe RSV lung infections. These are an RSV vaccine given during pregnancy, or one of two long-acting antibody injections given to the baby (nirsevimab or the newly licensed clesrovimab). In June 2025 the US Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices added clesrovimab as an option for babies under 8 months old who were not protected through maternal vaccination. No single option is preferred.
keyPoints: All infants should be protected against RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infection, either through maternal RSV vaccination in pregnancy or an antibody injection given to the infant.
Clesrovimab was recommended in June 2025 as an alternative to nirsevimab for infants under 8 months who are born during or entering their first RSV season.
The antibody injections are meant for babies who are not protected through maternal RSV vaccination.
No one product is preferred; the choice depends on parent preference, product availability, and when the baby is born relative to the RSV season.

items.title: Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) Vaccination and Assisted Reproduction Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 25 studies to see whether COVID-19 vaccination affects the outcomes of fertility treatment such as IVF. It compared thousands of vaccinated and unvaccinated patients. There were no statistically significant differences in pregnancy rates, number of eggs retrieved, fertilization, implantation or live birth. The authors concluded that COVID-19 vaccination is not associated with different fertility outcomes in people having assisted reproduction.
keyPoints: Clinical pregnancy rates were not significantly different between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients.
Number of eggs retrieved, fertilization rate, implantation rate and live-birth rate also showed no significant differences.
Results did not change when studies were split by country or vaccine type.
The review included 25 studies, with 19 reporting embryo transfer outcomes and 18 reporting ovarian stimulation outcomes.

items.title: Efficacy and Clinical Outcomes of mRNA COVID-19 Vaccine in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 11 observational studies covering more than 46,000 pregnancies in which women received an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine (almost all Pfizer). Side effects were mostly mild, such as arm pain, tiredness and headache, and were similar to those seen in women who are not pregnant. Stillbirth and preterm birth rates in vaccinated women were low, and the authors report that vaccination was linked to lower illness and death for mothers and babies. There were no randomised trials, so the findings come from observational studies only.
keyPoints: Local side effects after at least one dose included pain (32%), swelling (5%) and redness (1%).
Systemic side effects included fatigue (25%), headache (19%), muscle pain (18%), chills (12%), fever (11%) and joint pain (8%).
Among the vaccinated pregnancies, 0.03% ended in stillbirth and 3.68% in preterm birth, and average birthweight was 3,452 g.
The side effect pattern in pregnant women was similar to that in non-pregnant women, and one or both doses were linked to lower maternal and fetal illness and death.

items.title: Respiratory syncytial virus vaccination during pregnancy for improving infant outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled six trials with nearly 18,000 pregnant women to see whether an RSV vaccine given in pregnancy protects babies. RSV is a common virus that can cause serious chest infections in infants. The vaccine roughly halved the number of babies hospitalised with lab-confirmed RSV. It had little or no effect on birth defects or poor growth in the womb, but there may be a small signal for more preterm births that needs further study.
keyPoints: Maternal RSV vaccination reduced infant hospitalisation with lab-confirmed RSV disease (about 11 fewer per 1000 infants), based on high-certainty evidence.
There was little or no effect on congenital abnormalities (high certainty) and likely little or no effect on poor growth in the womb (moderate certainty).
Preterm birth may be somewhat more likely after vaccination (8 more per 1000 infants), but the evidence is very uncertain and needs further investigation.
Evidence on stillbirth, maternal death and infant death is low or very low certainty, with little or no effect seen so far.

items.title: Effectiveness and safety of COVID-19 vaccine in pregnant women: A systematic review with meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 14 observational studies covering over 360,000 pregnant women to look at COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy. Vaccinated women had fewer SARS-CoV-2 infections and fewer COVID-19 hospital admissions than unvaccinated women. No significant differences were found in complications for the mother or baby. The authors rate the certainty of the evidence as very low, so the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Vaccination during pregnancy was linked to fewer SARS-CoV-2 infections and fewer COVID-19 hospitalisations.
The benefit looked larger in women who were fully vaccinated.
No clear difference was found in intensive care admission, though the result was uncertain.
No significant differences were found in maternal or fetal complications between vaccinated and unvaccinated women.

items.title: Interventions to increase uptake of influenza vaccination in pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from seven randomised trials to see which approaches help pregnant women get the flu vaccine. Overall, the approaches tested made vaccination more likely than usual care. The clearest benefit came from educational approaches such as pamphlets, websites and short one-to-one talks.
keyPoints: Across seven trials, interventions made flu vaccination in pregnancy more likely than standard care (OR 1.78).
Educational interventions showed the clearest effect (OR 2.71).
Pamphlets, websites and brief one-to-one education can be effective tools.
Flu vaccination in pregnancy aims to protect pregnant women, their babies in the womb, and infants too young to be vaccinated.

items.title: The risk of miscarriage following COVID-19 vaccination: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined the results of 21 studies covering about 150,000 women to see whether COVID-19 vaccines raise the risk of miscarriage. Women who were vaccinated did not have a higher risk of miscarriage than women who were not vaccinated or who received a placebo. Rates of ongoing pregnancy and live birth were also similar between the two groups. The authors note the evidence is limited, mostly observational and varied in quality, so larger studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Women who received a COVID-19 vaccine did not have a higher risk of miscarriage than those who received a placebo or no vaccine (risk ratio 1.07, with a range of 0.89 to 1.28).
Rates of ongoing pregnancy or live birth were comparable between vaccinated and unvaccinated women.
The review included 21 studies (5 randomised trials and 16 observational studies) with 149,685 women.
The authors caution that the studies varied a lot and had some risk of bias, so larger population studies are needed.

items.title: Effect of COVID-19 vaccination on the outcome of in vitro fertilization: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 20 studies covering 18,877 people having IVF to see whether COVID-19 vaccination affects fertility treatment results. Vaccination made no difference to egg numbers, mature eggs, fertilisation, embryo (blastocyst) development, implantation or early (biochemical) pregnancy rates. Clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates were very slightly lower in the vaccinated group in the combined analysis, but the mRNA vaccine subgroup showed no significant differences on any measure. The authors conclude vaccination does not adversely affect IVF outcomes.
keyPoints: No difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated people in egg numbers, mature eggs, fertilisation, blastocyst rate, implantation rate or biochemical pregnancy rate.
Clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates were slightly lower overall (risk ratios 0.97 and 0.93), but the abstract reports no significant differences in the mRNA vaccine subgroup.
The authors conclude COVID-19 vaccination does not adversely affect IVF outcomes and hope this eases vaccine hesitancy for women planning IVF.

items.title: Burden of stillbirths among women vaccinated with COVID-19 vaccines: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 8 studies to estimate how often stillbirth happened among pregnant women who had a COVID-19 vaccine. About 5 in every 1,000 births were stillbirths, which the authors describe as a low rate. The studies differed a lot from each other, so the exact figure is uncertain. The authors conclude the results add to evidence that COVID-19 vaccination in pregnancy is safe.
keyPoints: The pooled stillbirth rate among vaccinated pregnant women was about 5 per 1,000 births.
The authors describe this as a low stillbirth rate.
Results varied widely between studies, and the confidence range was wide.
The authors say the findings support the safety of COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy.

items.title: Recommendations for Prevention and Control of Influenza in Children, 2023-2024
items.summary: This is guidance from the American Academy of Pediatrics for the 2023-2024 flu season. It recommends a yearly flu shot for all children from 6 months of age, unless there is a medical reason not to, to protect children and the wider community. The report also covers flu vaccination during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and flu tests and antiviral medicines for treatment and prevention. The abstract does not give details of what it says about pregnancy specifically.
keyPoints: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a yearly flu vaccine for all children from 6 months of age who have no medical contraindications.
Flu vaccination is described as an important way to protect children and the wider community.
The report includes a section on vaccination during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
It also covers flu testing, antiviral medicines for treatment and prevention, and ways to encourage vaccine uptake.

items.title: Use of the Pfizer Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine During Pregnancy for the Prevention of Respiratory Syncytial Virus-Associated Lower Respiratory Tract Disease in Infants: Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices - United States, 2023
items.source: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.journal: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.summary: US health advisers (ACIP and CDC) now recommend the Pfizer RSV vaccine (RSVpreF) for pregnant people, given as a single dose between 32 and 36 weeks of pregnancy. Its aim is to protect babies under 6 months old from serious RSV lung infections, since RSV is the leading cause of hospitalization in US infants. The vaccine is recommended during the RSV season, September through the end of January in most of the continental US. Babies need protection from either the maternal vaccine or an infant antibody injection (nirsevimab), but most do not need both.
keyPoints: RSVpreF vaccine is recommended as a one-time dose at 32-36 weeks of pregnancy to help prevent RSV-related lower respiratory infections in babies under 6 months.
In most of the continental US it is given seasonally, from September through the end of January.
Either maternal RSVpreF vaccination or nirsevimab given to the infant is recommended, but both are not needed for most infants.
All infants should be protected against RSV lung infection through one of these two products.

items.title: Intention to Receive COVID-19 Vaccine during Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 surveys covering almost 17,000 pregnant people to see how many planned to get a COVID-19 vaccine. About 47% said they intended to be vaccinated, and this varied a lot between regions. Those who had received flu or Tdap vaccines in pregnancy were more likely to plan on a COVID-19 vaccine. The authors say better shared decision-making and clearer public health messages are needed.
keyPoints: Around 47% of pregnant people surveyed intended to receive a COVID-19 vaccine.
Intention was lowest in Africa (19%) and highest in Oceania (48%).
Having had flu or Tdap vaccines in pregnancy was linked to about three times higher odds of planning a COVID-19 vaccine.
The authors note COVID-19 carries known risks in pregnancy and they found no evidence of risks from vaccination, and call for improved shared decision-making and public health messaging.

items.title: COVID-19 vaccine and pregnancy outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pooled results from observational studies that compared pregnant women who had a COVID-19 vaccine with those who did not. Babies of vaccinated women were no more likely to be smaller than expected for their age in the womb. Vaccinated women also had a slightly lower rate of premature delivery and fewer cases of non-reassuring fetal monitoring.
keyPoints: No difference was found in the chance of having a baby small for gestational age between vaccinated and unvaccinated pregnant women.
Vaccinated pregnant women had a slightly reduced rate of premature delivery.
Vaccinated women also had a reduced chance of non-reassuring fetal monitoring.
The studies reviewed were observational, not randomised trials.

items.title: Maternal and neonatal safety outcomes after SAR-CoV-2 vaccination during pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 13 studies covering about 56,000 pregnant people to look at whether COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy affects safety for mothers and newborns. It found no meaningful difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups for miscarriage, postpartum bleeding, fever after birth, hospital stay, birth weight or newborn Apgar scores. The authors concluded that vaccination showed no effect on these outcomes.
keyPoints: No significant difference in miscarriage risk was found between vaccinated and unvaccinated pregnant people.
No significant differences were found for postpartum hemorrhage, puerperal fever or length of maternal hospital stay.
Birth weight and the chance of a low Apgar score (7 or below at 5 minutes) were similar in both groups.
The analysis combined 13 studies with 56,428 patients.

items.title: The impact of COVID-19 vaccines on fertility-A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 29 studies to ask whether COVID-19 vaccines affect fertility in men and women of reproductive age. Sperm movement, sperm concentration and pregnancy rates were not meaningfully different before and after vaccination, or between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups. The authors conclude there is no scientific proof that COVID-19 vaccines impair fertility. The quality of the included studies was mixed, with most rated poor or moderate.
keyPoints: No clear difference in sperm movement or sperm concentration before versus after vaccination.
Biochemical and clinical pregnancy rates did not differ between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups.
No significant differences were found by vaccine type, including mRNA vaccines.
The authors found no scientific proof linking COVID-19 vaccines to fertility problems in men or women.

items.title: Safety of vaccines used for routine immunization in the United States: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 338 studies on the safety of vaccines routinely used in the United States for children, adults and pregnant women. For pregnant women, it found no evidence of increased risk of serious problems after the tetanus, diphtheria and whooping cough (Tdap) vaccine, including stillbirth. Across all groups, few links were found between vaccines and serious side effects, though very rare events are hard to study.
keyPoints: Pregnant women who had the Tdap vaccine showed no evidence of increased risk of key adverse events, including stillbirth (moderate certainty).
Across a large body of research, few links were found between vaccines and serious adverse events.
Rare events are hard to study, so some uncertainty remains.
Any side effects should be weighed against the protection vaccines provide.

items.title: Vaccines for preventing influenza in healthy adults
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 52 trials of over 80,000 healthy adults to see how well flu vaccines work and how safe they are. Inactivated (injected) flu vaccine probably lowers the chance of getting flu from about 2.3% to 0.9%. In one trial in pregnant women, a flu vaccine containing the 2009 pandemic strain protected about half of mothers and babies (up to 24 weeks old) against flu. The review found no trial data on protection against seasonal flu in pregnancy, and no clear link to serious side effects. The authors describe the protection in pregnant women and newborns as modest.
keyPoints: Inactivated flu vaccine probably reduces flu in healthy adults from 2.3% to 0.9% (moderate-certainty evidence).
In one trial in pregnant women, vaccine efficacy against pH1N1 flu was about 50% in mothers and 49% in infants up to 24 weeks.
Vaccination causes a small increase in fever (1.5% to 2.3%), and no link to serious adverse events was found.
Observational data showed no significant effect of flu vaccines in pregnancy on miscarriage or newborn death, but this evidence is less certain.

items.title: Prevention of Pertussis, Tetanus, and Diphtheria with Vaccines in the United States: Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP)
items.summary: This report pulls together the US vaccine advisory committee's existing advice on preventing whooping cough (pertussis), tetanus and diphtheria. It adds no new recommendations. For pregnancy, it advises a dose of the Tdap vaccine in every pregnancy, given between 27 and 36 weeks, even if the woman has had Tdap before.
keyPoints: Women are recommended to receive one dose of Tdap during each pregnancy.
The dose should be given from 27 through 36 weeks of pregnancy, whether or not Tdap was received before.
Babies and young children are recommended to have a 5-dose DTaP series, and adolescents one Tdap booster.
Adults who have never had Tdap are recommended to get one booster, then a Td booster every 10 years.

items.title: Prophylactic vaccination against human papillomaviruses to prevent cervical cancer and its precursors
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 26 trials (about 73,000 girls and women) to see whether HPV vaccines protect against cervical precancer and whether they are safe. In girls and young women aged 15 to 26, the vaccines clearly lowered the risk of precancerous changes, especially those caused by HPV types 16 and 18. Serious side effects were no more common than with placebo, and the trials did not show a higher risk of miscarriage. The trials were too short to measure actual cervical cancer, and long-term follow-up is still needed.
keyPoints: High-certainty evidence that HPV vaccines protect against cervical precancer in girls and women aged 15 to 26, with the biggest effect for HPV16/18-related lesions.
Protection was greater in those not already infected with high-risk HPV when vaccinated.
In women vaccinated at 24 to 45, there was no clear difference in precancer between vaccinated and unvaccinated women overall.

Serious adverse events were similar between vaccine and control groups (high certainty), and miscarriage risk was similar (high certainty); effects on congenital abnormalities and stillbirth remain uncertain.

items.title: Committee Opinion No. 718: Update on Immunization and Pregnancy: Tetanus, Diphtheria, and Pertussis Vaccination
items.summary: This guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists explains why pregnant women are advised to get the Tdap vaccine, which protects against tetanus, diphtheria and whooping cough (pertussis). Newborns are very vulnerable to whooping cough because they cannot start their own vaccines until about 2 months old. Having the vaccine in pregnancy passes protective antibodies to the baby. The abstract reports no evidence of harm to the baby from this type of vaccine.
keyPoints: One dose of Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy, even if the woman has had the vaccine before.
The best timing is between 27 and 36 weeks of pregnancy, as early in that window as possible, to give the baby the most antibody protection.
Tdap can be given at any point in pregnancy if needed, for example for wound care or during a whooping cough outbreak.
Family members and caregivers who have not had Tdap and will be close to a baby under 12 months should get a single dose.

items.title: The Effects of Influenza Vaccination during Pregnancy on Birth Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined results from many studies that looked at flu vaccination during pregnancy and birth outcomes. Women who had a flu vaccine (either the seasonal vaccine or the 2009 swine flu vaccine) had lower rates of preterm birth and low birth weight than women who were not vaccinated. No clear effect was seen on babies being born smaller than expected for their age. Most of the studies were observational, so they show an association rather than proof of cause.
keyPoints: Seasonal flu vaccine in pregnancy was linked to lower rates of preterm birth and low birth weight.
The 2009 H1N1 flu vaccine in pregnancy was also linked to lower rates of preterm birth and low birth weight.
No significant effect on babies being small for gestational age was found.
The review concluded that flu vaccination in pregnancy was associated with a decreased risk of preterm birth and low birth weight.

items.title: Impact of Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) and viral influenza vaccinations in pregnancy for improving maternal, neonatal and infant health outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether getting a Hib vaccine or a flu vaccine during pregnancy improves health for mothers and babies. Only two trials were found. The Hib evidence was very limited, from one small trial at high risk of bias. The flu vaccine trial was large and high quality, and it found fewer lab-confirmed flu cases in vaccinated women and in their babies, with no clear difference in other outcomes.
keyPoints: Evidence on Hib vaccination in pregnancy is limited, from one small trial at high risk of bias.
In the large flu vaccine trial, lab-confirmed influenza was about half as common in both vaccinated women and their babies.
No clear differences were found for pregnancy outcomes such as miscarriage, preterm labour or stillbirth, or for adverse systemic reactions.
The authors say more trials in different settings are needed for both vaccines.

items.title: Vaccines for women for preventing neonatal tetanus
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether giving tetanus vaccine to women of childbearing age or pregnant women protects newborns from tetanus. A full course of two or three doses clearly reduced tetanus cases and deaths in newborns, while a single dose did not give clear protection. The review's authors support vaccinating women in communities with a similar or higher risk of newborn tetanus. Pain at the injection site was reported more often with the vaccine in a small safety trial.
keyPoints: A two- or three-dose course of tetanus vaccine in women protected newborns from tetanus deaths (moderate-quality evidence).
A single dose did not give clear protection against newborn tetanus deaths (low-quality evidence).
Newborn tetanus cases were lower after at least one dose of tetanus vaccine (moderate-quality evidence).
Pain at the injection site was more common in vaccinated pregnant women than in those given placebo.

items.title: Effective probiotic regimens for bacterial vaginosis treatment and recurrence prevention: A systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 16 randomized trials (published 2014-2024) of probiotics for bacterial vaginosis (BV). One strain, Lactobacillus rhamnosus TOM 22.8, looked most effective: it improved Nugent scores (a lab measure of vaginal bacteria), vaginal pH and the mix of vaginal bacteria, and lowered how often BV came back. Other Lactobacillus strains also showed promise, and side effects were mild and went away on their own. The authors say small studies and varied outcome measures mean larger, better trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Lactobacillus rhamnosus TOM 22.8 (10 billion CFU a day for 10 days) was the most effective strain and dose, improving Nugent scores, vaginal pH and vaginal microbiota, and reducing BV recurrence.
L. crispatus, L. plantarum and L. acidophilus also showed treatment potential at doses of 100 million to 5.4 billion CFU a day, for between 6 days and 4 months.
Reported side effects were mild and self-limiting.
The review supports probiotics as an add-on or alternative BV treatment, but small trials and inconsistent outcome measures mean more research is needed.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of different drugs for the treatment of bacterial vaginosis: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.source: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
items.journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
items.summary: This review pooled 42 studies with 8,382 patients to compare treatments for bacterial vaginosis (BV), a common vaginal imbalance. Ornidazole by mouth looked like an effective option, and metronidazole and secnidazole caused more side effects than placebo, while probiotics caused fewer side effects than metronidazole. Vaginal sucrose and probiotics may be promising treatments, but the authors say more high-quality studies are needed to confirm this.
keyPoints: Oral ornidazole had a better clinical cure rate than clindamycin, secnidazole and probiotics, and may be an effective alternative for BV.
Metronidazole and secnidazole had more adverse reactions than placebo, while probiotics had fewer side effects than metronidazole.
Vaginal sucrose had a better cure rate than metronidazole, and metronidazole had a lower cure rate than probiotics.
Sucrose and probiotics are potential BV treatments that need to be confirmed by more high-quality studies.

items.title: The Role of Probiotics in the Treatment of Vulvovaginal Candidiasis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from six randomised trials of women with vaginal thrush (vulvovaginal candidiasis) who were given probiotics. Probiotics did not change how often tests still grew the yeast compared with a placebo. They did lower the chance of thrush coming back. The authors conclude probiotics may be a helpful alternative treatment, but the abstract does not rate the certainty of the evidence.
keyPoints: Six randomised controlled trials were included in the analysis.
Probiotics were no different from placebo for the rate of positive yeast cultures.
Probiotics were more effective than placebo at reducing recurrence of thrush.
The authors suggest probiotics could be an alternative treatment option for vaginal candidiasis.

items.title: Treatment for recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (thrush)
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at treatments for recurrent thrush (four or more symptomatic episodes in a year) in 23 small trials involving 2212 women. Antifungal treatment, taken by mouth or applied to the vagina, may reduce how often thrush comes back compared with placebo or no treatment. The evidence is low quality, and it is very uncertain whether tablets work better than topical treatments. The findings do not apply to pregnant women, women with diabetes or women with weakened immune systems, as these groups were mostly left out of the studies.
keyPoints: Oral or topical antifungals may reduce symptomatic recurrences of thrush at 6 and 12 months compared with placebo or no treatment (low-certainty evidence).
No clear difference was found between oral and topical treatment, or between different doses and treatment lengths (very low-certainty evidence).
Side effects were uncommon in both treatment and placebo groups, though they were poorly reported.
The results do not apply to pregnant or immunocompromised women or women with diabetes, and more research is needed on the best medicine, dose and frequency.

items.title: Probiotics are a good choice for the treatment of bacterial vaginosis: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trial
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials to see whether probiotics help treat bacterial vaginosis (BV) in adult women. Adding probiotics to antibiotics gave higher cure rates than antibiotics alone, and probiotics did better than placebo. Probiotics on their own were not clearly different from antibiotics. The authors say probiotics may help, but stronger evidence is needed.
keyPoints: Probiotics plus antibiotics worked better than antibiotics alone or with placebo across 14 trials (risk ratio 1.23).
Probiotics beat placebo in three trials, but the number of trials was small.
Three trials found no clear difference between probiotics alone and antibiotics.
Results varied with how the probiotic was given and the dose; oral L. rhamnosus did better than vaginal use in this analysis.

items.title: Guideline: Vulvovaginal candidosis (AWMF 015/072, level S2k)
items.summary: This German clinical guideline sets out how vaginal thrush (vulvovaginal candidosis) should be diagnosed and treated. About 70-75% of women get thrush at least once, and symptoms alone cannot reliably tell thrush apart from other causes of vaginitis, so the diagnosis should be confirmed before treatment. Common antifungal creams, vaginal tablets and oral tablets are generally well tolerated and work similarly well. Women without symptoms, and their partners, should not be treated.
keyPoints: Diagnosis should rest on symptoms plus seeing the yeast under a microscope, and be confirmed by a clinician before treatment starts.
Acute thrush can be treated with local antifungals (vaginal tablets, ovules or creams) or oral triazole tablets, and the different regimens give similarly good results.
Women with repeated Candida albicans thrush should have long-term, lower-dose maintenance treatment with oral triazoles.
In the last 6 weeks of pregnancy, antifungal treatment is advised to lower the chance of passing thrush to the baby, and local treatment is preferred in pregnancy.

items.title: Contribution of Lactobacillus iners to Vaginal Health and Diseases: A Systematic Review
items.source: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
items.journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
items.summary: This review looked at Lactobacillus iners, a common bacterium in the vagina, and what it does for vaginal health. It is often found in healthy vaginas but is also found in high numbers in bacterial vaginosis (BV). It seems to protect less well than other vaginal Lactobacillus species such as L. crispatus. The authors say more research is needed to understand its exact role.
keyPoints: L. iners is common in healthy vaginas but is also often found in high numbers in bacterial vaginosis.
It appears to be a transitional species that moves in after the vaginal environment is disturbed.
It offers less protection against vaginal imbalance than other Lactobacillus species such as L. crispatus.
Evidence links it to BV, sexually transmitted infections and adverse pregnancy outcomes, but its exact role is still unclear.

items.title: Screening for Bacterial Vaginosis in Pregnant Persons to Prevent Preterm Delivery: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force looked at whether testing pregnant people with no symptoms for bacterial vaginosis (BV) helps prevent preterm birth. For people not at increased risk of preterm birth, it found with moderate certainty that this screening gives no net benefit. For people at increased risk, the evidence is conflicting and not enough to say whether screening helps or harms.
keyPoints: Bacterial vaginosis is common in pregnancy, affecting an estimated 5.8% to 19.3% of pregnant women in the US, and has been linked to preterm delivery, early miscarriage, postpartum womb infection and low birth weight.
The Task Force recommends against screening for BV in pregnant people without symptoms who are not at increased risk of preterm delivery (D recommendation).
For pregnant people at increased risk of preterm delivery, current evidence is insufficient to judge the balance of benefits and harms of screening (I statement).
The recommendation applies only to pregnant people without symptoms of BV.

items.title: Oral versus intra-vaginal imidazole and triazole anti-fungal treatment of uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis (thrush)
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 26 trials (5,007 women) comparing tablets taken by mouth with creams or pessaries placed in the vagina for uncomplicated thrush. Both routes probably cure symptoms about equally well. Tablets probably clear the yeast itself a little more often, and more women preferred them, though that evidence was low quality. The trials overall had a high risk of bias.
keyPoints: There was probably little or no difference between oral and vaginal treatment in clearing symptoms, in the short or long term (moderate-certainty evidence).
Oral treatment probably improves mycological cure, meaning the yeast is no longer found, compared with vaginal treatment (moderate-certainty evidence).
Few women stopped treatment because of side effects with either route; vaginal treatments caused more local reactions, while oral ones caused more whole-body effects like stomach upset and headaches.
Oral treatment appeared to be the preferred option, but the data were poorly reported and the certainty was low.

items.title: High Global Burden and Costs of Bacterial Vaginosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled studies from around the world to see how common bacterial vaginosis (BV) is among women of reproductive age. About 1 in 4 women (23% to 29%, depending on the region) were affected. In North America, rates were higher in black (33%) and Hispanic (31%) women than in white (23%) or Asian (11%) women. Treating symptomatic BV costs an estimated US $4.8 billion a year worldwide, and the authors call for more research on its causes and on prevention and treatment.
keyPoints: BV is very common: 23% to 29% of reproductive-aged women had it across world regions.
In North America, prevalence was 33% in black women, 31% in Hispanic women, 23% in white women and 11% in Asian women.
Treating symptomatic BV costs an estimated US $4.8 billion a year globally.
The authors say more research is urgently needed on what causes BV and how to prevent and treat it lastingly.

items.title: Global burden of recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pooled eight population-based studies from 11 countries (over 17,000 women) to estimate how common recurrent thrush is, meaning four or more episodes in a year. It found that about 138 million women worldwide are affected each year, and around 372 million over a lifetime. Rates were highest in women aged 25 to 34. The authors say affected women need better care and better treatment options.
keyPoints: Recurrent thrush (four or more episodes a year) affects about 138 million women worldwide each year.
About 372 million women are estimated to be affected at some point in their lives.
The 25 to 34 age group has the highest rate, at about 9%.
The number of affected women is expected to rise to almost 158 million a year by 2030.

items.title: Probiotics for vulvovaginal candidiasis in non-pregnant women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether taking probiotics alongside usual antifungal medicine helps treat vaginal thrush in women who are not pregnant. It combined ten trials with 1656 women. Probiotics seemed to help symptoms and clear the infection in the short term and lowered the chance of thrush returning at one month. This did not clearly last in the longer term, and the evidence was low or very low quality.
keyPoints: Added to antifungal drugs, probiotics may have improved short-term symptom cure and short-term clearing of the yeast infection.
Thrush came back less often at one month, but the evidence for this was very low quality.
No clear long-term benefit was seen at one or three months after treatment.
Probiotics did not seem to raise the rate of serious or non-serious side effects.

items.title: Antibiotic treatment for the sexual partners of women with bacterial vaginosis
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether giving antibiotics to the sexual partners of women being treated for bacterial vaginosis (BV) helps the women get better or stops BV coming back. It pooled seven trials with 1026 people. Treating partners did not improve symptoms or lower the chance of BV returning, and partners taking antibiotics had more side effects, mostly stomach upset.
keyPoints: High quality evidence shows that treating partners with antibiotics does not make women's BV symptoms or clinical signs improve faster or more often than placebo.
Low quality evidence suggests partner treatment does not lower the chance of BV coming back in women.
Partners given antibiotics reported more side effects, most often gastrointestinal symptoms (low quality evidence).
Compared with no treatment at all, partner antibiotics also did not reduce recurrence or improve outcomes, though those results were imprecise.

items.title: Guideline: vulvovaginal candidosis (AWMF 015/072), S2k (excluding chronic mucocutaneous candidosis)
items.summary: This German guideline reviews how vaginal thrush (vulvovaginal candidosis) is diagnosed and treated. Thrush is usually caused by Candida albicans, and many standard antifungal creams, pessaries and oral tablets work equally well, clearing more than 80% of acute cases. Only about 35-40% of women with genital itching actually have thrush, so examination and a microscope check of vaginal fluid are important for diagnosis. Rarer yeast types and thrush that keeps coming back need different tests and longer treatment.
keyPoints: Only 35-40% of women with genital itching actually have thrush, so history, examination and microscopy are needed; a fungal culture is advised if results are unclear or thrush keeps recurring.

Vaginal polyenes, imidazoles and ciclopirox olamine, plus oral fluconazole or itraconazole, are equally effective and succeed in over 80% of acute cases; oral triazoles should not be used in pregnancy according to manufacturers.
Rarer types such as Candida glabrata and Candida krusei respond less well to usual antifungals and need different treatment.

Recurrent thrush can be controlled with long-term suppressive fluconazole, but about half of women relapse after it stops; self-treatment with over-the-counter products is discouraged because of frequent wrong diagnoses.

items.title: Antenatal lower genital tract infection screening and treatment programs for preventing preterm delivery
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for trials of screening pregnant women for common vaginal infections (bacterial vaginosis, trichomonas and thrush) and treating them, to see if this lowers preterm birth. Only one trial of 4155 women met the criteria. In that trial, screening and treatment before 20 weeks was linked to fewer preterm births (3% versus 5%) and fewer small babies. The evidence comes from a single trial, so more studies are needed.
keyPoints: One trial of 4155 women found fewer births before 37 weeks with infection screening and treatment (3% versus 5%).
Fewer preterm babies were born with low or very low birthweight, graded as moderate quality evidence.
Screening and treatment programs were linked to cost savings by preventing preterm births.
Only one trial qualified, and the authors call for more trials of different screening programs.

items.title: Vulvovaginitis: screening for and management of trichomoniasis, vulvovaginal candidiasis, and bacterial vaginosis
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline reviewed the evidence on diagnosing and treating three common vaginal infections: thrush (vulvovaginal candidiasis), trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis. It found that thrush is very common and that creams and tablets work equally well, while trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis are treated with the antibiotic metronidazole. It also notes that evidence for alternative remedies such as probiotics and vitamin C is limited, and that treating trichomoniasis in pregnancy helps prevent preterm birth.
keyPoints: Thrush affects about 75% of women at least once, and topical and oral antifungal azole medicines are equally effective.
Recurrent thrush means 4 or more episodes a year, and weekly oral fluconazole for up to 6 months after initial treatment improves success.
Trichomoniasis cure rates reach up to 88% with oral metronidazole, and treating the partner improves cure rates; a test of cure afterwards is not recommended.
Symptomatic bacterial vaginosis is treated with oral metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days, with vaginal gel or clindamycin as alternatives, and longer courses for repeated recurrences.

items.title: Antibiotic prophylaxis during the second and third trimester to reduce adverse pregnancy outcomes and morbidity
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled eight trials (about 4,300 women) that tested giving antibiotics to pregnant women in the second or third trimester to prevent problems like early birth. Overall, antibiotics did not lower the chance of preterm birth. The one exception was women who had a previous preterm birth and also had bacterial vaginosis (BV) in the current pregnancy, where early birth was less likely. The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to support routine antibiotics in pregnancy, partly because of possible bias and too little information on harms to babies.
keyPoints: Antibiotics given routinely did not reduce preterm birth overall (high-quality evidence).
Preterm birth was reduced in women with a previous preterm birth who had BV in this pregnancy, but not in those without BV.
Antibiotics lowered the risk of infection of the womb lining after birth (postpartum endometritis) and of gonococcal infection (moderate-quality evidence for endometritis).
The authors found not enough evidence to support routine antibiotics in pregnancy, and said possible harms to the baby are unclear.

items.title: Vitamin B12 supplementation for growth, development, and cognition in children
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 16 trials with 4083 children under 12 to see whether vitamin B12 supplements help growth, learning and development. B12 supplements clearly lowered rates of B12 deficiency and raised B12 levels in the blood compared with placebo. For height, thinking skills, motor skills and anaemia, there may be little to no difference, though this evidence was mostly low certainty. Very few trials reported on side effects, so little can be said about them.
keyPoints: Vitamin B12 supplements reduced B12 deficiency in children compared with placebo (high-certainty evidence).
B12 supplements probably raised blood B12 levels, by about 68.5 pmol/L on average (moderate-certainty evidence).
B12 may make little to no difference to height, attention and thinking, motor skills or anaemia (mostly low-certainty evidence).
Few trials reported adverse effects, and none did for B12 alone versus placebo.

items.title: Efficacy of different routes of vitamin B12 supplementation for the treatment of patients with vitamin B12 deficiency: A systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 13 studies (4,275 people) comparing three ways of taking vitamin B12 for deficiency: tablets by mouth, injections into a muscle, and tablets dissolved under the tongue. All three raised B12 levels, and the differences between them were not statistically significant. Injections ranked highest for raising B12, but the authors say this was not clinically meaningful, and the number of studies was limited.
keyPoints: Oral, injected (intramuscular) and under-the-tongue B12 all effectively raised B12 levels.
Injections ranked first for raising B12, followed by under-the-tongue, but the differences were not statistically significant.
No significant difference between routes was found for haemoglobin, other blood count measures or homocysteine levels.
The authors note that the limited number of studies restricted the strength of the comparisons.

items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of functional vitamin B12 status among adult vegans
items.summary: This review pooled results from 19 studies to see whether adults who follow a vegan diet are more likely to have low vitamin B12 than vegetarians or people who eat meat. Vegans had lower B12 in the blood and higher levels of markers that point to B12 not working properly in the body, compared with people who eat meat. Vegans who took B12 supplements had better results on every marker than vegans who did not. The authors say better ways are needed to make sure people on vegetarian and vegan diets get enough B12.
keyPoints: Vegan adults had lower blood B12 and higher homocysteine than people who eat meat, which points to a functional B12 shortfall.
Vegans also had lower B12 and higher homocysteine than vegetarians, though two other markers (HoloTC and MMA) did not differ between the two groups.
Vegans who took B12 supplements had better results on all the B12 markers than vegans who did not.
The authors call for better strategies and appropriate B12 supplement use among people following vegetarian and vegan diets.

items.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency and use of proton pump inhibitors: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 25 studies to see whether taking proton pump inhibitors (PPIs, common heartburn and acid-reflux medicines) is linked to vitamin B12 deficiency. People who took PPIs had slightly higher odds of B12 deficiency than non-users. However, the studies varied a lot and the effect was small, so the authors say the link is not clearly shown.
keyPoints: PPI users had slightly higher odds of vitamin B12 deficiency than non-users (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.16-1.73).
Most studies found no difference in blood B12 levels between PPI users and non-users.
The studies differed a lot from one another, and the effect was too small to show a clear association.
Better-designed long-term studies are needed to clarify the question.

items.title: B vitamins and prevention of cognitive decline and incident dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 95 studies (over 46,000 people) to see whether B vitamins help protect thinking and memory in later life. B vitamin supplements were linked to a very small slowing of cognitive decline, mostly in people without dementia and in trials lasting more than 12 months. Low folate and high homocysteine were linked to higher dementia risk, but low B12 or B6 levels and higher B12 or B6 intake were not.
keyPoints: B vitamin supplements were linked to slightly slower cognitive decline, with the benefit seen mainly in people without dementia and in trials lasting over 12 months.
Lower folate levels and higher homocysteine levels were associated with a higher risk of dementia and cognitive decline.
In adults aged 50 and over without dementia, higher dietary folate intake was linked to lower dementia risk (HR 0.61).
B12 or B6 deficiency, and higher intake of B12 or B6, were not linked to dementia risk.

items.title: Effects of Vitamin B12 Supplementation on Cognitive Function, Depressive Symptoms, and Fatigue: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression
items.summary: This review pooled 16 randomised trials with 6,276 people who did not have a clear vitamin B12 deficiency or advanced brain disorders. It looked at whether B12 supplements, alone or with folic acid and sometimes B6, help thinking skills, low mood or tiredness. No benefit was found for thinking skills or depression. Only one study looked at unexplained fatigue, so no conclusion could be drawn about that.
keyPoints: No evidence that vitamin B12 alone or B complex supplements improved any area of cognitive function.
No overall effect of the vitamins on depression scores.
Only one study measured unexplained fatigue, so it could not be analysed.
The authors conclude B12 supplements are likely ineffective for thinking skills and low mood in people without advanced neurological disorders or overt B12 deficiency.

items.title: Oral vitamin B12 versus intramuscular vitamin B12 for vitamin B12 deficiency
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether vitamin B12 tablets work as well as B12 injections into the muscle for people with low B12. It found only three small trials with 153 people in total. The evidence was low quality, but B12 levels rose similarly with both routes, and the tablets cost less. The trials did not report on symptoms or quality of life.
keyPoints: Low-quality evidence suggests oral and injected B12 raise blood B12 levels in a similar way.
Oral B12 cost less than injections in one trial, though this evidence was also low quality.
Very low-quality evidence suggests oral B12 appears as safe as injections.
No trial reported on symptoms of deficiency, quality of life, or how acceptable patients found the treatment.

items.title: Vitamin and mineral supplementation for maintaining cognitive function in cognitively healthy people in mid and late life
items.summary: This large review pooled 28 trials with more than 83,000 healthy adults aged 40 and over to see whether vitamin or mineral supplements protect thinking and memory. For B vitamins (including B12), the reviewers found they probably have little or no effect on thinking skills for up to 5 years, and possibly up to 10 years. Overall, no vitamin or mineral supplement showed a meaningful effect on cognitive decline or dementia, though the evidence is not strong enough for firm conclusions. Most participants were over 60, so little is known about starting supplements in midlife.
keyPoints: B vitamin supplements (folic acid, B12, B6 or a mix) probably have little or no effect on thinking skills in healthy adults, mostly in their 60s and 70s.
No vitamin or mineral supplement strategy was found to have a meaningful effect on cognitive decline or dementia.
Only long-term antioxidant vitamin use (beta-carotene, vitamin C) showed small signs of benefit, based on low-certainty evidence.
Very few studies reported on side effects or looked at supplements started before age 60.

items.title: Calcium, vitamin D, or combined supplementation to prevent fractures and falls: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pooled 69 trials with about 154,000 adults to see whether calcium, vitamin D, or both together prevent broken bones and falls. Most people studied lived in the community and were not at high risk of fractures or falls. Overall, the supplements made little to no meaningful difference to fractures or falls. The evidence was mostly moderate to high certainty, but there was less evidence for people at high risk or living in residential care.
keyPoints: Vitamin D alone had no effect on the risk of any fracture (high certainty).
Calcium alone (moderate certainty) and calcium with vitamin D (high certainty) showed little to no meaningful benefit for fractures.
Supplements also appeared to have little to no effect on hip fractures, other fracture types, or falls.
Evidence was limited for people at high risk of fractures or living in residential care.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation for prevention of vitamin D deficiency in preterm and low birth weight infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 34 trials (5012 babies) of vitamin D supplements in babies born early or at low birth weight. Giving vitamin D probably lowers the chance of vitamin D deficiency compared with giving none. Higher doses (800 IU a day or more) probably lowered deficiency more than lower doses, but probably raised the chance of too much vitamin D. Most trials had a high risk of bias, and the effects on bone health and growth are uncertain.
keyPoints: In preterm babies, vitamin D supplements (at least 200 IU a day) probably reduce vitamin D deficiency up to discharge or term-corrected age (moderate-certainty evidence).
In low birth weight babies born at or near term, weekly vitamin D probably reduces deficiency at six months (moderate-certainty evidence).
Higher doses (800 IU a day or more) probably reduce deficiency and secondary hyperparathyroidism more than lower doses, but probably increase vitamin D excess.
The review is uncertain about other effects on bone health, growth and illness, and whether higher doses affect high blood calcium.

items.title: 2024 Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia guideline for osteoporosis management and fracture prevention in postmenopausal women and men over 50 years of age
items.source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia
items.organisation: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia
items.summary: This is an updated Australian guideline on keeping bones strong and preventing broken bones in women after menopause and in men over 50. It encourages earlier spotting of poor bone health using personal risk factors and a fracture risk tool called FRAX. It says calcium and vitamin D supplements work better at reducing fracture risk in people who are actually low in these nutrients, rather than in healthy people living independently.
keyPoints: Earlier recognition of poor bone health is encouraged, using clinical risk factors and an absolute fracture risk tool such as FRAX.
Widespread population-based osteoporosis screening is not recommended in Australia because there is not enough evidence to support it.
Calcium and vitamin D supplements are more effective at reducing fracture risk in people with calcium and vitamin D deficiency, not in healthy people living in the community.
People at imminent or very high fracture risk are a group in whom early bone-building (osteoanabolic) treatment can be considered.

items.title: The Lebanese GRADE-based vitamin D guidelines: a paradigm for the MENA region
items.summary: A Lebanese expert panel reviewed the research and wrote guidelines on checking and supplementing vitamin D in adults. For most healthy adults living in the community, they suggest no routine vitamin D screening and no calcium and vitamin D supplements. For adults living in care homes or similar institutions, they suggest supplementing with calcium and vitamin D. Some higher-risk groups were identified as more likely to benefit from testing and supplements.
keyPoints: The panel suggests against routine vitamin D deficiency screening for adults, based on very low certainty evidence.
For community-dwelling adults, they suggest no calcium and vitamin D supplements, based on moderate certainty evidence.
For adults in institutions, they suggest calcium and vitamin D supplements, based on moderate certainty evidence.
If supplementing, they suggest a daily dose of 600-2000 IU rather than more than 2000 IU, based on very low certainty evidence.

items.title: Vitamin D and depression in adults: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 66 studies on whether vitamin D levels in the blood are linked to depression in adults. Most studies found that lower vitamin D goes along with depression, especially studies that measured both at a single point in time. Only a few studies followed people over time, so it is still unclear whether low vitamin D causes depression or whether taking vitamin D supplements could prevent it.
keyPoints: Overall, the studies showed an association between depression and vitamin D blood levels.
Most of the 66 studies (46) looked at people at one point in time, which cannot show cause and effect.
Only a few studies that followed people over time linked lower vitamin D to a higher risk of developing depressive symptoms or major depression.
It is not yet known whether taking vitamin D supplements could protect against developing depression.

items.title: The effect of vitamin D supplementation on primary depression: A meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 18 randomized trials in adults with primary depression to see whether vitamin D supplements ease depression symptoms. Overall, supplements gave a small reduction in symptom scores. The benefit was seen in people whose blood vitamin D level was already above 50 nmol/L, and not in those with lower levels. The trials differed in timing, country, dose and length, which may have affected the results.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplements gave a small overall reduction in depression symptom scores across 18 trials.
The benefit appeared in adults with blood vitamin D (25(OH)D) above 50 nmol/L.
No benefit was seen in adults with levels below 50 nmol/L.
The trials varied in dose, duration and setting, which may have hidden true effects.

items.title: Population-based interventions for preventing falls and fall-related injuries in older people
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at community-wide programmes meant to prevent falls and fall-related injuries in older adults, including offering free calcium and vitamin D3 supplements. Nine studies were included, but the evidence was very low quality, so the authors could not say whether these programmes work. One study found fewer fall-related hospital admissions among women offered calcium and vitamin D3, but the authors were unsure of this result.
keyPoints: Nine studies of community-wide falls prevention programmes were included, covering communities of between about 1,200 and 172,500 people.
In one trial, women offered free calcium and vitamin D3 had fewer fall-related hospital admissions, with no difference seen for men, but this finding was very low certainty.
The review found it uncertain whether community-wide multicomponent programmes (such as exercise, home changes and education) reduce falls or injuries.
The authors call for better-designed, larger trials, and no studies reported adverse events.

items.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines of the Latin American Federation of Endocrinology for the use of vitamin D in the maintenance of bone health: recommendations for the Latin American context
items.summary: A group of Latin American hormone and bone specialists wrote guidelines on using vitamin D supplements to keep bones healthy. They recommend supplements for adults aged 18 and over, including healthy adults, people with thinner bones (osteopenia), people with osteoporosis, and older adults living in care homes. Doses are meant to be tailored to each person, with blood vitamin D levels checked at set intervals and doses adjusted. The authors say more local data from Latin America is still needed.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplements are recommended for adults aged 18 and over, including healthy adults, people with osteopenia or osteoporosis, and institutionalized older adults.
Dosing should follow an individualized treatment plan.
Blood levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D should be monitored at set intervals, with doses adjusted based on results.
The panel stressed the need for local data and for considering regional geography, social and cultural factors.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation to prevent acute respiratory infections: individual participant data meta-analysis
items.summary: This study pooled the individual results of 25 trials (about 11,000 people aged from newborns to 95) to see whether vitamin D supplements prevent chest and airway infections such as colds and flu-like illness. Overall, vitamin D lowered the chance of having an acute respiratory infection. The benefit was clearest in people taking small regular (daily or weekly) doses and in people who started with very low vitamin D levels. Vitamin D did not increase serious side effects, and the authors rated the evidence as high quality.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplements reduced the risk of acute respiratory infections overall (adjusted odds ratio 0.88).
Protection was seen with daily or weekly doses, but not when one or more large single (bolus) doses were given.
The benefit was strongest in people with very low vitamin D levels at the start (below 25 nmol/l).
Vitamin D did not change the chance of serious adverse events, so it was considered safe in these trials.

items.title: Association between vitamin D supplementation and mortality: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 52 randomised trials with about 75,000 adults to see whether vitamin D supplements help people live longer. Overall, taking vitamin D alone was not linked to a lower chance of dying from any cause, or from heart disease. It was linked to a 16% lower risk of dying from cancer. The authors say more large studies are needed to know whether vitamin D3 specifically might lower overall death risk.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplements were not linked to lower death from any cause in adults (risk ratio 0.98).
No link was found with heart-related deaths or with deaths from other non-cancer causes.
Vitamin D supplements were linked to a 16% lower risk of cancer death.
Neither vitamin D3 nor vitamin D2 alone significantly lowered overall death risk; more large trials are needed for vitamin D3.

items.title: Italian Association of Clinical Endocrinologists (AME) and Italian Chapter of the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists (AACE) Position Statement: Clinical Management of Vitamin D Deficiency in Adults
items.source: Italian Association of Clinical Endocrinologists (AME) and Italian Chapter of the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists (AACE)
items.organisation: Italian Association of Clinical Endocrinologists (AME) and Italian Chapter of the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists (AACE)
items.summary: Italian endocrinology groups reviewed the evidence on vitamin D deficiency in adults and issued practical recommendations. They suggest a blood level of 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) is fine for most people, but that people at higher risk, including those who are pregnant or breastfeeding, should aim above 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L). Healthy people do not need routine testing, and routine re-testing during treatment is not suggested.
keyPoints: Vitamin D deficiency is common; 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) is considered appropriate for the general population, but levels above 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L) are recommended for people at risk.

People at risk, including those during pregnancy and lactation, those with bone, liver or kidney disease, obesity or malabsorption, and some older adults, should be screened with a 25-hydroxy-vitamin D blood test, but healthy people should not.
Besides a healthy lifestyle (mostly sun exposure), oral vitamin D2 or D3 supplements are recommended for people with proven deficiency and those taking bone-active drugs.
Routine monitoring during treatment is not suggested because vitamin D has a wide safety margin; the blood level can be checked after at least 6 months in particular conditions.

items.title: Interventions to Prevent Falls in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed ways to prevent falls in people aged 65 and older who live at home and are not known to have osteoporosis or vitamin D deficiency. It found that exercise programmes moderately reduce falls in people at higher risk, and that multi-part programmes help a little. Vitamin D supplements did not help prevent falls, and their overall harms were judged small to moderate.
keyPoints: Exercise programmes have a moderate benefit in preventing falls in older adults at increased risk of falling.
Multifactorial programmes (several approaches combined) have a small benefit and are offered selectively, depending on a person's history and preferences.
Vitamin D supplements had no benefit in preventing falls, and the task force recommends against using them for this purpose.
These recommendations apply to adults 65 and older living at home who are not known to have osteoporosis or vitamin D deficiency.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation in the prevention and management of major chronic diseases not related to mineral homeostasis in adults: research for evidence and a scientific statement from the European society for clinical and economic aspects of osteoporosis and osteoarthritis (ESCEO)
items.summary: A group of European bone-health experts reviewed whether vitamin D supplements help prevent or treat long-term illnesses that are not related to bones or minerals in adults. Low vitamin D blood levels are often linked to these illnesses, but clinical trials have given mixed results. The trials so far were often too small, used lower doses, or included people whose levels were already adequate. The group concluded there is not enough evidence to recommend vitamin D supplements for these illnesses.
keyPoints: Low vitamin D blood levels (below 50 nmol/L) are consistently linked to chronic diseases in observational studies, but this does not prove supplements prevent them.
Trials of vitamin D have given contradictory results, and large trials with sufficient doses are missing.
No recommendation can be made for using vitamin D supplements to prevent or treat chronic diseases outside the bones.
Raising vitamin D levels well above what bones need is not recommended, because safety has not been confirmed.

items.title: Association Between Calcium or Vitamin D Supplementation and Fracture Incidence in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers combined results from 33 randomized trials with over 51,000 community-dwelling adults older than 50. They looked at whether calcium, vitamin D, or both together lowered the chance of broken bones compared with placebo or no treatment. None of the supplements was linked to fewer hip, spine, non-spine, or total fractures. The authors say these findings do not support routine use of these supplements in community-dwelling older people.
keyPoints: Calcium, vitamin D, or both together were not linked to a lower risk of hip fracture.
No significant link was found with non-spine, spine, or total fractures either.
Results were generally similar regardless of dose, sex, fracture history, dietary calcium intake, or starting vitamin D level.
The authors conclude the findings do not support routine use of these supplements in community-dwelling older people.

items.title: Calcium plus vitamin D supplementation and risk of fractures: an updated meta-analysis from the National Osteoporosis Foundation
items.summary: Researchers combined results from eight randomized trials, with about 31,000 adults, to see whether taking calcium plus vitamin D lowers the chance of broken bones. People taking both supplements had about 15% fewer fractures overall and about 30% fewer hip fractures. The authors concluded the findings support using these supplements to reduce fracture risk in middle-aged and older adults. One limitation is that the analysis used data from a subgroup of the Women's Health Initiative study.
keyPoints: Calcium plus vitamin D was linked to a 15% lower risk of fractures overall.
Hip fractures were about 30% less likely with the supplements.
Results were similar across many different ways of checking the data.
The findings apply to middle-aged and older adults, both living at home and in care homes.

items.title: Lack of Evidence Linking Calcium With or Without Vitamin D Supplementation to Cardiovascular Disease in Generally Healthy Adults: A Clinical Guideline From the National Osteoporosis Foundation and the American Society for Preventive Cardiology
items.summary: Two US expert groups, the National Osteoporosis Foundation and the American Society for Preventive Cardiology, reviewed the research on calcium, with or without vitamin D, and heart and blood vessel health.
