They found moderate-quality evidence that calcium from food or supplements neither helps nor harms the risk of heart disease, stroke or death in generally healthy adults. Calcium intake below the upper safe limit of 2000 to 2500 mg a day was considered safe from a heart health standpoint.
keyPoints: Moderate-quality evidence shows no link, good or bad, between calcium (with or without vitamin D) and heart disease, stroke or death in generally healthy adults.
This applies to calcium from both food and supplements.
Intake up to the upper level of 2000 to 2500 mg a day is considered safe for the heart.

items.title: Vitamin D for the treatment of chronic painful conditions in adults
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether vitamin D supplements help adults with long-lasting (chronic) pain. It pooled 10 trials with 811 people, comparing vitamin D with placebo or other treatments. Overall, there was no consistent sign that vitamin D eased pain better than placebo, though the evidence was low quality. Side effects were uncommon and similar between vitamin D and placebo.
keyPoints: No consistent pattern showed vitamin D relieving chronic pain better than placebo (low quality evidence).
Side effects and people dropping out were uncommon, with no consistent difference between vitamin D and placebo (good quality evidence).
A large benefit of vitamin D across different chronic pain conditions is unlikely.
Whether vitamin D helps in specific pain conditions needs more research.

items.title: The 2024 Endocrine Society Guideline on Vitamin D: Comprehensive Summary and Critical Appraisal
items.summary: This article summarises and critiques the 2024 Endocrine Society guideline on vitamin D. The guideline concluded that vitamin D supplements lower rickets and chest infections in children, deaths in people aged 75 and over, pregnancy complications, and the move from prediabetes to diabetes. It recommends routine vitamin D for children and teens, adults 75 and over, pregnant women and people with prediabetes, without needing a blood test first. The review found the guideline was rigorous but left open questions, especially about doses and who it applies to.
keyPoints: The guideline recommends vitamin D supplementation for pregnant women, children aged 1 to 18, adults 75 and over, and people with prediabetes.
Supplements were found to reduce rickets and respiratory infections in children and pregnancy complications.
The suggested intake goes above standard dietary reference amounts and is given without a 25(OH)D blood test.
Critics point to unclear doses, differences from earlier guidelines, uncertainty about some groups, and the role of vitamin D blood testing.

items.title: Regimens of vitamin D supplementation for women during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 25 trials with 7008 pregnant women to see whether higher vitamin D doses work better than lower doses during pregnancy. Higher doses (more than 600 IU a day, or 4000 IU a day or more) may make little or no difference to pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth or low birthweight. Few side effects were reported, and no differences were seen between groups. Most of the evidence was low certainty, so the findings are not firm.
keyPoints: Doses above 600 IU a day, compared with up to 600 IU a day, may make little or no difference to pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth or low birthweight.

Doses of 4000 IU a day or more, compared with lower doses, may make little or no difference to pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes or preterm birth, and probably make little or no difference to low birthweight.
Few adverse events such as high calcium or too much vitamin D were reported, with no differences between groups.
The authors call for larger, better-designed trials with longer follow-up of babies and children.

items.title: The Effects of Vitamin D Supplementation During Pregnancy on Maternal, Neonatal, and Infant Health: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 66 trials (over 17,000 pregnant women) that tested vitamin D supplements in pregnancy. Supplements did not change the risk of preeclampsia, preterm birth, small babies or low birth weight. They may lower the risk of gestational diabetes and slightly raised average birth weight (by about 53 g). The authors say the benefits remain uncertain because the trials differed a lot and many had a high risk of bias.
keyPoints: No clear effect of vitamin D on preeclampsia, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age or low birth weight babies.
Vitamin D may protect against gestational diabetes (risk ratio 0.65 across 12 trials).
Average infant birth weight was about 53 g higher with supplementation.
25 of 66 trials had at least one area at high risk of bias, so benefits remain uncertain; better trials are needed in women with low vitamin D levels or higher risk.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation in pregnant or breastfeeding women or young children for preventing asthma
items.summary: This Cochrane review pulled together 18 trials (about 10,600 people) to see whether vitamin D given during pregnancy, breastfeeding or early childhood helps prevent asthma in children. Evidence that vitamin D prevents childhood asthma is limited. Moderate-certainty evidence suggests high-dose vitamin D during pregnancy likely lowers the chance of childhood wheeze, but it probably makes little difference to asthma itself. More high-quality studies are needed.
keyPoints: High-dose vitamin D in pregnancy or breastfeeding likely reduces childhood wheeze compared with a low or standard dose (moderate-certainty evidence).
High-dose vitamin D in pregnancy likely makes little to no difference to childhood asthma, eczema, airway infections or allergic sensitisation (moderate-certainty evidence).
Any vitamin D versus placebo in pregnancy may reduce early childhood asthma, but this came from one study and the evidence was low certainty.
Evidence on vitamin D given directly to infants and children was mostly low certainty, and safety (adverse event) evidence was very uncertain.

items.title: Efficacy of vitamin D supplementation on the incidence of preeclampsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 33 randomised trials with 10,613 pregnant women to see whether vitamin D supplements lower the chance of preeclampsia, a serious blood pressure condition in pregnancy. Women who took vitamin D had a lower risk of preeclampsia and of preterm labor than those given a placebo or standard care. There was no clear difference in low birth weight or newborn Apgar scores. The authors say more research is needed on effects for babies.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplements in pregnancy were linked to a 44.8% lower risk of preeclampsia (RR 0.55).
Preterm labor risk was about 30% lower in women who took vitamin D (RR 0.70).
Blood vitamin D levels rose significantly in the supplement group.
No clear differences were found in low birth weight or 5-minute Apgar scores, so effects on babies remain unclear.

items.title: Comparative effectiveness of prophylactic strategies for preeclampsia: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 130 randomized trials (about 113,000 pregnant women) to compare ways of preventing preeclampsia, a pregnancy condition involving high blood pressure. Low-molecular-weight heparin, vitamin D supplements, exercise, calcium supplements and aspirin were each linked to a lower risk of preeclampsia or pregnancy-related high blood pressure. The evidence was rated moderate to very low certainty, and the benefits of heparin, vitamin D and exercise varied between groups of women, doses and regions.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplementation was linked to lower risk of preeclampsia or pregnancy-induced high blood pressure (risk ratio 0.65).
Low-molecular-weight heparin, exercise, calcium supplements and aspirin were also linked to lower risk.
No clear differences were found between these effective strategies for preventing preeclampsia.
Aspirin and calcium results held up across subgroups, while heparin, exercise and vitamin D results varied by risk group, dose and area.

items.title: Effects of vitamin D supplementation on ovulation and pregnancy in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 20 randomized trials with 1,961 women who have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) to see whether vitamin D supplements help with ovulation and pregnancy. Women taking vitamin D were more likely to ovulate and to become pregnant, and had fewer early miscarriages and premature births. Some other measures, such as fertilization rate and pregnancy complications like gestational diabetes, showed no clear difference. The authors say the quality of the included studies was limited, so more high-quality trials are needed to confirm the results.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplementation was linked to higher pregnancy rates and higher ovulation rates in women with PCOS.
Early miscarriage and premature delivery rates were lower in the vitamin D groups.
Androgen (male-type hormone) and luteinizing hormone levels were lower with vitamin D.
No clear difference was seen in fertilization rate, gestational diabetes or gestational hypertension, and study quality was limited.

items.title: Relationship between vitamin D deficiency and neonatal hypocalcemia: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 11 studies, covering 452 newborns with low blood calcium and 2,599 with normal calcium. Newborns who were low in vitamin D were more likely to have low calcium. Low vitamin D in the mother during pregnancy was also linked to low calcium in the baby. The authors suggest vitamin D supplements may help lower how often this happens, but the studies only show a link and do not prove cause.
keyPoints: Newborns with vitamin D deficiency had higher odds of low blood calcium (odds ratio 2.87).
Mothers with vitamin D deficiency had babies with higher odds of low calcium (odds ratio 7.83).
The authors say vitamin D supplementation may reduce how often newborn low calcium occurs.
The analysis found a significant link between vitamin D deficiency and newborn low calcium.

items.title: Vitamin D Supplementation during Pregnancy: An Evidence Analysis Center Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics
items.journal: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of vitamin D supplements taken during pregnancy. Supplements clearly raised vitamin D levels in both mothers and babies. There was fair evidence that they may lower insulin resistance in the mother and slightly raise birth weight. They made no clear difference to preeclampsia, caesarean section, gestational age at birth or birth length. The authors say better dose-response trials are still needed to work out how much vitamin D is best in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplements in pregnancy raised vitamin D blood levels in mothers and in their babies, with good or strong evidence.
Evidence was fair that supplements lower maternal insulin resistance and increase birth weight by about 114 grams on average.
No clear effect was found on preeclampsia, caesarean section, gestational age or birth length.
Results varied a lot between studies for vitamin D levels, and the authors call for higher quality trials to find the best dose.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation for term breastfed infants to prevent vitamin D deficiency and improve bone health
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 19 trials (2,837 mother-baby pairs) to see whether vitamin D given to breastfed babies, or to breastfeeding mothers, helps prevent low vitamin D and supports bone health. Giving babies 400 IU a day may raise their vitamin D levels and lower the chance of vitamin D insufficiency. Giving vitamin D to breastfeeding mothers also raised babies' levels, but only in groups already at high risk of deficiency. The evidence was low to very low certainty, and there was not enough evidence to say whether either approach improves bone health or prevents rickets.
keyPoints: Vitamin D at 400 IU a day for breastfed babies, for up to six months, may raise their vitamin D levels and reduce vitamin D insufficiency.
Vitamin D given to breastfeeding mothers may raise their babies' vitamin D levels and lower insufficiency and deficiency, but all these studies were in high-risk populations.
Direct supplements for babies raised infant vitamin D levels more than supplements for mothers did, though the evidence was very uncertain.
There was not enough evidence on bone strength, rickets or side effects such as high blood calcium; certainty was low to very low for all outcomes.
keywords: does my baby need vitamin d

items.title: Clinical practice guidelines for vitamin D in the United Arab Emirates
items.source: Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
items.journal: Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
items.summary: This guideline looks at vitamin D deficiency in the United Arab Emirates and wider Gulf region, where it is very common. Hot weather, covering up, diet and low activity all make low vitamin D more likely. The authors reviewed published research and suggest daily vitamin D amounts for different groups, including babies, children, adults, older people, and women who are pregnant or breastfeeding.
keyPoints: For pregnant and breastfeeding women, 2000 IU of vitamin D per day is recommended, starting from the first trimester.
Breastfed babies are advised 400 IU/day up to 6 months, then 400-600 IU/day from 6 to 12 months, depending on diet and sun exposure.
Adults over 18 are advised 1000-2000 IU/day, and people over 65 are advised 2000 IU/day, all year round.
The aim of supplementing is to reach and keep a blood vitamin D level (25(OH)D) of 30-50 ng/mL.

items.title: Systematic Review of Vitamin D and Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
items.summary: This review looked at studies on vitamin D levels in pregnancy and high blood pressure conditions such as preeclampsia. Trials suggest that taking vitamin D together with calcium may help protect against preeclampsia. Studies that simply observe women are less clear, partly because they were done in very different ways, so no firm conclusion can be drawn yet.
keyPoints: Trial evidence supports a protective effect of combined vitamin D and calcium supplements against preeclampsia.
Evidence leans towards a higher risk of high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy when vitamin D blood levels are below 50 nmol/L.
Observational studies give mixed results because of differences in study design, definitions and how vitamin D was measured and reported.
Caution is advised with vitamin D dosing in trials because long-term safety data are lacking.

items.title: Updated clinical practice guidelines on pregnancy care
items.summary: These are updated Australian guidelines for health professionals giving antenatal care. One key change is a recommendation against routine vitamin D blood testing in pregnancy unless there is a specific reason to test. The guidelines say that testing everyone and then giving vitamin D supplements is not supported by evidence, because the benefits and harms of supplementation remain unclear.
keyPoints: Routine testing of vitamin D levels in pregnancy is not recommended unless there is a specific reason.
Testing all pregnant women and then giving vitamin D supplements is not supported by evidence, as the benefits and harms remain unclear.
Routine hepatitis C testing at the first antenatal visit is now recommended.
All pregnant women should be offered a chance to discuss weight change, diet and physical activity, and to be weighed at each antenatal visit.

items.title: Interventions during pregnancy to prevent preterm birth: an overview of Cochrane systematic reviews
items.summary: This overview pulled together Cochrane reviews of things done in pregnancy to try to prevent preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks). Only four of 36 intervention reviews showed clear benefit, and none showed clear harm. For vitamin D, one review found a possible benefit of vitamin D alone for women without pre-existing conditions, while another found a possible harm when vitamin D was combined with calcium and other minerals. Both vitamin D findings were rated as 'possible' rather than clear, meaning the evidence was not strong enough to be sure.
keyPoints: Four reviews showed clear benefit for preventing preterm birth: midwife-led continuity of care, screening for lower genital tract infections, zinc supplements, and cervical cerclage (only for singleton pregnancies at high risk).
Vitamin D supplements alone showed a possible benefit for women without pre-existing conditions such as diabetes.
Vitamin D combined with calcium and other minerals showed possible harm (more preterm birth) for women without pre-existing conditions.
No review reported clear harm, and the authors say their ratings are not clinical guidance, so individual choices should be weighed with a healthcare provider.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy: Updated meta-analysis on maternal outcomes
items.source: Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
items.journal: Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
items.summary: This review pooled results from 15 trials of vitamin D supplements taken during pregnancy. Women who took vitamin D had much higher vitamin D blood levels by the end of pregnancy than women who did not, though results varied between studies. Vitamin D, with or without calcium, may be linked to a lower risk of pre-eclampsia, but the authors say more studies are needed to confirm this.
keyPoints: Women given vitamin D had significantly higher vitamin D (25(OH)D) blood levels at term than those given placebo or no treatment, but results were inconsistent.
Vitamin D plus calcium was linked to a lower risk of pre-eclampsia in three trials (about 5% versus 9%).
Two trials of vitamin D alone suggested a lower pre-eclampsia risk (8.9% versus 15.5%), but the result was not clearly conclusive.
Two trials found no difference in gestational diabetes risk with vitamin D.

items.title: Intermittent fasting for adults with overweight or obesity
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 22 trials with 1995 adults with overweight or obesity to see whether intermittent fasting helps weight loss. Compared with regular dietary advice, intermittent fasting made little to no difference to weight loss or quality of life. Compared with doing nothing, it probably led to a small amount of extra weight loss. The evidence on side effects was very uncertain, and trials only followed people for up to 12 months.
keyPoints: Compared with regular dietary advice, intermittent fasting may make little to no difference to weight loss (low-certainty evidence).
Compared with no intervention or a waiting list, intermittent fasting likely leads to a small extra weight loss (about 3.4% of starting weight, moderate-certainty evidence).
Effects on quality of life and side effects were unclear, with very low-certainty evidence.
No trials reported participant satisfaction or diabetes status, and none followed people beyond 12 months.

items.title: Impact of Ketogenic Diet on Weight, Metabolic, and Endocrine Parameters in Women with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from seven studies of overweight or obese women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) who followed a ketogenic (very low-carbohydrate) diet. After the diet, the women lost weight, had lower blood sugar and insulin, and had better cholesterol-related and hormone measures, including lower testosterone. There was too little data to say anything about pregnancy outcomes. The authors say larger studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Women with PCOS lost weight and had a lower BMI after following a ketogenic diet.
Blood glucose, insulin and insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) went down, as did LDL cholesterol and triglycerides.
Testosterone levels fell and SHBG (a protein that binds sex hormones) rose, along with improvements in LH and FSH levels.
Data on estrogens, progesterone and pregnancies were too scarce to compare.

items.title: Managing obesity in children: a clinical practice guideline
items.summary: This Canadian guideline gives advice on how to support children living with obesity, using the best available research and the views of families and health care providers. It recommends that care start with a full assessment of the child and family. Lifestyle and psychological support that combines several approaches should be the foundation, and medicines or surgery may be considered as options in some cases. The certainty of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate.
keyPoints: Care should begin with a comprehensive assessment of the child and family.
Multicomponent behavioural and psychological programs should form the foundation of care (strong recommendation, very low to moderate certainty).
Medicines and surgery can be considered as options (conditional recommendation, low to moderate certainty), depending on availability, feasibility and acceptability.
Decisions should be shared between the child, family and health care providers, based on benefits, harms and family values and preferences.

items.title: Social jetlag and obesity: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 43 observational studies (over 230,000 people) to see whether 'social jetlag' is linked to body weight. Social jetlag means sleeping at very different times on work days and days off. People with more social jetlag tended to have a higher body mass index, more body fat, a larger waist and a higher chance of having overweight or obesity. The studies only show a link, not cause and effect, and results varied a lot between studies.
keyPoints: More social jetlag was linked to higher BMI, fat mass, percent body fat and waist size.
It was also linked to a higher chance of having overweight or obesity (odds ratio 1.20).
The studies were observational, so they cannot show that social jetlag causes weight gain.
The authors say more research is needed on cause, mechanisms, and whether keeping a regular sleep schedule helps with weight.

items.title: Comparative efficacy of exercise, diet and/or pharmacological interventions on BMI, ovulation, and hormonal profile in reproductive-aged women with overweight or obesity: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 95 trials (9,910 women) of women with overweight or obesity of reproductive age. It compared exercise, diet and medicines, alone and combined, on BMI, ovulation and hormone levels. Combining all three approaches did best for weight loss, ovulation and lowering male-type hormones such as testosterone. The authors note that over half the trials had a high or unclear risk of bias, so better-quality studies are still needed.
keyPoints: Diet plus weight-lowering drugs gave the biggest drop in BMI, and adding exercise gave a similar result.
Exercise plus diet plus ovulation-inducing drugs gave the biggest rise in ovulation rate.
Exercise plus diet plus weight-lowering drugs was the best option for lowering testosterone.
Results were similar when only women with PCOS were looked at.

items.title: The efficacy and safety of GLP-1 agonists in PCOS women living with obesity in promoting weight loss and hormonal regulation: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: Journal of Diabetes and Its Complications
items.journal: Journal of Diabetes and Its Complications
items.summary: This review pooled results from four randomized trials (176 women) of GLP-1 medicines, such as semaglutide and liraglutide, in women with PCOS who live with obesity. Compared with placebo, the medicines were linked to lower BMI, smaller waist size, lower triglycerides and lower testosterone. They made no clear difference to total cholesterol or insulin resistance (HOMA-IR). Where side effects were reported, 49 of 112 women had mild ones such as nausea and abdominal pain. The number of studies and women was small.
keyPoints: GLP-1 medicines lowered BMI by about 2.4 points and waist size by about 5 cm compared with placebo.
Triglycerides and total testosterone levels were also lower with the medicines.
There was no significant difference in total cholesterol or insulin resistance (HOMA-IR).
Of 112 women with side effect data, 49 had mild effects like nausea and abdominal pain.

items.title: Physical Activity and Excess Body Weight and Adiposity for Adults. American College of Sports Medicine Consensus Statement
items.journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
items.summary: This consensus statement from the American College of Sports Medicine reviews how physical activity fits into managing excess body weight and body fat in adults. It finds that weight loss and prevention of weight gain work best when activity builds up to at least 150 minutes a week of moderate-intensity activity, with bigger benefits for more activity. No single type of activity was found to be better than others for body weight. The statement also says activity programmes should be tailored to a person's sex, gender, age, background and circumstances.
keyPoints: Benefits for weight loss and preventing weight gain are likely greatest when activity builds up to at least 150 minutes a week of moderate-intensity activity, in a dose-response way.
High-intensity interval training does not appear better than moderate-to-vigorous activity for body weight, and light activity may help if it uses enough energy.
No single type of physical activity is better than others for weight, so a mix of activity types is recommended for wider health benefits.
Physical activity is supported alongside medical treatments for excess weight, such as medicines or bariatric surgery, when medically appropriate.

items.title: Effectiveness of Probiotics, Prebiotics, and Synbiotics in Managing Insulin Resistance and Hormonal Imbalance in Women with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS): A Systematic Review of Randomized Clinical Trials
items.summary: This review pulled together 11 trials testing probiotics, prebiotics or synbiotics (a mix of the two) taken for at least 8 weeks by women with PCOS. Supplements, especially synbiotics, were linked to better insulin resistance, blood fats and hormone levels, with high adherence and few side effects. However, the trials were small, all from Iran, and in overweight or obese women, so the results may not apply to everyone. The authors say larger, longer and more varied studies are needed before these supplements can be widely recommended.
keyPoints: Probiotic and synbiotic supplements improved insulin resistance markers (HOMA-IR, fasting glucose and insulin) in women with PCOS.
Cholesterol and blood fat levels improved, and hormone balance shifted (higher SHBG, lower total testosterone).
Synbiotics had stronger effects than probiotics or prebiotics alone, and side effects were minimal.
Small, short, homogeneous trials limit how far the findings can be generalised; more evidence is needed.

items.title: Interventions for weight reduction in obesity to improve survival in women with endometrial cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether diet and exercise programmes aimed at weight loss help women with endometrial (womb lining) cancer who are overweight or obese live longer. It combined 12 trials with 610 women. The trials were too small, too short and too low in quality to show whether these programmes help with survival, weight loss or quality of life. No serious harms were reported, but the true effect is currently unknown.
keyPoints: There is not enough high-quality evidence to say whether lifestyle and weight-loss programmes improve survival in women with endometrial cancer who are overweight or obese.
The programmes were not linked to significant weight loss or better quality of life compared with usual care, but the evidence was low or very low certainty.
The trials reported no serious harms such as hospital stays or deaths related to the programmes, and it is uncertain whether muscle and joint problems increased.
Larger, better-designed trials with follow-up of five to 10 years are needed.

items.title: AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on Pharmacological Interventions for Adults With Obesity
items.summary: The American Gastroenterological Association reviewed the evidence on weight-loss medicines for adults with overweight or obesity. The expert panel strongly recommends adding medicine to lifestyle changes for adults who have not lost enough weight with diet and exercise alone. It suggests several medicines for long-term use and suggests against orlistat.
keyPoints: Medicine is strongly recommended alongside lifestyle changes for adults with a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with weight-related health problems, who did not respond enough to lifestyle changes alone.
Semaglutide 2.4 mg, liraglutide 3.0 mg, phentermine-topiramate ER and naltrexone-bupropion ER are suggested for long-term use, based on moderate certainty evidence.
Phentermine and diethylpropion are also suggested, but the evidence for them is low certainty.
The panel suggests against orlistat and says there is not enough evidence yet on Gelesis100 hydrogel.

items.title: Effect of Diet on Insulin Resistance in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This review pooled 19 trials with 1193 women who have PCOS to see whether changing what they eat could improve insulin resistance, a common problem in PCOS. Diet was linked to better insulin measures, blood sugar and body measurements such as weight, BMI and waist size. The longer women followed a diet, the bigger the improvement. Compared with the medicine metformin, diet led to more weight loss and had similar effects on insulin.
keyPoints: Diet was linked to lower insulin resistance, fasting insulin and fasting blood sugar in women with PCOS.
A DASH-style diet looked best for reducing insulin resistance, and calorie-restricted diets looked best for improving body measurements.
Longer time on a diet was linked to greater improvement.
Compared with metformin, diet gave more weight loss and similar effects on insulin regulation.

items.title: Body weight management in overweight and obese breast cancer survivors
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 20 trials with about 2,000 women who were overweight or obese after breast cancer, to see how weight loss programmes work. The programmes led to small drops in body weight, BMI and waist size, and women reported better quality of life. Programmes that combined diet, exercise and emotional support seemed to work a little better than diet alone, though the evidence was low quality. There was not enough information to know whether losing weight affects survival or cancer coming back.
keyPoints: Weight loss programmes led to an average loss of about 2.25 kg, plus small drops in BMI and waist size (low-quality evidence).
Overall quality of life improved, and there was no increase in side effects (high-quality evidence for side effects).
Programmes combining diet, exercise and psychosocial support appeared to give bigger reductions than diet alone, but the evidence was low quality.
Results were similar regardless of ethnicity or menopausal status, but there was too little data to judge effects on survival or breast cancer recurrence.

items.title: Lifestyle changes for treating psoriasis
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 10 trials of lifestyle changes, such as low-calorie diets, exercise and education, for people with psoriasis. In people who were obese, a low-calorie diet may improve psoriasis and probably improves quality of life and lowers BMI compared with usual care. Adding exercise to a diet plan probably lowers BMI, but it was unclear whether it helped skin symptoms more than advice alone. The evidence ranged from low to moderate quality, and no trials tested quitting smoking or alcohol.
keyPoints: In obese people, a strict low-calorie diet may lead to bigger improvements in psoriasis severity than usual care (low-quality evidence).
Diet probably improves skin-related quality of life and lowers BMI compared with usual care (moderate-quality evidence).
Diet plus exercise probably lowers BMI more than information alone, but may make little or no difference to psoriasis severity.
Most people stuck with the lifestyle programmes, and no trials looked at smoking cessation, alcohol abstinence or time to relapse.

items.title: Interventions for supporting the initiation and continuation of breastfeeding among women who are overweight or obese
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether support such as education, peer or professional contact, or a breast pump helps women who are overweight or obese start and keep up breastfeeding. It found seven small trials with 831 women, mostly in the USA. The quality of the evidence was very low, so it is unclear whether any of these supports make a difference. The authors say better-designed trials are needed.
keyPoints: Women who are overweight or obese are less likely to start breastfeeding and tend to breastfeed for a shorter time.
Only one small trial (39 women) tested a breast pump, and it could not show whether it helped.
Six trials used education and social support (phone or face-to-face); results for starting and continuing breastfeeding were uncertain.
The authors conclude there is not enough evidence to say which type of support works best and call for larger, better-designed trials.

items.title: FTO genotype and weight loss in diet and lifestyle interventions: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from studies of diet and lifestyle weight-loss programmes in adults to see whether a common gene variant (FTO), linked to a higher chance of obesity, changes how much weight people lose. People carrying two copies of the obesity-linked version lost slightly more weight (about 0.44 kg more) than people with none. The difference was small, and the authors say more research is needed before this could be used in practice.
keyPoints: People with two copies of the obesity-linked FTO variant (AA) lost about 0.44 kg more on diet or lifestyle programmes than those with none (TT).
People with one copy (TA) did not lose a clearly different amount of weight.
The gene did not appear to stop people from benefiting from diet and lifestyle changes.
The authors say the clinical use of these findings needs further investigation.

items.title: Pharmacological management of obesity: an endocrine Society clinical practice guideline
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: The Endocrine Society, with two partner societies, wrote guidelines on using medicines to manage obesity. They conclude that losing weight can improve health for people with obesity-related risk factors and conditions. Medicines approved for long-term weight management can be a useful extra for people who have not succeeded with diet and exercise alone. Some common medicines for diabetes, depression and other conditions can cause weight gain or weight loss.
keyPoints: Weight loss can improve health for people with obesity-related risk factors and health conditions.
Approved weight-management medicines can help alongside lifestyle change when diet and exercise alone have not worked.
Many medicines for diabetes, depression and other chronic diseases affect weight, either up or down.
Where possible, choosing medicines with a favourable weight effect can help prevent and manage obesity.

items.title: Interventions for idiopathic intracranial hypertension
items.summary: This review looked at treatments for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), a condition that raises pressure around the brain and most often affects young women with obesity. Only two small trials were found, both testing the drug acetazolamide alongside a weight loss programme. Vision changes were similar with the drug and with placebo, though the drug showed some benefit for pressure, swelling at the back of the eye and quality of life. The evidence was low certainty, so the reviewers could not say whether acetazolamide or any other treatment clearly works.
keyPoints: Two trials (211 people) compared acetazolamide with placebo, with weight loss support given to both groups.
Change in vision was similar between the acetazolamide and placebo groups.
Acetazolamide gave a greater reduction in spinal fluid pressure and eye swelling, and better quality of life scores in one study, but also more side effects such as nausea, tiredness and tingling.
There is not enough good evidence to recommend or reject acetazolamide or other IIH treatments; more high-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Effective strategies for weight loss in post-partum women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 32 randomized trials of lifestyle programs (diet, exercise or both) in 1,892 women within 12 months of giving birth. Programs where women tracked their own progress, such as logging food or weight, led to more weight loss than programs without tracking. Programs combining diet and exercise worked better than exercise alone.
keyPoints: Programs with self-monitoring led to about 4.6 kg of weight loss, compared with about 1.3 kg without it.
Combining diet and physical activity led to about 3.2 kg of weight loss, compared with about 1.6 kg for physical activity alone.
Lifestyle programs that used both self-monitoring and a combined diet-and-exercise approach had the greatest weight loss in postpartum women.

items.title: Effects of mHealth-Based Lifestyle Interventions on Gestational Diabetes Mellitus in Pregnant Women With Overweight and Obesity: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 16 randomised trials with 7,351 pregnant women who had overweight or obesity. It looked at whether lifestyle programmes delivered through phones, such as apps, could help prevent gestational diabetes. Compared with usual care, these programmes were linked to fewer cases of gestational diabetes, less preterm birth and fewer very large babies. The authors say larger, better-designed trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Phone-based lifestyle programmes lowered the chance of gestational diabetes compared with usual care (odds ratio 0.74).
They were also linked to lower rates of preterm birth and of macrosomia (a very large baby).
Women in the programmes gained about 1.1 kg less weight during pregnancy on average.
Apps, programmes led by obstetricians, and programmes aimed at Asian populations showed clearer reductions in gestational diabetes.

items.title: Theory-based interventions aimed at promoting physical activity in pregnant women: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 11 randomized trials of programs designed to help pregnant women be more active, using methods based on health behavior theories such as goal setting and action planning. The programs modestly increased moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, slightly reduced weekly weight gain, and lowered the chance of gestational diabetes. Effects on total weight gain over the whole pregnancy, high blood pressure in pregnancy and preterm birth were unclear. The programs appeared to be safe.
keyPoints: Theory-based activity programs modestly increased moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (moderate certainty evidence).
Average weight gain per week of pregnancy was slightly lower, by about 0.06 kg per week (moderate certainty evidence).
Gestational diabetes was less common, with a risk ratio of 0.64 (high certainty evidence).
Effects on total weight gain, gestational high blood pressure and preterm delivery were unclear, and the programs appeared safe.

items.title: Incidence and factors influencing delayed onset of lactation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review combined 35 studies of about 19,000 new mothers to look at delayed onset of lactation, when milk 'comes in' more than 72 hours after birth. About 3 in 10 mothers (30%) had a delay. Several health and birth factors were linked to a higher chance of delay, and the authors say clinicians should watch for mothers at higher risk and offer support early.
keyPoints: About 30% of mothers had delayed onset of lactation (milk coming in after 72 hours).
Factors linked to delay included overweight or obesity before pregnancy, gestational diabetes, gestational hypertension, thyroid disease in pregnancy, caesarean birth, and a baby born early or small.
Less frequent breastfeeding, shorter daily sleep and not receiving breastfeeding guidance were also linked to delay.
Links with age, weight gain in pregnancy, anxiety, time of first feed and breast massage were unclear.

items.title: Risk factors for preterm birth: an umbrella review of meta-analyses of observational studies
items.summary: Researchers pooled the results of 85 earlier reviews covering 166 possible risk factors for preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks). Many links had been reported, but only seven were backed by robust evidence. These were amphetamine exposure, a single umbilical artery, maternal personality disorder, sleep-disordered breathing, a prior vacuum-aspiration abortion, low weight gain in pregnancy, and a gap of under 6 months after a miscarriage before the next pregnancy. The studies were observational, so they show associations rather than proof of cause.
keyPoints: Of 166 reported associations with preterm birth, only seven were supported by robust evidence.
Low weight gain in pregnancy was one of the seven robust risk factors.
Short spacing (under 6 months) after a miscarriage and sleep-disordered breathing were also on the list.
The authors say sleep quality and mental health are not routinely screened at prenatal visits and suggest they should be.

items.title: Efficacy of continuous glucose monitoring on maternal and neonatal outcomes in gestational diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
items.summary: This review pulled together six randomized trials (482 women) comparing continuous glucose monitoring, where a sensor tracks sugar levels all day, with usual finger-prick testing in gestational diabetes. Women using continuous monitoring had slightly lower average blood sugar (HbA1c) at the end of pregnancy, gained a little less weight, and had babies with slightly lower birth weights. No differences were seen in the other outcomes studied. The authors say the evidence is limited because there were few studies and they were small.
keyPoints: Continuous glucose monitoring was linked to slightly lower HbA1c at the end of pregnancy than finger-prick testing.
Women using it gained somewhat less weight in pregnancy, and their babies had lower birth weight.
No differences were found in the other maternal and newborn outcomes checked.
The evidence is limited by few and small studies, so larger trials are needed.

items.title: Association of Antenatal Diet and Physical Activity-Based Interventions With Gestational Weight Gain and Pregnancy Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 117 randomized trials involving about 34,500 pregnant women to see whether diet and physical activity programs affect weight gain in pregnancy. Women in lifestyle programs gained about 1 kg less on average and had a lower risk of gestational diabetes than women getting routine care. Diet-based programs showed the biggest effects on weight gain and on several baby outcomes. The authors describe this as level 1 evidence and support offering such programs in routine antenatal care.
keyPoints: Lifestyle programs were linked to about 1.15 kg less weight gain and a lower risk of gestational diabetes compared with routine care.
Diet-based programs had the largest effect on weight gain (about 2.6 kg less) and were linked to lower risks of preterm birth, large babies and neonatal intensive care admission.
Physical activity programs were linked to less weight gain and lower risks of gestational diabetes, high blood pressure disorders of pregnancy and cesarean section.
Less structured mixed programs, such as written information or behavioral support alone, reduced weight gain but not other outcomes.

items.title: Weight Gain and Nutrition during Pregnancy: An Analysis of Clinical Practice Guidelines in the Asia-Pacific Region
items.summary: Researchers reviewed 10 clinical practice guidelines on weight gain and nutrition in pregnancy from countries across the Asia-Pacific region. Most of them (9 of 10) were rated as low quality. The advice on how much weight to gain, how much extra energy to eat and which supplements to take also differed a lot from one guideline to another. The authors say the guidelines need to be improved so pregnant women get consistent, appropriate advice.
keyPoints: 9 out of 10 guidelines were rated low quality using a standard checking tool (AGREE II).
Recommendations on weight gain in pregnancy varied, including advice aimed at Asian populations.
Advice on diet, extra energy intake and nutritional supplements also varied between guidelines.
The authors conclude the guidelines need to be improved so pregnant women receive appropriate advice.

items.title: Weight gain during pregnancy: A narrative review on the recent evidences
items.summary: This review looked at how much weight women should gain in pregnancy, especially women who were living with obesity before pregnancy. Gaining too little or too much weight is linked to problems for mother and baby. Advice for women with obesity is still debated, and newer studies suggest targets should be personalised by obesity class (I, II or III).
keyPoints: Both low and excessive weight gain in pregnancy are linked to poorer outcomes for the baby.
Pre-pregnancy obesity is linked to higher risks of high blood pressure, gestational diabetes, cesarean section and a larger baby.
The 2009 Institute of Medicine target for women with obesity (11-20 lb) has been called too high by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
Very low weight gain or weight loss in pregnancy is linked to a higher chance of a small baby, so both upper and lower limits matter.

items.title: Prevention of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus and Gestational Weight Gain Restriction in Overweight/Obese Pregnant Women: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 23 trials with nearly 9,000 pregnant women who were overweight or obese early in pregnancy. It compared diet changes, physical activity, both together, and medication for preventing gestational diabetes and limiting weight gain. None of the approaches clearly prevented gestational diabetes, though physical activity and diet plus activity showed a hint of benefit. Diet, activity and the two combined all helped limit weight gain in pregnancy, while medication did not.
keyPoints: No intervention (diet, physical activity, both, or medication) significantly prevented gestational diabetes, though physical activity and diet plus activity showed a trend toward benefit.
Diet, physical activity and diet plus activity all significantly reduced weight gain in pregnancy; medication did not.
Combining diet and physical activity appeared to be the best overall choice for both preventing gestational diabetes and limiting excess weight gain.

items.title: Physical activity and gestational weight gain: a systematic review of observational studies
items.summary: This review looked at 21 observational studies to see whether being physically active in pregnancy is linked to how much weight a woman gains. Most studies found that more active pregnant women gained less weight overall than inactive women, though not every result was statistically significant. The authors say the evidence has limits, so no firm conclusions can be drawn yet.
keyPoints: All studies that looked at total weight gain pointed the same way: more physical activity was linked to less weight gain, although not all results were statistically significant.
Most studies on excessive weight gain found a significant link with some aspects of physical activity.
Results were mixed for how fast weight was gained each week, with some studies finding no link.
The authors say the evidence is limited and more consistent studies are needed.

items.title: Elite Athletes and Pregnancy Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.source: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
items.journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
items.summary: This review pooled 11 studies of 2,256 women to see how pregnancy goes for elite athletes who were competing right before they conceived. Elite athletes seemed less likely to have low back pain in pregnancy, but may be more likely to gain more weight than recommended. The evidence for both findings is weak, and there were no differences between athletes and other women for most other outcomes.
keyPoints: Low certainty evidence: elite athletes had lower odds of pregnancy-related low back pain than active or sedentary women.
Very low certainty evidence: elite athletes had higher odds of gaining more weight than recommended in pregnancy.
Low certainty evidence from two small studies noted three episodes of slow fetal heart rate after high-intensity exercise, which settled within 10 minutes of stopping.
No differences were found between athletes and controls for the other outcomes studied, and more research is needed.

items.title: Maternal exposures and the infant gut microbiome: a systematic review with meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 76 studies on what happens before birth that may shape a baby's gut bacteria. Factors linked to differences included antibiotics, probiotics, diet, weight before pregnancy, weight gain in pregnancy, diabetes and mood. In the combined analysis, antibiotics given during labour, maternal overweight or obesity, and gaining more weight than recommended in pregnancy were each linked to less variety in the baby's gut bacteria. Most studies were observational, so they show links rather than proof of cause, and study methods varied a lot.
keyPoints: Antibiotics during labour, maternal overweight or obesity, and excessive weight gain in pregnancy were each linked to lower diversity of bacteria in the infant gut.
Other factors reported to influence the infant gut microbiome included maternal probiotics, diet, diabetes and mood.
Most studies were observational, few followed babies over time, and stool sampling and analysis methods varied.
The authors say more standardised methods and collaboration are needed to understand this area.

items.title: Behavioral Counseling Interventions for Healthy Weight and Weight Gain in Pregnancy: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed research on counseling programs that help pregnant people gain a healthy amount of weight. About half of people in the US start pregnancy with overweight or obesity, and gaining too much weight in pregnancy is linked to problems like a larger baby, cesarean birth or preterm birth. The Task Force concluded with moderate certainty that these counseling programs give a moderate benefit. It recommends that clinicians offer them to pregnant people.
keyPoints: Gaining too much weight in pregnancy is linked to a large-for-gestational-age baby, cesarean delivery and preterm birth.
Counseling aimed at healthy weight gain has a moderate net benefit for pregnant people, based on moderate-certainty evidence.
Clinicians are recommended to offer effective behavioral counseling to pregnant people (a B recommendation).
Overweight and obesity at the start of pregnancy are common, affecting almost half of pregnant people in the US in 2015.

items.title: Probiotic treatment for women with gestational diabetes to improve maternal and infant health and well-being
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at nine small trials (695 women) testing probiotics against a placebo as a treatment for gestational diabetes. The trials could not show whether probiotics change the chance of high blood pressure in pregnancy, caesarean birth, or large babies, because the evidence was low certainty. Some blood markers of insulin resistance and inflammation improved, and no side effects were reported. The review concludes the evidence is too limited to guide practice.
keyPoints: Low-certainty evidence means it is unclear whether probiotics affect high blood pressure disorders of pregnancy, caesarean birth or large-for-gestational-age babies.
Uncertain whether probiotics change weight gain during pregnancy or total gestational weight gain.
Probiotics were linked to minor improvements in markers of insulin resistance and inflammation, and possibly to lower triglycerides and total cholesterol.
No adverse events were reported, but small trials and varied probiotics limit what the review can say; larger, better trials are needed.

items.title: Impact of maternal body mass index and gestational weight gain on pregnancy complications: an individual participant data meta-analysis of European, North American and Australian cohorts
items.summary: Researchers pooled data from 39 studies covering about 265,000 births in Europe, North America and Australia. They looked at how a woman's weight before pregnancy and how much weight she gained during pregnancy relate to pregnancy complications. Higher weight before pregnancy and higher weight gain were linked to higher risks of high blood pressure disorders, gestational diabetes and larger babies. The authors suggest that a healthy weight before pregnancy and healthy weight gain may reduce complications.
keyPoints: Higher pre-pregnancy BMI and higher weight gain in pregnancy were linked to more gestational hypertension, pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and large babies.
Preterm birth risk was higher at both lower and higher BMI and weight gain.
Women with obesity and high weight gain had the highest risk of any complication (odds ratio 2.51).
About 24% of pregnancy complications were linked to overweight or obesity, and about 32% of large babies to excessive weight gain.

items.title: Association of Gestational Weight Gain With Adverse Maternal and Infant Outcomes
items.summary: Researchers pooled data from nearly 200,000 pregnancies across 25 studies in Europe and North America to see how weight gain during pregnancy relates to problems for mothers and babies. Risk of problems such as preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, caesarean birth and preterm birth varied with both weight gain and the mother's weight before pregnancy. The study suggests different weight gain ranges for different starting weights, with lower ranges for women with obesity. The authors note these ranges were only modestly useful for predicting who would have problems.
keyPoints: Overall, 37.2% of women had at least one adverse outcome, ranging from 34.7% in underweight women to 61.1% in women with grade 3 obesity.
Estimated best weight gain ranges were 14.0 to under 16.0 kg for underweight, 10.0 to under 18.0 kg for normal weight, and 2.0 to under 16.0 kg for overweight.
For obesity, estimated ranges were 2.0 to under 6.0 kg (grade 1), 0 to under 4.0 kg (grade 2), and 0 to under 6.0 kg (grade 3).
The ranges had limited ability to predict who would have adverse outcomes, but may help inform prenatal counseling.

items.title: Metformin for women who are overweight or obese during pregnancy for improving maternal and infant outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether taking metformin (a diabetes medicine) during pregnancy helps women with obesity and their babies. It found three trials with about 1,000 women, all started early in the second trimester. Metformin did not change the chance of a baby being born large for their age and made little or no difference to birthweight or most other outcomes. It may lower weight gain slightly, but it caused more side effects, especially diarrhoea. The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to support using metformin for this purpose.
keyPoints: Metformin made no clear difference to the risk of a baby being born large for gestational age (high-quality evidence).
Women taking metformin may gain slightly less weight in pregnancy (about 2.6 kg less on average, low-quality evidence), though the result was uncertain.
Metformin probably makes little or no difference to gestational diabetes, and may make little or no difference to gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia.
Women taking metformin were more likely to have side effects, especially diarrhoea (high-quality evidence).

items.title: Dietary advice interventions in pregnancy for preventing gestational diabetes mellitus
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 11 trials (2,786 women) to see whether dietary advice in pregnancy can prevent gestational diabetes. Women who got dietary advice may have had a lower chance of gestational diabetes than those given standard care, but the evidence was very low quality and the result was not clearly certain. Women given dietary advice also gained less weight and had less pregnancy-induced high blood pressure, though this evidence was low quality. Low-GI advice was not clearly better than moderate- to high-GI advice.
keyPoints: Dietary advice versus standard care showed a possible trend towards less gestational diabetes (very low-quality evidence), with a possibly bigger effect in women who were overweight or obese.
Women receiving dietary advice gained about 4.7 kg less during pregnancy on average, and had less pregnancy-induced high blood pressure (low-quality evidence).
No clear differences were seen for caesarean birth, pre-eclampsia or perineal trauma.
Low-GI dietary advice made no clear difference to gestational diabetes or gestational weight gain compared with moderate- to high-GI advice.

items.title: Screening for gestational diabetes mellitus based on different risk profiles and settings for improving maternal and infant health
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether different ways of screening pregnant women for gestational diabetes (diabetes that starts in pregnancy) improve health for mothers and babies. It found only two trials, both from Ireland, with about 4,500 women in total. Screening every woman found more cases of gestational diabetes than screening only women with risk factors. There was no clear difference between screening in primary care and in hospital-based care, but the evidence was low quality, so no firm conclusions can be drawn.
keyPoints: Screening all women found more cases of gestational diabetes than screening only women with risk factors (low-quality evidence).
Screening in primary care versus secondary (hospital) care showed no clear differences in gestational diabetes, high blood pressure, pre-eclampsia, caesarean birth or newborn outcomes.
Neither trial reported on gestational weight gain, postnatal depression or later type 2 diabetes.
The authors say there is not enough trial evidence and call for larger, high-quality trials.

items.title: Effectiveness of Dietetic Consultations in Primary Health Care: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.source: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics
items.journal: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics
items.summary: This review pooled 26 randomized trials of one-to-one dietitian appointments for adults in primary care. Dietitian consultations appeared to help with diet quality, blood sugar control in diabetes, weight loss, and limiting weight gain during pregnancy. They did not show consistent benefits for cholesterol or blood pressure. The authors rated the evidence as fair for the benefits and limited for cholesterol and blood pressure.
keyPoints: Dietitian consultations in primary care appeared effective for improving diet quality and diabetes outcomes such as blood glucose.
They also appeared effective for weight loss and for limiting gestational weight gain (fair evidence).
Evidence did not consistently support dietitian counselling alone for improving blood fats or blood pressure (limited evidence).
The review covered 26 randomized trials with about 5,500 adults.

items.title: Macronutrient composition and gestational weight gain: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 56 studies on how what pregnant women eat relates to how much weight they gain. Eating more energy (calories) in pregnancy was linked to gaining more weight. The roles of protein, carbohydrate and fat were less clear and often inconsistent, and most of the studies were of low quality.
keyPoints: Higher energy (calorie) intake during pregnancy was linked to higher weight gain.
Results for protein and carbohydrate intake were inconsistent across studies.
Fat intake might be linked to weight gain, but the direction may depend on the type of fat, such as saturated fat.
No macronutrient was consistently linked to gaining too little or too much weight, and results were similar in high-income and lower-income countries.

items.title: Antenatal dietary education and supplementation to increase energy and protein intake
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 17 trials with 9,030 pregnant women to see whether diet education or food supplements that raise energy and protein intake help mothers and babies. Diet education looked helpful for some outcomes, such as fewer preterm births and low birthweight babies, but the evidence was low quality. Balanced energy and protein supplements seemed to help babies grow and may lower the chance of stillbirth, while high-protein supplements did not look helpful and may be harmful. None of these approaches clearly changed how much weight women gained in pregnancy, and the authors say the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Nutritional education was linked to lower risk of preterm birth and low birthweight and to higher birthweight in undernourished women, though the evidence was low quality.
Balanced energy and protein supplements probably raised average birthweight and lowered the risk of stillbirth and of babies being small for their gestational age (moderate-quality evidence).
High-protein supplements did not seem beneficial and were linked to more small-for-gestational-age babies in one trial.
No approach clearly changed weekly or total weight gain in pregnancy, and many trials had unclear or high risk of bias.

items.title: Real-world menstrual cycle characteristics of more than 600,000 menstrual cycles
items.summary: This study looked at 612,613 ovulating cycles from 124,648 users of a cycle-tracking app that records temperature and ovulation tests. The average cycle lasted 29.3 days, so the textbook 28 days is only an average. The phase before ovulation varied most (on average 16.9 days, usually between 10 and 30), while the phase after ovulation was steadier (on average 12.4 days, usually between 7 and 17). Between ages 25 and 45, cycles got slightly shorter, by about 0.18 days per year of age. Cycle length varied a little more from cycle to cycle in women with a BMI over 35. The authors note that ovulation day differs between women and cycles, so tracking body signs helps more than counting days alone when trying to conceive.
keyPoints: Average cycle length was 29.3 days across 612,613 cycles.
The phase before ovulation varied most (average 16.9 days, usually 10 to 30); the phase after ovulation averaged 12.4 days (usually 7 to 17).
From 25 to 45, cycles got about 0.18 days shorter per year of age.
Cycle length varied slightly more in women with a BMI over 35.
Ovulation day differs between cycles, so counting days alone is a rough guide to the fertile days.
keywords: how long is a normal cycle

items.title: Menstrual disturbances in various thyroid diseases
items.summary: This study from Japan checked period problems (missed periods, light or heavy periods, short or long or irregular cycles) in more than 2000 women with thyroid conditions, including an overactive thyroid (Graves' disease), an underactive thyroid, thyroiditis and thyroid nodules, and compared them with 105 healthy women. Overall, period problems were not more common than in the healthy women. They were more common when the thyroid problem was severe: women with a severely overactive thyroid more often had missed or very light periods, and about 35% of women with a severely underactive thyroid had period problems, compared with about 10% with a mild or moderate one. The authors conclude that period problems with thyroid disease are less frequent than once thought.
keyPoints: Across all thyroid conditions, period problems were not more common than in healthy women.
A severely overactive thyroid was linked with more missed periods (2.5% vs 0.2%) and very light periods (3.7% vs 0.9%) than a mild or moderate one.
About 35% of women with a severely underactive thyroid had period problems, compared with about 10% with a mild or moderate one.
Period problems in thyroid disease were less frequent than earlier thought.

items.title: The Menstrual Disturbances in Endocrine Disorders: A Narrative Review
items.source: International Journal of Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: International Journal of Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This narrative review summarises how hormone (endocrine) conditions affect the menstrual cycle. The glands involved include the pituitary, thyroid, pancreas, adrenal glands and ovaries. Across conditions such as an overactive or underactive thyroid, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), Cushing's syndrome and diabetes, the most common change was infrequent periods, with cycles longer than 35 days. The authors say that cycle length and the amount of bleeding can point to a hormone condition, and that more research is needed.
keyPoints: Thyroid problems, PCOS, Cushing's syndrome, diabetes and high prolactin can all change the menstrual cycle.
The most common change across these conditions was infrequent periods (cycles longer than 35 days).
Changes in cycle length or bleeding can be a sign of a hormone condition worth checking with a doctor.
This is a narrative review, not a systematic one.

items.title: Clinical and exercise professional opinion of return-to-running readiness after childbirth: an international Delphi study and consensus statement
items.summary: Runners who have had a baby often say there is little clear guidance on when to start running again. In this international consensus study, 118 clinicians and exercise professionals who work with postpartum runners answered three survey rounds; agreement was set at 75% or more. They agreed that after at least 3 weeks of rest and recovery, a gradual, individual return to running can be considered. Before starting, they recommend checking for medical and psychological concerns, current physical capacity (such as strength and pelvic floor symptoms) and past training. The authors say this is initial guidance from expert opinion and needs testing in research.
keyPoints: After a minimum of 3 weeks of rest and recovery, a gradual return to running can be considered, on an individual timeline.
Before running, check medical and psychological concerns, current physical capacity and training history.
Based on expert agreement (75% or more of 95 to 118 professionals over three rounds), not on trials.
The authors call it initial guidance that research still needs to confirm.

items.title: Clinical and exercise professional opinion on designing a postpartum return-to-running training programme: an international Delphi study and consensus statement
items.summary: This international consensus study asked clinicians and exercise professionals how to build a training plan for running again after childbirth. Across three survey rounds (118, 107 and 95 participants), they agreed on 42 of 47 statements. The plan should start with a period of relative rest, then increase duration and intensity gradually, begin with walk-run intervals and include strength training. It should be adjusted for muscle or joint pain, pelvic floor symptoms such as leaking or heaviness, sleep, mental health, breastfeeding and whether she is eating enough for her activity. Cost and access to experienced professionals can be barriers.
keyPoints: Start with relative rest, then build up duration and intensity gradually.
Begin with walk-run intervals and add strength training.
Adjust the plan for pain, pelvic floor symptoms (leaking, heaviness), sleep, mood, breastfeeding and energy intake.
Consensus was reached on 42 of 47 statements; it reflects expert opinion, not trial results.

items.title: Amenorrhea: A Systematic Approach to Diagnosis and Management
items.summary: This review for family doctors explains how to look into absent periods (amenorrhoea). Primary amenorrhoea means never having had a period; it should be checked if there is no first period by age 15, or 3 years after the breasts started to develop. Secondary amenorrhoea means periods that stop for 3 months after being regular, or for 6 months after being irregular. Causes include problems of the womb or vagina, the ovaries stopping early, the brain's hormone centres (for example from stress, low weight or a lot of exercise), thyroid and other hormone conditions, chronic illness, and pregnancy. The first steps are a pregnancy test and blood tests for FSH, LH, prolactin and TSH (thyroid); further tests depend on the findings. Missed periods from low energy intake can go with disordered eating and weak bones, and PCOS needs checks for metabolic and womb-lining risks.
keyPoints: No first period by 15, or 3 years after breast development started: see a doctor to check why.
Periods stopping for 3 months (or 6 months if they were irregular) should also be checked.
First tests: a pregnancy test and blood tests for FSH, LH, prolactin and thyroid (TSH).
Causes range from pregnancy and stress, low weight or heavy exercise to thyroid, pituitary or ovary conditions.
Missed periods from low weight or heavy exercise can go with disordered eating and low bone density.

items.title: MANAGEMENT OF ENDOCRINE DISEASE: Diagnosis and management of primary amenorrhea and female delayed puberty
items.summary: This review from paediatric hormone specialists and gynaecologists explains when a missing first period needs checking and why it can happen. The first period is a late step of puberty. Primary amenorrhoea means no first period by 15 in a girl who has otherwise developed and grown normally, or no signs of puberty at all by 13. A check should also be considered if there is no period 3 years after the breasts began to develop, or 5 years after if that happened before age 10. Causes include hormone problems in the brain or pituitary, the ovaries not working, other hormone conditions and differences in how the womb or vagina formed. With early diagnosis, the authors note, fertility can sometimes be achieved even when the cause cannot be cured.
keyPoints: No first period by 15 despite otherwise normal development, or no signs of puberty by 13: see a doctor.
Also check if there is no period 3 years after breast development started (5 years if it started before 10).
Causes include brain or pituitary hormone problems, ovaries not working, other hormone conditions and differences in the womb or vagina.
With timely diagnosis, a pregnancy may sometimes still be possible later even when the cause cannot be cured.

items.title: Contraceptive Failure in the United States: Estimates from the 2006-2010 National Survey of Family Growth
items.source: Perspectives on Sexual and Reproductive Health
items.journal: Perspectives on Sexual and Reproductive Health
items.summary: This study estimated how often each contraceptive method fails in real life (typical use) in the United States, using a national survey of 6683 women and 15,728 periods of method use, corrected for under-reporting of abortions. In the first year, IUDs and implants failed least often (about 1%), while condoms (13%) and withdrawal (20%) failed most often. Hormonal methods together, such as the pill, had a failure rate of about 6%, down from 8% in 1995. Typical use includes forgotten pills and other mistakes, which is why it is higher than the rate with perfect use.
keyPoints: First-year typical-use failure: IUD and implant about 1%.
Hormonal methods such as the pill, patch, ring and injection together: about 6% (8% in 1995).
Condoms about 13% and withdrawal about 20% in the first year.
All reversible methods together: 10% in 2006-2010, down from 12% in 2002.
keywords: how often does the pill fail

items.title: Typical-use contraceptive failure rates in 43 countries with Demographic and Health Survey data: summary of a detailed report
items.summary: This study used survey answers from women in 43 countries to estimate how often contraception fails in everyday (typical) use. In the first 12 months, failures per 100 episodes of use were lowest with implants (0.6), IUDs (1.4) and injections (1.7), in the middle with the pill (5.5) and male condoms (5.4), and highest with withdrawal (13.4) and calendar-based abstinence (13.9). The figures come from what women recalled and were not corrected for under-reported abortions, so they may be too low.
keyPoints: 12-month typical-use failures per 100 uses: implant 0.6, IUD 1.4, injection 1.7.
Pill 5.5 and male condom 5.4.
Withdrawal 13.4 and calendar methods 13.9.
Based on recalled survey data from 43 countries, not corrected for under-reporting.

items.title: Hormonal contraceptives and risk of ischemic stroke in women with migraine: a consensus statement from the European Headache Federation (EHF) and the European Society of Contraception and Reproductive Health (ESC)
items.source: The Journal of Headache and Pain
items.journal: The Journal of Headache and Pain
items.summary: Migraine, especially migraine with aura, is linked with a higher risk of ischaemic stroke (a stroke from a blocked blood vessel). European headache and contraception experts reviewed the evidence on whether hormonal contraception adds to this risk and agreed on statements for safe prescribing. The evidence is of low quality, but it suggests that combined hormonal contraception (with oestrogen) may raise the stroke risk further in women with migraine, especially migraine with aura. Their statements therefore put safety first, and they call for more research.
keyPoints: Migraine with aura is linked with a higher risk of ischaemic stroke.
Combined (oestrogen-containing) contraception may raise this risk further, especially with aura.
The quality of the evidence is low; the statements put safety first.

items.title: Contraceptive decision-making in women with migraine: integrating guidelines, vascular risk, and clinical practice
items.summary: This 2026 narrative review looks at how to choose contraception when a woman has migraine. Migraine with aura is consistently linked with a higher risk of ischaemic stroke, and combined hormonal contraception (with oestrogen) adds to it. Guidelines agree that combined methods should not be used with migraine with aura, while progestogen-only methods are considered safe. With migraine without aura, a low-dose combined pill may be considered for carefully selected women without other risk factors (such as smoking or high blood pressure), although progestogen-only methods are preferred when such risk factors exist. Some evidence suggests the desogestrel progestogen-only pill may reduce migraine frequency.
keyPoints: Migraine with aura: guidelines agree that combined (oestrogen) methods should not be used.
Progestogen-only methods are considered safe with migraine, with or without aura.
Migraine without aura: a low-dose combined pill may be considered if there are no other stroke risk factors.
The desogestrel progestogen-only pill may reduce how often migraines happen (limited evidence).
This is a narrative review.

items.title: Association between the number of eggs and live birth in IVF treatment: an analysis of 400 135 treatment cycles
items.summary: This study used the UK national register (HFEA) of 400,135 IVF cycles from 1991 to 2008 to see how the number of eggs collected and the woman's age relate to the chance of a baby. Overall, 21.3% of fresh IVF cycles led to a live birth. The chance rose with the number of eggs up to about 15, levelled off between 15 and 20, and fell above 20. Age mattered a lot: in 2006-2007, with 15 eggs collected, the predicted live birth rate was 40% at ages 18 to 34, 36% at 35 to 37, 27% at 38 to 39 and 16% at 40 and over. These are older averages; success rates have risen since.
keyPoints: Overall live birth rate: 21.3% per fresh IVF cycle (UK, 1991 to 2008).
The chance rose with egg number up to about 15 eggs, levelled off at 15 to 20 and fell above 20.
Predicted live birth rate with 15 eggs (2006-2007): 40% at 18-34, 36% at 35-37, 27% at 38-39, 16% at 40 and over.
Older data; national success rates have risen since.

items.title: Health insurance: maternity benefits (what Swiss basic insurance covers in pregnancy and after the birth)
items.summary: The Swiss Federal Office of Public Health (BAG) explains what basic health insurance pays for in pregnancy and after the birth. In a normal pregnancy it covers seven check-ups with a doctor or midwife, one ultrasound scan at weeks 12 to 14 and one at weeks 20 to 23, and the first-trimester test for the risk of trisomy 21, 18 and 13. More scans are covered in a high-risk pregnancy when the gynaecologist finds them necessary. Maternity services cost nothing extra: no deductible or co-payment, and from week 13 until eight weeks after the birth other medical care is free of cost-sharing too.
keyPoints: A normal pregnancy: seven check-ups and two ultrasound scans (weeks 12 to 14 and weeks 20 to 23) are covered.
The first-trimester test (nuchal scan at weeks 12 to 14 plus a blood test) for trisomy 21, 18 and 13 is covered.
A NIPT blood test is covered from week 12 if the risk of a trisomy is 1 in 1000 or higher.
Amniocentesis or a placenta biopsy (CVS) is covered if the first-trimester risk is 1 in 380 or higher, or if NIPT strongly suggests a trisomy.
No deductible or co-payment for maternity services; from week 13 until eight weeks after the birth none for other medical care either.
After the birth: a check between weeks 6 and 10, three breastfeeding-advice sessions and a 150-franc contribution to a birth-preparation course.
