items.title: Swiss basic insurance covers a first-trimester pre-eclampsia test from 1 July 2026 (KLV Art. 13 letter b quater)
items.summary: From 1 July 2026, Swiss basic health insurance pays for a first-trimester test for the risk of pre-eclampsia, a pregnancy condition with new high blood pressure and organ involvement that can be serious for mother and baby. The test is done at the routine scan at weeks 12 to 14 for women expecting one baby. It combines the mother's risk factors, her blood pressure, a Doppler scan of the blood flow in the arteries of the womb and a blood test for placental growth factor (PlGF). Depending on the result, the doctor prescribes low-dose aspirin to lower the risk. Until now, women at risk were picked by their risk factors alone; the BAG says the combined test predicts better and is recommended in Swiss and international guidelines.

items.title: Bone density scans (DXA): when Swiss basic insurance pays (KLV Annex 1, edition of 1 July 2026)
items.summary: Annex 1 of the Swiss health insurance benefits ordinance (KLV) lists when basic insurance pays for a bone density scan (DXA). It is not a screening test for everyone: it is covered for set reasons, such as osteoporosis that has already caused a fracture after a minor fall, long-term cortisone treatment, low sex hormones (hypogonadism), gut diseases that reduce absorption (for example Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, coeliac disease), primary hyperparathyroidism, HIV, aromatase-inhibitor treatment and anti-epileptic medicines. items.title: Swiss vaccination schedule 2026: vaccinations before and during pregnancy
items.summary: The Swiss vaccination schedule (BAG and the Federal Commission for Vaccination) recommends checking and completing vaccinations before every pregnancy, especially measles-mumps-rubella, chickenpox and hepatitis B. In every pregnancy it recommends a flu vaccine (any trimester), a pertussis (whooping cough) vaccine in the second or third trimester, preferably the second, whatever the time since the last dose, and a COVID-19 vaccine in the second or third trimester. An RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) is recommended once, not in every pregnancy, between weeks 32+0 and 36+0 when the due date falls between early October and the end of March, as one of two options to protect the baby; the other is an antibody injection for the newborn. Every pregnant woman should be tested for hepatitis B in every pregnancy, with few exceptions.
keyPoints: Before every pregnancy: check and complete MMR, chickenpox and hepatitis B vaccination.
In every pregnancy: flu vaccine in any trimester; pertussis (dTpa) in the second or third trimester, preferably the second; COVID-19 in the second or third trimester.

RSV: one dose of Abrysvo between weeks 32+0 and 36+0 if the due date is between early October and end of March; once only, not in every pregnancy; the alternative is an antibody injection for the baby.
Live vaccines such as MMR and chickenpox are not given in pregnancy; women who are not immune get them soon after the birth.
Hepatitis B test (HBsAg) in every pregnancy, unless immunity is reliably documented.

items.title: Nutrition before and during pregnancy and while breastfeeding: Swiss federal advice (BLV page, FAQ and brochure of August 2025)
items.summary: The Swiss Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office (BLV) advises taking folic acid tablets (400 micrograms a day) already before a planned pregnancy, to lower the risk of birth defects, and eating a varied, balanced diet. In pregnancy almost all nutrients can come from food, except folic acid and vitamin D; sometimes a supplement for iron, iodine or omega-3 fats is needed, to be discussed with the gynaecologist. Women of childbearing age, pregnant and breastfeeding women in Switzerland often get too little iodine: the BLV advises iodised salt, dairy and sea fish, and asking the gynaecologist whether an iodine tablet is needed. While breastfeeding it recommends vitamin D drops, enough omega-3 fats and avoiding alcohol. Its brochure (August 2025) adds: weight gain by starting BMI (11.5 to 16 kg at normal weight), about 250 extra kcal a day from month 4 and 500 from month 7, 1.5 to 2 litres of drinks a day, caffeine in moderation (for example 1 to 2 cups of coffee or 4 cups of black or green tea a day), no alcohol in pregnancy, limits for some fish because of mercury, and about 30 minutes of movement a day.
keyPoints: Folic acid tablets, 400 micrograms a day, from before a planned pregnancy.
In pregnancy, folic acid and vitamin D are the nutrients food alone does not cover; iron, iodine or omega-3 supplements only after talking with the gynaecologist.
Iodine: use iodised salt, have dairy products and sea fish, and ask the gynaecologist about an iodine tablet when trying to conceive, pregnant or breastfeeding.
Breastfeeding: vitamin D drops, omega-3 fats from oily fish, walnuts or rapeseed oil, and no alcohol (a small glass on a special occasion, then wait two hours before the next feed).
Soft cheese should be avoided in pregnancy.
Weight gain in pregnancy by BMI before pregnancy: under 18.5: 12.5 to 18 kg; 18.5 to 24.9: 11.5 to 16 kg; 25 to 29.9: 7 to 11.5 kg; 30 or more: 5 to 9 kg.
Energy: about 250 extra kcal a day from month 4 and about 500 from month 7 (normal weight); eat twice as well, not twice as much.

Drinks: 1.5 to 2 litres a day in pregnancy, at least 2 litres while breastfeeding; caffeine in moderation, for example 1 to 2 cups of coffee or 4 cups of black or green tea a day; avoid energy drinks and tonic.
No alcohol in pregnancy.
Fish: avoid marlin, swordfish, shark, Baltic salmon and Baltic herring; fresh or tinned tuna and imported pike at most once a week.
Movement: about 30 minutes a day, avoiding overexertion; low-risk activities such as swimming, walking, gymnastics or yoga.

items.title: Screening and management of gestational diabetes (SGGG expert letter 81, Gynäkologie 1/2024)
items.summary: The Swiss Society of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (SGGG) recommends an early check for diabetes that existed before the pregnancy at the first pregnancy check-up, with a fasting blood sugar or HbA1c test. Between weeks 24+0 and 28+0 all pregnant women are tested for gestational diabetes: the standard is a 75 g glucose drink test (OGTT) under set conditions, after at least 8 hours without food and starting between 6 and 9 am. Gestational diabetes is diagnosed if one value is at or above the limit: fasting 5.1 mmol/l, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/l or 2 hours 8.5 mmol/l. Women without risk factors can have a fasting blood sugar test first, which spares some of them the drink. After gestational diabetes, a diabetes test after the birth is advised.
keyPoints: First check-up: fasting blood sugar or HbA1c to look for diabetes that existed before the pregnancy.
Weeks 24+0 to 28+0: a 75 g glucose drink test (OGTT) is the standard test, fasting for at least 8 hours and starting between 6 and 9 am.
Limits for gestational diabetes: fasting 5.1 mmol/l, after 1 hour 10.0 mmol/l, after 2 hours 8.5 mmol/l; one value at or above the limit is enough.
Without risk factors, a two-step approach can be used: a fasting blood sugar test first, and the drink test only if needed.
After a pregnancy with gestational diabetes: a diabetes test after the birth, and support for breastfeeding.

items.title: Anti-D injections in pregnancy for RhD-negative women (SGGG expert letter 94, January 2026, replaces letter 68)
items.summary: The Swiss Society of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (SGGG) explains when a pregnant woman whose blood group is RhD negative needs an anti-D injection, which stops her body from making antibodies against an RhD-positive baby. At the first check-ups (weeks 8 to 12) every woman has her blood group, RhD status and an antibody screen checked. For RhD-negative women, a blood test between weeks 16 and 24 can read the baby's RhD status from the baby's DNA in the mother's blood; it is a genetic test, so she is counselled first and gives written consent on the lab form, and insurance pays for it once. If the baby is RhD positive, the woman gets an anti-D injection between weeks 28 and 30, and again after the birth. If the baby is RhD negative, no routine anti-D is needed in pregnancy, after bleeding or procedures, or after the birth; the letter says this spares about 40% of injections in pregnancy in Switzerland. Anti-D after the birth is given ideally within 72 hours, and can still be given up to 14 days later. This letter (January 2026) replaces letter 68 of 2020.
keyPoints: First check-ups (weeks 8 to 12): blood group, RhD status and a screen for blood group antibodies.

RhD-negative women: a blood test between weeks 16 and 24 shows the baby's RhD status; the society advises against doing it before week 16. It needs counselling and written consent, and basic insurance pays for it once.
Baby RhD positive: anti-D injection between weeks 28 and 30, and again after the birth, ideally within 72 hours (up to 14 days later if missed).
Baby RhD negative: no routine anti-D in pregnancy or after the birth, and none needed after bleeding or procedures; the newborn's blood group then does not need testing.

items.title: Group B streptococcus (GBS): swab at weeks 35 to 37 and antibiotics in labour to protect the newborn (SGGG clinical practice recommendation 86, 2024)
items.summary: Group B streptococci (GBS) are bacteria that live harmlessly in the vagina or bowel of many women, about 20% of pregnant women in Switzerland. During birth they can pass to the baby and, rarely, cause a serious infection in the first week of life. The Swiss recommendation (SGGG, approved by the Swiss Academy for Feto-Maternal Medicine) is to test every pregnant woman at weeks 35 to 37 with one swab from the lower vagina and the skin around the anus; no speculum is needed and women can take the swab themselves. Women who test positive get antibiotics through a drip from the start of labour or when the waters break, which lowers early infections in the baby by 80 to 90%. Treating GBS before labour is not advised, because it usually comes back. Antibiotics are also given without a swab after GBS in the urine in this pregnancy or a previous baby with GBS infection, and when the result is unknown and there is a risk factor (birth before 37 weeks, waters broken 18 hours or more, fever in labour). A planned caesarean before labour and before the waters break does not need GBS antibiotics.
keyPoints: Every pregnant woman is offered a GBS swab at weeks 35 to 37; a result older than 5 weeks counts as unknown.
One swab from the lower vagina and the skin around the anus; women can take it themselves.
GBS found: antibiotics through a drip from the start of labour or when the waters break; this lowers early infection of the baby by 80 to 90%.
No treatment before labour: the bacteria usually come back.
Antibiotics without a swab: GBS in the urine in this pregnancy, or a previous baby with GBS infection.
Unknown result: antibiotics if the birth is before 37 weeks, the waters have been broken 18 hours or more, or there is fever in labour.
Tell your team about a penicillin allergy: the lab then tests which other antibiotics work.

items.title: HPV vaccination in Switzerland: recommended ages, doses and costs (BAG and Federal Commission for Vaccination)
items.summary: The Swiss Federal Office of Public Health (BAG) and the Federal Commission for Vaccination recommend the HPV vaccine for all young people aged 11 to 14, girls and boys alike. In the cantonal vaccination programmes the vaccine is exempt from the deductible for people aged 11 to 26; the co-payment is still paid by the person.

items.title: Cervical cancer screening in Switzerland: who, how often and with which test (SGGG expert letter 97, June 2026, replaces letter 50)
items.summary: The Swiss Society of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (SGGG) recommends cervical screening every 3 years from age 21 to 70. From 21 to 29 the test is a cell test (Pap smear, cytology); from 30 to 70 it can be a cell test or an HPV test, each every 3 years. Doing both tests at the same time (co-testing) is not recommended for routine screening. Basic insurance still does not pay for the HPV test as the first screening test; an application was made in 2025, so women who choose it usually pay for it themselves. Switzerland has no invitation programme: women book the check themselves. Screening is not done before 21, whatever the age at first sex. It can stop at 70 after normal results (three normal cell tests in 10 years or two negative HPV tests in 6 years) and no earlier high-grade changes. HPV-vaccinated women follow the same schedule, and a pregnancy does not change it.

items.title: Cancer screening Swiss basic insurance pays for: cervical smear and breast screening mammography (KLV Art. 12e, version of 1 August 2026)
items.summary: The Swiss health insurance benefits ordinance (KLV, Article 12e) sets which screening tests basic insurance pays for. items.title: Breast cancer screening programmes in Swiss cantons: which cantons have one, who is invited and what it costs (Swiss Cancer Screening, 2026)
items.summary: Swiss Cancer Screening, the umbrella association of the cantonal screening programmes, lists which cantons run an organised breast cancer screening programme. items.title: IVF in Switzerland in 2024: how many women were treated and how often treatment led to a birth (Federal Statistical Office, BFS)
items.summary: The Swiss Federal Statistical Office (BFS) collects figures from all Swiss fertility centres. In 2024, 6,533 women had IVF or ICSI treatment, over 12,573 started treatment cycles, and 2,475 babies were born alive after these treatments. Of all the women treated that year, 47% became pregnant and 37% gave birth. Counted per embryo transfer, about 30% led to a birth (26% after a fresh transfer, 32% after a frozen one); counted per started cycle, about 19%. About one pregnancy in five ended in a miscarriage. Twins made up about 2% of births and there were no triplets. Women in treatment were 36.8 years old on average: 6% were under 30, 27% were 30 to 34, 43% were 35 to 39, 23% were 40 to 44 and 1% were 45 or older. The BFS tables do not show success rates by the woman's age, so for the effect of age other sources are needed, such as the UK register. These are national averages, not a personal chance; the fertility clinic can explain what they mean for her.

items.title: Combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch, ring): effectiveness, missed pills and migraine (FSRH clinical guideline, January 2019, amended October 2023)
items.summary: The UK Faculty (now College) of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare guideline on the combined pill, patch and ring. Used perfectly, about 0.3% of users get pregnant in the first year; with typical use, which includes late or missed pills, about 9% do, because the method depends on being used correctly every day. Implants and coils (IUDs) stay below 1% either way, because they do not depend on the user, so women choosing the pill should hear about them too. A combined pill counts as missed when it is more than 24 hours late; missing pills next to the 7-day break matters most, because it makes the break longer; the detailed steps are in the separate FSRH guidance on incorrect use. Vomiting within 3 hours of a pill, or severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours, counts like a missed pill. Women who have migraine with aura should not use combined methods (UKMEC category 4: an unacceptable health risk), because together they raise the risk of ischaemic stroke; with migraine without aura the combined method can usually be started (UKMEC 2), but new migraine after starting it is a reason to stop (UKMEC 3). The absolute stroke risk in young women stays low.
keyPoints: First-year pregnancy rate: about 0.3% with perfect use and about 9% with typical use (pill, patch and ring alike).
Typical use, other methods: progestogen-only pill 9%, injection 6%, male condom 18%, copper coil 0.8%, hormonal coil 0.2%, implant 0.05%.
A combined pill is missed when it is more than 24 hours late; pills missed next to the 7-day break matter most.
Vomiting within 3 hours of a pill, or severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours, counts as a missed pill.
Migraine with aura: combined pill, patch or ring should not be used (UKMEC 4) because of the higher risk of ischaemic stroke.
Migraine without aura: a combined method can usually be started (UKMEC 2); new migraine after starting it is a reason to stop (UKMEC 3).
Women who often miss pills can consider a method that does not depend on daily use, such as an implant or coil.

items.title: What to do after late or missed combined pills, a late patch or a late ring (CDC US Selected Practice Recommendations, 2024)
items.summary: The US CDC practice recommendations (2024) say what to do when combined pills are taken late or missed. A pill counts as late when less than 24 hours have passed since it was due, and missed after 24 hours or more. If one pill is late or missed (less than 48 hours): take it as soon as possible and carry on as usual, even if that means two pills in one day; no extra protection is needed. If two or more pills in a row are missed (48 hours or more): take the most recent missed pill now, carry on as usual, and use condoms or avoid sex until seven hormone pills in a row have been taken. If the missed pills were in the last week of hormone pills, finish them and start the next pack straight away without the break. If pills were missed in the first week and there was sex without a condom in the previous 5 days, emergency contraception should be considered. Patch and ring follow the same 48-hour rule. The UK FSRH uses the same 24-hour and 48-hour limits; her own pack leaflet can be stricter and then applies, and a pharmacist can help.
keyPoints: Late = less than 24 hours after the pill was due; missed = 24 hours or more.
One pill late or missed (under 48 hours): take it now, even two in one day, and carry on; no extra protection needed.
Two or more missed in a row (48 hours or more): take the latest missed pill now, carry on, and use condoms or avoid sex until 7 hormone pills in a row have been taken.
Missed in the last week of hormone pills: finish them and start the next pack without the break.
Missed in the first week with sex without a condom in the previous 5 days: emergency contraception should be considered (ask a pharmacist).
Patch or ring 48 hours or more late: put a new one on or in now and use condoms for 7 days; the pack leaflet can be stricter.

items.title: Fertility treatment 2024: trends and figures, including IVF birth rates by age (HFEA, UK national register, June 2026)
items.summary: The UK Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority (HFEA) reports every IVF cycle done in the UK. In 2024 the average birth rate per embryo transferred, using the woman's own eggs and counting fresh and frozen transfers together, was 30%, up from 20% in 2014. Age makes the biggest difference: it was 38% for women aged 18 to 34 and 8% for women aged 43 to 44. Most transfers (84%) used a single embryo, and the multiple birth rate was about 3%. The average age at starting IVF was about 35. The 2024 birth figures are preliminary and not yet fully validated. These are UK averages per embryo transferred, not a personal chance; the clinic can explain what they mean for her.
keyPoints: Birth rate per embryo transferred (own eggs, fresh and frozen together): 30% on average in 2024, up from 20% in 2014.
By age: 38% for women aged 18 to 34; 8% for women aged 43 to 44.
84% of transfers used a single embryo; the multiple birth rate was about 3%.
The average age at starting IVF was about 35.
The 2024 birth figures are preliminary; averages per embryo transferred are not a personal chance.

items.title: What counts as a normal period: cycle length, bleeding days and regularity (FIGO System 1, International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics 2023)
items.summary: The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) defines normal menstrual bleeding in the reproductive years with four measures. A normal cycle, counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next, lasts 24 to 38 days; shorter cycles count as frequent and longer ones as infrequent, and no bleeding at all is amenorrhoea. Normal bleeding lasts up to 8 days, spotting included. Cycles count as regular when the shortest and longest cycle differ by up to 7 to 9 days, depending on age (up to 9 days at 18 to 25 and 42 to 45, up to 7 days at 26 to 41); for girls under 18 and women over 45 there are no agreed limits. Flow is judged by the woman herself as light, normal or heavy. Bleeding between regular periods is not normal and is worth discussing with a doctor.
keyPoints: Normal cycle length: 24 to 38 days, from the first day of one period to the first day of the next.
Normal bleeding: up to 8 days, spotting included.
Regular: the shortest and longest cycle differ by up to 9 days at ages 18 to 25 and 42 to 45, and up to 7 days at ages 26 to 41.
No agreed limits for regularity under 18 or over 45.
Heavy flow is judged by the woman herself; bleeding between regular periods is not normal.

items.title: Folic Acid Supplementation to Prevent Neural Tube Defects: US Preventive Services Task Force Reaffirmation Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force checked the evidence on folic acid again in 2023 and kept its advice. Neural tube defects are serious birth defects of the brain and spine, affecting about 3000 pregnancies a year in the US, and many are caused by low folate. The Task Force is highly certain that folic acid supplements bring a substantial benefit. It recommends that everyone who is planning a pregnancy or could become pregnant takes a daily supplement with 0.4 to 0.8 mg (400 to 800 micrograms) of folic acid.
keyPoints: Updated (reaffirmed) in 2023; replaces the 2017 statement.
High certainty that folic acid supplements bring a substantial benefit in preventing neural tube defects.
Recommended for everyone planning a pregnancy or who could become pregnant: a daily supplement with 0.4 to 0.8 mg (400 to 800 micrograms) of folic acid (grade A).

items.title: Screening for Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy: US Preventive Services Task Force Final Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed screening for high blood pressure conditions of pregnancy, such as pre-eclampsia and gestational hypertension. These conditions are a leading cause of serious illness and death in mothers in the US, and they have become about twice as common since the 1990s. The Task Force concludes with moderate certainty that checking blood pressure throughout pregnancy has a substantial benefit, and recommends it for all pregnant women who do not already have high blood pressure.
keyPoints: Replaces the 2017 statement on screening for pre-eclampsia and now covers all high blood pressure conditions of pregnancy.
Blood pressure should be measured throughout pregnancy (grade B).
Moderate certainty that this screening has a substantial benefit.
High blood pressure conditions in US pregnancies roughly doubled between 1993 and 2016 to 2017.

items.title: Interventions to Prevent Falls in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed ways to prevent falls in people aged 65 and older who live at home and have a higher risk of falling. Falls are the leading cause of injury in older adults; in 2018 more than a quarter of over-65s in the US reported a fall in the past year. The Task Force concludes with moderate certainty that exercise programmes bring a moderate benefit, and recommends them. Programmes that combine several steps (for example checking medicines, vision and the home) bring only a small benefit overall, so the Task Force says they should be offered case by case, depending on past falls, other health conditions and the person's wishes.
keyPoints: Replaces the 2018 statement.
Exercise programmes are recommended for people 65 and older at higher risk of falls (grade B, moderate benefit).
Combined multi-step programmes have a small overall benefit and should be decided case by case (grade C).
In 2018, 27.5% of over-65s living at home reported at least one fall in the past year.

items.title: Testing and interpreting measures of ovarian reserve: a committee opinion
items.summary: This committee opinion from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine explains what ovarian reserve tests can and cannot tell. Ovarian reserve means the number of eggs left in the ovaries. It is estimated from hormone blood tests (such as AMH) and from features seen on an ovary ultrasound scan. These markers help predict how many eggs may be collected after ovarian stimulation for IVF, but apart from age they are poor predictors of the chance of getting pregnant.
keyPoints: Ovarian reserve means the number of eggs left, not their quality.
Markers include hormone blood tests such as AMH and features measured on an ultrasound scan.
They help predict how many eggs may be collected after stimulation.
Apart from age, they are poor predictors of the chance of pregnancy.

items.title: Cervical Cancer, Version 2.2026, NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines In Oncology
items.journal: Journal of the National Comprehensive Cancer Network
items.summary: This is the current version of the US cancer network (NCCN) guideline on cervical cancer. It covers how cervical cancer is diagnosed and staged, the principles of surgery, the main treatment options for early and advanced cancer, and a detailed overview of drug treatments. The abstract does not list specific recommendations.
keyPoints: Covers diagnosis, staging, surgery and main treatments for early and advanced cervical cancer.
Gives an overview of drug (systemic) treatments.
Replaces older versions such as Version 3.2019.
The abstract does not list specific recommendations.

items.title: Tobacco and Nicotine Cessation During Pregnancy: ACOG Committee Opinion, Number 807
items.source: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
items.organisation: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
items.summary: This guidance from US obstetricians (ACOG) explains the risks of tobacco in pregnancy and how to help women stop. Smoking in pregnancy is linked to cleft lip and palate, a baby who grows poorly, placenta problems, waters breaking early, low birth weight, ectopic pregnancy and more deaths around birth; children have more chest infections, asthma, colic and obesity. About 54% of women who smoke stop just before or during pregnancy. Stopping at any point helps mother and baby, with the greatest benefit before 15 weeks. E-cigarettes, vaping, hookahs and cigars are increasingly used, and ACOG advises stopping all forms. Care should be individual, with counselling, behavioural support and, where needed, medicines, and support should be discussed at prenatal and postnatal visits.
keyPoints: Replaces Committee Opinion 721 (2017).
Stopping smoking at any point in pregnancy helps; the greatest benefit is before 15 weeks.
About 54% of women who smoke stop just before or during pregnancy.
All forms of tobacco and nicotine, including e-cigarettes and vaping, should be stopped.
Support can include counselling, behavioural help and medicines, offered at prenatal and postnatal visits.

items.title: Menopause: identification and management (NICE guideline NG23, updated November 2024)
items.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
items.journal: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
items.summary: This is the UK national NICE guideline on recognising and managing menopause, including premature ovarian insufficiency (menopause before 40). It was updated in November 2024 and replaces the 2015 version. It aims to make the support and information people get during menopause more consistent. It is written for health professionals and for women, trans men and non-binary people registered female at birth who have menopause symptoms, and their families. The abstract does not list specific recommendations.
keyPoints: UK national guideline, updated November 2024; replaces the 2015 version.
Covers recognising and managing menopause, including premature ovarian insufficiency.
Aims to make menopause support and information more consistent.
The abstract does not list specific recommendations.

items.title: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine Consult Series #53: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy: Replaces Consult #13, April 2011.
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This US guidance from the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine covers intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP), a liver condition of pregnancy that causes itching and raised bile acids in the blood. It carries little risk for the mother but raises the risk of an early birth, meconium in the waters and stillbirth for the baby. The society recommends a blood test for bile acids and liver enzymes when ICP is suspected, ursodeoxycholic acid as the first medicine for the itching, and checks on the baby from diagnosis. It recommends offering birth at 36 weeks when bile acids are 100 micromol/L or higher, and birth between 36 and 39 weeks when they are lower, but no birth before 37 weeks on symptoms alone without a raised bile acid result.
keyPoints: ICP causes itching and raised bile acids; the main risks are for the baby (early birth, meconium, stillbirth).
Suspected ICP: blood test for bile acids and liver enzymes (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence).
Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line medicine for the itching (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence).
Bile acids of 100 micromol/L or more: birth offered at 36 weeks; lower levels: birth between 36 and 39 weeks.
No birth before 37 weeks for itching alone without a raised bile acid result.

items.title: Return of fertility after discontinuation of contraception: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.summary: This review pooled 22 studies of 14,884 women who stopped using contraception in order to see how quickly they became pregnant. About 83 in 100 became pregnant within the first year after stopping. The rate was much the same after hormonal methods and after an IUD, and neither the type of progestogen nor how long the pill had been taken made a clear difference. The authors conclude that using contraception, whatever the method or for how long, does not harm or clearly delay the ability to get pregnant afterwards. The evidence was not graded.
keyPoints: 22 studies, 14,884 women who stopped contraception.
About 83% became pregnant within 12 months of stopping.
No clear difference between hormonal methods and IUDs, or by how long the pill was used.
The authors conclude contraception does not harm or clearly delay later fertility.
